Until 1988, all employees were required to contribute to a pension scheme if an employer offered one. While the idea of a government-funded compensation scheme has not garnered wide support at Westminster, the government appears to have softened its position slightly. Miss Ann Widdecombe, a junior social security minister, said it would be 'irresponsible' for the government to consider such a fund before investigations into the disappearance of the missing Maxwell assets are complete - but she said nothing had been ruled out. As political pressure grows at Westminster, the group of 100 MPs is switching its focus from Whitehall to the City, and to the Bank of England in particular. They want the Bank to exert pressure on commercial banks to return some of the securities they received on behalf of Maxwell companies. Some ministers are joining forces with the pensioners' lobbyists to urge the banks to acknowledge their moral obligations. For their part, the banks say that they are studying the matter, but they point out that they accepted the securities in good faith and had no way of knowing that they were pension fund assets. Mr Field and Mr Page were encouraged when they saw Mr Peter Lilley, the social security secretary, recently by his undertaking to pass on their criticisms to the Bank of England. Last week, Mr Page wrote to Mr Norman Lamont, the chancellor, asking him to put pressure on the Bank to take a more active view of its supervisory role. The failure of Mr Robin Leigh-Pemberton, the governor of the Bank, to acknowledge publicly that the Bank played a rather too passive role in the Maxwell affair is likely to result in some uncomfortable questions from the group of MPs. The Bank's reluctance to become involved in seeking a solution is also likely to raise some uneasy questions about City regulation in general. 'If the Bank steps back from this it is saying it has no role in regulating the City: it would be entirely wrong for the Bank to step back. This strikes at the fundamental core of how the City runs itself and the basis on which transactions take place,' said Mr David Shaw, Tory MP for Dover and another leading member of the MPs' group. He said the entire structure of self-regulation in the City had been called into question, and described as 'profoundly unsatisfactory' the prospect of MPs shuttling about in taxis from one regulator to another in search of a single voice to speak for the City. His remarks echo the findings of the all-party social security committee of MPs in the last parliament. Its report on the Maxwell affair commented that the most striking result of months of hearings was that no single body or individual appeared to have full responsibility for monitoring pension fund activities. 'Pontius Pilate would have blushed at the spectacle of so many witnesses washing their hands in public before the committee of their responsibilities in this affair.' One of the main recommendations of the committee will now be implemented. Mr Lilley is about to announce a government review of pension law, although not specifically within the suggested nine-month timescale. The review will address the fundamental question of the status and ownership of pension funds, but is also set to include other select committee proposals such as: the appointment of independent custodian trustees to hold pension-fund assets, all with clearly designated ownership; the annual right of every pensioner to transfer his or her assets from a pension scheme to another recognised financial institution; and the right of pensioners and contributors to veto transfers of assets to another scheme. It is also likely to look at the concerns already voiced by Imro, about the difficulties of marrying trust law - the legal framework governing pension funds - and financial services legislation. The strengthening of the Occupational Pensions Board to police a new regime will also be considered. Now that a portion of the pensions industry has accepted that some sort of compensation fund is needed, one problem is the form the fund would take. The US, Japan and most European countries, including France and Germany, already have such funds. Setting one up in the UK would entail an overhaul of current pension law because the fund would insist that any scheme covered by it met minimum standards. Mr Brian McMahon, chairman of the National Association of Pension Funds, the industry trade association, has called for scheme members to be eligible to apply to the Investors Compensation Scheme set up under the 1987 Financial Services Act. The ICS allows investors to receive up to Pounds 48,000 in total compensation - a paltry sum compared with the potential benefits lost when a pension scheme collapses. The NAPF has also embarked on a feasibility study of a separate compensation fund. This would be an additional safety net for pensioners whose schemes had failed without sufficient assets to meet all liabilities. One proposal is that it be funded by a levy on all UK pension schemes - an idea which has proved divisive. 'On the basis of my postbag, there isn't much support for it,' Mr McMahon said. 'The postbag tends to be from the larger schemes who say they run good schemes. They don't want to bail out the likes of Robert Maxwell.' Clearly, neither the government nor the industry wants to pay for a compensation fund. The government is waiting to assess exactly how much funding would be needed and to see whether the banks will return some of the securities received on behalf of Mr Maxwell. The industry, on the other hand, wants to reassure pension scheme members that their savings will not disappear if a company fails, but it does not want to underwrite pension fund abuse by an open-ended commitment to a compensation fund. Over the longer term the government review will be of immense significance for an industry that has operated in an almost unregulated environment. But it will do little for the Maxwell pensioners because they would be outside the scope of any future legislation. Mr Page compared their position with that of passengers on the Titanic, if they had known that its sinking would lead to new international regulations about lifeboats and safety at sea. 'I'm sure they would be delighted that in future people would have more protection, but they are bound to be concentrating on their own predicament.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Leading Article: The next step in housing
DOC.TEXT: WHEN THE chancellor, Mr Norman Lamont, meets representatives of the leading building societies this afternoon, he and his ministerial colleagues will no doubt be given reassuring news about repossessions in the housing market. And there is indeed room for modest reassurance: while repossessions remain at historically high levels, the trend has unquestionably improved in the first few months of the year. Yet it could hardly have been otherwise. Since the government and the building societies agreed in December on a package of measures to help stabilise the housing market, nominal interest rates have fallen further and income support for mortgage interest has been paid direct to lenders, automatically reducing the risk that borrowers will go into default. In addition the societies have recognised the advantages of keeping overstretched mortgagors in the property. With the aid of counselling and renegotiation, otherwise shaky borrowers have been kept afloat to the benefit of both parties. What is clear at this point is that the improvement in the figures owes precious little to the attempt to encourage defaulting mortgagors to become housing association tenants in the former owner-occupied property. Those who have escaped the problems of the rented sector for the financial strains of home ownership appear singularly reluctant to rejoin the tenantry. The scheme has anyway been criticised for its legal complexity. And from the building societies' point of view the economics look unfavourable, since former owner-occupied property does not enjoy the grants that enable housing associations to charge low rents on new property. Enormous pressures That said, it is hard to see a chancellor who faces enormous pressures on public finances being prepared to contemplate the cost of equalising the financial position of these two forms of tenure. Nor does it seem likely that Mr Lamont will accede to the demands of those who would like to see his temporary relief against stamp duty extended beyond the summer. If it has failed to kick-start the market into a significantly higher level of transactions by now, its point has been lost. The question is why it has failed and what else the government should do, if anything, to help. By past standards the relationship between house prices and earnings, which was distorted during the boom of the late 1980s, is back to its long-term trend level. House prices appear affordable again. Yet buyers remain elusive. Affordable prices One explanation might be the caution-inducing persistence of high real rates of interest after a decade in which the personal sector doubled its indebtedness in relation to household income. Another could be that buyers expect prices to look even more affordable in due course. That is far from implausible if the first big fall in nominal house prices since the war causes the speculative investment premium in housing to disappear - an outcome that could be reinforced by the erosion of the real value of mortgage interest relief and the less favourable trend in household formation that is expected later in the decade. Against that background, house prices might well be expected to settle at a lower multiple of earnings than hitherto. A more tangible factor behind the low volume of transactions is that between half a million and a million buyers are reckoned to have a negative equity in their homes, whereby the mortgage exceeds the value of the house. They are stuck on the bottom rung of the housing ladder and unable to move. It is here that the housing market slump is doing economic, as well as social, damage. In the absence of a more flexible private rented sector, job mobility is reduced. Existing legislation prevents the building societies from transferring mortgages to a new property by stipulating that they cannot lend more than 100 per cent of value. Where housing equity is already negative this prudential requirement is academic. It also acts as a needless constraint on labour market flexibility. The chancellor should explore the case for a limited relaxation of the legislation to cope with this unexpected consequence of the collapse in house prices.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Leading Article: The isolation of Serbia
DOC.TEXT: THE HORROR of the human tragedy provoked by Serbia, first in Croatia and more recently in Bosnia-Hercegovina, has at last persuaded the international community to take action. Predictably, critics now maintain that the sanctions adopted by the United Nations Security Council last Saturday have come much too late and should have been approved at least nine months ago. But the necessary consensus was not forthcoming at the time and the US, in particular, made it plain that it did not want to get involved in a far-off ethnic conflict which did not seem to threaten wider international security. There is little point now in pursuing the argument whether the European Community is more to blame for its incapacity to solve the Yugoslav crisis in the first place, or the US, for washing its hands of the whole affair until outraged domestic public opinion forced the Administration to change its mind. What is certain is that international solutions to crises of this magnitude still require the involvement and commitment of the only remaining superpower, the US. In spite of the mixed results that international sanctions have had in the past and the bluster of Mr Slobodan Milosevic, the Serbian leader, who boasts that the Serbian economy can survive in spite of them, there is every indication that sanctions will bite deep. This is particularly true of the oil embargo, given that Serbia is dependent for some 75 per cent of its oil needs on foreign suppliers such as Russia, China, Romania and Angola. In the circumstances, it is hard to see how its military effort can be maintained indefinitely, though civilian users of cars and fuel will probably be made to pay the biggest price to keep the military machine going. Popular opposition Equally important will be the effect that shortages, the inconvenience caused to travellers by the suspension of international flights and the disappointment for a football-obsessed people of seeing its team banned from the European championship finals in Sweden, will have on national morale and Mr Milosevic's political standing. The demonstration in Belgrade at the week-end by some 50,000 anti-war protesters was an indication that popular opposition to his policies is growing, at least in the capital. The peace movement in Serbia, however, is mainly middle class-based. It would be an illusion to believe that it finds much of an echo in the rural Serb and Montenegrin population, not least the Serbs in Bosnia, who look upon the Belgrade government as their main protector and champion. Indeed, Mr Milosevic is far from being his own man in Bosnia, where the leaders of ultra-nationalist irregular Serbian military units are even accusing him of being too soft. Perverse effect There is clearly a risk, therefore, that UN sanctions could have the perverse effect of giving a boost to Serbian nationalism. Even if the Belgrade government were to have a change of heart as the result of international pressure, regional nationalist groups might well decide to pursue their crusade. The Yugoslav partisans demonstrated during the Second World War how effective they were at guerrilla warfare. If the international community were to wait until Serbia is economically exhausted or Mr Milosevic is overthrown, it could wait for a very long time. Sanctions must be given a fair chance to bring Mr Milosevic to his senses, but if they fail, what then? International military action can no longer be ruled out as a longer term option. As in the Gulf crisis, such operations would have to be sanctioned by the Security Council, though they would probably have to be undertaken by surrogate organisations such as Nato or the Western European Union. Military action should be restricted to air strikes against strategic targets. It would be most unwise to contemplate sending ground forces, since they might become stuck in Yugoslavia indefinitely and suffer politically unacceptable losses. But whatever action is finally decided, it is essential that it should be taken by the international community as a whole including the US, which alone has the clout to bring transgressors of international law to heel. Anything less, as has been proved conclusively, is doomed to failure.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Arts: A surrealist cast of symbols - Sculpture
DOC.TEXT: Phillip King, the lately retired Professor of Sculpture at the Royal College of Art, is now 58. He read Modern Languages at Cambridge before turning to sculpture, which he studied under Anthony Caro at St Martin's in the late 1950s, followed by a brief stint, around 1960, as an assistant to Henry Moore. Late vocation or not, his critical success was almost immediate. He was a particular star of Bryan Robertson's seminal New Generation show at the Whitechapel Gallery in 1965; a trustee of the Tate by 1967; CBE by 1974; ARA by 1977; and subject of a full retrospective at the Hayward Gallery by 1981. All the while there has been a constant stream of shows at home and abroad, regular solo shows of current work with the old Rowan Gallery, and significant contributions to group exhibitions. In short, King is a substantial and influential figure in his generation, an artist with a truly international reputation. Or is he? Any artist, in shifting the course of art in his turn, though by only a little, only adds to its impetus and the capacity of those who follow to shift it further in their turn. Our much vaunted British Sculpture, in received opinion our one consistent and truly significant contribution to the world's art in the 20th century, is carried on by other, younger hands. If King's reputation has lain somewhat in the shadows since the apparent zenith some 10 years ago or more, the show at the Yorkshire Sculpture Park, along with Tim Hilton's timely and invaluable monograph, affords us the proper occasion to bring it once more, quite literally, out into the light of day. King's work is, of course, no stranger to the open air, but with such public monuments as the 'Clarion' at Fulham Broadway, and the 'Diamond Sculpture' beside the road at Street in Somerset, it is more familiar in an urban of industrial than a rural context. Also, his early use of bright, unnatural colour and apparently insubstantial materials, and the long, inevitable practice of showing even the most monumental of the works inside the gallery, have conspired in the common belief that the true place for his sculpture is indoors. Only to the comparative few of his public, familiar with the sculpture garden of his long-time dealer, Alex Gregory-Hood at Loxley in Warwickshire, will this splendidly bucolic display in the park at Bretton Hall come as no surprise. Even to them, with so many definitive pieces on show, the urge to modify both expectation and judgment is irresistible. For what emerges is not just that these things look so much at home on the grassy slopes beneath the trees, but rather that brightly coloured or drab and natural, they display a remarkable consistency both in their imaginative preoccupation and formal development. The differences are clear enough: the hints at figurative reference in the earliest; the overt figuration in the latest works; and, in between, works in which formal and material considerations are over-riding. Yet, whichever it is, what brings it so to sit happily with the oeuvre at large is an unmistakable sense, not just of space occupied and articulated, but of a place established and enclosed. Given the open nature of so many of the structures in the purely formal sense, this may seem a somewhat contradictory thing to say but, even so, it holds good. Stonehenge may be open now to all the winds that blow, but its sense of enclosure and, more than that, of being enclosed to some purpose, is undeniable. And by how much is the same true of ruins of all kinds, whether of castles or cottages, temples, tombs, sacred graves? If King does not make the point himself, the works make it for him in a remarkable combination of sculptures, set out more or less across the slope and half-way down the hill toward the lake. On either side sit two works of 1977, 'Open Place' and 'Sure Place', each a low slanting structure, deceptively tumbled, of slabs of slate set into a steel framework. In between are two bright and open structures, arched and sprung, not so much higher and with the same scope across the ground. They could hardly be more different, and yet so very much the same: the dome, the canopy, the tent, the tomb. So back it is to those earliest things, to 'Genghis Khan' of 1963, dark blue against the green and what might be a great swirling cape or tent surmounted by an imperious set of heraldic antlers. On to the most recent things, to the clouds and the arcades and tumbled elements, redolent of Giacometti and de Chirico, Picasso and Miro: and again, King sets out the same contained space, though now a stage, as it were, on which to put his discrete surrealist cast of symbols - the hand, the ball, the moon. Those latest, openly surrealist works may seem something of an arbitrary break in the natural development, romantic as ever but a conscious rejection of the abstract and the formal. Shown as they are, however, in the pavilion in the upper garden alongside a group of the earliest things, colourful pyramids and cones fraught with a latent surrealism, they seem less so, less certainly than they did new and alone a year or two ago. Who knows where they may tend? But an artist in mid-career is the master of is own direction, and the professor, Emeritus now, has yet to collect his bus pass. Already the work comes together, all of a piece. There is plenty of time. Phillip King - Sculpture 1960-1991, Yorkshire Sculpture Park, Bretton Hall, Wakefield until August 31. The Sculpture of Phillip King by Tim Hilton, published jointly by Lund Humphries and The Henry Moore Foundation

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / People: Hanson to groom its media image
DOC.TEXT: Hanson, Britain's eighth biggest company, has recruited Aviva Gershuny-Roth, who made her name as a property marketing whiz, to improve its lacklustre media image. The 34-year-old Gershuny-Roth will report to vice-chairman Martin Taylor who has been the group's principal spokesman to date. Unlike most large companies Hanson has not spent much time grooming its media image because it felt its financial performance spoke for itself. Lord Hanson did hire Michael Shea, a former press secretary to the Queen, as director of public affairs in 1987. However, Shea has spent most of his time cultivating Hanson's contacts with Westminster rather than the City. As a consequence, when Hanson took a near 3 per cent stake in Imperial Chemical Industries last year, it was unprepared for the level of media attention - and criticism - that it received. It has been known for some months that Hanson has been seeking an in-house professional to handle its corporate communications. Nevertheless, Gershuny-Roth's appointment will surprise some Hanson watchers. For the last 15 months she has been involved in the marketing of Olympia & York's ill-fated Canary Wharf development in London's docklands and before that she spent nine years with Savills, the up-market firm of chartered surveyors. Although she is well regarded, her expertise in marketing property is not exactly an obvious qualification for looking after the image of a company such as Hanson which employs a workforce of more than 70,000 worldwide. ***** Steve Tibble, former director of research at Valin Pollen, has joined Richard Pollen & Co as a senior consultant.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / People: GA looks for change
DOC.TEXT: The promotion of Bob Scott to the board of General Accident Fire and Life Assurance, the UK operating board of the Perth-based insurance composite is symptomatic of the wind of change at the traditionally cautious Scottish company. An Australian who has spent much of his working life in New Zealand, Scott came into the GA fold following the takeover of NZI in 1987. He then moved to the UK in 1990 to spearhead a restructuring of the company's sluggish UK operations. Now 50, he is one of a number of younger executives to emerge at GA in recent years. The finance director, Barry Holder, is in his mid-40s. It has been a tough two years. GA has rationalised its branch structure, cutting over a thousand jobs, and has survived a confrontation with brokers over its determination to sell a greater percentage of its home and motor policies directly to the public. Yesterday's appointment is an indication that Scott has impressed the powers that be in Perth. After two years of heavy underwriting losses, GA's first quarter results were last month showing glimmers of a turnround in the company's UK performance.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Technology: Here's one for the road / Describing plans to co-ordinate Britain's street works
DOC.TEXT: If the road outside your house has just been resurfaced, you can be sure that it won't be long before someone comes along with a pneumatic drill and digs a hole in it. For years, street works have been poorly co-ordinated in the UK, with the gas, water and electricity boards and the local highway authority often ignorant of each other's plans. A marked improvement is likely from this October, however, when the New Roads and Street Works Act 1991 goes live. The new laws, replacing existing legislation drafted in the 1930s, will improve communication between utilities and increase the highway authorities' responsibility for co-ordination. Under the new Act, local authorities must keep a register of all street works, and from 1994 that register will be held on a computer. A single, national database will eventually hold details of all the country's street works and the list will be updated as utilities and highway authorities exchange information by electronic mail. Whereas under the old Public Utilities Street Works Act (Puswa), there are three kinds of road works - major, minor, and emergency - the electronic register will have to cope with a host of new definitions. Certain streets, for example, have been deemed 'traffic sensitive' and any street works on them would require a longer period of notice. The total number of messages which utilities and authorities send to each other is also expected to increase by as much as 50 per cent. This is because for the first time local authorities must give warning of anything that is likely to effect the motorist, be it a manhole inspection or the London marathon. Even though the computer system won't be ready until 1994, authorities must comply with the new Act from this October. While they wait, councils are having to develop interim systems which in most cases will be based on fax machines and the post. The thinking behind the computer system stems from 1985 when Puswa was heavily criticised by a government report which, among other things, called for a national Computerised Street Works Register (CSWR). Since then, highway authorities and utilities have been working to develop improved codes of practice, and their representative body, the Highway Authorities and Utilities Committee, has advised the government on what the CSWR should look like. A blueprint is now being developed for the Department of Transport (DTp) by KPMG Management Consulting, and a contract worth about Pounds 14m will go out to tender by the end of the year. The CSWR offers a chance to improve the accuracy of road work information. This should not be difficult as Puswa has been notoriously inaccurate - it is said to have records of road works in the North Sea, for example. Increased accuracy would mean fewer cases of contractors and utilities damaging plant by digging holes in the wrong places. Over the last few years, the National Joint Utilities Group (NJUG), which represents utilities collectively, has been trying to achieve this goal through a series of regional trials; and two of these, in Lothian, Scotland, and in Dudley, in the West Midlands, have been useful precursors to the CSWR. In 1982 Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council started a trail-blazing experiment which involved utilities sharing their mains records through centralised digital maps maintained by the council. When this system went live in 1985, damage to plant was cut by about 50 per cent almost immediately. From 1987, the council decided to use its digital maps as the foundation for a street works register which would chart the life of an excavation from the planning stage to the final reinstatement of the road and settlement of invoices. Holes in the road were defined by their co-ordinates on the maps to an accuracy of within one metre. The maps now hold records of about 45,000 holes. Dudley's system has drawn considerable international interest. However, it is too expensive to be sustained indefinitely and now the council is about to move to a post and fax system to comply with the new Act. The trial will have cost Pounds 2.5m, funded jointly by British Gas, BT, Mercury Communications, the DTp, the council, and the electricity supply and water industries. Another NJUG experiment managed to outlive its trial by being less ambitious and therefore cheaper. The system, known as Susiephone, started life at Lothian Regional Council as a message-relaying service with the slogan 'Dial before you dig'. By making a single phone call a contractor could inform all the utilities of an intended excavation and receive a complete picture of underground plant. Backed by a consortium of users including Scottish Power, British Gas (Scotland), BT, Mercury and local cable TV companies, Susiephone soon developed into a PC-based electronic messaging system. In addition, Lothian developed its own 'Puswa management system' which has many of the features of a rudimentary street works register. Susiephone was very successful but not sophisticated enough to meet the demands of the new Act. So the consortium returned to the drawing board and this year announced a new version based on modern workstations from the US company Sun Microsystems. The new Susiephone has been aligned with the requirements of the national CSWR. Lothian intends to use it as an interim system before the full CSWR arrives in 1994, and the consortium has signed a Pounds 400,000 deal with ICL which will develop the system for marketing to other UK authorities. Although utilities doubt that it could be used as a full CSWR, it is just possible that Susiephone could evolve into a national system. Both the Dudley and Susiephone groups will be invited to tender for the CSWR contract later this year. KPMG's specification for this contract is nearly finished and some features of the future system are beginning to emerge. A consultation paper issued to authorities and utilities last month by the DTp recommends a single national database built from a network of regional computers. It will support: electronic mail for giving notice of road works; software for co-ordinating road works; software for handling road-work inspections (from 1996). For improved accuracy, the CSWR will make use of a new National Street Gazetteer which will be the first complete list of all streets in the UK. Greater accuracy - to within metres - would be possible using digital maps. However, a Dudley-type system covering the whole country has been dismissed for the present. The technology is 'slightly too immature', says Richard Goodwin, project manager at KPMG. But Mike Bosworth, Dudley council's chief land surveyor, says the CSWR may eventually resemble Dudley's system. 'Our concepts are sound and I think the national system will develop into what we've got here at Dudley after 10 years,' he says. The DTp's consultation paper suggests the CSWR will be controlled by its users through a management board, which would appoint a computer company to operate the network. However, authorities and utilities are still considering forming a company in which they would be joint shareholders. In Scotland, the home of Susiephone, the big issue is whether to have a register separate from the rest of the UK. 'There's a fairly strong feeling that we should have a system located in Scotland,' says Sylvia Murray, principal policy officer with Cosla, the Scottish local authorities association. 'But being Scots it would be hard to argue against sharing a system based in Birmingham - if it were cheaper.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Pledge by Major on Brussels powers
DOC.TEXT: A CAMPAIGN to roll back 'unnecessary regulation' by Brussels was yesterday promised by Mr John Major as he set out his priorities for Britain's presidency of the European Community in the second half of this year. In a speech to the Ayrshire Chamber of Commerce, the prime minister promised to work unceasingly for a wider Europe that would embrace the emerging democracies of eastern Europe. His appearance in Scotland marked the first in a post-election series of visits to fulfil a pledge to make government from Westminster less remote from the people of Scotland. While reiterating his promise to 'take stock' of the pressures in Scotland for more self-government, he reaffirmed his absolute opposition to legislative devolution. Attacking the 'narrow nationalism' of the Scottish National party, he warned that devolution would be a 'step half-way across a chasm'. He linked Scotland's past and future prosperity to the role that Britain played in the EC. Separation would relegate Scotland from the heart of Europe to, at best, its outer fringe, depriving it of investment and influence. Mr Major, who used a trip to central Europe last to back the claims of Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary for EC membership, said that a wider Europe was vital to the peace and prosperity of Europe. 'It is not an optional extra.' He insisted that the government would not be content with arguing its corner defensively in the Community but would set out its own vision of the future. Britain would take as its starting point that the cardinal principle of the Community must be the free market. It would use its presidency to ensure that the single market was completed and then move on to try to limit the burdens the EC placed on business.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Solicitors face levy to meet sharp rise in fraud claims
DOC.TEXT: SOLICITORS IN England and Wales face a special levy of more than Pounds 1,000 this autumn on top of their annual insurance premiums to meet a big increase in professional fraud claims. The Law Society, the solicitors' governing body, also proposes tough restrictions on the right of solicitors to practise on their own. Dishonest sole practitioners are largely responsible for the rise in payments made by the profession's compensation fund from Pounds 11.7m last year to an estimated Pounds 20m this year. Much of the increase in claims stems from the increase in mortgage fraud involving solicitors. The Metropolitan Police have put the value of mortgage fraud involving solicitors at more than Pounds 1bn. The society disputes that figure. The compensation fund was set up by the society to meet claims - not covered by professional indemnity insurance - that result from the dishonest conduct of sole practitioners and cases where all partners of a firm have been dishonest. The profession already has to raise Pounds 178m this year for the solicitors' indemnity fund. To meet the growing cost of dishonest solicitors, the society is proposing to raise Pounds 50m for the fund this year. Solicitors who hold clients' money - partners - will each have to pay at least Pounds 1,591 made up of an annual contribution of Pounds 600 plus a special levy when they renew their practising certificates this autumn. Contributions to the indemnity fund will also rise significantly in the autumn. The contributions of sole practitioners will rise by 31 per cent and those of two-partner and three-partner firms by 18 per cent, while the contributions of most larger firms will remain the same. Sole practitioners will in future face bi-annual accounts checks by the society and restrictions on their right to handle clients' money. The society will also vote later this week on whether to cap payments out of the compensation fund at Pounds 50,000. The society is not keen to cap the fund in relation to private clients, as it feels that would be a public-relations disaster. It is considering a cap on payments to banks and building societies arising out of dishonest conduct by solicitors, on the ground that institutions should be more aware than individuals of the risks involved.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / BR to introduce station nurseries
DOC.TEXT: COMMUTERS will soon be able to park their children as well as their cars at 10 stations on British Rail's Network SouthEast. Just over half the places at the nurseries, paid for by BR and local employers, will be reserved for BR staff, but they will also be open to passengers. The first two, at Oxford and Wimbledon - purpose-built at a combined cost of Pounds 500,000 - are likely to open in July and provide a total of 100 places. BR says many more such creches might open around the country if the scheme is successful. Network SouthEast hopes to open a further eight during the next school year. BR hopes the nurseries will help in retaining women workers, cut absenteeism and increase efficiency. The number of employer-sponsored nurseries has doubled to 425 since the 1990 Budget introduced tax incentives. The BR move comes after Midland Bank's decision to end its creche programme last year. The bank had planned to open 300 nurseries by 1993, but stopped at 130. Last year a survey showed that, of 34 companies that had been planning nursery provision in 1989, only seven had started to operate creches. The BR nurseries will be run by independent companies and based on US railway creches. The 10 nurseries will be spread throughout the south-east region, almost certainly at sites that will serve each of the nine divisions of Network SouthEast. An additional London-based nursery is likely.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Pit deadline
DOC.TEXT: MINERS at Easington in Durham, one of only five remaining pits in north-east England, were yesterday given a further four weeks to improve their colliery's productivity. They were warned that only much improved performance would secure the pit's future beyond next March.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / London crime rises
DOC.TEXT: CRIME in London has risen by 11 per cent with the biggest increases being recorded in street crime and domestic violence, according to figures released yesterday. Street thefts increased by 36 per cent with 7,600 reported incidents in the year to the end of March. Only 6 per cent of muggers were caught. Reports of domestic violence increased by 46 per cent to almost 8,700.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Engineers warn on skills shortage
DOC.TEXT: FEARS of a skills shortage in the mid 1990s should not be abandoned because of the effect of the recession on manufacturers, the Engineering Employers' Federation said yesterday. That statement was made at the launch of a guide to help employers respond to the needs of women with caring responsibilities so as to recruit them and retain their skills

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Election boost for unit trusts
DOC.TEXT: THE general election result and new tax incentives led to the highest sales of unit trusts for 12 months, according to figures released today by the Unit Trust Association, John Authers writes. Total sales in April were Pounds 1bn, while the total number of unit trust accounts held rose for the first time since June 1990. Net sales, at Pounds 252.6m, were greater than for the entire first quarter, and reached their highest level since last September. Funds under management grew to Pounds 59.36bn, the highest figure since October, up from Pounds 55.98bn in March. This was also aided by the strong stock market performance in the weeks after the election. Increased tax concessions announced in the Budget for unit trust investment via Personal Equity Plans (Peps) also encouraged smaller investors into the market. Mr Norman Lamont increased the amount that can be invested annually in unit trust Peps from Pounds 3,000 to Pounds 6,000.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Customers 'ignorant' of water penalties
DOC.TEXT: MOST customers of water companies in England and Wales do not realise they are entitled to compensation if certain guaranteed service standards are not met, according to a survey. That can arise when it takes longer to restore a water supply than the customer has been warned; where there are supply interruptions of more than a set time; when an appointment on a day promised in writing is not kept; or when there is no answer to a complaint or inquiry within a specified time. Customers can claim a Pounds 5 cash payment or credit for each infringement. The survey is the first commissioned by the Office of Water Services (Ofwat), the industry's economic regulator, to discover what customers think about the standard of water and sewerage services and their priorities for improvements. Nearly a quarter of the 3,617 people surveyed by Mori between November last year and January 1992, thought water charges were 'fairly unreasonable' and 15 per cent thought their bills were 'very unreasonable'. Half thought the price they paid for water was reasonable, but more than three quarters were satisfied with the overall service. The findings come at a time of steep rises in water charges. Bills in England and Wales are due to rise in the next few years by an average of 5 percentage points above the level of inflation to pay for the industry's Pounds 28bn capital expenditure programme. The average rise this year is 9.3 per cent. Mr Ian Byatt, director-general of Ofwat, said it was important to know the opinions of the industry's customers, and the survey indicated where their priorities lay. The Customer Viewpoint. Ofwat, Centre City Tower, 7 Hill Street, Birmingham, B5 4UA. Pounds 5.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Business school director resigns
DOC.BYLINE: By IAN HAMILTON FAZEY, Northern Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: PROFESSOR Tom Cannon resigned yesterday as director of Manchester Business School, clearing the way for controversial plans by Manchester University to change the structure of management research and education in the city. The plans have already caused 14 private-sector representatives to resign from the business school's council. They demanded an inquiry by Mr John Patten, the education secretary. With Prof Cannon no longer available to lead the school's fight for greater autonomy from the university, Mr Patten is thought unlikely to intervene. Prof Cannon and the university yesterday agreed a statement to reduce the blow to the university's prestige caused by the high-level resignations - which were led by Sir Dennis Landau, chief executive of the Co-operative Wholesale Society. Prof Cannon, who had two years of his contract still to run, said a recent sabbatical had given him the chance to look into new areas of research which he would now pursue. The university appointed him to a part-time visiting chair in corporate responsibility. The university plans to federate the management education and research activities of the business school, the University of Manchester Institute of Science and Technology (Umist) and the university's department of accounting. They have sofar operated separately. Prof Cannon said a new ordinance brought in by the university to regularise financial accountability would alter the remit of the school's director and its council. The ordinance will in effect remove the business school's autonomy and abolish its council. The council's 14 lay members, who resigned, say the university does not understand the relationship needed between the public and private sectors in management education, which requires more autonomy from the university, not less. The university admitted in the joint statement with Prof Cannon that its relations with the business school have been difficult for many years - and well before Prof Cannon's arrival in 1989. It says they were forced into new prominence by the Education Reform Act, which required the university to define clearer lines of financial accountability. In what amounts to a public testimonial for Prof Cannon, the university says he doubled the size of the school, attracted record numbers of postgraduate students, improved the quality of its research, enhanced its academic reputation and achieved two years of record profits.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Trouble spot
DOC.TEXT: A welder working yesterday near London Bridge Underground station, where electricity, gas, water and tele-communications systems are being diverted so that they do not present a safety hazard, Richard Evans writes. The work follows the inquiry into the King's Cross Tube station fire, which made recommendations for safety improvements to be carried out at a number of London Underground stations. The project is likely to cause delays in Borough High Street, Southwark, until the end of the year while a temporary road is built over the existing carriageway. The safety work is expected to continue beneath the temporary road until 1994 One for the road, Page 15

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Lamont defies EC demands on VAT
DOC.TEXT: MR NORMAN LAMONT, the chancellor, came under strong pressure from the European Commission yesterday to abandon Britain's policy of refusing to accept legally binding minimum rates of value added tax throughout the EC. The Treasury signalled that it would be prepared to face a clash with the Commission over the issue. Mrs Christiane Scrivener, EC commissioner responsible for fiscal policy, warned that Britain would face a 'hard time' unless it agreed a compromise with its EC partners before the end of this month. She was speaking after meeting Mr Lamont in London about preparations for the next EC finance ministers' meeting to be held in a week's time. Mr Lamont used yesterday's talks to reaffirm Britain's firm line not only on VAT but also on excise duties on spirits sold throughout the EC. The UK wants to protect the Scotch whisky industry from possible increased duties in some EC states under plans to harmonise indirect taxes. Underlining a toughening of the sparring over indirect taxation, Mrs Scrivener hinted that Britain might put into jeopardy its hard-won right to maintain zero VAT on a range of everyday goods unless it backed down over the minimum rates question. 'We want the UK to realise that the situation is very serious,' she said. The Treasury flatly contradicted Mrs Scrivener's implicit threat that the zero-rate exemption might be at risk. Britain's zero VAT rates were guaranteed under the EC's sixth VAT directive, which could be changed only by unanimous decision of finance ministers, the Treasury said. The VAT tussle goes to the heart of Britain's desire to maintain maximum fiscal policy freedom in spite of growing economic integration. Mrs Scrivener said she was hopeful that a solution could be found before Britain took over the Community presidency in a month's time. Britain has agreed Commission plans for a Community-wide minimum VAT level of 15 per cent, to come into effect on January 1 next year with the establishment of the single market. But the UK has refused to enshrine the measure in a legally binding EC directive, on the ground that it would restrict the Treasury's freedom of manoeuvre. Mrs Scrivener said that other EC countries that had already decided to align their national VAT rates with the new rules were growing increasingly angry about Britain's VAT obduracy.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Routes to being considered for an honour
DOC.TEXT: THE WHITEHALL MACHINE: technically anybody can make a recommendation, but most come through the Civil Service grapevine. Each principal department has a subcommittee that sifts names and forwards them to a central honours pool run by the Cabinet Office. Names are then passed to 10 Downing Street and eventually to Buckingham Palace. THE QUEEN: has her own list for the Order of Merit and for some orders of chivalry. POLITICAL PARTIES: the principal route is through the whips' offices. Conservative Central Office feeds candidates to the chief whip - one of whose titles is patronage secretary - and after sifting they go to the Cabinet Office and on to 10 Downing Street. Nominations from opposition parties go the same way. THE PRIME MINISTER: can add or subtract from the lists the Civil Service supplies, and it is at that stage that glamour names, such as pop and sports stars, are added.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / PM sustains orders of vanished empire
DOC.BYLINE: By RICHARD EVANS, RICHARD DONKIN, JIMMY BURNS and ANDREW SLADE
DOC.TEXT: MR JOHN MAJOR'S dissol-ution honours on Saturday and the Queen's birthday honours list a week later will be trawled minutely for any hint they may give of the prime minister's intention to overhaul the complex and cumbersome honours system. The honours system is often defended as harmless and inexpensive fun, which occasionally rewards the outstanding and frequently the dull but worthy. Critics say the system represents Britain at its worst - snobbish, secretive and backward-looking - and that nothing illustrates its absurdity better than the titles awarded of commander, officer and member of orders in a non-existent empire. Nearly every state awards honours of some kind, but Britain is the only country to give honours that involve the recipients' changing their names or taking a parliamentary seat unelected. Similarly, only Britain has evolved a system of such arcane complexity that only a handful of senior civil servants, and presumably the Queen, fully understand its fine distinctions. Any shivers of apprehension in Whitehall and the Conservative party that imminent reforms might damage cherished expectations are likely to be premature - both the lists to be published this month promise to be solidly mainstream and traditional. Many hurdles have to be overcome before reforms are introduced, and the question remains whether the meritocratic Mr Major can overcome the support for the system in the Civil Service and in the government, where patronage can be a formidable weapon. How would potential rebels be kept in order if government whips could not rely on honours for the subservient and hints about life peerages to discipline troublemakers? And how would party coffers be filled? At least twice annually - with the new-year and the Queen's birthday lists - and more frequently in years when parliament is dissolved or a prime minister resigns - public worries about patronage are aired, then shelved. Mr Major has now to show he can disrupt this pattern. There are three areas Mr Major will have to reform if he is to meet the main criticisms - the way decisions are reached, which is regarded as too secretive; the ending of automatic honours; and the abolition of political honours. Although recipients are researched scrupulously, the secrecy means there is often no clear rationale behind decisions, and that leads to suspicions. For example, the relationship between businessmen who give large sums of money to the Conservative party and those who have received high political honours is close. During Mrs Thatcher's 11 years as prime minister, 17 private-sector industrialists were made peers - their companies had contributed more than Pounds 5m to the Tory party or a linked organisation. As Mr John Walker says in his book The Queen Has Been Pleased, that works out at Pounds 300,000 a peerage. He estimates that a senior industrialist doubled his chance of getting a peerage or knighthood after 1979 if his company donated to Tory funds. After the Lloyd George sale of honours in 1920, when the price of a peerage was about Pounds 100,000 (more than Pounds 1m at today's prices), a political honours scrutiny committee of three privy councillors was created to ensure that there was no further scandal. Mr Major is clearly against the award of automatic honours to civil servants and others simply because of seniority. The practice was introduced to reward poorly paid public servants, but pay is no longer poor in the higher reaches of the Civil Service. The awarding of automatic honours is less clear-cut outside the Civil Service. The heads of the Stock Exchange and the Securities and Investments Board, for example, can count on knighthoods, but one is not always bestowed on the chairman of the Lloyd's of London insurance market. Chairmen of the four clearing banks are virtually assured of a title, and the governor and his deputy at the Bank of England are also certain of honours. So-called political honours were abandoned by Lord (Harold) Wilson when he was prime minister in 1966 and were not used by Sir Edward Heath, his successor, to reward loyal and long-serving backbenchers. The tradition was revived by Mrs Margaret Thatcher and more than 100 knighthoods were given to Tory MPs during her premiership. Probably the worst job to have for anyone wanting to attract an honour is that of a profession is usually well represented in the lists, the world of entertainment is rarely recognised. Stars such as Benny Hill, Dick Emery and Tommy Cooper received no recognition, although they provided big export earnings through films and television series. There also seems to be some distinction in sporting honours. Cricket, rugby union and show jumping get proportionately many more honours than soccer, rugby league or snooker. Support for reform is widespread. Lord Hunt, a life peer and former secretary to the cabinet in the Callaghan and Thatcher administrations, said the system worked surprisingly well in identifying people who were not part of the establishment. 'But the idea that people should get honours simply because they have reached a certain level in the Civil Service is wrong.' What is not clear from Mr Major's hints of reform is the timing, and the signs are that nothing is imminent. It will depend on his judgment on whether the political dividend of radical change is seen to outweigh the aggravation caused within the government and in Whitehall.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Police case
DOC.TEXT: Alison Halford, an assistant chief constable for Merseyside, arrives at an industrial tribunal yesterday. Ms Halford told the tribunal that she endured 'years of misery' among senior police officers. She is claiming sex discrimination against the present chief constable; the home secretary; HM inspector of constabulary for the north-west; and Northamptonshire police authority. Ms Halford claims that, of nine applications for senior posts, she was shortlisted only twice and was never successful because she is a woman. The hearing continues today.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Decision on Ulster talks
DOC.TEXT: NORTHERN Ireland's political leaders agreed yesterday to spend a further two days trying to resolve a row over the timing of the Irish government's entry into the talks. There was little evidence that intensive talks in a sub-committee over the past few days had made significant progress towards resolving the deadlock. Sir Patrick Mayhew, Northern Ireland secretary, may decide to suspend the process, or he may announce unilaterally when the Irish government will enter. Yesterday, Sir Patrick and Mr Jeremy Hanley, the minister responsible for political development in the province, had talks with the party leaders before to a full plenary session. The Northern Ireland Office said it had been agreed that the sub-committee would continue to try to move the process forward before reporting back tomorrow. All parties were yesterday maintaining their pledge of confidentiality.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Discussion on aid for Names
DOC.TEXT: THE COUNCIL of the Lloyd's of London insurance market will consider a proposal to help some of the worst-affected Names at its monthly meeting tomorrow. However, Lloyd's said yesterday that there was no certainty that it would adopt any plan. An ad hoc committee has been considering possible schemes for several weeks. The adoption of any plan is likely to depend on the approval in a ballot of the market's 22,400 Names - wealthy individuals whose capital backs the market. The Names may have to meet much of the cost of any scheme through a special levy. Although most agencies - which manage syndicates and handle the affairs of Names - favour a bail-out plan, many of the Names are less enthusiastic.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / BSkyB and BBC confirm FA deal
DOC.TEXT: BRITISH Sky Broadcasting, the satellite television venture, and the BBC yesterday agreed a Pounds 75m deal with the Football Association for coverage of FA Cup matches and England's home internationals, Raymond Snoddy writes. The two broadcasting organisation are three years into a Pounds 30m four-year agreement with the FA. Yesterday's deal is for a further four years. The agreement yesterday follows the Pounds 304m deal last month between BSkyB, in which Pearson, owner of the Financial Times, has a stake, and the BBC for five years' coverage of the new Premier League's matches. The BBC will continue to have access under the agreement to one live game for each round of the Cup as well as the semi-finals and the final. BSkyB will have rights to one live game and one recorded game from each round and exclusive coverage of any semi-final replays. The deal is likely to arouse more anger from ITV, which says its bid for the BBC package alone was close to the combined BSkyB-BBC total. ITV is now left with an Pounds 8m-a-year agreement to cover the Football League, without the Premier League or the Rumbelows Cup.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Big double-glazing company fails: MP demands rapid inquiry by official receiver 'to ensure there has been no malpractice'
DOC.BYLINE: By IAN HAMILTON FAZEY, Northern Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: A DOUBLE-GLAZING com-pany started by founders of the collapsed Stormseal group has failed after less than 15 months. Northern Stock Plastics, which traded as Surestyle, was started with the assets of the Stormseal group. It has called in receivers, with a threat to about 500 jobs. Mr Mark Palios of Cork Gully, the receiver, said last night he hoped to have a preliminary estimate of Surestyle's debts today. Stormseal failed in January last year owing about Pounds 20m to unsecured creditors, including Pounds 500,000 to leading players in a snooker tournament it was sponsoring. Exact figures have not yet been calculated by Grant Thornton, Stormseal's receiver, and the inquiry has not yet been completed. More than 3,000 jobs were lost or affected. Stormseal and Surestyle were both founded by brothers Michael and Mark Sweeney, of Bury, Greater Manchester, where both businesses were based. The companies both used nationwide sales staffs paid on commission. High-pressure methods used by some of their salesmen had attracted criticism. The Sweeneys formed Surestyle as a 'phoenix' company after buying the Stormseal businesses from the receiver for Pounds 3m in February 1991. Mr Alastair Burt, Conservative MP for Bury North, last night called for a speedy inquiry by the official receiver 'to ensure there has been no malpractice'. He has written to Mr Neil Hamilton, trade and industry minister, about the time taken to complete the Stormseal inquiry. As a minister - in the social security department - he is limited in what he can say in public on constituency-related matters. Concern is understood to be increasing at Westminster about 'phoenix' companies - failed companies restarted by people who ran them before their collapse. Limited liability enables directors to leave the trading debts of a failed company behind and start afresh in the same business. There is no suggestion that the Sweeneys have done anything improper - they had to compete to buy Stormseal's assets. Some MPs, though, are asking whether people involved in a business failure should first be cleared by the receiver in order to start a phoenix operation with the same assets. Mr Michael Sweeney yesterday blamed Surestyle's collapse on the recession and 'unwarranted' bad publicity. He said that in having a second go at the business he and his brother had been trying to save jobs. Earlier this year a Teesside lecturer called on police to remove two Surestyle salesmen who refused to leave his home without a sales order. Surestyle later sacked them.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Warning by Bank on foreign mergers
DOC.TEXT: THE BANK of England warned banks yesterday of the dangers of buying a foreign bank or trying to develop into pan-European institutions. The management and cultural impediments of adopting either strategy 'appear to be overly daunting', Mr Brian Quinn, the Bank's director in charge of supervision, told chairmen of the world's biggest banks at the International Monetary Conference in Toronto. This year's conference chairman is Mr William Purves, chairman of Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, the Far Eastern bank that is trying to buy Midland Bank of the UK. Mr Quinn said cross-border deals similar to that proposed by Hongkong Bank would remain few and far between. He said it was 'unlikely that we will see any pan-European retail or wholesale bank or securities company established in the near future'. Mr Quinn pointed out that banks of different nationalities were tending to form looser alliances, such as sharing businesses. Some were taking minority shareholdings in each other or being jointly represented in some countries. He was sceptical about the benefits of such alliances. 'They appear to owe more to defensive or protective sentiments than to a clearly articulated strategy,' he said. Big US banks were encouraged by a speech from Mr Nicholas Brady, the US Secretary of the Treasury, in which he made a commitment to revive the White House attempts to reform the US banking system. 'Banks should be permitted to branch nationwide, diversifying their risk and increasing the competition in service.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Union chief warns on Labour party funding
DOC.TEXT: MR TOM SAWYER, deputy general secretary of the Nupe public-service union and a strong influence in the labour movement, warned yesterday that unions would be unwilling to provide funds for the Labour party if they had no say in its policy. Defending the unions' links with Labour, Mr Sawyer said there was a case for modernising the relationship and for unions not casting block votes on behalf of anonymous members. He cautioned: 'People who fund the party must have a say. While we fund the party we will have a say. It is as crude as that.' Mr Sawyer's comments - he even advocated retaining the electoral college for electing the leader - amount to a further blow to supporters of root-and-branch reform of the party-union link. They appeared to make the running in the immediate post-election period. His comments come a week after Labour's national executive committee set in motion an inquiry into the relationship with unions. It was Mr Sawyer, an NEC member and last year's party chairman, who proposed the inquiry. The executive of Nupe, the fourth-largest union affiliated to Labour, said in a statement yesterday that it rejected any notion that the union-party links should be broken. In a speech to the union's annual conference in Scarborough, Mr Sawyer criticised party members who sought to make the unions a scapegoat for the Conservatives' election victory. 'Don't blame the unions,' he said. 'And don't blame the staff or the party's advisers. If the campaign wasn't good enough, it was the politicians who were in charge of the campaign that failed.' Mr Sawyer also criticised fellow union leaders and others who began advocating a diminution of union influence immediately after the election. 'Too many who should know better are saying too many things about the election and the future of the Labour party without thinking.' Later, Mr Sawyer said: 'We are in danger of losing the collective approach of unions in policy-making structures.' The basis of the inquiry should be to safeguard the rights of the people who fund the Labour party. The electoral college that chooses who should be Labour party leader should stay, although it should be democratised, he said. That may put him at odds with Mr John Smith, likely to be the next Labour party leader, who has said that he wants future leadership contests to be decided on the basis of one-person-one-vote. Mr Sawyer said he would favour calls for an examination into the separating of union block votes so that the preferences of individual members could be reflected. Under the present system, each union casts all of its votes for one candidate or another. Mr Sawyer said unions should also maintain a presence on the national executive committee. They gave 'balance, breadth and working-class representation.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Concern at 'fragility' of training policy
DOC.BYLINE: By DAVID GOODHART and ANDREW ADONIS
DOC.TEXT: FURTHER evidence of govern-ment concern at the 'fragility' of its training policy is disclosed in a strategy paper by Sir Geoffrey Holland, permanent secretary at the Department of Employment. He says the 'initial enthusiasm' of the 82 Training and Enterprise Councils in England and Wales has been 'dented' and adds that not all Tecs are fully effective. The main anxiety mentioned in the paper is the ability of Tecs to work with the education service and meet the government's targets for skill levels among young people. 'There is a big (but declining) gap between the achievements of young people and the target achievement,' the paper adds. Sir Geoffrey says that a shortage of resources has prevented Tecs from playing a full part in stimulating growth in the Investors In People scheme. 'We need to address ourselves to how to transform IIP into the flagship it ought to be - and must be if we are to succeed,' he writes. On an institutional level the paper states: 'Tecs clearly need to develop rapidly and professionally their partnership with education . . . Few have made much progress in this area.' Sir Geoffrey also highlights the tension between meeting government training guarantees for the unemployed and achieving training targets for those in work. That has been echoed by many Tec chairmen, some of whom would like the freedom to transfer resources from the large schemes for the unemployed - Youth Training and Employment Training - to other training initiatives. Mr Tony Blair, shadow employment secretary, called for a thorough stocktaking of the success and failure of the Tec experiment but expressed opposition to any move to shift resources away from training the unemployed.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Bright lights
DOC.TEXT: Beneath London's West End, fitter Steve Flint puts the finishing touches to a 132,000-volt cable tunnel leading to an electrical substation built to meet the growing demands of the capital's entertainment district. The first electricity from the complex built below Leicester Square (see inset drawing) will soon be fed to businesses and homes throughout the capital's theatreland. The project has taken several years and was designed to prevent traffic congestion in the heart of the West End and to protect the environment in neighbouring streets. Taylor Woodrow, the substation's contractor, has been commended by Westminster City Council. Work has been carried out while Leicester Square was refurbished by the council.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / BT job loss move opposed
DOC.TEXT: THE MAIN union in BT, the telecommunications group, has voted not to co-operate with a scheme for redundant workers that would guarantee them three months' work after leaving the company. The annual conference of the NCU communications union voted to reject the scheme, fearing that it would lead to increased casual employment. BT hopes for 24,000 redundancies this year. Its scheme would provide leavers with a Pounds 1,000 training voucher and at least three months' work in the year after redundancy. The work would be arranged through Manpower and Skillbase employment agencies. BT says that although the idea of 'bridging' work before retirement or another job is not new, it has never been tried on such a scale for non-managerial staff. Those on the scheme would be employed by the agencies and receive at least 25 per cent of their last BT salary for the three months' work.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Lenders will defend record
DOC.TEXT: CHIEF executives of the top 10 UK mortgage lenders will today try to persuade ministers that they have managed to prevent evictions of thousands of homeowners unable to maintain mortgage payments. The Pounds 800m mortgage rescue programme announced last December has nevertheless so far failed to get off the ground. At the meeting will be Mr Norman Lamont, chancellor, Mr Peter Lilley, social security secretary, and Sir George Young, housing minister. They will tell lenders of their disappointment that only a dozen households seem to have been spared eviction by the mortgage rescue schemes agreed between lenders and the government. Lenders say legal and commercial snags have delayed full operation of the schemes, but that they have saved tens of thousands of homeowners from eviction by negotiating easier terms. About 275,000 mortgage borrowers were six months or more behind with payments at the start of the year, but evictions by the end of the year are likely to be close to last year's 76,000. That suggests that lenders have found ways of saving about 200,000 homeowners.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Smaller pay rises 'vital' says Heseltine
DOC.TEXT: PAY RESTRAINT is vital if Britain is to maintain its competitive position, Mr Michael Heseltine, trade and industry secretary, warned yesterday, Emma Tucker writes. In a speech attacking manufacturing wage rises for running at twice the rate of inflation, Mr Heseltine said lower pay settlements were vital if Britain was to 'build on the increase in competitiveness which we achieved in the 1980s'. He complained that manufacturing earnings were rising by an average of 8 per cent, almost double the inflation rate. 'Compared to the UK's 8 per cent, the increase in earnings in manufacturing in Germany last year was 6 per cent, in Japan 4 per cent and in the US just 3 per cent,' Mr Heseltine said at a London conference of business leaders. The Department of Employment says average earnings for the whole economy are still running at an annual rate of 7.5 per cent even though the level of pay deals has fallen significantly since last year. Economists expect the rate of average earnings to drop over the next few months as the high pay settlements of a year ago - when the inflation rate was above 6 per cent - drop out of the index.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Gas-fired power stations criticised
DOC.TEXT: NATIONAL Grid Company may refuse to take power from many of the new gas-fired power stations being built in England and Wales because of fears about the design of the stations, it said yesterday. National Grid, which owns and operates the electricity supply system, was responding to a statement from Mr Malcolm Edwards, former commercial director of British Coal. He said the new stations would be technically inferior to existing coal-fired stations. This will intensify the row over whether the 16 new stations now committed or being built were necessary. National Grid has warned that they would create a 60 per cent surplus of electricity by 1997. Mr Edwards said the new gas stations were less flexible than coal-fired stations and could not guarantee the stability of the system. He said those shortcomings arose from National Grid's failure to communicate the requirements for the design of the gas-powered stations to developers. That was supported by the contradictory comments from National Grid and developers of the new stations, he said. However, Mr Bryan Townsend, chairman of Midlands Electricity, rejected the claim. 'It's absolute rubbish,' he said. Midlands Electricity is involved in the biggest power station project on Teeside. Mr Townsend said that all new stations had been designed to meet requirements set out by National Grid in its grid code. 'If a plant is designed to meet the grid code, it won't have problems.' Mr Mike Eggleton of Yorkshire Electricity defended the new stations. 'Many of the new gas plant designs are more flexible than the large coal stations,' he said. Yorkshire Electricity is building a power station in south Humberside. National Grid said it was concerned that some of the gas-fired stations might not meet the system's requirements, even though they met the grid code specifications. That was because the code left room for interpretation and did not specify how flexible a new plant had to be. Mr Edwards predicted that National Grid would not be able to take more than half of the total power that all the new stations being built or committed would provide when demand was low without jeopardising the supply. That was good news for coal, he said. Even if gas were cheaper, it might replace the power generated by only about 20m tonnes of coal, rather than the 30m previously expected.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Broker accused of making false statement
DOC.BYLINE: By RAYMOND HUGHES, Law Courts Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: A STOCKBROKER falsely told Goldman Sachs, the US investment bank, in October 1990 that Maxwell Communication Corporation was about to file for bankruptcy, it was alleged at Knightsbridge Crown Court yesterday. Mr Andrew Collins QC, prosecuting, said Mr Peter Marks, a director of Branston and Gothard, made the statement, which he had known was untrue, to try to lower the MCC share price and make money for himself on dealings in the shares. Mr Marks has pleaded not guilty to a charge under section 47 of the Financial Services Act of making a misleading, false or deceptive statement to induce share dealing. Mr Collins said that soon after 8am on October 12 Mr Marks telephoned Mr Graham Ward, a Goldman Sachs marketmaker in London, and agreed to sell him 100,000 MCC shares at 136p. Three minutes later Mr Marks rang again and asked Mr Ward to call him back on a line on which calls were not tape-recorded. The return call was made by Mr Ward's superior, Mr Timothy Medland, whose recollection was that Mr Marks had told him that Mr Robert Maxwell would be filing for bankruptcy for MCC that day, or words to that effect. Mr Collins said: 'What was conveyed was a statement of fact that Maxwell was effectively going bust that day.' Shortly afterwards Mr Marks again telephoned Mr Ward and agreed to sell him a further 100,000 MCC shares at 133p. Mr Marks then bought 200,000 MCC shares at 134p to fulfil the sales. Mr Collins said Goldman Sachs had been one of the main buyers of Maxwell shares. If it had suddenly marked them down the price might have been expected to fall. Mr Ward said that in September and October 1990 Goldman Sachs had in general been buying, and as the MCC price had gone down Mr Ward had bought the stock on the instructions of a Goldman Sachs partner in New York. Cross-examined by Mr Anthony Scrivener QC, for Mr Marks, Mr Ward agreed that on October 12 Goldman Sachs had held 23,433,708 MCC shares and that dealing records appeared to show that on that day 1m MCC shares had been sold within Goldman Sachs. Mr Collins intervened to say the 1m shares had been sold to Goldman Sachs New York. Mr Medland said he had passed on what Mr Marks had told him to Mr Eric Sheinberg, Goldman Sachs managing director in New York. Mr Scrivener suggested to Mr Medland, now a stocktrader with Swiss Bank Corporation, that Goldman Sachs had 'a special relationship' with the Maxwell organisation. Mr Medland agreed. He said Mr Sheinberg had been the only person with authority over a special Maxwell share account. The trial continues today.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / Chambers offered single roof: Moves to merge two business organisations
DOC.TEXT: ON THE brink of the 21st century, the business organisations that have represented British companies since the end of the 19th are belatedly bringing themselves up to date. Plans for a merger between the Association of British Chambers of Commerce - founded in 1860 - and the National Chamber of Trade - established in 1895 - mark an important step towards consolidating the voice of smaller businesses. Their fragmented lobbying efforts have frequently been blamed for their ineffectiveness in influencing government policy. A merger would also represent an important boost to plans launched by the association just over 18 months ago to strengthen the chamber of commerce network. By linking with the NCT, which mainly represents retailers, the association would enhance its role as one of the country's big three national business groups, second to the Confederation of British Industry with 250,000 members and ahead of the Institute of Directors with 33,500 UK members. If the merger - in effect a takeover by the association of the less financially well endowed NCT - goes ahead in the autumn, it will end the confusion of two very similarly named organisations competing for public attention and for members in towns and cities up and down the country. The NCT draws a large chunk of its membership from 28 affiliated trade organisations representing among others booksellers, coal merchants and sports goods distributors. It also has 150 chambers around the country. The association heads a group of more than 100 chambers but is trying to improve patchy national coverage by creating a network of 55 core chambers. Around those will cluster smaller local chambers, some of them no more than social clubs. For the NCT, difficulties are even more acute. Average membership of local chambers of trade is 60 people. Even the largest six chambers of trade in towns such as Sheffield, Carlisle and Eastbourne have only 400 to 500 members. That compares with the larger chambers of commerce in London and Birmingham with 5,000 and 5,400 members respectively - although even those are tiny compared with the large, publicly funded Continental chambers. None of the chambers of trade is expected to have the resources to join the the association's core network. Both the association and the NCT have to cope with unaffiliated chambers that use the chamber title but are outside national membership for financial reasons or because they have fallen out with the national body. Although at first sight the addition of 150,000 new members to the association would be welcome to an organisation in the middle of a national recruitment drive to boost numbers from 83,000 to 150,000, many of the new members would be one-person businesses and corner shops. They do not conform to the association's target of dynamic businesses set on growth. They would, however, be welcome at a time when the association's own expansion programme has run up against the recession. With the impact of its recruitment drive yet to show through, the association is nursing a 7,000 loss in membership over the past two years. The association and the NCT have been trying for many years to merge. The two most recent attempts, in 1984 and 1986-87, failed because of differences of opinion about the relative weight of the two organisations in the combined group. So why do they now think they can get together? Mr Bernard Tennant, NCT director-general, believes it is because the association wants to fill an important gap in its coverage of UK industry sectors, namely retailing. The NCT is willing to accept a subordinate role as a retailing and small firms division of the association, prompted possibly by the sharp contraction in the number of smaller retailers in recent years - although not in its membership - and by financial constraints. The NCT still has a strong balance sheet but has made operating losses in the past two years because of a reluctance by member chambers to raise subscription rates. The association's reorganisation is being led by Mr Ron Taylor, a former head of Leeds chamber of commerce and the organisation's first director-general in living memory to have a chamber rather than a Civil Service background. Mr Tennant is a long-term member of the NCT's headquarters staff, who became director-general in 1987. The two men have known each other since the 1960s, when Mr Tennant also worked for the chambers of commerce. He later headed Bolton's chamber of trade, which, wealthier than the local chamber of commerce, invited the latter to take office space in its new headquarters. As the terms of the proposed merger suggest, that power relationship has changed.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 02 JUN 92 / World Trade News: French share in railway order for Bratislava
DOC.TEXT: BRATISLAVA, capital of the Slovak republic, has awarded a FFr3bn (Pounds 300m) contract to a consortium of two French companies and local partners to build a driverless commuter railway for the city, William Dawkins reports from Paris.
