Opening the conference in Johannesburg, Mr Mandela said members of the ANC were increasingly aware of the resource constraints that would face a future government, and that there would therefore be 'no quick fix to decades of apartheid destruction'. Mr Mandela said the Third World was littered with relics of liberation movements which had failed at the polls because of unfulfilled promises, lack of openness in policymaking and through adopting policies which their countries could not sustain. He said these were valuable lessons for the ANC to learn. Mr Mandela also gave notice, however, that the constitutional negotiation process in South Africa could be entering a difficult phase. The ANC and its allies were contemplating mass civil protests, possibly including a general strike, to place pressure on the government. He gave July as a deadline by which progress should be made in constitutional talks, and said the conference would consider activities 'to break the intransigence of the regime'. The four-day policy conference, being attended by 700 delegates, is the first such ANC conference since the drafting of the Freedom Charter at Kliptown in 1955. The charter, a romantic and aspirational document, has since taken on a totemic importance within ANC ranks. Ms Cheryl Carolus, a senior ANC official, said the task of the conference was 'to take that magnificent vision of ours, enshrined in the Freedom Charter, and make it tangible'. Mr Mandela also took time to reply to the provisional findings of the Goldstone Commission, a judicial inquiry into the causes of violence in the country. Judge Goldstone yesterday delivered a report in which he said the main cause of violence was the political struggle between the ANC and the mainly Zulu Inkatha organisation. Mr Mandela said the findings were superficial in two respects: attributing blame to the ANC and Inkatha was to ignore the role of the government and security forces in fostering this rivalry; and suggesting that the ANC and Inkatha were in the best position to stop the violence was to 'ignore the reality that it is the National party regime who wields state power'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Greek exporters take to the sea, air and narrow road - War in what was Yugoslavia, means finding new routes to European Community markets
DOC.TEXT: FOR GREEK exporters, war in the former Yugoslavia already means higher transport costs, fear of goods being hijacked and, for producers of oranges and cucumbers, a sizeable loss of business. International sanctions against Serbia are likely to pose further problems for Greek trade with the European Community, which last year accounted for two-thirds of total trade worth Dollars 25.8bn (Pounds 14.5bn). Until last summer, around 40 per cent of Greece's trade with its EC partners passed through Macedonia and Serbia. In the past 10 months, road haulage traffic through the northern Greek border has dropped by half, while trains to Belgrade and Munich no longer run regularly. Customs officials say that between 100 and 150 international long-distance TIR trucks used to cross the Yugoslav and Bulgarian borders every day. Now fewer than 70 go through. Most drivers prefer to take a slow two-lane road through Bulgaria rather than the Belgrade highway. Greek exporters and freight forwarders are spending time and ingenuity devising alternate routes to western Europe that avoid Serbia. Agreement was reached earlier this year on a new rail route to Austria through Bulgaria, Romania and Hungary. But problems of time-keeping and theft still loom large, says Mr Kriton Ioannides of Proodos, a Greek freight forwarder. 'Quality was lacking: not enough locomotives were available in Romania to be sure of keeping to schedule; rail freight theft is a problem in all east Europe countries,' he explains. Proodos, which imports white goods and cars by rail and exports fruit and vegetables, organised special trains to travel non-stop between Austria and Greece with an armed escort aboard. 'We had the train put together at the Austrian border and made sure that, if it stopped, it would be at a small station where the guards wouldn't be attacked,' Mr Ioannides said. Trains can reach Greece in 35 hours, the time taken on the old rail route through Croatia and Slovenia. Mr Ioannides says higher costs are not enough to deter traders if it becomes impossible to transit Serbia. Trucks now take a more expensive time-consuming route, using ferries to Italy from western Greek ports. But costs are up to 30 per cent higher for manufactured goods and up to 90 per cent higher for fresh fruit and vegetables at times when the bulk of a crop becomes available. At peak points in the season, especially summer when tourists' cars compete for space with trucks carrying grapes or peaches, not enough ferries are available. Also, the small western Greek ports are not equipped to handle large numbers of TIR trucks. An Igoumenitsa harbour official said: 'Even in January it was chaos here when the oranges were leaving. We don't have parking space for more than a handful of 20-tonne trucks.' Agricultural produce accounts for more than 20 per cent of Greek exports, with fresh fruit and vegetables the highest earners. But, last winter, orange exports to the EC fell by 38 per cent to 87,500 tonnes, according to Incofruit, the exporters' association. Cucumber exports were down by 37 per cent to 29,700 tonnes. Exports of oranges to eastern European countries rose by 22 per cent to 157,000 tonnes, but overall fruit and vegetable earnings still declined to Dollars 352m for the 1991-92 season, a 6 per cent fall from the previous year. Mr George Polychronidis, director of Incofruit, estimates that exports of oranges and cucumbers would have been 20 per cent higher if access to EC markets had been easier: 'We lost market share in the EC both because of higher transport costs and poorer quality because the produce was on the road an extra 24 hours. Sales to eastern Europe can't compensate because prices are much lower and the market is still very unstable.' Bumper harvests of cherries and peaches were expected this year, but these were too expensive to find markets easily in eastern Europe. Exporters on the island of Crete, which accounts for more than 50 per cent of Greek fruit and vegetable exports, are planning for the first time to air-freight produce, aboard charter flights taking European tourists home from holidays. After years of resistance to similar proposals, the Greek ministry of transport last week agreed that tourist charter jets could carry a limited amount of cargo. A report by the Chamber of Commerce in Heraklion, Crete's principal town, estimates that up to 750 tonnes of fruit and vegetables could be shipped each week to cities in Britain, the Netherlands and Germany. 'Air freight costs twice as much as road and ferry. But we think this can be covered by the extra value of fruit marketed within a few hours of being picked,' a Chamber official said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Japan warns US chip makers over imports pressure
DOC.TEXT: JAPAN'S electronics industry might reduce its purchases of US semiconductors if the US applies 'too much' pressure for increased imports, Japanese government officials warned yesterday. The warning follows Washington's decision to review the US-Japan chip pact and examine ways of improving exporters' access to the Japanese market, where the foreign share has hovered at 14 per cent for the past year. Tokyo fears chips will be targeted by Washington during the US presidential election campaign, in an attempt to show the Bush administration has been tough on trade with Japan. The two countries disagree over interpreting the pact, signed last year and replacing a 1986 agreement. Japan says the wording provides no market share guarantees; the US chip industry argues the pact needs at least 20 per cent foreign share by the end of this year. At the end of last year, the foreign share was 14.4 per cent, with little chance the 20 per cent figure will be reached. A Ministry of International Trade and Industry official said: 'If this review doesn't just look at market share and creates a better understanding about the long-term relationship between the two industries, we think it may have a good effect.' If Washington applied unnecessary pressure, the official said, Japanese companies would be 'discouraged' and might cut their purchases of foreign chips. He blamed the stalled market share on the slowing of the domestic economy and inability of medium-sized US makers to penetrate the Japanese market. The Electronic Industries Association of Japan (EIAJ), which is due to meet US chip industry representatives in Tokyo next week, said some US companies had sold their chips in Japan, but others have failed to meet customer specifications. 'A Japanese customer was looking for small and thin chips, but found US semiconductor companies could not make it. We are collecting stories like that,' the EIAJ said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Third world 'faces neglect from industrial nations'
DOC.BYLINE: By DAVID DODWELL, World Trade Editor
DOC.TEXT: DEVELOPING countries face a 'period of neglect' from the industrial north when trade and protectionism will be more important than aid or debt relief in shaping growth, Sir Peter Leslie, Commonwealth Development Corporation chairman, said yesterday, David Dodwell, World Trade Editor, reports. Presenting the annual report of the CDC, the UK government-controlled organisation channelling aid into private-sector projects in developing countries, Sir Peter said funds were flowing less freely to the third world now than in the 1970s and 1980s. Political and economic reform was the key to attracting investment, with good governance and an end to corruption important preconditions for aid. He noted the 'progressive disappearance' of British private investors in countries where the CDC operates, and warned the protectionist consequences of a failure of the Uruguay Round trade talks would have 'serious repercussions' on many of the 68 countries where the CDC has operations. New investment in 105 projects reached a record Pounds 157.3m in 1991, up from Pounds 145.9m in 1990, with less than 45 per cent provided from the UK government's aid programme. The majority (about Pounds 87m) came from profits earned on past CDC investments, lifting to Pounds 1.33bn total CDC investments and third world commitments. CDC income from investments rose to Pounds 86.9m, from Pounds 83.1m in 1990, leading to an operating surplus of Pounds 69.9m, up from Pounds 67.2m. Extraordinary profits of Pounds 22.3m from the sale of long-standing investments in Thailand and Singapore lifted the surplus transferred to reserves to Pounds 28.4m, almost four times the 1990 transfer of Pounds 7.7m. An extraordinary gain of Pounds 45m will be reported next year, following the sale in April of its shareholding in a Hong Kong container terminal.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Pepsico in Belarus bottle joint venture
DOC.TEXT: PRODUCTION OF Pepsi bottles will start later this year in the republic of Belarus under a joint venture officially announced in Moscow yesterday. The venture, named Belpak, is between Pepsico International and Eastman Chemical Company, both of the US, and Khimvolokno chemical company and MPOST synthetic textile enterprise, both of Mogilev, Belarus. The venture will make plastic bottles for soft drinks and is expected to produce Dollars 100m (Pounds 56.4m) of investment over the next five years from hard-currency earnings. The initial investment, which was said to be 'modest', was not disclosed. From the autumn, Belpak will produce polyethylene terphthalate resin (PET), a clear recyclable plastic used in making drinks bottles. Half the production will be used for Pepsi bottles in the former Soviet Union, while the rest will be exported to west and east Europe for hard currency. The hard currency profits will be split equally between the two US partners and the two Belarus enterprises. Production of the PET resin is expected to grow to 25,000 metric tonnes annually, equivalent to 500m 2-litre bottles a year. Pepsico, the leading soft drinks maker in the former Soviet Union, has a history of innovative agreements since opening its first facility there in 1974. It trades its soft drink for exports of Stolichnaya vodka and, in the past two years, commercial ships built in the Ukraine. Mr Donald Kendall, Pepsico's former chairman, said: 'There is no question that US and other western companies should come into this market now. People who wait for political stability or better convertibility of the rouble will lose out to others.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Government gives boost to home-grown capitalism
DOC.TEXT: THE focus of Hungarian privatisation is to turn inwards, to give preference to domestic over foreign investors, the government announced yesterday. Mr Tamas Szabo, Hungary's privatisation minister, launched a battery of measures designed 'to give a push to local investor demand'. The most concrete change in policy is an explicit commitment that domestic investors will be preferred over foreign companies in the case of similar bids, whereas price was previously the all-important factor. Further help for domestic investors who cannot afford to buy a state company outright will come in the form of concessional leasing or option arrangements. The new schemes will be financed partly by using Ft16bn (Pounds 110m) of the Ft57bn (Pounds 392m) of privatisation sale proceeds forecast for 1992. Hungary has also turned towards Czechoslovak-style privatisation schemes to spur domestic ownership by distributing some state property rather than selling it. The government is to hand over state assets to institutions such as universities, though mass distribution of shares to the public at large is still not on the agenda. The change of emphasis comes at a time when both the government and privatisation itself are increasingly unpopular and marks a concession to political pressure for home-grown and popular capitalism after two years in which Hungary has relied almost exclusively on foreign corporate investors to take property off state hands. Nine out of the top ten privatisations by value last year were to western companies. Mr Szabo said that it was necessary to favour domestic investors in order to preserve the overall momentum of privatisation at a time when public showed a 'tendency' to suspect foreign economic domination. A survey this month showed that opinion was divided on privatisation with 39 per cent in favour of selling off state industry and 34 per cent against. Public attitudes to foreign investment and privatisation have been coloured by their coincidence with a deep recession which saw gross domestic product fall by 10 per cent last year. Hungary has been, until now, the most welcoming of east European countries to western investment, a stance rewarded by Dollars 3.5bn (Pounds 1.97bn) in accumulated foreign direct investment, about 60 per cent of the total for the region as a whole. The inflow helped boost the private sector to 25-30 per cent of gross domestic product.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Italy's new president calls for reform
DOC.TEXT: MR Oscar Luigi Scalfaro, Italy's ninth president, yesterday took the unprecedented step of calling for a constitutional overhaul in his inaugural address to parliament. The only president to take an initiative of this kind, the 73-year-old former Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies left no doubt that he intended to encourage institutional reform and inject new morality into public life. 'I believe the president's task consists above all else in taking note of the popular will and, within the constraints of his powers, ensuring this is translated into valid and effective results,' he said. That popular will, he noted, had been expressed in the April 5 general election which saw the traditional political parties humiliated by a large protest vote. 'In this light, the president of the republic from this moment invites parliament respectfully but firmly to nominate a commission of the two houses with a brief to revise the entire institutional framework.' He also emphasised public morality, in a clear reference to the country's corruption scandals, notably in Milan. 'The misuse of public funds is a very serious matter, defrauding honest taxpayers and abusing citizens' confidence: there is no worse evil, no greater danger to democracy than the dirty involvement of politics with business.' Mr Scalfaro was elected on Monday as a compromise candidate proposed by his Christian Democrat party. He was backed by the four-party Christian Democrat-led coalition, as well as the former communist Party of the Democratic Left (PDS), as a candidate whose reputation was untainted by corruption. In his speech, Mr Scalfaro also warned of the need for urgent action on the country's deteriorating finances. He emphasised the risk of failing to converge with the rest of Italy's EC partners, adding: 'We are well aware that Europe cannot wait.' After being sworn in for his seven-year term, Mr Scalfaro drove to the Quirinale Palace where Mr Giovanni Spadolini, the interim president for the last month, formally handed over the keys of office. Mr Scalfaro, a long time widower and devout Catholic, inherits a 16th century palace with 1,200 rooms used by 30 former Popes, four kings and eight presidents. The total presidential staff numbers 796 with a budget of L207bn (Pounds 93.7m) a year. This may well be among the first items to be subjected to reform and austerity.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Russian role in Moldova underlined
DOC.TEXT: CHILDREN laid flowers yesterday on four fresh graves of Russian army officers who died in the fighting in Moldova's breakaway region of Trans Dnestr. The graves, in the central square of the region's capital, Tiraspol, seem to back up Moldovan claims that on May 19 parts of Russia's 14th army began to fight openly on the side of Trans Dnestr's Slavic separatists. The war of words escalated over the role of Russian soldiers in the fighting, as a man was reported killed and three injured in a fresh clash between the region's largely Slav national guard and Moldovan militia near the outpost of Bendery. On Wednesday, President Boris Yeltsin of Russia pledged that the 14th army would be withdrawn from Moldova, whose strong ties with Bucharest have aroused fears among the separatists that Trans Dnestr could one day be swallowed up in a greater Romania. The region declared independence from Moldova in September 1990. Mr Mircea Snegur, the president of Moldova, yesterday described Mr Yeltsin's move as 'a victory for commonsense', but said he feared Russian hardliners might block the withdrawal. The Trans Dnestr Womens' Defence Committee, which has been collecting weapons from unprotesting soldiers at Russian army barracks, said it had been assured by 14th army officials that the soldiers would not withdraw until the conflict was over. Over 100 people have died in the fighting in the past four months. A defiant Mr Igor Smirnov, president of the breakaway republic, said yesterday he expected soldiers and officers from the 14th army to remain in the region and join the Trans Dnestr armed forces. That manpower, combined with Trans Dnestr's strong industrial base which Mr Smirnov said is being geared to military production, would be enough to defend the republic if the 14th army pulled out, he said. Mr Smirnov said entire units of the 14th army might join the separatist side. Guarded by khaki-clad young men toting Kalashnikovs, Mr Smirnov said officers from the right bank of the Dnestr river, where Moldova has taken over most former Soviet forces, had defected to the Trans Dnestr military. Mr Smirnov did not deny Moldovan allegations that the war was costing Trans Dnestr 1m roubles a day but said that funds from Russian enterprises and individuals were offsetting the cost.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Danes wonder if it's time to get off the Eurowagon: Many voters are having second thoughts about EC unity
DOC.TEXT: FOR MANY Danes, Europe appears to be rolling in the wrong direction. A majority of them may be about to stop the unity bandwagon just long enough for their country to jump off. Next Tuesday Danish voters decide in a binding referendum whether to accept or reject the Maastricht treaty agreed last December. The vote represents the first direct test of public opinion on the European union treaty in any of the 12 EC member states. It poll will be followed by a referendum in Ireland on June 18, and, possibly, by one in France later in the summer. The Danes - traditional Euro-sceptics - are showing strong signs of post-Maastricht irritation. In the first three weeks of May, opinion surveys consistently showed small majorities against the treaty. A May 26 Gallup poll, however, indicated 41 per cent in favour, 39 per cent against. Mr Uffe Ellemann-Jensen, the foreign minister, and Denmark's most enthusiastic and tireless pro-Maastricht campaigner, dismisses as irrelevant speculation of a negative vote. 'None of it matters, for there will be a Yes. The Danish people have got too much sense to say No,' he declares. Even if Mr Ellemann is right, the pro-Europe vote seems almost certain to be much smaller than on the two previous occasions when Danes were consulted about European policies. In the 1972 referendum on EC membership, 63 per cent of votes were in favour of joining the Community. In 1986, in the poll on the Single European Act, 56 per cent of voters said Yes. There are many reasons for anti-Maastricht feeling. They range from complaints about the European Commission's strictures on sales of over-curvaceous cucumbers to fears that, in a federal Europe, Denmark will be dominated by 80m Germans. Critics of Maastricht advance arguments on policies which will not be directly implemented by the treaty. These include establishing a European army and proceeding to economic and monetary union (which Denmark would join only after yet another referendum). Above all, opposition focuses on worries about loss of sovereignty and self-determination, and general antipathy to the Brussels bureaucracy. Opinion polls indicate a striking gulf between the people and the political and corporate establishment. The Folketing (parliament) voted by a comfortable 130 votes to 25 to ratify the treaty. The trade unions, all the main business organisations and almost every newspaper of any consequence are urging the electorate to vote in favour. The voters appear unimpressed. The campaign against Maastricht is headed by the two parties which voted against in the Folketing. These are the populist right-wing Progress Party, which wants to keep the Community as it is, and the left-wing, erstwhile Marxist, Socialist People's Party. The opposition Social Democratic Party and the unions are in a particular dilemma. They support Maastricht, but two thirds or more of their normal supporters are against. The Confederation of Danish Trade Unions was even forced to cancel a pro-Maastricht demonstration in Copenhagen on May 22. It feared a repeat of events on May Day, when its chairman, Mr Finn Thorgrimson, had to break off his speech because of a barrage of catcalls and rotten fruit. If Denmark votes No on June 2, what would be the effect on the rest of Europe? As a first step, on June 3 the Irish government would be expected to ask the other members to reaffirm their commitment to the treaty. Although this would require a new treaty excluding Denmark, the signals are that the other 11 members of the Community will implement European union whatever the outcome of the Danish vote. Denmark might then have to accept an associate membership agreement along the lines of the European Economic Area deal with the Efta countries, according to Mr Henning Christophersen, the Danish EC commissioner. Legally as well as practically, a two-tier European union would create enormous problems. Denmark as a signatory to the Rome Treaty would be represented in some EC bodies but not others. Mr Niels Ersboll, the Danish secretary-general to the European Commission, argues that such an outcome would be unsustainable. Denmark would then, he says, be detached from the Rome Treaty institutions as well. Supporters of the treaty such as Mr Christophersen and Mr Ersboll ceaselessly deploy the argument that Denmark cannot afford to be left out on the Maastricht road. One obstacle may, however, be particularly difficult to surmount: far more women are against the treaty than in favour. Perhaps, quips Mr Ellemann-Jensen, because virtually all the people telling them to say Yes are men.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Mars loses a round in battle over ice-cream
DOC.BYLINE: By GUY DE JONQUIERES, Consumer Industries Editor
DOC.TEXT: MARS, the US-owned confectionery maker, yesterday lost a round in its legal battle over the European ice cream market when the Irish High Court ruled that the Anglo-Dutch Unilever group was entitled to bar Mars products from its retail freezer cabinets. The ruling follows a European Commission decision two months ago that Langnese-Iglo, a Unilever subsidiary, and Scholler Lebensmittel, another German ice-cream maker, were acting illegally by maintaining exclusive ties with German retailers which kept Mars products out of their stores. The Commission also reached an interim decision that exclusive freezer agreements operated by Unilever - Europe's biggest ice-cream maker - infringed EC competition law. Mars yesterday sought to overturn a two-year-old Irish court injunction preventing it from putting its ice cream into freezers owned by HB Ice Cream, an Irish Unilever subsidiary. However, the High Court said the injunction did not violate EC or Irish law. Mars said it would appeal against the ruling before the Irish Supreme Court and possibly in the European Court of Justice. It also expressed confidence that the EC Commission would decide formally to prohibit exclusive freezer agreements.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Poland to turn to secret past
DOC.TEXT: THE vexed issue of past collaboration with the communist secret police, which has never been properly aired in Poland, came to the fore yesterday, writes Christopher Bobinski from Warsaw. Mr Janusz Korwin Mikke, a deputy from the small right-wing UPR group, signalled that he would put a motion ordering the Interior Ministry to 'provide full information on government officials, senators, deputies, judges and lawyers who had worked with the SB security service between 1945 and 1992'. Initial reactions showed that it would get a majority. The Interior Ministry is quietly conducting such investigations.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Italian interim leader: Correction
DOC.TEXT: In the editorial comment on Italy on page 18 of the Financial Times of May 27, Mr Giovanni Spadolini was incorrectly described as justice minister instead of interim president of the republic.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Shanghai shock for bulls in China's stock market shops
DOC.TEXT: THE CHINESE, who have embraced share trading with wild enthusiasm, are having to get used to the concept of prices going down as well as up. Prices on Shanghai's stock exchange have dropped 19 per cent in the past three days, after the authorities attempted to ban investment syndicates suspected of ramping share prices. A week ago prices doubled in a single day when the exchange removed limits on daily price movements. The exchanges in Shanghai and in Shenzhen special economic zone, close to Hong Kong, have caught the imagination of the Chinese, many of whom have substantial savings and are looking for ways to put their money to profitable use. Many other cities, including Guangzhou, capital of prosperous Guangdong province, have applied to open stock exchanges. The authorities in Beijing are adopting a cautious approach and officials believe that any new exchanges approved will be in the north. Shanghai lists 'A' shares, which can be traded by Chinese, in only 14 companies, and 'B' shares, which can be traded by foreigners, in one of them. A further 15 'A' shares and six 'B' shares are listed in Shenzhen. With the opportunities for investment so limited, the prices of shares have soared. Although the exchanges have been open for 18 months, trading this year has become frenzied following Beijing's endorsement of accelerated economic reform and as a result of growing prosperity in the south. There is growing interest in the markets from investors in other provinces. Investors see share trading as a way to make quick money in a country which offers few profitable avenues for investment. Communist officials in provinces all over China see share ownership as a means to mobilise savings to back economic reform, to revitalise grossly inefficient state industries and to emulate the booming south. Many officials seem unabashed by the volatility in the existing fledgling markets, and the exchanges themselves are planning a large number of new listings. The mayhem in Shenzhen has seen one murder and hundreds of arrests as the authorities cracked down on gangsters who were fighting for places in queues outside brokers' offices - queue positions were being traded as well as shares. In Shanghai, one man committed suicide after losing 6,000 yuan (Dollars 1,000).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / World News in Brief: Paracetamol review
DOC.TEXT: Four out of every 10 attempted suicides by poisoning involve an overdose of paracetamol, a common cure for headaches, according to a study by doctors in Oxford. They call for an urgent review of paracetamol use.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / UN chief says no to troop relief for Bosnia
DOC.BYLINE: By MICHAEL LITTLEJOHNS, PHILIP STEPHENS and LAURA SILBER
DOC.TEXT: UNITED NATIONS troops should not provide protection for humanitarian aid efforts in Bosnia-Hercegovina, according to Mr Boutros Boutros Ghali, the United Nations secretary-general. The recommendation that the Security Council reject a European Community request for armed intervention came as diplomats put the finishing touches to a package of UN sanctions against Serbia to end the war. While acknowledging it was for the Security Council to make a final decision, Mr Boutros Ghali warned that it would require large numbers of UN troops to secure several hundred kilometres of roads and to establish a defensive perimeter around the Bosnian capital, Sarajevo. The city has been cut off by Serb militia and Yugoslav army troops in a bid to starve it into submission. There was a lull in the fighting around Sarajevo yesterday after heavy overnight clashes. In a bid to distance itself from the mortar attack on Sarajevo on Wednesday which left 17 people dead and 80 wounded, the rump Yugoslav presidency yesterday called on the UN to investigate the 'massacre'. However, diplomatic moves to impose mandatory sanctions could reach fruition as early as today, according to Mr John Major, the prime minister. Speaking in Budapest after talks on the crisis with Mr Joszef Antall, the Hungarian prime minister, Mr Major said that the sanctions were likely to include a trade embargo, a freeze on Serbia's overseas assets, severe restrictions on commercial flights, the suspension of all official sporting contacts and the break-off of scientific, technical and cultural co-operation. The terms of the resolution under discussion by UN ambassadors in New York also included provision for an oil embargo from the middle of next month if Serbia did not act to halt the fighting. Mr Major said that the precise terms of the resolution were still under discussion, 'But I hope it will be agreed by the United Nations by the end of this week . . . that it will be a binding and mandatory series of sanctions.' Mr Boutros Ghali urged the Security Council to bear in mind that authorising hostile action against 'certain factions' in Bosnia-Hercegovina could make it more difficult to secure the co-operation needed for the UN to fulfil its mandate in the protected areas in Croatia. A 'less ambitious possibility' would be to use UN troops to protect relief convoys between Sarajevo airport and distribution centres in the city, he said. A more promising course would be a determined effort to persuade the warring parties to conclude and honour agreements permitting unimpeded delivery of aid to 'all suffering civilians,' said the secretary-general. However, numerous efforts to secure ceasefires have failed after Serb militias and the Yugoslav army have prevented any supplies which have been sent from reaching Sarajevo. In Belgrade the Serbian Orthodox Church attacked the policies of President Slobodan Milosevic in an unprecedented open letter. The church, which had supported the nationalist politics of Mr Milosevic, yesterday appealed for his resignation and the formation of a government of national salvation. Greek exporters, Page 3

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Foreign Exchange (10): Poland sets the pattern - Eastern Europe's move towards convertible currencies
DOC.TEXT: FOREIGN exchange trading in the former communist world from the Elbe to the Pacific Ocean used to be either a state-controlled rip-off or a furtive, back-street affair with money changers who were often secret policemen in disguise. The Poles were the most blatant and competitive of black-market dealers and it was entirely appropriate therefore that Poland became the first of the post-communist regimes to make its currency, the zloty, internally convertible and turn foreign exchange dealing over to the private sector. Poland's trail-blazing liberalisation of its foreign exchange market was an essential element in the IMF-backed economic stabilisation programme which began on January 1, 1990. Backed by a Dollars 1bn currency stabilisation fund provided by western governments and financial institutions the exchange rate of the zloty was fixed at 9,500 to the dollar, the rate at which it was trading on the black market. To general surprise the once-despised socialist currency then appreciated in real terms for the next 17 months as the internal purchasing power of the zloty was eroded by inflation while its external value remained fixed. Then came the first devaluation in May last year followed by introduction of a crawling peg system which devalues the currency by around 1.8 per cent a month. While the central bank maintains this controlled floating regime, actual trading is carried out in thousands of privately-owned exchange booths and commercial bank counters equipped with real-time computer terminals which compete fiercely over their spreads to attract custom. The success of Poland's bold experiment in foreign exchangeliberalisation and internal convertibility was followed in a quieter way by several other former Soviet satellites. In no case, however, has full convertibility been introduced, involving capital account transactions and non-residents. Hungary also comes close to full convertibility in practice, however, with non-residents guaranteed the right to repatriate Forint earnings on direct and portfolio investments. But even Hungary maintains token limitations on residents obtaining foreign currency for business or travel purposes and it remains far easier to change hard currency into local currencies than vice versa. The introduction of varying degrees of internal convertibility throughout eastern and central Europe has been accompanied by the collapse of trade denominated in the now-defunct transferable rouble and a sharp rise in trade with hard currency markets. This has led to a corresponding increase in export-import financing and foreign exchange trading volume. Between the last quarter of 1989, which saw the destruction of the Berlin Wall, and the end of the second quarter of 1991 the three central European countries, Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary, which are now associate members of the European Community, saw their exports to the OECD area rise by between 13 and 35 per cent, with a corresponding rise in foreign exchange transactions. But the most important development in foreign exchange trading is due on July 1 when the Russian government takes the first big step towards introducing convertibility for the rouble. For decades the act of even taking rouble banknotes out of the Soviet Union was considered a serious criminal offence. Tourists and businessmen alike were only allowed to change money at a grotesquely over-valued rate while the gigantic bureaucracies which dealt with foreign trade were tied up in knots by an incredibly complex structure of foreign trade co-efficients and other bureaucratic nonsense. This created a thicket of differing exchange rates which bore no relationship at all to any concept of market value and made it impossible for the Soviet authorities to have any rational foreign trade policy. On July 1, all these various artificial exchange rates will be abolished and replaced by a single, albeit floating, rate of exchange. The idea is for the rouble to float for a few months to get an idea of its approximate market value and then to fix a central rate within a 7.5 per cent fluctuation band. This is expected 'sometime this autumn', according to Mr Georgy Matiukhin, the chairman of the Russian central bank. A huge amount of work remains to be done to train the necessary staff and set up the infrastructure required to ensure orderly foreign exchange trading across this huge country extending over nine time zones from St Petersburg in the west to Sakhalin or Vladivostok in the east, with key oil- and gas-producing, and therefore hard-currency-earning, Siberia in the middle. The new convertible rouble will be the currency of Russia, the largest, and potentially the richest, of the 15 former Soviet republics which made up the defunct Soviet Union . Those of the former Soviet republics who want to remain within the 'rouble zone' will have to play by the rules hammered out in the inter-republican central bankers' commission where Russia, with its huge energy and raw material resources, has the most influential voice. Russia's pre-eminence will be reinforced by the imminent steep rise in the rouble price of its energy and raw material exports to the other former Soviet republics. Those republics, like the Baltic states and Ukraine, which have no oil or gas of their own, will inevitably run up deficits with Russia. But Moscow's willingness to supply the necessary rouble credits will depend on the willingness of other republics to play by the new monetary rules which will accompany rouble convertibility. As the terms of trade move sharply in Russia's favour the other republics will have to step up exports to Russia and agree to tight monetary and other disciplines. In this way, Russia will almost certainly re-assert its hegemony over the former Soviet republics and enforce economic re-integration of the rouble zone through a combination of higher energy prices and convertibility. If this prognosis is correct the prospect of the former Soviet republics being able to introduce their own national currencies will be much reduced. Latvia was the first to introduce its own parallel currency in a move which the IMF described as 'economic suicide'. The other Baltic states, Estonia and Lithuania, have similar plans alongside the Ukraine which initially created a semi-Ukrainian currency by sticking coupons on existing rouble banknotes. This was essentially part of a rationing system to give nationals priority access to scarce food and other items, but plans are advanced for the introduction of the Hryvnia as a fully-fledged national currency. But the introduction of new currencies is shrouded in considerable controversy. Mr Matiukhin, diplomatically commented that in the beginning at least, the new currencies are likely to be as independent as the Scottish pounds, issued by several Scottish banks, but only under strict Bank of England control.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Foreign Exchange (12): Optimism about union dims - Europe has embarked on the arduous task of making Emu a reality
DOC.TEXT: THE DRAMA is over; now comes the hard work. After the excitement of the Maastricht summit at the end of last year which settled on the terms for European economic and monetary union, Europe has embarked on the arduous task of making Emu a reality. In its third and final phase, Emu is aimed at ushering in a single currency for a large part of western Europe. Monetary policy across the region would be set by a new European Central Bank (ECB). According to the Maastricht timetable, the final phase is to start up between 1997 and 1999. It would involve a core group of countries - not necessarily the whole of the existing European Community - with membership of the union set by which countries wish to join and how many meet the economic criteria. As a prelude to phase three, stage two of Emu is intended to start in 1994 with the creation of a European Monetary Institute (EMI). This body will be based on the existing committee of European central bank governors, and will oversee policy co-ordination and preparation for the final phase. Ultimately, the EMI would evolve into the ECB. Progress towards Emu has been disrupted by a variety of developments: Political arguments. In several community nations a debate has broken out - rather late, given the detail of the Emu protocol sketched out at Maastricht -about whether handing over monetary sovereignty to the new pan-European central bank is in their interests. Discussion along these lines will surface during the rest of the year, when the Maastricht treaty is due to be ratified in all 12 EC countries. Particular worries are being expressed in Germany - Europe's strongest economic power - over whether Germany's interests will best be served by giving up the D-Mark for the uncertainties of a single European currency. It looks as though the Maastricht terms will be subject to ratification by the German parliament around 1996. This will probably give Germany the same powers to opt out of Emu as Britain has by dint of the special treaty clause which it negotiated at Maastricht. Since an Emu without Germany would look like Hamlet without the Prince, the rumblings from Germany could easily scupper the project. High borrowing. Inflationary forces in several EC countries remain strong, much of this due to the rising prices sparked in Germany by unification in 1990. That has led the German Bundesbank to increase interest rates, leading to tight monetary policies across much of the rest of Europe and weakening growth prospects. As a result, several European countries, particularly Belgium, Italy and Ireland, may find it difficult to reduce government borrowing quickly enough to meet the tough fiscal targets set as part of the Emu timetable. According to the Maastricht fiscal policy criteria, countries should bring down their budget deficits to no more than 3 per cent of gross domestic product while outstanding government debt is required not to exceed 60 per cent of GDP. Effects of high interest rates. The high German rates have - due to Germany's anchor role in the European Monetary System - required other countries to keep their borrowing rates high also. Some regard this development as underlining the inherent lack of flexibility in semi-fixed or fixed exchange rate systems. They contend the problems would be still worse in a monetary union with only one currency for Europe. In the past year or so the problems of high German interest rates have been particularly intense for countries such as Britain, France and Italy which in all cases would probably have liked to cut rates to stimulate their flagging economies. Role of the ECB. There remains much work to be done on defining the powers of the bank - especially in the area of financial regulation and acting as a lender of last resort. If the bank is to function efficiently, it may also need to play a part in the area of pan-European fiscal policy, a role which could place it in conflict with national governments. Lack of economic convergence. Emu will make sense only if the nations that seek to enter a union have similar economic performances, as measured by criteria such as growth and inflation. The Maastricht protocol set out tough specific criteria that have to be met if countries want to join Emu. These include the stipulation that average inflation over one year in each member nation should be within 1 1/2 percentage points of the rate of the three or fewer European countries where inflation is lowest. But there is a question mark over the number of countries likely to make progress in moving closer to each other on such criteria. In particular, this could make it difficult for some of the southern European nations such as Portugal and Greece to qualify. If such countries made such a determined effort to meet the inflation criteria that they opted for policies which led to large rise in unemployment, then it could be argued that the social costs of meeting the Emu conditions are too high. Practical details. No one has worked out the arrangements for minting or printing the coins and notes of the new European currency units. Also to be settled would be the way in which pounds, D-Marks and francs - assuming these currencies are ultimately subsumed in a monetary union - are replaced by the new currency. The decisions would have to focus not only on ordinary transactions at the consumer level but on arrangements for financial markets covering currencies and bonds. Bearing in mind the huge disruption which can be entailed by just one nation changing currency - as happened in Britain in 1971 when it introduced a new decimal coinage - the potential for difficulties in this area could be immense. Emu optimists can, however, point to one area where the Emu process has got off to a reasonable start. The exchange rate mechanism of the European Monetary System has proved successful in keeping its 10 member currencies within set limits according to either 6 per cent or 2.25 per cent fluctuation bands. The ERM is a vital part of planning for Emu; assuming Emu proceeds as planned at Maastricht, ultimately the ERM should disappear to be replaced by a system of irrevocably locked exchange rates. In other words, the room for fluctuation in the current bands would be brought down to zero, leading to the single currency.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Foreign Exchange (11): Still only a distant dream / A look at prospects for the Ecu becoming widely used
DOC.TEXT: THE SEE-SAWING prospects of the Maastricht treaty on economic and monetary union (Emu) being ratified by all 12 EC parliaments this year have been reflected in the health of the Ecu, which the treaty set as Europe's single currency by the end of the century. The Ecu currency basket itself remains stable. Eight currencies that account for 80 per cent of the Ecu's weighting are within the narrow fluctuation band of the European exchange rate mechanism. In addition, Maastricht agreed to make no further changes in the Ecu's composition. This is not a major move, but one which will prevent a recurrence of the slowdown in Ecu market activity that used to precede the five-yearly revision of the Ecu basket. It is the Ecu bond market which has acted as a bellwether of Maastricht's perceived political fortunes. Just after Maastricht, Ecu bond yields decreased as investors took the long view that the Ecu would be just about as solid as the D-mark - simply because it would have to be, if Germany was going to let the former replace the latter. But in March, as doubts began to creep in about Maastricht surviving the referendum in Denmark and getting a two-thirds majority in the Bundestag, the spread between Ecu and D-Mark bond yields widened. The enthusiasm for Ecu bonds as a financial instrument stayed high this year. In the first quarter, primary issues totalled an impressive Ecu10.8bn, though down on the record Ecu14.9bn issued in the same period of 1991. The yield curve was filled at either end, with the French Treasury launching Ecu1.5bn worth of 30-year OAT notes and the UK Treasury issuing Ecu1bn worth of three-year notes. Over the past couple of years, the EC has stepped up its own Ecus issues, with balance of payments loans to Greece and eastern Europe and with European Investment Bank lending increasing to the latter region. EC central banks, too, are making more use of the official Ecu in intervention, buying and selling it against their national currencies. But there is still almost no private use of the Ecu. The past two years have seen minor advances, with the Eurocontrol air traffic control organisation starting to bill airline companies in Ecus, and some 18 European railway companies adopting the Ecu as the accounting unit between themselves. Yet, less than 1 per cent of EC exports are invoiced in Ecus. At this stage, therefore, the European Commission's dream of the Ecu becoming the world's top currency still seems distant. A 1990 Commission report forecast that Emu might, in various ways, lead to a flow into the Ecu of nearly Dollars 500bn. This, it speculated, could be the result of EC countries being able to dispense with Dollars 200bn in official reserves; An increase of Dollars 35bn in seigniorage (income derived from issuing interest-bearing assets) as non-Europeans decide to hold Ecus in cash as a store of value; Fund and portfolio managers diversifying into Ecus to the tune of perhaps Dollars 200bn; Increased use of the Ecu, roughly Dollars 60bn worth, in trade payments. The development of Ecu-denominated trade would reduce EC traders' foreign exchange risk, and give EC banks more scope to provide services in their own currency around the world. Though all this may be far off, there is at least growing interest in the Ecu in European Free Trade Association (Efta) countries, several of whom have applied to join the EC. Between October 1990 and June 1991, Norway, Sweden and Finland decided to peg their currencies to the Ecu; Austria, for its part, has attached the schilling to the D-Mark. Further afield, Iceland has apparently been weighing a link to the Ecu, even though the US dollar makes up 18 per cent of the trade-weighted currency basket it uses at the moment. Malta, which is an EC applicant, has not formally linked its money to the Ecu, but Ecu-component currencies have a majority weighting in the currency basket it uses. While it may make sense for central European countries to peg currencies to the Ecu, Warsaw, Prague and Budapest do not have the financial markets to handle such an operation. The three main Nordic countries would like associate membership of the European Monetary System, which EC states have so far resisted, partly because if they created such a status, it would be hard to deny it to others. Norway has, in fact, negotiated the essence of associate membership by organising swap credits with several EC central banks. Finland may want to do the same, particularly after its rocky start with the Ecu; it had to devalue the markka heavily against the Ecu this year. Sweden is still pushing for formal status as an EMS associate, to obtain a multilateral swap arrangement which would otherwise have to be negotiated bilaterally. But it is idle to think the Ecu will 'take off' outside the Community before it 'takes off' inside. Mr Andre Louw, one of the Commission's Ecu specialists, says there are still obstacles to greater use of the Ecu. Chief of these is that Germany still regards it as a currency index, not a true foreign currency. As a result, it is still not possible to write a cheque or contracts in Ecus which is enforceable in German courts. Some other countries, particularly Belgium, Spain (which only recently lifted exchange controls), Greece (which still has them), actually allow residents to perform in Ecus transactions that are not allowed in other foreign currencies. But Belgium, which has issued some Ecu coins as legal tender, does not allow companies to denominate their capital in Ecus. Luxembourg does, but only two firms have done so. Mr Louw also complains that banks, mistakenly, fail to promote the Ecu. 'When we get the Ecu, banks will lose from no longer being able to trade national (EC) currencies, but they will gain far more from an enormous increase in trading the Ecu against the dollar and yen, in Ecu deposit/credit banking and in Ecu bond trading,' he says. 'The problem is to generate a circuit, so that if you generate revenue in Ecu, you can spend it in Ecu.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Foreign Exchange (8): Drawing a line on currency / Profile of Simon Crane
DOC.TEXT: SIMON Crane spends his days looking out for abandoned babies, shooting stars, flags, pennants, crows and candlesticks. Mr Crane is a chart analyst, one of the much-maligned, but now indispensable technical observers of foreign exchange movements. The flags, babies and stars are different ways of describing the lines he puts on paper. Yet Mr Crane is anxious to avoid colourful language. It creates confusion over what chartists are about, he says. In Mr Crane's words, forex chartists aim to show where the risk or profit on a particular currency lies within a given period, and where the market is at that particular time. 'The market is a big playing field,' he says. 'Everyone knows where the ball is, and where the goalposts are. What they do not know is where the pitch is or just where the boundaries are.' The key to drawing charts is past performance. 'With a monotonous regularity, the same picture occurs,' says Mr Crane. Using a measurement of performance, the chartist aims to make a projection about what might happen in the future, he says. Critics of charts - who disparagingly refer to the discipline as the 'autopilot approach' - would hold that Mr Crane's job takes little account of the unquantifiable factors such as politics and sentiment affecting exchange rates. Mr Crane argues no chartist would ignore such factors. 'At the end of the day, you are analysing the psychology and dynamics of the market,' he says. 'There is no scientific method of interpreting charts.' However, there is one golden rule and that is: 'The market is always right'. Such a rule applies as much to fundamentalists as to chartists, he says, and each faction would be wrong to ignore the other. Differences of opinion merely fuel Mr Crane's enthusiasm. He maintains that among the 25 banks and corporations which his company - Crane Investment Analysis (CIA) - lists as clients, there are a healthy number who disagree with what he says. Yet they still come back, because most traders will not ignore the risk parameters as defined by detailed charts. 'We define where the resistance is, where the support is . . . and make a judgment as to how much pace is behind the current move.' On a given day, Mr Crane could work with hundreds of charts. The aptly-named CIA - Mr Crane keeps his methods secret even from close friends - deals also with the precious metals, capital markets and equity markets. However, the bulk of his analysis deals with currencies and capital markets. To the sceptics, Mr Crane says charting is likely to become an increasingly important tool for foreign exchange trading. Technical analysis is essential, he says, 'in a market place where a large percentage of any given currency move occurs over increasingly shorter time frames'; and in a market worth some Dollars 700bn a day and growing, according to his own calculations, traders will find it more and more difficult to ignore any help they can get.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Foreign Exchange (6): The Square Mile stays out in front / Discussing London's role as a leading financial centre
DOC.TEXT: THE CITY of London has long been proud, if not cocksure, of its reputation as a leading foreign exchange trading centre. Brochures published by the Corporation of London boast that London's Square Mile can still claim to be the world's leading international financial centre. But political and financial developments in Europe alongside Britain's general antipathy towards monetary union have led some to suggest that London's continuing dominance in foreign exchange trading is in question. The main concerns over London losing its competitive edge are that the European Central Bank will be located in another European city and that the British government will continue to be hostile towards monetary union. On closer examination, both concerns appear overblown. The Bank of England, anyway not yet resigned to the ECB going elsewhere, brushes off suggestions that London's dominant role in global foreign exchange trading would be weakened if another city were chosen to house the ECB. The Bank says London's underlying advantages will continue to give the City an edge over other European centres. After all, where the bank is located is less important than where it operates. In the US, the Federal Reserve is based in Washington, but operates mainly through the largest, most developed and highly securitised market - New York. The same would surely be true of Europe. According to the most recent survey of foreign exchange market activity carried out by the Bank of International Settlements in 1989, the City is only just behind Tokyo in total international banking business. In foreign exchange trading, the UK ranked first, with total daily foreign exchange transactions amounting to Dollars 187bn. This compared with turnovers of Dollars 129bn in New York and Dollars 115bn in Tokyo. In Europe, leaving aside London, only Zurich recorded a turnover of more than Dollars 50bn. On this basis, the Corporation of London says it is 'hardly surprising' that 'foreign banks have flocked to London, providing the essential cement to the international flavour of the City'. There are more than 500 foreign bank branches, incorporations or representative offices based in London's square mile. Perhaps the most prestigious of all is the latest international recruit, the headquarters of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, with shareholders from more than 40 countries. Although the Bank of England believes the City would weather the location of Europe's central bank outside the UK, it continues to argue strongly that it should come to London. In a speech earlier this year, Mr Robin Leigh-Pemberton, governor of the Bank of England, said it would be in the interests of the European Community to have its central bank placed in London. 'A single European currency would be one of the world's three major currencies, and would obviously be actively traded in centres around the world . . . London is one of the three major world financial centres, perhaps the only truly international centre and certainly the pre-eminent international centre in Europe, with a depth, variety and liquidity in its money and capital markets - which very much now embrace and are developing the Ecu - that will be vital to an effective single monetary policy,' he said. If the ECB does go to one of the so-called 'compromise' candidates, the 'Domesday' scenario is that much of London's foreign exchange trade will go with it. 'Much depends on what the European Central Bank actually does,' says Ruth Lea chief economist at Mitsubishi bank in London. 'Will it be just for committee meetings, or will it be a major operating unit?' Whatever its role, she dismisses the worst-case scenario; 'I think London will remain the biggest centre in Europe but it will inevitably lose an edge if the ECB goes elsewhere.' Mr Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International, says the Japanese bank is similarly unflustered at the prospect of London's future. 'There are enough reasons to be positive about London's role - liquidity is the key factor and London already has that plus a lot of expertise in foreign exchange. Its infrastructure as an international financial centre has already been proven,' says Mr Lyons. However, he cautions that even with these in-built advantages, the location of the ECB is still important and could yet affect London's position. 'If the ECB is based in a city which clearly doesn't have the potential to become the European financial centre, like Amsterdam for example, then there will be no threat to London, but if it goes to Frankfurt, which does have the potential, then that could pose some sort of problem.' As for Britain's antipathy towards monetary union, few in the City feel that London's position in foreign exchange trading would be put in jeopardy if Britain were to opt out of Emu. 'An awful lot of London's business is offshore business,' said a spokesman from the Bank of England. 'Because it is an offshore centre, there is every reason to believe it will continue to be one even if we were not in Emu.' There is also growing scepticism over the timetable for Emu set out in the Maastricht treaty. Many in the City view it as unrealistic, and are confident that no big financial houses would even consider making a move elsewhere in Europe while the future of monetary union looks so uncertain. In fact, worries over the attitude of the British government towards Europe are likely, at least for the time being, to be outweighed by the more comforting prospect of five years of political stability following the decisive victory of the Conservative party in the April general election, especially when compared with the relatively turbulent political outlook elsewhere in Europe. Other reasons tying financial houses to London are the exceedingly high costs now sunk into London. It would take some good reasons indeed for a company to undertake the enormous cost of relocating its European base.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Foreign Exchange (7): Risk-taking is his business -Profile of Julian Simmonds
DOC.TEXT: TUESDAY, mid-morning; Citibank's London foreign exchange dealing room is humming. Smart, young traders bark instructions to each other from opposite sides of the room, others gaze at flickering green screens, pensively twirling their telephone handsets. Presiding over the hubbub from a dealing post bang in the middle of the spot-desk, is Mr Julian Simmonds, Citibank's energetic managing director of foreign exchange and money markets in Europe. After almost 20 years in foreign exchange trading and sales, Mr Simmonds still approaches his job with the zeal of a newcomer. 'At the end of the day, I actually enjoy my job and I enjoy the people I work with. If I didn't, I wouldn't bother to get up in the mornings,' he says. Responsible for all of Citibank's foreign exchange and funding activities in Europe, Mr Simmonds' presence in the dealing room and the fact that he continues to take a position on currencies, is testimony to his love of risk-taking and ability to avoid, as far as possible, the administrative side of management. 'Like any other large organisation there is a real risk at senior levels of management of getting dragged away from your desk,' he says. 'One of my key challenges is to not allow myself to become engulfed in a sea of papers and meetings. You can't watch the market if you are stuck in meetings.' The approach means that he can stay in touch with his workforce and with Citibank's customers. Understanding customers' needs has become a key part of Simmonds' approach to forex trading. 'I don't believe the business of banking is any different from other service industries,' says Mr Simmonds. 'The product we are trying to sell is foreign exchange. I approach the challenge by thinking, what is it I want when I go into a mojor store to make a big acquisition?' One initiative has been to survey customers' needs through a questionnaire. Mr Simmonds reads every single return, tackling weak areas directly with the sales, trading and administrative teams. All this makes him a busy man. He is into the office by 7.45am and tries to be home by 6.15pm. When away from his desk, he regularly glances at a portable Reuters screen that he carries with him everywhere. At night he is frequently woken by traders keeping him in touch with his position. Two things help - he claims not to need much sleep and he has an understanding wife. Certainly Mr Simmonds, a vigorous 41, shows no sign of the 'burn-out' often associated with the frantic life of forex risk-takers. 'Burn-out comes from excessive alcohol and entertainment, not from the work,' he says. 'I am only prepared to entertain in the evenings where it is important, and wherever possible I try to involve my wife.' Family life is important. 'When the kids tell me about their latest crisis at school, it puts the job in perspective.' The only downside of the job to which Mr Simmonds is devoted, he says, is failure. 'But it's a risk business, and failing is something you have to learn to live with. 'You have to do what you think best in the business. If I buy dollars because I think the dollar is going up, and I make a mistake, then I can live with it. I am disappointed, but I can live with it,' he says.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Foreign Exchange (2): Well set to weather storms - Dollar
DOC.TEXT: THE DOLLAR has this year weathered some unexpected economic and political turbulence at home and abroad. This suggests that the US currency may be able to withstand any storms that lie ahead during the rest of 1992. Since January, the dollar has appreciated steadily against the currencies in the D-Mark bloc and against the yen in spite of disruptive and conflicting influences. On the negative side, the dollar been buffeted by a US economy that only recently appeared to be foundering in its attempts to pull away from recession, by declining domestic interest rates pressured lower by Federal Reserve policy eases, and by early and disturbing signs of President Bush's political vulnerability in election year. On the positive side, there has been rising interest rates in a Germany troubled by inflationary pressures and the complex economic and political repercussions of reunification, political turmoil and an apparently collapsing economy in the republics of the former Soviet Union, and economic slowdown and financial crises in Tokyo where stock values have plummeted, institutions have curtailed foreign investments and the seemingly all-powerful growth machine has begun to stall. Against this unsettling background, the dollar has charted an upward path. Since January it has appreciated 4 per cent against both the D-Mark and the yen, and 1.5 per cent against sterling. The view of analysts in New York is to expect a modest appreciation in the dollar over the rest of the year. The main reason for their bullishness is the US economy, which is forecast to grow at a steady rate of between 2.5 per cent and 3 per cent over the next eight months. In contrast, growth in the main European economies will be slower, while there are enough doubts about the outlook for the Japanese economy to also swing the forecasts in the dollar's favour. On the policy front, US interest rates look as though they have bottomed, while the more sluggish European economies could require some extra stimulus. This means yield differentials between the dollar and the D-Mark - which recently reached historic highs - should finally begin to narrow. There are two threats to this scenario. The Federal Reserve could cut rates once more if it thinks economic growth is not sufficiently robust. The likely trigger would be fresh news of weakness in the jobs market. The other danger is if the Bundesbank proves more hawkish about inflation. If industrial unrest forces employers to grant big pay increases, then the Bundesbank could keep policy tight. The near-term direction of Japanese monetary policy is harder to call. The conventional view is that slowing economic growth and continued financial instability will persuade the Japanese authorities to adopt a more accommodating monetary stance. However, there is an alternative prospect. This is that the policy remains unchanged, or even tightens, as the Japanese government bows to international pressure to reduce its bulging trade surplus by forcing the yen higher. Moreover, the signs are that Japanese fiscal, not monetary, policy will be eased in the immediate future, which could boost confidence in the economy and turn the slide in the growth rate. Add to that further declines in net outflows of Japanese capital (linked to stockmarket losses), and it is plausible that the yen will actually gain against the dollar. A big unknown on the horizon this year is US politics. A Bush victory in the November election, guaranteeing continuity of political and economic policy, would be the best possible outcome for the dollar. (This assumes, of course, that the nation and the financial markets do not fall for the charms of Texan billionaire and can-do businessman/politician Ross Perot, who is preparing to run as an independent.) Analysts have warned, however, not to expect a celebratory post-election surge in the dollar if Bush wins. All the currency risk, therefore, is stacked the other way, with the potential for the dollar to take a big hit at a hint of trouble in the Bush campaign. Yet the chances of a Democrat (or an independent) winning the presidency remain slim, in spite of those early hiccups in Bush's re-election drive. In his favour, Bush has an opposition still divided over the electability of its likely presidential candidate, Governor Bill Clinton of Arkansas, and an economy that is showing signs of achieving a sustainable recovery at exactly the right time. The election, however, is far enough away for the markets to ignore it for now. 'I'm not sure electoral expectations are factored into the dollar yet,' says John Lipsky, economist at Salomon Brothers in New York. 'It could be a bit like it was in the UK election, where the markets did not take it seriously until just before polling day.' Thus, barring any disasters felling Bush, the dollar should be free from electoral considerations between now and early autumn. International politics could also leave its mark on the dollar this year. The unstable situation in the Commonwealth of Independent States, has already given a short-term lift to the US currency, which is traditionally the safe haven for investors concerned by global political unrest.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Foreign Exchange (3): Stability amid turmoil - Yen shrugs off changes in the Japanese economy
DOC.TEXT: DOMESTIC financial and political turmoil and far-reaching global political change have left the yen remarkably unscathed over the past year. In the fiscal year 1991, the dollar averaged Y133, with the currency moving in a range of Y15, the second smallest fluctuation since it floated against the dollar in 1973. The currency has shrugged off significant changes affecting the Japanese economy such as long-bond yields falling from last year's 9 per cent to the recent 5.2 per cent, and the stock market down more than 55 per cent from its peak. The stock market scandals and political bribery allegations that shook Japan last year failed to rock the yen. The authorities have shown that they are able to stabilise currency markets. Earlier this year, the Bank of Japan and Federal Reserve Bank of New York were selling dollars in co-ordinated intervention. According to Mr Paul Summerville, economist at Jardine Flemings in Tokyo, increased information has also decreased currency fluctuation. 'Dollar/yen movements are becoming limited because information is discounted into the rate every day,' he says. However, the middle- and long-term trend in supply and demand points to a strengthening of the yen. Japan's current account surplus for the fiscal year to March 1991 surged by 167 per cent from the previous year to Dollars 90bn. Official figures disclosed a record surplus of Dollars 113bn in the trade account, and a surplus of Dollars 40bn in the long-term capital account, the first surplus since 1980. The long-term capital account surplus followed a sharp increase to Dollars 101bn in foreign net purchases of Japanese securities from Dollars 60bn. Foreigners bought a net Dollars 36.77bn in Japanese stocks, up from Dollars 15.92bn in fiscal 1990. Japanese investment in overseas markets has started to shrink, as excess liquidity has been squeezed out, and overseas and domestic interest rate differentials have narrowed. In 1991, Japanese direct investment was Dollars 23.6bn, down from Dollars 44.9bn, reflecting tougher financial conditions at home and the world recession. Long-term capital flows are expected to remain in surplus for Japan as Japanese investors continue to favour domestic investments and foreigners remain net buyers of Japanese equities, prompting Mr Robert Feldman, an economist at Salomon Brothers in Tokyo, to forecast that the yen will strengthen to Y115 against the dollar. In addition to payments surpluses, Mr Masao Susaki, head of research at the Bank of Tokyo, says that dollar/yen forward contracts affect the currency rate. 'Japanese exporters and speculators made positions in dollar selling forward contracts in the late 80s and have been rolling the positions over,' says Mr Susaki. He says investors and exporters will start selling the dollar against the yen from mid-1992. Mr Susaki expects the average dollar/yen rate to be around Y123 this fiscal year. Mr Hideki Furuya, senior economist at Sanwa Research Institute, says that economic fundamentals dominate the yen currency movements, and political and financial scandals tend to be secondary factors in the long run. Mr Furuya says that while the yen has weakened on the back of a slowing Japanese economy, recent economic figures indicate a gradual recovery. After declines in industrial production, inventory growth has slowed to a 7 per cent increase in March, down from a peak 13 per cent in December. Housing demand is showing signs of a recovery, reflecting the fall in interest rates on housing loans. The economy is also expected to benefit from the government's stimulatory package, which brings forward 75 per cent of this fiscal year's public works spending into the first half. According to Mr Furuya, this will have the same impact as an increase of Y3,000bn in spending. Reflecting the gradual recovery of the economy and a rise in long-term interest rates towards the end of the year, Mr Furuya forecasts the yen will rise to Y125. Mr Summerville, at Jardine Fleming, sees the D-Mark/yen rate averaging between Y70 and Y75 in fiscal year 1992.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Foreign Exchange (4): Shine starts to fade / Investigating the D-Mark's decline
DOC.TEXT: THE Deutsche Mark has lost something of its shine in recent months. Since the beginning of the year, what has traditionally been Europe's strongest and most stable currency has lost ground against the US dollar, against sterling, and and against other currencies in the European Monetary System. The slippage in the currency's value since the beginning of the year - from DM1.53 to nearly DM1.61 against the US dollar by the middle of May, from DM2.85 to DM2.93 against sterling over the same period - indicates a significant deterioration of sentiment. Whether this reassessment is the prelude to a more radical shift in perceptions remains to be seen. Many commentators take the view that the Bundesbank, arch-defender of monetary stability, has taken the right decisions and is undergoing problems amid the turbulence of this year's wage round. According to these analysts, the Bundesbank's determination to fight the battle against inflation is undiminished - and, more importantly, its credibility is intact. However, there is a minority view that the Bundesbank's determination to do battle with inflation has already faltered - but that the market has not yet cottoned on to this. According to this line of argument, when market perceptions catch up with the new and unfortunate reality, there will be a new and more permanent downgrading of the value of the D-Mark. The stark facts of the matter are that year-on-year inflation in Germany reached 4.8 per cent in March - more than twice the Bundesbank's target of 2 per cent. Money supply M3 - the broad measure which is a key indicator for the Bundesbank's monetary policy - grew at an annual rate of 9.75 per cent in the same month, again way above the Bundesbank's target range of 3.5 to 5.5 per cent. Has the Bundesbank done enough to counter these trends? Or, is it succumbing to international pressure and letting itself be bullied into keeping rates too low for Germany's domestic situation? The Bundesbank moved last December, raising Lombard and Discount rates by a half a per cent. At the time, the rise to 9.75 and 8 per cent (Lombard and Discount rates respectively) took investors by surprise. Economists expected at the most a rise of 25 basis points. The move to Germany's highest post-war interest rates was taken as evidence of the central bank's unwavering commitment to the goal of price stability. Reflecting the markets' confidence, Bund prices surged, with yields on 10-year long Bunds tumbling from well over 8 per cent to 7.75 per cent and lower. The psychology behind this paradoxical rise in bond prices in response to a rise in interest rates was due to investors' conviction that the Bundesbank had knocked inflation on its head once and for good. The rise would encourage the unions to behave responsibly in the forthcoming wage round and allow the Bundesbank to chop headline rates again by the third quarter. As events unfurled, this prognosis began to look optimistic. Unions - first the steel workers and then the public sector workers - showed themselves unwilling to defuse inflationary pressures by accepting pay increases below the level of real inflation. The powerful IG Metall union was also in sabre-rattling mood, and, like the public sector, settled for a basic 5.4 per cent. The consensus date for the lowering of rates crept backwards by the week - from late in the third quarter to the fourth quarter. From today's viewpoint, even the first quarter of next year looks extremely optimistic. Perhaps interest rates might have to go up again first. The Bundesbank has so far maintained its credibility, a fact reflected in a steeply inverted yield curve. Interest rates at the long end of the market are sharply lower than short-term rates, 150 basis points apart in fact, because the markets still believe the Bundesbank will win. And some argue that the Bundesbank has been right not to overreact to money supply figures which to a large extent reflect non-inflationary rebuild of eastern Germany. However, argues Avinash Persaud at UBS Phillips & Drew - under the headline 'Crumbling credibility?' - 'a number of new pressures may restrain the Bundesbank from responding to the worrisome acceleration in monetary growth. If these pressures are seen to influence the Bundesbank, market perception could evolve'. From being perceived as Europe's most active central bank, it could suddenly be seen as merely reactive, Mr Persaud argues, with dire consequences. Mr Persaud identifies three pressures on the Bundesbank policy-making, two international and the other domestic in nature. First, Germany's economy is slowing down, and may slip into recession - may the Bundesbank not be tempted to ease rates to stimulate growth? Second, the US has cut its own interest rates aggressively to kick-start its own and by extension the world economy - and it is attempting to bring pressure to bear on Germany to follow suit.
