Third, there are specifically European pressures on Germany: Germany's European partners are putting political pressure on the German government to keep rates low. As the former Bundesbank president, Mr Karl Otto Pohl, indicated in a recently published book, Bonn rode roughshod over the Bundesbank in 1990, forcing through better monetary union between the two Germanys at a much more generous exchange rate than the central bank wanted. At a time when Bonn does not want to rock the European boat, the Bundesbank may find itself under intolerable political pressure once again - this time to keep interest rates lower than required.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Foreign Exchange (5): Prognosis for pound is good -Sterling
DOC.TEXT: STERLING LOOKS set to enjoy a period of relative stability on world currency markets, amid a healthier outlook for the UK economy and the prospect of a settled political environment. Behind the reappraisal of the pound in recent weeks by many international investors was the Conservatives' surprise win in the April 9 general election. That removed the doubts of some market practitioners that sterling could face a devaluation within the European exchange rate mechanism and sparked an intense period of buying pressure. The pound's consequent rise against the D-Mark - from DM2.83 early in April to around DM2.94 a month afterwards - was the result of the strongest surge of support sterling since the UK joined the ERM in October 1990. Helping sterling has been the general sentiment that Britain is starting a slow recovery from its serious recession. Such a conclusion has been supported by several economic indicators in recent months, notably a sizeable 3 per cent quarter-on-quarter increase in underlying import volumes in the first three months of 1992. There is also the perception that Britain - unlike other European nations including France and Italy - faces a relatively long period without an election. As a result, purchasing support for the pound relative to other European currencies has been healthy. Sterling has also benefited indirectly from the problems facing the German economy as a result of unification. These appear to have weakened the role of the D-Mark in the ERM and have strengthened other currencies in the system. It was partly because of the markets' perception that the role of the D-Mark might have lost some of its importance that the pound weathered the interest-rate cut on May 5. The reduction brought UK base rates from 10.5 per cent to 10 per cent in the first such fall since September. It narrowed the gap between UK rates and the corresponding 9.75 per cent German Lombard rate to just a quarter of a point, the lowest level since 1981. For all the stronger tone of sterling, its rapid rise in the month after the election should be regarded in the context of the poor period in the six months before the poll. During this time, investors sold sterling in large volumes because of worries about a possible change of government and doubts about how long any UK recovery could be sustained. For much of this period, the pound languished as the ERM's weakest member. Can sterling's recent strength be sustained? Much depends on further progress in containing inflation. There are indications that inflationary pressures - which have lain dormant for much of the past 18 months because of the demand-limiting effects of the recession - may start to reappear over the next few months. That could weaken the demand of overseas investors for sterling and depress its value. Another question mark is over the pace of UK recovery. Assuming that the revival proceeds at a relatively sedate pace sterling's strength can be expected to hold. But if indications emerge that the economy is being thrown off bal-ance - such as through a surge in imports that would show up in a deteriorating trade position - then the pound could suffer. A third factor concerns the decision on whether to put sterling into the narrow, 2.25 per cent band of the ERM. The pound is only one of three currencies in the 10-currency system which are allowed to fluctuate against all the others in broad, 6 per cent bands. There has been speculation that the UK will enter the narrow band at its existing central DM2.95 rate over the next six months - a decision which would probably increase the attraction of sterling to international investors. A fourth issue is the direction of German interest rates. It is possible that the Bundesbank could decide to push up German borrowing costs in a further effort to dampen inflationary forces sparked by the surge in demand in the formerly communist eastern part. Even allowing for the reappraisal in many market practitioners' minds about the D-Mark's role in the ERM, such a move by the Bundesbank would almost certainly lead to a large switching of funds into the German currency, putting pressure on sterling. Finally, no one knows to what degree the role of the D-Mark in the ERM will change in a permanent way. There have been some suggestions that the D-Marks' central position in the mechanism could be taken over at some point by the French franc, on account of France's good inflation performance over the past year. To many economists such theories seem fanciful. Until the Bundesbank is replaced as Europe's most hardline central bank on inflation, then it appears Germany's role will remain dominant. On this thinking, it could well be that the UK has to get used to a more fluid pattern of interest-rate changes as part of membership of the system. Thus, even though Britain took the opportunity to cut rates in early May, if the Bundesbank were to tighten policy over the next few months the UK might have to raise them again to prevent sterling falling beneath its ERM floor. Such a move would underline the degree to which ERM entry has pushed responsibility over UK monetary policy away from London and towards the members of the Bundesbank council sitting in Frankfurt.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Foreign Exchange (1): Caught in the eye of a storm - Leading currencies have been buffeted by world upheavals over the past 18 months. A symptom of a recent uneasy calm has been a marked decline in the volatility of the so-called G3 exchange rates - the dollar, D-Mark and yen / Assessment of the future of currency markets in the light of economic and political events
DOC.TEXT: THE WORLD'S foreign exchange markets are caught in the eye of a storm. Leading currencies are suspended between geo-political pressures for change on the one hand and, on the other hand, institutional developments in the global banking industry and moves to greater integration in western Europe which argue for calm. A symptom of this unstable equilibrium has been a marked decline this year in the volatility of the so-called G3 exchange rates - the dollar, D-Mark and yen. The dollar's fluctuation range against the D-Mark in the first 4 1/2 months of this year was just 18 pfennigs as it moved between a low of DM1.50 and a high of DM1.68. This, according to Swiss Bank Corp, is less than half last year's trading range of 39 pfennigs and well below the 105 pfennig trading range recorded in 1985, when market conditions were especially turbulent. The movement of the dollar against the yen has been even more subdued - a mere 12 yen between a low of Y123 and a high of Y135, against fluctuation ranges of Y19 last year, Y35 in 1990, Y51.5 in 1986 and Y63 in 1985. The decline in exchange rate volatility has reflected a number of forces in the world economy and banking industry since the mid-1980s. Governments want more stable exchange rates. Although the Group of Seven countries - the US, Japan, Germany, France, Britain, Italy and Canada - no longer attempt to peg their exchange rates to each other as after the 1987 Louvre Accord, they act when necessary to combat excessive exchange rate movements. More important perhaps have been regional developments. In particular, the exchange rate mechanism of the European Monetary System has increasingly taken on the characteristics of a fixed exchange rate block. It has attracted new members (Spain, Britain and Portugal over the past three years) and acts as a centre of gravity for non-EC countries such as Sweden, Norway and Finland which peg their currencies to the European currency unit (Ecu) and are seeking closer links to the EMS. ERM rigidity has grown with the adoption last December at the EC's Maastricht summit of plans to move to Emu, or economic and monetary union, by the end of the decade. All industrialised nations put a high priority on combatting inflation. While there has been increased recognition that national economic policy measures must vary to take account of differing conditions, convergence towards low inflation has helped iron out one classic cause of exchange rate movement. Central banks have become more adept at managing intervention. They no longer defend specific currency rates, preferring instead to carry out smoothing operations in the exchange markets. These more refined tactics have deprived speculators of the 'one-way bet' that so often appeared when fixed or semi-fixed rates were defended, only to be abandoned under the pressure of speculative forces. These trends have been reinforced by developments in banking and among other market participants. In general, the currency markets have become more risk averse. Caution has grown with the approach of the end-1992 deadline for international banks to comply with stringent capital adequacy ratios, agreed in 1988. Loan losses incurred during the past three years of slow growth and recession have curbed banks' enthusiasm for speculative foreign exchange trading. But it would be wrong to assume that calm will endure in the foreign exchange markets. Following the collapse of communism and the end of the Cold War, the currency markets, like policy makers, are operating in a world where old certainties no longer hold good. The strength of the US economic recovery is unclear, as is the capacity of Germany to absorb the new eastern Lander without allowing inflation to run out of control. There are doubts whether the authorities in Tokyo will be able to stave off recession while managing the current problem of asset price deflation in Japan. Overshadowing these worries, is the unfathomable outlook for the republics of the former Soviet Union as they embark along the road to the market economy. Large-scale changes in exchange rate relationships may emerge once there are answers to these uncertainties. When determining exchange rates, the market has already begun to look much more closely at underlying economic and political factors than simply at nominal interest rate differentials or the trend lines drawn by chartists. Such considerations lie behind the late spring reappraisal of sterling and the French franc, which has allowed the authorities in London and Paris to bring their official interest rates almost down to German levels. The dollar's reaction to last December's interest rate changes in Germany and the US, when Germany pushed its rates to their highest peace-time levels since the 1930s and the US responded by cutting its discount rate to the lowest level for nearly a generation, provided an early example of this trend. After an initial downwards move, the dollar responded to the yawning 6 percentage-point interest differential in favour of the D-Mark by moving higher. Investors in this case looked beyond the immediate horizon and reasoned that the news was good for the US economy. They also assumed (wrongly as it happened) that the next move in dollar interest rates would be upwards. While fast-moving economic and political changes make smooth running currency markets more important than ever, the general decline in exchange rate volatility has been bad for profits. These factors have reinforced a tendency for trading in the leading currencies to become concentrated among a small number of big, well-capitalised players such as Citibank and Chemical Bank of the US, Union Bank of Switzerland and Barclays Bank of Britain. Trading in leading currencies takes place in a mature market, where information is very rapidly disseminated to all participants and competitive edge is hard to achieve. A strong customer base has become all important, not just for the business that it brings but for the insight it provides on exchange rates movements. As capital flows have supplanted trade flows as the engine of market activity, traders have had to develop more sophisticated services such as options and derivatives to win business from institutional clients. In this very competitive environment it seems that London has continued to build up its position as the world's leading foreign exchange centre, at the expense of Tokyo, where Japanese banks have been hard hit by the asset price fall, and New York, where a lack of liquidity, particularly on Fridays, has forced some foreign exchange banks there to function as niche players. But such concentration of muscle does not mean an absence of business opportunities elsewhere. Markets for so-called exotic currencies, from eastern Asia or Latin America, are becoming more prominent. They offer opportunities for smaller trading companies to operate on their own account and provide some of the excitement that used to characterise the foreign exchange market as a whole in the 1970s and 1980s. In a business that sometimes wonders whether it is in decline, trading in second line currencies will continue to grow. The historic currencies of western Europe may be destined to disappear if plans for Emu are fulfilled. But other currencies will gain importance as the ex-communist countries of eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union embrace the market economy and move towards currency convertibility.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Coventry (11): Labour-dominated scene - Economic successes for moderates
DOC.TEXT: THE LABOUR Party was returned with ease as the largest party in the recent local elections for the Coventry city council. In April, Mr Dave Nellist, who was expelled last year from the Labour Party, ran as an independent and this factor tended to dominate coverage of the general election for Coventry. These two developments may have created the impression that - seen from a distance - Coventry was a little like Liverpool: an industrial, predominantly working class city, faced with a struggle between the hard left and Labour Party moderates. In the event, Mr Dave Nellist, a popular local man who had built up a reputation as a good constituency member of parliament, was defeated in Coventry South East by the official Labour Party candidate, Mr Jim Cunningham. But it was a close-run thing - Mr Cunningham polled 11,902; Mr Nellist, Independent Labour, 10,551; while Mrs Martine Hyams polled 10,591 for the Conservatives - showing a seven per cent swing to the Tories from Labour since the 1987 election. At a local level, however, any faction-fighting within the Labour Party was not a consideration. The Conservatives did gain five seats at the expense of the Labour Party, but Labour still held an overwhelming 41 seats, with none going to the Liberal Democrats. Mr Bob Ainsworth, who won the Coventry North East seat for the Labour party says: 'The hard left or extreme left - or whatever you would like to call it -has never had much influence at a local level.' The Labour city council is widely seen as united and moderate council which has been the main driving force behind the successful diversification of the economy. Mr Jim Cunningham the new MP for Coventry South East, who was the leader of the council until his election, says: 'We realised in 1981 we had to change. We had to broaden the base from the car industry. The alternative was mass unemployment. We built the science park with the university; we took the initiative in building Westwood Park - Barclays Bank has moved to Westwood. If Barclays bank is prepared to move to Coventry, then it must be confident of the City's future.' Mr Cunningham says there was little opposition from within the Labour Party to these entrepreneurial policies - 'the only people to oppose us were the Conservatives. The government didn't like the idea of local authorities building science parks - they didn't like the idea of any public authority spending money on that kind of thing.' Mr Bob Ainsworth (Coventry North East) who is a former deputy leader of the city council says: 'We were able to get things moving in the early 1980s because - abnormally for a city council - we had a lot of assets. 'We owned most of the city centre and we had a lot of land. We were able to use this land to enter into deals with developers. It's a lot more difficult now, of course, because any land sales have to go mostly towards debt relief.' Asked whether the disturbances in the estate of Wood End in mid-May are not worrying and harmful for the image of a city still trying to attract new investment, Mr Cunningham says: 'Of course they are worrying - but it isn't just Coventry, is it? All the talk I have been hearing in the House of Commons is where is it going to be next. 'The basic problem in the inner cities is the young unemployed; many, in their late 20s, and without jobs, feel disenfranchised and let down. It isn't an ethnic problem, as has been suggested - the minorities are as badly affected as everyone else. 'The trouble is there isn't enough training: anyone connected with the Tec (Training and Enterprise Council) will tell you there are not enough funds.' Mr Ainsworth, who made his maiden speech on the subject of the Coventry disturbances, says: 'This kind of thing is going to happen until we have a proper urban policy. Unemployment in these estates is so very high and many people are unemployed for so long that it's socially acceptable not to work. These people are without a stake in society.' He continues: 'The tabloid press has exaggerated the disturbances - the police never lost control of the estate. There were not great numbers involved. 'The damage to property was not extensive. But yes, if the exaggeration is believed, then it could harm Coventry's attempts to attract new companies.' Mr John Butcher, a former government minister, the MP for Coventry South West and the only Conservative among Coventry's four MPs, agrees that the Labour-dominated council has done a good job in diversifying the economy: 'I would say that there has been a healthy partnership between the local authority, the educational bodies and the government. 'Now, of course, development of science parks and industrial estates will be more and more in the hands of the private sector.' In regard to disturbances Mr Butcher says: 'It has nothing to do with race, as has been suggested. The problem here is a few young people, known to the police, who decided to go on the rampage. The police have the situation under control. 'The encouraging thing is that older people on the estate want to see the young offenders dealt with. It is wrong to conclude from these events that Coventry has a law and order problem.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Coventry (12): A big effort to strengthen the China connection - Delegation due in Jun / The flow of goods and funds is growing
DOC.TEXT: COVENTRY has a gradually strengthening connection with China, evident in both the vehicle and leisure industries, with the flow of funds, goods and ideas moving in both directions. As far back as 1983, the City Council wanted to take advantage of what at that time was seen as China's 'open door' policy and, characteristically of a city very attached to the idea of twinning, linked-up with Jinan in Shandong province. That move came to very little and any hope that it might do so were shattered by the events of Tiannamen Square. But now the political atmosphere is changing. MGA Developments, the design and engineering company, has, purely on its own initiative, taken advantage of that. It has just completed in 27 months - against an industry norm of three or four years - a Pounds 7.69m contract to design and bring to production in China a 1.5 tonne truck for Tianjin Automotive Corporation. Production of the truck has started at the rate of 12,000 units a year. This will rise to 50,000 and over the life of the project, total production is expected to reach 500,000 units. Meanwhile MGA is seeking to win more contracts in China. It has completed a commission for the design of a four-wheeled drive vehicle and is negotiating for a further contract to bring it to production. It is also investigating another truck project. In the other direction, there is the strong possibility that Chinese funds will be invested in the council's project to bring the historic but deteriorating Coombe Abbey back to life. Coombe Abbey and the surrounding land is owned by the council but is just outside the city boundary. The Abbey is in need of repair and in its present state it has little practical use, but it is a pivotal part of a wider project which will see it restored as one of the focal points of a leisure project which will include a country hotel, a golf course with club facilities and a health centre. The council has gone into partnership with Lumley Castle, the Durham hotel company, but needs further equity funds. Now, China Construction International, a company which acts commercially but whose activities are ultimately controlled by the government, has expressed interest in providing Pounds 3m of equity for the Pounds 20m project. The matter may be settled next month when a delegation is expected. For the moment the council's dealings are through Trade Circle International, China Construction's agents in London. An investment of Pounds 3m could mean that China Construction would end up as the majority equity holder.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Coventry (8): Car maker's links go back over 50 years - Jaguar's long tradition in Coventry / In the late 1980s, Jaguar was producing 50,000 luxury cars a year in Coventry
DOC.TEXT: JAGUAR'S connections with Coventry go back a long time, almost to the origins of the motor industry, but question marks have recently hovered over whether the company will maintain its commitment to the city. Jaguar moved to Coventry from Blackpool in 1928. Under Sir William Lyons and his successors, it has survived with various partners and owners in Coventry for more than 50 years. The takeover in 1989 by the Ford group for Pounds 1.6bn and the impact on luxury car sales of the recession in the late 1980s has, however, made some employees question whether the company has a future as an independent marque, and what role if any Coventry would play. The company was hit particularly badly by the downturn in sales for its cars in the US. Exports account for something like two-thirds of sales. In the late 1980s, Jaguar was producing 50,000 luxury cars a year in Coventry, but last year output was only half that level and the company registered a loss of Pounds 226m in 1991. The battering that Jaguar took from the recession has led to a reduction in the total workforce from more than 10,000 in 1990 to 8,000 today. The numbers employed in the two manufacturing plants in Coventry has dropped to under 7,000. Reports at the time of the takeover that Ford executives were unhappy with low productivity at Jaguar has led to suggestions that production of engines would be moved elsewhere, and that assembly might also be transferred to other parts of the UK, or even to Europe, or, at the very least, that the Coventry plants could expect further drastic redundancies. Mr David Boole, the director of communications and public affairs for Jaguar, is at pains to dispel these unsubstantiated reports. 'Despite the softness of the market at the moment, Ford is convinced that there is a future market for luxury cars. 'The entry of Japanese manufacturers, Nissan and Toyota, have proved that. Ford are going to persevere with the Jaguar as an individual marque. 'Ford has has made a long-term commitment to Jaguar. It has said that it will invest Pounds 1bn in Jaguar. It is going to expand the product range, bring in new models, maintain the quality of Jaguars and improve efficiency.' One development being mentioned is the production a V8 engine for a new mid-series vehicle which would replace the XJ6 and compete with BMW. This does not mean, however, that the company will just be making bigger versions of Fords. Mr Boole insists also that Jaguar's future is inextricably bound up up with Coventry. 'Ford has made a firm commitment to remain in Coventry,' he says. Although there could be further job losses through natural wastage or increased automation, the numbers employed are not expected to decline substantially below the current figure of 8,000, and could even rise if the world economy improves. Over the next few years, Ford is looking to increase the numbers of cars produced to 150,000, tripling the peak output of two years ago. 'You are seeing the first smatterings of a recovery. Sales of Jaguars in April were 16 per cent higher that for the same month a year ago, compared with 9 per cent for the rest of the car market. 'Sales in the US were 2.5 per cent higher in April over the same month,' he says. But he does emphasise that despite the guarantees given, Ford will want to see productivity increases. Mr Boole feels that the Ford takeover will ultimately be seen as a good development, both for the Jaguar and for Coventry. 'The company enjoyed a sales spurt in the mid-1980s, particularly in the United States, but it was never really big enough to compete on a world scale. 'With a parent company developing a new generation of sports cars and saloons, and with enough 'muscle' to take full advantage of the market for these new models, it will be able to compete,' he says. 'That can only be good news for Coventry. It is part of Jaguar's tradition to be in this city.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Coventry (9): The roots go deep - Peugeot Talbot's community involvement
DOC.TEXT: A FEW weeks ago, a small community group in the Stoke area of Coventry needed access to a photocopying machine, to duplicate a newsletter. It turned for help to an unexpected quarter. In many areas the appeal would automatically have been made to the local authority, or one of its agencies. In Stoke, however, as in many other parts of the city, it is increasingly Peugeot Talbot, the French car manufacturer -the antecedents of which put down roots in the fabric of Coventry early this century - where such requests are heard. Roots - or Rootes - is the operative word, of course. Lord Rootes, as he later became, was one of the men who helped found the city's wealth on the motor car, and having prospered so much from the skills and hard work of the local people, he resolved to put something back. Perhaps the most public evidence of Rootes patronage in the city is the widely-respected University of Warwick, which despite its name is well within the city boundary, and which came into being thanks largely to the family's influence. Peugeot Talbot assumed the role of patron when it acquired the ailing UK business of Chrysler, which had absorbed Rootes Group some years earlier. Mr Dick Parham, the deputy managing director, concedes that the company's charitable efforts were permitted to wane in the years following the takeover, as the management wrestled with the more pressing problems of survival. Some four years ago there was a sea change in Peugeot Talbot's fortunes, and it became obvious that the company was riding the crest of a wave. At about the same time, Mr Geoffrey Whalen, the managing director, and his board members looked again at the company's place in the community. Mr Parham deliberately chooses small instances, like the offer to duplicate the newsletter, to illustrate Peugeot's belief that there is more to community involvement than cheque book charity - the glamorous and well-publicised business of allocating large sums for heart-rending causes. The story can be told in figures, of course - charitable giving last year of Pounds 181,000, covenants to hospitals, schools and community associations, lists of cars on long-term loan to deserving organisations. But the statistics alone leave the true nature of Peugeot's commitment in shadow. The whole issue is illuminated, and given character, by the people who work for the company, and who, from the boardroom to the shop-floor, immerse themselves in local affairs. SHOP-FLOOR workers are actively encouraged to involve themselves in local matters. The company, which already supplies four JPs to the local bench, recently asked for more volunteers to allow their names to go forward. Coventry's current lord mayor, Mr Dave Edwards, is an employee, as is the next mayor of Nuneaton, Mr Tony Lloyd. Among his many activities, Mr Whalen chairs the Coventry and Warwickshire Training and Enterprise Council, and has ensured that Peugeot Talbot personnel have been seconded to help with its work. Mr Parham is chairman of ADEPT - the Agency Developing Enterprise Partnership and Trust - which arose from the bishops' Faith in the City working party, and concentrates its work on the less privileged areas of the city. He was also instrumental in setting up the 'Spirit of Coventry' movement, which has now merged its interests with the newer, and like-minded, 'Coventry Is Making It' campaign. Other executives are engaged in similar work throughout the city - the purchasing director lends his expertise to the Coventry health authority, and the finance director serves as a governor at Hereward College, the city's national further education establishment specifically for the disabled. Links with education - and a desire to see employees enrich their lives in and out of the workplace - are strong at the company. The company sponsors Coventry Polytechnic's business school, helping to strengthen links between education and industry. It works closely with local schools and offers work experience to 16-18 year-olds. The firm has built a partnership centre, with an accent on foreign languages. Sporting ties are strong. The company sponsors Coventry City, Coventry Rugby Club, and Warwickshire Cricket Club - giving it a hand in the three most popular spectator sports in the area. On a broader front, Peugeot last year launched an assisted learning programme, allocating Pounds 250,000 for any studies - vocational or otherwise - to which employees are attracted, in the belief that anything which stimulates the learning habit will eventually enhance a fast-changing shop floor where the ability to pick up new skills quickly will be of crucial importance. By co-incidence, French has so far proved to be the most popular course, even for workers who do not need it for their jobs. But others have chosen to earmark their cash from the scheme in the pursuit of HGV licences, fork-lift truck skills - and even passing the standard driving test. 'We've made rapid progress over the past few years - but we've by no means finished. We can now give a lead, and harness the desire in the workforce to help in the community by having this effectively as part of the company's ethos,' Mr Parham explains.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Coventry (7): The city's largest employer - Coventry City Council has substantial property holdings
DOC.TEXT: COVENTRY City Council has long tentacles. This is not just a matter of the number of people it employs, or the extent of the services it provides. It also has substantial property holdings, more and more of which are likely to become the subject of joint venture developments with the private sector. At the same time, the Council's position as the city's largest employer suggests that it is a significant influence on the local labour market. It is in a position to act as a role model for the private sector, through, for example, the pursuit of active training policies and the practice of equal opportunity. Whether such influence will be sustained during a period in which increasing constraints are being placed on local government expenditure remains to be seen. Contrary to the national trend, the size of the Council's employment roll has actually increased over the last two years, although it is now starting to drift down. In 1990 the Council had, in the jargon, 12,982 full time equivalent employees. The latest figure, said Mr John McGuigan, the assistant chief executive, is about 14,000. The numbers are up to 300 fewer than a year ago, but, said Mr McGuigan, 'the progressive reduction has not been as dramatic as other authorities.' This is largely because Council staff have won contracts for rubbish collection, housing maintenance and sports and leisure facilities' management that had been put out to tender. But the total will drop as, for instance, further education passes away from local authority control and as spending cuts take effect. The spending cuts spring from the disparity between what the council wanted to spend and what the government thought it ought to spend. The government's standard spending assessment for Coventry for the 1992-93 fiscal year was Pounds 234.9m, an increase of 5.6 per cent over 1991-92; it was prepared to allow spending of Pounds 245.3m, but any spending over that second figure would have resulted in poll tax capping. The initial City Council spending proposal was Pounds 251.7m. It has thus had to shave that by Pounds 6.4m to avoid capping and, effectively, the imposition of a government budget on the city. It came through with Pounds 6.9m of cuts, after an anguished spending survey which put potential council economies into three categories: those which are politically unacceptable, those which the Council is unwilling to face but would have to, and those which it would have thought about doing anyway. The burden of the cuts fell on the education service - Pounds 5.38m - followed by personnel and administration, accounting for Pounds 1.24m, and transportation and highways, accounting for Pounds 1.14m. The financial position of the Council would have been stronger had it not lost Pounds 0.5m in property rents, because of the weakness of the property market and because of the necessity to make provision for failures to collect the poll tax. In both these regards, Coventry is not in a markedly different position from any other council in the UK. In fact, its position on poll tax collection has been better than most. Mr McGuigan estimated that about 10 per cent of the city's people had not paid anything at all. This is a relatively small proportion, given the political agitation about payment. There was, indeed, a local campaign waged against poll tax waged by Mr Dave Nellist, the former Labour MP for Coventry South East who fought the seat - vainly as it turned out - in the general election as an Independent. The council budget for 1992-93 assumes a six per cent non-payment rate. The council, best described as 'pragmatic Labour,' has played the poll tax issue quietly, as its label might suggest it would. Equally, it is adopting a pragmatic approach to development, especially where its own landholdings are concerned. It has dropped a passive approach of simply responding to private sector approaches which might be forthcoming on a particular piece of land, or on a particular social scheme. Instead, it has been identifying possibilities for development and making it clear that it is prepared to talk with anybody who is prepared to envisage a joint venture, the structure of which would have to meet certain broad criteria. These include long term partnership, as opposed to short term funding, and a readiness to meet council objectives as well as producing private sector profits. Cases in point include the search for a partner to run and develop Coventry Airport, the rehabilitation of Coombe Abbey and the creation around it of more leisure facilities (covered in an article on the China Connection; see facing page), a scheme to generate power from waste incineration, the enhancement of the area around Coventry Cathedral and the expansion of business parks around the outside of the city. Co-operation with the private sector is necessarily an integral part of Coventry's 1992 City Challenge bid. It is competing with other local authorities to win government funding of Pounds 37.5m, spread over five years, to revive the inner city wards of St Michael's and Foleshill. Within this bid there are three large schemes where private sector companies will play the major role. British Gas and Carroll Business Parks plan to reclaim the old Foleshill gas works for a new business park. Courtaulds and Inner City Enterprises wish to turn a vacant headquarters building into a centre for the clothing industry and a new enterprise centre. Ideal Homes and Moorfield envisage new homes and offices on a derelict part of the Coventry Canal Basin. For the Council, over and above the question of developing links with the private sector, the City Challenge bid is of fundamental importance. Its success or failure could speed or retard plans for revival in the poorest part of the city. If the bid is successful there will be an injection of central government funds. But if it fails there is likely to be less funding for the city from the government's Urban Programme. This is because the funds allotted to City Challenge by the government come out of existing budgets. So, more spending on City Challenge means less spending elsewhere.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Coventry (10): Valuable role in the city's economy -University of Warwick works closely with industry and commerce
DOC.TEXT: THE UNIVERSITY of Warwick, situated to the south-west of central Coventry has played an important role in helping the city's economy to grow and diversify. With 2,800 employees at the university and a further 1,100 in the neighbouring Science Park, it was ranked in 1990 as the ninth-largest employer in Coventry and third largest in the public sector. The university came into existence in the mid-1960s as one of the new, so-called 'plate-glass' universities (as opposed to ancient and red-brick universities.) It has 10,000 students enrolled on undergraduate, postgraduate, post-experience and distance-learning courses. The 34 academic departments offer a wide range of three and four-year undergraduate courses in the sciences, social sciences and humanities; and there are 1,300 postgraduates. The 2,000 undergraduate places on offer each year attract a total of 20,000 applicants. Around 8 per cent of those who graduated last summer from Warwick were still without a job by the end of 1991, according to a recent newspaper poll of unemployment among graduates from British universities. This compares with the national average of one in 10. Much interest in Warwick has centred not only upon academic achievement but on links with local industry and the role the university has played in developing the economy of Coventry and Warwickshire. As might be expected in an area with long associations with the automotive industry, the university is strong in engineering. For example, through Professor Kumar Bhattacharyy's, manufacturing group in engineering, the university has worked closely with the Rover Group in training and research, as well as with other companies. Through the advanced technology centre, which is part of the manufacturing group partnership, Warwick co-operates with both Rover and Rolls-Royce Motors in strategic research into automotive technology and new materials. The Warwick Business school, an integral part of the university, maintains close contacts with the local business community. The school's centre for small and medium-sized enterprises produces a twice-yearly business survey which contains important information for the local business community. The school has important links with the Coventry and Warwickshire Training and Enterprise Council. One of the region's commercial success stories is the University of Warwick Science Park. This was started in 1982 as a joint venture between the university, Coventry city council, Warwickshire county council and the then West Midlands county council. Its success was a factor in persuading the city council to locate its 100-acre Westwood Business Park, just across the road from the university. Today, the science park houses 65 companies, many in high technology fields. Dr John Wood, the Industrial Development Officer, says: 'The science park is a success in that there is a definite technology transfer. Approximately half the companies are involved in joint projects or consultancy. Not all science parks have achieved these links with universities, some have become just industrial estates.' Coventry Polytechnic, which next month should receive permission to become Coventry University, has also developed close links with the city's business community. The annual turnover the polytechnic is now around Pounds 46m, an increase of around 50 per cent in the past ten years. The revenue comes not just through government funding but also from overseas students and various private enterprises. There are 12,000 students attending the campus which occupies 18 acres in the city centre, next to the cathedral. There are 1,800 staff making the polytechnic, like the University of Warwick, a main employer in the city. There are close ties with local companies. Both Peugeot Talbot and Lucas provide support for posts within the polytechnic and fund specially-tailored courses. The polytechnic's wholly-owned trading company, Coventry Polytechnic Enterprises, is now in its third year of operation. Mr Charles Leonard, the head of commercial development who runs the company, estimates that it now accounts for around seven per cent of the polytechnic's revenue. Activities range from training to negotiating professional liability contracts and consultancy. One of the most publicised of the company's activities are its dealings with the former Soviet Union. More than 400 former Soviet nationals have been on training courses at Coventry. There is currently a group of Ukrainians at the Coventry sponsored by Allied Lyons and another group sponsored by De Beers. The Polytechnic has had to find private sponsorship for these trainees because the sponsoring countries no longer have the funds to send managers to Coventry. The Polytechnic has recently received Pounds 20,000 from the British Foreign Office 'know-how fund' to help set up mobile food kiosks in Moscow. The Vaz car plant (which makes Lada cars) has asked the polytechnic's help in setting its first commercial bank. The company is working on around 500 projects or contracts and is seeking more.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Coventry (5): Cost and access a spur for inward moves - The National Grid is among companies which have moved their operations to the Midlands city
DOC.TEXT: OFFICIALS AT Coventry City Council realised they would have to diversify the city's economy in the early 1980s. The recession of 1979-81 had been traumatic for Coventry, with around 53,000 jobs lost by 1982, compared with the mid-70s. Over this period, the dominant industries - car-making and related engineering - cut back their activities. In 1980, 46 per cent of the workforce was employed in manufacturing of some kind, most of in the automotive industry: it became obvious too that many of the jobs lost were not going to reappear when the economic cycle turned favourable. An economic development unit at the city council was formed in 1986, and from 1987 different kinds of companies began to move to Coventry. Equity and law Life Assurance Company had already moved some of its operations to Coventry in 1974, but the company, had been very much a lone beacon in the financial services sector. Coventry was seen as a manufacturing city, with the necessary related services being carried out in nearby Birmingham. The absence of a white collar culture meant that very little B1 industrial/office space was available for high technology or financial services companies. The situation began to change with the founding in 1982 of the University of Warwick Science Park, a 45-acre site owned by the university and developed jointly by the university and the city council. Today there are 65 companies, many of them high technology concerns, employing more than 1,100 people on the park. Another development, Westwood Business Park, was brought on stream in 1986. This 100-acre site which is close to the science park provided the breakthrough the city needed. Again, it was developed by the city council, but this time in conjunction with private sector developers. It has proved attractive to financial services companies: Barclays Bank, which now employs 850 people in Coventry, and RSA Examinations Board, which employs 130 people are two well known service companies which have moved operations to the park. The city council estimates that, in all, 157 companies have moved part or all of their operations to Coventry since 1987, creating 10,570 new jobs. This has meant that the percentage employed in manufacturing has dropped to 35 per cent. On the science park, some of the high-technology companies include Sun Microsystems, Buehler International, Telemecanique and Olivetti. Other companies which have relocated to Coventry include the National Grid employing 800 people at a new headquarters building; Midland Bank, which has established a regional data headquarters, and employs 250 people, the Department of Transport which has a regional administration unit involved in motorway widening, and which employs 130 people, and Mortgages plc, a financial services group, which employs 158. A successful diversification is thus clearly under way for a variety of reasons. The city does qualify for some government assistance as an intermediate development area, but it has not had new town or urban development status, and has not received large government grants to prime the pump for developers. The cheap cost of Coventry has, however, been a factor. In the late 1980s rents for offices were as low as Pounds 7 a sq ft compared with Pounds 15 for Birmingham. There was also an abundance of skilled labour following redundancies at car plants. Mr Myles Mackie, the investment and policy adviser at the city council, feels the accessibility of Coventry has also been important. He says, 'I know every town looking for investment claims it is the centre of England, but Coventry really is: we are the closest part of the Midlands to London - it's only an hour and 20 minutes by train. We're close to the motorways, but there is good internal access. The ring road actually works and there is little congestion in the city centre, unlike big cities, such as Birmingham.' But also important has been the ability of the local authority to provide the right kind of accommodation. The RSA Examination Board when it wanted to move out of London in 1988 appointed agents to find a new site. They found premises in Nottingham and Derby, but they were unsuitable because they were on industrial estates next to companies manufacturing. The Board wanted a clean business-like environment and the Westwood estate fitted the bill. Costs have risen since the late 1980s, and B1 business premises would now cost around Pounds 13 a sq ft., but this is still competitive with other relocation towns such as Milton Keynes, Peterborough and even Telford; 12 other industrial estates apart from the science park and the Westwood business park are open for business, representing several hundreds of acres of B1 space.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Coventry (6): Schemes have matured - Youth and adult training
DOC.TEXT: THE Coventry and Warwickshire Training and Enterprise Council was set up in September 1990. This was a difficult moment: it was a time when a key Coventry employer, Jaguar, was making large numbers redundant. The TEC has been able to take in some, but by no means all of the 1,000 or so employees made jobless at Jaguar, under its Employment Training programme. The ET scheme, together with the Youth Training Scheme, is one of the two major programmes which the Coventry and Warwickshire Tec like other Tecs has inherited from the government's Training Agency. The ET programme is designed for the older workers, who are thrown on to the labour market in mid-life and who run the risk without retraining of becoming long-term unemployed. YTS was designed for young people between the ages of 16 and 19 with the aim of giving them vocational qualifications. The programme for former Jaguar workers is rather special in that Jaguar is making facilities available for retraining and the Coventry Chamber of Commerce is also involved along with the Coventry and Warwickshire Tec. But the TEC has also had to absorb others made jobless in the recent recession. Mr Scott Glover, the chief executive of the Tec, says that there are around 3,000 people on the ET programme at any given time. He rejects suggestions that the ET programme has just become an easy way for long-term unemployed to pick up money with no real intention of taking a job. 'Seventy five per cent of thepeople we have interviewed, and this includes employers as well as people on the scheme, have said they feel the scheme has been very beneficial,' he says. He estimates that there is a successs rate of 25 per cent of people on the scheme finding new work - 'this is not high enough of course, but it is early days in the scheme and there has been a fierce recession.' Several millions of the budget of Pounds 25m is spent on adult training. Around 56 per cent of the total goes on youth training which is the other main programme inherited from the training agency. The idea is that young people of between 16 and 19 are given funds with which they can not support themselves exist but also buy some training - either on-job training or at a college or a combination of both - which will lead to a recognised national vocational qualification (NVA). There was much criticism of the youth training scheme (YTS) when it was administered by the Training Agency. It was said that some employers 'just used young people as cheap labour' and failed to give them training. Young people on the other hand saw the YTS as a government ruse to deny them their social security money or unemployment benefit, since acceptance of YTS money implied taking a job of some kind whether it entailed training or not. Mr Glover says: 'The schemes vary from area to area. But yes, I suppose in the early days the YTS was designed to get young people off the streets. But the schemes have matured. They are not known as the youth training schemes, but just youth training. Our surveys show that 75 per cent of young people involved in our programmes are receiving training of some kind which should lead to a vocational qualification.' The Coventry and Warwickshire Tec has not gone over to the voucher scheme adopted by other Tecs. Under this system, the young person is given a voucher or credit which can then be cashed in to buy training. Instead, the Coventry Tec goes in for what Mr Glover calls 'flexible funding.' This means giving the young person as much as possible to meet his or her training needs. 'We must recognise it takes more to train an engineer than it does a typist,' he says. Funding remains a problem. There are 310,000 people in Coventry and 480,000 in wider Warwickshire. The Pounds 25m is only a fraction more than the Training Agency was spending before the Tec was set up. BESIDES the two training programmes the Tec has also taken over the enterprise scheme and is responsible for small business. The Tec wants to to do more than perpetuate old schemes. The main thrust of its aims is closer targetting. By this is meant surveys to find out what are the skills needs of the area and a closer involvement with companies, local authorities, and educational authorities to try and match those skills with the right kind of training. One recent survey showed a need for, among other things: Drivers for heavy goods, fork lift and public service vehicles. In engineering - craft technicians and engineers. Tourism, catering and hotel staff. Management skills of all kinds. All forms of electricians and electronic engineers. All modern offices skills, eg computing and word processing. This survey was taken at a time when unemployment was over 12 per cent in Coventry although much lower in Warwickshire as a whole. It showed a considerable skills mismatch. The economy of Coventry has changed over the past decade with a diversification into high technology industries away from the dependence on engineering in the automotive industry. Nevertheless, the 200 largest companies still employ nearly 40 per cent of the workforce. It is expected that some of these companies will shed further labour and that there will be a high proportion of men and women in their 50s needing retraining. One scheme which the TEC is behind is to get big companies to use their facilities to train people from smaller concerns or from business start-ups. 'This all takes time. We are evolutionary, rather than revolutionary,' says Mr Glover. He stresses though, that the Tec does not want to be a provider of training itself but wants to be an enabler or facilitator. This means the main aim is to get local companies and education bodies involved - and keep them involved.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Coventry (4): The shake-out takes its toll - Manufacturing, the quality as well as the quantity of jobs on offer has decline / The decline of the manufacturing sector and the rise of the services sector leads to a mismatch of local skills
DOC.TEXT: ONCE upon a time, when the sun shone on the Coventry economy and never looked likely to set, city unemployment was about half of one per cent. That was in 1955. Now, nearly a generation of change later, the contrast is savage. Over the last six months, said the West Midlands Enterprise Board in latest analysis of unemployment in the old West Midlands metropolitan county, 'the highest rate of increase has been in Coventry where the jobless total has risen by 13 per cent, and the lowest has been in Birmingham where there has been a rise of 6.1 per cent. In the county as a whole, there has been a fall of 0.1 per cent over the last month and a rise of 8.5 per cent over the last six months.' Coventry, in other words, has been faring worse in employment terms than other parts of the West Midlands conurbation. However, within this generalisation, encapsulated in an overall unemployment rate of 14.1 per cent against a national average of 9.4 per cent, there are distinct local and sectoral variations. Firstly, men have suffered from redundancies to a greater extent than women. This is not a phenomenon peculiar to Coventry, but as the City Council noted last year, men were losing their jobs at twice the rate of women, confirming that 'the current recession is affecting mostly male full-time employment.' The latest jobless totals have a male unemployment rate of 18.1 per cent and a female rate of 8.0 per cent. Secondly, and this follows on from the first point, redundancies appear to have been taking place at a much higher rate in the manufacturing sector, where there is the highest incidence of full time male employment, than in the services sector, where there is a high level of female, part-time employment. The list of companies which have announced redundancies in recent months is full of household names: Alvis, British Coal, closing the last pit in the area; Courtaulds, Dunlop Aviation, Federal Express, GPT, Massey Ferguson, Matrix Churchill and so on. Third, the geographic distribution of unemployment in the city shows that some wards are markedly more affected than others - 'there is still a strong north-west/south-east divide,' observes the City Council, 'with much lower rates evident in the areas to the south and east of the city centre and very high rates within the inner city wards.' The worst affected wards are St Michael's and Foleshill, where male jobless rates run at 34.0 and 29.0 per cent respectively. They are also the wards where there is the highest concentration of ethnic minorities - Asian and Afro-Caribbean. Their male unemployment rate is twice as high as the white rate, and their female rate is three times higher than the white. It is these wards where, says Mr Trevor Cornfoot, head of economic development at the City Council, 'there is a real difficulty of trying to secure adequate employment.' Partly, he notes, this is because the wards are among the early industrialised areas of Coventry and over the last two decades there has been a succession of large factory closures, including Alfred Herbert, the machine tool manufacturer, and Morris Engines. Not surprisingly, the two wards are the setting of Coventry's City Challenge bid for new government urban renewal funding. The steady rise in unemployment, as the recession has bitten deeper, has taken place against the background of a decline in the working population, itself a movement in parallel with a declining population. Official estimates show that the total population is expected to decline to 296,000 by next year from 326,000 in 1979, while the working population will reduce to 177,000 by next year from 193,000 in 1979. But within these declining numbers there has been a perceptible shift in the nature of employment. The string of manufacturing redundancies of recent months has simply exacerbated a trend which has been apparent in varying degrees from the early 1970s: the lower importance of manufacturing and the higher importance of services in the employment mix. The 1989 employment census, coming after a decade of deep cuts in capacity, still showed, however, that 40 per cent of the workforce was employed in manufacturing, against a national average of 23 per cent. The present recession will have reduced that proportion further. Indeed, most local predictions suggest that unemployment will continue rising at least until well into the second half of this year and possibly into 1993. Given the cyclical nature of the engineering industry, broadly defined, the process of reducing dependence on manufacturing may provide a greater degree of employment stability. But there are two problems. The first is that, as a generalisation, jobs with wage rates which traditionally had supported a family have disappeared to be replaced by service sector jobs which offer less money. Labour surveys have shown that the likely maximum wage for office staff is about the median level for industrial earnings. They have also shown that, although basic pay for full-time working women is roughly two-thirds of the level of male pay, it is double the level paid to part time working women. The second problem is that the decline of the manufacturing sector and the rise of the services sector gives rise to a mismatch of skills. Service sector employers do not need people with expertise in industrial working. Given continued expansion of the Coventry services sector, finding new entrants to the labour force will assume a greater importance even as jobs are being lost. The pattern for employment trends has been set. Dr Michael Healey, principal lecturer in geography at Coventry Polytechnic, believes that, in terms of job creation in the city, three factors are likely to be evident over the coming years: there will be more part-time working, more flexible employment practices and, as the present jobless statistics have foreshadowed, there will be an even greater role for women. ---------------------------------------- WARD UNEMPLOYMENT ---------------------------------------- Ward Number % Bablake 587 8.8 Binley and Willenhall 1,376 13.8 Cheylesmore 838 11.7 Earlsdon 706 9.7 Foleshill 1,703 24.4 Henley 1,486 16.5 Holbrook 1,264 14.7 Longford 1,421 17.1 Lower Stoke 1,066 14.5 Radford 1,427 19.1 St Michael's 1,746 27.6 Sherbourne 928 12.7 Upper Stoke 1,033 13.4 Wainbody 360 6.2 Westwood 871 13.4 Whoberley 879 10.9 Woodlands 937 10.0 Wyken 968 10.4 District total 19,599 14.1 ---------------------------------------- Source: Coventry Labour Market Review. ----------------------------------------

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Coventry (2): A changing economic base - Manufacturing employment is concentrated in a small number of large companies
DOC.TEXT: SAFEWAY has a new supermarket on one of the western approaches to Coventry city centre. Nearby, a bridge with the name Alvis painted on it, spans the road. It is a natural historic juxtaposition, symbolic of changes in the city's economy, writes Paul Cheeseright. Alvis, the fighting vehicle manufacturer, owned the land where Safeway now operates, but it has slimmed down and moved out of the city centre: where once there was industry, there are services, a switch which is the single most important characteristic of the Coventry economy since the recession of the early 1980s. Retrospectively, it is clear that manufacturing peaked in 1966, but the critical years were between 1974 and 1982. 'During that period, Coventry lost 46 per cent of its manufacturing jobs - 53,000. A major shift took place in the local economy,' says Mr Michael Healey, principal lecturer in geography at Coventry Polytechnic and the author of numerous studies on Coventry's economic development. His research showed that nearly two thirds of the manufacturing job losses were caused by recession and changes in the industrial structure - 'Coventry suffered from the weakness of the national economy,' Mr Healey noted. Yet, despite the relative decline of manufacturing, the economic significance of industry remains huge, and the 1990s recession may also lead to permanent losses of capacity. Indeed, there are local fears - and Coventry is not unique in this respect - that the scale of the cutbacks, the reduced level of training, and financial difficulties in coping with any expansion in demand will mean that companies may not be able to respond quickly to an upturn in orders. Certainly skill shortages are expected to recur. This may be unduly pessimistic if only because the manufacturing base is held together now, as it was 20 years ago, by a relatively small number of companies. The 100 largest employers account for around 60 per cent of total employment in the city and within that 100, the top 15 account for around 45 per cent. These are not the sort of companies that necessarily have trouble with the bank manager. The three largest private sector employers are Jaguar, GPT and Peugeot Talbot, but the largest employer of all is Coventry City Council. Employment is highly concentrated, and in manufacturing is spread over a narrow range of sectors, primarily metal goods and engineering, with a particular emphasis on vehicle manufacture: the historic industrial base remains intact. WITH more than half of its jobs in manufacturing now in the control of companies headquartered outside the region, and frequently abroad, the Coventry economy has, however, been prey to global economic movement. There has not until recently been the leavening and diversity provided by local small companies. Nor indeed has there been the stability which comes from such diversity. But the shockwaves of the 1980s recession, the easy credit of the mid-1980s and a changing appreciation insouth-east England of Coventry's role in the national economy has set off change. Reli ance on a small range of manufacturers and a narrow range of products is diminishing. On the basis of information gleaned from VAT registrations, Coventry had, during the 1980s, an exceptionally high rate of business formation. There was a growth rate of 41 per cent. This was not only the highest of any district in the West Midlands but 12 percentage points greater than the national average. Surveys suggest both that the vast majority of the new businesses have been of local origin and in the services sector. The services sector has been expanded by inward investment. At a time when the south-east England economy was growing quickly, Coventry was seen as close enough to be convenient, and cheap enough to be attractive. Indeed, reports Mr Harvey Williams, regional spokesman for the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors, current office rents in and around Coventry for new or recently refurbished property are between Pounds 12 and Pounds 14 a square foot, compared with Pounds 17-18 in Birmingham and Pounds 40 in the south-east. Yet, Coventry's significance as an office centre should not be overstated - 'a large proportion of service functions have been back-office functions. 'I don't think we would see ourselves as in the position of Birmingham, saying we want to be some kind of financial services centre,' says Mr Trevor Cornfoot, the City Council's head of economic development. Coventry is instead becoming an office dormitory of the south-east. Many of the new jobs have gone to business parks on the periphery of the city, leaving the city council anxious to secure other forms of development in the centre, through, for example, the expansion of hotel, leisure and retail facilities. Yet, come what may, Coventry's future, like that of the West Midlands as a whole, is indissolubly linked to that of the engineering industry. The problem has been to secure the growth of companies which will at once diminish economic dependence on the traditional employers, widen the industrial base and provide the development opportunities for the technology of the next generation. The city council calculates that there are now 300 companies in Coventry engaged in high technology activities. One stimulus has been the University of Warwick Science Park, a centre of research and development for 54 companies of diverse origin - 'the science park has made a difference to the quality of companies entering the city,' notes Mr Cornfoot. In spite of all these changes, Coventry has not managed to compensate, at least in employment terms, for the de-industrialisation which took place during the late 1970s and the early 1980s. Although greater diversity carries the promise of greater stability, it is not clear, especially after taking into account the effects of the current recession, that the local economy has reached the stage where a new generation of growth is assured.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 29 MAY 92 / Survey of Coventry (1): Diversification points the way to greater stability - Although Coventry has large swathes of unused industrial capacity, the city continues to seek an infusion of new economic vitality from outside
DOC.TEXT: COVENTRY is the epitome of the UK's industrial cities: a mix of wealth and poverty, of pockets of grace in a suit of drabness, a dependence on the industries which inspired its growth but an increasing reliance on recent diversification, a population in overall decline, but including an enlarging ethnic minority. Smaller than Birmingham, Glasgow, Leeds, Liverpool or Manchester, Coventry is, nonetheless, like them in that it has been badly served by the first years of the decade. First the recession of the 1980s, a few brief years of recovery, and then headlong into another recession which has stunted aspiration. There are now, it is true, glimpses of recovery. Since the beginning of the year, most order books have stopped shrinking, but business surveys show that not only in Coventry but in the West Midlands region as a whole, there are large swathes of unused industrial capacity. The latest unemployment figures, and the news that car production in April was still running at a lower level than April 1991, show that the city is far from putting its problems behind it. Coventry is no longer 'car city' in the sense that it was in the 1960s and 1970s. In fact, its industrial base cracked in the 1980s recession. Its fortunes, however, are still tied to the motor industry, and not only the industry on a national scale. The success of the industry in carving out export markets has only emphasised the way in which Coventry is borne along on the waves of both the national and international economies. Jaguar's problems in the US markets are a source of worry, and Peugeot Talbot's growing share of the UK market a harbinger of future prosperity, but both are controlled from outside the region. Although the proportion of jobs in the manufacturing sector, dominated by engineering and particularly vehicle assembly, fell during the 1980s from 46 per cent to 34 per cent, and has continued to fall since, large industrial employers still are the main influence on the labour market. But that diminution in the importance of manufacturing is the key to the city's economic future. During the 1980s, Coventry started to change its spots. Creation of more small businesses, the appearance of high technology research companies around the edge of the city and a spate of inward investment were the start of a move towards a more balanced economy. Although headquarters offices were few and far between, Coventry won its share of back-office operations and, in effect, latched on to the industrial economy a new, but relatively low level, office economy. This movement, in turn, has allowed Coventry to weather the present recession in better shape than, otherwise, it might have done. Indeed, the major job losses of the last two years have not been in the services sector; they have been in manufacturing. It is an indication of the greater stability which springs from a larger basket of economic activity that home repossessions in Coventry have been running at 15 per cent below the national average. IT is a moot point whether Coventry will again recapture the importance it enjoyed as a manufacturing centre a generation ago, when the demand for its products seemed everlasting and abundant. Building a new city economy is not easy at the best of times, especially when there is a wider tendency of decentralisation. The drift from the country to the towns which started in the nineteenth century has gone firmly into reverse. Coventry's population began to grow sharply in the second half of that century and reached a peak of about 340,000 during the 1960s, the decade when manufacturing activity peaked. Since the 1970s it has been drifting downwards: manufacturing does not provide the work, the services sector has not fully made up the slack. The outlook for Coventry then is not one of major expansion, but rather to be a medium-sized city with, if the trends which became evident in the 1980s hold firm, a relatively prosperous but varied economy. There are both plus and minus signs. On the plus side is the re-invigoration of the motor industry, Jaguar's problems notwithstanding. This has been stimulated by the presence in the UK of Japanese carmakers and the gradual introduction of Japanese practices to enhance productivity. It has been emphasised by the increasing integration of British-based car makers and component manufacturers into international motor trade. But if the underlying factors needed to secure Coventry's continuing role in the motor industry are in place, the growing number of small high technology companies also offers the hope of industrial diversification into high value-added products. This is the significance of, for example, the University of Warwick science park. At the same time, the geographical position of Coventry, the relative cheapness of its property and land, should ensure that, once there are more solid signs of national economic revival, there will be a steady trickle of corporate refugees from south-east England. What happened in the 1980s should happen again in the 1990s. The challenge will be to have available an adequately trained labour force. The minus signs include the perception that Coventry is not one of the most attractive UK cities. The image of Coventry is of its inspiring cathedral and the gentleness of some its immediate environs. But a wider reality is the drabness of its 1960s architecture. While more jobs may come from inward investment, the vigour of the city will not be assured if the new arrivals want to live outside in the countryside. The future vigour of the city is, of course, dependent on factors other than that. Not least is the task of ensuring that its ethnic minority, largely Asian in origin and now accounting for around 30 per cent of the population, is not left out on a social and economic limb. THERE is the need, too, to banish the industrial detritus of the past, although, in this connection, Coventry does not have, like some of its industrial city peers, huge tracts of derelict land. These two sets of problems come together in the wards of St Michael's and Foleshill. Here, the ethnic minority is concentrated and male unemployment runs up to nearly 35 per cent. Housing in parts of the locality is the worst in Coventry, the industrial infrastructure is decayed, and crime rates are high. Health levels are low relative to the rest of the city, but the funds to make physical improvements, to train the lowly skilled and to provide jobs are in short supply. The city council does not have them and that is why it has made these two wards the subject of a bid for government funding through City Challenge 1992. But housing and unemployment problems spread to the estates in the outer suburbs. Indeed, the events of mid-May, when police clashed with youths on Wood End estate, one of the city's problem areas, were a blunt reminder of the consequences when the cocktail of idle hands, recalcitrant minds and warm weather is shaken too hard. For a city seeking inward investment, the clashes were not the most obvious advertisement.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / International Company News: Philips to buy rest of Super Club
DOC.TEXT: MINORITY shareholders in Super Club, the loss-making Belgian video rental chain, agreed yesterday to sell the company to its biggest shareholder, the Philips electronics group of the Netherlands. Philips, which holds 51 per cent of Super Club's shares, offered earlier this month to pay BFr150 (Dollars 4.40) in cash for each of the 8.4m shares which it does not already own. Shareholders were also offered the choice of receiving warrants on Philips shares worth about BFr225 each. A majority of 98 per cent of shareholders accepted Philips' terms at a meeting of Super Club's holding company in Geneva. The vote brings to an end a dispute between Philips and several key minority shareholders about the value of Super Club's shares. The Dutch company wanted 100 per cent control of the heavily loss-making Belgian group to carry out a thorough restructuring programme. At their peak in 1990, Super Club's unlisted shares were worth more than BFr5,000 each on the Belgian over-the-counter market. The shares plummeted after a swift expansion programme landed the company in debt. Philips took majority control last year after a series of bail-out operations. Philips' increasing involvement in the Belgian company had come as a surprise because of Philips' own financial difficulties, but Philips management has defended the investment, saying the video-rental business complemented the company's production of VCRs.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / International Company News: RJ Reynolds starts work on factory in Warsaw
DOC.TEXT: R. J. REYNOLDS Tobacco International has started work on a Dollars 33m cigarette factory in Piaseczno near Warsaw which is due to come on stream in the middle of next year and have an annual production capacity of 8bn cigarettes. The decision to build the plant is in contrast to the strategy of its rival Philip Morris which has offered to purchase the Krakow tobacco works which accounts for around one third of the country's output. Philip Morris, which recently bought the Czech cigarette monopoly, has a long-standing link with Krakow where it has has produced its Marlboro brand under licence since 1973. Last year output of Marlboro in Krakow reached 2bn cigarettes and Philip Morris is offering to invest Dollars 200m in the plant on top of the purchase price. The country's five state owned plants last year produced 90bn cigarettes while an estimated 10bn cigarettes are imported, many of them as contraband.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Nato hopefulon defence roles deal
DOC.TEXT: MR Manfred Worner, secretary-general of Nato, expressed optimism yesterday that the alliance would resolve its row over the role of the new European corps being set up by France and Germany. His statement at the end of a two-day meeting of Nato defence ministers - not including France - came amid increasing signs of reluctance by other European allies to commit themselves to joining the corps, as Bonn and Paris have invited them to do. 'I have no doubt that in the end we will find sat-isfying solutions, not only for France and the US but for all of the allies,' Mr Worner said. Much would depend on the detailed arrangements for the new 35,000-man corps, he added. Several allies including the UK and the Netherlands, have voiced concern that the Franco-German plan could undermine the transatlantic alliance. Mr Dick Cheney, US defence secretary, said Washington still had some 'unanswered questions about the new corps'. Foremost among these was how it would fit in with the role allotted to the Western European Union as the vehicle for developing Europe's defence interests. Belgium is seen as one of the most likely candidates for an expansion of the Franco-German initiative. But Mr Leo Delacroix, its defence minister, said it would join only if the corps were placed clearly under the political authority of the WEU. The military units which Belgium is considering assigning to the corps would be the same as it is earmarking for Nato's new rapid reaction forces. Spain, which like France stands outside Nato's integrated military command, remains interested in the Franco-German initiative, while Italy said it did not intend to join the corps but would make other units available to the WEU.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Fiat deal demands by Polish unions
DOC.TEXT: LAST-MINUTE union protests have dogged talks - expected to end today - between Fiat and the Polish government on the sale to the Italian motor company of a majority share in the FSM car plant. Union leaders at the Tychy plant, one of two in the FSM combine, were continuing to insist yesterday on being consulted about the terms of the agreement which Mr Giovanni Agnelli, Fiat's chairman, is expected to sign in Warsaw today. FSM at present produces Fiat's new Cinquecento model at Tychy as well as the 1970's Fiat 126 car at Bielsko Biala. Government officials are due at FSM in southern Poland today to outline the agreement to union representatives who are demanding there be no immediate job losses as a result of the deal. Three unions - Solidarity, the OPZZ (the old pro-Communist movement), and Solidarity 80 (a radical group) - are co-ordinating their protest at Tychy, which employs 7,000 of the factory's 23,000 workers. Tychy's unions are also demanding that the share of production costs devoted to wages remain at the same level as in Fiat plants in Italy and elsewhere. Under the deal, which was provisionally agreed last week, Fiat will invest Dollars 2bn and will ultimately control 90 per cent of the company's equity. It will be taking responsibility for FSM's outstanding foreign currency debts worth Dollars 500m, as well as sums due to domestic suppliers worth more than Dollars 200m. Fiat will add Dollars 180m into the company's capital and will cover FSM's losses for the next four years. Fiat has also promised to make new investments worth Dollars 850m.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / EBRD decides on strategy for Russia
