DOC.TEXT: Ian Irvine, deputy chief executive of Reed International, is the latest senior businessman to be sounded out for the top job in ITV - chief executive of the commissioning system for the new centralised network to be introduced next year. Irvine is an inspired choice. He is a serious businessman who would be able to handle the Pounds 500m or so a year programme budget. On top of that, as a former chairman of TV-am, he has at least a passing acquaintance with the colourful ways of Britain's commercial television. Pay is not a problem. For the right chief executive, up to Pounds 300,000 a year could be on the table. The only problem is that Ian Irvine is the latest in a long and distinguished line to say no. Some TV executives have been heard to ask plaintively how they can get their names taken off the list. Those considered capable of doing the job think it would be like sitting on the original bed of nails at the centre of 15 companies notorious for their inability to agree on anything. And those who actually want the job are by definition deemed irredeemably unsuitable. But there's plenty of time yet. ITV does not expect to have to take a decision before the end of May.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Observer: Plane words
DOC.TEXT: The power of the press. Observer reported yesterday that John Major was travelling around central Europe in an ancient chartered aircraft. Within hours his aides were promising things would be different in future. They revealed that Downing Street is negotiating with the RAF to provide a permanent customised jet to fly Major and his entourage around the world - Britain's equivalent of Air Force One. There is only one snag. The Treasury has yet to approve the several million pounds necessary to provide the prime minister with an aircraft befitting an international statesman.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Observer: Breaking the bank
DOC.TEXT: As Edinburgh muscles into the contest to house the European central bank, the city is at least showing a touch of realism. Unlike Luxembourg - which has dug up an arcane EC law dating from the mid-1960s to support its case for accommodating the new Euro-bankers lock, stock and barrel - the Scots are advocating the break-up of the institution even before it exists. The idea is that if bits of it were scattered around the community, Edinburgh would merit a share. Although the tactic has style, it is alas no satisfactory answer to the Germans - rooting noisily for Frankfurt - who argue that Britain's wishy-washy commitment to full monetary union puts the entire country in a poor position to claim the prize. But the real problem, closer to home, seems to be Ian Lang, the Scottish secretary. Far from fighting Edinburgh's corner in cabinet, all he has apparently produced so far is a feeble bureaucratic- sounding letter to the campaigners last month vouchsafing that the government would give Edinburgh's case 'the most careful consideration' - but only if it was decided to go outside London at all. Indeed the Conservative party as a whole is hardly leading from the front on the issue. Labour's shadow Scottish secretary Donald Dewar turned out to be the only politician to speak at yesterday's launch of Edinburgh's campaign. Not a single Tory minister, MP or as much as a councillor was in evidence. Meanwhile, the cooler heads in Scotland are hoping that the campaigning may at least give their capital a leg-up in obtaining some other (unspecified) EC institution as a consolation prize. In the meantime, there is no harm in giving the city's claim to be Britain's second financial centre a further thorough airing.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Leading Article: Risks of too much hot air
DOC.TEXT: THERE IS no such thing as a free breath. This is the point behind the debate on global warming at the Rio de Janeiro Earth Summit, starting next week. Anything that comes free of charge will be used to excess. So it is not difficult to accept, in principle, that as human activity increases, so will the costs of treating the air as if it were free. The difficulty is knowing how, and how far, to turn that principle into practice. The starting point must be the nature of the risks and the costs of reducing them. The latest World Development Report from the World Bank reports scientific estimates that mean global temperature might rise by between 1.5' and 4.5' Celsius, with a best guess of 2.5', as a result of the doubling of greenhouse gases above their pre-industrial concentrations. But the cost has been estimated at only about 1 per cent of US gross domestic product. This seems to be much ado about nothing. Things are not that simple. As Bill Cline points out in his study of global warming for the Washington-based Institute for International Economics, the doubling of greenhouse gases is expected to occur in the first half of the next century. But global warming is continuous. He offers a central estimate for global warming of 10' Celsius by 2300, with an upper limit of 18'. Six per cent of GDP is his best guess of the economic cost, with 20 per cent at most. More important, such a world would be radically - perhaps horribly - different from today's. Nevertheless, even with a low rate of discount, the case for strong action is not overwhelming. Nor, given the time scale, is it overwhelmingly urgent. But a benevolent and risk-averse global dictator would, undoubtedly, want to slow the build up of greenhouse gases, while mounting further studies of the risks. Carbon tax In a world with a multitude of very different states, reaching even so limited a decision requires much debate. The Rio summit is an excellent place to start. But the European Community's on-and-off-again carbon tax shows what is in store. A carbon tax is the right kind of policy. That said, the proposed tax of Dollars 10 a barrel would make little difference to the consumption of a commodity already taxed, on average, more than five times as heavily in the EC. Nor can much be said in favour of a tax that exempts the most energy-intensive industries. In short, the EC tax was a gesture. Now EC ministers have decided not to make that gesture. As a result, the EC's environment commissioner, Mr Ripa di Meana, has decided to make one himself, by not going to Rio. This may be farcical, but the EC has at least stirred things up. It has also shown how hard it will be to reach international agreements. The lesson applies globally, but more so. Hard issues The issues are hard. First, the setting of uniform targets for emissions cannot make sense in a world of radically different countries. Second, no global compact can be agreed and enforced that does not redress the grossly unequal use of the atmosphere. Last but not least, stabilising carbon dioxide emissions will hurt. The World Bank suggests starting with a modest precautionary policy, focusing on research into global warming, the elimination of subsidies to wasteful energy use and the development of renewable energy resources. Afforestation would be part of such a strategy. So would higher taxes on the use of fossil fuels. Should the dangers become clearer, property rights in carbon dioxide emission would need to be agreed, enforced and traded. But these would entail large redistributions of income. According to the World Development Report, the industrial world would have had to pay the developing countries Dollars 70bn to purchase 1988's level of emission, if the right had been sold at Dollars 25 per ton of carbon. In the long run, air could become expensive. The political reaction to that possibility has been illustrated by this week's EC imbroglio over the carbon tax. But Rio is only a first step. If something like the World Bank's precautionary programme were implemented now, along with intensified debate, leading in the long run to property rights in the atmosphere, Rio would be a breakthrough.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Low-tech risks for high finance: The pressures placed on the banking system by difficulties in the commercial property market
DOC.TEXT: If you had asked a central banker five years ago to identify the most worrying threats to the banking system, he would probably have talked at length about the accelerating pace of financial innovation and the proliferation of complex new financial instruments that were beyond the capacity of most bankers over the age of 40 to understand. How ironic that the chief threat in the 1990s comes from that most low-tech and comprehensible of assets, commercial property. The collapse of the UK property group Mountleigh, with outstanding debts of more than Pounds 1/2 bn, and now the likelihood of receivership or administration for the UK operations of Olympia and York of Canary Wharf fame, are just the latest in a series of items of bad news for the banks in property. The Canadian-based Olympia and York is admittedly in a category of its own, in view of its size and the complexity of its international financial arrangements. Yet the decision of the banks to retreat into receivership or administration at these two troubled groups demonstrates the difficulty of maintaining support operations where the agreement of numerous creditors is required. At the same time both these concerns have notably obvious things in common with other troubled property companies such as Heron International and Speyhawk, that are the subject of continuing discussions with their bankers, namely the presence of Barclays and Citicorp. For the battle-weary in the City, it is tempting to respond to this latest disaster with a rhetorical question: so what's new? It is now common ground that the commercial banks vetted individual risks in property lending without considering the implications for the whole portfolio of loans. It may seem hard today to grasp how Barclays' outgoing chairman, Sir John Quinton, could have shared responsibility for an unsustainable 35 per cent compound growth in the bank's property loan book in the six years to 1991, far faster than the other clearing banks, given that he had played a central role in running the clearing banks' lifeboat operation in the fringe banking and property crisis of the mid-1970s (see chart). Yet it has to be seen, say the apologists, in the context of the heady climate of the late 1980s. Nor was Barclays out on its own. Citicorp, once the world's biggest bank, operated even more impressively in the boom years as a kind of gigantic corporate centipede. If it shot itself in the foot, it consoled itself with the thought that there were ever so many feet to go. Alas, by last year it was down to four feet and the Bank for International Settlements had decreed that it must have eight to maintain the present volume of lending. Back to the gun room for further inspiration. As for the problems of the property market, the existence of a huge oversupply of space and of the related overhang of Pounds 40bn-plus of bank debt - three times the level, in real terms, of the last crisis in 1974 - has been discussed ad nauseam for two years or more. Why should the banking system suddenly be regarded as subject to an increased threat when its troubles have been so widely predicted? The answer is that some things have changed for the worse and not simply because the British clearing banks have yet to make substantial provisions against a new round of dud property loans. The banks are engaged in a debt work-out, similar to the one they conducted in the second half of the 1970s. Yet the economics of the work-out, in which property companies are nursed along under the best available management until the market turns up and property becomes saleable again at worthwhile prices, are very different this time round. Barclays provides an interesting case study. At the end of 1991 it had property and construction loans of Pounds 8.5bn in Britain and more than Pounds 11bn worldwide, compared with capital of Pounds 9.1bn. That may be modest by the standards of Japanese city banks, many of which have property exposure equivalent to two times their capital. But by any other yardstick it looks high. Sir John Quinton is nonetheless sanguine about his bank's ability to weather the property storm and argues that: at least 70 per cent of the bank's property loans are for completed, income-producing properties where the tenants have no problem in meeting debt service; all the bank's property loans were made at a discount to conservative valuations and many were made before the peak of the boom; a total of Pounds 40bn of bank debt is not large in relation to the property market's estimated overall value of around Pounds 180bn; the risk in the outstanding debt of the larger troubled property companies is widely spread around the whole international banking community, so the individual provisions and write-offs will be less than the size of the corporate collapses might seem to indicate; and when economic recovery restimulates tenant demand, institutional and other investors will readily provide Pounds 10bn of equity to refinance one quarter of the debt overhang. On that basis Barclays expects overall provisions not to exceed those in 1991 and possibly to emerge somewhat lower. And yet these seemingly reassuring points may not be quite as comforting as they appear at first sight. One fundamental difference between today's property collapse and the earlier one in the mid-1970s is the extent of the oversupply, not least in London offices. There is now 32.4m sq ft of empty office space in the capital, equivalent to 18 per cent of the total office stock, according to property advisers Debenham Tewson & Chinnocks. Investment Property Databank, a leading independent source of property market intelligence, estimates that central London office rents were plunging in the six months to March at an annualised rate of 32 per cent. Corporate landlords, including Britain's biggest, Land Securities, are increasingly finding that properties are let at rents that exceed today's increasingly depressed market values. The outcome is a radical shift in the balance of power in favour of the tenant. Oversupply, according to Mr Norman Bowie, a doyen of the chartered surveying profession, means that tenants are seeking to use their new bargaining power to win greater flexibility in the terms of leases. The market answer to this demand, says Mr Bowie, is shorter leases or leases with break clauses. In other words, the 25-year lease with upward only rent reviews - an inflationary ratchet if ever there was one - is no longer accepted without demur by tenants. So the lease structure that provided UK property with so much of its attraction as an institutional investment and a form of bank collateral is no longer uniform across the market. The banks' interest cover is thus under threat. Property let at rents above the prevailing market rate may deliver a lower rental income as leases fall in. And the changing pattern of leases may ultimately make the banks' collateral a less attractive asset to the institutional investors which Barclays expects to help refinance the Pounds 40bn debt overhang. In the meantime anecdotal evidence from the chartered surveying fraternity suggests that the valuations on which the banks placed so much faith in the boom are proving to have been far less conservative than the banks thought. Prospects on the revenue side of the work-out equation are thus becoming worse rather than better. And the problem is compounded by a fundamental change in the way the cost side now operates. Back in the mid-1970s, real rates of interest were negative at the most stressful point for property companies. Debt was eroding in real terms and inflation was providing some help for asset values. This time real rates are positive and the debt burden is actually increasing. So heavily indebted property companies are caught in a double bind, with London office rents plunging in nominal terms and the debt servicing burden rolling up remorselessly in real terms. It becomes harder with time to close the shortfall of revenue against income, as compound interest applies its punitive calculus to the figures. In the absence of a spectacular economic recovery to reactivate the property market, this means that things will probably get a great deal worse for the banks before they get better. The work-out will be a far more protracted affair than in the 1970s and the opportunity cost of putting more money into rescues will be higher. And there is still no sign that the insurance companies and pension funds will be ready to take the banks off the hook by rediscovering their appetite for commercial property. While Scandinavian-style bank nationalisations are not in question, there must be some doubt about the ability of the banking system to finance recovery. The problem is the huge degree of leverage in bank balance sheets. At Barclays, capital last year was equivalent to 8.7 per cent of risk-weighted assets, based on the guidelines of the Bank for International Settlements and the Bank of England. That 0.7 per cent surplus over the regulatory floor of 8 per cent is equivalent to Pounds 730m of retained profits. Just to put that in context, Barclays' dividend last year was uncovered and retained profits were negative to the tune of Pounds 96m after making provisions against property and construction in the UK alone of Pounds 245m -this, before the latest rash of announcements about Olympia & York and the rest. Barclays also wrote off more than Pounds 300m against the value of its own properties to reserves. Looked at from another perspective, Pounds 730m is equivalent to less than 7 per cent of the value of the total property and construction loan book. This implies that the capital safety net contains remarkably little slack. Such figures clearly raise questions about the ability of the banking system to finance an economic recovery, especially now that Japanese banks have been withdrawing from international markets. But provisions and write-offs are a notoriously impressionistic area of accounting; and the figures above assume that other things are equal, which may not be the case. With known losses in the rest of the corporate sector already substantially provided for and huge losses in overseas subsidiaries now running down, the underlying profitability of the clearing banks is potentially much healthier. Yet their capital ratios remain vulnerable to unexpected shocks. And the process of recovery will be slower and more painful than any clearing banker would wish. The British clearers can count themselves luckier than the Japanese city banks in that they have not been hit by a collapsing stock market as well as a collapsing property market. But that does not mean that the latest bout of trouble in property should give the authorities no cause for concern. Tomorrow: how doubtful property loans are causing strains in Japan's financial system. -------------------------------------------------------------------- BRITISH CLEARING BANKS' UK PROPERTY LENDING -------------------------------------------------------------------- Pounds m NatWest Barclays Midland Lloyds -------------------------------------------------------------------- 1986 997 1,197 632 unknown 1987 1,394 2,140 733 unknown 1988 1,931 3,195 1,301 unknown 1989 2,633 4,493 1,859 3,900 1990 2,813 5,265 1,880 4,300 1991 2,478 5,397 1,630 4,100 Compound growth 20 per cent 35 per cent 21 per cent -------------------------------------------------------------------- Source: IBCA --------------------------------------------------------------------

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Arts: Mad, Bad and Dangerous to Know
DOC.TEXT: On January 2 1815 Lord Byron awoke and found himself married: 'Good God, I am surely in Hell'. One feels the same watching Mad, Bad and Dangerous to Know, the life of Byron at The Ambassadors Theatre. One is forced to be intimate with someone one does not recognise. This distillation of extracts from Byron's letters, table talk, diaries and poems is neither mad nor dangerous. Neither is it quintessential Byron, far from the pan-European hero, exile and archetype who died at Missolonghi in 1824. The author-director, Jane McCulloch, an experienced writer of theatre-biography, spreads the action too thinly across the available material. The enterprise courts superficiality: 36 years of hard living, facile writing and stormy friendships cannot be compassed in two hours on stage. The play's problem starts with its chronological approach. McCulloch rightly wants one to know the extraordinary life, but in finding sequence, the play loses focus and depth. Each scene closes neatly, but does not help our understanding of Byron; instead it offers where he was and when. The interventions arrive clumsily: 'So here I am at Cambridge' (Byron), 'I like being Lady in Waiting to Queen Charlotte' (lover) or 'He was well aware that Don Juan would cause a stir' (narrator). The difficulties continue by ignoring Byron's misanthropy and melancholy, 'the deep midnight of the mind,' the sense that Byron's life, like Keats's and Shelley's before him, became a Romantic way of dying. The play lacks the shadows and inwardness, those essentials of Byronic man. It rarely touches on the misogyny - 'Do you know? I hate women' - which drove Byron to devote himself so much to loving and leaving. It is even more disappointing that Mad, Bad has moments of achieved success, particularly in the interchanges between Byron and Lady Caroline Lamb, in 'She Walks in Beauty', and in Byron's letter of 1813 warning that pleasure can be anticipated or recalled, never experienced. These scenes generate intensity and demand concentration. They need refining and fashioning. The lighting and music conspire to be culpably anodyne. Both are well but wrongly done: few changes of lighting give little visual variety; and in a play about Byron, why not one glimmering taper or midnight study scene? The music (settings of Byron's poems) is shapely, and accurately sung; but why not one contemporary line from Schubert or Beethoven? Mad, Bad and Dangerous to Know survives because of superb acting by both Derek Jacobi (Byron) and Isla Blair (the women and narrator). They redeem and carry what should be a much better show. Of course, Byron has a word for harsh reviewers: 'A man must serve his time to every trade Save censure - critics all are ready made.' Ambassadors Theatre, London. (071) 836 6111

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Technology (Software at Work): Consultant's critique
DOC.TEXT: Sometimes it pays to go against accepted practice. Steele & Company prefers to rent rather than buy computer systems. In accounting terms this make little sense. Since the rental company carries the depreciation charges, it must pass them on to the customer or make a loss. So the renter pays all the depreciation and has to add a profit margin on top. As a balance sheet manipulation technique, it has little to commend it either. Most auditors treat software as a form of consumable and write it off in the first year. Hardware is usually written down straight-line over three years. The residual value of three-year-old hardware is zero in most cases. It is only worthwhile if the rental adds some value. For short-term rentals this value is gained by the flexibility in obtaining and returning the equipment. Steele & Co gains its value from rental by the ties it creates with the system provider. Getting support on computers, once installed and running, is notoriously difficult. By renting, Steele forces the vendor to be more attentive to problems. It also frees them from risks of failure in high-cost items. Steele has also reduced the maintenance costs by a third. Usually, support contracts cost 15 per cent of the original purchase price. Steele is paying only 5 per cent of the capital value. Software is more akin to a subscription than a purchase. Every major PC software package is updated annually. Each update costs Pounds 50-Pounds 99 which is typically 10 per cent to 30 per cent of the retail price. Most users take these upgrades without question, providing a steady stream of revenue to the software developers. The problems in accepting new technology that Hankey describes are typical. Computer systems are binary both in their construction and in peoples' attitudes - either on or off, with nothing in between. A new system is seen as a panacea by some and a threat by others. As with any tool, the gains are realised only by perseverance and practice. Kevin Grumball The author is a consultant at Software Design and Construction, of Milton Keynes

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Technology (Software at Work): Extending the legal limits - Phil Manchester continues a series on getting the most out of software by describing how a firm of solicitors expanded its practice through better use of computers
DOC.TEXT: Like many other traditional professional organisations in the UK, Steele & Co, a firm of solicitors based in Norfolk, has had to come to terms with information technology quickly. Five years ago, the firm had a few PCs in its single office in Norwich and employed 20 staff. It now operates nine offices across Norfolk and Suffolk and employs more than 120 people. They are supported by a computer network which performs billing, provides word processing and administers accounts. An integrated network system, based on a mixture of proprietary and Unix systems, has given the firm an opportunity to find new ways to work. Most important of all, the system provides management accounting information which enables Steele to make the best use of its resources. Tim Hankey, Steele's financial controller, says that the firm's recent expansion would not have been possible without the computer network, which now forms the backbone of the practice. Steele operates in all the traditional areas of law - about 25 per cent of its income comes from conveyancing; 25 per cent from commercial work, 25 per cent from litigation; and 25 per cent private clients. But Steele's approach to running its business is not typical. 'We have a philosophy of small satellite offices feeding into a larger regional office and to a central administrative headquarters. This is a somewhat unusual philosophy for a firm of solicitors and it is only through the IT network that we can retain control,' Hankey explains. The network also allows scarce resources, such as legal specialists, to be shared out in the most efficient way. 'We can't have all of our specialists at every site. They are at a central or regional site and our general solicitors at the other ones,' explains Hankey. The current network is based on a Unisys 6000/60 which runs both CTOS and Unix. This is located at the headquarters in Norwich and connected to the outlying offices through dedicated lines leased from British Telecom. The technology at the outlying offices varies according to the local need. Some offices have a direct inquiry facility and others go through a TCP/IP Ethernet network connection. At the smaller offices, where access to the whole system is unnecessary, there is a single inquiry screen. Hankey has taken an unusual approach to data capture, which flies in the face of current thinking. Financial and timekeeping data are never entered directly into the system by the outlying offices. It is sent to the central administrative headquarters to be entered by specialist data entry staff. Hankey says that the main reason is to keep control over the integrity of the company's data. Transactions are recorded on sheets and faxed across to the central administration office every afternoon. Steele's software also has an unusual pedigree. TMA, its software supplier, acquired the rights to a popular solicitor's application package called Solacs and used it as the basis of a new package called Comptroller. But Steele wanted a more flexible version of the software and searched for other firms of solicitors with a similar need. 'We joined forces with a consortium of five other firms of solicitors and commissioned TMA to write a replacement. It was quite unusual for a firm of solicitors to take this sort of initiative.' The new package, called TMA-Sims, is written using a fourth-generation language called Progress, which brings particular advantages. The TMA package provides the standard application, and Progress allows users to write extra reports. Hankey says that this is where applications packages have fallen down in the past: 'You could not have the full range of reports that people want. But it is very easy to write reports with Progress. They have a feature called Fasttrack which lets you do programming on a portable computer and then send it down the line to the main system.' In addition to the standard administration software the network also supports other important functions. Terminals have access to office automation facilities - word processing, spreadsheets and communications - all supplied as part of the CTOS package. Steele rents every part of its system - including the software. Hankey says this brings financial benefits as well as allowing the company to maintain its technological edge. Carefully-timed upgrades mean that the company is always running an up-to-date system: 'We are in position where we don't own the hardware and don't want to. You could argue that after five years in strict cash terms you have nothing else to pay. But the technology will need replacing by then anyway. 'The other advantage we have found is that when the rental period expires - because hardware costs have come down - you are getting a much better specification of hardware for the same price. Not only that, with depreciation the value of the rental has gone down.' A rental agreement also brings other benefits: 'Renting ties the computer company to you. There is that syndrome where the salesman sells you something and does not need to come back to you. When you are renting, it is still their hardware and they have to look after you. 'We rent software too. Arguably it is even more important to rent software because you have constant upgrades. As an accountant I don't want the software as a capital asset on the balance sheet,' says Hankey. He is keen to expand the system and is currently experimenting with the use of facsimile and telex links so that every terminal in the system can send messages. There are also plans to make greater use of portable computers so that solicitors can work on the move and connect into the company network. Hankey uses a Unisys Powerport portable for his own report writing and to build small applications in the Progress language: 'We are using Progress to develop our own reports - which brings some advantages. On the big Unix box we have a run-time licence. But on the portable we have a full licence. This means I can develop things on the portable and then push them across to the Unix box.' Despite his personal enthusiasm for the technology Hankey is realistic about its effect on a company and believes that data integrity and trust in the system is paramount. 'We have auditors from the Law Society, the tax office and the DSS so the data must be absolutely correct. If there is a single error the whole system loses credibility.' But Hankey notes that there is predictable shift in attitudes about a new computer system when it is introduced: 'There is a very interesting cycle which occurs when you introduce computer systems. Day one - it is put in with great expectations and, after a month, people want to know where all of these fantastic reports are. After six months they still have not got them, because there is no history in the system. 'After a year, there is total rejection of it. But by the end of 18 months you can start producing comparative data and the users see information they have not seen before - fluctuations in work in progress or your debtors' position. After two years they start to believe that it is right because the trends which it has shown start to ring true.' * * * BUZZWORDS FOURTH-GENERATION LANGUAGES were devised so that non-technical computer users could build simple programs. They use plain English to state a user's requirements, for example 'Print Sales Report'. * * * RUN-TIME LICENCES refer to a type of agreement between software suppliers and purchasers. Suppliers do not sell software outright, and this licence gives the purchaser the right to use the package only in its final form. A full licence give the purchaser rights to develop the package further. * * * STEELE & CO COMPANY SNAPSHOT Steele & Company is one of a new breed of professional organisations which has based its business expansion plans on significant use of technology. The geographical spread of its operations in rural East Anglia has made good communications and careful use of computer systems a necessity. NATURE OF BUSINESS: The firm operates in all the standard areas of law including property conveyancing, litigation, probate and commercial work. TURNOVER: As a professional partnership, Steele & Company does not disclose financial data. TECHNOLOGY FILE SOFTWARE: The main administration and financial work is handled by TMA-Sims, a specially-developed package for solicitors, running under Unix. The office systems software is provided by Unisys's CTOS system and covers electronic mail, database query, word processing and spreadsheets. HARDWARE: The main system runs on a Unisys 6000/60 with 1.3 gigabytes of disk storage for the central database. Each satellite office is served by a number of Unisys CTOS systems, operating on a local area network. These can also act as terminals to the main system. The whole system serves 120 screens. COMMUNICATIONS: The satellite offices are connected to the main computer at the firm's headquarters, through leased BT lines. COSTS: Steele rents all software and hardware at a current annual cost of Pounds 170,000. Equivalent capital cost of the installation is estimated at about Pounds 700,000. Steele also pays an annual Pounds 35,000 maintenance cost for both software and hardware.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / The Cadbury Report: Self-regulation seen as the way forward -Industry voices support for code - Shareholders give a mixed reaction
DOC.TEXT: TWO assumptions underpin the recommendations of the Cadbury committee, published yesterday. One is that self-regulation, rather than statutory enforcement, is the best route to improving the way companies are run. The second is that financial markets, rather than external regulators, provide the toughest sanctions against companies that fail to reach accepted standards of corporate governance. Both rely on companies' willingness to comply - and on shareholders' readiness to shake off their traditional apathy and take a more active interest in the companies they own. Given past experience, neither can be taken for granted. The Cadbury committee was set up in response to a number of corporate scandals that cast doubt on the systems for controlling the way companies are run. The downfall of powerful figures such as Asil Nadir or the late Robert Maxwell, whose personal control over their companies was complete, raised fears about the concentration of power. The collapse of companies that only shortly before had received clean audit reports prompted renewed questioning over the part played by auditors in reporting to shareholders on their investments. It will be against those extreme cases that the success of the Cadbury recommendations will be judged. The backbone of the proposed system is an annual statement to shareholders on each company's compliance with a code of conduct, which lays down best practice for the running of companies. The code is voluntary: the report to shareholders will not be. The Stock Exchange - whose chairman, Sir Andrew Hugh Smith, sat on the committee - is expected to amend its rules for listed companies to require directors to report each year on whether they have complied with the code, and to give reasons if they have not. A company's auditors will then report on the directors' statement, to make sure shareholders are given a true picture. 'It will be quite easy to see which companies are cocking a snook,' said Mr Nigel Macdonald, a committee member and vice-chairman of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Scotland. 'The market has already rumbled the flagrant abuses.' The Cadbury recommendations should also flush out the less obvious cases, he said. Whatever sanctions are necessary will have to come from the financial markets. 'If most companies have an audit committee and one or two barons ignore it, their cost of capital will shoot up,' said Mr Macdonald. 'It's the reverse of Gresham's Law: good practice should drive out bad.' Around that central pillar the committee proposes a patchwork of measures that together would reinforce the system for running companies. The proposals should be seen as a package, the committee says, the strength of which depends on all the proposals' being accepted. Some, however, are unlikely to see the light of day for some time. Four possible amendments to company law are proposed: to limit directors' service contracts to three years; to make it easier for auditors to report fraud; to require directors to report on their systems of internal control; and for them to state explicitly in the annual accounts that their businesses can continue as going concerns (the last two should be looked at 'in the light of experience' of other recommendations in the report). However, no new companies legislation is planned. More likely to see the light of day in the short run are proposals that do not need a change in the law: for example, that the Stock Exchange should extend the interim reporting requirements for listed companies to include balance-sheet information and an audit opinion.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / The Cadbury Report: Code of practice relies on threat of public censure
DOC.TEXT: AT ITS heart, the Cadbury committee report on the Financial Aspects of Corporate Governance relies on the threat of public censure to force companies to improve the way they are governed and to tell shareholders more about their affairs. Sir Ron Dearing, chairman of the Financial Reporting Council and a member of the committee, concedes that the final document, presented as a draft for public comment, is a consensus view and will fall short of the sort of reforms that some have been seeking. The report, for instance, stops short of urging companies to give shareholders greater say over executive pay. It also does not challenge the House of Lords' ruling in the Caparo case that auditors have a duty of care only to a company's management, not to individual shareholders. Sir Ron said more radical reforms would not be complied with voluntarily and would therefore require legislation, which would stifle innovation and enterprise. He said: 'We felt in the end that the best way to go was the co-operative route encouraged by the Stock Exchange.' The main body of the report consists of a code of practice that seeks to force companies to disclose the extent to which they comply with the code and to explain themselves where they do not. 'Had such a code been in existence in the past, we believe that a number of the recent examples of unexpected company failures and cases of fraud would have received attention earlier and might have been avoided,' the committee says. The Stock Exchange, which was represented on the committee by Sir Andrew Hugh Smith, exchange chairman, intends to add a new rule to its 'yellow book' which will make such disclosure a listing requirement. The rule will take effect almost immediately and will cover accounts filed for the year ending December 31 1992 and beyond. The 19-point code of practice covers four main areas: responsibilities of boards of directors; the role of executive directors; the role of non-executives; and accounting controls and reporting mechanisms. Among its main points are: Corporate boards should have a clearly accepted division of responsibilities. When the roles of chairman and chief executive are combined, there should be 'a strong independent element' on the board, with an appointed leader. Non-executives should be of a high enough calibre and appointed in sufficient numbers to give their views weight on a board. The majority of them should be free of any business or financial connection with the company and it is advisable that they should not be eligible to participate either in stock option or employee pension schemes. Their nomination should be approved by the board as a whole and should be the result of a formal selection process. Non-executives should be able to seek financial or legal advice from professionals outside the company at company expense. The Companies Act should be amended to reduce the maximum period of a director's service contract to three years from the present five - a rule that may be circumvented with shareholder approval. Directors' pay should be determined by a remuneration committee composed wholly or mainly of non-executives. The remuneration of the chairman and the highest-paid director should be fully disclosed and split into their salary and performance-related-pay elements. The basis upon which performance-related pay is measured should be explained. Boards must establish effective audit committees within the next two years, composed entirely of non-executive directors, a majority of whom are completely independent of the company. The audit committee should be able to seek external professional advice and consult advisers. They should also meet at least annually with the outside auditors, without any executive board member present. Fees paid to audit firms for non-audit work conducted worldwide should be fully disclosed and regulations under the Companies Act should be reviewed and amended as necessary. Interim financial statements should include balance sheet information. Although it is not necessary for interim statements to be audited, they should be discussed with auditors, and Stock Exchange listing requirements should be amended to include that requirement. The accountancy profession is urged to draw up guidelines to guarantee a periodic change of partners involved in the preparation of any particular company's audit over a period of years. However, the committee rejected a proposal to change auditors every few years to prevent relationships between management and auditors from becoming too comfortable. Boards should state that it is a reasonable expectation that their company will continue as a going concern, with supporting assumptions or qualifications as necessary, and auditors should be required to report on that statement. The committee has urged the accountancy profession to develop guidance on the 'going concern' rule. Legislation may be an option if voluntary compliance appears ineffective. Although detecting fraud remains the responsibility of boards, the committee recommends new legislation allowing auditors to report suspicion of fraud to government authorities without breaching client-confidentiality rules implied by their contracts. Such laws are already in place for auditors for banks and other regulated entities. The committee also lays out what it believes to be the proper role of shareholders and their relation to boards of directors. In what is likely to be a disappointment to many institutional shareholders, the report said the committee considered, but rejected, a formal role for shareholders in the appointment of directors and auditors. The report noted that there had been suggestions that shareholders should be allowed to form committees that would have a say in the drawing up of director service contracts and the selection of external auditors. Mr Michael Sandland, chairman of the Institutional Shareholders Committee and a member of the Cadbury committee, said such committees often did not work because institutional investors were unwilling to turn over their proxies to be exercised by someone else. Other shareholder groups, though, have sought such a mechanism because individual shareholders typically held too few votes to force management changes. Instead, the Cadbury committee urges shareholders to back up its recommendations by 'requiring' companies they invest in to implement the code. The report also acknowledges the disparity in power between institutional and individual shareholders. It stops short of urging any mandatory public disclosure requirements when significant developments occur, although it urges companies to ensure that any 'significant' statements concerning their company are made publicly and are available to all shareholders. The report also suggests ways to use the annual meeting as a forum for shareholder concerns. It says: 'If too many annual general meetings are at present an opportunity missed, this is either because shareholders do not make the most of them or because boards do not encourage them to do so.' Possible ways forward include providing forms in annual reports in which shareholders could send in written questions before the meeting so that prepared answers could be given at the AGM. After the meeting, the board could circulate a summary of questions and answers to all shareholders.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / The Cadbury Report: Men behind the decisions
DOC.TEXT: THE Committee on the Financial Aspects of Corporate Governance was officially formed a year ago at the instigation of the accountancy bodies and the Stock Exchange. Mr Michael Lickiss, a partner at Grant Thornton and then chairman of the Institute of Chartered Accountants, Sir Ron Dearing, chairman of the Financial Reporting Council, and Sir Andrew Hugh Smith, Stock Exchange chairman, were its founding members. After discussions with the government, a committee with representatives from industry, shareholder groups and the accountancy profession was formed under the chairmanship of Sir Adrian Cadbury. Other members were: Mr Ian Butler, a member of the CBI Council. Mr Jim Butler, senior partner, KPMG Peat Marwick. Mr Jonathan Charkham, adviser to the Governor of the Bank of England. Mr Hugh Collum, chairman, 100 Group of Finance Directors, and finance director at SmithKline Beecham. Mr Andrew Likierman, Professor of Accounting and Financial Control, London Business School. Mr Nigel Macdonald, vice-president, Institute of Chartered Accountants of Scotland. Mr Mike Sandland, chairman, Institutional Shareholders Committee. Mr Mark Sheldon, vice-president, Law Society. Sir Dermot de Trafford, IoD chairman. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- MAIN POINTS OF CADBURY REPORT ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Companies must disclose extent of compliance with Cadbury code to maintain a stock exchange listing ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Board authority divided between chairman and chief executive. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Pay packages of chairman and highest-paid UK director should be disclosed in annual accounts split into salary and performance-related pay ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Each board should have an adult committee 'wholly or mainly' composed of non-executives ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Interim financial statements should be discussed with auditors although they need not be formally audited. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Audit committees should meet at least once a year with external auditors and without the presence of executive directors. -----------------------------------------------------------------------

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / The Cadbury Report: Proposals receive boardroom backing
DOC.BYLINE: By MICHAEL CASSELL and BETHAN HUTTON
DOC.TEXT: MANY boardrooms welcomed the Cadbury committee's proposals and said they were already far advanced in carrying out its main recommendations. There was general recognition of the need for a greater role for non-executive directors, and backing for a code of practice widely seen as having struck the right balance between prescription and the flexibility required within individual companies. Most companies believed the code would prove acceptable and had sufficient teeth to ensure that it was widely implemented. It was hoped that it would help minimise the prospect of legislation in areas covered by the code. Mr Graham Mason, director of company affairs at the Confederation of British Industry, said the committee had put forward practical answers to some of the key issues of corporate governance. It built on the concept of the unitary board and the existing means of promoting the accountability of directors. Mr Blenyth Jenkins, director of corporate affairs at the Institute of Directors, said the majority of companies already practised many of the recommendations but there remained 'a tiny minority which cocks a snook at good corporate principles and which need to be brought into line'. He said some companies were finding it increasingly hard to raise capital because of shareholder concerns about elements of their management policy. The document provided a clear framework against which they could be judged. Imperial Chemical Industries was confident that it operated according to most of the recommendations. Sir Denys Henderson is both chairman and chief executive but the company has appointed Mr Ronnie Hampel as chief operating officer. ICI already provides a breakdown between executive pay and bonuses, and all members of its audit and remuneration committees are non-executive directors. Sir Christopher Hogg, the chairman of two Courtaulds companies and of Reuters, said the findings would not present difficulties of compliance within his companies. He was relieved that it was not a revolutionary document and added: 'There was a danger it could have gone overboard in proposing new rules and regulations, making it hard for companies to work in a flexible way. I am mightily relieved it has not.' Mr David Prosser, chief executive of Legal and General, said his company, as an investor, believed in good corporate governance and 'ought to achieve it in our own house'. Legal and General complies with most of the proposals on non-executive directors. Mr Prosser added: 'Our interim report is discussed and reviewed by the auditors, although it is not fully audited. We do not publish a half-year balance sheet and do not really think it is necessary for most companies, but it would not be a problem for us.' Sir Nicholas Goodison, former Stock Exchange chairman and now chairman of TSB Group, said: 'I broadly welcome it. I think it is positive and I think it improves the level of corporate practice.' He said that since joining TSB he had introduced most of the practices recommended by Cadbury, particularly relating to non-executive directors. TSB audit and remuneration committees were entirely composed of non-executive directors, full details of all directors' salaries were published, with names, and divisions of responsibility between directors were made clear. Sir Patrick Meaney, who holds six non-executive directorships, including the chairmanship of Rank Organisation, said: 'There is nothing in it so outrageous or costly to provide sound reasons for rejection. They are par for the course for any self-respecting company.' Mr Tony Mitchard, chief executive of Avon Rubber, said the proposals 'made good sense' and his company, which already complies with some of the recommendations, would be happy to comply with its findings. Mr Mitchard said that audited interim statements 'would obviously cost rather more money by way of audit fees, and it would take a bit more time, but I do not think it would be too burdensome'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / The Cadbury Report: Labour attacks voluntary approach
DOC.TEXT: THE REPORT was greeted with some disappointment by Ms Marjorie Mowlam, who speaks for Labour on corporate affairs, but it was welcomed by ministers. Ms Mowlam questioned the efficacy of peer group pressure as a way of enforcing the code of practice and warned that the use of a voluntary code might amount to a 'recipe for inactivity'. She said: 'We have had best-practice codes before - from the Association of British Insurers and from the Institutional Shareholders Committee. I am not sure they ever go far enough.' She highlighted areas where she believed the report should have gone further, commenting on its 'rather vague' reference to companies finding new ways of working with shareholders. She said that it could have proposed simplified annual reports or training for shareholders. A further weakness was the report's comments on the role of non-executive directors because they did not address where they might be found and whether they should be trained. Ms Mowlam also commented that, if the report were serious in addressing the issue of boardroom pay, it would have recommended that annual meetings should be able to vote on directors' salaries. She was disappointed the report did not offer fundamental change, and warned that as business activity recovered in the 1990s, the same drawbacks would re-emerge. 'Practical guidelines should have been laid down,' she said. She welcomed some elements in the document, such as the proposed extension of statutory protection for auditors reporting reasonable suspicion of fraud. Mr Neil Hamilton, the corporate affairs minister, said the report was a valuable contribution to the debate on improving corporate governance. In particular, he applauded the idea of a voluntary code of practice, hailing it as 'an important step forward in improving corporate governance'. The Department of Trade and Industry emphasised that the report was a draft. The government would look again at it in the light of the comments it attracted.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / The Cadbury Report: Investors raise only two cheers
DOC.TEXT: OF ALL the interest groups participating in the corporate governance debate, perhaps no one has more to lose than institutional shareholders. It is they who suffer when bad management leads to corporate collapse. Unlike bank creditors, they are on the sidelines when receivers are called in to divide the remaining assets of a defunct company. Shareholders give the Cadbury report two cheers. While applauding the proposed code of practice and its frequent references to the role of shareholders as owners of companies, they expressed disappointment that, on several key issues, the report did not go further. Mr John Rogers, secretary to the investment committee of the National Association of Pension Funds, whose members manage more than Pounds 300bn in assets, said it clearly reflected the need to reach a consensus among its members' conflicting interests. 'However, it's better to have a lower common denominator that everyone can agree on than to have a higher standard that is ignored,' he said. Mr Rogers welcomed the proposal for a new Stock Exchange listing requirement tied to disclosure, saying that some companies might have perfectly valid reasons for not complying with certain aspects of the code and there was no reason to compel them to do so. Eventually, though, companies would find failing to comply with best practice was simply too cumbersome an exercise. Other shareholders were less optimistic about the effectiveness of the recommendations. The report's suggestion that shareholders would be able to require companies in which they invest to comply with the code was dismissed as improbable. 'If a shareholder sees value in a company, he's unlikely to sell the shares, no matter what kind of corporate governance it has,' said one institutional shareholder. 'And you only sell the shares when you think the company is on the way down, anyway, and you've approached management with your concerns and they tell you to sod off,' he added. Some fund managers expressed disappointment that they are not to be given a greater role in approving what are seen as some of the most contentious aspects of board policy. Those include directors' remuneration and selection of external auditors. Shareholders also expressed disappointment that the committee had not recommended legislation to make clear that auditors have a duty of care to shareholders, thus overturning the Caparo decision. In it, the House of Lords ruled that auditors had a duty of care only to managements and to shareholders generally - a view that effectively prevents individual shareholders from seeking restitution from an auditor over a faulty report. Shareholders noted that the desire for consensus had clearly forced the committee to water down some proposals that they had wanted most.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Researchers praise Dutch education
DOC.TEXT: HIGHER productivity in the Netherlands than in Britain owes much to the superiority of Dutch education and training, according to the National Institute of Economic and Social Research. In this month's National Institute Review, three researchers emphasise the relative inferiority of British workers in skill levels. Comparisons of manufacturing plants found Dutch productivity at least 30 per cent higher in engineering and more than 15 per cent higher in biscuits. The researchers highlight three contrasts: higher emergency downtime in British plants, reflecting poor standards of machine maintenance and diagnostic skill; greater difficulty in maintaining product quality; and higher shopfloor manning levels in Britain because of a comparative shortage of workers able to switch between tasks. The researchers say Dutch schools place greater emphasis on 'early systematic preparation for a career'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Economists predict growth will remain weak: Conservative election victory fails to brighten forecasts - National Institute says government expectations may not be met
DOC.BYLINE: By EMMA TUCKER and CHRISTOPHER FLOOD
DOC.TEXT: ECONOMIC growth in the UK will continue to crawl along at a weak level for the rest of this year and next, according to the latest Financial Times survey of forecasts on the UK economy. In spite of the Conservative party's election victory in April and a supposed renewal of confidence, economists have scarcely altered their growth forecasts since the election. Economists expect gross domestic product to grow 0.8 per cent this year. Even next year, GDP growth will not quite recover to the so-called 'trend' rate of about 2.5 per cent - the level at which the economy is thought to be able to grow without stretching productive capacity and provoking inflation. Forecasters project that growth will hover at about 2.4 per cent next year. The consensus from economists at 22 universities, intergovernmental institutions, independent think-tanks and City investment houses is that unemployment will continue to grow over the next two years, rising to 2.75m by the end of this year and to just under 3m by the end of next. Eight of the economists surveyed forecast that the number of jobless would reach 3m next year. Most are confident that the continued pressure on employment will bring down average earnings growth to below 7 per cent and reduce unit-wage-cost inflation. Projections for output this year are particularly gloomy. The consensus among the City economists is for output to fall by just less than 1 per cent. The overall average, at an increase of just under 1 per cent, is only slightly more cheerful. Investment is forecast to fall substantially this year but to rebound with force next year, consensus growth rate of about 4 per cent. Forecasters do not expect inflation to wither greatly from present levels. The average forecasts for this year and next, at well over 3 per cent for both years, are a long way off the Chancellor's desired rate of 2 per cent. The UK's trade deficit remains a big concern. Nearly all the economists surveyed predict a worse current-account balance this year than the Pounds 6.5bn deficit projected by the Treasury in the March budget - the consensus is for a deficit of Pounds 8.4bn - but their forecasts might be too benign in the light of the most recent current-account data. Figures for the first four months of this year, released earlier this week, may be revised substantially in mid June, when more detailed calculations of the first-quarter 'invisibles' are available. Goldman Sachs takes the rent-account balance. It predicts a deficit of Pounds 16.7bn next year, more than twice the size of some of the other forecasts. The forecasts for interest rates reflect the continuing constraints of the UK's membership of the European exchange rate mechanism. The average forecasts do not suggest that Britain will be able to cut its interest rates below German rates, although the idea is entertained by some economists. Mr Giles Keating of Credit Suisse First Boston says: 'I see no problem in UK interest rates falling below German, although this would be accompanied by sterling's being a little weaker within the ERM than it is now.' The gloomiest forecasts come from UBS Phillips and Drew and Professor Wynne Godley at Cambridge University. Prof Godley is the only economist to forecast negative GDP growth this year and has the lowest projection for growth next year. He predicts a PSBR of Pounds 33bn this financial year and sees unemployment surpassing 3m next year. UBS sees no growth this year, rising to 1.4 per cent next year. A much more bullish outlook comes from Mr Michael Knapp at BZW. He forecasts growth of 1.5 per cent this year and is the only economist to forecast that unemployment will fall next year. Mr Richard Jeffrey at Charterhouse Tilney believes that the bottom of the economic cycle was in the middle of the last year, with a pause before the election. 'I think the recovery will surprise people by its strength,' he says. Since the last FT compilation of forecasts in January, Hoare Govett is no longer included in the panel and Charterhouse Tilney and Yamaichi have been added. The OECD forecast has been included as a memorandum item only because it dates from last December and is therefore out of date. The OECD secretariat has prepared a new UK forecast but refuses to release it until the publication of the next OECD Economic Outlook at the end of June, by which time it will also be out of date.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Sales optimism reported
DOC.TEXT: OPTIMISM about sales among small businesses has risen markedly in the past three months, according to the latest NatWest Quarterly Survey of Small Business. A rise in sales is expected by 20 per cent more small business owners in the present quarter - April to June - than expect sales to fall. In the previous survey, 10 per cent more businesses expected sales to fall. Ms Jane Bradford, head of small-business services, said: 'The position is better than at any time since early 1991, suggesting the bottom of the cycle has passed.' Such optimism contrasted with actual sales performance, with 4 per cent more businesses reporting lower sales, unchanged on the percentage for the previous quarter. Most businesses still expect to reduce employment levels and cut investments in the present quarter, but the percentages involved are smaller. On balance, 4 per cent more businesses expect to cut jobs compared with 17 per cent in the previous quarter, while 6 per cent will cut investment compared with 14 per cent.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / EC budget increase is urged for EMU
DOC.TEXT: THE European Community needs a much larger budget to make a success of economic and monetary union, according to Sir Donald MacDougall, a former chief economic adviser to the UK government. Writing in the National Institute Economic Review, Sir Donald said countries might face 'a prolonged period of painful adjustment, with sluggish or even negative economic growth' if they did not have Community financial help after losing the power to vary exchange rates. Sir Donald, appointed by the EC Commission in the late 1970s to head a high-level study group on public finance and European integration, said the lack of a larger budget 'would run the risk of setting back, rather than promoting, progress towards closer integration in Europe'. His 1977 report advocated increasing the EC budget from the then 0.7 per cent of Community GDP to between 2 and 2.5 per cent over a decade.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Edinburgh joins contest for EC bank
DOC.TEXT: EDINBURGH yesterday pitted itself against Frankfurt, London and Paris, as well as Amsterdam and Manchester, in formally joining the acrimonious struggle to become the location of the European Central Bank. Edinburgh would like the whole of the new institution to come to the city. It believes its best chance of success, however, lies in persuading the European Community to disperse departments of the bank around member states, with Edinburgh becoming the home of an important sector. Under decisions taken at last year's Maastricht summit to achieve European monetary union by the end of the century, the bank would operate monetary policy across the community when the third stage of monetary union starts either in 1997 or in 1999. Decisions on siting of the bank should in theory be taken by the end of this year. London, Frankfurt and Paris are fighting to be the bank's home, with Amsterdam seen as a possible compromise candidate. Manchester is the only other British city to have put its hat into the ring. Last week Mr Norman Lamont, the chancellor, raised the hopes of centres other than London when he told the Commons that he believed 'that Britain - not London alone but other centres - will be the strongest candidate' to be the bank's headquarters. The campaign to bring all or part of the bank to Edinburgh was launched at a conference in the city attended by some 200 members of its financial community. A consortium of local authorities and economic development bodies is spending Pounds 250,000 on the campaign. Professor Donald MacKay, an economist who heads the economic consultancy Pieda, said European monetary policy would best be controlled by the bank from a financial centre where trading took place, which would rule out Edinburgh - but there was no reason why other functions, such as money transmission, accounting, research and collation of statistics, could not be located in Edinburgh. He said the city had considerable expertise in its financial community and good telecommunications, and was an inexpensive place to operate. He believed the bank would employ between 1,500 and 2,000 people in all, of which between 750 and 1,000 jobs would be in backroom functions of the kind that Edinburgh could hope to attract. Observer, Page 21

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Council watchdog urges rise in homes for rent
DOC.BYLINE: By JOHN WILLMAN and ALISON SMITH
DOC.TEXT: GOVERNMENT action is needed to remedy the shortfall in affordable housing for rent, according to a report published today by the Audit Commission. The local-government watchdog warns that there will be a growing shortfall in rentable properties at reasonable cost in the next few years. Ms Sheila McKechnie, director of the housing charity Shelter, said: 'We want the government to look again at the implications of the projected Pounds 1bn reduction in local-authority housing resources.' The Audit Commission's report, she said, 'reinforces Shelter's call for extra affordable homes as the only way to stop spiralling homelessness'. The commission says councils could do more to meet the demand for social housing from their existing resources, but that would still not eliminate the shortfall. Its report estimates that an additional 74,000 homes will be needed every year for the next 10 years to meet the demand. The commission is also critical of the government's encouragement of large-scale transfers of council homes to housing associations. It notes that such transfers have resulted in increased rents and more government costs in higher housing benefit. The government has promised housing associations sufficient finance to build 57,000 homes a year by 1994-95. But with local authorities expected to build only another 5,000 homes a year, there would still be a shortfall. Sir George Young, the housing minister, said the government supported the commission's recommendations on measures local authorities could take. He added that ministers were looking at a range of initiatives to bridge the housing gap. They included the use of the planning system to increase the supply of affordable housing, and - through housing associations - reducing the risks of letting for private landlords. Sir George did not dispute the Pounds 1bn figure for the reduction in local-authority housing resources, but pointed to increases in the budget for the Housing Corporation. 'We don't expect local authorities to build new family homes for rent,' he said. The commission says that the gap could be partly closed if local authorities made better use of their existing housing stock. It suggests that: Gaps between lettings are still unnecessarily long. Achieving the commission's target of three weeks (six weeks in London) would create 26,000 extra lettings and generate additional rents. Reducing the growing number of unlicensed tenancies would provide 7,000 new homes (mostly in London). Many councils fail to use their full entitlement to nominate tenants to registered housing associations. Councils could do more to encourage people to move into more suitable council homes - perhaps by increasing rent differentials so that people in unnecessarily large homes were encouraged to move. The report estimates that the backlog of maintenance and repairs to local-authority housing stock has fallen to about Pounds 8.5bn (down from Pounds 11bn in 1985). While the number of homes in the private sector lacking basic amenities has continued to fall, the level of homes in serious disrepair or unfit is stable. Developing Local Housing. Audit Commission. HMSO. Pounds 12.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / The good, the bad and the insanitary
DOC.TEXT: FOURTEEN resort and rural beaches failed to meet the environmental and safety standards laid down in new seaside awards announced yesterday by the Tidy Britain Group, a national agency for anti-litter issues. A total of 43 resort beaches were up to standard and received an award, and 14 received a premier award for good water quality. Six resort beaches - Thorpe Bay, Sutton on Sea, Hill Head, Littlehampton, Exmouth and Goodrington South Sands - failed. On Littlehampton, the judges spoke of 'the large quantity of sewage-related debris present on the beach'. The resort beach premier winners included: Bridlington North; Mablethorpe; Skegness; Sheerness Beach Street: Crinnis; Weymouth; and Woolacombe. Fifty rural beaches passed, 22 receiving premier awards, and eight failed.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Ford to sell stake in AC Cars
DOC.TEXT: FORD is to sell its stake in AC Cars, the Surrey-based specialist sports car company in which it took a 50.96 per cent stake for Pounds 1.3m nearly five years ago. The holding is being sold, for an undisclosed sum, to Mr Brian Angliss, AC Cars' managing director. He also controls Autokraft, a private company which holds the minority stake in AC Cars. Ford yesterday gave no explanation for its decision to return the holding, but said it would continue to assist AC Cars with the supply of engines and components for the AC Ace, a sports car under development for some time. Mr Angliss said last night that the sale had been agreed amicably. That is despite a long-standing apparent clash of cultures which led Ford in 1990 to seek the winding-up of AC Cars. The application is only now being withdrawn. Mr Angliss intends to seek a new partner to put the AC Ace into commercial production at volumes of 500-600 a year. AC, formed in 1901, is one of the oldest carmakers still in existence. It was attractive to Ford partly because it originally made the Cobra, a powerful Ford-engined sports car of the 1960s which became something of a legend. Ford will retain the right to the Cobra name in North America.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Reform of pensions law urged
DOC.TEXT: A THOROUGH overhaul of the legal basis for the UK's 400,000 occupational pension schemes was called for yesterday by the chairman of the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation, one of the City's investment regulators. The comments of Mr George Nissen in a speech to a London conference appeared to have been prompted by the plight of Maxwell pensioners, although he did not mention the late Mr Robert Maxwell by name. 'There has never been an attempt to establish an occupational pension scheme system set in a sound, purpose-built legislative framework,' Mr Nissen said. Referring to a parliamentary investigation of the handling of pension and other trusts nearly a century ago, he said: 'The problems that existed in 1895 are still with us today. 'The existing system should be reviewed and the results of that review used in establishing a sound . . . system on a firm legislative foundation.' Mr Nissen also complained that responsibility for the running of pension schemes was spread between too many agencies. 'The number of agencies and professionals involved in the administration is so great and their responsibilities so unclear that cracks were almost bound to develop,' he said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / School tests attack
DOC.TEXT: NATIONAL tests for seven-year-olds should be scrapped and replaced with teacher assessments, the National Association of Head Teachers urged at its conference.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Wales wins EC aid
DOC.TEXT: WALES WAS yesterday granted Pounds 96m in EC aid. Mr Bruce Millan, regional policy commissioner, said: 'Wales has suffered severely from the problems of industrial restructuring of the coal and steel industries and the recession.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Construction orders rise
DOC.TEXT: THE CONSTRUCTION industry showed signs of improvement in the first quarter of this year with total orders rising by 3 per cent on the previous three months, according to the Environment Department. Orders were up 14 per cent compared with the first quarter of 1991, when the construction industry was feeling the full impact of the savage downturn in property development.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / New limit boosts unit trust Peps
DOC.TEXT: A CHANGE in Personal Equity Plan rules has led to a record inflow into unit trust Peps. Mr Norman Lamont, the chancellor, announced in the Budget that Pounds 6,000 could be invested in a unit or investment trust Pep this tax year. The previous limit - except for investment trust new issues - had been Pounds 3,000. About 230,000 unit trust Peps were opened between April 6, the start of the tax year, and May 1, according to the Unit Trust Association. The Pounds 151m invested in April was a record monthly figure, pushing the total invested to Pounds 2.3bn, spread across 996,000 accounts.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Liquidator for investment firm
DOC.TEXT: THE Securities and Investments Board has appointed a provisional liquidator of RCI Portfolio Managers, a member of the Financial Intermediaries and Brokers Regulatory Authority. RCI, run by Mr Andrew Clive, had about 50 clients and investments of about Pounds 2.5m. According to SIB, the firm appears to be insolvent. In March, SIB directed RCI, which operated from Putney, London, not to carry on further investment business.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Bank of England faces action threat
DOC.TEXT: THE Bank of England faces the threat of industrial action from members of the Bifu finance union for making 41 computer staff compulsorily redundant. 'These are the first compulsory redundancies in the Bank's history,' said Mr Jim Lowe, Bifu assistant secretary. 'Staff are disgusted at the complete lack of consultation. Industrial action has not been ruled out.' The job cuts follow the Bank's decision to contract work out to computer services company Hoskyns. Bifu's information technology staff committee, which represents all IT staff at the Bank, is meeting this morning to decide what action to take.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Berry aims to sue Manpower for Pounds 1/2m
DOC.TEXT: THE FORMER chairman of Blue Arrow is to sue the company for about Pounds 500,000 in connection with his legal fees for the two Department of Trade and Industry inquiries into its activities, John Mason writes. The move by Mr Tony Berry follows the issuing of a writ in the High Court by City law firm D. J. Freeman. The firm, which acted for Mr Berry during the inquiries into the 1987 Blue Arrow rights issue, is claiming Pounds 234,817 in unpaid fees. Mr Berry will contest the action and also sue his old company, which has been renamed Manpower, for his total legal costs. Mr Berry says he has paid Freeman approximately Pounds 300,000. The money sought by Freeman is a balancing item. Although indemnified by Manpower for the DTI inquiries as a condition of his resignation in 1989, Mr Berry says he has yet to be reimbursed for any of the legal fees incurred. Mr Mitchell Fromstein, Manpower's chairman, said the company's decision on how much and when to pay Mr Berry depended on the outcome of the still unpublished second report. He believed the company had met Mr Berry's legal fees from the first inquiry.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Behind the scenes disputes in the Labour Party
DOC.TEXT: A GLIMPSE of the behind-the-scenes disputes in Mr Neil Kinnock's shadow cabinet emerged last night as the three candidates for Labour's deputy leadership debated the party's future, Ivo Dawnay writes. Mrs Beckett, Mr Gould and Mr Prescott all admitted that they had expressed serious reservations over the leadership's unwillingness to adopt sharp cuts in defence expenditure. In the three-way debate organised by the Fabian Society, they disagreed over how the leadership had responded to the UK's membership of the European exchange rate mechanism and the longer-term goal of monetary union.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 28 MAY 92 / Gould refuses to concede fight for Labour leadership
DOC.TEXT: MR Bryan Gould, a candidate for the leadership and deputy leadership of the Labour party, insisted yesterday that he would not concede the contest to take over from Mr Neil Kinnock, even though he admitted that there was a danger of 'falling between two stools' in running for both posts. In a press conference to launch 'An Agenda for Change', as part of his rolling manifesto, Mr Gould criticised as 'somewhat undemocratic' claims from Mr John Smith's camp suggesting that the leadership contest was already over. Mr Smith's standing among the constituency parties was, he said, 'a matter of conjecture'. He warned that it was 'slightly disturbing' for Mr Robin Cook, Mr Smith's campaign manager, to claim that Mr Smith already had majority support in the contest when voting will not take place until mid July. Mr Gould said that the contest for the deputy leadership was more difficult to read than that for the top job. However, the perception seemed to be that Mrs Margaret Beckett was losing ground among Labour MPs and constituency parties, and might finish in third place. He was confident that he would win in a final ballot against Mrs Beckett or Mr John Prescott. Acknowledging that some people would not wish to vote for him for both posts, Mr Gould urged those who wanted him to be leader to carry that view through to the deputy leadership election as well. 'The real question is: do they want me in a leadership team?' he said yesterday.
