Exploration Company of Louisiana jumped 16 to 88p on further consideration of an announcement at the end of last week about prospects for the East Riceville field in South Louisiana. Mr Tony Alves of ExCo Louisiana's UK broker Henderson Crosthwaite said initial tests suggested that the field could add 100p a share to the company's present net asset value of 60p. Take profits advice from a number of securities houses and worries about increased oil/fuel prices saw British Airways fall 7 to 307p. One of the houses, Kleinwort Benson, said all BA's recent good news was now in the price and an 'uncertain economic background, increased competition and continuing weak premium traffic' in the coming year meant little upside in the price. There was more trouble for Eurotunnel as the chairman of French contractor Bouygues said talks to compensate the builders were deadlocked and added: 'We cannot rule out that Eurotunnel might go bankrupt.' The group's shares were steady at 370p. Mountleigh's demise failed to have a dramatic effect on the property sector, the receivership having been widely expected in the market. Only Speyhawk, a developer also in acute financial straits, retreated on reflection, dropping 4 to 9 1/2 p. However, selected banks suffered on worries over their exposure to Mountleigh. Barclays fell 9 to 383p, NatWest 7 to 354p and TSB 6 1/2 to 144p. The worst kept secret in the leisure sector, that Forte is close to selling its catering subsidiary Gardner Merchant, was still being denied by the hotel group at its agm yesterday. However, analysts said the uncertainty was affecting the shares, which declined 3 to 236p, with returning talk that Forte will need a rights issue if it fails to make a disposal. Dealers suspected a possible switch as leading supermarket chain Argyll Group gained 3 to 349p while Tesco lost 4 to 263p in an otherwise thin sector. Goldman Sachs was particularly keen on Argyll, in spite of market disappointment at recent results, noting that its Safeway subsidiary is the second most profitable food retailer in the UK. DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / London Stock Exchange: Poor trade figures upset share prices
DOC.TEXT: A PROMISING start by London's equity market to the last period of the three-week trading account was halted in its tracks by a disappointing set of UK trade figures for April and a steep opening decline by Wall Street. The trade figures were greeted with widespread dismay by marketmakers, who quickly gave the leaders the red pencil treatment, chopping prices across the board and prompting a hefty reversal in the FT-SE 100-share Index. Up more than 12 points within two hours of the opening, the index moved into negative ground soon after the economic data emerged, and remained under pressure for the rest of a quiet session to close a net 10.4 off at the day's low of 2,704.6. Ironically, it was the oil and gas sector, among the market's poorest performing areas for around 18 months, that helped prevent an even steeper fall by the Footsie. Last week's Opec agreement on output resulted in crude oil prices edging back over the Dollars 20 a barrel mark yesterday and produced keen support for the sector. The day began on a subdued note, with the Footsie opening around seven points higher, mainly due to the strength of the oil sector and a number of individual stocks such as Cable and Wireless, Welcome and SmithKline Beecham. But with little genuine retail buying interest evident and the trade figures coming in much worse than had been expected, the market turned off sharply as a flurry of profit-taking and institutional selling appeared. Dealers pointed out, however, that the market's attendance was well down on normal levels, as many operators took advantage of the good bank holiday weather with extended breaks. One estimated that perhaps as many as a quarter of the usual number of fund managers had stayed away. 'The marketmakers wanted the market down, got their excuse with the trade figures and Wall Street and they got their way,' said one senior salesman. The Footsie's poor performance was accompanied by equally poor turnover figures for equities. Volume yesterday fell to 404.3m shares, the lowest since the general election. Figures published by the Stock Exchange revealed that the value of customer business last Friday totalled Pounds 937.8m. On four out of the five trading sessions last week retail business fell below the Pounds 1bn level. With the volume of business showing distinct signs of shrinking and summer looming, many market traders are beginning to question the likelihood of a flurry of takeover activity and spate of rights issues widely forecast after the Conservative election victory. The oil sector provided the best individual Footsie performance in Lasmo, which rose more than 4 per cent, closely followed by BP, British Gas and Shell. The rises followed what Mr Steve Turner, energy specialist at Smith New Court, described as 'the most unambiguously bullish Opec meeting since July 1990, when Opec announced its intention to move to a Dollars 21 a barrel market price'. TSB took the dubious honour of being the worst Footsie performer, dropping 4.3 per cent.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets (America): Dow declines on higher oil price prospect
DOC.TEXT: Wall Street THE prospect of higher oil prices, following a change in Saudi Arabia's pricing policy, triggered fears of inflation and depressed US equity prices yesterday, writes Karen Zagor in New York. The Dow Jones Industrial Average ended 22.56 lower at 3,364.21. Declines led rises by about two-to-one after moderate New York SE volume of about 198m shares. The Standard & Poor's 500 slipped 2.61 to 411.41, while the Nasdaq composite lost 4.65 to 575.65. The pressure on prices started early in the day, following reports in the Wall Street Journal that Saudi Arabia had apparently changed its pricing policy and that crude oil prices might rise by as much as Dollars 3 a barrel later in the year, spurring fears that higher prices might lead to an escalation in inflation. In late trading, the July crude oil contract on the New York Mercantile Exchange was quoted Dollars 1.06 higher at Dollars 22 a barrel. In addition, sentiment was dampened by an unexpectedly sharp rise in the May consumer confidence index, which further quelled hopes of an immediate interest rate cut. The May index weighed in at 71.6, above the 68 the market had expected. Energy issues dominated big board trading, with some attaining 52-week highs. The activity was spurred by reports that Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter, had changed its pricing policy and planned to bring it in line with the Opec producers who want higher prices. Since the end of the Gulf war, the sector has suffered because of weak oil and natural gas prices. Exxon forged ahead Dollars 3 1/2 to Dollars 64, USX-Marathon Dollars 1 5/8 to Dollars 23 7/8 , Mobil Dollars 3 5/8 to Dollars 67 and British Petroleum's ADRs Dollars 2 5/8 to Dollars 60 5/8 . Oil service shares also benefited from the prospect of increased crude prices. Halliburton rose Dollars 5/8 to Dollars 29 7/8 , Baker Hughes Dollars 1 1/8 to Dollars 23 3/4 and Schlumberger Dollars 3 5/8 to Dollars 68 1/2 . The boost for crude oil prices was a blow to the transportation section, the Dow Jones Transportation Average tumbling 15.69 to 1,360.80. AMR, parent of American Airlines, declined Dollars 1 3/8 to Dollars 64 3/8 , Delta Air Lines Dollars 1 1/2 to Dollars 57 7/8 and United Airlines Dollars 3 1/4 to Dollars 118 3/4 . Merck receded Dollars 1 3/8 to Dollars 49 1/2 . The company recently implemented a three-for-one stock split. It has declared a regular 23-cent quarterly dividend on the split shares. General Motors and Ford lost Dollars 1 1/4 to Dollars 38 and Dollars 7/8 to Dollars 43 1/4 respectively. GM reported mid-May US car sales of 94,323, up from 82,312 a year earlier. US truck sales rose to 51,790 from 43,233. Ford's mid-May car and truck sales also improved from the previous year. Canada TORONTO gained ground yesterday and closed at the day's best after oil futures shot higher on Opec's decision to freeze output at second quarter levels. Gold shares climbed on expectations that strengthening crude oil prices will spur inflation. The TSE 300 composite index rose 12 points to 3,382.3 and advances outscored declines by 308 to 263 after volume of 25.1m shares valued at CDollars 271.7m. Imperial Oil led the energy group, rising CDollars 2 1/8 to CDollars 44 3/8 on volume of 196,000 shares as the sector's index climbed 2.2 per cent.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Foreign Exchanges: Confidence figures boost dollar
DOC.TEXT: EVIDENCE from the US that consumers grew more confident about the economy in May boosted the dollar. The US currency perked up during European trading after news that the Conference Board's consumer confidence index rose to 71.6 in May from a revised 65.1 for April. Mr Neil MacKinnon, chief economist at Yamaichi Bank, said: 'The consumer confidence figures were extremely good news for the dollar. The very strong pick-up suggests that consumers are getting ready to spend again.' By mid-afternoon the dollar had recovered early losses to stand at DM1.6115, from DM1.6060 just before the confidence data were released. It rallied to Y129.33 from a Y128.75 low and a Y129.25 start. But in later trading it lost ground to end at DM1.6090, nearly a pfennig down from Friday's DM1.6185 close. The dollar firmed in New York to close at DM1.6127 and Y129.50. Although the confidence data were welcome news for the dollar, analysts warned that it would not be sufficient to enable the currency to break out of its DM1.6050 to DM1.6250 range. Other US economic statistics yesterday were less encouraging - existing home sales fell by 0.3 per cent in April compared with March - and the wide interest rate differential between the dollar and the D-Mark continues to obstruct the US currency's progress. Meanwhile, sterling was unmoved by news that the UK's current account deficit almost doubled last month. The sharp deterioration in the figures for April were ignored by the foreign exchange markets, traders said. Mr Peter Luxton, senior economist at Barclays, commented: 'There was absolutely no interest. Sterling held absolutely rock steady when the news came out.' There were suggestions that the pound would test its central EMS rate of DM2.95 this week. According to traders, the steadiness of the UK currency - which finished the day at DM2.9425 - stemmed partly from positive long-term prospects for sterling, notably the dwindling possibility of another base rate cut on the horizon, and partly from the fact that the big rise in imports was concentrated in areas such as capital and consumer goods which suggested a recovery in confidence. The French franc also nudged higher, improving to FFr3.3602 per D-Mark from FFr3.3620. Traders said the French currency was underpinned by a comment from Mr Michel Sapin, the French finance minister, that he would not lower interest rates except as part of a co-ordinated move with other countries. This positive sentiment was reinforced by news that France's economy grew by 1.1 per cent in the first quarter compared with the previous quarter.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Money Markets: Rates creep higher
DOC.TEXT: NEWS that the UK current account deficit deteriorated sharply in April sent a shiver through the money markets. Rates firmed after figures from the Central Statistical Office showed that the current account deficit widened to Pounds 1.06bn in April, significantly higher than the City's consensus forecast of Pounds 600m. The deficit - the result of a surge in imports and dwindling exports - followed the previous month's deficit of Pounds 591m. While the foreign exchange markets were unruffled by the ballooning trade gap, the money markets - described by one trader as 'a beacon of sanity' - reacted adversely. The key three-month interbank rate rose 1/8 percentage point to 10 1/16 per cent, while the rate for six-month money firmed to 10 per cent from a close of 9 15/16 per cent on Friday. The September sterling contract fell by eight basis points during the day. It opened at 90.37, but touched a low of 90.28, where it hovered in late trading. The downward movement in sterling futures suggests that the market is less sure of a base rate cut before September. Today's levels still allow for a 1/4 point cut in base rates, but according to Mr Nick Parsons of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, a drop below 90.25 would mean that the market had given up any hope of a base rate reduction before the autumn. Short-term cash rates came under heavy pressure during the day because of a log-jam in the market, which meant it failed to meet the Bank of England's big shortage. In the morning the Bank forecast a shortage of Pounds 1.7bn but provided only limited liquidity in the early rounds of its operations. The forecast was later revised to around Pounds 1.6bn and morning assistance came to Pounds 791m, including Pounds 124m of band-1 bank bills at 9 7/8 per cent. The shortage was later revised upwards to Pounds 1.8bn. The Bank operated again, purchasing Pounds 705m of bills, including Pounds 670m of band-1 bills at 9 7/8 per cent and Pounds 35m of band-2 bills at the same rate. Late assistance of Pounds 125m brought overall intervention operations to Pounds 1.6bn. As a result overnight rates soared to 22 per cent, where they finished the day. German call money firmed slightly yesterday to 9.50/60 per cent from 9.45/55 per cent. Dealers expect the Bundesbank to hold rates stable.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: Algeria to sign exploration deals
DOC.BYLINE: By MARK NICHOLSON, Middle East Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: ALGERIA IS on the verge of signing a fresh batch of oil and gas exploration agreements, according Mr Nordine Ait Laoussine, the oil minister, who said the government is discussing new ventures with six foreign companies. Speaking after last week's Opec meeting, Mr Ait Laoussine said: 'We will be able to announce very shortly several exploration agreements'. The oil minister said Algeria's ambitious oil and gas expansion plans, accelerated late last year by law changes to encourage foreign investment, could entail investment worth Dollars 20bn by the end of the century in a drive to boost output to meet European demand. Mr Ait Laoussine also said Algeria would open a bidding process for up to 12 new oil concessions in July. He added that, if should talks with some of the six companies currently involved in negotiations - including US, European and Japanese groups - were not be concluded by then, he might include blocs in the next round. He hoped to offer fresh territory for bidding every six months. 'We would like to cover all the sedimentary areas with bidders,' he said. The country - which is also a leading producer of gas, liquified natural gas and condensates - hopes to raise output from some 1.8m b/d of oil equivalent to some 2.5m b/d by the turn of the century. Mr Ait Laoussine said Algeria had signed contracts to export almost 60bn cubic metres of natural gas a year - the most the country can comfortably sustain, he explained - and was expanding facilities to meet that target. With reserves of 3 trillion (million million) cu m of gas, the minister said recently that Algeria hoped to become Europe's major gas supplier over the next decade. In Vienna he pointed out that Algeria needed to explore gas fields in the country's south which, he said, had been largely neglected. On oil, Mr Ait Laoussine said there was a 'definite need to increase the exploration effort' in Algeria, which at present pumps 770,000 barrels a day. Official studies estimate that Algeria faces a decline in sustainable output to between 500,000 and 300,000 b/d by early next century without new oil finds. Algeria presently has just over 9bn barrels of exploitable reserves. The government late last year substantially revised its foreign investment laws in the hope of attracting foreign capital into its hitherto protected oil sector. The changes permitted output sharing agreements, improved exploration terms and cut tax and royalty rates. Atlantic Richfield (Arco) this month became the first foreign company since the law changes to sign contracts with Sonatrach, the state oil company, to explore for oil and gas.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: Brent oil price breaks through Dollars 20 barrier
DOC.TEXT: NORTH SEA oil prices broke through the Dollars 20-a-barrel barrier to reach a six-month high following the unexpected agreement by the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries in Vienna last week to roll over its second-quarter output ceiling. Saudi Arabia had widely signalled its intention before the meeting to press for a rise of 1m barrels a day. In the event it agreed to maintain the existing ceiling of 22.98m b/d. Brent crude for July delivery rose 90 cents to Dollars 20.45, the highest price since December last year. 'The market has been very firm, on the conclusion that last week's agreement marks a fundamental shift in Saudi oil policy,' said Mr Peter Gignoux, head of Smith Barney's energy desk in London. 'It looks as if there is further pent-up demand, and we could see it reaching Dollars 21 in the short-term.' He warned, however, that it might be premature to talk of a 'fundamental' shift in Saudi policy, or of longer-term increases of Dollars 2 or Dollars 3 in the Brent price. Mr Mehdi Varzi, oil analyst at Kleinwort Benson, believed that the agreement 'epitomised Saudi Arabia's willingness to move into line with the Opec majority' and treat Dollars 21 a barrel for the Opec basket of crudes as a real target. That would mean a Brent crude price of around Dollars 23. Analysts point out that Saudi Arabia may indirectly have achieved as much as it wanted without needing to raise the ceiling. The agreement allowed for an increase of 300,000 b/d in Kuwaiti production, while Saudi Arabia said it would continue to produce slightly more oil than it was officially allocated. Most estimates put Opec's true second-quarter output at about 23.5m b/d, likely to rise to 24m b/d by the end of the third quarter. That would effectively be in line with both Saudi wishes and the lower end of expectations of third-quarter demand. However, stock-building before the winter is likely to boost third-quarter demand by at least 500,000 b/d and keep prices firm. Beyond that, observers feel that Saudi Arabia's actions may be explained by short-term political factors - such as a desire to avoid another clash with Iran. The kingdom may also have decided to flex its political muscles and demonstrate the control it - and Opec - can still exert on oil prices before next month's Earth Summit in Rio. Opec is firmly opposed to EC proposals for a carbon tax which it believes would badly hurt its revenues.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Government Bonds: Jump in consumer confidence index upsets Treasuries
DOC.BYLINE: By KAREN ZAGOR and SARA WEBB
DOC.TEXT: LONGER-DATED US Treasuries tumbled yesterday in response to reports that crude oil prices might climb as much as Dollars 3-a-barrel this year. The market was also shaken by signs of an improving economic climate from a surprisingly large increase in the May consumer confidence survey. In late trading, the Treasury's bellwether 30-year bond was down 15/16 at 101, yielding 7.906 per cent. Shorter-dated maturities fared better, with the two-year note losing a more moderate 5/32 to yield 5.326 per cent. The Federal Reserve entered the open market to arrange two-day system repurchase agreements when Fed Funds were trading at 3 15/16 per cent. The adding operation was widely expected and was seen as a technical move to meet requirements. Traders started liquidating positions in longer-dated bonds late last week, on reports that Federal Reserve policy-makers had decided not to take immediate steps to cut short-term interest rates. The selling accelerated yesterday following the release of the consumer confidence index for May, which rose to 71.6 per cent from a revised 65.1 per cent in April. Players had been looking for a May reading of around 68 per cent. The April index was previously reported as 64.8 per cent. FRENCH government bonds fell by over a quarter of a percentage point yesterday as Mr Michel Sapin, the finance minister, dashed hopes of a cut in interest rates. Mr Sapin suggested that a cut in French interest rates would have to be part of a co-ordinated move. The comments were taken to mean that France would not act unless the Bundesbank cuts German interest rates - a scenario which few traders expect to see in the short term. A strong first quarter GDP figure, showing growth of 1.1 per cent, also reinforced the view that France is unlikely to cut rates soon, traders said. The yield on the 10-year benchmark bond - the 8 1/2 per cent bond due 2002 - moved from the opening level of 8.49 per cent to 8.56 per cent by late afternoon. The Matif futures contract fell from 108.88 to 108.56. Elsewhere in Europe, the government bond markets drifted lower in dull trading. German bond futures fell from the opening of 87.89 to end at around 87.73, wiping out early gains. Bunds rose briefly early in the day, following the release of better-than-expected inflation data for the western German state of Hesse. Consumer prices in Hesse rose 0.3 per cent in the month to mid-May, and by 4.1 per cent on the previous year. THE UK government bond market dropped due to the combination of disappointing trade figures and worries about supply. A worse-than-expected current account deficit in April of Pounds 1.06bn, compared with Pounds 591m in March, pushed down gilt prices, with longer-dated issues falling between a quarter and a half of a percentage point. The benchmark 11 3/4 per cent gilt due 2003/07 fell from 118 17/32 to 118 1/16 . JAPANESE government bonds slipped in late trading, following the initial fall in US Treasury bonds and ahead of the monthly government bond auction. The Ministry of Finance is expected to auction about Y800bn of 10-year bonds, probably today. Traders said the June issue was expected to carry a slightly lower coupon of 5.6 per cent, compared with 5.7 per cent in last month's auction. 'A 5.6 per cent coupon isn't exactly bad news, but it might dampen retail interest,' said one dealer. The yield on the benchmark government bond - the No 129 - opened at 5.495 per cent and closed in Tokyo at 5.515 per cent. However, it then moved to 5.54 per cent in London, trading as the US Treasury bond market fell. Traders report a shift out of short-dated bonds into the long end of the market recently, and expect this trend to continue over the next couple of days. News that the long-term prime rate would be raised by 0.3 percentage points to 6.3 per cent, with effect from June 1, had little impact on the bond market, dealers said. The key September futures ended at 101.68, down from 101.80 on Monday, on a volume of 29,382 contracts.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Capital Markets: BNZ climbs 30% and lifts dividend
DOC.TEXT: THE BANK of New Zealand yesterday reported a 30 per cent improvement in net operating profit to NZDollars 171.1m (USDollars 92m) for the year ended March 1992 and increased its dividend from three to four cents a share. But company officials declined to comment on speculation that the bank would soon have new owners. Mr Syd Pasley, chairman, told a news conference it was inappropriate for him to comment on the prospects of a sale. BNZ's share price has risen by 22 per cent in the past month, partly on expectations of improved profits, but mostly on rumours that the government was about to sell its 58.2 per cent stake in BNZ. The NZ government attempted to sell the bank in 1987, but pulled out of the market because bids were too low. Since then the state has twice had to inject capital to rescue the bank. Mr Pasley said the bank had been successfully reshaped during the past three years. Last year's profit equated with 21.1 per cent on ordinary shareholders' funds.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Capital Markets: Oil groups may form mutual insurer
DOC.TEXT: SEDGWICK, the UK insurance broker, and Price Waterhouse, the accountants and management consultants, are joining forces in a bid to help leading European oil and gas companies form a new mutual insurance company. The new mutual, which could have a capital base of more than Dollars 50m and a minimum of 15 members, would provide extra insurance capacity in the specialist energy insurance market, where rates have increased and capacity diminished following recent losses. Since December, Sedgwick and Price Waterhouse have conducted feasibility studies and intend to hold more detailed talks with their clients within the next two weeks. No company has yet agreed to join the proposed mutual, but both organisations report a general feeling of support from their clients for the concept. 'We believe the support is there. We are literally having clients say to us 'when can we have it?',' said Mr Chris Mundy, director of marketing at Sedgwick Energy, the broker's specialist subsidiary. 'We would like to think we would be putting together a cast iron proposal within the next four to six weeks,' he added. Mr Mundy said there was an urgent need for action because of the contraction in available capacity. Sedgwick's 200 clients include British Petroleum, Shell and Mobil. Several oil majors which have North American interests are already part of a mutual company, Oil Insurance Ltd (OIL), which was formed in the late 1960s. Hit by losses such as the explosion of the Piper Alpha rig in the North Sea in July 1988, specialist energy insurers, including syndicates at Lloyd's of London, have increased rates and reduced the amount of cover available. Last year, buyers faced rate increases of between 15 and 200 per cent.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Capital Markets: Fletcher Challenge to dip into loss
DOC.TEXT: FLETCHER CHALLENGE is to write down its Australian and New Zealand property portfolio by NZDollars 400m (USDollars 215m) in a move that will force an unexpected loss on the company for this year. It says that the write down, intended to comply with international accounting practices, will push the company into a loss of about NZDollars 155m for the year ending June 1992, instead of a predicted NZDollars 300m profit. The news stunned the New Zealand stock market. Analysts had been braced for a write-down at the company's 48 per cent owned Australian property arm, Jennings. However, analysts had not expected write downs on the company's other property involvements. Mr Hugh Fletcher, chief executive, said the write-down did not represent cash outflows, and would not affect the group's ability to pay a prudent dividend. The board expects to pay a total dividend of 14 cents, compared with 27 cents in 1990-91. Included in the write-down is some NZDollars 50m as a result of the decision by the Jennings group to write off ADollars 74m (USDollars 56.92m) of its involvement in the ADollars 650m Southgate development in Melbourne. Fletcher Challenge said this provoked it to write off NZDollars 350m from its other property investments. That represents 29 cents a share, or eight per cent of net asset backing. The group forecast an end-June asset backing of NZDollars 4.13 per share. Year-end assets per share will now be NZDollars 3.70, broadly in line with the NZDollars 3.68 of end 1990-91. A main reason for the heavy write-down was a wish to conform with US accounting practices as far as New Zealand accounting standards and law would allow. Mr Fletcher said that the increasing overseas ownership in the company, which now stands at 40 per cent and the overseas origin of debt, were related factors. He said the write-down would allow investors to focus on the group's competitive strength and the potential for recovery in its four businesses of pulp and paper, energy, building and rural servicing 'secure in the knowledge that adequate provision had been made for the group's property exposures.' Mr Fletcher said that the company still expected to sell NZDollars 750m worth of assets this year. There were no plans for future cash issues. Next year's results were expected to benefit from improvements in most markets, he said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Capital Markets: TNT remains in the red but reduces borrowings
DOC.TEXT: TNT, the international transport group, has remained in the red for the third quarter of 1991-92 but has significantly reduced its borrowings. The company yesterday announced a loss of ADollars 44.4m (USDollars 33.6m) for the nine months ended March, against a half-year loss of ADollars 23.4m and a loss of Dollars A18.5m in the previous corresponding period. But the company said earnings continued to be heavily affected by abnormal items, most latterly associated with the flotation of the GD Express Worldwide venture in the US which raised about ADollars 400m. Abnormals added a ADollars 40.9m loss in the latest nine months, compared with ADollars 48.2m previously. Before abnormals and tax there was a profit of ADollars 23.2m, against ADollars 55m. Helped by the GD Express sale, TNT more than halved its interest bill in the period to ADollars 41.7m. Borrowings had been reduced by ADollars 898.5m. Despite the recession, the group increased revenue in Italy, GD Express Worldwide, domestic operations in Germany and Spain, the European contract logistics business and the TNT shipping and development group, the company said. Revenue was steady in the UK and the US, while declines were experienced in Australia, Canada and Brazil. TNT said the company's half-owned domestic airline operations, Ansett and Eastwest, had incurred losses in the period. 'While there is no question as to the underlying worth of TNT's investment in Ansett, it is possible that Ansett may reassess, at year-end, the value of its investment in Eastwest in the light of the current confused airline policy situation,' TNT said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Capital Markets: Sappi proposes Dollars 250m offering
DOC.BYLINE: By PAUL ABRAHAMS and PHILIP GAWITH
DOC.TEXT: SAPPI, the South African pulp and paper company, plans to raise about Dollars 250m through share issues on the London, Paris and Frankfurt stock markets. The offer, the largest by a South African company since trade and investment sanctions were lifted, will go ahead in June. Gencor, one of South Africa's largest conglomerates and owner of a controlling interest in Sappi, will underwrite the issue for up to the South African rand equivalent of Dollars 115m. The offer will be partly used to finance Sappi's DM396.5m (Dollars 240.30m) acquisition of 90 per cent of Hannover Papier, a German fine paper group. Hannover had existing obligations of DM370m at the end of last year. The acquisition is part of Sappi's strategy of reducing its dependency on the South African market, Mr Eugene Van As, executive chairman, said. The group wants to move increasingly into European high-margin specialty papers, but this would be impossible without closer links to customers, he says. Sappi expects about half the shares to be taken up in South Africa and half in Europe. US investors may be put off by the continuing sanctions imposed by 13 states and 74 municipalities. The consequent losses in those markets may be greater than potential gains of doing business with South Africa. The issue is being lead-managed by SG Warburg.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Capital Markets: Top Japanese insurers report fall in profits
DOC.TEXT: JAPANESE non-life insurance companies were hit by sharp increases in underwriting losses stemming from last September's typhoon damages and declining investment income. Non-consolidated net premium income for the year ended March at the top five Japanese non-life insurers - Tokio Marine & Fire, Yasuda Fire & Marine, Mitsui Marine & Fire, Sumitomo Marine & Fire, and Nippon Fire & Marine - rose 6.8 per cent as a result of brisk sales of car and compulsory auto liability insurances. But all five companies reported falls in pre-tax and after-tax profits. Only Tokio posted an operating profit. Net insurance payments for the five companies jumped 27.7 per cent to Y1,857.3bn (Dollars 14.35bn), due to a rise in car accidents and the surge in claims from typhoon damages. Non-operating profits were squeezed due to lower interest rates and the stock market slump. The companies also faced a sharp rise in redemptions for the savings type insurances.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Sharp fall at Mitsubishi Materials
DOC.TEXT: MITSUBISHI Materials, a leading Japanese maker of metals and ceramics, posted a 25.7 per cent decline in pre-tax profits to Y20.3bn (Dollars 156m) for the year to end-March. Net profits also plunged, by 20.2 per cent, to Y32.8bn on a special gain related to land sales. Weak sales of gold and declines in demand and prices for other metals amid the domestic economic sluggishness were behind the poor profit performance. In contrast, aluminium can sales posted gains due to increasing environmental concerns. The company, which changed its name from Mitsubishi Metal after merging with Mitsubishi Mining and Cement in December 1990, posted a 3.5 per cent sales gain for the year to Y787.8bn. However, in the period ending in March 1991 cement sales relating to a subsidiary involved in the merger contributed for only four months. Calculated at the same rate over the entire period comparable turnover for the year just ended was off Y113bn, Mitsubishi Materials said. For the current term, Mitsubishi Materials expects a partial recovery in metals demand as well as continued gains in its aluminium can operations. Sales are forecast to gain 4 per cent to Y820bn and pre-tax profits 3 per cent to Y21bn. However, in the absence of further land sales net profits are seen falling 69 per cent to Y10bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: KDD held back by stock losses
DOC.TEXT: KDD, Japan's international telecommunications company, said a rise in revenues from its international telephone service helped boost sales in the year to March, but profits were affected by losses on its securities holdings. Non-consolidated sales for the year grew 1.6 per cent to Y244.5bn (Dollars 1.89bn), while non-operating profits increased by 14.2 per cent to Y19.4bn. However, pre-tax profits rose by just 0.2 per cent to Y26bn. Lower corporate taxes lifted after-tax profits by 4.6 per cent to Y14.1bn. KDD, which posted sharp declines in sales and profits in the previous year due to competition in the international telecommunication business and lower rates, said cost controls helped operating profits. The company recorded Y2.7bn in losses on securities holdings due to the decline in the Tokyo market. Interest received fell 32.5 per cent to Y2.8bn, while interest on securities declined 53.3 per cent to Y865m. Dividends received fell 37.8 per cent to Y293m. Legislative changes to allow foreign ownership of KDD shares - now prohibited - are under way, and KDD said foreign investors would be able to buy its shares during this fiscal year. For the current year to March 1993, KDD expects a 3.7 per cent rise in pre-tax profits to Y27bn on a 5.9 per cent increase in sales to Y259bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: US machine tool orders down 9% as exports lag
DOC.TEXT: THE US machine tools industry suffered a 9.4 per cent decline in orders in April, compared with the month before, but the level of orders still showed a recovery against the depressed orders of a year ago, writes Alan Friedman in New York. Orders for the industry were Dollars 220m in April, down from Dollars 243m in March, according to the Association for Manufacturing Technology, a US machine tool trade organisation. But the orders were 13.6 per cent higher than the Dollars 193.7m achieved in April 1991. The industry's main problem is garnering export orders. Export orders were 37.6 per cent lower in April than in the same month last year, while domestic orders rose by 29.7 per cent year-on-year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Avesta holding talks with British Steel
DOC.TEXT: AVESTA, the Swedish stainless steel group, has said it is holding talks with British Steel on possible co-operation, but it intended to remain an independent company, Reuters reports from Stockholm. Avesta said in a brief release through the Stockholm bourse that further information was expected within a few weeks. In 1991, Avesta made a loss of SKr248m (Dollars 43.5m) after financial items on turnover of SKr7.39bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: O&Y bank creditors post gains
DOC.TEXT: BANK of Montreal (BMO) and Bank of Nova Scotia, Canada's third and fourth biggest banks respectively, lifted second-quarter earnings despite their sizeable exposures to troubled property developer Olympia & York. BMO, which disclosed CDollars 318m (USDollars 267.2m) in loans to O&Y, boosted net earnings to CDollars 143.5m, or CDollars 1.07 a share, in the three months to April 30, from CDollars 128.4m, or CDollars 1.01, a year earlier. The improvement was due largely to a slower rise in expenses than in revenues, and to a substantial growth in lending volumes, especially to small and mid-sized businesses. Total assets have jumped by almost 8 per cent in the past year to CDollars 104.2bn. BNS's earnings advanced to CDollars 171m, or 75 cents a share, from CDollars 163.3m, or 73 cents, in the same period last year. The bank ascribed the rise to wider margins as interest rates continued to decline. BNS has lifted its fiscal 1992 loan loss provisions by CDollars 200m, or 45 per cent, to reflect its exposure to O&Y and to other troubled borrowers. Its exposure to O&Y stands at CDollars 630m. Its second-quarter provision of CDollars 110m is unchanged from the previous three months. The provision in the second quarter of 1991 was CDollars 85m. Non-performing loans, net of provisions, rose to CDollars 1.87bn on April 30 from CDollars 1.74bn three months earlier. The bank did not disclose how much of this increase was accounted for by O&Y loans. BMO has classified its entire O&Y portfolio as non-performing, but has left its forecast for fiscal 1992 loan losses unchanged at CDollars 500m. The bank said that its loans to O&Y were secured by specific office buildings, which continue to generate cash flow, and by listed marketable securities. It is not involved in the Canary Wharf project in London or in any of O&Y's large syndicated financings. Although they are among O&Y's biggest lenders, the Canadian banks are generally well-equipped to absorb substantial losses. BMO reported that its risk-weighted capital-to-assets ratio improved in the second quarter to 9.1 per cent from 8.5 per cent three months earlier. BNS's capital ratio has edged up to 8.6 per cent from 8.5 per cent. Olympia & York's creditors are gradually stripping away the secrecy that was once the property developer's hallmark. The Toronto-based company, whose Canadian operations were placed under court protection two weeks ago, has made public for the first time the cash flows of its Canadian properties. The data is contained in a 26-page affidavit submitted in response to a court order which was granted last week at the request of the creditors. The company was also due to provide various groups of lenders with more detailed information by late yesterday, including projections of future cash flows.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Revlon to sell 20m shares in move to pay down debts
DOC.TEXT: REVLON, the US cosmetics and consumer products company taken over by Mr Ronald Perelman, the corporate raider, after a bruising bid battle in 1985, is coming back to the stock market. The New York-based company announced yesterday that it planned to transfer its cosmetics, skin care, fragrance and personal care operations to a new subsidiary company, 'New Revlon'. It will then sell 20m shares in this subsidiary to investors, via an initial public offering. Shares sold to investors via the flotation will account for just under one-fifth of New Revlon's equity. Revlon Inc, the parent company, will own the remaining 82.2 per cent, and will continue to be controlled by Mr Perelman. Revlon said that funds raised via the flotation would go towards paying down debts, Revlon said that the maximum offering price in the IPO filing was Dollars 19 a share, which would raise Dollars 380m before expenses. Yesterday, Moody's, the Wall Street rating agency, said it had placed Revlon's existing publicly-traded debt securities under review for a possible upgrade. Moody's said it was 'focusing on the extent proceeds from the new equity issue will be used to reduce debt levels, the resulting financial flexibility at Revlon and the ability of the remaining Revlon businesses to generate cash to service debt going forward in a very competitive operating environment'. Revlon was founded in 1932 by the eccentric Mr Charles Revson. The Dollars 1.8bn takeover by Mr Perelman was a quintessential 1980s deal, heavily dependent on junk bond financing and borrowed money. Since then, however, a good deal of debt has been paid down via the flotation on a minority interest in National Health Care Group, another subsidiary, and via the sale of Max Factor and Betrix cosmetics to Procter & Gamble for Dollars 1.14bn. According to recent analysts' reports, Revlon's debt had fallen from Dollars 2.38bn at December 1990, to Dollars 754m (on a pro forma basis) at year-end 1991. The Equitable Life Assurance Society, the US life insurer which is converting from mutual status to a shareholder-owned company, announced yesterday that it plans to sell 43.5m shares to investors. It estimates that the initial public offering price will be between Dollars 11 and Dollars 14 a share, raising up to Dollars 600m. In addition to shares being sold in the IPO, The Equitable is distributing shares to its policyholders and to Axa, the French insurer which injected Dollars 1bn into the ailing US company last year. At the end of the process, Axa will hold between 40 and 49 per cent of The Equitable's shares.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Fulcrum cash offers closed
DOC.TEXT: Fulcrum Investment Trust has announced that its cash offers for its own shares have closed. The investment trust was due to be wound-up between 1991 and 1994 but has been seeking to extend its life via a rights issue and placing. The cash offers of 10.75p per capital share and 40p per income share were an alternative to the restructuring proposals. They have been taken up by 17 per cent of capital shareholders and 0.64 per cent of income shareholders.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Slough makes Pounds 43m deal in Germany
DOC.TEXT: Slough Estates, the UK property group, has made a Pounds 43m forward sale of a department store in Cologne's main shopping precinct to an unnamed German institution. This is the largest deal completed by Slough in Germany, where it has operated since 1974. The 94,000 sq ft property, bought by Slough in 1988, has been pre-let to Ludwig Beck, a Munich-based retailer, and is set to be finished in the autumn of 1993.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Woodchester plans to give full service
DOC.TEXT: Woodchester Investments, the Dublin-based small-ticket leasing and finance group, has changed its name to Woodchester Credit Lyonnais Bank. The move reflected what Mr Craig McKinney, Woodchester chairman, described as the group's 'ambition to develop a full retail banking service in Ireland'. The group intended to acquire 'around 40 to 50' retail banking outlets in Ireland 'to be in a position to offer services that Credit Lyonnais offers elsewhere in Europe'. Mr Jean Yves Harberet, president of Credit Lyonnais, said his bank's tie-up with Woodchester 'opens a window in Europe for the development of Woodchester's leasing business'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Frogmore pays Pounds 15m for shopping centre
DOC.TEXT: Frogmore Estates, the property company, has bought a shopping centre in Hertfordshire from Norwich Union for Pounds 15.2m. The 73,000 sq ft Spires Shopping Centre in Barnet, which was opened about three years ago, has a rent roll of Pounds 1.64m, giving Frogmore a yield of 10.8 per cent. Five empty shops will increase the annual income to about Pounds 1.8m when let. The deal brings Frogmore's spending this year to over Pounds 40m. It said it was increasing its weighting in retail property, which it believed would be the first sector to recover. Frogmore, which fought off a takeover bid a year ago, said its ability to buy on historically high initial yields vindicated its earlier policy of eliminating borrowings by selling property.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Evered finance director resigns
DOC.TEXT: Mr John Ford, finance director of Evered Bardon, the aggregates group, since September 1985, has resigned. Mr Peter Tom, group chief executive, said Mr Ford's departure reflected Evered's current policy of consolidation after rapid expansion in the late 1980s. 'John is a financial director more suited to acquisitions. He wanted to go off and do other things. We've parted the best of friends,' he said. In February, Evered announced the disposal of two non-core businesses, and three others in the US are up for sale. Cash raised will be used to reduce gearing from 70 per cent towards 40 per cent.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Kelsey holds 8p in face of interim loss
DOC.TEXT: Kelsey Industries incurred a loss of Pounds 119,000 in the six months to March 31 but expects to be profitable in the second half. However, it is certain the year will not match the Pounds 1.44m pre-tax made in 1990-91, warned Mr Brian Arbib, chairman. The interim dividend is held at 8p - the halfway profit was Pounds 1.11m last time - but the rate of the final (18p) will be decided at the appropriate time. The group, a maker of roofing materials, audio and video accessories, and solder, saw signs that the business climate, both in the UK and North America, was changing slightly for the better.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Whitecroft sells engineering side
DOC.TEXT: Whitecroft has effectively reduced its borrowings by Pounds 1.97m via the sale of Silcoms, its sole precision engineering subsidiary. This is a further step in the disposal of peripheral activities and allows management to focus on operations in lighting, building products, medical cotton fibre and textiles. In the year to March 31 1992 Silcoms made pre-tax profit of Pounds 383,000, its net tangible assets were Pounds 721,000, and book value of property Pounds 551,000. The purchaser was Bolton Engineering, owned by the present directors of Silcoms, together with 3i Group. Consideration for the sale was Pounds 1.35m and Whitecroft received a dividend of Pounds 75,000.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Little change for Andrews Sykes
DOC.TEXT: Increasing profitability from smaller subsidiaries enabled Andrews Sykes Group to improve in the second half and produce a pre-tax profit of Pounds 1.2m for the year to March 31. That compared with Pounds 1.32m last time. Turnover fell to Pounds 56.8m (Pounds 62.6m) and operating profit to Pounds 3.44m (Pounds 4.29m) but interest charges were cut to Pounds 2.24m (Pounds 2.98m). Profit was struck after redundancy costs of Pounds 208,000, against last year's Pounds 941,000 for redundancies and reorganisation. Mr David Hubbard, chairman of this plant hire group, said cash flow continued to be strong and bank borrowings were reduced by Pounds 3.3m with gearing falling from 110 to 89 per cent. Further action was taken to reduce overheads and staff numbers had been cut by 14 per cent during the year. After a substantially heavier tax charge, earnings per share fell to 1.2p (3.2p). The final dividend is 3p for a maintained total of 4.4p.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Monks net assets marginally ahead
DOC.TEXT: Net asset value of The Monks Investment Trust stood at 409p as at April 30, a marginal increase from 399.5p over the year. The trust increased its holdings in Europe and south-east Asia but its US portfolio was reduced following a sharp decrease in oil holdings. Net revenue amounted to Pounds 5.76m (Pounds 5.81m), equal to earnings of 7.43p (7.48p). A same-again final dividend of 4.7p maintains the total at 6.7p.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: CRT pays Pounds 1.5m for Reach-a-Teacha
DOC.TEXT: CRT Group has paid Pounds 1.5m to acquire Reach-a-Teacha, which trades as Wetherby Training Services and provides open learning materials principally in office, secretarial and computer training. Wetherby operates through 160 franchised locations throughout the UK, together with a small number of overseas franchises. For the year to April 30 it made a pre-tax profit of Pounds 263,000 from turnover of Pounds 929,000. The acquisition was made via the Pitman Training Group subsidiary. The consideration was met by the allotment of 659,000 ordinary shares, the issue of Pounds 399,800 bank guaranteed unsecured loan notes, and Pounds 220,000 cash.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Kitty Little tumbles Pounds 0.31m into the red
DOC.TEXT: A pre-tax loss of Pounds 306,000 was announced by Kitty Little Group, the USM-quoted maker of fragrant gifts, air fresheners and self-selection reading glasses, for the 11 months to December 31 1991. For the 12 months to end-January 1991 there was a profit of Pounds 167,000. Mr Grahan Webster, chairman, said that on a pro rata basis sales in the fragrance division fell by 37 per cent and losses there were Pounds 285,000 (Pounds 514,000 profit). Shardan, the toilet bag manufacturer, incurred losses of Pounds 108,000 (Pounds 106,000) after provisions for slow moving stock and bad debts. However, following the acquisition of the minority interest in Magnivision - now KL Eyecare - and the stock and goodwill of Ready Readers, both companies had reported profits. Turnover amounted to Pounds 4.23m (Pounds 6.8m). Net interest payable fell to Pounds 224,000 (Pounds 369,000) and the company is concentrating on reducing bank borrowings further by keeping a close control of working capital requirements. Losses per share amounted to 1.96p (0.19p earnings) and there is no dividend (0.575p).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Mezzanine Capital net assets up 3.7%
DOC.TEXT: Mezzanine Capital & Income Trust 2001, which specialises in acquisitions in the US, increased the net asset value of its income shares by 3.7 per cent to 110.1p over the year to March 31. A final dividend of 7.25p is proposed, to give an unchanged total of 14.5p.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: JMD cuts losses to Pounds 89,000
DOC.TEXT: JMD Group, the greeting cards maker and novelty products merchandiser, cut its pre-tax loss from Pounds 1.11m to just Pounds 89,000 in 1991. The USM-quoted group made a profit of Pounds 74,000 (Pounds 527,000) before exceptional charges of Pounds 163,000 (Pounds 150,000), and last year before loss on discontinued activities of Pounds 1.49m. Sir Cecil Burney, chairman, said there was still a need to rebuild liquidity but he remained encouraged by the performance of Downpace, which was a good cash generating business and returned profits before management charges and tax of Pounds 400,000 in the year. Turnover fell to Pounds 3.34m (Pounds 4.69m). Losses per share were 0.05p (1.44p).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Drayton English decreases
DOC.TEXT: DRAYTON ENGLISH and International Trust has seen its unquoted portfolio suffer badly from the UK recession, leading to a number of write-offs and provisions. Its net asset value fell from 108.4p to 66p over the 12 months ended April 5 1992, although that had improved to 71.5p by the end of April. Gross income for 1991-92 dropped from Pounds 6.07m to Pounds 4.4m, and net revenue from Pounds 2.69m to Pounds 1.69m. Earnings per share were 0.71p (3.16p) and the final dividend is cut to 0.6p (2.3p) for a total of 1.2p (3.2p). Resources were being focused into the UK quoted smaller company sector, which currently accounted for 60 per cent of the portfolio. Two other Drayton trusts have also reported their results: Drayton Recovery, which began trading last October, produced gross revenue of Pounds 931,000 for the period to April 30 1992, and net revenue of Pounds 594,000 for earnings per share of 7.19p. An interim dividend of 2p is declared; a special of 2p has already been paid. Net asset value at April 30 was 98.9p. Drayton Blue Chip, which began trading in March 1991, finished with gross revenue of Pounds 1.8m for the period ended March 31 1992. Net income reached Pounds 1.12m for earnings per share of 8.88p, and the final dividend is 5.495p to make 8.4. Over the six months to March 31 1992, net asset value fell from 89.4p to 60.5p.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Center Parcs to build holiday village in France
DOC.TEXT: Center Parcs, a subsidiary of Scottish & Newcastle, the brewery and leisure group, is building a holiday village in France at a cost of Pounds 75m. Set in 300 acres of parkland near Sologne in the Loire Valley, the village will comprise villas, a leisure complex, shops and restaurants. It is expected to open in 1993, create 450 full and part-time jobs, and cater for a potential 300,000 visitors a year. Mr James Merrington, corporate affairs director, said approval was expected shortly on a new UK site and negotiations had started with Belgian authorities on another possible development. The Sologne Center Parc will bring to 13 the number of complexes in Britain, France, Belgium and the Netherlands. Scottish & Newcastle's leisure division -which includes the Pontins holiday group - last year made pre-tax profits of Pounds 65.5m on turnover of Pounds 300m.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Mercury Asset advances 15% despite provisions
DOC.TEXT: MERCURY ASSET Manage-ment, the fund management group 75 per cent owned by SG Warburg, achieved a 15 per cent rise in pre-tax profits last year despite substantial provisions on two investments. Pre-tax profits in the year to March 31 rose from Pounds 56.4m to Pounds 65.1m, reflecting the group's success in holding down costs. While turnover jumped by Pounds 14.6m to Pounds 154m, costs rose by less than Pounds 1m to Pounds 99.6m. Mr Peter Stormonth Darling, chairman, said that investment in systems in previous years to make the group's back office operations more efficient had accounted for the low cost increase. However, the group announced provisions of about Pounds 5m on two investments at March 31, holding back its advance. Some Pounds 3m of this was a write-down on its investment in Jupiter, a fund management group in which MAM bought a 27 per cent stake for Pounds 7m last year. About half of that provision might be written back because the value of MAM's holding had recovered since the year-end, Mr Stormonth Darling said. A further provision of more than Pounds 1m was made against a holding by MAM in Isosceles, which it had taken on to its own books when unable to place the shares with investment clients. Funds under management rose by Pounds 2.7bn to Pounds 40bn. The Pounds 2bn of new money under management, down from the record Pounds 3bn taken on the previous year, reflected the slower rate at which cash was flowing into UK pension funds. Earnings were 25.4p (22.8p) basic and 25.1p (22.1p) diluted. A final dividend of 8.9p is proposed, for a total of 11.5p (10p adjusted).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Brown Shipley to raise Pounds 43m in disposal
DOC.TEXT: BROWN SHIPLEY, the merchant banking group, is to sell two of its subsidiaries. The group, which posted pre-tax losses of Pounds 3.34m in the year to March 31, 1991, confirmed yesterday that overall losses for the year ending March 31, 1992 would be 'substantial'. It will earn some Pounds 33m from the sale of its profitable insurance broking arm to Holmwoods Group, a company formed by the arm's senior management. The sale of Brown Shipley's offshore company to Standard Bank Investment Corporation of South Africa (SBIC) will net a further Pounds 10.25m. Holmwoods, which has been advised by J O Hambro Magan, is to pay Pounds 30m in cash plus two deeply discounted loan notes with aggregate nominal value of Pounds 3m and final redemption dates in 1997 and 1998. CINVen, manager of Pounds 600m of pension funds for British Coal, British Rail and Barclays Bank Pension Funds, will provide 70 per cent of the equity backing for the venture. Senior debt behind the deal has been underwritten by the Bank of Scotland. Holmwoods specialises in providing insurances for private schools and colleges in the UK and the US, where it trades as AWG Dewar. Its other activities include marine, corporate and personal insurance broking. The insurance broking subsidiary was a profitable part of the Brown Shipley group. Unaudited profits in the year to March 31, 1992 amounted to Pounds 3.5m, including exceptional items of Pounds 340,000, when shareholders' funds amounted to Pounds 5.1m. SBIC's payment for the offshore company is subject to an adjustment based on the net assets of the offshore group, which specialises in banking, stockbroking, investment management and fiduciary services, primarily from its base in Jersey. Discussions are also taking place with Woodchester Investments about the terms of the sale of Lease Management Services, Brown Shipley's leasing subsidiary. A memorandum of understanding has been exchanged. Brown Shipley said its 'accounts for the full year ending March 31, 1992 would include sharply increased provisions for bad and doubtful debts, resulting in a substantial overall loss. Against this background the directors will not be recommending a final dividend.' Observer, Page 19

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Japanese computer makers fall below expected earnings
DOC.TEXT: JAPAN'S computer and semi-conductor makers yesterday reported worse-than-expected earnings for the fiscal year just ended. The parent companies of NEC, Toshiba, Mitsubishi Electric and Fujitsu announced falls in pre-tax profits ranging from 43.1 per cent to 68.6 per cent. They blamed the poor performance on a weak semiconductor market and, in particular, falling prices for the latest generation of memory chip, the 4Mbit, on which they may never recoup their investments. Sharp reported a smaller drop in profits - 11.9 per cent - although along with other makers of consumer products, it reported a fall in demand for audio-visual equipment. Most of the chip makers' factories are running at well below capacity. Toshiba, for example, produces about 300m of the 4Mbit chips, instead of the planned 500m each month. In the past year, the price of those chips has more than halved, to Y1,400 (Pounds 5.90) each. As a result, Japanese companies which have dominated the memory chip market in recent years, are cutting back on new semiconductor investment. NEC said the industry had been hit by global recession and falls in domestic capital expenditure and consumer spending. Fujitsu, the world's second largest computer manufacturer, is hoping for a 25 per cent rise in profits, to Y50bn. Mitsubishi Electric reported flat parent sales of heavy machinery, industrial products and automation equipment. Air-conditioners were the best-selling consumer line, but audio-visual equipment sales were weak. DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / S&P gloomy on US property losses
DOC.TEXT: STANDARD & POOR's, the credit rating service, yesterday offered a gloomy assessment of the likely impact on US banks of loan losses from the depressed US commercial property market. The S&P study warned that notwithstanding improved first-quarter 1992 earnings at a number of US banks, the worst was not yet over. S&P said it believed 'that the problem loan workout period will be protracted and that the losses will have a long tail, reaching substantially higher levels than they have to date'. The report sought to dispel the idea that the effect of the worldwide property depression on the US banking industry was waning. The recent bankruptcy filings by Olympia & York of Canada were cited by S&P as 'a vivid confirmation that real estate (property) markets have not begun to recover or stabilise'. Senior US bank executives have said in recent months they expect the level of bad debt provisions caused by commercial property loans to remain at the same level this year as in 1991. But the S&P report claimed that reserves at many banks are not yet adequate to cover prospective commercial property losses. S&P predicted that 'the overhang of losses will continue to be a significant drain on (banking) industry earnings over the next few years'. The report said that S&P's outlook for bank ratings remains stable, with several banks unlikely to receive a ratings upgrade in the near term. S&P cited the experience of banks in Texas during the late 1980s property slump as a worst-case scenario, and noted that loan write-offs at some Texas institutions reached the level of 30 per cent of commercial property loan portfolios. The ratings service described as 'disturbing' that the level of non-performing property loans at New York City banks was reaching the 40 per cent range. Loan losses would not be as high in other regions as they were in Texas and the southwest, and should represent about 15 per cent of the original loan portfolio value of most banks. The loan losses could, however, reach the level of 25 per cent of outstanding property loans at some banks, S&P said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / EC weakens environment plans
DOC.TEXT: THE European Community's position at next week's Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro looks set to fall well short of what environment commissioner Carlo Ripa di Meana has proposed, and his own attendance at the summit was last night in doubt. Environment ministers of the 12 yesterday agreed to sign the Climate Change convention, due to be agreed in Rio, but they did not agree to endorse politically the European Commission's plan to tax energy as a means of curbing CO emissions, even though no EC state opposed the proposal. Nor were they able to agree on a timetable for nearly doubling development aid to a minimum of 0.7 per cent of gross domestic product to help developing countries adopt more environmentally sound development strategies. Taken together, this is a limp posture when set against what Mr Ripa de Meana had defined as the minimum 'dowry' the Community should take to Rio. The Commission's plan is to stabilise CO emissions at 1990 levels by 2000, through an energy tax equivalent to Dollars 10 a barrel of oil equivalent. Mr Ripa di Meana says the EC can only deliver half that target without a tax. The plan won strong support yesterday from Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Italy. The first four attacked the Commission for making introduction of the tax conditional on the US and Japan adopting similar measures. France and the UK reserved their position behind procedure, since the Commission overshot its deadline in producing the detailed draft directive, which it will look at today. 'The UK position remains that when we see it, we will study it in detail,' Mr Michael Howard, UK environment secretary, said of the tax plan.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / The Lex Column: SG Warburg
DOC.TEXT: It may be gratifying for SG Warburg to unveil Pounds 71m of previously hidden reserves, but that also creates a large slice of additional capital on which it has to make an acceptable return. Yesterday's annual results show that only Pounds 3m would have been added to hidden reserves in 1991-92 had they still been in place. So the extra capital may prove something of a millstone, although Warburg will need to be well-capitalised to meet EC securities company regulations. That in turn creates a requirement for a steady flow of large issues, whatever conditions in the market, if the capital is to be used efficiently. Net return on capital last year was only 12 per cent. Mercury Asset Management's provisions against its investments in Jupiter Tyndall and Isosceles are a real but transitory embarrassment. More worrying is the fact that, thanks to pension fund holidays, it only attracted some Pounds 2bn of new money last year. Since it cannot continue to cut costs for ever, MAM must break into the nascent European pension fund market to secure future growth. The chances are that a smooth operator such as Warburg can cope with these problems better than most. But the road ahead is difficult. A yield of 4 per cent offers only limited compensation for investors, even if the scare surrounding February's so-called profit warning was overdone.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / The Lex Column: Mountleigh
DOC.TEXT: It is not entirely clear why the banks should have pulled the plug on Mountleigh, as opposed to any of the other walking wounded in the UK property sector. The lenders, to be sure, already have their hands on most of the available security, and have no obvious incentive to throw Pounds 56m of good money after potentially obstreperous bondholders. Mountleigh, though, is hardly unique in this respect. Perhaps in the end patience simply ran out with a company whose conspicuous extravagance had become a symbol of the late 1980s and whose top-heavy 14 man board was disparagingly but aptly described by one small shareholder at the last annual meeting as a football team with three reserves. Judging by the market's calm reaction to the news yesterday, it may be that the wider implications are indeed slight. After all, everyone knew that Mountleigh's assets had to be sold to repay its debts: all that has happened is that the administrator rather than the company will now get on with the task. The problem with this cosy theory is that the timetable for disposals will now presumably be that much tighter, the risk being that today's forced sellers ultimately become the market. With very few signs of a pick-up in demand vendors in the commercial property sector may prove to be behaving as unrealistically as home owners throughout most of last year. The banks have to balance the cost of further rescues against the damage to confidence and the impact on their balance sheets of letting other companies go bust. It is a delicate and dangerous game.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / The Lex Column: UK economy
DOC.TEXT: Any lingering doubts that recovery is under way should have been dispelled by yesterday's trade figures showing import volume grew an underlying 4 1/2 per cent in the three months to April. That, however, is about the extent of the good news. It might be possible to interpret the import surge as a sign that recovery is already robust, but that would scarcely be consistent with other available data. The depressing conclusion is that even a weak recovery is enough to push the trade figures heavily into the red, possibly because loss of capacity during the recession has left the economy with bottlenecks. Granted, a large trade deficit does not matter in the short term because foreign money is flowing abundantly into post-election Britain. There is a reasonable chance that the estimates for invisible earnings, which have been running at Pounds 300m a month since the start of the year, will be revised upwards. By contrast, export performance has not yet been affected by any slowdown that may hit the rest of Europe as a result of the Bundesbank squeeze. Heavy inflows into the gilts market may have created a breathing space but adjustment will be inevitable before long. Since ERM membership gives the UK little independent control over its monetary policy, the brunt will have to be born on the fiscal side.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / The Lex Column: Dowsing the grid
DOC.TEXT: Whatever the outcome of the latest government inquiry, a national grid for the UK water industry is likely to remain a distant prospect. Practical objections aside, it is perhaps worth recalling that the principal attraction of privatising water was to remove the industry's capital spending requirements from public sector finances. It is scarcely conceivable that the government would approve the huge increases in spending needed to build a national supply network. By way of example, the 50 miles of the London ring main is costing Thames Water around Pounds 250m. Granted, the issue of who would pay for the grid is clouded, but there is little chance of the companies stumping up. As the forthcoming results season will remind them, consumers already face steady real increases in water bills. The case for further rises is unlikely to appeal to politicians. Nor would investors in water shares have much to cheer about. In addition to capital costs, there would be ongoing operating expenses for pumping water around the country. Should UK rainfall return to historic levels, a large project might end in embarrassment. All the same, the politicians' surge of interest could have beneficial effects. If the regulator agreed, water companies' spending on improvements to their leaking underground pipes could be brought forward at the expense of other work. In time, that would ease the supply problem. A faster introduction of metering might have the same effect on consumption. Water company chairmen have long maintained that their biggest problem is consumers' wasteful attitude to the resource. Changing that is perhaps a sufficient long-term challenge for the industry. More immediately, the shares will doubtless be supported by a regulatory regime that still allows dividends to be increased at roughly twice the average market rate.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / EC moves closer to trade ban on Serbia as Major speaks out
DOC.BYLINE: By PHILIP STEPHENS, LAURA SILBER and JUDY DEMPSEY
DOC.TEXT: THE European Community last night moved closer to a trade ban and other sanctions against Serbia as officials of the 12 member nations, meeting in Brussels, agreed on recommendations to ministers. The drive for sanctions gained further momentum as Mr John Major, visiting central Europe, condemned the role of Serbian forces in provoking ethnic conflict in breakaway Yugoslav republics. Before leaving Warsaw for Prague, the prime minister called for mandatory United Nations sanctions to force an end to the fighting. British officials travelling with Mr Major said ambassadors of UN Security Council nations in New York had prepared a draft UN sanctions resolution against Serbia. But France was said to be resisting the inclusion of oil trade in any package of sanctions. The officials gathered in Brussels left open whether the EC should act alone or through the UN. Their recommended package of sanctions will be scrutinised at a meeting of EC ambassadors today, but EC ministers might not meet until next week to decide on it. Mr James Baker, US secretary of state, called at the weekend for tough sanctions against Serbia, and both the US and Canada have cut air links with Belgrade. EC countries and the US have already announcing withdrawal of diplomats from Belgrade. Mr Major made clear Britain was pressing for mandatory measures including an oil embargo, a break in civil air links with Belgrade and more general trade sanctions. He was aware when he made his remarks that France is reluctant to agree to significant sanctions. But he indicated Britain was determined to press ahead regardless. His calculation is that Paris will not in the end be able to resist international pressure for sanctions. Mr Major set out a series of conditions which the west should demand before lifting a threat against Serbia. They included a ceasefire in the breakaway republic of Bosnia-Hercegovina, Serbian action to control its irregular forces, resumption of constitutional talks and guarantees to let refugees return home. Echoing the hard line taken by Washington on international sanctions, Mr Major demanded also that troops of the Yugoslav federal army be withdrawn from the republic of Croatia. Diplomats in Brussels said France wanted any trade embargo, particularly on oil, to be channelled through the Security Council. France argued that because the EC supplied only about 10 per cent of Serbia's oil, an embargo would work only if backed by such countries as Iran, China and Russia. In an effort to head off the campaign for sanctions, Serbia promised to 'do its utmost' to get humanitarian aid to Bosnia. At the same time Mr Andrei Kozyrev, the Russian foreign minister, announced a deal in Sarajevo to reopen the blockaded city's airport. He said a ceasefire would take effect today so that emergency supplies of food and medicines could be flown in. The airport has been under blockade since early April, first by the federal army and now by Serbian irregulars.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Abolition of UK visa requirements for Polish tourists
DOC.TEXT: John Major yesterday announced the abolition of UK visa requirements for Polish tourists and increased Britain's financial aid to Warsaw - moves designed to underline his commitment to Poland's eventual membership of the EC. Report,Page 2

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / ITV to issue writ over soccer deal
DOC.BYLINE: By RAYMOND HUGHES and RAYMOND SNODDY
DOC.TEXT: THE ITV companies last night said they planned to issue a writ today against the new Premier League for alleged breach of confidence. ITV failed yesterday in its attempt in the High Court to get an injunction to block the Pounds 304m five year joint British Sky Broadcasting-BBC deal for football television rights, which would have given ITV the chance to increase its Pounds 262m bid. But Mr Trevor East, ITV's executive producer for football said after the hearing: 'We are encouraged to hear that the High Court believes we have an arguable case for breach of confidence, and therefore we plan to issue a writ tomorrow against the Premier League for damages that we believe could be substantial.' ITV claimed it had been put at an unfair disadvantage because its bid had been leaked to BSkyB by Mr Rick Parry, the league's chief executive, just before the meeting on Monday last week when the Premier League clubs considered the offers. Mr Justice Ferris said the league had clearly indicated it would not be prepared to consider a new offer from ITV and it could not possibly be right to make an order forcing it to do so. The judge added that ITV could return to court for a full hearing of its case and the court might take a different view - 'although I very much doubt it'. Mr Frank Barlow, chairman of BSkyB, said the decision had confirmed his faith in British justice. Mr Barlow, who is also managing director of Pearson, which has a significant stake in BSkyB and owns the Financial Times, described the unsuccessful ITV attempt to obtain an injunction as 'an act of despair'. BSkyB rights to live Premier League games - the BBC will show recorded highlights - would 'open up a whole range of commercial options', Mr Barlow said. He declined to elaborate. One option is to make Premier League football available without extra charge on Sky Sport to encourage the public to buy satellite dishes. New revenue would then come from persuading them to subscribe to film channels. Another option is to scramble Sky Sport and charge a Pounds 5 per month subscription fee for it from the outset and move, at a later stage, to pay-as-you-view for top matches. After yesterday's hearing Mr Parry said he was relieved by the outcome. 'We have achieved a demonstrably better deal for the clubs and the league as a whole - and that was the only issue from our point of view,' he said. Mr Christopher Carr QC, for ITV, had argued that the contract with BSkyB had been procured by breach of confidence. Mr Parry had 'communicated sufficient of the terms of the ITV bid to enable BSkyB to formulate a new claim which took account of the ITV bid'. That had breached an implied term that ITV's bid would be treated in confidence and not revealed to a rival bidder. Mr Carr claimed that the league and BSkyB had finalised their contract 'with unseemly haste' on Thursday in an attempt to defeat any High Court action. In evidence read to the court, Mr Parry said he had told Mr Sam Chisholm, BSkyB's chief executive, of ITV's offer - though not the figure. Spitting contest, Page 17

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Observer: Spice of life
DOC.TEXT: A group of ladies is taking afternoon tea on the balcony of the local golf club while their spouses play a competition round. Missing his final putt a player lets out a string of expletives which cannot but be overheard. Result: a complaint to the committee about the disgraceful language. Decision: ladies are banned from taking tea on the balcony during competition matches.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Observer: Driving force
DOC.TEXT: The last amateur cricketer to lead a county championship winning side, Colin Ingleby-Mackenzie, faces a challenge of a different order as head of the management buy-out team at insurance brokers Holmwoods. Ingleby-Mackenzie, who won national sporting fame when he led Hampshire's successful side during the late 1950s and early 1960s, is skippering the Pounds 33m move for Holmwoods, a subsidiary of merchant banking group Brown Shipley which has hitherto specialised in finding insurance for private schools. Already solidly profitable, it seems well placed to take advantage of the increasing flexibility with which public-sector schools are being run. Among the 50-strong management team involved in the buy-out is another former county captain, Nick Pocock, a successor of Ingleby-Mackenzie at Hampshire, while Carl Openshaw, director of finance and development, is a third cricketing buff - albeit a Kentishman.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Observer: Backing group
DOC.TEXT: 'If you shake my hand on a deal then you had better be absolutely bloody sure you know what you are shaking it for' is the latest Peter de Savary message. Observer hopes the movers and shakers behind BusinessAge also know what they have let themselves in for. Tom Rubython, who has created the new magazine - featuring the said de Savary as its cover story - out of the embers of the late Management Week, is certainly amazed. 'The investors have left it completely to us. It's very odd, isn't it?' Rubython, former editor of Management Week, which folded in December, had the idea of approaching 2,000 subscribers of the ill-fated publication to see if they would invest in the new venture. A total of Pounds 900,000 was raised from 171 backers. One name featured in the Sunday Times list of Britain's 300 richest men sent Pounds 300,000 on condition his identity remained secret. Most reader-investors, who together control 80 per cent of the equity, have invested between Pounds 100 and Pounds 10,000. With such a disparate range of shareholders, Rubython is convinced he will have total editorial freedom. But not everyone will be completely satisfied with the new magazine. In a letter published in the first issue, John Gammon of Hawkshead Consultants said he was disappointed with Management Week because there were too many articles about the likes of Donald Trump and Madonna. And what is on page 66 of BusinessAge? Madonna: America's Smartest Businesswoman.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Observer: Class-conscious
DOC.TEXT: A charter has come to the aid of Citizen Major.
