On his first foreign trip since the election victory, the prime minister is travelling around Central Europe on an aircraft more used to ferrying holidaymakers on cut-price package tours. When Major decided three weeks ago to travel to Poland, Hungary and Czechoslovakia, the RAF regretted there were simply no VC10s available to accommodate him and his entourage. So John and Norma find themselves on an ancient BAC 1-11 chartered from British Air Ferries. When introduced in the 1960s, the aircraft was undoubtedly ahead of its time but in more recent years has been consigned to the Stansted-Jersey holiday run. Major may be unphased by having to sit in economy just a few rows ahead of the travelling press. But the class-conscious political hacks have already pledged themselves to decorous silence if on future trips the man of the people opts for an aeroplane more appropriate to their status.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Observer: Pohl's golden opportunity
DOC.TEXT: Canadian financiers with fingers in the property pie are hardly flavour of the month among the international banking fraternity these days. But Peter Munk, Toronto entrepreneur par excellence, is clearly different. How else has the smooth-talking, fine-wine-loving Munk managed to lure Karl Otto Pohl onto the board of his gold, oil and property holding company Horsham Corporation? Since stepping down from the Bundesbank, Pohl has lined up an impressive string of blue-chip directorships - including Bertelsmann, Unilever and Royal Dutch Shell. Having turned down hosts of other worthy causes, he was obviously in the market for a touch of excitement. But what, in turn, can the owner of American Barrick, a leading North American gold producer, and Clark Oil, a US Midwest oil refiner, want with a former German central banker, however noted? A Hungarian emigre who has been in Canada for more than 30 years, Munk still retains a soft spot for Europe and Europeans. He has a ski chalet at Klosters, and another prominent German, Nato secretary-general Manfred Worner, was a guest of the Munks on his most recent Canadian trip. Never dull on the subject of French wines, Munk would like Pohl's reputed ability to be able to distinguish between 200 sorts of grappa. And while he would not primarily be seeking advice on the gold or oil markets, Munk must undoubtedly be hoping the new big name addition to the board will grease the wheels of a recent foray into Germany. Horsham owns 195 hectares on the outskirts of Berlin which it wants to turn into a business park and entertainment complex and has its eyes on other properties. Pohl's help should be invaluable in the search for financial partners - and tenants.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Leading Article: Italy's need for reform
DOC.TEXT: IT SOMETIMES seems to take a shock to make Italians realise that urgent action is required to avert a national crisis. It needed such a shock, in the form of popular indignation at the murder of the courageous anti-mafia magistrate, Mr Giovanni Falcone, to shame Italy's squabbling politicians into electing a new president. The insults hurled by mourners at Mr Falcone's funeral against leading politicians, including Mr Spadolini, the justice minister, reflected growing public outrage at the incapacity of the authorities to clamp down on the mafia's overlords. Thanks mainly to the efforts of individual judges prepared to risk their lives, successive crime and corruption scandals have brought to light the links between the mafia and some sections of the political establishment and the police. Until recently, corrupt practices were associated mainly with the Christian Democratic party, the ruling party throughout most of the post-Second World War era. But arrests made in the latest corruption scandal in Milan have demonstrated that the cancer has spread to other political groups, particularly former prime minister Bettino Craxi's Socialist party. So it is hardly any wonder that the Italian people have become more and more disillusioned with the old guard of politicians. The voters fired a powerful shot across their bows in the general election at the beginning of last month, when they deprived the outgoing four-party coalition of its overall parliamentary majority. The long-dominant Christian Democrats won less than 30 per cent of the overall vote for the first time. Signally failed The result was widely interpreted not only as a rejection of the old political parties - no fewer than 16 parties are represented in the new parliament - but as a desire for a reform of a political system which has signally failed to provide stable government. The farcical scenes which characterised the early rounds of the presidential election this month were a reversion to old-style Italian political practices and a negation of what the electorate appears to want. But the one positive outcome of the assassination of Mr Falcone is that it has brought the politicians to their senses. The business of forming a new government can now begin in earnest. The choice of Mr Oscar Luigi Scalfaro as president appears to be a good one. While he is a veteran member of the Christian Democratic party, his support has come from all parties. Above all Mr Scalfaro has a reputation for incorruptibility and is thus the man for the moment. Although his powers as head of state are strictly limited, he has considerable influence on the government-building process. That is important at a time when speed and good judgment are of the essence. Main tasks One of the new president's main tasks will be to persuade the politicians and the country as a whole that Italy has no more time to waste. Though a signatory of last year's Maastricht Treaty, Italy has yet to persuade its European partners that it can fulfil either the conditions of the projected economic and monetary union or the political union. It is still a very long way from meeting any of the economic convergence criteria laid down for full membership of Emu. More fundamentally, its partners must wonder whether it will be able to enforce the directives and other Community-wide legal instruments laws agreed collectively. The remedies are not difficult to find. Tough measures must be taken to bring the public deficit and debt under control, to cut subsidies to state industry and to reform the pensions system. Equally important is the fight against corruption and gangsterism. An important part of the solution will be an agressive programme of privatisation. This can only be done by a strong government, requiring a radical reform of the present electoral system. The fundamental condition for achieving all this is political will, which has so far been lacking. That resolution may now be provided by pressure from a people who seem finally to have had enough of political instability and corruption. Italy's politicians must be made to understand that there is no room for further procrastination.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Arts: Jenufa - Opera at Glyndebourne
DOC.TEXT: Glyndebourne brings back its 1989 production of Jenufa. Three years ago it was already a noble achievement; now it must be deemed one of the festival's unarguable triumphs, superlatively well sung, played, acted and conducted - an experience of 'small-house' Janacek opera, close-meshed in ensemble, that proves almost too much to bear. Stumbling back at the end, blinded by tears and stirred to the marrow, into the civilised Glyndebourne world of Pimms and picnic baskets may be one of life's odder experiences. It is certainly one of British opera's most meaningful and valuable. The tone of the revival - urgent in momentum, never driven in pace - is set by the musical direction of Yakov Kreizberg, the young Russian making his British debut. On this showing he would appear to possess a talent for genuinely dramatic opera-conducting of a rare order. The sonorities drawn from the LPO are no longer refulgently Straussian and string-based, as they were first time round, but athletic, woodwind-dominated - lots of lyrically insistent oboe and plangent bassoon to the fore - and stamped by an airy clarity of texture that lets through the voices and allows the angular phrase-nuggets to soar. The cleaned-up Mackerras-Tyrrell edition used by Glyndebourne sounds not just leanly magnificent but fiercely right; the pulse-beat of the music, keen yet steady, is made indistinguishable from that of Nikolaus Lehnhoff's severely beautiful staging. The two leading sopranos of 1989, Roberta Alexander in the title role and Anja Silja as the sextoness, have returned to the production, to its incalculable benefit. They find in its acutely judged confines an ideal space for creating character through voices and bodies. Miss Silja's gaunt tragic radiance was from the first on the highest level of music-drama, a triumph of sweeping imaginative perception fully realised; now Miss Alexander is every bit her equal, with sweet yet sinewy singing and a heartbreaking quiet warmth of bearing. The two play to each other's strengths with glorious freedom, subtlety and generosity. When they are on stage together, alone or alongside Menai Davies (grandmother), Angela Hickey (mayoral wife) and Elen ap Robert (Karolka), all superb, Jenufa demands to be accounted the great Woman's Opera. But since Kim Begley's heroically sung Laca and Kurt Schreibmayer's trimly handsome Steva (a touch unsteady of voice at climaxes) arrive at the same full-blooded roundness of characterisation, it is in the end Janacek's sublime honesty of vision that Glyndebourne celebrates. In repertory until July 17

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Arts: Philadelphia Orchestra
DOC.TEXT: For the London stopover on their European tour the Philadelphia Orchestra brought a refreshingly unhackneyed programme to the Festival Hall. There was none of box-office-safe Beethoven or Brahms with which visiting orchestras too often shore up their concerts - the big romantic symphony was Skryabin's Second, and the orchestral showpieces placed before it were Elgar's concert overture In the South and Casella's Paganiniana. The current tour is the last the orchestra will undertake with Riccardo Muti as Music Director; he leaves at the end of the current season to be replaced by Wolfgang Sawallisch. On the evidence of Monday's concert Muti will bequeath to his successor an ensemble as fine as any in the world at present. There are no detectable faults in any department of the orchestra; the sound is supple and refined, founded upon a wonderfully homogeneous string section, with wind principals, brass as much as woodwind, of limpid phrasing and elegant individuality. The personality of the orchestra is never intrusive; it offers carte blanche to a conductor who knows his stuff to apply his own characterisations and nuances. The sound world on offer, though, is not one to suit precisely every part of the orchestral repertory. In this particular programme that mattered not at all, particularly with Muti's bracing attacks on rhythms and dynamics to add contours and life to the immaculate surfaces. Casella's four-movement suite was an innocuous start. Commissioned to celebrate the centenary of the Vienna Philharmonic in 1942, it was hardly born under a lucky star, and does little but run the departments of the orchestra through some showy neoclassical paces. In the South has long been a Muti party-piece; he conducted it in London during his years with the Philharmonia, and has preserved the freshness and vigour of his approach intact. There was a real Mediterranean tang to its flavours, intense theatricality in its extraordinary depiction of the might of the Roman empire, a daring sweep and thrust to the phrasing. It is the most (Richard) Straussian of all Elgar's works, and delivered without English pastoral preconceptions becomes a thrilling piece of orchestral description. The longueurs of Skryabin's Second are less easy to transmute; a work which never says anything in eight bars which could profitably be extended to 80 needs all the care and attention a conductor can provide. Muti gave the impression of believing in every one of its blasts of rhetoric; even the C major finale, piling banality upon banality, was given its full measure. Earlier the langourous melodies and queasy modulations had been sifted and coloured most beautifully by the Philadelphia strings; a better case for the work could not have been made. After such a peerless demonstration of orchestral virtuosity, an encore was inevitable - an orchestral arrangement of a piano Notturno by Giuseppe Martucci, a favourite piece of Toscanini as Muti told us from the rostrum, and played here with hushed eloquence and burnished tone.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Arts: Malvern Festival
DOC.TEXT: The Malvern hills threatened to ring with unaccustomed music at the weekend, as thousands of hippies gathered for an impromptu festival. This is the home of Edward Elgar and the uninvited visitors had taken over the very area where the great English composer conceived some of his finest music. By coincidence it was also the central weekend of the official Malvern Festival. As one might expect, Elgar is traditionally the presiding spirit in the hall at Great Malvern which bears his name. This year, however, the festival programme has featured Robert Simpson as Composer in Residence. Four of his works received premieres, funded entirely by the festival after other sources failed to come up with finance: a symphony, a string quartet and concertos for flute and cello. Simpson has always been concerned with the renewal of classical forms and these four pieces have imposed on them his usual rigour of form. The Eleventh Symphony is lighter than its immediate predecessors. Simpson has written for a chamber orchestra and made a conscious effort to keep the textures transparent. The symphony lasts half an hour. It is in two movements, the first slow and moody like Shostakovich, the second playful at first, then forcefully dramatic. The teasing final pay-off, in which the brooding music is swept aside with a flick of the wrist, recalls the end of the Fourth Symphony of Beethoven. The symphony was written for the conductor, Matthew Taylor, towards whom the composer was generous with his praise, but the City of London Sinfonia performed as if it had yet to get the technical difficulties under its belt. On Sunday, the orchestra returned to give the first performance of the Flute Concerto, now conducted by Richard Hickox and with Susan Milan the eloquent soloist. Of the two premieres which I heard, this was the more attractive. The flute writing is delightful, delicately balanced between decoration and substance; the structure is novel. From a fanciful scherzo-like opening, the concerto slowly winds down until it metamorphoses into an intimate quintet, producing a thought-provoking ending as the music turns ever more pensively in upon itself. The loss made on mounting the premieres means the festival will be returning to more traditional fare next year. Elgar is the likely focus of attention - bands of roving hippies notwithstanding.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Arts: Spitting contest for grown men - Television
DOC.TEXT: Does soccer sometimes seem to you little more than a spitting contest for grown men? Does it strike you as absurd that they spend all that energy producing, typically, a one-nil score? Are you appalled at the way tackled players fling themselves to the ground and go through pantomimes of agony until they realise nobody is watching? Then, like me, your first reaction to the news that ITV was stitched up by BSkyB (or Sky as we shall call it) with the sly assistance of the BBC ('Yes let's sling a brick through their window why don't you') may have been quiet satisfaction. At last they are taking away this infantile exhibition and sticking it on a separate channel where we won't have to watch it. There are, of course, second thoughts. For a start, there is a lot of soccer outside the Premiere League and, as the BBC proved when it lost the athletics and boxing contracts which had previously given it the top contests, it is possible to make fairly impressive bricks with low grade straw, if you happen to be an outstanding programme maker with a lot of experience and a well established tradition of sustaining the sports infrastructure. So, even viewers without a dish are likely to find quite a bit of this awful game still on their screens. Secondly, though the consensus is that Sky has achieved a great coup, the proof of the pudding will be in the eating: Pounds 304m is a huge sum, and not all the big sports deals of recent years have proved profitable to television. Most significantly, perhaps, the deal is the most vivid example yet of what the Thatcherites meant when they talked about bringing free market economics to television. In the very week that the BBC's top management was told yet again that it would have to cut more staff and introduce further economies to justify its claim on the licence fee - Pounds 80 a year, or less than Pounds 6.70 a month for two television channels and five radio networks - we learn from Mr Rupert Murdoch's Sunday Times that, thanks to the Sky coup, 'by next year homes wanting to watch football are likely to be paying an average of Pounds 22 a month for the privilege' to Mr Murdoch's Sky TV. Thus what was, until recently, available as cheap viewing for everybody under the much derided BBC/ITV duopoly is to become a Pounds 22-a-month 'privilege' for those who can afford it. Is this really an improvement in British life? If the deal does work, dish sales do shoot up, and Sky does bring in that pay system, two groups will presumably benefit greatly: the clubs in the Premiere League, and Sky shareholders. . . which include those of us on the FT who took up share options in the parent company, Pearson, long before it became one of Sky's main shareholders. It would be short-sighted or dishonest, or both, to pretend changes of this sort are due exclusively to the actions of politicians. The days of wavelength scarcity with the resultant automatic domination of public service broadcasting are gone. It is possible today to have entire channels dedicated to sports: anyone with a Sky dish pointing at the Astra satellite is already receiving three. The relationship between viewers and, say, football clubs is affected as much by developing technology as by politicians. However, politicians can greatly help or hinder, and it is impossible to avoid the feeling the present lot are intent upon helping outfits such as Sky. I had hoped to be able to turn from soccer to the arts, specifically to BBC2's season under the awkward umbrella title 'Commissions And Collaborations', and declare 'There, you see? Thanks to its popular base that's what the BBC can do, and does do, and ought to be encouraged to go on doing, because nobody else has ever managed to do it better, and nobody else has done it (well or badly) at such low unit costs'. But of course life is rarely so simple: 'Commissions And Collaborations' turns out to be a decidedly odd mixture. Some of its items are certainly fresh and exciting. For instance Cross Channel, a half hour programme choreographed by Lea Anderson and directed by Margaret Williams, is one of the best television dance programmes (dance specifically created for television) that I have ever seen. The all-female Cholmondeleys go to Calais while the all-male Featherstonehaughs camp on the white cliffs of Dover, and around this Anderson creates a delightfully funny ballet of the banal: the men using all the gestures of the car packers on the ferry, the women reading newspapers on the boat, the men building human pyramids the way people do on beaches. Everything works, from the music to the brilliant ice-cream colours, and above all the way in which television is exploited to expand the potential of dance. Location shooting is a huge advantage. At one point the girls, for some reason in white debs' dresses from the 1950s, dance in a hotel corridor in Calais while the boys are performing on the English cliffs: the music is the sole common strand, but that is all that is needed to bridge the Channel. Nearly the same can be said for two or three of the five-minute programmes in the 12-strong Dance House which started last night and is currently appearing each night at 7.55. Programme 5 created by Belinda Neave and Peter Mumford makes good use of television's tricks: slo-mo, constant replay, a sequence in which a dancer goes tumbling down a passage, the invisible edits making it seem as though the passage and consequently the dance are endless. In No. 10 Kim Brandstrup and Ross MacGibbon offer a 5-minute Cinderella, reminding us (and, it must be hoped, some of the other programme makers) that narrative is not something to be ashamed about. Best of all is the last piece, by Aletta Collins which, like Cross Channel, has the advantage of location filming, good music and humour. Too many of the others were made by people who seem to have been unaware that they were working in television. Had they spent an hour watching the pop videos on MTV or Lifestyle's Satellite Jukebox, both available to owners of Astra dishes, they would have seen Wacko Jacko or his sister, or Mylene Farmer, and realised that there is already a lot of dance expertise on television. In The Mystery Of Dr Martinu, Ken Russell appeared to have retrogressed to some point before A Song Of Summer, his unforgettable programme about Delius made for the BBC 24 years ago. The Billboard Project seems downright contrary; it may make sense for a broadcasting organisation to support orchestras since they make programmes, but why pay artists to produce ersatz ads for street hoardings instead of working in television? If artists must be induced to ape advertisements why not television commercials? Artists' Journeys look like conventional art appreciation programmes, the quality depending largely on the charisma and articulacy of the presenter, Avigdor Arikha being inspiring on Velasquez but Jim Dine (next Sunday) somewhat gnomic and private on Munch. These programmes do not look like a carefully planned season, they look like an odd assortment shoved together under one umbrella as an afterthought in the hope of creating extra publicity. Some are good, some are poor, and the billboard exercise seems a questionable way to spend licence fees (assuming that is where the money came from). Despite all that, 'Commissions And Collaborations' contains programmes of a sort which it is difficult to imagine will ever be produced by the sort of organisation which intends to charge you Pounds 22 a month solely to watch soccer.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Business and the Environment: Too few fish in the sea / Describing why the livelihood of New England fishermen is threatened by reduced quotas
DOC.TEXT: Sonny McIntire, an aging Maine fisherman, drew his boat into harbour with a visible frown on his face. Together with his two sons, he inspected their daily catch, then slowly shook his head. 'We put out twice the traps we used to and catch half as many lobsters,' he said sadly. McIntire's complaints are echoed throughout the once-thriving fishing villages that dot New England's jagged coast. The fishing industry, an important part of the region's economy, has been thrown into chaos as fishing trips bring in ever shrinking yields. The reason for the problem is simple - there are too many fishermen in the sea. During the 1970s and 1980s, the federal government saw fishing as the perfect way to stimulate the New England economy. It offered low interest rates on boats, and tax incentives for anyone wanting to get started. The region applauded the efforts as a way to boost a pollution-free industry. But no one was prepared for the ecological disaster which followed. Marine biologists say the situation has never been more critical, and that the bio-mass of some stocks - particularly haddock and redfish - has dwindled to less than 10 per cent of its original level. Now, the fishermen find themselves caught in a painful situation. To make more money, they need to catch more fish, but to increase the number of fish in the ocean they have to catch fewer. Despite the hard times, fishermen say they are still managing to scrape out a living, but that could soon change. Federal laws set to go into effect soon would cut the region's fishing quotas to just a fraction of their former levels. 'It could put most of us out of business,' said Joe Testaverde, a Gloucester fisherman. New England fishermen are especially bitter about proposals to slash their tuna quota. Prodded by the International Commission for Conservation of Atlantic Tuna, the US government agreed to cut its bluefin tuna harvest 10 per cent by 1993. Moreover, the National Marine Fisheries Service decided to increase quotas for recreational tuna angling. 'I just don't understand,' said McIntire, who switches from lobster to tuna during the summer months. 'Weekend fishermen could just catch and release, but we need to make a living.' Sports anglers catch some 40 per cent of the 65,000 tuna landed in the US each year, according to Andrew Applegate, analyst at the New England Fisheries Management Council. The catch has been well in excess of their legal quota, since recreational fishermen are subject to little government monitoring. Because they overrun their limits by such a large margin, recreational fishermen have successfully argued that their quotas are too small. Over the next few months, their official limit is set to more than double. William Fox, assistant administrator of fisheries, insists recreational fishermen have not been given preferential treatment. 'They will suffer more than commercial fishermen from some of the new rules, including ones which forbid the landing of smaller fish,' he says. The bluefin tuna, a fast, crafty fish which can reach up to 12 feet in length, has attracted the attention of environmental activists around the world. Because the fish can migrate large distances - some marine biologists claim to have tracked the fish over thousands of miles - ecologists formed an international commission to help protect the species. The bluefin is popular with sportsmen because it is notoriously difficult to catch. The fish is popular with commercial fishermen for another reason: it is extremely profitable. Most of the tuna landed in the US is sold for about Dollars 10 a pound to consumers in Japan, who consider the bluefin a delicacy. Since the giant fish reaches about 700-800 pounds, a single catch can yield Dollars 8,000 or more. The International Commission for Conservation of Atlantic Tuna has been pushing for more controls on tuna fishing for at least a decade. A widely-agreed 10 per cent quota reduction represents one of its biggest victories, but the commission continues to battle for even stricter controls. The reduction in tuna quotas is just one of the problems facing New England fishermen, though. Two US environmental groups, the Audubon Society and the Conservation Law Foundation, entered a lawsuit last year against the National Marine Fisheries Service for allowing the stocks of groundfish - such as cod and haddock - to fall to dangerously low levels. In response to the lawsuit, the federal government asked the New England Fisheries Management Council to come up with new rules to revitalise the fish population. The council proposed halving the number of days fishermen can spend at sea, a suggestion which angers the fishermen. In the New England fishing village of Gloucester, fishermen attended a public meeting recently where they presented an alternative plan. The Gloucester Plan, as it has been dubbed, accepts some reductions in fishing, but far less than those proposed by the Management Council. After the meeting broke up, the fishermen and their families lingered to air their concerns. 'They say 'get another job' but there is no other job,' said Daniel Sullivan, who works on one of the boats in the area. Unemployment in the Gloucester, at 15 per cent, is one of the highest in Massachusetts. Some New England fishermen call for federal subsidies to help buoy them through the crisis. Others favour the use of hatcheries and investment in the development of better fishing technology to reduce the rates of fish mortality on the seas. 'Many of the fish die unnecessarily,' admits fisherman Joseph Cracchiolo. 'They are too small to sell, and we have to throw them back in the sea dead. If we had better equipment, that wouldn't happen.' The National Marine Fisheries Service, however, believes hatcheries would be ineffectual. Moreover, they warn that tighter fishing quotas could be in the pipeline. Most fishermen know that something needs to be done. But they worry that if they cut back further, they will be forced to get out of the business altogether. For many, who have been in fishing families for four or even five generations, the thought is painful. 'It's a way of life,' said McIntire, whose great-grandfather, grandfather and father forged a living as fishermen off Maine. 'I just hope that whatever happens, it will be fair.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Business and the Environment: Phosphates aim for clean bill of health
DOC.TEXT: Phosphates, thought to be environmentally criminal ingredients in detergents, might get a reprieve if efforts to clear their name are successful. Initial concern about phosphates in detergents - which act primarily as a water softener - dates back to the late 1960s when Lake Erie in the US 'bloomed' with an unusually strong growth of algae. Detergents were blamed. Similar blooms now occur throughout the world and are part of a process called eutrophication (rich in nutrients). These blooms have been blamed on unusually high amounts of phosphates getting into rivers and lakes via sewage systems and from farms. The algae consume the oxygen in the water and deny it to other water life, such as fish, which then die. Sometimes the algae rot and can be poisonous if eaten by animals. Most 'green' detergents exclude phosphates and declare this on the label. The phosphates are replaced with higher levels of surfactants (the cleaning agent) or alternatives are used. Italy and Switzerland have banned phosphates from household detergents but the UK government has called for more research before it makes up its mind on the subject. In Stockholm, on the other hand, city authorities encourage citizens to use detergents that contain phosphates. At the heart of the argument is the EC's directive on municipal wastewater treatment which should be implemented by 1998. This stipulates that sewage works in areas suffering from eutrophication must install strippers to remove most of the phosphates from the treated water. Phosphate supporters argue that detergent-based phosphates contribute only a small amount to the total quantity of phosphates in the water supply. Most comes from agriculture and other constituents of sewage. Furthermore, the substance is more efficient than alternatives. Zeolite, a substitute, tends to form a sludge which can reduce the efficiency of sewage works. If phosphates in sewage can be removed by stripping - and possibly re-used as a fertiliser - then it makes sense to use the substance in detergents. This argument is backed by evidence which shows that phosphate bans in Switzerland and Italy have not solved those countries' eutrophication problems. The amount of detergent used in Switzerland has increased since the phosphate ban because householders have used more to compensate for reduced cleaning power. Those who argue against phosphates say the EC directive will take nearly a decade to be implemented and then strippers will only be sited in some areas. They point to evidence gathered by the National Rivers Authority in the UK which identifies eutrophication as a big problem in an area of southern England which was previously unaffected. There is no clear winner in the argument. The UK government commissioned a report on the issue which concluded that there was insufficient evidence to ban phosphates. The government then consulted industry and environment groups and found little agreement on the issue. It commissioned more research and allowed manufacturers to continue using phosphates. But environment groups have, for the most part, abandoned phosphates as a campaign issue. Most of the confrontation on the subject is now taking place within the industry. Last year in France, for example, Rhone-Poulenc, a chemicals group, took Henkel to court for promoting its phosphate-free detergent, Le Chat, as good for the environment. The court found in Rhone-Poulenc's favour and fined Henkel FFr150,000 (Pounds 15,000) for each infringement of the judgment.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Scotland gains a voice of its own in Brussels
DOC.TEXT: SCOTLAND yesterday gained representation in Brussels when Mr Ian Lang, the Scottish secretary, launched a body designed to help Scottish organisations and businesses make the most of the European Community. Scotland Europa is a hybrid - neither the embassy of an independent Scotland nor the official representative office of a European region, but a subsidiary of Scottish Enterprise, the official development body. It is a joint venture between the public and private sectors and is expected to pay its way from fees and rent within three years. Although Scotland Europa houses representatives of Scottish Enterprise, the main job of its chief executive - Mr Grant Baird, a canny 49-year-old who was until recently chief economist of the Royal Bank of Scotland - is to act for the members he signs up. They include bodies such as Glasgow Chamber of Commerce, Edinburgh University and the Scottish Trade Union Congress, and companies, of which the first three to sign up are ScottishPower, Scottish Hydro-Electric and Glasgow-based BP Exploration. The organisation is the product of several years of argument about how Scotland should best be represented in the EC without infringing the prerogatives of the Foreign Office and arousing the anxieties of the Treasury about costly duplication of facilities. About 35 European regions already have offices in Brussels to keep abreast of developments in the EC and lobby for their interests. The most influential are said to be those of the German Lander, which report back to the Land governments and legislatures. The UK government decided that Scotland could not have a regional office because of its status as part of the UK, which is a unitary state. Germany, on the other hand, is a federation. The Scottish Office makes its representations in Brussels through the UK's permanent representative office in Brussels, UKREP, which is part of the Foreign Office. Even Mr Bruce Millan, the former Labour Scottish MP who is the EC regional development commissioner, said yesterday that this was the right way for Scotland to deal with the Commission. He admitted, though, that he would personally prefer Scotland to have its own devolved parliament and thus separate representation in Brussels. Some observers of regional activities in Brussels have warned that Scotland Europa, because it lacks the status of an official government body in Brussels, will lack influence when it tries to fulfil its aim of trying to increase the flow of EC funds to Scotland. Yet even before the setting up of Scotland Europa, whose creation follows hard on the heels of Brussels offices for Northern Ireland and Wales, Scots had been effective in obtaining EC funds. Strathclyde Regional Council, Scotland's largest local authority, has had an office in Brussels for several years and is at present coming towards the end of implementing a Pounds 300m programme of regional aid. The Highlands and Islands are dotted with European flags denoting EC-funded projects. The idea is that as Scotland Europa gains more members - it has about 20, with a further 10 being courted - it will become the centre of a network of intelligence on the likely effects for Scotland of what is going on in the Community. Members of Scotland Europa can purchase Mr Baird's time, depending on the level of their subscriptions, to investigate new Commission proposals and make representations about them. He admits that his agenda will largely be dictated by his clients rather than following a predetermined strategy. However, in one sense there is already a network of intelligence-gathering on Scottish interests in Brussels. Scotland Europa is handing out a booklet with the names, positions and telephone numbers of all Scots known to be working in the Commission and the Belgian capital. With cheerful allusions to the Mafia, it calls the network Scotia Nostra.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Pounds 8m grant to Tayside Region
DOC.TEXT: THE EC's Regional Development Fund announced an Pounds 8m grant to the Tayside Region, centred on Dundee, yesterday to top up Pounds 3.5m private funding and Pounds 13m from central and local government. The Tayside programme is designed to promote jobs, transport links and businesses.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / A matter of striking a balance: The new trade minister discusses his objectives
DOC.BYLINE: By DAVID DODWELL andAND RALPH ATKINS
DOC.TEXT: MR Richard Needham, the new trade minister, is anxious to deflect criticism of Britain's export performance. He treads a balanced path between reassuring businessmen worried by trade deficits and avoiding overt backing for a more interventionist government policy. After a month in his job, the new man at the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) is sufficiently astute not to criticise his predecessors but believes that in promoting UK exports there has to be a more constructive relationship between the DTI and industrialists. It would be churlish to make too much of the fact that his predecessors made similar noises and made light of the steady deterioration in relations with industry. Yesterday Mr Needham faced top exporters concerned at the lack of support and frustrated by the government's preference for seemingly endless bright public-relations ploys - such as last September's export initiative to Venezuela, or the Kuwait 'task force' aimed at winning business after the Gulf war. Exporters would rather have help on export finance or the use of more aid funds to boost exports. Britain's export performance is not as bad as critics claim, Mr Needham says. The long-term decline in Britain's share of world trade has stabilised. The UK exports the equivalent of Pounds 1,800 a person a year. Japan manages only Pounds 1,000. The volume of UK exports has grown significantly faster in the last year than many other leading industrial countries. 'That gives us a base on which we can build,' he says. When he was Ulster's economy minister he was regarded as interventionist, a charge he does not deny, but he rejects any suggestion that he wants a greater injection of public money into industry, talking instead of working in 'partnership'. While his statements suffer from cliche, he does strive to give them substance. 'What the DTI can do . . . in many parts of the world is to work together with industry to ensure that if there are orders out there, that they are got by us.' Support should not just be forthcoming in officially sponsored export drives but also when the DTI negotiates on the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, within the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development or on the European single market, he says. The government, he adds, should be seen to be backing winners and encourage industry 'to feel that they have got that backing. That 'backing winners' principle is going to be very important.' He was unwilling to offer any pledges to increase the support that government gives to exporters to sell goods in volatile or difficult markets. UK industrialists complain regularly about the limited availability of medium and long-term export-credit cover and the high cost of export-credit insurance premiums, which they regard as unfair handicaps on exports. Yet there is not even a hint that Mr Needham will try to meet their complaints. He is sympathetic, if uncompromising. 'Not everyone is going to get what they want, but at least if you have a partnership and there is a large degree of trust and confidence it is much easier, in those circumstances when things don't always go right, to ride the squalls.' Such backing for exporters extends to spending time on helping to restore the image of industry and selling the idea of industrial benefits to young people. 'The last great exposition of British industrial might was in 1851 . . . Ever since then, the whole atmosphere and attitude of the establishment towards industry has declined, right through the education system, through the Civil Service, through the professions and so on. Now I believe that that is starting to come back.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Needham issues pledge to exporters
DOC.TEXT: THE PROMISE of a fresh dialogue between the government and exporters about how to improve the performance of British exports was made yesterday as a six-strong delegation from the British Exporters' Association (Bexa) met Mr Richard Needham, the trade minister. Mr Needham agreed to meet the exporters in three months' time to update them on what the government was doing and to hear their concerns. The Department of Trade and Industry said the new minister found the meeting 'helpful and useful'. Bexa said it believed that the dialogue would 'lead to a comprehensive understanding of our mutual objectives in maintaining and developing the international competitiveness of the UK export industry, for the overall benefit of the country's economy'. The delegation was led by Mr Keith Johnson, the chairman of its industry section. The association said it had not previously had a dialogue with ministers. Differences between exporters and the government were consistently highlighted last year over the government's sale of the insurance services group, the short-term credit insurance arm of the Export Credits Guarantee Department. More generally, exporters have expressed a view that the UK government is not doing as much as its foreign counterparts to promote British exports. Earlier this month, a memorandum from Bexa warning ministers of the risk that the UK was turning into 'a screwdriver-assembly economy' was leaked to the Labour party. While just a general and introductory discussion, yesterday's meeting still focused on export services provided by the government, including the role of the continuing ECGD. In the past few years, trade ministers have often committed themselves to listening to, and working in partnership with, British industry, while in practice relations have become progressively worse.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Government retreats on teacher training plans
DOC.TEXT: THE GOVERNMENT has partly retreated from controversial proposals to shift secondary-level teacher training in England and Wales from training institutions to schools. Mr John Patten, education secretary, yesterday announced modifications to plans by his predecessor, Mr Kenneth Clarke (now home secretary), to impose a 20 per cent ceiling from September on the college-based component of courses for the postgraduate certificate of education. The ceiling will instead be a third, to be achieved by 1994. That will raise the school-based component of courses from a current average of 18 weeks to 24 weeks - out of the 36 weeks that the courses run. Higher education institutions, and the government's Council for the Accreditation of Teacher Education, expressed strong opposition to the original plans. They feared that the move would undermine college education departments and impose an excessive load on schools selected for training. Mr Patten said: 'It is important to give trainee teachers as much school-based training and experience as possible, without imposing unnecessary burdens on heads and senior teachers.' He added: 'In striking the balance at 24 weeks I believe that I am setting a tough but fair requirement . . . I expect practising teachers to be more fully involved in the design of courses and in the assessment of students than they are at present.' In a letter to Sir William Taylor, chairman of the accreditation council, Mr Patten said the government would not be issuing guidelines on the amount of money schools should receive from teacher-training institutions for their contribution to courses. Universities and polytechnics, which run most of the courses, warned of widespread closures of education departments if they were forced to pass to schools most of their income from training courses. Mr David Hart, general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers yesterday accused the government of an incoherent approach to the future organisation of schools. He said ministers kept changing their minds on such key issues as selection at the age of 11 or whether to allow mass opting-out of schools from council control.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Old Masters hold their class: Saleroom
DOC.TEXT: OLD MASTER pictures have survived the downturn in the art market better than most sectors and both Sotheby's and Christie's held encouraging auctions in New York at the weekend. Sotheby's was particularly cheered by a sale that totalled Dollars 15.4m (Pounds 8.45m) with 13 per cent unsold. The top price was Dollars 1.48m (Pounds 814,000) for a previously unknown painting by Canaletto of Venice's Grand Canal looking south-west. To attract bids in what is still a convalescent market, Sotheby's had put a temptingly low estimate on the work of about Dollars 500,000. The auction contained a group of paintings from the collection of Jaime Ortiz-Patino including another Venetian view, of the Church of San Giorgio Maggiore, by the other great 18th-century recorder of the city, Guardi, which sold within forecast for Dollars 1.26m. 'A Village Wedding Dance', by Pieter Brueghel the Younger sold for Dollars 577,500 and another 'lost' painting, 'Boethius and Philosophy', by the 17th-century Italian artist Mattia Preti, which carried a Dollars 60,000 estimate, sold for Dollars 506,000. Sotheby's noticed stronger buying from private American collectors. All told, Sotheby's raised Dollars 29.4m for Mr Ortiz-Patino from its auctions of furniture, silver and paintings from his collection. That comfortably exceeded its pre-sale estimate of Dollars 22m. Christie's main achievement in its Old Masters auction was selling all 31 paintings offloaded as surplus stock by the J. Paul Getty Museum in Malibu, California. They totalled Dollars 3.33m. Top price in the sale was 'The Bathers' by Francois Le Moyne, which had been estimated at Dollars 60,000 but which sold to a London dealer for Dollars 451,000.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Jaguar to introduce three-year warranties
DOC.TEXT: JAGUAR is preparing to sharpen competition in UK and continental European luxury car markets by introducing three-year, 60,000-mile warranties from June 1. Such warranties have been standard since the mid 1980s on new cars sold by Europe's prestige carmakers in the highly competitive North American market. In Europe, the norm for BMW, Mercedes, Jaguar and other non-Japanese prestige cars is a one-year, unlimited-mileage warranty, with some manufacturers offering additional years at extra cost. The decision to launch the extended warranty follows an intensive effort at Jaguar, which is owned by Ford, to improve quality and productivity. Mr Roger Putnam, sales and marketing director, said that the move would give Jaguar 'an important advantage over our competitors' in the UK and on the Continent. BMW (GB) said last night that the company would be studying the move but gave no indication that it might alter its own warranty terms. Japanese manufacturers such as Toyota and Mitsubishi already offer two or three-year warranties throughout Europe. The warranty move comes as Jaguar has begun returning to a five-day working week on its saloon car lines.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Violence sparks fears of summer rioting: The background to clashes with the police in Coventry
DOC.TEXT: POLICE in Coventry are analysing extensive video footage and expect over the next few days to make more arrests after a series of clashes with youths a fortnight ago and over the three days of the holiday weekend. So far, 75 arrests have been made. Outbreaks of violence in Coventry, involving the stoning of police, attacks on fire engines, the use of petrol bombs, arson and stealing, have aroused fears in the Midlands and elsewhere that UK cities may be poised for a lawless summer. Mr Robert Ainsworth, Labour MP for Coventry North-East, where some of the disorder erupted, told the Commons in his maiden speech: 'Our cities are in great danger.' Mr Robert Evans, chairman of British Gas, told a recent Birmingham conference: 'Companies cannot afford to ignore the problems of economic regeneration in their local communities.' The Coventry areas where the clashes took place are quite different. Wood End, scene of the first clash of youths with police, is an outer-city council estate of low-rise homes, notorious locally for its decay in human and physical terms. Hillfields, where there was disorder last weekend, is an inner-city area where the unemployment rates are the highest in Coventry and housing conditions are described by the city council as 'the worst in the city'. The two areas have poverty in common. Although half the Hillfields population is black, neither of the series of disturbances pitted one racial community against another. Rather, youths, white in Wood End, both white and black in Hillfields, have been attacking the symbols of authority. To that extent the outbreaks were similar, although they do not seem to have been connected. The gap in time between the series of incidents in Wood End and Hillfields did not suggest that one series set off the other. The catalyst for the disorder at Wood End is clear: the police made one of their periodic forays to stop illegal motorcycle riding through the estate and met resistance. At Hillfields, there was no clear reason for the outbreak, although recently the police have been acting against drugs and prostitution and therefore might be said to have been attacking local vested interests. In both cases the delicacy of the police position was clear. The police had to be seen to be acting against local lawbreaking, if only to dissipate pressures from residents to set up their own vigilante groups. Once attacked, the police, from their own point of view, had to react: there could not be a no-go area where the police writ did not run. If the police came down too hard, though, there was the chance that the antagonism of the youths - gangs of up to 40 in Hillfields and more than double that number in Wood End - would be exacerbated, thus storing up trouble for other warm nights. For the moment the question of authority seems to be resolved. In Hillfields yesterday police patrolling was normal and in Wood End the motorcycling terrorism has abated. Yet the question of why the authority should be contested, why the youths are so antagonistic, remains. Mostly the youths are unemployed or truants. There is an established coincidence between lawlessness on the one hand and unemployment and deprivation on the other. A Coventry City Council report on Wood End last year noted high levels of family breakdown, of child neglect and of debt. More recently the council has stated that in Hillfields, a district which has suffered 'substantial economic decline' and where there is 'limited access to jobs and higher education', the crime levels 'are among the highest in the city'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Education programme at Ford improves industrial relations
DOC.TEXT: AN EDUCATION programme at Ford has significantly improved industrial relations at the motor company, according to senior managers and union leaders. Mr Jack Adams, deputy general secretary of the TGWU general union and the senior Ford negotiator, said the Education and Development Assistance Programme (EDAP) had been responsible for keeping last year's pay talks to one day - the first time this had happened for many years. Last year was also the first year in which no strike threat was made. EDAP, in which Ford pays up to Pounds 200 a year for each employee's after-work education, is run by local committees on which union and management representatives have an equal say. In the magazine of the Involvement and Participation Association, Mr Adams says union-management co-operation on the project had caused 'suspicions on both sides to diminish'. EDAP, which was set up in 1988, allows employees to study any subjects except those which have a direct bearing on their jobs. Mr John Hougham, Ford's personnel director, told the magazine: 'We have had experience of working together, of learning together, of co-ownership, of joint acceptance of responsibility, of actually sharing an enormous enthusiasm for what we are achieving.' A report by the Ruskin College Trade Union Research Unit emphasises that EDAP has not only improved union-management relations but also the relations between employees themselves. It adds that the company will benefit from easier recruitment and retention and concludes that EDAP is a model of what 'social partnership' could achieve.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / DoE predicts a sharp fall in spending on training
DOC.DATELINE: GOVERNMENT spending on the country's two largest training schemes
DOC.TEXT: Youth Training and Employment Training - will fall sharply in real terms in 1993-94, according to internal Department of Employment estimates. The cut, partly for demographic reasons, is expected and follows similar cuts over the past two years. YT is likely to be cut from Pounds 851m in 1992-93 to Pounds 845m in Pounds 1993-94 and ET, for unemployed adults, will rise slightly in nominal terms, from Pounds 807m to Pounds 818m, but not enough to cover inflation. The leaders of the 104 Training and Enterprise Councils, which administer YT and ET in England and Wales and spearhead the government's training initiative, will try to resist the cuts in the spending discussions with the Treasury and the Department of Employment which begin next month. The Tecs' main priority is to win greater flexibility for the way they spend their money. They want more money to be based on 'outputs' - the number of people who achieve specified qualifications, or jobs - rather than 'inputs', the number of people who start courses. People currently finishing ET courses have little more chance of finding a job than people who do not do ET at all. Lord Stockton, chairman of Centec in central London and unofficial spokesman for Tec leaders, said Tecs wanted freedom to offer ET training to people who have been unemployed for only three months, instead of the current threshold of six months. Tecs also want more flexibility on the length of courses, arguing that some people need shorter but higher-quality courses and others longer but lower-level. 'Inflexibility has exacerbated the funding problem,' Lord Stockton said. Tecs are keen to divert as much money as possible from big training schemes for the unemployed to the demanding Investors in People training standard for people already at work. The government is also keen to push Investors in People but will not allow Tecs to abandon the guarantee of a training place for all people under the age of 25. Some London Tecs have still not agreed their budgets with the Department of Employment for the current year but are expected to do so in the next few weeks.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Talks venue adds Pounds 5m to EC presidency cost
DOC.TEXT: BRITAIN's six-month presidency of the European Community, starting on July 1, will cost up to Pounds 5.5m more as a result of the decision to hold the Heads of Government summit in Edinburgh rather than in London. The Foreign Office said yesterday that the meeting will cost Pounds 6.4 million to stage in Edinburgh, compared with an initial estimate of Pounds 900,000 for holding it in London. However, the Foreign Office added that even had the summit stayed in the capital that figure would have been higher. The decision by Mr John Major, the prime minister, to hold the EC leaders' summit in Edinburgh was taken in the run-up to the general election with the aim of reinforcing his adherence to the Union with Scotland. A large part of the extra cost for staging the meeting in the Scottish capital will come from renovating Holyroodhouse, where the talks will be held. The cost of different locations has been taken into account by the Foreign Office in deciding on venues for the other council meetings and informal talks, all of which are expected to be held in London. A further Pounds 3.4 million has been set aside to cover the costs of the six-month presidency.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Coal advisers
DOC.TEXT: BRITISH COAL said last night it intended 'at the appropriate time' to appoint Samuel Montagu, the merchant bank, as financial advisers over government plans to privatise it.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Prince issues defence warning
DOC.TEXT: THE Prince of Wales has issued a veiled warning over the extent of defence cuts. In a foreword to an officially sanctioned book about the British Army in the Gulf, he says that the armed forces face their most profound changes for 40 years and hopes Britain will always be able to help others in a crisis. The Shield and the Sabre. Nigel Pearce. HMSO. Pounds 19.95.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Security design urged for buildings
DOC.TEXT: POLICE yesterday launched a campaign to incorporate crime prevention into the design of commercial buildings. Secured by Design, an initiative that originally applied only to new residential properties, has been extended to new and renovated commercial properties. Last year there were 550,000 commercial and 600,000 domestic burglaries but police say that simple measures, such as good lighting for footpaths and car parks, can deter burglars. Properties that meet police guidelines will be able to have the Secured by Design logo used as a selling point.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Lib Dems seek water statement
DOC.TEXT: THE LIBERAL Democrats are to urge Mr Michael Howard, environment secretary, to make a Commons statement on the drought when parliament returns next week. Mr Simon Hughes, the party's environment spokesman, said an average of 20 per cent of total water supply leaked away before reaching customers' taps. His comments came after Mr Howard announced a review of water use. Lex, Page 20

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Little sign of revival in house lending
DOC.TEXT: THERE IS little sign of a revival in the housing market, according to lending figures produced by the Building Societies Association, Philip Coggan writes. Although evidence from estate agents had suggested that confidence in the housing market had improved since the general election, the April lending figures, which included three post-election weeks, were lower than those for March. Mr Mark Boleat, director general of the Building Societies Association, said: 'The fall back indicates that buyer confidence has not yet been fully restored to the housing market. There is evidence that the general election had a temporary depressing effect on activity.' On the savings side, the building societies had net receipts of Pounds 212m last month, after an outflow of Pounds 172m in March. Mr Boleat said those figures were 'relatively low' for a month that was usually favourable for building societies. The April inflow last year was Pounds 1.337bn. Gross mortgage lending was Pounds 2.988bn, Pounds 133m lower than in March and down from Pounds 3.308bn in April 1991. Net new commitments were Pounds 2.764bn, compared with Pounds 3.456bn in March and Pounds 3.530bn in April 1991. Mr John Wriglesworth, building societies analyst at stockbroker UBS Phillips & Drew, said the savings figures were 'terrible', adding that 'it looks as though 1992 is going to be the year for societies to struggle to get retail receipts'. He added that he had evidence to suggest the market had picked up in May.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Leader of Names attacks militants
DOC.TEXT: MR PETER NUTTING, a prominent Names' leader and a member of Lloyd's Council, the insurance market's governing body, yesterday launched a ferocious attack on more militant Names' leaders. Mr Nutting, who earlier this year led a successful campaign for compensation by nearly 1,000 Outhwaite Names, resigned his chairmanship of the Lloyd's Names Association's Working Party on Friday. He said: 'It is becoming increasingly apparent that some leaders and members of the committees of some action groups are involved in a highly organised and well orchestrated campaign of vilification against Lloyd's, its council and most of those who earn their living on the market.' Mr Nutting is particularly critical of legal efforts by Names - individuals whose assets back underwriting - that are designed to win injunctions to prevent Lloyd's drawing down their deposits in order to pay insurance losses. He said such action 'strikes at the foundations of Lloyd's'. Although UK Names have so far been unsuccessful in two separate efforts to win injunctions, an American Name was granted an injunction by a Denver court last week. The Lloyd's Names Association Working party has been involved in discussions with Lloyd's about a bail-out scheme to help Names facing severe underwriting losses. However, it has not been supported by the biggest Names association, the Gooda Walker Names Action Group, which has more than 2,100 members. The Gooda Walker Names' chairman, Mr Alfred Doll-Steinberg, is backing another effort to win injunctions for his Names and has been critical of Mr Nutting's more moderate approach. Mr Nutting also says that action groups should postpone any action until the Lloyd's reviews are complete. Mr Nutting said: 'I believe a number of action groups would be well-advised not to confuse activity with action which is in most cases premature and in some cases counter-productive. I strongly urge all members of action groups to reject the leadership of extremists.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Ulster talks stalled by infighting
DOC.BYLINE: By RALPH ATKINS and Our Belfast Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: ROWS between Northern Ireland's Unionist and nationalist leaders last night appeared to have seriously - perhaps fatally - undermined the government's four-week-old attempt to resolve the province's political future by dialogue. In spite of a series of meetings with local political leaders during the day, Sir Patrick Mayhew, Northern Ireland secretary, seems to have failed to reach agreement on when to move to the next stage of the agreed talks schedule - the point at which the Irish government would take part. Instead, a sub-committee has been set up to try to resolve the dispute. The delay - which in effect means losing a week out of the 12 set aside for talks - and the apparent anger of Unionist and nationalist leaders, suggests that the initiative may not get any further. Nobody will want to be seen as the first to walk away from the negotiating table, however. The talks have concentrated on finding agreement on a devolved government in the province. The nationalist and Unionist positions have been so far apart, however, that little common ground appears to have been agreed. 'Strand two' of the talks - on relations between north and south - was supposed to start at Sir Patrick's discretion but 'within weeks' and once 'substantial progress' had been made. The two requirements have proved mutually exclusive. Negotiations on issues rather than procedure have lasted far longer this year than during a similar initiative last year, and the participants have largely maintained the promised confidentiality - a sign that some goodwill remains. Mr John Hume, leader of the nationalist Social Democratic and Labour party, urged a swift move to strand two while Mr James Molyneaux and the Rev Ian Paisley, the two unionist leaders, want to stay at strand one. Unionists have been horrified by SDLP proposals for a government in the province that would include commissioners appointed by the Dublin government and the European Community. The army was at the centre of fresh ill-treatment allegations yesterday after a clash with civilians in Londonderry. Police and army investigations have been launched into an incident in the republican Shantallow area on Monday.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Cadbury Schweppes to move its headquarters
DOC.TEXT: CADBURY Schweppes, the confectionery and soft drinks maker, is to move its group headquarters to Berkeley Square in London's Mayfair. The letting of a 51,500 sq ft building, reportedly at Pounds 55 a sq ft, is thought to be the most valuable deal signed in the West End since the property market went into steep decline in late 1990. 'The demand for good buildings has definitely come back in the West End,' said Mr Geoff Marsh of Applied Property Research, a research group. Several potential tenants were looking for property in the area as a result of a revival of confidence after the general election and a feeling that rents would not fall any further, he said. He did not expect other parts of London to see a similar revival. Cadbury has signed a 25-year lease for the newly refurbished building in the north-east corner of Berkeley Square. At present, the company is based in Connaught Place, west London. The Berkeley Square building belongs to Randsworth Trust, a subsidiary of Randsworth Acquisition, which went into administrative receivership earlier this year. It has been on the market, at an asking rent of Pounds 70 per sq ft, for about a year. Debenham Tewson & Chinnocks, property adviser, estimates that 7.5m sq ft of offices are available in the West End, giving an availability rate of 14 per cent for the area.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / London office glut worsens
DOC.TEXT: EMPTY OFFICE space in central London increased by 5 per cent in the first quarter of this year to stand at 34.2m sq ft - enough to fill London's Centre Point tower 190 times over. The proportion of empty offices in the capital now totals 18 per cent, according to Debenham Tewson & Chinnocks, property advisers. That record availability figure is largely responsible for the severe decline in central London property values since 1990. Debenham Tewson believes that the rise in vacant property over the past two years is coming to an end. It said: 'Availability will fluctuate about its current level until the end of the year, when it will start to fall gradually.' The rise in availability was inclusion of large developments at Ludgate in the City and East India Dock in Docklands, which together contributed more than 800,000 sq ft of space. Recovery is being hampered by the low level of demand. The rate of take-up in the first quarter of this year was the same as last year, with about 2m sq ft of offices let. Media companies and government departments were the most important sources of demand. Debenham Tewson expects the low level of demand to continue because it believes office employment in central London will fall in the short term. It expects the amount of new offices becoming available to vary between 3m sq ft and 4m sq ft a quarter for the rest of the year. That is a sharp reduction from the levels of 1990 and last year, when the quarterly average was about 7m sq ft. Construction starts in the first quarter of this year were just less than 500,000 sq ft, one of the lowest quarterly levels since 1986. The report highlights the poor quality of much of the available space. It says that older, second-hand buildings in fringe locations may be converted for residential uses. 'Given the poor prognosis for central London office employment over the foreseeable future, there will be growing pressure to identify alternative uses for apparently unlettable offices,' the report adds. Central Offices Research, Spring 1992. Research & Information Services, Debenham Tewson & Chinnocks, 44 Brook Street, London W1A 4AG. Pounds 25.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Pounds 1m gems in BCCI dispute
DOC.TEXT: WHILE depositors with Bank of Credit and Commerce International attempt to increase their compensation from Abu Dhabi, a fresh legal battle has started in London - over the fate of jewels belonging to Mrs Rabia Abedi, wife of the bank's former president. The tug-of-war over the collection of diamonds, emeralds and South Sea Island pearls, valued at almost Pounds 1m, started yesterday at City of London magistrates' court but must now go to the High Court for a resolution. The gems, seized by police last year and displayed in court, include a pair of gold earrings, each inset with 16 Indian rose-cut diamonds, with nine-diamond pendants and three-pearl tassels. The police seized them as part of the Serious Fraud Office investigation into the collapsed bank and were yesterday asking for a court order over who should maintain possession of the collection. They were supported by lawyers for Touche Ross, the official liquidators, who argued that they had a claim on the jewels since Mr Agha Abedi, the former BCCI president, had purchased them with the bank's money. The liquidator's counsel told the court that both the Abedis were now resident in Pakistan. Should the jewels be allowed out of UK jurisdiction, they might never return. Counsel for Mrs Abedi said the police had seized the collection illegally. Mrs Abedi had issued a writ against the SFO for their return and proceedings would start in the High Court, he said, arguing successfully for the magistrates' court proceedings to be adjourned indefinitely. Detective Superintendent Jerry Ohlsen of the City fraud squad said an order was necessary because of the cost to the City police of keeping the jewels in a Barclays Bank vault. The police had decided that, in the circumstances, their own vault was too insecure.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Collor on offensive over brother's claims
DOC.TEXT: PRESIDENT Fernando Collor de Mello of Brazil yesterday apologised to the nation for the crisis caused by allegations of corruption and drug abuse levelled against him by his younger brother. In a nationwide television and radio address Mr Collor said he was apologising for the 'outcry caused by the insensitive and false declarations of my brother Pedro'. Appearing pale and tense, he said: 'I've come to the conclusion that, however painful it may be for me and my family, I cannot leave the country without answers, without knowing the truth. As president my personal feelings must be sacrificed because Brazil comes above all.' The Brazilian Congress was still voting yesterday evening on whether to open a parliamentary inquiry into the accusations against Mr Collor and Mr Paulo Cesar Farias, the businessman whom Mr Pedro Collor alleges operates as the president's 'front-man'. The Democratic Movement party (PMDB), Brazil's largest party, announced it would vote in favour of such a probe. An inquiry could delay consideration of important economic projects. The financial markets continued to fall yesterday morning, with the main Sao Paulo exchange dropping 5.5 per cent after a poll by the Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper showed that a majority believes the accusations. Of those polled, 43 per cent called for the president's dismissal. The latest inflation indices also suggested that inflation is heating up and is expected to reach 22.5 per cent this month. However, by lunchtime the markets seemed to have calmed, encouraged by the president ruling out the possibility of resigning or impeachment and by his apparent decision to move on to the offensive by launching a police inquiry and legal proceedings against his brother for 'moral damage'. After the afternoon recovery the Sao Paulo index ended the day just 0.3 per cent down. The attorney-general has called on Mr Pedro Collor to present immediate proof of his allegations and to hand over a video tape on which he elaborates the charges.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / White House approves genetically-altered food
DOC.TEXT: US biotechnology companies will not need special approval to market food products they develop, as long as they do not drastically alter the genetic make-up of the food, the White House said yesterday, Reuter reports from Washington. The policy proclamation decrees that genetically engineered foods - emerging strains ranging from tomatoes to cucumbers and melons - are not inherently more dangerous than other products and do not need extensive pre-marketing tests. The Food and Drug Administration, which regulates most US foods, will not require identifying labels on genetically altered products under the new policy. The policy decision was expected and fiercely opposed by some consumer watchdogs, on health and safety grounds. But the White House rejected their fears that fruits and vegetables genetically altered to produce tastier, more nutritious or longer-lived produce might be dangerous. Under the policy the FDA will require pre-market testing only if products are altered in such a way that safety issues are raised. One example might be if a new product was unlike anything that had been safety-tested before.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Perot clears way for tilt at presidency
DOC.TEXT: MR Ross Perot will step down next week as chairman and chief executive of Perot Systems, clearing his way for an independent run at the US presidency. A formal declaration is expected later next month. Mr Morton Meyerson, a business associate, will take over the corporate offices of the computer services company which had revenues of about Dollars 200m (Pounds 112.9m) last year. Mr Perot will remain on the board. The Texas businessman has so far contributed about Dollars 1.25m to finance his prospective campaign, including Dollars 850,000 in April alone. He has said he is willing to spend more than Dollars 100m. So far his supporters have officially registered him on the presidential ballot in only seven states, with five more due later this week. But there seems little doubt that petitions on his behalf will get him on all 50 states, plus the District of Columbia. He had made this a pre-condition for running for president.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / US car sales exceed forecasts
DOC.TEXT: STRONGER than expected figures for US consumer confidence and car sales yesterday indicated that the uncertain economic recovery is becoming more firmly established. The signs of stronger domestic growth, together with fears of higher oil prices, contributed to a sharp fall in bond prices on Wall Street. The Conference Board, a New York business analysis group, said its closely-followed index of consumer confidence rose to 71.6 this month, against 65.1 in April and a low of 47.3 in February. Sales of domestically made cars jumped to a seasonally-adjusted annual rate of 6.7m in the middle of the month, compared with analysts' forecasts of sales of 6m. Sales were running at an annual rate of only 5.7m in the first 10 days of May. Sales of light trucks also rose sharply, to an annual rate of 4.9m against 3.7m at the start of the month. Car sales are seen as a key barometer of public confidence. The failure of sales to revive earlier in the year was one of the main reasons for fears of an unusually weak recovery. The increase in consumer confidence was also larger than expected. However, the index remains well short of the 100 plus level normal in a healthy recovery. Mr Fabian Linden, for the board, said the improved figures left 'little doubt that the economy is at long last recovering'. The Federal Reserve reached the same conclusion last week when it decided against further interest rate cuts. For the first time since August the Fed reportedly shifted to a neutral monetary stance, abandoning its bias towards lower short-term rates. More than a quarter of respondents to the Conference Board survey said they expected improved business conditions over the next six months, against less than 10 per cent expecting worse conditions.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Courts and cash tax limits of the power of prayer: Problems of strategy and finance inthe Christian Science church
DOC.TEXT: CHRISTIAN Science reading rooms are usually calm, quiet places befitting a religion that emphasises the power of prayer. But beneath the surface, the Boston-based First Church of Christ, Scientist has been riven by a debate over strategy, finances and leadership. At the centre of the US-based religion's problems has been an ambitious attempt - now partly abandoned - to build a miniature media empire. The effort, started in the 1980s, has cost dearly and dented the church's finances. Distressed at this and the manner in which those finances were being handled, some senior figures resigned earlier this year. They included John Hoagland, one of the principal forces behind the media expansion, who stepped down as one of three trustees of the Christian Science Publishing Society. Since then an uneasy lull has descended and the external spotlight on the church's affairs has dimmed. But, with three events scheduled to take place over the next month, it seems unlikely that matters will stay subdued. For a start, lawyers will appear in a probate court today, attempting to assert the church's right to a Dollars 98m (Pounds 55.3m) bequest against competing claims from the Los Angeles County Museum of Art and Stanford University. Meanwhile, the First Church of Christ, Scientist - known to Christian Scientists as the 'Mother Church' - is preparing a comprehensive report on its finances. This should reach members by the annual meeting on June 8. And there is still the vexed question of what the Christian Science movement does with its 'Monitor Channel', the US cable operation which caused many of its financial difficulties in the first place. A deadline of June 15 has been set for its sale, and if a buyer cannot be found the operation will close. This all represents unwelcome publicity for a movement founded by Mary Baker Eddy, then Mrs Patterson, in 1866. The 45-year-old New Englander, who lived near Lynn in Massachusetts, suffered bad internal injuries after a fall. She attributed her subsequent recovery to the invocation of divine power through prayer, and spent the rest of her life spreading a gospel of Christian healing. The church itself was formed in 1879. However, its early years were marked by organisational upheavals, and what emerged was a structure which differed significantly from that of other organised forms of Christianity. Today, most Christian Scientists have dual membership, both to a local democratically-run 'branch' church, and to the Mother Church, governed by a 'self-perpetuating' board of directors. The religion has long been active in the publishing world - starting with The Christian Science Journal, which Mary Baker Eddy founded in 1883. However, for most of this century its flagship operation has been the Christian Science Monitor, a respected daily newspaper with strong international coverage and a predominantly secular approach. Reputation notwithstanding, the Monitor has been the victim of falling circulation recently. It sells 108,000 copies a day, a third down on a decade ago. It was in the mid-1980s that the Mother Church started to build up a broader range of media operations. It began to produce TV and radio news programmes, acquired a TV station in Boston, and started to transmit shortwave radio broadcasts worldwide.
