The most ambitious project, however, was the Monitor Channel, a 24-hour news and current events channel. This began to air in early 1991 and, at one stage, employed several hundred people. These wide-ranging media operations required substantial subsidies from the church. Detailed estimates of the losses have varied substantially, but it is generally acknowledged that the aggregate annual deficits ran into tens of millions of dollars. That, in turn, has prompted much internal debate about the expansion strategy. Some Christian Scientists have viewed this as a justified extension of the church's activities. Others have argued that the effort was diverting the religion from its core principles, at worrying cost. In the event, financial outlays and the growing dissension put an end to the ideological debate. The church, having borrowed money from its pension fund to back the Monitor Channel, announced on March 9 that it would shed the operation. Today church officials say that efforts to find a buyer are continuing and note that representatives were out in force at a big trade show recently. However, if a new owner is not secured by June 15 they are emphatic that the channel, already reduced to minimal technical staff, will simply shut down. This complex interplay of finance and ideology has not been confined to the media expansion. Earlier this century a heavy-going book, The Destiny of the Mother Church, was written by a Mr Bliss Knapp. Like his parents, Mr Knapp was a prominent member of the Mother Church, and the book was published privately in 1947. The Mother Church regarded the work as ideologically suspect and declined to treat it as 'authorised' literature. But, under a bequest set out before his death by Mr Knapp and his immediate relatives, the church stood to receive millions if it reversed this policy by 1993. Late last year it did indeed decide to make the book available in print through the Christian Science Publishing Society. It now sells in reading rooms for Dollars 15. Whatever the real motivation for this change of heart, some Christian Scientists have had misgivings, suspecting that the Mother Church was abandoning principles for the sake of money. In fact, the funds have not been forthcoming immediately. The two alternative beneficiaries, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art and Stanford University, are still seeking to determine whether the Knapp bequest conditions have been met by the Mother Church. And there, in uneasy fashion, matters stand. 'We put a lot of stock in the power of prayer,' comments one church member, trying to explain that the very secular spotlight which has been turned on the church misreads the more spiritual approach of the membership to the church's difficulties.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Egyptians protest at Israeli air strikes
DOC.TEXT: EGYPT yesterday called on the US, Russia and the United Nations to press Israel to end the air strikes on guerrilla targets in south Lebanon which continued yesterday and which have sharply raised tensions in the region over the past week. In an unusually strong statement, the Egyptian Foreign Ministry condemned what it called Israel's 'flagrant aggression' against Lebanon and called on it to 'desist immediately'. It said the UN and the two sponsors of the Middle East peace negotiations - the US and Russia - should intervene with Israel to prevent any damage to the peace process. Shortly after the Egyptian statement Mr Boutros Boutros Ghali, the UN secretary general, expressed concern that the escalation of violence could jeopardise Middle East peace efforts. He deplored the loss of innocent life and urged restraint. Egypt, the only Arab country to have made peace with Israel, is worried that the violence in south Lebanon could escalate out of control. Fears have been expressed of a clash between Syria and Israel, although Israeli leaders yesterday signalled that they did not expect such an outcome. Israel launched repeated rocket strikes yesterday morning on positions held by Hizbollah, the Iranian-backed Moslem fundamentalist militia fighting Israel's occupation of a 'security zone' inside Lebanon. Four guerrillas and one civilian were wounded. It was the third wave of air attacks carried out by Israeli forces since a Hizbollah force last week overran a post held by the South Lebanon Army, Israel's surrogate militia, which polices the zone. In one attack on a Hizbollah leader's house, his wife and two small daughters were killed. The attacks included strikes on positions in areas under Syrian control. Syria was reported to have boosted its troop concentrations in Lebanon after the attacks and its foreign minister, Mr Farouk al-Sharaa, said Syria would have 'no option but to fight' if Israel 'imposed war'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Japan tops foreign assets league: Tokyo's net overseas holdings rise to record Dollars 383bn
DOC.TEXT: JAPAN last year regained its position as the world's largest holder of net foreign assets, despite the turmoil in Tokyo's financial markets. Japan's net overseas assets rose 16.8 per cent to a record Dollars 383.1bn (Pounds 216.40bn) at the end of 1991, overtaking Germany's total of Dollars 345.4bn, according to figures published yesterday by the Ministry of Finance. Japan held the top spot for five years from 1985, before losing it to Germany in 1990. Economists said the figures highlighted Japan's continuing ability to invest abroad, even though some of its financial institutions have been hit by the slump in the Japanese stock and property markets. The balance of Japan's gross short-term investments overseas declined slightly - by 0.4 per cent to Dollars 759bn - because of cuts in financial market investments by Japanese banks. Banks have been reducing foreign assets to try to meet standards for capital adequacy set by the Bank for International Settlements. However, the balance of gross long-term investments rose 13.8 per cent to Dollars 1,247.9bn, thanks to continuing investments in foreign securities, in direct investment such as factories, and in loans made under Official Development Aid (ODA) programmes. Taking short- and long-term investments, Japan increased its total gross foreign assets by 8.0 per cent to Dollars 2,006.5bn. Foreigners' investment in Japan also grew, with the balance of gross inward investment rising 6.1 per cent to Dollars 1,623.4bn. Foreigners' long-term investments soared 39.5 per cent to Dollars 647.4bn, as investors poured funds into Japanese stocks and bonds, hoping to take advantage of the slump in the Japanese equity market. Foreigners' holdings of Japanese securities rose 32.7 per cent. Foreigners' short-term assets declined by 8.4 per cent to Dollars 976.0bn, as investors switched funds from short-term instruments, such as yen-denominated bank deposits, into equities. The disparity in flows of direct investments increased once again - with an increase of Dollars 30.3bn, Japan's total direct investments rose to Dollars 231.8bn. Foreigners investments in Japan rose a modest Dollars 2.4bn to Dollars 12.3bn. Japan's June long-term prime rate has been increased by 0.3 points to 6.3 per cent, Reuter reports from Tokyo. The long-term credit banks and the Ministry of Finance were divided over what the June long-term prime rate should be. Bank officials said they wanted to raise the rate by 0.3 percentage points in line with the yield on the latest five-year bank debentures, while the MoF said it was opposed to a 0.3 point increase on concerns about its possible negative impact on the economy. The increase was the first in 11 months. The rate was last raised by 0.2 points to 7.9 per cent in July 1991.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Li Peng urges ties with US
DOC.TEXT: Chinese Premier Li Peng yesterday urged the chairman of the US-based Boeing aircraft manufacturer to work for an end to trade disputes between the US and China, AP-DJ reports from Beijing. The comments were made in the run-up to the June deadline for the US to renew Beijing's most favoured nation (MFN) trade status, which allows China low tariffs on goods exported to the US. The Chinese premier said he expected Boeing 'to make fresh efforts toward the removal of trade frictions and the further restoration and expansion of relations between China and the US,' the Xinhua News Agency quoted Li as saying. Boeing and China signed three contracts last year for China to buy 29 jetliners valued at more than Dollars 1.4bn (Pounds 772m).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Satellite TV accord near
DOC.TEXT: A convention on copyright law and neighbouring rights in trans-frontier satellite broadcasting moved a step closer to finalisation yesterday when an informal ministerial meeting of the 27-nation Council of Europe backed the broad lines of its text, writes Karen Fossli in Oslo. Ms Aase Kleveland, Norway's culture minister, said that the amended text of the proposed convention provided a basis for finalisation at a meeting of the Committee of Ministers in November. The purpose of the convention is to clarify the legal position of authors, composers, performers and broadcasters in the face of uncertainties stemming from the proliferation of satellite television broadcasting, the Council of Europe explained.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / World Trade News: US-Israeli chip venture
DOC.TEXT: National Semiconductor, the US semiconductor chip manufacturer, has agreed to work with the Israeli government and Israeli companies to establish a joint venture company in Israel, writes Louise Kehoe in San Francisco. The joint venture would take over the existing National Semiconductor facility in Migdal Haemek in Israel and develop an independent semiconductor manufacturing business. National Semiconductor would own 19.9 per cent of the proposed entity, while the government of Israel would own 26 per cent. A consortium of Israeli electronics companies would own the remaining 54.1 per cent. In a joint statement, the partners said they are enthusiastic about the prospects for this venture, and for the opportunities it presents to contribute to the technological leadership of the local electronics industry in Israel.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / World Trade News: UK and Netherlands sign gas agreement
DOC.TEXT: The UK and the Netherlands yesterday signed a treaty which will lead to the first export of UK gas to continental Europe later this year, a move seen as a possible first step in the development of a European energy market, writes Neil Buckley in London. The treaty gave the go-ahead to development of the Markham Field, operated by a Dutch subsidiary of Lasmo, the UK oil exploration and production company. The field, with reserves of 700 bn cubic feet, straddles the UK/Netherlands median line, requiring inter-governmental agreement on the development plan, allocation of reserves, and issues such as safety and inspection, before the field could be developed. Gas will be exported from the North Sea field via a pipeline to Den Helder, in the Netherlands. The majority will be sold to Gasunie in the Netherlands, with the rest going to Wintershall in Germany.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Ericsson in Dollars 42m mobile phone deal
DOC.TEXT: ERICSSON, the Swedish telecommunications company, announced yesterday it had signed a contract worth Dollars 42m (Pounds 23m) for the extension of the mobile telephone network in the Guangdong province of China with additional capacity for 55,000 subscribers, writes Robert Taylor in Stockholm. After signing the contract in Stockholm, Mr Lars Ramqvist, the company's president, urged the Swedish government to ease its current trade restrictions with China which were imposed after the Tiananmen Square massacre nearly three years ago. The company itself has arranged the financing of the deal because Sweden's public aid credit body - Bits - has not been allowed to provide the kind of credits that were needed. Mr Ulf Dinkelspiel, the Swedish trade minister, said yesterday that the government was considering whether to ease the existing restrictions but he could give no timetable of when they were likely to be abolished. The new deal for the Guangdong mobile telephone network will be implemented during the first quarter of next year, Ericsson said. The original installation began in 1988 and covers 95,000 subscribers.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Honda announces first motorcycle venture in China - The Japanese company's willingness to commit capital to the joint venture company is a measure of its confidence in the Chinese market
DOC.TEXT: HONDA Motor of Japan yesterday announced that it would establish the first motorcycle production joint venture in China, which is quickly becoming one of the world's most lucrative motorcycle markets. The Honda announcement of a joint venture in Guangzhou, in the south, is likely to be followed by a similar project by Yamaha Motor, which at present is negotiating the terms of a production venture with Chinese government organisations. Honda already has technical assistance projects with Chinese partners in four cities, but its willingness to commit capital to the Dollars 17.6m (Pounds 9.7m) joint venture company, Wuyang-Honda Motors (Guangzhou), is a measure of its confidence in the Chinese market. The Japanese company will have a 35 per cent stake in the project, with state-run Guangzhou Motorcycle taking the majority stake. Honda will also have three representatives on an eight-member board. Using an existing factory, the joint venture company expects to produce 50,000 motorcycles of 125cc engine capacity in the first year, and plans to double the output by 1995. Production will begin in August and the new company will have 1,500 employees. The exact number of motorcycles in China is unclear, but the Japanese industry estimates that there were 1.8m units sold last year and that the total number is around 7m. Sales in 1990 are reckoned to have been between 1.1m and 1.2m. Honda's technical assistance projects, which began operations in 1982, produced about 224,000 bikes last year, and the total this year, including the new joint venture, will be about 330,000. This is expected to rise to some 500,000 by 1995. 'The market is booming at the moment, so we don't plan to use the new factory for exports,' a Honda official said. However, a shift in political winds could hurt the motorcycle market, as the Communist Party limited sales after crushing the pro-democracy movement in 1989. The party was apparently annoyed that motorcyclists played an active role in the demonstrations and police were ordered to confiscate riders' licences.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Danish poll shows swing to EC treaty
DOC.TEXT: A late swing in favour of the Maastricht Treaty on European Union appears to be taking place among Danish voters who go to the polls on June 2 to vote in a binding referendum, writes Hilary Barnes in Copenhagen. The latest Gallup poll suggested a majority of 41 per cent were in favour of the treaty, with 39 per cent against.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Bosnian minister campaigns for US hearts and minds
DOC.TEXT: WHEN Haris Silajdzic, the indefatigable foreign minister of Bosnia-Hercegovina, arrived in Washington last month, he had one aim: to jolt the US out of its indifference towards the violence and ethnic fighting in his country. For nearly a year, the US has relied on the European Community to shoulder the burden of the war in the former republics of Yugoslavia. The tall and dapper Mr Silajdzic, 47, has changed all that. 'James Baker (US secretary of state) agreed to meet Silajdzic,' a US state department official said. 'Baker had already been briefed many times by Larry Eagleburger, and Brent Scowcroft, both of whom were diplomats in Belgrade in the 1960s and had close connections with Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic. Silajdzic had a lot of work to do, a lot of records to put straight. . . . Baker didn't know what hit him last month.' The official said Mr Silajdzic spelt out to the secretary of state how Serbia was trying to destabilise Bosnia's newly-won independence, and how both Croatia and Serbia were conniving to divide Bosnia. His sensitivity towards ethnic problems and the dangers they bring was fostered during his university days at Pristina, the capital of the province of Kosovo, whose ethnic Albanian majority has long been in conflict with its Serbian overlords. Before his appointment to the foreign ministry in 1990, Mr Silajdzic was an academic in Sarajevo. His speciality is international relations. 'Silajdzic impressed upon Baker that this was no local war in a far away place. He argued that the Balkans could go up in flames, involving Greece and Turkey, two Nato allies,' another US official said. Mr Silajdzic returned to Washington 10 days ago, with considerable difficulty. Serb irregulars and the Yugoslav federal army have been allowing no one in, or out of, Sarajevo airport. Capitalising on his growing friendship with Mr Baker, the Bosnian foreign minister then started swinging the American media behind him. His articulate manner, helped by his impeccable English which he learned while doing a doctorate in the US, put Bosnia-Hercegovina and its Moslems on the map. He has also won much support among the tens of thousands of Moslem refugees who have sought refuge in neighbouring Croatia. 'He is a kind man, and a great man,' said Mr Shefko Cengic, a 32-year-old refugee from Sarajevo. 'Let's hope American support is backed by deeds as well.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Polish President Walesa challenges centre-right minority government to resign
DOC.TEXT: PRESIDENT Lech Walesa yesterday challenged Poland's centre-right minority government to resign, writes Christopher Bobinski in Warsaw. In a letter delivered to parliament during the closing hours of a day-long visit to Warsaw by Mr John Major he declared he had lost 'confidence' in the cabinet led by Prime Minister Jan Olszewski. The prime minister, appointed in December, showed no immediate sign that he was thinking of resigning.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Major drops visa requirement in gesture to Poles
DOC.BYLINE: By PHILIP STEPHENS, BETHAN HUTTON, ARIANE GENILLARD
DOC.TEXT: MR John Major announced the abolition of UK visa requirements for Polish tourists yesterday and increased Britain's financial aid to Warsaw. The gesture was designed to underline his commitment to Poland's eventual membership of the European Community. After talks with Polish leaders in Warsaw, Mr Major said he would use Britain's presidency of the EC in the second half of this year to commit the Twelve to allowing Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary to join the Community. He said membership of the EC was not practical in the short term. Poland is locked in twin political and economic crises, heightened last night when President Lech Walesa declared he had 'lost trust in the present government'. All three countries are still making a painful transition to market economies. Mr Major, however, emphasised his determination that the Community should not remain a 'rich man's club', suggesting that the EC should set the turn of the century as a firm target for their inclusion. His announcement, after talks with Mr Walesa and Mr Jan Olszewski, the Polish prime minister, that Britain will abolish visa requirements for Polish visitors to the UK ended a long-running dispute between the two governments. In the past Britain has argued that, because of the large Polish communities in the UK, many visitors have stayed on as illegal workers. Some 200,000 Poles live in the UK. Many have relatives in Poland who want to visit. Complaints have centred on long delays in granting visas, excessive bureaucracy, the number of people rejected and the charge for visas, which at about Pounds 20 can be more than a week's wage in Poland. Last year 47,350 Poles applied for UK visas, and 5 per cent were turned down. The announcement was welcomed by Polish community organisations in the UK. Mr Mieczyslaw Hampel, administrator of the Polish Social and Cultural Association in London, said: 'In general we are very pleased'. Mr Major said the UK would increase financial aid for Poland by Dollars 14m (Pounds 7.7m). The money will finance small business development. Ariane Genillard in Prague writes: Mr Vaclav Havel, the Czechoslovak president, will urge the EC to speed the process of admitting east European countries when he meets Mr Major today. Faster integration with the EC would lessen the risk of violence in the east, he said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Dutch MPs vote to legalise brothels
DOC.TEXT: The lower house of the Dutch parliament voted yesterday to legalise brothels and introduce permits for brothel-keepers to enable local councils to regulate prostitutes' working conditions, writes Ronald van de Krol in Amsterdam. The new law is likely to go before the upper house in the autumn. It will clear the way for the previously unenforced ban on brothels to be lifted in early 1993.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / French charge man in Bakhtiar murder
DOC.TEXT: A French judge yesterday detained and charged an Iranian suspected of involvement in the murder of former Iranian prime minister Shapour Bakhtiar, in France last August, officials told Reuter. Zia Sarhadi, 25, extradited hours earlier from Switzerland, was charged with being an accomplice. Mr Bakhtiar, Iran's last premier before the Islamic revolution, was stabbed to death at his home near Paris. France is holding three other suspects, all Iranians.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Sweden forecasts a slow recovery
DOC.TEXT: Sweden has reached the bottom of its three-year slump in manufacturing output, but the country's economic recovery is going to be slow and weak, according to the latest forecast published yesterday by the Confederation of Swedish Industries, writes Robert Taylor in Stockholm. The employers' organisation said it would take Swedish industry until the end of the decade to return to the levels of production it achieved in 1989. Yesterday, Sweden's central bank announced a sharp deterioration in the country's balance of payments deficit in March to SKr3.3bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / France welcomes sign of recovery
DOC.TEXT: INDICATIONS of a sharp recovery in the French economy in the first quarter of this year have been warmly welcomed by Mr Michel Sapin, the finance minister, who has predicted that this year's growth rate may well exceed the 2 per cent previously forecast by the government, writes Ian Davidson in Paris. French GDP grew by 1 per cent in the first quarter of this year, according to official figures, and by 2.8 per cent on a year-on-year basis, twice as fast over this period as the rest of the industrialised world. Exports provided the main motor of the recovery, expanding by 4.3 per cent in the first quarter or by 9.7 per cent against last year's opening period. Household consumption has been more hesitant, with an increase of 0.7 per cent during the quarter. The black spot remains corporate investment, which dropped for the sixth quarter in a row, this time by 0.6 per cent.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Waigel says no to Emu subsidies
DOC.BYLINE: By CHRISTOPHER PARKES and DAVID WALLER
DOC.TEXT: GERMANY'S finance minister, Mr Theo Waigel, rejected suggestions yesterday that European Community members should be subsidised to help them meet the economic targets set as a condition for taking part in European monetary union (Emu). He also promised to set a good example of the necessary self-discipline when he tables his own budget on July 1. 'Member states need constant pressure from the convergence criteria in order for them to make the necessary adjustments at home,' the minister told a conference in Frankfurt. Mr Helmut Schlesinger, the Bundesbank president, said it would be prudent for a future European central bank to set monetary goals and minimum reserve requirements for banks. Mr Waigel said there was no mention of a convergence fund in the Maastricht treaty, which established the ground rules for economic, monetary and political union by the end of the decade. Subsidies to help poorer members meet the criteria could be counter-productive. He had already proposed his measures for controlling Germany's rising deficits, and gave assurances that his budget package for 1993 would be no more than 2.5 per cent higher than that for 1992. Mr Waigel will today discover how much help he can expect in his much-vaunted 'hard-as-nails' budget policy at a meeting between leaders of the ruling coalition and the opposition Social Democrats. The main aim of the talks, which follow further setbacks for the mainstream parties in elections in Berlin at the weekend, is to reach an understanding on financing economic recovery in the east. Meanwhile, the Bundesbank stood by its own strict criteria. Mr Otto Issing, the central bank's chief economist, said there would be no change in its money supply growth targets, which come up for review this summer. Revision would undermine the bank's credibility and arouse 'mistrust', he told a Bundesbank seminar. He acknowledged the rapid expansion of the broad M3 measure, up 8.8 per cent in the first four months of this year compared with the bank's target corridor of 3.5-5.5 per cent. The Bundesbank had to bring them closer into line, he said. Even so, he added, the target was only a 'rough guide' and in the past had been met only around 50 per cent of the time. However, according to Mr Hans Tietmeyer, the bank's vice-president, expansion of the money stock and the current 'far too high' rate of inflation ruled out any interest rate reductions 'in the foreseeable future'. Speaking in Singapore on Monday night, he said an inflation rate of 2 per cent must again become the benchmark for the next few years. Recent pay deals of around 6 per cent were still not satisfactory in terms of anti-inflation policy, although Mr Waigel's plans for controlling public spending were the correct course. Inflation during May is expected to be steady at around 4.5 per cent on an annual basis. A drop to below 4 per cent is widely expected in July, when excise duty increases imposed last summer drop out of the reckoning.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Banks asked to provide Pounds 500m for Canary Wharf
DOC.TEXT: BANKERS to Canary Wharf are being asked to provide another Pounds 500m loan facility to keep the project owned by Olympia & York Developments out of the hands of the receivers and to build the Jubilee Line Underground extension to Docklands. This is far more than the banks originally hoped they would have to provide. However, bankers said yesterday they were cautiously optimistic that the loan package would be approved. The 11 banks, which include Citibank of the US, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, Credit Suisse of Switzerland, Credit Lyonnais of France, Royal Bank of Canada, and Barclays and Lloyds of the UK, are reconciled to honouring O&Y's agreement with the UK government to provide Pounds 400m towards the costs of extending the Jubilee Line. On the other hand, they are counting on the government to rent 500,000 square feet of office space at Canary Wharf for more than 2,000 civil servants. 'We need the government to sign up for the space at the same time as we sign the loan agreement', said a banker. Bankers have been persuaded by the government that it cannot subsidise the project by taking the space at an uneconomic rent. However, they believe the Pounds 15 a square foot price being offered is a commercial rate. The government's negotiations with the banks are being co-ordinated, on behalf of the prime minister, by Lord Wakeham, the Lord Privy Seal. A banker involved in the negotiations admitted the Canary Wharf lenders faced sizeable losses on the loans they had already made to the project. 'But there is a good chance that over a 10-year period we might recoup some of those losses if Canary Wharf is kept afloat', he said. To date, banks have provided a core loan of Pounds 566m to Canary Wharf and a finance lease of Pounds 58m. There is also a separate Pounds 450m loan from four Canadian banks and Pounds 100m from the European Investment Bank. The 11 bank creditors must at the very least agree to provide Canary Wharf with an additional interim loan facility of Pounds 20m by the end of the week if the company is to avoid filing for insolvency protection in the UK. Their plan would be to approve the full Pounds 500m by mid-June. The Pounds 500m has two elements: Pounds 300m is needed to furnish the buildings, provide inducements to potential tenants, complete the small amount of construction work outstanding on phases 1 and 2 of the project and pay the Pounds 100m first two tranches of O&Y's contribution to the costs of building the Jubilee Underground line. Another Pounds 200m is required to meet interest payments to banks on existing loans. However, the banks will try to find outside investors who would refinance individual Canary Wharf properties. If they succeed, the Pounds 200m facility would still be needed as a guarantee to these outside investors that their interest will be paid. S&P gloomy on US property losses Page 21 O&Y bank creditors post gains Page 25

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / World News In Brief: Habib dies
DOC.TEXT: Philip Habib, the former US special envoy in the Middle East, died of a heart attack on a private visit to France. Habib, 72, helped arrange the meetings that led to the 1978 Camp David peace accords.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Stock & Currency Markets
FT 27 MAY 92 / Disposal of Mountleigh UK property may take years
DOC.BYLINE: By VANESSA HOULDER, ROBERT PESTON and PAUL CHEESERIGHT
DOC.TEXT: THE DISPOSAL of Mountleigh's Pounds 400m UK property portfolio could take years, according to KPMG Peat Marwick, the receiver appointed on Monday. Mr Stephen James of KPMG said he had already received interest from potential purchasers. But he stressed that there would be no immediate 'fire sales'. 'It may take years to unravel,' he said. Receivers were also appointed yesterday to 21 UK subsidiaries. As the complexity of repaying Mountleigh's creditors became clear, bankers warned that other property companies were likely to collapse in coming months. 'The worst may be yet to come in the UK property market', said a senior banker with loans outstanding to Mountleigh. Mountleigh has two main borrowing facilities. A syndicate of nine banks, whose agent is Barclays, has provided Pounds 329m. Also in the syndicate are Credit Suisse of Switzerland, Citibank and Bankers Trust of the US, Unibank of Denmark, Credit Lyonnais of France and three UK banks, Royal Bank of Scotland, National Westminster and Lloyds. There is a much smaller Pounds 38m syndicated loan, whose agent is Citibank. There are also two overdraft facilities, taking Mountleigh's total bank borrowings to more than Pounds 400m. In addition, it owes bondholders Pounds 144m. Mr James said it would take several days to decide what should be done with the UK property portfolio. Although the property is generally well-let, it includes several development sites. The largest properties in Mountleigh's UK portfolio are the Merry Hill shopping centre at Dudley in the West Midlands, the Camberley shopping centre in Surrey and a half share in the Criterion centre in London's Piccadilly Circus. The Richardson brothers, who developed Merry Hill and sold a controlling interest in it to Mountleigh, said they might be interested in repurchasing the shopping centre. Mr Don Richardson said: 'If we could get some arrangement on price we couldn't let a good deal pass by.' London office glut, Page 7 Lex, Page 20 Interest in Merry Hill, Page 23

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Trade gap widest since 1990: April imports surge prompts fears over whether recovery can be sustained
DOC.TEXT: BRITAIN'S trade and current account deficits widened unexpectedly last month, pointing to increased activity in the domestic economy but casting doubts over whether the recovery can be sustained. The visible trade deficit jumped from Pounds 891m in March to a seasonally adjusted Pounds 1.36bn in April, the highest since August 1990. The Central Statistical Office estimated that the deficit on current account, which includes a projected Pounds 300m surplus from 'invisible' trade such as services and transfers, increased last month to Pounds 1.06bn, the biggest since January last year, from Pounds 591m in March. Imports, when measured in volume terms and minus oil and so-called erratic items such as aircraft, ships, oil rigs and precious stones, set a new record in April. While some economists said the jump in imports was a welcome sign of recovery, others expressed concern that import volumes had already recouped the recession-linked decline before any real recovery in the economy had become apparent. Yesterday's figures cast some doubt on the UK's ability to maintain strong economic growth in the medium term without experiencing the constraints of a widening trade deficit. 'The figures bode ill for the sustainability of the recovery,' said Mr Leo Doyle, an economist with Kleinwort Benson, the UK merchant bank and securities group. At the Treasury, however, a spokesman pointed out that some pick-up in imports was to be expected as the economy recovered. He said exports were still strong and warned that monthly trade figures could be erratic. The April deficits were much higher than the City's consensus forecasts of Pounds 600m for the current account and Pounds 900m for the visible trade account. They reflected a sharp 3.5 per cent increase in the value of imports to Pounds 10.15bn last month. Exports, at Pounds 8.79bn in April, were 1.4 per cent lower than in March. However, exports, although down last month, have been running at a historically high level. The volumes for both exports and imports in the latest three months are the highest ever recorded. The deficits had a mixed impact on financial markets. Shares were marked down on the news and continued lower partly because of falling prices on Wall Street. The FTSE-100 index, up 12.1 points before the announcement, closed at 2,704.6, down 10.4. Sterling, protected by relatively high interest rates and membership of the European exchange rate mechanism, shrugged off the bad news and gained against both the D-Mark and dollar. At the London close, the Bank of England's trade weighted sterling index was 93.1, up 0.3 on Friday's close, while the pound closed 0.5 pfennigs higher at DM2.9425 and up 1.35 cents at Dollars 1.828. In New York, the pound closed at Dollars 1.825 and stood at DM2.94225 in late trading. DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Yale chief quits to build US schools for profit
DOC.TEXT: THE PRESIDENT of Yale University, Mr Benno Schmidt, is resigning to lead a controversial project aimed at revitalising US education by building a national network of profit-making private schools. Mr Schmidt, a 50-year-old law scholar, is to become president and chief executive of the Edison Project, the brainchild of Mr Christopher Whittle, a Tennessee entrepreneur best known for his Channel One TV news programme beamed to classrooms. The project plans to break the mould of US education by creating 1,000 technologically advanced schools offering pre-school to high school education. Mr Whittle hopes to open 100 of the schools by 1996 and the rest by 2010. It aims to rethink the assumptions behind conventional schooling - from the length of the school day to classroom teaching methods. The Whittle schools hope to capitalise on deep-seated worries about the quality of America's state schools. A series of recent tests has shown US students languishing at the bottom of international league tables in subjects such as maths and science. The schools plan to charge fees of about Dollars 5,500 (Pounds 3,000) a year, roughly the average cost per child in the state school system. They expect to generate healthy profits by using fewer teachers and support staff than public schools and by making better use of new technology. About a fifth of pupils at the schools would be needy students funded by scholarships. The project has initial financing of Dollars 60m from a consortium including Whittle Communications, Mr Whittle's company, Time-Warner, Philips Electronics and Associated Newspapers of the UK. The Edison Project closely parallels the Bush administration's 'America 2000' initiative, which is financing pilot projects to design a new breed of public schools. Mr Schmidt will head a design team that includes Mr Chester Finn, a former top aide at the Department of Education, and Mr John Chubb, a fellow at the Brookings Institution and co- author of Politics, Markets and America's Schools, an influential book that made a powerful case for more competition and parental choice in US education. Mr Schmidt's surprise departure was the latest of several recent blows for Yale, which has lost two other senior officials in recent months. It recently announced controversial plans to close several academic departments in an effort to curb a Dollars 12m budget deficit.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / AT&T to pay Russians Dollars 60 a month
DOC.TEXT: AMERICAN Telephone & Tele - graph hired 100 fibre optics scientists and technicians from the Russian Academy of Sciences in Moscow yesterday at the bargain salary of Dollars 60 (Pounds 34) a month per scientist. The one-year renewable contract, which begins next Monday, puts AT&T among the first US companies to have found a way of using the wealth of talent left behind in the break-up of the Soviet Union. Corning, the glass company, also yesterday announced it had signed joint research accords that would employ more than 100 Russian scientists on basic research projects in glass. It is understood to be paying the scientists about the same salary as AT&T. The scientists working with Corning will research silicate, phosphate and fluoride glass, as well as conducting research into optical materials and devices. The AT&T deal calls for the Russian team to work full-time in Moscow, under subcontract, in co-operation with the 100-strong fibre optics team in the US of Bell Laboratories, its research centre. Bell said the deal was worth 'a few hundred thousand dollars', and would include funds for travel by the Russian scientists to the US on brief visits. Bell will provide funds to the Russian Academy's General Physics Institute to buy equipment for the research projects, which are expected to focus on developing high-strength fibres and metallic coatings on optic fibres. Dr Kumar Patel, executive director of Bell Laboratories, said the equipment to be supplied, including some laser systems that are a generation old, would not violate any Cocom restrictions on the export to Russia of sophisticated US technology. 'At present there is no intention of transferring the latest fibre optics technology to Russia,' Dr Patel explained. Fibre optics has become a crucial telecommunications technology, rapidly replacing copper cabling as the medium of choice for high-speed digital transmissions, ranging from telephone to computer systems. The deal includes an unusual intellectual property rights agreement. This will allow the Russian institute to retain patent rights within Russia for any products developed during the research, while Bell Laboratories has the patent rights for the rest of the world. In March, Sun Microsystems of California enlisted a team of 50 former Soviet defence researchers to work on supercomputer applications. They are believed to be getting even lower pay than the AT&T subcontractors. The US administration itself recently finalised a contract with 116 nuclear scientists at the Kurchatov Institute of Atomic Energy in Moscow to help in the development of develop a fusion reactor. These scientists are believed to be receiving around about Dollars 65 a month.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / London Stock Exchange: Equity Futures And Options Trading
DOC.TEXT: A DULL day in stock index futures saw the June contract drift lower in afternoon trading as an aimless market looked to a weak Wall Street as its focus, writes Christopher Price. June opened at 2,733, and an initially lively start saw the contract squeezed up, reaching 2,744 by 10.30am. However, this proved to be the high point of the day, as interest drifted away. Although it still managed to trade at a slight premium to fair value for the rest of the session, the story was mundane as June slid with the cash market. The poor UK trade figures added to the negative tone. A declining Wall Street, pressured by faltering US bond prices, further undermined June. The contract ended at 2,713, down a net 26, and around its estimated fair value. Turnover reached 6,361 contracts. However, in after-hours' trading, June was under further pressure, slipping to an estimated two-point discount to fair value. Among traded options, turnover was boosted ahead of expiry day for a number of series. Lasmo was the top stock option, with 3,378 contracts dealt and the August 240 series particularly busy. Hanson and Cadbury-Schweppes which also expire today were also busy. Total turnover was 28,923 lots compared with 26,595 on Friday.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets (Europe): Northern consolidation after recent uptrend
DOC.TEXT: SLIGHT weakness, or consolidation after recent gains ruled in northern Europe yesterday, but Milan and Madrid both managed to close higher, writes Our Markets Staff. FRANKFURT settled for a moderate consolidation, the DAX index closing 4.91 lower at 1,806.66 after a 0.25 rise to 725.26 in the FAZ at midsession. Volume fell slightly from DM7.7bn to DM7.6bn. The more broadly based FAZ index, which has lagged behind the blue chip DAX during the market's recent rally, actually hit a new 1992 high yesterday. Not all of its constituents were so lucky. Lufthansa, the airline which produced poor results earlier this month, hit a new low of DM126.50, down DM5.50 yesterday compared with a 1992 high of DM181.50. In a similar, but less severely disappointing category, the engineer, Deutsche Babcock, dropped DM3.70 to DM163. Generally, pre-bourse optimism generated by a slowdown in inflation in the state of Hesse failed to result in follow-up buying orders; and Hesse's fall from an inflation rate of 4.5 per cent in April to 4.1 per cent in May was countered later by Baden-Wurttemberg, where the rate rose from 4.3 to 4.4 per cent. Nevertheless, there was more confidence about economic recovery prospects and an eventual fall in interest rates; utility companies, interest rate sensitive, bucked the weaker trend with RWE rising DM3.70 to DM413.20. In engineering MAN rose another DM7 to DM397 on good prospects for the current year and, in banking, Bayernhypo rose DM5 to DM412.50 on what was conventionally put down to good first quarter results; Ms Barbara Altmann, of B Metzler in Frankfurt, said the figures were in the price and that financial technicians were buying the shares for the dividend about to be paid. PARIS seemed to be slightly unnerved by the capital increases announced by Bouygues yesterday and Alcatel Cable on Monday, with Lafarge Coppee rumoured to be in line for a FFr5bn issue in the near future. As a result the CAC-40 index lost 16.67 to 2,029.58 in turnover of some FFr2.34bn. Bouygues, FFr13 off at FFr632, was also reported as saying that negotiations between Eurotunnel and its contractors were deadlocked which could threaten the survival of the project. Eurotunnel was 50 centimes weaker at FFr37.85. Alcatel Alsthom, parent of Alcatel Cable, lost FFr9 to FFr649 on news of its subsidiary's capital increase; Lafarge shed FFr6.60 to FFr374.40. However, one of the biggest losses on the day was recorded by LVMH as the market reacted to Monday's news that the outlook for 1992 was not promising. Its shares closed down FFr110 or 2.6 per cent to FFr4,085 with some analysts saying that 1992 earnings will have to be downgraded. Oil stocks continued to buck the market with Elf up FFr1.50 at FFr398.40 and Total rising FFr5.30 to FFr267.80. MILAN extended its rally to a fourth session, the Comit index closing 1.56 higher at 497.25 following the election of Mr Oscar Luigi Scalfaro as president on Monday. Volume was estimated at around Monday's L113bn. Industrials tried to take the initiative again, but largely failed to do so. Fiat closed L59 higher at L5,394 but slipped to L5,355 on the kerb. AMSTERDAM weakened slightly in late trading and the CBS Tendency index closed down 0.1 at 130.9. Royal Dutch saw strong foreign interest, gaining Fl 4.20 to Fl 158.60. Elsewhere Nedlloyd, which holds its annual meeting today, was 50 cents weaker at Fl 60.50, Buehrmann-Tetterode suffered from profit-taking and shed Fl 1.10 to Fl 52.40 and Elsevier lost Fl 1.70 to Fl 113.50. Hunter Douglas, which announced that it is to begin trading in London, was up Fl 1.90 at Fl 74.20, while Fokker lost 50 cents to Fl 34.80 as Deutsche Aerospace said that it hoped to complete its acquisition of a 51 per cent stake by mid-June. STOCKHOLM was cautious ahead of the Electrolux first-quarter results, which arrived after the close. The Affarsvarlden General index fell 6.7 to 991.1, with turnover moderate at SKr434m. Electrolux, the white goods major, saw its B shares lose SKr4 to SKr283 ahead of profits which were about 10 per cent below expectations. The real loser of the day was the banking and finance sector, which fell by 3.6 per cent; analysts said that the decline was due more to program trading than any new discouraging news. MADRID was held up by Telefonica's surprise news, after Monday's close, that it would lift its 1991 dividend to Pta59 from Pta55. Its shares closed up Pta25 at Pta1,165 while the general index put on 0.20 to 258.90 in low volume of some Pta5.8bn. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- FT-SE EUROTRACK 100 - MAY 26 Hourly changes ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Open 10 am 11 am 12 pm 1 pm 2 pm 3 pm close 1203.54 1202.52 1200.03 1198.49 1197.93 1197.89 1198.31 1198.37 Day's High 1203.64 Day's Low 1196.12 May 22 May 21 May 20 May 19 May 18 1197.48 1187.57 1187.62 1180.66 1184.41 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Base value 1000 (26/10/90). -----------------------------------------------------------------------

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets (Asia Pacific): Nikkei falls 1.9 per cent after bleak earnings reports
DOC.TEXT: SENTIMENT deteriorated yesterday after bleak earnings reports, and share prices lost ground on small-lot profit-taking and index-linked selling, writes Emiko Terazono in Tokyo. The Nikkei average ended 350.36, or 1.9 per cent, down at 18,204.64. It had opened at the day's high of 18,519.67, falling to a low of 18,203.53 in the afternoon. Volume picked up a little from 189m shares to 200m. Dealers remained on the sidelines on the final trading day for May delivery, while most investors waited for corporate results. Mr Kaoru Shimura at Sumitomo Life, a leading life insurer, said current price levels were too high to buy, but too low for profit-taking. Declines led advances by 581 to 342, with 193 issues unchanged. The Topix index of all first section stocks slipped 11.87 to 1,371.83, but in London the ISE/Nikkei 50 index edged up 0.96 to 1,085.16. Towards the close, the Nikkei's downswing was accelerated by selling pressure in the futures market, which prompted arbitrage-unwinding. Traders said market participants have started to become cautious towards next month's expiry of the June futures. Mr Richard Clayton at County NatWest said low liquidity in the September contract could affect the rolling over of arbitrage positions. Speculative theme stocks remained firm, with Morinaga Milk Industry, the most active issue of the day, rising Y8 to Y860. Okamoto Industries advanced Y40 to Y1,390. Trust banks, which announced weak results for the past fiscal year, retreated. Pre-tax profits at the seven trust banks fell by 34 per cent, due to thinner profit margins and sharp falls in commission revenues. Some trust banks announced cuts in dividends, and investors have become wary of their deteriorating loan portfolios. Mitsui Trust & Banking fell Y31 to Y830. Nippon Telegraph and Telephone receded Y9,000 to Y633,000. The company posted a 15 per cent decline in unconsolidated pre-tax profits for the last fiscal year, and forecast that profits will drop 24 per cent to Y267bn for the current year to March 1993. Electronics issues, which have reported sluggish earnings with some companies expecting a slow recovery, lost ground. Sharp, which expects a 7 per cent decline in pre-tax profits for the current year, fell Y70 to Y1,260. In Osaka, the OSE average dipped 44.98 to 20,911.50 in volume of 12.7m shares. Small-lot profit-taking amid low volume depressed share prices. Nintendo lost Y200 to Y10,800. Roundup MARKET rumours lifted Hong Kong and Singapore yesterday in a mixed day for the region. HONG KONG broke through 6,000 and stayed there this time, hitting a third record high in four days as the Hang Seng index rose 58.97 to 6,052.08. Turnover was again strong, totalling HKDollars 5.7bn after Monday's record HKDollars 6.4bn. One stimulus was the rumour that Hong Kong Land, the colony's premier landlord, had sold one of its office buildings in the central business district for a price above market value. The company declined to comment but the stock rose 40 cents to HKDollars 13.30, and its parent, Jardine Matheson, gained HKDollars 2 to HKDollars 59.50. SINGAPORE was subject to widespread rumours that interest rates may be lowered by another 0.25 of a percentage point, and the Straits Times Industrial index closed 23.34, or 1.6 per cent, higher at 1,494.29 as turnover jumped from SDollars 70m to SDollars 159m. Traders were surprised by the strength of the market, which grew in intensity towards the last hour. This prompted the belief that buying came from UK funds. MANILA rose as the market looked forward to the likely victory of former defence secretary Mr Fidel Ramos in the presidential elections which took place on May ll. The composite index added 8.07 at 1,440.91 after Monday's 53-point climb. BANGKOK fell as investors waited for a new coalition government to take shape following the resignation as prime minister of Mr Suchinda Kraprayoon. The SET index relinquished 12.84, or 1.7 per cent, to 729.58 in moderate turnover of Bt3.9bn. TAIWAN lost ground after midsession when selling pressure was triggered by falls in many of the small, speculatively oriented shares which had played a leading role in the market's recent rally. The weighted index dropped 94.33, or 2 per cent, to 4,540.00. AUSTRALIA's All Ordinaries index dipped 9.9 to 1,674.2 in turnover of ADollars 158m, compared with Monday's ADollars 143m. Brokers said investors were waiting for today's ANZ Banking half-year results. BOMBAY had a dull day. After the scandals which have rocked Indian equity markets recently, a lack of initiative yesterday was reflected in a fall in the BSE index of 106.55 to 3,298.74. Volume was described as poor, with only limited institutional interest.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets: South Africa
DOC.TEXT: INSTITUTIONAL interest remained focused on blue chips as the industrial index set another record high, up 24 to 4,659. Strong buying helped lift the overall index 11 to 3,720 but the gold index was down 16 at 1,105.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets: Hope ascendant in bullish Hong Kong
DOC.TEXT: With hopes of an interest rate cut pushing the Dow to a record level, and the pay settlement by metalworkers and employers in Germany sending the DAX to a 21-month high, sentiment was generally bullish last week and the FT-Actuaries World Index gained more than 1 per cent. All was not well everywhere, Finland registering the steepest fall in the index. Insurers and banks were the main casualties. Helsinki has been fairly erratic since the stamp duty tax on share transactions was removed at the start of the month, and after a flurry of interest the market has retreated into lethargy. However, Kleinwort Benson's latest monthly review says there should be a further stimulus once all foreign ownership restrictions are removed, possibly by the autumn. Other Scandinavian markets, with the exception of Denmark ahead of next month's referendum on the Maastricht treaty, had a good week. In particular, Sweden is looking strong, with Astra active last week on a better than expected first quarter. Elsewhere in Europe, Italy recovered, the Comit index rising by nearly 3 per cent on Thursday following Fiat's announcement of a Dollars 2bn joint venture with FSM, the Polish car maker. The market should get another short-term boost once the political impasse has been resolved; this is now a little nearer after Monday's election of a new president. Looking to Asia, Hong Kong stood out as the star performer, in spite of beginning the week in negative territory as the Olympia & York troubles led to selling of property issues. However, traders soon put this behind them as hopes of a further easing in interest rates, fulfilled on Friday, pushed the Hang Seng index to new highs. The percentage point cut in the prime rate surprised the market, and analysts had no hesitation in forecasting that the index will soar. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- MARKETS IN PERSPECTIVE ----------------------------------------------------------------------- % change % change % change in local currency** sterling** in US Dollars** 1 Week 4 Weeks 1 Year Start of Start of Start of 1992 1992 1992 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Austria +1.36 -1.98 -20.12 +7.75 +3.97 +0.83 Belgium -0.69 -0.11 -2.64 +4.71 +1.32 -1.73 Denmark -1.05 +0.29 -6.20 -5.18 -7.66 -10.44 Finland -5.28 -0.07 -23.92 +7.47 +4.24 +1.09 France +1.07 +2.96 +13.13 +15.85 +13.80 +10.36 Germany +3.24 +1.58 +3.98 +12.48 +8.71 +5.42 Ireland +0.34 -2.79 -0.79 +0.91 -1.51 -4.49 Italy +5.21 -1.85 -10.25 +0.87 -2.01 -4.97 Netherlands +0.98 +0.29 +7.06 +10.36 +6.71 +3.49 Norway -0.26 +5.40 -12.86 +10.07 +7.24 +4.00 Spain -0.34 +3.92 -6.72 +6.00 +4.70 +1.53 Sweden +2.89 +5.49 +2.80 +15.52 +13.29 +9.87 Switzerland +0.10 +3.00 +13.62 +14.99 +7.90 +4.63 UK +1.19 +2.96 +10.63 +10.42 +10.42 +7.10 EUROPE +1.44 +2.25 +6.62 +10.57 +8.64 +5.36 Australia +1.36 +4.36 +7.68 +1.37 +4.13 +0.98 Hong Kong +3.17 +10.54 +53.64 +37.79 +42.79 +38.48 Japan +1.69 +3.63 -28.51 -20.73 -21.07 -23.45 Malaysia -0.08 -0.42 -6.79 +2.42 +13.94 +10.50 New Zealand +1.02 +5.96 -4.69 +0.45 +2.58 -0.51 Singapore -0.44 +4.01 -2.13 -1.09 +1.05 -2.00 Canada -0.49 +0.62 -3.49 -3.68 -3.92 -6.82 USA +0.91 +1.33 +10.82 -0.61 +2.47 -0.61 Mexico +0.38 -4.39 +69.39 +19.11 +20.34 +16.71 South Africa -0.16 +9.94 +19.52 +7.39 +0.17 -2.86 WORLD INDEX +1.24 +2.40 -3.12 -3.42 -2.79 -5.73 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- ** Based on May 22nd 1992. DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / World Commodities Prices: Market Report
DOC.TEXT: London COCOA prices continued to decline, second position July sinking to a new 16 1/2 -year low of Pounds 546 before closing at Pounds 547 a tonne. Dealers said there was no sign of significant producer selling. Manufacturers were also inactive. A quiet week appears in prospect with a French holiday tomorrow likely to limit business further. In contrast robusta COFFEE closed around the day's highs, also in quiet trading. Prices were aided by a lack of sellers. Caution was evident ahead of this week's producer meetings at the ICO, starting today, and there was little sign of any Indonesian selling. New York arabicas were ahead at midday. On the LME NICKEL moved ahead; the close was considered constructive by technical traders, signalling further gains today. COPPER again met resistance on any rise to the Dollars 2,240 level for three-month metal, dampening trading interest. In Chicago WHEAT held modest gains at midday, supported by news of crop damage in western Kansas because of record cold there during the US Memorial Day weekend. Also bullish was news that Russia bought a large share of soft red winter wheat in its total purchase of 860,000 tonnes of EEP wheat. Compiled from Reuters

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: Farmer's Viewpoint - From farmyard to fuel tank / Agriculture could become a driving force for industry and transport
DOC.TEXT: AS LONG ago as 1912 the man who invented the 20th century's most economic motor engine, Rudolph Diesel, said: 'The use of vegetable oils (as fuel) may be negligible today but such products could very well become as important as mineral oil and coal tar products'. The concept of using farm crops as a source of motive power is therefore hardly new. Indeed in Mr Diesel's day, in spite of his inventions, most transport was based on genuine live horsepower and the animals derived their energy from hay and oats. So perhaps it was easier for him to conceive of a similar source of power for his engines than it is for the present generation more used to relying on non-renewable fossil fuels. The question is, why are we still using up precious reserves of crude oil when we could be running our tractors, lorries and cars on fuel derived from crops grown afresh every year on farms? Moreover, if we were using such low-carbon fuels the level of air pollution would be much reduced and both the environment and human health would benefit. The reason, of course, is the relative cost. As a rough rule of thumb it would be necessary for the price of oil to rise by a factor of three or, alternatively for the price of farm based fuels produced from EC-grown crops to come down by two thirds, for the relative costs of the two products to correspond. Clearly oil is too cheap and the cost of growing non food crops too high for the environmentally attractive idea to be viable. No one would wish to see the price of oil rise by the necessary amount for fear or provoking world recession, And farmers could not afford to grow the appropriate crops at such a reduced return. But times may be changing. Last week's Brussels agreement on reform of the European Community's common agricultural policy, for instance, will mean that the prices farmers get for crops like cereals, oil seed rape and in due course, sugar beet, will be much closer to world levels, in other words, lower. The fact that there will be compensation for the loss of income should be viewed separately. The relevant point is that it will be cheaper for industry, or whoever, to buy crops from farmers and this will narrow the gap between them and fossil fuels. A few weeks ago the EC proposed and the UK government accepted that a carbon tax, designed to encourage consumers to use the fuels that cause the least air pollution, should be imposed to raise the cost of the fossil fuels mainly responsible for the problem. The proposal has not yet been endorsed by community environment ministers, but the delay appears to be only technical and to do with drafting. Assuming that this is the case, while the speed of introduction and the initial extent of this tax remains to be determined, it is likely to become EC policy and over time will raise the price of fossil fuels. Meanwhile it has also been agreed that the levels of excise duty charged on so-called 'bio-fuels' , that is those derived from vegetable sources, should be limited across the community to 10 per cent of those charged on the fossil fuels they replace. Add all these measures together and it is clear that the cost gap which existed only weeks ago is now much smaller, always accepting of course that this is the result of political manipulation rather than market forces. It might not be too fanciful to believe, however, that the environment and green policies in general will continue to receive favourable treatment by governments for the foreseeable future. The community would not be treading a new path if it developed a bio-fuel industry. In fossil fuel-starved Austria for instance such an initiative is already well advanced. Farmers grow oil seed rape and sell it at government subsidised price to processors who convert it into fuel for tractors and lorries and then sell it back to them. The performance of the vegetable-powered vehicles is said to be only marginally lower than it would be with fossil-based diesel and the conversion from one to the other can be done in any farm workshop. How much the success of this venture relies on aid from the Austrian government is not immediately clear but lack of other sources of fuel was clearly the motivation and at least it has proved it can be done. Neither is diesel fuel the only one that can be replaced from farm based sources. In Brazil, another country without its own fossil fuel resources, many of the country's cars run on fuel derived from alcohol made from sugar cane. It can also be made from maize or wheat starch and during the 1970s oil crisis US fuel companies set up plants to manufacture what they called 'gasahol'. Now that the oil price has fallen it is seldom seen but the technology exists and given a favourable cost comparison could be reactivated. Moreover there are many other as yet unexploited industrial uses for farm crops. It is well known that it is possible to manufacture plastic from wheat starch. What is more the product is bio-degradable, making it environmentally desirable. Disposable nappies made from farm based starch are already being widely used in the US as are engine fuel filters and absorbent gels. They too have superior environmental properties compared with fossil based equivalents and after use need not be buried in landfill sites but can be composted and returned to the soil as an organic fertiliser. There is even a type of printer's ink made in the US from soya bean oil. Presumably it enables journalists to eat their words if the need arises. Could it be that non-food uses of farm crops is an idea whose time has come? Will the combination of global environmental concern and the realisation that reserves of fossil fuels are finite persuade governments to take the extra step, now shorter than ever before, to make such enterprises viable? Certainly it will have to happen sometime - when the oil runs out. It would be potentially disastrous if the present concern about surplus food production that prevails in the EC were to blind politicians to the opportunities that could be provided by efficient, cheap, renewable crop production.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: Ekofisk production halted after fire
DOC.TEXT: NORWAY'S OIL industry watchdog yesterday ordered the closure of the big North Sea Ekofisk oil and gas complex pending clarification of the cause of a brief fire which broke out on Monday night in an air filter on one of the field's platforms. 'We have informed Phillips Petroleum that oil and gas production from the Ekofisk complex will have to be shut down until we have a reasonable explanation for the cause of the fire. Phillips will have to formally apply to the directorate to reopen production from the field,' explained Mr Jan Hagland, an NPD official. The field produces about 250,000 barrels of crude a day, but three nearby fields - Valhall, Gyda and Ula - which produce a combined 330,000 b/d will also be affected as their output is transported by pipeline to the Ekofisk field centre. Also affected by the closure is about 1bn cubic feet of gas per day which is transported from the Ekofisk complex to Emden, Germany to supply a consortium of European gas buyers. Mr Hagland said that a team of NPD experts is assisting Phillips in seeking to determine the cause of the fire. The fire occurred just hours ahead of an earlier planned maintenance shutdown by Phillips in which Ekofisk production would have been shut down for approximately 90 hours. Mr Hagland said that if the Ekofisk closure was maintained over an extended period it could have implications for production from the giant Statfjord and Gullfaks fields, which have combined oil output of just over 1m barrels a day.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: Producers plan palm oil defence
DOC.TEXT: INDONESIA AND Malaysia are to meet next month to discuss setting an international standard for crude palm oil. The Philippines has also been asked to attend the discussions, which are in response to concerns over the high-cholesterol content of palm-oil. An official of the Indonesian Palm Oil Producers Association said yesterday the meeting would set a minimum standard for crude palm oil exports and was needed 'to counter the allegation' over high cholesterol levels. Indonesia has achieved dramatic growth in palm oil production from about 700,000 tonnes in 1980 to an estimated 2.9m tonnes last year. Exports have risen rapidly from just 300,000 tonnes in 1980 to about 1.46m tonnes in 1990, itself a 50 per cent increase over the previous year. A recent report by the US embassy in Jakarta estimates that 715,000 hectares were harvested during 1990, but that a further 400,000 hectares had been planted 'ensuring steady gains in production in coming years'. Industry officials say a further 100,000 to 150,000 hectares is being planted every year. Industry officials estimate production of 3.2m tonnes this year, rising to up to 3.7m tonnes in 1993 and 4.9m tonnes by the end of the decade. Indonesia exports of palm oil and kernel totalled USDollars 329m last year, up from Dollars 216m the year before. The Netherlands accounts for about one-third of exports, while other important buyers include China, Kenya and the UK. Palm oil demand will exceed supply for the second consecutive season in 1991-92 (October-September), despite steadily increasing production, according to the Oil World newsletter, reports Reuter from Hamburg. World production is expected to rise by 740,000 tonnes to 11.94m tonnes in 1991-92 but usage will jump 1.12m tonnes to 12.33m tonnes.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: CBoT wins approval for scrap steel futures trading
DOC.TEXT: THE COMMODITY Futures Trading Commission has approved a scrap steel futures contract for the Chicago Board of Trade. Scrap steel is not traded on any other futures exchange. The CBoT plans to make the scrap contract the first on its new electronic order-matching system called Project A. The screen trading system, now under development, will be a local area network for launching new futures and future-options or listing low-volume products. Mr William O'Connor, the exchange's chairman, said: 'Ferrous scrap futures are just the sort of market Project A is meant for'. The ferrous futures contract will for 100 tonnes of either shredded or bundled scrap and will have the trade months of March June, September and December. The minimum price movement will be 25 cents a tonne or Dollars 25 a contract. The daily limit on price movements will be set at Dollars 10 a tonne. Delivery against the contract will be made on the basis of tendering shipping certificates issued by scrap processors and approved by the exchange.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Capital Markets: Demand for Latin American debt intensifies
DOC.TEXT: THERE is little sign of slowing in the Latin American debt market, with new borrowers queueing to tap international investors for funds and bankers introducing new structures to investors thirsty for high-yielding investments. Last week, Uruguay became the latest Latin American sovereign borrower to tap the international bond market, following Mexico, Venezuela and Argentina. It raised Dollars 100m over three years in a deal lead-managed by JP Morgan. Next in line is probably Columbia. Bankers said yesterday the country was also hoping to raise Dollars 100m, and was in talks with new issue firms. Most expected a bond issue of between three-years and five-years maturity, priced to yield between 2.75 per cent and 3.25 per cent more than US Treasury bonds. Uruguay's issue was priced at the bottom end of this range. However, while Latin American countries are still obliged to pay substantially more than most European or US corporations, the cost of funds has fallen sharply since the market re-opened to them in late 1990. For example, Nafinsa, the Mexican state financing agency, borrowed at a yield spread of 350 basis points over Treasuries in 1990, but today would pay closer to 220 basis points. At the same time, dollar interest rates have fallen sharply. As yield spreads on straight Latin American bonds have fallen, bankers are designing new structures offering investors higher-yielding, but potentially more risky, investments. For example, Credit Suisse First Boston yesterday launched a Dollars 75m two-year bond issue backed by a holding of Venezuelan debt conversion bonds, securities issued as part of the country's Brady debt restructuring agreement with commercial bank creditors. Although similar private placements have taken place, the deal is the first public Eurobond issue collateralised on Latin American debt. The deal offers a high return, with a yield spread of 370 basis points over US Treasury bonds. Bankers said yesterday a new two-year Eurobond issue by Venezuela would offer a yield spread of perhaps 200 basis points. However the high return reflects a higher risk. The cash to repay bondholders in 1994 will be raised from the sale of the underlying Venezuela bonds in the secondary market. If the secondary market price of the conversion bonds falls substantially, the sale might not generate enough funds to repay holders of the new bonds in full. Warrants on bonds have also been offered to investors keen for leveraged exposure to Latin American credit risk. Last week, Paribas Capital Markets launched an issue of warrants offering investors the right to buy Brazilian 'multi-year deposit facility agreement' (MYDFA) bonds - instruments based on Brazil's commercial bank debt and already traded between financial institutions. Again, while the potential rewards of leveraged exposure to Brazilian credit risk are great, so are the risks. Yesterday, the secondary market price of Brazilian MYDFA bonds sank from a shade over 40 per cent of face value to 37 1/2 per cent, following accusations of corruption levelled against President Fernando Collor. The Paribas warrants offer the right to buy the bonds at 40 per cent. Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), the state oil company, will hold off for a couple of months on placing more bonds on the international markets, AP-DJ reports. The move is being made because demand for bonds has dropped sharply, thanks to the continuing appearance of political instability in the country following a failed February coup attempt. PDVSA is in the middle of a five-year, Dollars 48bn investment plan.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Bonds: NTT CDollars 200m issue leads activity in subdued start to week
DOC.TEXT: THE international bond market started the week in a more subdued mood, following the flood of new issues last week. However, moderately sized and cautiously priced deals were launched in Canadian dollars, sterling, French francs and Australian dollars. In the Canadian dollar sector, Nippon Telegraph and Telephone came with an anticipated CDollars 200m five-year issue, lead-managed by Goldman Sachs. The 8 1/2 per cent paper was re-offered to investors at the fixed price of 99.785, where the yield is 48 basis points more than Canadian government bonds. The deal was NTT's fourth in the Canadian dollar sector of the Eurobond market, and it has built a strong following among continental European retail investors. The proceeds of the issue were swapped back into yen. Participants in the deal reported strong buying for bonds, which were viewed as being sensibly priced. By the close of trading in London, the deal stood at a yield spread of 46 basis points. Municipality Finance, the local government financing vehicle of Finland, launched its debut in the sterling sector of the market. It launched a Pounds 100m five-year issue, jointly lead-managed by UBS Phillips & Drew and Credit Suisse First Boston. The 9 1/2 per cent bonds were reoffered at a fixed price of 99.43, at which level the yield spread over UK government bonds was 34 basis points. This was seen as tight by participants for a little-known borrower. Municipality Finance is best remembered by some investors for a debut Ecu issue launched last September which has since performed poorly. However, the joint lead managers underwrote around 90 per cent of the deal and reported steady buying from continental European investors keen to buy sterling bonds at a healthy yield pick-up over government paper. UBS quoted the bonds at a yield spread of 34 basis points by the close. Another debutante was KFW, the top-rated German government-backed financing agency, which launched its first French franc issue. The FFr2bn 8 3/4 per cent 10-year deal was lead-managed by Credit Lyonnais and offers a yield of 35 basis points more than French government paper. International investors are keen buyers of French franc assets, and the deal appealed to institutions keen for additional yield over government bonds but wary of buying of lower credit quality. By the close of trading, the yield spread had narrowed to 31 basis points. Deutsche Bank launched a ADollars 100m six-year issue, hoping to capture flows from maturing Australian dollar Eurobonds, which amount to ADollars 750m over the next month. The paper carries a 9 per cent coupon, seen as necessary to attract retail buyers into the deal, but was issued 102, an unusually high premium to face value. Less full fees of 2 per cent, the level at which underwriters owned the bonds, the paper yielded 23 basis points more than Australian government paper. Tintas, a Brazilian paint company, launched a Dollars 40m two-year Eurobond issue yesterday, despite the turbulence of domestic financial markets following accusations of corruption against President Ferdinand Collor. The deal is lead-managed by ABN Amro. The Turkish government is rescheduling almost half the commercial bank debts of the loss-making Turkish Iron and Steel Works (TDCI) by securitisation, Reuter reports from Istanbul. State minister, Mr Tansu Ciller, said the six Turkish banks involved would receive state bonds after rescheduling TL1,000bn of TDCI's TL2,200bn debt bearing a compounded interest burden of 135 per cent. Turkish inflation presently runs at 74 per cent.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Capital Markets: Fanuc shows first fall in five years
DOC.TEXT: FANUC, the Japanese maker of numerical control devices and other machine tools equipment, yesterday reported its first profit fall in five years and warned that earnings would slide further in the current year. For the 1991 fiscal year group pre-tax earnings fell 25.4 per cent to Y52bn (Dollars 401.8m). The company predicted that earnings will decline by 29.3 per cent to Y36.9bn in the current fiscal year. The company blames the setback on Japanese companies' continuing reduction in spending on industrial facilities. Net profit decreased by 20.1 per cent to Y30.1bn, and it is predicted to fall to Y20bn in fiscal 1992. Sales were down by 15.6 per cent to Y155.8bn, reflecting a 20 per cent fall in orders. Fanuc expects a further 9.4 per cent decrease in turnover in fiscal 1992 largely due to the sluggish Japanese economy. Shiseido, the cosmetics company, posted a 7 per cent rise in consolidated sales to Y553.3bn for the year to end-March, on strong demand of higher value cosmetics and hair treatment products.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Equity Issues: Reliance offering a test case
DOC.TEXT: INVESTORS in the emerging markets will be keeping a close eye on the Dollars 100m international equity offering from Reliance, the Indian petrochemical company, as a handful of other Indian companies prepare to raise funds in the international markets. The Reliance equity offering was due to be priced either late last night or in the next couple of days. The shares are expected to be priced at about Rs250, (the lower end of the pricing range) compared with the closing price of Rs300 in Bombay yesterday. The Reliance equity offering marks the first time that foreign investors have been allowed to invest in a share offering by an Indian company. However, there are three other Indian companies hoping to launch international offerings within the next couple of months. Grasim, a cement and fibre producer controlled by the Birla family, is expected to launch its Dollars 100m offering around the middle of June, with Citicorp and Merrill Lynch as the joint lead managers. Also in the pipeline are share offerings of about Dollars 100m each from Essar Gujarat, an iron company, and Tata Iron and Steel (TISCO), India's largest private steel manufacturer. Merrill Lynch is lead manager for Essar Gujarat, and Credit Suisse First Boston has been appointed lead manager for the Tisco deal. The Reliance issue has attracted strong interest, particularly from Asian funds, despite the current stock market scandal in India. 'Fund managers don't want to miss out on this issue,' said one London banker. 'People will be learning about the Indian market with Reliance.' However, some investment bankers warn that India could suffer if it ends up as the latest 'vogue' emerging market. 'Investors have been so country-of-the-week oriented,' complained one US banker. 'The foreign investors just want to be first-in and first-out.' While bankers expect the Reliance issue to be a success and comfortably over-subscribed, most will be watching to see whether investors hold the shares long-term in their portfolios or whether they simply take their profits and run.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Capital Markets: HK, Canadian groups to buy Novatel assets
DOC.TEXT: NORTHERN TELECOM, the Canadian telephone equipment maker, and Hong Kong's Techtronic International are expanding their cellular business by separately buying most of the assets of Novatel Communications, the troubled group owned by the province of Alberta. Novatel, which is one of North America's leading cellular equipment suppliers, has been a heavy burden on Alberta taxpayers. The two buyers will pay a total of CDollars 66.8m (Dollars 56m) but the provincial government estimates its total investment in Novatel at CDollars 566m. Northern Telecom will pay CDollars 38m for Novatel's cellular radio systems division, including installations in North and South America, and the Caribbean. The company has also promised to convert one of Novatel's two factories into a wireless research centre in Calgary.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Sumitomo Heavy ahead 5.6% at pre-tax level
DOC.TEXT: SUMITOMO Heavy Industries, a leading Japanese shipbuilder and steelmaker, posted a non-consolidated 5.6 per cent increase in pre-tax profits to Y4.23bn (Dollars 32.8m) for the year to end-March. Gains in financial items accounted for the rise at the pre-tax level. However, the company suffered its first drop in operating profits in four years as a result of higher costs, with a decline of 14.3 per cent to Y11.8bn related to products sold. The value of Sumitomo Heavy's short-term securities portfolio plunged Y41.9bn to Y93.7bn. Net profits were off 13.6 per cent at Y3.5bn because of an extraordinary loss resulting from suspended printing machine manufacturing and sales activities.
