The company, which no longer counts shipbuilding as its main activity, has diversified into construction, cargo handling and injection molding. It delivered six mid-sized ships during the period. Machinery sales declined 1.9 per cent to Y81.5bn, while orders were up 4.8 per cent at Y91.9bn. Shipbuilding, steel frame and defence equipment sales were off 1.4 per cent at Y86.8bn, and orders fell 47.1 per cent to Y68bn. Standardised and mass-production machinery turnover fell 2.8 per cent to Y80bn and orders declined 10.3 per cent to Y72bn. Quantum and other equipment sales jumped 87.6 per cent to Y38.8bn and orders by 76.3 per cent to Y48.6bn. This year, Sumitomo Heavy expects sales to rise 4.5 per cent to Y300bn, while pre-tax profits are expected to slip 6 per cent to Y4bn and net profits by 28 per cent to Y2.5bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Launch date for Sony's Mini Disc
DOC.TEXT: SONY, the Japanese consumer electronics group, said yesterday it planned to introduce its Mini Disc portable player, a miniaturised version of the compact disc, in Japan by November 1 and in main overseas markets by Christmas. The Mini Disc is competing against the Digital Compact Cassette (DCC) as the next-generation recording system with the audio quality of the compact disc (CD). Sony, which is seeking a new popular product to reverse its fall in earnings for fiscal 1991, hopes the Mini Disc will repeat the success of its Walkman cassette player, with the Mini Disc replacing cassettes in the same way the CD has succeeded the long-playing record. The Mini Disc will be the first compact disc system able to record as well as play. Sony said it would price the Mini Disc at Y80,000 (Dollars 617) for a record/playback model and Y60,000 for a playback-only version. Pre-recorded mini disc albums would cost about the same as CD albums, which is Y2,500 in Japan, while blank discs would be about Y1,000. Matsushita recently announced it would market its first Digital Compact Cassette (DCC) player in Japan on September 21. The DCC table unit would be priced at Y135,000. A portable DCC player is scheduled to be launched next spring at a lower price. The DCC technology, which uses a cassette tape, was developed by Philips of the Netherlands. Analysts believe that the Mini Disc may have gained a competitive edge over the DCC, at least in the Japanese market, because of its lower price and its compact disc format. 'The failure of digital audio tape (Dat) indicates that consumer interest in the use of cassette tape is waning, while the preference for compact discs is growing,' says Mr Chuck Goto, an analyst at S. G. Warburg Securities. The price of the Mini Disc must still fall further to penetrate the mass market, he adds. However, Mr Barry Dargan, deputy head of research at James Capel in Tokyo, believes there is still consumer resistence to both the Mini Disc and DCC systems, with the most popular alternative being a recordable standard-size compact disc. 'The advantage with the Mini Disc is that it is at least a step in that direction.' Sony said it has signed licensing agreements with 22 hardware manufacturers for Mini Disc technology. They include many of the main Japanese and Korean consumer electronics companies. Eight companies have signed similar agreements to produce recorded software and 10 to make blank discs.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Embraer cuts workforce as aircraft demand falls
DOC.TEXT: EMBRAER, the state-owned Brazilian aeronautics company set for privatisation, is to reduce its 8,200-strong work force by 30 per cent. The company's factory will remain idle until June 4, and about 5,200 employees will join another 2,600 who have been on paid leave since March. Depressed international demand for aircraft had led to the cuts, the company said. Production of Embraer's leading product, the 30-seat turboprop Brasilia, is still projected to reach 36 units this year but output dropped from 48 units in 1990 to 31 last year. The worldwide recession, especially in the US, has been taking its toll on the company. In 1991, sales reached just Dollars 402m; exports accounted for Dollars 271.5m of the total. In 1990, overall sales were Dollars 582m and exports Dollars 365m. Brasilia sales account for half of Embraer's receipts, and the depressed market was evident in the results for 1991, when the company lost Dollars 235m. In 1990, it suffered a loss of Dollars 265m. Analysts warned, however, that comparisons between 1990 and 1991 results for Brazilian companies were difficult due to changes in accounting regulations.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Japan's top shipping lines slip but competitors show gains
DOC.TEXT: NIPPON Yusen (NYK) and Mitsui OSK Lines, Japan's two biggest shipping companies, have reported lower pre-tax earnings for 1991-92, but expect profits to increase this year. In contrast, their three closest domestic competitors - Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha, Navix Line and Showa Line - all posted sharp profits gains for the year ended March 1992. Reduced interest payments helped boost the profitability of Kawasaki, Navix and Showa, although the latter two expect lower earnings this year. Both NYK and Mitsui OSK blamed their earnings declines on foreign exchange losses. NYK's pre-tax profits dropped by 2.7 per cent to Y14.1bn (Dollars 109.3m), although sales rose by 6.8 per cent to Y569bn due to a recovery in liner and tramper operations. Net profits rose 26.8 per cent to Y6.5bn due to lower taxes. The dividend was unchanged at Y4. NYK predicts that pre-tax profits in the current year will rise 6.1 per cent to Y15bn, while sales will increase 3.7 per cent to Y590bn due to its recent takeover of Nippon Liner System. Net profits are expected to decrease by 8.1 per cent to Y6bn. Mitsui's pre-tax profits fell by 31.7 per cent to Y7.4bn, although sales rose by 5.5 per cent to Y480.9bn. It noted that liner operations to Europe had returned to profitability, while losses on North American routes were halved due to increased shipments of consumer products. Net profit fell by 60.9 per cent to Y2.3bn, but the dividend was left unchanged at Y4. Mitsui expects sales in fiscal 1992 to rise to Y500bn as the liner operations improve to the break-even point with growing shipments of raw materials. Pre-tax profits will also increase to Y10bn, while net profit will reach Y5bn. Kawasaki was the only top Japanese shipping company to record an increase in sales and pre-tax profits. It expects the upward trend to continue this fiscal year. Navix and Showa had lower sales, reflecting reduced rates for tankers and iron-ore tramps. But their pre-tax profits rose. Navix attributed the 166 per cent increase in pre-tax earnings to Y3.4bn to the dividends received in return for the sale of ships. Navix and Showa expect the situation to be reversed this year, with higher sales but lower pre-tax profits.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Philips says price of DCC tapes to match CDs
DOC.TEXT: PHILIPS, the Dutch group, and Polygram, the music recording company in which it owns a 79 per cent stake, yesterday announced the prices of digital compact cassette (DCC) tapes would be similar to the prices of compact discs currently being sold, writes Michiyo Nakamoto. Polygram also announced a list of musicians - featuring Bryan Adams, U2 and Fine Young Cannibals among the pop set, and Pavarotti and von Karajan from the classical world - whose music would be available on DCC when the system is launched in September. The company plans to have about 500 music titles ready when DCC systems become available. The pricing of pre-recorded music on the new digital cassettes has been an important issue in the industry and one which many observers believe will be a key factor determining the success of or failure of the DCC. If much of the pre-recorded music on DCC is priced at levels similar to the price of compact discs, they will be substantially higher than the price of analogue audio-cassettes, which they are intended to replace. In the UK, the current price of a hit album on compact discs, at Pounds 14.99 (Dollars 27.13) at leading retailers, has already attracted consumer criticism as being excessively high. It compares with a retail price of Pounds 8.99 for a hit album on analogue tape.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: National Bank of Kuwait in profit
DOC.TEXT: NATIONAL Bank of Kuwait (NBK), the largest of Kuwait's six commercial banks, managed to make net profit of 44.2m Kuwaiti dinars (Dollars 151m) in the two years 1990-1991, despite the disruption of its operations by the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait, AP-DJ reports. The results came in accordance with directives to local banks to combine the two years' results. The last full-year result of the bank was in 1989, when it announced a 13 per cent rise in its net profit to 34.2m dinars.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Seiko set back by poor market for watches
DOC.TEXT: SEIKO, a leading maker of watches and clocks, suffered a sharp fall in profits after being hurt by weak demand for its main line of watches and at its jewellery operations The company recorded a 26.4 per cent drop in pre-tax profits to Y3.6bn (Dollars 27.9m) for the year ended March, its first retreat since the 1987-88 fiscal year. Seiko noted that consumer demand for high-priced goods had dropped precipitously during the current economic slowdown. Sales for the period dipped 2.3 per cent to Y298.7bn, while net profits advanced 7.6 per cent to Y1.5bn. Domestic sales were off 2.5 per cent at Y187.1bn, while exports fell 1.9 per cent to Y111.6bn. By division, sales of watches slipped 2.6 per cent to Y178.5bn and clocks 2.1 per cent to Y44.5bn. Jewellery turnover was off 4.6 per cent at Y26.7bn, although other items staged a 0.1 per cent gain to Y49bn. For the current period, Seiko expects the positive effects of price stability in Japan to be more than offset by continued weakness in corporate earnings and the stock market. Sales are expected to rise 0.4 per cent to Y300bn, while pre-tax profits are forecast to slip 2.6 per cent to Y3.5bn and net profits 1 per cent to Y1.5bn. Kandenko, Japan's largest electrical engineering company, reported solid gains in unconsolidated sales and profit for the year to end-March, Kyodo reports from Toyko. Net profit increased 14.1 per cent over the previous year to Y12.36bn, or Y105.82 a share, up from Y102.50. Pre-tax profit also rose 14.5 per cent to Y29.40bn on sales of Y520.23bn, up 8.2 per cent.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Tobishima in the red despite sales gain
DOC.TEXT: TOBISHIMA, the Japanese general contractor which has appealed to banks for interest rate cuts on its debts of Y1,000bn (Dollars 7.75bn), blamed an after-tax loss of Y44.3bn on charges related to the company's restructuring. Sales during the year rose 9.8 per cent to Y460.6bn. However, the company said the general awareness of its financial problems may unnerve potential clients and, as a result, orders for the current year were expected to fall by 14.5 per cent to Y420bn. Tobishima is shifting back to its core business of contracting and away from hotel and resort development, which led the company into financial difficulty during the late 1980s. Officials from Fuji Bank, its main bank, are overseeing the restructuring plan. For the current year, Tobishima's pre-tax profit is expected to double to Y3bn, while the company is aiming for an after-tax profit of Y500m. Kumagai Gumi, the general contractor, reported a 24.7 per cent fall in pre-tax profit to Y38bn on a 4.7 per cent decline in sales to Y1,145bn which followed a decision to cut its exposure in the international market. The construction industry is hoping the government's plan to accelerate budget spending, and perhaps to announce a supplementary budget later this week, will bolster earnings. Kumagai is expecting sales this year to remain at around Y1,150bn, while pre-tax profits are forecast to fall a further 21 per cent to Y30bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: ABSA turns in earnings of R491m in first full year
DOC.TEXT: ABSA, South Africa's largest banking group, reported attributable earnings of R491.4m (Dollars 174m) in the year to March, the first full year of the group's existence. ABSA was formed in early 1991 from the merger of the United Building Society, Allied, Volkskas and part of the Sage group. A further merger, early in 1992, with the Bankorp group, confirmed ABSA's status as South Africa's largest banking group in terms of assets. The effects of this second merger, which is still being carried out, are not reflected in the current results. The timing of the first merger invalidates comparison with earlier results. The net interest margin was R2.3bn, but set against this was a very large provision of R451m for bad and doubtful debts. Other operating income was R974.5m, leaving total operating income of R2.85bn. Operating expenditure was R2.2bn. Total assets of ABSA rose by 8.5 per cent to R56.2m - in line with the industry, but a 6 per cent drop in real terms. Mortgage loans represent 33 per cent of total assets, reflecting United and Allied's roots as building societies. Total advances in the group came to R42bn. Commenting on the rationalisation, Mr Herc Hefer, chairman, said the group had exceeded expectations by achieving net cost savings of R98m. These arose mainly from the integration of the support services of Allied, United and Volkskas. There were three main phases to the rationalisation which included consolidating the group's insurance interests and related financial services, and integrating support and technical services. Mr Piet Badenhorst, chief executive, said the bad debt figure reflected the fact that the level of provisions in the group had been upgraded to the standard maintained at United. Slightly more than half of the provisions relate to Volkskas. He said the group's exposure to the agricultural sector - currently in the grips of a severe drought - was in line with that of its competitors. Earnings per share rose by 15.2 per cent to 107.6 cents and the dividend was lifted to 39.5 cents from 36 cents. The policy is that the dividend cover, now up to 2.7, should reach 3. Mr Hefer said despite the poor operating climate, further rationalisation savings should help lift profits in the coming year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Deere remains pessimistic after weak second quarter
DOC.TEXT: DEERE & Co, the US equipment maker, continued to struggle with a sluggish worldwide market for agricultural and construction machinery. For its second quarter, ended April 30, it reported net income of Dollars 44m, or 58 cents a share, sharply down from Dollars 73.1m, or 96 cents, in the same period last year. Worldwide sales and revenues decreased 3 per cent to Dollars 1.86bn from Dollars 1.93bn. The operating results reflect lower production and sales volumes, partly because of the poor market and partly because of the company's efforts to reduce inventories. Buyer incentives remained high, given competition in the industry, and these promotions cut into margins. While the second-quarter results were an improvement on the net loss of Dollars 19.9m, or 26 cents a share, during the first quarter, Mr Hans Becherer, chairman, warned that the company's outlook this year for the equipment market was 'less positive'. Deere will thus reduce its production tonnage by 7 per cent this year compared with last year's levels. While farm and industrial equipment accounted for about 70 per cent of the company's second-quarter sales, lawn and grounds care equipment sales were the only bright spot, picking up by 21 per cent to Dollars 261m from Dollars 216m last year. Second-quarter results in Deere's other divisions fared better. Net income of its credit operations rose to Dollars 25.8m from Dollars 22.1m last year and net income from insurance and healthcare operations was Dollars 10.9m, up marginally from Dollars 10.4m a year ago. Worldwide net income in the first six months was Dollars 24.1m, or 32 cents a share, compared with net income of Dollars 30m, or 39 cents, last year. Net sales and revenues for the first six months were Dollars 3.31bn, down 2 per cent from Dollars 3.36bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Komatsu hit by housing slump
DOC.TEXT: KOMATSU, the Japanese construction equipment manufacturer, has reported a 50.6 per cent fall in consolidated pre-tax earnings to Y41.9bn (Dollars 324.8m) for the fiscal year ending March 31. The profit slide and a 7 per cent decline in sales to Y919.8bn were blamed on weak demand for construction equipment in Japan, the US and Europe as housing starts were hit hard by recession. Komatsu predicted that pre-tax profits would level off at Y42bn in the current fiscal year on higher sales of Y950bn, while net profit would increase to Y15bn from Y10.9bn. Sales of construction equipment, which account for almost two-thirds of total sales, fell by 12.3 per cent to Y579bn. However Komatsu recorded sales growth in other business areas that it has been developing in an attempt to diversify. Revenues from industrial machinery, including machine tools, rose by 1.5 per cent to Y87.9bn. Turnover in the electronics division climbed by 7.5 per cent to Y54.9bn, while civil engineering and construction services increased by 11 per cent to Y86.2bn due to the steady expansion of public sector projects.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Sumitomo Electric in 6.7 percent decline
DOC.TEXT: SUMITOMO Electric Industries, Japan's leading producer of electic wires and cables, reported its first annual profit fall in nine years with pre-tax earnings declining by 6.7 per cent to '35.8bn (Dollars 277.5m), writes John Burton. Net profit in fiscal 1991 dropped by 5.5 per cent to Y19bn. Despite the fall and a prediction that earnings will level off in fiscal 1992, Sumitomo will raise its dividend by Y1 to Y10. Sales grew by 2.4 per cent to Y800.4bn. Revenues from electric wires and cables fell by 3 per cent to Y398.1 because of lower copper prices.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Bouygues to raise fresh capital
DOC.TEXT: BOUYGUES, one of the world's largest construction groups, is to raise FFr1.04bn (Dollars 180m) of new equity capital, the first leading French quoted company to launch a big rights issue in the present stock market rally. The group is to issue 1.712m new shares at FFr610 each, a 5.4 per cent discount to yesterday's opening price, to help 'pursue the development of its mainstream activities and its diversification in France and abroad,' said Bouygues. It was interested in buying parts - but not all - of Elbo, the east German construction group being privatised, said Mr Martin Bouygues, chairman. He predicted the group's profits would rise this year from last year's FFr635m net on turnover of around FFr64bn, about the same as in 1991. Stockmarket analysts had expected Bouygues to take advantage of the recent strength of its share price, up by 20 per cent from mid-February, the start of the stock market rally, to a peak of FFr675 in mid-May. However, the share price fell FFr19 to FFr626 by yesterday afternoon, on fears that the rights issue would dilute earnings per share. Other leading French groups will soon follow Bouygues' example while share prices continue their strength, said Mr David Harrington, research analyst at James Capel in Paris. Bouygues has not had a rights issue for six years and was thought undercapitalised in relation to total assets. Its debts stood at an estimated 46 per cent of shareholders' funds at the end of last year. Nearly three quarters of the issue, FFr744.2m, will be reserved for French shareholders, with the remainder for international investors. Subscriptions will be open from May 28 to June 16. Alcatel Cable has already said it is planning to raise up to FFr1.5bn next month. Others thought likely to benefit from an injection of fresh equity capital include Michelin, the indebted tyre maker, Moulinex, the household appliance group, and Ciments Francais, the construction materials supplier.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Norway's top savings banks show advance
DOC.TEXT: NORWAY'S top 34 savings banks, which represent 80 per cent of the combined assets of the savings banks, yesterday reported a sharp improvement in first-quarter performance, helped by improved net interest earnings, lower operating costs and cheaper funding by the central bank. According to the Savings Banks' Association, the banks boosted first-quarter net interest income to NKr2.64bn (Dollars 418m) from NKr2.55bn last year. Other operating income rose by NKr50m to NKr450m while operating costs were reduced to NKr1.87bn from NKr2.04bn. Combined first-quarter credit losses were slightly up by NKr30m to NKr860m, however, while the 34 banks' combined operating profit improved to NKr360m from NKr80m in last year's first quarter. The Savings Banks Association yesterday reiterated sharp criticism of the amount of state support issued last year to prop up the country's top three commercial banks, saying it was undermining competition. The association singled out Christiania Bank, which was acquired last year by the state after its equity capital was wiped out by massive losses.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Electrolux posts sharp decline to SKr253m
DOC.TEXT: ELECTROLUX, the Swedish household appliances multinational, announced a sharp drop in profits (after financial items) for the first quarter of the year to SKr253m (Dollars 43.41m) from SKr414m for the same period of 1991. Income for the first quarter of last year included a SKr184m capital gain for divestments in the company's commercial services business area. If that is excluded the group made a 10 per cent improvement in its profits for on-going operations for the first quarter. A 2 per cent growth was recorded in sales to SKr19.46bn from SKr19.23bn in the same period last year. The earnings per share after full tax dropped to SKr0.20 from SKr3.60 in the first quarter of last year. The shareholders yesterday approved Electrolux's decision to maintain its dividend at SKr12.50 per share. In his address to the shareholders Mr Leif Johansson, president, said the restructuring programme of the past two years with the closure of 10 plants and a cut of 15,000 in the workforce had 'radically improved the production structure as well as productivity'. He added that inventory costs dropped by more than SKr1bn last year with a 'significant improvement in the cash flow'. He said Electrolux was moving into a phase when it would devote more resources to selling in existing markets as well as intensifying the search for new ones. Electrolux said that the European market for its products had slackened during the first quarter especially in the Nordic countries, but it added that there were also signs of stagnation in Germany. By contrast demand in the US market increased for household appliances but from a low base in the first quarter of last year. Overall profitability in the group's household appliances division rose.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Thyssen tumbles 11% to DM203m
DOC.TEXT: NET profits at Thyssen, the German steel, engineering and trading group, fell 11 per cent to DM203m (Dollars 123m) in the first half of the current year. While group sales rose 1.7 per cent to DM18bn, turnover from the core steel business continued downwards and the volume of incoming orders taken by all divisions fell 0.5 per cent to DM19.1bn. Sales of capital goods rose from DM5.14bn to DM5.81bn. Net earnings of DM203m, compared with DM227m in the first six months of 1991 and DM363m in 1990, matched market expectations, and reflected the continuing weakness of international and domestic markets. Meanwhile, the group is rationalising its existing businesses and looking for acquisitions or partnerships which will reduce its dependence on the highly-cyclical steel and heavy engineering markets. Mr Heinz Kriwet, chief executive, said recently it was interested in telecommunications or consumer goods. The group's two main steel businesses, Thyssen Stahl and Thyssen Edelstahl, which yesterday reported substantial sales declines to DM5.09bn and DM1.53bn respectively, are to be merged later this year in an attempt to prune costs. Klockner-Humboldt-Deutz, the engines and agricultural machinery maker, yesterday forecast a 'negative result' for the first half of 1992 but said it expected to return to profit by the end of the year. Sales in the first four months had fallen to DM960m from DM1.17bn in the comparable period of 1991. Meanwhile the company plans to increase its capital base before its current authorisation runs out in mid-1995, according to Mr Werner Kirchgasser, chairman. Timing of the issue of new shares would depend partly on the condition of capital markets and partly on the group's ability to improve its earnings significantly. Krupp's takeover of Hoesch, and the creation of a new force in the European steel industry, has been given the go-ahead by the European Commission. Krupp has also announced the proposed terms for buying in the Hoesch shares it does not own. The merged group, with sales of about DM30bn and 100,000 employees, would still be smaller than the community's four steel giants, the commission said, and market domination was not an issue. The two companies have agreed the final terms for the takeover, which include Krupp's offering 13 of its shares plus DM6 in cash for every 10 Hoesch shares. Although no details are available of how much Krupp paid for its 51 per cent stake, the total value of the deal is estimated at over DM1bn. The final formalities are expected at an extraordinary general meeting at Hoesch on July 27.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Canadian bank lifts provisions
DOC.TEXT: BANK OF Nova Scotia has boosted its fiscal 1992 loan loss provisions by CDollars 200m (USDollars 168m) or 45 per cent, to reflect its exposure to Olympia & York and other troubled borrowers. The bank, Canada's fourth biggest, nonetheless reported a small increase in second-quarter earnings, with the extra write down exactly offset by a recovery in third world loans. As a result, the second-quarter provision of CDollars 110m is unchanged from the previous three months. The provision in the second quarter of 1991 was CDollars 85m. Although they are among O&Y's biggest lenders, the Canadian banks are generally well-equipped to absorb substantial losses. BNS for instance, reported that its risk-weighted capital-to-assets ratio improved in the second quarter to 8.6 per cent from 8.3 per cent a year earlier. Net earnings rose to CDollars 171m, or 75 cents a share, in the three months to April 30, from CDollars 163.3m, or 73 cents, a year earlier. The improvement was largely due to wider margins as both domestic and foreign interest rates continued to decline. Return on equity slipped, however, to 16 per cent from 17.6 per cent. BNS disclosed earlier that its total exposure to O&Y is CDollars 600m. But with the loans largely secured by prime office buildings and marketable securities, the bank said that it expects 'substantial recoveries'. Total non-performing loans, net of provisions, rose to CDollars 1.87bn on April 30 from CDollars 1.74bn three months earlier.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / International Company News: Swissair sells holding in Kuoni
DOC.TEXT: SG WARBURG SODITIC, the Geneva subsidiary of the British merchant bank, has purchased the 35.8 per cent stake in the Swiss travel group Kuoni held by Swissair, the Swiss national airline, and sold it to European institutional clients. Terms were not revealed, but following the announcement of the transaction the price of Kuoni bearer shares rose SFr1,100 to SFr23,900, valuing the Swissair stake at SFr119.9m (Dollars 81m). The sale has been rumoured for some time as part of a Swissair programme to sell off peripheral activities. 'By pulling out of Kuoni, Swissair is underlining its intention to concentrate on its core businesses, the transport of people and goods, and related services,' the airline said. Mr Luigi De Carlo of Warburg Soditic said that one quarter of the shares were placed with Swiss institutions. The remainder were placed with institutional customers elsewhere in Europe. Warburg's view was that the shares were undervalued and that the wide distribution of the Swissair stake would raise liquidity and investor interest. The Kuoni-Hugentobler Foundation still has absolute control of Kuoni, with a 52.6 per cent voting stake.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Radio Clyde tunes in to 57% increase after Forth purchase
DOC.TEXT: RADIO CLYDE Holdings, which since its merger with Radio Forth last year broadcasts to all the main cities in Scotland, increased pre-tax profit by 57 per cent, from Pounds 707,000 to Pounds 1.11m, in the six months to March 31. Turnover at the USM-quoted group advanced to Pounds 6.62m, reflecting the all-share acquisition completed in April last year. Because of the extra equity, earnings per share rose only 1p to 8.3p. The interim dividend is held at 3.25p. Mr John Bowman, finance director, said the original Clyde group made operating profits of Pounds 798,000. Forth added Pounds 261,000, while Buzz FM, a Birmingham station aimed at a younger audience, lost Pounds 89,000. Clyde had only recently taken effective control of Buzz after spending about Pounds 750,000 over 18 months to buy 97 per cent of it. Interest received amounted to Pounds 143,000 and the group had Pounds 2.5m cash at the half-way stage, compared with Pounds 3m last year, with Buzz accounting for the difference. Mr James Gordon, chief executive, said local advertising revenue, which accounted for 70 per cent of the total, rose by 8 per cent year-on-year and had reached a record level. Growth in national advertising was 5 per cent and there had been some encouraging signs in April and May. The group, which has missed out in the bidding for the first two national commercial radio stations, said it would not bid for the third speech-based one. It was continuing to look for other areas in which to invest. An extraordinary charge of Pounds 270,000 rose from a change in accounting treatment for Satellite Media Services, in which it now has a 28.6 per cent stake. An anticipated sale had fallen through, leading to the accounting change. The business was close to breaking even and the sale of the stake was not being actively pursued.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: ICL appoints advisers in run-up to flotation
DOC.TEXT: ICL, the UK-based computer manufacturer in which Fujitsu of Japan has a majority stake, has appointed advisers in the run-up to its proposed flotation on the London stock market. It said yesterday that it had appointed Schroders as merchant bankers and Cazenove as lead broker, assisted by Warburg. The search for financial advisers has been under way since the beginning of the year. Fujitsu paid Pounds 743m for an 80 per cent stake in ICL two years ago; at the time it said it would float at least 25 per cent of the company in London within five years at a minimum price of 225p a share, giving ICL a tag of not less than Pounds 1.2bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Mowlem serves Pounds 18.5m writ on Eagle Star
DOC.TEXT: THE long-running dispute between John Mowlem, the construction group, and Eagle Star, one of Britain's biggest insurance companies, has escalated further with Mowlem serving a writ for loss and damages exceeding Pounds 18.5m. The action arose following claims by Mowlem that it was wrongfully dismissed as management contractor on the Carlton Gate development of luxury flats in Maida Vale, north London. The contractor was dismissed in 1989. The developer, Carlton Gate Development, was half-owned by Eagle Star, a subsidiary of BAT Industries. The balance was held by a banking consortium led by Security Pacific EuroFinance. When it was put into receivership in December 1991, Mowlem accused the company of behaving 'deplorably' and of taking the action to avoid its financial obligations. Shortly afterwards, an arbitrator found that Mowlem had been wrongfully dismissed and awarded it Pounds 12.25m plus costs. The company said that virtually none of the award had been paid. Mowlem is pursuing separately a claim for Pounds 1.1m against Phippen Randall & Parkes, the project architects, which it claimed had wrongfully deducted money from payments properly due to the contractor. Mowlem alleged the architects had also unlawfully conspired with Eagle Star to terminate the management contractor's Carlton Gate contract. Both parties, according to Mowlem, had wrongfully interfered with, and procured a breach of, its contract. Phippen Randall & Parkes said it had acted properly throughout the project and was fully confident that any tribunal would reach the same conclusion. Eagle Star said it refuted all the allegations made by Mowlem in its 'spurious and mischievous' writ and would vigorously defend its case.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Price increases help East Surrey rise 42%
DOC.TEXT: EAST SURREY Holdings, the small water supply company based in Redhill, has announced a 42 per cent increase in pre-tax profits, helped by price increases and a lower interest charge. But the company has warned that a hosepipe and sprinkler ban in force since March may have to be extended if rain levels are low in the autumn. 'Our bore holes are now at the levels we normally expect for the end rather than beginning of summer,' said Mr Ian Foster, managing director. East Surrey lifted profits from Pounds 3.91m to Pounds 5.54m in the year to March 31. It heralds the start of the month-long reporting season for the 25 water supply companies and 10 privatised water services companies in England and Wales. Turnover increased 30 per cent to Pounds 21.9m (Pounds 16.9m). Mr Foster said the steep increases in profits and sales reflected the last year of East Surrey's high K allowance, the amount of increase allowed above the rate of inflation. K was set at 16 per cent last year, following 16.5 per cent in 1991. This high allowance was designed to bring companies such as East Surrey in line with the privatised water services companies and prepare for heavy capital expenditure programmes. East Surrey's K allowance has been reduced to 2 per cent for this year, although the company has agreed with Ofwat, the water regulator, that price rises will not be above inflation. East Surrey warned that the rate of growth of its water business could now slow. Operating costs rose to Pounds 15.4m (Pounds 11.6m). Most of the increase was due to extra spending on underground mains which need upgrading. Capital expenditure rose to Pounds 6.8m (Pounds 6.5m). Interest costs fell to Pounds 982,000 (Pounds 1.34m) following a debenture repayment. Earnings increased to 38.7p (26.6p). The company is recommending a final dividend of 6p (5p) to give a total of 9.56p (8p), an increase of 19.5 per cent. East Surrey expanded its non-regulated business with two acquisitions, including a small water treatment company. But non-regulated turnover remained at under Pounds 1m, although Mr Foster said growth could be rapid. The company said unbudgeted expenditure of Pounds 8m may be needed in 1994-95 to meet EC standards on water quality and pesticides. Tests are under way to assess the final cost of compliance.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: The Battle For Midland - Chairman defends Hongkong Bank's management record
DOC.TEXT: MR WILLIAM Purves, chairman of HSBC Holdings, yesterday defended Hongkong Bank's record and ability to manage a global bank and told shareholders that the planned merger with Midland Bank was in Hong Kong and China's best interest as well as theirs. Speaking at the bank's annual meeting Mr Purves said the merger with Midland would create an international banking group that would be exceptionally well capitalised. Shareholders would be able to participate in a growing international group with considerable potential, he said. Hongkong Bank's planned acquisition of Midland has not found favour among Hong Kong investors. Many have criticised the plan to create a global bank, saying the experience of the 1980s has underlined the difficulties of such a strategy. But Mr Purves responded to these criticisms yesterday and said Hongkong Bank had long experience in managing operations that span the globe. What it envisages with the merger with Midland 'is materially different from other attempts to establish global banks.' 'Our approach is different because our organisation has always been built on a series of separate franchises in a variety of countries. 'What links these franchises is our commitment to international banking - and our highly efficient technology through which we deliver competitive products.' Meanwhile, the bank said that Lloyds Bank's complaint to the US Federal Reserve over Hongkong Bank's request for a 'fast track' approval of its acquisition of Midland was 'yet another spoiling tactic'. It was the third letter on this issue that Lloyds had sent the Fed, it said. The bank would be writing to the Fed in due course pointing out that the merger did not involve the acquisition of significant banking assets in the US. It will also cite the Fed's quick approval of Deutsche Bank's purchase of Morgan Grenfell as precedent for a timely determination. In a separate announcement yesterday Hongkong Bank revealed its long-foreshadowed board restructuring. It has moved to a two-tier structure with HSBC Holdings overseeing the bank's global operations and the separate, overlapping, board for Hongkong Bank focusing on the bank's interest primarily in the colony. Among new significant appointments is Baroness Lydia Dunne's elevation to non-executive chairman of HSBC. Lady Dunne is an executive director of Swire and also on the board of Volvo. Mr Victor Li, the 27-year-old son of magnate Mr Li Ka-shing, has joined the board of Hongkong Bank following his father's recent departure.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Merry Hill interests the Richardsons - Mountleigh shopping centre may revert to former majority owners
DOC.TEXT: DON AND Roy Richardson, the twins who developed the Merry Hill shopping centre and sold a controlling interest in it to Mountleigh, could again emerge as the majority owners. 'If we could get some arrangement on price we couldn't let a good deal pass by,' Mr Don Richardson said yesterday, contemplating the implications of Mountleigh's collapse and anticipating that the receiver, at some stage, will sell off Mountleigh's interest. The Richardsons do not expect the receiver to dispose of the centre, the jewel in Mountleigh's somewhat tarnished UK property crown, at firesale prices. 'If he did, we'd be the first there,' Mr Richardson observed. The attraction - at a price - for the Richardsons is clear. Rents are higher than when they sold it, the capital value undoubtedly less. About 25m shoppers a year visit Merry Hill, near Dudley - indeed, it was packed yesterday. After the MetroCentre in Gateshead, it is the second largest shopping centre in Europe. But the ownership of the Merry Hill shopping centre, itself part of a wider development under construction in an enterprise zone since 1982 and involving also offices and an industrial park, is complex. The adjacent developments are largely owned by the Richardsons. The shopping centre ownership, however, can be split at least five ways. The first point is that the Richardsons still have a direct interest, the exact extent of which they have not and will not disclose. The second is that when the Richardsons, in December 1990, sold Mountleigh an interest for a sum which, again, they would not disclose, but which Mountleigh latterly valued at Pounds 160m, the payments were staged. Some payments remain outstanding, but they are secured against part of the property. Had Mountleigh managed to sell its interest to Hammerson, the UK property group, and O'Connor Group of the US, earlier this year, at least some of the takings would have found their way to the Richardsons. The third facet of the ownership is the existence of the Richmount Laser Trust, set up by Mountleigh and the Richardsons, to attract private investors seeking tax shelters through the purchase of a property in an enterprise zone. Part of the Merry Hill shopping centre is owned by the Trust. Fourth, during the years of the centre's development - over four years to the completion of the last and biggest phase in 1990 - a series of individual transactions were completed with the retailers. Some own their freehold. Others are on leases of 99 and 999 years. Others again have shorter leases: the terms of some of them are related to turnover. The fifth slice of ownership is that of Mountleigh. It is estimated that of the whole it is probably about 80 per cent. But that is not to say it owns 80 per cent of all the 260 shops on the 1.85m sq ft of retailing space at the centre. While it might own the building, the retailer may have spent twice the value of the building's shell on the interior. Given the fragmentation of the ownership and the presence of the Richardsons in the background, the sale of the Mountleigh interest in Merry Hill is likely to be a lengthy affair. It is likely to be made more complicated by fears that it might be on contaminated land, one of the reasons given for the collapse of the Hammerson-O'Connor purchase. The shopping centre is on the site of old railway sidings, next door to the old Round Oak steelworks, which closed in 1984. The Richardsons are building an office complex next door to the shopping centre on the Round Oak site. But the land has not been designated by anybody as contaminated and the Contaminated Land Register in which it was feared that it might appear does not yet exist.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: IRG urges bid rejection
DOC.TEXT: IRG, the Irish plastic packaging manufacturer, has advised its shareholders to reject the IPounds 22m (Pounds 20m) bid by Barlo, an Irish radiator manufacturer. Mr Brendan O'Kelly, chairman, said the share-exchange bid - 55 Barlo for every 20 IRG - 'offers IRG shareholders only 40 per cent of the combined business'. He said that of the combined entity IRG would contribute 79 per cent of turnover, 54 per cent of pre-tax profits and 51 per cent of net assets. 'Your board believes this Barlo offer is inadequate and accordingly cannot recommend that shareholders accept it', he stated. IRG announced a 23 per cent fall in pre-tax profits from IPounds 2.9m to IPounds 2.2m, on turnover marginally down to IPounds 55.9m (Pounds 56.4m) for 1991. Earnings per share fell to 12.2p (16.8p). The dividend is held at 6.2p with a final of 4.45p. The bid closes on June 4.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: A hostage to its UK parent's lost fortune / A look at the future of Galerias Preciados, the failed group's Spanish retail arm
DOC.TEXT: AS GALERIAS Preciados, Spain's second largest retail chain, prepares to change owners for the fifth time in 10 years following the collapse on Monday of Mountleigh, its UK parent, at least one group of employees will not be too concerned about their future. They are the 300 staff at the large Galerias store on Madrid's prestigious Calle Serrano who last Christmas won Pta12bn (Pounds 65.2m) in the country's biggest lottery. For the remaining 7,200 Galerias employees in each of its 29 stores around Spain, the future is once again heavy with speculation and concern. The administrative receivership of Mountleigh makes it 'inevitable' that Galerias would have to be sold, Mr Tim Hayward, one of the Peat Marwick receivers at Mountleigh, said in Madrid. Mr Hayward, who is in Madrid to outline the receivership at Mountleigh to senior Galerias management, also said one potential buyer had made an offer for the chain. It is believed this bid is being organised in New York and may involve Mr Nelson Pelz and Mr Peter May, the US investors who bought control of Mountleigh in late 1989 and subsequently sold half of their 22 per cent stake. Mr Michael Babcock, an American managing direc- tor appointed last year by Mr Pelz and Mr May, has also suggested he might try to look for support to buy the chain and it is highly likely that there will be other bidders. One possibility is Marks and Spencer, which has recently opened two stores in Spain and may be looking for more sites. But M and S is unlikely to want all 29 Galerias stores. Analysts say it will be difficult to put a price on the company. It is said to have debts of close to Pounds 200m and last year, under new American management, slipped back into losses after three profitable years. Galerias' biggest creditor is probably Mountleigh itself, which has guaranteed and raised some Dollars 150m (Pounds 85m) on Galerias' behalf in the past two years, principally in London. 'It is not our intention to ask for the immediate repayment of that money,' said Mr Hayward. 'It is our desire that Galerias continue to operate as a going concern and we hope to be able to see it into safe hands.' Galerias, which was yesterday trying to reassure suppliers and employees that its operations would not be affected by the Mountleigh receivership, has changed ownership four times already in the past 10 years. The chain was owned by the Rumasa banking and trading group which the Spanish government expropriated in 1983. It was subsequently sold on by the government to the powerful Cisneros family of Venezuela and, in 1987, to Mountleigh. Since its expropriation the group has made money only in the three years it was under the control of a management appointed by Mr Anthony Clegg, Mountleigh's founder. In the 1990-91 year sales rose 34 per cent to Pta97.6bn compared with 1987-88, while income had increased 36 per cent to Pta33bn. The new management under Mr Babcock has spent heavily on trying to take the chain up-market, refurbishing stores and on advertising. Although accounts for the last financial year, to April 30 this year, have not been published, and Galerias was not available for comment yesterday, sales growth is understood to have slowed to just 0.5 per cent while expenses have risen sharply. The group is thought to have ended last year with a loss of Pta3.8bn after net profits of Pta1.2bn in 1990-91. To combat its rising costs Galerias has been trying, with only partial success, to sell and lease back some of its stores. It has had some successes - although leasing has sent costs soaring - but as the Spanish economy has slowed down, so have property prices. Galerias' problems in selling its two sites in Barcelona are one measure of the problems it faces.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: British Gas silent on hive off speculation
DOC.TEXT: BRITISH GAS yesterday refused to confirm or deny speculation that the company might hive off its regional businesses or float its exploration and production business. The reports helped the shares gain 6 1/2 p yesterday to 257p. The group announced in January that it was undertaking a fundamental review of its operations, following continued pressure from Ofgas, the industry regulator and the Office of Fair Trading to introduce more competition into the gas market. Analysts suggested that it might be more sensible to sell off its supply businesses in advance of increased competition in the market, and allow shareholders to benefit, than simply to wait for its market share to be eroded. Another option would be to float the company's Pounds 4bn exploration and production arm. Speculation that British Gas might be considering such a move emerged again this weekend following the publication of an interview with Mr Cedric Brown, senior managing director at British Gas, despite Mr Brown's refusal to comment. Mr Brown has been tipped to become chief executive, if that role is relinquished by Mr Robert Evans, currently both chairman and chief executive. Mr Steve Turner, industry analyst at Smith New Court, and one of those who has suggested that a break-up would be in British Gas's best interests, said he believed such speculation was premature. 'British Gas faces the task of hiving off its pipeline business before the end of the year. It would be irresponsible for the company to undertake major restructuring before that has been achieved, and until the regulatory debate about returns on the pipeline business has been settled.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Jupiter Tyndall's reconstruction plan for CST
DOC.BYLINE: By PHILIP COGGAN, Personal Finance Editor
DOC.TEXT: Jupiter Tyndall, the fund management group which is battling for control of the Pacific Horizon Investment Trust, has announced proposals for the reconstruction of CST Emerging Asia, another of the trusts in its stable. The plan is to issue shareholders with zero coupon convertible unsecured loan stock for nine-tenths of the nominal value of their existing shares. CST would then tender for 60 per cent of the zero culs, allowing investors to liquidate a substantial proportion of their holdings. It is hoped that this plan would narrow the discount to net assets on which CST shares trade. SG Warburg has estimated that a package of one share and 9 culs would have a value equivalent to 90 per cent of the trust's net asset value.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: JS Pathology in possible bid talks
DOC.TEXT: JS Pathology, the clinical laboratory, yesterday said it was in talks which could lead to a bid, following a 33 per cent jump in its share price to 153p. Mr Eric Rothbarth, finance director, said the talks were friendly although they had been instigated by the other party, believed to be a medical services corporation. The subjects discussed did not necessarily mean a bid, he added. An announcement is expected within the next few weeks.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Management buy-out at Sharelink
DOC.TEXT: SHARELINK, one of the UK's three big private client stockbrokers, has been bought out by its managers for an undisclosed sum. The group, which regularly handles more than 10 per cent of the bargains on the UK stock market, was launched in the late 1980s with backing from BT, which owned 64.7 per cent of the company. Albert E Sharpe, the Birmingham-based stockbroking group, had 31.3 per cent. The sale reflects BT's aim of concentrating on its core telecommunications business. The buy-out, agreed at the weekend, is being backed by Foreign & Colonial Ventures and CINVen, which invests on behalf of the British Coal and British Rail pension funds. As part of the deal Mr David Jones, chairman, will increase his stake in the company from 4 per cent to 20 per cent. Sharelink, which conducts business over the telephone or through a postal service, was launched as a low-cost rival to existing stockbrokers, and has won a market share equal to the two other leaders, Barclays and NatWest Stockbrokers. Mr Jones was fresh to the stockbroking world when he approached BT with the idea for Sharelink in 1986. His vision of a low-cost, automated dealing service has helped to reshape the UK's retail stockbroking industry, forcing other brokers to reduce their own cost bases to compete. Sharelink made profits of Pounds 2.6m in the year to March 31 1991 and slightly less in the year to this March, though profits have yet to be disclosed.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Lasmo offer likely to raise Dollars 30m more than expected
DOC.TEXT: SHARES IN Lasmo, the UK oil exploration and production company, gained 8p to 207p on news that it expects to receive Dollars 30m (Pounds 16.9m) more than expected from the offering of its Canadian and US refining and marketing business. Including other factors, Lasmo could earn about Dollars 175m more from the disposal than previously estimated. Lasmo announced at the beginning of the month that it planned to float the US downstream assets of Ultramar, the oil company it acquired in a Dollars 1.2bn takeover last year. But a revised prospectus lodged with the US Securities and Exchange Commission raises the price of the equity offering to between Dollars 590m and Dollars 680m, an increase of some Dollars 30m over the previous price range. Proceeds from debt offerings remain unchanged at Dollars 400m, and together with inter-company debt of Dollars 80m to be repaid, Lasmo will receive an estimated Dollars 1.07bn to Dollars 1.16bn from the public offering. This would put the estimated total net proceeds to Lasmo from the disposal of the downstream businesses - including the refining and marketing businesses, ships, and financial and property assets - at between Dollars 1.35bn and Dollars 1.44bn, compared with a previous net estimate of Dollars 1.17bn and Dollars 1.27bn. The proposed offering will go before an extraordinary meeting of shareholders for approval on June 10. Lasmo disappointed the stock market in March with a sharp drop in pre-tax profits from Pounds 48.8m to Pounds 28.8m, with gearing up to 83 per cent. The company hoped to reduce its Dollars 1.2bn debt burden by selling off Ultramar's downstream assets, but has so far been unsuccessful, and opted instead for a flotation. However, initial pricing details showing a potential book loss again disappointed the City, sending the share price tumbling 21p. Lasmo made a small contribution to reducing its debts last week by selling half its 57 per cent shareholding in Lasmo Canada for a profit of about CDollars 38m (Pounds 17.5m). The 10.1m shares were owned by its wholly-owned Lasmo International and Lasmo Oil Development (Canada) subsidiaries. The deal, arranged by Gordon Capital Corporation, priced the shares at CDollars 8.25, producing an aggregate consideration of CDollars 83.2m before expenses. A share purchase warrant attached to the shares entitles holders to buy Lasmo's remaining shares in Lasmo Canada for CDollars 8.75 at any time up to December 15 1993. If the warrants were exercised in full, that would entail a further profit to Lasmo of about CDollars 42m, and result in the disposal of its entire interest in Lasmo Canada.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Pounds 750m ticket tipped for MFI
DOC.TEXT: THE BUILD-UP to the planned July flotation of MFI, the furniture group with heavy debts going back to a 1987 management buy-out, has gathered momentum with the issuing of new forecasts for profits and potential market value. County NatWest, which is advising the company on the flotation, estimated that trading profit for the 12 months to the end of April was Pounds 70m, up from Pounds 48.6m, and forecast Pounds 100m for this year. CNW said that if the group were given a rating in line with the stores sector, its market value would be Pounds 750m. An important assumption is that the flotation proceeds will reduce the group's debts of about Pounds 500m to Pounds 100m, giving annualised interest costs of little more than Pounds 10m. In 1990-91 interest payments totalled nearly Pounds 80m, sending the group to a pre-tax loss of Pounds 24m. It took on debt of Pounds 491m in 1987 during the buy-out from Asda which valued the group at Pounds 718m. Asda retains a 25 per cent stake. Mr Derek Hunt, chairman, said Pounds 20m was paid off before a refinancing in August 1989. Borrowings went back up to Pounds 503m, which is the figure expected in the April 1992 accounts. Since then a further Pounds 15m has been paid off. Mr Hunt and other directors, who own 3 per cent of the company, and 350 managers, could gain several million pounds from the flotation, depending on the value. MFI, with about 13 per cent of the UK furniture market, has benefited from the collapse of such rivals as Lowndes Queensway and ELS, while Magnet, another highly geared buy-out, has run into severe difficulties. Mr Hunt said MFI had improved its operating margins without raising prices by increasing efficiency and through turnover growth in the second half of the year. CNW estimates sales of Pounds 640m compared with Pounds 620.7m. Mr Hunt hoped that after the flotation the number of banks involved in lending money to the group could be reduced from 39 to three. The pathfinder prospectus and full-year results are expected to be announced on June 11.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Price war checks advance at Blacks
DOC.TEXT: CUT-THROAT competition helped dampen the profits advance at Blacks Leisure, the camping goods and sportswear company, which yesterday announced a Pounds 200,000 rise to Pounds 3.7m for the year to February 29, on sales 18 per cent higher at Pounds 70.4m. Mr Simon Bentley, chairman and chief executive, said one of the group's star performers of 1991 - the distribution of LA Gear goods - had suffered from US wholesalers dumping stock at much reduced prices in the UK. Retail profits had also declined in the face of 'one of the severest recessions this century' and price-cutting promotions from competitors. Trading remained tough in the first half of the current year, Mr Bentley said. 'There has been no sign of an improvement.' However, some of the adverse conditions had been eliminated - such as the dumping practice which had cost the company at least 30 per cent of LA Gear sales. The distribution operation improved overall profits before interest and tax by 14 per cent to Pounds 4m, largely on the back of a record rise in the sale of Fila brand goods. The figures included a marginal contribution from Quaser, the sports goods company acquired for Pounds 1.9m in shares in January. The fashion and textiles division, now part of distribution, incurred a 'small loss' for the year. Mr Bentley said Blacks' longer-term plans included selling this business which supplies retailers such as Burton and Etam. The retail operation, which sells camping and sporting goods, increased outlets by nine to 69, and consumed Pounds 3m of the group's Pounds 3.7m capital expenditure. Profits before interest and tax tumbled from Pounds 3m to Pounds 1.93m as margins came under pressure from competitive price-cutting. The Pounds 4.7m rights issue in June, which helped cut debt from Pounds 10m to Pounds 5.8m by the year-end, resulted in lower earnings per share of 9.82p (11.6p). The final dividend is maintained at 2.25p, resulting in a 10 per cent rise for the year to 3.35p. COMMENT Simon Bentley is determined to prove that Blacks' chequered past is dead and gone. Organic growth and development of existing brands is the key, he says, so Blacks does not expect to open retail stores this year. He also emphasises that Blacks now has an in-house brand in Quaser, endorsed by Gary Lineker. That endorsement could give a hefty boost this summer, if the football hero scores just two more goals. That would make him England's highest scoring player and kick into action a massive advertising campaign for the brand. Such a windfall might offset gloomy noises about current trading and fears that Blacks may lose its licence to distribute LA Gear when it expires in 1994. Nevertheless, it might be better to wait for the outcome of the important summer months before acting. House brokers are forecasting flat profits of Pounds 3.75m, with a prospective p/e of 10.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Spurs confirms sale of Paul Gascoigne
DOC.TEXT: The Pounds 5.5m sale of Paul Gascoigne, the England international footballer, to the Italian club Lazio was confirmed yesterday by Tottenham Hotspur, the quoted football club. Tottenham expects to get about Pounds 5m of the proceeds, which would wipe out its debt. Before Mr Alan Sugar, who also chairs Amstrad, and Mr Terry Venables, former team manager, bought the company nearly a year ago, borrowings peaked at about Pounds 15m.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Coca Cola adds Canada mixer
DOC.TEXT: Coca Cola & Schweppes Beverages has added Canada Dry to its range of mixer drinks, ending nearly 40 years during which Ginger Ale was bottled by Britvic Soft Drinks, the joint venture between Bass, Allied-Lyons, Whitbread and Pepsico. The new licensing arrangement will leave Britvic free to launch its own five flavour range of mixers in September.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / SG Warburg reveals its hidden reserves
DOC.TEXT: THE FULL hidden reserves of SG Warburg were revealed for the first time yesterday as the UK's leading merchant banking group reported full-year profits in line with expectations at Pounds 166.3m. Warburg said that a year ago its hidden reserves totalled Pounds 70.9m, equivalent to nearly 10 per cent of its disclosed shareholders' funds of Pounds 719m at the time. European legislation would have forced disclosure two years from now, but Lord Cairns, Warburg chief executive, said the group preferred to pick the moment that suited it best to make the announcement. Most of the larger UK merchant banks have now voluntarily disclosed their secret reserves, a traditional tool used by banks to smooth out profits. Warburg said it had never used secret reserves to bolster its profits, though losses on Rolls-Royce in the mid-1970s and local authority swaps two years ago had been set against these reserves. Had it maintained the reserves this year, reported profits would have been Pounds 3m less. The level of reserves, above most expectations, eased the mild disappointment that the stock market felt at the group's performance in the year to March 31. After reporting profits of Pounds 89m in the first half, Warburg slipped to Pounds 77m in the second, due in particular to the lack of corporate finance activity before the UK general election in April. It had issued a profits warning in February. Profits for the year as a whole were up by nearly a quarter from the restated Pounds 135.2m of the previous year. This was largely because of the spate of rights issues by UK companies in the first half, followed by an international equity raising later in the year, including the Pounds 5bn sell-off of BT shares by the government. Mercury Asset Management, the majority-owned fund management group, increased pre-tax profits from Pounds 56.4m to Pounds 65.1m. Lord Cairns said: 'A large number of decisions were quite clearly being deferred due to uncertainty about the election.' The group managed a return on its enlarged disclosed reserves of 18.9 per cent, up from a restated 16.4 per cent the year before and still well short of the average 25 per cent it hopes to achieve in the long-term. Lex, Page 20; MAM, Page 22

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Frank words from French entrepreneur: Jean-Luc Lagardere of Hachette and Matra talks to William Dawkins
DOC.TEXT: Jean-Luc Lagardere's image as one of France's top self-made men has recently taken a knock, but he is as resilient as ever and swears his strategy remains valid. Mr Lagardere almost takes relish in countering the widespread criticism of his latest scheme, which he argues has been poorly understood since being unveiled earlier this month. Unkind spirits have condemned the merger of the two companies he controls - Matra, the transport, telecommunications and defence group, with Hachette, France's leading international publisher - as panic. Some see it as a way to use profitable Matra to pay for the FFr3.55bn (Pounds 359.7m) losses clocked up by La Cinq, the now defunct television station which Mr Lagardere bought for Hachette 18 months ago. The 64-year-old Mr Lagardere recognises this as the most serious setback in his career. Others see it as an eccentric attempt to find common interests between unrelated businesses or a cynical attempt to fend off possible bids. Mr Lagardere forcefully denies these claims. 'People take me for either an idiot or a hooligan. I believe I am neither one nor the other,' he says. 'You don't tie someone with a broken leg to a healthy person and expect them to go faster . . . I won't tell you that there is a synergy between magazines and missiles . . . but that's not the point.' So what is the point? The big advantage of the merger is that it will allow both sides to draw cashflow centrally for investments in each of the nine activities in which they are jointly present, he says. There will be big head office and administrative savings, but that is a secondary gain. The project is in line with his mostly successful business strategy, Mr Lagardere insists. He has always believed that any business that cannot guarantee very high sales volumes must diversify to survive. It must be ready to adapt, to take risks, close lossmakers when the risks get too great, seek partners where it can no longer compete alone - as Matra is doing in telecommunications - and move into new areas. The merger will help both groups by making them financially stronger and more flexible, he argues. 'I have always been convinced that one cannot make a group live eternally on a single product. You need an enormous effect of mass to do that . . . Look at Dassault,' he says, referring to the aircraft group where he trained as a designer of prototypes in the 1950s. 'Nobody could have succeeded better at what they are doing, and yet they have not sold a single military aircraft outside France for the past four years.' Mr Lagardere's Dassault years marked him in all kinds of ways. His engineering roots are evident in the way he sketches graphs to illustrate his points. The experience also bought him into close contact with Matra, then a single product company supplying missiles to Dassault, now much more diversified with innovations including the Espace family and the VAL automatic metro. Matra's controlling shareholder invited him to take over as managing director at the age of 34, which Mr Lagardere did on condition that he got carte blanche. The same shareholder supported Mr Lagardere's takeover of Hachette in 1980. From the start, Mr Lagardere has been driven by two main impulses. First, the urge to create a great company, which he attributes to a passion to redress France's wartime humiliation; and second, the realisation that as an entrepreneur he must take investment risks, but cut his losses if the company's life is threatened. Clearly, he argues, multi-product companies can spread risks more easily. 'When we took over La Cinq, it was losing money, but I reckoned that these were not losses but investments. I have always said that once an investment becomes a loss, it is time to cut. If I had continued with La Cinq in 1992, the fatal risk for the group would have been real.' He points out that Hachette will be easily recapitalised before the merger with Matra, so there is no question of robbing the electronics group to bail out Hachette. Neither was there any question of hoping that the French state would bail out the television station. Mr Lagardere has always taken pride in belonging to none of the political or financial power networks that bind corporate France together. So he could expect no special favours. 'I have never stepped into that world, never. I have always known how to work with the establishment, but I keep my distance,' he says. In other countries, a La Cinq-type disaster might have provoked the resignation of the chairman. Yet Mr Lagardere has, if anything, strengthened his position by putting the new merged group under the control of a societe en commandite par actions, a share partnership in which the partners, headed by Mr Lagardere, have unlimited personal liability for losses but are almost unsackable. 'On the subject of resignation, even in England it's not so simple . . . I used to have a motor racing team with Jackie Stewart as driver. It happened that one day he lost a Grand Prix. But we didn't replace him at the next race because he had won 10 previously.' If chairmen were sacked every time they made a mistake, 'business would become a game of massacre, in which those who succeeded would be the ones who did nothing. My idea of business is that one must dare to take risks,' he says. Mr Lagardere dislikes pressure for short-term performance, something which he could produce by selling assets. 'Unlike some people who I will not name, that is not my idea of entrepreneurship,' he says. Suggestions that the commandite structure artificially protects management overlook the fact that the partners' personal liabilities are very real, he argues. 'For me, it is a profession of faith to make money and to stay independent . . . Institutional shareholders should say to themselves that Lagardere is obliged to make money, for all his personal fortune is in it. Unless he is mad or a masochist, he must make money.' Whether or not you believe his strategy of pooling his businesses to give them the strength to diversify, Mr Lagardere is and will remain a driven man.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Oil groups may form mutual insurer
DOC.TEXT: SEDGWICK, the insurance broker, and Price Waterhouse, the accountants and management consultants, are joining forces in a bid to help leading European oil and gas companies form a new mutual insurance company. The new mutual, which could have a capital base of more than Dollars 50m (Pounds 28m) and a minimum of 15 members, would provide extra insurance capacity in the specialist energy insurance market, where rates have increased and capacity diminished following recent losses. Since December, both Sedgwick and Price Waterhouse have conducted feasibility studies and intend to hold more detailed discussions with their clients within the next two weeks. No company has yet agreed to join the proposed mutual, but both organisations report a general feeling of support from their clients for the concept. 'We believe the support is there. We are literally having clients say to us 'when can we have it?',' said Mr Chris Mundy, director of marketing at Sedgwick Energy, the broker's specialist subsidiary. 'We would like to think we would be putting together a cast-iron proposal within the next four to six weeks,' added Mr Mundy, who said that there was an urgent need for action because of the contraction in available capacity. Sedgwick's 200 clients include British Petroleum, Shell, Amerada Hess and Mobil. A number of oil majors which have North American interests are already part of a mutual company, Oil Insurance Ltd (OIL), which was formed in the late 1960s. Mr Richard Titley, chairman of Sedgwick Energy, said the new mutual would 'complement OIL by focusing on European assets.' Hit by losses such as the explosion of the Piper Alpha rig in the North Sea in July 1988, specialist energy insurers, including Lloyd's syndicates, have increased rates and reduced the amount of cover available. Oil companies, especially those in the North Sea, have massive insurance exposures, sometimes in excess of Dollars 2bn. Last year buyers faced rate increases of between 15 and 200 per cent, and Sedgwick expects the tightness in the market to continue. 'Capacity is going to be diminished,' added Mr Titley.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Major drops visa requirement for Polish tourists to Britain
DOC.BYLINE: By PHILIP STEPHENS and BETHAN HUTTON
DOC.TEXT: MR JOHN MAJOR announced the abolition of UK visa requirements for Polish tourists yesterday and increased Britain's financial aid to Warsaw. The gesture was designed to underline his commitment to Poland's eventual membership of the European Community. After talks with Polish government leaders in Warsaw, Mr Major said he would use Britain's presidency of the EC in the second half of this year to commit the 12 to allowing Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary to join the Community. Mr Major said membership of the EC was not practical in the short term. Poland is locked in twin political and economic crises, heightened last night when President Lech Walesa declared that he had 'lost trust in the present government'. All three countries are still suffering from the painful transition to market-based economies. Mr Major, however, emphasised his determination that the Community should not remain a 'rich man's club', suggesting that the EC should set the turn of the century as a firm target for their inclusion. His announcement, after talks with Mr Walesa and Mr Jan Olszewski, the Polish prime minister, that Britain will abolish visa requirements for Polish visitors to the UK ended a long-running dispute between the two governments. In the past, Britain has argued that, because of the large Polish communities in the UK, many visitors have stayed on as illegal workers. Some 200,000 Poles are resident in the UK. Many have relatives in Poland who want to visit. Complaints have centred on long delays in granting visas, excessive bureaucracy, the number of people rejected and the charge for visas, which at about Pounds 20 can be more than a week's wage in Poland. Last year, 47,350 Poles applied for UK visas, and 5 per cent were turned down. The announcement was welcomed by Polish community organisations in the UK. Mr Mieczyslaw Hampel, administrator of the Polish Social and Cultural Association in London, said: 'In general we are very pleased'. Mr Antoni Zniderycz, secretary of a branch of the Polish Ex-Combatants Association, said: 'Our main argument was that we who stayed by the side of England for many years during the war were the first to deserve that kindness from the British government.' Mr Hampel expressed some worries that young people might exploit the relaxation to work illegally, but other leaders played this down. 'If anything it would be a short-term problem, not a long-term problem. Everybody knows there is unemployment in this country,' said Mr Alojzy Gajdzik, chairman of the Polish Parish in south-east London. Mr Major flew to Prague last night on the second leg of his four-day tour of central Europe. At a joint press conference earlier with Mr Olszewski, he indicated that he intended to press for a much stronger political dialogue between Poland, Hungary and Czechslovakia and the EC. Foreign ministers from the three countries will be invited to a meeting of the EC council and the three heads of government will attend joint talks in London during the British presidency. Mr Major said the UK would increase financial aid for Poland by Dollars 14m. The money will finance small business development.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / EC weakens environment plans ahead of Earth Summit in Rio
DOC.TEXT: THE European Community's position at next week's Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro looks set to fall well short of what environment commissioner Carlo Ripa di Meana has proposed, and his own attendance at the summit was last night in doubt. Environment ministers of the 12 yesterday agreed to sign the Climate Change convention due to be agreed in Rio. But they did not agree to endorse politically the European Commission's plan to tax energy as a means of curbing carbon dioxide emissions, even though no EC state opposed the proposal. Nor were they able to agree on a timetable for nearly doubling development aid to a minimum of 0.7 per cent of gross domestic product to help developing countries adopt more environmentally sound development strategies. Taken together, this is a limp posture when set against what Mr Ripa de Meana had defined as the minimum 'dowry' the Community should take to Rio. The Commission's plan is to stabilise CO emissions at 1990 levels by 2000, through an energy tax equivalent to Dollars 10 a barrel of oil equivalent. Mr Ripa di Meana says the EC can only deliver half that target without a tax. The plan won strong support yesterday from Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Italy. The first four attacked the Commission for making introduction of the tax conditional on the US and Japan adopting similar measures. Spain, Portugal and Greece insisted that conditionality was vital to protect EC industry. France and the UK reserved their position behind procedure, since the Commission overshot its deadline in producing the detailed draft directive, which it will look at today. 'The UK position remains that when we see it, we will study it in detail,' Mr Michael Howard, UK environment secretary, said of the tax plan.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Letter: Fund's financing too low fully to realise east Europe objectives
DOC.TEXT: Sir, As Mr John Major, the UK prime minister, visits Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Poland this week, he may see something of what Britain is doing, through the Know-how Fund, to help build institutions at the heart of their economies. Because the transformation of these countries entails massive disruption, the strength of these fledgling institutions will be severely tried in the years ahead. If they do not stand the strain, the consequences will not be limited to central Europe. In all three countries, the Know-how Fund has been so successful in attracting good projects and so quick in approving them that its budget is stretched to its limit and, in one case, beyond that limit. This is a tribute to a good concept, well administered. But justified pride should not mask the fact that the present level of financing is too low. When Mr Major speaks to his hosts of political co-operation between their governments and the EC, his words will ring hollow if he cannot assure them that the Know-how Fund will be increased to a level commensurate with the economic risks to their political stability and our responsibilities as a nation that did so much to inspire the reforms they have undertaken. Roger Garside, Garside, Miller & Associates, City Business Centre, 2 London Wall Buildings, London Wall, London EC2

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Letter: Automatic not for the sensible ecologist
DOC.TEXT: Sir, Having commendably recommended diesel engined cars because of their higher fuel efficiency ('Motoring: Diesels for sensible ecologists', May 23), Stuart Marshall's assertion that a car with automatic transmission 'is ideal for the 1990s' is a complete contradiction of what a 'sensible ecologist' should go for. It has long been known that automatic transmission consumes 7 to 8 per cent more power than a car with manual exchange. Unless there is some health or medical reason for saving the driver the minute effort of using a gear lever, surely the great majority of drivers at all interested in saving the environment from unnecessary pollution and in minimising consumption of irreplaceable fuel should avoid this expensive and unnecessary luxury. Using, say, a pint of fuel per hour to obviate such a very slight personal effort seems to me to be nothing short of an ecological crime. Archie Kidd, Archie Kidd (Thermal), Seend, Melksham, Wiltshire SN12 6NX

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Letter: MP no Euro sceptic
DOC.TEXT: Sir, Philip Stephens's description of Labour MPs who voted against the Maastricht Bill as '61 of the party's Euro-sceptics' is an unresearched generalisation ('Tories shrug off backbench revolt on Maastricht', May 22). I voted against and am by no means a Euro-sceptic - quite the reverse. I voted against because the 'British version' of the treaty seeks to create a Europe which pays no attention to the social needs and the employment rights of ordinary workers employed or unemployed. In fact, it negates the clear implications in the change of title from European Economic Community to European Community. That is not the sort of Europe I want to see.
