The interests of most of my constituents focus on the Social Chapter 'which in our case we have not got'. Our European colleagues have all got a much better deal - the deal that I want for Britain. I voted against the Bill because I am a Euro-enthusiast, not a Euro-sceptic and I believe more than a few of my new colleagues did the same. Colin Pickthall, House of Commons, London SW1A 0AA

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Foreign Affairs: Bosnia's tragic example - Security arrangements in Europe underpin renewed international interest in Yugoslavia's civil war
DOC.TEXT: You might think, from public statements made in the past two days by American and European statesmen, that their top priority was doing something effective to halt the fighting in Bosnia-Hercegovina. Speaking in Lisbon on Sunday, Mr James Baker, the US secretary of state, was eloquent on the subject: 'There are 35,000 diabetics now who have no insulin. There are 6,000 women and babies who have no medicine, baby formula or milk . . . Anyone who is looking for a reason not to act, or arguing somehow that action in the face of this kind of nightmare is not warranted at this time . . . is on the wrong wavelength.' This from a man who stalwartly refused to contemplate any kind of sanctions against Iraq before August 2 1990, in spite of evidence that Saddam Hussein was guilty of chemical warfare and other gross violations of human rights; a man famous for staying all of seven minutes in south-eastern Turkey in April 1991, when it was flooded with Kurdish refugees. By Monday, Mr John Major had taken up the theme, calling on the EC to take measures against Serbia well beyond a token protest. Meanwhile, the Portuguese foreign minister had promised that the EC would 'not allow those responsible for the bloodshed to go unpunished', and Mr Klaus Kinkel, the new German foreign minister, dotted the i: 'It must be said clearly who is responsible. The Serbians are responsible.' No doubt that is true. Reporters on the spot are certain that Serbian militias in Bosnia are working in tight collusion both with Serbia itself and with the Yugoslav army, to achieve exclusive Serb control of about two-thirds of the republic's territory and expel the other ethnic communities. 'Ethnic cleansing' is the euphemism for this procedure, which has been applied also in the Serb-controlled areas of Croatia, and to a smaller extent by the Croats in areas that they control. But of course it was not invented by either Serbs or Croats. The Armenians are doing the same in Nagorno-Karabakh. The Turks did it in northern Cyprus. The Israelis did it in parts of Palestine in 1948, and again on a smaller scale in 1967. The Czechs did it in the Sudetenland, the Poles in Silesia, Pomerania and East Prussia, after 1945. Greeks and Turks did it to each other in 1922-3. Ever since ethnicity began to be invoked as a basis of statehood, people trying to build or preserve states in disputed areas have been tempted, as a last resort, to clear those areas by force of people whose ethnic identity renders their loyalty suspect. Mr Baker and his European 'allies' are right to be horrified, but it is doubtful whether any of them really believe they can stop it. 'We are really talking about the need - maybe - to do something next time,' says an unnamed US official quoted in the international press. 'Everyone in the loop concedes that Yugoslavia is a past case already.' It is an unworthy thought, but difficult to resist once it has occurred to you, that the argument is not really about what should be done in the former Yugoslavia but about future security arrangements in Europe. It was perhaps no coincidence that this heightened awareness of the horrors of war in Yugoslavia hit the headlines on the very day that France and Germany agreed to push ahead with their proposal for a 35,000-man joint army corps, intended to be the nucleus of a future European army. It was last Friday, remember, that President Francois Mitterrand and Chancellor Helmut Kohl made their announcement in La Rochelle, and it was that very night that Mr Baker, after conferring with Mr Major, suddenly called on 'the civilised world' to start thinking about political, diplomatic and economic action against Serbia, and then added: 'If measures in those fields should fail, then and only then it would be my view to take a look at questions involving military matters.' The beauty of this formulation is that it raises the possibility of military action only when other measures have been tried and failed. By then, of course, the Serbs would have more or less completed their 'ethnic cleansing', and might even value the arrival of a 'peacekeeping force' which would make it more difficult for armed Croats or Moslems to infiltrate the 'cleansed' area. The Turks have found a UN force very useful for that purpose in Cyprus, and it was clearly in that spirit that the Serbs agreed to have one in Croatia - although they are now in trouble with the UN for trying to finish off the 'cleansing' operation after the UN troops arrived. To be really cynical, one could argue that the prevention of ethnic cleansing is a task unachievable by any military intervention short of a full-scale occupation and administration, but that ethnic cleansing itself is a useful, perhaps even essential, precondition for a successful 'peacekeeping' operation, which classically involves the interposition of a neutral force along a clear line of demarcation between two sides. Now think back to last summer, when the fighting in Yugoslavia started. Victory in the Gulf War had reasserted the US's military supremacy and indispensability, but the Europeans, aided by US public opinion, had bounced President Bush into intervening in Kurdistan, from which he was trying to extricate his troops as fast as possible. Meanwhile the Europeans were wrangling among themselves and with their Nato allies about the institutional framework for closer European defence cooperation: should it come under Nato or should it be an aspect of the new European Union? In other words, should America have a say in it or not? Yugoslavia was no longer a stake in the cold war, and the US concluded it was an area of limited strategic interest, where involvement carried significant risks but offered few worthwhile benefits. The Europeans were proclaiming a new 'common foreign and security policy'. Let them try their luck. The Europeans tried, with the results we now see. Meanwhile a compromise was reached, at the Nato summit in Rome last November and then at Maastricht in December, on European defence: it would be done through the Western European Union (WEU), which was to be both 'an integral part of the development of the European Union', and 'a means to strengthen the European pillar of the Atlantic Alliance' - the latter remaining 'the essential forum for consultation among its members'. Although the French and German governments insist that their joint corps, which other WEU members are invited to join, will 'contribute to the reinforcement of the Atlantic alliance,' it is clearly regarded by the US, and by the British and Dutch, as a breach of the spirit of last year's compromise. That is why it is such a good moment for the US to rub Europe's nose in the reality of its political incompetence and military irrelevance, by drawing attention to a crisis it has conspicuously failed to solve, and by hinting at a military intervention which, without Nato's help, it would be quite unable to organize. Yet I wonder if it is a wise thing to do. When Europeans have had time to think about it, they may decide to take the task of building a force which would be less dependent on the US more seriously.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Letter: Banking practice is not a 'sham'
DOC.TEXT: Sir, Your rather gratuitous quotation ('Islamic bank opens in Jakarta', May 15) of a 'local banker' that profit payments by Indonesia's new Islamic bank are 'a sham' is very much unappreciated. A newspaper of your quality surely has many qualified staff who are aware that the issue for Moslems is not what conventional bankers consider to be interest, but what Allah considers to be 'riba'. Interest as paid in the normal course of most bank loans and deposits is, indeed, riba. But, here in America, Moslems find that a number of transactions are riba free, and yet still defined as interest by authorities. For instance, were I to sell goods on consignment at a profit, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) would define the profit as interest. Or were I to lease equipment to a manufacturer under an Islamically acceptable lease, my accountant would define my income to the IRS as 'interest'. In neither case would there be an iota of riba, a stain of sham. I could cite many more examples. Let's see what services Bank Muamalat Indonesia offers, and then we will have a basis for judging whether or not they are a sham. I suspect that they will not be a sham. Please don't cast aspersions unnecessarily. Abdulkader, president and publisher, FP Publications, 27957 Ridgebluff Court, Rancho Palos Verdes, California 90274, US

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Letter: London as financial centre of EC
DOC.TEXT: Sir, If London is to have any hope of becoming the EC financial centre there is no more than a four-week window of opportunity to clear up the Lloyd's mess. The Council of Lloyd's is caught in a cruel dilemma. If the LMX spiral practices are legal and defended as such then the effect will be even more disastrous than if they are declared illegal. The sheer inequity of this practice will soon be obvious to all. It cannot be kept hidden that the LMX 'pyramid' process is flagrantly to the benefit of the brokers (and Lloyd's indirectly) at the expense of the Names. Condoning this practice, even if legal, will mean that the traditions of the City of London render it unacceptable as a financial centre because exploitation is not sufficiently ruled out. It is also very likely that the 1982 Lloyd's Act will be challenged in the European Courts of Justice as being contrary to basic human rights. To expect Lloyd's to regulate itself is like asking turkeys to regulate Christmas. The case will be an acute embarrassment to the government, which will be put in the impossible position of having to condone dubious practices. At this point it will become obvious that London is not fit to be the financial centre of Europe. Allowing turkeys to behave as ostriches will not solve the dilemma. It may just not be too late for resolute action by the government. Inquiries that are too late in reporting are not sufficient resolute action. Edward de Bono, L2 Albany, Piccadilly, London W1V 9RR

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / The strain and pain in Spain: The path to convergence with leading EC economies is tough
DOC.TEXT: If Spaniards thought that their transition to democracy in 1977, their entry into the European Community in 1986 and the growth of the economy ahead of the single market next year entitled them to enjoy the fruits of success, they are now being disabused of the idea. Tomorrow, a half-day general strike will probably shut the country down. Another full-day stoppage is planned for October. The nation's political pulse has suddenly quickened as the government, having dawdled through its third term until now, has launched a raft of policies to lock the country more tightly into Europe - policies that directly threaten the political power of Spain's trade unions. Their focus is convergence with the leading Community economies and the government's determination that Spain becomes a founding member of European economic and monetary union in 1997 or, at the latest, 1999. Spain wants to be a founder member because it fears that otherwise it will be left behind in the second tier of European development, along with Greece and Portugal. To get there, Spaniards are being asked to make another huge social and economic effort and, for the unions at least, the price is too high. For its part the government is certain that it has the country on its side. 'Spain now has an historic opportunity to form part of a process of political integration in the most developed, rich and, maybe, the most socially advanced part of the world,' said Mr Carlos Solchaga, the finance minister, to parliament recently. Convergence with strictly defined macroeconomic criteria was the centrepiece of the Maastricht Treaty in December. To join the founders of Emu, Spain has to cut public-sector deficits from 4.4 per cent to 3 per cent of gross domestic product; bring long-term interest rates to within two points of the lowest in the EC; take the peseta into the narrow band of the European Monetary System's exchange rate mechanism by 1994; hold public-sector debt below 60 per cent of GDP; and cut inflation to within 1.5 points of the three best performers in the EC. Spain's public debt as a percentage of GDP is one of the lowest in the Community, but it faces an uphill battle against inflation, which has risen from an annual 5.5 per cent at the end of 1991 to 6.5 per cent now. Worse, last year's public-sector deficit of Dollars 25bn is being fuelled by spending on infrastructure and social provisions such as health and education by both the central government and the country's 17 autonomous regions. The government's need to borrow is, in turn, the chief cause of the country's high real interest rates, now hovering at about 6 per cent. For Mr Solchaga, the prime minister's commitment to Maastricht has been a blessing. The finance minister has for years been keen to cut deficit growth and to discipline the economy. More often than not, he has been prevented from doing so by the left-wingers who dominate the Socialist party administration. Now Mr Felipe Gonzalez, the prime minister, has been told bluntly by his finance minister that unless Spain radically cuts spending, it will not be able to meet Maastricht's convergence targets. For a man who has dedicated 10 years in government to putting Spain at the EC's top table, not converging is a shocking prospect. He appears to have given Mr Solchaga carte blanche to achieve his goal. By March, Mr Solchaga had his Convergence Plan ready. He had two main targets: the country's employment agency, Inem, and the body that administers the national health system, Insalud. In the past three years Inem, which runs unemployment offices and pays benefits, accumulated a deficit of Dollars 4bn, which was due to rise to Dollars 6bn by the end of this year. As economic activity has slowed, employers are not renewing the short-term job contracts introduced by the government in 1985. The number of people eligible for benefits has increased sharply. Less than a week after publishing his Convergence Plan, Mr Solchaga decreed sharp cuts in the amount of unemployment benefits payable and doubled the time required to qualify for benefits to a year. The measures could save Dollars 4bn this year but the unions have responded with a programme of strikes and increasingly vitriolic verbal assaults on the government. In the words of one union leader: 'It is the biggest attack ever on the workers by a democratic Spanish government.' On the healthcare front, Mr Solchaga also plans to implement sweeping reforms of a system that has overspent its budgets by a total of Dollars 6bn since 1988. Notably, the civil servants who manage the budgets are to become contracted executives who, for the first time, will face dismissal if they do not meet financial targets. Insalud, the central buying monopoly for the hospitals, is to be run as a business and will be phased out as health planning is devolved to regional governments. Unions see the moves to streamline health administration as a first step to privatising it. Together, the Inem and Insalud deficits account for more than 1 per cent of GDP and the attack on them is fundamental to Mr Solchaga's Convergence Plan. But he has also infuriated the left and the unions by establishing goals that go beyond Maastricht's requirements. Where Emu says public deficits should be lower than 3 per cent of GDP, Mr Solchaga has committed Spain to 1 per cent. The finance minister's fervour stems from a fear of two things. First, the possibility that Emu may not happen in the light of German worries over giving up the D-Mark; second, his long experience of his party increasing spending ahead of elections. By the end of 1994 Spaniards will have voted in municipal, regional, general and European elections. For Mr Solchaga, these two factors mean 'the government is doing no more than any responsible government would do, even without Maastricht'. It was inevitable that the unions would oppose the programme. As a result, a united stance by the Socialist party is crucial. To achieve this, Mr Gonzalez has been forced to breathe life back into the political fortunes of the deputy party leader, Mr Alfonso Guerra. He resigned as deputy prime minister last year in the wake of a scandal involving political favours to his businessman brother in Seville. Mr Guerra has always had a tight hold on party organisation, and his power has rested in his ability to control the nominations of election candidates. A general election must be held by October next year and Mr Gonzalez seems to have made a simple trade. Mr Guerra will be allowed to manage the election in return for ensuring party solidarity behind convergence. Both Mr Gonzalez and Mr Solchaga have publicly hinted that they would rather lose their parliamentary majority than forego the Convergence Plan. Against this, union efforts to mobilise support against the Socialists seem doomed. 'There is a risk,' says Mr Nicolas Sartorius, a leader of the United Left (IU) party, the biggest of the left-wing parties, 'that the strikes may backfire'. Public transport strikes in Madrid and Barcelona in the spring irritated the public, while the decree on unemployment benefits has excluded a much abused scheme that pays benefits to unemployed farm workers in the regions of Andalucia and Extremadura. This scheme virtually captures the large rural vote in these regions for the government. The problem the unions have in trying to generate sympathy is that the context in which the benefit cuts have been made is convergence, and the idea of becoming a leader in Europe is popular in Spain. The unions have thus been forced to try to win support over two tangential threats. The first is a strike law which will restrict union freedom to call and implement strikes; the second has been a decision by the government to freeze all subsidies to public sector companies at current levels. The unions are not alone in the firing line of reform. Mr Solchaga also has the professions and the trades in his sights. Prices in the service sector are rising at roughly double the rate of inflation and he is looking for ways to strip away protective traditions which fix fees and entry into many occupations. If Mr Solchaga's overall strategy sounds bold, the government is confident that it has adequate public backing, particularly from the growing numbers of Spaniards who count themselves as middle class. In 1985, for example, 39 per cent of polled Spaniards said they were middle class. By last summer, that figure had risen to 51 per cent. The government, then, is playing to the economic and European aspirations of a majority of voters, and the only criticism it will listen to now comes from economists sceptical of its ability to put the Convergence Plan into practice. Mr Jaime de Pinies, chief economist at the merchant bank Banco Santander de Negocios, says he believes 1992 and 1993 will be 'low credibility years' for the plan. An election is looming and Mr Solchaga will be under great pressure not to cut spending too much. Also, the plan requires Spain to grow faster than the Community average, while committing it to cutting inflation and deficits in the absence of any real signs of an international economic upturn. Although wage settlements are averaging about 7.5 per cent this year - a full point down on 1991 - several economists wonder whether Mr Solchaga may have bitten off more than he can chew. 'The achievement of these objectives (3 per cent inflation by 1996 and a public deficit of 1 per cent of GDP) seem far from realistic, and carry an important sacrifice in terms of employment and real economic growth,' said a recent report by the Madrid-based Analistas Financieros Internacionales. Mr Solchaga, though, has one and a half tricks up his sleeve to counter the pessimism. Peseta entry into the narrow band of the ERM would require cuts in interest rates, and could encourage exports and stimulate the economy. The half trick is a Spanish invention called cohesion. At Maastricht, Spain managed to persuade its partners to create a 'cohesion' fund to channel extra Community funds to poor member countries seeking to restructure their economies. It was agreed this would be established by 1994. Madrid is now battling to bring the date forward to the end of this year. However, Mr Gonzalez will need all his charm to get this money flowing Spain's way in the face of German and British opposition. 'We need this money,' says Mr Carlos Westendorp, the minister for Europe. DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Leading Article: Mr Lamont's objective
DOC.TEXT: THE RE-ELECTION of the Conservatives did not resolve the dilemmas of British economic policy. It merely changed the time horizon. The government is now able to take a strategic perspective. Such a perspective would be unnecessary if there were no choices left to make. But there are a few, even if the unmentionables - leaving the ERM or a realignment of sterling - are ignored. With sterling in the wide bands, the government can vary interest rates a little and public spending and taxation rather more. The question is what to do with its freedom. The chancellor of the exchequer has given his answer. He told the annual dinner of the Confederation of British Industry last week that Britain should aim to match Japan's inflation performance, which is about 2 per cent, if it wants to be 'a first-rank commercial power'. This sounds very attractive. But one might ask whether a current account deficit of Pounds 3.2bn in the first four months of 1992, for much of which the economy was in the seventh successive quarter of decline, is consistent with being a 'first-rank commercial power'. The official view is that the external position of a country is of no significance. Since the authorities also argued that the monetary expansion between 1986 and 1988 was a private phenomenon of limited policy concern, this view is not convincing. A 'first rate commercial power' in recession, but with a current account deficit, probably needs a real exchange rate depreciation. With realignments ruled out, low inflation is the sole route to that goal. Mr Lamont's target for inflation is not mere hubris. It is a goal that must be achieved, the sooner the better. Necessary pain This suggests that the high interest rates of today, not to mention efforts to put public spending back under control, represent necessary pain. So should Mr Lamont whisper sotto voce thanks for the monetary consequences of German unification and watch as British inflation - now merely back to where it was before the Lawson boom - is slowly dragged down to respectable levels? After all, under today's 5 per cent underlying rate of inflation, sterling would lose three quarters of its purchasing power in 30 years. This is not respectable. His choice is not so simple. What has made the disinflationary process effective is also what makes it so dangerous: the consequences of high interest rates on an economy whose banks, property companies and households took a huge bet on inflation not so many years ago. Mountleigh is the latest, but certainly not the last casualty from that period. Debt deflation There is only one answer to debt deflation: low short term interest rates, the answer supplied by the Federal Reserve in the US. But the sluggish US recovery suggests that a powerful debt deflation can only be overcome by a far more aggressive central bank than anything on offer in the UK. So what should the government choose: as much monetary restraint as possible, to get inflation down, or as little as possible, to get the economy moving again? Lower interest rates do appear desirable. Disinflation is in train, whatever happens to interest rates in the short to medium term. Maybe interest rates can even fall a sliver below German levels, which are themselves unlikely to fall for quite a while. High German interest rates do at least virtually guarantee that the loosening in the UK will not be overdone. Yet whatever the government now chooses, the legacy it inherits from its own and its predecessor's errors ensures that the outcome will be unhappy: underlying inflation will not fall as fast as the government hopes; recovery will not be as strong as it might wish. More important still, even when underlying inflation has at last been driven down to low levels, strong growth may well not ensue. Like the British public, the government has taken a gamble. The public bet on inflation. The government has bet on the ERM. It has bet that the weak balance of payments position will not constrain future growth; it has bet as well that a heavily indebted economy will return to health despite high real interest rates. Only time will tell whether the gamble will work. Even a newly re-elected government can only do a little more than hope.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Book Review: Cards up their sleeves
DOC.TEXT: VENDETTA: American Express and the smearing of Edmond Safra By Bryan Burrough HarperCollins Dollars 25 hardback, 477 pages HOUSE OF CARDS: Inside the Troubled Empire of American Express By Jon Friedman & John Meehan GP Putnam & Sons Dollars 24.95, 262 pages During the 1980s few US companies enjoyed such rapid profits growth and success as American Express. And few company chairmen were as lionised as Jim Robinson, the soft-spoken and courtly Atlanta banker's son who moved effortlessly between Wall Street and Washington. After being named chairman in 1977 Mr Robinson appeared to be constructing a financial services supermarket as he steered American Express from one acquisition to another. To the company's traditional charge card and travellers cheque products were added an array of sister businesses that ranged from stockbroking and investment banking (Shearson Loeb Rhoades, Lehman Brothers, E F Hutton) to private and commercial banking (Mr Edmond Safra's Trade Development Bank) to the cable television business (Warner Amex Cable). The good times for American Express coincided with the rise of the free-spending yuppies in the 1980s. Consumer spending kept rising - and with it the number of holders of the Amex green card, the gold card, and even the platinum card - until the company had some 36m cardholders worldwide. But American Express began facing a far harsher environment at the end of the decade. In retrospect, its once grand strategy now seemed more an ad hoc series of opportunistic acquisitions that had produced an unwieldy conglomerate. Its purchase of E F Hutton in late 1987, for example, came shortly after the Wall Street crash and led to heavy 1990 losses at Shearson Lehman Hutton. The new Optima card, a downmarket venture in the credit card sector, was by Amex's own admission poorly managed. By 1991 Optima was mired in credit losses. By early 1992 - after a year in which Optima accounted for more than 50 per cent of the Dollars 697m rise in credit loss provisions in the card division - Amex admitted its need to strengthen its capital base. Worse still, the core business of cards had been affected not only by the Optima losses but by rising numbers of retailers who were steering customers away from the Amex card and protesting the company's high fee structure. For Mr Robinson it must all seem like a bad dream. Critics say his 1980s diversification strategy has begun to disintegrate: the cable business was disposed of in 1985, just before it turned profitable. In 1984, a year after the purchase of Trade Development Bank, Mr Safra had broken with Amex (TDB itself was sold in 1990). And in 1989 Mr Robinson had to make a humbling public apology and a donation of Dollars 8m to Mr Safra's favourite charities when it emerged that persons employed by Amex had engaged in a smear campaign against Mr Safra. Now, as Mr Robinson and American Express are coming in for criticism over the company's business strategy in US media and financial circles, two new books add to the controversy. Yet neither provides enough analysis to answer the key question: what really went wrong? The first to be published is a chronologically ordered narrative called House of Cards. The book tries to present itself as an expose of Mr Robinson, who is dismissed as a power-hungry lightweight. However, the book is superficial and at times gratuitously salacious. This is a shame because House of Cards might have been - had it contained a bit more analysis - a more authoritative look at a fascinating company that lately has seemed to be somewhat adrift. Vendetta is another story. This is a well written and heavily detailed account of the way in which some distinctly unsalubrious operatives were deployed in the late 1980s by an aide to Mr Robinson to investigate Mr Safra. Vendetta recounts how they ended up smearing the secretive Swiss-based banker, thus costing Amex an enormous amount in terms of image and reputation. Vendetta has brought Bryan Burrough, author of the best-selling Barbarians at the Gate, a Dollars 50m libel suit from the former aide to Mr Robinson who eventually resigned because the Safra affair occurred 'on my watch'. The libel suit, however, does not concern the book, but rather an article published by Burrough in The Wall Street Journal. The book's great strength is as a colourful yarn that chronicles some questionable behaviour committed in the name of an otherwise reputable US corporation. Its weakness is that it hints at Mr Robinson's direct involvement in the Safra affair, but never quite manages to make the charge stick. The real value of both books is less in their revelations than in their underscoring of the problems that have caused Mr Robinson and Amex to come under such scrutiny. Mr Robinson may yet put things right, but for now the company's image - perhaps its most precious asset - looks somewhat tarnished.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Arts: Today's Television
DOC.TEXT: A promising evening. BBC2 continues its series of five-minute Dance House programmes, a film choreographed by Jacob Marley, known for his work with the Pet Shop Boys (7.55). Channel 4's consumer series Check Out 92 returns with a programme which asks why, even after the recommendations following the 1985 Manchester air disaster, safety measures which have been understood for decades (rear facing seats for example) are still, apparently, being ignored by the Civil Aviation Authority (8.30). In the week before Czechoslovakia's general election, Dispatches reviews the state of the country's economy and discovers that many of those now running large businesses were communist bosses not long ago (9.00 C4). BBC2's re-run of the drama about politics, Edge of Darkness reaches its penultimate episode (9.25). Inside Story offers what sounds like a harrowing documentary about Baragwanath Hospital in the South African black township of Soweto where 100 victims of assault arrive every night (9.30) BBC1).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Arts: Book prize
DOC.TEXT: The UK's biggest literary prize, worth a basic Pounds 30,000, was announced yesterday. To be known as the David Cohen British Literature Prize it will be awarded biennially, starting in 1993, to a living British writer in recognition of a lifetime's achievement, writes Antony Thorncroft. The Arts Council, which has been instrumental in setting up the Prize, will award an additional Pounds 10,000 to the winner who will use it to commission a new work from a younger writer.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Business and the Environment: Regional issues get support
DOC.TEXT: As world leaders prepare to discuss global environmental problems at the Earth Summit in Rio, the UK government has been told by its Advisory Committee on Science and Technology (Acost) to focus environmental research more on local and regional issues. An Acost review of UK environmental research programmes concludes that the concentration of funds on global issues such as climate change 'could starve initiatives in other areas'. Acost recommends 'a move over time to greater focus on local and regional issues, many of which are pressing problems (for instance, waste management and land remediation)'. It points out that huge sums will be spent tackling local pollution over the next decade - for example Pounds 28bn by the UK water industry - and says 'research could produce cheaper or better ways of improving these local and regional environmental problems'. Total public spending on environmental research is Pounds 200m a year on a narrow definition - and as much as Pounds 400m a year on a very wide definition. The lower figure would represent 5 per cent of total government R&D, a similar level to other industrialised countries. The biggest single area of spending is the physics of the global atmosphere, which consumes about Pounds 55m a year. Total spending on water pollution, including oceans and seas, lakes and rivers, amounts to Pounds 40m. At present much environmental research focuses on the scientific processes that determine the system being studied. As these become better understood, Acost says, the emphasis should switch to investigating the specific impact of changes on the environment and remedial measures that can be taken to combat undesirable changes. The report was written by an Acost committee chaired by Robert May, professor of zoology at Oxford University. Environmental Research Programmes, an Acost Report. HMSO. Pounds 11.95.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / The Week In Luxembourg: Milking the Community cow - European Court
DOC.TEXT: Dairy farmers who were paid a premium by the European Community to take a five-year holiday from milk production are entitled to damages for lost income they would have received during the period under the EC additional milk levy quota, the European Court of Justice (ECJ) ruled last week. The Court said the Community must compensate the farmers because they had accepted a temporary EC non-marketing premium for a period chosen by Dutch and German authorities under 1984 EC milk rules which the ECJ had already ruled invalid because they breach Community law on protection of legitimate expectations. The ECJ held that the Community had incurred liability because of its failure to take account of the specific situation of the producers affected without invoking any higher public interest. The extent of damage to be compensated was the loss of income that would otherwise have been earned. Income earned from alternative occupations had to be deducted in mitigation. Interest was awarded at the rate claimed but at a maximum of 8 per cent. The farmers were not entitled to further damages under a 1989 amendment to the milk rules which allowed producers a provisional quota. Although the 1989 amendment was equally invalid, the breach of EC law on protection of legitimate expectations was not sufficiently serious to entitle them to compensation because the Community legislature had considered all relevant interests in making its legitimate economic policy choice. All dairy farmers in the same situation as those in last week's test cases will be entitled to claim damages caused by invalid EC rules on the additional milk levy quota introduced in 1984, but not for any loss caused by the failure of the 1989 rules to allocate sufficient quota. However, those involved have as much as a year to agree the calculation of the amount of damages, in accordance with principles laid down by the Court. So while final adjudication in the event of disagreement is reserved to the Court, further delay and complications are likely before any dairy farmers are compensated. Mulder and others v Council and Commission, Joined Cases C-104/89 and C-37/90, FC, 19 May 1992. Last Friday, ECJ president Ole Due refused the European Commission's application for interim measures against the UK in a case concerning the scope of the monopoly enjoyed under EC law by the five UK Milk Marketing Boards (MMBs) over 'milk produced and marketed without processing'. The UK says the monopoly covers all forms of liquid milk for direct human consumption including skimmed and semi-skimmed milk. The Commission disagrees, claiming that the MMBs' exclusive rights are limited to whole milk. The ECJ president, who customarily decides interim measures cases alone, did not examine the merits of the dispute, rejecting the Commission's application on the ground of lack of urgency. In particular, he held that the milk producers concerned had sufficient safeguards that the status quo would be maintained until judgment by the full court without danger of serious and irreparable damage. He accepted undertakings by the MMBs not to enforce any rights over skimmed or semi-skimmed milk until the ECJ's final decision. Commission v UK, Case C-40/92 R, Order of the President of the Court, 22 May 1992. Permissible national controls - auditors The ECJ has delivered another significant judgment for the professions, and in particular auditors, building on earlier indications of the kind of national controls which member states may impose on individuals or companies established in one member state when they provide services or are engaged as employees in a second member state. In accordance with EC rules on establishment, an auditor authorised to practise in Luxembourg under Luxembourg law, and employed by an authorised Luxembourg company, may not have his authorisation removed simply on the ground that he no longer satisfies the condition of Luxembourg law which restricts authorisation to auditors established in Luxembourg, when he moves his centre of operations to Germany, and is employed by a German company related to his Luxembourg employer. However, the Rome Treaty rules on free movement of workers and freedom to provide services permit Luxembourg to require the auditor to comply with certain rules which can be objectively justified in the public interest and are equally applicable to Luxembourg auditors, if the requirements in the member state where he is established are not equivalent. In the current case, this meant that, within its own territory, Luxembourg could require compliance with rules objectively necessary to ensure professional rules applicable to auditors are observed, and require an effective presence and a permanent infrastructure in Luxembourg as well as the supervision of an auditor's compliance with professional ethics. Ramrath v Minister of Justice, Case C-106/91, 6CH 20 May 1992. Cheaper German roads The ECJ had condemned a German law, previously suspended in 1990 by interim order of the Court, increasing the tax imposed on heavy lorries using Federal roads. The tax was held to infringe the Rome Treaty's 'standstill' rule prohibiting the introduction of new road transport measures with the direct or indirect effect of discriminating against transport from other member states. The discrimination resulted from the fact that, while German road hauliers were subject to the same increase, they received a reduction in motor vehicle tax which was not shared by those from other member states. This judgment will save road hauliers of all member states the additional costs when crossing Germany, in particular, to eastern Europe. Commission v Germany, Case C-195/90, FC 19 May 1992. Other cases In four cases of less general significance, the ECJ rejected cases brought by Greece challenging the clearance of its 1987 CAP accounts (Case C-385/89) and by the Commission against Germany unsuccessfully claiming that German rules infringed the Treaty rules on free movement of goods by applying stricter rules to eye drops as a result of defining them as medicinal products instead of as cosmetics (Case C-290/90). The court upheld the Commission in finding that the Netherlands had failed to implement correctly, within the time laid down, the 1982 directive on risks of certain big industrial accidents (Case C-190/90) as well as interpreting certain terms in the directive on the treatment of employees in the case of the transfer of undertakings in the special context of certain Dutch social work foundations (Case C-29/91). FT Commercial Law Reports Following the introduction of the European Court column, FT commercial law reports now appear on Wednesdays, Thursdays and Fridays. There will be no European Court column next week as the court is not sitting. All dairy farmers in the same situation as those in last week's test cases will be entitled to claim damages caused by invalid EC rules on the additional milk levy quota introduced in 1984

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Construction Contracts: Radio system for Africa
DOC.TEXT: A contract worth about Pounds 1m has been won by RACAL RADIO, Reading, Berkshire, to supply and install the main HF radio system for use along the full length of the Tazama oil pipeline in Africa. Funded by the African Development Bank, the contract was awarded to Racal by Tazama Pipeline following an international competitive tender. The order calls for the supply and installation of eight 1kW HF radio systems for voice and data transmission, including Group 3 fax, with the hub station located at N'dola, Zambia. Refurbishment of antennas and training support are also part of the package. The systems to be supplied are Racal Adaptive Communications Equipment (RACE), with an HF installation being located at the six pumping stations along the pipeline and at the main control installations at each end. The pipeline runs a total distance of 1,710 kilometres from the port of Dar-es-Salaam, Tanzania, to the refinery at N'dola. The Tazama eight-system HF network requirement forms the intial phase of what is expected to grow into a larger order. A future phase is likely to include the introduction of a Racal-designed automatic, remote dial-up telemetry acquisition capability, enabling the pipeline control station in N'dola to monitor the inlet and outlet pressures at each of six pumping stations. In the current contract the monitoring requirement is met by voice reporting or by manual data messaging. Delivery is due to be complete by the second half of the year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Construction Contracts: US oil equipment project
DOC.TEXT: WEIR MATERIALS has been awarded a contract, initially worth Pounds 5m, to supply specialist components made from its supersteel Zeron-100 to three oil projects in Alaska. It is the largest export order won by the Weir Group company since it was set up four years ago, and is the first time it has supplied equipment to the Arctic regions. Weir Materials will supply pipes, fittings and flanges to the Point Mclntyre project, the Lisburne field expansion and the Prudhoe Bay development. The order has been placed by Arco Alaska Inc and its partners BP and Exxon. Contract delivery is scheduled for this summer. Initial orders will be serviced by a British and European manufacturing consortium co-ordinated by Weir Materials. The company has already signed agreements to transfer manufacturing and fabrication technology for Zeron-100 to steel mills in the United States with the aim of establishing an indigenous manufacturing capability.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Construction Contracts: Pounds 5.5m awards for Ashby
DOC.TEXT: ASHBY & HORNER JOINERY has received orders totalling Pounds 5.5m. The two largest contracts are very different. One is for the joinery work required in the restoration of the 17th century Uppark House, a National Trust property near Petersfield, West Sussex. The other major contract, a little more unusual, although not unique for this P&O company, is the fitting out of the 1929 luxury motor yacht Jezebel: Work on the 248 ft yacht is being carried out for DML(Devonport Management Ltd) to the designs of yacht designer Jon Bannenberg. All the main items will be made at Ashby & Horner Joinery's works at Thurrock and then installed in the yacht at the Devonport Royal Dockyard in Plymouth over the next 18 months. The work includes all the interiors to the owner's and guests' main accommodation. This includes the saloon, dining room, library and staterooms with bathrooms. The lift interiors and the common areas in the owner and guest accommodation are also part of the contract. Ceilings will have veneered perimeters and lacquereed cof fered centres. Covered fabric panels with special features will adorn the walls. High quality carpets, timber parquet and marble will be used for the flooring, either separately or in a combination of all three. Jezabel is currently in dry dock and has been stripped down to the bare hull for survey and any repairs needed before the reconstruction starts. Although she will be fully equipped with modern systems, the vessel's original style and character will be carefully recreated.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Construction Contracts: Scottish hospital work
DOC.TEXT: HALL & TAWSE, the const ruction division of Raine Industries, has won hospital development contracts worth Pounds 7.3m. An orthopaedic centre and two operating theatres are being built at Woodend Hospital in Aberdeen by Hall & Tawse Scotland. The contract, worth Pounds 3m, also includes refurbishment of the hospital's theatre block. Hall & Tawse Southern has won a Pounds 1.7m contract to refurbish Southampton General Hospital, carrying out extensive repairs and renewal to the buildings' roofs and windows. The same Hall & Tawse company has also been awarded a contract to construct a private hospital in Reading for Independent British Hospitals. The project at Coley Park, which will take 55 weeks to complete, will provide 69 bed spaces.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Construction Contracts: Export orders won by ML Aviation
DOC.TEXT: ML AVIATION, a subsidiary of ML Holdings, has recently been awarded an order for defence products. This brings the total won since October to Pounds 16m. Over 80 per cent of the orders are for export customers and were won against international competition. ML Aviation, which incorporates ML Wallop Defence Systems, is a UK manufacturer of infra-red decoys, aircraft weapon carriage and release equipment, and naval decoy systems. The orders included in the list are: over Pounds 4m of airborne infra-red decoys for the Far East and Europe; over Pounds 4m of aircraft bomb racks and missile launchers from McDonnell Douglas for Harrier 2 AV8B for the US Marine Corps and from BAe for Hawk for various export customers; and Pounds 3.5m of naval decoy systems and ammunition destined for Asia and the Middle East. The company is also to supply Pounds 1m of Special Forces equipment for the United Kingdom's Ministry of Defence and the Gulf area.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Construction Contracts: Business park scheme
DOC.TEXT: Birmingham Midshires Building Society has appointed four Midlands-based companies to develop its new Pounds 9m headquarters at Pendeford Business Park. Wolverhampton-based Mason Richards Partnership has been appointed as architects for the project. Clarke Bond Partnership of Birmingham has been appointed to oversee the structural engineering work. RW Gregory & Partners has been employed to act as mechanical and electrical engineers. Francis Groves, another Birmingham-based firm, will act as quantity surveyors. Birmingham Midshires plans to invite tenders for the main building contract from a list of nominated companies. A decision on the successful company will be announced in August.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / People: Worldwide liaison from St Helens
DOC.TEXT: Pilkington's new group legal adviser, from the beginning of June, is a keep-fit fanatic - who once ran hilly marathons in under three hours and took part in an Everest expedition. He has now turned his energies to windsurfing - and to managing the legal resources of Pilkington worldwide. David Bricknell, 43, joined the UK glassmaker in 1974 from Slaughter & May. He was company secretary from 1981 to 1989; and is currently manager of the group legal department and number two to Tony Hartley, 62, who retires at the end of the month after a 33-year stint at Pilkington. Bricknell explains that while he only wished to alter 'one paragraph of the job description', the emphasis of his task has changed - away from licensing, which once consumed a lot of time but is now under a separate team within technology management. He will hence be freer to concentrate on 'worldwide liaison'. 'With only 20-25 per cent of our business based in the UK, we have to rely on local (legal) advisers a lot,' says Bricknell who was closely involved in the 1980 purchase of Flachglass in Germany. 'And the scale of both costs and damages these days means this dimension of the business has to be managed in as tight and disciplined a way as any other expenditure.' While the headquarters for much of the European operation has moved to Brussels - causing a furore in St Helens - Bricknell is part of the small corporate headquarters concerned with global strategy that remains in Lancashire. ***** David Roycroft is to be appointed head of corporate affairs at Pilkington from July. He is currently director of marketing at ITN and was formerly in the diplomatic service where his appointments included three years as deputy private secretary to the Prince of Wales. ***** Timothy May has been appointed company secretary of EUROCAMP on the resignation of Martin Kinsey. ***** Tim Bowdler, md of Cape Architectural Products, is also appointed md of CAPE Building Products on the resignation of Sandy Hutchison. ***** John Kelly, at present md of Associated Leisure, has been appointed chief executive of Cashcard Systems. ***** Karen Richardson, a partner in Travers Smith Braithwaite, has been appointed solicitor and company secretary of REED INTERNATIONAL. ***** BLENHEIM GROUP has appointed Philippe Delhomme, formerly financial director of Habitat France, financial director of its French subsidiary; Paul O'Reilly, formerly group financial controller of Avis Europe, financial director of its US subsidiaries; and Mike Fletcher, formerly md of Johnson Fry, md of its UK operations. ***** Stephen Crossan and Roy Knowles have been promoted to the board of CHORLEY ENGINEERING, part of BET Plant Services. ***** Rod Taylor, human resources general manager for marketing and operations staff at British Airways, is appointed director of human resources at SEARS. David Garth, head of group personnel is to become director of human resources for Sears womenswear division.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / People: Non-executive directors
DOC.TEXT: Mair Barnes, md of Woolworths, at ABBEY NATIONAL. ***** Bryan Toye, chairman of Toye & Co, as deputy chairman of FUTURAMA SIGNS. ***** Sir David Orr has retired from RTZ. ***** Jeffrey Rowlay has retired from NEXT. ***** Michael Davies as chairman of NATIONAL EXPRESS; Ray McEnhill remains chief executive. ***** Derek Kingsbury, chairman of Fairey, as chairman of GOODE DURRANT. ***** Derek Roberts has resigned from NEWMARKET VENTURE CAPITAL.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / People: Hooley resigns from Butte
DOC.TEXT: Bill Hooley, who, in January last year signed a three-year, Pounds 71,500-a-year contract as managing director of Butte Mining, a London-listed company, has resigned. The announcement about his departure follows news last week that Butte, which has not made a profit since it was floated five years ago and has a present market value of about Pounds 5m, had started a legal action in the US claiming Dollars 325m damages. Butte has been advised to conserve its resources to ensure it has the cash to fight the legal battle and has therefore decided to halt temporarily its exploration and mine development operations. 'Bill is a mining engineer and he prefers digging holes in the ground. He feels he is an overhead we don't need,' says a spokesman. No replacement managing director will be recruited. The cash conservation effort has also seen David Lloyd- Jacob, the executive chairman, agree to take only half the Pounds 100,000 a year guaranteed by his three-year contract. Hooley will work for Butte four days a week as a consultant in Australia where he went after it took over two small companies there. Previously he had worked with Dallhold Resources. ***** MIKE OTTY was taking something of a leap into the unknown when he decided to move from trying to set up an electronic rival to Glass's Guide, the UK motor trade's used car price 'Bible', to taking a job with Al Habtoor, a Dubai-headquartered conglomerate active throughout the Gulf. That was nine years ago, and not long after he had parted company with car maker Peugeot Talbot as its sales operations director in the UK. Dubai had seemed a sunnier prospect in more ways than one, as the UK motor trade and industry continued a long struggle to emerge from its early 1980s recession. Initially, Otty signed up to help Al Habtoor increase its network of motor distribution businesses in the Emirates, and which now include such illustrious names as Rolls-Royce. But although making the leap, Otty was destined to land firmly on his feet: this month he was appointed a group managing director under chairman Khalaf Al Habtoor. From now on, vehicles will form only a part of his remit. The others include construction, hotels, trading - and even marble and perfume.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Management: A coalition versus a dictator / Learning from experience that shareholders have a hard fight ahead if they want to fire the management
DOC.TEXT: Bad managers have been eyeing their shareholders with anxiety recently. Over the last 18 months the big institutional investors have shown themselves willing to remove managements which are not performing well. The trend has been greeted with general applause: onlookers argue that the institutions have found a new spirit at last. However, this view is mistaken. There is no new spirit. The apparent revolt by the institutions is just another aspect of the recession. The weak economy has exposed bad management and has also made it difficult for institutions to sell shareholdings. The decline in takeover activity has also put the spotlight on management, as companies which might otherwise have been predators have been forced to turn their resources inwards. Most cases of bad management unfold slowly. For instance, at Brown & Jackson, the discount retailer, and at Great Western Resources, the oil and gas group, institutional pressure has led to a change of chairman. But the circumstances leading up to the changes took a year or more to unfold, during which time the share prices declined steadily. Many people have argued that institutions should act more quickly. However, the balance of power between managements and their shareholders is heavily skewed in the former's favour, making quick action in most cases difficult, if not impossible. The typical fund manager runs a portfolio of between 50 and 150 stocks, and looks at up to 100 new stocks a year for possible investment. Other calls on his time include reports to investors, marketing presentations and internal management meetings. He will not be able to spend more than a few days a year on any one stock. Suppose you are a fund manager who feels the management in one of your stocks has taken the wrong track. You have a choice: change the management or sell the stock. If you wanted to adopt the first route, what would be involved? Your first port of call would be the management itself to unearth information and air your concerns. But the managers are unlikely to accept your criticisms. They will plead deeper understanding of their business, a plea that you cannot refute. You are not convinced, so you contact fellow institutions. Many will not share your concerns; after all, this is not a headline case. Some shareholders are bound to agree with you, although most of them will be intent on selling the stock, not on causing a revolution in the boardroom. To go on, you need to speak for 10-15 per cent of the company (assuming there are no big blocks supportive of management). If you get to this level, you have done well: you have got the support of say three of the top five institutional shareholders in the company. Now the real task begins. You need time because there is now going to be a serious fight. You are not just challenging management decisions, but the very livelihoods of the managers. The stakes for them are much higher than for you, and they will fight hard. They also have money on their side: the board will activate the whole corporate finance panoply - auditors, lawyers, merchant bankers, stockbrokers, public relations consultants. Each will depict a good management doing its best. Their presentations will be authoritative because they are based on hard information from inside the company. Some changes in policy may be announced, together perhaps with the sale of a subsidiary. Are these sufficient for you? If not, check how the rest of your ginger group views them. It is important to maintain cohesion. The management's presentation is now being wheeled around the uncommitted institutional shareholders. Meanwhile, you are having to make your case without a battery of advisers. The company may be able to spend hundreds of thousands of pounds on professional fees, but your budget is likely to be close to zero. It will be hard to convince the trustee of your fund to allocate fund money for professional fees. Nor will your own company be an easy touch. Even if you do raise some money for professional fees, the other fund managers you have enlisted may be unable to do so. Your cohesiveness becomes more fragile. You lack experience of this type of exercise. Fund managers are listeners, not persuaders. Even if you have a flair for presentation, it will be difficult to match the management's arguments because you are working only on the basis of the information they have given you. Most debilitating of all, you are a coalition facing a dictator. The management will react quickly and decisively to each turn of events, whereas the fund managers, who work for different firms, may find decisions difficult to arrive at, especially when the writs start flying. Even if you have found the time, and can manage without the money, how about the visibility? How does your marketing director feel about your efforts? Corporate governance may be a good thing, but it tends to draw clients' attention to your bad investments. The next problem is the likely reaction from your other investments. In future, their managements may prove less willing to be open with you. Beware your own chief executive. Does it look wise, from where he sits, to put your firm in the spotlight? In reality, this sort of battle rarely happens, and for good reasons. At every stage there is only one rational course of action for the fund manager: sell the stock. If you cannot, you will have to wait for a takeover bid. Failing that, wait for the bad management to become so acute that the board itself sorts the problem out. Only if none of these solutions is possible will the odds be sufficiently in the fund manager's favour to make it worth exercising shareholder power. The author was corporate finance director of Fidelity Investments until earlier this year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Management: Discretion is the better part of valeur / A look into the mystery of French bosses' pay, and finds they are doing nicely
DOC.TEXT: Ask a senior French executive how much he or she is paid and you are likely to be shown the door. The French have a catholic distaste for talking about private money, reflected in company disclosure laws which oblige employers to tell no one but the taxman how much their top people are paid. So some guesswork is needed to work out who gets what. Recent estimates by Towers Perrin, the pay and personnel consultancy, suggest that directors of companies with over FFr1bn (Pounds 100m) turnover pull in the second highest gross salaries in the world - between FFr2m and FFr2.5m. This is well behind their criticised US counterparts. Yet in net terms, France's top people get a less impressive pay packet - around FFr764,000 annually - behind the Germans, British and Japanese, after the high tax and social security charges for which France is renowned. Quoted companies are not, as in Anglo Saxon countries, obliged to publish the boss's salary, though they do have to declare in the annual report the sum of the top directors' pay. So it is that the Compagnie Generale des Eaux, the water distribution to construction giant, rumoured to be a generous rewarder of top people, reveals in its 1990 annual report that it paid FFr28.8m to its top 20 directors, an average of FFr1.44m each. The average is misleading, since the chairman, Guy Dejouany, is rumoured to earn above the odds. However, the chairman's salary is unlikely to be the whole story. He will typically receive top-ups from a number of foreign subsidiaries, usually small amounts set just under the income tax-paying threshold in each of those countries. This is an entirely legal tax avoidance technique, explain consultants. On top of this, French directors tend to hold more non-executive board seats on other companies than their Anglo-Saxon counterparts, believes Heidrich and Struggles, the leading headhunter. They pick up a fee every time, sometimes amounting to an impressive total. Some senior corporate figures sit on more than half a dozen company boards, an essential part of the networks of influence and patronage that bind together the higher echelons of French finance and industry. Not surprisingly, the biggest groups are reputed to pay the best directors' fees, or jetons de presence. Compagnie Generale des Eaux paid FFr1.45m to 12 non-executive directors, in 1990, an average of FFr120,000 each. Then come benefits in kind. Here French companies use share options much less than their British counterparts, and are less generous with company cars, but tend to be more willing when it comes to other perks. These include chauffeurs (pure status symbols, given that being driven to work in traffic-jammed Paris usually takes much longer than going by metro). Another popular perk is a company-owned flat rented out to the senior executive at a cheap rate. This is a valuable perk in France because rental allowances are taxed like normal income. However, the tax authorities are prepared to countenance a reasonably cheap rent on a company owned property, so allowing the executive to pocket the difference between the subsidised and commercially realistic rent free of tax. Anecdotes abound on French companies' generosity in expenses for receptions, seminars in the Bahamas and management meetings in Tuscan villas - although it is hard to get companies to admit to such open-handedness. In keeping with directors' coyness over the size of their salaries, secrecy also surrounds the way in which pay is set. In the private sector, a small committee of two or three of the most influential administrators decide the chairman's salary in private. The figure is communicated to the boss alone, and remains a mystery to other board members, including - crucially - the staff representatives which every French company above a certain size must include on its board. In state-owned industry, which includes seven of France's 10 top companies, the system is different. Here it will be up to the government minister responsible - usually industry or finance - to settle the chairman's salary. On the whole, public sector company chairmen are paid less than their opposite numbers in the private sector because the benchmark ministers use is the pay of civil servants. This tradition is coming under strain, however, as state owned companies increasingly employ executives from the private sector or acquire privately owned companies. Francis Lorentz, chairman of the state-owned computer group Bull, is said to earn rather less than some of his ex-private sector staff. Consultants believe the French top salary system is under pressure to become more open, as French industry becomes more international. Companies with share quotations on Anglo-Saxon markets, for instance, may have to give as much information as their overseas counterparts. Examples include Elf Aquitaine, the oil and gas group, its rival, Total, and Pechiney, the aluminium and packaging group, which have New York quotations. However, all three say their chairmen's salaries are still confidential. Old traditions take a while to die.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Jobs: Swiss slide below the Brits - How executive pay varies across Europe
DOC.DATELINE: IT cannot be denied any longer
DOC.TEXT: the ski-lift has definitely gone into reverse. Over nigh on a decade of comparing the buying-power enjoyed by European executives, I became so used to seeing the Swiss soaring high above everybody as to doubt they would ever be knocked off the peak. Indeed, such was their supremacy that even when the Spanish and the Luxembourgeois edged above them 12 months ago, I felt sure they would be back at the top this year. How wrong I was may be seen from the table over to the right: they have been overtaken by their counterparts in yet another four nations, including the United Kingdom. But before commenting further, I'll explain how the table works. As in previous years, it is drawn from the annual survey made by the Wyatt consultancy group's arm in Brussels. The latest version covers 1,470 companies of assorted sizes and activities in 17 European countries, and gives supplementary data on the United States and Turkey. Of the 17 countries, Belgium supplies the biggest sample of companies with 230, the smallest sample being Luxembourg's 36. The study also gives information on pay and perks for nine kinds of specialist directors as well as chief executives, divided into company-turnover bands. All of which is of course far more than I have room for. Anyone wanting the full report can obtain it, at a price, from either Jean-Pierre Becquet at 273 Avenue de Tervuren (Box 4), 1150 Brussels, Belgium; tel (02) 771 99 10, fax (02) 762 37 43: or Don McClune at 21 Tothill St, London SW1H 9LL; tel 071-222-8033, fax 071-222 9182. My extracts are confined to chief executives and just two sorts of other directors, of finance and of personnel, across companies of all sizes in each land. And I have included only the dozen best-paying countries, converting the currencies into sterling at the London closing rates on May 20. In each case, the table gives basic salaries, total money pay including bonuses, and a rough measure of buying power. The three 'lower quartile' columns refer to the executive who'd be a quarter of the way up from the foot of a ranking of all in the same job and land, the 'median' trio to the one mid-way, and the 'upper quartile' trio to the one a quarter way down from the top. Then come the standard averages. The buying-power is calculated by taking the total cash pay, deducting the particular country's normal tax and social security charges for a person with the specified income who is married with two dependent children, then adjusting the resulting net pay in line with Wyatt's index of international variances in executives' living costs. Alas, it is a loosely approximate measure at best. The reason is that, since survey companies evidently find it impossible to devise a gauge of housing costs that is consistent across different countries, that central item of spending is left out of account. Nevertheless the index is the best measure available of what pay is worth, and the countries are ranked by the average buying power of the three executives listed. On that criterion, the Spanish hold the top place they gained last year, with the Italians leapfrogging into second place over the Luxembourgeois who rank above the French by dint of paying the two specialist directors better. That is also why the Swiss are higher than the Austrians, although both are now below the UK and in the lower half of the ranking. Among the rest, the Belgians have regained the slight lead over the Dutch which they lost 12 months ago.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Hopes rise amid trade gloom
DOC.TEXT: THERE is a small crumb of comfort in yesterday's worse-than-expected UK visible and current-account trade figures for April. The respective Pounds 470m increases between March and April in the seasonally adjusted visible trade deficit to Pounds 1.36bn and in the provisionally estimated current-account deficit to Pounds 1.06bn suggest that UK domestic demand is reviving at last. The first-quarter decline in gross domestic product, disclosed last week, may mark the end of the recession. The bad news in yesterday's figures from the Central Statistical Office is that the UK's trade figures have taken a sudden turn for the worse long before recovery has become firmly established. There were no such deficits at this stage of the business cycle after the recessions of 1973-75 or 1979-81. Nor could the CSO's statisticians find any extraordinary factors in yesterday's figures to explain the worsening trend. On what is often considered the most reliable indicator of underlying trends - trade volumes minus oil and so-called erratic items such as aircraft, ships, oil rigs and precious stones - UK exports continued to grow in the three months to April. They were 2.3 per cent higher than in the three months from November to January and 4.2 per cent higher than between February and April last year. However, import volumes less oil and erratics were 4.3 per cent higher in February to April than in the previous three months, and 7.4 per cent higher than in the February to April period last year. Import volumes in the latest three-month period have been growing at roughly twice the rate of export volumes. Trade between Britain and its European Community partners has been especially disappointing in recent months. Exports were only 0.8 per cent higher in value terms in the three months to April than in the November to January period. At the same time, imports from other EC countries grew by 4.4 per cent. Britain's exports to Germany, the UK's biggest trading partner, were virtually unchanged in the latest three months, while imports from Germany rose by 5 per cent compared with the preceding three months. Between March and April, UK imports from Germany rose by 4.5 per cent while exports to Germany fell by 9.5 per cent. Another concern was the way the increase in imports last month was fairly evenly spread across all product categories. According to Mr Kevin Gardiner, UK economist at Warburg Securities in London, the import figures were 'pretty punchy and flagging a widening deficit to come'. One month's figures can - as the Treasury always points out - be deceptive. It may be that last month's 3.5 per cent jump in imports into the UK reflected wholesalers' and retailers' expectations of an increase in UK demand rather than an actual rise in demand. In that case, the April trade figures may be a reflection of increased stocks. If, on the other hand, the figures reflect genuine strong demand for imported goods, they pose serious questions about how far the UK's recovery from recession can be sustained before it runs into a balance-of-payments constraint. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- CURRENT ACCOUNT (POUNDS BN) ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Visible Trade Balance Less oil Current and Invisibles Balance Total erratics Exports Imports Balance ----------------------------------------------------------------------- 1990 -15.4 -18.6 -21.0 102.0 120.7 +3.2 1991 -4.4 -10.1 -13.4 103.7 113.8 +5.7 Qtr 2 -0.2 -2.2 -2.9 26.0 28.2 +2.0 Qtr 3 -1.2 -2.3 -3.5 26.4 28.8 +1.1 Qtr 4 -0.6 -2.6 -3.5 26.3 28.9 +1.9 Nov -0.3 -1.0 -1.3 8.7 9.7 +0.6 Dec -0.1 -0.7 -1.0 9.0 9.7 +0.6 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- 1992 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Qtr 1 -2.2 -3.1 -3.6 26.2 29.3 +0.9 Jan -0.9 -1.2 -1.3 8.3 9.4 +0.3 Feb -0.7 -1.0 -1.1 9.0 10.0 +0.3 Mar -0.6 -0.9 -1.1 8.9 9.8 +0.3 Apr -1.1 -1.4 -1.4 8.8 10.2 +0.3 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Invisibles for January to April 1992 are projections. DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Five regional radio permits to be offered
DOC.TEXT: THE RADIO Authority announced yesterday that it is planning to advertise five regional commercial radio licences covering up to 4.5m adults in the autumn. They will be advertised in areas where FM frequencies are available. The regional stations, in addition to Radio Authority plans for three national commercial stations, will cover central Scotland, north-east England, the west Midlands, north-west England - the largest - and the Severn estuary, covering south Wales and Avon. The Radio Authority said applicants would have to offer something different from existing radio stations in the area. The way is clear for those wanting to offer thematic stations offering a particular music format. Mr Peter Baldwin, director of the Radio Authority, sees the new regional stations as a way of offering other parts of the UK some of the commercial radio choice available in London. The formal announcement about the stations came as the Radio Authority yesterday published a consultative document on the re-advertisement of 55 independent local radio licences that expire by February 1995. The authority plans to begin the re-advertising process and complete it by the end of 1993. The controversial element of the plan is to advertise AM and FM frequencies separately. Many local stations have been running dual-frequency transmissions served by a single news operation. The Radio Authority may decide that an existing local station should keep only one of its frequencies. Mr Baldwin believes that there is likely to be a reasonable degree of stability but that each case will be judged on its merits. If two frequencies are awarded in a particular area to two different companies then it will be up to them to decide what economies of scale are possible through co-operation. Senior executives of the Radio Authority are also due to meet Mr David Mellor, National Heritage secretary, next month to discuss the future of radio in the UK. The Radio Authority would be horrified if, as some are suggesting, BBC Radio 1 and Radio 2 should take advertising at a time when national commercial stations offering classical music, pop and speech are trying to establish themselves.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Call to strengthen Commons groups
DOC.TEXT: THE cross-party Commons committees that shadow government departments should be given greater powers to call the prime minister to account, Mr Michael Meacher, a member of Labour's shadow cabinet, said yesterday. In a speech at a Labour rally as part of the party's leadership contest, Mr Meacher said that the committees should have a new role in relation to the prime minister. The prime minister should be answerable to the relevant committee if he intervened on a departmental matter, and the committees should be able to ratify or stop important public appointments in their areas, he said. Mr Meacher also called for the committees to be given stonger powers to summon ministers to give evidence. The departmental committees themselves have not yet been appointed since the election. Although the government's business managers are trying to get them established, there are some fears at Westminster that they might not be able to start work until the autumn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Trafford Park in line for Pounds 45m investment
DOC.BYLINE: By IAN HAMILTON FAZEY, Northern Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: A SERIES of related agreements between Asda, Varity Holdings, Amec and Trafford Park Development Corporation is expected to lead to Pounds 45m of investment during the next five years, with up to 1,550 new jobs and more than 1m sq ft of new factory space. The developments will lead to Varity, the troubled international farm and industrial machinery group, which owns Massey-Ferguson and Perkins, leaving the Trafford Park industrial estate in Greater Manchester. Worldwide distribution of Perkins replacement parts will be relocated to the former steelworks town of Irlam, still within the corporation's area. A new 17-acre warehouse and office complex in Irlam will be run by Caterpillar Logistics Services, which will handle Massey-Ferguson and Perkins warehousing. The principal part of the agreement involves the redevelopment of 70 acres of former Massey-Ferguson land in the main Trafford Park area. Varity is selling 30 acres to Asda for a shopping development, with the development corporation acquiring the rest. Varity and the corporation have negotiated an agreement with Amec Properties for phased redevelopment of the site, starting next year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Security-aware design urged for buildings
DOC.TEXT: POLICE yesterday launched a campaign to incorporate crime prevention into the design of commercial buildings. Secured by Design, an initiative that orginally applied only to new residential properties, has been extended to new and renovated commercial properties. Last year there were 550,000 commercial and 600,000 domestic burglaries, but police say that simple measures, such as good lighting for footpaths and car parks, can deter burglars. Developers are to be encouraged to consult police crime prevention experts at an early stage and to incorporate security features in building specifications. Properties that meet police guidelines can then be marketed using the Secured by Design logo as a selling point. Advice from police architectural liaison officers will be free, and the publicity campaign is being sponsored by lock-makers and other providers of security equipment. Crime-prevention officers recommended that even the layout of an estate, whether commercial or residential, should be planned with security in mind. Barriers should create well defined 'defensible space' around estates and individual properties.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Exchange grows heated over computers / A look at why market makers are again becoming angry over plans for new technology
DOC.TEXT: NOT since the Seaq quote-distribution system expired with a whimper during Big Bang in 1986 has there been such a fuss over Stock Exchange technology. The immediate cause is the exchange's decision, announced last month, to pass responsibility for running its computer operations to Andersen Consulting, one of the world's largest business consultancies. The contract, worth between Pounds 10m and Pounds 15m a year to Andersen over the next five years, is of a kind known in the computer business as 'outsourcing'. The exchange's 305-strong data-processing staff were transferred overnight on to Andersen's payroll and the consultancy has agreed to meet stiff terms on service delivery and performance. It has also agreed to work in partnership with the exchange to 're-engineer' the market support systems, implementing modernisation plans which the exchange's top management has had in place for some time.
