Outsourcing is increasingly popular with large companies anxious to concentrate on their core businesses rather than run large and expensive data-processing operations. Since the announcement, however, Mr Peter Rawlins, the Stock Exchange's chief executive, has found himself under fire. Some critics say he has given away the heart of the exchange's operation with its technological capability. Others say that Andersen was unfairly favoured when the contract was awarded without competitive tendering. The latter point to the fact that until 1983 Mr Rawlins was an Andersen partner, admittedly on the accounting rather than consultancy side. Mr Rawlins gives such insinuations short shrift, arguing that Andersen was selected on merit after four months of intense evaluation and that the decision was taken by the full board of the Stock Exchange. The conflict has tended to obscure the real issue. The exchange's sprawling systems undoubtedly should be replaced urgently, but is what Mr Rawlins has in mind the best way forward and has his vision of the future the support of the members? The exchange's computer systems for collecting and distributing price information and settling bargains have grown piecemeal over the years. They have been a victim of a continuing uncertainty within the membership over the exchange designing and building its own technology. Aconsequence has been erratic funding and a lack of management vision. Seaq, for example, the centrepiece of the 1986 move to electronic marketmaking, was a string-and-sealing-wax solution put together in too much of a hurry. The central database, Epic, on which the rest of the operation depends, is 16 years old. There are eight different and incompatible kinds of hardware in use: IBM, DEC, Tandem - even some old Modcomp machines kept going only by cannibalising others for spare parts. The exchange uses eight different programming languages with an emphasis on Pascal - which is used elsewhere mostly for scientific and technical computing. A simple business change such as earlier opening can take nine months to implement. There are nine different networks. Mr Rawlins complains: 'We are drowning in wires; the people we are really enriching is BT.' Maintaining and running the systems costs Pounds 52m a year exclusive of property costs - more than a quarter of the entire exchange's operational costs. In short, the present systems are too costly and inflexible to allow the exchange to provide an economic service or remain competitive in global terms. Mr Rawlins' plan envisages an 'open systems' solution: standard hardware, standard software and a single, common network. He estimates that such a solution could cut costs by up to 40 per cent. One drawback is that the existing system cannot simply be thrown away - it is supporting the markets reliably, if inefficiently, and nothing can be allowed to interfere with day-to-day trading. Mr Rawlins says that all possible ways of re-engineering the critical systems were investigated before Andersen was selected. An internal solution was rejected because of a lack of resources. Facilities management - using an outside firm to manage the existing systems -did not seem to offer cost savings. The exchange was determined to keep control of the systems. Mr Rawlins says: 'These systems are the market. We have to keep control.' He does not, however, enjoy the total confidence of his membership. Many suspect that the real thrust behind his plan is the development of an order-driven electronic exchange - perhaps along the lines of the system Andersen built for the Swiss Options and Futures Exchange. Some critics fear that that would effectively spell the end of the existing market-making system in London. Indeed, the exchange has just launched a wide-ranging review of the marketmaking system which it introduced at the time of Big Bang. The abrupt way in which the Andersen contract was awarded has done nothing to allay such fears.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Greenpeace criticises Earth Summit agenda
DOC.TEXT: GREENPEACE, the environ-mental activist organisation, has accused organisers of next week's Earth Summit of allowing it to be 'hijacked by industry' and failing to include in the conference agenda any controls on industrial activities. At a press conference in Rio de Janeiro, Mr Kenny Bruno, co-ordinator of the Greenpeace Hazardous Export/Import Project, said the Summit had 'adopted industry's line that first world corporations have the capacity to spread environmentally sound, sustainable technologies thoughout the world'. The truth was that they remained 'the primary creators of dirty, dangerous and unsustainable technologies and are at the root of all the world's main environmental problems.' Mr Bruno accused companies of 'greenwash', which he said meant 'hiding environmentally destructive practices behind environmental images and language stolen from the ecological movement'. In a report Greenpeace examines the records of big companies which Mr Bruno claims 'are proclaiming environmentalism' while continuing to cause damage.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Consumer confidence growing in US
DOC.TEXT: US CONSUMER confidence registered its third consecutive monthly increase in May, reinforcing other signs of a gradual economic recovery, Michael Prowse writes from Washington. The Conference Board, a New York business analysis group, said its index of confidence rose to 71.6 this month, against 65.1 in April and a low of 47.3 in February. The increase was larger than expected, but left the index short of the 100-plus level normal in a healthy recovery. Mr Fabian Linden, for the Board, said the steady rise in confidence left 'little doubt that the economy is at long last recovering'. The stronger figures follow the Federal Reserve's decision last week that lower interest rates were not needed to sustain the recovery. For the first time since August the Fed reportedly shifted to a neutral monetary stance, abandoning its previous bias towards lower short-term rates. More than a quarter of respondents to the Board's survey said they expected the business outlook to improve over the next six month.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Approval for gene-altered food
DOC.TEXT: US biotechnology companies will not need special approval to market food products they develop, as long as they do not drastically alter the genetic make-up of the food, the White House said yesterday, Reuter reports from Washington. The policy proclamation decrees that genetically engineered foods - emerging strains ranging from tomatoes to cucumbers and melons - are not inherently more dangerous than other products and do not need extensive pre-marketing tests. The Food and Drug Administration, which regulates most US foods, will not require identifying labels on genetically altered products under the new policy. The policy decision was expected and fiercely opposed by some consumer watchdogs, on health and safety grounds. But the White House rejected their fears that fruits and vegetables genetically altered to produce tastier, more nutritious or longer-lived produce might be dangerous. 'The US is already the world leader in biotechnology and we want to keep it that way,' Mr Dan Quayle, vice-president, said when announcing the policy. Under the policy the FDA will require pre-market testing only if products are altered in such a way that safety issues are raised. One example might be if a new product was unlike anything that had been safety-tested before. The guidelines should be a boon for agricultural biotechnology companies, which have fretted for years that pre-market approval of genetic goods might be required. There are about 2,000 biotechnology companies in the US, but only about 10 per cent are involved in the food sector. New techniques like cell-cloning or gene-transfer have raised hopes of hardier breeds, but also some fears. The Foundation for Economic Trends, run by Mr Jeremy Rifkin, a consumer activist, filed a petition with the FDA on May 18 asking for tight rules on biotechnology.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Dual approach to electricity sell-offs
DOC.TEXT: SOUTH-EAST Asian nations are moving towards a dual approach to privatisation and restructuring of their electricity supply industries, the Financial Times Asian Electricity Conference was told yesterday. The pattern evolving among key members of the Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) - Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines - was for independent, private power generators in competition for electricity sales with the state utilities, and for the longer-term restructuring of the state companies aimed at selling their shares on the region's stock exchanges. The pace is being set by Malaysia's state utility Tenaga Nasional Berhad, 23 per cent of whose shares were recently sold by subscription to institutions and individual investors in the country's biggest state-sector share flotation. Trading in the shares on the Kuala Lumpur stock exchange is imminent. Mr S. Samy Vellu, the Malaysian energy minister, said the flotation had been substantially oversubscribed and more shares could go on the market soon if a strong price was established. Other Asean nations have their own privatisation programmes, but their approach tends to be to invite independent power generators to set up alongside national utilities. Restructuring of the state companies would come later, and a cautious approach would be taken to any sell-off of state assets, the conference was told. Mr Artono Arismunandar, Indonesia's director-general of electricity, said his country already had a lot of private-sector power operating alongside the PLN, the state utility, but most was for own-use in industrial estates and company towns. The country aimed to boost sale of surplus private power to the national grid and to invite new private power generators to share in new projects. Mr Danilo Cantiller, economics department manager for the National Power Corporation of the Philippines (NPC), said his country had an open-door policy to private-sector power generating companies to supplement the output of the NPC. Enabling legislation declaring that the PLN was no longer a natural monopoly was passed in 1987. A study of the possible break-up and privatisation of the NPC was being undertaken. Mr Piyasvasti Amranand of Thailand's National Energy Policy Office said the abolition of trade unions at the Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand several years ago had made it possible for the authority to consider some form of privatisation.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / East Timorese gets 10 years
DOC.TEXT: AN EAST TIMORESE student was yesterday sentenced to 10 years in jail for his part in a non-violent protest against the massacre of more than 50 pro-independence activists by soldiers in East Timor last November, reports William Keeling in Jakarta. Mr Joao Freitas de Camara was found guilty of organising a protest in Jakarta on November 19. He was charged with subversion.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Keating has to reshuffle cabinet
DOC.TEXT: AUSTRALIAN Prime Minister Paul Keating yesterday announced a cabinet reshuffle forced on his government by the resignation last week of his most powerful and influential strategist, Senator Graham Richardson, reports Emilia Tagaza in Canberra. The reshuffle, though minor, is another setback for Mr Keating. One of the ministerial posts was filled by someone who is likely to unseat another of his staunchest supporters in parliament, the Speaker of the House of Representatives, Mr Leo McLeay. The new minister for consumer affairs, Miss Jeanette McHugh, has represented a seat which was recently abolished in a redistribution ahead of the next election. Most voters in her constituency were moved to Mr McLeay's electorate. It is understood Miss McHugh is determined to get the seat back from Mr McLeay. Senator Richardson resigned last week after reports that he might have supported a relative's shady activity in the Marshall Islands. He was instrumental in delivering votes to Mr Keating in his leadership challenge to former Prime Minister Mr Bob Hawke last year. His resignation, together with an increased budget deficit, threaten whatever political gains Mr Keating made in the last four months. Senator Richardson's former position as minister for transport and communication has been filled by Mr Bob Collins.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Thailand's acting rulers lift state of emergency
DOC.TEXT: THAILAND'S acting government yesterday lifted a state of emergency imposed on Bangkok and four surrounding provinces during violent confrontations between pro-democracy demonstrators and troops last week. The authorities banned public gatherings under the state of emergency, but protesters ignored the order. At least 48 people were killed by the armed forces before the king of Thailand brokered a compromise and Gen Suchinda Kraprayoon, the prime minister, was forced to resign. The five-party coalition government which appointed Gen Suchinda bowed to popular pressure on Monday and approved constitutional amendments demanded by the opposition to reduce the power of the military. Yesterday the pro-military coalition appeared to be on the brink of falling apart as its members attempted to choose a new prime minister and faced demands for the punishment of the senior military officers responsible for the shootings. Various solutions are being aired, including a new coalition which would bring in some of the opposition parties, and the possibility of new elections. There is widespread concern the military will feel cornered by demands for retribution and stage a coup d'etat. Opposition parties have asked the constitutional tribunal to rescind an amnesty decree signed by Gen Suchinda which pardons demonstrators and those who gave the troops the order to shoot.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Fall of the tireless salaryman: Signs of a decline in Japan's famed work ethic
DOC.TEXT: HAVING bickered with his daughter over the choice of daytime television dramas, the holiday-stricken salaryman grabs his golf clubs and heads for the driving range. In the cartoon's next frame, he slices the ball, smashing a window in an adjacent house. In the end, not knowing where to turn, he seeks refuge back at the office, behind his faithful desk. Once the hero, portrayed in the glorious style of socialist realism, the factory and office 'warrior' dedicated to building a strong Japan has become a media-mocked buffoon, lacking in social skills, alienated from his family, and comfortable only in the company of his desk. Young Japanese laugh at the thought of emulating him, and company managers are aghast at the pointed criticism that has skewered the salaryman. The salaryman's fall from grace is part of a larger debate over the fate of the country's famed work ethic, said to be under siege by modern comforts and a creeping, corrupting individualism. This theory is partly inspired by the recurring nightmare that Japan has 'peaked', that the economy is in quickening decline and that directionless Japanese youth will lead the country into mediocrity. Mr Akio Morita, Sony chairman, regarded as Japan's Prince Charles for his sometimes lofty though not irrelevant observations, relaunched the debate a few weeks ago with an unexpected confession that employees are underpaid and overworked. He said companies have failed to recognise that the era of aggressive growth has passed and, essentially, should be more caring and sharing. The timing of Mr Morita's comments, just before the annual wage bargaining season, drew gasps of disbelief from other executives who saw the Sony boss as loading the heavy artillery for the unions. However, Japanese unions are weaker than at any time in recent history and quickly agreed to small pay rises after a half-day ceremonial strike by train drivers, who later offered humble apologies for the inconvenience caused. With wage negotiations out of the way, Japanese executives have felt free to express their opinions on the work ethic, and not all disagree with Mr Morita. Meanwhile, Mr Kiichi Miyazawa, the prime minister, has just received two reports from special committees drafting a New Economic Plan to better balance the priorities of GNP growth and lifestyle. One report urged that Japan become a 'lifestyle superpower', as opposed to a military or economic superpower. And, as one way of attaining this distant goal, recommended that the country's commuter trains, famed for those white-gloved guards who shove excess passengers into already crammed carriages, be 10 per cent less crowded. Another committee found, as committees have in the past, that the present economic structure focuses too much on the company and too little on the consumer, and that while statistically wealthy, Japanese do not feel affluent. But this government committee went further, encouraging the individualism that is widely seen as a threat to 'groupism', company loyalty, and the work ethic. 'We must make Japan a society in which people can attain a better quality of life, an equitable society where every citizen can both appreciate a comfortable and leisurely lifestyle, and have equal opportunities to develop an individual sense of values,' the report recommended. A survey of 2,125 corporate executives by the Keidanren, the employers federation, showed support for shorter working hours and recognition that the salaryman did not have a leisurely lifestyle. This executive support was tempered by the beliefs that Japan 'cannot afford' to reduce the working week and that Japanese had an innate love of work. But a majority of executives also said this 'love' was fading among younger workers, the shinjinrui or new breed, who see no role model in the middle-aged, desk-bound salaryman. By repute, the ethic-less younger generation will take holidays, swap jobs, and refuse to compromise personal interests for the company good. The changes are more in attitude than action. A separate survey of 10,000 residents by the prime minister's office found, across all age groups and both sexes, that only 24 per cent thought personal fulfilment more important than the national interest, though among males aged between 25 and 29, the figure was 39 per cent. Yet graduates' choice of companies this year showed a clear bias towards the neatly drawn career path and lifetime employment offered by the typical large company and the bureaucracy. Meanwhile, the onset of recession has encouraged the electronics makers, which pioneered the unorthodox practice of mid-career hiring, to reduce this intake to a few specialist staff. 'I thought about working in a small company or starting my own business, but it was safer to work for a big financial company,' said a graduate who joined Yamaichi Securities a year ago. He did not particularly like the work or the weight of the hierarchy bearing down on him, but 'I don't really have a choice'. Rather than young Japanese breaking the social contract, some troubled industries are now tempted to lay off staff. Securities companies increased their employees by 41.6 per cent over the four years to 1990, and the mid-sized brokers, most bruised by the stock market collapse, are trying to find a way to close branches without making staff redundant. The government, meanwhile, will soon have to reschedule the official timetable for the reduction of working hours. The aim was to get the official average working year down from 2,050 hours to 1,800 hours by next year. Unpaid overtime pushes the total as high as 3,000 hours in industries such as banking. But, in the Keidanren survey, 44 per cent of companies were not sure that the 1,800 target could be reached by the end of the century. 'One's life is made up of time, and this should be better understood,' explained a sympathetic executive at Coal Resources Development, a coal importer. But the case of another resources company is more illuminating - Mitsubishi Oil became suddenly famous two years ago when news surfaced of a scheme to fine employees who did not take their full complement of holidays. The truth is that the scheme involved only seven employees in one small section of the crude oil import division. Last year, four of the seven workers failed to take a total of 14 days' holiday and the Y14,000 in fines went to buy beer and sake for their end-of-year party.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Chiefs, Indians and Rabuka go to polls in Fiji: Bullets or ballots, this time Fiji's military ruler wants to take power in an election
DOC.TEXT: MAJOR General Sitiveni Rabuka has taken power in Fiji twice since 1987, each time at the point of a gun. This week, he hopes to take power again, through the more unpredictable mechanism of the ballot box. Almost exactly five years after Mr Rabuka's first armed intervention, Fijians are voting in a general election organised by an interim civilian government. The election will almost certainly return the ethnic Fijian Soqosoqo ni Vakavulewa ni Taukei (SVT) party, led by Mr Rabuka, as the largest parliamentary group. But it seems unlikely to resolve the underlying tensions among Fiji's 345,000 ethnic Fijians, 340,000 Indians and 35,000 Europeans, Chinese, Polynesians and other races. The army took power in May 1987 in the name of ethnic Fijian nationalism, claiming that a coalition government dominated by Indians was making Fijians second-class citizens in their own country. It was a message which made Mr Rabuka a hero to many ethnic Fijians, especially when the army intervened a second time to torpedo a compromise agreement which would have given the coalition a continued role in government. But by focusing on a single cause of tension, the nationalist rhetoric obscured the underlying reasons for the coup, which had at least as much to do with regional and class conflicts as with race. The election of the coalition gave Indians a leading role in Fijian government for the first time since their forebears arrived to work on sugar plantations during British colonial rule. But the coalition also contained a number of ethnic Fijians representing the trade-union based Fiji Labour party, which wanted to reduce the influence of the chiefs, the traditional leaders of ethnic Fijian society. Furthermore, many of the Labour MPs came from the west of Viti Levu, Fiji's main island, which has long resented the influence of the eastern-based chiefly establishment. The constitution drawn up by the interim government seeks to entrench ethnic Fijian political domination by reserving 37 of the 70 seats in the lower house of parliament. Indians have been allocated 27 seats, and other races five; one is reserved for the Polynesian island of Rotuma. In addition, the prime minister must be an ethnic Fijian, and veto power on many issues has been given to a senate composed entirely of ethnic Fijians selected by the Great Council of Chiefs, a traditional advisory body. The constitution also seeks to entrench village values by over-representing rural ethnic Fijians at the expense of urban voters who are more likely to oppose chiefly influence. In effect, the system is a compromise between Mr Rabuka and Fiji's elder statesmen, Ratu Sir Penaia Ganilau, the former governor-general who is now president, and Ratu Sir Kamisese Mara, the interim prime minister. Both chiefs are believed to have argued for a less confrontational approach to the Indian community, while supporting the objective of buttressing chiefly influence. However, the voting system means the SVT can only govern alone if it wins almost all the ethnic Fijian seats. That is unlikely to happen, mainly because of growing support for the more extreme Fijian Nationalist United Front (FNUF), which has called for the expulsion of Indians. The SVT could also lose some seats to the multiracial All National Congress, which would probably line up with Indian opponents of the constitution. The arithmetic is complicated by the Labour party's promise that its MPs will boycott parliament, which would lower the threshold for a working majority. But the most likely outcome is a hung parliament in which the FNUF holds the balance of power. If that happens, Ratu Sir Penaia will almost certainly have to appoint Mr Rabuka head of an SVT/FNUF coalition government, which would be a frightening prospect for many Indians. Indian business leaders say such an outcome could lead to a further wave of emigration as better-off Indians follow the example of the 23,000 largely professional workers who left after the coups of 1987. However, most Indians appear willing to stay provided there is no repetition of the inter-racial violence which followed the first coup in 1987. Many have extensive business interests which they would be reluctant to abandon. In the longer term, both ethnic Fijians and Indians say the country has a bright future if it can achieve stable government and maintain the strong growth in tourism and manufacturing it has enjoyed under the interim government. On present trends, that is likely to happen in the early years of the next century. Meanwhile, voters must wait until Sunday to learn the result of the week-long election, which is taking place on more than 300 islands scattered over more than 700,000 square kilometres of the South Pacific. This time, Mr Rabuka must wait too.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / World Trade News: SA bank expands in Mideast
DOC.TEXT: South Africa's biggest bank, ABSA Bank, has announced the establishment of links with 15 financial institutions in Bahrain's offshore banking centre to try to finance trade between the two areas, Reuter reports from Manama. Mr Stephanus Smith, head of ABSA's international banking services, said all of the Bahrain-based banks he visited agreed to open foreign exchange lines and most were also prepared to consider placing money market lines for offshore finance at the South African bank's disposal. He said this would bring the total of Middle East banks ready to do business with ABSA Bank to around 40. Gulf states have not formally lifted sanctions against South Africa but deals which took place for years are gathering momentum as apartheid is dismantled.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / World Trade News: US set to spill beans on its EC oilseeds 'retaliation' - Dollars 1bn in sanctions being considered in Washington to offset 'unfair' European subsidies
DOC.TEXT: THE BUSH administration is debating a list of Dollars 1bn in sanctions it is threatening to impose on European Community products in retaliation for the EC's oilseeds regime which the US claims has cost it billions in soyabean sales. Foods, wines and beer are likely to head the list, but a number of US officials believe it might provoke a greater outcry if industrial products are included. The question has been forwarded to the Bush cabinet for discussion, perhaps as early as this week, after an interagency group committee was unable to agree. For its part, the EC has yet to decide how to respond to the US threats. It is said to be considering a compensation proposal. Complicating the issue is the agreement reached last week by the EC farm ministers to reform the Common Agricultural Policy, and the possibility that the changes ultimately will at least partly address US complaints by reducing EC oilseeds production. The US made public its intention on April 30 to impose sanctions after the EC blocked a report finding that EC oilseeds subsidies were illegal under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. The EC indicated that it would accept the report at a Gatt Council meeting in June and at the same time propose a remedy. Meanwhile, the Bush Administration, unasked, is getting industry's ideas. The National Association of Wheat Growers, for example, has recommended new tariffs on pasta and wheat gluten to level the 'uneven playing field'. US imports of EC pasta, made from heavily subsidised wheat, have increased 70 per cent in the past decade. Both the Uruguay Round and the oilseeds dispute are expected to be on the agenda when Mr Frans Andriessen, the EC commissioner in charge of trade, and other EC officials meet today with Mr James Baker, the US secretary of state; Mrs Carla Hills, the US trade representative, and Mr Edward Madigan, the US agriculture secretary. Without a breakthrough Mrs Hills is likely to roll out a list containing Dollars 2bn in sanctions for 30 days of public comment, after which the list will be pared. Mrs Hills talks of how she was promised 'with a handshake' that the subsidies would be 'fixed' in time for the 1991 growing season. US patience has been 'rather endless,' she said, but if the Gatt process is to have any credibility, she must act. The role of domestic politics cannot be dismissed. Mrs Hills says President Bush has clung fast to his free-trade principles, though only 35-40 per cent of US farmers support his position in the Uruguay Round. There are no senators who do not have farmers in their districts, she said. 'There are some districts that are 100 per cent agricultural and could indeed tip the election.' The EC oilseeds programme, which set Community prices at about double the prevailing world levels, was designed to draw Community farmers away from surplus grain production. Between 1980-1990, EC producers more than tripled the land area devoted to EC production of rapeseed, sunflower seed and soyabeans, and boosted planting from 4m to 13m acres. At the same time US exports of soyabeans fell 63 per cent. In 1987 the American Soyabean Association gave up waiting for farm reform in the Uruguay Round to solve the problem and filed a case against the EC oilseeds regime, which the US trade representative took to the Gatt. After many delays, a Gatt panel concluded in 1990 that the subsidies impaired the advantage the EC had promised when in 1962 it agreed to 'bind' its oilseed import tariffs at zero duty. After more postponements, the EC revised its oilseeds regime. Instead of making payments to oilseeds processors for using EC oilseeds, it would make them directly to EC farmers. In the US view, this was an improvement because the regime no longer discriminated against foreign oilseeds, but it still subsidised production and thus devalued the advantage promised when zero tariffs were negotiated. The US returned to the Gatt, where a panel again found against the EC oilseeds regime. The EC blocked adoption of the panel's report on April 30 but promised a 'concrete proposal' for settlement before the June 1992 Gatt Council meeting. The US indicated that it would impose sanctions if the proposal was not satisfactory. EC officials, who complain that the US is impatient and impulsive, say the Bush administration is acting 'totally without justification' and lacks legal basis because the oilseeds report is still pending. American officials see the EC as consistently delaying the inevitable; they believe that by blocking the panel report the EC is violating the spirit of the Gatt and they have the right to take action.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Caretaker government imposes further three-month freeze on capital spending in Italy
DOC.TEXT: ITALY'S caretaker government yesterday imposed a further three-month freeze on capital spending projects in a symbolic gesture to answer the EC's recent harsh criticism of the country's public finances, writes Robert Graham. In January, the government imposed for a six-month period a series of stiff requirements for approval of capital spending projects to hold down the public sector deficit, which was rising beyond 10.5 per cent of GDP. The main effect of this measure was to permit the Treasury to scrutinise all large investment requests and withhold approval unless ample justification was provided. Yesterday's cabinet meeting extended this procedure until September. The saving will be little more than L1,000bn (Pounds 452.7m), against this year's projected deficit of more than L165,000bn. But the authorities were anxious to signal to Brussels that public spending would be closely monitored while a new government is being formed.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Italian 'Mr Clean' emerges from a dirty fight: Mr Oscar Luigi Scalfaro, the new president, is the product of compromise
DOC.TEXT: MR Oscar Luigi Scalfaro, who will be sworn in as Italy's ninth president on Thursday, has a personality and style in sharp contrast to his predecessor, Mr Francesco Cossiga. Courteous, devoutly Catholic, and formal, the new president, 73, could not be more different from the loquacious and unpredictable Mr Cossiga. Although both have come to the presidency from the ruling Christian Democrat party, Mr Scalfaro has always kept his distance from the inner cabals - unlike Mr Cossiga. Mr Cossiga rejoiced in his self-appointed populist role as 'the man with a pick-axe', chipping away at a political system in urgent need of reform. Mr Scalfaro projects the image of an impartial father figure, steering the ship of state along the path of reform with the limited powers available to the head of state. Mr Scalfaro was taken on as a 'Mr Clean'. Indeed, eyebrows have been raised by his ultra-conservatism. When chosen as speaker of the chamber of deputies after the April 5 general election, he had his office sprinkled with holy water and in the past is credited with telling a woman in a restaurant her decollete was too revealing. Perhaps not surprisingly he and Mr Cossiga can scarcely speak to each other. Mr Cossiga was deeply affronted when Mr Scalfaro became the new speaker against his express wishes - a key element in the latter's resignation on April 25, two months before his seven-year term was complete. In his brief period as speaker, Mr Scalfaro impressed with his scrupulous impartiality. When voting for the presidency began on May 13 he was considered a potential compromise candidate, but it required 16 voting sessions of the joint houses of parliament to endorse him in the final round (there were 1,010 potential voters). Although this may have seemed an unnecessarily long period to elect a new head of state when the country was without a government, the election process was treated by the parties as a dress rehearsal for the formation of the next government. Thus the first three sessions tested whether the outgoing four-party coalition of Christian Democrats, Socialists, Liberals and Social Democrats could rely on their members to fall behind the leadership choice. This failed, as the Christian Democrats in particular were deeply divided. The Christian Democrats then played their main card, proposing Mr Arnaldo Forlani, the party secretary general, in the fifth and sixth vote. He mustered no more than 479 votes, short of the 508 majority, and should have won 60 votes more if all the coalition had backed him. The failure of Mr Forlani was crucial. He received insufficient support because he was too openly identified with a discredited system of Christian Democrat-controlled power, out of touch with the reforming mood of the country. The rebuff applied equally to another Christian Democrat heavyweight, Mr Giulio Andreotti, the outgoing prime minister. Unable to unite his party, Mr Forlani resigned last Friday. The Forlani resignation symbolised the impotence of the ruling coalition and allowed the search for a Christian Democrat compromise 'institutional' candidate in the form of Mr Scalfaro. Mr Scalfaro received 672 of the 1,002 votes present. This included the vote of the former communist Party of the Democratic Left (PDS), the radicals and the Greens, but not the republicans, who were upset that their strong front-runner, Mr Giovanni Spadolini, the interim president, was passed over. This voting alliance demonstrates that the politicians have taken on board the public demand for electoral and institutional reform evident in the big general election protest vote. The politicians were also conditioned in their choice by the need to present a 'clean' candidate in the light of growing public unease over the Milan corruption scandal.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Belgrade softens line on Bosnia to avoid sanctions
DOC.BYLINE: By LAURA SILBER and JUDY DEMPSEY
DOC.TEXT: BELGRADE yesterday launched a diplomatic offensive to stave off international sanctions by trying to distance itself from the war being waged by Serbian forces in Bosnia-Hercegovina. Mr Branko Kostic, the acting president of the Serb-dominated Yugoslav presidency, wrote to Mr Boutros Boutros Ghali, the United Nations secretary general, appealing to all sides to allow the reopening of the airport in Sarajevo and stop the bombardment of the Bosnian capital and Mostar (in southern Bosnia). His move followed similar conciliatory statements overnight from the federal presidency and government. The airport has been under blockade since early April, first by the federal army and now by Serbian irregulars. Western diplomats said the statements represented attempts at improving public relations rather than concrete steps to end the killing and destruction in Bosnia. 'It is hot air,' said one diplomat. 'The presidency could take some real steps. For example, it could order the Serbian army to hand over its weapons.' Mr Kostic dismissed as 'psychological pressure' the possibility of western military intervention. 'I think foreign countries will find it difficult to decide to send soldiers to our country because of the possibility of them coming back in coffins,' he said. As Bosnian radio yesterday reported a lull in fighting around Sarajevo, the Croatian President Franjo Tudjman has capitalised on the international pressure which is mounting on Serbia by calling fresh parliamentary elections. The announcement by Mr Franjo Gregoric, the Croatian prime minister, coincides with a revival in support for the ruling conservative Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), led by Mr Tudjman. The HDZ won the republic's first free elections in April 1990. Although Mr Tudjman has publicly supported the territorial integrity of independent Bosnia, he has consistently backed plans by Bosnia's nationalist Croats, led by Mr Mate Boban, and Bosnia's Serbs, led by Mr Radovan Karadzic, to divide the republic between Serbia and Croatia. This would leave the Moslems without a homeland. Members of Croatia's opposition parties say international attention on the war in Bosnia, and criticism of Serbia, has also allowed Mr Tudjman to crack down on the media. Mr Vladimir Seks, a parliamentary deputy, who was recently appointed state prosecutor, has pressed charges against prominent members of the opposition and journalists. They include Mr Ivan Zvonimir Cicak, head of the Croatian Peasants Party, Mr Milorad Pupovac, head of the liberal Serbian Democratic Forum, and Ms Jelena Lovric, a journalist at Danas, the Croatian weekly. Under the criminal code, anyone found guilty of disseminating false information, or causing disturbances of the public peace, can be imprisoned for up to five years.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Commonwealth of Independent States
DOC.TEXT: From today, the FT is dividing its coverage of the constituent republics of the former Soviet Union between the European and International news pages. Coverage of the central Asian republics - that is, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan - will be carried on International; Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Moldova, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Georgia will remain on Europe. This new division is designed to reflect the different regional and political contexts in which the member states of the Commonwealth of Independent States are developing.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Walesa asks parliament to create new cabinet
DOC.TEXT: PRESIDENT Lech Walesa said yesterday that he had lost confidence in the government of the prime minister, Mr Jan Olszewski, and asked the Polish parliament to create a new cabinet, Reuter reports from Warsaw. Capping weeks of pressure on Mr Olszewski's minority cabinet to resign, Mr Walesa sent a letter to the speaker of the Sejm (lower house) saying he had withdrawn his support for the government because it was destabilising state structures. 'I lost confidence in the government and this forces me to withdraw my support for it. I propose that solutions aimed at creating a new cabinet are undertaken (by parliament),' Mr Walesa said in a letter.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Bonn fails to satisfy US on new corps
DOC.TEXT: GERMANY has failed to overcome US objections to setting up a Franco-German army corps despite providing assurances that obligations to Nato will not be affected. Mr Dick Cheney, US defence secretary, discussed the European Corps' role with Mr Volker Ruhe, German defence minister, before a Nato planning meeting here yesterday. US officials said questions remained unanswered about the 'ultimate allegiance' of the corps, launched officially at last week's Franco-German summit. However, Mr Ruhe said later that the meeting of Nato defence ministers produced 'no revolt' against the plan. Germany was one of several allies expressing broad support for proposals to enable the nine-nation Western European Union (WEU) to make use of military formations which also had a Nato role. The Netherlands and Italy backed UK proposals to make a range of both multi-national and national forces available to the WEU. Mr Malcolm Rifkind, UK defence secretary, said in a recent policy statement that the Franco-German corps could play a part as one of the formations available, alongside forces already existing in the Nato structure. WEU foreign and defence ministers are expected to agree an outline forces plan at a meeting in Bonn on June 19. Belgium and Spain, which are both considering joining the Franco-German corps, are discussing with other allies how else they might contribute to the WEU initiative. Britain has said that the use of forces by the WEU should be subject to prior Nato consultation. However, it is understood to view this as a precautionary measure to ensure that forces can be spared for operations outside the Nato area, and not as a US right of veto over WEU operations. The US is anxious to ensure that forces continue to be trained for their Nato role. However, WEU members, who are in the process of setting up a planning cell for military contingencies, foresee holding some exercises of their own. The Nato ministers also held preliminary talks on providing peacekeeping forces for the 52-nation Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe (CSCE). Nato is agreed on the principle of making its resources and organisation available for such operations if the CSCE takes on a regional UN peacekeeping mission.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Soviet communist party to go on trial: Old regime likened to Nazis as Moscow prepares to judge Lenin and his heirs
DOC.TEXT: THE communist party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) was yesterday sent for trial for violations of the constitution of the Soviet Union, the state which it created. The trial, timed for July 7, will be a public judgment on the darkest chapters of the history of the USSR since the 1917 revolution. Mr Andrei Makarov, the legal counsel of Mr Boris Yeltsin, the Russian President, set the tone when he likened the CPSU to the German Nazi Party - many of whose leaders were put on trial at Nuremberg after the last war. Mr Gennady Burbulis, Mr Yeltsin's top aide, said after the decision of the Constitutional Court that further action might be taken against specific leaders of the CPSU. The decision of the court to, in effect, put the Party's history on trial came ironically as a result of a suit brought to the court by communist deputies, alleging that President Yeltsin's decrees banning the CPSU and the Russian Communist Party after the August coup were unconstitutional. This was countered by a cross suit brought by Mr Oleg Rumyantsev, leader of the Social Democratic Party, that the CPSU had violated the Soviet constitution. The collegium of judges on the bench decided to unite both suits in one - to the vociferous protests of the many once senior communists in the court - including Mr Yegor Ligachev, formerly number two in the politburo to Mr Mikhail Gorbachev, and Mr Vladimir Ivashko, Mr Gorbachev's deputy at the time of the coup. The judgment, described by Mr Burbulis as 'brilliant', means that even if Mr Yeltsin's decrees are ultimately judged unconstitutional, the country will be convulsed by promised revelations on the party's murderous past. Mr Gorbachev, the party's last general secretary and, in his role as president, the man who presided over its dissolution, was not himself in court. Mr Burbulis hinted that the court's decision would damage the former president's efforts to rehabilitate himself when he said: 'I doubt he will now engage in further political activity.' Mr Valery Zorkin, the court's chairman, ruled that former party leaders, including Mr Gorbachev, could represent the party if they wished. Mr Yeltsin's side had argued that the party had no legal standing in the court because of the ban on its activities. Mr Sergei Shakhrai, legal aide to Mr Yeltsin, has already given a hint of the evidence to be brought against the party when he produced a document on Monday which showed that the CPSU had authorised shipments of weapons in 1975 to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, the most militantly terrorist of the groups within the Palestinian Liberation Organisation. Mr Yeltsin said yesterday he would not resign from office during his current term but did not plan to stand for a second spell in 1996, according to Itar-Tass news agency.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / CIS moves another step nearer break-up
DOC.BYLINE: By JOHN LLOYD and DMITRI VOLKOV
DOC.TEXT: THE Commonwealth of Independent States took a step closer to dissolution yesterday when defence ministers of most of its member states agreed to limit their joint military command to strategic nuclear weapons. This means that the navy and air force, including the Black Sea fleet whose possession is disputed between Russia and Ukraine, will now be divided among the member states, with the bulk of it falling to Russia. Mr Ivan Bizhan, Ukrainian defence minister, said all nuclear weapons had been removed from the Black Sea fleet three weeks ago. Talks have begun between Ukraine and Russia on the division of the fleet but there is no resolution in sight. Marshal Yevgeny Shaposhnikov, the head of the CIS command, said the CIS would continue to maintain and control the nuclear forces until they were all returned to Russia. The other states with nuclear weapons - Belarus, Kazakhstan and Ukraine - have agreed to do this by mid-1994. There still appears to be disagreement between Russia and Ukraine on the precise control of the nuclear warheads. General Leonty Kuznetsov, head of the Russian general staff, said Russia had been delegated responsibility for putting the nuclear forces on alert - and said that acts adopted by Ukraine on administrative control of the nuclear warheads 'put their safety in doubt'. Marshal Shaposhnikov said the forces remaining under CIS control were the strategic missiles; the strategic nuclear bombers; nuclear missile-carrying warships; the anti-missile systems and the technical back-up to the nuclear force. Mr Boris Yeltsin, Russia's president, called last night for urgent talks on the worsening conflict between national guards and forces of the Russian minority in Moldova. Mr Mircea Snegur, the Moldovan president, warned on Monday that his republic might have to declare a state of war with Russia because of alleged involvement of the Russian 14th army on the side of Russian forces in the self-proclaimed TransDnestr republic in the east of Moldova.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Survey of Korea (10): Sharper edge needed - Industry seeks a wider technology base
DOC.TEXT: SOUTH KOREA'S rapid rise to a position in the world's top league of semiconductor producers is testimony to its ability to acquire, develop and manage high technology. Yet having scaled such technical heights in one of the most demanding industrial fields, it is in danger of lagging behind its competitors in the deployment of technology in the more mundane industries that make up the bulk of its export sector. 'Increasing the level of technology in every field of industry is our top priority,' says Mr Choi Gak Kyu, deputy prime minister and head of the Economic Planning Board. 'Every industry needs to upgrade its technology. We must deepen our industrial structure by substituting domestic output for imports of components and materials.' That industry is intent on applying more technology to offset higher labour costs is evident from a surge in factory automation equipment imports, much of it from Japan. These have been rising at annual rates of 20 per cent or more in recent years, according to government statistics, and could amount to more than Dollars 1bn in 1992. Nor is there any doubt that technology transfer forms a part of virtually every industrial deal with foreign companies, though some observers doubt whether that such technology is always fully absorbed and efficiently employed. The growing network of government research laboratories boasts 'many people who are as good as any in the world', according to western diplomats. And industry spending on research and development has risen sharply in recent years. But there are question-marks over the corporate sector's R&D efforts. Some observers point to the behaviour of many of the big companies in 1986 and 1987, when they were flush with cash. The profits then went mainly into speculative property and stock market dealings rather than into R&D. Some Korean companies, such as Samsung Electronics, have earned international reputations for being at the cutting edge of semiconductor technology. But the evidence is less clear that companies across the board are investing the very large amounts in pure research and product development which would be needed to lessen their ties to foreign, and especially Japanese suppliers of components and high value equipment. Mr Duck Soo Han, director general of the industrial policy bureau at the Ministry of Trade and Industry, accepts that the 'technology gap won't be solved easily'. But he contends that a combination of tax incentives, a government policy to encourage collaboration and the importation of key foreign technologies will help. In addition, the government has identified strategic industries which it believes will be the basis for South Korea's future competitiveness. These include the following: new generations of semi-conductors, including the development of a 64 Megabit Dram by 1993 and a 256 Megabit Dram by 1996; development of a variety of high definition television equipment, including HDTV monitors by 1993, transmission technology by 1994 and flat panel displays by 1997; the commercialisation of a multi-media computer by 1994. Some critics, however, contend that the government plan is over-ambitious. One European engineer familiar with the HDTV programme, for example, believes that 'only a half a dozen Korean engineers really understand the technology.' Mr Choi denies that the high technology effort is spread too thinly, noting that Korea's priorities fall well short of those in more developed countries, where the emphasis is on 'fine chemicals, aerospace, biotechnology and new materials'. He adds that 'decisions on R&D projects should equally consider economic viability as well as technological feasibility.' The relatively thin layer of engineering talent in the country has caused some companies to search widely for new recruits. One of the most technologically advanced companies, Samsung Electronics, is seeking to lure Korean-Americans back to their former homeland. It is also trying to hire Russian scientists and engineers, either individually or as a team, though it has so far failed to reach any agreement. 'We don't care what nationality a person is,' says Mr Hun Kim, a senior Samsung executive. But such sentiments may not be heard in the corridors of other Korean conglomerates, which have a reputation for being highly nationalistic. They also have a reputation - among many western business executives atr least - of being less than respectful of intellectual property rights and for being reluctant to pay for foreign technology. This is particularly the case when they are buying the innovative engineering services which will be needed in ever-larger amounts, according to Mr John Lyle, Seoul branch manager of HW Structures, part of the UK's Hawtal Whiting Group. He believes that the 'complexity of design and development is rarely understood at government or senior management level', in large part because Korean industry has had a manufacturing bias. 'There is still an emphasis on importing licensed technology and manufacturing ready-made designs,' he says. 'Purchasing innovative engineering services costs money and sometimes the effort needed to develop these skills is not understood by Korean companies.' But Mr Lyle believes Korean companies are beginning to understand that 'if you pay yesterday's prices, then you get yesterday's technology'. The sheer size and dominance of Korea's big companies can also deter technology transfer. Dr Berthold Leibinger, president of the German Machinery and Plant Manufacturers Association, the VDMA, said recently in Seoul that German medium-sized companies found it hard to find suitable Korean partners. 'It's very difficult for a German company with 500 or even 2,000 employees to deal with a Korean one employing 50,000,' he notes. Government policy is to encourage the start-up of small, innovative technology-based companies. But there may still be more than a grain of truth in the joke which asks: 'What is the first thing a Korean entrepreneur does?' The answer is: 'He goes to the States.' Mr Choi at the EPA accepts that the shortage of small specialist suppliers is a weakness which must be overcome, in part through a recently announced loan programme. But government officials believe long-term technological competitiveness can only come through the reform of the chaebols into more focused entities.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Survey of Korea (11): The All-Korean car is still some way off - The motor industry is striving to reduce dependence on foreign suppliers
DOC.TEXT: SOUTH KOREA'S car manufacturers offer a case study of the challenges which face the country's industry as a whole. All need to upgrade technology, lessen dependence on foreign suppliers, diversify markets and establish new relationships with their labour unions. And they need to overcome a period of economic uncertainty, both at home and in their main export markets. The myriad alliances, technical co-operation agreements and joint ventures that bind Korea's carmakers to the world's leading manufacturers will remain a hallmark of the industry for years to come. The advent of an 'all-Korean' car created from a 'clean sheet of paper will have to await the next century', says one western expert. But the need to reduce dependence on foreign, and particularly Japanese partners or suppliers for everything from basic designs to key components is a priority for all manufacturers. So, too, is the need to move away from a manufacturing bias, towards greater emphasis on higher value activities such as design and product development. Such a task will be neither easy nor cheap. 'Unlike Japan, Korea has only pockets of automotive expertise', says Mr John Lyle of the UK's Hawtal Whiting Group of consulting engineers. 'When we started (in Korea) we noticed our clients' engineers did not gain much by studying the design process because priority was given to developing products quickly.' However, companies such as Hyundai, the industry leader, have invested heavily in research and development facilities, where 'massive teams are using state-of-the-art technology to develop new vehicles,' according to Mr Lyle. He predicts that the effort will result in 'a new range of Korean products in the next five years', including light commercial vehicles and heavy trucks. 'They will all be new designs or vehicles based on better platforms than exist now,' he says. The emphasis on independent projects stems in part from Korean dissatisfaction with the high cost of royalties paid to foreign suppliers and the limitations of technology transfer through the main international alliances in the industry - Hyundai with Japan's Mitsubishi, Kia with Ford and Mazda and Daewoo's now-defunct link-up with GM. But few observers expect that Korean companies will be able to catch up in all areas. 'Great advancements have been made,' says Mr Dong Wha Lee, director of the Korea Autombile Manufacturers Association, who cites the introduction last year of a Hyundai-developed engine, and similar programmes in place at Kia and Daewoo. But he concedes that the industry 'still lags behind' its international competitors in many areas. These include systems such as air bags, anti-lock braking systems and four-wheel drive. Perhaps more worrying for Korea's technology effort, however, is the international trend towards less environmentally damaging cars, the development of which is beyond Korea's technical capabilities. The quantum leap in the technical quality of Korean cars in recent years has been matched by moves to upgrade their image in key export markets, though that effort suffered badly when labour disputes affected the build quality of Hyundai cars sold in the US. Mr NM Kim, Hyundai's managing director for export marketing, acknowledges that 'we have a perception problem in the US', where export sales dropped from 260,000 units in 1986 to a current rate of just over 120,000 a year. But he argues that the launch of the Elantra, which some experts describe as 'Korea's first good car', will improve Hyundai's US image. Mr Kim also believes that Korean manufacturers must move away from the 'price-value market strategy', which has focused on undercutting the price of rival products.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Survey of Korea (9): Obstacles to growth / A look at efforts to unblock the infrastructure
DOC.TEXT: SIT behind a crawling container truck choked by diesel fumes and dust on the 400km from Seoul and Pusan, and one becomes aware of the large sums of money South Korea needs to spend on improving its inadequate infrastructure. The journey along the congested highway between the country's two biggest cities can be tedious. In Seoul, the capital, congestion is even worse. The exhaust fumes of 1m cars hangs like a pall over the city for much of the year. Traffic jams cost hundreds of millions of dollars in lost production time adding to the discontent of a people that wants its standard of living to rise in line with economic growth. The metropolitan area of Seoul houses 18m people, 43 per cent of the country's population, and accounts for 59 per cent of South Korean manufacturing output. Pusan in the south east is the country's biggest seaport. Traffic between the two cities, therefore, is large. Central government has estimated that road congestion in 1990 cost the country Won1,200bn (Dollars 1.7bn) in wasted energy and lost time. The main Seoul-Pusan rail link has already reached maximum capacity increasing the potential for road congestion as distributors are forced to use container lorries. South Korean infrastructure in many areas is struggling to cope with the rapid growth in the economy. Delays in cargo handling at the ports of Pusan and Inchon are estimated to have cost the country a further Won700bn (Dollars 1bn) in 1990. Kimpo airport, South Korea's leading airport handling 85 per cent of international passengers and 95 per cent of air freight, is forecast to reach its maximum capacity in 1996. The need for increased infrastructure spending is undeniable. Without higher investment production bottlenecks will intensify and inhibit future growth. Social unrest also is likely to increase as living standards come under increasing pressure from inadequate services. The government, in a bid to co-ordinate spending plans, has established a special task force under the president, the Planning Agency for Social Infrastructure Development (Pasid), to identify priority projects. One of its major aims is to encourage greater investment away from over-crowded cities to less economically successful areas, particularly the south west of the country. Improvements in transport are regarded as essential. The task force has proposed that Won40 trillion (Dollars 52bn) be spent by central government on infrastructure between now and 1996. More than half of this is planned to be invested in roads and railways. About Won19 trillion (Dollars 24.6bn) is expected to be spent on constructing 450km of new roads and upgrading a similar length of existing roads. The programme includes beginning work on three new motorways. The most important is a 353km expressway, costing Won3 trillion, between Seoul and Mokpo in the south west, the region which has been identified by the government for expansion. In the past, heavy emphasis has been placed on connecting Seoul with other cities. The latest crop of motorways will instead connect regional cities with each other including a 289km highway between Ch'unch'on and Taegu costing Won2 trillion and a 160km motorway between Taejun and Chinju. Investment in the south west will be further aided by the expansion of Kwangyang which is intended to become a major seaport. There are also plans for increased spending water services, power generation and land development. The government hopes that this will encourage the private sector to invest in new factories, offices and homes in the south west as well as other less developed areas. A further Won8 trillion (SDollars 10.3bn) is expected to be invested between now and 1996 on upgrading and electrifying South Korea's railway network including starting work on a high speed rail link between Seoul and Pusan which is expected to cost Won5.8 trillion (Dollars 7.5bn) when it is completed towards the end of the century. Other high speed rail routes are planned including a link between Seoul and Mokpo but these programmes have still to be allocated a budget. There is also substantial investment planned in improved water and sewerage facilities, a trebling in the size of the Seoul subway system and a large power station building programme. As a result central government spending on infrastructure as a proportion of GNP is forecast to almost double from 1.7 to 3 per cent between 1991 and 1996. About Won7 trillion is planned to be spent on improving drinking water and installing new water services. The government intends to extend sewage treatment from about 35 per cent of the population to about 70 per cent by the mid-1990s. The Ministry of Energy and Resources, which has a separate budget funded out of a special petroleum revenue tax, plans to invest Won70 trillion by the year 2000 on new power stations and transmission equipment. The country currently runs nine nuclear power stations. Last year, these provided nearly half the country's electricity. By the year 2000, South Korea expects to have another 11 nuclear stations either built or under construction, making it one of the world's biggest users of nuclear power. Funding such a vast programme will not be easy. Rising inflation caused by over-heating in the economy means that the Korean government is seeking to slow down the overall rise in construction output while leaving infrastructure spending plans intact. Restrictions on the issue of building permits for private residential and commercial development have been introduced in a bid to reduce activity. The controls which had been expected to be lifted in the Spring have been extended. They are expected to remain in force at least until the end of the year - such is the difficulty of restricting rises in construction output which has been blamed for the doubling of the country's annual inflation since 1985. The aim is to restrict real increases in construction output, after allowing for inflation, to between 3 per cent to 4 per cent a year between now and 1996. Current forecasts are that total construction output will rise by 7 per cent in real terms this year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Survey of Korea (6): Unnatural silence - Why the stock exchange is still subdued
DOC.TEXT: KOREA'S reputation as the land of the morning calm may strike visitors caught up in one of Seoul's rush hour traffic jams as singularly undeserved. But it sums up the mood on the Korean stock exchange (KSE). Its performance this year has been subdued despite the infusion of funds from abroad after the limited opening of the market to foreign investors in January. The composite index has hovered around the 600 level for much of the year, compared with an all-time high of 1,008 in April 1989. Interest rates at around 16 per cent, a relatively low GDP growth rate of about 7.5 per cent and political uncertainty surrounding December's presidential election explain the poor performance, according to local brokers. Their foreign counterparts say the same factors have put off many international investors, who have also been deterred by the remaining government restrictions on their activities. These include a 10 per cent limit on foreign ownership of individual shares and a three per cent ceiling on holdings in a Korean company by any single foreign investor. Other barriers to greater foreign participation include a requirement to secure an investor identification number and a capital gains tax which has proved to be a big deterrent to investors from Germany, Japan and Hong Kong, countries which do not have double taxation treaties with South Korea. Some foreign investors have also been annoyed at having to trade under their real names, rather than through the usual nominees, though it appears that this requirement is being eased, according to Mr Peter Thorn, the chief representative in Seoul of brokers WI Carr. Another factor which has dampened the interest of those investors who missed the first wave of buying is the fact that foreign holdings in the most liquid stocks quickly reached their ceiling, forcing latecomers to pay a premium in the over-the-counter market. Ministry of Finance officials note, however, that only 18 companies out of the 688 listed have reached their foreign quotas. Ministry figures show that foreigners invested Dollars 917m as of May 6, while withdrawing only Dollars 125m. The net foreign position at the end of April represented just 0.73 per cent of the market's capitalisation, suggesting that government fears that a 'wall of Japanese money' would be used to pick off the choicest bits of Korean industry were overstated. The lacklustre performance of the composite index so far this year conceals sharp price rises in the shares of some smaller companies, a sector in which foreign buyers have been particularly active. Mr Thorn notes that the shares of some smaller companies are trading on 'multiples of only six, seven or eight and are extraordinarily cheap'. The low price/earnings ratios are largely the result of the sector having been ignored by domestic investors, who have traditionally focused instead on the absolute price of the more liquid shares of large companies. Foreign infatuation with the smaller companies has struck a welcome chord with the government, which is keen to encourage greater capital flows to small and medium-sized businesses as part of its policy to reduce the economic dominance of big conglomerates. The initial pattern and volume of investment from abroad has also done much to calm government fears over the impact of market liberalisation, and has strengthened the hand of those officials who would like to see the stock exchange opened more widely to overseas funds. Mr Philip Smiley, branch manager of Jardine Fleming Securities in Seoul, says: 'The commitment shown by most foreign investors to stay in the market' has largely dispelled government worries that 'hot money' from abroad would wreak havoc in the domestic economy. But few brokers, whether foreign or domestic, expect radical reforms to replace the government's cautious approach. 'The officials have learned much over the past three or four months', says Mr Thorn. 'The Ministry of Finance is now saying to brokers 'how can we make things better?' But there is still a reluctance to give up control.' The government is under pressure from foreign brokers to raise the 10 per cent limit on overseas ownership to 25 per cent, according to Mr Duncan Ross, manager of Baring Securities in Korea. But a senior finance ministry official countered that 'it is a little hasty to talk about expansion after only five months', and said investors 'should not expect such a decision this year'. The lack of movement on the issue is unlikely to stop the steady inflow of foreign funds, but it leaves the KSE standing out among other Asian markets, such as Hong Kong, where large international investors can move in and out of big blocks of highly liquid stocks with ease. US-based investors, in particular, have been put off by the lack of opportunities to invest Dollars 5-10m in one stock, according to Mr Smiley. The fact that Erisa-regulated US pension funds have been unable to comply with Korea's standing proxy rule, which conflicts with accepted American practice, has also been a barrier to US investment. But Ministry of Finance officials say a change in the rules this month should solve the problem. Nonetheless, US investors represented 20.2 per cent of total foreign investment at the end of April, while their British-based counterparts accounted for 42.3 per cent. New Zealand, through which some Hong Kong money is reportedly funnelled to avoid the Korean capital gains tax, represented 14.2 per cent of the total. But Japanese investors had come forth with little more than Dollars 1m, according to the ministry. The simplification or removal of the remaining regulatory restrictions will continue to be a top priority of the government, according to Mr Kim Tae-hyun, the director of the Ministry's Securities Policy Division. But he concedes that there has been 'no progress' on the avoidance of double taxation for Japanese, German and Hong Kong investors.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Survey of Korea (8): The advantages of North-South links - How to restore industrial competitiveness
DOC.TEXT: IF South Korea's industrialists had their way, the hesitant diplomatic dalliance between North and South would give way to an early economic bearhug. The most optimistic of the southern visionaries see close economic links with the North as the basis for a resurgence of international competitiveness. Such co-operation, say its proponents, would give South Korea the best of two seemingly contradictory economic worlds. First, it could restore Korea's declining competitiveness in traditional export items such as footwear and clothes by shifting production to the North, instead of to low wage countries in Southeast Asia. The application of even modest South Korean technology to the North's abundant supply of cheap and disciplined labour would lead to big productivity gains, say many Seoul economists. They believe that once such low-end but still lucrative export markets were secured, South Korean industry would be more confident about undertaking risky investments in high-technology areas. A by-product of the process would be the economic upliftment of 20m North Koreans, who would constitute a virtually captive consumer market for the south's industry. In addition, southern access to the North's mineral and other natural resources would lessen its dependence on imports, while defence spending, which constitutes a quarter of government expenditure, could be reduced substantially. Such a rosy scenario, however, assumes an orderly development of links with the the North, rather than any sudden lurch towards unification and the attendant risks of massive economic dislocation. And it may underestimate the difficulty of working within the North's troubled economy. Figures from the Economic Planning Board (EPB) in Seoul suggest that North Korea's gross national product shrank by 3.7 per cent in 1990, when it was hit by raw material and oil shortages caused by a change from barter to hard currency trade with the former Soviet Union. Mr Byung-Bae Kim, director of the EPB unit monitoring the North's economy, guesses that growth last year was 'at best at a standstill'. The government-funded Korea Development Institute estimates that the North's GNP was Dollars 27.3bn in 1990, about a tenth of the South's, while GNP per head was Dollars 1,273, a fifth of the Dollars 5,569 official figure for South Korea. Trade between the two economies has been minimal, and has generally been carried out through third countries such as China, Japan and Singapore. EPB figures for intra-Korean trade last year indicate that the South received Dollars 166m worth of goods - mostly non-ferrous minerals, gold, silver and coal - while sending Dollars 26m worth of mainly chemicals, textiles and home appliances to the North. Mr Kim says the growth of direct trade will depend on the pace of North-South talks this year, though a tentative agreement has been reached to set up a clearing account to facilitate greater exchanges. However, agreements on the avoidance of double taxation, commercial arbitration and the protection of investments will be required before Seoul approves the first joint ventures, he says. The need for additional negotiations has not put off southern industrialists, especially those who believe they can create on their own doorstep a Korean version of southern China's fast-growing Guangdong province. Mr Kim Woo-Chung, founder and chief executive of Daewoo Group, made a much-publicised trip to the North last January, during which he tentatively agreed to set up joint ventures in a number of light industries at the special economic zone which North Korea has proposed building at the port of Nampo. He also discussed mining projects and a scheme in which 10,000 North Korean workers would be used on a Daewoo contract to build a highway in Pakistan. The other big conglomerates, including Hyundai, whose founder was born in the North, are said to be equally keen despite a lack of hard information about the state of North Korean industry. Daewoo's Mr Kim Woo-Chung reported that productivity at the factories he visited seemed to be about half that of equivalent plants in the South, though he predicted that North Koreans would have little difficulty in adapting to more modern technology. Rivalry among the Korean conglomerates (and possibly foreign companies) to secure North Korean partners is likely to be heightened by the fact that most industrial sectors have only a few main companies, thus encouraging early link-ups. The Seoul government says it will gauge the success of small-scale joint ventures before approving any big industrial projects or partnerships with the North. And it will need to know much more about the soundness of individual North Korean companies, says Mr Kim at the EPB. But Pyongyang has made it clear that it has an ambitious development agenda of its own. Mr Kim Dal-hyon, the North Korean deputy prime minister responsible for the economy, said recently that Pyongyang would welcome broader foreign investment. He said the invitation included investment from the US although that would have to await a resolution of the nuclear issue and the lifting of a US ban on most commercial contacts with the North. Such statements, however, indicate just how far the North Korean government is prepared to go to attract foreign investment, which it believes can be confined to the SEZs or other specific areas, such as proposed tourist developments in mountainous areas revered by both North and South Koreans. South Korean companies accept that that will be the pattern for the first projects. But many economists in Seoul doubt whether Pyongyang can keep the bulk of its population isolated from foreign influences for long, especially as industrial logic will dictate the location of any large-scale projects. In the longer term, the focus for South Korean and foreign investment in North Korea could switch to the Tumen River basin along the border with China and Russia. A plan put forward by the United Nations Development Programme calls for the phased construction of a cross-border free trade zone near the mouth of the river. The zone would then serve as the base for developing the vast natural resources of the sparsely-populated hinterland of the region. Regular talks, which include South Korean and Mongolian representatives, are being held on ways of developing such a zone, which the UNDP estimates could cost Dollars 30bn over 15-20 years. That kind of talk clearly excites South Korean companies. It also pleases their government, which views any development that promises the orderly opening up of the North as positive. 'Recent events in Germany show us that unification can take any form and can proceed at any speed,' says Mr Kim at the EPB. 'There will always be a painful transition, but the costs can be much lower if the process is orderly.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 27 MAY 92 / Survey of Korea (7): World's fifth city - The population boom has put strains on Seoul
DOC.TEXT: WHEN Seoul marks its 600th anniversary as the Korean national capital in 1994, it will also be celebrating its position as the fifth biggest city in the world with a population approaching 11m. The city's role as an important Asian urban centre is expected to grow during the next decade, especially if the two Koreas are reunited. By 2001, its inhabitants are expected to number 14m. But Seoul's phenomenal and rapid expansion since the end of the Korean war in 1953 has brought a host of urban ills in its wake. 'Our biggest problems are transportation, housing, pollution and refuse collection,' says Seoul Mayor Rhee Hai-won. Those problems stem from the population explosion the city has experienced in the past 35 years. While the city's population stood at 1.5m in 1955, it swelled rapidly thereafter as the country embarked on a massive industrialisation programme, with factories concentrated in the main cities. As early as 1963, the population had already doubled to 3m and the city's boundaries were also doubled to accommodate the inflow of people moving from rural areas. The result was the transformation of Seoul from a compact city of traditional one-storey wooden houses into an urban sprawl dominated by high-rise buildings and the brownish haze of air pollution. In the process, Seoul has lived up to its name, which means capital in Korean, by becoming the focal point for all aspects of Korean society. The greater Seoul region, which also includes the port city of Inchon and other towns in the surrounding province of Kyonggi, has more than 18m people, accounting for almost 45 per cent of the South Korean population. The region is responsible for more than half of the national economic output, with 60 per cent of the country's industrial facilities located there. Besides being the political, corporate, financial and media capital of South Korea, the Seoul region has almost three-fifths of the nation's universities and close to half its theatres. The speed of the city's growth has defeated earlier attempts to control its development. Urban planning 'was difficult because conditions were changing so quickly,' explains Mayor Rhee. The city adopted in 1990 a master plan that establishes guidelines until the turn of the century.
