DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Foot soldiers dig in for war of attrition - Alison Smith gauges the mettle of Westminster's Euro-rebels
DOC.TEXT: UNDETERRED by their failure to stop the bill last night, the cross-party bands of Euro-rebels will be fighting on - and fighting to win - as the legislation proceeds through Westminster. Once it became clear that Labour would try to block the bill only and specifically on the grounds of opposing the UK's opting out of the social chapter and economic and monetary union - a course which would not attract any Tory rebels - the Euro-sceptics knew they would not be able to stop it in its tracks. At last week's Tory Euro-sceptics' dinner at the Carlton Club - even before the numbers of rebels had hardened - the talk was of tactics during the bill's committee stage, when MPs as a whole will be able to discuss it in detail and propose amendments to it. The critical question for the rebels will be whether they can devise an amendment which could unite elements as disparate as the Labour frontbench and hardened Euro-sceptics such as Sir Teddy Taylor on the Tory side. In any event, there is certain to be an attempt to propose a referendum, and though this might lead the pro-European Liberal Democrats to vote with some Tory Euro-sceptics, it may be difficult for the Labour party to agree. The two options open to the rebels for handling the bill are co-operation or delay. With co-operation, perhaps four full days would be set aside for discussion of the main issues. There are votes, which they are likely to lose, but at least the arguments would have been given a hearing. But if the rebels - or even a small minority of them - decide to filibuster in a bid to delay the bill, then the government might seek to impose a timetable on discussion, perhaps by then with popular support from backbenchers on both sides of the Commons. Alternatively, it could simply threaten a later summer recess. Though either route ends in the passage of the bill, both parties have been making strenuous efforts to minimise the rebellion. Particular pressure has been applied to new MPs, with more success on the Tory side than on the opposition. Mr Llew Smith, the Labour MP for Blaenau Gwent, used his maiden speech to explain why he was going to vote against the bill instead of following the party line of abstaining. Mr Nick Harvey, the new Liberal Democrat MP for Devon North, abstained rather than following his colleagues in voting for the bill. More generally, reminders that none of the rebels seemed to have mentioned to the electorate just a few weeks ago that they were planning to vote against party policy have been coming from the two frontbenches. There have also been touching appeals to logic, party unity and detailed argument when in many cases the view held is more instinctive and high-flown. On both sides, the rebels include a few figures, such as Mr John Biffen and Mr Peter Shore, whose seniority even those wholly unsympathetic to their stance say gives the rebellion 'a bit of class'. 'I don't feel as though I'm backing a loser,' said one senior rebel, 'but I'm not sure we'll win in my lifetime.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Royal visit to a British corner of Spain
DOC.TEXT: IF EVER there was a good time to be British in Spain, it was yesterday in Seville - when the Prince and Princess of Wales arrived to celebrate British Day at Expo '92. Pipe bands and the band of the Royal Marines marched in front of a huge glass waterfall. The Royal couple walked around a yacht built by British Steel and waved to the crowd. The Red Arrows zoomed overhead but were invisible because the walkways have over-hanging shrubs to keep out the sun. Inside Britain's pavilion, which is British territory for the summer, visitors are greeted by Elizabeth, who says: 'I'll be your navigator today.' The Expo theme is Discovery. In front of a bank of about 400 screens filled with images of Britain, Elizabeth said she was going to take the visitors on a journey 'to a country you think you may know well'. But first, some questions. Did we think the British were unemotional? Did we think they loved tradition more than technology (this as the pipe band struck up again outside)? Did the British value dignity more than dynamism? In a theatre high in the steel tube and glass pavilion, an actor did an elaborate and impressive mime to sound and lights. In the often-used US portable pavilion things were hopeless. The hamburgers were cold and there were no hot dogs. One of the pavilions belongs to Cruzcampo, a local brewery owned by Guinness. The royals never made it to Cruzcampo, but the managers were hoping the Red Arrows might drop in for a pint. Unfortunately they were last seen heading south, maybe back to Gibraltar, another bit of territory owned by Britain.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / 400 Names face average Pounds 80,000 loss
DOC.TEXT: ABOUT 400 Lloyd's Names will learn this week that they must pay an average of more than Pounds 80,000 each to meet losses sustained since 1983 by syndicate 387, which specialised in offering stop-loss reinsurance policies to other Names. Syndicate 387's losses for 1989 alone amount to Pounds 32.93m - more than five times the size of its stamp or capital base, and one of the worst results produced by any of the 401 syndicates trading at the Lloyd's insurance market in 1989. Lloyd's is expected next month to report a loss of between Pounds 1.6bn and Pounds 1.8bn for 1989, according to the latest estimates. The affairs of more than 70 per cent of the syndicate's Names were handled by agencies linked to the Lime Street agency. Names will be asked to meet the losses by mid July. The syndicate was formerly managed by the Gooda Walker agency, which went into liquidation last October. Many of the Names - individuals whose assets back underwriting - already face severe underwriting losses as a result of their membership of syndicates managed by Gooda Walker, Rose Thomson Young and other agencies which underwrote spiral reinsurance business, in which syndicates and London market companies reinsure each others' exposure to catastrophe loss. Syndicate 387's present managers, GW Run Off, have called in cash to meet losses on five separate underwriting years, 1983, 1984, 1985, 1988 and 1989. All have been left open because of uncertainty about future claims. Losses for the five years amount to Pounds 54.93m. Mr Ralph Sharp of GW Run Off said that the deterioration on the earlier years was because of increasing losses from pollution and asbestos-related claims, many of which emerge many years later. The losses for 1989 could eventually amount to more than Pounds 43m, according to Mr Sharp. In the years from 1983 to 1989 the syndicate's membership ranged from 239 to 448, but many were members in more than one year. In 1989 a handful of Names committed between Pounds 30,000 and Pounds 40,000, and face losses of up to Pounds 300,000 each. An early-day motion concerning alleged malpractice by professionals at Lloyd's was withdrawn from the Commons order paper yesterday. The motion had been tabled by two Tory MPs - Mr Paul Marland, MP for Gloucestershire West, and Mr Henry Bellingham, MP for Norfolk North West.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Freight may use fast Channel link
DOC.TEXT: MR JOHN MacGREGOR, trans-port secretary, yesterday raised the possibility of head-on competition between railway companies for freight traffic through the Channel tunnel. Mr MacGregor announced in a written Commons answer that the planned Pounds 4bn high-speed link between London and the tunnel would be designed to carry freight as well as passenger trains. It had been expected that the link would carry only high-speed passenger trains while all tunnel freight traffic used BR's existing tracks to the Kent coast. The effect of yesterday's announcement is that operators of freight trains will have a choice between two routes to the tunnel: the existing lines owned by BR (or a privatised version of it) and the new line which the government has said will be built and owned by an independent private developer. The transport department said yesterday that it was not strictly necessary for the high-speed link to carry freight trains because there was enough capacity on the existing network for all anticipated freight traffic. This meant that two freight tracks would not be added to the two passenger tracks because the extra Pounds 2bn cost could not be justified. But the department could not rule out the possibility that demand might be greater than forecast, for example, if a second Channel tunnel were built. It has therefore decided on the relatively low-cost option of incorporating passing loops into the railway so that high-speed passenger trains can overtake slower freight trains. It is not yet clear, however, whether a private-sector developer will be found to build the line or when it will open.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / PowerGen and Trafalgar plan rail terminal
DOC.TEXT: POWERGEN, the electricity generator, and the Business Parks subsidiary of Trafalgar House, the shipping, construction and property group, emerged yesterday as potential sponsors of an independent railfreight terminal after British Rail has been privatised. The two companies plan to develop a business and distribution centre based on a railfreight terminal at Hams Hall near Coleshill, north-east of Birmingham. Hams Hall is one of two sites in the west Midlands considered suitable by Railfreight Distribution, BR's international freight arm, as Channel tunnel terminals. The other, promoted by the Black Country Development Corporation, is at Bescot in Walsall. PowerGen said it was assuming Railfreight Distribution would choose Hams Hall, 'but if it does not we will seek an independent operator for the terminal'. Development of the terminal would take place regardless. Railfreight Distribution expects to choose a site at the end of next month. But the future of Railfreight Distribution is unclear. Under plans to privatise BR, Railfreight Distribution would be sold off. Whether it would be sold as a single entity or in blocks has yet to be decided. The transport department says the government wants to see a number of freight operators on the rail network. The Hams Hall terminal would be capable of handling 1m tonnes of freight a year by 1995, according to PowerGen and Trafalgar House. It would occupy 50 acres of a 890-acre redundant site owned by PowerGen. The two companies plan to develop 350 acres of the site. Hams Hall would be the largest commercial property project in the Midlands and would create what the companies called a 'Pounds 380m facility' providing 7,000 jobs. The rail terminal would have private sidings and 5.5m sq ft of warehousing and manufacturing space. The site is beside the Birmingham-Nuneaton railway line and the Birmingham-Derby line runs across part of it. Hams Hall is next to the M42 motorway and close to the M42-M6 junction.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Paying price of peace dividend: David White on the battle for survival at two naval dockyards
DOC.TEXT: BRITAIN'S two main naval dockyards are fighting a highly politicised battle for survival. The private-sector companies which have been running the yards since 1987 believe their fate will be sealed within the next year. When the two refit yards - Devonport Royal Dockyard at Plymouth and Rosyth Royal Dockyard in Fife - were placed under private-sector management in 1987, the change was hotly contested by unions. Both yards have been through heavy redundancy programmes paid for by the government. At Devonport, with an annual turnover of about Pounds 270m, jobs have fallen from more than 11,000 to just over 5,000. Rosyth, with a Pounds 180m turnover, has cut the number of jobs from about 6,000 to 4,200. The Ministry of Defence, which still owns the facilities, guaranteed the managers a 'core programme' for refitting surface ships and submarines - about two thirds of naval work with the rest being put out to competition or carried out by the Royal Navy's maintenance yard at Portsmouth. The programme has now been substantially reduced. Fleet numbers are being cut, some vessels have been paid off early, and the latest ships need less frequent work. Devonport Management (DML), a consortium in which the main partners are Brown and Root of the US, Balfour Beatty (part of BICC) and Weir Group, says its warship refit work has been cut by 45 per cent compared with the original programme. Mr Mike Leece, managing director, thinks the whole naval industry - shipbuilding and refit - will provide no more than 11,000 to 12,000 jobs in the late 1990s compared with 30,000 in the mid 1980s. The crucial decision under consideration at the MoD is on new refuelling and refitting facilities for nuclear-powered submarines. Refitting of the UK's Polaris ballistic-missile submarines is done at Rosyth and work on nuclear-propelled 'hunter-killer' submarines is split between Rosyth and Devonport. Both DML and Babcock Thorn, the management consortium at Rosyth, believe the logical option is to concentrate this work in a single site. Cranes and lorries are already busy at the Rosyth yard on a facility known as RD57 to accommodate Trident submarines, the successors to Polaris. Plans include two dry docks and an integrated refuelling site. About Pounds 50m has already been spent, and the overall cost was originally put at Pounds 450m. DML says it could provide similar facilities for less than Pounds 200m and that the extra work would greatly increase its efficiency. Babcock Thorn is discussing a low-cost alternative to its original plan at Rosyth which it says would reduce the further spending needed there to Pounds 150m. Both yards have diversified into areas such as refurbishing rail stock and boat building, but both see their future pinned to submarine business. The MoD is due to tell them by October 5 whether it proposes to renew their contracts, which expire in April 1994. Both dockyards are next to naval bases - another area under review at the MoD. DML argues that the Navy, needing to find substantial savings in support costs, cannot sustain three bases in the south - Plymouth, Portsmouth and the smaller establishment at Portland - and that the whole complex could be at risk, affecting 10,000 jobs. Mr Leece says: 'At the end of the day one of us is going to pay the bloody peace dividend.' SIGNIFICANT delays and cost overruns in the refitting of naval vessels at the Devonport and Rosyth dockyards have been highlighted by the National Audit Office, the public spending watchdog. In a report published yesterday the audit office underlined the problems of high overhead costs and excess capacity at the yards and said the defence ministry must determine how much of the facilities it would need in the long term. The report recognises that commercial managers had improved efficiency but said there was no way of assessing the net savings achieved since the MoD handed over the running of the yards. The audit office calculates that under-utilised staff and facilities at the yards cost Pounds 53m in 1990-91. Ministry of Defence: Operation of the Royal Dockyards under Commercial Management. HMSO. Pounds 7.80.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Staple defends staff and his predecessor's record
DOC.BYLINE: By ROBERT RICE and JOHN MASON
DOC.TEXT: IN SPITE OF criticism of the Serious Fraud Office over the collapse of the second Guinness trial and its handling of the Blue Arrow prosecution, the new director appears relaxed about the SFO's ability to do the job. At a press conference yesterday following publication of the SFO annual report Mr George Staple mounted a staunch defence of the competence of his staff and the record of his predecessor, Mrs Barbara Mills QC, now the director of public prosecutions. Before the Roskill fraud trials committee report, prosecution of serious fraud was a problem. The SFO had changed that, Mr Staple said. The SFO's conviction rate rose last year from 63 per cent to 66 per cent. The office prosecuted 58 people in 28 trials. Twenty defendants were jailed. Nevertheless, he admits to the strains on his department of coping with the burgeoning of cases of detected fraud. The increased value of the cases being reported has led to the raising of the SFO's limit for taking on new cases from Pounds 2m to Pounds 5m. This is in spite of a big increase in the SFO's budget, which rose from Pounds 13.2m in 1990-91 to Pounds 17.8m last year and Pounds 21.2m this year. Much of this increase was a result of having to mount the BCCI and Maxwell inquiries. 'If we had the funds no doubt we could prosecute more cases - there is a lot of serious fraud about,' Mr Staple said. 'But that is up to the government. I feel we are doing enough to be a real deterrent.' Confronted with the debate on how regulators and the legal profession should best tackle the problems of combating white-collar crime, Mr Staple believes that because the SFO is less than four years old it is not the time for fundamental change. He rejects an enhanced regulatory role for the office giving it powers similar to the Securities and Exchange Commission in the US. The existing demarcations between the SFO, Department of Trade and Industry and the Stock Exchange work well at the moment and should not be tampered with, he said. There are changes to trial procedures which he would like to see to counter some of the criticism of the length of recent cases. The defence should be forced to disclose its hand at a much earlier stage. That would allow the prosecution to refine its case thereby reducing the overall length of the trial. He denied that this would amount to a further erosion of a suspect's right to silence. A procedure for agreeing non-contentious evidence in advance of the trial would also save time, he said. But he rejected the suggestion that the SFO itself could make the greatest contribution to cutting the length of cases if it abandoned its approach of throwing the book at defendants and concentrated on the best six or 10 counts. 'The SFO is bound by the Crown Prosecution Services' code which requires us not to charge people on the fringes of a cases only the people at its core,' he said. 'And, equally, we are required not to overload the indictment. But we can't be put in a straitjacket. These cases are big and they are complex. Justice often requires a number of defendants and a number of charges.' Mr Staple did not reject out of hand the introduction of some form of plea bargaining in serious fraud cases.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Call for gas strike
DOC.TEXT: UNION negotiators for 37,000 white-collar workers at British Gas will next month press for a strike ballot over the company's 4 per cent pay offer.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Sales of life assurance up
DOC.TEXT: SALES of life assurance products rose substantially in the first quarter of this year, the Association of British Insurers said yesterday. Single-premium business - which often increases during a recession as consumers look to invest redundancy payments - rose by 85 per cent compared to the same period last year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Performance pay likely to spread
DOC.TEXT: THE traditional annual pay rise will virtually vanish in the financial services sector within two years, according to a survey published yesterday. KPMG Peat Marwick, the management consultants, found that 75 per cent of companies in the sector had introduced performance-related pay and predicted that this would increase to more than 90 per cent in the next two years.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / More charities submit accounts
DOC.TEXT: A TOTAL of 46 per cent of Britain's registered charities submitted accounts to the Charity Commission last year in response to its drive to improve administration of the sector. This compares with only 11 per cent in 1989. Under the new Charities Act, financial controls will be strengthened and the commission believes a target of obtaining accounts from 80 per cent to 90 per cent of charities can be achieved by 1994. The commission concluded 397 inquiries into charities last year as a result of public complaints and its own monitoring, and irregularities were discovered in 129 cases.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Reduction in capital spending
DOC.TEXT: CAPITAL spending by UK manufacturing industry fell 4 per cent in real terms in the first quarter of this year, indicating no easing of the recession in investment. According to the latest provisional seasonally adjusted estimate from the Central Statistical Office, real capital spending, which includes expenditure on leased assets, was 11 per cent lower than in the same period last year. The decline followed falls of 2.75 per cent and 0.5 per cent respectively in the final and third quarters of last year but was less steep than the 8 per cent drop registered in the first quarter of last year. Northern Ireland had one of its worst years for attracting overseas investment last year, the Industrial Development Board, the province's main jobs agency, said yesterday.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Opt-out school loses bid to be selective
DOC.TEXT: THE FIRST application for an opt-out comprehensive to become a grammar school was rejected yesterday by Mr John Patten, education secretary. Castle Hall School in Mirfield, West Yorkshire, wanted to become selective and change its age range from 9-13 to 11-18. It is understood that Mr Patten rejected Castle Hill's application because it had no record of teaching the planned age range, there was no proper financial scheme and no clear curriculum planning. The decision was greeted with fury at the school where 91 per cent of parents voted in favour of the application. It was reported last night that Mr Patten may face a legal challenge from parents over his decision. Editorial Comment, Page 16

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / DPP defends decision on W Midlands police
DOC.TEXT: MRS Barbara Mills QC, the director of public prosecutions, has replied to critics over her decision not to prosecute West Midlands Serious Crime Squad officers. In letters in today's issues of the Independent and The Guardian newspapers, she acknowledges the public disquiet about criminal justice but defends her decision that there was insufficient evidence for officers to be prosecuted. In the Independent she says: 'There is an enormous difference between poor supervision and sloppy management practice, and criminality. This point appears not to have been appreciated in much of the reporting of the matter.' The Crown Prosecution Service could only support criminal proceedings when there was 'sufficient, substantial, admissible and reliable evidence to provide a realistic prospect of conviction'. Mrs Mills' decision not to prosecute any officers of the former West Midlands Serious Crime Squad followed an investigation by West Yorkshire Police into allegations of corruption, fraud, perjury and faked evidence and several successful appeals against convictions on its evidence, including that of the Birmingham Six.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / SFO probes payroll company
DOC.TEXT: THE Serious Fraud Office is investigating how Payroll Services, a private payments company, allegedly diverted more than Pounds 24m of PAYE and National Insurance payments from the Inland Revenue and may have invested in a string of properties and a Spanish villa. Payroll Services, based in Sutton, south London, which serves more than 500 banks and financial institutions around the capital, went into provisional liquidation last month after the Inland Revenue discovered that one of the companies had fallen badly behind on its tax payments. Touche Ross, the accountancy firm acting as provisional liquidator, said the SFO is also investigating Payroll Services's parent, the Wren Group, where some of the money was allegedly transferred, and the directors of the companies. The Inland Revenue is understood to have extended an informal moratorium on the payment of these missing taxes. But it says Payroll Services' clients - which include a number of London offices of large Japanese and European banks - will have to make a second tax payment if the missing funds are not recovered. Payroll Services is one of a number of groups that have grown rapidly in recent years as smaller companies contract out the monthly payment of salary, PAYE and national insurance. The company handled more than Pounds 30m of such payments each month. According to the Touche Ross report, Wren Group appears to have invested in 55 properties, some of them residential, while Payroll Services owned a Pounds 75,000 villa in Spain. Mr Terence Wright, who owns all but one of Payroll Services's shares, is among a number of directors being pursued by Touche Ross. Among Wren Group's assets is an office building in Sutton which is nearly fully let to a number of smaller companies on short leases. Among the other subsidiaries of the Wren Group are a photographic company; a distributor of hydraulic parts and equipment; a property refurbishment company and an insurance broker. Last month the Bank of England called for provisional liquidators to be appointed to a financial arm of George H. Jackson, Payroll Services's Sutton-based auditors, which had carried on 'a banking-type business', Touche Ross said. The arm had been operating without the required Bank of England licence.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Grandson of 'Tin King' sells silver: Saleroom
DOC.TEXT: SOTHEBY'S started in New York on Wednesday to dispose of the most important art collection it has handled for two years - the silver, furniture and Old Masters of Jaime Ortiz-Patino, the grandson of Simon Patino, the Bolivian 'Tin King'. In the first session, devoted to French furniture, all the 103 lots sold for a total of Dollars 15.9m (Pounds 8.67m). The excellent provenance, rarity, and quality of the furniture on offer led to competitive bidding from private collectors and dealers, and total proceeds exceeded Sotheby's high estimate. The top price was the Dollars 1.98m paid by a private European collector for a Louis XVI ormolu mounted mahogany commode, painted with floral designs, and signed Joseph. It was made around 1770 and is attributed to Boullee. It is one of the few examples of top quality painted and veneered 18th century French furniture to have survived. A highly ornate Louis XIV table a ecrire, decorated with Chinese scenes, which had been estimated to sell for about Dollars 500,000, was bid up to Dollars 1.87m. A pair of Louis XVI ormolu mounted Boulle marquetry and Japanese lacquer commodes, signed by Levasseur, made Dollars 1.705m. Jaime Ortiz-Patino has been appointed adviser in Europe to the Bolivian government and is moving from a large house in Geneva to a small house in London. As a result he is selling some of his collection which should bring in at least Dollars 30m. Sotheby's jewels sale in Geneva brought SFr23m (Pounds 8.57m). A diamond necklace, made in London around 1900, unusual in that it is still intact, and heavy with fin de siecle opulence, sold for Pounds 380,297. The liquidators of BCCI pulled off a rare coup at Bonhams yesterday when they sold two sheet gold plaques over an iron core, 4 1/2 inches in diameter, dating from around 350 BC, for Pounds 187,000, as against a Pounds 20,000 top estimate. The plaques show a horsed warrior spearing an enemy and were made in Bactria, near modern day Iraq. Eight smaller plaques sold for Pounds 24,200. All were bought by a London dealer.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Murdoch gave TV soccer deal full support
DOC.TEXT: MR RUPERT MURDOCH, chief executive of News Corporation, promised English football's new Premier League the backing of 'the whole company' in the battle over TV rights. Apart from owning 50 per cent of British Sky Broadcasting - the satellite television consortium which on Monday won rights to broadcast 300 live Premier League matches over five years - Mr Murdoch also owns five national newspapers. The combined BSkyB-BBC offer was worth a total of Pounds 304m compared with a final ITV offer of Pounds 262m. Pearson, owner of the Financial Times, has a stake in BSkyB. According to one of those at Monday's league meeting - Mr Rick Parry, Premier League chief executive - those present had been guaranteed the backing of News International, News Corp's UK subsidiary, and 'the personal commitment of Mr Murdoch'. Mr Michael Grade, chief executive of Channel 4, said that, if true, the Murdoch promise was not 'the level playing field or the new spirit of competition envisaged by the Broadcasting Act'. Mr Greg Dyke, chairman of ITV Sport, said he had written to Sir John Quinton, chairman of the Premier League, asking for Monday's decision to be set aside. Mr Parry, however, said the decision was 'irrevocable.' Yesterday, Mr Alan Sugar - chairman of Tottenham Hotspur, a Premier League club, and of Amstrad, which sells satellite dishes - conceded he had spoken to BSkyB on the day of the meeting but that the company had already been informed of the new ITV offer. Mr Sugar said nothing unfair had happened on Monday. 'There was never an official tender offer date. Mr Parry always made it clear to both parties the latest offer status. Both companies had up to the last minute to make their final offer and they did,' Mr Sugar said. 'ITV had been soliciting each chairman with an envelope including their final offer at the doors of the meeting.' At the meeting, Mr David Dein of Arsenal had asked that Mr Sugar abstain from voting because he was a manufacturer of satellite equipment. Mr Sugar offered to do so but the club chairmen and chief executives present decided by 20-1 to allow him to vote. Mr Dyke said ITV Sport felt it had been misled. 'We are told that when the meeting started at 10am the bids were very close. 'However, by one means or another, BSkyB learned of the size of our bid and was allowed to increase their bid.' Mr Sam Chisholm, chief executive of BSkyB, yesterday expressed surprise that ITV wanted the bidding re-opened.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Jump in lending suggests growing confidence
DOC.TEXT: SIGNS that confidence among businesses and consumers is improving were boosted yesterday by news that bank and building society lending roselast month. The Bank of England said lending by banks and building societies to the private and corporate sectors - M4 lending - grew by Pounds 5.1bn in the month. The sharp jump suggested an increase in building society loans for house purchases. Economists warned against reading too much into one month's figures, and said much of the growth was a rebound from March, when companies and individuals made repayments totalling Pounds 400m net. It was the first time since 1982 that repayments on bank and building society lending outstripped new loans. The modestly encouraging news from the Bank was backed by figures from the British Bankers' Association, the trade body for Britain's nine biggest banking groups. The figures showed that lending by the association's members to the private sector grew by Pounds 2.6bn last month, the largest rise since the statistics began a year ago. This increase followed a net repayment by the private sector of almost Pounds 1.75bn in March. According to the association's figures, lending to individuals for house buying grew by Pounds 402m compared with a rise of Pounds 197m in April last year. The figures also showed that consumers continued to repay debt. Last month consumers repaid a net Pounds 43m on personal loans including overdrafts, loans for cars, and credit card loans, compared with a rise of Pounds 103m in April last year. Within the company sector, bank lending to securities dealers grew by Pounds 306m, to wholesalers by Pounds 200m and to manufacturers by Pounds 196m. Those figures were offset by net repayments from leasing, construction and property companies. 'One should never draw conclusions from one month's figures since they may be erratic,' said Lord Inchyra, association secretary-general. 'It is particularly difficult in a month like this, where there is a very large seasonal adjustment, to point to any clear signs of an upturn in the demand for credit.' Figures for money supply growth were in line with expectations. Narrow money, or M0, which comprises mostly notes and coins in circulation and represents underlying demand pressures, rose 0.4 per cent last month to give a 2.3 per cent increase for the year. M0 growth in the year to March it was 2.2 per cent. M4 rose by 0.8 per cent last month, bringing the year-on-year growth rate to 5.7 per cent. Lex, Page 18

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Company register reform is urged
DOC.TEXT: CHAMBERS of Commerce are to press the government to support the establishment of a mandatory trading register for all companies along the lines already adopted by many EC countries. Representatives of the chambers are to meet Mr Michael Heseltine, trade and industry secretary, on June 8 to seek ministerial backing for a wide-ranging overhaul of the system of registration. The initiative is designed to simplify and speed up the process of company licensing and registration and to improve the flow of commercial information available. Mr Richard Brown, director of policy for the Association of British Chambers of Commerce, told the association's conference in Brighton that British companies faced heavy burdens of compliance. The report of an association working party on the issue presented to the conference says there is widespread confusion and ignorance, particularly among new businesses, about regulatory and licensing requirements. Mr Brown said British companies had to compete with a culture which sought to inhibit business and had to deal with regulatory bodies which sometimes appeared set on preventing the creation of wealth. There was, he claimed, considerable scope for streamlining the process of obtaining registration or licences. The chambers were proposing - in place of the existing piecemeal approvals - a network of trading formalities centres where the registration process would be co-ordinated. The centres would provide a 'one-stop' entry point at which all businesses could quickly establish the necessary procedures for compliance. Chambers say many business opportunities are lost because of the 'information gap'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Foreign banks await securities scam fall-out
DOC.TEXT: WITH INDIA'S financial markets in disarray as a result of irregular securities trading, foreign banks are nervous that in the fall-out from the country's worst financial scandal they could face a further setback to their expansion plans. Foreign banks dominate the interbank securities market from which Mr Harshad Mehta, the Bombay broker, and others raised large sums for stock market speculation. These institutions face the charge that it was their more innovative and aggressive trading practices that produced the environment in which abuses flourished. The two oldest foreign banks - Standard Chartered, the British-based bank, and ANZ Grindlays, the former UK bank now Australian-owned, - are seen to have had inadequate controls over their securities dealing. Standard Chartered has announced provisions of Pounds 50m for losses in its operations. Grindlays is believed to be exposed on Rs5bn to Rs6bn (Pounds 97m-Pounds 116m) of transactions, though ultimate losses could be substantially less. Foreign banks, which account for 6 to 7 per cent of bank deposits, had hoped to be a big beneficiary of financial deregulation - both through setting up new investment banks and through more branch offices. Part of the suspicion of foreign banks stems from the different compulsions under which they act compared with the state-owned banks. The state banks - though this is now beginning to change - had as their primary function allocating credit at government direction. They were not too worried about their balance sheets. The foreign banks are increasingly profit-driven and in search of new opportunities to improve earnings in a tightly regulated banking system that provides little room to manoeuvre. The local state-owned banks used the interbank market to purchase securities in line with statutory liquidity requirements, laid down by the Reserve Bank of India, the central bank, that they hold a proportion of their deposits - until recently 38 per cent - with the Bank in government paper. Foreign banks, however, actively traded in the market. They swapped securities of differing interest rates and maturities to improve yields; they sought to prevent the depreciation of their portfolios when interest rates moved; and they looked to trading profits. They also introduced new instruments into the market - such as the banker's receipt, a promissory note issued by a bank to pledge delivery of securities. Fraudulent and uncovered banker's receipts lie at the heart of the scandal. Over the last 18 months nationalised banks have come under pressure to improve their balance sheets as a first step to financial reform. Interest rate changes became more frequent - with the beginnings of deregulation, rates were moving more in line with inflation. Both foreign and state-owned banks responded with increased trading. A new generation of brokers - of whom Mr Mehta is the symbol - entered the market pressing new techniques and cutting new deals. Mr Mehta is an approved Reserve Bank broker in the securities market. Many were not. A year ago the stock market took off on a boom that was to treble the value of the Bombay Stock Exchange index. The temptation grew to syphon funds from trade in government debt to make share purchases on the stock market. In this hothouse atmosphere, central bank supervision was inadequate and carelessness crept into trading. The Reserve Bank's own ledger of security transfers - maintained by hand - fell well behind. Banks failed to verify with each other the authenticity of banker's receipts. Smaller banks - most prominently the Bank of Karad, which now has problems meeting its obligations - issued receipts of a size out of proportion with their assets. Some foreign banks are patting themselves on the back that they have got away unscathed. 'Its a tribute to our systems and our procedures,' said one. But in such an unruly market those who escaped had luck on their side. Mr Manohar Jethnand Pherwani, head of the state-owned National Housing Bank, who resigned last week when investigators discovered that Rs7bn was missing, died yesterday of a heart attack. Once known as the 'Big Bull' of the Bombay bourse, he was credited with developing an equities mania among Indians.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Israeli air raids kill nine guerrillas in Lebanon
DOC.TEXT: ISRAEL'S war with the pro-Iranian Lebanese Shia Moslem Hizbollah escalated yesterday when Israeli aircraft twice bombed Hizbollah targets in Lebanon, killing nine guerrillas and wounding 20. Unconfirmed reports said that one of the dead was an Iranian revolutionary guard. The bombing raids and helicopter gunship attacks on two Shia villages in southern Lebanon constituted the most serious Israeli offensive against Hizbollah since the violence following Israel's assassination of the group's leader, Sheikh Abbas Musawi, in February. A Hizbollah delegation had met Syrian Vice-President Abdel-Halim Khaddam in Damascus on Wednesday night. Syria has supported Hizbollah's 'resistance' operations against the Israelis. The first Israeli bombing raid yesterday targeted a Hizbollah base at Janta, just three miles west of the Syrian border, renewing fears that Syria could be drawn into the Hizbollah-Israeli conflict. The current fighting began on Tuesday, when Hizbollah militiamen overran a hilltop position of the South Lebanon Army (SLA), Israel's proxy militia in southern Lebanon. Reuter adds from Jerusalem: The Israeli army said it was checking Palestinian claims that undercover troops had shot and wounded seven children on Wednesday, during a Palestinian election campaign in the occupied West Bank city of Nablus.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Stand-off in Thai power struggle: The confrontation between the people and the military is far from over
DOC.TEXT: THAILAND'S political crisis is not yet over. After three days of violent confrontations between the government and pro-democracy demonstrators, Bangkok was returned to its normal state of noise and congestion yesterday by the timely intervention of King Bhumipol Adulyadej. The compromise brokered by the king late on Wednesday between Gen Suchinda Kraprayoon, the prime minister, and Mr Chamlong Srimuang, leader of the opposition campaign, has halted the violence and given businesses the chance to recover from the week's chaos. This forced reconciliation of enemies in the presence of the monarch, however, is only an interim solution. It is now up to the two sides to achieve the seemingly impossible task of satisfying both the political ambitions of the military establishment and the democratic aspirations of the Thai people. Yesterday neither side showed much willingness to yield. As 3,000 protesters emerged from jail yesterday under an amnesty announced by Gen Suchinda - some still wearing clothes stained with the blood of dead comrades - they insisted that the prime minister would have to resign and even go into exile. On his own admission, 40 people were killed in the disturbances, although unofficial tallies put the death toll higher. All over the capital, residents expressed relief that the violence had ended but said it would take a long time to heal the emotional scars left by the sight of Thai soldiers gunning down civilians in the city centre. 'Anger' was the word most commonly expressed, and opposition parties are demanding that Gen Suchinda and his government should be held accountable for the actions of the army. The sense of continuing conflict was underlined by a reference in one Bangkok newspaper to missing protestors as 'pro-democracy MIAs', an abbreviation usually reserved for soldiers missing in action. King Bhumipol's intervention has left the ball in the government's court. After meeting the king, Gen Suchinda promised to arrange for parliament to meet next week to rush through an amendment of the constitution, one of the opposition's main demands. They want the constitution changed to reduce the power of the military-appointed senate and reserve the premiership for an elected member of parliament, but it is unclear how far the pro-military coalition which appointed the unelected Gen Suchinda is prepared to go down the path of reform. Indeed, it was the coalition's hesitation on the constitutional issue which contributed to the violence in the first place. The five parties in the government, having conceded the need to change the constitution, appeared to be backtracking just before the disturbances erupted on Sunday night. King Bhumipol implicitly criticised Gen Suchinda on this point in his audience on Wednesday. Throughout this week the members of the coalition, having won the elections in March with the help of vote-buying in the provinces, have either remained silent or made undiplomatic statements which have grated on the ears of the more sophisticated population of Bangkok; the capital voted overwhelmingly for Mr Chamlong in the elections. Gen Suchinda dismissed his opponents as communists or Buddhist heretics. Mr Samak Sundaravej, deputy premier, responded to a question about the killing of anti-government protestors by saying: 'Let me ask you something. Why didn't anybody blame President George Bush when he sent troops to invade other countries?' And Mr Arthit Urairat, speaker of the lower house of parliament, drew an angry reaction from doctors and patients at a Bangkok hospital when he and other coalition MPs visited injured protesters and handed them tins of evaporated milk. Nor is it clear if Gen Suchinda is prepared to resign or if the coalition would then choose somebody acceptable to replace him. After the loss of so many lives, the demonstrators are determined to win at least a modest victory. They have warned that the protests will resume if their demands are not met by parliament, but government MPs apparently do not share the same sense of urgency. It was announced yesterday that although parliament would meet on Monday it would not consider constitutional amendments until Friday. 'I think it's going to be very jittery over the next few days,' said one western diplomat in Bangkok. Even if a compromise on the constitution can be reached, there is no sign of a solution to the much deeper problem of the military's long-standing involvement in politics and business. The generals have seen their freedom of action constrained in recent years by the growing confidence of civilian politicians. Thailand, however, did not resolve the issue of military interference when the king intervened to change the government after riots in 1973, and neither he nor anybody else is likely to do so now.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / French missile bid stirs row: George Graham on US anger at Thomson-CSF's move to buy missiles division of US defence contractor
DOC.TEXT: THOMSON-CSF, the French state-controlled defence electronics group, has provoked a storm in Washington over its efforts to buy the missiles division of LTV, the US steel and industrial group operating under bankruptcy protection. The Committee on Foreign Investment in the US (CFIUS), a review body chaired by the Treasury, this week decided to launch a full investigation of the deal under the Exon-Florio rules, introduced in 1988 to give the president the power to block or reverse any foreign acquisition that 'threatens to impair the national security'. But, even before the formal CFIUS review has begun, Thomson-CSF has come under fire from Congress. The French group's representatives have been grilled by a series of hostile Congressional investigative committees. Two of the Senate's most senior members, Senator Robert Byrd of West Virginia and Senator Lloyd Bentsen of Texas, have sponsored a bill to ban the deal. The Bush administration's decision on LTV's missile business - which is involved in top-secret US military programmes, such as the Losat anti-tank missile and the MLRS anti-artillery missile system - could foreshadow US policy on an expected wave of foreign acquisitions in sensitive technology areas. As military purchasing budgets shrink, the US defence industry is restructuring. Some industry executives estimate that 100 subsidiaries, divisions or units of defence contractors are up for sale. Many of these are likely to interest foreign buyers. 'The LTV case offers the president an opportunity to demonstrate that, in fact, he has a strategy for America's defence industrial base in the post-Cold War era,' said Senator James Exon, co-author of the Exon-Florio rules. LTV at first agreed in February to sell its missile and aircraft business as a whole for Dollars 355m to a consortium formed by Lockheed and Martin Marietta, two leading US defence contractors. In April Thomson-CSF bid Dollars 280m for the missiles division, coupled with a Dollars 120m bid for the aircraft division from Carlyle Group, a Washington-based merchant bank headed by Mr Frank Carlucci, the former defence secretary. After a round of bidding, the New York bankruptcy judge presiding over LTV awarded the two units to Thomson-CSF and Carlyle for a total of Dollars 450m. Opposition to the Thomson-CSF-LTV deal focuses on three points of concern: The security of secret US military technologies. Thomson-CSF's state ownership, which its competitors fear could give it unfair subsidies, cheap capital and political advantages. Hostility to France, which has been described by senators as 'aggressive', 'stubborn' and 'cocksure', and accused of widespread industrial espionage against the US. Thomson-CSF has already begun discussions with the defence department about measures to protect US secrets. These include a 'special security arrangement' by which classified information would be placed under the control of a special committee of US citizens with the necessary security clearances. Pentagon officials appear, however, to be happy with this kind of arrangement only up to the 'Secret' level of classification. In past foreign acquisitions involving 'Top Secret' or 'Comsec' classifications, the Pentagon has insisted that control of the company be placed in the hands of a voting trust or of proxies. 'It has to become a passive ownership or it doesn't fly,' said Mr Donald Atwood, deputy secretary of defence, last month. Mr Daniel Tellep, chairman and chief executive of Lockheed, argues that even proxies or voting trusts are inadequate protection, since it is at the level of a company's engineers that technology is transferred. Mr Carlucci retorts that Thomson-CSF engineers already have access to their US pany's participation in US programmes, such as the US Army's MSE battlefield communications system based on Thomson-CSF's Rita system. 'Thomson-CSF already bids on defence department contracts. It has at least 20 classified contracts now. The only question is whether it should bid offshore or onshore,' he says. On the issue of government ownership, Thomson-CSF has an even harder task defending itself. 'What we have here is a policy problem involving government involvement in the free enterprise system, and the two are like oil and water,' said Mr Norman Augustine, chairman and chief executive of Martin Marietta. More troubling, however, is the extent of anti-French sentiment displayed in the tussle over the LTV deal. Senator Fritz Hollings of South Carolina is perhaps the most overtly xenophobic member of the Senate, but his gibes are usually directed at the Japanese and the Koreans. Of the French, he said: 'We love each other. I've stood on tables all over France singing the Marseillaise.' But in a barbed exchange with Mr Carlucci, he placed France alongside Iraq in his pandemonium. 'I couldn't possibly see General (Norman) Schwarzkopf being employed by Saddam Hussein to train his troops. Why should we allow you to come in now as a former Secretary of Defence and take over our defence technology for France?' he said. The old days of ever-expanding military budgets are over, however. Today's procurement budgets may not sustain even a single domestic supplier in many areas of defence technology, let alone competing suppliers. The alternative to foreign acquisition may, for many US defence companies, be shutdown.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / White House rejects charge of Iraq cover-up
DOC.TEXT: SENIOR members of the Bush administration yesterday angrily rejected Congressional charges that the White House was trying to cover up improprieties related to more than Dollars 4bn of loans to Iraq by Italy's Banca Nazionale del Lavoro. In testimony before the House of Representatives banking committee, Mr Lawrence Eagleburger, deputy secretary of state, attacked the committee's release of classified documents which, he claimed, had led to 'distortions of the record, half-truths, and outright falsehoods, all combined into spurious conspiracy theories and charges of a cover-up.' He was referring to a series of Bush administration documents made public by Mr Henry Gonzalez, committee chairman, who has argued that the documents show a pattern of administration financial assistance to Iraq and possible knowledge of the secret BNL loans, made from the bank's branch at Atlanta, Georgia. Mr Gonzalez criticised President George Bush for failure to provide Congress with a series of BNL-related documents. In reply, Mr Eagleburger said the administration would not permit the further release of documents without fresh assurances that they would be kept confidential by Congress. Mr Eagleburger and Mr John Robson, deputy treasury secretary, testified that there had been insufficient evidence of any Iraqi wrongdoing in the BNL affair, in November 1989, for a senior White House meeting to block the extension of Dollars 1bn of separate, government-guaranteed loans to Baghdad. Mr Eagleburger stated that these US government-guaranteed loans for Iraqi purchase of US agricultural goods were seen by the Reagan and Bush administrations as a tool to moderate Iraq's President Saddam Hussein. 'It didn't work,' admitted Mr Eagleburger. Mr Edward Kelley, a member of the Federal Reserve's board of governors, made clear that, at the White House meeting, the Fed had firmly opposed more US export credit loan guarantees for Iraq because of concern about the BNL case and Iraq's credit-worthiness.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Farm Reform in Europe: German minister stands his ground against farm lobby
DOC.TEXT: GERMANY'S battle-hardened agriculture minister, Mr Ignaz Kiechle, must have known he was on a hiding to nothing. On Tuesday, the German farmers' union demanded that he fight the proposed reforms 'with all his might, and even use his veto if necessary'. So it was hardly a surprise that Baron Constantin von Heereman, president of the German farmers' organisation, the Deutscher Bauernverband (DBV) for the past 23 years, denounced the package yesterday as 'intolerable'. 'We are in favour of reform, but not the one which Kiechle is accepting,' he declared. 'They get a 5 per cent plus wage rise in the public sector, and we get 35 per cent minus for the cereal farmers: it is unacceptable.' That comes on top of a drop in farm incomes in 1990-91 of 16 per cent, and little better than stagnation in the current year, according to official figures. The DBV predicts another real loss of some 21 per cent in 1991-92. For once, however, Mr Kiechle seemed to be standing his ground against his own farming lobby, strongest above all in his native Bavaria. He described the DBV and its members as 'day-dreamers who have no idea of agricultural political necessities'. Mr Kiechle fought his corner in Brussels with his usual tenacity, but the key change in Germany's position was that he did not appear willing to use his veto. Two factors seem to be behind that relaxation in Germany's staunch defence of the CAP: a desire to reach a deal in the Gatt round, above all before the Group of Seven world economic summit in Munich in July, to be chaired by Chancellor Helmut Kohl; and the advent of huge east German farms to German agriculture, requiring a whole new set of policy priorities. German agriculture is no longer so dominated by small farmers - above all by part-time farmers. A whole new category of huge factory farms on the eastern model have now to be taken into consideration. Most are effectively bankrupt now, but they have to be given the incentive to recover. Mr Kiechle wanted a cereal price cut of 15-20 per cent maximum. In that, he was seeking to defend western Germany's relatively small and high-cost farmers, fearful that if the EC support price were dropped too far, they would be unable to compete with French cereal farmers, themselves driven out of the export market. He has been forced to accept a 29 per cent cut, although he will be allowed to pay substantial compensation to his farmers. Germany was happy to go along with Britain in calling for the compensation to be paid to big farms as well as small - thanks to the existence of the eastern farms. The compensation comes in two ways: Mr Kiechle has won the right to keep paying income support measures this year to replace the 3 per cent VAT rebate which expired last year. That is a German national measure - a clear distortion of the agricultural common market, and therefore an important concession. The second form of compensation is that payable to all EC farmers in exchange for a 15 per cent reduction in their arable land. Mr Kiechle was determined that the payments should be allowed for an indefinite period. But even then, his farmers are suspicious. 'The farmers are naturally sceptical about whether the compensation will be lasting,' an Agriculture Ministry official said yesterday. 'Lasting could mean five years, or it could mean 10 years.' Or as one diplomatic observer of German agriculture put it: 'The farmers know they are being paid to do nothing. That is a very vulnerable position to be in.' The EC reforms bring German agriculture face to face with some unpleasant realities. 'They have to restructure their agriculture and lower their overheads,' an independent analyst said. 'That means they are going to have to go further down the road towards the industrialisation of agriculture - which is anathema to Mr Kiechle.' The irony is that perhaps Mr Kiechle will not be around to implement it. He is widely expected to be a casualty of the next cabinet reshuffle in the autumn, finally abandoned by his friend and admirer, Chancellor Kohl, in the interests, no doubt of 'agricultural, political necessities'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Farm Reform in Europe: Wary US takes longview of outlook for grain
DOC.BYLINE: By NANCY DUNNE and BARBARA DURR
DOC.TEXT: FOR THE past decade, US officials have cajoled, threatened and spent billions on agriculture export subsidies in an effort to convince the European Community to phase out farm supports. When the news arrived yesterday in Washington of a deal to begin reform of the Common Agriculture Policy, the reaction was subdued. The immediate response to the agreement was 'mass confusion, maybe long-term hope and maybe long-term heartburn', said Mr Paul Drazek, a spokesman for the American Farm Bureau. He thought CAP reform 'could be the most significant development in the grain trade in the last 30 years,' but he cautioned that its importance 'would depend on how much less production and dumping' there was likely to be. Grain market experts also expressed some scepticism about how a CAP subsidies cut of 29 per cent, instead of the 35 per cent proposed by the European Commission, would be received by Washington in this electoral year. Many farm lobbyists who advise Mrs Carla Hills, US trade representative, say they will not support any Uruguay Round deal which weakens proposals by Mr Arthur Dunkel, Gatt director-general for deeper subsidy cuts. There is already so much uncertainty in the grain markets because of the changes in eastern Europe that the impact of CAP reform - stretched out over years - is likely to be less important than a drought in Mongolia or snow in Brazil. In Chicago, there was reluctance to predict any price effects on grains. CAP reform was 'certainly encouraging,' said Mr Martyn Foreman, an analyst with Agrivisor, a market advisory service of the Illinois Farm Bureau. 'It would put some underpinning in world prices.' Past US Department of Agriculture studies have forecast a rise in grain prices in the event of a 35 per cent cut in European subsidies, but Mr Daniel Basse, director of market research at AgResource in Chicago, said the USDA was assuming demand would remain constant, a premise that not all analysts share. Even without CAP reform, the outlook for commodity prices is murky, experts believe. Much depends on countries like China and the Commonwealth of Independent States. This year, the CIS wheat crop looks to be 12m tonnes larger than last year's 73m tonnes. China is both the largest wheat producer and importer (94m tonnes and 16m tonnes, respectively, are predicted) but it can easily curb imports, as it has in the past for political reasons. According to Mr Basse, the effects of lower EC prices would not be felt at the earliest until next year's crops. Eventually, reductions in EC grain production and less dumping of excess grains on world markets could help raise exports, particularly of wheat, from other grain producers. Countries such as Canada, Australia and Argentina were considered more likely to see the benefits on exports than the US given that Washington has competed with Europe on export subsidies while other countries have not. Mr John Sault, agricultural counsellor of the Australian embassy in Washington, said his country had been caught in the crossfire between the EC and the US export subsidies, pushing Australian traders out of their traditional markets such as the former Soviet Union and China. CAP reform gave some hope that former markets could be regained.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Farm Reform in Europe: Britain welcomes levelling of field
DOC.TEXT: BRITISH FARMERS yesterday welcomed the end of the uncertainty surrounding their businesses. Their main complaint about the original plans to reform the CAP was that they discriminated against the UK, which has much larger and more efficient farms than the rest of Europe. Much of the original discrimination against British agriculture appears to have been cleared away. In particular, farmers with large acreages will be relieved at the demise of a proposal to limit the amount of set-aside land on which compensation is paid. This was the biggest stumbling block for the UK during the negotiations. 'It would appear that John Gummer has achieved quite a remarkable victory on behalf of all UK arable farmers,' the managing director of one large company said yesterday, delighted that Britain had not been left at a disadvantage to smaller European competitors. Under the reform proposals 15 per cent of the arable land will be put into set-aside. Farmers will then qualify for compensation for the 29 per cent cut in EC cereal prices. This would imply a compensation figure of about Pounds 200 per hectare. The Ministry of Agriculture said that Pounds 230 a hectare had originally been proposed for a 35 per cent cut in cereal prices, and a later proposal to cut prices by only 27 per cent would have given Pounds 175 a hectare compensation. Britain has gained further concessions within the reform package, particularly for sheep farmers in the so-called 'less favoured areas', or uplands, where the original proposals limited the number of ewes eligible for subsidy to 750. UK farm incomes, however, will continue to fall from already low levels. Booker Farming, which farms and advises on 45,000 acres in England, predicted earlier this year that the income of a top quality 500-acre farm in the UK would fall from Pounds 20,000 to only Pounds 3,500 under the original MacSharry proposals. While the impact of the latest package will not be so severe, it could still cut the farm income in half. Mr David Naish, president of the National Farmers Union, agreed yesterday that many farms were already under severe financial pressure, but he was prepared to accept lower prices if the UK was on an equal footing with the rest of Europe. As long as the reform package treated all farmers the same, 'we have got to learn to live with it,' he said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Babcock in Pounds 56m Greek deal
DOC.TEXT: GREECE'S Public Power Corporation (PPC) has awarded a Dr19.6bn (Pounds 56m) contract to Babcock Energy Systems, the British engineering company, to upgrade a power station at Lavrion, near Athens, writes Kerin Hope in Athens. The PPC intends to help reduce atmospheric pollution in Athens by developing generating capacity outside the city and converting diesel-fired units to natural gas during the 1990s. The project involves transferring a steam turbine from the Keratsini power station in Athens to Lavrion, 40 miles from the capital, which will steam link to two existing gas turbines to form a combined cycle unit, raising the plant's capacity from 114 to 180 MW.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Total in Russian oil agreement
DOC.TEXT: TOTAL, the French oil group, has signed a production-sharing agreement with Komineft, the Russian oil company, for the Khariaga field. The deal will involve investment of Dollars 400m (Pounds 218m) over two and a half years to bring the field on stream, with total investment likely to be Dollars 1bn over the life of the field. Total will be the operator in the development of several geological layers of the Khariaga oilfield, located in the Timan Pechora basin, west of the Urals near the Arctic circle. Reserves are estimated at approximately 250m barrels, with production likely to be around 35,000 barrels a day. An agreement was signed in the presence of the governor of the Nenets territory, where the Khariaga field is situated, but is subject to Russian Federation government approval. Total has signed two previous deals with Russian partners to bring western oil drilling technology to boost yields from fields not yet producing.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Easier access to Japan urged for foreign groups
DOC.TEXT: A GROUP of visiting British executives yesterday called on the Japanese government to ensure that foreign companies have the same access in the country as Japanese companies have in the UK market. The six-company group - headed by the Duke of Kent and Mr Michael Perry, the chairman of Unilever, and including executives from Glaxo Holdings and SG Warburg & Co - presented a list of proposals to Japanese industry representatives and the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (Miti). In an 'Agenda for Action by Japanese Business', the executives expressed confidence that British companies will expand Japanese market share 'unless that market is distorted for political reasons or because of excessive bias towards Japanese domestic suppliers.' However, Mr Perry said the delegation, in Tokyo as part of the Priority Japan campaign, does not regard Japan as a 'problem' but as an 'opportunity'. He added that UK industry does not 'want to argue about the rules of the game'. UK exports to Japan fell from Pounds 2.63bn in 1990 to Pounds 2.26bn last year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Slovenia looks to Community for new markets
DOC.TEXT: THE war in the former republics of Yugoslavia is forcing Slovene enterprises to find alternative trading partners among European Community countries as a means of compensating for lost markets in the region. However, Slovene officials warn that capital inflows will not increase unless Slovenia re-establishes trade links with its southern neighbours. Until 1990, over 30 per cent of Slovenia's exports were with the former Yugoslavia, while about 70 per cent were divided between Comecon, the now defunct socialist trading block, and western European countries. But following an embargo by Serbia on Slovene imports in 1990, and ensuing war in neighbouring Croatia last year, Slovene exports to the former Yugoslavia have fallen to 15 per cent of that previously. The loss of markets in the former Yugoslavia, and the war, has led to a sharp drop in industrial production, which last year fell by 15 per cent, and will fall a further 12 per cent this year. Unemployment has risen to 101,000, up from 9 per cent to 11 per cent of the labour force. However, inflation is falling thanks to a strong monetary policy implemented by Slovenia's central bank. Inflation was running at 25 per cent a month last October, but by April it had fallen to 5 per cent. Mr Feri Horvath, head of Slovenia's Chamber of Commerce, said Slovenia, which declared its independence last June, must seek new markets because the republic is too small to be able to attract large amounts of foreign investment to foster growth. Renault, French car manufacturer, which assembles cars in Slovenia, and Siemens, German-based mechanical and electrical goods maker, which has a joint venture with Iskra, Slovenia's electronic and telecommunications manufacturer, have used Slovenia as a base for exporting to other parts of Yugoslavia, as well as to western Europe. 'We have recently signed bilateral trade agreements with Croatia and Macedonia,' said Mr Horvath. 'We want to normalise relations with the other republics,' he added. In the meantime, Slovene enterprises, particularly those in the furniture, electronics, paper, and white goods sector, are exporting to European Community countries. Exports for the first quarter amounted to Dollars 941m (Pounds 513m), and imports totalled Dollars 752m. Last year, total exports of goods reached Dollars 3.9bn, and imports, Dollars 4.1bn. 'Our enterprises are beginning to find new markets,' said Mr Horvath, adding that Germany, Italy, France and Austria are now Slovenia's main trading partners. Mrs Vojka Ravbar, Slovenia's deputy foreign minister, who earlier this week headed a trade delegation to the UK, said enterprises will have to become even more competitive after privatisation. Parliament is now discussing a privatisation bill.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / EC backs radical farm reform: Deep cuts in price support expected to boost Uruguay Round talks
DOC.TEXT: THE European Community last night agreed on the most radical overhaul of the Common Agricultural Policy in its 30-year history. It followed up with a challenge to the US to match the Community's deep cuts in farm price support and to join in trying to reach a conclusion of the Uruguay Round world trade talks. The EC agreement, greeted as historic by nearly all Community farm ministers, should lead to the end of food mountains in Europe, lower retail food prices and give EC farmers more stable incomes and a sharper competitive edge. Accord was reached in the face of continued resistance from Italy over its milk quota. Mr Ray MacSharry, EC agriculture commissioner, said: 'We have charted a different course after 30 years.' Mr Louis Mermaz, French agriculture minister, hailed the accord as 'a fundamental change from traditional (EC) agriculture towards a competitive model, with, of course, compensation for our farmers'. Mr John Gummer, UK farm minister, called it 'a major breakthrough which will bring the Community into line with the rest of the world'. Mr MacSharry's blueprint for reform, unanimously opposed when it was unveiled 18 months ago, finally won acceptance this week after four days and three nights of negotiations. Italy, although in agreement with the reform, held out until last night for retrospective validation for part of its illicit excess milk production. Italy, entitled to produce 9m tonnes of milk by the EC, in fact produces 11.5m tonnes. By dawn yesterday, however, Mr MacSharry had assembled a clear majority, partly by offering a range of concessions. The Portuguese presidency of the EC put the package through under the weighted majority voting system. Mr Arlindo Cunha, Portugal's farm minister, said: 'We took our political courage in our hands.' Mr Giovanni Goria, Italy's farm minister, said Rome would take the dispute to June's Lisbon summit of EC heads of government. At the centre of the package is a 29 per cent cut in cereals prices over three years, which should lead to cheaper feeds for livestock, enabling a 15 per cent cut in beef price supports, and a 5 per cent cut in the butter price. Sheep and beef will now be subject to quotas like milk. The cuts are designed to move EC agriculture towards world prices. Farmers are fully compensated for them directly, but big farmers have to take 15 per cent of their land out of production to get these payments. The cuts should eliminate export subsidies almost entirely by 1996-97. This, and the EC's new ability to guarantee restraints on production, should give momentum to the Uruguay Round negotiations between the US and EC, due next week. Mr MacSharry said: 'We can say, with our chests out and our heads held high, and with pride, that you (the US) match what we have done, and then we can get progress.' A spokesman for the US trade representative said: 'We are hopeful that reform would bring the EC's internal prices closer to world prices, and promote greater and fairer competition in EC and world markets. Also, we hope that the (CAP) agreement would allow the EC greater flexibility in the multilateral agricultural reform effort under way in the Uruguay Round.' Early today New Zealand, a member of the Cairns Group of agricultural exporting nations which has been critical of the EC, gave a cautious welcome to the agreement. . Mr Philip Burdon, trade minister, said: 'It's a good sign, but it's not a black and white picture.' Mr MacSharry insisted that the US should now accept the EC's demands that its direct compensation payments to farmers be allowed under General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (Gatt) rules for subsidies which do not increase production and therefore distort trade. Farm reform in Europe, Page 4 Editorial comment, Page 16 A grain of sense, Page 16 Lex, Page 18 Commodities, Page 34

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Stock and Currency Markets
FT 22 MAY 92 / Major gives warm welcome to accord
DOC.BYLINE: By PHILIP STEPHENS and DAVID BLACKWELL
DOC.TEXT: MR JOHN MAJOR gave an enthusiastic welcome to the farm talks deal yesterday. He said an agreement on reforming the Common Agricultural Policy would be good for farmers, consumers and the future of world trade. Although consumers will have to wait until the middle of the decade before benefiting from cheaper food prices, British farmers welcomed the end of the uncertainty surrounding their businesses. 'It would appear that John Gummer (agriculture minister) has achieved quite a remarkable victory on behalf of all UK arable farmers,' the managing director of a large farming company said. He was delighted that Britain had not been left at a disadvantage to smaller European competitors. Speaking in the House of Commons, Mr Major said that the deal was good news for the British farmer, for the British consumer, for the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade negotiations, for world trade and for many developing countries. He congratulated Mr Gummer on his negotiating stance during the marathon Brussels negotiating session. The prime minister made it clear that the accord was closely in tune with the thrust of Britain's own proposals, which were designed to protect farmers while progressively reducing the EC's massive stocks of agricultural products. Whitehall officials said that the proposed shift towards a system of farm payments tied to supporting incomes rather than paying for surpluses could provide the background for a deal with the US in the stalled Uruguay round of world trade talks. More specifically, they welcomed the fact that the proposals to compensate cereals farmers for taking land out of production took account of the much larger average size of British farms. Labour warned that the reforms were as likely to fail in reducing surpluses as previous efforts had been. Mr David Clark, shadow agriculture minister, said that the only effects would be that 'the cost to the UK taxpayers will increase in each of the next few years; the consumer will not benefit; farmers will get large pay-offs.' While Britain's farmers expressed relief that uncertainty had been resolved, reaction in France was tougher, where farmers condemned the deal and said that they would take to the streets immediately in protest. German farmers said subsidy cuts would lead to collapse in many farm regions, which would be hit by drastic price cuts in grain and other crops. Italian farming lobbies reacted angrily to reforms which left their country out in the cold. 'This is a completely unsatisfactory deal,' an association of farmers said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / Tories shrug off backbench revolt on Maastricht
DOC.TEXT: THE LEGISLATION to ratify the Maastricht Treaty on European union passed its most important parliamentary hurdle last night as the government shrugged off a rebellion by anti-federalist Conservative MPs. The House of Commons voted by an overwhelming majority of 336 to 92 to endorse the deal negotiated by Mr John Major on closer European integration. Some 22 Conservative rebels opposed ratification of the treaties on European and Monetary Union, arguing that they represented a further step along the road to federalism and a handful of others abstained. Mr John Biffen, a former cabinet minister, was among those refusing to back Mr Major. But the government's discomfort was matched by acute embarrassment among the Labour leadership after 61 of the party's Euro-sceptic MPs rejected instructions to abstain and instead voted against ratification. A Labour amendment calling on the government to opt-in to the social policies adopted by the other 11 EC countries was defeated by 360 to 261 votes. The backing for the government at the end of the two-day debate followed a strong defence of the Maastricht accord by Mr Douglas Hurd, the foreign secretary. He argued that it had produced a treaty which 'more closely mirrors British priorities than any of its predecessors'. Emphasising that the intergovernmental structure of the agreement had halted the march towards more centralised decision-making, Mr Hurd said Britain now had 'a real chance' to shape the EC's institutions. He stressed that the prospective enlargement of the Community to include northern European states would not force Britain to concede further changes in those institutions before the proposed review in 1996. Mr Norman Lamont, the chancellor, meanwhile sought to reassure Conservative MPs that the staged process of monetary union did not threaten the government's rights to decide independently Britain's tax and spending levels. Sir Edward Heath, the former prime minister, enlivened the debate with a stinging if thinly-veiled attack on the views of his successor in Downing Street, Mrs Margaret Thatcher. But he combined criticism of 'bigoted' and 'xenophobic' attacks on Germany with criticism of Mr Major for not going far enough to embrace closer integration. The Tory rebels indicated that they intended to continue to harry the legislation when it moves to its detailed committee stage early next month. A group of five Tory MPs last night tabled a series of amendments designed to stall progress. One amendment calls for an advisory referendum before Maastricht is enacted while another aims to limit severely the government's ability to strike deals in Brussels without the consent of parliament. Parliament, Page 10

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / World News in Brief: Pounds 25,000 prize
DOC.TEXT: Jung Chang won the Pounds 25,000 NCR book award for Wild Swans, her autobiographical account of China's shift from feudalism to a republic. The award is for non-fiction.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / World News in Brief: Tobacco's toll
DOC.TEXT: More than a fifth of people in developed countries will die from smoking-related diseases, according to an Imperial Cancer Research fund study in the Lancet. In the UK, 400 people a day die as a result of tobacco.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / World News in Brief: Doubts over school tests
DOC.TEXT: Last summer's first national school tests for seven-year-olds gave 'unreliable' results for at least one pupil in five, the schools inspectorate said. Editorial comment, Page 16; Application rejected, Page 8

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / World News in Brief: Prisoner surrenders
DOC.TEXT: Police called off a manhunt for escaped prisoner Keith Hanger, 29, after he gave himself up at Grendon Underwood jail, Bucks. He is wanted for questioning in connection with the murder of Alan Kearley, whose body was found in a car near Christchurch, Dorset.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / World News in Brief: Shark stays put
DOC.TEXT: Bill Heine won a six-year planning battle to keep an 18 ft glass fibre shark on the roof of his Oxford home when the Department of the Environment upheld his appeal against an Oxford City Council order. The DoE inspector said the system must make some small allowance for 'the dynamic, the unexpected and the downright quirky.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 22 MAY 92 / World News in Brief: Nigerian violence spreads
