Westpac's brutal accounting treatment also throws down the gauntlet to its competitors in an Australian banking industry still wracked by a 1980's lending spree to the country's remarkable crop of failed entrepreneurs; notably Mr Alan Bond, Mr Christopher Skase and Mr John Spalvins. National Australia Bank is due to report interim results today, followed by ANZ next week. However, widely varying write-off and provisioning approaches have long been a feature of the Australian banking industry. Westpac's action suggests that anything less dramatic by rival banks may mean that they will meet stock market disapproval. In its latest full year, National wrote off Dollars A955m (USDollars 729) in bad loans and raised problem loan provisions to Dollars A3.9bn while corresponding figures for the ANZ were Dollars A1.04bn and Dollars A3.6bn. The stock market is likely to demand much more 'blood on the floor,' mindful that on an international scale, the Australian banks can afford bigger write-offs. They enjoy comfortable capital adequacy ratios, especially the all important Tier 1 measure. Even after yesterday's deck-clearing, Westpac is claiming a Tier 1 ratio of 5 per cent against the 4 per cent minimum demanded under central bank regulations. National boasted a Tier 1 ratio of 7.6 at the end of last year, with ANZ on 6 per cent. Even so, Westpac's decision not to have it's ADollars 1.2bn rights issue underwritten was surprising; especially in the light of some worrying information buried in the fine print of yesterday's announcement. The fine print showed that the big write-downs have reduced the company's net asset backing from Dollars A5.66 to Dollars A3.75 a share, but 74 cents of that valuation is in future income tax benefits which are not allowable for capital adequacy purposes. As a consequence, on a strict interpretation, Westpac's asset backing is perilously close to the Dollars A3 price of the rights issue. The shares closed at Dollars A3.89 in Sydney yesterday. Westpac's managing director Mr Frank Conroy put a brave face on the results yesterday, pointing to an improvement in core profitably. He noted that operating earnings before tax totalled Dollars A687m in the latest half. Although that was a decline on the Dollars A892m recorded for the corresponding six months of last year, it was higher than the Dollars A655m earned for the second half of 1990-91. Mr Conroy said that the bank did not expect any negative response from the ratings agencies, and shortly afterwards Moody's confirmed all Westpac's ratings. 'We do anticipate a positive reaction as we proceed with the capital raising and the bank's performance continues to improve'. 'I want the market and the media to have no misunderstanding on the following points: I can assure proprietors, staff and customers that our reviews have been thorough and conservative. The bank is sound, and what we are reporting today will increase our financial strength. We expect a sound profit in the second half and we can look forward to the future with confidence,' Mr Conroy said. Analysts, however, were less than happy last night as they digested the enormous breadth and impact of the Westpac statement. Some were puzzled that the property exposure involved properties with a book value of Dollars A6.3bn. Some analysts' estimates put Westpac's total property exposure in excess of ADollars 12bn. Much of Westpac's property exposure is held through the Australian Guarantee Corporation (AGC) subsidiary which made a loss of Dollars A719m and has necessitated an Dollars A850m capital injection from the parent. Mr Conroy said that AGC's affect on the group was actually more serious than it appeared on paper because a number of the finance arm's problems had been transferred to the bank. 'If you include Bill Acceptance Corporation, Westpac General Finance in the UK, and the cost of the support arrangements from the bank, AGC and its related activities accounted for Dollars A1.1bn of the Dollars A1.67bn group half-year loss,' he said. He added that the bank would reduce AGC's exposure to major property developments and would turn its attention to specialist activities. Mr Conroy's final comments on AGC underlined, if they did not understate, the plight of the entire group. 'Of course mistakes have been made,' he said. 'Hopefully we have learnt from them.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Sega lifts profits and increases dividend
DOC.TEXT: SEGA Enterprises, the video game and toy maker, doubled profits to Y33.5bn (Dollars 251.87m) for the year to end-March. Unlike most Japanese companies, it sharply increased its dividend. Comparisons are made difficult by a change in the company's accounting year, but sales rose from Y106.6bn to Y213.3bn on strong demand for Sega games in the US. After-tax profit was dragged down to Y14bn by the settlement of a US patent dispute over image-display technology, which resulted in the company writing off Dollars 28.67m of the agreed Dollars 43m payout to a US inventor. The only other disappointment was the impact of the Tokyo share price collapse on short-term holdings of stocks, which are showing unrealised losses of Y235.8m, up from Y25.5m at the end of March last year. The increase came in spite of the company almost halving its short-term holdings to Y1.35bn. Even though Sega apparently paid the Dollars 28.67m out of its cash reserves, these rose, from Y29bn to Y72.5bn, following a surge in US sales during the Christmas period, when it took market share from the industry leader, Nintendo. Yesterday's results came as Sega of America, the US subsidiary of the parent company, and Sony Electronic Publishing announced a marketing agreement. Under the deal, Sony will produce and market Sega video games and interactive entertainment, Reuters reports. Sony Electronic will develop games for all Sega cartridge-based platforms. The deal also provides opportunities for the development of Sega titles through Sony Pictures Entertainment and Sony Music Entertainment.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Toyo Sash slides 28%
DOC.TEXT: TOYO Sash, Japan's top maker of aluminium housing products, revealed a 14.6 per cent drop to Y32.5bn (Dollars 244.36m) in non-consolidated pre-tax profits for the year to end-March. Net profits also fell sharply, by 28.6 per cent to Y14.8bn, although sales climbed a modest 4 per cent to Y481bn. A sharp drop in demand in the second half - reflecting the nation's stock market troubles - and a private sector spending downturn were behind the profit retreat, the company said. Sales of housing sashes, which account for over half of company sales, grew 1.1 per cent to Y280bn. Building sash sales increased 10.6 per cent to Y148bn, due largely to the introduction of new products for high-rise structures. Turnover of housing equipment and other products also gained 11.5 per cent to Y14bn. But construction material sales were off 0.2 per cent to Y38.7bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Black warns Daily News of job losses
DOC.TEXT: MR CONRAD BLACK, chairman of the Daily Telegraph group, yesterday informed trade union leaders at the New York Daily News that he would want to cut 700 jobs if he acquired the newspaper. Mr George McDonald, president of the Allied Printing Trades Council, a coalition of nine unions, said representatives of Mr Black mentioned the prospective job cuts at a 'get-to-know-you meeting.' Mr John Campi, spokesman for the Daily News, said that Mr Black on Tuesday submitted a bid for the famous New York tabloid acquired last year by the late Mr Robert Maxwell. The bid was believed to be for Dollars 75m (Pounds 42m). Mr McDonald seemed untroubled by the job cuts mentioned by Mr Black's representatives. 'It's just a proposal. They'll say it's negotiable, otherwise we can't do business. Black wants the paper and we want our jobs,' he said. The unions gave up about 800 jobs last year when Mr Maxwell acquired the paper. Mr Mortimer Zuckerman, publisher of US News and World Report, is another prospective buyer of the Daily News.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Toray slides despite improved fibre sales
DOC.TEXT: TORAY Industries, Japan's leading synthetic fibre maker, yesterday posted falls in consolidated earnings for the full year to March. It blamed sluggish demand for its synthetic fibres, and lower profits at its construction affiliate, writes Emiko Terazono in Tokyo. Pre-tax profits fell 11.4 per cent to Y64bn (Dollars 481.20m) on a 6.5 per cent rise in total sales, to Y976.7bn. After-tax profits fell 26.2 per cent to Y27.7bn. The company's fibre sales grew 10.1 per cent to Y489.9bn. However, the company said demand for nylon used in tyre cords and fishing nets declined. Sales of chemicals and new businesses declined 0.5 per cent and 2.4 per cent respectively. Nylon resin sales slowed because of sluggish demand from the automotive and electronic industries. Polyester film sales also decreased because of low demand and increasing price competition from film for magnetic tapes and industrial materials. Sales of the housing and engineering division rose 7.8 per cent to Y219bn, but operating profits fell 3.2 per cent to Y7.6bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Carter Hawley stems losses
DOC.TEXT: CARTER Hawley Hale, the California-based department store group operating under Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, suffered a net loss of Dollars 20.37m, or 70 cents a share, in the first quarter to May 2, compared with a loss of Dollars 32.39m, or Dollars 1.12, in the same period last year, Reuter reports from Los Angeles. Reorganisation costs were Dollars 3.59m, down from Dollars 7.96m. Sales rose to Dollars 433.62m from Dollars 430.11m last time.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Hewlett-Packard throws down the gauntlet to IBM
DOC.TEXT: HEWLETT-Packard has launched a bold challenge to IBM by introducing a new class of high-performance computers that will represent a cheaper alternative to conventional mainframe computers. 'Mainframes based on old and proprietary technologies can't match the flexibility or cost-efficiency of H-P's new systems, which provide similar performance at one-fifth the cost,' Mr John Young, president and chief executive of the US computer system maker, said. H-P is building on the momentum of its sales of workstations and minicomputers which helped boost first-quarter earnings, announced earlier this week, by 40 per cent. Its shares rose Dollars 1 1/8 to Dollars 75 1/4 . The company is now targeting IBM's traditional stronghold in the corporate data processing centre. H-P introduced nine new 'corporate business servers' with performance up to 75 per cent better than its current high-end machines - and more powerful than 90 per cent of installed IBM mainframe systems. However, it has yet to subject its new computers to standard benchmarking tests. The new systems incorporate the same reduced instruction set computing (Risc) technology that is at the heart of H-P's computer range and will run the same applications programs. Four models are designed to run H-P's version of the Unix operating system, while five run H-P's proprietary operating system. With its new products, H-P hopes to play a leading role in the trend toward reducing the size of data processing systems by off-loading applications from room-sized mainframes onto networks of smaller computers. More than 46 per cent of mainframe computer users are taking such steps, according to a survey late last year by Dataquest, the US market research firm. H-P stressed the cost advantages of its new systems, which the company believes will appeal to companies trying to limit spending in the weak economic environment. An IBM mainframe computer with a performance equivalent to H-P's fastest model costs five times as much to operate, H-P claimed. The cost of ownership includes the initial purchase price of the system and peripherals, software and support for a three-year period. Cost savings include lower systems prices, ranging from Dollars 335,000 to Dollars 925,000, about a fifth the cost of IBM's latest mainframes. Other factors reducing costs include lower power consumption and reduced support personnel requirements. Not included in this calculation, however, is the potentially high price of converting applications to run on the H-P systems. To ease the conversion process, H-P has persuaded several leading mainframe computer software developers to produce new versions of their programs to run on H-P computers. Despite all the advantages that H-P claims for its new computer systems, the company must still prove its ability to address market segments where it has little presence. These will include the financial services sector, telecommunications industry and government markets. 'The world mainframe market is Dollars 50bn. We only have to win a modest share of that market to be very successful,' maintains Mr Lewis Platt, H-P executive vice-president and head of the Computer Systems Organisation.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: American Airlines denies holding talks with KLM
DOC.TEXT: MR Robert Crandall, chairman of American Airlines, yesterday quashed rumours that the US carrier had been in talks with KLM Royal Dutch Airlines over some form of partnership, possibly involving the purchase of a share stake. Breaking from American's normal policy of not commenting on merger rumours, Mr Crandall said: 'There is no KLM deal - it's absolutely made up.' Earlier this year, merger talks between KLM, the Dutch flagship carrier, and British Airways broke down. Recent newspaper reports have suggested that KLM might have found an alternative suitor in American. Back on the domestic front, Mr Crandall acknowledged the serious competitive problem posed by Southwest Airlines, a small low-cost carrier which competes in a number of short-haul markets. He said American was looking at various options to deal with the situation. These included the possible withdrawal from some markets it serves or 'introducing a re-defined product . . . where our full feature service is more than our customers want or need.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Insurance claims from LA riots reach Dollars 775m
DOC.TEXT: COVERED insurance claims from the Los Angeles riots are unlikely to rise much higher than the Dollars 775m estimate reported yesterday by insurance trade groups, industry officials said, Reuters reports from Los Angeles. 'We're pretty confident the Dollars 775m will be an all inclusive number,' Ms Patricia Lombard, spokeswoman for the Western Insurance Information Services, said. Among insurance companies Farmers Insurance Group estimated its insurance losses at Dollars 70m from about 800 claims filed so far, mostly for businesses. Allstate Insurance has so far received more than 440 claims totalling Dollars 24m, a spokesman said, adding the company's largest losses were for vehicles vandalised or destroyed. Transamerica Insurance Group has received about 130 claims totalling about Dollars 13m, the company said. State Farm, a mutual insurance company, expects its claims to total about Dollars 41m from 1,100 claims. The company added it had so far paid out Dollars 7m. California's FAIR plan, an insurance industry pool, had received 514 claims totalling Dollars 37.4m, it said. Ms Lombard said the industry was moving quickly to settle the claims in the riot-torn area. 'A lot of people have been given partial payments already,' she said. 'Companies are geared up and they want to deal with it as quickly as possible.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Salomon agrees Dollars 290m settlement in bond scandal
DOC.TEXT: SALOMON Brothers, the Wall Street securities house, yesterday agreed to pay Dollars 290m in fines and compensation to settle charges relating to its alleged illegal activities in the US Treasury markets between 1989 and 1991. Criminal charges, however, will not be filed against the firm, although criminal investigations of individuals and other firms involved in the Salomon case continue. In an additional penalty against Salomon, the firm was suspended for 60 days from engaging in transactions with the New York Federal Reserve. The New York Fed said it would resume trading with Salomon on August 3, when its previous ban on the firm bidding in Treasury auctions for customers - imposed immediately after the scandal broke last August - will also be lifted. The suspensions, however, do not affect Salomon's status as a primary dealer in government securities with the Fed, which it retains. After yesterday's settlements were announced, Salomon said that it would take a pre-tax charge of Dollars 185m in the second quarter of this year, which, with the Dollars 200m set aside last year, will go towards covering the cost of the penalties and legal costs related to the roughly 50 private lawsuits that have been filed against the firm in the wake of the bond trading scandal. The Dollars 290m settlement ends a 10-month joint investigation launched by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the Federal Reserve and the Justice Department in August 1991, when federal authorities discovered that members of Salomon's bond trading desk had faked customer orders and bid beyond government limits in Treasury auctions. The SEC also said yesterday that during the investigation it was discovered that in August 1989 another primary dealing firm secretly bid for Dollars 3.5bn in government securities on Salomon's behalf by concealing the real identity of the bidder in its records of the transaction. Officials at the SEC declined to identify the primary dealer involved. There was no comment on what action might be taken in light of the discovery. Of the money Salomon has agreed to pay for its actions, Dollars 190m represents fines and forfeitures for violating US securities laws, and Dollars 100m will be placed in a fund to compensate victims of the violations. The settlement, however, does not affect the private lawsuits filed against Salomon by clients and individuals who claim they suffered losses because of the firm's activities. The penalties imposed on Salomon yesterday were generally regarded by analysts as sizeable but not threatening to the firm's survival. The news was certainly well-received on Wall Street, with Salomon shares jumping Dollars 2 7/8 to Dollars 33 1/2 .

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: O&Y in talks on tax payments
DOC.TEXT: OLYMPIA & York has funnelled so much cash out of its profitable US buildings in recent months that it has asked authorities in New York for temporary relief on municipal tax payments which fall due on July 1. O&Y said yesterday it was exploring 'options' with the New York City administration, and was likely to reach an agreement in the next week. About USDollars 75m in property tax payments fall due on July 1. Although only four of O&Y's 12 New York buildings have cash flow problems, the company has diverted every spare dollar from its US operations to the cash-starved Canadian parent and the Canary Wharf project in London. O&Y hopes that last week's Ontario court order, which freezes its Canadian debt obligations under the Companies' Creditors Arrangements Act (CCAA), will give it sufficient breathing space to replenish the coffers of its US operations. Its ability to do so partly depends on petitions to be brought by bondholders in the Ontario Court of Justice today to exclude some of the developer's most prized Canadian buildings from the CCAA order. The bondholders' move to reverse the order has wide implications for all forms of non-recourse finance. The bonds were issued by single-purpose companies with no recourse to O&Y Developments, the parent. The bondholders had previously assumed that they would be insulated from the parent's liquidity crisis. The bondholders will argue that their claims should be separated from those of O&Y's other creditors and that they should be at liberty, if necessary, to seize rents from the buildings to cover overdue debt-service payments. The CCAA order issued last week covers a total of 28 entities besides the parent company. They include First Canadian Place, O&Y's 72-storey flagship in Toronto, as well as other buildings in Toronto, Calgary and Ottawa. The application is likely to be opposed by O&Y's bank lenders, whose claims on the projects in question generally rank behind the bondholders. However, some of the banks which provided a Dollars 2.5bn jumbo loan to O&Y are expected to raise concerns of their own about the CCAA order. The banks contend that the order in its present form permits O&Y to channel surplus cash from its Canadian assets to the US and UK operations, which have not been brought under court protection. The banks will also mount a separate court challenge today against the amount of collateral provided by the developer to its Canadian lenders. The international group is seeking to assert its rights to the security pledged on a Dollars 100m loan advanced earlier this year by four Canadian banks.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: BHF bank shows 30% improvement
DOC.TEXT: THE OPERATING profits for Berliner Handels-und Frankfurter Bank, the Frankfurt-based merchant bank, advanced 30 per cent in the first four months of the current year compared with the previous corresponding period. Partial operating profits - excluding the contribution from trading - increased by 21.5 per cent, Mr Klaus Subjetzki, outgoing senior partner, told the bank's annual meeting. Total assets climbed by 5.2 per cent to DM28.1bn (Dollars 17.6bn), while interest income was up 5.5 per cent and commission income up 20 per cent. The results are in line with strong results from other German banks which have also reported good figures for the early part of the current year. The results follow a record year for the German banking sector and suggest that there has been only a moderate slowdown in loan demand in spite of a sharp downturn in German economic activity. The sector is also benefiting from a recent improvement in conditions in the domestic stock market.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Ferguson Intl declines 43% to Pounds 6.63m
DOC.TEXT: Adversely affected by trading conditions world-wide, but particularly in the UK, Ferguson International Holdings saw pre-tax profits fall 43 per cent from Pounds 11.6m to Pounds 6.63m in the year to February 29. Group trading profits on continuing activities were down 20 per cent to Pounds 9.7m, an improvement on the 28 per cent reduction at halfway. Boosted by two acquisitions - Interstate Cable Enterprises of the US and Globus Druck of Germany - turnover on continuing activities rose 6 per cent to Pounds 114.9m. Interest payable was cut by 56 per cent to Pounds 1.1m (Pounds 2.54m) and there were exceptional costs of Pounds 1.6m relating mainly to the closure of Harkwell Labels & Tags. Extraordinary charges of Pounds 1.14m derived from the disposal of non-core businesses. Earnings emerged at 13.5p (22.7p) per share and the directors have proposed holding the final dividend at 8.25p for a maintained 12.5p total.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Henderson seeks Pounds 20m from trust launch
DOC.TEXT: Henderson, the fund management group, is seeking at least Pounds 20m from the launch of an investment trust specialising in European equities. It is the second new European investment trust to be announced this week. Henderson EuroTrust will have a split capital structure, with 75 per cent of the issued capital in ordinary shares, and the rest in zero-dividend preference shares. It is hoped that this structure will stop the shares from moving to a discount to net asset value. The company has a 10-year life until the annual general meeting of October 2002, when the zero shares will be redeemed at 70p. This is equivalent to a gross redemption yield of 10.2 per cent. Projected initial gross yield on the ordinary shares is 5 per cent. During the launch issue only packaged units, consisting of one ordinary share and one zero at a price of Pounds 1, will be available.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Union Discount
DOC.TEXT: Union Discount, the London discount house, yesterday announced that its wholly owned subsidiary had decided to cease trading in non-core activities comprising trade bills, currency deposits and foreign exchange. The withdrawal from these activities, which have shown losses in recent years, will involve the loss of 19 jobs in Edinburgh and Manchester.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: REA Holdings falls
DOC.TEXT: A fall in pre-tax profits from Pounds 1.23m to Pounds 883,000 was announced by REA Holdings, the plantation holding company, for 1991. Turnover improved to Pounds 76.9m (Pounds 66.4m) but increased cost of sales resulted in lower operating profits of Pounds 5.38m (Pounds 5.84m). Earnings emerged at 4.1p (10.8p) and the dividend is unchanged at 4p.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Essex Furniture
DOC.TEXT: Essex Furniture is raising Pounds 1.3m net by way of a rights issue mainly to fund expansion prospects. The issue is on a 1-for-3 basis at 43p. This compares with yesterday's closing price of 52p, down 4p. The directors and families own 79 per cent of the capital and have renounced rights to the issue in favour of clients of Williams de Broe.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Dunedin Worldwide
DOC.TEXT: Net asset value per 25p share of Dunedin Worldwide Investment Trust stood at 569.7p on April 30. That compared with 595.3p six months earlier and with 578.9p at end-April 1991. After-tax revenue for the half year to April 30 declined from Pounds 1.53m to Pounds 1.23m, equal to earnings of 3.61p (4.5p). The interim dividend is again 2.4p and the directors anticipate a maintained final of 7.1p.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Ralston Inv Trust
DOC.TEXT: At the March 31 year-end the net asset value per share of Ralston Investment Trust stood at 60.25p, compared with 63.25p a year earlier. Net revenue fell 18 per cent from Pounds 459,000 to Pounds 377,000. The trust said that the portfolio of listed equities rose in value but this was outweighed by the need to write-down certain unquoted holdings, the value of which was now Pounds 580,000. The final dividend is again 1.275p for a total of 2p (2p). Earnings were 1.57p (1.91p).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Cupid doubles
DOC.TEXT: A full year's contribution from Pronuptia and three months from Youngs helped Cupid, the USM-quoted bridalwear and nurserycare company, to achieve more-than-doubled profits in the year to end-March. From turnover up by Pounds 5.38m to Pounds 14.7m, pre-tax profits came through at Pounds 982,000, against Pounds 411,000 last time. Pronuptia, the bridalwear retailer, was acquired in December 1990 for some Pounds 3m. Youngs Formal Wear was bought for about Pounds 1.65m in December 1991. Earnings improved from 6.5p to 9.1p and the dividend is being increased to 3.25p (3p). An extraordinary charge of Pounds 115,000 (nil) related to professional fees incurred in an aborted acquisition attempt.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Martin Currie
DOC.TEXT: Martin Currie European Investment Trust had a net asset value of 85.1p per share basic at April 30 compared with 86.4p a year earlier. Diluted, the value was 87.7p, against 88.7p. Net revenue for the year fell to Pounds 74,000 compared with Pounds 308,000 for the 14 month period to April 1991. Earnings amounted to 0.32p (1.34p) per share and a dividend of 0.2p (1.1p) is recommended.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Baggeridge Brick
DOC.TEXT: Profits of Baggeridge Brick, the West Midlands-based brickmaker and supplier of building materials, fell from Pounds 1.07m to Pounds 761,000 pre-tax for the half year ended March 31. Turnover totalled Pounds 11.9m (Pounds 13.3m). Interest accounted for Pounds 649,000 (Pounds 819,000) and tax for Pounds 251,000 (Pounds 364,000). Earnings worked through at 1.29p (1.79p) and the interim dividend is a same-again 0.75p. Operating profits of the land filling operations rose to Pounds 546,000 (Pounds 193,000) while those from building materials fell to Pounds 864,000 (Pounds 1.7m).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Wardell Roberts
DOC.TEXT: Difficult economic conditions throughout the year in the UK and later in the Irish Republic left pre-tax profits at Wardell Roberts, Dublin-based food processor, 15 per cent lower at IPounds 2.42m (Pounds 2.2m) in the 12 months to March 31 against IPounds 2.86m. Turnover fell to IPounds 45.1m (IPounds 48.1m) including IPounds 3.89m (IPounds 10.5m) from discontinued activities. Earnings per share came out at 8.4p (10.6p) and a maintained final dividend of 1.936p is proposed for a total payment of 3.206p (3.146p). There was an extraordinary charge of IPounds 2.59m relating to the withdrawal from the poultry business in the UK.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Chamberlin & Hill slips to Pounds 1.43m
DOC.TEXT: CHAMBERLIN & HILL yes-terday reported a 10 per cent fall in annual profits but pointed to an improvement in the second half. It backed this up with a 0.25p increase in the final dividend to 4.25p. Shares in the iron castings, electrical conduit and switchgear company rose 33p to 130p. Sales in the year to March 31 fell to Pounds 19m (Pounds 19.5m), interest payable rose to Pounds 124,000 (Pounds 79,000) and pre-tax profits amounted to Pounds 1.43m (Pounds 1.59m). Earnings came through at 15.28p (16.64p) and the total dividend is 6p (5.75p).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: US buyer for ASH's surveillance division
DOC.TEXT: AUTOMATED Security (Holdings), which supplies burglar alarms and other security products, is selling its electronic and television surveillance wing to a US company for Pounds 150m. The loss prevention business, which includes till monitoring to prevent theft by shop staff and the new TVX system using a tiny video camera, is being sold to Sensormatic, a supplier of electronic security systems listed on the New York stock exchange. It is acquiring a business that made Pounds 11.1m trading profit last year on sales of Pounds 60.2m. Net assets before the deduction of borrowings were Pounds 68.5m in November. It is being sold debt-free. ASH previously tried to float off this wing. More recently, it tried to sell part of the leasing portfolio to reduce debt. The cash consumptive nature of the business had raised concern among analysts. Mr Tom Buffett, chairman, said the sale would wipe out the group's debt and 'take away balance sheet concerns'. At the end of November, ASH's net borrowings were Pounds 95m. The group still has about Pounds 60m of convertible capital bonds. ASH made Pounds 23.2m pre-tax profit last year and the first fall in 19 years came as a shock to the market, further undermining the share price. This had fallen from more than 300p two years ago to 81p in March. The recovery continued yesterday with an 11p rise, though the announcement did not come until after the market closed. ASH's remaining security systems business made a trading profit of Pounds 35.1m on sales of Pounds 119m last year. The deal should lift the interest burden on the remaining business. Mr Buffett said the deal marked an alliance between the two groups. He would become non-executive vice-chairman of Sensormatic. The initial payment of Pounds 50m cash is expected to be followed by another Pounds 100m from the proceeds of a public offering of securities by Sensormatic.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Net assets fall 16.9% at Land Securities
DOC.TEXT: LAND SECURITIES, the UK's largest property company, suffered a 16.9 per cent fall in its net assets in the year to end-March, which its chairman described as 'the most difficult period for the property industry that I can remember'. 'High real interest rates, over-borrowing in both the personal and corporate sectors, the over-supply of accommodation, particularly in central London and, until recently, political uncertainty, all took their toll,' said Mr Peter Hunt, chairman. But the company stressed its financial strength, which was underlined by a 5.7 per cent increase in pre-tax profits from Pounds 215.2m to Pounds 227.5m in the year to March 31. The company owns Pounds 4.3bn of property, the value of which fell 12.6 per cent during the year. Its borrowings of Pounds 1.52bn, up from Pounds 1.27bn, correspond to gearing of 43.2 per cent, which is relatively modest for a property company. The fall in net assets per share from 668p to 555p was mainly blamed on the central London market, which has been particularly badly hit by recession and oversupply of space. Properties in the West End and Victoria were worst affected, falling 21.3 per cent in value, while those in the City fell 17.6 per cent. Elsewhere in the UK, the value of shops and offices fell 2.8 per cent. The value of out-of-town retail property increased 9 per cent; industrial and warehouse property increased 0.7 per cent. Mr Hunt criticised the government for neglecting central London's transport systems, describing the priority given to Docklands transport as 'ridiculous'. He is also lobbying the government to remove the 'patently unfair' rate charges on empty buildings. Earnings increased 5.7 per cent to 32.62p. A final dividend of 15.75p makes a total of 21.75p for the year. See Lex

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Fiat in deal with Polish carmaker
DOC.BYLINE: By TONY ROBINSON and JOHN GRIFFITHS
DOC.TEXT: FIAT HAS signed a preliminary agreement to acquire a 90 per cent stake in Poland's Fabryka Samochodow Malolitrazowych (FSM), the country's largest producer of small cars, in the largest ever foreign investment in Poland. The deal will lift the Italian carmaker's investment in Poland to Dollars 2bn (Pounds 1.1bn), but in terms of investment in eastern Europe, it remains far behind the Dollars 6.9bn which Volkswagen is investing to aquire a 70 per cent stake in Skoda, the Czechoslovak carmaker. Formal approval between the Polish government, which will retain a 10 per cent stake, and the Italian group is expected by May 28. Last October Fiat signed a memorandum committing it to take a 51 per cent stake in the company. Under this scheme up to 30 per cent of the shares would have been allocated to the company's 20,000 employees. During negotiations between the two groups since the October accord, the Polish government has argued that Fiat should absorb the group's substantial domestic debt, believed to be more than Dollars 100m. In return, the Polish government offered a higher stake and larger financial commitment. Of the Dollars 2bn committed to the project, some Dollars 800m has already been spent, mainly on bringing into production the Cinquecento, Fiat's new small car which is being built by FSM at a rate of 160,000 cars a year. Under yesterday's agreement, signed between Mr Andrzej Olechowski, the caretaker Polish finance minister, Mr Renato Ruggiero, Fiat's deputy chairman, and Mr Paolo Cantarella, Fiat Auto's managing director, production of the Cinquecento will be expanded to 240,000 units a year. Fiat will also invest in a new model to replace the Fiat 126, another small car built for Fiat by FSM. Fiat believes that if it did not sign while Mr Olechowski was still acting finance minister the future of the deal would have been in doubt. Mr Olechowski, a former trade minister and central banker, resigned as finance minister earlier this month in protest against a parliamentary vote that would have increased government spending and pushed up the budget deficit.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Governor of Bank waives bulk of his 28% pay rise
DOC.TEXT: MR Robin Leigh-Pemberton, governor of the Bank of England, was given a 28 per cent pay rise to Pounds 198,446 in 1991-92, but he decided to waive all but 6 per cent of the increase. Last year, Mr Leigh-Pemberton was widely criticised for accepting a pay rise of nearly 17 per cent in the year to February 1991, while urging pay restraint on the public. Bank directors yesterday defended their decision to give the governor a 28 per cent rise while the government and the Bank were encouraging companies to make low pay awards. 'There's no way I would apologise for that,' said Mr Gavin Laird, general secretary of the Amalgamated Engineering and Electrical Union and a member of the Bank's remuneration committee which set Mr Leigh-Pemberton's salary. 'I believe in the rate for the job,' Mr Laird went on to say. 'My only complaint was I felt he should have taken the money.' A Bank official said Mr Leigh-Pemberton's decision to forego most of the rise was 'entirely his own decision'. The Bank refused to say whether Mr Leigh-Pemberton had waived any of his wage rise in the current year as well. After waiving Pounds 34,135 of the rise, Mr Leigh-Pemberton was paid Pounds 164,311 in 1991-92. The 6 per cent increase was in line with that of the bulk of his staff. Other executive directors of the Bank saw their remuneration increase by 13 per cent on average. None of them has waived their entitlement to the additional money. Sir Adrian Cadbury, chairman of the Bank's remuneration committee and a campaigner for improved corporate management practices, said it was essential for the Bank's health that the pay of senior directors should not fall too far behind the private sector. He said the committee, which includes Sir David Scholey, chairman of merchant bank SG Warburg, and Sir Brian Corby, who retired yesterday as president of the Confederation of British Industry, had established a framework in 1988 for moving the directors' pay nearer to a 'semi-market rate'. 'We realised we could not get the pay rates to the proper level all in one go,' he said. Instead, the committee decided to recommend sizeable pay increases in each of the succeeding few years. In November 1990, the committee fixed the precise amount of the 1991-92 pay rise, opting for a 28 per cent increase for Mr Leigh-Pemberton, even though there were clear signals from the government that prominent public figures should set an example by accepting lower pay rises. Sir Adrian said it was vital that the Bank should be in a position to recruit outsiders to its top jobs, so its pay levels should be competitive. But it was difficult to find a private sector equivalent of the governor. Stricter standards call, Page 10

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Standard Chartered makes Pounds 50m provision: UK-based bank suffers high losses in India
DOC.BYLINE: By DAVID HOUSEGO and ROBERT PESTON
DOC.TEXT: STANDARD CHARTERED, the UK based international bank, is being forced to make a provision of Pounds 50m to cover losses by its Bombay branch from securities deals. It is therefore likely to emerge as one of the two biggest losers - with the Australian-owned ANZ Grindlays - in India's worst financial scandal. Standard said last night that a senior team of bank executives, recently sent over to India from London, is 'investigating the possibility that losses may have been incurred in its Bombay branch as a result of transactions in breach of the group's established control procedures entered into to finance stock exchange dealings'. Its total exposure to this form of stock exchange finance is Pounds 100m. Although it could not quantify how much the eventual loss will be precisely, it was making a Pounds 50m provision against possible losses, it said. According to bankers, Grindlays is also likely to face significant losses. Nine state-owned Indian institutions including State Bank of India, Canara Bank, United Bank of Calcutta, Karad Bank and National Housing Bank are also vulnerable to substantial losses. Yesterday, representatives of several banks spent a second day at a round-table conference in Bombay seeking to reconcile their accounts in the interbank securities market. As banks embarked on what is the massive task of reconciling the backlog of securities transactions, the Reserve Bank of India, the central bank, announced that it had suspended four of the employees from the office which has responsibility for registering transfers of government securities. The bank took the unusual step because of what it called 'procedural irregularities in the upkeep of the register'. Until now the register has been maintained by hand. Standard Chartered said it had brought a six-man team to India to verify the daily records of its securities department over the past six months. The bank does not exclude fraud. 'We cannot rule it out,' it said. Mr S. Venkitaramanan, the governor of the Reserve Bank, has supporters who point to his role in bringing to light the abuses in the securities market. But there are also many bankers who hold the central bank governor ultimately morally responsible for inadequate supervision of a market that has grown explosively. Mr Harshad Mehta, a Bombay broker who has been suspended by the Bombay Stock Exchange authority, was questioned by the Central Bureau of Investigation for the first time yesterday. While the authorities are pursuing him, they also seem to be opening the door to a settlement that would allow him to meet at least part of his outstanding obligations through transferring shares. US court ruling, Page 28

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Economic Viewpoint: Two per cent inflation and slow recovery
DOC.TEXT: In last Monday's Economic Viewpoint, I argued that the only way to discover whether, and how far, British interest rates could move below German interest rates within the constraints of the ERM was to 'suck it and see'. That is, the Bank of England should move them down gradually and be prepared to go into reverse if sterling came under pressure within its ERM band. Why has not the Bank of England so far attempted this? One answer is that these are early days. It is only since the April 9 election that there has been this room to experiment; and there has already been a half point cut in base rate to 10 per cent. A further reduction of half a point - or two further cuts of a quarter point - would take the UK rates a shade below German rates and into the experimental zone. There are also, however, domestic arguments for caution about cutting basic rates, which need to be discussed, but not necessarily endorsed. In line with my usual practice of leaving the heavier economics to the second half of my articles, I shall start off with the partisan political case. The chart shows UK output in relation to the trend of productive capacity. The numbers just give an order of magnitude. The trend line is meant to give an idea of where output might be if inflation is not accelerating, and production is growing in line with capacity. During the period in the late 1980s, when the thick line, indicating actual output, was above the dotted trend line, there was pressure on productive capacity, with inflation rising and the balance of payments gap widening. Somewhere towards the end of 1990, output reached a sustainable level, as overheating was giving way to recession. Since then, output has been well below the sustainable level, recession has been prolonged, but inflation has fallen. The Bank of England expects a slow recovery. This means not merely that output will stay below the trend line, but that the gap shown by the shaded area between output and productive potential will continue to widen. Indeed, according to some definitions it would not be a real recovery. The prospect is nevertheless quite pleasing to some in government. The logic of the case is this. The upturn in the late 1980s came too early and went too far. Therefore, the 1992 election had to be fought under the handicap of a corrective recession. If output can be kept comfortably below capacity for a couple of years, there can be a growth spurt in the pre-election period without any inflationary overheating. The GDP line would then start to move up smartly towards, but still not reach, the trend line. Thus there could be a pre-election boom without too much inflationary danger; and after the next election the government will try to stay nearer the trend line. I am perhaps over-rationalising a desire to do in this parliament the opposite of what was done in the last; but the proposition should be discussed. There are two objections to this approach. First, it is immoral to have recessionary conditions unnecessarily prolonged and unemployment unnecessarily high to arrange a pre-election boost. Second, it will not work politically. The errors of the late 1980s were honest lapses and arose from policies such as credit deregulation, which were worthwhile for their own sake, and were corrected when they were diagnosed, despite the political risks. The electorate sensed this and still preferred the Conservatives to the alternative. If, however, they sense that they have gone through unnecessary years of stagnation and are then being bribed by a deliberate and unsustainably rapid expansion, the government will be out on its ear, however weak the opposition. Now let me turn to the economic case for preferring a slow recovery. I had described the subject of this article to colleagues needing to know in a rush as 'the Bank of England's case for continuing the recession'. This served as shorthand, but may be unfair in view of the May Bulletin's statement that 'high interest rates in Germany have obliged other countries in the ERM, especially those in the narrow band, to maintain higher interest rates than domestic considerations would, for the most part, have dictated'. I defy anyone to tell me whether or not the Bank of England is saying that UK interest rates are higher than it would like. What then is the domestic economic case for maintaining a substantial and widening 'gap' between output and productive capacity? It is to achieve an inflation rate which the chancellor, Norman Lamont, has described as 'not only below the European average, but as low as the best in Europe, measured on a comparable basis'. He quantified this objective as '2 per cent'. When UK output fell below the trend line near the end of 1990, the underlying inflation rate was still much too high, even allowing for lags. If this is to be reduced, output must fall below the trend line and stay there until a sufficient improvement in inflation is in the pipeline. And if the amount of slack is not merely high, but increasing, inflation will come down that much faster. The case for continuing to pile on the agony is that UK inflation is still a good deal higher than it appears in the headline rate, which is distorted by the timing of mortgage interest reductions. The underlying rate is still about 5 1/2 per cent, a good deal higher than Germany's, for all the Schadenfreude. UK producer price inflation, which is now running at 2 per cent to 3 per cent a year, is doing much better; but in leading competitor countries it is below 1 per cent. How strong are the arguments for suspending this aim until something like 'stable prices' has been entrenched? Common-sense observation suggests that it is much more difficult to squeeze out the last few percentage points of inflation than to get down to 4 or 5 per cent. An inflation rate of 2 per cent is less than the creeping inflation that prevailed in the Bretton Woods period and less than anything known in the lifetime of most of the population. To achieve it would involve a clampdown on the costs of the half of the economy that is sheltered from international competition such as construction, property rents and other services. We have moved a long way from the traditional economic objective, which would have been to stabilise the movement of output as near to the trend line as possible. As this is well beyond the half-way point of my article, I can add that some might have described this objective as 'minimising a quadratic loss function' - or flattening out booms and slumps. Even if the Treasury wants to forget about stable growth rates, it may simply not be able to maintain the margin of slack required for inflation to fall as low as it would like. For if demand remains slack for too long, capacity can be retired and workers become so discouraged that they leave the labour force. Such people have little disinflationary influence. It is reasonable for the chancellor to seek to publicise a lower rate of inflation than he expects to get. If he becomes a 'Stormin' Norman' for 2 per cent, he may be able to lock in 4 per cent. But serious disinflation objectives are best stated in terms of internationally traded goods and services; and the reluctance of the sheltered sectors to follow suit is best treated by competition and other supply-side activities.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Observer: Uneasy riders
DOC.TEXT: Every observant motorist knows of the existence of the little publicised Society for Dangerous Driving at Slow Speeds. The biggest membership faction in Britain seems to be teachers meandering home in mid-afternoon. Things are different in Rio de Janeiro, where the society's rolls have just been swelled by several hundred motor-cyclists, given to inching along in line abreast and intermittently bumping into one another if not falling off unaided. Early theories that they must be apprentice Hell's Angels turned out wrong. They are in fact police in training to serve as outriders for the motorcades of the heads of state due to attend the Earth Summit in Rio next month. The necessary skills are rare in the city where motorbikes are normally few and far between, and although the police are doing their best to learn, they clearly have a long way to go. Still, a pile-up of more than 100 heads of state would be something to be seen.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Observer: Outside bet
DOC.TEXT: If you want to understand the Danes, go to Ghana. That tip for anyone betting on the outcome of Denmark's impending referendum on the Maastricht Treaty, comes from Britain's former ambassador there Sir James Mellon, now chairman of Scottish Homes. He has just marked his long love affair with the country, which began with his first visit as a teenage hitch-hiker in 1948, by publishing a book in Danish called Og gamle Danmark . . . (the first two words meaning roughly: 'And as for dear old'). But in it he reveals that it wasn't until his foreign office duties involved him with the Ashantis in Ghana that he twigged how to fathom the Danes. He suddenly realised that they are not so much a nation as a tribe, with the tribe's much greater exclusiveness - which would seem to lead him to expect them to turn the treaty down. The tribal exclusiveness makes them touchy about the idea of international co-operation, especially if it threatens to interfere with what they see as their Danishness, he writes. 'That seems to be precisely the worry that many Danes have about European Union. The very word 'union' suggests an unwelcome intrusiveness.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Observer: Indigestion
DOC.TEXT: David Mellor, the minister of fun - and a lot of serious things as well - may spoil the appetite of certain BBC governors and bureaucrats over a working dinner tonight. They spent all yesterday beavering away deciding what the BBC is up to. Let's hope they come up with an answer that will satisfy the secretary of state for the national heritage. For Mellor is determined the BBC is not going to be propped up like a stately building or nurtured in perpetuity like a museum. 'They are going have to it all to do,' he warned, reverting to football-spiel. Observer assumes the haute cuisine at the Lucknam Park hotel does not rise to bombe surprise.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Observer: Tale of woe
DOC.TEXT: Having spent the last two years graphically depicting the impact of recession on its membership, the Confederation of British Industry yesterday poured out its own, sorry tale of financial hardship. The organisation's expanded accounts for 1991 show that an operating surplus of Pounds 756,000 in 1990 turned into a deficit of Pounds 188,000 last year -a performance the CBI tries to pass off as an achievement in these tough times. But having preached the need for moderation on pay throughout the darks days of 1991, the CBI also disclosed that its own salary roll - despite a standstill in the numbers employed - rose by a healthy (some might say well above average) 12 per cent during the year. At least Sir John Banham, the retiring CBI director general, did not personally add to the organisation's swelling pay costs. Yesterday, he was again reminding people how he has consistently refused any pay rise during the slump - which puts Bank of England governor Robin Leigh-Pemberton's much trumpeted self-denial firmly in its place.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Observer: Expansionary policy
DOC.TEXT: The gang of five atop the Bundesbank has been feeling the pinch. Germany's central bank directorate, reduced last year from the previous complement of seven by the death of Ottomar Werthmoller, was also depleted by the more headline-grabbing resignation of Karl Otto Pohl, the then president. While Pohl was happier with no more than six wise men, which reduced room for dissent, his successor Helmut Schlesinger frets that five is too slender for comfort. With officials often spread all over the world speechifying - and one fifth of the policy-makers in the shape of Johann Wilhelm Gaddum off administering the bank's affairs in east Germany - the president gets nervous that there'll be no one left to mind the store. So, with the holiday season upon him, Schlesinger is agitating to fill the two vacancies pdq. While Bonn has the last word, it can take recommendations from the central bank. Observer hears that both posts will be filled by 'technicians' - with an announcement due any time, perhaps even after today's regular council meeting. The late Werthmoller's post seems likely to be taken by Wendelin Hartmann, a safe pair of hands who as chief of the Bundesbank's admin- istrative department has to most practical intents and purposes been doing the job in recent months. He appears to have finished a short head in front of one Hans-Jurgen Siegmund from the Hamburg central bank. But will the Pohl vacancy also be filled by someone from inside the bank? Since Karl Otto was always going to be a hard man to follow, it might be best not to make the attempt. Why not just settle for yet another bureaucrat?

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Letter: Future view
DOC.TEXT: Sir, There are several points one could make about Joe Cryans' letter (May 16), but I would make just one. Canary Wharf may currently appear as 'one of the more visible mistakes of the markets', though, no doubt it seemed a good decision at the time. Perhaps it is worth saying that neither the 'New Right' nor, perhaps, the 'Old Left' is infallible. And, who knows, future generations may thank us for our wisdom and foresight in building such a wonderful office complex. J H Bescoby, 4 Bishops Court, Knoll Hill, Bristol, BS9 1NS

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Life with Captain Bob
DOC.TEXT: MAXWELL'S FALL By Roy Greenslade Simon & Schuster Pounds 4.99 Among the least edifying spectacles of the aftermath of Mr Robert Maxwell's death was the speed of the overnight conversion of his flagship newspaper, the Daily Mirror, from docile servant to exposer of the publisher's many sins. The newspaper that had proclaimed Mr Maxwell a 'giant with wisdom' was to go out of its way to condemn him as a devil. The Mirror's exposes ranged from stories of widespread buggings of senior executives to mock-up photographs of Mr Maxwell with the white hair he would have had if he had not had it regularly dyed dark brown by his Savoy barber. Maxwell's Fall is the book that Mr Maxwell did not ban; he died before its publication. Its author, Roy Greenslade, is a former senior executive of Mr Rupert Murdoch's Sun and Sunday Times, who accepted the editorship of the Daily Mirror in January 1990. He left 14 months later after agreeing a generous severance payment and a confidentiality clause designed to prevent Greenslade from ever publicly speaking ill of Mr Maxwell. Greenslade argues that only someone who has been 'sullied by working closely with Maxwell' can share in the exhilaration of release felt by Mirror journalists, past and present, at the news that Mr Maxwell's body had been found floating off the coast of the Canaries. The book certainly records a cathartic experience, a genuine attempt to understand a part of the author's past that he had either ignored or overlooked. Why an experienced journalist like Greenslade, who had worked for a rival Murdoch tabloid, volunteered to work for Maxwell in the first place is a mystery. Claiming to have some sense of Mr Maxwell's dishonesty as a person, but unsuspecting about his financial improprieties, Greenslade initially considered himself capable of taking on Maxwell the idiosyncratic bully and of imposing himself as an editor. The book lists several episodes in which Greenslade portrays himself as having successfully stood up to Mr Maxwell by defending some of his staff from sacking, and overriding his employer's attempts to dictate a story or headline. On one occasion, for example, Greenslade refused to fill up his front page with the news that Mr Maxwell had bought two Israeli football clubs. On another he ignored Mr Maxwell's telephoned 'tip-offs' - erroneous as it turned out - that six members of the British cabinet were about to resign over the Tory leadership contest. In the end, however, Greenslade found himself increasingly impotent in the midst of 'Maxwellia' - the crazy, disorganised, cruel and corrupt world Mr Maxwell created. Mr Maxwell never forgave his editor for a memorable interview Greenslade gave to the British newspaper trade's weekly magazine, the UK Press Gazette, which cast gloom over the future sales of tabloids such as the Mirror. Along the way there were moments when Greenslade chose silence rather than protest. In one of the best-written human episodes in the book, he describes Mr Maxwell's public humiliation of a secretary. 'Never has an extrovert with an overweening sense of self-importance and the thickest of skins, lacking even a tiny perception of the word embarrassment, got to control a newspaper group and use it so flagrantly for his self-aggrandisement,' reflects Greenslade. It is not merely the man himself whom Greenslade criticises. His business moves come under attack too. Perhaps the only commercial decision for which Greenslade believes Mr Maxwell did deserve praise was his move into colour printing before his rivals. The decision boosted advertising revenue, enhanced the editorial content of his newspapers and eventually forced the rest of Fleet Street to follow suit. Apart from that single episode this is the story of irrational and improvised decision-making by a newspaper publisher who insisted on controlling the expenses of his editorial staff, while lavishly wasting his companies' resources on personal promotion. The blurb on this paperback boasts that Greenslade's book is the first account since the publisher's death of the full monstrous story. In fact several financial chapters seem to be the result of a skilful cuttings job on material already published in newspapers, rather than the product of original investigation. As such it puts the key in the door, but fails fully to unlock the mystery of the whys and wherefores of Mr Maxwell's dealings or to assign responsibilities to family members, employees, and financial institutions. As for Mr Maxwell's personal history, Mr Greenslade adds little to what can be gleaned already from Tom Bower's The Outsider, although he is adept at pointing out the contradictions between Bower's unofficial biography and the official account written by Joe Haines. Greenslade suggests that Mr Maxwell commited suicide under pressure over his collapsing business empire but fails to indicate where the evidence might come from to back this up. Neither does he explain why the Daily Mirror, under his editorship, did not probe into Mr Maxwell's pensions fund when its rival the Daily Mail did. The chapters focusing on Greenslade's first-hand experiences of Mr Maxwell are what gives this book its particular value, and raises it above the level of a mere attack on his labyrinthine financial dealings.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Arts: The Family Reunion - Theatre
DOC.TEXT: In 1951, TS Eliot reflected on the 'intentions, failures, and partial successes' of his plays. He rightly said of The Family Reunion: 'After what must seem to the audience an interminable time of preparation, the conclusion comes so abruptly that we are, after all, unready for it.' This throws down the gauntlet to both audience and director, and his challenge has been met in a bold, exciting production at the Leicester Haymarket. Putting a difficult verse drama on the Haymarket main stage calls for nerve and invention: Reunion gets both from director Julia Bardsley and designer Aldona Cunningham. The out-of-kilter country-house set works with the discordant soundtrack (Andrew Poppy) to conjure feelings which, according to Eliot, 'which we can only detect' from the corner of the eye. Frequent changes of state indicate the shiftings of consciousness implicit in Eliot's text. Reunion, based on Aeschylus and cut for Leicester, traces the return of Harry to his ancestral home. There, a chorus of aunts and uncles, a harridan of a mother and a jilted sweetheart await him. He has been haunted by 'furies' ever since his wife fell to her death from an ocean liner; he searches for peace with himself and his dying mother. Eliot wrote Reunion in 1939, midway between Murder in The Cathedral and Four Quartets. It shares technical similarities with both, and was subject to his rigorous verse-drama aesthetic. While he felt that he overvalued the verse, neglecting plot and character, Eliot managed to write speech rhythms which make one cease to be conscious of the play's verse form. This production strives to stay in touch with those rhythms: 'In an old house there is always listening . . . We do not like to walk out of a door and find ourselves back in the same room.' Eliot was later to rue the chorus and the furies. But here, two coups of stagecraft involving both make the evening. The furies are terrifying children dressed as Harry's relatives, and appear in a wonderfully frightening sequence; they reappear in a psychodrama of Harry's past. The exorcised furies become 'the friendly ones'. The fine acting of Rory Edwards (Harry) and Paola Dionisotti (his sage aunt Agatha) sends tap-roots into the subconscious. Even her dangerous lines 'May the weasel and the otter be about their proper business' find a place amidst the evil in the dark. The chorus is an apt melange of insight and stupidity, conveying their uncertainty and their knowledge; the reflective passages should be quieter. This is intelligent directing which tackles Eliot head on. If the production overreaches itself, it does so to compass Eliot's scope; for he knew that art was the imposition of credible order upon ordinary reality which elicited a perception of order in reality. Leicester Haymarket Theatre (0533 539797) until June 6

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Arts: Such stuff as dreams are made on - Cinema
DOC.BYLINE: By NIGEL ANDREWS and STEPHEN AMIDON
DOC.TEXT: THE LONG DAY CLOSES (12) Curzon West End WAYNE'S WORLD (PG) Empire Leicester Sq DON'T TELL MOM THE BABY SITTER'S DEAD (PG) MGMs West End, Odeon Kensington DEF BY TEMPTATION (18) Prince Charles Terence Davies's The Long Day Closes, like his Distant Voices, Still Lives, is a dream of what film-making could be like. Davies is telling us another story from his past: his boyhood memories of life with Mum (Marjorie Yates) in mid-1950s Liverpool, when the bliss of family life and of discovering the movies (The Robe, Private's Progress, The Lady-killers) was poisoned only by an eleven year old's first taste of life at a new Catholic school. It is not what Davies tells, it is how he tells it. He must never have listened to sensible cinematic advice in his life. The film has no coherent story; there are long silences interspersed with cryptic dialogue or impromptu singalongs; and the images mix the real with the surreal. In one scene a fantasised sailing ship splashes real spray at hero Bud (Leigh McCormack as the young Davies) as he daydreams in a classroom. In another, he sees his own face in a school window: but it is not a reflection, it is a new image of himself about to flash us forward into a new scene. The Long Day Closes is a miracle of rebel imagination over movie manners. Since Davies's first film Trilogy, a three-part suicide note shot in black and white with BFI money, he has put colour and humour into his work. And a dazzling sensuality. He turns his recreated postwar Liverpool, painstakingly mocked up at London's Rotherhithe Studios, into a dreamscape part beautiful, part brutalist. Changing daylight weaves shifting traceries on worn carpets. Rain lends a silver pointillism to a street outside a cinema. (As abruptly and dramatically as it comes, it is cut off.) And lyrical tracking-shots travel not just between streets but between years, lubricated by Davies's invocation of hallowed movie dialogue lines. 'In those years they had time for everything' (The Magnificent Ambersons); 'Mrs Wilberforce, I understand you have rooms to let' (The Ladykillers). Some filmgoers resist or even resent film-making so determinedly impressionistic. Even though their own minds operate in this free-associative way almost every minute of their lives, they think films should tell neat linear stories. But just look at one scene that turned this filmgoer incandescent with joy. The boy sits on a staircase silently musing. All that 'happens' is that the lighting on his face changes three times. The scene has no takeaway message, the boy's thoughts and feelings are not spelled out in over-voice. But the profundity and serendipity of changing human mood has never been more simply, vividly caught. Davies only falters, briefly, when he harks back to the messianic miserablism of Trilogy. It is a good black joke to follow Mum's wistful 'I wonder what 1956 will bring' with a shot of nailed feet on a cross. (Cue Bud's entry into his new school.) But the round of lice inspections and bleak cruelty, with more helpings of religious symbolism, is too overtly querulous. We feel hectored. Worse, we feel we have been smuggled into Davies's mind by the non-denominational beguilements of the film's early scenes in order to be his anti-Catholic storm troopers when he needs us. Far more haunting is a single, inexplicable nightmare image at home. A pair of hands reach out from behind Bud's bed and clasp his head. Nothing leads to the scene, nothing leads away: it is for the audience to join the emotional dots. Here and in the film's use of music to challenge or ironise the visuals, and in the ingenuity of the visuals themselves like the halo-ing back-light on Bud's head in class that suddenly wobbles to become a movie projector beam, Terence Davies proves that he is not just a good film-maker, he has the makings of a great film-maker. Wayne's World provides the most convincing argument since Network for throwing your television out of the window. It follows the antics of two young American couch potatoes, Wayne and Garth (Mike Myers and Dana Carvey), as they present their public access TV chat show, an anarchic combination of mindless babble of the 'party on, dude' variety, woebegone special guests and lots of heavy metal music. When not on air, Wayne and Garth stumble through the world in a permanent electronic thrall - quoting TV adverts, lip synching to the radio, dreaming of the girl in the rock video. Their idea of witty dialogue is for one to exclaim 'No Way]', whereupon the other counters by saying 'Way]'. The film was born as a regular skit on America's Saturday Night Live comedy show, where it provided an often hilarious depiction of a generation of youth unable to conceive of anything that is not bounced off a satellite or channelled through loudspeakers. It is a shame that Myers, the show's creator, felt it had to be stretched out to a movie format - the plot, involving a venal network producer trying to take over the show, is nonsense, while the satire quickly achieves saturation point in a series of gags which will try the patience of most viewers. To make matters worse, there are continual references to television commercials and programmes unavailable over here. This is not to say that there are not some funny moments, though the overall impression the film leaves you with is that the telecommunications revolution is over, and the machines have won. A far less distressing view of American youth is on display in Don't Tell Mom The Babysitter's Dead. The film's plot is more or less deducible from its title: a harried single mother of five decides to take a few months off in Australia, leaving her children in the care of a tough old sitter, who promptly dies, whereupon the eldest child (Christina Applegate) must take charge of the family. The carefree 17-year-old soon shows her worth by bluffing her way into a high-paying position in the fashion industry, managing to hold the family together while at the same time winning the heart of the boy in the hot dog delivery van. What starts out as a potentially chaotic teen comedy soon turns into a gormlessly charming coming-of-age story that comes down firmly in favor of honesty, hard work and traditional family values. The distributors of Def by Temptation claim that it is 'the best black vampire movie since Blacula', an assessment I am not prepared to argue with, having missed all the other black vampire movies. Unfortunately, first time writer/director James Bond III has made a film which is hard to praise in many other ways. It tells the story of a young divinity student who travels to New York City for a vacation, only to find himself doing battle with a female vampire barfly who tries to tempt him away from his faith. Despite some spirited acting by Bill Nunn and Kadeem Hardison, the film's pace too uneven and its goriness too unconvincing to make it very scary. It is not that Bond is without talent - he just has failed to stretch his low budget to adequately cover the horror genre.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Arts: Patagonia/The Fastest Clock in the Universe - Theatre
DOC.BYLINE: By ALASTAIR MACAULAY and DAVID MURRAY
DOC.TEXT: Telling your own history is an important way of showing that you have some pride in yourself. Patagonia, presented by the Welsh group Brith Gof, is less about that distant land than about the 153 Welsh settlers who sailed there in 1865 and whose descendants remain there, still speaking Welsh - mixed with Spanish and a little English - holding eisteddfodau, singing festivals and Welsh newspapers. Part documentary, part performance art, Patagonia does honour to both Wales and to pioneers. Its first parts remind me a lot of Martha Graham's greatest work, the 1944 Appalachian Spring. Like that, this shows the bare frame of a new homestead against an open sky, the two women and two men of the new community, their relationships and the religious practices they have brought with them. But Patagonia is not a dance work, and it celebrates to a considerable degree the way these Welsh Patagonians have kept the Welsh language alive. I have no Welsh, but hearing the musicality of this Welsh, whether in speech or in song, was one of the evening's pleasures. This work is about history, the development of a community through the generations and its commemoration of its past. We not only see and hear the rites and customs of these emigres, we hear detached commentary too. A narrator figure - who sits, with his back to us, at the front of the auditorium, using the front of the stage as his desk - and the four onstage performers tell isolated stories of specific families and their houses. We hear how 'She is the museum. Women always carry the history,' how even these Welsh became 'true conquistadors,' how 'In a land where nothing rots, history spreads itself,' and how one of these stories was told to (among others) Bruce Chatwin and became chapter 17 of his In Patagonia. All of this is affecting and stimulating, and the simple elegance of the staging is often marvellous. The four-part singing is excellent, the speaking has dignity, the main gestures have breadth and power. The use of sand on the floor provides a source of beautifully ambiguous symbolism - sand as locale, sand as time, sand as omnipresent intrusion. Best is the way that the staging frequently shows us two or more acts at the same time or in quick succession. There are, however, a few longueurs, even though the work lasts only 70 minutes. Certain inventories of local life become ponderous, and the slow-motion treatment of one dramatic episode manages to be both dull and obscure. But Patagonia, a frequently poetic work, won my immediate respect and interest. Brith Gof is a group new to me; I hope to encounter more of its work before long. It is the first offering in the excellent three-week Barclays New Stages season at the Royal Court, which presents some of Britain's leading work in performance art, new dance and/or music theatre. Philip Ridley's new play at the Hampstead Theatre until June 13 is short and sour, variably funny and intermittently gripping. In outline the scenario might suggest Joe Orton, but neither the writing nor the sentiments echo that cheerful subversive at all. Structurally, the play is much nearer to Pinter's Birthday Party - and not only because Ridley's centrepiece too is a sinister party. Here, the birthday is Cougar Glass's 'nineteenth': we gather he has had several of those already. He lives with his sugar-daddy 'Captain Tock', a cultivated, tragically balding antique dealer who likes clocks (Cougar hates them, and cultivates nothing but his quiff and his artifical tan). The parties are a device for luring beddable youths home; in due course the Captain will make an excuse and leave. The latest unknowing prey is Foxtrot Darling (Ridley's way with names is all his own), for whom Cougar has become a a big-brother substitute. Foxtrot arrives with not only a deeply unwelcome birthday gift, but his pregnant fiancee Sherbet Gravel too; they call each other 'Babe' indiscriminately. The Captain decides to remain, while Cougar leaves off his languid macho preening and goes into a long, silent seethe. Sherbet soon sizes up the situation all too well, and her bright chat turns again and again to reflections upon mortality. Eventually there is a ghastly eruption, staged for maximum theatrical impact by the director Matthew Lloyd. Jonathan Coy (I think that is his real name) plays the Captain with some delicacy, if slightly too much hair, and Con O'Neill (ditto) seethes well. The kids are expertly cartooned by Jude Law, the lamb to the slaughter, and clever Emma Amos. As tough old Cheetah Bee, the landlady of this semi-converted factory (picturesquely devised by Moggie Douglas), Elizabeth Bradley makes the most of her two appearances with Zimmer frame. They all give the play a grounding in a plausible East End reality which Ridley's text barely suggests, dreamily abstract as it often is. Curious exercise] If it bears a moral, it seems too obvious to mention; but perhaps there is a real-life Cougar out there somewhere, who is meant to be pilloried here.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Technology: Cutting through the red tape - How fragmented sectors, such as machine tools, can realistically carry out joint R&D
DOC.TEXT: Over the past few months, Europe's machine tool builders have been engaged in characteristically low-pro-file talks with the European Community about a possible industrial policy. In the depths of a recession that has damaged competitiveness, the industry hopes for some stimulus to investment by its customers in manufacturing, but also wants the EC to help create the conditions that might address some of its longer-term problems. At the top of the list is a very different approach to research and development - aimed at stimulating better co-operation between companies in the most strategically important areas of R&D, and improving the unhappy relationship between the industry and EC-funded research programmes. The outcome of the talks is far from clear, but the industry's approach raises questions about the nature of R&D in a fragmented, intensely competitive industry of some 1,500 independent producers. How does such an industry achieve a balance between 'R' and 'D' when most companies concentrate exclusively on the D? Where does the R get done, and how does the industry benefit? How much R is necessary anyway? For many machine tool builders, development work that is not linked to a specific product or technology is rare, and 'blue-sky research' taboo. But new materials, relatively new processes such as laser-cutting and the trend towards standardisation of control systems, motors and drives all argue for a significant research element in R&D. Inevitably, though, the recession has reduced the ability of machine tool builders to do much more than plough their own development furrows. Consequently, increased co-operation on higher levels of research - broad-based and 'pre-competitive' but not 'blue-sky' - has become an even higher priority for producers, users, institutions and universities. But the industry and the EC industrial research infrastructure is poorly matched. Most machine tool builders, for example, believe the structure and content of the EC's Brite/Euram industrial research projects make it difficult for them to participate. 'The research is too far removed from the market place to allow the formulation of projects that can be useful in the medium- or short- term,' says Mike Bright, chairman of Brighton-based FMT Holdings. 'It's the Plesseys, Siemens & Philips who are obtaining the funds. The SMEs (small and medium-sized enterprises) are not getting a look in, and it's causing quite a concern.' Tony Balding, managing director of Norwich-based Beaver Engineering Group, cites the intimidating amounts of paperwork involved in applying to join an EC project. He warns too that small companies which do participate may find their pace is inhibited by larger, slower-moving partners. Continental machine tool companies have similar complaints. Sandvik of Sweden has participated in Brite/Euram via EC subsidiaries, but Clas Ake Hedstrom, president of the Sandvik Coromant metal-cutting tools division, says that results have been limited so far, and some programmes are taking longer than was originally anticipated. The problem for the machine tool industry is that such EC projects were set up to focus on what Nigel Eldred, chief executive of Amtri, the UK machine tool research organisation, calls 'macro-technology'. Consequently, small companies which have traditionally carried out strictly targeted development work find it difficult to leap into these broader-based projects. However, the industry has reason to hope that EC-funded research may soon become more user-friendly. Jean Heymans, secretary general of Cecimo, the European machine tool trade association umbrella body, says the EC's current Framework programme for Brite/Euram projects will be much more geared to industry than to blue-sky research.
