Cecimo, whose talks with the EC are backed by its 12 member countries, is pushing for a policy designed to improve the SMEs' access to R&D programmes through measures such as increased funding for their projects, simplified administrative procedures and enlarged Craft-type programmes. Craft, an offshoot of Brite/Euram and currently at the pilot stage, is likely to be more market-oriented than Brite/Euram itself, and could appeal to SMEs. Administrative procedures should be simpler but, according to one UK machine tool official, 'there will still be a whittling down process, and unless you know the ropes, you haven't got a hope in hell'. As long as the machine tool industry retains its current structure, though, there will always be companies which will find it hard to benefit from the EC's largesse - some Ecu 500m (Pounds 350m) spent on Brite/Euram in 1989-92 and Ecu 670m budgeted for the overlapping 1990-94 programme. But the industry can, and is, participating in the pan-European Eureka R&D initiative, launched in 1985. This is intended to be more market-related than Brite/Euram, but projects are narrower in scope and rely on funding by national governments. Speed is probably the biggest factor prompting some companies to consider bilateral agreements on development rather than become involved in a long-term project which offers little opportunity to cover administrative costs and could be tantamount to 'buying a headache,' says Eldred. But at least one larger UK machine tool company is happy to be taking part in a Brite/Euram project, even if it did take months to get off the ground. Jones & Shipman, the Leicester-based grinding machine manufacturer, is investigating the potential of cubic boron nitride for precision cylindrical grinding at high wheel speeds via a four-year Brite/Euram project based at Aachen. The diversity of the project's participants is a new trend for machine tool research and one which many observers believe should be encouraged. Apart from Aachen University's machine tool research department, the other partners are Brussels-based Diamond Boart, manufacturers of super-abrasive wheels, and a user - the vehicle-parts and electricals group Robert Bosch. In the UK, which has traditionally lagged behind continental Europe in harnessing R&D carried out by companies, universities and government-funded research institutions, Amtri has been the catalyst behind a unique project that follows a similar approach. The Pounds 15m Machine Tool Technology and Materials Processing Programme, supported by the Department of Trade and Industry, brings machine tool customers, producers and part suppliers together in a series of separate projects such as high-speed spindle research. The aim is for all the technologies being developed in the programme to be combined in a 'multi-function machine tool'. Eldred sees a key role for Amtri as a 'networker' to link companies with universities and other bodies, and to keep its ear close to the ground in relation to other European centres. As companies and institutions begin to take a more international approach to research partnerships, the next step is to help develop a more effective 'network of networks' in Europe, according to Derek Palethorpe, Amtri's director of operations. The overall aim should be to produce a more co-ordinated, broad-based approach to R&D in the European machine tool industry. In the background is competition from Japan, which has always outshone rivals on product development and exploitation but is also becoming more interested in multidisciplinary international research. Japan's proposed research project into intelligent manufacturing systems, for example, is intended to have international participation. Some European observers worry, therefore, that it may be no more than a Trojan horse feeding on Europe's remaining areas of superiority in machine tool innovation. At the same time, industry critics say, more mergers and cross-border co-operation among European machine tool builders would develop a mentality that is better suited to participate in the higher reaches of EC research. At least they would have more resources to handle the red tape.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Technology: Self-help on open systems
DOC.TEXT: An initiative to promote 'open' computer systems among UK small- and medium-sized businesses is being orchestrated by the Department of Trade and Industry as its Pounds 12m open systems technology transfer programme ends this month. The DTI has already held meetings with a number of large computer suppliers who have pledged their support for a broad programme of measures to disseminate information about open systems and their benefits. The list includes ICL, IBM, Digital Equipment, Hewlett Packard, AT&T, Easylink, Unisys and Uniplex. While details of the initiative remain to be settled, it seems likely it will include a 'hotline' number which companies will be able to call for independent advice. It is also likely to develop guidelines which will define a set of attributes for openness which could be compared with suppliers' offerings. Open systems are based on commonly accepted industry standards and usually imply computers that can easily be connected together and run software from any supplier following open systems rules. Open systems offer significant possibilities for cutting costs once the move from proprietary designs has been made, but DTI studies show that while the message is well understood among very large companies - BP, Marks & Spencer and Lucas are enthusiastic supporters of the initiative - medium-sized and small companies are frequently confused by differing messages from suppliers and have difficulty obtaining independent information on which to base decisions. They are often too small to be able to afford to join one of the big league self-help organisations such as the Butler Cox Foundation. The DTI intends to inject some Pounds 2m in pump priming funds over the next two years but otherwise will confine itself to acting as 'honest broker' among the various factions and suppliers which make up the open systems movement. The idea is for the industry to take the lead in speaking to customers with a single, unambiguous voice about open systems. The DTI initiative is backed by lobby groups including X/Open, Uniforum UK, Unix International and the National Computing Centre.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Management (Marketing & Advertising): Getting corporate projection in the Cannes - Professionals who beat a path to the film festival but never watch the movies
DOC.TEXT: George Eccles managed to get to the showing of the movie 'Braindead', but was soon slumbering. He observed the on-screen cannibalism and decided he could use the sleep instead - 10 days' of marketing his accountancy firm at the Cannes film festival is exhausting work. Not to be at Cannes these days is more of a marketing than a social gaffe. Europe's film industry now has an annual turnover of Dollars 1.4bn; this year, three of the main four prizes went to European movies. None of those are likely to match the commercial success of the latest US box office hit, 'Wayne's World', which took more than Dollars 100m in its first two months. Yet closer EC political and economic ties offer the prospect of greater co-production funding and distribution deals within the community. That in turn creates a need for more efficient marketing. How to achieve that is an open question; one answer for many is to go to the film, music and television festivals held annually at Cannes. Some 20,000 people go to considerable trouble to get to the Cannes festival but many do not see even one film. Instead, they pay inflated prices for accommodation and services to join in a 10-day marketing jamboree which they hope will result in cinema-associated business. The marketing moves at Cannes are mostly down to old-fashioned direct selling, focused almost entirely on rented hotel suites and the esplanade where the US, Canadian, Japanese and European pavilions house producers, tax lawyers, accountants and assorted other fixers, all renting space or sponsoring the pavilions to market their services. Even the economic development department of Gwynedd county council in Wales was there, dishing out brochures announcing: 'Fairytale lands . . . The Great Wall of China . . . The dark depths of Transylvania . . . Gwynedd has the film location you're looking for'. Eccles heads the media group at accountants, Coopers & Lybrand Deloitte. For him, Cannes is 'a trade and marketing event. We are here to serve existing clients and get new ones. It's impossible to know how much new business we attract by being here. But we are now working for a client who has acquired cable rights in Nigeria. He said he came to us because he picked up one of our brochures in Cannes 11 years ago.' Coopers spends more than Pounds 20,000 to mount an exhibition with five staff at Cannes. Eccles says it is 'very difficult for accountants to market ourselves and our activities. We can't do blanket television advertising, so we have to pick our marketing opportunities much more carefully.' This year was the first at Cannes for Howard Bass, a partner at Ernst and Young's New York office; clearly it will not be his last. 'We have at least 20 large clients here this year and it's important for them to see us. 'The cinema industry is a huge business for us, worth perhaps Dollars 100m a year, so the investment of perhaps Dollars 60,000 to bring a small team here and set up an exhibition is definitely worthwhile.' But much more than that, Bass has a choice of spending perhaps Dollars 25,000 on a full-page advertisement in a glossy trade magazine which few might read, or to shake hands in the most direct form of marketing available. He opts for the latter and intends expanding Ernst and Young's exhibition at Cannes 1993. The European pavilion is organised annually by Button Eventures, part of the Reed group. For Steve Jaggs, UK marketing manager for Agfa, the film stock producer which is sponsoring the European pavilion, it is a vital aspect of his marketing strategy. 'Cinema is something of a cottage industry and a people business, so conventional advertising is not so appropriate.' Jaggs says that some 20 per cent of Agfa's costs in the UK are on marketing but he spends 70 per cent of his budget on event sponsorship and support for professional cinema organisations, and only 30 per cent on conventional advertising. He hopes that by being highly visible at Cannes, Agfa will stick in the mind of producers and film companies thinking of purchasing stock. If Cannes provides a marketing forum for business, it is equally attractive as a centre for marketing new productions and forging contacts. Nicholas Steil, general manager of Euro Aim, an EC-funded organisation, regards Cannes as the centre for plugging in to the European film industry. In the end, 'Braindead' - in which 'a zombie mother interferes with the course of true love' - will probably fade alongside hundreds of other movies shown at Cannes. But the movie business itself is set to expand both in Europe and elsewhere. And as European integration speeds up, the leisure industry may find that marketing events become an increasingly important means of making both contacts and profit.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Management (Marketing & Advertising): Burnt by over-exposure in the Sun - Norwich Union has been fined Pounds 50,000 by Lautro
DOC.TEXT: Financial services, it must be said, are not like floor wax. The fact that four out of five housewives agree is not likely to persuade viewers to purchase a complex financial product which may require investment over half a lifetime. Because the losses from choosing the wrong product can be great, there are firm rules for what financial services firms can and cannot tell the public about their products. Last week, Lautro, the self-regulatory body for the life insurance industry, slapped a Pounds 50,000 fine on Norwich Union for misleading advertising - along with a bill for Pounds 15,000 in costs - underscoring the seriousness with which breaches of advertising codes are viewed. The fine was the first ever imposed by Lautro under powers it received last autumn. The offending ad was a four-page pull-out in the Sun newspaper in April 1991. Lautro's main objection was that the advertisement looked just like the Sun's editorial pages, and so gave the impression that it was a journalist's account of a new product. Furthermore, the ad, promoting a 15-year savings product, implied that premium payments would remain constant when, in fact, they would rise by 20 per cent per year for the first five years in order to give the right investment returns. The ad also offended by suggesting that the illustrated investment returns were conservatively estimated and were likely to be far larger in practice. Although such breaches are worrying, they are rare. According to Kit Jebens, chief executive of Lautro, instances of misleading advertising have fallen over the past two years. Indeed, only one of the eight or nine disciplinary cases still before Lautro involves misleading advertising. Most of the others concern companies' failure to control their so-called 'tied agents'. These are sales agents who are self-employed but who agree to sell the products of one company exclusively. Significantly, Norwich Union's ad was not placed by the company itself, but by one of its tied agents. The agent, a company called 'SunCare' was a subsidiary of Sedgwick Group, the financial services broker, and was set up for the sole purposes of running the advertisement. The company has since ceased operations. Companies are becoming aware of the high cost of misleading advertising and steer clear of it, Jebens said. While Norwich Union has earned the first fine, others have had to bear the cost of rewriting their advertising, notifying clients of advertising errors and in some cases, they have been forced to refund customers. The regulation simply says that advertising must be 'fair, clear and not misleading'. But that rule is backed up by guidelines which ban the design of ads which are identical to a newspaper's editorial copy. Other rules forbid companies from playing down certain information - such as a 'health warning' that past investment performance is no indication of future returns. But while regulators may have stamped out the worst excesses in published advertising, they have been far less successful in controlling the informal, verbal advertising that goes on in private between a potential customer and a commissioned sales agent. 'That's where the real sales pitch goes on,' said Jean Eaglesham, money policy manager at the Consumers' Association. CA has sent actors posing as potential customers to gauge how much misleading advertising goes on in private. A recent CA survey of 40 mortgage lenders found that all 'were selling endowment policies very hard and were giving inaccurate information to consumers.' For instance, the sales agents - employees of banks and building societies - told buyers that endowment insurance policies were guaranteed to pay off a mortgage upon maturity when in fact, they are not. 'I don't really know what you can do about that,' Eaglesham said. 'It really needs radical reform of the commission system.' The commission system, under which sales agents are allowed to keep a portion of the premium payments from new customers, encourages a hard sell, critics say. The life industry has adamantly opposed any reform of the commission system, saying it would be a disincentive to sales agents and that people who need insurance simply would not be encouraged to buy it. Jebens admits that there is some merit in that view. 'Remuneration systems are partly at fault here,' he said, 'but there's not a lot you can do about it'. Commission, he says, is a commercial matter and cannot be subject to regulation. But Eaglesham argues that until misleading advertising transmitted by word of mouth is made as costly as that delivered in print, there is little incentive for companies to stop. Indeed, SunCare, Norwich Union's sales agent, signed up 4,500 new customers with its ad in the Sun - and earned a commission on every one.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Rivers watchdog criticised on cash
DOC.TEXT: MPs HAVE strongly condemned the National Rivers Authority for weaknesses in financial management that led to wasted expenditure of Pounds 1m and the resignation of its first chief executive. A report from the Public Accounts Committee published yesterday criticises the Environment Department, Lord Crickhowell, chairman of the NRA, and his board for failing to keep a sufficiently close eye on the water pollution organisation's expenditure. The primary reason for the outspoken criticism was evidence that rules for spending large sums of money had been ignored in fitting out the NRA's new head office in Bristol. The project resulted in the wasting of about Pounds 1m out of a total cost of Pounds 2.65m, and the resignation last June of Mr John Bowman, chief executive, with a pay-off of Pounds 125,000. Two other senior executives received written warnings for ignoring the financial procedures laid down for the NRA. In July, 1990, the NRA engaged Corporate Design Interiors (CDI) to advise on relocating and to help choose contractors. It was also one of three firms asked to tender for the Pounds 12,000 contract to design the layout of the new offices. The NRA then decided to combine the design contract with a much bigger one for fitting out the building. Instead of asking several firms to tender, it considered only two that had bid for the much smaller design job. The Pounds 2.65m contract went to CDC, a sister company of CDI, without Lord Crickhowell, Mr Bowman or the NRA board being told. An internal inquiry found that had the job been properly managed it would have cost only Pounds 1.6m. The NRA said last night there had been 'serious shortcomings' in the management of fitting out the Bristol head office, which resulted in poor value for money. Financial Management and Control in the National Rivers Authority; HMSO; Pounds 10.75.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Kinnock calls for re-think on 'opt-outs'
DOC.TEXT: THE PROMOTION of 'co-ordinated expansion' during the UK presidency of the Community was urged on the government yesterday, by Mr Neil Kinnock, the Labour leader. Opening the debate for the opposition, Mr Kinnock argued that such an approach was the only way 'to ensure vitality and confidence in western Europe and to promote stability, hope and strengthened democracy in Eastern Europe'. The certainty of growing interdependence between EC countries made it essential, he said, for the government to work towards promoting balanced development and social cohesion. He called on the prime minister to abandon his 'opt-out mentality' and re-emphasised Labour's broad support for the treaty, He also emphsasised its opposition to opting out of the social chapter and economic and monetary union. These 'opt-outs' are at the heart of the party's 'reasoned amendment' to the bill. But if that amendment fails, Labour policy is to abstain on whether the bill should proceed. That policy came under fire during the debate from some Labour backbenchers. Mr Kinnock called the terms in which minsters had attacked the social chapter 'absolute fantasies' and warned that the government had indulged in such fictions because it needed the false threat of disruption to cover up its desertion of duty in failing to secure better rights for British workers. He said Britain was the example that poor labour conditions did not mean necessarily superior economic performance, and called on ministers to end efforts to make Britain 'the labour market bargain basement of Europe'. Turning to economic and monetary union, he warned the government that as early as 1994 it would have to make specific proposals so that preparatory decisions could be taken. 'They won't be able to opt out of that', he said. While Mr Kinnock was heard in a crowded Commons with little interruption, there was discomfort for the Labour front bench from Mr Peter Shore. The former Labour cabinet minister called the party's apparent readiness to let the EC decide the future size of public borrowing under a Labour government 'a total disgrace', and warned that opposition MPs had a duty to vote against the bill itself. He ridiculed the briefing from the party's Treasury frontbench team that the mention of goals of sustainable growth and high employment early in the treaty put those aims on a par with the aims of economic and monetary union, and price stability in particular. Mr Shore said the government had evaded the central issue of where Britain should go when a majority of other EC member states wanted a different - federal - destiny. Mr Tony Benn (Lab Chesterfield) said it would be absolutely wrong for a step of such magnitude to be taken without consulting the people who - because of the transfer of more decision-making to Brussels - would lose democratic rights. Mr Austin Mitchell (Lab Great Grimsby) said the Bill would get a second reading tonight not because the argument had been won but because the Labour leadership had 'allowed it to go through'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: PM resists Tory Euro-sceptics
DOC.TEXT: ASSURANCES by Mr John Major, the prime minister, that the Maastricht treaty marked the beginning of a reversal of the 'centralising trend' in the European Community failed to satisfy prominent Conservative backbench critics in the Commons last night. Mr William Cash, MP for Stafford and one of seven Tory backbenchers who called for the rejection of the Bill implementing the treaty, insisted that it was a 'very centralising measure'. A former cabinet minister, Mr John Biffen (C Shropshire North) also expressed 'considerable reservations' about the treaty. He contended that it contained a great deal of senseless commitment to centralism. In a confident speech opening the two-day debate on the Bill, the prime minister maintained that the treaty marked 'an important change in direction' by enabling agreements to be reached by the member states of the European Community outside the confines of the Treaty of Rome which established it. Dealing with another issue that has caused considerable concern on the government back benches, he strongly reaffirmed Britain's determination to maintain frontier controls to guard against illegal immigration from non-EC countries, and to combat terrorism, crime and the traffic in drugs. Mr Kenneth Baker, the former home secretary, argued that the issue of immigration controls was one on which Britain could afford to make no concessions and should fight in the courts if necessary. Sir Teddy Taylor (C Southend East), a leading critic of the EC, and Mr Peter Shore (Lab Bethnal Green and Stepney), a prominent opponent of the Maastricht treaty, warned that the government's position on frontier controls may be subject to legal challenge. The prime minister promised Britain would 'fiercely' contest such proceedings, citing the 1987 single European Act. He said Britain would co-operate within the framework of international law, but outside the framework of EC law. Emphasising the significance of the distinction, Mr Major said: 'Any dispute would go to the International Court of Justice, not the European Court of Justice.' The prime minister said the Maastricht treaty provided for those to be dealt with either under the Rome treaty or through intergovernmental co-operation. It also recognised that there might be circumstances in which 'the member states can act better on their own'. Underlining the negotiating objectives he achieved at the Maastricht summit, Mr Major said the treaty set 'exactly the framework' Britain wanted for economic and monetary union. It ensured 'an absolute right' for the UK parliament to decide later, at a time of its own choosing, whether Britain should move to the third stage of economic and monetary union. The prime minister hit out at Mr Neil Kinnock, the Labour leader, for his condemnation of the carefully negotiated provision giving Britain the right to decide whether or not to join a single currency. Those who supported Mr Kinnock's view, he said, were commiting themselves to 'enter a single currency now in unknown economic circumstances in the future, with the Community at an unknown size and with economic convergence at an unknown level'. Mr Major dismissed Labour's denunciation of the government's refusal to accept the social chapter. He said signing the chapter would have removed from British employers and their employees the right to determine working conditions. Mr Ray Whitney (C Wycombe) argued that the tenor of the debate was out of tune with the mood of the country. He said people outside the House were more disposed to accept the reality of Britain's relationship with Europe. In a maiden speech, Mr Iain Duncan-Smith (C Chingford) warned that the treaty kept the door open to federalist centralisation and an uncompetitive Europe which was clearly moving in the wrong direction from the rest of the world. Sir George Gardiner (C Reigate), who described himself as a 'Euro-pragmatist', said his support for the European ideal had never embraced a federalist structure. He deplored the efforts being made by some to force the EC step by step into a 'federal centralised straitjacket'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Lib Dems to support Maastricht treaty
DOC.TEXT: MR Paddy Ashdown, the Liberal Democrat leader, said that although the Maastricht treaty had failed to provide democratic accountability for the European institutions it created, his party would still support the bill. The Liberal Democrats believed the treaty was 'a step forward that must be taken and that it would be a disaster for Britain and for Europe were it not to be ratified'. At Westminster last night, the party's MPs voted to replace European affairs spokesman Sir Russell Johnston as deputy leader with Treasury spokesman Mr Alan Beith.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Smith and Gould clash in debate
DOC.TEXT: THE RIVAL candidates for the Labour leadership clashed last night in the first and, possibly, the only head-to-head confrontation before the electoral college ballots on July 18. Their performances in a Fabian Society debate eschewed acrimony and were held by many to have amounted to a draw. However, several rounds of applause for Mr John Smith's staunch avowals of Labour's first principles may just have given him a points victory over his rival, Mr Bryan Gould. The loudest accolade came for the shadow chancellor's dismissal of a suggestion that the party should appeal baldly to electors' self-interests. 'The philosophy of democratic socialism is about a moral view of life . . . if there is no morality in it it is not worth having,' he said. Mr Gould won acclaim too when he made clear that altruism was not enough and that Labour needed to find new ways to appeal to a new and wider electorate. Arguing that one path to victory was to defuse the concentration of power among vested interests, he cited the aphorism: 'The great advantage of socialism is it removes the need to be altruistic.' In the event, the clearest exposition of the differences between the two men came in their opening statements. Mr Smith spoke of building an opposition from the anti-Conservative majority. Promoting his plan for a Commission on Social Justice to examine tax and benefits, he argued: 'We face a new challenge of designing a strategy for social justice and economic opportunity that will benefit the minority, while gaining the votes of the majority that will have to pay for it.' Mr Gould offered a lightly veiled critique of his rival as a 'one last heave' candidate. The leadership needed someone with the experience to fight beyond Labour's heartlands who could offer 'distinctive and positive reasons why people should vote Labour.' That would involve a commitment to run the economy differently and challenge monetarist orthodoxy, he said. The differences between the two men in much of the question session that followed was mostly mood music. On Europe, Mr Gould rejected a purely 'monetarist' approach in the convergence towards economic and monetary union. Mr Smith, instead, stressed the need to discuss that question while progressing to the EMU goal. On party reforms, Mr Smith argued that there should be a role for MPs in a future leadership electoral college, whereas his opponent said a one-member, one-vote system would lessen union unease. Both agreed on the need for constitutional reform, especially devolution and a consideration of electoral reform. Mr Gould put greater emphasis on the need to promote full employment before a redistributive tax policy, whereas Mr Smith suggested that such a goal, although desirable, was no substitute for a clearly argued case for redistribution.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Evans seeking to oust Labour whip
DOC.TEXT: MR JOHN EVANS, the doughty anti-Militant campaigner, was first out of the traps yesterday in the race to contest the post of Labour's chief whip with the incumbent, Mr Derek Foster. Within minutes of the campaign timetable being announced, the St Helens North MP said his candidacy aimed to shake up the party's management of parliamentary business, which, he claimed, 'was frequently criticised for lacking logic or dynamism'. Mr Jeff Rooker, the Birmingham Perry Barr MP, also confirmed yesterday that he was discussing a bid with his colleagues. But the odds are still on Mr Foster, who has held the post in spite of a series of challenges since 1985. He is said to enjoy the tacit support of Mr John Smith, now seen as a certainty for election as party leader. Under the timetables announced to the parliamentary Labour party yesterday, nominations for chief whip and the PLP chairmanship will open on June 18 and close on June 25. An exhaustive ballot will begin on July 9, repeated, if necessary, for each week that follows with the last-placed name dropping out, until one candidate has secured 50 per cent of the vote. That means the race will be completed before the electoral college meets to conclude the leadership issue on July 18. For the shadow cabinet elections, party officers have agreed a complex arrangement that opens nominations on July 9 and closes them before the leadership result is known on July 16. Voting for the 18 places will take place up to July 23 to allow MPs to take account of the outcome. Some MPs were complaining yesterday that the planning for the chief whip and party chairmanship contest - each ex-officio shadow cabinet posts - further helps the incumbents as backbench MPs must 'bid' for select committee places -in effect, decided by recommendations from the whips' office - from today.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Thatcher warns on transfer of power
DOC.TEXT: FROM BEYOND the Commons, Mrs Margaret Thatcher again entered the European debate yesterday, warning that the EC should have acted more vigorously in dealing with what was Yugoslavia, and that the Maastricht treaty was particularly flawed in its transfer of powers to a centralised bureaucracy, Alison Smith writes. In an article in the current issue of The European newspaper, she supported the government's line in strongly resisting any attempt by other EC member states to dilute or remove border controls to deal with international crime, immigration and terrorism. The plight of what was Yugoslavia was used as an example of how the provisions of the Maastricht treaty are 'not in tune with the instincts of the people', who would like to help but see that the EC can do nothing. Among the treaty's other failings, the article said, is that it would not ensure or enhance democratic government because of the power it transferred away from nation states, extending the areas of Community authority and of majority voting. Mrs Thatcher said she was 'very concerned' that the larger role of the Western European Union in European defence arrangements might send the wrong message to the United States about whether the EC wants American troops to continue to be stationed in Europe. The treaty's failure to tackle European protectionism and thus improve world trade was also attacked. On the subject of border controls, she defended the position she negotiated, saying it is a matter of 'good faith (which) once lost is hard to regain' that the other EC countries stand by the general declaration attached to the Single European Act. The Act said that the provisions for free movement of goods and persons would not affect measures that individual countries thought were needed to control immigration from outside the EC as well as to combat terrorism and international crime.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Scots MPs backing referendum delay debate
DOC.TEXT: INCENSED SCOTTISH Labour MPs delayed the start of the two-day Maastricht debate by some 25 minutes yesterday, deploying a series of parliamentary devices to stall scheduled Commons business. The ruses culminated with Mr John McAllion, the Labour MP for Dundee East, forcing a vote on the technical matter of whether 'strangers' or non-MPs should leave the chamber. The Tories were the 'strangers' referred to, he said, claiming the government was denying Scotland 'its democratic right' to a referendum on its constitutional future. The disruption followed a stormy session of Scottish questions in which the government ridiculed repeated Labour and Scottish National party demands for a referendum. To have such a referendum now on 'vague and unspecific philosophical concepts' would prove nothing and achieve nothing, Mr Ian Lang, Scottish secretary, said, claiming the demands were being made only to cover the confusion over constitutional change in Labour ranks. Prior to the general election, he said, Labour opposed a referendum and planned to impose a Scottish assembly. The government was considering whether there were ways of 'continuing to make the government of Scotland responsive to Scotland's needs without undermining the unity of the UK.' Mr Donald Dewar, shadow Scottish secretary, said there was 'major room for improvement and a shift in the balance of power towards Scots running their own affairs within this country.' Mr Alex Salmond, the SNP leader, said that the real reason the government would not hold a referendum was that it had no confidence that its position would 'carry the day'. Mr Jim Sillars will stand down as deputy leader of the SNP when the the post comes up for re-election in September. Mr Sillars, who lost his seat at Glasgow Govan in the general election, said he intends to remain active in the party.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / The Finance Bill: MPs ready to enact Budget
DOC.BYLINE: By EMMA TUCKER, RICHARD WATERS, ANDREW TAYLOR and ALISON SMITH
DOC.TEXT: THE FINANCE Bill, published yesterday, enacts most of the Budget announced by Mr Norman Lamont, the chancellor, in March. The bill is likely to survive its parliamentary stages intact, although, since the government majority is now just 21, there is scope for Tory backbenchers to push their hobbyhorses, possibly winning some concessions. It is difficult to predict where controversy might arise, but building societies were already reacting angrily yesterday to the fact that the government has not changed its stance on the societies' claim that they were taxed twice during the introduction of composite-rate tax in the late 1980s. Leeds Building Society said Clause 52 might spell the end of its attempts in the UK courts to recover what it claims is Pounds 57m of overpaid tax. Mr Mike Blackburn, Leeds chief executive, said: 'No single word adequately describes the action the government is proposing. It is outrageous and offensive to the rule of law. It makes a mockery of the Citizen's Charter and shows the Inland Revenue's Taxpayer's Charter is not worth the paper it is written on.' Last year's Finance Bill contained retrospective legislation preventing Leeds and others from following in the footsteps of the Woolwich, which had won a similar action. This year's retrospective legislation might close the door for good on action in the UK courts. If so, Leeds said it was prepared to take the matter to the European Court of Human Rights. The dispute stems from efforts by the government to bring building societies' tax payments, previously made annually, into line with the banks, which make their returns on a quarterly basis. About seven sessions are expected to see it through to a third-reading debate beginning in early July. It should pass into legislation around the middle of July. The new bill follows the Finance Act, which was given Royal Assent on March 16 and enacted the Budget's more controversial elements, including the new 20 per cent income tax rate on the first Pounds 2,000 of taxable income and excise duty changes. The bill is due to be debated in the Commons on June 2. Finance Bill. HMSO. Pounds 13.10. LABOUR is likely to raise the issue of stamp duty on house sales during discussion of the Finance Bill, Andrew Taylor and Alison Smith write. The move comes amid concern from housebuilders and estate agents that reintroducing stamp duty may halt a fragile recovery in the housing market when the concession ends in August. Industry leaders have been lobbying the government to try to get the concession on properties priced between Pounds 30,000 and Pounds 250,000 extended. The concession was introduced at the end of last year to encourage the housing market. Some Tory backbenchers have said that the government would find it difficult to re-impose the duty unless the housing market was showing clear signs of recovery. Treasury ministers have made clear that there is no question of extending the holiday.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / The Finance Bill: Ex-rebel is 'no sloppy interventionist' - The former health minister who will guide the proposals through the Commons
DOC.TEXT: THE Treasury is regarded as the rightwing redoubt of Mr John Major's government. Mr Norman Lamont, the chancellor, is as dry on economic policy as any member of the cabinet. Mr Michael Portillo, the chief secretary, is as close as anything the Thatcherite wing of the party has to an heir-apparent. But every rule has its exception. In the case of the Treasury it is Mr Stephen Dorrell. The financial secretary, charged over the next few weeks with piloting the Finance Bill through the Commons, is now firmly established among the rising stars in the middle ranks of Mr Major's administration. The responsibilities of the third-ranking member of the Treasury team include the detailed tax work involved in Budget-making along with a brief to give substance to Mr Major's pledge to create a nation of savers and share owners. He is also the minister directly responsible for privatisation, competition and de-regulation. More immediately, Mr Dorrell's oversight of the Civil Service means that he will have to grapple with what is shaping up as a bitter clash over pay with the Whitehall unions. His boyish looks belie a grasp of economics as well as politics that have allowed the 'wringing wet' rebel of the early 1980s to become the Treasury minister of the 1990s. If he proves his mettle over the next two or three years, the reward should be a place on the shortlist for the next batch of entrants to Mr Major's cabinet. It is quite a turnround for the 40-year-old MP for Loughborough, the youngest of the Tory arrivals at Westminster in 1979. He spent most of the first half of the 1980s rebelling against his government's economic strategy. He was once driven by Mrs Thatcher's faith in monetarism to describe his party as 'the better of two evils'. When Mrs Thatcher appointed him to the whips office in 1987, colleagues at Westminster saw it as an inexplicable act of forgiveness by the prime minister. Mr Dorrell, long an acolyte of Mr Peter Walker, is refreshingly unfussed about a past that embraced public opposition to Treasury cuts in unemployment benefit and repeated defiance of Mrs Thatcher's opposition to the European exchange rate mechanism. In the present government the latter view - which in 1986 prompted a public rebuke from Mrs Thatcher - has served to strengthen the relationship he forged with Mr Major during his spell as the whip responsible for Treasury affairs. Like most attached to the One-Nation strand of Toryism, the financial secretary's thoughts on economic policy have moved on: 'We all change, don't we, as we respond to new influences. So, yes, they (his opinions) have changed'. Not all. He is still firmly wedded to the concept of a welfare state that is more than a basic safety-net for the very poorest. 'I'm personally totally committed to the principle, for example, that health and education are services that we should seek to provide not as a safety net but as a universal service . . . and they don't come free.' As the former health minister who spent much of the past two years defending the NHS reforms, though, he is convinced that those services cannot be immune from the disciplines of the private sector. 'What we need to be doing is constantly testing which (public services) have to remain in the public sector and ensure that the efficiency of those which do remain there is constantly tested.' An official who worked with him attests that he is 'no sloppy interventionist'. A large shareholder in and former manager of his family's textile business, Mr Dorrell insists that he has always been committed to low direct taxation to sharpen the incentives that drive wealth creation. He insists that there is no contradiction between the government's pledge for better public services and his responsibilities as financial secre-tary to find new ways of reducing the tax burden. He displays little of the evangelical zeal of those in the party - including Mr Portillo - who believe that a renewed drive to cut income tax must be given priority over virtually all else. Pressed on the right balance between public spending and taxation, Mr Dorrell retreats to the pragmatic response that there is no 'final state of knowledge' on where the line should be drawn. He comments: 'Life isn't like that'. Closer to home, Mr Dorrell is cautious about how the government will live up to its promise to entrench the habit of saving among the less affluent as well as the wealthy. This year's finance bill is unspectacular in polit-ical terms, the left-overs Mr Dorrell's Treasury officials can be expected to explain that, even with the next budget still nine months off, it is not quite as easy as it looks to manipulate the tax system to turn us into a nation of savers. For now, he is reluctant to pre-empt anything that Mr Lamont might have in mind on the tax front. He is apparently unsure how to persuade a sceptical City to support the government's efforts to provide new incentives for individual shareholders. That should not prove too much of a handicap to a man who is as astute a politician as he is hard-working as a minister. It does no harm these days to be seen as the young face of Majorism.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / The Finance Bill: Capital gains to company cars: the bill in detail
DOC.TEXT: THE GOVERNMENT yesterday set out the policies and effects of the 69 clauses and 17 schedules of the Finance Bill. CUSTOMS AND EXCISE Abolition of fiscal frontiers: Clause 1 and Schedule 1 make provision for Customs to fix the point at which the requirement to pay excise duty takes effect. Clause 2 makes provision for Customs to repay excise duty where the commissioners are satisfied that goods chargeable with duty have not been, and will not be, consumed in the UK. Clause 3 and Schedule 2 are designed to protect the revenue derived from excise duties, for example ensuring that duty is payable when goods leave a warehouse and creating an offence of taking preparatory steps with a view to evasion of duty. Clause 4 limits Customs enforcement powers in relation to people or goods entering or leaving the UK, so as not to prevent, restrict or delay their movements between member states. Clause 5 enables Customs to exercise powers in relation to transfer passengers travelling by air when they reach their eventual UK destination. Other provisions: Clause 6 abolishes excise duty on matches and mechanical lighters. Clause 7 makes provision to exempt members' clubs and similar societies from liability to bingo duty. Clause 8 modifies arrangements for determining the recommended retail price on which the ad valorem element of cigarette duty is based. Clause 9 rectifies minor omissions in regulations that will, after introduction of the beer end-product duty system, make beer duty a preferential debt. Clause 11 sets rates of vehicle excise duty for classes of heavy goods vehicle which will be able to operate in the UK from January 1. Clause 12 repeals provisions relating to exemptions from vehicle excise duty for disabled people. Clause 13 makes minor changes to arrangements for special vehicle registration marks. VALUE ADDED TAX Clause 14 and Schedule 3 introduce changes to VAT law necessary for completion of the single market. Clause 15 ensures that matches remain chargeable with VAT at the standard rate when excise duty on matches is abolished. CAR TAX Clause 16 and Schedule 4 amend the Car Tax Act 1983 in preparation for completion of the single market. INCOME TAX, CORPORATION TAX, AND CAPITAL GAINS TAX Lower rate: Clause 17 makes technical consequential changes following the introduction of the 20p lower rate of income tax. Married couples allowance: Clause 18 and Schedule 5 set out arrangements for couples to agree to allocate the allowance to the wife or to share it or for the wife to opt for it to be split equally, with effect from April 6 1993. Corporation tax charge and rate: Clause 19 sets the main rate of corporation tax for the financial year 1992 at 33 per cent. Clause 20 sets the small companies' rate at 25 per cent. It also sets at one 50th the fraction used for calculating marginal relief for companies whose profits are in a band above the profits limit for the small companies rate. That will be equivalent to a marginal rate within the marginal relief band of 35 per cent. Capital gains tax: Clause 21 provides that, where appropriate, a rate equivalent to the lower rate of income tax will apply in charging an individual's gains to capital gains tax. Groups etc: Clause 22 and Schedule 6 amend the definition of share arrangements for group relief and other tax purposes. It treats options to buy and sell shares, in some circumstances, as if they had been exercised. Clause 23 makes minor changes to ensure that a company leaving a group cannot manipulate the provisions to avoid paying capital gains tax on certain assets previously transferred to it by other members of the group. Charities etc: Clause 24 reduces from Pounds 600 to Pounds 400 the minimum limit for charitable donations qualifying for tax relief under the Gift Aid scheme. Clause 25 relaxes the rules for tax relief for certain charitable covenants. Clause 26 extends the power for the Inland Revenue to inspect charities' records of Gift Aid donations. Interest, dividends and distributions: Clause 27 changes rules for including interest paid to people who are not ordinarily resident from returns to the Inland Revenue. Henceforth, separate declarations of non-ordinarily resident status will not be needed. Clause 26 is required to implement the EC parent/ subsidiary directive, which eliminates the double taxation of dividends and abolishes withholding taxes on them when they are paid to a parent company in another member state. The clause excludes from the charge on both paying and collecting agents' dividends paid by a company that is not resident in the UK to a company that is resident. Exclusion is subject to the latter company's controlling, either directly or indirectly, not less than 10 per cent of the voting power in the former company. Clause 29 amends requirements for companies providing vouchers for dividend payments, so that the shareholder will receive a voucher in all circumstances, including electronic transfer. Securities and deposits: Clause 30 and Schedule 7 take securities out of the charge on deep gain securities where they may deliver a deep gain only by operation of their event of default or event risk clauses. Clause 31 and Schedule 8 prepare for 'dematerialised' certificates of deposit under new arrangements that will eliminate in most cases the creation of paper certificates. Clauses 32, 33, 38 to 44 and 54 implement the EC mergers directive, which defers certain capital-gains charges that might otherwise arise on a cross-border reorganisation. Clause 32 brings capital gains provisions concerning share exchanges fully into conformity with the requirements of the directive. Employee shares: Clause 33 removes the tax charge that can arise on the trustees of an Employee Share Ownership Trust as a result of a share-for-share exchange. Clause 34 removes the charge to tax special benefits received by employee shareholders where benefits are available to at least 90 per cent of shareholders and a majority of shares are held by people who are not employees. Business expansion scheme: Clause 35 ends relief under the BES for shares in unquoted trading companies after the end of 1993. Clause 36 makes it easier for BES companies that raise money for private rented housing to have a property management subsidiary. Clause 37 makes it easier for them to operate mortgage rescue schemes. Transfers of trade: Clause 38 defers capital gains charges where a company resident in one member state transfers all or part of UK trading operations to a company resident in another member state in exchange for securities issued by the transferee company. Clauses 39 and 44 permit the UK to tax gains accruing where a UK resident company transfers a branch or agency situated in another member state to a company resident in a third member state. Relief will be given for any tax that, but for the EC Mergers Directive, would have been payable in the member state where the branch or agency is situated. Clause 40 introduces amendments to the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 consequential upon Clauses 38 and 39. Clause 41 replicates the relief available under Clause 38. Clause 42 replicates the relief available under Clause 39. Clause 43 is consequent upon Clauses 41 and 42. Double taxation relief: Clause 44 in relation to Clauses 39 and 42, provides for double taxation relief on the basis of the tax that would, but for the Mergers Directive, have been payable in the member state where the branch or agency is situated. Clause 45 contains provisions necessary to implement the EC Arbitration Convention, which sets up a mechanism for resolving transfer pricing disputes within the Community. Miscellaneous: Clause 46 introduces lower car fuel scale charges to tax the benefit of free diesel fuel provided by employers for employees' private use in company cars. Clause 47 brings the activity of transporting oil or gas directly abroad from an offshore field within the corporation tax 'ring fence', so that the relevant costs may offset companies' UK oil production profits. Clause 48 and Schedule 9 extend to a friendly society incorporated under the Friendly Societies Act 1992 tax exemptions currently available to unincorporated societies registered under the 1974 Friendly Societies Act. Clause 49 changes, in certain circumstances, the rules for charging rent to income and corporation tax in order to prevent manipulation of those rules to secure a tax deferment. From March 10, where rent is payable in arrears - directly or indirectly - between connected persons, the recipient will be chargeable to tax in a particular chargeable period on the rent that has accrued in that period, and not as at present on the rent the recipient was entitled to receive in that period. Clause 50 modifies, from a date to be appointed, the tax treatment of maintenance payments to take account of the Child Support Agency. Clause 51 and Schedule 10 alter the arrangements for accounting for tax deducted by paying and collecting agents (mainly banks end stockbrokers) from foreign dividends and interest. From October 1 1992 the tax is to be paid to the Inland Revenue within 14 days of the end of the month in which it is deducted. The schedule also abolishes the statutory remuneration agents receive from the Inland Revenue. Clause 52 confirms rates of tax charged on building societies, banks and other deposit takers under the former composite rate tax arrangements for the years 1986-87 to 1989-90. Clause 53 and schedule 11 make tax changes affecting insolvent companies in compulsory liquidation that were carrying on a deposit-taking business. Losses brought forward and certain expenses can be offset against income arising from the trade after it has ceased. CAPITAL ALLOWANCES Clause 54 defers capital allowance balancing charges and other balancing adjustments where Clauses 39 and 41 apply. Clause 55 provides for relief for capital expenditure on computer software. Clause 56 and Schedule 12 amend capital allowances legislation applying to expenditure on buildings constructed in enterprise zones. The Schedule remedies a defect in existing legislation that denies enterprise zone allowances to a purchaser of an unused building who buys it after expiry of the 10-year life of the zone. It also provides that allowances will be available on buildings sold within two years of being brought into use. It restricts enterprise zone allowances to expenditure incurred within 10 years of the expiry of the zone. Clause 57 increases from Pounds 8,000 to Pounds 12,000 the limit on the cost of business cars above which capital allowances and tax relief for lease rentals are restricted. Inheritance tax: Clause 58 increases the starting point for inheritance tax to Pounds 150,000. Clause 59 and Schedule 13 make changes to the rates of relief from inheritance tax for certain business assets and farmland - the higher rate from 50 per cent to 100 per cent, the lower rate from 30 per cent to 50 per cent. Shares dealt on the Unlisted Securities Market are treated as unquoted for the purpose of the relief. Petroleum revenue tax: Clause 60 and Schedule 14 provide petroleum revenue tax relief for transporting oil or gas directly abroad from an offshore field and make various consequential changes to the PRT rules. General and special commissioners: Clause 61 allows the lord chancellor to change the names of tribunals that hear tax appeals. Clause 62 and Schedule 15 allow the lord chancellor to introduce procedural rules for hearing tax appeals. Those are planned to came into effect in April 1993. They will include powers for the special commissioners to award costs where either party has acted unreasonably, and to publish selected decisions. Miscellaneous: Clause 63 and Schedule 16 provide for continuity of tax treatment of Northern Ireland Electricity. on pre-privatisation and reorganisation into successor companies. Clause 64 removes the double charge to gas levy and PRT that would otherwise arise when a PRT-exempt contract for sale of North Sea gas ends at a fixed date predetermined in the contract. Clause 65 amends Section 8 of the Treasury Bills Act 1977 to remove the requirement that Treasury bills be countersigned by the comptroller and auditor-general, bringing them into line with other government debt instruments. Clause 66 removes the requirement to publish National Loans Fund and Public Works Loan Board interest rates in London and Edinburgh Gazette each time they are changed.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / CBI calls for series of interest rate cuts
DOC.TEXT: THE Confederation of British Industry yesterday called on the government to pursue small but regular reductions in interest rates. It suggested they might soon be capable of falling below those of Germany. The CBI said further cuts in the cost of money would be possible without prejudicing the UK's position in the exchange rate mechanism if Britain's improved performance on inflation continued. The organisation emphasised the need for caution but said interest rates could be cut in the short term by as little as a quarter of 1 percentage point to 'test the water' in foreign exchange markets. Sir David Lees, chairman of the CBI's economic and finance policy committee, told the organisation's governing council that continued cuts in interest rates were the most important step towards encouraging the economic recovery that appeared likely in the rest of the year. Sir David said the CBI wanted to see sterling join the narrow bands of the ERM, but there was no immediate pressure to do so, given the progress made in cutting interest rates and the prospective improvement in UK competitiveness in Europe. Sir David emphasised that headline inflation in the UK was already below that of Germany, where it was on a rising trend. He stressed that a change of perception would be needed to establish the view that UK interest rates could be below those of Germany. There was, he added, some evidence that that was already taking place, but it could be easily jeopardised by 'too hasty an approach to interest rate reductions'. Sir Michael Angus, who retired as chairman of Unilever two weeks ago, was yesterday elected president of the CBI for the next two years, succeeding Sir Brian Corby.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Teacher vacancies well down
DOC.TEXT: THE NUMBER of teacher vacancies in England is sharply down on last year according to government figures released yesterday. The overall vacancy rate has fallen by nearly two thirds since last year - from 1.5 per cent of all posts to 0.6 per cent - taking the number of unfilled posts to 1,955. Overall teacher numbers are slightly up at 394,000. The altered trend is particularly marked in London, where the vacancy rate has fallen to 1 per cent, its lowest since 1988 - and the lowest for secondary schools since 1984. Vacancies in science subjects fell by two thirds, but the decline in other shortage subjects was below par. Maths vacancies were down by half, and unfilled posts in modern languages declined by only a third. High levels of graduate unemployment account partly for the renewed attraction of teaching, but substantial real pay increases in the past two years, and promotion and bursary schemes to attract students in shortage subjects, may also have made an impact. Lady Blatch, schools minister, said: 'Any lingering claims that the national curriculum cannot be delivered in full because of teacher shortages should now fade away.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / 'Signs of life' in housing
DOC.TEXT: THERE has been a widespread increase in confidence among potential house buyers and sellers since the general election, according to a survey of almost 100 English and Welsh estate agents, published today. The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors, which conducted the survey, said the number of people making inquiries about properties for sale has risen since polling day. 'The clearest signs of recovery are coming from East Anglia, where increased sales are reported, particularly in Norwich and Peterborough,' it said. 'The London housing market, worst hit by the property slump, also shows greater signs of life, with more people house hunting and a detectable rise in optimism. After several false starts, a recovery in the housing market is at last within sight.' The institution warned that it would take a long time before house sales returned to normal levels. The survey said 30 per cent of agents reported price falls in the three months to the end of April, compared with 68 per cent who said prices had remained static. Most agents expect prices to lag, even if sales increase this year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Rare fine art finds healthy market: Saleroom
DOC.TEXT: THE WORLD'S fine art markets are in overdrive this week, with important sales in London, New York, Geneva and Madrid. The results have been generally encouraging, with collectors competing for rare and exceptional works of art. At Christie's in London yesterday, The Camerarius Florilegium, an exceptionally rare manuscript, sold for Pounds 638,000 - comfortably above its high estimate of Pounds 500,000. The manuscript depicts 473 ornamental plants and 194 leaves that were in the garden of the German botanist Joachim Camerarius in the late 16th century. It is the only known surviving record of the contents of a garden of this period. The buyer was the Oxford dealer Rosenthal, bidding on behalf of a continental European - presumably German - institution. In New York, Christie's sold the late Mr Bill McCarty-Cooper's collection of tribal art. Mr McCarty-Cooper had been adopted at the age of 36 by Mr Douglas Cooper, who possessed one of the finest collections of 20th century French art. Under his influence, Mr McCarty-Cooper assembled an excellent collection of tribal art, which raised Dollars 3.27m (Pounds 1.8m) on Tuesday, with 11 per cent unsold. A Fang male reliquary figure, 19 3/4 in high, carved about a century ago in what is now Gabon in Equatorial Africa, sold for Dollars 550,000, at the bottom of its estimate. A rarer Fang female reliquary figure beat its target at Dollars 440,000. Pacific art was the most sought-after sector and a Fijian headrest, estimated at up to Dollars 20,000, sold for Dollars 77,000. Sotheby's noticed Colombian bidders for the first time at its auction of Latin American art in New York. This has been a strong market for the past two years, but on Tuesday some of the leading artists, including Botero, Matta and Lam, were out of favour. The Mexican Diego Rivera remains popular, though, and his Mujer con Alcatraces, depicting a peasant clutching a vast bunch of lilies, sold for Dollars 2.8m (Pounds 1.5m), the second-highest auction price paid for Rivera, indeed for any Latin American painting. The sale totalled Dollars 7.5m (Pounds 4.1m) but was 34 per cent unsold. Edmund Peel in Madrid had mixed success with his auction of Spanish Old Masters. A Goya portrait was unsold at Pounds 1.15m - although there were hopes of a deal after the auction - but a still life of flowers by Juan de Arellano made a record Pounds 673,000. A Gainsborough drawing owned by the late Lord Clark is to be sold at Christie's on July 14. A Peasant Family Going to Market is estimated at up to Pounds 400,000, but may approach the record Pounds 616,000, which Christie's set for a Gainsborough drawing last year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / BNFL to cut further 550 jobs
DOC.BYLINE: By IAN HAMILTON FAZEY, Northern Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: BRITISH Nuclear Fuels (BNFL) is to shed at least 550 jobs at its Capenhurst uranium enrichment plant, in north-west England, because of the collapse of the world market since the cold war ended. The job losses are in addition to 400 last year, and a further 500 jobs are under threat because of technological improvements. BNFL also announced plans to sell enriched uranium worldwide through a new joint venture with counterparts in the Netherlands and Germany. Enriched uranium has been treated to increase the proportion of uranium-235, the isotope that sustains chain reactions. BNFL produces U-235 by turning uranium into a gas, then centrifuging out the heavier atoms of the unwanted U-238 isotope. Enriched uranium is used in nuclear power station reactor rods and for military purposes. The end of the cold war has cut military requirements and opened the world market for reactor rods to Russian producers with low labour costs. BNFL said yesterday: 'There is now worldwide oversupply and the competition is becoming cut-throat.' BNFL, a public limited company with the government as its sole shareholder, said it would have lost Pounds 6m in the current year had it tried to carry on. It is negotiating to convert Urenco, its partnership with Ultra-Centrifuge Nederland, of Almelo, and Uran-Isotopentrennungs Gesellschaft, of Julich, Germany, into a company. Urenco was formed in 1971 after the British, Netherlands and West German governments agreed to co-operate on commercial exploitation of the gas centrifuge process. Ownership of the new venture will be split equally. Capenhurst's military and civil uranium enrichment operations are being split, with 600 staff being temporarily 'parked' in a new subsidiary until they can be transferred to the European company. The other 550 staff will stay with BNFL to dismantle and decommission Capenhurst's old diffusion plant and carry on making enriched uranium for the Ministry of Defence until the contract to do so expires next year. Fewer than 100 people are likely to be needed at Capenhurst in five years, when Urenco should have developed new, labour-saving technology.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Bank seeks tougher standards
DOC.TEXT: THE Bank of England is pressing for a change in international banking regulations to ban banks from branching outside their home countries if they fail to meet certain standards. The Bank's tough stance in talks with other regulators on the Basle Committee for Banking Supervision emerged yesterday when the Bank published its annual report and a separate report of its supervisory activities. It is understood that Mr Brian Quinn, the Bank's representative on the Basle committee, hopes that by the end of the year bank supervisors from the big industrial countries will have agreed to radical changes in the 1983 Basle Concordat, which lays down a regulatory framework. Mr Quinn is believed to support a proposal that bank supervisors should ban bank branches from their countries if the branches' owner fails to meet standards laid down in the concordat. In the wake of last year's closure of Bank of Credit and Commerce International, a change in the concordat is likely to be that international banks should submit to being regulated worldwide by at least one supervisory authority. A second change to the concordat would be that banks must meet the international capital adequacy standard, the Basle ratio, intended to ensure that banks are robust enough to withstand shocks. The Bank's reports contain much information on its work and views. Highlights include: The Bank criticises the 'lending criteria' observed in the 1980s. UK banks expanded their lending portfolios very rapidly in that period and have recently suffered big losses on those loans. The Bank says it has encouraged UK banks to review their procedures for making loans. However, it is adamant that in a market environment it would have been inappropriate to prevent the banks from making such mistakes. It discloses that it became concerned last year that small banks might run into serious difficulties. Many small banks' access to liquid funds became severely reduced because local authorities, public-sector corporations and other professional investors transferred their deposits to bigger banks. They made the transfers because of fears that small banks might fail as a result of big losses on loans. Their concerns became even greater after the closure of BCCI. The Bank of England kept a very close watch on the small banks in this period and believes they handled the crisis prudently. A few decided to wind down their business in an orderly way and all were urged by the Bank to explore whether they could reduce dependence on volatile sources of deposits. The Bank made an operating profit of Pounds 166m in the year to February 29 1992, 3 per cent up on the previous year. From that it paid the UK Treasury Pounds 67.6m, down from Pounds 81.5m. The number of authorised banking institutions operating in London fell from 530 to 518. The Bank of England revoked the banking licence of only one institution, BCCI. The fall in authorisations was the result in part of mergers of banks and reorganisations of international banking groups. The Bank reiterates its view that the banks do not operate a cartel in the small-business loan market. Nevertheless, it is concerned that small-business customers may find it difficult to shop around for a new bank because of technical difficulties in terminating an existing bank relationship. However, the Bank believes that competition in the small-business loan market has increased greatly in the past decade, with the entry into the market of TSB Group and foreign banks and the growth of the Scottish clearing banks. It has given those views to the Office of Fair Trading, which is deciding whether Lloyds Bank's proposed bid for Midland Bank should be referred to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission. The Bank gives aggregated figures for the trading results of the big UK banks - Barclays, National Westminster, Lloyds, Midland, Standard Chartered, Royal Bank of Scotland, Bank of Scotland and TSB Group. They show that the banks collectively made record provisions to cover losses on loans of Pounds 6.8bn, up from Pounds 4.1bn in 1990. The running costs of the banks as a percentage of total income fell, ending a trend which began in 1985. USE of the Pounds 20 note is increasing rapidly, according to the Bank of England's annual report. In the past year, 489m Pounds 20 notes were issued, compared with 252m the previous year. The Pounds 10 note remains the most commonly issued denomination, with Pounds 5.74bn worth of them in circulation, compared with Pounds 5.29bn for the Pounds 20 note.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Retail sales in April show modest rise
DOC.TEXT: HIGH STREET sales rose modestly in April, suggesting that consumers returned to the shops after the election - but not in large numbers. The volume of retail sales in April grew by 0.8 per cent compared with March. City analysts had been looking for more robust figures after a late Easter and widespread claims of a spending surge after the election. Although April's figure was slightly disappointing, it followed a revised 1 per cent fall in sales recorded in March. The three-monthly trend continued to show volumes of sales still declining. In the three months to April, retail sales fell by 0.3 per cent compared with the previous three months. Compared with a year ago, the volume of sales fell by 0.5 per cent. Evidence that consumers are feeling more confident is gradually gathering strength. Earlier this week, the Confederation of British Industry reported the highest retail sales for two years in its quarterly survey of the distributive trades industry. The Treasury said the April figure was mainly a rebound from the fall in March, and more evidence was needed to assess the exact state of consumer demand in the post-election period. According to yesterday's figures from the Central Statistical Office, sales by food retailers rose 0.2 per cent in the three months to April and those by mixed retailers 0.1 per cent. Sales by non-food retailers fell 0.6 per cent. In the non-food sector, however, sales of household goods rose 2 per cent in the latest three months and were up 1 per cent compared with the same period a year before. Clothing and footwear sales fell 3 per cent in the latest three months compared with the three months to January. In value terms, sales in the four-week April period totalled a non-seasonally adjusted Pounds 10.5bn, which was 4 per cent higher than a year earlier. Mr Bill Martin, chief UK economist at UBS Phillips & Drew, said yesterday's figures reinforced his view that consumer demand would be exceedingly slow to revive. Yesterday's figures were the first since measures designed to improve the accuracy of economic statistics were introduced by the CSO. Previously, 3,500 retailers supplied data on a voluntary basis, but 5,000 are now obliged to respond.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Lamont entered BCCI row
DOC.TEXT: MR NORMAN LAMONT, the chancellor, was forced to intervene in a dispute relating to the defunct Bank for Credit and Commerce International between members of the Bank of England's board of banking supervision, it was disclosed yesterday, Robert Peston writes. The lay members of the board were concerned that Mr Robin Leigh-Pemberton, the Bank's governor, was likely to breach banking secrecy standards when being interviewed last year about the collapse of BCCI by the Commons Treasury and Civil Service Committee. After widespread criticism, Mr Leigh-Pemberton wanted to give a detailed account of the Bank's role to the committee. The board's lay members felt that Mr Leigh-Pemberton was proposing to disclose more than was allowable under the Banking Act. The board's function is to review all aspects of the Bank's supervisory work under the act. The chancellor was called to adjudicate on the issue. In the event, he backed Mr Leigh-Pemberton, who on July 26 submitted to questioning by the Commons committee. It was the first time in the board's four-year existence that the chancellor had been called to settle such a dispute. The incident is alluded to in an annexe to the Bank of England's Banking Act report - in which every year it discusses its role as a supervisor - which was published yesterday. In the Bank's annual report, also published yesterday, Mr Leigh Pemberton said he believed the Bank's decision not to close BCCI till last year - and all its other actions over the years as supervisor of UK operations - were 'correct at the time they were taken'. The annual statement of the Deposit Protection Board, which is linked to the Bank of England and provides insurance against possible losses to holders of bank deposits, was also released. The board said it had increased its borrowing powers to Pounds 125m in order to meet claims for compensation from depositors at BCCI's UK offshoot. The Bank expects the board to have to pay out no more than Pounds 95m to BCCI depositors.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / SRO is named
DOC.TEXT: THE proposed new self-regulatory organisation for retail investment business is to be named the Personal Investment Authority.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Satellite TV sales 'overstated'
DOC.TEXT: THE SIZE of the satellite television market in the UK has been significantly overstated, according to a report. GFK Home Audit, a market-research company, says 1.6m homes had satellite television by the end of last year. That figure compares with the 1.8m estimate by Barb, which produces the official viewing figures, and a figure of 2.1m quoted by Continental Research, a research company regularly quoted by the Financial Times and British Sky Broadcasting, the satellite television network in which Pearson, owner of the Financial Times, has a stake, The GFK figure was based on interviews with 10,000 people last June and updated with data from GFK Lek-Trak, which monitors more than 8,000 electrical retailers. GFK Home Audit Report. Tel. 0932 354911. Pounds 500 plus VAT.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Tory MP Names attack Lloyd's
DOC.BYLINE: By DAVID OWEN and RICHARD LAPPER
DOC.TEXT: A GROUP of Tory back-benchers called yesterday for criminal proceedings 'if and where necessary' against any malpractice at the Lloyd's insurance market, David Owen and Richard Lapper write. The four MPs, three of whom are Names at Lloyd's, included Mr Paul Marland, MP for Gloucestershire West. They met Mr Neil Hamilton, a junior trade and industry minister, and urged independent regulation of Lloyd's. They also argued that the authorities at the market were failing to honour the Lloyd's Act because they were not looking after the interests of outside Names. Names are the individuals whose assets back underwriting at the market. The trade and industry department described Mr Hamilton's meeting with MPs and a subsequent meeting with Mr David Coleridge, Lloyd's chairman, as 'essentially a listening exercise'. The MPs left Mr Hamilton with detailed questions about Lloyd's, and suggested that he put them to Mr Coleridge. Their questions covered Lloyd's brokerage charges and costs and the solvency of the market. They asked if the Lloyd's central fund was still adequate to cover all Lloyd's cashflow difficulties in the light of the forthcoming judicial review (being pursued by some Names). Mr Marland yesterday tabled a Commons early day motion alleging that professionals at Lloyd's had 'favoured themselves and their close relations' as well as other Lloyd's professionals by 'placing their own business on highly profitable and safe syndicates ahead of outside Names'. The motion mentions five leading professionals and notes that none is a member of any of the catastrophe reinsurance syndicates managed by such agencies as Gooda Walker, Feltrim, Devonshire and Rose Thompson Young. It says, however, that some of the five placed external Names on those syndicates. The five are Mr Coleridge, chairman of Lloyd's and of the Sturge agency; Mr JM Donner, chairman of Donner Underwriting; Sir Peter Miller, chairman of Thomas R. Miller; Mr JP Tilling, chairman of Gravett and Tilling; and Mr Murray Lawrence, chairman of Murray Lawrence Members' Agency. SG Warburg, the merchant bank, confirmed yesterday that it had been appointed by Lloyd's to advise on 'narrow technical issues' arising from work under way on a plan to help Names hardest hit by recent losses. Warburg said yesterday that it was not playing a broad advisory role but would be assisting on an ad hoc basis. Lloyd's appointed the bank earlier this month. Mr Alan Lord, Lloyd's chief executive, announced at the end of April that it was examining the possibility of providing financial assistance to Names facing severe underwriting losses.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Housing may be cut from RPI
DOC.TEXT: HOUSING costs may disappear from the retail prices index if Britain is to bring its measure of inflation more closely into harmony with other European Community countries. Half the EC's member states make no allowance for housing costs in their calculations of the main inflation rate - only the UK and Ireland include mortgage interest payments. Other countries, such as Germany, measure home-owning housing costs with an 'imputed rent' system - the cost is treated as if the properties had been rented. That approach was used in Britain until 1975 but dropped because the private rented sector was too small and unrepresentative a market on which to base the housing costs of most of the population. At the International Conference of Labour Statisticians in 1987, the International Labour Organisation recommended that countries should provide an all-items index that excludes shelter in order to ease international comparisons. The ILO said that although the exclusion of shelter from the all-items index would not eliminate all the differences encountered when making such comparisons, it would make rates of price change more comparable across countries. The recommendation stemmed partly from concerns about the different methodologies used to calculate housing costs, but another concern was that housing markets were distinctive to different countries. Whether because of rental controls or tax incentives, markets did not behave in an identical manner. Although Eurostat, the EC's statistical office, has looked at the issue of the harmonisation of inflation measures across the EC, little has yet been heard of any definite proposals. A report published by Eurostat in 1989 suggested that imputed rents could be used as the yardstick for measuring owner-occupiers' housing costs.
