The Confederation of British Industry, which criticises the inclusion of mortgage interest payments in the calculation of the RPI, says that would not be difficult to implement in the UK, since imputed rents are already used in the UK's national accounts for measuring owner-occupiers' housing costs.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / A pervasive influence on the economy: The impact of the retail prices index and the way in which it is calculated
DOC.TEXT: THE RETAIL Prices Index has become a pervasive influence in many aspects of the British economy. That is in spite of the existence of various other measures of inflation - such as the GDP deflator, the producer price index for manufactured goods and the pensioner price index - which may have theoretical advantages or be more suited to particular purposes. The RPI has become the dominant measure because it is rapidly available (by about the middle of the next month), is adjusted in scope to reflect changing spending patterns and is protected from undue political interference by an advisory committee that includes independent members. The RPI has an unrivalled effect on the level of pay increases - the average level of pay rises is invariably close to the latest inflation rate. Many wage bargainers, particularly among trade unions, would resist reforming the RPI, but they would probably have little option but to continue to use it as the main yardstick in negotiations. Mr Norman Willis, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, said yesterday: 'Mortgage rates are part of the cost of living. If costs go up and are not reflected in the RPI then that would produce a horse laugh.' But Mr Alastair Hatchett, of the Incomes Data Services pay research group, believes negotiators would use the official RPI, however it was calculated. Mr Peter Ball, deputy director-general of the Engineering Employers Federation, said: 'There would be a lot of hot air spoken if the formula changed but eventually people would follow it.' A change in the RPI calculation would present difficulties for a sizeable minority of companies that have negotiated long-term pay deals linked to inflation. Those are far less popular than they were in the late 1980s, but most car manufacturers, including Ford and Vauxhall, still favour two-year deals, as do British Airways and the Civil Aviation Authority. If the method of calculation were to change, there might be argument in some companies over what the second-year rise should be. Mr Hatchett said clauses laying down that inflation would be as calculated at the time of the agreement were likely to grow in popularity, but would be based on the assumption that the RPI as currently constituted would still be available - which was by no means certain. A potentially sensitive area is the impact of RPI changes on social security benefits, including state pensions, unemployment benefit, income support and housing benefit, which are upgraded annually according to the RPI. Any suggestion that the government was trying to suppress statistical evidence of rises in living costs would create a political storm. But in some respects an index excluding mortgage interest would be a more suitable determinant of the level of social security benefits. Regulation of utility prices has also become an important area for the application of the RPI. It forms the benchmark for regulating BT's main prices, for example. The price formulae are being reviewed by Oftel, the telecommunications regulatory body, but it is almost certain that the RPI will continue as the benchmark. Oftel has resisted switching to another index, arguing that RPI is the only inflation measure widely understood. BT and Oftel had no comment yesterday on the merits of excluding mortgage interest payments from the RPI. It is thought, though, that in the long run such a change would have little effect on the company's finances. Ofgas, the industry regulator that devised the formula controlling British Gas's price rises to domestic customers, said it was unlikely to revise the formula if the RPI figure was calculated differently. The RPI similarly plays a central role in the complex formula used for water charges. The Office of Water Services said it was assumed that water companies would have to take account of any new method of calculating the RPI before deciding charges. Investments such as index-linked gilts depend on the RPI for their value. Index-linked gilts showed modest gains in prices yesterday, as investors reacted to the possibility of the proposed change - both the repayment value and the interest on the gilts are linked to changes in the RPI. Prospectuses for index-linked issues have a clause saying that, in the event of a 'fundamental change' in the calculation of the RPI which would have a 'materially detrimental effect' on stockholders, the stock might have to be redeemed. Since the index-linked issues currently trade at a discount to their inflation-adjusted value, that would be expensive for the government. According to the Bank of England there are about Pounds 19bn of index-linked gilts in issue. Since prices excluding mortgage costs are rising faster than the RPI, it would be hard to argue that a change would be 'materially detrimental'. National Savings said its index-linked savings certificates, which rise according to the RPI, would simply adjust to reflect any change in the index's constituents. Indexation clauses also crop up in occupational pensions legislation. Limited price indexation - inflation-proofing parallel with the RPI with a ceiling of 5 per cent - applies to deferred pensions payable to workers who leave a company before retirement age. The same protection will one day be applicable to pensions in payment - legislation is on the statute book but has not yet been implemented. There is a pensioner price index that excludes housing and has consequently been rising more rapidly than the RPI recently. This PPI is not applied to pension benefit, although the changes might mean it would move more closely in line with the RPI. Additional reporting by Philip Coggan, Michael Smith, Hugo Dixon, Richard Evans and Neil Buckley

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Threat to maternity-benefits plan
DOC.TEXT: A VOTE by the European parliament to give women throughout the EC at least 14 weeks maternity leave at 80 per cent of pay is likely to be overturned by European social affairs ministers next month, Mrs Gillian Shephard, employment secretary, indicated yesterday The UK objects to the scale of the maternity benefits voted for by the European parliament earlier this month. The government is prepared, however, to accept reduced maternity payments equivalent to the level of sick pay. In theory, the social affairs council of ministers may attempt to push through the higher level of benefits on a qualified majority vote. To do so might, however, jeopardise a compromise Mrs Shephard is offering on measures to curb the working week. The European Commission's working-time directive would mean a maximum 48-hour week - a ceiling unacceptable to the UK. Mrs Shephard says she would now accept amendments enabling workers to choose to work more than 48 hours if they want to. The issue is also due to be discussed by the social affairs council next month. On the maternity benefits proposals, Mrs Shephard said she had met Mr Jose da Silva Peneda, president of the EC social affairs council, in London on Tuesday. He had given his backing to the UK's position on the level of benefits, she said. Long negotiations on levels of maternity benefits were concluded at the end of last year at the social affairs council. A delicate compromise of 14 weeks benefit at sick-pay levels was finally agreed, although the UK abstained because it objected to the issue's being treated as a health and safety matter and therefore subject to qualified majority voting. That compromise has now been upset by the higher level of benefit voted for by the European parliament. Present UK maternity benefits provide for six weeks pay at 90 per cent of earnings plus 12 weeks at sick pay rates of about Pounds 45 a week. However, the only women to qualify for those full rates are those who have worked for the same employer for at least two years by the 15th week before the birth. The EC rules would cut the qualifying period to 12 months.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Sir Peter Gregson: Correction
DOC.TEXT: IN A LIST of top civil servants, on Page 12 of yesterday's Financial Times, a picture of Lord Gregson incorrectly accompanied an item about Sir Peter Gregson, permanent secretary to the Department of Trade and Industry.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / OFT condemns secrecy in credit decisions
DOC.TEXT: LENDERS should be required to tell would-be borrowers why they have been rejected, the Office of Fair Trading said yesterday. It said it would consider whether legislation was needed if lenders could not agree on a voluntary disclosure format. The OFT added in a comprehensive report on the practice of credit scoring that it would consult the credit industry on a format to let customers know why their requests for credit had been refused. 'Should it prove impossible to implement this change by voluntary agreement, the office will consider whether a legislative solution is appropriate,' the OFT said. Credit scoring systems allocate points to various characteristics of a potential borrower. The characteristics, which include age, occupation and residential status, are meant to have a correlation with an individual's likelihood of repaying credit. While bank and building society lenders usually inform applicants that they have been refused credit on the basis of a previous adverse credit report, they do not specify what the decision is based on. The British Bankers' Association called the OFT's report 'a very balanced contribution to the discussions'. It said, however, that lenders were reluctant to tell those rejected for credit on the basis of low credit scores the specific reasons for the decision. For one thing, it said, such information could assist a subsequent fraudulent application. Also, a low score often reflects several factors and those may be known only to the credit scorer, often an outside company. Sir Gordon Borrie, OFT director-general of fair trading, said the confusion and secrecy of the credit process was itself evidence of a difficulty. 'Of course, lenders have the right to decide whether or not to grant credit,' he said. 'But that right does not justify secrecy in the decision-making process beyond the need for lenders to protect themselves from fraud.' In its report, the OFT rejected the assertion that providing more information would encourage fraud. It cited the US Equal Opportunity Credit Act, which for years has allowed rejected credit applicants to learn the basis of lenders' decisions, and said there was very little evidence that those reports had led to fraud. The US experience also suggested that it would be fairly easy to develop software packages that will help lenders to inform credit applicants of the reasons for their low credit score. The OFT urged lenders to develop methods to detect incorrect information, to offer applicants a simple explanation of how credit scoring works and to give information about appeal procedures to those who have been rejected.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Nissan UK chiefs sent for trial
DOC.TEXT: TWO SENIOR executives of Nissan UK charged with multi-million-pound tax evasion were yesterday sent to the Old Bailey for trial. Mr Michael Hunt, 58, assistant managing director and deputy chairman of the former importer-distributor of Nissan vehicles, and Mr Frank Shannon, also 58, the company's finance director, are alleged to have cheated the Inland Revenue out of Pounds 170m. It is alleged that the money found its way to them after false invoices were filed for freight payments. Magistrates at Worthing, West Sussex, committed the men for trial at the Central Criminal Court. Mr Hunt, of Hove, East Sussex, and Mr Shannon, of Brighton, East Sussex, were remanded on conditional bail until the trial. Mr Hunt was granted bail on condition that he lives at his present address and gives the Inland Revenue 72 hours notice if he travels abroad. He has also given the court sureties of Pounds 200,000. Mr Shannon was granted bail on the same conditions and his sureties were worth Pounds 225,000.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / TUC threatens to bar AEEU entry
DOC.TEXT: THE Amalgamated Engin-eering and Electrical Union will be told today that it will be unable to affiliate to the Trades Union Congress if it goes ahead with a merger between its electrical section and the breakaway union Cabin Crew 89. Mr Norman Willis, TUC general secretary, and Mr Rodney Bickerstaffe, TUC president, will tell AEEU leaders that affiliated unions should not associate with breakaway unions. Cabin Crew 89 was formed three years ago by 5,000 former members of the TGWU general workers' union. Mr Bill Morris, TGWU general secretary, has said that the TGWU will leave the TUC if the merger between Cabin Crew and the EETPU electrical section of the AEEU goes ahead. Talks between the EETPU and Cabin Crew began before the electricians merged with the AEU engineering workers at the start of this month. Although most AEU executive members would be against a Cabin Crew merger, Mr Paul Gallagher, EETPU general secretary, said last week that he would not allow other unions to run AEEU affairs. The talks were already likely to be tortuous before the Cabin Crew issue emerged. Since the EETPU was expelled from the TUC in 1988, it has merged with several breakaways from unions, most of which want their former members back. Moreover, leaders of both the AEU and the EETPU had questioned the value of TUC affiliation. AEEU leaders have agreed not to go ahead with the Cabin Crew merger while TUC discussions continue. However, a merger is not possible until later in the year because Cabin Crew will have to ballot its members about the move. Mr Gavin Laird, AEEU general secretary, who will attend today's talks, said yesterday he was anxious to create a climate that would enable the EETPU to rejoin the TUC. The leadership of the Balpa airline pilots' union is to be contested between Mr Chris Darke, who has been recommended for the general secretary's job by the union's executive, and Mr David Lebrecht, an assistant general secretary.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Shephard creates women's policy unit
DOC.TEXT: MRS GILLIAN SHEPHARD, the employment secretary, yesterday announced the creation of a group to advise her on women's issues. Its first task will be preparing to carry out the manifesto pledge on after-school and holiday child care. She said the schemes would be set up through the Training and Enterprise Councils, and emphasised that the approach to dealing with barriers to women at work would be through persuasion. 'I don't think compulsion; legislation; extra burdens do anything to help the cause of women,' Mrs Shephard said. She did, however, indicate that she had already talked to the Equal Opportunities Commission, and would look at its conclusions on how existing legislation was unsatisfactory. A cabinet committee on women's issues will be created from the ashes of the former ministerial group on the subject. Members of the group to advise Mrs Shephard are: Lady Elspeth Howe; Ms Joanna Foster, who chairs the EOC; Ms Sue Slipman, director of the Council for One-Parent Families; Baroness Denton, a trade and industry minister; Ms Sue Rostad, chairman and managing director of Poppies UK, a franchise cleaning company; Mr Peter Davis, chairman and chief executive of Reed International; Ms Sheila Forbes, group personnel director of Storehouse; Ms Kay Coleman, chief executive of Harvey's & Co (Clothing); Mr Graham Millar, managing director of Rowntree Mackintosh Confectionery; Dr Susan MacRae, senior fellow of the Policy Studies Institute; Sir Bryan Nicholson, chairman and chief executive of the Post Office; and Ms Margaret Seymour, who runs Seymour Swimming Pool Engineers.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Momentum of recovery still in doubt: The strength of upturn from economic recession in the US
DOC.TEXT: FEW US forecasters envisage a repeat of last year, when a promising economic recovery unexpectedly ground to a halt late in the summer. That said, this week's report of a 17 per cent fall in housing starts in the single month of April is not the kind of statistic destined to bolster confidence in the economy's underlying momentum. The drop in starts was partly a reaction to strong advances in preceding months. But it was much more severe than expected, and by no means the only discouraging news. Consumer confidence and car sales are still depressed; claims for state unemployment insurance remain stubbornly high. The Federal Reserve, meanwhile, is again embarrassed by sluggish monetary growth, a problem that has plagued it for two years. M2, the main measure of broad money, is only just above the lower limit of its 2.5-6.5 per cent growth target. The signs of continuing fragility are offset by positive indicators, such as last week's report of a solid rise in industrial production in April, the third consecutive monthly gain. Employment and retail sales have also risen substantially since the year began. Few economists are thus inclined to revise their forecasts, which mostly point to growth of about 3 per cent at an annual rate in the second half of the year. But the negative indicators are fuelling demands that the Fed buy a little extra insurance by nudging the federal funds rate (the cost of money in the interbank market) a quarter-point lower, to 3.5 per cent. A move in the next few weeks would exploit fully the scope for lower short-term rates created last December when the Fed cut the discount rate a full percentage point to 3.5 per cent. The discount rate is the rate at which the Fed lends to banks, but it is of largely symbolic significance because banks rarely borrow from the central bank. Analysts believe another small cut in the federal funds rate would be helpful because it would probably trigger a half-point cut in banks' prime lending rates to 6.0 per cent. This would reduce the cost of a range of consumer and business loans. Encouraging recent figures for inflation are seen as enhancing the Fed's room to manoeuvre. The core consumer price index (food and energy excluded) is still rising at an annual rate of nearly 4 per cent, but other measures, including the gross domestic product deflator and an index of employment costs, point to an underlying inflation rate of perhaps only 3 per cent. The counter-argument is that short-term rates are already at their lowest level for a generation. The Fed regards the failure of long bond yields to decline significantly below 8 per cent as the more important brake on economic growth. The risk in cutting short-term rates further, with the recovery already under way, is that expectations of inflation will rise, putting upward pressure on bond yields. The Fed's failure to move yesterday probably indicates that it believes further easing would be counter-productive in the absence of more conclusive evidence of economic weakness. In the short run, growth estimates are likely to be revised up. Last week's report of a sharp rebuilding of corporate inventories in March is expected to prompt an upward revision of GDP in the first quarter, to show growth at an annual rate of 3 per cent rather than 2 per cent. This would be by far the best performance since President George Bush took office early in 1989. Some bulls, such as Mr Robert Brusca, chief economist at Nikko Securities in New York, regard the first-quarter expansion as a launching pad for faster growth - perhaps 4-5 per cent at an annual rate later in the year. But others are more cautious. The fact that inventories have already rebounded, say economists at JP Morgan, the New York bank, undercuts a potential prop for growth in the second quarter. Trade figures released yesterday were a warning that higher imports may siphon off some of the stimulus from rising domestic demand. The trade deficit widened to Dollars 5.8bn in March from Dollars 3.3bn, largely because of a 4.5 per cent increase in imports. Residential housing was the one sector of the economy to stage a 'normal' recovery in the past year. Rapid growth of personal consumption spending - another strong motor in the first quarter - reflected special factors such as tax rebates and an unsustainable fall in personal saving. The consumer is likely to remain inhibited by historically high ratios of debt to income. The biggest difference between this year and last is the substantially lower level of short-term interest rates and a significant strengthening of corporate balance sheets. This greatly reduces the risk of a 'triple dip' into recession. But the Fed and other policy-makers would be unwise to take the health of this erratic recovery for granted.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Perot scores with write-in primary votes
DOC.TEXT: TWO MORE easy presidential primary victories for President George Bush and Governor Bill Clinton in the US on Tuesday have again been overshadowed by evidence of Mr Ross Perot's growing political appeal in the Far West and nationally. However, the Texan businessman was himself embarrassed yesterday by a published report in which Senator Warren Rudman, a Republican from New Hampshire, expressed his annoyance that Mr Perot seemed to have hired a private investigator to make 'unauthorised inquiries' about his background. Mr Rudman had been viewed as a possible vice-presidential running-mate for Mr Perot, but said he had no interest in the prospect now. The primary story from Oregon and Washington state was familiar. Mr Bush scored 76 and 83 per cent respectively, against 22 and 13 per cent for Mr Pat Buchanan, his remaining nominal challenger for the Republican nomination. The president won 53 delegates in the two states to Mr Buchanan's five, further padding his already sure majority to take to the party convention. Mr Clinton took 50 per cent of the vote in Oregon and 51 per cent in Washington, against former California governor Jerry Brown's respective 35 per cent and 29 per cent, with former Massachusetts senator Paul Tsongas, who has pulled out of the race, winning 11 and 16 per cent. Washington state names convention delegates in separate caucuses. The 29 Mr Clinton won in Oregon give him more than 1,850 of the 2,145 needed for the Democratic nomination, which he may well secure in the final primaries - including those of California, Ohio and New Jersey - on June 2. Primaries next week, in Kentucky and Mr Clinton's native Arkansas, do not award enough delegates to put him over the top. However, in both the Democratic and Republican primaries this week, there was evidence of a surprisingly large write-in vote for Mr Perot. Neither state is obliged to disclose such votes immediately, but a CNN exit poll suggested Mr Perot's support exceeded 10 per cent in Oregon and might have carried some rural counties in Washington. That said registered Democrats in Oregon preferred Mr Perot to Mr Clinton by 45 to 41 per cent. On the Republican side, 49 per cent went for Mr Bush and 40 per cent for Mr Perot. The Pacific north-west has long been fertile ground for iconoclastic, outsider politicians. In 1968, Oregon voted for Senator Eugene McCarthy over Senator Robert Kennedy. Several recent local polls have put Mr Perot ahead of the current pack. The NBC-Wall Street Journal survey, out yesterday, had Mr Bush in the lead with 35 per cent, followed by Mr Perot at 30 per cent and Mr Clinton with 27 per cent. Moving closer to a formal declaration of candidacy, Mr Perot has now filed a 123-page financial disclosure statement with the Federal Election Commission. This does not reveal a net worth - assumed to be over Dollars 3bn - but points to recent annual incomes from investments ranging from about Dollars 25m to as much as Dollars 130m. It suggests he has mostly been a conservative investor of his private wealth, being heavily into tax-exempt municipal and utility bonds as well as property, with some hedged bets in stock and currency options, and venture capital partnerships. It was, according to the FEC, easily the largest such statement of wealth received from a presidential aspirant. It underlines his ability to finance a campaign from his own pocket without recourse to federal funds. The question of Mr Perot's ability to buy the presidency, as it were, may become an issue late in the year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Developing countries look for better deal on trade - Why the Generalised System of Preferences is regarded as only a qualified success
DOC.TEXT: RICH and poor countries are meeting in Geneva this week to look at ways of strengthening the preferential trading arrangements for developing nations under the so-called Generalised System of Preferences (GSP). The GSP, first introduced in 1971 under the auspices of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (Unctad), provides for countries to reduce or waive normal customs duties for Third World imports. As Unctad shows in its latest review of the system, the GSP has been a qualified success. On the plus side, there are now some 15 schemes in operation, giving preferential trade treatment to more than Dollars 60bn (Pounds 33bn) worth of exports a year from over 100 developing countries. Preferential imports into the OECD countries grew roughly twice as fast as total imports between 1976 (when the US introduced its scheme) and 1989 (the most recent available year). Product coverage has been expanded, and an increasing number of poor countries are benefiting from the schemes. That suggests the GSP is working as intended: promoting development through trade. But both sides concede the system also has serious weaknesses. Unctad estimates that in 1989 only half the Dollars 226bn worth of imports from developing countries subject to duties were covered by the GSP schemes - mostly manufactures and semi-manufactures. Only half of those actually received preferential treatment. In addition, because the scheme is designed to encourage industrial exports, advanced developing countries have grabbed the lion's share of the benefits. The US dropped the four Asian 'tigers' - Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan and South Korea - from its scheme in 1989. Even so, the top 10 beneficiaries accounted for over 80 per cent of GSP benefits granted by the US the following year, with Mexico alone garnering a quarter. Overall, the top 10 beneficiaries account for more than 60 per cent of GSP preferences. The 40-plus least developed countries (LDCs), which are most reliant on traditional commodity exports, had preferential exports in 1989 of a meagre Dollars 710m, or just over 1 per cent of total GSP exports by all developing countries. To remedy these deficiencies, developing countries, supported by the Unctad secretariat, are pushing hard for broader product coverage of the GSP schemes. These currently exclude many agricultural products and often 'sensitive' industrial goods such as textiles and footwear, the traditional springboards for industrialisation. Third World nations also see expanded coverage as partial compensation for the reduction in the value of preferences that will inevitably follow from the general lowering of tariffs now being negotiated in Gatt's Uruguay Round of global trade talks. But for the first time developing countries openly acknowledge that the quid pro quo for broader product coverage will be 'graduation' out of the GSP schemes for the most successful Third World exporters. Australia is to follow the US in graduating the Asian 'tigers' from 1993. With the writing on the wall, developing countries are backing Unctad proposals to draft multilateral 'graduation' guidelines in a bid to prevent gross disparities between schemes and protect countries from arbitrary delistings due to protectionist and other pressures. In practice, many Third World nations see advantages in orderly graduation in spreading GSP benefits more equitably. The indirect effects can also be important. In Asia, the US decision has already led to plans for substantial direct investment by South Korea and Taiwan in Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia to take advantage of trade preferences these countries still enjoy in the American market. The meeting is also discussing ways of remedying two other major defects in the GSP scheme. The first is the fact that the schemes differ in operation as well ascoverage. Thus the same good can satisfy origin rules for one scheme and not for another. More difficult to tackle are differences due to the use of GSP benefits to pressure countries over policies. The EC withdrew GSP benefits for a time from South Korea in a row over intellectual property protection. The US routinely threatens to withdraw benefits to countries whose trade policies it dislikes or which deny basic worker rights. Green criteria may be added if US environmentalists have their way. The second problem is the negation of GSP benefits by non-tariff measures, which Unctad reckons (based on 11 OECD schemes) affect over one-fifth of dutiable imports from developing countries. These measures can take the form of quotas or ceilings, which limit benefits from preferences, or of anti-dumping or anti-subsidy duties which can wipe them out altogether. In the 1980s the World Bank voiced the views of many development experts that the Third World had made a 'Faustian bargain' by relying on trade preferences that could be withdrawn at will rather than playing an active role in multilateral trade talks. This week's meeting has revealed a new consensus that, while the GSP and other preferential arrangements are no panacea, and certainly no substitute for Gatt, they are a useful and worthwhile form of development assistance in their own right.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / World Trade News: EC warned not to cut tariff on chips
DOC.TEXT: THE EUROPEAN semiconductor industry would be unlikely to survive if it dismantled its 14 per cent tariff on chip imports, a report by the industry market research group Dataquest says. The EC is being pressed by the US and Japan to dismantle the tariff. It is the only main industrial region that has kept tariffs on semiconductors. The US, Canada and Japan suspended theirs in 1985. The EC Commission has offered to cut the 14 per cent tariff on imports of integrated circuits by a third, to 9 per cent, in exchange for reciprocal lowering of trade barriers. Such a cut could sharply reduce competitiveness of the European industry and is unlikely to lead to lower prices. The declining trend in European manufacturers' own share of their market and low market prices of many chips in Europe have created a situation where dismantling the tariff overnight 'is likely to spell the death of the European semiconductor industry,' Mr Byron Harding, industry analyst at Dataquest, asserts. The EC, the US and Japan are discussing the issue in Gatt's Uruguay Round. Calls have come from within the US to reinstate the suspended 14 per cent tariff on chip imports if Europe fails to cut its tariff. EC chip users have been urging a cut in the tariff, which, they say, damages their competitiveness. The study indicates that despite the EC tariff on imports, prices of certain chips in Europe have been as low as, or at times lower, than prices in other main markets. This is because foreign makers are ready to sacrifice profit to revenue, to boost European market penetration, Mr Harding believes. * EC Semiconductor Tariffs and Related Issues. Published by Dataquest.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Mexico link for Trafalgar
DOC.TEXT: TRAFALGAR House Construction, part of the UK property, engineering, shipping and hotels group, is forming a new company with Sidek of Mexico to take advantage of the expanding Mexican construction market, writes Andrew Taylor. The joint venture based in Guadalajara will begin with a large order book in the resort development and leisure sector, Trafalgar House said. The new company, Grupo Sitra, would be able to call on Trafalgar's bigger technical and operational facilities to work on infrastructure and industrial projects. Mr Barry Myers, Trafalgar House director responsible for construction, said industrial investment in Mexico was expected to rise as North American Free Trade talks led to reduced trade barriers between the US and Mexico.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Investors 'avoiding cheap-labour states'
DOC.BYLINE: By DAVID DODWELL, World Trade Editor
DOC.TEXT: FOREIGN investors are no longer hunting for cheap labour in developing countries - they want big markets, quality infrastructure and high skill levels, according to the International Finance Corporation, the World Bank's private lending arm. Strongest growth in private investment has occurred in Chile, Papua New Guinea and Thailand over the five years from 1986 to 1990, the study shows. All three countries saw private investment more than doubled. The strongest magnets for foreign direct investment are also countries with high savings, the IFC says in its third annual study of trends in private investment in developing countries. 'Most of the countries whose savings ratios improved, typically by virtue of cuts in the public sector deficit, show a strong investment response by the private sector,' it says. Foreign investment has grown in the past decade, now accounting for 10 per cent of all private investment in the 40 developing countries examined. Low labour costs 'have been of diminishing importance', largely because they account for a dwindling share of overall manufacturing costs, on average 10-15 per cent. 'Foreign investors are strongly influenced by structural factors such as market size, the quality of infrastructure, the level of industrialisation and the size of the existing stock of foreign investment,' the report adds. Foreign investors display a 'herd' mentality in following where others have invested. This is partly because the presence of other foreign companies raises the likelihood of reliable suppliers and a pool of trained labour. Political risk has not deterred investors where returns are sufficiently high.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Assurances sought on EC access
DOC.TEXT: SIXTY-FOUR developing countries which have a trade and aid treaty with the European Community will seek further assurances of continued preferential access to the Community for important commodities when both groups meet in Jamaica today. They will also be seeking more EC financial assistance. Ministers representing the African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) group and the EC will examine ACP concerns about the effects on trade and aid of the creation of a single European market next year, and the move towards deregulation of international trade under current Gatt proposals. Mr Ralph Maraj, Trinidad and Tobago's foreign minister and president of the ACP ministerial council, said the Lome Convention, the treaty between the ACP and the EC, will have to be re-examined in the light of global changes such as the dismantling of centrally-planned economies, the collapse of apartheid, the 're-emergence of South Africa on the world stage', and the 'current international bloc politics portrayed by the Ecu, yen and dollar zones'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / World Trade News: New HK trade commissioner
DOC.TEXT: BRITAIN'S new trade commissioner in Hong Kong - equivalent to Britain's ambassador to the territory - is to be Mr Stephen Day, a career diplomat who has for the past five years been ambassador in Tunisia, writes David Dodwell. Hong Kong's anomalous colonial status, under which the governor is the queen's representative in the territory, but at the same time speaks for Hong Kong rather than Britain, makes Mr Day the UK's top spokesman for British interests - particularly those of business. Hong Kong is the UK's 15th largest export market and an important springboard for business in the region. UK visible exports to Hong Kong in 1991 were Pounds 1.38bn. The value of the market would be even greater if invisibles, and goods transiting Hong Kong for China, were included.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Thailand's revered king has his day
DOC.TEXT: BEFORE every show in Thai cinemas the audience rises for the national anthem and for a faded film showing King Bhumipol Adulyadej - officially dubbed the 'working monarch' - inspecting worthy rural projects throughout Thailand in unremarkable civilian clothes. The frowning, bespectacled man visiting irrigation canals in the countryside looks like an ordinary, if particularly serious, Thai citizen. But both he and the institution of the monarchy are revered by his subjects to an extraordinary degree. Thailand became a constitutional monarchy in 1932 and the king's legal powers are severely circumscribed. Yet he is regarded as a mediator and arbiter of last resort at times of national crisis. Like the government, the pro-democracy demonstrators who have confronted the army in the past four days of disturbances in Bangkok have repeatedly and publicly emphasised their loyalty to the king. Thai academics appealed to the 64-year-old king to intervene, as he did in 1973 by meeting the leaders of the discredited authoritarian government and student demonstrators, and finally by appointing a new administration. Last night the king finally stepped in. State television showed him giving an audience to Gen Suchinda Kraprayoon, the embattled prime minister, Mr Chamlong Srimuang, on Monday, and Mr Prem Tinsulanonda, prime minister from 1980 to 1988 and now an adviser to the king. The three men crawled into the room on their knees while the king sat on a sofa - as a mark of respect for the monarch his subjects are obliged to keep their heads lower than his. Breaking his silence on the crisis, the king told the prime minister and opposition leader: 'If you both continue to seek to win, in the end the country will lose.' He urged them to turn to each other and seek compromise. King Bhumipol has been on the throne for 42 years. Born in the US in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where his father was studying medicine at Harvard, he went on to cultivate interests ranging from photography and jazz to boat-building and painting. As he grew older he developed an interest in rural development, initiating more than 1,000 projects in the countryside and reinforcing his popularity among the peasantry. Although the king is held in profound respect - public criticism of the royal family is forbidden and it is not unknown for people to be convicted of lese-majeste - he is aware of the limitations of his power and of the danger of different factions attempting to manipulate him. 'I am called a king, but my duty - you have noticed - is not the duty of a king,' he said in a BBC interview 10 years ago. 'We keep in the middle, neutral and in peaceful co-existence with everybody,' he said then when asked about his involvement in politics. 'We could be crushed by both sides, but we are impartial. One day it would be very handy to have somebody impartial.' That day arrived yesterday.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Peace in Beirut hit by storm over reconstruction: The battle over a Dollars 2.65bn plan to transform a ravaged city
DOC.TEXT: PLANS to reconstruct the war-ravaged heart of Beirut have generated a controversy as fierce as any which marked the 1975-90 civil war. If successful, the Dollars 2.65bn plan will transform 135 hectares of desolate ruins into skyscrapers, condominiums, parking lots and shopping malls, complete with a 40-storey, twin-tower World Trade Centre, an opera house, museums, an artificial island and a palm-lined avenue wider than the Champs-Elysees. The dispute has been the subject of television documentaries and impassioned newspaper columns. It promises to generate legal battles for decades to come. Opponents have staged sit-ins and spread allegations of malpractice against proponents of the plan, many of whom have ties to the Lebanese-born Saudi billionaire Mr Rafiq Hariri. Landlords claim that expropriation of their buildings in exchange for shares in a property company constitutes theft and that archeological treasures will be buried. Conflicting views of Lebanon's past and future, of the rights of individuals and the public good, are tinged with religious and class prejudice. Opponents also object on aesthetic grounds to the architectural design, which Lady Yvonne Cochrane, the aristocratic president of the owners' and tenants' association, labels 'the dream of a retarded adolescent.' Advocates insist that failure to carry out the project would doom the city's centre to being a perpetual slum inhabited by refugees and squatters - and prevent the rehabilitation of the entire country. 'The law has been passed,' says Mr Fadel Shallak, president of the Council for Development and Reconstruction (CDR), the organisation responsible for creating the new Beirut. 'These people who are still arguing six months later are a continuation of the civil war. They lack discipline. They think they are more important than the state. In doing these designs, we have tried to express the future of a strong Lebanese state.' Opponents say the plan contravenes the Lebanese constitution, which protects private property. In exchange for their stake in the city centre, 127,000 landlords and tenants are offered 50 per cent of the shares in a real estate company to be formed pending completion of a financial assessment. The other half will be owned by investors, who will initially contribute capital equal to the assessed value of the land. The company is tax exempt for 10 years, and capital will be increased as building progresses. Over the next 25 years, the real estate company will sell off its property. The CDR argues that no other solution could resolve claims of landlords and tenants; the latter say they are being forced into a partnership with third parties they do not know and who are not legally committed to completing the project. Although he avoids publicity, Mr Hariri is the central character in the saga. The 47-year-old son of Sunni Moslem farmers from the southern Lebanese port city of Sidon emigrated to Saudi Arabia 27 years ago. In a local-boy-makes-good story that has endeared him to his supporters and aroused the scorn and suspicion of his detractors, he won the favour of Saudi Arabia's King Fahd, purchased the French construction giant Oger and proceeded to build much of modern Saudi Arabia. Mr Hariri founded the Mediterrannee banking and insurance group and owns significant shares in a half-dozen other international banks. This year he established a media holding company for his radio stations and two planned television stations. He established in 1984 a foundation which pays university fees for 12,000 Lebanese students every year. According to one of his aides, he contributes Dollars 87m to charities in Lebanon every year. For his acolytes, Mr Hariri is a disinterested philanthropist; his enemies say he is buying off public opinion - and the country. Lebanese President Elias Hrawi lives in a building that is owned and maintained by Mr Hariri. Mr Shallak, who began working for Mr Hariri in 1978, says that the CDR is an independent, government-financed organisation, in spite of the fact that Mr Hariri has made clear his intention to subscribe to the legally allowed maximum of 10 per cent in the Beirut real estate company, paid for renovation of the CDR's new headquarters and personally bankrolled two master reconstruction plans, one for Beirut, the other for all of Lebanon. The largest engineering consultant in the Middle East and the eighth biggest in the world, the Lebanese company Dar Al-Handasah was given responsibility for the Beirut plan. The Dollars 7.5m contract for the national plan was split between Dar Al-Handasah and the US company Bechtel, which refused to send any of its staff to Lebanon. Invitations to tenders for the first three years of their Dollars 4.5bn national plan will be issued this month. The Lebanese Parliament last autumn passed a law giving the CDR wide powers. 'We are free of all red tape and bureaucratic procedures,' says Mr Shallak. 'It is in our bye-laws that we should be given freedom to do our job.' He is sensitive to accusations of conflict of interest, but says 'sometimes we have to make a choice between what is good for the country and nice formal aspects.' Under the direction of the CDR, Oger Liban, Mr Hariri's company, is supervising the dynamiting of unsafe buildings in the old city centre. Before the work started, Mr Samir Rebeiz, an architect, photographed every building. Although many no longer exist, he continues to classify them according to historical period, architectural style, urban value, present condition and the feasibility of restoration. 'Only 10 per cent of the buildings were actually unsafe,' he says. 'They had to destroy them to maximize the number of offices and apartments they can build.' Mr Rebeiz particularly regrets the destruction of medieval vaulting in the Tawile and Ayass souks, a 17th-century stone structure with a crenellated roof, and an 18th-century Greek Orthodox monastery. He says that the master plan would raze vestiges of the medieval city walls and build over an area where ancient Canaanite artefacts were found before the civil war. The CDR has asked Unesco to carry out archeological studies in line with Dar Al-Handasah's master plan and invited the Lebanese Department of Antiquities to excavate parts of the city. But archeologists say they have been given permission to work only in 3m-wide segments of an unpromising area with a high water table and six metres of surface sewage. Mr Henri Edde, the Lebanese architect in charge of 200 Dar Al Handasah consultants working on the Beirut project, brushes off the criticism: 'Can you imagine that such a huge project would not have opposition? When the French built the Pompidou Centre and the Louvre Pyramid there was an outcry. Prince Charles argues with architects. We are not responsible for the destruction of these buildings. It was the fighters in the war who did it. The people who are now screaming 'Stop the bulldozers' didn't try to stop them. If they delay reconstruction or make it impossible, they will be judged by history.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Filipinos show distaste for graft and patronage: The presidential poll results are demonstrating a break with traditional politics
DOC.TEXT: WHOEVER wins the drawn out battle for the Philippines presidency, the result will represent a repudiation of the traditional politics of patronage. Analysts say the cry for a new type of leadership was evident in the heavy turnout in what is regarded as the most peaceful and free election the country has seen, despite complaints of fraud by some candidates. By last night Mr Fidel Ramos, of the Lakas-National Union of Christian Democrats coalition, was still in the lead. With 43 per cent of the 26.7m votes counted, he had 2.56m votes against 1.95m for Mrs Mrs Miriam Defensor Santiago, of the People's Reform Party. Both Mr Ramos and Mrs Santiago had occupied various public offices - he is the former armed forces chief-of-staff and defence secretary, while she used to be a court judge and immigration commissioner. Neither has held any elected position before. Political analysts say the voter acceptance of Mr Ramos and Mrs Santiago represents a rejection of the old-style politics of patronage and largesse that had become fodder for corruption in the bureaucracy. Corruption in government has been tagged as one of the main reasons for the Philippines' inability to improve standards of living - 65 per cent of the 62m Filipinos live below the poverty line - despite its resource-rich economy and a steady flow of foreign aid. Mrs Santiago pegged her campaign on an anti-corruption crusade while Mr Ramos promised 'people empowerment' that will expand citizen participation in government affairs. Their camps projected each candidate as a 'fighter' - Mr Ramos against coup plotters who had repeatedly tried, but failed, to grab power from President Corazon Aquino, and Mrs Santiago against 'the evil' of corruption. In the rest of the field of seven Mr Eduardo Cojuangco of the Nationalist People's Coalition stood third with 1.85m votes. He is viewed largely as a remnant of the autocratic government of deposed dictator Mr Ferdinand Marcos, but has not done as well as foreign observers had expected. Mr Ramon Mitra, of the dominant Laban ng Demokratikong Pilipino (LDP) party, had been unable to shake off his image as a paragon of traditional politicians, disparagingly referred to as trapos (old rags). He defeated Mr Ramos in an LDP straw vote last November, but Mr Ramos left the party that Mr Mitra helped organise in 1986 after his petitions for an investigation of fraud charges were ignored. Also trampled by the rush against traditional politicians was the career of Mr Jovito Salonga, former Senate president, who stood on a strong nationalist theme. Mr Salonga had topped all senatorial elections that he ran in since the 1970s, but at the age of 71, his appeal to the voters had obviously waned , although he continues to enjoy enormous support from the intellectuals and certain middle-class niches. By demolishing the traditional basis for political alignments, however, the May 11 poll may have also created new elements that could be a drag to the new administration. Mr Joseph Estrada, a film actor who became senator in 1987, appears almost certain to clinch the vice presidency. Mr Estrada was originally one of the eight contenders for president but in late March he joined Mr Cojuangco's camp as the Marcos crony's running mate. Mr Estrada's nationalist beliefs could run into the more cautious approach of Mr Ramos or Mrs Santiago. This fundamental difference could turn him to another 'wallflower' vice president. Most of the country's presidents since the 1950s had little use for their elected vice presidents who belonged to rival political parties. Even In the bicameral congress, the majority most of those winners ing the election are from the LDP. In the race for the 24 seats in the Senate, the latest count showed the LDP winning at least 17. The results for the 200-member House of Representatives will become clear by this weekend, but many of the known LDP stalwarts were reported ahead leading in their constituencies. The bias against traditional politics extended to the voting in the Senate. Another political upstart who originally gained popularity as a movie and television actor, Mr Vicente Sotto III, appears to be headed to become the runaway top-notcher from among the 168 candidates. Analysts see this also as further evidence of voter preference for 'fighters' - as vice-mayor of Quezon City, a Metro-Manila suburb, he led a campaign against drug abuse. Observers are unanimous in crediting the Filipino people who jammed the polling centres as the 'real winners' in the election.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Japan's land prices show record fall
DOC.TEXT: A SURVEY of Japanese urban property values has found a 12.3 per cent fall in residential prices in the six months to the end of March, the largest fall in the post-war period and an indication of the severe pressure on financial institutions which have been big lenders to the property market. The Japan Real Estate Institute said the national land price index, including commercial and industrial property, fell by 1.9 per cent during the same period to 108.4, the first decline in 17 years. The institute's survey is regarded as a lagging indicator, and the 12.3 per cent fall in the urban residential index to 83.8 does not reflect the dramatic price plunges in some sectors, particularly the condominium market on the fringes of Tokyo and Osaka. Some Osaka condominiums have fallen in price by more than 40 per cent over the past year, following a spate of speculative building from the late 1980s until 1990, when there were a record 1.7m housing starts in Japan. The figure fell to 1.37m in 1991, and property agents say demand appears to have bottomed for well located apartments selling for around Y40m (Pounds 169,000). Housing starts in March were 2.6 per cent lower than the same month in 1991, and leading apartment builders say their fast growing stock of unsold apartments appears to have peaked. However, developers holding highly priced properties in areas that were thought feasible sites at the peak of the speculative era remain in serious financial difficulty, and officials at the real estate institute indicated that national property prices would continue to fall in coming months. The institute found that the residential price index in central Tokyo was down 12.2 per cent to 83.1 over the six month period, while in Osaka, the index fell 14 per cent to 78.1 and in Nagoya, it was 2 per cent lower at 118.2. Reuter adds: Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry yesterday released revised figures showing a fall in industrial production in March of 2.6 per cent from the previous month.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / India's satellite launch success
DOC.BYLINE: By K K SHARMA and REUTER
DOC.TEXT: INDIA yesterday successfully launched a satellite into orbit using a locally developed rocket. The launch follows two failures four years ago. The launch of the rocket, the third version of the 'augmented satellite launch vehicle', took place at the Sriharikota launching station of the Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro), north of Madras. The satellite is part of a series launched by the Indian government for research purposes. Although designed by Isro, components for the rocket and the satellite were obtained from various sources, including the US which last week banned exports to Isro because it had bought cyrogenic rocket technology from Russia. The ban is bound to slow India's space programme which the government claims is for peaceful purposes and not for development of missile technology, as the US alleges. Prof U R Rao, chairman of Isro, said after the launching that it was a 'total success'. The two tasks of proving the functioning of the rocket and orbiting the satellite had been completed successfully, he said. India issued charges yesterday against the head of a Sri Lankan Tamil guerrilla group for the murder a year ago, of Mr Rajiv Gandhi, the former prime minister, Reuter reports from Madras. The special investigation team looking into Mr Gandhi's killing on May 21, 1991, charged Mr Velupillai Prabhakaran, head of the Tamil Tigers, and his intelligence chief, Mr Pottu Amman. India has asked Sri Lanka to arrest and extradite Mr Prabhakaran.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Kings fall out over Jerusalem shrine
DOC.TEXT: IN ONE of those arcane and highly personalised disputes that swirl about the Arab world, King Fahd of Saudi Arabia and King Hussein of Jordan find themselves in potentially bitter competition over renovations to Islam's third holiest shrine after Mecca and Medina. It is not clear who will emerge with the privilege of paying for repairs to the Al Aqsa mosque and other holy places in Jerusalem, but the Saudi monarch, whose personal wealth is put at Dollars 18bn, certainly has the wherewithal. The contest of the custodians of Islam's holiest shrines - the dispute owes more to past rivalries than present differences - began earlier this year when Unesco appealed for help to restore Al Aqsa's distinctive gold dome and marble facade on the site where the Prophet Mohammed, according to Moslem belief, ascended to heaven. King Fahd responded swiftly, offering Dollars 70m for renovations to all Islamic sites in Arab East Jerusalem. King Hussein, whose Ministry of Religious Endowments is still responsible for Jerusalem's Islamic holy places, felt obliged to try to match the Saudi monarch's largesse where Al Aqsa is concerned. He offered Dollars 8.25m, and battle was joined. Not that the two men are likely to be consulting each other. King Fahd has not spoken to his Jordanian counterpart since King Hussein expressed sympathy for Iraq's position early in the Gulf crisis. And worse from Jordan's point of view, Saudi Arabia has cut off aid that had helped to keep the impoverished Hashemite kingdom afloat. Behind the battle of the dollars lies a complex story of family rivalries that date back to early this century when Abdul-Aziz Ibn Saud, the warrior-founder of the House of Saud, drove the Hashemites from their strongholds in the Hejaz along the west coast of what is now Saudi Arabia, including Mecca and Medina. King Hussein re-opened wounds during the Gulf crisis when he asked subjects to refer to him as Sharif Hussein in memory of his great-grandfather, Sherif of Mecca, who helped inspire the Arab revolt against Ottoman Turks in 1916. The dispute among Arab royalty has been further complicated by Egyptian intervention, and more recently by the Palestinians in the person of Mr Yassir Arafat, chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organisation who is risking an unholy row with King Hussein over his apparent endorsement of the Fahd offer. Egypt's press reported this week that Egyptian engineers, working under the auspices of Saudi Arabia, were being despatched to Jerusalem to examine the Islamic sites. Jordan, which controlled East Jerusalem and the West Bank until the 1967 war, was not amused, and strong criticism was voiced in its press. Enter, at this point, Mr Arafat, who expressed his deep gratitude this week to King Fahd. 'In the name of our struggling Palestinian people. . . we would like to express our many thanks and brotherly gratitude for your wise decision,' he said in a message to the Saudi monarch. Cynical observers might suggest Mr Arafat was trying to curry favour with wealthy Saudis whose anger at PLO support for Iraq in the Gulf crisis knew almost no bounds.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Bonn will defend east's shipbuilders
DOC.BYLINE: By ANDREW HILL and CHRISTOPHER PARKES
DOC.TEXT: THE German government said yesterday it would fight European Commission proposals to cut capacity in the ailing east German shipbuilding industry. The Commission agreed plans to lift the ceiling on state aid to 36 per cent of contract value for yards opened before October 1990. All aid would have to be paid before the end of 1993. But yards will have to be closed and jobs cut to ensure shipbuilding capacity in the new German Lander falls by 40 per cent before the end of 1995. Other Community shipbuilders, notably the Spanish, have campaigned hard against relaxing the rules for the east German yards. The Bonn Economics Ministry said it could accept the increase in the ceiling, which compares with an EC-wide limit of 9 per cent for production aid. But a spokesman added: 'In the light of cuts already undertaken, reduction of capacity on this scale will give us great difficulties.' The proposals will be discussed by EC ministers next month. Germany alone will be unable to block agreement by a majority of other member states. The Commission said its proposals were in line with policy in other member states and that apart from the increased ceiling, the normal rules on aid to shipyards would be applied. Lightning strikes among printers hit production of yesterday's German newspapers after Tuesday's arbitration talks failed to produce a pay deal. IG Medien, the main union involved, and one of the most militant in Germany, said it would call a strike ballot immediately if there was no result from conciliation talks scheduled for today. Further disruption was expected last night. The threat of strikes also loomed over paper manufacturing yesterday.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / New German justice minister sworn in
DOC.TEXT: Germany's new justice minister is sworn in at parliament's meeting in Berlin yesterday. Mrs Sabine Leutheusser-Schnarrenberger succeeds Mr Klaus Kinkel, now foreign minister.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / All eyes on German money supply: The broad M3 measure has clearly grown more quickly than the Bundesbank would like, writes Andrew Fisher in Bonn. Exactly why is not quite so evident
DOC.TEXT: IN THE PAST, not many people bothered with the German money supply figures. German monetary stability was taken for granted. Those who watched to see if the Bundesbank's carefully set monetary targets were met were only the economists, bankers and financial market traders. But that was before the costs of reunifying Germany knocked the country's public finances sideways, with the money supply trend becoming a key factor in its high interest rates. The Bundesbank lifted rates in December to levels uncomfortably high for the rest of Europe, where economies remain weak, and foreign politicians and executives are acutely aware of what German money supply means for business abroad. Today, when M3, the broad monetary aggregate, is racing away at a near double-digit annual rate - twice the centre point of the target range for this year of between 3.5 and 5.5 per cent - and inflation is higher than in Britain and France, Germany's money supply is one of the most closely watched financial indicators. However, while M3 clearly has grown much faster than the German central bank would like, it is not so evident why. In March, the growth rate was an annual 9.4 per cent after 8.6 per cent in February and 8.9 per cent in January. The rate is expected to slow, but there is little likelihood the Bundesbank will meet its target. The April figures will be out in the next few days. Curiously, M3 was already out of line at the start of the year; the target is based on the average for the fourth quarter of 1991, but December's rapid growth put the 1992 starting point well above that level. Nevertheless, the Bundesbank does not intend to make the target range higher simply to make it easier to reach. Its goal for M3 (comprising mainly cash, savings, and short-term deposits) is a firm expression of its intent to maintain stability. Past targets have not always been met, but they acted as beacons of monetary resolve to the financial world. Why is the target not being met now? What's more, does it really matter? Each year, the Bundesbank assesses Germany's potential for economic growth and adds a few percentage points for expected inflation and the rate of monetary circulation. The result is the M3 goal, with the range representing acceptable upper and lower variations. This time, however, unification has upset the calculations. The bank's determination to stick to its target range is its counter-strategy to the high, and inflationary, state spending and borrowing wave embarked on to support the east German economy. Most of the funds going from west to east still finance consumption rather than productive investment. Even so, investment in the east is moving ahead. It is this factor which is mainly behind the steep rise in the money supply. The benefit is that such spending represents the rebuilding of east Germany. But much of it is subsidised by soft loans, grants, and subsidies. Thus, credit demand from the private sector, up at an annual rate of 12 per cent in the past six months, is less subject to the Bundesbank's control. Also helping propel M3 along more quickly than usual are: lower profit levels, leading companies to borrow more at a time of economic slackness to finance investments; increased lending for consumption and residential property deals; and the effect of high interest rates in encouraging funds to be placed in short-term deposits. All this points to the question of how seriously M3's growth should be taken. The bank lifted interest rates by an unexpectedly high 0.5 percentage point in December, making it harder for other European countries to put theirs down at a time when their economies needed a stimulus (although Britain and France have just done so). Now, Germany's Lombard rate is at 9.75 per cent and the discount rate at 8 per cent. The longer money supply keeps expanding quickly, the less likely the Bundesbank is to cut rates. Inflation has moderated to an annual rate of 4.5 per cent in March, but the Bundesbank is obviously unhappy about wage trends and the vigour of M3. Moreover, the German economy, though flaccid after a lengthy period of growth, is resisting world recession and is expected to perk up in 1993. So high interest rates, in the Bundesbank's view, do not carry the risk of torpedoing the economy. Of immediate concern is the impact of monetary growth on inflation, which the bank wants to see below 4 per cent this year and around 2 per cent later. In its January report, the Bundesbank stressed its legal obligation to regulate money supply and credit to safeguard the D-Mark. It noted: 'There is also a growing worldwide conviction that central banks should primarily ensure stable prices. In this connection, managing the money stock is of crucial importance, for there is broad agreement that inflation is a monetary phenomenon in the long run.' In the 1970s, the average rise in the money supply outpaced real potential growth in the economy by more than 6.5 per cent. This was accompanied by high inflation; prices increased by an annual average of 5.5 per cent. In the 1980s, M3 grew less rapidly and so did prices. These days, the link is less straightforward, partly because the D-Mark now floats against the dollar; this influences import costs and delays the influence of the money supply. 'Prices have tended to follow the growth of the money stock with a lag of about two to three years,' the bank said. So the full effect of what the Bundesbank is doing now may not show through for some time. For those abroad chafing under high German rates, patience may thus be the only response to the Bundesbank's stern policies.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Consumer credit rise adds to Bundesbank fears
DOC.TEXT: THE BUNDESBANK yesterday again voiced concern about the rapid expansion of German money supply, coinciding with a strong rise in consumer credit, and weak growth in capital formation. In spite of adjusting its calculation of money supply growth in March downwards, from an estimated 9.75 per cent to a corrected annual rate of 9.4 per cent, the central bank emphasised that the expansion had accelerated again: from a rate of 8.9 per cent in January, 8.6 per cent in February, and now 9.4 per cent in March. At the same time it published figures for the growth of west German private indebtedness for consumption in 1991, showing that it expanded by DM28.6bn (Pounds 9.7bn), compared with DM23.7bn in 1990, DM21.1bn in 1989, and only DM13bn in 1988. The other particular concern expressed in the Bundesbank's monthly report is the failure of capital formation to match the growth in credit to the private sector, underlining the fact that credit is being used primarily for consumption. The trend reflects in part the massive transfers of capital from west Germany to the east, to finance consumption rather than a corresponding expansion in investment there. But it also shows that western consumers are financing their spending increasingly from credit, and not income - and that easterners are rapidly acquiring the habit. The pessimistic tone in a series of articles by the bank's economics department underlines the determination of its governing council to maintain a tight monetary policy until the growth of money supply and inflation are brought down. Even the fact that industrial production in the west expanded by 3 per cent in the first quarter, compared with the last quarter of 1991, was discounted: year on year, the growth was only 1 per cent, and the reason for the strong recovery was a combination of unnaturally low production at the end of last year, and a very mild winter, outweighing the normal seasonal adjustment. The independent German Economics Institute (DIW) in Berlin published its own estimate yesterday of real 3 per cent growth in gross domestic product in the first quarter - in spite of the fact that GDP in eastern Germany actually fell by 2 per cent. The institute said that a sustained recovery in the east German economy was still not in sight, although, thanks to the high level of earning from 'commuters' travelling to west Germany to work, the gross national product of the east actually increased by 4 per cent compared with the first quarter of 1991.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / European corps units to remain separate
DOC.TEXT: FRANCE and Germany have agreed that their European defence corps, to be set up by President Francois Mitterrand and Chancellor Helmut Kohl tomorrow, will consist of separate national units under a joint command. Germany has rejected a French proposal to assign troops fully to the corps in peacetime, insisting that they remain 'nationally assigned' just as they are in Nato, Bonn officials said yesterday. The corps is nonetheless seen as an important move in creating a European defence identity, within Nato and complementary to it, but also capable of being used in non-Nato operations within and outside the territory of the alliance. The corps will be set up 'in the perspective of European union', and put under the umbrella of the nine-nation Western European Union. It is clear, however, that the German troops in the corps may not be able to participate in all its potential operations because of the constitutional restriction on combat missions outside the Nato area. Mr Volker Ruhe, German defence minister, believes it will be possible to agree on a change in the constitution allowing use of German troops in United Nations peace-keeping operations, without geographical restriction, by the end of the year. But he admits it could be 10 years before they take part in other activities. The Franco-German agreement provides for three precise uses of the corps: the common defence of the Nato allies, the maintenance and restoration of peace, and humanitarian missions. A planning staff will be set up in July, and the corps should come into existence in 1995, with a headquarters in Strasbourg. From the German point of view, a major benefit will be in bringing the French troops in the corps openly under the Nato umbrella for the defence of the allies. Europe's new muddle army, Page 20

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / US takes up offensive against Serbia: Washington revokes landing rights as UN considers sanctions
DOC.BYLINE: By JUDY DEMPSEY and LAURA SILBER
DOC.TEXT: THE US yesterday revoked landing rights for JAT, Yugoslav airlines, signalling the beginnings of a much wider diplomatic offensive to isolate Serbia. 'Serbia has gone beyond the bounds of what is tolerable,' a senior western diplomat said. He added that members of the Islamic Conference, which includes Arab countries, Malaysia, Pakistan and Indonesia, were shocked at the cruelty inflicted on the Moslems in Bosnia-Hercegovina, and what might happen to them in (Serbian-controlled) Kosovo. Pressure to impose a comprehensive package of sanctions increased as masked Serb gunmen yesterday held hostage in a sports stadium 5,000 people who are mostly Moslem women and children. They are trying to escape from the fighting in Sarajevo, the Bosnian capital. Western diplomats said the UN is considering a range of sanctions. These include blocking off Serbia's air and surface transport links, imposing an oil embargo and freezing Serbia's Dollars 2.9bn in assets which were in western banks at the end of last year. But he did not say how these sanctions would be implemented, and warned of the difficulties in implementing them. Some western diplomats said UN troops, backed by an air-defence system, should be sent to gain control of Sarajevo airport. 'This has been mentioned. But, as yet, there is no concrete proposal on the table,' a diplomat said. The UN still faces opposition from countries, including Russia, (it has traditional Slav connections with Serbia), India, a prominent member of the non-aligned movement, and Greece, which opposes independence for the former Yugoslav republic of Macedonia. 'With growing pressure from the Islamic Conference, and the appalling evil of the war, there is growing consensus to slap sanctions on Serbia and make them stick. Serbia must be stopped. The war must not spread,' a western diplomat said. Yesterday gunmen fired a mortar at UN peace-keepers trying to free Moslem refugees held hostage by Serbs outside the embattled city of Sarajevo. It was the latest in a rash of assaults on international relief and peace-keeping personnel in the Balkan state. A volunteer for the International Committee of the Red Cross died on Tuesday in a rocket attack on a humanitarian aid convoy. Yesterday Serb irregulars demanded the delivery of food to besieged army barracks in the centre of Sarajevo in exchange for the release of the hostages held in Ilidza, a Sarajevo surburb. Earlier Radio Sarajevo said Serb irregulars were launching mortar attacks on the city of Bihac in northwestern Bosnia from the surrounding hills. It said the railroad station was repeatedly hit. Hundreds of thousands of people are stranded in the city without water or electricity. Food supplies are nearly exhausted.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / EC forces Italy to think anew
DOC.TEXT: A SPECIAL cabinet meeting of the outgoing Italian government has been called tomorrow to examine the economy following the EC's blunt warning that the country risked being unable to meet the requirements for economic and monetary union if it did not put its finances in order. The meeting will be little more than a symbolic act as the outgoing Christian Democrat coalition has been operating since last month's general election in a caretaker capacity. Yesterday Mr Guido Carli, outgoing treasury minister, sharply rebuked Italy's politicri'The populist nature of the political parties ..has allowed a system of public finances where free hand-outs are widespread and where .citizens never pay what they should for the services they receive.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Swiss cultures clash over request to join Community: The decision, says Ian Rodger, has aroused both joy and suspicion
DOC.TEXT: THE SWISS government's decision this week to make an early application to enter the European Community may turn out to be a case where Swiss French logic crumbles before Swiss German stubbornness. Reaction to the decision has certainly been very different in the country's two main linguistic communities. In French-speaking Romandy, which has long had a cosmopolitan culture, there was near-unalloyed joy; in the more inward-looking German-speaking cantons suspicion prevailed. Neue Zurcher Zeitung, Zurich's leading newspaper, relegated the news to page 21 and grumbled about the 'undignified' way it leaked out. Even strong advocates of joining the EC worried that the move was premature and risked undermining public support for two other Europe-related plans which are to be put to plebiscites later this year. Most Swiss business leaders believe that their country must have closer ties with the EC if the country's economy is to thrive, but they suspect that the only way to convince the independent-minded German-speaking majority is by proceeding very gradually. That had also been the strategy until last October of the federal government. With the governments of the other six member states of the European Free Trade Association (Efta), Bern was negotiating a trade agreement with the EC to create a European Economic Area (EEA). Even that would be tough enough for many Swiss to accept. The idea was that the Efta countries would take on the four freedoms of the EC's single market, meaning Switzerland would open its doors to EC workers and home buyers and remove several mechanisms that protected professionals and many businesses from EC competitors. If all that was accepted and implemented, there would be plenty of time to try to cajole the Swiss into joining the EC itself. And even if they ultimately decided not to join, the Swiss economy would already be getting virtually all the benefits of membership. But in October, the government announced that joining the EC was official policy and that the EEA should be considered only a step towards it. From there, it was, as Swiss President Rene Felber said yesterday, only logical to actually send in an application. Coming when the country is approaching two plebiscites on the EEA treaty, this decision had the appearance of an attempt to get a Euro-bandwagon going. In September, a referendum is to be held on a proposal to spend SFr30bn (Pounds 11.1bn) to dig two new rail tunnels through the Alps. This is part of the EEA agreement intended to resolve the long-running dispute over transit rights through Switzerland and Austria for EC lorries, and it was always going to face strong opposition from both environmentalists and people worried about the cost. Then, probably in December, the referendum on the EEA treaty itself will be held. Both a majority of the population and a majority of the 26 cantons must approve the proposals. Most cantons are German-speaking and their lingering suspicion of international organisations was shown on Sunday when they approved by only the slimmest of margins a proposal to join the International Monetary Fund. The IMF would not directly hurt any Swiss. The EEA, on the other hand, would cause considerable upheaval, especially among the small and medium-sized businesses that are the core of the Swiss German economy. As Mr Pierre Borgeaud, president of the national business association, Vorort, pointed out, 'the feeling of being threatened is most strongly felt in eastern (German-speaking) Switzerland'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / ITV wants Pounds 304m football deal reopened over late offer
DOC.TEXT: THE independent television companies are pushing to reopen the Pounds 304m satellite television deal with English football's new Premier League because British Sky Broadcasting was allowed to submit a secret last-minute improved offer to freeze out ITV. At least one football club chairman is calling for an official inquiry because of what he said was the unfair and unethical way the negotiations were concluded. The agreement in principle - heads of agreement are now being drawn up - is controversial because only viewers with access to satellite or cable television will be able to see live Premier League matches. Chairmen and chief executives of the new league, which starts in August, voted on Monday by the narrowest possible margin in favour of a joint BSkyB-BBC deal worth Pounds 304m over five years. Two of the 22 clubs present abstained and six voted against. The agreement in principle needed two-thirds support. A detailed ITV offer worth Pounds 262m over five years was delivered by hand between 8am and 9am on Monday by Mr Trevor East, executive director of ITV football, to Mr Rick Parry, chief executive of the new league, and Sir John Quinton, its chairman, who is also chairman of Barclays Bank. Mr Parry handed out copies of the ITV offer to the premier league executives as they arrived at London's Royal Lancaster Hotel for the 10am meeting. Mr East says that just before 10am he overheard Mr Alan Sugar, chairman of Tottenham Hotspur football club and of Amstrad Consumer Electronics, the principal maker of satellite dishes, making a telephone call from a booth in the hotel. 'He was very excited. He was saying things like: 'Don't you understand. You don't seem to have taken it in. These are the figures. You've got to get something moving quickly.''
