According to Mr East, the Amstrad chairman concluded by saying: 'Blow them out of the water.' Asked yesterday if he had called BSkyB with details of the new ITV offer, Mr Sugar said: 'It's none of your business who I was talking to. I might have been talking to my girlfriend.' BSkyB, it is believed, was also tipped off by sources other than Mr Sugar that the ITV bid had narrowed the gap between the two sides. ITV, which wanted 30 live games a season compared with the 60 in the BSkyB deal, believes that if the difference had been less than Pounds 10m a year the clubs would have accepted the greater visibility that ITV would have given the new league. A new BSkyB offer was put together at the last moment and sent to Mr Parry, who did not join the meeting until nearly 10.40am. Mr Parry then relayed the offer orally - there was no accompanying paperwork. According to those present, no clue was given that there had been a last-minute offer and ITV was given no chance to respond with a new offer. Mr Greg Dyke, chairman of the ITV Association and chief executive of London Weekend Television, said yesterday Mr Parry had said on four occasions that everything would be all right for ITV. Requests for a chance to make a presentation to the league chairmen came to nothing. Mr Sam Chisholm, chief executive of BSkyB, a consortium in which Pearson, owner of the Financial Times, has a significant stake, last night declined to confirm or deny a last-minute revised offer. Editorial comment, Page 20 Yorkshire TV results, Page 26

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Thailand's king seals accord to end violence
DOC.BYLINE: By VICTOR MALLET and PETER UNGPHAKORN
DOC.TEXT: THE KING of Thailand last night sealed an agreement between the government and pro-democracy demonstrators to end four days of confrontation in which at least 40 people have been killed. King Bhumipol Adulyadej, the country's 64-year-old constitutional monarch, summoned Gen Suchinda Kraprayoon, the prime minister, and Mr Chamlong Srimuang, the opposition leader arrested on Monday, and told them to make peace for the sake of the people and the economy of Thailand. Both Gen Suchinda and Mr Chamlong were seen on television crawling on their knees into the presence of the king. In a televised address soon afterwards, Gen Suchinda said Mr Chamlong was being freed, along with all others arrested during the bloody clashes. MrChamlong, sitting alongside him, appealed to protesters to refrain from violence. The agreement will bring relief to Thais and to foreign investors, although there are still many uncertainties. Most Thais think Gen Suchinda will have to step down and may even have to leave the country after presiding over the shooting of protesters, but he and his supporters appear reluctant to relinquish control. Gen Suchinda, the former armed forces chief appointed as premier by a coalition of pro-military parties which won elections in March, is not an elected MP and is likely to have to resign within a month. He may choose to stand in a by-election to retain his post, although he has previously rejected this course. He said that he would ask parliament to meet on Monday to amend the constitution, one of the key demands of the demonstrators, who want to reduce the influence of the military in politics and restrict the post of prime minister to elected MPs. Mr Chamlong, himself a former army general but a man noted for his campaigns against corruption, told Thais: 'I ask you not to support any people who are being disorderly, so that the situation can return to normal as fast as possible.' He added: 'The situation has eased because of the good offices of the king.' King Bhumipol told the two men to use the good offices of Mr Prem Tinsulanonda, prime minister between 1980 and 1988 and one of his closest advisers. 'You, especially you two, General Suchinda and Major General Chamlong, must turn towards each other and not confront each other in order to solve this problem,' the king said. 'In the end people no longer know why they are fighting. All they want is to win and this is dangerous.' Before the midnight announcement of a deal, there had been feverish speculation in Bangkok that Gen Suchinda would be overthrown by disaffected colleagues in the military. Bangkok remained under a night curfew after the king's intervention and troops continued to patrol the streets. But thousands of demonstrators manned barricades around the Ramkamheang University in the capital's north-east in defiance of the curfew. Gunshots could be heard elsewhere, even after Gen Suchinda's announcement. Undimmed loyalty, Page 4

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / EC farm policy on verge of wide-ranging reform
DOC.TEXT: THE MOST radical reform of the European Community's Common Agricultural Policy was within reach last night as EC farm ministers were locked in a second night of hard bargaining. Agreement on the reform would send a signal that the Community is at last serious about restraining its chronic overproduction of food - now running at about 20 per cent over consumption and rising. A deal could also clear the way for a conclusion of the Uruguay Round negotiations to liberalise world trade. These talks have been stalled for the past 18 months because the US and other agri-exporters regard EC commitments to cut farm subsidies as inadequate. As well as clearing the food mountains, the reform could bring cheaper food. It could also gradually bring about a cleaner rural environment by making intensive farming less economically attractive. Independent estimates calculate that the reform could cut Ecu15bn-Ecu20bn (Pounds 10.5bn-Pounds 14bn) off EC food bills, with 15-20 per cent cuts on pork and poultry, 15 per cent reductions on beef, 7 per cent cheaper butter and 3 per cent off bread. Mr John Gummer, the UK agriculture minister, predicted that a CAP reform deal was 'more likely to be late tonight than next time'. Mr Louis Mermaz, representing France, the EC's agri-superpower, said that in broad terms 'we accept the proposal . . we are very satisfied'. The main obstacle to a deal was a brewing north-south row over demands by Italy, Spain and Greece for the right to produce more milk than they are allowed under the EC quota system - which none of the three has rigorously applied. Their partners appeared likely to concede to Spain and Greece, as relative newcomers to the EC, but remained obdurate on Italy. Ministers were last night taking turns to negotiate bilaterally, on this issue and other loose ends, with the European Commission and EC presidency, before regrouping for a final push at about 4am. Mr Ray MacSharry, EC agriculture commissioner, and Mr Arlindo Cunha, Portuguese farm minister currently chairing the council of ministers, reached a compromise yesterday morning which preserved the radical structure of the Commission's blueprint and offered a number of sweeteners to farm interests. The reform includes subsidised prices cut towards world market levels, and full compensation paid directly to the farmer. For all but small farmers this refund is conditional on their taking 15 per cent of their land out of production. This scheme should slice into oversupply while buttressing farm incomes. 'What we are involved in here is a totally different philosophy to what has existed for 30 years,' said Mr MacSharry. The main cut is likely to be a 29 per cent reduction on the subsidised price of cereals over three years. This will virtually eliminate the export subsidies at the core of the Uruguay Round impasse and looks set to be endorsed in spite of the misgivings of Germany, whose inefficient agricultural sector has dictated the high prices of the CAP. Mr Ignaz Kiechle, the German farm minister, appears to have come to this meeting with instructions to do a deal, and last night said he was ready to conclude the reform debate. Basis for a deal, Page 38

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Stock and Currency Markets
FT 21 MAY 92 / Major and Thatcher clash over Maastricht: Prime minister's assurances contradicted by predecessor
DOC.TEXT: A CLASH of views between Mr John Major and Mrs Margaret Thatcher over Maastricht's impact on European Community powers last night jarred with government attempts to control today's expected revolt by Tory MPs over the treaty's ratification. Mr Major's predecessor as prime minister flatly contradicted his assurance to those Conservative MPs worried about a European super-state that Maastricht 'marks the point at which, for the first time, we have begun to reverse that centralising trend'. In The European newspaper today, Mrs Thatcher writes that Maastricht 'passes colossal powers from parliamentary governments to a central bureaucracy'. Mr Major, like Mrs Thatcher, favoured stiff resistance to the threatened loosening of UK border controls. But his comments amounted to a rebuff to his predecessor, implying she had overseen moves towards centralisation, while he had reversed the trend. He said the 1986 Single European Act and its accompanying declaration recognised Britain's concern to keep border controls in order to stop terrorism, illegal immigration and drug smuggling. Mr Major told Euro-sceptics that Britain would 'fight for that position' even if the dispute went to the European court. In her article, Mrs Thatcher said she was 'amazed when I hear it suggested that it (the declaration) does not have the force of law and can be ignored. Upholding it is a matter of good faith and good faith, once lost, is hard to regain'. Up to 20 or 30 Conservative MPs, some heartened by Mrs Thatcher's interventions, together with possibly a higher number of rebel Labour MPs, are expected to vote against the government tonight. One potential rebel, Mr John Biffen, former Conservative cabinet minister, expressed 'considerable reservations' about the centralising impact of Maastricht. But the bill is likely to pass its second reading comfortably. Labour MPs are supposed officially to abstain and Liberal Democrats will support it. Government whips have stepped up the pressure particularly on new Tory MPs, warning that careers would be wrecked by opposing, or abstaining on, the bill. Mr Major sought to appease critics, saying that 'what we kept out of the Maastricht Treaty is as important as what is in the Treaty'. There was no Social Chapter, no diminution of Nato's role, no word 'federal', and Britain retained 'an absolute right' to decide in its own time whether to move to the third stage of economic and monetary union. He added: 'Many in this house and throughout the country have expressed anxiety that decision-making in the Community is becoming too centralised. In fact, many of the issues which are most problematic for us . . . are ones that arise from the application of the original Treaty of Rome, not the Maastricht Treaty.' Mr Major stressed the importance of the legally binding text he secured at Maastricht on 'subsidiarity' - the principle of decisions being made at the lowest possible levels. If necessary, Britain could take disputes over its implementation to the European Court of Justice, he said - angering those Scottish Labour MPs calling for devolution. The prime minister quoted Mr Jacques Delors, European Commission president, as saying that, 'if a success is to be made of Maastricht and the single market, the Commission will have to comply fully with the principle of subsidiarity. Indeed its future existence depends on this'. Mr Neil Kinnock, the Labour leader, urged the prime minister to end his 'opt-out' mentality. But the opposition front bench also had to face tough criticism from its own Euro-sceptics as the debate continued. DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (16): From office to mosque - Religious affairs
DOC.TEXT: MR HAMDI MERT's office, complete with the standard portrait of Ataturk above his desk and the Turkish flag beside it, looks exactly like that of any other senior government official. With a departmental budget this year of TL 2.3 trillion (Pounds 200m) and 84,000 personnel, it is a substantial government department by Turkish standards. A glance outside the window, however, at the giant dome of the Kocatepe Mosque, complete with an inscription in Arabic letters, quickly reminds visitors that Mr Mert's office is not quite like any other department of state. He is deputy president of the Department of Religious Affairs, the state body which administers all Sunni Shi'ite religious activity in Turkey, but is also a spiritual body. About 69,000 of the department's staff are hodjas (clergymen) serving mosques. From time to time, Mr Mert himself puts aside his grey suit and tie and dons religious garb. He then leads prayers in the mosque (where the president and prime minister may be among the worshippers) and delivers sermons. Is this a contradictory situation in a state which claims to be secular? No, says Mr Mert. He believes that some sort of secularism, in the sense of a division of duties between spiritual and worldly affairs, arises naturally from the Islamic religion itself. His superior, the President of Religious Affairs (PRA) is a direct successor of the Seyhulislam, the traditional head of the Sunni Islamic clergy in the Ottoman Empire. Religious and political boundaries, as elsewhere in the Middle East, tend to overlap. As Mr Mert sees it, the duty of the PRA is to attend to the religious side of citizen's lives and to instil a sense of unity. 'We are all Muslims,' he says, 'no matter what particular rite of Islam we happen to observe.' He also believes in inter-faith dialogue: the PRA holds meetings with representatives of other religions, including Christianity, from time to time. 'Turkey is the only secular country in the Muslim world. We Turks are both Muslim and secular, but the west doesn't seem to accept this fact,' he says. Some Christian clergy serving the less than 1 per cent of Turkish citizens who are non-Muslims but include ancient and exotic linguistic groups such as the Chaldians and Syriacs alongside the better-known Greeks and Syriacs, challenge this view. 'How can you call a country secular where religious education is compulsory?' asks one Catholic priest, pointing out that during the 1980s, Islamic religious education in schools was made compulsory not just to secular Turks but also for non-Muslims. After discreet lobbying by the French, the obligation was suspended two years ago. Mr Mert says, however, that he believes that religious instruction is a moderating force. 'Religious fanatics tend to come from those who do not attend the religious vocational schools,' he says. There has been a steady expansion of religious education in Turkey over the last decade. About 350,000 students are now enrolled in religious secondary schools, alongside the western-style lycee system, and they are now allowed to enter universities though not the military cadet schools afterwards. Alarm at growing fundamentalism, however, is less strong in Turkey today than it was before the Gulf War. Turkey's western middle class is no longer as fearful as it once of being swamped in a tide of religious revivalism. 'Fundamentalism has peaked in this country,' says one Istanbul professor confidently. It is, nonetheless, still a powerful force. Religious groups collect funds to sponsor mosque-building and religious schools in the Turkish-speaking republics of the former Soviet Union. Proposals to revive the fetva, a formal Islamic comment on whether a course of action is correct or not from the religious point of view, were mooted recently and strongly condemned in the press. The High Islamic Council, a committee of senior clergy and theologians, has also been reactivated after more than a decade. Mr Mert denies Turkish press reports that the council is planning any kind of religious reformation, something that some Turkish nationalists have hankered after since Ataturk's days. 'Our religion is an unchanging system. We believe it is the final revealed religion, so reform is out of the question,' he says. He is more coy about a surprising initiative taken by the PRA in the last six months: the opening of a formal dialogue with representatives of non-Sunni Moslems in Turkey. About one in five of all Turks are Alevis, a version of Twelver Shi'ism. Alevis do not worship in mosques but in cemevis or community houses, where food and wine are passed around, and members of the congregation speak in turn, rather as in a Quaker meeting, and there is dancing. In addition, Alevis have an awkward relationship with the state. They are given no money to finance their mosques or clergy - and their children have to receive Sunni religious instruction in school. There are deeper tensions below the surface. Alevis strongly supported the secularising reforms introduced by Ataturk and they tend to vote for centre-left political parties against Turkey's right-wing majority. Some Sunnis regard Alevis as non-Moslem (though Mr Mert says he is not among them) and there were outbreaks of intercommunal fighting before the 1980 coup when Sunnis attacked Alevi immigrants in some towns. The attacks were promptly and effectively suppressed by the Turkish military, but they reawakened old communal memories going back to the day in the 16th century when the Sultan Selim the Grim slaughtered 40,000 Alevis in a single night, accusing them of support for the Ottoman empire's Iranian enemies. 'Some sort of recognition will have to be given to this country's largest religious minority before much longer,' says one Alevi intellectual in Ankara. Cultural associations - such as one to commemorate the work of Pir Sultan Abdal, a politically radical folk poet who was hanged by the Ottoman authorities - are now emerging, where only a few years ago plays and poems about Pir Sultan were officially banned. The dialogue with the state has exposed differences inside the Alevi Community between conservatives (who seem to favour the new dialogue) and radicals who suspect the PRA's motives. The ancient tensions may be disappearing, but they are doing so only slowly.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (17): The neighbours are suspicious - The biggest project in the Mediterranean
DOC.TEXT: THE FIRST kilowatt of electricity is expected to be generated later this year as engineers open the flood gates onto the first of the eight Swiss-built turbines installed on the massive USDollars 4bn Ataturk dam complex in southern Turkey. This dazzling engineering achievement has become a symbol of Turkey's industrial self-reliance and long-term planning. It has also engendered the suspicion of Turkey's neighbours downstream on the Euphrates. The south-east Anatolian project or Gap, as it sometimes better known, is currently the largest development project in the Mediterranean. When fully implemented, it will comprise 22 dams and 19 power stations, providing a third of Turkey's projected energy needs. It will account for half of the country's irrigated land, with around 1.7m hectares under irrigation. The project and the services attracted to the area in its wake will create jobs for some 5m people. Since the foundation stones were laid in 1981 the Gap project has absorbed USDollars 9bn. By 2005 Turkey is set to spend a further Dollars 23bn while another Dollars 10bn will be needed to complete the project sometime in the next century. The burden on the Turkish economy has been enormous. To date, almost all of the funds have been raised by the budget without the assistance of donors wary of touching a project which involves a riparian dispute. Indeed, many economists believe it has been the single largest factor behind Turkey's 70 per cent rate of inflation. Every year, the Gap absorbs 10 per cent of total government outlays, which does not include the subsidies and investment incentives given to private business to move to the area. 'What we would like to see is all the power stations complete by 2005,' says Mr Olcay Unver, president of the Gap authority in Ankara. The politicians also have few doubts. Both Turgut Ozal, the president and Mr Suleyman Demirel, the prime minister, are engineers. As a young electrical engineer, Mr Ozal cut his teeth working on the Keban dam. For this reason, the project seems destined to be finished. When Gap was first conceived, it was seen primarily as a way of providing alternative sources of energy in the wake of the 1972 oil crisis. The project was also set to transform this dry south-eastern corner of Turkey. Today, the environmental effects are less clear. The social and political benefits have still to be demonstrated, but Turkey's large construction groups have gained invaluable experience. This is now paying dividends in former Soviet republics and other regions. The centrepiece of the project is the Ataturk dam, the fifth largest in the world. It is close to completion. 'We need two or three average years and the reservoir will be full,' says Mr Mustafa Buke of the state hydraulic corporation DSI. Engineers estimate, given the unusually heavy snow fall this winter, that the water level could reach the required 513 metres by November and the first turbines could then be brought into action. The current level is around 503 metres. When it reaches 526 metres, the twin Urfa tunnels will start to irrigate some 250,000 hectares on the Haran plain close to the Syrian border. Officials no longer hold out great hopes that it will contribute much to resolving the crisis for the region's Kurdish-speaking population. They seem increasingly disenchanted with the politicians in Ankara and now provide growing support for the Kurdish Workers Party (PKK), fighting for a separate state in south-east Turkey. The social benefits are also being reassessed. Officials say they hope only to be able to stabilise the current population and stem the trend of urban migration which has had such a devastating effect on city services in Istanbul and Izmir in recent years. It is not even certain that the project will help hasten the redistribution of land. Many officials concede that as the areas move to more intensive farming methods and the need for greater scale economies, there may be a case for the concentration of land holdings, giving the aghas or hereditary feudal landlords even more control over the area. Internationally, the Gap project has also met with criticism. In 1987 Turkey and Syria signed a protocol which guaranteed that 500 cubic metres a second would pass across the shared border. The agreement stipulates that the deal will last for as long as the reservoir is being filled 'or until a permanent sharing of the water can be agreed'. The sides have not met since July 1990, before the Gulf War, the last occasion for the trilateral technical meeting between Turkey, Syria and Iraq. Iraq in theory is due to host the next meeting in Baghdad but, while its international isolation continues, that may be some way off. The Syrians' concern is that Turkey's plans could jeopardise the efficiency of their own hydro-electric dams which provide 75 per cent of the country's power generation. Damascus also worries about the downstream effects of pollution if Turkey uses pesticides and fertilisers in its irrigated land. It argues that the Ataturk dam will take all the rich silt from the water and thus make it less useful for downstream irrigation. However, Turkish officials point out with some justification that the Syrians started work on their own Taqba dam some 10 years before the foundations were laid for the Ataturk, with similar effects. The Syrians' long-term fear is that water could be used as a political and strategic weapon. This explains their reluctance to attend last year's planned international water conference to have been held in Istanbul which was consequently cancelled. Because of Syrian misgivings, many of the prospective international donors have fought shy of the Gap project. The World Bank extends close to Dollars 1bn to Turkey every year, but has rules which exclude it from lending on a project involving a water dispute between riparian neighbours. Japan withdrew a Dollars 600m irrigation proposal. A Japanese official confirmed that Tokyo would be unable to extend financing until a solution was achieved over the water issue. 'This water is not a present of nature. We have to import equipment to clear the snow. This means spare parts. We have to employee people,' says Mr Ferruh Anik, the director general of DSI. 'Every Turkish citizen has a tax on his water. This is not free water. What the Syrians and Iraqis are getting now: that's free water.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (14): What to eat - and where to find it - Food
DOC.TEXT: THIS YEAR'S pistachio crop is in, and the barrows of Eminonu are weighed down by these deliciously salty nuts. Fresh dates have arrived from Tunis in the Misir Carsi - the Egyptian market. In Pandeli's, high above the Spice Bazaar, where in Ottoman times the merchants sat watching for the grain ships to arrive from Alexandria, tourists are now eating artichokes so huge they simply discard the leaves. They then tuck into Black Sea turbot and a quince compote doused in kaymak, the clotted cream made from buffalos' milk in the Belgrade Forest nearby. As the blossom of the Judas tree falls on the slopes of Eyup, the city's cooks look forward to the new season's ingredients - 'Napoleon' cherries as big as golfballs, figs from Izmir, and the wild Ottoman strawberries which are ever harder to find. Perhaps the prize ingredient is the aubergine, which finds its way onto restaurant tables in hundreds of different guises - as 'Patlican Salatasi,' a delicious wood-smoky paste, or 'Beykoz Kebab' where it is wrapped around tender chunks of milk-fed lamb. The best-known aubergine dish is the one swimming in olive oil, called 'Imam Bayildi' which, so the story goes, caused the Imam to 'faint' it was so mouthwatering. The variety does not stop there. In winter you can find quail and woodcock, and steaming cups of sahlep, a warming drink made from dried orchid root, which they serve on the ferries. Best of all is the Lufer from the Bosphorus. Some think this fish rivals the Scottish salmon. Stambouli's will tell you it betters it. Locals eat where they always have, in the numberless small lokantas throughout the city. Businessmen still lunch at the Borsa near the old Stock Exchange at Sirkeci, or at Haci Abdullah's and Haci Salih's on Istiklar, formerly la Grande Rue de Pera. The better-heeled often go to the Divan Hotel where the Circassian chicken should not be missed. In Istanbul it will be hard to go hungry - there is always the Doner Kebab sold at every street corner or the rows of charcoal braziers underneath the Galata Bridge where grilled fish is served on bread still warm from the ovens. Turkey's food is as varied as the many subjects of its former Ottoman empire -refined and sophisticated after 500 years of culinary indulgence. Today it is widely acknowledged as one of the world's great cuisines. The Sheraton Tower on Taksim Square was one of the first to offer traditional menus. Revan, its restaurant, is renowned, and today takes its cooks from Bolu, a town still famous for supplying chefs to the palace kitchens in Ottoman times. Even the newcomers are waking up to what local cooking offers. Swiss Otel, Kempinski and Movenpick have recently opened, and already provide a wide range of international cuisine, from Chinese to French & Japanese. The race is now on to bring the glories of Ottoman cooking to their tables. Kazan at Movenpick is set to open later in the summer. A Turkish restaurant is also planned at the Swiss Otel, with its staggering view of Topkapi, the Blue Mosque and Aya Sofia to the Sea of Mamara beyond - breathtaking at sunset. Kempinski has recently restored the Ciragan Palace where Mr Joachim Schmitt, the food and beverage manager, is endeavouring to rediscover the court cuisine of Istanbul. Original recipes of the palace kitchens are being translated with the help of 90-year-old grandmothers, today the only people who can still understand the imperial Turkish. The Ciragan could not be a more authentic location. This vast and ornate 19th century palace on the Bosphorus is where Sultan Abdul Hamid II kept his unwanted brother locked up for 30 years - just about enough time to try out the recipe books.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (12): Controversy on how to cut the deficit -Tax reform prospects
DOC.TEXT: FOR ONCE, all economists are in agreement. Turkey's yawning public sector deficit is the key cause of today's inflation. But questions of precisely how big the deficit is and how to reduce it leave the country - and its economists - divided. Official Turkish statistics show a public sector borrowing requirement equivalent to a record 13 per cent of GNP in 1991. World Bank calculations which strip out the contributions of public sector banks and financial institutions put the financing requirement higher still, at 14 per cent. If inflation is allowed for, the figure falls to 8.4 per cent but still shows a clear jump in 1991, as it did in the previous election year of 1987. Buying votes is a traditional pastime for local politicians. It was, in other words, a tainted chalice which the Demirel government inherited. The new government quickly declared a 1992 target of reducing the PSBR from 13 per cent to 8.8 per cent. It also decided that increasing tax revenues would be the central plank of its policies. But there continues to be a major controversy over whether the measures it has proposed are adequate. Initially, Mrs Tansu Ciller, the minister of state responsible for the economy, talked of tax reform. One adviser, taking this message seriously, suggested a new tax on wealth. But this caused such an outcry that he left his job. It soon became clear that major reforms would be left for the future and that the present would concentrate on minor reforms such as a withholding tax on government interest payments, and reducing the tax loopholes for banks. In addition, the government announced a tax amnesty, a measure which attracted more criticism than might have been expected given the fact that in the past two decades Turkey has averaged one such amnesty every 28 months. The amnesty helped the Treasury by bringing in revenues which would not otherwise have been paid. Its effects were felt in April, but despite this, at the beginning of this month, the Treasury's borrowings from Turkey's Central Bank stood at TL26,000bn (Dollars 4bn), only 17 per cent below its legal limit for the year as a whole. The public sector thus finds itself with its back to the wall and facing a simple but awkward choice. Does it increase its borrowings from its domestic capital markets, thereby driving up interest rates at a time when it is seeking to reduce inflation? Or does it increase the prices of goods and services produced by the state - which also makes inflation look as if it is rising? A tax reform might alter the ground rules. At present the overall level of taxation is around 19 per cent of GNP, around one half of the OECD average of 37 per cent. Further, while there are a few highly publicised top tax payers, including Madame Manukiyan, the local brothel queen, the large rural population is exempt from direct taxation. Further, indirect taxation accounts for a disproportionate share of tax revenue. However, the underlying issue which the present government, like all its predecessors, has yet to face, is the extreme overstaffing of the central government and associated state economic enterprises. The Turkish prime minister is, directly and indirectly, probably the largest employer in the west. Ankara's present privatisation programme appears unlikely to alter this. Attempts to balance Turkey's budget are likely to remain a key issue throughout the 1990s and inflation to prove a stubborn target. David Tonge is general manager of IBS Research and Consultancy, which helps international companies build up business in Turkey and publishes Doing Business in Turkey, a 600-page updated reference guide.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (15): Take a fiver for a visa - Businessman's guide
DOC.TEXT: Travel FOR THE European businessman reaching Turkey is easy, involving just a short flight and a range of routes and airlines, including the much-improved Turkish Airlines. The British are particularly well served, with Londoners able to choose whether to travel and then work half the day, or vice versa. But the British have to obtain a visa, which requires giving a Pounds 5 note -no cheques accepted - to the police officer on arrival. Inside Turkey, Istanbul and Ankara are connected by regular air services and, for the more curious, an overnight train. In winter the train is recommended, not least because those who chose the site of Ankara's airport disregarded a shepherd's warning that he often lost his sheep in the fog. Other cities are also accessible by air, at reasonable prices. On land, car hire is expensive, but taxis are cheap. Make sure the driver restarts his meter, and do not be surprised when those in Ankara charge the night rate for travel to and from the airport. Do be surprised, however, if the driver understands your destination. He may well be from out of town and, unlike his London counterpart, will not have had to do 'the knowledge'. The A-Z of Istanbul is a good investment. It will also help you minimise your time in the town's impressive traffic jams. Accommodation No longer a problem in any of the major cities in Turkey. In Istanbul, the Swissotel and on the Bosporus, the Kempinski, are impressive while the Hilton and Sheraton have their devotees. Also just opening, are a Movenpick and Conrad. Good value can be obtained at the Divan, Marmara and Nippon. In Ankara, the Hilton and Sheraton rise side by side, with the Sheraton well served by the Ankara Business Centre. (Tel 420 3040). Telecommunications These are now good, with direct dial available from most hotel rooms. However, the Turkish PTT likes to challenge the user's ingenuity. Its latest move has been to change all Ankara numbers beginning with 1 so they now begin with 4 and all Istanbul numbers beginning with 1 so that they now begin with 2. Contacts Most major Western countries have commercial sections at both their embassies in Ankara - chasing state contracts - and their consulates in Istanbul. There are a number of Chambers of Commerce, of which the French is among the most active, and the British is good on agency information. The Austrian and German federations of industry have representatives in Istanbul. The Americans are also strong. On the Turkish side, foreign investors are advised to contact Yased, the Association of Foreign Capital Co-ordination (Tel 272 5094), and foreign traders, to explore the range of services offered by DEIK, the Foreign Economic Relations Council (Tel 243 4180), which is particularly strong on relations with the Commonwealth of Independent States. Independent consultants and research companies include IBS who are also authors of the 600-page service, Doing Business in Turkey (Tel. 231 0481). Other publications worth following are the OECD's annual surveys on Turkey; the monthlies - Business International's Turkey Monitor (London 071 493 6711) and the independent Turkey Monitor (London 081 881 3199), and Cornucopia, a striking Istanbul arts and life magazine (Istanbul 248 3607). Entertainment The Bosporus and old Istanbul are unique. Leave time to wander up and round them, or call on the Kahriye with its superb mosaics on the way to the airport. Ankara has less to offer but its castle and Museum of Anatolian Civilisations are interesting.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (13): Investors go elsewhere -Stock Exchange
DOC.TEXT: TURKS HAVE been living with high inflation for so long that they tend to take it for granted. Yet nowhere does the damage to the economy show more clearly than in the country's stock exchange at Istanbul. The market was set up in its present form in 1986 and, despite Turkish misgivings about unfettered capitalism, the bourse has established itself as a permanent feature of the country's business scene. Small investors quickly took to the idea that there are times when company stock can offer a better return than more familiar investments in gold, foreign currency, or one-year bank deposits. The number of companies whose shares are traded and the number of shares traded has also been rising rapidly. The average number of shares traded each day rose from 6,224 in 1990 to 18,345 in 1991. Despite the striking increase in volumes, the market's best days came as long ago as the summer of 1989 when it was one of the best-performing markets anywhere. The last notable rally was in February last year. For most of the first quarter of this year, the index has lingered around the 4,000 mark. In April, Turkey was stuck at the bottom of the emerging markets performance chart. Yet the country has obvious investor potential. Why the lacklustre performance? For much of the winter, political uncertainty was widely given as part of the reason for the market's sluggishness. But Mr Demirel and his team have turned out not to be foes of the exchange. Quite the opposite: the coalition government plans to raise more funds than its predecessor did through privatisation operations. The main reason for the market's dull performance is that local investors - most of them small short-term investors - have been putting their money into other investments, ranging from treasury bonds to foreign currency deposits, which offer a better return under present circumstances. Considering that Turkey had something of a recession last year in which manufacturing industry grew by only 2.6 per cent (a dire figure by the standards of the last two decades), things might be worse. There have been few share price collapses, but cement companies, the market star performers in 1991, have done less well recently, and food and beverage stocks have tended to lead the market. All this is fairly discouraging to foreign investors, at least for the time being. 'They are going to be loath to invest in Turkey until they see some sign of a sustainable decrease in the country's inflation rate,' says Mr Peter Bennett, portfolio manager of Morgan Stanley's Turkish Investment Fund which is listed on the New York Stock Exchange. He believes that sooner or later, Turkey will have to follow most of the Latin American countries and take steps to bring down inflation and that until then the market will not be able to tap its full potential. That would mean a government decision to bring inflation well below 20 per cent: something which does not seem to be in prospect at the moment, even though some economists forecast a slight dip in Turkish inflation by the year end. Meanwhile the government has pushed through legislation which should help the market grow. Companies will be able to raise funds by issuing futures and asset-backed securities provided they have an approved rating. The Capital Markets Board will be given new powers to curb irregularities by brokerage houses, including the issue of forged share certificates. Abuses such as insider dealing will become punishable for the first time and independent auditors will be made responsible for any deficiencies in company accounts.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (10): Cities try to close gap with Europe - The quality of life in Ankara and Istanbul
DOC.TEXT: NEARLY 11m of Turkey's 58m inhabitants live in two cities, Ankara, the national capital, and Istanbul, Turkey's main business centre and largest city. The citizens of Ankara and Istanbul make up the overwhelming majority of Turkey's political and business class, its civil service and intelligentsia, and its growing consumer middle class. They also pay most of the country's taxes. Until the late 1980s, however, it is probably fair to say that conditions in both cities were more reminiscent of the third world than of the typical European metropolis. Migration from the countryside enlarged their populations by around 6 or 7 per cent each year. Most of the new arrivals lived in vast shanty-town districts. Services and urban infrastructure were correspondingly poor. Interruptions in water and electricity supplies were more or less routine. Public transport was limited and there was little public housing development or planning. Since the late 1980s, this picture has been changing. For a start, the pace of migration has slackened slightly, though Ankara's 2.8m inhabitants are still growing by an estimated 100,000 a year and Istanbul's 8m population rises by over 6 per cent annually. More importantly, the population of the two cities has come to expect improved services. In both Ankara and Istanbul, social democrat mayors are struggling to improve basic utilities such as water, sewerage, gas supply and transport. There have been some striking successes. The previous Motherland party administration in Istanbul under former Mayor Bedrettin Dalan (who has since switched parties and represents Istanbul for the ruling True Path party in the present parliament) installed the city's first ever sewage treatment plant and managed to improve the water supply. In Ankara, the city's council, under a joint venture with British Gas, has fitted 200,000 homes to take Siberian natural gas. A second stage is planned shortly. As a result, this winter was Ankara's first without heavy air pollution for half a century. 'My aim is to bring conditions in Ankara at least to the level of the nearest European capital cities, such as Athens, over the next three to five years. Ankara is going to be one of the best cities in the region,' says Mr Murat Karayalcin, the capital's mayor. In pursuit of this goal, Mr Karayalcin has drawn up a masterplan to take the city, until now something of a Cinderella among those in the Mediterranean basin, through to 2015 and is embarking on a range of projects, from a light rail system and metro through to a new cultural and exhibition centre. The city's annual budget of TL7 trillion (Dollars 1.2bn) includes investment spending of between TL2-3 trillion. Spending on infrastructure has overtaken that on new housing for the first time in Ankara's post-war history. Revenues come almost entirely from a central government block grant: municipalities in Turkey have very limited ability to raise cash through local taxes. The Ankara metropolitan municipality has also started tapping syndicated loans on the international market and earlier this year raised Dollars 230m in bonds and now has a credit rating in Frankfurt and Tokyo. The challenge of developing Ankara, however, is relatively modest compared with Istanbul, a city which takes in up to 500,000 rural migrants a year and which has become a vast sprawling megalopolis, part of a conurbation in which one can drive for over 50 miles without seeing the countryside. 'We would like to see the government developing new industrial centres in other parties of Turkey such as Zonguldak and Bolu and in the eastern Black Sea around Trabzon and Artvin to take some of the migrant pressure off Istanbul,' says Mr Icen Bortucene, the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality's deputy secretary-general. Istanbul's development budget this year will be around TL5.9 trillion, and it already has an international debt burden inherited from the mid-1980s, costing it around Dollars 600m a year to service. 'It is relatively small. We certainly are not fearful about further foreign borrowing for important projects,' says Mr Bortucene. Asked how the city plans to spend its cash, Mr Bortucene has a simple answer. 'We want to make life less intolerable for the ordinary citizen. Quite simple investments in transport for example could stop large numbers of our people losing up to three hours a day travelling to work and back. Transport at present is so poor that sometimes you see clerical workers hitching lifts to and from work.' Like Ankara, Istanbul is also building its own light rail mass transport. A first stage of 8km has already been completed and work is currently under way to build a 26km extension. Work on a second tramway system also starts this month, while the city's bus fleet has taken on an extra 800km capacity with the purchase of a 845 new buses. Again like Ankara, Istanbul's planners are ambitious. The city is competing with other international cities to host the Olympic games early in the next century. 'We want Istanbul to be a world metropolis, serving not only Turkey but also the world as a whole. Its international economic, trading and political importance has changed enormously since the break up of Soviet Union,' says Mr Bortucene. Shortage of cash is, however, not the only problem standing in the city's way. The sprawling megalopolis is run by an equally unwieldy administration, working more or less along Ottoman lines with paper dossiers travelling slowly between departments inside the city's vast municipal headquarters. Reliable statistics are scarce. Istanbul does not appear to have the tightly focused urban development plans which have been produced in Ankara. It also has other problems - including a powerfully entrenched local underworld or mafia - which if it exists at all in the capital is far less effective. Mr Bortucene believes some sort of administrative overhaul is long overdue, especially in management and information technology. 'We lack a good management information system, especially where specific projects are concerned,' he says. Just how swiftly such changes can be achieved remains to be seen. On the other hand, Istanbul is a genuinely powerful and rich industrial city, where average per capita income is around Dollars 10,000, much closer to the income levels of a developed country than to those of the rest of Turkey - even if income distribution is highly uneven. That fact seems to be slowly driving the city to close the gap with Europe.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (11): Aiming to rise to the top - Profile, Mayor Karayalcin of Ankara
DOC.TEXT: FEW JOBS in Turkey are quite as thankless as that of mayor of Ankara. Trying to satisfy the insatiable expectations an electorate for rapid benefits in the quality of life while having to rely on inadequate financial and administrative resources is a daunting prospect for even the most ambitious politician. None of the mayors of the Turkish capital in the last 15 years has served more than one term in office and none has made a successful transition to national politics. Even Mr Bedrettin Dalan, the ultra-popular Motherland party mayor of Istanbul in the 1980s, sits as a backbencher in Mr Demirel's True Path party. At seven o'clock in the evening on a typical working day, Mr Murat Karayalcin, Ankara's social democratic mayor, still has a chaotic and gruelling schedule ahead of him. Crowds of visitors mill around in the anteroom to the mayor's office. The streets outside are even more chaotic: in normal times they are the main arteries for the city's traffic. Now, they have been closed to traffic for months. Only a few of them will make it to the relative calm of the mayor's inner sanctum, a grandiose dark-panelled room inherited by Mr Karayalcin from his predecessors. Once inside they meet a quiet, unpretentious social democrat, who plays down political antagonisms between himself and his predecessors and has more the flavour of the civil servant or technocrat about him than that of Tammany Hall. Yet Mr Karayalcin is clearly an ambitious man, who is pledged to making Ankara one of the best cities in the region and is widely tipped as an eventual leader of Turkey's social democrats some day if he ever does make the transition to national politics. Meanwhile Mr Karayalcin is trying to leave lasting imprint on a teeming city of 2.8m people. Though much smaller and more orderly than Istanbul, Ankara lacks some of its rival's advantages: it is not primarily a business centre but an administrative capital. There is much less wealth around and also a less glittering cultural life, though Ankara has been a large and important city since pre-Roman times. Like most of his voters, Mr Karayalcin was not born in the city he now presides over, but was brought up on the Black Sea coast, arriving in Ankara in his late teens for high school and university. He cut his political teeth in student politics in the late 1960s and early 1970s and graduated from the political science faculty of Ankara University, the training ground of the Turkish civil service. In the middle 1970s, he spent two years at the institute of development studies of the University of East Anglia in the UK studying urban-biased models for economic development. He retains fairly strong links with the UK. When the social democrats were in office in Turkey at the end of the 1970s, Mr Karayalcin became an undersecretary in the Ministry of Rural Affairs and then worked in the city's municipal administration and was appointed head of Batikent, a large co-operative housing development on the west of Ankara, organising the construction of 200,000 housing units. The aim behind the Batikent project was to develop services and housing well outside the traditional boundaries of Ankara and so relieve pressure on the congested centre of the city. A year or two after the project got going, the 1980 Turkish military coup swept away the country's civilian political system. The social democrat mayor of Ankara was replaced by a retired general whose most striking action as the capital's mayor was to order that all the houses in the citadel should be painted blue, apparently to discourage rodents. Mr Karayalcin kept a low profile through the years of military rule and unlike almost every other social democrat official managed to remain at his post. The Batikent project moved ahead. When democracy began to make a gradual return to Turkey in 1983, Mr Karayalcin rejected advances from the Motherland party and joined the newly-founded Social Democracy Populist party (SHP) of Mr Erdal Inonu and in 1989, he ran successfully for mayor. He has generally supported Mr Inonu, rather than his rivals in the fierce factional in-fighting which dogs the SHP. 'Life is difficult at the moment for social democrats all over the world, not just in Turkey,' says Mr Karayalcin. 'We have to work out some sort of practical response to the ideological challenges we are facing.' As mayor however Mr Karayalcin's sights have been set on less contentious matters such as infrastructural projects, ranging from the conversion of Ankara's gas supply to natural gas to new light rail and road systems. He is a good administrator and the changes have meant less disruption to the daily life of the capital's population than has been the case in Istanbul. Nevertheless, his fortunes are clearly bound up with the future of Turkey's ailing and bitterly divided social democratic movement. Mr Karayalcin sees a fresh chance to reunite it in current efforts to revive the pre-1980 Republican People's Party, shut down along with other parties by the military junta in 1981 in what Mr Karayalcin describes as a legal disaster. 'Its closure was a mistake and putting it right would be a suitable opportunity to reunite the left-of-centre in Turkey,' the mayor says. Founded by Ataturk, modern Turkey's founder and national hero, in 1923, the RPP was Turkey's largest party in the 1970s and none of its post-coup successors has ever managed fully to take its place. The parliamentary centre-left in Turkey is currently divided into four or five bickering factions, split between three parties. So does Mr Karayalcin plan to go into national politics? Asked directly about his intentions, he replies cautiously: 'A politician always has to be ready to take on any position and rise in his own party as high as he possibly can.' If he ever does go into parliament, he may eventually emerge as a consensus candidate for the eventual succession to Mr Inonu. But that is unlikely to be in the lifetime of the present parliament. In the meantime, Mr Karayalcin will have his work cut out making Ankara into the fairest capital city of the Mediterranean.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (8): Banks start to catch up - The growth potential of the market
DOC.TEXT: 'WE ARE the 73rd bank in the country,' explains Mr Ibrahim Betil, chairman and chief executive of Bank Ekspres, a new Turkish bank which has just opened its doors in Istanbul's business district. Until last year, Mr Betil was general manager of Garanti Bankasi, one of Turkey's larger private sector banks. Then he decided to strike out on his own, raising Dollars 16m in capital from a group of like-minded private investors, a move which is something of a novelty in Turkey where private sector banks tend to be offshoots of an industrial empire owned by a single individual or family. Over the next five years his game plan is to target medium-sized corporate customers and the retail banking market and build up a branch network of between 40 and 50 branches, thereby establishing Bank Ekspres as one of the main players in the Turkish market. It is an extremely ambitious goal even for a banker who is already well-known in his own market. Mr Betil, however, is not alone in believing in the growth potential of the Turkish market where each year sees a few more hopefuls, usually one-branch trade finance boutiques, being granted banking licences. Why is there so much interest in a banking sector whose operating conditions, judged by the standards of the rest of the world, look extremely daunting? Because of Turkey's runaway inflation, interest levels are almost stratospheric. The inter-bank overnight interest rate at the end of April was 66.7 per cent. One-year retail deposits can earn up to 81 per cent from some banks and US dollar deposits 11 per cent. Corporate borrowers pay between 100 and 120 per cent. Borrowing rates have actually fallen in the last year because customers are hard to find. The margin may look still wide but it isn't. According to Mr Erol Sabanci, vice-chairman of Akbank, Turkey's most profitable bank, required reserves, taxes and staff costs eat up nine-tenths of every hundred lira held by a Turkish bank. 'Deposit costs are just not under control,' Mr Sabanci says. Banks make money not by lending but by holding treasury bonds or other operations of which trade finance is the most lucrative. There is, nevertheless, frantic competition for deposits, especially from the smaller banks. Deposit rate competition was introduced in Turkey in the late 1980s. Though the large banks currently pay between 71 and 73 per cent on one-year deposits (and between 55 and 60 per cent even on one-month money), the smaller banks can beat this by as much as six percentage points. Not surprisingly, once in a while savers get nervous in this market. In early January, savers lined up outside branches of one of the smaller Istanbul banks. The scare proved groundless and short-lived, but quite a few savers seem to have been willing to forgo a year's interest just to get their money back. There have been no actual bank failures since the first half of the 1980s, though the treasury monitors each bank's balance sheet and from time to time stages discreet operations to help banks out of trouble. There can also be other surprises. In mid-April, Ziraat, the state-owned agriculture bank which is Turkey's largest, abruptly moved its rates to depositors up by two percentage points, to the dismay of its main competitors, Akbank and Turkiye Is Bankasi. Just why Ziraat selected this moment to move seems to be something of a puzzle. Mr Sabanci identifies high operational costs and low working capital as chronic problems of the banking sector. In theory, all Turkish banks are now moving gradually towards the international standards set by the BIS for capital adequacy. In practice, the strengths of the banks are rather more difficult to assess. Ziraat this year has moved, for example, from being audited by the Turkish offshoot of Coopers & Lybrand, to a small local accountancy house. Mr Sabanci points out that the capital bases of many of Turkey's larger banks look distinctly less impressive when real estate and equity holdings are deducted, though this is not a requirement under the BIS rules. The fact that the Turkish banking sector can be measured against international standards is, nevertheless, a sign of how far it has come in the last decade - and its success not just in piloting its way through a hyperinflationary environment, but also in coping with high levels of non-performing corporate debt throughout the 1980s. Though most banks are still owned by industrial groups, there are some changes in attitudes towards non-banking subsidiaries. Turkiye Is Bankasi, for example, has sold off stakes in three subsidiaries in the past two years, including most recently its stake in Unilever's Turkish offshoot, which went to the international parent company for an undisclosed price. Most of the infrastructure of a modern banking sector has been set in place, though foreign bankers identify some continuing weaknesses. 'Taxes on inter-bank transactions are still holding back the inter-bank market. With taxes on transactions and volumes, not on revenues, you do not get a deep inter-bank market and without that bankers cannot develop derivative products and sophisticated financial instruments to eliminate costs,' says one American bank in Istanbul. However, some parts of the banking sector are becoming much more like large banks in a modern country. Akbank, set up after World War II, has already overtaken the other large private sector and the public sector banks in profitability and will probably pass in them in asset size in a few more years. It has a notably less bureaucratic atmosphere than that which still prevails among some of its rivals. At one of Turkey's largest banks last month, the deputy chief executive folded his arms and confessed nervously to the Financial Times: 'I am just an appointed clerk. You can't expect me to be able to comment on anything.' But at the retail end of the market, changes are under way, driven by the emergence of a consumer middle class and expectations of higher standards of service than in the past. The dozen or so largest banks are developing modern cheque clearing and money transmission houses. An automated clearing house is being set up with a pilot stage in Istanbul which will offer clearing one day in Istanbul and three days across the entire country. A new inter-bank electronic funds transfer scheme began operating on April 1 for corporate and retail customers, and BKM, an inter-bank ATM network service, has also been launched. Turkey has virtually nothing in the way of credit reference services. So a limited debit card service which is being set up operates with all transactions being authorised by computer at the point of sale. Nevertheless, the plastic card market is growing rapidly. BKM expects that there will be around 10m cards, the vast majority of them cashcards for use in automatic teller machines, in circulation by the end of this year. That sort of rapid expansion, originally led by the Yapi ve Kredi bank, is proving to be more profitable than the other large banks expected.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (9): Where cost control counts - Profile, Akbank
DOC.TEXT: BE THEY large or small, most Turkish banks operate from glitzy modern headquarters designed to suggest vast opulence. Not so Akbank. Its headquarters are a distinctly unpretentious 1950s building on a busy street in Istanbul's Findikli district. 'The moment you set foot in that building you know you are in an environment where cost control counts,' says one foreign banker in the city. Eschewing the glitter, Ak, set up in 1948 and owned by the Sabanci Group, one of Turkey's two main conglomerates, has set its sights over the past two decades firmly on containing its costs and raising its profits. In doing so, it has risen from the ranks of the smaller and medium-sized banks with 30 branches to become of the dominant players in the country's financial system with 599 branches. Still smaller by asset size than its main competitors, Turkey Bankas and Yapi ve Kredi, Akbank was still far ahead of both last year with TL1,342bn (Dollars 265m) in post-tax profits, up from TL733bn in 1991. Assets at the end of 1991 were Dollars 3.65bn. For the past seven years, Akbank has come out ahead of the rest of the banking market in terms of net profit. Return on average assets was 9.17 per cent last year and return on equity 57.7 per cent, figures which places Akbank well ahead of many other European banks and not just its Turkish competitors. 'It is fairly clear now that Akbank is on the way to becoming dominant in the Turkish financial services sector,' says the general manager of another Istanbul bank. The results are achieved by fairly old-fashioned banking methods, combined with a determination to see the bank and its profits grow. 'Other banks tend to be satisfied with their results. We are not content,' says Mr Erol Sabanci, the bank's vice-chairman and dominant figure. During the mid-1980s, when most Turkish banks ran into trouble by lending to companies which could not pay them back, Akbank managed to keep its non-performing loans below 1 per cent of its loan book or less: no mean achievement for a bank which is owned by and closely associated with a large industrial group. 'We have known most of our customers for 20 or 25 years. We tend to be cautious about lending to new businesses unless we are very sure about what sort of management they have behind them,' says Mr Sabanci. The same caution applies to new types of banking business into which Akbank has moved in the past decade. It entered the field of trade finance and merchant banking for example, by setting up a joint venture with Banque Nationale de Paris and Dresdner Bank. In the UK it has a subsidiary, the first Turkish bank in London, Ak International, with paid up capital of 65m. When it became clear at the end of the 1980s that large Turkish banks would have to invest heavily in money transmission and information technology in order to tap the potential of an emerging domestic retail banking market, Ak watched and waited to see how the experiments of its rivals would fare. 'There are advantages in going second or third into a new market,' says Mr Akin Kozanoglu, the bank's head of retail operations and information technology. 'We were doubtful whether or not automated teller machines would be appropriate in Turkey for example," Once convinced that there were indeed profits to be made in retail banking, Ak pushed ahead, setting up a network of 300 ATMS and spending up to Dollars 100m a year on software development, through its own software house, Aknet, and developing on-line real time computerised links with all its branches. As a result Akbank customers now enjoy some facilities not generally available to European consumers: for example, they can dial a debit card number and learn the balance of their account over the telephone. The move into modern retail banking has brought other changes, especially in the bank's management structure. 'Akbank used frankly to be a one-man show, with most of its top managers relatively insignificant figures compared to Erol Sabanci,' says another banker. 'You can see that he is now consciously trying to replace the one-man show with young executives who are intended to be the backbone of a new management team for the future.' It may sound like a potentially difficult transition for a bank which was only a small family business little more than a generation ago. But other bankers point to the strong corporate culture which Mr Sabanci has developed at Akbank. 'Akbank executives rarely move to other banks, and they tend to understand what is expected of them much better than bankers in the other large banks. It is an old-fashioned outlook, but also a very tightly focused one. If you want to explain why Ak is probably going to go on outperforming the competition, I think that tight focus is the main reason,' says one banker.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (7): Patience is a virtue - Relations with the European Community
DOC.TEXT: THE SAGA of Turkey's relationship with the European Community is now nearly 30 years old, but the final outcome is still unclear. The reasons behind the failure to consummate this long and often difficult courtship are anything but simple. A complex mixture of economic, political and even ideological factors continues to bar the Community's door to the entry of a country whose strategic value to the west was already indisputable during the cold war and whose geopolitical importance has, if anything, increased following the collapse of the Soviet Union and the Communist system. Successive Turkish governments, basing themselves on the argument that the EC-Turkey Association agreement of 1963 specifically mentioned the possibility of Turkey's eventual accession to the Community after a 22-year transitional period, have never wavered in their ultimate objective. They have insisted that by virtue of its strategic geographical situation, its major contribution to western defence and the secular vocation bequeathed to it by the founder of the modern Turkish state, Kemal Ataturk, Turkey's fundamental eligibility for full membership could not be questioned. Most EC member states, however, have never adopted such a straightforward attitude. Though they have not said so frankly, it is an open secret that there have always been serious reservations in the Community about the desirability, or even feasibility, of integrating an Islamic state in the EC. For Turkish President Turgut Ozal, that is the real reason why his country has made so little headway in its attempts to join the Community and that all the other obstacles enumerated by the Community are no more than pretexts. President Ozal is doubtless as mistaken in his incomplete analysis as those who claim that Turkey's Moslem religion is a factor of no importance or relevance whatsoever. Turkey's chequered political history over the past three decades, including a military coup as recently as 1980, its poor human rights record over much of the period, its relative underdevelopment, its failure to implement some of the key provisions of the association agreement and its protectionist economy, all provided sufficient grounds for putting off any decision on its membership. All these considerations, together with others of a much wider nature arising out of the profound changes that had taken place in Europe following the collapse of communism and the desire to give priority in the EC's enlargement policy to the European Free Trade Association and eastern European countries, were set out in the European Commission's 'opinion' at the end of 1989 on Turkey's formal application for membership made two years earlier. Most of the points made are as valid now as they were two years ago. The Commission stressed that, since 1980, the Turkish economy had made 'a remarkable leap forward'. Its GDP had increased by an average of 5.2 per cent a year for the period 1981-88, compared with only 2 per cent for the Twelve. Indeed, it reached more than 9 per cent in 1990, before falling back to about 2 per cent last year. Exports, including notably manufactures, had increased very rapidly and their structure had been diversified. And in 1988 Turkey had managed for the first time since the war to register a current account surplus, a result which was to be reversed two years later, however. So much for the good news in the Commission's 'opinion'. The other side of the coin was that, with a fast-rising population which would eventually be greater than that of any Community member state - an estimated 68m in the year 2000 - Turkey's general development was substantially lower than the European average. Purchasing power was still only one-third of the Community average. Both its industry and agriculture were characterised by very major structural disparities, the level of industrial protectionism was very high, while social protection was much lower than in the EC. In addition, the rate of inflation was several times higher than in the Community - an understatement, given that it reached 70 per cent last year, and only marginally less the previous two years - and the rate of unemployment was extremely high. For good measure, the Commission threw in a number of political reasons why it would be inopportune for Turkey to be granted early membership. While conceding that Turkey now had a parliamentary democracy 'closer to Community models', and that it had made progress in the human rights field and the respect for minorities, 'these had not yet reached the level required in a democracy'. It also stressed that the various disputes with Greece, in particular over Cyprus, were additional obstacles to Turkish membership. In short, the Commission concluded that it was not convinced that the adjustments which would confront Turkey if it were to become a Community member could be overcome in the medium term, despite the positive features of recent developments in Turkey. Whereas it was difficult to argue with many of the Commission's economic arguments, the Turks were particularly irritated by the fact that the Commission was laying down a new set of ground rules for the opening of membership negotiations with Ankara. By stressing that it could not take any decision until after the implementation of the Single European Act in 1993 and until it had fully examined the implications of enlargement for the further development of the Community, taking into account all actual or potential applications for membership, the Commission appeared to have found a new reason for stalling. Indeed, Ankara rightly concluded it was being relegated in the list of applicants behind Efta and the Eastern European countries. If Mr Suleyman Demirel's government has recently adopted a more philosophical attitude towards EC membership, it is partly because the new administration is more realistic than its predecessors about the substantial macro-economic and structural adjustments that still need to be made before Turkey can participate in a European economic and monetary union and before its industry, except for the modern textile sector, can face the full blast of EC competition. Turkey's new status as a pole of attraction and role model for the new central Asian republics, with which it shares a common cultural, linguistic and religious tradition, has also given it a fresh regional political and economic vocation. While no Turkish politician or official seriously believes that there is any real long-term alternative to membership of the EC, which already provides a market for 53 per cent of Turkish exports and is the source of 48 per cent of its imports, it is now accepted in Ankara that Turkey is unlikely to become a full member of the Community until the early part of the next century. Its hopes, in the meantime, reside in the 'substantial measures' proposed by the European Commission to help Turkey's economic and political modernisation process and to prepare the path to its eventual membership. These include the completion by the beginning of 1996 of a customs union between the EC and Turkey, the activation of the Association Agreement's 4th Financial Protocol providing Turkey with Ecu600m (Pounds 420m) of financial aid, the full association of Turkey with the EC's Mediterranean programme and the stepping up of the Community's industrial and technological aid to Turkey. Most of the member countries are no longer prepared to tolerate the political veto of some of the most important of these measures by Greece, which has linked them to a settlement of the Cyprus problem. Though not denying the importance of a Cyprus solution for Turkey's long-term links with the Community, Britain, which takes over the EC presidency in the second half of this year, is particularly anxious to revitalise the EC's relationship with Turkey as quickly as possible. Indeed, there is a growing feeling in Community countries that Turkey has reaped a poor reward for its steadfast loyalty to the western alliance and that Ankara needs to be reassured that it has not been permanently rejected by the European partners it has wooed for so long.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (6): Horizon shifts to central Asia - Foreign Affairs
DOC.DATELINE: ONCE ONE of the world's great imperial powers, Turkey
DOC.TEXT: like Britain and France - has never lost its conviction that it has a special role to play in international affairs. Yet, in spite of its strategic position at the hinge of Europe and Asia, these ambitions have been frustrated since the final collapse of the Ottoman empire in 1923, by Turkey's economic under-development, its political instability including three military coups in the last 30 years and the restraints imposed on its freedom of action by the military might of its former Soviet neighbour. True to the ideas of the founder of the modern Turkish state, Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, Turkey has consistently attempted to project a western, secular image, in spite of the fact that the vast majority of its inhabitants are Moslems. Until very recently, however, its western allies have looked upon it essentially as a rampart against Soviet military expansion, rather than as an equal partner sharing their own democratic principles and traditions. The considerable progress that has been made over the last few years to transform Turkey into a genuine multi-party democracy, a market economy and a society in which civil liberties and human rights are guaranteed are beginning to change international perceptions, in spite of continuing criticisms of the government's treatment of the country's Kurdish minority. The European Community's gates will probably remain shut to Turkey until the beginning of the next century (the reasons for which are examined in the other article on this page). But, at a time when Turkey's international credibility can no longer be based mainly on its former cold war role of anti-Communist bastion and defender of Nato's south-eastern flank, it has suddenly emerged as an invaluable partner of the west in preserving regional political stability and preventing Iran from extending its influence and its particular brand of Islamic fundamentalism throughout the area. The Turks have found completely new foreign policy horizons opening up in the aftermath of the cold war and the dissolution of the Soviet Union, which has led to the independence of central Asian republics, such as Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Tajikistan. All these republics, with the exception of Tajikistan, speak Turkic languages and share a common cultural and religious tradition with Turkey. Though they have shown no desire - as yet, at least - to become part of a pan-Turkic union, they look upon Turkey, with its comparatively advanced economy and mixed secular, Islamic tradition, as a model they would like to follow. Their overtures have been followed up with alacrity by Ankara. Turkey has offered help to modernise the central Asian states' telecommunications and transport networks, has started beaming special Turkish-language TV programmes to its 'sister states,' is giving scholarships to enable central Asian students to study in Turkey and has even proposed aid for the introduction of the Latin alphabet in states which have used the cyrillic version ever since their incorporation in the Soviet Union. So far, so good. All this cultural aid is more than welcome in most of the countries of the region, where Islam and secularism find no difficulty in cohabiting in an atmosphere relatively free of tension, as in Turkey. But Iran and Saudi Arabia are pursuing a similar goal, in which religion plays a much bigger, if not predominant part. Iran's proselytising zeal, backed by the distribution of tens of thousands of copies of the Koran, is nowhere more in evidence than in Azerbaijan, the only one of the mostly Sunni-dominated republics in which the Shia Moslems are in the majority. This competition for the hearts and minds of the former Soviet transCaucasian and central Asian republics is equally intense in the economic sphere. During a recent tour of the region, Mr Suleyman Demirel, the Turkish prime minister, generously offered some Dollars 1bn worth of loans and export credits. However, Turkey can ill afford such largesse, given the need to put its own inflation and debt-ridden economic house in order. Certainly, oil-rich Iran and Saudi Arabia are much more capable than Turkey of granting substantial financial aid to the poverty-stricken central Asian region. Indeed, the Turkish leaders are constantly stressing that their country has neither the ability nor the desire to act alone in the region, however much it has taken the cultural high ground in wooing the central Asian states. It is well aware that Turkey's own contribution can be no more than a drop in the ocean compared with the total western financial aid required by the region and that the problem is further complicated by the priority that has been given by western donor countries to aid for other, politically more important parts of the former Soviet Union, such as Russia. For the Demirel government, the new focus on central Asia is clearly seen as a useful means of diverting public opinion from more long-standing and intractable problems such as the Kurdish problem and its implications for Turkey's relations with Iraq and Syria, its tense relationship with Greece and and the closely connected issue of EC membership. These problems will not go away, however. Though Turkey, largely thanks to President Turgut Ozal's persistence in the face of strong domestic opposition, fully supported the US-led anti-Iraq coalition in the Gulf War, it did so with a heavy heart. Iraq was one of its principal trading partners before the Gulf conflict and Iraq exported much of its oil through a pipeline across Turkey, before Ankara turned off the taps. Though it has no intention of contravening the United Nations Security Council's economic embargo on trade with Iraq, it is no secret that Turkey would like to see an early end to sanctions. 'Our sincere wish is to see Iraq come back to the world community as soon as possible,' Mr Hikmet Cetin, the Turkish foreign minister said in an interview. 'Turkey is the country most affected, economically, politically and socially by the sanctions (apart from Iraq). We have calculated that Turkey lost about Dollars 15bn during the crisis and is continuing to do so.' Nor is there much official or public enthusiasm about the continuing presence of US, British and French aircraft on Turkish air bases near the Iraqi border, which are acting as a deterrent against any attempts which might be made by President Saddam Hussein to oust the country's Kurdish population from its protected zone in Northern Iraq. The chances that the Turkish parliament will authorise in June an extension of this so-callled 'Operation Comfort' for another few months are considered to be good. But there can be no guarantee that this permission will be forthcoming indefinitely, or indeed, for very much longer.
