At the same time, Turkey's European relations continue to be bedevilled by apparently insoluble disagreements with Greece over Cyprus, the northern part of which has been occupied by Turkish troops since 1974, the Aegean continental shelf, territorial waters and air space and Greece's refusal to give the green light to the EC's financial aid to Turkey. Though there has been some improvement in the bilateral atmosphere since Mr Constantine Mitzotakis's government came to power in Greece and since the meeting of the Greek and Turkish prime ministers in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year, there is, as yet, very little light at the end of the tunnel. The only hope lies in the renewed efforts of the United Nations secretary-general to finalise a deal on Cyprus this summer. For, as the Greeks constantly emphasise, it is Cyprus which holds the key to better Greek-Turkish relations. Yet it is clear that Ankara would rather accept a continuation of tense relations with Greece than an unsatisfactory settlement which failed to guarantee the equal rights of the Turkish population within a Cypriot federation.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (5): Slow moves on asset sales - The public deficit is spiralling, but privatisation is being held up
DOC.TEXT: TURKISH POLITICIANS rarely discuss the issue with the zeal you find in eastern Europe, or in Argentina where reformed Peronists are now rolling back the frontiers of the state. Today in Ankara, with a coalition government at the helm, the debate about privatisation has been hijacked by bureaucratic infighting, and the opposition of vested business interests, concerned at the growing foreign presence in the country's economy. It has always been easier to make the economic case for the privatisation of Turkey's state-run industries. The state's interests in 235 enterprises, either as the majority shareholder, as an affiliate or a minority partner in a privately-managed concern, are responsible for up to a third of the public sector borrowing requirement, which in 1991 was running at around 12 per cent of GNP. They account for almost half of all fixed investment in Turkey and employ close to half a million people. Mrs Tansu Ciller, the economics minister, has still to convince her cabinet colleagues of the need for swift remedies if Turkey is to contain the spiralling public deficit which is the main cause of the country's 70 per cent rate of inflation. The former Bosphorus University professor seems increasingly estranged from the bureaucrats whose job it is to carry out her policy. The problems have been exacerbated by her public differences with Mr Cavit Caglar, the state minister who has repeatedly challenged her views on the economy. In the eight months since the election, the government has yet to give a clear signal on the issue. The current privatisation programme is centred on the sale of the government's minority stakes in a number of privately managed companies, the details of which were already approved under the last government. While moving ahead, it is little more than a revenue-raising exercise and does nothing to transform the structure and ownership of Turkish industry. Moreover, there are no plans regarding the main lossmakers - the railways, the ports authority, Tek (the power utility), the grain board, the coal corporation and the tobacco and alcohol monopoly. A World Bank report called for a radical restructuring of the state sector. Tusiad, the Turkish businessmen's association, also called for strong action. The Bank suggested that many of the state companies would have to be closed down. Others would be restructured, by selling their distribution and marketing arms. All of the state enterprises needed to be brought under the commercial code to instil the discipline of the market and allow the managers to make decisions about price. Two months ago, in a somewhat desperate gesture, Mrs Ciller asked Peugeot, the French carmaker, to consider locating its new investment in the old mining town of Zonguldak on Turkey's Black Sea coast. However, the French company is expected to stick to its original plan to build the plant near Izmir. The loss-making state-owned Zonguldak coal corporation, with its payroll of close to 50,000 miners, is one of the principal drains on the Turkish exchequer. In April, after several months of exhaustive discussion, the Turkish cabinet cleared the way for the creation of a new body to handle the disposal of state assets. The idea was to put the state enterprises under the control of an independent authority drawn from political but also academic, business and labour circles. The plan was to restructure the companies in preparation for a sale to the public. However, the powers of Toyok, as the agency is known, have been severely curtailed. The council of ministers retains an effective veto on key decisions, such as the closure of plant and staff redundancies and lay-offs. The privatisation programme was launched by the former Motherland party government in 1986. The gains have been modest. Total revenue from the sale of state assets either by public offering, by block share sales or flotations on the Istanbul stock market, comes to less than USDollars 1bn. Turkey's bid to revive the programme has now met with opposition from businessmen, worried at foreign encroachment in a number of key industrial sectors. The problem is in part a practical one. Turkey's infant stock exchange will find it difficult to digest a large-scale flotation of state-owned assets. On the other hand, few Turkish groups are in a position to raise the sort of cash required to buy state shares in block, which is currently the government's favoured method. In the short term, foreigners may prove the only buyers ready to invest. This year, the newly-created Public Participation High Council, the agency entrusted with handling the sale of state assets to the public, expects to raise Dollars 868m. Officials talk of selling off parts of PTT, the Turkish telecommunications monopoly. The government says the company's cable, TV, car telephone and computer networks are earmarked for disposal. Mr Yasar Topcu, minister of transport, has all but ruled out the sale of Turk Hava Yollari (THY). Any early moves to sell off Petrol Offisi, the state's petrol products retailer, and Tupras, the state refineries corporation, have also been put back. Mr Ustun Sanver, head of the high council, says the government may sell some Petrol Offisi gas station outlets. In the case of the refineries, the government is more likely to look for a foreign investor to form a joint venture with the existing plant. In addition to the cement companies, Mr Sanver hopes to raise Dollars 25-27m from the sale of block shares in Polinas Plastik, a packaging producer; Seker Sigorta (insurance); Istanbul Demir Celik, a mining concern; Turk Tractor, an agricultural machinery business; Trakmak, its marketing arm; and Turk Otomotiv, the car parts manufacturer. Several state companies are to be re-offered to the public, after the PPHC rejected earlier bids. These include Ray insurance, Gima department store and Meysu, a fruit juice and food producer. Mr Sanver expect these sales will realise Dollars 28-34m. There are plans for the public offering of the government's remaining 49 per cent of Netas, which is part-owned by Northern Telecom of Canada. Mr Sanver says preparations are under way for the sale of block shares in Teletas, the telecommunications industry; AEG-ETI, the electric transformer maker; Guneysu, the fruit juice producer; Tofas, the Fiat joint venture assembly and its marketing arm; Aksaray Azmi, flour producer and Ankara, the flour and bread producer. In January, Citibank organised the sale of 51 per cent of Ipragaz for Dollars 65m to the French company Primagaz. In March, Sabanci - Turkey's largest industrial conglomerate - paid Dollars 22.5m for an 87 per cent stake in Nigde Cimento, a local cement producer. Cement has become the cause celebre with the French taking a commanding position after the purchase by Societe Ciments Francais (SCF) of five state-owned companies in 1989. Lafarge Coppee, the world's second largest cement producer, and Societe Vicat have also entered the market. It was Mr Suleyman Demirel, the prime minister, who opposed the sale to SCF, arguing it contravened a 1987 law on privatisation as the shares had not first been offered to domestic investors. This month the role of foreign capital is again expected to come under scrutiny when the PPHC offers block shares in a further 11 cement companies. Mr Sanver says the cement sale is open to all investors, local and international. Any hiccup at this stage could badly damage Turkey's privatisation programme.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (4): Parliament comes back to life - Politics / A change in mood
DOC.TEXT: YOU MIGHT think, looking at the political scene in Turkey, that nothing much has really changed. The politicians have the same old faces. The issues are little different from a decade ago. Even the excuses sound familiar. But Turkey is experiencing an important change in mood. Amid signs of increasing political violence, and a deteriorating economy, parliament - so long ignored under the previous government - is enjoying a renewed lease of life. The 450-seat National Assembly is today the most eclectic gathering of Turkish political opinion in the country's history. In all, there are six parties representing every strand, from radicals of the Kurdish minority to Islamic fundamentalists and extreme nationalists on both the right and left wing. In many countries, such a fiery political cocktail would be a recipe for disaster. In Turkey a consensus has emerged, with a coalition government of conservative and social democratic parties pushing ahead with what promises to be the most thoroughgoing reform programme since Ataturk founded the republic in the 1920s. The man responsible is Mr Suleyman Demirel, the prime minister and leader of the right-of-centre True Path party, DYP. He knows only too well the vicissitudes of Turkish politics. Six times prime minister before, he was twice ousted by the military, the last occasion being in 1980. The prime minister's bid to restore the effectiveness of parliament is something of a personal crusade. More practically, it allows him to ignore the constant jibes of President Turgut Ozal who has repeatedly used his office for partisan political purposes in a bid to undermine the growing public support for his long-time rival. This uneasy cohabitation with President Ozal casts a deep shadow over Turkish politics. But Mr Demirel has provided the president with just enough rope to hang himself, by dangling the threat of a series of corruption files, where official impropriety is alleged. The prime minister's tactics are in some ways merely reflect the situation that he does not have a sufficient majority to unseat the president by changing the constitution. But many colleagues believe this measured approach to Turkey's problems underlines Mr Demirel's determination not to rock the political boat. At 68, Mr Demirel wants to lay to rest his turbulent reputation and secure an honourable place in Turkey's history. The real question is whether he can match his enthusiasm with the necessary urgency to push badly needed legislation through the house. The result of the election in October, while reconfirming the strength of the conservative vote in Turkish politics, did not provide Mr Demirel with the outright majority he wanted. True Path emerged as the country's largest party, winning widespread support particularly in the small towns of the Aegean and central Anatolia. But the outgoing Motherland party, ANAP, also did better than expected, polling strongly in the big cities where it successfully harnessed the votes of the business community with its image of a modern western-oriented Turkey. The election result also underlined the demise of the left in Turkey with the Social Democratic Populists, the main left-of-centre party, only too happy to accept Mr Demirel's offer to form a coalition. The party has still not resolved its leadership crisis, with Mr Deniz Baykal making a series of so far abortive bids to replace Mr Erdal Inonu, the SHP leader. Local elections on June 7 in many parts of Turkey are expected to reinforce these trends. A strong swing to the DYP might even persuade the prime minister to go to the country in the autumn in search of a clear mandate. It is too early to claim what is happening is the renaissance of Turkish democracy, as the government suggests. But parliamentary sessions now receive extensive television coverage. The deputies have probably never worked so hard. Indeed, the legislative timetable is now so congested that the speaker has had to shelve plans for an early recess. The politicians may find themselves confined to smoky committee rooms well into the summer months. To visit one of the many state ministers who share offices in the old prime ministry in Ankara's Kizilay district is to run the gauntlet of a throng of farmers, relatives and free loaders, all waiting for jobs and other official largesse. Mr Demirel indulges the electorate with regular audiences in the prime ministry where, if you can brave the military police on the door, any Turk can make his point to the prime minister - a custom which seems to have more in common with the consensus-building traditions of Arab politics. Another feature of the new parliament is the return of a number of familiar faces from Turkey's turbulent political past. Mr Bulent Ecevit, the former socialist prime minister, regained his seat in the mining town of Zongludak. Mr Alpaslan Turkes, leader of extreme right-wing Turkish Labour party is also back. The happy triumvirate is made up by Mr Necmettin Erbakan, the Islamic leader who espouses, among other things, an Islamic common market and an Islamic Nato. There are newer faces too, including the attractive radical Kurdish deputy, Mrs Leyla Zana, who created such a stir when giving her oath of allegiance at the opening of parliament wearing a headband in tricolour of the banned Kurdish Workers Party, PKK, which is fighting an increasingly violent separatist war in Turkey's south-east region. She was one of 22 radical Kurdish deputies who stood on the Social Democratic ticket - 18 of whom have now resigned. In the shifting sands of Turkish party politics, some of the other recent alliances are already coming unstuck. Mr Erbakan and Mr Turkes, bedfellows during the election, have already gone their separate ways. The landscape could soon be changed further if parliament approves a draft bill submitted in April which would lift the restrictions on political parties banned following the 1980 military coup. That would allow these political groups to lay claim to extensive property impounded under the military order. There is talk of reconstituting the centre-left Republican's People's Party, founded by Ataturk. There has even been some debate about allowing a Kurdish party - a suggestion first made by Mr Mesut Yilmaz, leader of ANAP.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (2): Market reserves its judgment - The economy / There are still clouds on the horizon
DOC.TEXT: LATE LAST year, when Mr Suleyman Demirel's coalition government took office, many Turkish businessmen made little secret of their misgivings. For Mr Demirel was last in power 12 years earlier, when inflation soared to three-digit figures, Turkey suffered its worst-ever balance of payments deficit and industry was paralysed. Nearly six months on, the market is still reserving its judgment, but it is clear that times have changed. The Suleyman Demirel of the 1990s believes in privatisation, realistic exchange rates and - in theory at least - fiscal reform. Turkey does not look as if it is about to be plunged into a fresh economic crisis. That said, there are still plenty of clouds on the horizon. Though Turkey is managing to keep its external payments under control and last year ran a surplus of Dollars 272m on its current account, the economy failed to shake off a recession which began with the Gulf War. Gross National Product grew by only 0.3 per cent in 1991 in an economy where growth has averaged between 5 and 6 per cent a year over the past three decades. Worse still, inflation went up to 71.1 per cent from 60.4 per cent in 1990 and from the middle of the year, monetary disciplines were abandoned as it became clear that there would be a general election. Six months on, monetary self-restraint has not returned. Consumer prices jumped by an alarming 9 per cent in January, by 5.4 per cent in February and 4.9 per cent in March, taking inflation to 78.7 per cent for the previous 12-month period. Does this mean that Turkey is on the way to triple-digit inflation? Probably not, says Mr Deniz Gokce, professor of economics at the Bosphorus University in Istanbul. He predicts that inflation will slacken this year though probably not as sharply as official forecasts, but that GNP growth will also be relatively disappointing. On the other hand, Turkey's balance of payments seems to be under control despite a foreign debt burden of around Dollars 43bn. Turkey's trade deficit fell by 20 per cent in 1991, largely because demand for imports was very slack. Exports rose by 4.9 per cent to Dollars 13.6bn (1990: Dollars 12.96bn) while imports dropped by 5.7 per cent from Dollars 22.3bn to Dollars 21.04bn. As a result, the trade deficit was down from Dollars 9.3bn in 1990 to Dollars 7.4bn. Despite this improvement, foreign currency reserves held by the central bank have slipped by about Dollars 1bn from Dollars 5.1bn at the start of the year to Dollars 4.08bn, mainly because Turks are selling Turkish liras and buying foreign currency as the local currency plummets ever further and faster against the US dollar and the Deutschemark. The main reason for the currency's ever-faster decline appears to be the widening public sector deficit. The 1992 budget has been set at TL208 trillion, and an unchanged TL32 trillion deficit is planned, a target which bankers drily describe as 'implausible' since it would mean a reduction of about a third in the deficit in real terms at a time when government spending is shooting upwards and public revenues are languishing. Official projections are that tax revenues should be TL175.9bn, or about four-fifths of total government revenues. Around TL3.5 trillion will be raised from privatisations. Whether things will work out quite like this is another matter. There are few candidates for quick, profitable privatisations and the government does not seem to have the stomach to introduce unpopular new taxes in what may, after all, turn out to be another election year. The government announced a new package of tax reforms and other economic measures on January 17. The main feature appears to be a sharp increase in indirect taxation. It has also launched a controversial tax amnesty, intended to enable the Treasury to get at least part of the unpaid taxes it is owed. Both sets of measures have yet to prove their effectiveness. The government wants to press ahead with privatisation operations, but five agencies will not be sold off: TMO (the state grain organisation); TEK (the electricity authority); PTT; TCDD (state railways); and Tekel, the alcohol and tobacco monopoly. The trouble is that this list includes the main loss-makers. If these cannot be privatised, perhaps some of them at least - for example, the Zonguldak coal mines - could be shut down. That solution would please international agencies such as the World Bank, but it is probably too radical for Mr Demirel to contemplate. The burden of public sector losses is a heavy one. Most of Turkey's larger industrial enterprises were set up by the state between the 1930s and 1950s and were never designed to run at a profit. More than TL11,997bn was lost by 18 state industries in 1991. The top loss-makers were TEK (the electricity authority) which lost TL4,326bn, TCDD (state railways) TL3,269bn; and the Turkish Coal board (TL3,264bn) and the TD (iron and steel works which lost TL2,619bn). But not all the public sector industries make a loss. Eight state industries made money: Tekel, the state alcoholic beverages and tobacco monopoly made a profit of TL1,378bn, while TPAO, the petroleum prospecting agency made profits of TL1,289bn and the Post Office made TL1,229bn. The complaint most generally heard is that Mr Demirel's economics team makes grandiose promises but is short on a focused economy strategy. Mrs Tansu Ciller, minister of state in charge of the economy, does not seem to have the clout (or familiarity with the labyrinthine ways of the Turkish bureaucracy) to match the men who dominated the Turkish economy in the Ozal era. Instead she seems to be losing ground to Mr Cavit Caglar, another minister of state and president of the High Council on Credit and Mr Tevfik Altinok, the undersecretary of the treasury and foreign trade, a veteran treasury official who has spent most of the past decade working in Istanbul with Koc, Turkey's largest industrial conglomerate. Few of the new appointees have the international whizz-kid touch which distinguished the top economic officials in the Ozal era and though statism is out of fashion as an economic philosophy in Ankara, there also seems to be little enthusiasm for exposing the economy to more competition, particularly from the outside world, though on the foreign trade front, Turkey is pledged to achieving a customs union with both the European Community and Efta by 1996. Only one of Mr Ozal's men, Mr Rusdu Saracaoglu, the 43-year old central bank governor, has survived and his prospects look uncertain. The hardest choices probably still lie ahead. If Mr Demirel truly wants to stabilise the economy, he is going to have to turn a deaf ear to the pleas of state employees and farmers for more pay. A fresh round of public sector pay negotiations got under way this spring and the coalition government's social democratic minister of labour is planning changes to the law which would give unions much more power than they have enjoyed in the past. Agricultural support prices may prove an even trickier issue. Mr Demirel's main power base is the farming population of western Turkey. Once upon a time, Turkish farmers could count on the government to hold agricultural support prices high, allowing (untaxed) rural incomes to rise. The military and Mr Ozal put a stop to that way of doing things after the 1980 coup. If Mr Demirel reverses that trend this summer to please the farmers, Mr Altinok and the Treasury will face a gruelling time in 1993. But there is no way that the main reforms of the 1980s can be reversed, even if there is still plenty of scope for opening up the economy to genuine market competition.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Survey of Turkey (1): A worrying indecision - Though the country has enhanced its reputation as a stable influence in a volatile region, Mr Suleyman Demirel, the prime minister, faces growing pressure to deliver on his electoral promise of political and social reform
DOC.TEXT: IT MIGHT seem like a sentimental indulgence, but the Turks are greatly flattered that their country, once dismissed as the sick man of Europe, is now held up as a model by the newly-emerging states of central Asia. Today the attentions of these distant cousins is welcome vindication of Turkey's own moves to look west, a policy set in motion by Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, which has taken on a new urgency in the last decade. The recognition is particularly timely during a period of deepening troubles at home, where indecision at the centre threatens to spoil Turkey's best efforts at reform. A resurgence of urban terror groups provides a chilling reminder of the political instability which led to the military's intervention in 1980. Inflation is running at more than 70 per cent, with the next wage round looming. More worrying, for the first time, the Kurdish problem challenges the very basis of this nation state carved from the ruins of Ottoman empire. But Turks are great survivors and no politician better illustrates this than Mr Suleyman Demirel, the veteran conservative who became prime minister for the seventh time following the general election last October. His return 12 years after he was ousted by the military - for the second time - is seen as the best hope of restoring the country's fortunes. The coalition government he leads is described by one western ambassador as 'the most reform-minded, liberal and democratic in Turkey's history' - not such an extravagant claim given Turkey's recent political turbulence. Mr Demirel is best described a patronage politician, never more at home than when manipulating the small business and farmer groups which control his DYP party. Today he has also developed a strong instinct for the populist gesture, epitomised by his election slogan to build the police stations out of glass. It remains to be seen whether his fragile coalition has the self-assurance to administer the radical reforms which Turkey so badly needs. The search for consensus between Mr Demirel's True Path party (DYP) and the Social Democratic Populists (SHP) of Mr Erdal Inonu is already proving painfully slow. Even when legislation makes it through cabinet, it is destined for a rough ride in parliament where deputies are enjoying the restoration of those traditional powers largely ignored by the former government. However, with Turkey taking on the presidency of the Council of Europe this month, the prime minister is pushing on a broad front of political and legal reforms before the summer recess. A draft bill on human rights has been submitted. Its main provisions aim to combat the prevalence of police torture, which continues to be the single greatest blight on Turkey's image abroad. Labour laws are being tailored to bring the country in line with International Labour Organisation conventions, while proposals for the country's Kurdish minority follow Turkey's signature of the 1990 Paris Charter on human rights. Mr Demirel faces a number of other challenges, domestic and foreign. On its borders, Turkey confronts growing instability in the Caucasus, with accompanying fears that it could be drawn into defending the rights of Moslem against Armenian. In North Iraq, the evolution of some sort of autonomy for the Kurds might encourage similar aspirations from Turkey's own Kurdish minority. In Europe, Turkey is anxious not to be isolated by the process of economic and political union. The Turks have been associate members of the European Community since 1963, but the current government increasingly accepts that chances of full EC membership in the foreseeable future are slim. At Maastricht, Turkey was offered associate membership of the nine-nation Western European Union defence association, while the Greeks were invited to become full WEU members. Given Turkey's long-standing disputes with Greece, the legacy of more than 600 years of shared history, the government will have a hard task recommending the EC's offer to parliament. There are problems, too, on the EC trade and investment front. More than half Turkey's trade is with the Community and Turkey is still broadly on target for customs union with Brussels in 1996. But there are renewed calls for protectionism from Turkish business groups concerned at the growth in foreign competition which has resulted from liberalisation. There are even those who question whether Turkey will ever implement all the tariff cuts necessary for customs union, particularly given its needs on the revenue side. Turkey alone cannot resolve these issues, and Mr Demirel acknowledges that, to receive a better hearing, Turkey must first tackle a series of domestic problems that increasingly impinges on relations with the world at large. This has been dramatically shown by the Kurdish issue which has taken on an international dimension since allied intervention to help the Iraqi Kurds. Recognising this, the government has embarked on a new policy initiative. A package of economic measures is being introduced to tackle the south-eastern region's high unemployment, while a Kurdish institute and two Kurdish newspapers have been established. The government's junior coalition partners, the SHP, are now openly debating the broader constitutional question of devolved powers as a means to win back moderate Kurdish opinion and undercut support for the rebel Kurdish Workers Party (PKK). The authorities are steering a narrow course, offering liberal reform, yet giving the military an apparent carte blanche to combat the separatists. This could prove a difficult line to maintain as the PKK intensifies its campaign to force further reprisals from the security forces. Mr Demirel has the added disadvantage of a simmering feud with Mr Turgut Ozal, who became president in 1989 after dominating Turkish political life for most of the 1980s. It is on the Kurdish issue that the president has been most vocal, urging Mr Demirel to introduce Kurdish television for the south-east where the majority of Turkey's 10m Kurds live. The president has also used his veto to block key appointments and openly voiced disagreement with the government on a number of issues, particularly on the economy where he has accused the coalition of undoing the good work of the past decade, when he was prime minister. Turkey's economy is in recession. While the population increases by 2.2 per cent every year, Turkey's gross national product grew in 1991 by 0.3 per cent, the slowest rate in more than a decade. This year the picture will be barely improved. While Turkey remains the least taxed of OECD economies, all talk of tax reform flounders. Privatisation of the government's minority shares in privately-run companies still leaves the giant utilities and the other main loss-making enterprises burdening the exchequer. On the key issue of wages, so instrumental in Turkey's export drive in the 1980s, the unions are using SHP support to win further concessions, which economists fear could result in a loss of competitiveness for Turkish industry. The policy indecision is now filtering through to the money markets, where confidence in the Turkish lira looks increasingly shaky. A major intervention by the central bank in the first quarter of this year under-lined the vulnerability of the Turkish lira. Stability will be especially critical now that Turkey is going to the commercial markets for more than USDollars 1bn and floating bonds for the first time since 1990. Meanwhile, Mrs Tansu Ciller has progressively lost her authority as chief economics minister. Her inexperience in dealing with the bureaucracy has surfaced in a series of embarrassing public disagreements with Mr Rusdu Saracaoglu, the central bank governor and one of the few top civil servants to have survived the change of government. Turkey's promised land is some way off. For many of the country's 58m inhabitants, a 10-year diet of economic deregulation has been hard to digest. High inflation is eroding the standard of living of those on fixed incomes. Investment has dropped while foreign and domestic business waits to see whether Mr Demirel has the necessary courage to deal with Turkey's fundamental problems, and allow it to regain its natural position as leader in the region. Unless the government can tackle the question of the economy, all Turkey's problems will get worse. If it fails to do so, even the Central Asian republics could look elsewhere for their model - a prospect that neither the west nor Turkey relishes.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / London Stock Exchange: Hanson rumour lifts BP
DOC.BYLINE: By CHRISTOPHER PRICE and JOEL KIBAZO
DOC.TEXT: THE MARKET was set alight in early trading with rumours that Hanson had moved to buy the Kuwait Investment Office's 9.8 per cent stake in British Petroleum - provoking speculation that the conglomerate was setting its sights on the troubled oil company. No basis could be found for the story, although the repercussions acted on both companies' shares all day, with BP up 10 at one stage before retreating to close at 261p, a gain of 5 on the day. After an initial rise, Hanson slipped back to close 3 off at 228 1/2 p. A bulky 22m shares were traded in BP. Most analysts were sceptical that Hanson would consider BP, either as an investment or a bid, because of the illogical fit with its present strategy and portfolio - although a trader said yesterday's story was the third in recent weeks linking the two groups. Argyll retreats Food retailer Argyll Group was one of the worst performers among the FT-SE 100 constituents as its results failed to excite and a large line of stock looking for a home held down the share price. The full-year figures were within market expectations, but after last week's sparkling results from rival J. Sainsbury, the lack of surprises yesterday dulled the response. The stock was further undermined by a securities house having some problems placing 3.5m Argyll shares. However, turnover of 10m shares by the close, more than twice the usual volume in the stock, suggested that the house was finally successful. While the increased dividend helped sentiment, Argyll's current trading was below some forecasts. One analyst also complained that the group concentrated too much at its presentation on plans for the Lo-Cost supermarket operations rather than on the upmarket Presto chain. The shares declined 10 to 357p. Composite insurer Commercial Union, which reported first-quarter results yesterday, and launched a preference share issue, retreated 6 to 504p as word went round the market that Sun Alliance was about to place its stake in CU of around 14.5 per cent. Among those to discount the talk was Mr Steven Bird, of Smith New Court, who said the stake was 'unlikely to be placed at the moment'. The market was, however, pleased by the trading performance at CU, which revealed losses 20 per cent lower at Pounds 19.2m, and at the same time launched a Pounds 100m preference share issue, to be placed through Hoare Govett and Cazenove, to finance expansion. BZW said it remains a seller of the shares 'because we believe they are over-distributed on the dividend front and are trading above net asset value'. On the bull side, Smith said: 'The company has got a superior underwriting record. Unlike others in the sector, it is looking to make substantial profits in two years time.' Profit-taking weakened Sun Alliance, which finished 3 lower at 321p in spite of an upbeat annual meeting. Well-received results from Land Securities lifted the stock and other leading property shares, although there was little news to cheer those looking for a revival in the sector. Mr Graham Stanley at County NatWest said: 'There were glimmers of hope in the retail market outside of the south-east, but these were cancelled out by the depressing picture elsewhere, particularly in the central London office market.' He has reduced his profits forecast for next year to Pounds 233m from Pounds 239m, citing the cost of the group's move away from offices and more into retail. The shares rose 9 to 440p. Some investors looked to switch out of Land Securities, preferring instead British Land, up 11 at 214p, MEPC, 9 ahead at 346p, and Slough Estates, also 9 to the good at 196p. In spite of figures below expectations, Ranks Hovis McDougall moved ahead as spurious bid talk was again heard. Analysts were particularly disturbed by the downbeat theme adopted by the company on present trading conditions, plus the 62 per cent fall in milling and breadmaking revenue. Smith New Court pared its current year profits forecast by Pounds 7m to Pounds 98m, while Nomura reduced its estimate by Pounds 12m to the same amount. Next year, they forecast Pounds 105m and Pounds 109m respectively. The shares put on 5 to 234p. Brewer Bass turned in positive interim results, the shares advancing 11 to 631p. County NatWest is looking for Pounds 528m for the full year and Pounds 638m in 1993. Talk of a price war in the food retail market led to weakness in the sector. J. Sainsbury slipped 2 1/2 to 465p, Tesco 8 to 280p and Kwik Save 5 to 625p. Asda, however, continued to benefit from bid talk, edging 1 1/2 higher to 33 1/4 p in volume of 28m. The creeping pace of recovery in the hotel market was behind two forecast downgrades in Forte, which dipped 4 to 245p. Kleinwort Benson cut its current year estimate by Pounds 10m to Pounds 115m, while another house was reported to have come down to Pounds 125m. Turnover in Pilkington rose to 11m and the shares firmed 2 to 161p, after two blocks of 7.7m and 2.7m respectively went through the market. The bulk of the volume was said to have arisen from BZW selling the remainder of the 31m shares bought from BTR earlier this month. The reiteration of a buy recommendation by Kleinwort Benson on Inchcape boosted the stock, which climbed 12 to 513p on turnover of 1.8m. Bowater rose 12 to 850p. The shares are favoured by BZW, which has issued a weighty document on the stock that is due to land on investors' desks today. The broker lifted its current year forecast by Pounds 3m to Pounds 155m and the following year's by Pounds 12m to Pounds 188m. Fears that bankers to Eurotunnel could withdraw funding unless the company settles a dispute with the tunnel's contractor TML by August hurt the shares, which shed 8 to 380p. British Airways continued to bask in the glow of its spectacular results aired on Tuesday. The shares added 13 at 380p on some 10m traded. A badly handled order in NFC caused the shares to lose part of an earlier gain. They ended 9 up at 282p. NEW HIGHS AND LOWS FOR 1992 NEW HIGHS (300). DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets (Europe): Daimler helps Frankfurt to 21-month high
DOC.TEXT: APART from some weakness in Scandinavia, continental bourses were mostly firmer, writes Our Markets Staff. FRANKFURT rose to a 21-month high as domestic and foreign investors responded to this week's engineering and construction pay deals, and positive comments from Daimler-Benz on Tuesday. Volume rose to DM9.9bn from DM7.2bn. After a 6.84 rise to 717.40 for the FAZ index at midsession, the DAX ended 24.24, or 1.4 per cent higher, at 1,787.50, its highest close since August 3, 1990. Some analysts expect it to approach its all-time, March 1990 high of 1,976.43 within six months. Optimism hinged largely on Daimler's expectation that 1992 results will be above those of 1991. In a broadly based gain taking in carmakers and chemicals, steels and some engineers, both Daimler and AEG were boosted by the former's statement that it did not expect to book an AEG loss in 1992. AEG rose DM6 to DM212 and its parent by DM16.50 to DM804. Construction stocks liked the wage deal, and forecasts of further growth in the sector. Bilfinger & Berger led them up with a rise of DM24.80 to DM1,060. Retailers were mixed: Karstadt put on DM24 or 3.8 per cent to DM655; but Douglas closed DM26 lower at DM615 on a forecast of flat or lower earnings this year, after an early rise of DM14 to DM655 on higher profits for 1991. PARIS inched higher after Tuesday's drop but dealers said investors were getting cautious after the market's recent rally. The CAC-40 index ended up 7.71 at 2,030.84 in modest turnover of FFr2bn. Alcatel Alsthom was one of the day's more prominent losers, as the stock touched a low of FFr639 before closing FFr12 to FFr646 on news that it had placed 10m American Depositary Shares in the US at Dollars 23 5/8 each, which traders said was the equivalent to FFr635 in the French share price. In the afternoon, it was reported that a block of 290,000 American Depositary Rights in Elf Aquitaine were traded at Dollars 36 1/8 . In Paris, the shares closed FFr5.20 higher at FFr387.10. MILAN was enlivened by industrial stocks. The Comit index rose 2.21 to 475.01 in turnover estimated at L95bn after L76bn on Tuesday. Olivetti added L112 or 3.7 per cent to close at a 1992 high of L3,144, while Fiat broke through L5,000 on the kerb, having closed L19 higher at L4,960. Montedison added L10 to L1,475. The banking sector recovered as Banca Commerciale Italiana (BCI) rebounded L49 to L2,967 after its 4 per cent plunge on Tuesday. AMSTERDAM's CBS Tendency index rose 0.8 to 130.2 on foreign institutional interest. There was active buying in Buehrmann-Tetterode on reports of a buy recommendation from a UK brokers and it closed up Fl 1.70 or 3.5 per cent to Fl 49.80. KLM remained a favourite on renewed speculation that merger talks with BA had been reopened. It gained 70 cents to Fl 40.10. Polygram rose 70 cents to Fl 50.90 on news that it had formed a joint venture with Universal Pictures for the distribution of films in the US, while Heineken took comfort from the hot weather in Europe and was Fl 2 stronger at Fl 165. ZURICH brokers said that continuing high Swiss interest rates were keeping some investors away. The market gave up some earlier gains on a lack of buying interest, as the SMI index of leading shares rose 5.4 to 1,933.4 in quiet trading. Winterthur bearers fell SFr20 to SFr3,350. After the close the insurer said it would raise dividends after an 112 per cent increase in 1991 profits, and that it was opening up its share register to foreigners. STOCKHOLM was little changed as in Astra led most blue chips higher, balancing declines in domestic stocks and Volvo, where the B free fell SKr8 to SKr423 after Tuesday's SKr248m first quarter loss. The Affarsvarlden General Index rose 0.9 to 999.3 in heavy turnover of SKr900m. Astra accounted for SKr360m of total turnover, as the B unrestricted shares advanced SKr19 to SKr547 after Tuesday's favourable first quarter earnings report. The company also raised its forecast for full year profit growth to more than 25 per cent. BRUSSELS was firmer as dealers squared positions on the last day of the forward account. The Bel-20 index advanced 4.05 to 1,224.19. Petrofina rose BFr75 to BFr11,400 ahead of today's dividend payment. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- FT-SE EUROTRACK 100 - MAY 20 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Hourly changes ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Open 10 am 11 am 12 pm 1 pm 2 pm 3 pm Close 1185.44 1186.14 1186.46 1188.02 1188.59 1188.43 1187.94 1187.62 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Day's High 1188.97 Day's Low 1185.37 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- May 19 May 18 May 15 May 14 May 13 1180.66 1184.41 1171.24 1179.98 1187.91 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Base value 1000 (26/10/90). -----------------------------------------------------------------------

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets (Asia Pacific): Late fall in futures causes Nikkei to change course
DOC.TEXT: LATE afternoon profit-taking and arbitrage-related selling erased initial gains, and share prices lost ground in tandem with the futures market, writes Emiko Terazono in Tokyo. The Nikkei average was down 79.18 at 18,674.93 after a high of 18,927.64 in the morning and a low of 18,635.89 in the afternoon. Investors were encouraged at the start by the overnight high on Wall Street, and sought issues with favourable earnings prospects. However, share prices receded in the afternoon as a fall in the futures market prompted arbitrage selling. Volume declined to 300m shares from 340m. Rises retained a narrow lead over falls by 497 to 488, with 155 issues unchanged. The Topix index of all first section stocks shed 1.20 to 1,394.51, and in London the ISE/Nikkei 50 index ended just 0.66 up at 1,107.10. Traders said that, in the short term, the market looked vulnerable because of the high margin activity recently, especially in speculative or 'theme' stocks. In the longer term, however, fears of a loss of support at the 18,000 level seem to have subsided. Corporate results have had a substantial effect on some stocks. Surprises on the negative side stem from losses on securities investments and real estate development. Investors have been discouraged by losses at companies which had been known for their profitable business operations. Shares in Sekisui Chemical, which reported a 17 per cent fall in pre-tax profits due to losses at its financing affiliate, have dropped 21 per cent since the results were announced two weeks ago. It closed Y29 down at Y871 yesterday. Sato Kogyo, the civil engineering group, slipped Y70 to Y1,080. The company suffered an extraordinary loss of Y2.3bn in its last fiscal year due to loan guarantee payments to a resort construction affiliate. On the other hand, better than expected earnings announcements were appreciated. Nippon Meat Packers, which saw a 4 per cent rise in pre-tax profits to Y28.5bn on a 7 per cent increase in sales to Y585bn, responded with a gain of Y30 to Y1,770. Short-term trading in theme stocks led activity. The most active issue of the day was Mitsubishi Kakoki, an industrial waste water treatment equipment maker, which rose Y90 to Y1,190 on the environmental theme. Traders are also promoting the stock as an Aids-related issue, due to increasing sales of its condom production facilities. In Osaka, the OSE average gained a slight 0.73 at 21,348.15 in volume of 20.5m shares. Roundup THE Pacific Rim was generally firmer as international funds were switched out of Thailand into neighbouring markets. HONG KONG rose sharply on speculation that interest rates would be cut by the weekend. The Hang Seng index advanced 111.52 to 5,753.76 in turnover of HKDollars 3.91bn. HSBC Holdings led the rally, rising 75 cents to HKDollars 44 on news that the Bank of England would not object to the group's proposed bid for Midland Bank. BANGKOK rallied on bargain hunting following Tuesday's 8.9 per cent drop. The SET index gained 9.53 to 677.37. SEOUL lost ground, with sentiment depressed by rumours that the tax affairs of some individual investors were to be investigated. The composite index fell 8.06 to 579.91 in turnover of Won400bn. MANILA was stronger on selective buying of commercial and industrial stocks. The composite index appreciated 19.25 to 1,358.20 in turnover of 182m pesos. Philippine Long Distance Telephone gained 25 pesos to 1,090 pesos. TAIWAN extended Tuesday's advance and the weighted index put on 59.18 to 4,560.00 in turnover of TDollars 30bn. KUALA LUMPUR's composite index climbed 3.18 to 594.09 in turnover of MDollars 138m. Telekom moved ahead 20 cents to MDollars 12.70, with some 549,000 shares traded. AUSTRALIA advanced in strong trade. The All Ordinaries index gained 15.7 to 1,682.0 in turnover of ADollars 205m. Westpac shed 5 cents to ADollars 3.89 before reporting a loss of ADollars 1.67bn for its fiscal first half. The bank also announced an ADollars 1.2bn rights issue. Elsewhere, BHP moved forward 14 cents to ADollars 14.28 and News Corp put on 48 cents to ADollars 22.10. SINGAPORE's Straits Times Industrial index rose 3.07 to 1,472.87 in dull trade, with most institutional interest focused on Hong Kong. NEW ZEALAND declined as investors took profits. The NZSE-40 index retreated 5.26 to 1,547.43 in NZDollars 19.4m turnover.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets: New equity inflow weighs on Milan - Rights issues are being criticised for their timing and quality
DOC.TEXT: It is a measure of the bad sentiment on the Milan bourse that last Friday's 38 per cent cut in Fiat's ordinary share dividend was greeted with relief rather than rancour. So negative have attitudes towards Italian equities become that even the wildest rumours are being given credence. The possibility that a bellwether company like Fiat might swell the list of rights issues overhanging the market was one of the factors behind last week's plunge in the Comit index through the psychologically important 480 barrier. In the event, Fiat produced neither a rights issue, nor a dividend to be paid partly in shares and in cash - the other possibility haunting brokers. The news helped the market regain some ground at the start of the new trading account on Monday, but the recovery was short-lived. In spite of Fiat's temporary relief, Milan remains shell-shocked. While trading volume has risen above L100bn (Dollars 83m) on most days, almost every Societa di Intermediazione Mobiliare (Sim), Italy's new broking and fund management hybrid, is thought to be losing money on equities. Funding moves are the latest culprits. How, brokers ask, can companies expect the bourse to absorb trillions of lire in rights issues when trading is barely ticking over? In the past three weeks, Italcementi, Ras and Assitalia have announced big rights issues amounting to L1,776bn. Meanwhile, Iri, the state holding company, hopes to raise around L1,750bn by a secondary placing of shares in the Stet telecommunications holding group. Further down the line are likely flotations of Iri's Finmeccanica engineering arm, Eni's Agip and Snam subsidiaries, and just possibly, Iri's Ilva steel-making subsidiary. It is Iri's plans, bunched in the second half of the year, which have most depressed the market. Hit by the clampdown on government funding, Italy's biggest state holding company has turned to the market in virtual desperation. With its cash-raising ambitions in mind, some private sector companies may be trying to nip in first. Sentiment was already depressed before the latest money-raising cycle. Disappointing 1991 company results and limited scope for improvement in 1992 had crushed the market. Politically, delays in electing a president and forming a new government have postponed the likelihood of Italy getting to grips with its myriad economic problems. Foreign investors have taken cover, while domestic mutual funds have failed to step into the breach. Equity holdings by Italian unit trusts have reached a historic low as funds have switched to bonds or cash. Last month, the funds' net equity sales amounted to L150bn. The latest cash calls have been attacked both for their insensitive timing and poor quality. While Italcementi's purchase of control of Ciments Francais was applauded, its subsequent two-part rights issue was not. The company is charging the same price for ordinary and non-voting savings shares in the first half of the deal, while it is only offering non-franchised savings shares in the second. The move by Ras, Italy's second biggest insurer, which is controlled by Allianz, of Germany, to raise more than L800bn through a mixed share and warrant bond issue was equally unpopular. Its claim that funds were needed to build up the life insurance side was viewed sceptically, and the price of Ras's savings shares collapsed. Lack of information and poor investor preparation were the criticisms levelled at Iri for its Stet deal. In other circumstances the transaction might have gone down well: once completed, Iri will have only 53 per cent of Stet's ordinary shares and just 1 per cent of the savings stock, bringing true privatisation within sight. By half-heartedly releasing the news on the eve of a public holiday, however, and just days after repeated denials that such a transaction was imminent, Iri left the market feeling bitter and misled. With no sign of an upturn in investor confidence, and a host of public sector flotations to come this year, it is a lesson companies need to learn fast.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets: South Africa
DOC.TEXT: LIGHT buying interest in the afternoon helped lift Johannesburg shares off early lows. Falls in De Beers and Anglo pared the overall index by 15 to 3,667, while the industrial index recovered 2 to 4,563. The gold index lost 18 to 1,121.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: Saudi oil minister fails to turn up at Opec summit
DOC.TEXT: MR HISHAM NAZER, the Saudi Arabian oil minister, yesterday failed to turn up at the ministerial summit of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries in Vienna in a move which surprised and disconcerted other delegations, but which the Saudis said signalled no change in the Kingdom's oil policy. A Saudi delegate said that Mr Nazer was simply 'a little bit exhausted' after an intensive series of overseas meetings. Although some oil analysts suggested that Mr Nazer's absence, his first from an Opec meeting since he replaced Sheikh Yamani as the kingdom's oil minister in 1987, could be interpreted as a 'slight' towards delegations favouring a higher-price Opec policy, diplomats in Riyadh who met Mr Nazer yesterday said they believed he may genuinely have been over-tired. The diplomats said that there was no indication that Mr Nazer's post as oil minister was threatened, or that his absence indicated a shift in oil policy from Riyadh. They said he had appeared intent on making the trip to Vienna when they met him, but that 'he had no appetite for the journey'. Mr Nazer, they said, had spent 25 hours without sleep during talks late last week in Kuwait between EC ministers and those of the Gulf Co-operation Council on which the EC's proposed carbon tax was high on the agenda. Saudi Arabia is leading an Opec lobby against the imposition of such a tax. Mr Nazer's place at the summit was taken by Mr Fayez Badr, a minister of state with responsibility for the Saudi Ports Authority and a man with no clear oil expertise. Saudi Arabia has widely flagged before the Opec summit, which begins in earnest today, that it would be seeking a 1m barrels a day rise in the cartel's production ceiling for the third quarter from the 22.98m b/d agreed for the second in February. Iran, among several other delegations, opposes such a move and would prefer to see Opec restrain output to force prices towards the cartel's formal reference price of Dollars 21 a barrel. Mr Gholamreza Agazadeh, Iran's oil minister, told reporters curtly yesterday: 'I want a cut in the ceiling.' Oil analysts suggested that Mr Agazadeh may have simply been stating an opening bargaining position for the talks and that a cut in the February ceiling was unlikely. But many equally suggested that Mr Nazer's absence might indicate that Saudi Arabia would be likely to press less forcefully its argument for a rise in the ceiling for the third quarter and that, despite its opening position, the Kingdom may settle for a roll-over of the present ceiling. Saudi Arabia estimates the call on Opec crude to reach 24.2m b/d for the third quarter, but actual production for the second has neared 23.5m b/d rather than the nominal February figure, due largely to Kuwait's accelerated output and a Saudi refusal to cut production below 8m b/d - as was notionally allocated.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / World Commodities Prices: Market Report
DOC.TEXT: ALUMINIUM closed ahead on the LME after three-month metal hit stiff resistance around Dollars 1,360 a tonne. The overall steadier trend was prompted by a constructive close on Tuesday and by speculative interest. TIN came under profit-taking and technical selling in the afternoon, prompted by the failure of three-month metal to test Dollars 6,300 a tonne after hitting a new 18-month high of Dollars 6,290 in the morning. But the selling was well absorbed, with underlying interest evident below Dollars 6,250. PLATINUM held at Dollars 361 an ounce on the London bullion market after earlier falling on reported Middle East sales and a technical correction to Tuesday's rally. Analysts said the market had been overbought on its rise to Dollars 364, but sentiment was bullish on Nymex, where platinum futures were higher at midday, again outperforming Comex gold and silver. Optimism that economies worldwide are recovering sparked buying. Analysts also cited continued concerns over the availability of supply in the physical markets. Comex GOLD futures were weaker at midday on selling by players disappointed at the failure to surmount resistance levels on Tuesday. Compiled from Reuters

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / World Commodities Prices: Wool
DOC.TEXT: The importance of selection in realising better prices for wool was illustrated at the Goulburn auction in Australia on May 20. Better style merino fleece of good length and soundness attracted very good competition and prices moved up by 10 to 30 cents a kg. compared with the previous week. Otherwise the market was firm. The market indicator rose 6 cents to 588 cents a kg. Offerings in all primary producing markets are declining in selection and quality at this stage of the season, with drought a contributory factor leading to lower offerings this season.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: Newmont's gesture fails to convince gold market - Why the producer's symbolic purchase has so far not succeeded in lifting prices
DOC.TEXT: IT WAS meant to be a big, symbolic gesture by Newmont Mining, North America's biggest gold producer. Newmont wanted to send, with a flourish and fanfare, a clear message to the market and other producers that it was sure the gold price was at or very near its lowest point. Newmont bought 375,000 troy ounces (or 11.7 tonnes) of gold at a cost of nearly Dollars 126m on April 29 - the day the gold price was fixed in London at its lowest point for six years. But the impact of the news was dampened because it became fouled up by US stock market disclosure regulations. These forced the group to include details of the gold deal in its report on financial results for the first quarter. The gold deal was completed on the day those results were due to be revealed and Newmont was obliged to tell its shareholders immediately. After all, it was locking in a net profit of more than Dollars 40m. However, even allowing for the lack of razzmatazz accompanying Newmont's announcement, some gold bulls have been disappointed by the market's reaction. Newmont bought its gold at Dollars 335.95 a troy ounce, and two weeks later the gold price still languishes at Dollars 337.30, near its lowest for 16 years in real terms, when inflation is taken into account. Some bullion dealers were also perturbed by the comparative lack of impact Newmont's buying spree had on the market at the time. Sellers, particularly from Europe, swamped Newmont's attempt to give the gold price a push in an upward direction. However, as the price had drifted to a low of Dollars 333 an ounce on April 29, Newmont managed to lift it by a dollar or two. Some observers contrast this with the market's reaction in February 1988 when Newmont announced it had completed the biggest gold loan ever - of 1m ounces or 31 tonnes. Perhaps unfairly, this move was blamed for starting the steady fall in the gold price which continued through the following four years. In a gold loan operation a mining company borrows metal from a commercial bank or syndicate which has, in turn, borrowed some from a central bank. The mining company then effectively sells the gold in the market for cash which is then used for a designated purpose. In the opinion of some analysts, Newmont signalled in the most dramatic way in 1988 that the gold price had reached its peak and, once the news was out, the price took a tumble. Mining companies pay back gold loans, both principal and interest, usually in gold but occasionally in cash. Gold loans are mainly used to finance new gold mining projects, but Newmont's was arranged to take advantage of the low interest rates offered, roughly 3 per cent at that time, compared with the money markets. The group was under tremendous pressure to reduce the burden of its Dollars 1.6bn debt, most of it taken on to ward off the unwelcome overtures of marauders led by Mr T. Boone Pickens, the well-known corporate raider. Newmont bought gold at Dollars 449 an ounce for its five-year loan and was repaying at the rate of 62,500 ounces a quarter. By the end of last year about half the loan had been repaid. Mr Jim Hill, Newmont's vice president, corporate relations, says the company 'is neither disappointed nor surprised' by the reaction so far to its announcement about the early repayment of the rest of its gold loan. 'Gold analysts reacted very positively,' he says. 'We felt that, whereas the gold price might go down a few more dollars, the trend from now on would be up. So we decided to pay off our gold loan and lock in a net profit of about Dollars 100 an ounce.' Newmont is not the only producer to repay a gold loan before the due date. And an analysis by Ms Jessica Jacks, analyst with the RTZ Corporation, the world's biggest mining company, shows that at the end of 1991 total gold loans outstanding involved 330 tonnes compared with 391 tonnes in December the previous year. Therefore a net 60 tonnes of gold (1.9m ounces) was repaid last year. Yet a large number of professionals operating in the gold market seem to believe that the price has not yet touched bottom. Most of the commodity funds, for example, are selling the metal short - they have contracted to sell gold they do not yet own in the expectation that they will be able to buy it at a lower price when they need it. Sceptics also point out Newmont's move seems to bear the mark of Sir James Goldsmith, the Anglo-French financier, who is one of the greatest bulls of gold. Much of his fortune is wrapped up in Newmont. His General Oriental Investments, where he has a two-thirds stake, owns 42 per cent of Newmont. Sir James is also chairman of the group's new strategy committee. Yet it is clear Newmont did not just play a hunch. Mr Paul Maroni, Newmont's chief financial officer, lists some of the factors pointing to a gold price rise soon: production is tailing off; new gold is expensive to find and to produce; demand from the jewellery industry (which has been buying more gold than is newly-mined each year) remains buoyant. Mr Maroni suggests those producers who continue to sell when the price rises -and effectively 'cap' any substantial increase - are mainly high-cost producers who could not survive without this form of insurance. The time will come when their ability to survive will be called into question, he suggests. Also, the extraordinarily high level of gold sales from the former Soviet Union which helped to drive down the price in the past two years cannot continue because its stocks have almost run out and production is now relatively modest. Mr Maroni says there is also a potential 'wild card' which might benefit gold - a 'meltdown' of the world's financial system. Sir James has recently forecast such an event, which he suggests will see investors returning to the security offered by gold. Mr Maroni echoes this view: 'We don't think the world financial system is in very good shape.' Leaving that 'wild card' aside, many analysts agree with Mr Maroni's analysis. Ms Rhona O'Connell, analyst at Williams de Broe, part of the Banque Bruxelles Lambert group, says: 'We agree with the view that this is the bottom of the gold market.' But she warns: 'Recovery will be a slow and painful process.' Mr Andy Smith, analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland, also says the gold price is likely to be higher at the end of the year than it is today - perhaps by Dollars 30 or Dollars 40 an ounce. 'But it won't move for a month or so and it might not stay there when it gets there.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: Basis of a deal on radical CAP reform in sight
DOC.TEXT: THE fifth attempt this year to synthesize the vested interests of the EC farm sector around a genuinely radical reform of the creaking Common Agricultural Policy was finalised early yesterday morning, giving the basis for a deal. Although it festoons most member states with sweeteners to help them digest severe cuts in subsidised prices, the structure of the European Commission's bold attempt to overhaul the CAP is still intact. Mr Ray MacSharry, the EC agriculture commissioner who has cajoled, bludgeoned, and horse-traded with the 12 farm ministers for 18 months to bring them this far, said yesterday: 'What we're involved in here is a totally different philosophy to what has existed for 30 years.' Agreement is now in view - and as ministers settled into their second consecutive night of negotiations, there was hope for a deal either today or tomorrow. Yet despite general conviction that the fifth compromise paper presented by the Portuguese presidency constituted the basis for settlement, a major North-South row over plans to concede more milk quotas to Spain, Italy and Greece gathered pace through the day and could delay the denouement. The central element in the overnight compromise was the cereals price. Mr MacSharry persuaded the Portuguese presidency to retrace its steps and deepen the planned cut in subsidised grain prices to 29 per cent. The Commission had wanted to drop the cereals price by 35 per cent, from Ecu155 per tonne now to Ecu100, though it drew its public line at Ecu105, with the tacit understanding that Ecu108 a tonne was its limit. Mr Arlindo Cunha, the Portuguese farm minister, had tried to break the logjam by moving towards Germany, which insisted on settling as near as possible to the 20 per cent cut in domestic subsidies demanded by the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (Gatt) to conclude the stalled Uruguay Round. Mr Cunha last month proposed Ecu112 per tonne, and received an unprecedented and public rebuff from Mr MacSharry. On Tuesday they split the difference and settled at Ecu110 - a 29 per cent cut close to the 30 per cent the Commission had always set out to achieve, with a 1 per cent psychological sweetener to enable Germany to feel it was in the '20s'. The compromise on cereals looked set to harden into a deal acceptable to the Twelve last night, opening the way to agreement on the rest of the reform structure for which it is the foundation. It will enable a market with a production overhang of around 20m tonnes (as well as similar amounts in intervention stockpiles) to come back into balance. It will make EC grains competitive, without the need to dump abroad, and should all but eliminate cereal export subsidies - the real rock on which the Uruguay Round is foundering. Within the CAP reform structure itself, it will enable significant price cuts in the livestock and dairy sectors, which will be part compensated by lower cereal feedstock prices. The Commission also won back its own compromise position on how the scheme is to operate. In essence, the reform moves away from price support towards direct payments to farmers. All farmers will get a full refund of the price cuts paid directly to them, contingent for all but small farmers to their taking 15 per cent of their land out of production. All farmers will also get compensation for this 'set-aside', whereas the Commission had wanted to bite further into overproduction by excluding the biggest farms. Ministers had also rejected the Commission's plan to monitor set-aside by individual farms, which Mr MacSharry and his colleagues insist is the only way of making farmers take responsibility for their production. The presidency opted instead for county-size regional units - but on Tuesday the Commission got the individual farm unit reinstated. Senior officials say farmers will eventually bridle if they are penalised as a region because some farmers within it flout the land in production limits. These officials believe they have established a transitional regime to the effective controls they were seeking. Against this, scattered over the compromise are concessions for dried fodder and cereals grown for silage; for France's maize growers and the South's hard wheat growers; for tobacco producers and hill sheep farmers. Germany, which is likely to be allowed to pay a one-off national subsidy to its farmers this year, has also been granted special treatment for the eastern Laender. Some formula of future yield will be the yardstick for compensation for price cuts there, against fixed, past production reference periods for the rest of the EC - another critical weapon in the fight against oversupply. Ireland has scored a signal victory with an easing of what was to have been a very severe contraction of the intervention regime, which currently absorbs about four fifths of its beef produce. The compromise recognises the fact that Irish (and French) farmers slaughter their herds later in the year, and ensures they do not lose out in case those who slaughter earlier get into what will be finite stockpiles first. The UK, which at times over the last 18 months has suggested MacSharry was trying to refashion EC agriculture on a backward Irish model, was said by Irish farm minister Joe Walsh to be seeking the same regime for Northern Ireland. A British special case - providing half-subsidy for sheep farmers in disadvantaged areas over the 1,000 per flock limit - was also in the compromise, although British ministers were fighting for more. But the extra milk quota for Italy, Spain and Greece remained a big stumbling block, opposed by the UK, Netherlands, Denmark, Belgium and Luxembourg. This was enough to block the concession, but as the evening wore on, it seemed likely that all but the three recipients would come out against it. 'It's going to be very hard to get round that one,' predicted Mr David Curry, the UK deputy agriculture minister. The three countries have applied the milk quota regime only loosely, and are looking for extra quotas to soak up some of their existing excess production. The Commission reasons that this is a worthwhile price if these countries are now obliged to implement and monitor quotas. There were few signs last night that such reasoning was percolating through the rest of the Council.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Accountancy Column: Explaining the mixed record of global penetration
DOC.TEXT: SOMETIMES the simplest calculations can provide the most revealing results. Among 300 dense pages of statistics and graphics in a new compendium of accountancy data*, one table sticks out from the rest, showing the relative grip of accountants on national economies. As the table shows, dividing accountancy fee income by gross domestic product (1990 figures) throws up tremendous variations. If the US economy is -as sometimes claimed - being drained by lawyers, then accountants cannot be far behind. Elsewhere, the patterns are equally revealing, ranging from a low of 0.01 per cent of GDP in Japan to a peak of 0.63 per cent in Ireland. Lafferty's 'International Accounting Databook' puts a brave face on the proportions at the lower end of the spectrum. 'On the assumption that the accounting firms in other countries will be able to develop in the same way as British, Irish, Dutch and Swiss firms, it would appear that the potential world market for accountants' services is enormous,' it says. 'For example, the Italian market could increase 20-fold.' The Sony chairman, Mr Akio Morito, who has recently been outspoken in his criticism of the role of accountants in senior positions in business, might put a rather different perspective on the figures, and be gratified at his country's lowly position. At the other extreme, explanations for the position of Ireland and the Netherlands are hard to come by. Switzerland is also very high, at 0.5 per cent of GDP. This, the report suggests, may reflect the wide range of services offered by Swiss firms, as well as relatively easy access to outside capital. On home ground, theories are rather easier to develop. The UK comes in third highest, at 0.54 per cent. The survey suggests that the power of the profession reflects the UK's history as the birthplace of accountancy. It argues that the large number of companies subject to statutory audits and their control of the 'insolvency franchise' leads to the substantial fees generated. The firms have also been free to develop roles as tax advisers and general business consultants. 'Accountants are moving away from being a profession,' says Michael Lafferty, editor in chief of Lafferty Publications, 'they are becoming a business.' It no doubt also reflects the important role in the UK played by capital markets and the industries they sustain - corporate finance, financial reporting, due diligence work and so on - which are in their infancy across continental Europe. By comparison, tax and insolvency work in other countries including the US and Scandinavia is controlled by the legal profession and produces far less income for accountants. In some countries there are restrictions on accountants' business which may restrict the volume and value of work they conduct, such as compulsory rotation of auditors, or bars to prevent auditors conducting non-audit work. Overall, there is obviously a clear relationship between fee income generated and the number of qualified accountants. This raises the question of which came first: the accountants or the work to satisfy them? The Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales has about 97,720 members and this is rising by 2.9 per cent per year - considerably faster than GDP. In addition, the four other professional accountancy bodies have more than 70,000 members. Only Ireland can compete with that figure in Europe. There, 0.597 per cent of the population were certified or chartered accountants in 1990, against 0.572 per cent in the UK. (Third, at just 0.275 per cent, was Gibraltar.) Mr Andrew Colquhoun, chief executive of the English Institute, says: 'I see accountants as part of the invisible infrastructure essential to making a market economy work. They have a real economic role for invisible earnings - although it is difficult to quantify.' Analysts could nevertheless have a field day scrutinising the over-staffing of accountancy firms across borders, by examining countries in which professional fees as a proportion of GDP exceeded the number of practising accountants per capita. They might also do more to assess the contribution the firms truly make to national product - since there seems to be little clear correlation between the proportion of GDP consumed, and economic growth rates in the countries shown. Other figures in the Lafferty compendium bear witness to the remarkable growth and change taking place in accountancy firms around the world. Fee income from the main accounting networks in 1991 grew by 13.4 per cent worldwide. Fee income shot up by more than 17 per cent in Europe, compared with just 2.6 per cent growth in the US, making the markets now almost identical in size: the US and Canada together contributed Dollars 14,096m last year, against Dollars 13,833m in Europe. Gross fees per partner from the firms in the top networks averaged just over Dollars 1m, and ranged from Dollars 1.45m in Germany to a low of Dollars 750,000 in Japan. There are plenty of other statistical manipulations that could be done on the figures - enough, in fact, to keep an army of unemployed accountants busy for months. No doubt Mr Morito would be among those recommending that they might more usefully spend their time retraining in different, more useful, skills. *International Accounting Databook. Pounds 545. Lafferty Publications, The Tower, IDA Centre, Pearse Street, Dublin 2, Ireland.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Construction Contracts: Refurbishment work on power lines
DOC.TEXT: New power contracts totalling Pounds 12.1m have been awarded to the transmission division of EVE GROUP. They are led by four projects for extensive refurbishment work on power lines in England from all three divisions of the National Grid Company. For NGC northern division, the transmission division is carrying out a Pounds 1.97m refurbishment of the L2 400kV South Humberside line from Keadby to West Burton, and a Pounds 1.4m refurbishment in Nottinghamshire of the northern part of the L34 and L3 DC1 lines between High Marnham and Thurcroft, which follows the previous award of work on the southern part by NGC central division. A Pounds l9m contract for refurbishment of the southern half of the L2 400kV line between Keadby and West Burton in Lincolnshire has also been placed by the NGC central division. NGC southern division has commissioned from the transmission division a Pounds 1.7m refurbishment for its L2 400kV line, including fibral earthwire, between Laleham and west Weybridge in Surrey. Midlands Electricity has also placed a Pounds 1.9m contract with Eve's transmission division for the rebuilding of the 132 kV lines at Meaford and Stoke-on-Trent. Other clients include East Midlands Electricity and South Wales Electricity, the PSA in Kent and Oxfordshire; British Gas Southern at Basingstoke; the Port of London Authority; AT&T Network Systems; Telecom Eireann and Vodafone.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Capital Markets: Spain launches Ecu250m MTN issue
DOC.TEXT: THE ALREADY hazy distinction between traditional Eurobonds and medium-term note issues was further blurred yesterday, when Spain launched Ecu250m two-year paper under its MTN programme, writes Simon London. The issue, fully underwritten by Lehman Brothers and the four other dealers to the programme, is the largest of its type in the Euromarket. An MTN programme provides a legal framework under which a borrower can issue bonds in a range of currencies and maturities. MTN issues are normally small and not underwritten, with dealers placing paper where they can identify pockets of demand for securities. However, increasingly large bond issues are being made under the umbrella of MTN programmes. Until yesterday, the largest issue was a Dollars 153m deal launched by Eurofima.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Bonds: Toyota launches record Dollars 1bn Eurobond deal
DOC.TEXT: TOYOTA, the Japanese motor group, launched its Dollars 1bn Eurobond issue yesterday, the largest offering by a company in the international bond market and the second large deal to hit the market this week after the Province of Ontario's Dollars 2bn global offering on Tuesday. The deal was well received in the market, with syndicates reporting strong demand for the AAA rated paper. The five-year bond has a coupon of 6 7/8 per cent and was launched at a fixed reoffer price of 99.58 to yield 38 basis points over the five-year US Treasury bond, but in the course of trading the yield tightened to 35-36 basis points, traders said, with the bond priced at 99.50-99.55. Nomura and Merrill Lynch, the joint lead managers, said the deal was fully-placed, with European pension and insurance funds buying about 40 per cent and the rest going to Japanese and other Far Eastern investors such as investment trusts. The deal was seen as fairly priced, and traders said the combination of a bullish tone in the underlying government bond markets yesterday and the fact that the lead managers had two full days in which to market the issue contributed to its success. Toyota is one of several Japanese companies which currently face having to refinance equity warrant issues. The US dollar sector of the international bond market saw a heavy load of issues yesterday, with a Dollars 100m deal from Telebras, the Brazilian telecommunications group, and a Dollars 500m deal from Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken, the large Swedish bank. Telebras' five-year bond carried a coupon of 10 per cent and was priced to yield 365 basis points over the US Treasury bond, which dealers say should make it appeal to investors in search of high-yielding paper. Dealers point out that successive Telebras bond issues are being priced more aggressively: a three-year bond from the same borrower launched in February was priced at 450 basis points over the three-year US Treasury bond.
