'The market for LDC debt has come in dramatically in recent months, and you can now price these deals more aggressively provided there is a 10 per cent coupon,' claimed one dealer. S-E Banken increased its bond offering from Dollars 300m to Dollars 500m shortly after the deal was launched. Credit Suisse First Boston, the lead managers, said the five-year bond was priced at 78 basis points over the US Treasury, narrowing to 76 basis points over. The bond was trading at about 99.90 by late afternoon and the proceeds were swapped into floating rate dollars to produce a floating rate asset with a coupon of Libor plus 45 basis points. Outside the dollar sector, Credit Local De France launched a FFr2bn zero coupon issue which, with a maturity of 15 years is the longest-dated zero coupon bond in this currency sector. BNP, the lead managers, claimed there was strong demand for long-dated zero-coupon issues: retail investors buy this kind of paper for tax reasons while institutional investors are more likely to buy it for the combination of maturity, currency and leverage. Launched at the reoffer price of 28.299, the bond traded at 28.27-28.32 by late afternoon.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Capital Markets: Commercial Union joins preference share issuers
DOC.TEXT: COMMERCIAL UNION yesterday became the latest in a line of UK financial sector companies to strengthen its balance sheet without resorting to a rights offer by issuing preference shares. Although the Pounds 100m issue is the first in recent years by a UK insurance company, banks and building societies are increasingly turning to preference shares for quasi-equity funding. Until last year, preference share issues were very rare. Most companies preferred to issue either straight equity or debt securities. Bank of Scotland was the only issuer, tapping the market in 1988 and 1990. However, last September National Westminster Bank raised Pounds 140m capital from an issue of undated preference stock. In February, it was followed by Bank of Ireland, which raised Pounds 110m. Building societies have followed a similar route by issuing Permanent Interest Bearing Shares (Pibs). Like preference shares, Pibs pay a fixed dividend, have no redemption date and are deeply subordinated in the manner of equity. Preference shares are popular with financial sector borrowers because they count as core capital for regulatory purposes. Financial institutions have been able to improve balance sheet ratios without asking shareholders for additional funds. Commercial Union said that yesterday's issue would count as core capital under both current UK government regulations and draft EC directives for the insurance industry. As a result, the company's solvency ratio - the ratio of premium income to capital used by investors and regulators as a measure of balance sheet strength - improved from 41 per cent to 44 per cent. In the late 1980s, Commercial Union had a solvency ratio comfortably over 50 per cent. Preference capital is more attractive because the cost has fallen steadily in line with interest rates. Because preference shares pay a fixed rate of interest, they are priced against UK government bonds. For example, Commercial Union's preference shares pay a gross annual rate of 11.5 per cent, compared with 12 per cent on the National Westminster paper issued last autumn. In contrast, the cost of 'pure' equity capital has remained high. Corporate financiers noted yesterday that equity investors had not scaled back expectations of dividend growth substantially from the levels of the late 1980s. Mr Peter Foster, general manager for finance at Commercial Union, said: 'We had no urgent need for capital, but the issue gives us permanent additional capital at a cheaper rate than equity over the long term.' However, bankers are not predicting a rush of new preference issues. The market for preference shares remains limited to UK institutional investors with long-dated liabilities, such as pension funds and insurance companies. Moreover, insurance companies are loathe to buy paper issued by their competitors. Not all insurance companies with declining solvency ratios will be able to tap the market.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Capital Markets: Factory automation group confident
DOC.TEXT: ALLEN-BRADLEY, the factory automation company owned by Rockwell of the US, hopes to double its share of the market for computer numerical control (CNC) equipment over the next five years, according to Mr Don Davis, president. Leadership of the world market for CNC equipment, used to run machine tools, has passed from the US to Japan and Germany over the past 15 years, in line with trends in the machine tool industry. However Allen-Bradley plans a comeback. Earlier this year it launched a new CNC range, the 9/Series, which Mr Davis hopes will help it raise world market share from about 6 per cent. 'I would be very disappointed if we can't double that,' he said. Mr Davis admitted Allen-Bradley had struggled in the past because of the dominance of Japan's Fanuc, which has about 50 per cent of the world CNC market, and Germany's Siemens. CNC is crucial in factory automation, and is increasingly bought by the machine tool industry as a package. 'I can't say we will regain leadership, but a lot of customers are looking for an alternative,' Mr Davis said. The new range had been well received in Japan and Germany, respectively the largest and second largest machine tool producers. Allen-Bradley has until now had difficulties penetrating both these markets, but it now plans to expand its presence. It has largely missed out on the CNC market in Japan and eastern Asia, which account for between 35 and 40 per cent of consumption and could become increasingly important as machine tool builders in countries such as Taiwan and South Korea seek to increase exports. Mr Davis also hopes the CNC business will be strengthened by a recent reorganisation combining CNC and all other motion control products into a new division based in Italy. The move coincides with Allen-Bradley taking full control of Osai A-B, a CNC joint venture with Olivetti. Allen-Bradley, formerly privately-owned, was bought by Rockwell for Dollars 1.6bn in 1985, after a keenly-contested auction. The US aerospace, electronics and vehicle parts group narrowly beat a bid from Siemens. The deal brought Rockwell a new 'leg' and Allen-Bradley financial stability in an era of intensifying competition. Mr Davis said the two companies were just beginning to see real benefits, in technology terms, from the takeover. Apart from joint developments, including work on so-called 'fuzzy logic' - software that can help make a decision from unclear information - Rockwell had helped Allen-Bradley in advanced areas such as neuro-networks and artificial intelligence.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Capital Markets: EBRD plans to set up finance advisory brokerages in E Europe
DOC.TEXT: THE EUROPEAN Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) plans to set up two corporate finance advisory boutiques in Eastern Europe which may eventually be launched as financial institutions in the private sector. Mr David Hexter, head of the EBRD's Financial Institutions Group, said the bank is keen to establish the new corporate finance advisory brokerages, as these would help to select and identify new projects in Eastern Europe for the EBRD and others. The two projects still need the EBRD board's approval. The projects would require only a small amount of capital at first. Once they were established as fully fledged financial institutions, however, the EBRD said it would probably reduce its involvement by selling, or by reducing its participation. Mr Hexter said: 'In both cases we have identified locally committed people who are prepared to run with the idea'. The EBRD plans to provide help such as credit analysis, training, and computer systems. He added that ideally the EBRD should play the role of a 'catalyst', encouraging foreign banks to participate in banking joint ventures. Mr Hexter, who previously helped to set up banking ventures in Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary while he was working at Citibank, said that he was impressed by the willingness of Eastern European bankers to learn and to adapt to market conditions. The EBRD is working to develop banking systems in many Eastern and Central European economies. An estimated 90 to 95 per cent of the banks in the region are state-owned. The EBRD wants to promote the development of private sector banks.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: House products group tumbles 28%
DOC.TEXT: TOYO Sash, Japan's top maker of aluminium housing products, revealed a 14.6 per cent drop to Y32.5bn (Dollars 244.36m) in non-consolidated pre-tax profits for the year to end-March. Net profits also fell sharply, by 28.6 per cent to Y14.8bn, although sales climbed a modest 4 per cent to Y481bn. A sharp drop in demand in the second half - reflecting the nation's stock market troubles - and a private sector spending downturn were behind the profit retreat, the company said. Sales of housing sashes, which account for over half of company sales, grew 1.1 per cent to Y280bn. Building sash sales grew 10.6 per cent to Y148bn, due largely to new products for high-rise structures. Turnover of housing equipment and other products also gained 11.5 per cent to Y14bn. However, construction material sales were off 0.2 per cent to Y38.7bn. Toyo Sash, which sells all of its products domestically, is planning to change its name to Tostem after July 1, to reflect a shift to more diversified housing products manufacturing. The company said the outlook for the current year for another official discount rate cut was unlikely to push housing investment sharply higher and spark a rebound in its results. Toyo Sash expects a 6 per cent gain in sales to Y510bn. Pre-tax profits are expected to rise 1.5 per cent to Y33,000bn, and net profits 11 per cent to Y16,500bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Mitsubishi Petrochemical falls heavily
DOC.TEXT: MITSUBISHI Petrochemical, a joint venture between Mitsubishi and Royal Dutch Shell, suffered a 35.6 per cent drop in pre-tax profits, to Y30bn (Dollars 225.56m), for the year ended March. The economic slowdown in Japan and abroad, and inventory adjustments cut petrochemical demand, the company said. Lower product prices were also accompanied by higher operating expenses. Sales at Mitsubishi Petrochemical, Japan's industry leader, were off 6.4 per cent to Y407bn, while net profits declined 40.2 per cent to Y15.4bn. By sector, sales of resins were up 1.6 per cent to Y167bn and fine chemicals 34.8 per cent to Y27bn. Sales of plastics, however, fell 18.6 per cent to Y161.5bn and special chemicals 1 per cent to Y50bn. The company's current assets declined 31 per cent to Y348bn, including a fall from Y186bn to Y118bn in cash holdings and from Y42bn to Y35bn in investment securities.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Toray edges lower despite improved fibre sales
DOC.TEXT: TORAY Industries, Japan's leading synthetic fibre maker, yesterday posted falls in consolidated earnings for the full year to March. It blamed sluggish demand for its synthetic fibres, and lower profits at its construction affiliate. Pre-tax profits fell 11.4 per cent to Y64bn (Dollars 481.20m) on a 6.5 per cent increase in total sales, to Y976.7bn. After-tax profits plunged 26.2 per cent to Y27.7bn. The company's fibre sales grew 10.1 per cent to Y489.9bn. However, the company said demand for nylon used in tyre cords and fishing nets declined. Sales of chemicals and new businesses declined 0.5 per cent and 2.4 per cent respectively. Nylon resin sales slowed because of sluggish demand from the automotive and electronic industries. Polyester film sales also decreased because of low demand and increasing price competition from film for magnetic tapes and industrial materials. Sales of the housing and engineering division rose 7.8 per cent to Y219bn, but operating profits fell 3.2 per cent to Y7.6bn. Toray's non-operating deficit widened by 47 per cent to Y11.9bn, as interest and dividends received fell 24.4 per cent to Y18.6bn. The company's cash and deposit balance plunged 23.8 per cent to Y100bn. The company also posted extraordinary losses on stock holdings of Y2.1bn. For the current year to March 1993, Toray expects further price competition to squeeze earnings, and forecasts a 2.4 per cent drop in consolidated pre-tax profits to Y63bn, on a 4.4 per cent rise in sales to Y1,020bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Japanese builder down sharply
DOC.TEXT: HASEKO, a leading Japanese condominium-builder, was hit by the worsening domestic economy. Reporting a sharp drop in profits, the company pointed to an especially harsh environment in the real estate and construction industries, with investment down sharply in office buildings and large apartment complexes. It posted a non-consolidated Y25.2bn drop in pre-tax profits, to Y25bn (Dollars 187.96m), and a 42.8 per cent fall, to Y8bn, in net profits in the year ended March. Sales increased 1.5 per cent to Y529bn. Haseko's construction sales were up 6.8 per cent to Y328bn, and management income 3 per cent to Y19.4bn. Design management sales, however, fell 9 per cent to Y7.1bn. Real estate was down 7 per cent to Y174bn. Order receipts declined 33.4 per cent to Y280bn. Haseko drew down current assets Y47bn to Y839bn, including a drop in cash reserves of Y32bn to Y96bn and a sell-off of its entire Y1.5bn securities portfolio. Current liabilities were off Y85bn to Y646bn. With no signs of a pick-up in private capital investment or consumer spending, it expects continued hard times for construction orders and real estate activities. For the year ended March 1993, it expects its first sales decline in nine years, of 9.2 per cent to Y480bn. Pre-tax profits are also seen falling 40 per cent to Y15bn, and net profits 54 per cent to Y6.5bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Yamaha blames sluggish demand for 29% decline
DOC.TEXT: YAMAHA, the world's leading musical instrument maker, logged a 37.6 per cent drop in non-consolidated pre-tax profits, to Y6.8bn (Dollars 52.6m). Net profits fell 29.4 per cent to Y2.8bn in the year ended March. Both figures were down for the second consecutive year. The Shizuoka-based company blamed sluggish demand for pianos and other musical instruments for the declines. Overall, sales for the year edged up 0.1 per cent to Y383.7bn after a slight decline the previous year. Domestic sales, however, gained 1.3 per cent to Y272bn, despite weak demand for synthesizers and other electrical instruments. The negative effect of the yen's rise contributed to a 2.8 per cent drop in exports, to Y111.5bn, despite the start of piano shipments to Steinway of the US during the second half of the year. Piano sales fell Y7.4bn to Y60bn, electronic instruments Y3.2bn to Y68bn and audio equipment Y3bn to Y29bn. Sales of other instruments gained Y1.4bn to Y50bn. Yamaha's current assets slipped Y12.6bn to Y150.6bn, including a drop of Y518m in its securities holdings, to Y890m. For the year to next March, Yamaha expects sales and profits to decline further, largely because of a planned shift of household equipment operations to a subsidiary. Pre-tax profits are expected to fall 48 per cent to Y3.5bn and net profits 47 per cent to Y1.5bn, on a sales drop of 10 per cent in sales to Y345bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Indonesian banks in merger discussions
DOC.TEXT: TWO of Indonesia's largest banks are discussing a merger in what, bankers believe, may be the first step in the restructuring of PT Astra International, Indonesia's second largest public company. The banks, Bank Danamon and Bank Summa, are the country's second and 11th largest respectively, excluding the five state-owned commercial banks. Bank Summa is part of the Summa Group which, bankers say, is controlled by the Soeryadjaya family. The family owns about 75 per cent of Astra, which is responsible for over half of Indonesia's total vehicle sales, in addition to interests in financial services, timber and agribusiness. Brokers estimate, however, that vehicle sales have declined more than 40 per cent since 1990. Last month Astra, which has a market capitalisation of Rp3,025bn (Dollars 1.5bn), announced 1991 net profits of Rp210bn, down 11 per cent on 1990. Brokers are forecasting a further 15 to 20 per cent fall in profits this year. Astra had total borrowing of Rp2,247bn (over 50 per cent short-term) at the end of 1991. 'The merger itself has not been discussed by the board (of Bank Summa). It is up to the shareholders,' Bank Summa said yesterday. It would not confirm local press reports that Summa has received a Rp100bn loan from Danamon. Bankers say a merger may be tripartite and include Universal Bank, Indonesia's 14th largest private bank and one 51 per cent-owned by Astra International. Bank Danamon's total assets are estimated at about Rp3,700bn. It had a pre-tax profit in 1991 of Rp75bn. Bank Summa, with current assets of Rp1,700bn, recorded pre-tax profits last year of just Rp3bn, brokers say. Bankers believe Summa has been hit by clients defaulting on car purchase loans and a sharp fall in the property development market. Shareholders recently injected Rp300bn into the bank to enable it to meet a capital adequacy requirement of 4.75 per cent of total assets.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Abitibi-Price to sell paper distribution units
DOC.TEXT: ABITIBI-Price, 80 per cent owned by the Reichmann brothers through Olympia & York developments, is selling its printing and industrial paper products distribution business in Canada and the US to Alco Standard for CDollars 340m (USDollars 285.7m) cash. The deal includes four Abitibi units: Inter City Papers, Barber Ellis Fine Papers and Price Daxion in Canada and Whitaker Carpenter in the US. Mr Ron Oberlander, president of Abitibi, said the proceeds will be used to reduce Abitibi's debt. He stressed that Abitibi had no intention of paying a special dividend. 'We are carrying out our strategy to sell non-core businesses,' he said. 'The four businesses now being sold have annual sales of CDollars 850m, are profitable and represent most of our diversified products group.' Last year Abitibi, one of North America's largest newsprint producers, had sales of just over CDollars 3bn. Mr Oberlander said Abitibi wants to sell its building products business, several paper converting units and an office products distributor when the timing is right.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Seagram faces 'difficult year'
DOC.TEXT: SEAGRAM'S main wine and spirits businesses face a 'very difficult year,' Mr Edgar Bronfman, chairman of the international drinks group, said yesterday, Reuters reports from Montreal. After the annual meeting, Mr Bronfman declined to say how the 1992 results would compare with the previous year's earnings of USDollars 727m, or Dollars 7.67 per share, which had showed a small decline from 1990.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Macy's plans to close eight stores
DOC.TEXT: RH MACY is to close eight underperforming department stores by August 1 in order to strengthen its overall performance, AP-DJ reports from New York. The US stores group, in Chapter 11 of the US bankruptcy code, said the decision to close the stores followed a review of the company. The review was based on several factors, including unsatisfactory profitability and productivity, a declining sales trend and a lack of growth potential in the market. Macy's has notified the bankruptcy court and its creditor groups of its decision.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Honda hit by fall in domestic sales - Changes planned to give local management more autonomy
DOC.TEXT: HONDA Motor, the Japanese car maker, yesterday reported a 1 per cent fall in consolidated pre-tax profit to Y130.76bn (Dollars 1.01bn), and announced changes to its management structure to give executives in the US and Europe more autonomy. In common with other Japanese car makers, Honda has suffered from the downturn in the domestic market, where new registrations were 5.1 per cent down January to April, compared with the same period last year. But the company is still planning to expand its share of foreign markets. It said net profit for the current year is likely to fall by about Y5bn from last year's Y64.9bn, itself down 14.9 per cent, partly because of costs related to the commencement of UK production, scheduled for this October. A series of management promotions and title changes have created four clear divisions of Honda's car business, covering Japan, the US, Europe and 'others,' with each of the regions apparently given more control over local design, research and marketing. 'We felt that we had to make our management more flexible in these regions. Basically, the international car market is very stable, with no area promising rapid growth, and we have to adjust to this stable growth era,' Honda said. The company's consolidated sales rose 2.1 per cent to Y4,391bn, with a 3.9 per cent increase in car sales and a 2 per cent fall in revenue from motorcycles, even though there was a 6.4 per cent increase in sales by volume. The company said motorcycle sales were helped by strong demand from other Asian countries, although revenue was hurt by an appreciation of the yen. Parent company pre-tax profits, more exposed to the weak domestic car market, fell by 21.3 per cent to Y66.9bn on a 4 per cent increase in sales to Y2,911bn. For the current year, the parent is expecting slight sales growth at Y2,920bn and profits flat at Y67bn. 'We are not very optimistic in our estimations for the domestic market this year. Total sales in the market will probably be at the same level as last year's 7.43m units. Sales will be at that level or a little lower,' the company said. The company sold about 669,000 cars in Japan last year, unchanged from the previous period, 953,000 in the US, up from 952,000, and 196,000 in Europe, up from 173,000, while the 'others' accounted for 143,000, an increase of 22,000 units. As with many leading Japanese companies, Honda is planning to reduce capital spending, with the target this year Y200bn, down from Y237.8bn last year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Maple Leaf Foods advances 31% despite weak markets
DOC.TEXT: MAPLE Leaf Foods, the Canadian food-processing subsidiary of the UK's Hillsdown Holdings, has again overcome weak markets to post a 31 per cent rise in first-quarter earnings. Net earnings from continuing operations climbed to CDollars 12m (USDollars 10), or 15 cents a share, from CDollars 9.2m, or 14 cents a share, a year earlier. Sales dropped to CDollars 638m from CDollars 747m, due largely to the surgery which has transformed Maple Leaf, formerly Canada Packers, over the past 18 months into a more tightly focused and aggressive company. Mr Charles Bowen, recently appointed chief executive, ascribed the improved earnings to continued cost-cutting, lower interest expense and wider margins as a result of a greater emphasis on value-added products. The company earned net interest of CDollars 1.9m this year, compared with debt-service charges of CDollars 3.7m in 1991. Maple Leaf, which has virtually no long-term debt and net cash reserves of over CDollars 200m, has recently switched its focus from reorganisation to expansion. It has signed a flour-milling joint venture with ConAgra, the big US agri-business group. The company reported sharply higher first-quarter earnings from its milling opera-tions. Maple Leaf has also proposed buying out the minorities in Corporate Foods, its baking subsidiary, as a first step towards North American expansion.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Mitel reduces annual loss to CDollars 5.7m
DOC.TEXT: MITEL, the Canadian telecommunications equipment maker controlled by British Telecom, has enjoyed its best quarter in several years, but posted a loss for fiscal 1992 as a whole. The company, based in Ottawa, also warned that, despite a return to profit in its fourth quarter, strong competitive pressures remain. It indicated it was unlikely to repeat the past three months' results for at least the next half-year. The net loss for the fiscal year ended March 27 was CDollars 5.7m (USDollars 4.78m), or 12 cents a share, compared with a CDollars 107m loss, or CDollars 1.41 a share, in fiscal 1991. Revenues slipped to CDollars 406.1m from CDollars 431.3m. Operating losses, excluding extraordinary charges, were cut from CDollars 31.8m to CDollars 8.1m. The fourth quarter, however, produced a CDollars 5m profit on record sales of CDollars 121.7m. Much of the recent improvement is due to intense efforts to contain costs. Sales of the GX5000 office switchboard more than doubled to CDollars 7.1m last year. BT has been seeking a buyer for the past two years for the 51 per cent stake in Mitel it bought in 1985.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Swissair and Austrian Air to operate joint offices
DOC.TEXT: SWISSAIR and Austrian Airlines are to operate jointly customer service offices in their two home countries from November 1 as part of a programme to intensify co-operation and reduce costs. The remaining offices, including agencies of the two airlines in border towns of neighbouring countries, will be operated by the home airline. Passenger and cargo handling at Swiss and Austrian airports will pass to the home carrier from September 1. Austrian Airlines and Swissair, together with Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS), formed the European Quality Alliance in 1989 to share facilities and improve their competitiveness. The three recently set up jointly operated stations in some eastern European cities. Further links among the three were possible, said Mr Otto Loepfe, chief executive of Swissair, but he ruled out mergers. 'Generally we have said that, short of merger, all possibilities are open,' he said at a Zurich press conference.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: De Benedetti in Hungary deal
DOC.TEXT: COFINEC, the central European investment vehicle of Mr Carlo De Benedetti, the Italian financier, has taken control of Kner, a Hungarian printing group. The move is Cofinec's latest step towards its goal of building a Hungarian packaging business with annual turnover of Dollars 100m. Cofinec - controlled by Mr De Benedetti's Cerus investment arm - and the Hungarian Investment Company - the country fund managed by John Govett of the UK - bought 85 per cent of Kner in an investment worth Dollars 20m. The acquisition follows last year's purchase of Petofi, Hungary's most important packaging producer. Cofinec said that Petofi was in the international equity market and that a transaction would be announced soon. The Petofi offering comes after investments by the Hungary country funds and international institutions such as the Hungarian American Enterprise Fund and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. Petofi was the first industrial company in eastern Europe to receive credit from the EBRD, which has given priority to eastern Europe's underdeveloped packaging industry. Mr De Benedetti's group has been encouraged by rapid improvements in productivity and exports at Petofi. It is looking to build a more extensive packaging and printing business in central Europe. 'Hungary is still a low-cost country and close to markets which we want to penetrate very much,' explained Mr De Benedetti yesterday. 'This started as an investment opportunity and turned into a business opportunity.' Mr De Benedetti also said that Olivetti, the Italian computer company he controls, was working on additional orders for systems from Hungarian banks. Olivetti already has a contract with Hungary's National Savings Bank. However, Mr De Benedetti said that Olivetti was not planning any acquisitions in eastern Europe, in spite of a recent decision by International Business Machines to take a minority stake in Muszertechnika, Hungary's leading computer company.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Court ruling angers Price Waterhouse
DOC.TEXT: PRICE WATERHOUSE, the New York based accountancy firm, has been angered by an Arizona court decision calling upon it to pay Dollars 338m in damages to Standard Chartered Bank of the UK. The ruling, late on Tuesday, relates to negligence in past audits of a US bank acquired by Standard Chartered. The jury decision, which blamed Price Waterhouse for negligence and breach of fiduciary duty, is thought to be the biggest award ever levied against an accountancy firm in the US. The court finding stems from a lawsuit brought in 1988 by Standard Chartered. The suit claimed Price Waterhouse had failed to identify and report 'material deficiencies' in the loan portfolio and internal controls system of United Bancorp, an Arizona bank bought by the UK bank in 1987. Standard Chartered paid Dollars 335m for United, made heavy losses, and 18 months later sold it to Citicorp for Dollars 207m. The UK bank's lawsuit claimed that Price Waterhouse was negligent in its 1985 and 1986 audits of United Bancorp. Price Waterhouse admitted yesterday its insurance coverage would cover an amount of more than Dollars 100m in damages, but not the full Dollars 338m awarded by the court. Ms Erica Baird, a Price Waterhouse executive in New York, said, however, that 'our net worth is greatly in excess of the difference'. Ms Baird described the court decision as 'outrageous'. She said Price Waterhouse had played no role in the 1987 acquisition by Standard Chartered. 'I am confident we will never pay this award,' she said. In a memo to Price Waterhouse partners in the US, Mr Shaun O'Malley, chairman, called the verdict 'unfair and unjustified'. He said Price Waterhouse would move immediately for a new trial. Price Waterhouse said it was heartened that the Arizona jury had not found it guilty of violating the state's Civil Racketeering Act, which would have permitted damages to be trebled to more than Dollars 1bn. Mr O'Malley called the verdict 'completely contrary to the evidence' and claimed that United Bancorp's 1985 and 1986 financial statements 'were presented fairly even with the benefit of hindsight'. The Price Waterhouse chairman also assured partners that 'knowing the risks of a jury trial, we have been preparing for all contingencies and believe we can have the judgment stayed, pending appeal'. In London, the UK sister firm is facing a separate and unrelated charge of negligent auditing, this one contained in a writ filed by the liquidators of the Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI). Price Waterhouse has denied the charges contained in the BCCI-related writ, which claims Price Waterhouse was negligent as an auditor of BCCI and failed to spot serious irregularities in audits it performed before 1987.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / International Company News: Polygram, Universal in film venture
DOC.TEXT: POLYGRAM, the London- based music and entertainment company which is 80 per cent owned by Philips of the Netherlands, has formed a joint venture with Universal Pictures of the US for the distribution of films in North America. The North American distribution venture marks a further step in the company's efforts to increase its presence in the film industry. The joint venture, to be called Gramercy Pictures, will be based in Los Angeles. It is aimed at marketing medium-budget films supplied by both Polygram and Universal. The company intends to handle the release of an initial eight films a year, with more expected as the joint venture grows. PolyGram and Universal, which is part of MCA, the US film subsidiary of Matsushita of Japan, will continue to handle their own distribution in markets outside North America. The new company was formed because the partners believe the marketing of medium-budget films requires a different approach than the saturation advertising often available for big-budget, blockbuster films. 'Many good movies, with enormous box office potential, require a more nurturing marketing and distribution process. This new company was especially created to do just that,' said Mr Tom Pollock, chairman of the MCA Motion Picture Group. PolyGram said the joint venture was part of the company's Dollars 200m programme of investment in the film business. The investment programme was announced in September, when Polygram took majority control of two film production companies, Propaganda Films and Working Title. At the time, Polygram said that its plans for distributing medium-budget films in the US might involve setting up such a joint venture company.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Henderson launches Pounds 20m European investment
DOC.TEXT: HENDERSON, the fund management group, is seeking at least Pounds 20m from the launch of an investment trust specialising in European equities. It is the second new European investment trust to be announced this week. Henderson EuroTrust will have a split capital structure, with 75 per cent of the issued capital in ordinary shares, and the rest in zero-dividend preference shares. It is hoped that this structure will stop the shares from moving to a discount to net asset value. The company has a 10-year life until the annual general meeting of October 2002, when the zero shares will be redeemed at 70p. This is equivalent to a gross redemption yield of 10.2 per cent. Projected initial gross yield on the ordinary shares is 5 per cent. During the launch issue only packaged units, consisting of one ordinary share and one zero at a price of Pounds 1, will be available. Total launch expenses have been fixed at 4.5 per cent, with an annual management fee of 0.85 per cent. The trust is aimed at small investors, via brokers, and smaller institutions. The fund has a minimum holding in bonds of 15 per cent, and can invest up to 10 per cent of its assets in derivatives. It hopes to use this combination to deliver both income and capital growth. The prospectus will be available on June 8, and applications for Personal Equity Plans will close on June 22. The offer closes on June 30, with dealings in the shares starting on July 6.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Ferguson International declines to Pounds 6.63m
DOC.TEXT: ADVERSELY affected by trading conditions world-wide, but particularly in the UK, Ferguson International Holdings saw pre-tax profits shrink by 43 per cent from Pounds 11.6m to Pounds 6.63m in the year to Feb-ruary 29. However, Mr Denis Cassidy, chairman, said he had detec-ted 'some encouraging stirrings' in trading since January and especially in March and April. Trading profits were eroded in all of Ferguson's four legs. Mr Cassidy singled out the recessionary impact on UK retailers for the falls in the labels and hangers divisions - down 20 per cent to Pounds 4.7m (Pounds 5.88m) and 15 per cent to Pounds 2.63m (Pounds 3.08m) respectively. The chairman cited the tightened advertising expenditure for the decline in printing and publishing, which suffered the deepest fall - 44 per cent to Pounds 815,000 (Pounds 1.45m). Trading profits of the communications components side, supplying cable TV parts in the US, slipped to Pounds 1.56m (Pounds 1.7m), but showed a 47 per cent return on capital employed and was, said Mr Cassidy, a strong cash generator. Group trading profits on continuing activities were down 20 per cent to Pounds 9.7m, an improvement on the 28 per cent reduction at the halfway stage. Boosted by two acquisitions - Interstate Cable Enterprises of the US and Globus Druck of Germany - turnover on continuing activities rose 6 per cent to Pounds 114.9m. Interest payable was cut by 56 per cent to Pounds 1.1m (Pounds 2.54m) and there were exceptional costs of Pounds 1.6m relating mainly to the closure of Harkwell Labels & Tags. Extraordinary charges of Pounds 1.14m derived from the disposal of non-core businesses. Earnings emerged at 13.5p (22.7p) per share and the directors have proposed holding the final dividend at 8.25p for a maintained 12.5p total.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Shares fall on Pounds 2.2m loss at Henry Barrett
DOC.TEXT: SHARES in Henry Barrett Group fell 6p to 26p yesterday, close to an all-time low, after the the steel and industrial fasteners company announced an interim loss and expressed caution about the immediate outlook. Barrett, which has been forced to rein back after rapid expansion in the 1980s, reported a pre-tax loss of Pounds 2.19m in the six months to February 29, compared with a profit of Pounds 272,000. Turnover fell to Pounds 49.4m, against Pounds 57.4m, which included Pounds 11m relating to discontinued activities or businesses for sale. Mr James Barrett, group chief executive, said stockholding and industrial fasteners were profitable. But the construction division, mainly involved in structural steelwork, lost money because of pressure on margins. 'We're looking for margin not volume recovery,' he said. Losses per share were 3.47p (earnings 0.37p) and no interim dividend is being paid. However, the company said it would pay a nominal final dividend because several shareholders are trusts which have to sell shares if no dividend is paid. Barrett has continued to sell loss-making businesses, leading to an extraordinary charge of Pounds 2.7m. Last month Park Pallet, which is involved in materials handling, was sold for Pounds 168,000. Exceptional charges of Pounds 295,000 covered redundancies in ongoing businesses. Once Barrett's disposals and cuts are complete, the workforce will fall to 800, compared to 1,350 a year ago. Net borrowings remained high at Pounds 19.9m at the end of the period, equivalent to 87 per cent of shareholders funds (74 per cent). Mr Barrett said gearing should fall towards 50 per cent by the year end as cash flow was expected to turn mildly positive and some property sales were pending. Interest costs were unchanged at Pounds 1.18m.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Price war cuts RHM to Pounds 49m
DOC.TEXT: RANKS HOVIS McDougall, the UK's largest baker, yesterday revealed the effects of the deepening bread price war with a sharper-than-expected 36 per cent drop in interim pre-tax profits to Pounds 48.5m. The group also indicated that trading in the second half remained difficult and said annual profits would be significantly lower than last year. Analysts, surprised at the depth of price-cutting and at difficulties in RHM's US market, cut full-year forecasts from Pounds 110m to between Pounds 95m and Pounds 98m. Although the company had warned in January of lower profits, analysts said the indications were that price-cutting was deepening. Mr Paul Coker, managing director, said the company intended to pursue volume, even at the expense of margin. 'If you haven't got volume you haven't got a business,' he said. RHM, which entered the bread price war in the new year, had begun to rebuild the volume lost when it refused to cut prices last autumn, Mr Coker said. Turnover for the six months to February 29 rose by Pounds 7.4m to Pounds 773.7m. RHM did not intend to close any more of its 18 bakeries, he added. 'If there has to be capacity taken out, others can do it.' The milling and bread baking division, the group's largest business which includes brands such as Hovis, saw pre-tax profits drop by 62 per cent to Pounds 12.6m. The cakes business, home of Mr Kipling, also suffered from price-cutting and profits fell from Pounds 7.4m to Pounds 5.1m. In the US, RHM suffered the effects of higher peanut prices and a surplus of tomatoes, which resulted in a squeeze on ketchup margins. Pre-tax profits in North America fell by 84 per cent to Pounds 900,000. Both grocery products that and food services increased profits through cost-cutting and rationalisation, Mr Coker said. Earnings dropped by 35 per cent to 9.6p but the interim dividend is maintained at 3.82p. COMMENT RHM's shares proved remarkably resilient despite the results yesterday, closing up 5p at 234p. This has less to do with bullish sentiment than the fact that RHM maintained the interim dividend, making the yield a healthy 8 per cent. Yet, on full year estimates dividend cover falls to about 1.5 times - compared with a sector average of more than two times - and only marginally higher for 1993. There is also the threat that RHM is not generating enough profit to make the pay-out and it will have to use cash balances to do so. On full-year forecasts of Pounds 95m, the prospective p/e of 12.1 times leaves little reason to buy. Given next year's outlook there appears to be even less reason to hold.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Currie has 65% of Pacific
DOC.BYLINE: By PHILIP COGGAN, Personal Finance Editor
DOC.TEXT: MARTIN Currie Pacific Trust said that it has received more than 65 per cent acceptances for its offer for Pacific Horizon Investment Trust, which is managed by Jupiter Tyndall. Valid acceptances have been received for 65.79 per cent of the ordinary shares and 44.55 per cent of the warrants. A further 4.92 per cent of ordinary shareholders and 6.46 per cent of warrant holders have sent in acceptances, which are in the process of being validated. The offer has been extended until June 2. Jupiter Tyndall has been battling to block the takeover and has assembled a 25.1 per cent stake in the trust's warrants. Last week, it voted down a resolution which required a 75 per cent majority of warrant holders. As a result, Martin Currie dropped an improved offer for the ordinary shares of Pacific Horizon. Jupiter has said that it will put forward its own propo-sals to enhance shareholder value and enable share and warrant holders to receive cash for all or part of their holdings. Jupiter has a 15.4 per cent stake in the ordinary shares and has said that it will not accept the offer, thus preventing Martin Currie from passing the 90 per cent mark at which it could compulsorily acquire the outstanding shares. In these circumstances Jupiter says that the rights of the warrant holders will have to be substantially enhanced; Martin Currie Pacific says it has received legal advice that this is not the case.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: All-round growth lifts Compass
DOC.TEXT: RESILIENT demand helped Compass Group, the catering and hospitals concern, to increase pre-tax profit by nearly 10 per cent, from Pounds 15.5m to Pounds 17m, in the six months to March 29. Turnover advanced at a similar rate to Pounds 177m (Pounds 161m). Mr Francis Mackay, chief executive, said both divisions had achieved record sales and profits. In contract catering, operating profit rose to Pounds 13.5m (Pounds 12.7m) on sales of Pounds 146m (Pounds 132m). The margin was reduced by a large contract with British Telecom, announced at this time last year. It contributed about Pounds 20m to turnover but the margin was much lower than with established contracts. Fewer new contracts were signed and more were lost as sites closed, leaving a net gain of only seven. Redundancies also reduced traffic through some canteens. Opportunities were opening up in public sector hospitals and schools. The catering market in health and education was worth about Pounds 3.3bn, more than twice the corporate market. However, only 5 per cent was contracted out compared with 50 per cent in the business sector. The purchase of four hospitals early in 1991, taking the total to 15, helped the healthcare division to increase operating profit to Pounds 6.3m (Pounds 5.6m) on sales of Pounds 29.1m (Pounds 26.1m). Although average occupancy fell from 57.5 to 50 per cent because of the acquisitions, improved efficiency enabled overall margins to rise slight-ly. Net debt fell to Pounds 36.5m, against Pounds 41.1m at the year-end. However, last year's acquisition-led spending bulge was in the first half, whereas most of this year's investment in hospital expansion will come in the second half. Earnings per share rose to 16.8p (15.4p) and the interim dividend goes up to 4.19p (3.85p). COMMENT While scope remains for improving margins at BT and the acquired hospitals, short-term growth in catering will be limited by the lagging recovery in employment and by the time taken to win public-sector contracts. A move on to the continent also looks medium-term, unless some acquisition is in its sights. Market rumours have resurfaced that it may be interested in its rival Gardner Merchant. While Forte would consider a rich offer, Compass is unlikely to pay over the odds and there would be a monopoly issue in the UK, where the two have 50 per cent of the corporate market. A full-year pre-tax profit of Pounds 35m gives a prospective multiple of about 15 on yesterday's close of 519p, down 8p as expectations were a little dampened. While Compass has no trough to bounce back from, it deserves a premium for its sustained growth record and for the bright prospects in both its markets. After a good run, the shares still look a strong hold.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Monument to sell stake in gas field
DOC.TEXT: Monument Oil and Gas, the independent exploration and production company, has agreed to sell its 3 per cent interest in the Markham gas field in line with its strategy of disposing of licences in which its interest is relatively small. Wintershall (UK) is paying some Pounds 10.4m cash for UKCS License P701. This includes the reimbursement of certain development costs incurred by Monument. The agreement provides for adjustment of the settlement subject to a redetermination of field interest between the participants.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Miller hit by write-down of Pounds 6.5m
DOC.TEXT: Pre-tax profits of Miller Group, one of the UK's biggest privately-owned construction companies, tumbled from Pounds 10.75m to just Pounds 537,000 in 1991 as the recession continued to hit property values. The figures were struck after an exceptional provision of Pounds 6.45m arising from land and property write-downs and the closure of a specialist subsidiary. This followed an exceptional provision of Pounds 3.5m in 1990. The group has interests in civil engineering, general construction, mining property development and housebuilding. It recently appointed Mr David Cawthra as chief executive to assist with its expansion plans. Mr Cawthra was previously chief executive of Balfour Beatty, the construction arm of BICC the large engineering group. Turnover of Miller last year was virtually static at Pounds 238.03m against Pounds 235.38m. After tax of Pounds 210,000 (Pounds 4.16m) and dividends the group suffered an overall loss of Pounds 314,000 (Pounds 5.91m profit). Mr James Miller, chairman, stressed the strength of the company's balance sheet.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Young & Co's Brewery advances to Pounds 5.59m
DOC.TEXT: YOUNG & Co's Brewery, the south-London based independent brewer, increased profits by 11 per cent to Pounds 5.59m pre-tax in the year to March 28. Trading profits rose by 17 per cent to Pounds 8.03m on turnover 16.4 per cent ahead at Pounds 68.14m. Earnings declined from 28.38p to 27.51p but a final dividend of 7.5p (7p) lifts the total to 14.5p - a rise of 11.5 per cent. Trading profits were helped by the Pounds 12m acquisition last August of the HH Finch chain of 22 pubs and six wine bars and restaurants. These outlets contributed profits of Pounds 541,722 on turnover of Pounds 5.39m. Additional borrowings increased interest charges from Pounds 1.83m to Pounds 2.68m. Revaluation of the com-pany's property assets at the year end resulted in a surplus of Pounds 18m over book value. Sales of assets during the year realised gains of Pounds 244,000.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Yorkshire TV 55% ahead to Pounds 9.36m
DOC.TEXT: YORKSHIRE Television yester-day announced a 55 per cent increase in pre-tax profit to Pounds 9.36m for the six months to the end of March. Sir Derek Palmar, the Yorkshire chairman, yesterday described the result as a good increase in a period of recession that reflected the group's decentralised divisional structure 'which encourages management at all levels to maintain constant pressure to reduce costs in all areas.' The result was achieved on turnover ahead from Pounds 95m to Pounds 102m. Yorkshire, like other ITV companies, benefited from the government's decision to reduce the exchequer levy in the last year of the old franchises before the survivors started paying the Treasury the money they bid to retain their franchises. Yorkshire's profit before levy rose from Pounds 11.6m to Pounds 12.7m but the company only paid Pounds 3.38m in levy in the half year compared with Pounds 5.61m in the same period last year. Mr Clive Leach, Yorkshire's managing director, said that the rise in operating profit had been the best in ITV. Yorkshire, a company in which Pearson, owner of the Financial Times, has a 20 per cent stake, successfully retained its licence against two rivals but with a bid of Pounds 37.7m a year. The payments, in monthly slices, start in January together with 7 per cent of qualifying advertising reven-ue. Mr Leach said yesterday that Yorkshire had already achieved its 1993 cost structure - eight months ahead of schedule. The company had a net cash balance of Pounds 13.1m at the end of March. Earnings per share improved from 10.1p to 16p and the interim dividend is being maintained at 3.3p. Yorkshire said yesterday that there had been vigorous discussions with some advertisers designed to 'raise the value of the company's airtime in the market to bring it more in line with our high audience delivery in preparation for 1993.' Despite difficulties Yorkshire improved advertising revenue to Pounds 75.8m (Pounds 71m) and the sales of programmes increased by 8.7 per cent from Pounds 23.87m to Pounds 25.95m. Margins however remained depressed and further steps were being taken to improve profitability. Yorkshire said the outlook for advertising revenue was encouraging and the company was confident that its position as a strong ITV licensee was assured. The share price rose 3p to 193p.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: A future based on a dual-track strategy for growth - Vital changes that have transformed Courtaulds
DOC.TEXT: IN HIS new headquarters in London's west end Mr Sipko Huismans was in ebullient mood as he announced an 8 per cent improvement in Courtaulds' full year profits. The move to the smart new offices symbolises the changes at Courtaulds since it demerged its textiles operations two-years ago, according to Mr Huismans. 'We've moved the group from a tired, beaten up textile company in dingy surroundings into a modern up-to-date entity which has taken a grip of its destiny,' he says. 'We were described as a rat-bag of industries ripe only for takeover. Now we have demonstrated we have critical mass.' Courtaulds' ability to shrug off the recession has been dependent upon tight financial controls and its ability to manage high-margin businesses, Mr Huismans says. The company has cut its workforce from 23,550 last year to 22,700 and further cost savings are inevitable. Any company executive who reckons his company is efficiently run is a fool, argues Mr Huismans. Courtaulds has managers who cannot manage and there is lots more room for profits improvements, he adds. For the future, Mr Huismans has developed a dual-track strategy for growth through the exploitation of a new material called Tencel and through the replication of businesses on a global scale. Geographical expansion will mainly be in the Far East. He says he is not looking at diversification in any circumstances and that any acquisitions would be add-ons. Mr Huismans says that during his tenure, he would like to more than double turnover in the Far East. At present the region generates about 6 per cent of sales and he would like it to reach 15 per cent. Mr Huismans, who has been chief executive for nearly two years, reckons managers can achieve about four or five things over about half a dozen years before running out of steam. Meanwhile, Tencel, a man-made fibre aimed at the high-quality cotton market, remains one of Courtaulds' chief hopes. Its main advantage is that it does not need dry cleaning, can be laundered like cotton, but unlike cotton it can be produced when needed. A first Tencel plant, costing about Dollars 85m, is on-stream and should make every existing plant for cellulose fibres obsolete, according to Mr Huismans. The process also has a minimal environmental impact, he adds. He wants Courtaulds to reap the full benefits from Tencel, rather than setting-up co-marketing agreements. As for threats, the main one - according to analysts - is a Taiwanese investment for additional viscose production in the US which threatens to flood the market there, potentially undermining margins of between 20 and 25 per cent. But Mr Huismans reckons any investment would not come on stream for five years and the permits for the necessary pulp plant have not even been given yet. 'We've made mistakes,' admits Mr Huismans. 'I can name half a dozen without even thinking.' When pressed for examples he says it would be invidious to give details, but adds that all of them were because the group failed to understand the market or underestimated the reaction of the competition. 'In the end, you have to be an optimist, otherwise you end up as a gilts investor,' he concludes.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Courtaulds improves 8% to Pounds 201.4m
DOC.TEXT: COURTAULDS, the specialist materials group, yesterday reported an 8 per cent increase in pre-tax profits to Pounds 201.4m for the year to March 31, writes Paul Abrahams. Mr Sipko Huismans, chief executive, said the difficult economic conditions of the past two years were showing some signs of easing. The results were achieved on a turnover of Pounds 1.94bn compared with Pounds 1.91bn. The tax charge in the UK was Pounds 24.6m (Pounds 21.5m) while non-UK tax was Pounds 21.7m (Pounds 18.2m). Earnings per share increased from 36.5p to 38p. A final dividend of 9.35p makes a 13p (12p) total. The improved results mostly reflected a sharp rise in the films and fibres division where operating profits surged from Pounds 61m to Pounds 74m on turnover of Pounds 647m (Pounds 667m). Mr Huismans said the improvement resulted from the withdrawal from loss-making businesses such as carbon-fibre, advancements in the demand-supply balance and productivity gains. Operating profits at the coatings division increased from Pounds 56m to Pounds 59m on turnover of Pounds 678m (Pounds 640m). More than 20 per cent of sales growth was in the Far East. The worldwide marine business performed well, but results at protective coatings were described as sluggish. Performance materials were adversely affected by the poor state of the civil and military aviation industries. Weak demand in the US construction industry also affected the sealants market. The division made operating profits of Pounds 12m (Pounds 15m) on turnover of Pounds 183m (Pounds 179m). The packaging division reported operating profits of Pounds 25m (Pounds 21m) on turnover of Pounds 244m (Pounds 235m). Mr Huismans said margins had increased to take the overall return on sales to 10.2 per cent compared with 8.9 per cent last year. He added that greater efficiency and an improving mix of business had helped. The chemicals division made an operating profit of Pounds 42m (Pounds 38m) on turnover of Pounds 233m (Pounds 232m). The acetate operations had recovered from difficult operating conditions in the first half of the year and cigarette tow, used for filters, had continued to expand and make good margins.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: GPG declines to Pounds 2.39m
DOC.TEXT: GPG, Sir Ron Brierley's UK investment company yesterday announced a fall in pre-tax profits from Pounds 9.46m to Pounds 2.39m in the year to March 31. The company blamed lower interest earnings of Pounds 693,000 (Pounds 2.94m) and a lack of abnormal items, against Pounds 5.8m last time. Profits before interest and abnormals increased from Pounds 728,000 to Pounds 1.69m. The shares have been suspended since December 1990 because the company was thought to be a 'shell'. Attempts to lift the suspension had so far proved unsuccessful. Sir Ron complained of a 'Kafkaesque, impenetrable bureaucratic maze' at the Stock Exchange.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Grosvenor Inns joins USM with an Pounds 8.1m tag
DOC.TEXT: GROSVENOR INNS was yesterday launched on the USM, with 6m ordinary shares being placed by Rea Brothers at 105p. Dealings in the shares will begin on May 27. With the net proceeds of Pounds 5.7m, Grosvenor is to expand its portfolio of pubs by acquiring two London pub retailing operations - Slug & Lettuce, a group of 13 pubs, seven of which trade under the Slug & Lettuce name, for Pounds 4.46m cash, and the Hutchison Houses, two City pubs, for Pounds 640,000 cash. At the placing price Grosvenor is valued at Pounds 8.1m and the shares being placed represent about 78 per cent of its enlarged capital. Broker to the issue is Panmure Gordon. The acquired 15 pubs will boost Grosvenor's total estate to 30. On a pro forma basis, the net assets of the enlarged group will be about Pounds 7m. Mr Tim Thwaites, non-executive chairman, previously worked with the four executive directors at Grand Metropolitan. Mr Thwaites was managing director of Chef & Brewer and then chairman of Whitbread's retail division. Mr Peter Whitehead and Mr Gary Pettet are joint managing directors. The former left GrandMet in 1985 to establish Cromwell Taverns with Mr Michael Mills, Grosvenor finance director. The latter became a Cromwell director in 1988.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Commercial Union raising Pounds 100m and counts bomb cost
DOC.TEXT: COMMERCIAL UNION yesterday signalled its intention to increase its share of the UK insurance market by raising Pounds 100m through a preference share issue. The group, the most successful of the UK's composite insurers in recent years, also reported reduced pre-tax losses for the first quarter of 1992 and could be back in the black by the end of the year. Net losses (after reinsurance recoveries) from damage caused by the IRA bomb to CU's London headquarters and other buildings in the capital amounted to Pounds 15m, which would be taken in the second quarter. CU said it hoped to move back to its headquarters in a year. Pre-tax losses for the three months to March 31 amounted to Pounds 19.2m, compared with Pounds 24.2m, but losses per share rose to 5.3p (4.3p) after a charge for tax and minorities of Pounds 3.9m against Pounds 4.5m credit. Cazenove and Hoare Govett are brokers for the issue of Pounds 100m cumulative irredeemable preference shares, which have been placed. Mr Tony Wyand, executive director, explained that the intention was to reinforce the capital base in view of the rapid growth of the group's life business and the hardening in the UK non-life market. The extra capital would strengthen solvency and allow CU to increase non-life premium income by between Pounds 200m and Pounds 300m, he added. In the UK where rates have been increased for most lines income rose by 24 per cent to Pounds 473.2m (Pounds 380.1m), while total premiums rose by 16 per cent to Pounds 1.28bn (Pounds 1.11bn) According to Mr Stephen Bird, analyst with Smith New Court, CU was the only composite expanding its market share. Premium growth was particularly rapid in UK private motor, up 52 per cent to Pounds 48.9m, and London market marine and aviation (up 44.1 per cent to Pounds 80.2m). CU is also bullish about its life business, reporting new business growth of 46 per cent and an increase in life profits to Pounds 27m (Pounds 26.5m). Life premiums now account for 35 per cent of business compared with 18 per cent in 1982 and the group aims to increase the share to 50 per cent by the end of the decade. See Lex and International Capital Markets

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Willis Corroon hit by lower interest rates
DOC.TEXT: Lower interest rates and continued flatness in US insurance rates were the main factors pegging back profit growth at Willis Corroon, the insurance broker, where pre-tax profits dipped by 4 per cent to Pounds 42.1m in the first quarter. Brokerage and fee income rose to Pounds 165.6m (Pounds 146.5m) in the three months to March 31, with an underlying growth of 3 per cent when the effects of acquisitions and currency movements are stripped out), contributing to higher turnover of Pounds 175.1m (Pounds 163.7m). However interest and investment income fell to Pounds 13.1m (Pounds 18.4m) and expenses rose to Pounds 142m (Pounds 126.5m). Underwriting claims fell to Pounds 6.3m (Pounds 12.6m), leaving operating profit at Pounds 39.9m (Pounds 43m). The share of associates' profits rose to Pounds 3.4m (Pounds 2.5m) and interest payable fell to Pounds 1.2m (Pounds 1.5m). Mr Roger Elliott, executive chairman, said: 'Conditions for our UK operations have improved . . . (but) there is no evidence of such an improvement emerging in the USA.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Quadrant reorganisation will reduce staff by 220
DOC.TEXT: QUADRANT Group, the photographic materials and video company, yesterday announced it is to close three photo-processing laboratories with the loss of 220 jobs. The laboratories, in Chalgrove, Braintree and Yate, are being closed as part of a reorganisation of Quadrant's photo-processing business. The division, which mainly provided photo-processing for estate agents, has been affected by recession and the slump in the property market. Quadrant has decided to continue to market the estate agency services, but transfer the processing to ColourCare International, a subsidiary of London International Group. Quadrant also reported pre-tax profits down from Pounds 2.78m to Pounds 1.41m for the year to February 29. Turnover fell to Pounds 51.9m (Pounds 54.5m). At the operating level the loss was reduced from Pounds 386,000 to Pounds 360,000. Net interest receivable fell by Pounds 1.3m to Pounds 2.08m. The final dividend is again 2.35p for an unchanged total of 4p. The company said Lord Rees, the former cabinet minister, will become chairman 'when his existing commitments permit'. He will replace Mr Robert Brothers, who will also retire as chief executive officer in favour of Mr Andrew Douglas, chief operating officer.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Bass advances 20% to Pounds 271m
DOC.TEXT: A REDUCTION of Pounds 48m to interest charges of Pounds 27m enabled Bass, the UK's leading brewer, to raise half-year pre-tax profits by 20 per cent from Pounds 225m to Pounds 271m. Apart from the benefit of reduced borrowings due to the rights issue, the result was helped by the deferral of capital investment programmes 'pending more favourable opportunities' though spending still rose from Pounds 166m to Pounds 252m. Mr Ian Prosser, chairman, said that while consumer confidence appeared stronger in the UK, there was 'little evidence of any increase in demand in our principal markets.' Earnings per share for the six months to April 11 fell to 22.5p (22.7p). But the interim dividend was increased to 5.25p (4.95p). Operating profits rose marginally to Pounds 286m (Pounds 282m) on turnover down slightly at Pounds 2.23bn (Pounds 2.25bn) in spite of the disposal of 1,500 pubs. The brewing division benefited from reduced costs and lifted operating profits from Pounds 83m to Pounds 99m on turnover of Pounds 843m (Pounds 820m). Strong gains in the free trade limited the overall decline in beer volumes to 2.3 per cent against a 4.4 per cent fall in the market. Tennent's pilsner and super lagers, and Bass, Stones and Worthington ales increased volume sales. The charge for bad debts was raised from Pounds 4.7m to Pounds 9.7m. Britvic, the soft drinks business, held turnover at last year's level of Pounds 205m, but profits fell to Pounds 7m (Pounds 8m) after increased marketing costs. Profits from pubs fell by 25 per cent from Pounds 118m to Pounds 88m - about Pounds 21m of the decline was accounted for by pub disposals. The group has now sold, or agreed sales on, all but 290 of the 2,740 outlets it is required to free under government orders. The sales, at average prices 20 per cent above book value, have raised Pounds 380m gross, of which Pounds 125m was accounted for in the half year. The introduction of electronic sales equipment in the group's 3,000 managed pubs will increase costs during the next two years, but is expected to reduce staff by 700. Leisure operations showed a 31 per cent increase in operating profits to Pounds 34m (Pounds 26m), due mainly to the performance of the enlarged chain of bingo clubs. Holiday Inn Worldwide raised operating profit by 26 per cent to Pounds 54m (Pounds 43m) on turnover of Pounds 255m (Pounds 274m). Revenue per available room in managed hotels in the US increased 2.2 per cent, against a 0.2 per cent rise in the franchised hotels. In the rest of the world, the improvement was 3.4 per cent and 5.2 per cent respectively. COMMENT Headline profits may owe a lot to the interest charge reduction, but there are some encouraging signs at the trading level. Bass has retained 70 per cent of the beer volumes in the 2,450 pubs it has sold and is gaining strength in the rest of the free trade. Business through free trade pubs is 10 per cent higher, and there has been a 7 per cent improvement in the take-home market. The figures suggest the gains are not being made by giving the beer away. In present conditions, a 5 per cent improvement in Holiday Inn margins is quite an achievement, and promises rapid progress when the recovery eventually comes. Analysts are forecasting full-year profits of about Pounds 570m, a 33 per cent increase. On a prospective p/e of 13.4, the group stands at a 10 per cent discount to the market and appears significantly under-rated.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Sun Alliance in closer ties with top Swiss insurer
DOC.TEXT: SUN ALLIANCE, the UK's largest insurance company, will today sign an agreement with Helvetia, one of Switzerland's top five insurers, to jointly develop international commercial lines business. The deal, which the managing director designate of Sun Alliance International, Mr Peter Foreman, expects to sign in St Gallen, Switzerland, today, formalises a co-operation agreement which has been in existence for ten years. It should boost the profile of both companies in the highly competitive market for providing multinational companies with worldwide insurance programmes. Increasingly companies with strong international networks - such as American International Group, Zurich, Union des Assurances de Paris and Allianz - have been able to dominate the market. British companies, which lack comparable international networks and do not have the available available to make acquisitions, have been increasingly forced to join forces with international rivals. Sun Alliance itself has forged links with Taisho of Japan and Lucky Insurance Company of South Korea, while both Royal Insurance and Commercial Union have also formed long-term links with Japanese companies. Sun Alliance also has less formalised accords with Vesta Group in Norway and Atlantica in Sweden. More recently Royal agreed to merge its European operations outside the UK with Aachener and Munchener of Germany and Fondiaria of Italy. According to Mr Paul Cusition, manager international insurances at Sun Alliance International, says that by acting more closely together the companies have already been able to win the custom of one Swiss multinational. Mr Cusition says that the arrangement is seen as long-term and strategic. Contracts signed by the two companies allow for a six month notice period if either party opts to terminate the deal. Mr Cusition says it will strengthen Sun Alliance's ability to service multinational clients in both Switzerland and Germany, where the Swiss company is well represented.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Speyhawk sees no reason for share price increase
DOC.TEXT: SPEYHAWK, the property company with liabilities which exceed its assets by Pounds 70m, yesterday stated that it saw no justification for the increase in its share price. The shares closed yesterday at 18 3/4 p, up from 17p. This compares with a low of 2 1/2 p at the start of last month, when the company announced a Pounds 216m annual loss and restructuring talks with its banks concerning more than Pounds 300m of debt. When it announced the result, it said that 'the lead banks have agreed in principle to proposals for a restructuring covering Speyhawk's entire bank debt . . . the principles of which are at an advanced stage of negotiation'. Speyhawk said yesterday its position was unchanged. One analyst ascribed the share price surge to speculators who were unaware of the gravity of the company's financial state.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Fund managers take stock of weighty issues: The availability of investment cash for the equity market
DOC.TEXT: Every time the equity market hits new highs company finance directors rub their hands in glee. The higher the market, the more they can raise through rights issues or flotations. Last week BICC, the UK cables and construction group, took advantage of the rise in its share price since the election to launch a Pounds 154m rights issue, taking the total value of rights issues so far this year to more than Pounds 1bn. It is not only quoted businesses that are looking to take money from the stock market. There is a lengthening list of private companies planning to sell their shares. And the government is not missing out either. Its privatisation programme may be going through a quieter patch, but the exchequer's coffers still need filling and gilt sales will be higher than for many years. All these calls on the market could begin to put a strain on investors' cash. The fear is that if their available cash is all absorbed by capital raising issues, there will not be sufficient money invested in existing shares to keep the market rising. The 'weight of money' argument is an old favourite in the stock market, often used to support forecasts of rises or falls in the market when commentators have run out of other reasons. The argument depends on weighing up the supply of cash available to invest against the demands on that cash. If supply exceeds demand, the theory goes, the market will rise. However, accurate figures for both sides are hard to forecast, with official statistics for last year subject to revision. Mr Mark Brown, strategist at UBS Phillips & Drew, the stockbroker, has estimated the notion-al excess demand for equities in real terms since 1978. His chart suggests there is an increasing level of excess cash to invest which he says is a favourable influence on the equity market. On one side of the scales is the money coming into the market as institutional investors, such as pension funds and insurance groups, receive cash to invest. Although pension funds' cash inflows have been depressed by contributions, holidays and redundancies, the picture is brighter among insurance companies, for instance as people set up personal pension schemes. Between them institutional investment reached Pounds 38.3bn in 1991. Estimates are for a similar level this year. There are other sources of funds. Private investors may also increase their holdings of UK equities, either directly or through unit trusts. And there is the hope that takeover activity will increase with cash bids allowing recipients to reinvest the proceeds in the market. However, the current uncertainty on this side of the balance relates to overseas investors. It is hard to forecast how much money is flowing into the UK stock market from abroad, but the consensus is that since the general election, flows have been significant. County NatWest, the securities house, estimates foreign purchases of gilts alone total Pounds 4bn since the election. Large international securities houses have been advocating clients switching their investments into the UK. The day after the election, for example, Morgan Stanley advised its clients to increase the proportion of assets invested in the UK by 5.5 percentage points to 14 per cent, moving from an underweight to overweight stance as the UK accounts for 11 per cent of the value of European equities. Weighing down the other side of the balance, the biggest call on the market will be gilt sales. The public sector borrowing requirement, which was Pounds 13.9bn in 1991-92, is forecast to more than double in the current year. Following the election, the Bank of England moved fast to sell new gilts, and there are a lot more to come. Last year net gilt sales were nearly Pounds 11bn; this year they are expected to near Pounds 30bn. The increase in gilt sales will more than offset a decline in money raised in privatisations. Even these will not dwindle completely as there are many calls due from earlier partly-paid privatisations such as the electricity companies and the BT sale. Rights issues took more than Pounds 10bn from the stock market last year but may raise less this year as much work has already been done on restructuring balance sheets. Companies have been attracted to the corporate bond market too, as yields have fallen, although many of these securities are bought by international investors. New issue activity will jump however. Names such as MFI, GPA, 3i, The Daily Telegraph group will be joining the stock market. There is also the unusual sale of shares by Wellcome Trust in Wellcome, the pharmaceutical group, which may involve a Pounds 4bn issue. But with overseas demand expected to be high and the trust aiming to reinvest the proceeds in the stock market, this could add cash to the UK market rather than take it away. There is to some extent a self-correcting aspect to the mechanism. If there are too many rights, the market will sag, so discouraging other companies from making issues. A sudden fall in the market would put off flotations. And as Mr Brown admits, the equity market did well last year, in spite of a high level of rights issues. By contrast, it did badly in 1990 when there was in theory much spare cash. Institutions allowed their cash holdings to increase in 1990 and then ran them down again in 1991. However, this year most stock market strategists expect a Pounds 10bn or Pounds 15bn shortfall in available cash compared with the likely level of bond and equity issues, if purchases by overseas investors are excluded. At present it seems that foreign investors can more than plug the gap, meaning that the equity market could go higher. But foreign investors can be fickle and on their own they do not provide a sound basis for a bull market.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Resilient Argyll advances by 25%
DOC.TEXT: THE continued resilience of food retailers to recession was yesterday underlined by Argyll Group, which runs the Safeway, Lo-Cost and Presto chains, as it posted a 25 per cent gain in annual pre-tax profits to Pounds 364.5m. These followed similar substantial profits increases in recent weeks from two other big food retailers, Tesco and J. Sainsbury. However, the market was worried that cost increases were currently outstripping same-store sales gains and Argyll's shares fell 10p to 357p. Sir Alistair Grant, chairman, said as a result of the low-inflation environment in the 1990s, far more attention had to be paid to increasing productivity. 'We will have to industrialise the way we run our stores,' he said. Efficiencies would come from better management of its supply chain. The company is testing sales-based re-ordering systems. This year saw the extension of sales scanning equipment to all Safeway stores. In the year to March 28, Argyll's sales breached the Pounds 5bn mark for the first time climbing 6 per cent to Pounds 5.04bn. Operating profits climbed 16 per cent to Pounds 331m as a result of the widening of operating margin from 6.3 per cent to 7 per cent. Capital expenditure was Pounds 442m as Argyll opened 17 Safeway stores. This year 25 stores are due to open with spending projected to increase to Pounds 550m. Interest income - including Pounds 2.5m in dividends from its shareholdings in two mainland European retailers, Ahold and Casino - was Pounds 33.5m. This was considerably higher than the previous year's Pounds 5.5m income because of the cash inflow from last June's Pounds 387m rights issue. The company received Pounds 78.3m in extraordinary income from the settlement of its legal claim against Guinness over the Distillers bid. The taxman took Pounds 19.8m of the Pounds 100m settlement while Pounds 1.9m disappeared in legal costs. Earnings per share grew 12 per cent to 24.2p. A final dividend of 6.55p will lift the annual payout by 15 per cent to 9.75p. This set of results marked the fifth year since Argyll acquired the Safeway supermarket chain. Under its ownership, Safeway's sales have increased threefold and profits sixfold. 'We are quite proud of what we have achieved,' said Mr David Webster, deputy chairman. Lex, Page 22

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Barclays pulls out of US retail banking
DOC.TEXT: BARCLAYS BANK yesterday unveiled plans to sell off its 65-branch New York retail banking operations in a move that will mark the UK bank's withdrawal from the US retail banking business. The buyer of the Barclays operations is the Bank of New York, the 17th largest US bank with 223 retail branches in the New York area. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the New York bank is believed to be paying between Dollars 25m (Pounds 14.10m) and Dollars 50m for the Barclays branch network, which comes with Dollars 3.2bn of assets. The UK bank's total North American assets are Dollars 22bn. The 65 branches being acquired come with Dollars 2.9bn of deposits and Dollars 2.1bn of loans. Barclays declined to say what portion of these loans were classified as non-performing. The deal is expected to close by October. The Barclays move comes 21 years after the British clearer first began building up its US retail banking operations. It has been selling off a series of US consumer finance businesses and retail branches since the 1989 sale to Wells Fargo of its 50-branch California operations. Heavy bad debt provisions - stemming largely from problem property loans - caused Barclays' US holdings to suffer a total loss of Pounds 217m in 1991, compared with a Pounds 20m profit in 1990. Barclays' bad debt provisions in the US last year more than doubled at Pounds 339m. Mr John Kerslake, Barclays chief executive in the US, yesterday explained that, in terms of the bank's strategy 'to concentrate on serving the corporate and institutional markets', the New York retail branch banking network 'does not fit into that strategy'. Banking analysts stressed that Barclays, in common with other non-US banks such as National Westminster Bank, had found it increasingly difficult to manage a profitable branch business in the US. Barclays has been directing its strategy away from retail and middle market clients. For the Bank of New York, which has Dollars 40bn of assets and total deposits of Dollars 29.2bn, the acquisition of the Barclays network is considered a good fit.
