Both the Barclays and Bank of New York branches are concentrated in suburban New York areas such as Westchester and Long Island.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Westpac announces record loss
DOC.TEXT: WESTPAC Banking Corporation, Australian's biggest trading bank, has declared the largest loss in the country's banking history following a massive increase in property loan writedowns. The dividend has been cut and the capital base strengthened through a ADollars 1.2bn rights issue. It yesterday disclosed a ADollars 2.6bn (USDollars 1.96bn) turnround for the half year to March, sending it to a pre-tax loss of ADollars 2.32bn against a ADollars 313.4m profit last time. The bank's bottom-line loss was ADollars 1.67bn after a ADollars 713m tax credit and adjustment for minorities, compared with a ADollars 218m profit previously. The three-for-10 renounceable rights issue is at ADollars 3 a share. The issue will not be underwritten, and the price compares with Westpac's close of Dollars 3.89 in Sydney yesterday, down 5 cents. Mr Frank Conroy, managing director, said the bank anticipated a 'sound' profit in the current half and would pay a 12 cents a share interim dividend, against 15 cents last time. This rate was expected to be maintained for the full year. He said the Reserve Bank supported the company's conservative approach and had confirmed that, even after provisions, Westpac would satisfy official capital adequacy requirements. The Westpac loss follows bad and doubtful debt write-offs of ADollars 2.65bn, an increase from ADollars 579m last time. More than ADollars 2.1bn of write-downs reflect revaluations of the ADollars 6.3bn property portfolio. Mr Conroy said average revaluations were 34 per cent below book value. Westpac has also taken a much more pessimistic view of its 'problem' loans, increasing provisioning from 28 to 47 per cent, raising their value from ADollars 6.4bn to ADollars 8.2bn, or more than 10.6 per cent of the company's total risk-adjusted assets. Mr Conroy said shareholders would benefit in two ways. 'First, with the values recognised as current market value, the bank can implement a strategy of orderly disposal. But I stress the word orderly. There will be no fire sales or dumping of property on the market. 'Second, as the size of our property problem reduces, the burden on future profits from these non-performing assets will reduce.' Lex, Page 22; Background, Page 31

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / The Lex Column: UK economy
DOC.TEXT: So much for the UK's post-election boom. Yesterday's retail sales figures confirmed anecdotal and survey evidence suggesting consumers hardly rushed to the shops following the Tory victory. Perhaps the odd bottle of champagne boosted the food sector. Clothing and footwear were up, but a drop of 1.4 per cent in household goods sales was disappointing. Even though the effect of Budget tax cuts and lower interest rates will be felt from this month, there is not much sign of the consumer-led recovery which Mr Norman Lamont now urgently needs to meet his modest forecast of 1 per cent growth this year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / The Lex Column: Land Securities
DOC.TEXT: The net asset value of Britain's biggest property company may have fallen 17 per cent last year. But Mr Peter Hunt, LandSecs chairman, is in the relatively happy position of having lost less of his shareholders' money than most of his peers. The shares have outperformed the property sector by 15 per cent over the past 12 months, a deserved reward for his consistent refusal to heed the siren calls of those urging a more aggressive stance. The idea that they will now underperform should not go unchallenged, but, on the basis of the gloomier net asset value forecasts for this year, the shares are on a tight discount.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / The Lex Column: Commercial Union
DOC.TEXT: Yesterday's placing of Pounds 100m of irredeemable preference shares is the clearest sign yet that CU is moving off the back foot. The company was forced to become risk averse in the mid 1980s after disastrous losses in the US, a policy which, as it happens, enabled it to avoid most of the mortgage guarantee problems now haunting its competitors. Emboldened by a more encouraging first quarter, CU is now in a position to take a more aggressive stance on new premium growth. Shareholders might not have been easily persuaded to put up the money themselves, and would certainly have demanded a heavy price. But they are still entitled to ask whether the chosen instrument best suits their interests. The advantage is that the shares will count as capital for solvency margin purposes - taking this ratio from 41 per cent at the end of the first quarter to 44 per cent - while the gross rate of 11.55 per cent is almost a half-point cheaper than that recently paid by Halifax building society on a similar issue. The claim that ordinary shareholders' returns are being attractively geared up will depend on whether the UK general insurance cycle really is on the turn. Certainly the tentative conclusion from the composite insurance results of the last week or so is that better premium rates are at last sticking in most classes of business. The recovery, though, looks set to be long and slow and the risk for CU is in picking up dud accounts. Its UK general insurance premiums increased by no less than 26 per cent in the first quarter, against a 2 per cent fall at General Accident and a single-figure increase at Royal.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / The Lex Column: Westpac
DOC.TEXT: It is difficult to escape the conclusion that something has suddenly gone terribly wrong at Westpac, Australia's largest bank, after yesterday's ADollars 2.65bn provision. Non-accrual loans rose 26 per cent in the past six months; loans with interest more than 90 days overdue rose 63 per cent. The bank has come unstuck on international loans to the Maxwell empire, Olympia & York and Macy's, but most of the problems are in domestic property. After outside valuation of its property exposure, it has increased its provision rate from 28 to 47 per cent. Yet there is a chance that yesterday's announcement marks the beginning of the end of Westpac's troubles. Having been slow to provide as the property market fell, it has now leap-frogged some of its competition. Strictly speaking, its ADollars 1.2bn rights issue is unnecessary. After the provisions its capital ratios would still fall within the rules set by the Bank for International Settlements. With the extra equity, the ratios will be within the Australian norm. It thus looks as though the bank is positioning itself for recovery. Overheads have been cut by 1 per cent in the past year. The provisions rate should fall from now on. It may even be possible to write back some of the latest provisions. That would allow for more flexible management of the loan portfolio. The proviso remains, though, that there should be no further falls on the Australian property market. This risk will increase if other banks follows Westpac's example and raise provisions to the point where they can afford to sell property assets cheaply. Similar behaviour by banks in the US has certainly slowed property market recovery there.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / The Lex Column: A Safeway forward
DOC.TEXT: After yesterday's 25 per cent pre-tax profits increase from Argyll, it seems safe to conclude that the effect of recession has been to accelerate polarisation in the food retailing sector. Thanks in part to their successful rights issues last year, Argyll, Tesco and Sainsbury are now able effectively to bar rivals from developing competitive superstore chains. Marks and Spencer is in a category of its own on the high street. The rest have moved downmarket, where the returns are less attractive, or have simply gone backwards. As for the future, Argyll plans to open 25 Safeway superstores this year and again in 1993. It has Pounds 170m of cash in hand, although the preponderance of new stores in the more expensive south will push up its store opening costs and pull down its still impressive 30 per cent return on investment. Last year it grew faster than the competition. Its margins are ahead of Tesco's and a mere point below those of Sainsbury. Management is investing more time in non-Safeway operations, the Presto and Lo-Cost chains where it believes there is significant room to seize more market share. Granted, yesterday's figures were not quite as spectacular as Sainsbury's last week - hence, perhaps, the market's reaction in marking down its shares by 3 per cent. But there was no mistaking Argyll's confident tone. Given their recent record, the shares deserve better than a multiple below the market average.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / New inquiry into police service promises big shake-up in ranks
DOC.BYLINE: By ALAN PIKE, Social Affairs Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: WIDESPREAD changes to Britain's police service are likely to result from an inquiry announced by Mr Kenneth Clarke, the home secretary, yesterday. The inquiry will examine many areas of police organisation including its roles, responsibilities, career and rank structure, and pay. The service's centralised pay structure could be replaced by one based more on individual performance. Mr Clarke is under pressure to contain levels of spending on the police, which are high compared with other public services, and to improve management and efficiency. He announced the inquiry, which will report within a year, in a speech to the Police Federation conference at Scarborough. 'I believe that I should not simply charge into yet more change,' he said. Any decisions should be taken on the basis of an open, well-informed and independent assessment. The inquiry was well received by the conference and Mr Alan Eastwood, federation chairman, said: 'We have nothing to fear and much to gain.' After Mr Clarke had spoken, however, some delegates voiced reservations. 'I believe this is a cost-cutting exercise,' said Sgt Mike Bennett, chairman of the federation's Metropolitan Police branch. Some police forces are already modernising their management structures, and Mr Clarke said he intended to maintain the current 'direction and momentum of change for the better'. He made clear, however, that the inquiry would look specifically at rank structure - which means it is likely to consider whether the service is top-heavy with senior officers - as well as at pay. 'Is a blanket increase in pay to every rank and every officer, irrespective of type of work or competence, really the best way of reimbursing the police for the huge spectrum of work that they do?' asked Mr Clarke. The members of the inquiry team and their precise terms of reference will be announced within six weeks.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Letter: Pointers to an economic upturn
DOC.TEXT: Sir, I refer to Peter Marsh's article 'How To Figure Out The End of Recession' (Management, May 18). If one accepts the thesis that it is small business which generates underlying growth in the economy and creates employment, then statistics on new business start-ups and liquidations/insolvencies will provide a valuable indicator. There are many sources of this information and I would like to highlight one set of figures which may be of interest, new company formations. Limited companies are predominantly private rather than public and small rather than large. New company formations may therefore provide a useful indicator of start-up activity. Year on year growth in new company formations was the norm until the year ended March 1989. Over the most recent three years numbers have progressively fallen and we are yet to see an upturn. When and if an upturn occurs, maybe this will be an important indicator that the UK is moving out of recession. M Whitwell, chief executive, Jordan and Sons, 21 St Thomas Street, Bristol BS1 6JS

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Letter: Children's charity fears about World Bank priority for poorest (2)
DOC.TEXT: Sir, Your leader on the World Bank's World Development Report ('Development and the environment', May 18) is generally perceptive and well taken. There is however one jarring note. Speaking of environment problems you say: 'Fortunately, their solution does not require a global compact; it requires, first more development ..' The implication is that 'more development' does not require a global compact. I think on reflection you will agree this would be thoroughly wrong. Even if one accepts that 'more development' is to a large extent the responsibility of the developing countries, the history of the past two decades shows only too clearly that the lack of a global compact and of effective global economic management has had a great deal to do with the setbacks to development which many developing countries have experienced. 'More development' in an unfavourable international environment is a near-impossible task. I very much doubt that the World Bank's report would support this implication of your article. H W Singer, Institute of Development Studies, University of Sussex, Brighton, BN1 9RE

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Letter: Children's charity fears about World Bank priority for poorest (1)
DOC.TEXT: Sir, The recognition by the World Bank that the global environment debate has largely ignored the most serious problems facing developing countries ('Environment debate 'ignores plight of poor'', May 18) should be given a guarded welcome. Many individuals and organisations, including Save the children, will support the 'priorities for action' listed in the World Bank's World Development Report. These include stress on the need to address the problems of lack of clean water and adequate sanitation. That the welcome should be 'guarded' is because of fears about the priority which will be given to that list of priorities. Throughout the 1980s the World Bank played a dominant role in promoting structural adjustment policies in many developing countries. Save the Children and other organisations argued that the effects of such policies on the most vulnerable in society, particularly children, should be considered in advance. The World Bank and International Monetary fund were urged to adopt policies which would seek to improve the productivity and income of the poor and were told that services vital for the most vulnerable should be reinforced. Despite the welcome comments in the World Bank report, particularly on the need for education for women, fears remain that the World Bank sees concern for the poorest as something which can be tacked on to an otherwise unchanged policy of economic adjustment. Save the Children hopes that these fears are unfounded. International institutions must recognise that human and environmental objectives, like the needs of mothers and children, must be at the centre of an integrated, longer-term development policy. Nicholas Hinton, director general, Save the Children, Mary Datchelor House, 17 Grove Lane, London SE5

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Letter: Roads are not free
DOC.TEXT: Sir, You say ('Privatisation plus for BR', May 19) that 'state-owned railway tracks endure charges while users of state-owned roads go free'. With due respect, that is nonsense. There used to be a road fund into which all owners of vehicles paid an annual contribution called the road fund licence. They still pay it, but the government purloined that money for other uses and changed the name of the tax to hide the fact. Ken Gardner, member, European Communities economic and social committee, Bishop's Orchard, Oakley Green, near Windsor, Berkshire SL4 5UN

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Letter: Second class citizens of the sky
DOC.TEXT: Sir, Martyn Thomas, in his letter (May 19) concerning maintenance of national customs and border control for non-commercial aircraft flying between European countries, was right in upbraiding the UK. But he should also condemn the two EC commissioners, Martin Bangemann (industrial policy) and Sir Leon Brittan (competition) for their inaction. Both are aware that a person can today drive his car from the Netherlands to Belgium or from Belgium to France without passport control, but if the same person flies his aircraft from the self same countries to the other, customs and border controls apply and are likely to apply in all EC countries in 1993. My 750,000 members between them operate some 70,000 light aeroplanes, microlight aircraft, gliders, balloons, helicopters, etc. These aerial vehicles are used primarily for sport and recreation. Their pilots will, just like business travellers in their light aircraft, become second class European citizens left to face time and money wasting border controls at designated customs airports, unless the EC commissioners take action. The concept of the single European market will be meaningless unless national customs and border controls for road, rail, sea and air within the EC are abandoned. Frederick O Marsh, president, Europe Airsports, 1 Rue Montoyer, Bolte 12, 1040 Brussels Belgium

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Leading Article: RPI RIP
DOC.TEXT: THE BRITISH pride themselves on scoring own goals; and nowhere is this more true than in economic statistics. The Retail Prices Index has probably been responsible for more own goals than most. The particular fatuousness of the RPI lies in the fact that when the government increases interest rates to combat inflation, the immediate impact is to make inflation even worse. This arises because mortgage interest rates feature in the RPI. There is an equally adverse effect when interest rates are reduced. The net result is to produce violent swings around the trend. Governments would have to grin and bear it if the RPI represented some kind of final truth. But to present the RPI as an accurate measure is simply laughable. Most countries do not count mortgage interest payments. Instead, house prices or rents enter one way or another. With the gradual revival of the rented market in the UK, this method might be used for the British RPI. It is therefore good, if belated, news that the chancellor is to refer the treatment of owner occupiers' housing costs to the Retail Prices Index Advisory Committee. But loud cheering is not the order of the day, for there are fundamental fallacies behind the RPI and the Advisory Committee. The first is that there is a single method of measuring the price level of goods and services which is equally suitable for economic policy, uprating benefits, updating taxes, indexing gilts and using in pay negotiations. It is for instance often argued that the RPI has an inflationary bias because prices would appear to rise by about 2 per cent a year simply as a result of quality improvements in products included in the index. But if 2 per cent were docked off social security benefits for this reason, hardship would soon result, as the majority of hidden quality improvements probably take place in products such as hi-fi systems beyond the reach of beneficiaries. But the biggest anachronism of all is the Advisory Committee itself, which is a survival of the 1960s and 1970s, and represents many vested interests who are determined to get as much out of cost-of-living compensation as possible. Better to leave the job to the Central Statistical Office, subject to ministerial supervision and parliamentary scrutiny. If anyone fears that the government would then tamper with the index for political reasons, he or she need only glance at the immense powers of the cabinet secretary to make sure that the rules of the game are obeyed. And if anyone believes that the cabinet secretary's disapproval would remain discreetly hidden, he has a lot to learn about how government works in the world's oldest semi-democracy.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Leading Article: Soccer it and see
DOC.TEXT: WHILE the British parliament yesterday debated the pros and cons of European integration, the streets of London assumed a continental air. Baking sun, waving flags and the sing-song accents of Spanish and Italian football fans added to the cosmopolitan feel. The European cup final was in town. But the British were only spectators, a fitting finale to the dismal standard of football in this year's English football league. Last Sunday against Brazil, England's national team was made to look leaden, prompting from the manager an uncharacteristic footballing understatement, that his squad 'lacks individual flair'. Yet while Europe's politicians ponder and prevaricate, the people's sport is pushing out to new borders. Yesterday the European Football Union (UEFA) decided that clubs from Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia can enter European competitions; the republics of Slovenia, Croatia, Ukraine and Georgia are knocking on the door. European integration is the key to English football's salvation. The trend towards big clubs and European competition is commercially unstoppable. That the contract to televise English football has apparently been awarded to a European-based satellite company is a sign of things to come. Europe may not have a single currency by the end of the decade, but it certainly should have a European soccer league. The top few English clubs will then have to emulate the skills of continental Europeans, or get beaten by them every week.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Europe's new muddle army: Plans for military co-operation will have to disentangle overlapping forces and command structures
DOC.TEXT: It did not look such a great idea. Putting together a Franco-German brigade of 4,200 soldiers took three years' preparation. When it was inaugurated near Stuttgart in 1990, senior French officers admitted it would take somewhat longer before anyone would consider sending the brigade into combat. Two French regiments, two German battalions; one kind of beret but different codes of discipline, pay structures, radio systems, ammunition. Headquarters staff spoke French to each other one day, German the next, occasionally resorting to English. Le Monde dubbed it the unite-gadget, the gimmick unit. The French army seemed happy to keep it small. Yet the apparently fanciful experiment has become the embryo of a grand project. At their summit starting today in La Rochelle, President Francois Mitterrand and Chancellor Helmut Kohl are set to agree the blueprint for a joint corps, starting at about 35,000 men, ready in three years and intended as the nucleus of a future European army. For now, it is the nucleus of a disorderly tangle involving Europeans and Americans in intense diplomatic exchanges on the nature of European defence initiatives and their impact on Nato. The arguments are not about the principle of joint forces, but how they should be organised and who they should take orders from. They are not yet about what these forces might actually do in crises like Yugoslavia's. Ideas for new military combinations have been taking shape for about two and a half years. They arise from two distinct perspectives - Nato restructuring and development of the European Community. For Nato, multinational groupings were the best way it could keep a cohesive military structure after losing the enemy that for 40 years provided its reason for being. Almost all its members were cutting defences. Combined formations could rationalise these forces and make the continued presence of foreign troops in Germany more acceptable to the Germans. At the same time, the US was contemplating progressively bigger reductions in its troop levels in Europe - currently being halved to 150,000, with further withdrawals widely expected. By common accord, Europe had to take more responsibility for its own defence. Since relatively small forces were now required to be ready at short notice, it was logical that these should essentially come from the Europeans. Other notions of joint European defence - maybe, one day - on a more grandiose scale, were meanwhile appearing on the EC's horizon in the build-up to last December's Maastricht summit, coinciding with Nato's strategy review. Convergence was always going to be difficult, however. The EC had always left defence to Nato. There was a defence body straddling the two, the Western European Union (WEU), consisting of nine members of both the EC and the alliance, but it enjoyed no public profile, had been dormant for much of its existence, and had no troops. Nato, always busy trying to patch over its internal strains, was meanwhile searching for a new purpose, and Washington was going to be edgy about any attempt to rock the boat. And then, as always, there was the complicating factor of France. It is where Nato used to have its headquarters, has five other Nato allies on its borders, but for 25 years has had no part in the allied military hierarchy or in its joint military planning. It is now the nation most eager to carry the flag for Euro-defence. Nato got in first. A year ago, Britain leapt at the suggestion by General John Galvin, Supreme Allied Commander Europe (Saceur), that it should head a new rapid reaction corps of at least four divisions: 70,000 men. It would be a Nato force, but could also provide units for a European reaction force; commanders would just swap their Nato hat for a WEU hat. Under the WEU's wing, the forces could be sent outside the Nato area - something on which Nato has never reached a consensus. France saw the plan as a crude bid to pre-empt its own efforts to create a European defence structure that would be something more than a by-product of Nato. The Germans participated in the plan, but thought they had been stampeded by the British. When France and Germany came out with their own plan for a joint corps in October, the reaction from Washington and London was even sourer. Some other European allies shared their concern that it could undermine the alliance, in particular loosening the cement which since the 1950s had kept Germany at the heart of Nato. The UK, anxious not to alienate the US, contests the logic that Nato's role should decline proportionately as Europe's defence role increases. Some other EC partners are also cautious about the Franco-German plan, including the Dutch and Portuguese. But, one senior British diplomat says, for most European countries 'it is very difficult to tell the French to get lost'. Behind the careful compromises worked out at Nato's Rome summit in November ('the development of a European security and defence role . . . the enhancement of the role and responsibility of the European members') and the tantalisingly hedged ambitions endorsed by EC leaders at Maastricht in December ('the eventual framing of a common defence policy, which might in time lead to common defence') lie two fundamentally different approaches. For the French, it is prudent for Europe to make preparations independently of the US. From a British viewpoint, that is the kind of attitude that will make the US leave. Nato has constantly reiterated the need for a continued 'North American presence' in Europe. Canada, which up to now has shared this transatlantic function with the US, dealt allies a nasty surprise in February by saying it would pull its small remaining force out altogether. Keeping US forces, even at much reduced levels, is seen as providing the crucial linkage to Nato's ultimate defence guarantee, the US nuclear 'umbrella'. US involvement in Nato also stands as a more general emblem of transatlantic co-operation. Gen Galvin describes his post as 'America's seat at the table in Europe'. Sensitivity to this US view has led Nato allies to shelve the idea of appointing a European Saceur for the first time. Instead, Gen Galvin will hand over next month to another US army officer, Gen John Shalikashvili. As part of the military overhaul, the number of Nato commands is being been reduced, but Americans hold on to the two top posts - the supreme commands for Europe and the Atlantic - and to the southern Europe command in Naples. The paradoxical result is that, while Nato is being redesigned to take on a more European complexion, the US has a bigger share of the top military jobs. Britain opposes setting up any parallel European command structure - confusing, it says, and a waste of money. The WEU is, however, to have a contingency planning staff of 40. The WEU is being brought into service because it is there. The body once had an incipient military organisation but handed it over when Nato was formed. It embodies a firmer commitment than Nato's for allies to come to each other's aid. But its own military involvement has not gone beyond co-ordinating some Gulf naval operations. Britain wants it to be balanced halfway between Nato and the EC. But the language of Maastricht ties it more closely to the Community, as 'an integral part of the development of the European Union' and the executor of EC decisions that have defence implications. The WEU is set to co-ordinate closely with the Community, moving its secretariat from London to Brussels and opening its membership to other EC states. European Nato allies outside the Community may only join as associates. Mr Malcolm Rifkind, the UK defence secretary, last week spelt out initial proposals for forces that might be made available to the WEU. How big they were would be up the WEU, but there would be no standing forces and the organisation would draw on existing headquarters. He accepted that the Franco-German corps could be well suited for the task but only as one of a number of available units. France is lobbying hard to persuade other WEU members to give the corps more substance by joining. But there are few immediate candidates. Belgium is the most likely - the reason for a lightning visit there by Mr Rifkind on Tuesday - but appears still to be hesitating. Britain says clearly it will not join, but would contribute other forces for the WEU. These could include the existing UK-Netherlands amphibious force and the air-mobile division which Britain, Germany, Holland and Belgium are jointly forming as part of Nato's rapid reaction corps. But Nato would have first call on the troops. Mr Rifkind allowed that the WEU might be called on to act within Europe, but only when Nato chose not be engaged. It was 'hard to conceive of significant combat operations in Europe where Nato would not be involved'. The Germans, alert to the worries of the US and other allies, have given firm assurances that their own troops will remain assigned to Nato. The French foresee arrangements under which the whole corps could be placed under Saceur's wartime operational control. This is clearly distinct from assigning French troops automatically to Nato. But the Germans say the corps promises to associate France more closely with Nato's military partners, to Nato's benefit. The Bonn authorities meanwhile appear to see the corps as a possible way of easing the constraints on German military involvement abroad, something that the constitution is usually read as precluding. Still unclear are the corps' relationship to the WEU - the US fears it may create yet a third layer of military control - and its geographical scope. 'It seems odd,' admits Mr Willem van Eekelen, the WEU secretary-general, 'to argue to the French and Germans to make these forces available for everything except defence of their territory'. WEU foreign and defence ministers are expected to approve outline plans for putting troops at the organisation's disposal when they meet in Bonn on June 19. But it will all take time to clarify, and even then it will be an agreement on means rather than ultimate aims. Through the conceptual wrangling, the diplomatic niceties and the recondite arguments can be glimpsed a familiar spectacle of the old European military powers jockeying for influence.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Leading Article: Forward from Maastricht
DOC.TEXT: MR JOHN Major claimed yesterday, in opening the House of Commons debate on the Treaty of Maastricht, that the treaty 'marks for the Community an important and vital change of direction', in that it had 'for the first time begun to reverse the centralising trend', and to move decision-making power back towards the member states. He was elegant enough not to dot the i, but this was in fact a neat and telling response to the criticisms of his predecessor, who signed the Single European Act in 1987. 'You allowed the centralising Euro-steamroller to continue on its way,' he was saying to her in substance, 'whereas I have not merely stopped in its tracks but obliged it to change direction'. Thus he made much of the fact that the provisions of the treaty relating to foreign and security policy, justice and home affairs do not figure in the bill now before the House, because they are not modifications of the Treaty of Rome, do not affect the law or institutions of the EC as such, and therefore do not impinge directly on the law of the United Kingdom. Instead they are separate 'pillars' of the European Union, in the form of international agreements among the member states to co-operate in certain specific matters. Disputes arising from them, Mr Major said, could if necessary be brought before the International Court of Justice (which can only arbitrate in disputes between states), but not before the European Court (whose judgments, which may involve private firms or individuals, take precedence over those of domestic courts). Subsidiarity enshrined Mr Major also stressed the treaty's enshrinement of the principle of subsidiarity in EC law, in what he believes are legally binding terms - although these terms are in fact much too abstract for anyone to predict with confidence how the court will interpret them when they are put to the test. His basic message was clear: the dragon of centralising federalism has been slain, and the way is now clear for Britain, during its presidency in the second half of this year, to take the lead in a chastened and more pragmatic Community, which will at last give due priority to the interests of a wider Europe, opening negotiations with the EFTA countries and preparing the way for the admission of those further east. Yet Mr Major's own speech contained some clues which show that things will not in practice be that simple. He drew the House's attention to the fact that there could be no increase in the EC's resources without British agreement, and he served notice that he had 'no intention of agreeing' to any reduction in the rebate on Britain's contribution. Cohesion fund The fact is that the Community's southern members regard an increase in resources as a priority. Only this week a Spanish minister served notice that Spain will block the process of admitting new members unless it gets agreement on the early introduction of the 'cohesion fund' agreed at Maastricht to help the poorer member states prepare for economic and monetary union. This entails an increase in resources, as proposed by Mr Jacques Delors in February. The full Delors package may not go through, but any increase will sharpen the determination of other member states who are net contributors, notably Germany, to insist on a reduction, if not outright abolition, of Britain's rebate. Argument on these homely questions, not to mention predictable hand-wringing and recrimination over the corpse of Yugoslavia, will take the edge off any grand British design to give the Community a new lead. It is true that in many other member states the ratification process has produced a lively debate, which outside Britain had been notable for its absence in the period before Maastricht; and it is true that in the process some of Britain's anxieties about the erosion of national sovereignty have found an echo elsewhere in the EC. But the next stage of the institutional argument will not, as Mr Major seems to think, be about the transfer of powers to or from Brussels. It will be about the best method of taking decisions on matters already admitted to be of common concern, in the context of an expanding EC membership; and the more members there are, the harder it will be to leave any important issue at the mercy of a veto by any one of them.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Arts: Today's Television
DOC.TEXT: There is in Britain, particularly among the more influential, a widespread, albeit vague, feeling that it is highly dangerous to keep on proving that people have been wrongly convicted and wrongly imprisoned; it undermines faith in the police and the law. Even the eminent judge Lord Denning has expressed such thoughts. But it will surely be a dark day if journalists ever end their investigations, cease revealing such miscarriages of justice, and stop serving as a last resort for the desperate. Rough Justice comes up with yet another instance - Dave Smith and the Bordon Baseball Bat Murder - where it seems that the wrong person may have been jailed (10.00 BBC1). Radio has an interesting evening. At 7.05 Radio 3 starts the first broadcast performance of John Buller's new opera BAKXAI, relayed live from the London Coliseum. The Oath That Binds Us (7.20 Radio 4) tells of two doctors who trained at Birmingham University in 1938 and met again after a life spent in different countries. In Analysis (8.00 Radio 4) Peter Hennessy tries to work out what a fourth successive Conservative administration may mean for the way we are governed.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Arts: Bach cantatas - Music
DOC.TEXT: On so exquisite a summer's evening as Monday's it was all the odder to enter the Queen Elizabeth Hall and submit oneself to a selection of Bach cantatas, music that is manifestly intended for liturgical use. Yet there was nothing gloomy and fusty about these period-style performances by the Orchestra and Choir of the Age of Enlightenment, under Ivan Fischer. To the contrary, everything was light and air and colour - colourful drama, indeed, to quote the title of the six-concert series devised by Sir William Glock, of which this was the first (the second was last night). Each programme affords two or three of the vastly numerous (nearly 300) and varied cantatas along with a selection from the motets, concerti and orchestral suites (there are two other conductors involved, Rene Jacobs for the second pair of concerts, Barthold Kuijken for the third). Monday's programme attracted a virtually full house, as 'authentic' baroque performance usually does these days, whatever the weather. The first of our three cantatas, No. 110, 'Unser Mund sei voll Lachens', written for Christmas Day 1725, was an apt and festive opening chorus, despatched with bright irresistible crispness and panache. Cantata No. 104, 'Du Hirte Israel, Hore' (1724) followed, bringing the mellow oboes d'amore to the fore as well as tenor and bass vocal soloists. The latter, Michael George, gave an affecting account of his lilting pastoral aria, whose instrumental bass parts Fischer brought out with a discreet complementary pungency. The double 12-part choir (with the merest continuo accompaniment) produced a poised, compact but dramatically expressive polyphony in the short motet, 'Komm, Jesu, Komm]' (BWV 229). The fourth Brandenburg Concerto was done without conductor and with sprightly soloists: recorder players Catherine Latham and Anthony Robson, violinist Elizabeth Wallfisch (leader of the OAE), who executed the fast decorative scales of the first movement in a fine spray of virtuosity. After the interval we were treated to the plaintive sombre funerary colours of the motet 'O Jesu Christ, Mein's Lebens Licht' (BWV 118) and the graphic St. Michael's Day cantata No. 130, 'Herr Gott, dich loben alle wir' (1724). The opening choral-instrumental movement was rendered with keen, brilliant pointing of rhythm; tenor Christoph Pregardien's gigue-like duet with Lisa Beznosiuk's flute was charming. Bach cantatas are wonderful things: full of the bracing inventiveness of his Passions, without their longueurs, and never two the same. My appetite is whetted for the rest of these splendidly conceived concerts.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / People: Oxford picks from its own
DOC.TEXT: Clark Brundin, vice-chancellor of Warwick University, has been appointed to head Oxford University's new school of management studies - which promises to be a bright addition to management education in Britain when it admits its first batch of MBA students in 1994. The post goes with the presidency of Templeton College, the university's existing management institute where the new school will be built. After headhunting for more than a year, Oxford has, as ever, resorted to one of its own. Brundin trained as an engineer in the United States, but most of his academic life has been spent as a fellow of Jesus College, Oxford. An assiduous committee man, he ended up as chairman of the university's Board of Faculties before decamping to Warwick in 1985. Until recently he was also chairman of Anchor Housing, England's largest charitable provider of sheltered accommodation for the elderly. Brundin has a demanding job ahead. Templeton needs some Pounds 40m to get its management school off the ground. As yet it has only Pounds 5m - a sizeable chunk of it from Peter Moores, son of the pools supremo, after whom the directorship of the school is named. ***** David Kaye, a retired partner of Andersen Consulting, has been appointed Dean of the City University Business School in London. ***** Alan Brew has been promoted to be executive director of Landor Associates, the international design consultants, and based at Landor's headquarters in San Francisco. A former Financial Times journalist, Brew joined Landor from the FT in 1985 as marketing director of the newly-opened London office. Peter Farnell-Watson is to become managing director in the UK.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / People: Sales menu for Haagen-Dazs
DOC.TEXT: Haagen-Dazs, the ice cream company which runs naughty advertising campaigns, has appointed a new sales director in the form of Steve Ramsay to spearhead the drive to increase the product's availability in the UK. Ramsay, 36, who has a sales and marketing background at Paulig and Nestle, will be responsible for pushing Haagen-Dazs both through grocery supermarkets and food outlets; the company recently concluded deals with the Hilton and Scandic Crown hotels to put the ice cream on their menus. Ramsay has already bolstered the sales team through a series of top appointments and says he will explore new opportunities to develop the company's long-term market position in the premium ice cream sector.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / FT Law Report: Russian ship's arrest was unjust
DOC.TEXT: KHERSON Queen's Bench Division (Admiralty Court): Mr Justice Sheen: May 1 1992 A CARGO claim which is both an action in rem against the ship and an action in personam against the shipowners, arises out of the same cause of action and is between the same parties as proceedings in the same matter which have already been started in personam by the cargo-owner in the courts of a country which is party to the 1968 Brussels Convention. Therefore, under the terms of the Convention, the UK court must decline jurisdiction in favour of the foreign court and where that court would have refused to order the arrest of the ship, security provided to obtain its release from arrest in the UK must be returned. Mr Justice Sheen so held when declining jurisdiction to hear a claim by the owners of cargo carried on Kerch, and ordering the discharge of security provided by the shipowners to obtain the release of her sister ship, Kherson, from arrest. HIS LORDSHIP said the cargo-owners claimed damages for breach of a contract for the carriage of a cargo of oil on Kerch, from Rosario to Rotterdam, in 1990. Kerch was owned by a Georgian state company. On September 26 1991, the cargo-owners issued a writ in rem naming 16 ships belonging to the shipowners. On January 23 1992, the writ was renewed for 12 months. On March 27 1992, Kherson, a sister ship, was arrested at Felixstowe. The shipowners applied for an order that the court decline jurisdiction and that the ship be released. During the hearing, the court was told that the shipowners had acknowledged service of the writ. The action then became an action in rem and in personam. Kherson remained under arrest until April 3, when she was released on the provision of security. The action then ceased to be an action in rem against the ship. It now proceeded solely in personam. On October 5 1990, the cargo-owners told the shipowners' Rotterdam agent that if security was not provided they would arrest Kerch, which was then in Rotterdam. The Rotterdam agent informed the cargo-owners that there was a treaty between the USSR and the Netherlands which prohibited arrest if the shipowners chose domicil in the Netherlands. The effect of the treaty appeared to be that if a party contemplated commencing an action arising out of use of a ship, the other party might 'elect domicil' on the plaintiff's territory. When he had elected domicil an action in personam could be brought against him that territory, but the ship could not be arrested. The parties to the treaty would ensure compliance with the judgment. On October 5 1990, the shipowners chose domicil in Rotterdam. On October 9, the cargo-owners's agents wrote accepting the choice of domicil and stating that they refrained from arresting Kerch as security 'because according to the bilateral agreement, the Soviet Union is to make sure . . . .a verdict rendered by the Rotterdam District Court is to be carried out'. The shipowners contended that that exchange of letters was evidence of an agreement that the claim should be brought in the District Court of Rotterdam. They relied on article 17 of the Convention on Jurisdiction and Enforcement of Judgments in Civil and Commercial Matters 1968, which was given the force of law in the UK by the Civil Jurisdiction and Judgments Act 1982. Article 17 provided that if parties domiciled in a contracting state had agreed that the courts of a contracting state were to have jurisdiction, 'that court shall have exclusive jurisdiction'. The letter of October 9 1990 was not an agreement that the Netherlands courts were to have jurisdiction. By accepting the shipowners' choice of domicil, the cargo-owners established the right to commence legal proceedings in Rotterdam should they wish to do so, and prevented the shipowners from withdrawing their choice of domicil. That was not an agreement that the Netherlands court should have exclusive jurisdiction. Article 17 did not apply. As the cargo-owners had not had an opportunity to serve any of the ships named on the writ before October 4 1991, they decided to commence an action in Rotterdam. When they took that step they were aware they were not entitled to arrest one of the ships in the Netherlands, because of the treaty. Article 21 of the 1968 Convention provided that where proceedings 'involving the same cause of action and between the same parties' were brought in different contracting states, 'any court other than the court first seised shall . . . decline jurisdiction'. The cargo-owners disputed that article 21 applied to an action in rem. They submitted that a cause of action in rem was not the same character as a cause of action in personam. Also, it was said, the action was not between the same parties because it began as an action in rem and, after the shipowners acknowledged service, it continued as an action in rem as well as in personam. The action was founded on and involved the same cause of action as the Rotterdam proceedings (see The Deichland (1989) 3 WLR 478, 500). There were differences in character between an action in rem and an action in personam, but there were no differences between the essential elements of the cause of action in the two types of proceedings. As to whether two sets of proceedings were between the same parties, in The Nordglint (1988) 1 QB 183,201, Mr Justice Hobhouse said an action in rem was not an action between the same parties as an action in personam. He said 'it will only become an action between the same parties when and if a shipowner, liable in personam, chooses to appear in the action and defend it'. The court agreed. As Lord Justice Lloyd said in El Tawwab (1991) 1 Lloyd's Rep 205: 'The whole point of the action in rem is that it is an action against the ship itself . . . and not a personal action against the owners.' When a writ in rem had been served on the ship, if the owners did not acknowledge service, the action proceeded solely against the ship. If the shipowner acknowledged service, the action proceeded from that moment both in rem and in personam. Judgment would be in rem and in personam. The effect was that in so far as the judgment was in rem, it would be satisfied out of the proceeds of sale of the ship. Insofar as it was in personam, the plaintiff could not make double recovery, but could enforce it by attaching the defendant's assets as he could with any other judgment against a person. The only differences between an action which was both in personam and in rem (because the ship remained under arrest) and an action solely in personam, lay in the remedies available to a successful plaintiff and the procedure to obtain those remedies. The Rotterdam action and the present action involved the same cause of action. The two actions were between the same parties. Accordingly, article 21 applied and the court must decline jurisdiction in favour of the Rotterdam court. Now that the ship had been released, the court's decision as to return of the security must be the same as if she had remained under arrest. In October 1990, the cargo-owners refrained from arresting Kerch because of the treaty. If the cargo-owners had commenced proceedings in Rotterdam in October 1990 and refrained from arresting Kerch because of the treaty, the UK court would have regarded it as an abuse of its process if they had thereafter arrested a sister ship within the jurisdiction in respect of the same claim. The USSR had been dissolved, but Russia had assumed the treaty obligations. The security provided by that treaty was regarded by the Netherlands as adequate for its own national shipowners, and that was recognised by the cargo-owners in October 1990. In those circumstances it would have been unjust to keep Kherson under arrest. The UK court would have ordered her release. Accordingly, the cargo-owners were ordered to return the security. For the cargo-owners: Timothy Saloman (Clyde & Co). For the shipowners: Charles Macdonald QC (Lawrence Graham).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / People: Spending a bit of money on pubs
DOC.TEXT: Ross Cope, formerly with specialist mortgage provider First Mortgage Securities, is the new treasurer of Inntrepreneur Estates (IEL), the pub investment company set up last year by GrandMet and Foster's. He is an expert in securitisation, or repackaging debt as saleable securities, and is looking forward to bringing 'a novel financing technique into the pub market'. At First Mortgage Securities he had been treasury director, funding and securitising UK mortgages; hence Cope, 44, claims to be one of a small clutch of people 'who have actually done it rather than simply talk about it'. But while the funding side may have been a success, the specialist mortgage providers that sprang into life during the boom years of the 1980s, have been particularly badly hit by repossessions, and are narrowly eyeing their future commitment to the market. As a technique suitable for thinly capitalised companies, securitisation should work for IEL, which owns pubs and leases them out on 20-year contracts. One of Cope's tasks will be to refinance the Pounds 1.32bn loan taken out at IEL's inception. An accountant who had a spell as treasurer of Girobank, he is a fan of GrandMet's concept of managing pubs as properties in their own right. 'After a month in the new job, I have worked out how you spot Inntrepreneur pubs. They are the ones that look up-market, with a bit of money spent on them - basically they don't look like pubs.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / People: Developments at Supasnaps
DOC.TEXT: DIXONS is famous for selling the latest electronic gizmos through its Dixons and Currys retail outlets but is less well known for running the Supasnaps chain of film processing stores. There is good reason for this; Dixons has traditionally remained pretty quiet about the performance of its 354-store Supasnaps chain which has proved lacklustre in recent years. This week, however, the parent company has moved to reshuffle Supasnaps senior management. Colin Glass, 35, managing director of Supasnaps, has been elevated to the post of chairman and will also join the Dixons Stores Group board as marketing director. 'I will be focusing on developing the Dixons and Currys brand propositions and where they stand on the high street,' he says. His position at Supasnaps is filled by Elizabeth Fagan, 34, previously responsible for the company's buying and marketing functions. She joined Supasnaps from Boots in 1990. ***** Trevor Murch has been appointed managing director of NEI Parsons, the Newcastle-based subsidiary of Northern Engineering Industries, designing and manufacturing turbine generators for power stations. An engineering science graduate from Brasenose College, Oxford, and a Harvard MBA, Murch, 42, is currently president of Bristol Aerospace of Winnipeg, Manitoba, also part of the Rolls-Royce Industrial Power division. He was previously managing director of NEI Peebles, the Edinburgh-based producers of power and distribution transformers. ***** Anette Lawless has been appointed company secretary of PEARSON on the retirement of George Collett. ***** Robert Hawley, managing director of Northern Engineering Industries within the Rolls Royce Industrial Power Group, has been appointed chief executive of Nuclear Electric from June 15. Frank Ledger, deputy chairman, retires at the end of June. Brian George, chief executive of the pressurised water reactor group, becomes executive director of planning and construction on the retirement of Sam Goddard. ***** Gordon McGlone, previously md of Beverlac Fine Foods, is appointed commercial director of Elkes Biscuits of Uttoxeter, part of NORTHERN FOODS. ***** John Fleming has been appointed operations director of The MAYFLOWER CORPORATION; Geoffrey Codrington takes his place as md Ribbons, a Mayflower subsidiary; he moves from Bendix Safety Restraints. ***** Marie Blackburn has been promoted to group company secretary of ARGOS.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: NRA criticised over expenditure
DOC.TEXT: MPs HAVE strongly condemned the National Rivers Authority for weaknesses in financial management that led to wasted expenditure of Pounds 1m and the resignation of its first chief executive. A report from the Public Accounts Committee published yesterday criticises the Environment Department, Lord Crickhowell, chairman of the NRA, and his board for failing to keep a sufficiently close eye on the water pollution organisation's expenditure. The primary reason for the criticism, which is extremely outspoken for a parliamentary committee, was evidence that rules for spending large sums of money had been ignored in fitting out the NRA's new head office in Bristol. The project resulted in the wasting of about Pounds 1m out of a total cost of Pounds 2.65m, and the resignation last June of Mr John Bowman, chief executive, with a pay-off of Pounds 125,000. Two other senior executives received written warnings for ignoring the financial procedures laid down for the NRA. In July, 1990, the NRA engaged Corporate Design Interiors (CDI) to advise on relocating and to help choose contractors. It was also one of three firms asked to tender for the Pounds 12,000 contract to design the layout of the new offices. The NRA then decided to combine the design contract with a much bigger one for fitting out the building. Instead of asking several firms to tender, it considered only two that had bid for the much smaller design job. The Pounds 2.65m contract went to CDC, a sister company of CDI, without Lord Crickhowell, Mr Bowman or the NRA board being told. An internal inquiry found that had the job been properly managed it would have cost only Pounds 1.6m. It also said that the NRA's own board needed to be more vigilant on spending. The NRA said last night there had been 'serious shortcomings' in the management of fitting out the Bristol head office, which resulted in poor value for money.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / BR not at fault over most train door deaths
DOC.TEXT: BRITISH RAIL was largely exonerated by the Health and Safety Executive yesterday over the large number of deaths caused by passengers falling out of the doors of moving trains. At least 75 per cent of the deaths since 1984 were attributable to suicide attempts, drunkenness or misbehaviour, the executive concluded. Of the 25 per cent for which no explanation had been found, some may have happened because door locks had jammed open or because doors had not been properly closed, the executive said. It acknowledged that it had been unable to link any of the deaths it investigated to either of those causes. The investigation was launched last year because of public disquiet over the 165 train-door deaths between 1981 and 1990 - the largest single cause of passenger fatalities over the period. The executive concluded that a door lock properly engaged would never come open during a journey in normal service. However, it established that in certain circumstances, lock bolts could jam, and very slight pressure from inside the train could cause the door to open. A spot check of 140 doors had identified two in a dangerous condition, the executive said. It criticised BR for not adopting maintenance procedures to ensure the integrity of locks. BR responded by saying that all slam-door InterCity trains would be fitted with automatic locks over the next three years at a cost of Pounds 15m. It said it had also improved maintenance procedures and was taking steps to improve staff and passenger awareness of the importance of closing doors properly.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Satellite TV market 'overestimated'
DOC.TEXT: THE SIZE of the satellite television market in the UK has been significantly overstated, according to a report. GFK Home Audit, a market-research company, says 1.6m homes had satellite television by the end of last year, compared to the 1.8m estimate by Barb, which produces the official viewing figures, and a figure of 2.1m quoted by Continental Research, a research company regularly quoted by the Financial Times and British Sky Broadcasting, the satellite television network in which Pearson, owner of the Financial Times, has a stake, The GFK figure was based on interviews with 10,000 people last June and updated with data from GFK Lek-Trak, which monitors more than 8,000 electrical retailers, including a sample of independents retailers. 'The GFK Home Audit provides the most accurate record yet of home satellite ownership and suggests that there has been a substantial overstatement of the market,' said Mr John Ramsbottom, managing director of GFK. Mr Ramsbottom said his figures were supported by close comparison of film channel viewing in his panel with figures produced by BSkyB. Mr John Clemens, chairman of Continental, which puts the present number of homes with satellite dishes at 2.4m, yesterday stood by his figures, which are based on interviews with more than 4,000 adults every month. Continental said its end-of-year dish figure was 1.95m - the 2.1m figure includes homes served by a communal dish. Mr Clemens said Lek-Trak data consistently underestimated the number of satellite dishes in the UK. GFK Home Audit Report. Tel 0932 354911. Pounds 500 plus VAT.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Business creation
DOC.TEXT: NEARLY 480,000 small businesses started up in the UK last year, the third-highest annual figure, National Westminster Bank said yesterday. However, there was a sharp decline from a plateau in the second half.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Murdoch gas field output purchased
DOC.TEXT: KINETICA, the independent gas supplier, has purchased the entire output of the Murdoch gas field in the North Sea. The company, a joint venture between Conoco, the North Sea producer, and PowerGen, the UK electricity generator, already supplies more than 1,000 sites in the UK. The Murdoch field has reserves of 320bn cu ft, and is expected to have a peak production rate of 140m cu ft a day.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Fraud charges shake Brazil's first family
DOC.TEXT: BRAZILIANS, great lovers of soap operas, are glued to a real-life drama involving the presidential family in a battle which could threaten governmental stability. The row erupted with the allegation by Mr Pedro Collor that his older brother, President Fernando Collor, had been collaborating to help his campaign treasurer and friend to accumulate wealth through fraudulent means. Mr Pedro Collor says he has compiled a dossier on Mr Paulo Cesar Farias (known as PC), elaborating alleged frauds which could incriminate the president, and has put it on a video-tape now in a safe-deposit box in a New York bank. He accuses Mr Farias of having taken Dollars 15m from the Dollars 100m Collor campaign chest for the 1989 presidential election, and of then using his friendship with the president to cream off commissions for the award of government contracts. Mr Farias strongly denies the allegations, which a presidential aide claims were provoked by the younger brother's envy of the elder. However, the row caused the stock markets to fall 5 per cent on Monday, and forced Mrs Leda Collor, the family matriarch, to intervene to prevent a threat to government stability. After intense family efforts to silence Pedro failed, Mrs Collor announced on Tuesday night that she was sacking her youngest son Pedro from running the family media empire in their home state of Alagoas, in the far north-east, claiming that he was 'suffering a serious emotional crisis.' Yesterday, Mr Pedro Collor was visiting a doctor for a certificate of sanity. He insists he will not drop his campaign until 'PC is behind bars'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Democrats seek probe over Iraq support
DOC.TEXT: A GROUP of influential Democratic members of the US Congress is seeking the appointment of a special prosecutor to investigate possible wrongdoing by the Bush administration in its support of President Saddam Hussein of Iraq, before his August 1990 invasion of Kuwait. The House of Representatives judiciary committee said yesterday it planned to hold a hearing on whether to name an independent counsel. This follows allegations by Mr Henry Gonzalez, chairman of the House banking committee, and others in Congress, that the administration is trying to cover up its misuse of government loan guarantees that Iraq had obtained for agricultural purchases, but then used to acquire military goods and technology. At the core of the matter is an alleged abuse of loan guarantees for supposed agricultural exports to Iraq that were financed by the branch in Atlanta of Italy's Banca Nazionale del Lavoro (BNL). The BNL affair is beginning to attract widespread attention in the US media, with the approach of the trial of Mr Christopher Drogoul, former BNL Atlanta manager accused of making more than Dollars 4bn of improper loans to Iraq from his branch. The trial, due to begin on June 2, was yesterday postponed to June 22. Documents obtained by the Financial Times show that a substantial part of these loans helped Iraq's nuclear, chemical and missile projects.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / New challenge made to German currency role in the EMS
DOC.TEXT: THE FRENCH franc is just as important as the D-Mark in the European Monetary System, Mr Jacques de Larosiere, governor of the Bank of France, said yesterday, issuing a fresh challenge to the anchor role of the German currency in the EMS, writes William Dawkins in Paris. The future single European currency would be built around all its members and not just the D-Mark, the central bank governor said. Mr de Larosiere's remarks, on the eve of the Franco-German summit, underline France's efforts to make the franc a strength to rival the D-Mark before the projected single currency comes into effect by the end of this decade. 'The franc is not in the D-Mark zone,' he said. Nobody could deny that the D-Mark had been the anchor of the European Monetary System for years, said Mr de Larosiere. But 'we are now coming to a phase in our monetary relations where there is much more equality between countries and where France's performance is rather better than its partners,' he said. France, Denmark and Luxembourg were the only countries currently able to fulfil all the criteria for monetary union, he pointed out. 'So the notion of this mono-currency anchored on to the D-Mark gives way to the real necessity for a collective anchor and a common monetary policy,' he said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / Azerbaijan may pull out of CIS
DOC.TEXT: THE NEW leadership in Azerbaijan yesterday vowed to take the republic out of the Commonwealth of Independent States. Mr Abulfaz Elchibey, leader of the dominant Popular Front and the favourite candidate to win presidential elections due on June 7, said 'Azerbaijan will not be part of the current CIS, there is no doubt about that'. Popular Front leaders refused to accede to a collective security pact signed by six of the CIS members in Tashkent last week, seeing it as a threat to the republic's security. They believe Russian influence helped reinstate the former communist president, Mr Ayaz Mutalibov, for 24 hours last week before he was forced to flee. The conflict between Armenian and Azeri forces, which has spread from Nagorno Karabakh in Azerbaijan to the northern tip of the Azeri autonomous republic of Nakhichevan within Armenia, is causing growing concern to neighbouring Turkey and Iran.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / World News in Brief: Fiat in Polish venture
DOC.TEXT: Italian carmaker Fiat is to pay about Pounds 1.1bn for a 90 per cent stake in a joint venture with Polish carmaker FSM, the biggest investment in Poland by a western company.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 21 MAY 92 / UK Company News: ICS Group - Correction
DOC.TEXT: Industrial Control Services Group, the electronic safety systems manufacturer, was wrongly referred to as International Control Services in yesterday's Financial Times.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Show trial of Croats by Serb military
DOC.TEXT: FRANZ KAFKA would have felt at home yesterday in the first floor courtroom in Belgrade's main military courthouse. Seven pallid prisoners, all looking bewildered and one obviously mentally disturbed, sat facing five military judges, whose uniforms were decorated with from two to five stars. Above them the eternal flame, the communist emblem of the defunct Yugoslav federation, was still firmly fixed to the wood-panelled walls. A row of seven clean-cut military policemen in camouflage uniforms separated the defendants from the spectators and some scowling Belgrade journalists. The main witness, who was present at the hearing, cursed and jeered at the seven: 'Ustashe animals', using the Serbian epithet for Croats. The men, Croat nationals, who are accused by the Yugoslav army of war crimes and taking part in an 'armed uprising against Yugoslavia,' are the principal players in what may herald the start of a series of show trials. The seven are Croats from a village near Vukovar, the devastated city in eastern Croatia. They are accused of crimes last autumn at the height of the army siege of the town. The crimes range from murder to 'endangering the security of the Socialist Federated Republic of Yugoslavia'. The defendants, who face the death penalty, are being tried by a military court although they are all civilians. A guilty verdict looked predetermined as most of the defendants were not allowed to choose their own defence lawyers. Instead they were awarded 'defence' counsels from the ranks of embittered Serb refugees from Croatia. Mrs Nadezhda Danilovic, a defence lawyer from Belgrade, yesterday raised objections to the military tribunal, saying that the court was not authorised to try Croat, now foreign, citizens. Defence lawyers fear that Serbia's state-controlled media will use this and other trials to pump up hatred of Croats in order to channel popular resentment at the collapsing economy. The official media spew a steady stream of racist propaganda about non-Serbs. A western diplomat said: 'We are not questioning the right of Serbia to try war criminals if it is based on real evidence. But there is also a legal and moral responsibility to try criminals from their own side.' Mrs Danilovic says the trial may mark the beginning of a wave of show trials. She says the defendants are being tried for heinous war crimes, although Yugoslavia was never officially at war with Croatia. But if a wave of trials begins in Serbia, it is likely to be matched in Croatia, where resentment of the perceived seizure of its territory by Serbia, runs high. Serbs living in Zagreb, the capital of Croatia, have expressed fears that the government will use them as scapegoats.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / International Company News: Astra surges on strong Losec sales
DOC.TEXT: ASTRA, the Swedish pharma-ceutical company, boosted pre-tax profits by 40 per cent to SKr1.063bn (Dollars 185.2m) in the first quarter of 1992 from SKr757m in the corresponding period of 1991. The company again forecast that profits for the full year would rise between 20 and 25 per cent to over SKr4bn. Sales for the quarter climbed 35 per cent to SKr3.7bn from SKr2.7bn, while profit per share rose by 45 per cent to SKr5.55 from Skr3.85. Sales of Losec, the company's highly successful stomach ulcer drug and the main competitor of Glaxo's Zantac, increased by 72 per cent in the first quarter to SKr991m from SKr577m, with the biggest markets being in Germany, France and Britain. Total sales of Losec (including those made through licence-holders in the US, Italy and Spain) reached SKr1.550bn from SKr880m. Astra's asthma agent Pulmicort enjoyed a 57 per cent sales increase in the first quarter to SKr414m against SKr264.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / London Stock Exchange: Lasmo hit by broker revision
DOC.BYLINE: By CHRISTOPHER PRICE, PETER JOHN and JOEL KIBAZO
DOC.TEXT: OIL exploration company Lasmo was the worst performing stock yesterday in the FT-SE 100 Index and one of the weakest in the London market following a sharp profits forecast downgrading by securities house SG Warburg. Warburg argued that unless the company cuts its dividend, halves its exploration budget and takes Pounds 5m off its overheads it will lose Pounds 30m this year. It said Lasmo needed to reduce its total dividend to a nominal penny from 8.5p. Lasmo fell 18 to 199p with more than 8.8m shares traded. The revised forecast follows a similar exercise on Enterprise last week, when Warburg lowered its underlying earnings prediction by Pounds 16m to Pounds 78m, inclusive of Pounds 30m profits from asset disposals. County NatWest followed yesterday with a forecast cut from Pounds 86m to Pounds 72m for Enterprise, and estimated asset disposal profits at only Pounds 25m. It also advised clients to reduce holdings. Enterprise slipped 5 to 421p. Next optimism A healthy trading statement from Next helped sentiment in a positive retail sector anticipating improved official figures today. Next shares rose 4 1/2 to 88 1/2 p in volume of 6.8m. Chairman Lord Wolfson said at the group's annual meeting that retail sales in the first quarter were ahead by 10 per cent from last year's corresponding period. Although some observers pointed out that Next's sales last year were particularly flat, the rise followed similar noises from Burton last week. The market also expects a moderate increase in retail sales figures due today. Burton gained 2 to 50p, Boots 3 to 467p and Kingfisher 2 to 563p. Dixons advanced 6 to 271p and Amstrad rose 3 1/2 to 40 1/2 p, both partly on the back of the BSkyB football deal. Bank approves bid Approval by the Bank of England for Hongkong and Shanghai Banking's bid for Midland Bank prompted renewed support for the UK clearer. The statement triggered talk that Hongkong Bank would launch a dawn raid today for Midland stock in order to take its stake above 15 per cent. However, banking analysts said this was unlikely as Hongkong Bank is not allowed to buy stock in the market at a price lower than the bid price. Midland gained 4 to 397p. The possibility that rival suitor Lloyds Bank - up 8 at 432p - may not get a toehold caused analysts to cast around and look for another likely target for Lloyds. They alighted on Royal Bank of Scotland, pinpointing the value of its Direct Line Insurance subsidiary. Royal Bank climbed 7 to 205p. Figures at the bottom end of expectations prompted profit-taking in BOC, which dropped 15 to 703p. The gases and healthcare group announced half-year profits of Pounds 162.7m, up from a previous Pounds 144.7m but against analysts' forecasts of between Pounds 163m and Pounds 166m. The company said signs of an upswing were patchy and limited to a few segments of its global industrial gases markets. Smith New Court lowered its full-year profits forecast by Pounds 5m to Pounds 355m and was advising clients to switch into ICI which, it said, offers good value up to 1400p. ICI eased 5 to 1361p. Turnover in Hanson was boosted as a number of the conglomerate's directors exercised share options. Lord Hanson reduced his holding to 6m shares after selling 2.5m at 232 1/2 p. In the market, the shares eased 2 1/2 to 231 1/2 p with 10m traded. There were also 9.1m warrants traded. Body Shop retreated 12 to 308p as rumours of a critical television programme circulated. Talk of the sale of Gardner Merchant, Forte's catering subsidary, refused to die away ahead of today's results from rival caterer and potential purchaser Compass Group. The latest talk has the Pounds 500m subsidiary being broken up, with the UK side going to management and Compass taking the European operations. Both Forte and Compass shares were unchanged yesterday. Slightly disappointing results from Allied-Lyons saw the shares marked down 8 to 652p. Worries over the Carlsberg deal and the brewery group's cash flow -with City anxiety over the possibility of a rights issue refusing to go away - also persisted. Mr Graeme Eadie at County NatWest moved to a buy position on Allied, however, citing solid margins and good recovery prospects. 'The new management team is on course to deliver superior earnings growth over the next two years,' he said. Nervousness ahead of today's results from Bass left the shares down 12 at 619p. Selling in the US was said to have been behind a fall of 21 to 984p for Wellcome. Glaxo recovered 13 to 748p. Figures from Swedish competitor Astra, particularly on Losec, the direct competitor to Glaxo's anti-ulcer drug Zantac, were good but in line with forecasts. British Airways raced up 15 to 302p in brisk trade of 18m shares, making it the best performer in the FT-SE 100 Index. The company reported full-year profits up 119 per cent at Pounds 285m, and a 20 per cent rise in the dividend. Analysts moved quickly to upgrade current year forecasts to around the Pounds 409m mark. P & O benefited from the positive mood surrounding BA and gained 11 to 536p. A gloomy annual meeting at Ocean Group sent the shares tumbling 27 to 311p. British Steel eased 3 to 81p. There was talk in the market that the recent price increases for steel are not holding and that the company is being forced to sell to European customers at pre-April 1992 prices. Williams Holdings added 6 at 360p, with suggestions in the market that the share price was being massaged in preparation for a deal or acquisition. A line of GEC stock that has been overhanging the market was said to have held down the shares, which lost 2 1/2 to 230 1/2 p. However, 8m shares were traded in big blocks at 230 1/2 p a share, suggesting that the overhang had now been largely cleared. Board changes at Southern Water were welcomed by the market, the stock adding 12 at 411p in a positive water sector, where Panmure Gordon advised investors to stay 'overweight'. Building materials group BPB Industries gained 6 to 187p in heavy turnover of 3.6m as BZW moved to a buy stance. MARKET REPORTERS: Christopher Price, Peter John, Joel Kibazo. DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / London Stock Exchange: Equity futures and options trading
DOC.TEXT: BID talk in Asda, in the traded options market, created substantial interest in an otherwise dull day for derivative markets, writes Joel Kibazo. Turnover in the London Traded Options Market reached 29,821 contracts, a big improvement on Monday's 19,926, with the bulk of the day's business carried out in stock options. Volume in the FT-SE 100 option was negligible at 4,922 lots. Asda was the top traded stock option as takeover talk returned. There was a total of 7,051 contracts traded, with the July 35 calls - in which 3,670 lots were dealt - the busiest series. This was followed by British Airways, which reported good profits that led to a clutch of profit upgrades. It traded 2,961 lots. Hanson, BT and Lasmo, in which dividend cuts are forecast, were also busy. In stock index futures, dealers talked of a dull session with June trading in a narrow range for a large part of the day. June opened at 2,727, which proved to be the high point of the day. Buying interest at the lower levels was modest, with economic statistics and Wall Street having no effect on the day's trading. June finished at 2,717, down 12 from the previous session and around 9 points above its estimated fair value premium to cash of about 8. Turnover was a poor 4,649.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets (America): Hopes of another rate cut lift Dow to record
DOC.TEXT: Wall Street US SHARES, after trading in a narrow range on either side of opening values through most of the day, sprang to life yesterday afternoon and rose to a record level as investors responded to growing expectations of a further cut in interest rates in the wake of poor housing numbers, writes Patrick Harverson in New York. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 21.96 at 3,397.99, a shade above its previous all-time high of 3,397.58 set on May 11, but turnover on the New York SE was light, with 189.4m shares changing hands. The Standard & Poor's 500 climbed 3.56 to 416.37, while the Nasdaq composite of over-the-counter stocks gained 1.52 to 578.05. The day opened with the news from the Commerce Department that housing starts fell 17 per cent in April, more than three times the decline forecast. The drop in housing activity would normally have depressed stocks, but the fact that the data increased the likelihood of an easing of policy by the Federal Reserve restricted the damage. Market sentiment was also aided by a fresh decline in bond rates, which in the case of the benchmark 30-year bond yield, fell to 7.75 per cent. Upjohn rose Dollars 7/8 to Dollars 35 3/8 in turnover of almost 690,000 shares after the US Food and Drug Administration panel voted to allow the company to continue marketing its controversial Halcion insomnia drug. The ADRs of British Airways forged ahead Dollars 3 5/8 to Dollars 55 3/4 in active trading after the company reported a 119 per cent jump in earnings for the fiscal year ended March 31. Dayton Hudson climbed Dollars 3 1/4 to Dollars 62 1/4 on first-quarter net income of 40 cents a share, against 39 cents a year ago and above the consensus of analysts' forecasts.
