Relations between the managers and the Prince grew frosty early in 1990 after an article appeared in a German magazine accusing Petersen and his team of gross mismanagement and manoeuvring themselves to take control of the fortune when the Prince died. Formally, the Prince stood by his employees, but the old trust and confidence was gone and the managers' freedom to act was henceforth strictly circumscribed. By the middle of the year, Petersen and Crain had left of their own accord and shortly afterwards Levedag was fired. For the managers, the saga did not end with their departure from the Schloss, nor even with the Prince's death in December 1990. The Princess attacked them in numerous press articles, one of which in September last year alleged that they had systematically manipulated the Prince's accounts to pay themselves big bonuses. Petersen and his former colleagues hit back, suing both Gloria and a number of publications, claiming a systematic attempt to destroy their professional reputations. The Princess counterattacked by filing criminal charges against the managers. Late last month, the Princess quietly backed down: a statement issued in Frankfurt said that the House of Thurn und Taxis had dropped its allegations against the former managers. Both sides abandoned the lawsuits launched at each other; Levedag, who was sacked outright, obtained compensation and all the managers successfully won payment of unpaid bonuses due under their contracts. This attempt to subject a large family fortune to professional management discipline has not been good either for the fortune or the managers. While Petersen landed on his feet, taking up a post last year as managing director of the Wasserstein Perella investment bank in Germany, Crain has only recently found a new job with a French investment group in Frankfurt. Levedag is believed to be on the brink of taking up a new post. Meanwhile a distinctly press-shy Princess Gloria presides over a family fortune which is believed to be shrinking at much the same rate as it was before the ill-fated experiment with professional management.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Business and the Environment: Tall tales grow in the forest
DOC.TEXT: The UK's forestry policy has left the country with a subsidised crop of mature trees whose value is often so low that they cost more to cut down than to sell, according to a report* published recently by the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF). It suggests that new ways of valuing trees could lead to future generations being left with forests which they want and need, rather than serried ranks of densely planted, environmentally unfriendly conifers. WWF says that wildlife hates densely planted conifer forests, which allow little light to the forest floor, leaving no ground cover, no animals or insects, and consequently no birds. Conifers can also make the soil acidic and leave it unsuitable for growing anything but the same type of tree. The UK Forestry Commission has already started trying to put a value on the benefits of forestry apart from the value of the timber. It points out that it is far from easy to evaluate such things as landscape conservation, carbon fixing and job creation in rural areas. There are now signs, WWF believes, that economic analyses of forestry projects are attempting to describe what it calls 'the wider social returns,' such as environment costs and benefits. Policy changes include the replacement of tax incentives with targeted grants, as well as new planning procedures. Andrew Christie Miller, chairman of Timber Growers United Kingdom, the trade organisation for private woodland owners, thinks the WWF report brings together all the aspects of work being done to try to provide economic justification for subsidised forestry. While there are plenty of grants available in the UK, the level of planting in the UK has dropped to the lowest level since the Second World War. In the private sector in late 1980s, 25,000 hectares per annum were being planted, but this has now slipped below 10,000 hectares per annum. *Trees and the Treasury. Valuing Forests for Society, by R. Worrell. WWF United Kingdom, Panda House, Weyside Park, Godalming, Surrey GU7 1XR.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Business and the Environment: Life beyond the Earth Summit
DOC.TEXT: At next month's Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, the world community has an historic opportunity to move forward in a spirit of global partnership to meet the challenges that will define our common future. Sadly, the agreements to be signed at this historic meeting are hollow shells of the original proposals, with little assurance that there will be any real change in policy or practice, and meagre hope that the environmental crises they are intended to confront will be slowed. Regrettably, it was the intransigence of the US negotiators that weakened the accords. For example, the climate change convention was to unite the world in efforts to stabilise emissions of carbon dioxide, the principal cause of global warming, at 1990 levels by the year 2000. Instead, principally because of President Bush's opposition to these targets and timetables, the treaty to be signed contains only vague language and no specific goals. This means that world leaders gathering in Rio must, even now, begin looking beyond the Earth Summit, to build a new global consensus that will create stronger agreements and real progress. We need to create a mechanism to ensure that the parties to the climate convention will meet regularly to strengthen their commitments in the light of scientific developments. We also need to support calls for increased energy efficiency and for increased reliance on renewable energy sources. We must establish a strong and effective mechanism to carry forward the agreements reached at the Earth Summit. I have suggested establishing a Stewardship Council to deal with matters relating to the global environment, just as the Security Council now deals with matters of war and peace. Or we could establish a tradition of annual environmental summit meetings. Heads of nations must commit themselves to improving overseas development practices to ensure that the projects are sustainable. One of the best ways of doing this is to increase the transparency of lending practices so that local communities and non-governmental groups have the opportunity to comment on proposals. Working voluntarily, we must use every treaty and alliance, every tactic and strategy, every plan and course of action to halt the destruction of the environment and to preserve and nurture our ecological system. What is needed is a plan - call it a Global Marshall Plan for the environment - that combines large-scale, long-term, carefully targeted financial aid to developing nations. Some strategic goals are obvious. For example, world population should be stabilised, with policies designed to create the conditions necessary for the so-called demographic transition - the historical change from a dynamic equilibrium of high birth rates and death rates to a stable equilibrium of low birth rates and death rates. This change has taken place in most of the industrial nations and in few of the developing nations. We also need to develop environmentally appropriate technologies - especially in energy, transportation, agriculture, construction and manufacturing. We must rethink the economic 'rules of the road' by which we measure the impact of our decisions on the environment. We need to establish a system of economic accounting that assigns appropriate values to the ecological consequences of routine choices made by individuals and companies, and macroeconomic choices by nations. Governments need a new generation of agreements that will embody the regulatory frameworks, enforcement mechanisms, incentives, and mutual obligations necessary to make the overall plan a success. These agreements must be sensitive to the vast differences of capability and need between developed and developing nations. Finally, what is needed is an ecological perspective that does not treat the Earth as something separate from human civilisation. Looking at the whole means looking at ourselves. If we do not see that we are a powerful natural force like the winds and tides, we cannot see how we threaten to push the Earth out of balance. The author is a US senator. His book, Earth in the Balance: Forging a New Common Purpose, is published this week by Earthscan. Price Pounds 14.95.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Inside Whitehall: A society now not so secret - Yesterday the government cut secrecy at the heart of Whitehall, revealing the membership of cabinet committees whose very existence was previously not even acknowledged. The cloak is being removed from how decisions are made and who makes them
DOC.TEXT: LIGHT was was shed on some of the darker recesses of Whitehall secrecy yesterday, but Mr John Major's latest exercise in open government had an air of studied understatement about it. Sir Robin Butler, secretary to the cabinet and head of the Civil Service, who lifted a corner of the veil of secrecy surrounding Whitehall, is not a man who is given to grand gestures. The exercise, launched by Mr William Waldegrave in his capacity as chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, was designed to illuminate the instinctively secretive Whitehall establishment that Sir Robin runs for his political masters. It was a partial success. The publication of details of the cabinet committees at the heart of government - and of the detailed instructions to ministers on how to operate the machinery - provided a valuable insight into the way Britain is run. Yet, as Sir Robin was obliged to acknowledge, the picture remains far from complete. For those unaccustomed to the intricacies of Whitehall decision-making, the first message of the documents is that very little of the business of government is conducted at full meetings of the cabinet. The weekly sessions on Thursdays rarely last more than 90 minutes. With occasional exceptions, ministers report on their activities or float ideas rather than become entangled with the minutiae of policy-making. Most decisions are instead taken by much smaller groups of ministers - sometimes within the framework of the cabinet committee system published yesterday, and just as often in still smaller ad hoc groupings. They provide the infrastructure to support the all-important doctrine of collective responsibility: the unbreakable rule that once a decision has been taken it must be publicly supported by all ministers, whatever their private views. It was the official committee structure that Mr Waldegrave and Sir Robin unveiled - the 16 standing committees and 10 sub-committees that have authority to take decisions on behalf of the cabinet. The four most important - on home, foreign, domestic and legislative affairs -were officially acknowledged by Mrs Thatcher. While the existence of the others has long been an open secret, technically their activities have remained secret. Their membership confirms what has long been known about the Whitehall power structure: for example, that the chancellor or chief secretary, and frequently both, have places reserved on virtually every committee in their roles as guardians of the public purse. The prime minister heads nine of the main groups. Those interested in personal power plays will notice that Mr Michael Heseltine is well represented in his capacity as president of the board of trade. He has secured also Mr Major's agreement to an upgraded ministerial committee dealing with industrial issues. The prime minister has curbed Mr Heseltine's ambitions, though, by giving the group a neutral chairman in the person of Lord Wakeham and by including Mr Norman Lamont as its next most senior member. Lord Wakeham, the lord privy seal, lives up to his reputation as chief political fixer with the chairmanship of several committees on which departmental rivalries run deep. Mr Waldegrave's principal role as minister for the Citizen's Charter has won him a place on all the important domestic committees. So in theory, the interested observer should be able to trace the main decisions of government through the cabinet machinery. That machinery in turn should guarantee each member ample scope to ensure that his or her voice is heard before important decisions are reached. Unfortunately the reality is not quite as simple. Much of the most sensitive business of government is done not in the cabinet committee system but by smaller ad hoc groups with interests in particular policy issues. Sometimes those are established alongside the standing committees, gaining the title 'Misc' or 'Gen'. On other occasions, such groupings can exist outside any formal structure, limiting the capacity of most members of the cabinet to influence important decisions. In her second and third terms, Mrs Margaret Thatcher came to rely almost exclusively on 'Misc' committees and ad hoc gatherings to buttress her authority. Mr Nigel Lawson, the former chancellor, only once managed to secure a broad ministerial discussion on the European monetary system. The issue eventually tore Mrs Thatcher's government apart, but it never reached full cabinet. Questions of procedure make clear that a senior minister's ability to force full cabinet discussion of any particular issue is tightly circumscribed. Except in the case of a battle with the Treasury over funding, such a request must first win the support of the relevant committee chairman. Even then, the prime minister can reject it. Yesterday's documents make no reference to the role of Mr Richard Ryder, the chief whip, who has ex-officio membership of all the main groups. Mr Ryder, the prime minister's agent in much of the behind-the-scenes bargaining between ministers, wields considerable but officially unacknowledged influence across Whitehall. Mr Waldegrave insisted yesterday that Mr Major's decision to publish the details signalled his determination to use the formal committee system. However, senior colleagues say he will find it difficult to avoid the attractions of the ad hoc approach to settle the competing claims of Whitehall departments. In such circumstances, the standing committee might become little more than a mailing list for high-level documents. Sir Robin acknowledged that open government extends only so far. The cabinet office will periodically update the list of committees to include details of ad hoc groups, but will not announce their establishment at the time. Without any apparent hint of irony, Sir Robin said such announcements might be 'misleading'. In fact, he is anxious to ensure that outsiders cannot delve too deeply into the process of decision-making. More particularly, he wishes to discourage the appearance in public of differences of opinion between ministers. Mr Gus O'Donnell, the prime minister's press secretary, made clear yesterday that he would not help journalists to track decision-making through the Whitehall machine by revealing when the committees meet. In terms of open government, Mr Major has so far shone a torch rather than a searchlight into Whitehall. But at least there is some light.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Inside Whitehall: Lobbyists welcome cabinet disclosure
DOC.BYLINE: By ALISON SMITH and RICHARD EVANS
DOC.TEXT: YESTERDAY'S cabinet committee disclosures were widely welcomed as a sign of greater openness. Knowing how and by whom collective decisions are made is already the common currency of those who make their living lobbying government, or whose business depends on it. Big organisations such as the Confederation of British Industry and the Institute of Directors - and large companies with sophisticated lobbying and public-relations sections - thought the move would make little practical difference because much of the information was already available to them. Mr Nigel Clarke, a director of GJW, a political consultancy, said that the publication itself was of limited value. 'Anyone involved in this area already knows these things exist,' he said, 'and it does not require the mind of Solomon to work out who's on them. None the less, Dr Ann Robinson, head of the policy unit at the Institute of Directors, said: 'I welcome more open government because it means better government.' Political lobbyists agreed in hoping the disclosures represented a greater readiness by the government to consult interested organisations. Mr Peter Luff, Tory MP for Worcester and a consultant with the lobbying company Good Relations, expressed a view shared by industry in welcoming the move as 'demystifying' relations with government. He thought it would have a salutary effect on lobbying companies. He said some sold information that encouraged clients to believe they obtained through 'conspiratorial' means, rather than relying on selling good advice about how to make a persuasive case to government. The reforms are likely to help the small-business sector, where expertise is not as great, and where specialist lobbyists are sometimes brought in to provide information that will now be readily available. Mr Stephen Alambritis of the National Federation of Self-Employed and Small Businesses said the disclosures would be helpful in indicating which ministers were interested in certain subjects. In general, though, he did not think the current pattern of getting policies across would change much - small businesses, for example, would still be channelled through the Department of Trade and Industry and the relevant minister. Businesses and the lobbyists agreed that it was more important for them to know how to lobby effectively at an early stage, before a subject appeared on any cabinet committee's agenda. That was more important than discovering the identities of members of cabinet committees. Mr Clarke described much lobbying as going over policy details with middle-ranking departmental civil servants - 'where the decision starts'. Both categories also agreed, however, that while it would be helpful to know when cabinet committee meetings were taking place, so relevant points could be made, they could see why the government had decided against it. That was because of the danger that ministers could be swamped with too many approaches by the lobbyists. They had clearly come close to sharing a Whitehall view of the world before yesterday's disclosures.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Lilley boost for Maxwell MPs
DOC.BYLINE: By ALISON SMITH and NORMA COHEN
DOC.TEXT: MPs CAMPAIGNING on behalf of the Maxwell pensioners have been encouraged by the prospect of early publication of the report into the affair by the Securities and Investments Board (SIB). Mr Richard Page and Mr Frank Field, on behalf of the all-party group of MPs supporting the pensioners, had a 'constructive and cordial' meeting yesterday with Mr Peter Lilley, the social security secretary. They believe that pressure from Westminster has caused the government to take a more active approach to the affair. The two MPs were pleased that Mr Lilley undertook 'willingly' to pass on to the Bank of England the concern expressed that the banks were not making enough effort to identify assets, and their view that the recent comments of Mr Robin Leigh-Pemberton, the governor, had been unhelpful. Mr Page said afterwards that they had had the impression that the government expected to receive the SIB report within the next two to three weeks. They expect it to be published, enabling decisions to be taken before deadline at the end of next month when the next tranche of trusts have said they would be unable to pay pensions. The MPs told Mr Lilley that the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (Imro), felt it had not been given proper authority because of the difficulties of marrying trust law with the financial services regime. The meeting coincided with a claim by the Maxwell pensioners' group that 6,000 Maxwell pensioners stand to lose three quarters of their monthly payments by September unless the government acts. Mr Kenneth Trench, chairman of the Maxwell Pensioners Action Group, said the government had an obligation to help pensioners because of maladministration by government departments in their oversight of Mr Robert Maxwell's activities. By June, 5,000 Maxwell company pensioners will lose half their monthly pension payments and 240 members of one Leeds-based scheme are now getting no payments whatsoever.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Major fights off Maastricht rebel
DOC.BYLINE: By IVOR OWEN, Parliamentary Correspondent and JUREK MARTIN
DOC.TEXT: MR JOHN MAJOR, the prime minister, emerged unscathed in the Commons yesterday from a preliminary skirmish with one of the prominent Tory backbench opponents of the bill giving effect to the Maastricht treaty on European Union. Mr Christopher Gill (C Ludlow) - one of the two dozen or so Tory backbenchers expected to refuse to support the bill's second reading in the Commons tomorrow night - called for ratification of the treaty to be delayed until outstanding differences on a number of key policy issues had been resolved. He said the prime minister would never be in a stronger bargaining position to secure assurances on immigration, the retention of border controls and limiting Britain's contribution to the European Community Budget. Mr Gill argued that all those issues and the controversy over the EC's working time directive should be settled before the treaty was ratified. The prime minister replied that Mr Gill had raised a number of important - and in many ways, 'tendentious' - issues relating to the existing provisions of the Treaty of Rome - which established the EC - and not directly to the Maastricht treaty. He assured the House: 'In all these matters we will fight to preserve British interests up to, during and after ratification of the Maastricht treaty.' Another leading opponent of the bill, Mr Nigel Spearing (Lab Newham South), also sought to delay its passage by arguing that it should not be debated until the government had provided MPs with a consolidated version of the Treaty of Rome that reflected the changes resulting from the Maastricht treaty. Miss Betty Boothroyd, the Speaker, said the bill was perfectly in order. It was for the House to decide whether or not it should be passed. THE US Defence Department stated yesterday it considered the case 'closed', Jurek Martin writes from Washington. Mr Pete Williams, the spokesman, said: 'For our part, the US government has gone to extraordinary lengths to co-operate with the British investigation.' He insisted that what happened was an accident, stemming from 'a difference of interpretation' in communications between US pilots and British troops. But two US Congressmen said yesterday they had directed the House armed services investigations subcommittee to open a preliminary inquiry into the deaths of the nine British soldiers. 'We are not sure how much we can do to resolve the discrepancies between the American and British accounts of the events,' said Representative Nicholas Mavroules, a Democrat from Massachusetts who chairs the subcommittee. Mr Mavroules said that if there was a 'reasonable chance' of answering questions about the incident, the subcommittee could conduct a full inquiry.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Docklands 'option'for civil servants
DOC.TEXT: SENIOR civil servants throughout Whitehall had been informally reminded that any prospective departmental moves should take account of the 'attractive options' that might be on offer in Docklands, Downing Street said yesterday. In line for a move to Docklands are the departments of the environment and transport, whose Marsham Street offices in Westminster are due to be demolished next year. Ministers continue to emphasise that any move to Docklands would have to be made on value for money grounds and not as a 'bail-out' for troubled Canary Wharf developer Olympia & York.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Lib Dems press on environment
DOC.TEXT: THE Liberal Democrats yesterday called on Mr John Major to apply 'all his international negotiating skills to the full' at next month's Earth summit in Rio de Janeiro, Ralph Atkins writes. The party also launched a cross-party appeal for a Commons debate beforehand. Mr Paddy Ashdown, party leader, said preparatory negotiations for the summit had gone in the wrong direction. He proposed stabilising carbon dioxide emissions at 1990 levels by 1995, increasing resources for family planning in developing countries and 'Red Cross' style immunity for those engaged in environmental clean-up operations.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Prescott wins Oscarin battle over lunch
DOC.TEXT: IF AN ability to raise the spirits of party activists is the chief goal for Labour's leadership candidates, Mr John Prescott should abandon his campaign to be deputy leader and run for the top job. Yesterday, the Manufacturing Science and Finance union welcomed all four leadership contenders to address its annual conference in Bournemouth and, to the surprise of some, it was the shadow transport secretary who went home with the Oscar. Yet the day was also replete with ironies. This, after all, was the judgment of the largely leftwing delegates of a union representing thousands of Tory-voting white-collar workers, while the affluent south coast resort town appeared wholly oblivious of the passionate debate on the future of socialism taking part in its midst. Each candidate played his or her part in character. Mrs Margaret Beckett used her 15-minute address to play the gender card, making the case for a fresh appeal to women voters. Mr Bryan Gould, an MSF member, sold himself as the 'ideas candidate' but was in danger of losing his audience in a sophisticated argument about devaluation, referring to the gold standard and sterling M3. Battling against the effects of lunch on the 300-odd delegates, Mr John Smith's 18-page speech was respectfully if unspectacularly received. And before Mr Prescott appeared, it was widely held that Mr Gould was the narrow points victor. However, that was not to reckon with the pugnacious MP for Hull. Squinting, ad-libbing and at times tripping over his text, he none the less injected the right note of indignant exasperation that prompted repeated bursts of applause. Mr Prescott's basic thesis remained unchanged. What the party needed, he said, was someone to grab it by the scruff of the neck and shake up its organisation. With characteristic plain speaking, he went on to bash the Tories and the press, with a sideswipe at the party leadership for good measure. 'There is much talk of the need for new radicalism and new vision in the Labour party - not that I resist new ideas - but I'm firmly convinced that, adequately presented, our historic values remain as true today as ever.' Where the other candidates won barely 30 seconds of respectful sedentary applause, Mr Prescott ended with a full minute of standing ovation. It was a triumph of a kind. But as a long-time champion of electoral reform reflected, in the Pavilion Theatre's upper circle: 'Under proportional representation, he could be leader of that sort of party and bring a lot of union influence to bear . . . in opposition.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: PM rules out protest in 'friendly fire' deaths
DOC.BYLINE: By ROBERT RICE and RALPH ATKINS
DOC.TEXT: THE GOVERNMENT signalled yesterday that it would take no action against the US pilots involved in the deaths of nine UK soldiers killed by 'friendly fire' in the Gulf war. Mr John Major indicated to MPs that he did not believe the incident justified a protest to Washington over its role in protecting of the pilots. While lessons had to be learnt, he said, 'I hope we won't lose sight of the fact that those were American pilots risking their lives alongside our troops in a battle against a common enemy and to liberate Kuwait.' Speaking after an Oxford inquest ruled on Monday that the nine were 'unlawfully killed', the prime minister faced pressure by Mr Neil Kinnock, the Labour leader, to use his authority to ensure the victims' families had the full truth. Mr Major replied: 'I'm not in a position to provide any more information.' Mr Malcolm Rifkind, defence secretary, later admitted that in the immediate aftermath of the Gulf war, 'there was some confusion and uncertainty about what exactly happened'. While the war had ended in February, the US Marine Corps had not answered points raised in the Ministry of Defence inquiry until July 10, he said. However, Ministry of Defence officials said that all available information was now in the hands of the victims' families. Mr Rifkind said the UK was working closely with its allies to ensure that in future, 'the risk of troops firing on their comrades is minimised'. Meanwhile, Mrs Barbara Mills QC, director of public prosecutions, has asked to see all the relevant documents held by the Oxford coroner and the MoD on the incident. The DPP's office said yesterday that Mrs Mills would consider the papers in detail to see whether there was sufficient evidence to bring criminal charges against the two US pilots allegedly responsible. Her office repeated though, that there was no power to prosecute a foreign national in England and Wales for any offence of murder or manslaughter allegedly committed abroad.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Flat-rate pension rebates 'too costly'
DOC.TEXT: TAX REBATES to encourage young people to opt out of the state earnings-related pensions scheme (Serps) should be reduced and larger rebates offered to older people, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. The institute concludes in a study of financial arrangements for personal pensions that the present system of flat-rate tax rebates costs the government more in forgone revenue than it can ever save on social security payments. 'There is no particular reason to favour younger workers over older,' the institute concludes. By the time an individual has reached the late 40s, it is no longer advantageous to hold a personal pension and policyholders would be well advised to opt back into Serps, says the institute. The age at which the advantage disappears depends on whether the personal-pension holder is male or female and on the assumptions of investment returns earned on contributions. The government has ruled out age-related rebates, arguing that they would not provide enough incentives for young people to opt out of the system and that they would be too confusing. Much of the life assurance industry, which markets personal-pension plans, opposes any move to age-related rebates. The government has said it will offer additional incentive payments only to personal-pension holders over 30 from April next year. The rebate will still be insufficient to discourage older people from rejoining the state scheme, the study says. Pension scheme sponsors need to increase contributions as members of schemes grow older, the institute says. Thus lower contributions are needed for younger members and higher ones for older members. The government's present flat-rate rebates allow young people to buy a more generous personal pension plan than they could achieve by remaining in Serps, but the contribution is too small for older people to maintain personal pensions. The institute also notes that transaction costs on personal pensions can significantly reduce returns to policyholders. The institute concludes that between a third and a fifth of contributions to a scheme can be eaten up in charges. The Personal Pensions Stampede. Institute for Fiscal Studies, 7 Ridgmount Street, London WC1E. Pounds 20.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / 'The prime minister must be the final judge': Code of conduct for members of the government Warning on conflicts between private investments and public duties
DOC.TEXT: THE GOVERNMENT yester-day issued the guidelines on conduct that are given to each minister on taking office. On investments, the document urges ministers to 'order their affairs so that no conflict arises or is thought to arise between their private interests and their public duties'. Where there is doubt about an interest, 'it will almost always be better to relinquish or dispose of the interest, but in such cases the prime minister must be the final judge'. The document shows that Westminster and the City are miles apart in their approach to handling the many potential conflicts of interest that arise between private investments and public duties. City institutions generally take a permissive attitude: directors and other senior staff are allowed to own shares in companies they advise, for instance. Yet any dealings have to be disclosed internally - and many houses operate a policy of allowing staff to trade only with prior approval from a central compliance officer. Ministers are subjected to one general rule - that they avoid all conflicts of interest. Investments that could give rise to conflicts, or perception of conflicts, should be disposed of. Such guidance looks idealistic. 'It would be nice if you could see all conflicts in advance,' says Mr Colin Condron, compliance officer at Barclays de Zoete Wedd, the investment bank. He suggested that one route for ministers might be to ban investments in equities, or restrict them to investment trusts. Alternatively, ministers could be required to put their shares into 'blind' trusts, under which they are not given any information about their investments - one of the suggestions in the document for ministers who have a wide range of investments. Even that may not save ministers from embarrassment: 2 1/2 years ago, Mr Cecil Parkinson, then transport secretary, was forced to issue a denial that he had been involved in insider dealing after share trans-actions undertaken by brokers WI Carr in the name of his nominee account. The official guidelines to ministers say they should declare to colleagues any private interest if they have to discuss public business in any way affecting it. They should also 'remain entirely detached from consideration of that business'. There is no formal restriction - other than the normal rules on MPs' interests, on former ministers taking up posts or other private-sector interests - 'although they should naturally avoid any course which would reflect adversely on their or the government's reputation for integrity or the confidentiality of its proceedings'. On taking up office, the document says, ministers should give up any other public appointment. Directorships: Ministers must resign all directorships when they take up office, the document says. The exceptions are directorships in private companies established in connection with private family estates - and charitable organisations, unless there is a possible conflict of interest. Partners in professional firms should cease any role in day-to-day management of the firm's affairs, but need not dissolve their partnership or allow their annual practising certificate to lapse. 'It is not possible to lay down precise rules applicable to every case,' the document says. 'Ministers in doubt about their personal position should consult the prime minister.' Investments: Ministers cannot be expected to dispose of all investments. But if a minister holds a controlling interest in any company, the considerations are similar to those governing the holding of directorships. The document points out that an investment in concerns closely associated with a minister's department may create the danger of an actual or apparent conflict of interest arising from exercise of powers or other influence in a way that affects the value of the investment or from dealings where there may be reasonable suspicion that the minister has special knowledge. Ministers called upon to exercise any power or discretion or other influence that could give rise to an actual or apparent conflict of interest should delegate to another minister, and should take no part in the preparation or reaching of any relevant decisions. Ministers are bound by the provisions of the Companies Securities (Insider Dealing) Act 1985 in relation to the use or transmission of unpublished price-sensitive information obtained by virtue of their ministerial office. Ministers are also urged to avoid speculative investments about which they have, or may be thought to have, early or confidential information likely to affect the price. Ministers 'will wish to consider whether or not investments of their (minor) children and their spouse should be treated similarly to their own'. The document stresses that it is for ministers to judge what action they need to take in respect of investments, but they should record any action in a minute to the permanent secretary of the department. Membership of Lloyd's: The prime minister, the chancellor of the exchequer, the trade and industry secretary - and DTI and Treasury ministers responsible for matters relating to Lloyd's - should not be underwriting members of Lloyd's. Any such minister who has been an underwriting member should not exercise statutory powers affecting Lloyd's - or any syndicates, brokers or agents with which he or she is connected - until all syndicate years for which he or she was an underwriting member have been closed or until he or she has reinsured all liabilities in such a way that he or she has no further interest in their performance. A law officer who is an underwriting member of Lloyd's, or who still has open syndicate commitments in respect of past membership, should not tender advice on the formulation, application or enforcement of legislation relating to Lloyd's. It is 'inappropriate' for other ministers who are members of Lloyd's to take an active part in the management of the affairs of syndicates of which they are members. Ministers who are Lloyd's Names may be required to suspend underwriting risks in any area in which their departments have responsibility. Every minister is required on appointment to a first or subsequent ministerial office to obtain the prime minister's permission before continuing a connection with Lloyd's, however nominal. Any minister wishing to establish any such connection during his term of appointment should likewise obtain the prime minister's permission to do so. The secretary of the cabinet is required to keep a list of ministers who are members of Lloyd's. Cabinet business: Cabinet and ministerial-committee business is defined as consisting mainly of matters 'which significantly engage the collective responsibility of the government because they raise major issues of policy or because they are of critical importance to the public' and questions on which there is an unresolved argument between departments. Chairmen of ministerial committees are urged to limit references to the cabinet. The only automatic right of appeal is if Treasury ministers are unwilling to accept expenditure as a charge on the reserve. The document says the internal process through which a decision has been made should not be disclosed. Decisions reached by the cabinet or ministerial committees are binding on all members of the government. Ministers and the law officers: It will 'normally be appropriate to consult the law officers' in cases where: The legal consequences of action by the government might have important repercussions in the foreign, European Community or domestic field. A departmental legal adviser is in doubt concerning the legality, constitutional propriety or vires of proposed legislation or administrative action. There is a particular legal difficulty that may raise political aspects of policy. Two or more departments disagree on legal questions. By convention, written opinions of the law officers, unlike other ministerial papers, are generally made available to succeeding administrations. Opinions of or advice from the law officers must not be disclosed outside government without their authority. Accountability: Each minister is responsible to parliament for the conduct of his or her department. Public appointments: In considering candidates for public appointments, ministers should pay particular attention to securing, on merit, proper representation of women and members of ethnic minorities on public bodies. Acceptance of gifts and services: It is 'a well established and recognised rule' that no minister should accept gifts or services from anyone that would, or might appear to, place him or her under an obligation. The same principle applies if gifts etc are offered to a member of their family.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Commanding officer of British forces in N Ireland visits troops
DOC.TEXT: Commanding presence: Lieutenant General Sir John Wilsey, commanding officer of British forces in Northern Ireland, visited troops outside Coalisland, County Tyrone, yesterday after soldiers and youths clashed on Sunday. He refused to comment on demands by the Dublin government for the withdrawal of the Parachute Regiment from the province. The call by Mr David Andrews, Irish foreign affairs minister, followed several days of unrest in the town, culminating in the confrontation on Sunday when three civilians were shot. Paratroopers were kept off the town's streets yesterday after protests over the soldiers' behaviour. Lt Gen Wilsey spoke to troops outside the town as metal detectors were used to find a machinegun stolen during the unrest.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / RPI housing factor review
DOC.TEXT: THE GOVERNMENT has ordered a review of the way housing costs are treated in the retail prices index, Mr Norman Lamont, the chancellor, announced yesterday. In a parliamentary written answer, he disclosed that the government was referring the treatment of owner occupiers' housing costs to the retail prices index advisory committee, the body that advises the chancellor on the method of construction and compilation of the RPI, the UK's main index of inflation. The move follows widespread criticism inside and outside parliament of the method of measuring the cost of housing, which is based on mortgage interest payments. A particular complaint has been the way the method makes the RPI rise in response to higher interest rates when those are introduced to control inflation. That has knock-on consequences for wage negotiations and other costs. The inclusion of mortgage interest payments in the RPI has also been criticised because they involve a large element of investment and because they can be seen as measuring the cost of credit, while no other type of credit charge is included in the index. Only Britain and the Republic of Ireland among European Community member states include mortgage interest payments in their main inflation measures. Six EC countries make no allowance for owner occupier costs. The chancellor's advisory committee is already investigating how the council tax, holiday spending and new cars should be treated in the RPI.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Rivera landscape sells for Dollars 1.21m: Saleroom
DOC.TEXT: A LANDSCAPE painting by the Mexican artist Diego Rivera, 'Paisaje de Toledo', giving a Cubist impression of the countryside around Toledo in Spain, sold for Dollars 1.21m (Pounds 661,202) at Christie's in New York on Monday night. It was bought by a Mexican dealer and reflects the strong current demand for Mexican art. The auction totalled Dollars 7.75m and was 24 per cent unsold. 'The Temptation of St Anthony', a Surrealist work by Leonora Carrington, made Dollars 440,000, an auction record for the artist. Christie's sales of modern illustrated books and 20th-century decorative arts in Geneva on Monday were less successful, with both nearly 50 per cent unsold. The top price was the Pounds 37,218 paid for an autographed manuscript by Jean Cocteau, Cherchez Apollon, illustrated with three sketches. Sotheby's also had difficulties, this time with tribal art in New York. The most important lot, a rare Benin bronze head of a leopard, dating from the 17th century and estimated as worth as much as Dollars 500,000, was unsold. There was little demand for medium-quality works, but an object from New Guinea, a Middle Sepik River suspension hook, sold for Dollars 159,000, at the top of its target. The auction brought in Dollars 1m, with 52 per cent unsold. Silver remains a healthy market and in Geneva an auction of European silver totalled Pounds 2.5m and was more than 87 per cent sold. A French silver gilt toilet service made by Francois-Daniel Imlin in Strasbourg in 1825 for Stephanie, Grand Duchess of Baden, a protegee of Napoleon, sold for Pounds 228,461. A French silver soup tureen and cover, made by Jean-Baptiste de Lens in Paris in 1736, far exceeded its forecast at Pounds 191,744.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / April public sector borrowing requirement biggest since 1987
DOC.TEXT: THE public sector borrowing requirement for April was Pounds 3.6bn, including privatisation proceeds of Pounds 0.6bn. That is the biggest April deficit since 1987. The figure was slightly lower than expected but economists warned that Britain was still heading for a record deficit in fiscal 1992-93. Most expect the PSBR in the new financial year - which started last month - to reach Pounds 30bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Working by ethnic groups surveyed
DOC.TEXT: SELF-EMPLOYMENT is far higher among some ethnic minorities in Britain than among white people, accounting for 22 per cent of the Pakistani and Bangladeshi communities, according to the Department of Employment. The rate for white people is 13 per cent. However, ethnic minorities have an overall rate of self-employment of 16 per cent, with the West Indian community down at only 7 per cent. Self-employed members of ethnic minorities are more likely to create jobs for others, with 40 per cent having employees, compared with 31 per cent of whites. The figures are from the department's Labour Market Quarterly Report, published yesterday by the Sheffield-based Skills and Enterprise Network. The report says a difference is also emerging in self- employment patterns between men and women. There were 3.1m self-employed people last year, compared with 1.9m in 1979 - an increase of 65 per cent; but the number of self-employed women rose by 109 per cent, double the rate of increase for men. The reports says that in the 10 years from 1981 the number of self-employed women who employed others rose by 49 per cent, or 3 1/2 times the 14 per cent rate achieved by men. The idea that a large proportion of the self-employed are unskilled jobbing builders or labourers is fading. In 1981 nearly two fifths of those who were self-employed had no qualifications, but that had fallen to just over a quarter by last year - and that was a proportion of a much bigger total. However, the proportion with qualifications at degree level rose only slightly, from 10.5 per cent to 11.3 per cent. The report draws a distinction between self-employment and owner-management of a limited company, where directors are classed by the Inland Revenue as employees. It is therefore difficult to estimate how many small businesses there are, although the number is put at 3m.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Acquisitions steady in first quarter but total value falls
DOC.TEXT: ACQUISITIONS in the UK remained steady in the first quarter of this year but the value of transactions fell. There were 124 transactions with an estimated total value of Pounds 2.2bn in the first quarter of 1992, according to figures released yesterday by the Central Statistical Office. The total value of initial payments on acquisitions of UK industrial and commercial companies was down Pounds 2.1bn on the last quarter of 1991, when there were 130 transactions, and down Pounds 11.1bn from the 1989 peak. Independent companies were involved in 72 of the sales, and subsidiaries in 52. There were no mergers. Thirty transactions were valued at more than Pounds 10m and 49 at less than Pounds 1m. The largest were the acquisition of Steetley by Redland, valued at Pounds 624m, the sale of IEP (Automotive) to Inchcape Overseas for Pounds 363m, and Bowater's purchase of DRG for Pounds 201m. Cash expenditure accounted for 58 per cent of the total, ordinary shares for 41 per cent, and fixed-interest securities for the remaining 1 per cent. Cash has comprised more than half of expenditure in every quarter since the stock market crash of October 1987. The figures omit cross-border acquisitions. Shareholders of quoted companies in the east Midlands have fared better over the past year than the companies themselves, according to an analysis published yesterday by KPMG Peat Marwick, the accountancy firm. The analysis covered the published results of 74 companies, and showed that while, on average, pre-tax profits fell 5.1 per cent and earnings attributable to shareholders fell 19 per cent, shareholders received a 17 per cent increase in dividends. KPMG says 11,500 people have lost their jobs in the region in the past year. Turnover of the companies in the survey totalled more than Pounds 19bn, and was 2 per cent higher than in 1990-91. East Midlands plc. KPMG Peat Marwick, St Nicholas House, 31 Park Row, Nottingham NG1 6FQ. Free.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Bank notes optimism over recovery: The Quarterly Bulletin cautions that the revival is likely to be slow
DOC.TEXT: CAUTIOUS optimism is back in fashion in Threadneedle Street. The Bank of England in its latest quarterly bulletin says: 'The prospects for recovery now appear better than for some time.' It warns, though, that prospects are 'by no means uniform throughout the economy, and the pace of recovery is likely to be slow, depending on the course of the world economy and the impact of domestic and international financial fragility'. Although the Bank believes output in Britain fell slightly in the first quarter, it has taken heart from a recent recovery of business and consumer confidence and the better mood of financial markets since the election. Together with the May 5 cut in bank base rates to 10 per cent from 10.5 per cent, 'these developments are encouraging and herald the prospect of an end to recession,' it says. But the report also makes clear that much remains to be done if the UK is to have as successful an economy as many of its rivals abroad. For that reason, the Bank lays great emphasis on Britain's fulfilling the convergence criteria of the Maastricht Treaty on economic and monetary union by 1996, when the European Community is due to discuss the possible move to the third and final stage of Emu. The Bank expects the present counter-inflationary stance will enable the UK to meet the Maastricht terms on inflation and interest rates, but it has doubts about the government's capacity to bring the ratio of the general government deficit to the GDP from about 5 per cent at present to the Maastricht level of below 3 per cent by the 1995-96 fiscal year. The ratio of government debt to national income is likely to rise until 1995-96, which the Bank says would be the longest such rise for about 40 years. Achieving the 3 per cent ratio 'will require firm control of public expenditure'. The government should therefore set 'a credible medium-term target for public spending and borrowing'. The Bank also urges greater efforts to lower inflation. It warns that direct comparisons of consumer price trends between the UK and its EC partners can be too flattering. It says that there is 'no room for complacency' over earnings trends, even though average earnings growth has moved more into convergence with that in the UK's partners in the exchange rate mechanism of the European Monetary System. 'Continued downward pressure on costs will be essential', especially if Britain is to make the most of export opportunities. Here, too, there is some additional cause for worry. Strong exports helped to support output through much of the recession, but weakness in overseas markets is 'now contributing to the uncertainty surrounding the strength and timing of recovery' in Britain. The pace of recovery will depend far more on progress in easing personal and corporate debt burdens and developments in the property market. The Bank notes that the fall in interest rates from 15 per cent in October 1990 'has not yet significantly strengthened confidence.' The personal sector continued to increase its savings in the first quarter while its gross income gearing ratio - the measure of households' gross interest payments as a percentage of disposable income - was still high at 13 per cent at the end of 1991 compared with its 1990 peak of 14 per cent. The Bank suggests that falling house prices were one factor explaining the public's muted response to lower interest rates. House repossessions were another concern. The commercial property market is also likely to remain depressed as premises are completed and add to existing excess supply. The Bank notes that office rents fell by more than a fifth up to the end of 1991, while one estimate puts the drop in rental values for all properties in the City of London at 38.9 per cent last year. Corporate defaults have caused the banks greatly to increase their provisions against bad debts. But the Bank says risk asset ratios remain well above internationally agreed standards and there is no sign that bad debts are causing banks to curb their lending. Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin, May 1992. Vol. 32, No 2. Subscription details from Bulletin Group, Economics Division, Bank of England, London EC2R 8AH.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Barry Reamsbottom elected general secretary of CPSA
DOC.TEXT: Barry Reamsbottom was yesterday elected general secretary of the CPSA, the biggest Civil Service union. He will take over the Pounds 43,000-a-year job on June 1, when Mr John Ellis, general secretary since 1986, moves to head the Council of Civil Service Unions. Mr Reamsbottom, 43, has edited the union's newspaper for the past five years.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Long-term jobless total rises
DOC.TEXT: THE NUMBER of people unemployed for more than one year rose by 94,000 in the quarter to April to reach 841,000, the highest since October 1988. The 286,000 increase since April last year is the biggest yearly rise since 1982. Mrs Gillian Shephard, the employment secretary, regretted the increase but pointed out that long-term unemployment was still only two thirds the level it was five years ago. She also said that the number of very-long-term unemployed, people unemployed for more than five years, was at the lowest level since January 1985. All regions suffered an increase in long-term unemployment with the largest percentage increases in south Wales, the south-east - including London - and East Anglia. Among those aged 18 to 24, the figure has risen 168,300, the highest level since April 1988. The Unemployment Unit, a lobby group, said the long-term unemployed were becoming a larger proportion of the unemployed, rising from 25 per cent to 31 per cent in the past year. The unit also pointed to the fact that the main Department of Employment training schemes do not cater for the long-term unemployed. Employment Training, for unemployed adults, concentrates on those unemployed for between six months and one year. Mr Tony Blair, Labour employment spokesman, said: 'We are storing up a legacy of bitterness, discontent and frustration that is damaging to social cohesion.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Output rise fuels hopes of upturn
DOC.TEXT: SPECULATION that the UK economy is on the verge of recovery was fuelled yesterday by news that manufacturing output rose in the first quarter of the year. The increase of 0.3 per cent over the preceding quarter in the three months to the end of March was the first three-monthly rise in output since the recession began. It followed six successive quarterly declines. The figures, from the Central Statistical Office, gave rise to optimism among economists, but they said it was still too early to pronounce the recession over. In spite of the quarterly rise, and two successive monthly rises, manufacturing output remained 2 per cent below levels of a year ago and 7.5 per cent below the high point recorded in the second quarter of 1990. On a monthly basis, manufacturing output rose by 0.2 per cent in March after a 1.1 per cent increase in February. Overall industrial output - manufacturing plus energy - fell by 1 per cent in the first three months of the year compared with the previous three-month period. That was mainly due to a big drop in energy output, which fell by 4.3 per cent in the first quarter. The Treasury said economic growth would become firmly established this year. 'Today's economic figures suggest the fall in manufacturing output may have ended and growth will become firmly established during 1992,' it said. Mr Gordon Brown, Labour's trade and industry spokesman, said economic prospects for the summer and autumn remained weak. Four of the seven components in manufacturing showed an upturn in the first quarter. Output of the 'other manufacturing' sector, which covers paper, printing and publishing, rose by 1.4 per cent compared with the previous quarter and output of metals rose by 1.1 per cent. Production of food, drink and tobacco rose by 1 per cent. There was a small decline in engineering output, although on a monthly basis output in the sector has risen for two successive months. Within engineering, car production rose by 4 per cent compared with the previous quarter. Chemicals was the only sector to show a big improvement in output compared with a year ago. Output grew by 5.3 per cent in the three months to the end of March compared with the same period a year ago. The CSO said that was almost entirely attributable to the strong performance of the pharmaceuticals industry. Output of the consumer goods industries rose 1.3 per cent in the first quarter compared with the previous three months, with the highest rise in the sector coming from cars. Production of investment goods, considered a lagging indicator, fell by 1.5 per cent in the first quarter and intermediate goods by 2 per cent. Economists agreed Friday's first-quarter gross domestic product would still be negative in spite of yesterday's manufacturing output figures, because of the fall in energy and water supply.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Boulogne freight link
DOC.TEXT: THE Folkestone-Boulogne cross-Channel ferry route, closed by Sealink Stena Line at the end of last year, is to be reopened to freight traffic in mid June by a new shipping company, Opale Ferries. The company, formed by a group of mainly French investors led by the Boulogne Chamber of Commerce, has chartered a Canadian freight ferry with capacity for 50 lorries. Opale believes there is enough demand among long-established users of Boulogne to justify the service in spite of competition from the Channel tunnel. Passenger services were restored to the route last month through Hoverspeed's SeaCat catamaran service. North Sea Ferries has ordered two Pounds 31m freight ferries for its Hull-Rotterdam route. Associated British Ports, which owns the port of Hull, is to build an Pounds 11m roll-on roll-off terminal to serve them.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / IT sector warns of skills shortage
DOC.TEXT: THE UK faces a shortage of information technology skills which might lead to an exodus of computer software and service companies, according to leading IT companies. Mr Paul Aspin, southern region industrial business manager for International Business Machines, said: 'Companies can now base themselves wherever in the world the relevant IT skills are, and use international networks to transmit data from there.' Mr Aspin, who is also a board director of West London Training and Enterprise Council, warned that unless the relevant skills were developed, the IT industry would move to continental Europe and elsewhere. Investment in IT training per person in the UK is half that in Japan, according to Mr Peter Bonfield, chairman and chief executive of ICL, the computer group. Lack of training by companies has meant that people who have the skills are poached by companies at increasingly higher pay levels. Dr Phil Blackburn, chief executive of the West London Tec, said: 'Short-term recruitment ends up eating up funds that would be more effectively allocated to long-term training.' The Tec yesterday launched the IT Skills Forum, for which it has targeted Pounds 1m to be spent on joint projects with members of the forum, such as IBM, ICL and British Airways, to ensure that skills are developed. As part of its programme, it is conducting a skills survey to track the emerging skills needed by users. The first phase of the survey has disclosed that 90 per cent of IT users have no data processing or IT department responsible for transmitting skills. The survey also reveals that most people who learn to use computers do so by sitting next to someone with experience.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Jaguar reveals 2-stroke project
DOC.BYLINE: By KEVIN DONE, Motor Industry Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: JAGUAR, the UK luxury carmaker, has developed a prototype two-stroke engine which might enter production in the next decade. The surprise disclosure of the project represents a pioneering step among European luxury carmakers. Several of the leading volume carmakers are developing two-stroke engines for small cars. Jaguar, a subsidiary of Ford of the US, said yesterday that development of the compact and lightweight V6 engine was the result of a 4 1/2 -year research programme. Its engineers have worked with Orbital Engine of Australia, the company that leads the development of two-stroke technology, and with Queen's University, Belfast. Mr Ron Lee, Jaguar manager of engine development, said the prototype 3.2-litre V6 was 40 per cent lighter than a comparable 12-cylinder engine but could give the same output. The company's present engine ranges comprise a 5.3-litre V12 and 4.0-litre and 3.2-litre six-cylinder engines. It is developing a V8 engine range, codenamed AJ26, which is planned for launch in 1996. Jaguar is expected to decide this summer whether the new engine will be made at one of its existing Midlands sites or at a Ford engine plant. Jaguar said that the next stage in the two-stroke engine project would be a full-scale development programme in Australia with Orbital. The company said it aimed to produce a 350 brake horsepower demonstrator engine in the next two years. Jaguar's work has included the performance testing of a three-cylinder development engine. According to the company, two-stroke engines might offer significant benefits to luxury carmakers because they would be substantially lighter and much more fuel-efficient than the present generation of large car engines.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / EC urged to free energy market
DOC.TEXT: URGENT action is required to quicken the pace of energy liberalisation throughout Europe, Mr Tim Eggar, the energy minister, said yesterday. Mr Eggar said he would press for the quick introduction of a free energy market when he meets European Community energy ministers in Brussels tomorrow. He was speaking at a conference in London organised by the Confederation of British Industry and the Confederation of Norwegian Business and Industry. His comments suggested that energy liberalisation might be a theme when the UK takes over the EC presidency in July. The UK leads the way in deregulation of electricity and gas industries, but may face strong opposition in pushing for greater liberalisation from countries such as France and the Netherlands. Mr Eggar said industry and 350m consumers across Europe would have 'everything to gain' from cheaper gas and electricity, with only a handful of vested interests likely to be losers. He suggested there was a 'striking contradiction at the heart of Europe'. 'It is quite extraordinary that we have been spending so much time making sure that goods can cross frontiers but we apparently find it impossible for gas and electricity to flow across frontiers.' He said significant disparities still existed between electricity and gas prices in different European countries. He also warned that European industry might find it impossible to compete with the rest of the world unless energy prices fell, as they were in the liberalised markets of the US and Japan. Mr Eggar said arguments that electricity and gas were natural monopolies, and that only monopolies had sufficient economic security to undertake large investment programmes required by energy projects, had been proved wrong by the liberalised UK electricity market, and the gas market in the US. He also countered claims by opponents of energy liberalisation that it would require a 'huge centralised regulatory bureaucracy'. Regulation could be left to member countries operating within an agreed framework.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Lamont maintains stance on VAT
DOC.TEXT: BRITAIN yesterday maintained its opposition to legally binding European Community rates of value added tax, delaying a decision on the issue until next month at the earliest. EC ministers were unable to agree on a series of directives enshrining last June's political agreement on indirect tax and excise rates. The UK sees no need for legislation that would set a minimum standard VAT rate of 15 per cent, and has specific difficulties in agreeing directives on harmonised alcohol and tobacco duties. Mr Norman Lamont, the chancellor - probably the only person who can sanction a change in the British stance - left Brussels before yesterday's debate on indirect tax. Ministers also postponed a decision on the capital adequacy directive, which would harmonise prudential standards for banks and investment firms. The Portuguese presidency hopes for agreement at next month's meeting of ministers. The Advertising Association, which represents 26 leading advertising trade bodies, today steps up its lobbying of the government, MPs and members of the European parliament for further and wider deregulation within the EC.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / BBC offers rise below inflation
DOC.TEXT: THE BBC HAS angered unions by offering more than 25,000 staff an annual pay rise below the current rate of inflation. The corporation's offer for the year from the beginning of August is 3.7 per cent, with a guarantee that nobody will receive a rise worth less than Pounds 300. There is also a Pounds 75 increase in the London allowance, bringing it to Pounds 2,190. The deal would cost Pounds 21.5m a year on the BBC's pay bill of Pounds 590m. The pay offer, which applies to members of the Bectu broadcasting union, the NUJ journalists' union and the AEEU electricians' union, comes on the eve of a BBC governors and top management conference to consider the corporation's future role. Bectu, which represents about 14,000 BBC staff, asked for 3 percentage points more than inflation - at present 4.3 per cent - and a minimum salary of Pounds 7,500. Mr Neil Fraser, head of BBC Radio Scotland, is leaving the corporation after 24 years 'to pursue other programme interests', it was announced yesterday.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Channel 5 bidding row returns to High Court
DOC.TEXT: THE LEGAL battle between Five TV and TV-am over their planned bids for the Channel 5 franchise returns to the High Court today amid considerable bitterness. Mr Bruce Gyngell, chairman of TV-am, believes the integrity of the breakfast television company has been tarnished and is determined to pursue the issue for as long as it takes to clear the company's name. On May 5, Five TV issued a writ against TV-am, which is leading a consortium called The Entertainment Channel, for alleged breach of contract. Five TV, whose shareholders include Mr Moses Znaimer, founder of City TV in Toronto, said TV-am had signed a confidentiality and exclusivity deal preventing it from bidding for Channel 5 with anyone else. Five TV was horrified when TV-am signed an agreement to bid for the franchise in a consortium including Time Warner, the international media company, and Mr Conrad Black's Daily Telegraph group. It meant that a rival was in possession of most of Five TV's confidential plans. Mr Gyngell emphasised that Mr Stratis Zographos, his finance director, had signed what he took to be a normal confidentiality agreement and had not noticed a line blocking any investment in a rival Channel 5 bidder. Mr Gyngell has denounced the clause as a 'restraint on trade', although on May 8 in the High Court TV-am gave an undertaking that it would give Five TV notice before it concluded any agreement to bid for Channel 5. The legal action is delaying any serious attempts at bringing together the rivals to form a single consortium, which would almost certainly be in a position to bid the minimum Pounds 1,000 a year for the franchise. In the Five TV camp are Thames Television, Sony Entertainment, the parent of Columbia and Tristar Pictures, and CanWest, an international broadcaster. Several leading shareholders in the two consortia believe the start-up costs are so high that Channel 5 will be viable only if any bid is uncontested. Apart from the legal action, there is a gulf between the programme plans of the two groups, with Five TV placing greater emphasis on local news and The Entertainment Channel thinking more in terms of a single national channel. As soon as the two sides leave the High Court, the talking may start in earnest before the deadline of July 5.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Names take fresh action on deposits
DOC.TEXT: LLOYD'S Names yesterday launched two new attempts to prevent the authorities at the insurance market from drawing down on their deposits to meet losses. In the High Court Mr Justice Potts gave leave to six Names - individuals whose assets back underwriting at the mar ket - connected with the Gooda Walker Action Group, which represents more than 2,100 Names, to seek a judicial review of Lloyd's. In yesterday's hearing Mr Alan Newman QC, for the Names, argued that Lloyd's had 'failed properly to have regard to the interests of members' when making the cash calls and drawdown procedures. Mr Alfred Doll-Steinberg, chairman of the Gooda Walker group, said: 'We look forward to exposing the parlous state of Lloyd's regulation to the cold light of judicial scrutiny for the first time in its history.' Solicitors Bentleys Stokes and Lawless are advising the group. Judicial reviews are actions against public or semi-public bodies which are alleged to have failed to observe their - often statutory - duties. In a separate action, Withers, solicitors acting on behalf of the Distressed Names Spiral Action Group, issued 10 writs against the Gooda Walker, Feltrim, Rose Thomson Young and Devonshire agencies yesterday. The writs are regarded as test cases and allege negligence by the agents. They also claim that the spiral reinsurance transactions - deals in which Lloyd's syndi cates and London companies reinsure each other's high-level exposure to catastrophe risks - were entered into 'without the authority of the Names involved'. Withers said yesterday that it had been advised by counsel that Names have a 'very strong if not overwhelming prima facie case for negligence in respect of the underwriting business of the Rose Thomson Young agency'. Both actions aim to obtain injunctions to prevent Lloyd's from drawing down on the deposits that all Names must lodge when they join Lloyd's to meet insurance losses. Last month more than 800 Names, represented by solicitors Michael Freeman, failed to obtain injunctions.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / US banks face probe into racial lending
DOC.TEXT: FEDERAL banking regulators are investigating the lending records of 266 US banks suspected of having discriminated against customers from minority groups. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), which regulates a number of federally chartered banks, said yesterday the banks had been asked to reply to Washington by the end of the week. 'We have been investigating for several months and a number of banks have received letters saying we are looking into racial disparities in lending,' an OCC official said. The OCC said the mortgage lending records were being scrutinised after officials found a disproportionate rejection rate by some banks of mortgage applications from minority groups such as black and Hispanic Americans. The practice is known colloquially as 'redlining,' a term based on the notion of bankers drawing a red line on a map around neighbourhoods they do not wish to lend to. Other federal bank regulators also examining the issue include the Federal Reserve Board and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). If the OCC decides that a bank is guilty of discrimination it may employ a series of sanctions, ranging from administrative or civil penalties to limiting the institution's ability to expand its operations or open new branches. The Bank of Boston, one of the leading banks operating in the depressed New England economy, has claimed it will make Dollars 3bn (Pounds 1.6bn) of new business loans over the next five years in an effort to stimulate the region's economy. Banking analysts are sceptical, however, that the bank can fulfil such a forecast. The bank described the claim as a projection of loan demand, rather than an actual commitment to make the loans.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Plebiscite may break logjam over second term for Menem
DOC.TEXT: ARGENTINA'S government has threatened to hold a plebiscite later this year to force Congress to reform the constitution and allow President Carlos Menem to run for re-election in 1995. The constitution forbids presidents from holding consecutive terms. However, the opposition Radical party is opposed to Mr Menem's re-election when his present six-year term ends. The conservative UCD party, the government's ostensible ally, is split over the issue. Senator Eduardo Menem, the president's brother and head of the Senate, said: 'Since it appears that some political forces are against the reform, I think it would be correct to consult the people directly.' A plebiscite would not have force of law, but the government is confident of wining a 70 per cent majority, which would intimidate Congress into supporting reform. Constitutional amendment has become Argentina's leading political issue. Mr Eduardo Bauza, secretary general of the presidency, warned that 'undoubtedly we are heading towards a plebiscite' unless the opposition co-operates by approving reform. A two-thirds majority of Congress is needed to convoke a constituent assembly. Mr Menem's fixation with re-election as he approaches the middle of his term is creating political uncertainty. Analysts warn that a constituent assembly could introduce social clauses that hinder economic reform. The president has said constitutional reform will not deflect his commitment to free-market policies. But his claims that he is not directly involved in a reform campaign are not widely believed. Re-election has obsessed Argentina's civilian presidents. The only leader to win re-election was Juan Peron in 1952, but the amendment was scrapped after the army toppled him in 1955. Mr Raul Alfonsn, Mr Menem's predecessor, also tried to change the constitution but the Peronists blocked his efforts.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Sales of Halcion given go-ahead by FDA panel: Sleeping pill seen as safe when used as prescribed
DOC.BYLINE: By KAREN ZAGOR and PAUL ABRAHAMS
DOC.TEXT: HALCION, the controversial sleeping pill made by Upjohn, has been found by an advisory panel to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to be safe and effective when used as prescribed for short-term treatment of insomnia. The panel recommended that the world's best-selling sleeping pill remain on the market in the US, in spite of studies showing that it produces higher rates of anxiety and memory impairment in some patients than similar drugs. The panel recommended clearer labelling of the drug's possible side-effects. The FDA is not obliged to follow the panel's recommendations but is expected to abide by them and allow Halcion to remain on the market. Upjohn believes a final decision could be made within two to six weeks. The panel said data did not confirm more alarming side-effects. It was fears that Halcion induced a substantially higher number of these, particularly depression and memory loss, that led to the drug being banned in a number of countries, including the UK, Norway, Finland, Bermuda and Argentina. Restrictions have been imposed on dosing levels in France and Spain. A German Health Ministry panel has not yet reported. In the UK, a final decision on the ban is expected by the start of next week, according to Upjohn. Although the UK accounted for only a small part of Halcion's sales, the ensuing publicity hurt the drug's sales around the world. These declined by 39 per cent during the first quarter of this year. Last year Halcion accounted for Dollars 237m (Pounds 133.8m) of Upjohn's Dollars 3.4bn sales. Shares in the US company firmed Dollars 7/8 to Dollars 35 3/8 at the close on the New York Stock Exchange yesterday. The stock was trading at about Dollars 47 3/4 before Halcion sales were suspended in the UK last September. At the FDA panel meeting, the company said it would conduct a study of 10,000 patients in a further attempt to allay fears about the drug's safety. The panel had recommended additional studies to determine the safest and most effective dosage.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 20 MAY 92 / Mulroney to pursue tough line on trade
DOC.TEXT: CANADIAN Prime Minister Brian Mulroney visits the White House today in a climate marred by bitter trade disputes and concern that the US is drifting deeper into isolationism. It is just seven years since President Ronald Reagan and Mr Mulroney sang 'Irish Eyes are Smiling' together and swore their mutual allegiance to the free market. But clearly the world no longer seems 'so bright and gay'. Mr Reagan has left centre stage and - if the polls are correct - Mr Mulroney and President George Bush soon could be joining him in political retirement. Mr Mulroney seems to find Mr Bush no less genial personally than his predecessor, but the political realities dictate a tougher line on trade from Ottawa. However, the atmosphere will be lightened by a US Commerce Department decision last week to cut its proposed countervailing duty on Canadian softwood lumber from 14.8 per cent to 6.51 per cent. Mr Derek Burney, Canadian ambassador to the US, said the move would 'help lower the temperature,' but insisted the ruling was 'a tortured attempt to manipulate the facts in order to substantiate a pre-ordained result'. The case will head the list of trade grievances, along with skirmishes over duties on Canadian-made Hondas, beer and magnesium. The Uruguay Round of trade liberalisation talks is on the agenda. Mr Mulroney would request 'the same kind of flexibility' on agriculture trade talks that the US was demonstrating toward the European Community, Mr Burney said. There are two new problems to discuss. The White House last week requested a dispute settlement panel under the Free Trade Agreement to investigate Canada's wheat pricing methods. Mr Mulroney may now request a panel to examine US agriculture export subsidies. The Canadian prime minister is also expected to emphasise the necessity of US leadership on aid to the former Soviet Union, in advance of Russian President Boris Yeltsin's visit to Canada and the US in June.
