Sir Marcus is regarded as a populist rightwinger who campaigned discreetly but actively, particularly among the new intake. His victory coincided with a strong performance by the right wing Conservative '92 group in elections for the 1922 executive committee. Among the successful candidates was Mr John Townend, Tory MP for Bridlington and Euro-sceptic. Mr Onslow was a old-school Tory, happy with traditional procedures. The votes in the 1922 elections are not published, for instance. One minister agreed that he was, 'good at the frosty answers'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Major issues stern warning on spending
DOC.TEXT: THE PRIME minister yesterday warned the cabinet that this year's public-spending round would be especially tight. Details of Mr Major's caution to his colleagues were released as it emerged that Mr Michael Portillo, the new chief secretary to the Treasury, will call in 14 ministers for unprecedented talks on departmental budgets soon after Whitsun. Mr Major's warning, at the end of a 75-minute cabinet meeting, was clearly a deliberate effort to dampen expectations of extra departmental funding as the costs of high unemployment bite into exchequer revenues. Downing Street took the unusual step of relaying his message yesterday, adding that the prime minister had said it was 'right for the chief secretary to examine all spending proposals very rigorously'. While such admonitions are not unusual, Mr Major's efforts to lend his weight to his chief secretary and Mr Portillo's move to call in ministers - months before the final round of bilateral negotiations in September - underline the high level of concern. On Wednesday Mr Norman Lamont, the chancellor, insisted in a Commons debate on the economy that he was sticking to his forecast of a Pounds 28bn public-borrowing target this year. Speculation has been mounting among City analysts, though, that that, along with next year's Pounds 32bn figure, may have to be revised upwards. Mr Major is determined that borrowing should be reduced sufficiently to allow room for further income tax cuts towards the end of this parliament. But with yesterday's unemployment level showing 2.7m jobless, there are doubts whether a forecast average rate of 2.4m for the current financial year can be achieved. For every 100,000 jobless over that figure, the government must find Pounds 330m to cover unemployment and other benefits this year, rising to Pounds 360m in 1994-95. Civil servants now privately concede that the strain on the social security budget is substantially higher than first expected. The official word remains that there is no spending crisis, but rather that departments are being made aware of the insistence on good housekeeping. Efforts are under way to speed up the implementation of policies to contract out public-sector services and push through privatisation plans. A leaked letter from Mr Portillo to Mr Kenneth Clarke, the home secretary, earlier this month illustrated how ministers are also under pressure to improve productivity in their departments. Ministers are expected to have filed their bids for departmental budgets by about the end of this month. After their meetings with the chief secretary after Whitsun, the horse trading will begin in earnest after the summer recess and be completed in September before the autumn statement in early November. If ministers fail to reach agreement with Mr Portillo, they will face the humiliation of going to the so-called Star Chamber, where senior Cabinet ministers adjudicate on disputed issues. The last meeting was in 1986.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Openness may reign at the FO
DOC.TEXT: FOREIGN Office papers, held for more than 30 years but so far unpublished, could be released under a review announced by Mr Douglas Hurd, the foreign secretary. An internal committee will be set up to look at papers, including documents on Nazi deputy leader Rudolf Hess, but there were no indications that any particular papers would be released. The review is part of the government's promise to increase openness. Mr Hurd said: 'The culture of secrecy went too wide. The presumption should be that information is released unless there are compelling and substantive reasons of national interest to withhold it.' The Foreign Office refused, though, to confirm whether the review had yet been set up or who would chair it. An official would said only that it would be carried out by the Foreign Office's library and record department, headed by Mr Richard Bone. Mr Hurd said the government had made progress in eliminating secrecy. Criticisms of the 1989 Official Secrets Act had been misplaced. 'Fevered imaginations produced predictions of authors restrained, silence imposed and editors jailed. Nothing of the sort has happened. On the contrary, news has spread through Whitehall that secrecy for its own sake is no longer a virtue,' he said. But he dismissed calls for a Freedom of Information Act as 'a mechanistic approach to reform which produces conflict rather than progress'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Thatcher to cite fears of federalism
DOC.TEXT: MRS Margaret Thatcher, the former prime minister, will today set out her fears over the European Community's institutions and moves to federalism in a speech her aides said should avoid an explicit intervention into Conservative MPs' rows over the Maastricht treaty. Underlining tensions over the Commons' debate on Maastricht next week, Mr Roger Knapman, Tory MP for Stroud, last night lost his job as unpaid parliamentary private secretary to defence minister Mr Archie Hamilton, after telling government whips he could not support the treaty. Such strict discipline before, rather than after, a vote is rare at Westminster. Mrs Thatcher's high-profile address in The Hague will include some praise for Mr John Major, and is expected to steer clear of direct references to his handling of the Maastricht deal. But she will be sharply critical of the federal ambitions of Mr Jacques Delors, the European Commission president. Ministers, however, will be braced for coded messages in Mrs Thatcher's words and for her stepping into the Conservative party's battles when she answers questions afterwards. Speaking in Munich yesterday, Mrs Thatcher said that the former Soviet Union and eastern Europe were part of a trend away from centralised bureaucracy and towards co-operation between national governments. 'It is for individual countries to decide what powers they cede to the (European) Community,' she said at a meeting of the International Securities Market Association. Her aides said that today's speech to the European Research Centre was 'not a parochial speech about Britain' but a 'thoughtful' consideration of Europe in a world context. She is expected to put particular emphasis on promoting economic prosperity through world trade. Mrs Thatcher will not shrink from renewing her traditional attack on the erosion of the sovereignty of national parliaments and on the aspirations of Mr Delors. Mr Major provided some encouragement to Tory Euro-sceptics in the Commons yesterday by saying that Britain would not accept EC proposals to remove border controls under the single European market.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Councils face delay over budget targets
DOC.TEXT: THE COUNCIL tax looks likely to run into trouble in its first year because the announcement of next year's overall local-government spending will probably be delayed. Meanwhile, ministers faced criticism when Mr Michael Howard, the environment secretary, announced that the government intended to 'cap' 10 councils' spending this year. Each July the government usually announces the maximum amount it believes local government should spend in the following financial year (total standard spending) and the total amount of external support through government grant and the business rate. This year, though, The Department of the Environment believes the statement may be delayed until October. The likelihood of a hold-up is being interpreted as a sign of how tight the coming public spending round will be. Environment ministers consider it vital to secure a reasonable revenue support grant for next year so that the first year of the council tax does not produce the sharp rises in bills that bedevilled the first year of the poll tax. One difficulty is that ministers still lack detailed information about the tax base for the council tax, under which bills will be based largely on the value of property in one of eight bands. The valuation exercise is not expected to be completed until the end of next month at the earliest. Until its results are available, ministers will have difficulty in knowing the scale of the transitional relief scheme they will want to put in place. A further complication is that the extra money to go to local authorities to take account of their new duties in providing community care has yet to be decided. The government is still considering whether to prohibit councils from spending the grant on other services. Mr David Blunkett, Labour's local-government spokesman, said that the Department of the Environment and the Treasury were 'locked in a battle which will leave local government the loser'. In the Commons, Tory and opposition MPs alike criticised the environment secretary's decision to cap the 10 councils' spending. Mr Howard said the move would mean reductions in the average poll tax in the 10 areas from Pounds 58 a payer in Basildon to Pounds 3 a payer in Gloucester, benefiting 1.8m payers. The councils have 28 days to challenge the decision. Tory backbenchers were among those who warned that the limits on spending would mean cuts in services. The Labour-dominated Association of Metropolitan Authorities condemned the capping arrangements. When provisional capping criteria were set, the association said, that led almost all the other authorities to cut their budgets to avoid being capped. Mr Alan Howarth and Mr James Pawsey, Tory MPs for Stratford-on-Avon and for Rugby and Kenilworth respectively, joined Labour colleagues for Warwickshire in urging Mr Howard to relax the cap on Warwickshire. Mr Pawsey warned of the risk of 'a strongly adverse effect on the services being offered'. Mr Howard said he would look carefully at any representations made to him about the impact of standard spending assessments on capping, and that they were continually kept under review. ---------------------------------- CAPPED COUNCILS ---------------------------------- Authority Control ---------------------------------- Basildon Con Hillingdon Con Warwickshire Con Greenwich Lab Lambeth Lab Middlesbrough Lab Cheltenham Lib Dem Gloucester No overall Gloucestershire No overall Langbaurgh No overall ----------------------------------

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Astra skill centre cuts attacked
DOC.TEXT: THE NUCPS Civil Service union reacted angrily yesterday to the news that Astra Training Services, which took over the bulk of the 60 skill centres privatised in 1990, had announced to staff a further three rounds of closures and redundancies. Rochdale, Somerset and Redmouth centres are to close, and other redundancies totalling 70 were announced. That follows the announcement four weeks ago of the closure of three centres and 162 redundancies. 'This tactic of announcing such closures is roundly condemned by the NUCPS,' said Tony Gallagher, national officer of the union, which is in annual conference at Blackpool. 'It's not the first time but the third consecutive mid-conference announcement when the union officials are away from the workplace.' He further condemned the government underfunding of employment training, which Astra considers the reason for such cuts. 'Privatisation has been disastrous for the providers and those in need of training. It's a national disgrace that should be condemned by all.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Pricing gap emerges in bank fees
DOC.TEXT: SOME HIGH street banks' charges to small-business customers are substantially higher than their rivals', according to a survey of banking business charges published by the consultancy Rochester Research. The pricing gap is particularly wide between Lloyds and Midland, the two banks locked in a takeover battle. Lloyds emerges as the most expensive bank for small businesses and Midland the cheapest. The survey was carried out in bank branches in Kent but its findings are valid for the UK as a whole. Rochester says some Lloyds small-business customers would save at least 20 per cent if they banked with Midland. It has forwarded a copy of its report to the Office of Fair Trading, which is considering whether to refer Lloyds' bid for Midland to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission. Lloyds said yesterday it was unfair to compare its prices with Midland's when predicting what customers of a merged bank might pay two years from now. 'We have made it clear that the kind of cost savings which would then be possible would clearly benefit the customer,' Lloyds said. The bank declined to say why its charges were higher than those of the other banks. The survey says a small business with 80 transactions on its account each month would find itself paying Pounds 39.50 a quarter more in charges if it banked with Lloyds rather than Midland. For a customer writing 60 cheques a month, paying six bills by standing order and another six by direct debit, and receiving eight credits, Lloyds would charge Pounds 187.50 compared with Midland's Pounds 147.90. The charges of the other big clearers are closer to Midland than Lloyds. A NatWest customer would pay Pounds 159.60 for identical services and a Barclays customer Pounds 156.20. Lloyds scores better than other banks with its Premier Interest Account, in which businesses can hold funds. Business Banking in the Medway Towns. Rochester Research, Readers, Millcroft Road, Cliffe, Rochester. Pounds 5.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Social policy think tank to be relaunched
DOC.TEXT: THE SOCIAL Market Foundation, a think tank founded by supporters of the now defunct Social Democratic party, will be relaunched today with the backing of Mr David Sainsbury, one of Britain's wealthiest businessmen and a leading supporter of the SDP until its demise. The foundation will promote discussion of social policy in the framework of a capitalist market economy. The social market ideas espoused by Christian Democrats in Europe have attracted increasing interest among Conservative thinkers such as Mr Chris Patten. The foundation's new board includes two Conservative MPs who entered the Commons at the last election after serving as advisers to the prime minister: Mrs Judith Chaplin, who was Mr Major's private secretary, and Mr David Willetts, who was director of studies at the Centre for Policy Studies, the Conservative think tank founded by Lord Joseph and Mrs Thatcher. Mr Andrew Tyrie, a former Treasury adviser who worked for Mr Nigel Lawson and Mr Major, also joins the board. The board includes a wide range of other interests, including Mr Samuel Brittan, an assistant editor of the Financial Times, Professor John Kay of the London Business School and Ms Sue Slipman of the National Council for One-Parent Families. Reflecting the drift of many leading lights of the SDP towards Mr John Major's Conservative party, the foundation will be chaired by Lord Skidelsky, an SDP life peer who has recently taken the Conservative whip in the Lords.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / District privatises tax work
DOC.TEXT: COLLECTION of local taxes and the payment of benefits is to be contracted out to the private sector by East Cambridgeshire district council, in one of the first successful competitive tender for a local-authority white-collar function. The council sought competitive tenders for the collection of poll tax and business rates - and council tax when that is introduced next year - and the payment of housing benefit and poll tax benefit. The contract, worth Pounds 3.5m over five years, has been awarded to Capita Group from this month. The council's 23 revenue collection and benefits staff have chosen to transfer to Capita, and the service will continue to be provided from the existing premises. If service targets are exceeded, Capita will be paid a performance bonus. If standards are not met, their fee will be reduced. Capita already works under contract for more than 20 local councils in chasing up poll tax payments by phone, but this is the first contract involving the entire revenue collection and benefits payment service. Competitive tendering is due to be extended to a wide range of council professional and technical services under legislation passed in the last parliament. Details of the scope of such contracting out and the timetable are due to be announced soon, after officials have considered more than 500 submissions on a consultative paper issued last autumn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Approach to debts criticised
DOC.BYLINE: By JOHN WILLMAN, Public Policy Editor
DOC.TEXT: BUILDING societies, utilities and local authorities are exacerbating consumer debt troubles by their heavy-handed and inflexible approach, according to the National Consumer Council. In its annual survey of advice centres, the government-funded council says that difficulties over paying for essential services such as water, housing and fuel form a high proportion of cases requiring help. The troubles brought to advice agencies are often linked in cycles that are difficult to break. For example, people who have difficulty in paying bills may be asked for a deposit in advance, which they cannot afford. The council points out that consumers on low incomes often have to pay more for essential services such as gas and electricity. Pre-payment meters, which are helpful to consumers on a limited income, are more expensive than quarterly billing. The National Consumer Council also blames suppliers and local authorities for delays and errors that posed further obstacles to consumers. The collection of the poll tax has been particularly difficult, with confusing billing methods and unclear instructions. The recession appears to be leading to a tightening-up on debt collection procedures, according to the survey. The council gives a warning that lack of understanding and inflexibility about renegotiating repayments often made debt delays worse. The council concludes that 'with a little patience, understanding and with sensible budgeting, most consumer debts can be repaid'. Advice Monitor. National Consumer Council, 20 Grosvenor Gardens, London SW1W 0DH. Free.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Anger at BCCI allegation by MP
DOC.TEXT: THE Abu Dhabi majority shareholders of the collapsed Bank of Credit and Commerce International reacted angrily yesterday to allegations made in the House of Commons naming a senior adviser in the sheikdom as having benefited from fraudulent transactions. The allegations made by Mr Keith Vaz, the Labour MP for Leicester East, named Mr Ghanem Faris Al Mazrui, one of the most senior advisers to Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan al-Nayhan, the ruler of Abu Dhabi, as having gained from a 'no risk' share deal. The claims had been made before in the Section 41 Report on the BCCI fraud prepared by Price Waterhouse, the bank's auditors. The report prompted the Bank of England's closure action on July 5 last year. But Mr Vaz's decision to reiterate the allegations in the Commons, drawing the information from a new report prepared by Norton Rose, lawyers advising British-based creditors of the bank, reopened the wound at a critical stage for the Dollars 1.7bn provisional compensation agreement with Abu Dhabi negotiated by Mr Brian Smouha, the Touche Ross chief liquidator of BCCI. The High Court has adjourned the hearing into the liquidation until June 8 for creditors to seek 'clarification' of the deal. The unofficial creditors committee is seeking a better deal than the one on offer. Abu Dhabi said yesterday Mr Mazrui had been given no guarantee, indemnity or similar assurance that his transaction in shares in the BCCI group, which occured in 1986, would be risk-free. The details, said Abu Dhabi, had been voluntarily disclosed by Mr Mazrui to Price Waterhouse and the investigation committee set up by the majority shareholders. It said that at no time before April 1990 did Mr Mazrui know of fraudulent activities by BCCI management.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / South bears brunt of big increase in unemployment: More defence industry jobs lost
DOC.TEXT: THE BRUNT of April's sharp rise in unemployment was borne by the southern regions of the UK, although the number of people out of work rose in all parts of the country except Northern Ireland. The rise was sharpest in the south-west, where a 0.3 per cent monthly increase in the number of jobless brought the total to 201,800. In the south-east, including London, unemployment rose by 0.1 per cent, bringing the rate of unemployment to 10.2 per cent. There were also sharp increases in the west Midlands and north-west, but economists suggested yesterday that the southern half of the country would continue to suffer the biggest monthly increases in unemployment as pressure on the service sector persis-ted. In Northern Ireland the level of unemployment remained unchanged in April compared with the previous month. Nevertheless, the rate of unemployment - at 14.3 per cent - remained the highest in the country. The overall weakness of the labour market was further reflected in a rise in the rate of male unemployment to 12.8 per cent from 10.1 per cent a year ago. Female unemployment remained significantly lower, rising to 5.2 per cent in April compared with 4.4 per cent a year ago. The level of female unemployment, and consequently overall unemployment, may be much higher, since many married women whose husbands work are not eligible for benefits and hence do not show up in the figures. Job vacancy statistics worsened with the number of unfilled vacancies, which account for about a third of all vacancies in the economy, falling by 7,900 to 119,600 - 2,200 fewer vacancies than in April last year. The Department of Employment said that over the past six months Jobcentre vacancies had risen by 2,700 a month on average. Employment in the manufacturing sector continued to decline. The number of employees in manufacturing in the UK fell to 4.5m, a fall of 26,000 on the month. Employment in the sector has fallen by 297,000 in the year to March, compared with a fall of 239,000 in the previous year. Measured on a quarterly basis, an improving trend in manufacturing employment was reversed in the three months to March. In the third and fourth quarters of last year manufacturing employment fell by 65,000 and 59,000 respectively compared with a fall of 101,000 in the second quarter. In the latest three months, employment in manufacturing industries fell by 72,000.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Earnings rise continues: Reasons for the upward surge in wages - Average pay increases 7.5%
DOC.TEXT: THE upward 'blip' in UK average earnings, announced yesterday, can be explained by various special factors but still puts into sobering perspective the controversy over a 5.4 per cent pay offer to Germany's public-sector workers. Germany, of course, is paying for reunification. But the figures make clear that Britain can afford no complacency over its pay-setting arrangements. In spite of a sharp reduction in inflation and the new discipline that ERM membership is supposed to impose on the manufacturing sector, UK manufacturing earnings are rising faster than all but three OECD countries: Portugal, Greece and Italy. According to the government's own figures, UK manufacturing earnings in March were rising at an underlying rate of 8.25 per cent. The latest available figures for other large countries include 6.6 per cent in Germany, 4.3 per cent in France, 2.7 per cent in the US and 1.7 per cent in Japan. The underlying rate of increase in average earnings for the economy as a whole was 7.5 per cent in March, more than 3 percentage points above inflation. That is the same rate as February after an upward revision of that month from 7.25 per cent to 7.5 per cent. That figure disguises a jump of more than 10 per cent in earnings in many sectors between February and March. There are two main reasons for that. One is that many companies paid bonuses in March, earlier than usual, to save their better-paid employees from the effects of a possible Labour government's tax increases. The other is that some workers will have received two pay rises in the 12 months to March. In March last year, when inflation was 8.24 per cent but heading down quite rapidly, employers were trying to postpone pay settlements. This year inflation is relatively stable, and is even expected to rise slightly, so employers have been settling promptly. Apart from those 'special factors', it should be remembered that average earnings represent pay increases over a 12-month period, so the current figure still includes pay rises from the middle of last year when inflation was considerably higher. Nevertheless, employers and the government have been expecting average earnings to fall significantly, along with inflation, for nearly a year, without any luck. Average earnings were rising at a rate of 7.75 per cent in July last year, only 0.25 per cent above the March figure. Even more worrying, there are signs that pay settlements - which have been falling more rapidly - may be hitting a floor between 4 per cent and 5 per cent. Settlements are usually a percentage point or 2 below earnings increases because they exclude bonuses and overtime pay. The Confederation of British Industry is still reporting pay freezes for companies in special difficulty. The CBI, however, said settlements in manufacturing in the first quarter of this year rose from 4.2 per cent to 4.3 per cent. Some pay analysts are speculating that average earnings may not fall below 7 per cent at all, in the present cycle, if the recovery does pick up in the next few weeks. That would mean an increase in overtime and other bonuses. This view is probably too pessimistic and the recent low settlements from the banking sector suggest there is still downward pressure on pay. Even so, the latest 'blip' certainly serves to highlight the fact that Britain still has a pay difficulty both in the public sector - where settlements are running at about the German level of 5.4 per cent - and in the private sector.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Yorks businesses see signs of recovery
DOC.BYLINE: By IAN HAMILTON FAZEY, Northern Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: BUSINESS in the Yorkshire area and Humberside is beginning to show signs of recovery but prospects are still fragile, the region's Confederation of British Industry council said yesterday. There have been signs of further improvement since the regional trends survey was compiled. Mr Peter Barker, chairman of the regional council, said the most recent evidence was of domestic orders increasing for some companies and being at least stable for the majority. 'If the indicators on output and orders strengthen over the coming months - and if businesses maintain the pressure on costs which now appears to be bearing fruit - we should be able to discern a turning point and the beginning of the recovery,' Mr Barker added. He said the process would be slow, with definite signs elusive for some time. Confidence was crucial, but the general election had strengthened it. CBI members do not, however, expect employment prospects to improve. The region is likely to have Britain's smallest year-on-year decline by the end of June, but that will still be 2.8 percentage points.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Government may face legal action over 1989 dockworkers' strike
DOC.TEXT: THE BRITISH government may face legal action in the European Court of Human Rights by unions over the behaviour of employers in the 1989 dockworkers' strike. An independent study published by the TGWU general union found that, of 63 port employers, just 15 fully respected the human rights of striking dockworkers. The study calls on the TGWU to ask the Trades Union Congress to take the case against the government, concerning Associated British Ports (ABP), to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR). It argues that ABP breached the rules on collective redundancies. Rulings by the ECHR are binding on British courts.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Johnson Matthey wins tax plea
DOC.TEXT: JOHNSON MATTHEY, the precious metals company, yesterday won its appeal against the Inland Revenue to receive tax relief on Pounds 50m granted to it for the rescue of Johnson Matthey Bankers, its former subsidiary, seven years ago. The Bank of England rescued the bank, which ran into difficulties on its commercial loans business, by buying its shares for Pounds 1. The rescue was conditional on a Pounds 50m cash injection from Johnson Matthey. Five law lords unanimously upheld the company's argument that the Pounds 50m was a 'revenue payment' and hence deductible for corporation tax purposes. Lord Templeman said the payment was solely to enable Johnson Matthey to continue trading, because its own platinum-trading business would have collapsed if Johnson Matthey Bankers had closed. The Pounds 50m was not paid to persuade the Bank of England to buy worthless shares in the bank, but to persuade it to rescue it and allow Johnson Matthey to survive. A payment to preserve an existing business was attributable to revenue, the lords stated. The Revenue had argued that the Pounds 50m was a 'capital payment' to enable Johnson Matthey to get rid of a capital asset, and liable to tax.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / 'Green' rules alarm companies
DOC.TEXT: NORTHERN companies in sectors under pressure from environmentalists are concerned that their prospects are being threatened by the cost of compliance with over-hasty legislation. A survey published yesterday highlights strong discontent among manufacturers with the Department of Trade and Industry. It was based on interviews between December last year and February this year with chairmen, chief executives and managing directors from 62 of the largest private-sector employers in north-east England and Cumbria. Many felt that DTI ministers lacked understanding of the support that manufacturers needed. Business leaders in sectors such as energy and food also felt the government had failed to define its policy or shape European Community legislation to the advantage of UK companies. Companies in sectors under environmental pressure, such as plastics and chemicals, food and drink, pharmaceuticals and energy, also voiced great frustration at the complexity of UK and EC environmental regulation. The survey, A Business Agenda for the North, was prepared by Price Waterhouse, the accountancy firm, and the economic research office of the Northern Development Company. It says there is strong satisfaction with the region's further and higher education institutions.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Tighter tax rules on equity note payments
DOC.TEXT: LEGISLATION is to be introduced by the government which, with effect from midnight last night, will prevent multinational companies avoiding liability for UK tax on payments made under equity notes - perpetual debt instruments where the loan is not repaid. Mr Stephen Dorrell, financial secretary to the Treasury, said in the Commons that the Finance Bill to be published on May 20 would include provisions to prevent the exploitation of a recent ruling by the special tax commissioners arising from a double taxation agreement. They decided certain payments under equity notes were interest for tax purposes. Mr Dorrell said the Inland Revenue was considering an appeal against the ruling. He also announced that new clauses to be introduced in the committee stage of the bill to confirm the existing basis for taxing life assurance companies. They had been made necessary by the claims made by some companies that the existing basis could not apply when a trading loss was incurred.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / MoD given Iraqi supergun sections
DOC.TEXT: SECTIONS of the Iraqi supergun were yesterday delivered to the Ministry of Defence, more than two years after they were seized by UK customs officials. Ministry scientists are understood to be planning experiments with the parts.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Complaints against police increase
DOC.TEXT: THE Police Complaints Authority handled 7,953 cases last year, a rise of 9 per cent on the previous year, although serious cases fell by 15 per cent to 4,330. The most common complaints were of assault, incivility, irregular procedures and neglect of duty. One in 10 cases led to action being taken.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Charges allege Pounds 1.3m fraud
DOC.TEXT: MR Malcolm Johnson, a businessman, appeared before City of London magistrates yesterday charged with eight counts of fraud involving more than Dollars 2.4m (Pounds 1.3m). It followed his extradition from Austria on Wednesday after a request by the Serious Fraud Office. The charges against him include obtaining Dollars 2.4m by deception from Postel Investment Management by purporting that shares in Duralite Manufacturing were shares in a properly constituted company with assets of over Dollars 20m. Mr Johnson, 43, of Betchworth, Surrey, was remanded on conditional bail until July 9.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Scottish hospitals seek trust status
DOC.TEXT: ABOUT 16 hospital units or groups have notified the Scottish Office since the general election of their interest in obtaining trust status. One unit has submitted a formal application. Of the 56 hospital units in Scotland, two became trusts on April 1 and a third is poised to become a trust next year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Pay deal for NHS blue-collar staff
DOC.TEXT: NATIONAL Health Service blue-collar workers have accepted an offer worth 4.9 per cent on the pay bill. The 180,000 workers, who include domestics, porters and catering and laundry staff, will have their increase backdated to April 1. The lowest-paid will receive increases of up to 6.7 per cent. The settlement is consistent with a recent pay increase for white-collar NHS workers but below the average of 6.5 per cent awarded to doctors and nurses after pay-review recommendations earlier this year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Banknote theft probed by police
DOC.TEXT: EIGHT people have been arrested by police investigating the alleged theft of money from the Bank of England's depot at Debden, Essex, where old banknotes are destroyed. Scotland Yard said a large quantity of cash had been recovered but did not reveal the amount. The arrests by officers of the Company Fraud Squad and No 9 Regional Crime Squad were made yesterday at three addresses in Loughton and one at Chelmsford, Essex. The four men and four women arrested were released on police bail pending further inquiries. Neither the police nor the Bank would confirm a report in today's Daily Mail that up to Pounds 50m may have been stolen from the depot.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Lloyd's inquiry to end in mid-June
DOC.BYLINE: By DAVID OWEN and RICHARD LAPPER
DOC.TEXT: SIR DAVID Walker will complete his inquiries into alleged malpractices at Lloyd's of London by mid-June and will hand his report to the insurance market's authorities on July 1. That timetable emerged after a meeting yesterday between the Securities and Investments Board chairman and three Conservative MPs. When Sir David was appointed in February it was stated that he would take at least two months to complete his task. It has also emerged that a report into the loss-making Feltrim syndicates - the first of a number of loss reviews being conducted by Lloyd's - will not be ready until August. It had been expected that the investigations, which are being co-ordinated by Sir Patrick Neill QC, would be ready earlier this year. Yesterday's meeting came as the government was accused by the Labour party of mounting a cover-up of malpractice at Lloyd's in an attempt to protect its 21-strong Commons majority. Mr Peter Hain, Labour MP for Neath, called for a debate on the market's troubles and said there was evidence that 'the Council of Lloyd's - in discussion with the Department of Trade and Industry - was involved in an attempt using institutional finance to bail out Lloyd's Names including MPs'. A DTI official said yesterday that he had 'absolutely no knowledge' of the discussions referred to by Mr Hain. Mr Paul Marland, Tory MP for Gloucestershire West and a Lloyd's Name, joined Mr Hain in calling for a Commons debate on the ground that there was increasing evidence that the market was breaching the Lloyd's Act. Mr Marland expressed satisfaction with the meeting with Sir David, which he had attended along with Sir Gerard Vaughan, Conservative MP for Reading East, and Sir Michael Marshall, Tory MP for Arundel. In a separate development, Lloyd's Names who benefited from the out-of-court settlement in the Outhwaite case yesterday won another legal victory. After a two-day hearing in the Commercial Court Mr Justice Saville ordered Lloyd's to pay the Pounds 116m directly to the 987 Names party to the settlement agreed in February. Last month Lloyd's blocked direct payment of the settlement to Names by insisting that money be paid to its premium trust funds - the funds into which all underwriting money earned by Lloyd's underwriters is paid. The complication arose because some Names who benefited from the Outhwaite action are also members of loss-making syndicates - such as those managed by the Feltrim and Gooda Walker agencies - and have outstanding liabilities from those separate underwriting activities. In the cases of those Names, Lloyd's intended to offset settlement monies against these other liabilities. Mr Anthony Boswood QC, representing the Names, said that the decision had caused Names 'grievous financial hardship'. Lloyd's said it will not appeal.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Press wins praise from watchdog
DOC.TEXT: THE threat of govern-ment-imposed statutory controls on the press appeared to recede yesterday as the Press Complaints Commission praised the press for supporting the industry's code of practice. The commission, which replaced the Press Council in 1990, said in its first annual report that the press, especially the tabloids, had given it strong support. The Calcutt Committee on Privacy, supported by the government, made clear that the commission would be the last chance for the newspaper industry to avoid statutory intervention. Lord McGregor of Durris, commission chairman, said the newspaper industry had passed the 'stiff test' of showing that self-regulation can work. 'I am sure that the ethical standards embodied in the code will now be observed cumulatively, expansively and irreversibly,' he said. The commission emphasised yesterday that: Most complaints raising apparent breaches of the code of practice had been resolved directly with editors without the need for adjudication. No newspaper or periodical had repeated the same or a similar inaccuracy or misleading report brought to the commission's attention. The commission's formal adjudications had been observed. Lord McGregor also emphasised in his report the 'astonishingly small number of complaints made against news-papers in general and popular national daily and Sunday newspapers in particular'. During its first year, the commission had 1,396 communications from the public. There was judged to be no prima facie breach of the code in more than 37 per cent of cases. Of the complaints in which there was a formal adjudication, 43 were upheld and 48 rejected. Lord McGregor paid tribute yesterday to the work of the two tabloid editors who are commission members - Miss Patsy Chapman, editor of the News of the World, and Mr Brian Hitchen, editor of the Daily Star. He said it was unjust to suggest their presence was like 'putting criminals on a committee to reform the criminal law'. He added: 'We owe a great deal to Mr Hitchen and Miss Chapman, who have been criticised most unjustly.' Mr Hitchen said yesterday that a new code of practice for the paper's own journalists, underlining points in the industry code, had been completed this week. It placed considerable stress on intrusion and Mr Hitchen said his staff had been told: 'Don't do anything you would not like done to you.' Lord McGregor warned the press against complacency. He said: 'I can't believe the press will be so foolish as to relax on a feather bed and think that what the government said two years ago will be forgotten, because it won't' Mr David Mellor, the National Heritage secretary, is expected to review the first 18 months of the commission within the next few months. Press Complaints Commission annual report. 1 Salisbury Square, London EC4Y 8AE

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / ITV proposes to block re-runs by rival broadcasters
DOC.TEXT: THE NEW ITV network plans to buy rights to programmes for up to 15 years to keep them out of the hands of rival broadcasters. Mr Greg Dyke, chairman of the ITV Association and chief executive of London Weekend Television, said yesterday that ITV wanted to buy the right to show a programme three times over 10 years. There would also be an option for a further five years. 'What we are trying to do is defend ITV and not find its programmes used against it,' Mr Dyke said. He was speaking as ITV published the details of the new centralised ITV network and the proposed contracts that will govern programme commissioning and purchase in the future. The new policy on buying rights is expected to be investigated by the Office of Fair Trading in addition to its general responsibility under broadcasting legislation to ensure the network arrangements are open and fair. Mr Dyke said the ITV companies did not want to fall into the trap of networks in the US, where re-runs of their old programmes shown by independent stations and on cable television had eaten into audience share. The ITV move to control rights and often keep programmes on the shelf for years will undermine hopes that a secondary market will develop in the UK for the rights to programmes already shown once on national commercial television. The strategy will prove controversial with independent producers, who want to keep as many of the secondary rights in programmes as possible to sell in other markets. Mr Dyke said yesterday ITV would if necessary be prepared to pay more to guarantee full rights to programmes, and added that it was very much a buyers' market for programmes. ITV might end up 'buying less or not buying at all' from producers who did not want to sell 10-year rights. If approved by the OFT, the new policy, which would take effect from September next year, might have a significant effect on Channel 4, which has scored significant ratings successes with repeats of popular ITV programmes such as the detective series Inspector Morse. In future, the ITV network will be put together by a centralised system run by a chief executive and a network director, who will be spending an annual programme budget of about Pounds 500m.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Phone codes may cost industry Pounds 3bn: Telecom managers association urges Oftel to delay for at least two years proposals on extra digit for numbers
DOC.TEXT: CHANGES planned for telephone codes may cost industry more than Pounds 3bn, according to an organisation representing large telephone users. The Telecommunications Managers Association (TMA) has urged Oftel, the telecommunications regulator, to shelve proposals to introduce new codes in spring 1994 for at least two years. Oftel announced last September that all codes would have the digit '1' inserted after the initial '0' to cope with a shortage of telephone numbers, caused by growing competition in telephone services and increased demand for numbers. For example, Birmingham's 021 code would become 0121 while London's 071 and 081 would become 0171 and 0181. Its Pounds 3bn estimate of the cost takes into account modifying - or even scrapping - equipment, reprinting stationery and advertising the change. The TMA's objections have already stopped Oftel from giving final approval for the code change - Oftel's internal estimates put the cost at only Pounds 200m. A national campaign to alert customers, due to have started at the beginning of this month, was postponed at short notice. The delay is worrying parts of the industry. BT, Britain's largest telecommunications group, and the Telecommunications Users' Association, another user group, believe any further delay will give customers even less time to prepare for the change. In addition to the high cost of the planned change, the TMA has told Oftel that it would not even meet the difficulty of a shortage of numbers and that, in a few years, there would be further number changes and yet more disruption. Instead of a wholesale change to codes, it has proposed a stopgap scheme to buy time while Oftel examines whether there is a better long-term solution. The TMA's idea would involve taking codes from rural communities, where there are few users, and reallocating them to the areas with a shortage. Its fears of further disruption are confirmed by the fact that BT has recently put a proposal to Oftel that would involve more than a million customers in five cities changing both their codes and numbers. Numbers in Leeds, Nottingham, Bristol, Sheffield and Leicester would change from six digits to seven, while their current codes would be replaced with prefixes from the series '0111', '0112', '0113'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Sony and Thames join bid for Channel 5
DOC.TEXT: THAMES Television and Sony Pictures International have joined the Five TV consortium to bid for the Channel 5 licence. The agreement, about to be announced, means that there are now two powerful, potentially well funded groups competing for the new national channel capable of reaching about three quarters of the population. Last month TV-am, Mr Conrad Black's Daily Telegraph group and Time Warner, the world's largest media group, signed an agreement in principle to bid for the new channel. Last week another announced bidder, Mr Silvio Berlusconi's Fininvest group, decided not to go ahead. In addition to Thames and Sony Pictures, the parent group of the Columbia and Tristar Hollywood studios, Canwest Global Communications, a Canadian-based international broadcaster, has signed heads of agreement to join Five TV. Canwest's interests include a stake in TV3, the new television channel in New Zealand. The Five TV consortium was founded by Mr Chris Rowley, a former IBA executive, Primetime the independent production and distribution group, and Mr Moses Znaimer, founder of City TV in Toronto, who will be chief executive. The decision by Thames Television to take a stake in a Channel 5 bidder is a further sign of the company's desire to remain a broadcaster. The company, which was outbid in last year's competitive tenders for new ITV franchises, ceases to be an ITV broadcaster at the end of December. It has already announced the setting up of a satellite channel in a joint venture with the BBC. Thames is likely to take only a 15 per cent stake in Five TV, the maximum allowed to retain its independent producer status. Channel 5 will be an expensive project to get off the ground because the winner of the licence will have to pay for its own transmitters and the cost of retuning 3m video recorders, which will suffer interference from the Channel 5 signal.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Space satellite sent into new orbit
DOC.TEXT: INTELSAT last night successfully propelled its Dollars 157m telecommunications satellite into a temporary orbit, preparatory to moving it into its operational orbit. The satellite is to be lowered into its final orbit in time for it to start work this summer. This followed its rescue by US astronauts during the first three-man space walk. The mission to save the satellite has brought Nasa, the US space agency, its most sensational success since its re-organisation that followed the explosion of the shuttle Challenger in 1986. It had taken three tries before the astronauts, travelling at 17,000 miles an hour, were able to snatch the elusive satellite on Wednesday night. They set aside the bulky 'capture bar' which had been unsuccessfully employed to snare the the 4.5-tonne satellite, and caught it by hand. Once it was brought into the shuttle bay, the astronauts attached a new 12-tonne rocket motor and prepared it. The mission was performed at the behest of a consortium of 22 countries which own and operate the global communications satellite system. Intelsat paid Dollars 150m up front and unreturnable to Nasa because the satellite is expected to reap more than Dollars 1bn in business. So strong was its faith in Nasa - which has never failed on six previous missions to repair or recapture errant satellites - that Intelsat failed to insure the mission, which would have added about Dollars 43m to its costs. The entire Shuttle flight is reckoned estimated to have cost about Dollars 1bn. Nasa officials have been extolling its worth.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Accord on BCCI attacked by senator in US
DOC.TEXT: THE proposed Dollars 1.7bn settlement for creditors of the collapsed Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI) came under fire in the US senate yesterday as Senator John Kerry, who has been investigating BCCI, described the proposal as 'unfair'. He made his remarks to Mr Brian Smouha, the BCCI liquidator, who gave his first Congressional testimony on the BCCI affair. The senator, at a foreign affairs sub-committee hearing, called into question the settlement - by which the government of Abu Dhabi would pay BCCI creditors between 30 and 40 cents in the dollar - because creditors would be forced to waive their rights to bring any legal action against Abu Dhabi. The government there is the BCCI majority shareholder. Mr Kerry also criticised Abu Dhabi for its failure thus far to supply US authorities with key BCCI documents and with former executives of the bank being held under house arrest. The senator said the BCCI creditors 'deserve to know that, if there are deep pockets that fleece them, they have the right to take action.' He added: 'You have to understand who is responsible for the BCCI affair before you strike some deal that wipes this all away. I would call this an unfair trade practice.' Mr Ahmed al Sayegh, a director of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company and a member of the government's BCCI working group, said Abu Dhabi had no involvement in the frauds perpetrated by BCCI. He added that Abu Dhabi is in talks with the US Justice Department over the possibility of making available BCCI documents and witnesses now in Abu Dhabi. Mr al Sayegh also criticised former BCCI auditors Price Waterhouse as 'negligent', and said the accounting firm 'should accept responsibility for their failure to uncover the true position year after year.' Mr Smouha responded to Mr Kerry's criticism by saying that what he had sought was to 'negotiate a commercial solution.' The settlement, which will be reviewed at a UK high court hearing in June, will need to be approved by BCCI creditors and courts in the UK, Luxembourg and the Cayman Islands. A former top prosecutor claimed in earlier testimony to the sub-committee he had been impeded last year by the Justice Department in his efforts to obtain documents and bring indictments against BCCI. Mr Dexter Lehtinen, US attorney in Miami until four months ago, complained that, despite numerous written requests to Washington, the department declined to give him permission to enforce subpoenas demanding crucial BCCI documents about the bank's Luxembourg and other non-US operations. Anger at MP's claim, Page 10

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Partial reprieve for owl
DOC.TEXT: THE US administration yesterday gave a partial reprieve to the northern spotted owl, but proposed sharp reductions in the conservation areas set aside for the threatened species, writes George Graham in Washington. It also agreed to allow logging in a portion of the ancient Oregon forest that provides the bird's habitat. The Endangered Species Committee agreed to let the federal Bureau of Land Management sell timber on 13 parcels of land, although logging there might jeopardise the owl's existence. Only once, in 1979, had the committee by-passed the Endangered Species Act by granting such an exemption. The Interior Secretary proposed a plan to cut the federal land set aside for the birds from 5.4m to 2.8m acres.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Star wanes for the 'upstart' investor from Bombay
DOC.TEXT: TO MILLIONS in Bombay, the success of Mr Harshad Mehta in making the jump from low-paid office clerk to financial magnate, and self-proclaimedly largest taxpayer in the country, has provided proof that there is an escape from urban squalor. But Mr Mehta is now under investigation by police for alleged improper use of money from the interbank market in government securities to fund his equity dealings. His rise and fall mirrors the best and the worst of the Bombay stock market. As the market climbed this year from under 2,000 on the Bombay Stock Exchange 30-share index to a peak in April of 4,467 largely under the pressure of Mr Mehta's relentless buying (yesterday it closed 36.65 lower at 3,394.48) he became the symbol of the path to easy wealth. In Bombay's rather stuffy financial community, he was an upstart. The son of a cloth trader, he was proud of having done badly at school and college. He mocked the Indian education system by describing himself as a 'B Com, 37 per cent'. He quit working for an insurance company in 1982 and set up a portfolio investment company called by the characteristically aggressive name of Growmore. He liked the wealth that came from success - buying a large fleet of cars, and installing himself in a bungalow overlooking the sea that has a small golf course attached. The establishment eventually accepted him. Shortly after being raided by income tax officials, he was invited by state-owned television to offer his budget night comments. He was immensely well-connected among politicians, bankers and senior civil servants - buying and selling shares for them in transactions that could now come under close scrutiny. He became a legend for the way he could push up share prices, focusing on what he considered undervalued shares and sticking with them. Mr Mehta purchased 5 per cent of Associated Cement Corporation - helping to push up its share price from Rs350 at the beginning of 1991 to an April peak of Rs11,500. He bought similar 5 per cent portfolio stakes in other groups such as Appollo tyres or Piramal luggage - driving up their price as well. Part of Mr Mehta's success was that he knew the inner mechanism of an archaic market structure. The other reason was that he never seemed to lack funds. Last month part of the reason for this emerged when State Bank of India, the largest commercial bank, discovered that it had paid out Rs6.2bn (Pounds 122m) for securities or bankers' receipts (promissory notes in the interbank securities market) which it had never received. State Bank forced Mr Mehta to settle his account - a move that showed up the strains in Mr Mehta's finances. He seems to have turned to help from National Housing Bank, headed by Mr M J Pherwani, who has since resigned. A large cheque issued by National Housing Bank to ANZ Grindlays, India's biggest foreign-owned bank, was endorsed on the back to be credited to Mr Mehta's account. Mr Mehta is a quiet 37-year-old, full of charm. He holds his own in conversation, partly because of the power of his wealth. But as police investigators hover around him, he will have great difficulty in preserving all that he has gained.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Ramos and Santiago level in poll battle
DOC.TEXT: THE BATTLE of nerves among leading candidates in last Monday's Philippine general election heightened yesterday as counting of votes proceeded at a snail's pace. The camp of Mr Fidel Ramos, the administration-backed candidate for president, yesterday claimed it would fortify its slim lead over Mrs Miriam Defensor Santiago once the returns from nine of the country's 13 regions were tallied. Mr Ramos' Lakas-National Union of Christian Democrats party said Mrs Santiago's lead in metropolitan Manila and other urban centres could easily be offset by Mr Ramos' winning margins in the nine regions. Mrs Santiago, however, said votes from the countryside 'will further widen' her lead in the Media-Citizens Quick Count, an independent tabulation sanctioned by the watchdog Commission on Elections. (Comelec). Other estimates put Mr Ramos slightly ahead. The camp of Mr Eduardo Cojuangco, third in the count, yesterday also expressed confidence of emerging as winner. Vice President Salvador Laurel, trailing in the seven-member field, conceded defeat. Mr Ramon Mitra, Speaker of Congress, also acknowledged he had no real chance of success.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Pakistan raises tax base to cut budget deficit
DOC.TEXT: THE Pakistani government yesterday announced an annual budget containing new taxes to narrow its deficit while claiming that it intends to carry on with liberalisation of the economy. The measures did not appear to hit ordinary poor Pakistanis directly, as costs for domestic consumption of basic needs including food, electricity and water were untouched. Among measures announced to raise additional revenues of PR6.8bn (Pounds 152m) under the central excise budget, telephone call rates were raised by some 30 per cent. A 5 per cent duty was also introduced on unprocessed fabrics exported from Pakistan. An additional tax was announced for owners of cars of over 1,000 cc to encourage use of smaller vehicles. Mr Sartaj Aziz, finance minister, said in his budget speech that the government intends to widen the sales tax net to include items such as air-conditioners, ammunition and photographic equipment. Computerisation is to be used to improve efficiency of the tax system to broaden the tax base. Successive Pakistani governments have been unable to prevent large-scale tax evasion due to widespread corruption in assessment and collection systems. The government hopes for an additional PR3.62bn annually from improvements in collection of income, wealth and property taxes. Some incentives were also announced for the private sector, in an effort to continue with liberalisation of the economy. The budget provided details of a five-year plan under which a tax rate of 66 per cent for banking companies would be reduced to 55 per cent, and for publicly held companies from 44 per cent to 30 per cent. Tariffs ranging up to 90 per cent were reduced by 10 per cent on import of refrigerators, televisions and washing machines. Yesterday's budget appeared to be an attempt by the two-year-old government of Mr Nawaz Sharif to avoid measures which would be unpopular among the majority of the population. Most Pakistanis are not likely to be hit by such measures as increased telephone costs or car tax. But the government appeared to have made no headway on difficult decisions such as cutting the large defence budget.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Tortuous undoing of apartheid: South Africa's complex constitutional 'summit'
DOC.TEXT: 'Fine to warm, with storms brewing' THAT was how Mr Thabo Mbeki, one of the chief constitutional negotiators of the African National Congress, characterised the prospects for success at talks today on the political future of South Africa. When white, black, coloured and Indian South Africans meet today at the Convention for a Democratic South Africa (Codesa), the multi-party forum shaping the country's constitutional future, they will be tackling the central questions of post-apartheid politics: how will power be distributed in the new South Africa? Will there be majority rule or power-sharing? By Saturday night, the 19 parties to Codesa may have agreed to form a multi-racial interim executive which would bring blacks to power for the first time in 350 years. Such a government would include the ANC (the largest black group), the ruling National party (which represents most whites and probably a majority of coloureds and Indians), and the powerful Zulu party Inkatha, as well as parties from the nominally independent black 'homelands', the liberal Democratic party and smaller ethnically-based parties. It would remain in office until elections were held for an interim national assembly, probably early next year. But before they can strike a deal on the interim executive, the 200-odd delegates to today's plenary session of Codesa must either resolve the issue of how a new constitution is to be drawn up - or agree to differ on it for the moment. The bottom-line positions of the two main parties - the National party, which continues to demand what would in effect be a white veto in the constitution-making body, and the ANC which wants decisions taken by a two-thirds majority - reveals a big gap which they were yesterday frantically attempting to close. Since last December, five Codesa working groups have met for at least two days weekly to seek agreement on removing obstacles to free political activity, on interim government, on the shape of a constitution-making body, on the future of the homelands, and on implementation. They have spawned sub-committees, technical committees, steering committees and management committees, which have struggled for thousands of hours to reach consensus. Their deliberations, reported in confusing detail in the local press, have alternately baffled and bored ordinary South Africans. And though they can claim to have made progress, only the upcoming plenary will determine whether there is breakdown or breakthrough. On some important issues, consensus has already been achieved. At the first plenary session of Codesa last December, the two sides agreed on a 'declaration of intent' which committed them to a multi- party political system with 'freedom, equality and security for all', an independent judiciary, a bill of rights, separation of powers among the executive, the legislature and the judiciary with appropriate checks and balances, proportional representation, and an end to racial discrimination. The Inkatha Freedom party, which refused to subscribe to the declaration last December, has now said it will sign, after an amendment which raises the possibility of federalism. Since then, the working groups have agreed to restore South African citizenship to the residents of the homelands of Transkei, Ciskei, Venda and Bophuthatswana, and agreed 'in principle' that they should be re-incorporated into the republic (though the wording is vague and the deal fragile). They have agreed on the structure of the interim executive, to be called the Transitional Executive Council (TEC), which would include a representative from each of the 19 Codesa parties and take decisions by an 80 per cent majority. The council would be a sort of 'super cabinet' with powers to compel the existing cabinet (which would remain in office) to comply with its decisions. But its scope would be limited: the council would not run the government, but deal only with levelling the political playing field in the run-up to multi-racial elections, ensuring joint control over the security forces, the state media, the electoral process and some aspects of foreign affairs. The council, which would be appointed by Codesa, could take office within two or three months. But the ANC has said it will block it until agreement is reached on the constitution-making body which would both draw up a new constitution and make ordinary laws during the transition to democracy. That may be within reach today and tomorrow, but only by postponing the most contentious issues - powers of regional government, the supreme authority of central government, joint control of security services - until later. Yesterday the two sides were still fighting over the size of the majority needed in the constitution-making body. The ANC wanted that body to take decisions by a two-thirds majority, while the National party is demanding a 75 per cent majority, which would in effect give it and its allies (whites and other conservatives), a veto over the constitution. Though the percentages appear close, the dispute is substantive: the final figure will determine whether blacks have the power to write what is essentially a majority-rule constitution, or whether whites and other minorities can entrench minority protections. If talks break down, the ANC will probably mount a campaign of mass protest, including a national general strike, which will lead to more civil disruption. The National party, for its part, may not easily buckle under the pressure. But in the end, both parties concede they will return to the negotiating table with the same political problems to solve, the same backlogs of economic development, the same burden of joblessness - and even less time in which to solve them.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Keating accused of hampering probe into alleged corruption
DOC.TEXT: THE FUTURE of two senior members of Australia's federal Labor government was in doubt yesterday after Mr Paul Keating, the prime minister, demanded a written account of their relationship with a businessman facing criminal charges in the Marshall Islands. Separately, Mr Keating was accused by a Western Australian royal commission of hampering investigations into alleged corruption between Labor politicians and local businessmen by blocking access to tax records. The allegations mark the end of a five-month honeymoon period during which Mr Keating has increased Labor's opinion poll rating to within three percentage points of the opposition conservatives. The government trailed by 18 points when he replaced Mr Bob Hawke in December. The most serious allegations revolve around Senator Graham Richardson, the transport and communications minister, whose brother-in-law, Mr Greg Symons, is on trial for forgery in the Marshall Islands, a US protectorate in the Pacific. Mr Richardson admits meeting Mr Symons in his office, writing a letter of introduction for him, and telephoning Mr Amata Kabua, Marshall Islands president, after Mr Symons was arrested. It later emerged that Senator Kerry Sibraa, Senate president, wrote to the Australian embassy in Washington in November, urging the diplomatic service to help arrange meetings for Mr Symons with US officials. Both senators deny wrongdoing, but the affair has left Mr Keating open to allegations of protecting political allies. In Perth, Mr Tony Templeton, counsel assisting the royal commission, said investigations into the collapse of Mr Laurie Connell's Rothwells merchant bank had been limited by Mr Keating's refusal to allow access to tax records. Mr Keating said he refused access on the advice of Mr Trevor Boucher, the tax commissioner.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Libya claims renunciation of terrorism
DOC.TEXT: LIBYA claimed yesterday that it was renouncing terrorism but again refused to hand over the two men accused by the US and Britain of responsibility for bombing a PanAm aircraft over Scotland in 1988 which killed 270 people, writes Our Middle East Staff. Mr Ibrahim Mohammed Beshari, Libyan foreign minister, said in Indonesia, where he is attending a meeting of the non-aligned movement, his country's laws prevented extradition of the two suspects. A foreign ministry statement issued similtaneously in Tripoli referred only to the second part of UN Security Council's Resolution 731 which called on Tripoli to cut all links to terrorist groups.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Islamic bank opens in Jakarta
DOC.TEXT: Indonesia's first Islamic bank opens today with the express support of President Suharto and other leading members of the government. Bank Muamalat Indonesia will not offer interest rates but will instead pay 'profits' accrued from deposits, writes william Keeling in Jakarta. 'It's a sham, really. Profit payments are interest rates under a different name,' said one local banker. Critics argue that the timing of launching the bank, which has a capital of Rp100bn (Pounds 27.6m), is designed to boost the Islamic credentials of the ruling Golkar party in the first week of an election campaign.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Seoul adds to Hyundai squeeze
DOC.TEXT: THE South Korean government yesterday threatened new credit sanctions against Hyundai a day before Mr Chung Ju-yung, the founder of the conglomerate, formally launches his independent presidential campaign. The Office of Bank Supervision (OBS) said it would bar Hyundai from making new investments or acquiring real estate unless it collects Won202.7bn (Pounds 145m) Hyundai lent to the Chung family earlier this year. The Chung family is believed to have used the funds to help finance creation of the Unification National party, which is expected to nominate Mr Chung today as its candidate in the December presidential election. Hyundai recently promised it would recover the loans by the end of the year, but the OBS said the money should be repaid by this summer. Hyundai has suffered credit restrictions as a result of the dispute. It believes that it recently lost a contract to build the Tsing Ma bridge for the Hong Kong airport project because the squeeze on its credit undermined confidence in its financial position.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Tear-gas attack on Phola Park squatters' camp
DOC.TEXT: Residents of Phola Park squatters' camp near Johannesburg try to escape yesterday from a tear-gas attack during a police and military raid on the camp, an area of continuing factional violence. The latest turmoil came as Amnesty International, the international human rights organisation, warned that talks on South Africa's future were taking place 'against a background of increasing political violence and terror in the black townships, squatter camps and on commuter trains.' Amnesty also says the South African government has not taken firm enough action to end involvement by the security forces in torture and political killings. Unless they are brought to justice, 'the current climate of fear and high loss of life will continue, threatening prospects for a democratic transition in South Africa.' Amnesty notes that 'not a single prosecution has yet resulted' from any official inquiries into police and military complicity in assassinations of black activists.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Boeing wins Dollars 600m Malaysian order
DOC.TEXT: MALAYSIA Airlines yesterday placed firm orders worth Dollars 600m (Pounds 339m) with Boeing of the US for 17 737-400 twin engine aircraft. The deal comes at a time when general demand for narrow-body jets remains sluggish. Boeing plans to reduce monthly production of 737s from 21 to 14 aircraft from October, to adjust to the weaker market. The deal with Malaysia Airlines involves 12 new orders for 737s and the conversion of five earlier options. It brings to 45 the number of 146-seater 737-400 jets the Kuala Lumpur carrier has ordered, making it Boeing's biggest airline customer for this aircraft. The airline plans to use the new aircraft to expand its domestic and regional services. The new aircraft will be powered by CFM56-3 engines made by the CFM International joint venture between General Electric of the US and Snecma of France. Boeing has also delivered the last of its 707 Awacs (Airborne Warning and Control System) aircraft to the Royal Air Force. Production of the 707 Awacs ended last year and Boeing is now offering a militarised version of its twin-engine 767 airliner as the future Awacs airframe. Rolls-Royce jet engine sales to China have been boosted by an order for three Fokker 100 aircraft from China's Civil Aviation Administration (CAAC). The UK group will supply Tay 650 engines to power CAAC's twin-engine Fokker 100 airliners.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Nynex plans Japan-UK fibre optic cable
DOC.TEXT: A CONSORTIUM of international investors, led by Nynex, the north-east US regional telephone group, is considering installing the world's longest undersea fibre optic telecommunications cable, costing Dollars 1bn (Pounds 565m) and stretching from Britain to Japan. The group will outline plans next week to officials from many leading telephone companies. It aims to hold a further meeting in the autumn, to try to persuade the companies to buy capacity on the cable. Nynex stressed that the project was still in the early planning stages, with details of the cable's route, landing points and financing still to be worked out. Other members of the consortium are Marubeni, the Japanese trading company, Dallah-Al Baraka, a Saudi Arabian bank, and Gulf Associates, a New York-based firm specialising in Middle Eastern business. Some 95 per cent of the telecommunications traffic between the UK and Japan currently goes by satellite. The only cable linking the two regions via the Middle East is one between Singapore and France. This is a co-axial cable, which is less efficient than fibre optic cable. However, a second fibre optic cable is being built. The proposed Nynex cable would have much greater capacity than the Singapore ones. Its 120,000 circuits would be capable of carrying 600,000 simultaneous conversations. Fibre optic signals are much clearer than satellite ones, and do not suffer from time delays. The Nynex venture, known as Fibreoptic Link Around the Globe (Flag), would aim to complete the cable in 1996. It would have 14 landing points along the route. Nynex, one of the 'Baby Bell' telecommunications companies formed from the 1984 anti-trust break-up of American Telephone and Telegraph, has been conducting feasibility studies for two years. The move follows its failure to get US approval for a transatlantic cable between the UK and New York, because of the strict anti-trust court rules governing the 'Baby Bells'. These rules would not apply to a cable which did not land in the US.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Export credit rates review
DOC.BYLINE: By DAVID DODWELL, World Trade Editor
DOC.TEXT: THE premiums Australia's exporters pay to insure against default by foreign buyers are under review, with higher rates possible on trade with riskier countries, according to the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation. According to Mr Graham Nottle, manager of the Treasury and Loans division of EFIC, the review is due to be complete by the end of June: 'The objective would be to move to a more market rate of premium,' Mr Nottle noted: 'We are adjusting premiums with policy holders. They may not pay more, but may take on more risk themselves.' The Australian review follows recent decisions by Hermes, the leading German export credit agency, and the US Eximbank, to adjust their premium structures.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Globe-trotting Czechs seek new markets - The search to replace Soviet sales
DOC.BYLINE: By ARIANE GENILLARD and ANTHONY ROBINSON
DOC.TEXT: THE SEARCH by Czechoslovakia for new markets last month took President Vaclav Havel to Japan and South Korea while his prime minister, Mr Marian Calfa, set off for South Africa at the head of a 50-strong delegation of Czech and Slovak businessmen. Such top-level globe-trotting reflects the urgency of finding new export outlets to replace the former high dependence on Soviet trade. But it also marks a desire to re-establish a presence in global markets beyond the European Community and attract new investment to update Czechoslovakia's product range and increase the attractiveness of its exports. Until this happens the country remains locked into its existing pattern of exporting a wide range of relatively low- or medium-technology engineering and consumer goods while importing energy and raw materials from the former Soviet Union and more sophisticated investment and consumer goods from the west. Despite these product limitations, willingness to trim margins and easier access to the EC and markets of the European Free Trade Association (Efta) have already made western Europe the main market for Czechoslovak exports. This has helped offset the loss of the former Soviet bloc trading system Comecon, which accounted for 61 per cent of overall trade in 1989 but less than 30 per cent last year. Growth in trade with the west however has not yet been strong enough to compensate for the collapse of Comecon. Total exports of 321bn koruna (Dollars 11bn) in 1991 were 94 per cent of their 1990 level and nearly 30 per cent down on the Dollars 14.3bn of 1989. Imports have shrunk even more sharply to Dollars 10.1bn from Dollars 13.2bn in 1990. Lower imports reflect both a recession which cut gross domestic product by nearly 15 per cent last year and the shift away from energy-intensive, polluting heavy industry. Imports of crude oil from Russia, for example, dropped from 16m tons in 1989 to 11m tons last year. With imports dropping faster than exports, Czechoslovakia's balance of trade recorded a 25bn koruna surplus in 1991. The collapse of exports to the former Soviet Union in particular has deepened the domestic recession, especially in Slovakia with its heavy concentration of arms factories and other plants geared specifically to the old Soviet market. Within the lower overall volume, however, trade with EC markets grew strongly, to account for 40.7 per cent of Czechoslovakia's total exports last year compared with 24 per cent in 1988. A third of imports came from the EC, against only a quarter from the former Soviet Union, although imports from the former Comecon countries as a whole were virtually identical to the EC share at 32.2 per cent of the total. The trend towards closer integration in the EC is expected to continue as Czechoslovakia, along with Hungary and Poland, reaps the benefits of a recent association agreement with the EC. Germany, which accounts for two-thirds of the estimated Dollars 800m foreign capital invested in Czechoslovakia last year, took 19.4 per cent of Czechoslovak exports and supplied 20.1 per cent of all imports in 1991. It is expected soon to replace the former Soviet Union as the largest single export market. But the influence of the German-speaking world does not stop with Germany. Austria and Switzerland are also becoming important trading partners. In 1991, Efta, of which they are members, accounted for 10 per cent of Czechoslovakia's total trade. Business with Efta countries is expected to be boosted by a recent trade agreement which takes effect on July 1. But, as indicated by the official visits to Asia and Africa, and the opening soon of a trade office in San Francisco to supplement existing offices in New York and Washington, Czechoslovakia is also looking further afield. Until now trade with the Pacific rim countries has been minimal. Czechoslovak exports to Japan for example were a mere Dollars 71m last year, mainly traditional consumer goods such as Bohemian glass and porcelain and hops for brewing Japanese beer. Exports to South Korea were only Dollars 8m. Japan traditionally likes to boost trade links before following up with investment, and in the long run the main purpose of the high-profile state visit to both Japan and South Korea was to raise Czechoslovakia's profile as a profitable venue for investment. Africa was also neglected under the old regime, with trade limited mainly to shipments of military materiel in obligatory support of Moscow's support for revolutionary regimes.
