At the same time, he was at pains to underline the distinction made in the treaty between the 'core functions' of the Community's institutions and those areas, such as foreign policy, immigration and the fight against drugs, terrorism and crime, which remained subject to intergovernmental co-operation. On the controversial issue of EC frontier controls, Mr Garel-Jones said the UK accepted that there must be 'no systematic controls' over the movement of Community nationals.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / World News in Brief: Dissident loses job
DOC.TEXT: Conservative MP Roger Knapman lost his unpaid job as parliamentary private secretary to defence minister Archie Hamilton after telling whips he could not support the Maastricht treaty. Parliament, Page 11

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / World News in Brief: Prisoners in rooftop protest
DOC.TEXT: Prisoners were demonstrating on a roof at Winchester prison, Hampshire last night after a jail disturbance in which 20 young offenders barricaded themselves into a wing of the prison.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / World News in Brief: Riots in Lagos
DOC.TEXT: Police fired teargas to break up crowds in the Nigerian capital, Lagos, as they protested for a second day against poverty and fuel shortages, attacking banks and offices in the main business area.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Survey: FT Traveller, Genoa (10) - Part of the fabric of life / Wine, Vine cultivation on the steep and windy slopes of the Cinque Terre requires strong leg muscles and a head for heights
DOC.TEXT: 'YOU NEED a passion to do it. Many only keep up the tradition out of respect for their parents.' So Mr Nello Capris, a leading Genoese wine expert, describes the task of vine cultivation in the wild Cinque Terre, where strong leg muscles and a head for heights are as much pre-requisites for success as green fingers with the grape. Producing wine on the steep and windy slopes of the Cinque Terre, the five small villages just north of La Spezia, around 75 miles south of Genoa, is, says Mr Capris, 'a heroic task'. The narrow terraces perched along the near-vertical hillsides plunging down towards the sea offer little scope for mechanisation. Much of the work, including the carrying, is still done by hand. 'No one could keep a family solely on the income from growing wine,' he explains. 'Growing vines is now virtually all part-time work, either done as a second job or left to those who have already retired.' In spite of the immense difficulties, the wine business has not eroded, like many of the harsh hillsides which face the sea. For growing wine is part of the fabric of life in a region which, in spite of its immense tourist appeal, still depends largely on traditional sources of income for its livelihood. Without their vineyards, the five villages which make up the remote Cinque Terre would still be magnets for visitors on account of their ragged beauty and commanding views, but part of their magic would be lost. It is largely because of tourism that the two white wines of the Cinque Terre - Cinqueterre and Sciaccetra - are among the best known of all Liguria's produce, in spite of the relatively small quantities produced visitors buy the fruity Cinqueterre or, to a much lesser extent, sweet Sciaccetra dessert wine, in much the same decorative three-bottle cardboard packs as are found in other locations where tourism and wine-growing go hand in hand like Rudesheim on the Rhine or the villages south of Strasbourg in Alsace. Like their counterparts elsewhere in Italy, the growers of the Cinque Terre have recently woken up to the possibilities of 'agro-tourism'. Largely united in the Co-operativa Agricoltora Cinqueterre, the local growers are now starting to convert some of the small abandoned shacks dotted around the hillsides into basic accommodation for visitors. Tourists searching for five-star luxury should look elsewhere. But the provision of electricity and running water to the huts, traditionally used for storage and even temporary accommodation for workers on outlying vineyards, could appeal to the thousands of walkers and ramblers who descend on the region each year. Meanwhile, for the local economy, converting the huts could persuade visitors to stay for longer than the usual day-trip, which contributes little revenue to the community. By combining their interests, the members of the co-operative have helped to maintain an industry marked by a steady decline in the past. 'The problem is that the population is getting older, and the young people are drifting away. You can't change it,' says Mr Capris. Economic pressures make it increasingly difficult for younger members of wine-growing families to maintain the family business. The co-operative may not be able completely to reverse the tide, but it is at least trying to make the best of what is left. Agreement has already been reached with some local growers to give the co-operative the right of first refusal over their land should they decide to go out of business. Meanwhile, the co-operative, which comprises around three quarters of the local producers, has also strengthened their lobbying powers when it comes to outside bodies. Most recently, they secured funding from the European Community to install around 30 narrow mini-railways up some of the steepest local slopes to make the task of transporting grapes after harvest less of an endurance test. The Cinque Terre is the best known of the wine-growing areas of Liguria, but the region as a whole is as unfamiliar to most Italians as it is to foreigners on account of its limited output. Producing only around 300,000 hectolitres of wine a year, Liguria is one of Italy's smallest wine-growing zones, representing barely 0.5 per cent of national output. However, it is slowly gaining ground, reckons Mr Capris. Quality has improved, especially over the past decade. 'Ligurian wine was not always produced that professionally. It didn't always look good, nor keep well. Now we've managed to convince more top restaurants to take local wines, and they've been pleased with their choice,' he says. Like much in Liguria, the wine-growing region forms two sides of an arc with Genoa at its head. Although most of the wine business is concentrated in two areas around Albenga to the west and La Spezia to the east, even Genoa itself has some wines. The city's wines do not merit being classed among Italy's top-drawer 'Denominazione di Origine Controllata' (DOC) rating. However, they are ranked one notch down the scale as table wines coming from a strictly defined geographical region. Even that may seem surprising to those who remember that the local white Valpolcevera was known for decades as the standard tipple for Genoa's thirsty dockers. 'Mornings would start with a swig of wine and continue in much the same way all day,' jokes Mr Capris. However, change is now on the cards for Genoa's local wine, as well as for Verminto di Ne and Bianco di Verici, two other local whites. Subject to a variety of approvals, including the European Commission, the local wines will eventually all be called Golfo del Tigullio, a name harking back to the inhabitants of the Gulf of Genoa in pre-Roman times. While wines from around La Spezia, including the Cinque Terre and the nearby Colli di Luni stretching south to Tuscany, account for around half Liguria's output, wines from areas to the west of Genoa form much of the remainder. The Rossesse di Dolceacqua DOC, produced in about five villages around Ventimiglia on the border with France, accounts for a fraction of that total. The red wines, similar to the well-known Barolo from Piedmont to the north, have been produced for centuries and are strong and mature quickly. But rather than seeking out obscure growths, visitors to Genoa would do well to remember the names of Pigato and Vermintino, two of Liguria's most commonly found wines, which make up the bulk of the output from the western Riviera. The two whites are 'classic Ligurian wines', says Mr Capris, light and fruity. 'Some experts even claim to detect a a hint of salt, brought in from the sea,' he adds, somewhat sceptically. Both wines, along with the less familiar red Rossesse, form part of the 'Riviera Ligure di Ponente' DOC, which is concentrated around Albenga. Surprisingly, little or no wine is produced from the shady valleys in the hinterland behind Genoa and the other coastal resorts. The relatively high altitude of the Apennines and the cool temperatures are the main culprits, although depopulation has also played a role. 'There were few people there before, and there are even fewer now,' notes Mr Capris. As in parts of the Cinque Terre, many smaller or less accessible vineyards have been abandoned or sold. The Italian legal system, which requires an estate to be split between all the heirs, has not helped, as holdings have been divided into increasingly small fractions over the years. And Liguria's harsh geography, with a lack of land which can be cultivated easily, has encouraged new owners to convert fields once devoted to wine to other, more profitable or essential, uses. Although a law now exists to give tax advantages to farmers amalgamating wine-growing plots, human interests often come into play. 'Ligurians are very individualistic. Even setting up the Cinque Terre co-operative was a herculean task,' says Mr Capris. The economic pressures on growers are particularly evident around Albenga, one of the few parts of Liguria where the coastal strip broadens out from a thin belt, sandwiched between the mountains and the sea, into a sizeable area of flat, easily arable land. Here, the competition is from horticulture, which is already dominant further to the west. Growing flowers is not only less labour intensive and more easily mechanised, but more profitable, too. Such factors mean Ligurian wine will always remain a speciality in Italy. The difficulties of growing vines in the region are reflected in the price of grapes, which, at around L2,000 a kilo, is almost three times as high as in neighbouring Piedmont. Those costs are naturally mirrored in the price of a bottle of Ligurian wine, which at around L8,000-L10,000, is above the Italian average. However, local growers are not despondent, particularly in view of the greater recognition they have received over the past 10-15 years. And for visitors who want to impress their Ligurian hosts, a gift of Sciaccetra, which weighs in at around L50,000-60,000 a bottle, should go down particularly well.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Survey: FT Traveller, Genoa (9) - Football's year to remember / Sports, The Columbus festivities in 1992 include international cycling, water polo, athletics, roller skating and sailing events
DOC.TEXT: IN A COUNTRY totally dominated by football, Genoa is certainly no exception. It was here in 1893 that a group of British subjects founded the first Italian sporting society, the Genoa Cricket and Athletic Club, at the local British consulate. The cricket and athletics gave way to association football, and today the city is divided between Genoa, the club that descended from the society of yore, and Sampdoria, the side that brought home the Italian championship title last season. The title was captured by a team revitalised through the investments of chairman Paolo Mantovani, who in just over 10 years pushed what had long been considered 'Genoa's other team' to success against clubs backed by the largest business empires in Italy (Agnelli's Juventus and Berlusconi's Milan). Whether sustained by a prestigious past or more recent successes, the Genovese are first and foremost grandstand 'supporters': impassioned, sometimes even sombre, always extremely fair - and rather satisfied with results in 1992. For the first time in their history, both teams have been involved at the highest levels of international tournaments at the same time. While the Genoa club missed out on the UEFA cup, it had the consolation prize of playing in the semi-finals and achieving two historic victories against Liverpool. Meanwhile, the Sampdoria fans are busy organising their expedition to Wembley, where their team will battle Barcelona for the Champions' Cup. But the 1992 sporting year in Genoa will not be dominated by football: the Columbus festivities include international cycling, water polo, track and field and sailing events. The Genovese have become aware that the Columbus festival offers an opportunity for relaunching the city, and that sport can encourage the process. So they have partly overcome their traditional reluctance to embark on relatively risky investments. In the case of sports, the financial caution of public authorities and private sponsors even went so far as to penalise activities in which the city was once outstanding. One of the chronic problems afflicting sports in Genoa is a lack of management, facilities and space in which to build arenas and playing fields. The city is now trying to remedy this problem which, for example, resulted in the loss of a basketball team, Emerson, and the shift of the water polo centre to the nearby Riviera, which has better facilities. Other lost opportunities include a world swimming tournament, the baseball World Cup and international boxing, motorcycling and sailing events, and probably the finals of the volleyball World League. So, while the Genovese await new facilities (which will include a new sports arena and the new 'Sciorba' multisports centre), they are seeking to make the most of what they have. In the events that did not escape in 1992 they have demonstrated a new enthusiasm: speed of execution and managerial capacity on the part of organisers and a great deal of interest from the public. The big sport in February was track and field, first with the CUS Genoa Trophy, which attracted international athletes such as Leroy Burrell, the American runner, and Jamaica's Merlene Ottey, both favourites to win sprint gold medals at this year's Olympic Games to be held in Barcelona. This was followed by the three days of the European Indoor Championships, a testing ground for the Olympics, marked by the first participation of teams from Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia. The latest event, following the World Under-20 Fencing Championships last month, was the departure of the Columbus '92 Quincentenary Grand Regatta, with the participation of Spain, Portugal, the UK, Puerto Rico, the United States and, of course, Italy. One hundred and fifty veteran ships, including 25 school vessels, will undertake six legs from Genoa to Liverpool, where they are due to arrive between August 13 and 16 after covering 9,300 miles of ocean sailed in the name of Columbus. One of the organisers of the regatta is the Yacht Club Italiano of Genoa, one of the world's prestigious sailing clubs, which for more than a century has been helping to uphold the city's maritime tradition. Founded in 1879 with the patronage of King Humbert I, the YCI has provided outstanding figures in world sailing, such as the late Beppe Croce, who succeeded Peter Scott as president of the International Yacht Racing Union. With Giovanni Novi at its helm today, the club boasts around 1,000 members who were able to meet the rigorous membership requirements. The most illustrious include leading businessmen such as Raul Gardini, Carlo Bonomi, Gianni Verasi and Giorgio Falck. Genoa will also be the scene of an international cycling competition this year: in addition to the Apennine Tour earlier this month, the Tour of Italy will once again start out from Genoa (May 22-25) after a 12-year absence, with the first pink jersey awarded in the name of Columbus. The APT tennis tour will be in Genoa from June 15 to 21 with the IP cup (won last year by Carl-Uwe Steeb). Thereafter the city will host the World Rollerskating championships (September 3-6), thanks in part to Ingrid Van Marie, the multiple international title winner and Genovese by adoption. Young athletes, ranging from six to 14 years of age, will take part in the national finals of the Youth Games from October 4 to 10; there are 8,000 Italian participants (plus 1,000 Spanish and American guests), who will compete in events scattered throughout the Ligurian region. The final awards ceremony of the Games will be held in the new Expo area inside the port.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Survey: FT Traveller, Genoa (8) - Highs and lows amid the diversity / City guide, Haig Simonian takes a stroll around Genoa to view the contrast between its classic and modern architecture
DOC.TEXT: STAND with your back to elegant via Roma, facing Piazza De Ferrari in the heart of Genoa, and you could be in any well-kept Edwardian city, with the newly-cleaned civic buildings opposite proclaiming their wealth and well-being. The first surprise comes to your left, where the 'new' Carlo Felice opera house demands a closer look. The arcade along via Roma and the imposing portico on the square instantly bring to mind a classical theatre, perhaps a little touched up of late, But it is the huge fly tower, thrusting 200 feet into the sky, which gives the game away. Post-modernism is the theme in architect Aldo Rossi's striking design for one of the best known landmarks, which was partly destroyed in 1944 and only reopened to the public late last year. The fly tower has been the most controversial part of the generally well-received project. A close second came the series of windows and balconies which look over the stage inside. The shuttered windows, evoking the exteriors of a typically Genovese street, led to loud protests from the purists. But the overall effect, which gives the audience the impression it is looking at real life from the outside, is eye-catching and effective. On the same square, but with its baroque main facade just round the corner in Piazza Matteotti off via San: Lorenzo, is the lavishly restored Palazzo Ducale, the best example of the Columbus-led urban revival now taking place in the city. The scaffolding covering the former seat of Genoa's Doges is only just coming down to reveal white walls and gilded ornamentation. The sumptuous interior, not yet open to the public, will provide a new exhibition and meeting space akin to the restored Palazzo Grassi in Venice. A few steps down the hill is the Cathedral of San Lorenzo, another architectural gems. Its splendid Gothic facade, in multilayered marble, leads into a majestic interior, with a fine rose window and a wealth of intricate carving. If Genoa from Piazza De Ferrari evokes civic glories, the city seen from the top-floor balcony of the renamed and revamped Terrazza Colombo lends a wholly different perspective. The 31st floor viewing gallery of the skyscraper in Piazza Dante offers commanding views over the hills, city and harbour. At the foot of the building is the heavily restored Porta Soprana, a medieval city gate, near to which are the remains of what is believed to be Columbus's house. What is revealed from the terrace is more like modern Marseilles than an ancient Italian city. The sprawling port and ageing 1950s' buildings nearby, which would have counted as skyscrapers in their time, strongly recall the French port. The third place to see Genoa's diversity is beside the Loggia dei Mercanti, also still covered in scaffolding, in Piazza Banchi in the thick of the old town. Here the impression is of casbah rather than cosmopolitan metropolis. The area, which some Genovese shun by night, is a maze of narrow alleys and ancient, often delapidated buildings. The atmosphere is Neapolitan, if not distinctly Middle Eastern, the exotic flavour heightened by the large numbers of north African immigrants. Genoa claims to have the biggest historic centre of any city in Europe and, for anyone wandering around this area, it is easy to believe. So far, there are only small islands of restoration. One day, there may be more, although beautifying the area could, ironically, detract from its seedy charm. However, sea change in Genoa's attitude towards its architectural heritage is already apparent at the Columbus exhibition site nearby, where four of the old 16th Century bonded warehouses have been lavishly restored. Finally, there is the modern, high-rise Genoa of the San Benigno office complex, which includes the multi-storey World Trade Centre and a number of other glass boxes in its midst. The truth is that Genoa is full of contrasts. What could be more striking than the difference between the solid 16th Century palazzi of via Garibaldi, one of the finest streets in Italy, and the narrow lanes of the old town only minutes away? Via Garibaldi is rightly viewed as Genoa's architectural crown, with each building, many now turned into banks, more splendid than the next. Their history goes back to the 16th Century, when wealthy patrician families, many of them in the banking business which made Genoa famous alongside its trade, compete with one another to build splendid palaces, rather like the rivalry between the elite of Tuscan towns such as Florence and Siena a century earlier. Much remains, and a number of the buildings also contain fine art collections. The most obvious contrast of all is that of Genoa's differing heights. From the harbourside to the top of town by the Castelletto is a long walk. But once up on the Belvedere terrace, from which there is another fine view over the rooftops out to sea, the effort proves worthwhile.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Survey: FT Traveller, Genoa (7) - An annual Mecca for sailors / Fairs, The October Boat Show is one of the biggest events of its kind in the world and attracts around 350,000 visitors
DOC.TEXT: PERCHED on the delta of the river Bisagno on land rescued from the sea, Genoa's fair symbolises much about its host city. With the Mediterranean its immediate neighbour and the city centre just minutes away on foot, the fair highlights the advantages and disadvantages of Genoa's geography. For while the setting may be unbeatable, the narrow site offers little scope for expansion. In spite of its limitations, the fair comes into its own for 10 days each October, when it hosts the International Boat Show. One of the biggest events of its kind in the world, the Boat Show attracts around 350,000 visitors, more than half from outside Genoa and around 20,000 from abroad. The figures for the Boat Show are impressive, with more than 800 exhibitors and 1,500 boats on display in every corner of the narrow site. The biggest boats are reserved for Hall B, which, with its four-storey height, can take big sailing boats up to 32 metres long, masts and all. Bigger vessels, which are also seen regularly in Genoa, have to stay on the water in the specially-built marina used as additional exhibition space during the show and rented out to local sailors for the rest of the year. Having the marina at hand means Genoa can offer much the same amount of exhibition space as its bigger international rivals. Although the boat shows at Dusseldorf and Miami are about the same size, no other exhibition of its kind offers the same combination of sophisticated interior facilities and external possibilities on the water, says Mr Giuseppino Roberto, the fair's secretary-general. The Boat Show, which will celebrate its 33rd anniversary this year, used to be held in February until it was shifted to October in 1972. 'The choice of October was very fortunate. Although it is at the end of the season, it is still very much late summer in Liguria, meaning the weather is very pleasant and people want to come to look at boats,' says Mr Roberto. He is less communicative about the competitive factors which may also have forced the change. Boat shows have become big business in rich European countries and in the US. Apart from Dusseldorf and Miami, Genoa also faces rivals in London, Paris, Barcelona and a number of the Scandinavian countries. The decision to hold a boat show in Genoa reflects the thinking behind the creation of the fair in the mid-1950s. Building started in 1959, and the first Boat Show opened in 1962. 'With Genoa's traditions as a seaport, the original idea was to create a big event concentrating on communications, especially on a cultural level,' Mr Roberto recalls. However, early 'communications fairs' showed the concept had little commercial validity, he admits. It was a different story for the Boat Show, which gave Liguria's recreational shipbuilders a chance to show off their wares and the region's sea-loving public the opportunity to gawp and, sometimes, to buy. But while exhibiting boats turned out to be a swift success, the fair had to dream up other commercially-viable attractions. Many have fallen by the wayside, but two - Tecnhotel and Euroflora - have become established events. The first is devoted to the hotel business, while the second, held every five years, is a huge horticultural extravaganza. The success of both fairs illustrates the importance of presenting shows which have some local roots. With its huge tourist business and thousands of hotels along the Riviera, Tecnhotel fulfils a clear need. Likewise, staging Euroflora, which pulls in around 700,000 visitors for its 10-day run, is appropriate for Genoa given the Riviera's role as Italy's horticultural heart. Tecnhotel, which now has an additional fair on contract furnishing tacked on, began in 1965, while the first Euroflora was held in 1966. The most recent show, held last year, understandably had a Christopher Columbus theme, with the focus on the plants and flowers of north America, says Mr Roberto. While the Boat Show, Tecnhotel and Euroflora are Genoa's three big international events, the city also holds a variety of other, more specialised, fairs. Riabitat, held every two years, concentrates on the businesses of restoring and modernising buildings. Restoration often features as a side event at many big international building fairs. But no other city has an event devoted solely to the subject, says Mr Roberto. 'It's particularly appropriate if you think of Italy, with its historic city centres, where there is a culture of building which must last for centuries.' More recently, the fair has come up with Auto Story, a specialist exhibition of prestige and veteran cars, now in its second year. The fair has had a good reception from the public and car dealers, he says. But in a business noted for its competition, both internationally and between fairs in their own countries, Genoa will have to carry on thinking up new ideas if it is not to rely exclusively on its three big international events, one of which, after all, is only held twice a decade. The fair recognises, but may not have yet met, the challenge. Domestically, both the Milan and Bologna fairs are appreciably bigger in terms of size and prestige. Genoa ranks roughly on a par with cities such as Turin, Verona and Bari, all of which have around the same amount of space available and which all hold at least one event of international importance, as well as many other shows of more local interest. But in some ways, the priority for Genova is to hold its own, implies Mr Roberto. Surprisingly, the fair is not seen as a potential profit-maker for the city. Rather, he takes pride in the fact that it has generally managed to balance its books. Small surpluses in the past 10 years have been used to improve the facilities, with L12bn being spent on creating the marina and L8bn on modernising the congress centre. However, the L15bn investment now needed to upgrade facilities and improve essential services such as electricity and water will have to come from outside sources. 'The big profits come from big events which draw over 50,000 visitors. We don't have many of those,' Mr Roberto admits. 'Our aim is more towards providing an overall benefit towards the city.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Survey: FT Traveller, Genoa (6) - Symbol of lost opportunities / The Harbour, The flag of privatisation is now flying highest at the port - surprisingly, for a former centre of hard-left politics
DOC.TEXT: IN A CITY renowned for its reserve, nothing provokes an argument faster than the port. For its critics, the port symbolises decades of politicised management, bungling and lost opportunities, notably in failing to come to terms with containerisation. Added to that has been a reluctance to confront restrictive labour practices, which led to high costs and an inevitable downward spiral of lower competitiveness and steady decline. From 51m tonnes in 1980, cargo handled fell to 44m last year, including oil and related products, which comprised more than half the overall tonnage in 1991. Meanwhile, the number of dockers has dropped to just over 1,000 from more than 7,000 15 years ago. To some extent, the argument has already been won. Even the port's management, concentrated in the 13th Century Palazzo San Giorgio, admits Genoa must adapt or die. What they add is that change is already well under way. Surprisingly for a former centre of hard-left politics, it is at the port that the flag of privatisation is now flying highest. Under plans originally drawn up in 1984, and subsequently refined, the Port Authority is bringing in private companies as partners in a number of joint ventures within the traditional port area. Meanwhile, at Voltri, six miles to the west, a L180bn scheme is under way to build the biggest container terminal in the Mediterranean, with the Port Authority as only a junior partner to private sector capital. The Port Authority has singled out seven activities in the old port in which it wants private-sector participation, explains Mr Rinaldo Magnani, a former dock worker and ex-president of Liguria, who is now its chairman. The terminals include fruit, general bulk cargoes, fertilisers and roll-on roll-off transport. The most likely private sector shareholders will be the big companies already using the facilities, he explains. So far, Coeclerici, a leading trader and fruit importer, has joined forces with the Port Authority at the fruit terminal, Ferruzzi and two other private companies are participating on the ro-ro side, while the Camelli group has come in for bulk cargoes. 'We're trying out a concept which could eventually be applied to other Italian ports too,' says Mr Magnani. Sceptics say the decision to turn to private companies has come more out of desperation than desire given the sorry state of the port's finances and the financial pressures on the Rome government, which has been so generous towards Genoa in the past. Much of the expected L300bn investment in the terminals is supposed to come from the private sector. The biggest single investment - some L75bn - is going on the cruise and ferry terminal, while L20.5bn is earmarked for the specialised bulk cargo terminal and L47.5bn for ro-ro. If the scheme for the terminals is ambitious, that for Voltri is bigger still. Here, the Port Authority has joined forces with Fiat - a traditional bogey of the hard left in Italy. Together, they have set up a new company, Voltri Terminal Europa (VTE), in which Sinport, a subsidiary of Fiat's Cogefar-Impresit civil engineering arm, has 95 per cent of the shares and the port the rest. Significantly, overall management will be left to Sinport, which has been given the concession to run Voltri from the Port Authority, which controls the land. When it opens next year, Voltri, covering more than 1m square metres, will be able to handle three 'jumbo' container ships simultaneously. Volume in the first year is forecast to reach 100,000 containers, rising to 250,000 in 1995 and 500,000 by the year 2000. But ambitions for Voltri do not end there. Mr Magnani says the eventual aim may be to float VTE on the stock market, while other big industrial shareholders may also be brought in. Such partners could include leading Far East shipping groups, such as Evergreen, say local industry sources. Negotiating long-term contracts with big Far Eastern shipping companies is part of the Port Authority's strategy. 'I know there's a lot of interest,' Mr Magnani says. He wants the new facility to become a 'point of reference' in the Mediterranean, especially given Europe's steadily rising level of imports from the Far East. The Port Authority plays on Genoa's proximity to Europe's main markets, which can be reached easily via the adjoining motorway and rail network. By offloading at Voltri, shippers from the Pacific, sailing via the Suez canal, would save about a week's journey time compared with using established container terminals in northern Europe such as Rotterdam. In spite of having recently returned from an extensive Far Eastern marketing trip, Mr Magnani will not comment on how close Voltri has come to signing long-term contracts with big 'round-the-world' shipping groups. Nor will he reveal whether such companies might become future shareholders in VTE. However, he draws attention to the fact that a canny group like Fiat is unlikely to have commited so much money to Voltri if it were unsure about the outcome. Mr Magnani admits Voltri may take some business away from the port's two existing container terminals. However, he notes the facilities are complementary rather than competitive. Voltri will be able to berth appreciably bigger ships than can dock in Genoa now. He also points to the growth of 5-6 per cent a year forecast for Mediterranean traffic. So, while the old port may lose some business, it should remain busy, he claims. More important, the lower costs of using Voltri thanks to deregulated labour could provide a salutary stimulus for altered working practices among the port's existing dockers. Surprisingly, Mr Magnani is reticent when it comes to assessing the effect of Voltri on Marseilles and Barcelona, the two other big container facilities in the western Mediterranean with which it will compete. 'I don't say we should be competing with them. Rather, we should be winning back the business that now goes from Milan to Rotterdam, instead of coming to Genoa,' he says. But will Genoa, still bearing the stigma of rotten industrial relations for many shippers, be able to rise to the new challenges? For many Genoese businessmen, the port's conversion to the cause of privatisation is hard to swallow. Mr Riccardo Garrone, the chairman of the ERG petroleum group and a leader of the city's business community, responds with scepticism mixed with hope. His doubts are largely based on the way in which the port has been run in the past. 'The wrong people were in charge. When motorways were being built all over Europe, making other, more reliable, ports competitive in spite of being further away from the main markets, Genoa failed to react.' The port has undoubtedly lost ground. La Spezia to the south now handles appreciably more containers, although it is less conveniently placed for the big cities of northern Italy. Even smaller ports such as Savona have gained at Genoa's expense. Mr Garrone focuses on the lack of internal competition and transparency as the port's biggest problems in the past. Though showered with government money, the cash went to cover the losses caused by its myriad inefficiencies rather than being ploughed into investments for the future. Meanwhile, the regular doses of state funds cushioned dockers and even businesses connected with the port from feeling the harsh winds of competition, he thinks. Mr Garrone hopes that part-privatisation and the development of Voltri will mark a new chapter. But he warns that they will only succeed if there is genuine competition between port operators. For Mr Garrone, one of the gravest mistakes of the past was that the port was run by a single, largely unaccountable entity. Privatisation is definitely 'a step ahead. But there must true competition' if the schemes are to succeed, he stresses.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Survey: FT Traveller, Genoa (5) - A room with a view of the sea / Hotels, City centre accommodation is being improved but many visitors still prefer to go further afield
DOC.TEXT: POORLY served until recently by top hotels, Genoa has used the Columbus Exhibition to spur both rebuilding and new construction in a bid to offer business travellers more choice. The closure some years ago of the Colombia, Genoa's member of the Aga Khan's luxury CIGA hotels chain, has made the lack of top hotels more evident than ever. However, business visitors should note that the Colombia is supposed to re-open as a residence, which could be useful for those planning a longer stay. While the options within the city are now improving, the limited range and the fact that Genoa's leading hotels are often booked up months in advance for big events such as the annual Boat Show, means many visitors prefer to look outside town. For those not facing early-morning appointments in the city centre, staying somewhere along the coast could be a positive boon. And all the seaside towns except Portofino have good rail links with Genoa. Running from west to east, and beginning in Genoa itself, here is our choice: The high rating for the down-at-heel Savoia Majestic, facing the Colombia on the other side of Principe station, seems to stem primarily from the fact that none of the guide books which recommend it highly have been there recently. The hotel has also suffered from the general shift in Genoa's city centre from Principe station in the west to Brignole further east. Well located between the two is the Jolly Plaza. Even with building work to revamp the hotel still under way, it is surprisingly characterful by the Jolly chain's normally bland standards. There is also a car park nearby. Ten minutes away on foot is the Bristol, set under the arcades of busy via 20 Settembre. For some, the sombre hotel, all red leather upholstery and restrained colours, exudes the atmosphere of a London club, and typifies Genoa's Anglo-Saxon leanings. I found it depressing. Just by Brignole station in the new Corte Lambruschini complex is the Star, completed last year, and striking for its angular architecture. The hotel, expensive by local standards, is all a modern businessman's base should be - and little more. A range of facilities is available for conferences of up to 580 people as well as smaller meetings, and there is underground parking. The absence of a hotel at Genoa's small Christopher Columbus airport should be corrected towards the end of this year with the opening of the big new Sheraton. It may be worth a try, in spite of the inconvenient location. Substantial facilities for meetings and conferences are also planned. Outside the city, visitors should look exclusively along the eastern Riviera, rather than the industrialised immediate west. The choice starts at the small town of Nervi, now incorporated within Genoa itself, and runs down to the Portofino peninsula. Nervi itself, six miles from the city centre, is a quiet resort of considerable charm once away from the busy main road running above the town. None of its hotels is in the luxury class, but most are pleasant, especially the small Pagoda, in spite of its disappointingly utilitarian room furnishings. Lying in a small park on the edge of Nervi's public gardens, it even has its own path leading to the lovely seaside promenade. Camogli, 16 miles from Genoa and coming just before the Portofino peninsula, offers the Cenobio dei Dogi, a historic old hotel full of atmosphere overlooking the sea in its own grounds. Rapallo, Santa Margherita Ligure and Portofino itself are all on the eastern side of the peninsula, and offer a wide choice of hotels. Rapallo, with 26,000 inhabitants, is as much a small town as a seaside resort. Its leading hotel is the Grand Hotel Bristol, often confused with the hotel of the same name in Genoa. Built by the British early this century and expensively restored eight years ago, the Bristol is an unfortunate case of money ill-spent, Mirror glass cladding on the back and a range of garish colour schemes within may have been the last word in chic when commissioned. They could even become a 'feature' within a few decades. However, the effect today is pretty dire. Rooms are comfortable, with commanding views across the bay, and there are good meeting and conference facilities. Santa Margherita offers two luxury hotels, as well as a long list of more modest accommodation. Both the Imperial Palace and the Grand Hotel Miramare are set in fine grounds and face the sea. The town itself is first and foremost a resort, as evidenced by the many pleasure craft in its pretty harbour. However, it can become unpleasantly crowded on sunny weekends, and especially during the peak Sunday afternoon passeggiata. Three miles down the peninsula on a narrow, twisting road where drivers must fight the temptation to admire the view if they are to avoid head-on collisions, is Portofino. Called the Splendido, one hotel stands out above all else in the region, Genoa included. Justly feted in an industry known for its hype, the Splendido is one of those places guests do not want to leave. Set in a beautiful terraced garden high above Portofino, with views down to the harbour, sea and neighbouring hills, it is an ideal place to wind down - as witnessed by the large number of well-heeled Italians who regularly return at weekends. Of course, luxury accommodation, manicured grounds and a ratio of almost 100 staff for just 63 rooms do not come cheap. Yet the quality is so high and service so good as to make even the Splendido's extremely weighty bills seem reasonable in the circumstances. And guests can always console themselves that the hotel, now owned by the Venice Simplon Orient Express (VSOE) subsidiary of the Sea Containers group, is still appreciably cheaper than either the Cipriani in Venice or the Villa San Michele in Fiesole, VSOE's two other Italian hotels, both of which, especially the latter, are likely to provoke Latin American standards of debt for those contemplating an extended stay.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Survey: FT Traveller, Genoa (4) - An international meeting place / Conferences, The new Congress Centre in the old cotton warehouses gives the city a high-tech, purpose-built venue
DOC.TEXT: WHEN Confindustria, Italy's employers' federation, held its most recent congress earlier this year, it opted for Genoa. But rather than meeting in some well-established centre, the 2,000-odd delegates found themselves occupying the stalls of the Carlo Felice opera house. The choice of Genoa, and the theatre, probably reflected a desire to promote the city in Columbus year. And many of the delegates would undoubtedly have been keen to see the lavishly-restored theatre, which has received heaps of publicity. But it also demonstrated Genoa's lack of a suitable venue. Only with the opening of the new Congress Centre in the converted old cotton warehouses, which form part of the Expo site, will Genoa be able to boast a high-tech, purpose-built venue of its own. Converting the cotton warehouses, built by the British at the beginning of this century, has been a race against time, with workers in the building virtually up to a minute before its formal opening with the annual shareholders' meeting of the Banca Popolare di Genova. However, visitors are likely to be impressed. With its twin halls on either side of a central stage, the centre offers flexible seating for up to 1,500, along with a series of smaller auditoria seating up to 400. There is also a huge amount of exhibition space on the four floors. Typical of the iron and brick port architecture of the era, the long, thin cotton warehouse stretches for almost a quarter of a mile along the Molo Vecchio wharf jutting out into the harbour. While the exterior has been largely preserved, much of the interior has been transformed. The final section housing the conference centre has been gutted. From its upper floors, delegates will be able to look over the port, while a smaller building alongside houses all the services, such as sophisticated air conditioning, needed for a new conference centre. The complex even has its own telecommunications centre for live teleconferencing. The congress centre has already lined up five big international conventions to run concurrently with the Christopher Columbus exhibition, as well as a range of seminars and lectures. All will focus on maritime issues, including environmental protection and preservation, as well as legal matters. The creation of the congress centre means Genoa now has two venues for conventions, not counting the opera house, which is likely to revert to full-time cultural use. Over at the fair, the convention centre offers facilities for up to 800 in its largest auditorium, while a smaller hall can accommodate around 400 delegates. Further facilities are available at a number of hotels in the city, notably the Star, hard by Brignole station in the Corte Lambruschini complex. However, conference-goers should have an even wider range of choice come October, when a new hotel is expected to open near the airport, with a range of meeting halls of its own.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Survey: FT Traveller, Genoa (3) - Families dominate the scene / Business, For many, Genoa still means steel and shipbuilding, though both have shrunk beyond recognition
DOC.TEXT: THE traditional split in Genoa's business community between a public sector concentrated in engineering and a private sector specialising in shipping and trade has been eroded as a result of the crisis in heavy industry and the part-privatisation of the local steel industry. But the broad distinction is still valid. In spite of repeated shrinkage, the giant IRI state holding company remains Genoa's biggest employer. Its Finmeccanica engineering arm controls Ansaldo, the city's leading heavy engineering group, whose roots under the Perrone family go back to the early days of Italy's industrialisation. Ansaldo has taken some heavy knocks in recent years, notably after the 1987 referendum ban on nuclear power, making the company's nuclear power division redundant virtually overnight. In spite of that and competition from bigger international rivals such as Siemens and ABB, Ansaldo has bounced back. Its Genoese operations are in energy, transportation - especially rail equipment and signalling - and heavy engineering. Finmeccanica's other big Genoese offshoot is the Elsag Bailey precision engineering group. Often presented as one of Italy's high-tech jewels, the reality is slightly less extravagant. However, the company, which makes a range of specialised equipment for factory automation, mechanised letter sorting and various other purposes, has grown rapidly through acquisitions. After buying the US Bailey group, more than half of sales now come from abroad, a point stressed heavily in the group's stock market flotation last year. For many, Genoa still means steel and shipbuilding, though both have shrunk beyond recognition. The lavishly renovated headquarters of Ilva, the state steel group, in an Art-Deco palace in the posh Carignano district, must count as one of Italy's most impressive corporate headquarters with its starkly contrasting white interiors, black leather furniture and halogen lighting. Ilva's remaining industrial activities, based in the Cornigliano industrial zone west of the port, are another matter. Most basic steelmaking has long been moved to southern Italy, while part of the Cornigliano plant has been privatised. Plans are now in hand to convert much of the remaining industrial wasteland into a business park for smaller industrial and service companies as part of Ilva's ambitious but controversial 'Utopia' project. Most closely identified of all the public-sector companies with the Columbus Exhibition is IRI's Italimpianti subsidiary, which masterminded the L500bn building and general contracting project for the Expo site. Based in a distinctive pencil-shaped tower (the Mattitone) near the western docks, Italimpianti was merged this year with Italstat, another IRI subsidiary, into a new group called Iritecna. The aim was to create a large Italian group combining engineering, contracting and construction skills and able to compete with foreign rivals such as Germany's Mannesmann and Philipp Holzmann on big overseas infrastructure projects. However, Iritecna has so far failed to emerge from the political controversy and management in-fighting that mar many of its public-sector counterparts. Many of its problems, like theirs, stem from having too many bosses and criss-crossing responsibilities. So while the dream behind Iritecna remains laudable, it will only be realised if IRI's chairman Mr Franco Nobili, who has a building background, manages to knock heads together and unblock the difficulties which have so far paralysed what should be Italy's champion in the international building and general contracting field. Genoa is no longer the Italian base for the international oil majors, though the port remains the country's leading terminal for importing refined products, which are then distributed nationally or sent on via a direct pipeline to Switzerland and Germany. The only big private-sector oil operator left is the Garrone family's ERG group. Mr Riccardo Garrone, the chairman, is a pugnacious 56-year-old who assumed control as a youngster after his father died in 1963. Under him, ERG has grown into Italy's biggest private-sector oil group, with more than 2,000 petrol stations and about 6 per cent of the market. But even its Genoese activities have slimmed down in recent years. Though based in the towering World Trade Centre by the docks, most of its industrial operations are now elsewhere, with a big refinery in Sicily and other offices in Rome. Genoa remains the nerve centre for top management, concentrated in the family holding company. Mr Garrone himself, a keen hunter, is an entrenched critic of the city's left-wing politicians, whom he accuses of having caused its decline. At last month's general election, he failed to win a seat in the Senate as a candidate for the small Republican party. However, his local prestige - and lavish spending, according to his critics - was enough to lift the party's share of the vote to 15 per cent from around 4 per cent normally, in spite of competition from Mr Guido Carli, Italy's treasury minister, and other candidates. Genoa's foremost representative in shipping and trade is the privately-owned Camelli group. Somewhat confusing in its structure after a spate of recent takeovers of small stock market quoted companies, it now comprises five main branches. Camelli concentrates on oil trading, as well as having some refining and distribution capacity. Gerolimich, a quoted subsidiary, controls various industrial stakes, both directly and through Unione Manifatture, which is also quoted and is best known for owning the company making Sweda cash registers. Other recent acquisitions include Navigazione Alta Italia (NAI) in shipping and Rodriquez, a shipbuilder famous for its fast catamarans. Jointly owned by the Camelli family and by Mr Luigi Regis Milano, who masterminds its affairs, critics say the group now needs to simplify its structure after the string of takeovers. Meanwhile, trading in the shares of a number of the quoted subsidiaries is still suspended. Among Genoa's other top private companies are the Costa group, now most familiar for its cruise ships which ply the Caribbean and Mediterranean. Costa Crociere, quoted on the bourse, is all that is left of what was once one of Italy's foremost private companies, which rivalled and even surpassed giants such as Fiat and Pirelli. Mr Angelo Costa, a former boss, ranks as one of the most famous former chairmen of Italy's Confindustria employers' federation in the early 1950s. The group's decline is closely associated with that of the port in the 1970s. But the cruise business has led a partial comeback in recent years and resulted in a string of orders for huge new vessels - albeit at the cost of a substantial rise in debt. Completing the list of the city's big shipping and trading families are the Clericis, whose link with former British partners, the Coes, is enshrined in the name of their Coeclerici group. Their Bulkitalia subsidiary owns a fleet of bulk carriers, which used to be jointly owned with the big Ferruzzi group. However, Mr Giacomo Clerici, universally known as Jack, bought out Ferruzzi's then boss, Mr Raul Gardini, to take sole control. Now in his 80s, Jack Clerici, whose mother was British, ranks as one of Genoa's grand old men. His international links, particularly with the former Soviet Union, have won him a reputation akin to that of the legendary Mr Armand Hammer in the US. Mr Giovanni Battista (Gaimba) Parodi is probably Genoa's least known businessman to outsiders. But for many Italians from the city and beyond, he counts as one of the richest men in the country. His operations include the quoted Acquedotto de Ferrari Galliera group, which distributes half the city's drinking water, and a number of activities in the construction business, as well as a range of financial holdings, including stakes in big quoted companies such as Pirelli. The Parodi family's Genoese roots go far back. The former Banca Parodi was one of the regional institutions swept up in the founding of the Bank of Italy, and Mr Parodi is today on the board of the central bank. Another of the grand old men of Genoa, Mr Parodi is every inch the retiring millionaire. Famous for his modest lifestyle, his quirks reportedly include being chauffeured in a tiny Fiat mini-car and occupying the former servants quarters in a family-owned Palazzo in the majestic via Garibaldi. The Romanengo family has come to prominence outside Genoa only relatively recently. Last year, its Sci property group was floated on the bourse. Having already made a mark on the city's skyline with developments such as the World Trade Centre and other buildings in the big Centro San Benigno project, Sci, in which Mr Garrone's ERG group now has a 12.75 per cent stake, is now extending its property development activities abroad.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Survey: FT Traveller, Genoa (2) - Famous son repays his home town / Columbus Exhibition, The attempt to cash in on Genoa's most celebrated mariner has been done with true Italian panache
DOC.TEXT: SOMEWHERE underneath the flyover, not far from the container lorries and next to the apparently interminable road works is the horseshoe-shaped piece of Genoa's old harbour housing the exhibition on Christopher Columbus, Ships and the Sea, the reason for the city's present jamboree. The attempt to cash in on the Columbus business has been done with true Italian panache, meaning constructive chaos. The paint may still be wet in patches, the mortar not quite set on every stone, but the exhibition should open on time. That in itself will be an achievement considering the landscape of cranes, pick-up trucks and pneumatic drills that dominated the scene until just a few weeks back. The project turned into a race against time after early construction work unearthed the remains of 12th and 14th Century port installations just where the aquarium was supposed to go. In came the archaeologists and out went the blueprints as the site had to be redrawn. In the end, the aquarium and other linked buildings were shifted 50 metres out to sea. 'We knew all along it wouldn't be ready on time,' says Mr Gianfranco Medri, the managing director for the L750bn Expo project. 'The experts said it would take five years to have the aquarium fully functioning. We've done it in less than three, even if all the tanks won't be full yet. But then, we started a bit late.' Europe's biggest aquarium, and the second largest in the world, is just one of the attractions which the Columbus '92 Exhibition hopes will pull in the crowds to its redeveloped 12-acre site, just minutes from the city centre. Looking out to sea, visitors will be struck by the restored old cotton warehouses, now converted into a congress centre and exhibition space, to their left. On the right, another long jetty shoots out to sea. It will incorporate the boat-shaped Italian pavilion and the aquarium behind it. Straight ahead is a huge spider-like structure, the Bigo, rising from the water, which has become one of the exhibition's symbols. Recalling a giant ship's crane, it is the brainchild of Genovese architect Renzo Piano, best known as one of the two partners behind the Pompidou Centre in Paris, who has had overall responsibility for the design of the exhibition site. Yet, in spite of all the money and effort behind it, the exhibition is still having difficulty getting noticed. Pipped at the post by Seville in Spain, which has used the 500th anniversary of the discovery of the New World to mount a vast international extravaganza, Genoa has had to look for niches to justify its belated attempt to honour its most famous son. The resulting event, which is not just about Columbus, but on the more general theme of 'ships and the sea', has turned out worthy, with a stress on scientific research and international conferences, but rather dull. 'Seville is a very different thing,' says Mr Merdi. 'Their intentions are completely different. The site alone is 10 times bigger than ours.' Wishful thinking? The existence of the much bigger Seville show, which also started earlier, and the blanket promotion lavished on it, has obliged the Genovese to think hard about what their Columbus celebration is all about. 'Ours is based on culture. It's designed to appeal to more thoughtful visitors who will appreciate the exhibits but be just as interested in the redevelopment of the old port,' he argues. Genoa, perhaps making virtue out of necessity, stresses its show is neither Eurodisney nor Seville. For sheer fun, better to head for the outskirts of Paris. And if the aim is to gawp at a huge international exposition of the old school, housed in mind-boggling buildings, Spain is the best destination. But for those who are content with a more limited, and rather more intellectual treat, Genoa could fit the bill. Of course, the exhibition is not without its popular attractions, notably the aquarium. Likewise the crane, which incorporates a 60-metre revolving glass lift to hoist visitors aloft to admire the harbour and city from the sort of perspective more familiar to a young midshipman up the mast of his vessel than a mariner of today. But the feature in Genoa is more the general redevelopment project and Renzo Piano's aim to 'open the waterfront again and reunite the city with the sea' than providing the fun of the fair. The unspoken rivalry with other big European attractions this year and Genoa's much more modest means and space are among the reasons why the project has already excited local tempers, especially over how many people will actually come. The debate has been fuelled by the city's local newspaper, Il Secolo XIX, whose family owners favoured a rival scheme to promote the project. The Expo's organisers are banking on between 3m and 3.5m visitors during the Expo's three-month run. Others are more sceptical. They question how many people, especially from outside the city, will be drawn to an event which, for all its merits, is short of really big attractions for the general public. And many claim the L25,000 entrance fee is steep for what is on offer. 'I'm not expecting a big rush from the start,' says Mr Medri. 'We haven't gone in for the sort of blanket promotion used by Seville and Eurodisney. I think that approach can be counter-productive as people tend to get fed up with being bombarded by promotional publicity.' He hopes interest in Genoa's show will grow steadily through word of mouth. 'Things will start moving after the first two weeks,' he says. But, in a familiar refrain, he admits that 'we set off late with the promotion'. The bulk of visitors will come from Genoa itself or the immediate region. Around two thirds will be Italians, the remainder foreigners, either from nearby France or others visiting the Riviera for their summer holidays. The projections recognise that few will be coming to see Genoa itself, in spite of all the city's efforts to smarten its appearance. Almost all the Italian visitors will be day-trippers, and the publicity has been specifically designed for them. Apart from the Genovese themselves, the organisers expect the exhibition to appeal to millions of Italians from big cities such as Milan and Turin, both less than two hours away by train or car. 'We certainly don't expect they will all sleep in hotels in the city,' notes Mr Medri. But once the holiday season starts, he hopes for a wider public as holidaymakers along the Riviera may be tempted to desert the beach and spend a day seeing the exhibition for themselves. But the debate about numbers is probably irrelevant when considered against the exhibition's wider aims. True, it should provide some entertainment for the Genovese and their neighbours for a few months this spring and summer. But more important is the event's role in promoting the rediscovery of a rundown part of the city, yet lying cheek by jowl with some of its finest houses and shops. Though not on a scale with harbourside redevelopments in cities such as Baltimore, where hundreds of acres have been revived and whole new entertainment zones created, the Genoa exhibition has also been planned with the future of the city in mind. More than 80 per cent of the site will remain untouched after the exhibition closes on August 15, compared with the large-scale demolition which usually follows a big international event of its kind. Once over, visitors will even be able to see archaeologists at work on the port installations: it was their discovery which delayed plans for the aquarium. But the main contribution of the exhibition will be to have made the Genovese themselves take their city more seriously. Irrespective of the attendance figures, the exhibition has triggered off an architectural revival, with restoration schemes going well beyond the old port itself. So, while Genoa may have served Columbus badly when it failed to finance his expedition across the Atlantic, its most famous son has repaid his former home handsomely today.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 15 MAY 92 / Survey: FT Traveller, Genoa (1) - A look back to the future / First Impressions, Nowhere else do the normally chauvinistic Italians play so strongly the foreign card
DOC.TEXT: 'TO UNDERSTAND Genoa, you have to understand the British,' is the cliche regularly quoted to any remotely Anglo-Saxon visitor to Italy's biggest port, now belatedly rediscovering its cultural heritage as an instrument to counter years of economic decline. Nowhere else do the normally chauvinistic Italians play so strongly the foreign card. And nowhere else is the link so close with the UK. From Genoa's heyday in the early Middle Ages as a mercantile city-state and traditional rival of Venice, the relationship stretches through centuries of two-way trade and a flow of tourism and culture which has tended to move more in one direction than the other. Always important for the British in their Mediterranean commerce, the arrival of the Suez Canal made Genoa a vital stop for points further east as well, notably India. Soon, the British aristocrats, who had already discovered the mild breezes and jasmine gardens of the Riviera on either side of the city, were joined by less titled, but equally well-heeled, Britons who made the city and its surroundings a staging post on their way to India and beyond. Sojourns in Riviera watering holes became more than just a way of avoiding the beastly British winter. For those either returning to the UK from the colonies or just setting out, a spell on the Riviera became an acceptable way of adjusting to the climatic changes ahead. Climate and culture also appealed to the region's most famous British visitors, the Romantic poets. The bay of La Spezia, 75 miles south of Genoa, is still sometimes sold to the tourists as the 'Bay of Poets'. Byron used to swim regularly in Portovenere, just north of La Spezia. In 1822, the Shelleys rented a small house near the village of Lerici opposite. Sailing along the coast from Leghorn to La Spezia on his way home Shelley drowned. With the bicentenary of his birth this year, the number of British literary tourists is bound to surge. Genoa still makes much of its Anglo-Saxon links, a factor often cited today to explain its charms and failings. For fellow Italians, the Genovese are a dull lot; cool and reserved, they speak a barely comprehensible dialect and seldom display the extrovert verve usually associated with their fellow nationals. Like the Piedmontese to the north, they are also known throughout Italy for a caution with money which is associated more with the Scottish than the English. The Anglo-Saxon air still hangs over parts of the city, though more in terms of manners and society than art or architecture. Though exaggerated by their fellow Italians, the tradition of reserve remains. Genoa's rich do not flaunt their wealth like those in Milan and especially Rome. Money is suggested rather than seen behind the high hedges and wrought-iron gates of their big villas perched on the hills near the Staglieno cemetery towering over the city. Visitors to Genoa are often carted off to Finollo, an old-fashioned tie and shirt maker on elegant via Roma, to savour for themselves the city's Anglo-Saxon air. The dark and narrow store, full of ties in regimental stripes, certainly recalls some of its counterparts in London's Jermyn Street. But it is a measure of popular misunderstanding about the UK that the shop, whose proprietors seem to have confused the distant politeness of the British with a patronising smugness, verging on the rude, should so often be used as a showcase. Such self-satisfaction is at the heart of many of Genoa's problems, which have dogged it for decades and which partly explain why its corner of the famous economic triangle with Milan and Turin has shown signs of lapsing. 'Genoa's error is a bit like the problems of the British,' says Mr Carlo Da Molo, chairman of Italgas, one of Italy's leading companies, and a born Genovese. Over the past three decades, the city failed to adapt to changing economic circumstances and continued to rely heavily on the port as its main source of livelihood. 'They didn't appreciate that things were changing', says Mr Riccardo Garrone, a leading Genovese businessman whose ERG group is the biggest private-sector petroleum company in Italy. The complaints are levelled as much at the state as the private sector. After the Second World War, public money poured into the bomb-scarred city to rebuild heavy industry and set up new activities, notably in steel. Meanwhile, more cash was ploughed into the port, as much in later years to cover inefficiencies and restrictive labour practices as to adapt to new trends, such as containerisation. Change came only when the political balance tilted away from the hard left, which dominated both the port and local politics, or when the inefficiencies of both became too obvious to ignore. The bell began to toll for the steel industry in the late 1960s, when production started to shift to southern Italy. Though largely a political decision, the move was also in recognition of the fact that Genoa's narrow coastal strip, bounded by mountains and the sea, hardly lent itself to the development of large-scale, integrated steelworks. Meanwhile, shipbuilding suffered at the hands of cheaper foreign competition, and production of the biggest vessels was eventually concentrated elsewhere. Yet, the accusation of short-sightedness is levelled as strongly at Genoa's private sector. Geared to shipping and trade, the city boasts next to no private-sector industry, apart from the small Piaggio aircraft group and the remains of the now partly-privatised steel business. Showing native caution, Genoa's businessmen tended to stick to what they knew best, maintaining their traditions as merchants rather than entrepreneurs. Others suffered indirectly from the slow decline of the port. 'There were no industrialists in the private sector,' says Mr Garrone. 'And the big private companies that did exist were too divided among themselves to organise as a lobby to press for change'. Arguably, the development of much better communications from the late 1950s, with excellent motorway links between Genoa and the big cities of the north, may have encouraged the tendency towards individualism. Local businessmen, frustrated by left-wing politics locally, may have preferred to invest in the growing areas of Lombardy and Piedmont to the north rather than Genoa itself. Others may have chosen the less legal, but well-trodden, route to Switzerland for their flight capital. 'Our refinery had to be closed because its chimneys released private-sector smoke,' recalls a still bitter Mr Garrone. 'But the fumes from the Italsider steelworks were good, because they were public-sector fumes,' he says angrily. 'Mind you, as soon as it went private, it also came under attack.' Though most critical of the hard left councils which governed Genoa for years, he sees the city's recent past as having been tainted with a general hostility to the private sector that went beyond the Communists to influence other political groups, too. The changes in Genoa today may be too sudden and dramatic to last. But the optimists hope financial stringency in the public-sector will prove salutary in stimulating a concentration only on activities which are viable. At the port, partial privatisation of some operations and the construction of a huge new container terminal at Voltri to the west have offered the chance of regaining a role as the foremost trading post in the Mediterranean. Meanwhile, local politics have taken a significant move towards the centre with the arrival of a soft-left council two years ago. Looking ahead, many Genovese point to the Christopher Columbus exhibition as providing the spur to regenerate after decades of delay. Further off, but even more important in its potential economic effect, is the planned high-speed rail link with Milan. That could cut the journey time from two hours to around 40 minutes. But rather than seeing themselves as potential losers to their bigger neighbour to the north, the Genovese are confident their city will be the clear beneficiary from such an improvement in communications. The link would make the coast far more accessible to northern Italians, for whom Genoa would be the gateway. It may not trigger the development of new heavy industry, but the high-speed line could be just the incentive for creating the new service sector activities the city is looking for.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Cronite stake - Correction
DOC.TEXT: AFE, the French engineering company, yesterday said it owned or had agreed to acquire 26.1 per cent of Cronite, the Birmingham engineering company for which it has mounted a Pounds 7.3m recommended bid, and had undertakings in respect of a further 3.6 per cent. In yesterday's Financial Times, Mr James Lindsay-German, Cronite's chief executive, mistakenly stated that AFE spoke for 40.8 per cent.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Lloyd's faces satellite claim
DOC.TEXT: UNDERWRITERS AT Lloyd's of London stand to pay claims of around dollars 20m (pounds 11.2m) if attempts to resuce the Intelsat VI satellite are unsuccessful. Astronauts from the space shuttle Endeavour were scheduled to make a final effort to rescue it last night. Lloyd's underwriters insured the rescue mission on behalf of a number of Intelsat's 122 partners. The policy, 45 per cent if which is placed in Lloyd's, covers dollars 44m of the dollars 147m cost of the rescue mission.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Exam results
DOC.TEXT: INDEPENDENT schools are to collate and publish their A-level results for the first time this year. The Independent Schools Information Service plans to publish summary results for 570 schools at the end of August.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / World News in Brief: Radioactive seaweed
DOC.TEXT: Radioactive seaweed has been found on beaches near the Sellafield nuclear reprocessing plant. British Nuclear Fuels said the radioactivity levels posed no danger to the public. Freedom for atomic agency, Page 8

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / UK Company News: TI declares Pounds 504m Dowty bid final - Only unlikely appearance of white knight would affect offer
DOC.TEXT: TI GROUP, the specialist engineering company, yesterday turned the heat up on bid target Dowty by declaring its Pounds 504m offer final. Mr Christopher Lewinton, TI chairman and chief executive, said that the original 4 for 15 share offer, which values the bid at 186p and its cash alternative of 175p, fully valued Dowty. By taking the unusual step of making its first offer final, TI is confident that it was pitched high enough to see off potential rival bidders. However, it retains the right to increase its offer in the increasingly unlikely event that a white knight emerges with a rival bid. Mr Bruce Ralph, chairman of the aerospace and information technology group, said there was nothing new in TI's document, which still presented Dowty shareholders with an offer that was too low. As part of the defence, which is expected early next week, Dowty is likely to reveal an estimate of profits and earnings for the year ended March 1992. Stockbrokers have estimated profits between Pounds 18.5m and Pounds 22m - giving earnings of 4.1p to 5.4p - down from Pounds 60.6m in 1991. Mr Ralph said he was glad the phoney war was over and warned that some analysts might be embarrassed by their low estimates of 1991 earnings. Dowty will also try to slow the momentum TI has developed in the three weeks since it launched its hostile bid by focusing its shareholders on the strengths of its future order book and its development programmes. Late yesterday Dowty also said that Mr Christopher Bunker would no longer be joining in August as finance director from Westland, the helicopter manufacturer where he holds the same position. In what Mr Ralph called a humanitarian gesture Dowty had agreed to Mr Bunker's request not to join Dowty in the middle of a bid. In his letter to Dowty shareholders yesterday, Mr Lewinton repeated that the Cheltenham-based company had lost its way after diversifying into information technology. He said he recognised the problem from when he joined TI in 1986 and found that TI - formerly Tube Investments - had diversified from its core businesses into Raleigh bicycles and consumer products. TI has been refocused and built into an international group. The acquisition of Dowty would provide a third aerospace leg to add to the tubes and seals businesses. Dowty has two weeks to produce its first defence document and 28 days to convince its shareholders of the strength of its management. Dowty's shares fell 6p to 181p on news of TI's final offer while TI shares fell 1p to 697p.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Africa pledge by developed nations
DOC.TEXT: LEADING industrialised nations assured Africa yesterday they remained committed to rescuing its fragile economies, despite increased competition for aid due to changes in eastern Europe and the former Soviet bloc, Reuter reports from Dakar. The Netherlands minister for development cooperation, Mr Jan Pronx, told the annual meeting of the African Development Bank it was difficult to see where resources required to assist growth and attack poverty would come from, without more effective rescheduling of debt. 'In the view of the Netherlands, we still have to strive for a write-off debt of all least-developed countries,' he said. Representatives of other industrialised states stopped short of endorsing a need for new debt relief schemes, but chorused their intention to stand by Africa. 'My country is committed to remaining engaged in this continent,' declared Mr Olin Wethington, assistant secretary for international affairs at the US Treasury. Mr Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji, Nigeria's finance minister, said debt relief now provided 'a glimmer of hope', but Africa's economic plight was alarming. He proposed that concessions which multilateral aid agencies allowed to the poorest countries should be extended to the less well-off, middle-income states. But Mr Wethington told a news conference that Washington was reluctant at this stage to agree to such a proposal. He outlined at the meeting a two-pronged approach by his country in its economic relations with Africa in the post-Cold War world. While helping to meet social and economic needs, it would stress the value of democracy and market-based economies, and favour changes to promote the private sector. 'The long-term future lies with encouraging private enterprise,' he told reporters. 'The private capital markets will be able, in the long term, to provide resources that will exceed those available through official channels.' Mr Alhaji urged industrial countries to open their markets. 'At present, excessive subsidies to agricultural products of the developed economies create the double-edged sword which keeps our farm products out of their markets and, at the same time, depresses markets for our products,' the minister said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Press freedom call to CSCE meeting
DOC.TEXT: INTERNATIONAL news organisations and Unesco told the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe yesterday that its promotion of press freedom in Europe could affect other parts of the world, AP reports from Helsinki. 'Everyone has the right to freedom of opinion and expression. . . . without interference. The CSCE can make these hopes a reality,' said Mr Leonard Marks of the Washington-based World Press Freedom Committee. 'Established democracies now have an unparalleled opportunity to give help and guidance to the new democracies as they build their new highways of freedom,' he said. The committee is a co-ordinating group of national and international news organisations. Mr Marks urged delegates in a plenary session of the 52-nation security and human rights conference to adopt a 10-point charter rejecting censorship and other restrictions on information and the movement of journalists. 'If a democracy is to be firmly rooted, there must be no law infringing the freedom of the press,' he said. The charter, approved in January 1987 at a London conference on censorship problems, outlines principles designed to permit free, independent news media to function effectively. It says journalists should be free to travel over national borders and their visa applications should 'be handled promptly'. Mr Frederico Mayor, Unesco's director-general, said in a message read to the delegates by an aide that freedom of the press is one of the most essential components of a democratic society.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Ukraine tells Crimea to end independence bid
DOC.TEXT: THE UKRAINIAN parliament yesterday tried to brake Crimea's separatist drive by suspending its declaration of independence and planned referendum. Mr Leonid Kravchuk, the Ukrainian president, warned of 'bloodshed' and 'a tragedy in relations between Ukraine and Russia' if Crimea's separatist bid was not halted. Mr Kravchuk and the Ukraine parliament stopped short of dissolving the Crimean parliament and calling new elections but it set May 20 as a deadline for the Crimean legislature to annul its own declaration of independence and revoke plans to hold a referendum on August 2. The Ukrainian parliament did not specify the measures it would take if Crimea fails to comply, but the parliament did instruct Mr Kravchuk to use 'all necessary means' to restore constitutional order in Crimea.
