Advouch sends each of its clients a weekly activity report with a bundle of vouchers stapled to publications in which their advertisements have appeared. Without a voucher from Advouch stating that the booked advert has appeared correctly, the advertising agency can refuse payment to the publication. The whole process is about establishing trusted verifications, thus reducing cash-flow problems for all concerned. Computer technology has enabled Advouch to find a niche in an increasingly complex market; it is also enabling marketing directors to find their own niches among consumers who blithely pass by the 80,000 outdoor poster sites in Britain. NOP Posters, part of the MAI information services group, has just launched a new service with its subsidiary, Pinpoint Analysis. Called Posterpin, the service costs between Pounds 15,000 and Pounds 40,000 a year. For that, subscribers get a desk-top processor from which to obtain a wide range of information on poster sites including details of consumer expenditure, wealth indices and consumer demographics. They can also scan maps of a specified area, pinpointing poster sites, who owns them, how many panels they have and their availability. Users of the system will be able to call on a database to give the numbers of - for example - premium canned lager drinkers living in the area. According to Pinpoint the new service 'offers not just a mapping procedure but also useful marketing information'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Accountancy Column: Laying it on the line for future auditing standards
DOC.TEXT: A BOLD red line slices across the black and white cover of the exposure drafts issued earlier this week by the Auditing Practices Board. To certain senior accountants contemplating the birth pangs of the new standard-setting regime, it represents more than a simple design feature. It was at an 'awayday' conference for members of the Auditing Practices Committee at the Gatwick Hilton three years ago that Mr Graham Stacy, a technical partner with Price Waterhouse (and now representing the firm for its work as auditor to the collapsed Bank of Credit and Commerce International), purposefully picked up a red felt-tipped pen. With it he drew a horizontal line across a blank flipchart. Above it he a placed a wiggly line, and on top of that a second straight line running along the peaks. The lowest line represented existing auditing standards; the middle one, the quality of auditing actually achieved by the large accountancy firms; and the top one, the firms' own ideal standards. 'Some members of the committee were arguing that we should set auditing standards very high to give firms something to aim for,' he recalls. 'I said the big firms always have to keep their own standards far higher, so even when they fall short of perfection, they are still clear of the minimum. Otherwise they won't be able to survive.' 'Stacy's red line' - which has become part of the folklore at Price Waterhouse - has jumped sharply up the page following the publication of the first salvo of proposed documents from the Auditing Practices Board (APB) on Tuesday. It also stands as a symbolic high-water mark below which the old Auditing Practices Committee (APC) has drowned. The APC may have seemed a significant step forward when it was created to draw up coherent guidelines in the late 1970s, but a decade later it was looking very stale. That was the main conclusion of discussions held by the APC at the same Gatwick venue, and in a widely-leaked letter penned afterwards by Mr David Tweedie, the final chairman of the APC and now chairman of the Accounting Standards Board, and Mr Ian Brindle, his predecessor and now senior partner at Price Waterhouse. The APC was underfunded, unwieldy and undemocratic. It was far too secretive in its operations. And its decision-making was continually being slowed down by its owners, the six members of the Consultative Committee of Accountancy Bodies: the Institutes of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, in Scotland and in Ireland, the Chartered Institutes of Management Accountants and of Public Finance and Accountancy, and the Chartered Association of Certified Accountants. The new, improved APB, which began operations early last year, looks in much better shape to address the criticisms facing auditors in the 1990s, even if it is still owned by CCAB. There are 18 voting members - of which half are not practising accountants - and four observers. A series of working groups is beginning to tackle an ambitious series of future auditing standards. 'Exposing' the drafts for public comment and focusing on users of accounts as the APB's customer is a prudent if obvious step. The process of producing in plain English just two types of statement - standards (which are mandatory) and practice notes (which are best practice on emerging issues) - is a welcome relief from the range of confusing edicts with varying degrees of authority that were loftily pronounced in the past. On the downside, criticism of the APB's tardiness in getting to work over the last year are somewhat petty. A more significant concern - how independent the body can be - can only be judged over time. But its refusal to tow the line of the accountancy firms - which argued against the expanded audit report it has now put forward - bodes well. In place of a meaningless, pro forma paragraph that has been almost universally ignored, the auditors' report in companies' accounts will from next year become a dense and detailed page of text, which users of financial information will do well to turn to very early in their perusal. Some will see the proposals as defensive. Much of the text will still have a standard - albeit lengthier - format. A good chunk (if not provided elsewhere in the accounts) will spell out that it is the directors and not the auditors who are responsible for the accounts being true and fair. The number of qualified audit reports (present in just 6 per cent of UK companies last year) is likely to fall, because auditors will no longer be required to qualify companies facing 'material' or 'fundamental' uncertainties in the following 12 months, provided they are satisfied that disclosure of these elements in the accounts is adequate. That will at least ensure any remaining qualifications are unequivocal, rather than in terms of unqualified approval 'subject to' certain items, as the current guidelines allow. At least on paper, auditors are being given greater powers to actively use their skills to detect these uncertainties, and cast their judgment forward as well as back across the previous year to which the financial statements relate. While the qualification will be lost, the proposed audit report will have a section flagging the uncertainties in compensation. But that raises two potential difficulties. First, the definition of 'fundamental' is likely to generate intense debate. The draft guidelines cite examples such as cash flow problems, inadequate borrowing facilities, major litigation and large debts falling due. Assessment of their significance may well prove highly contentious. Second, it will be difficult to tell how far companies will accept disclosure of these fundamental items in the new-style auditors' report. Theoretically, each would currently result in a qualified audit report. In reality, directors fight very hard to resist a qualification, and may have been able to conceal some important information from their shareholders up till now as a result. The hope is that some of these uncertainties that might previously have just escaped attracting a qualification will now be clearly flagged. But companies may fight equally hard to prevent disclosure, arguing, for example, that it would jeopardise their commercial position. A separate but vital point is the relationship between the APB and the Accounting Standards Board. The proposed auditing guidelines do nothing to clarify what constitutes 'true and fair' in accounts. Until new ASB standards have dealt with what Mr David Tweedie calls 'accounting fiddles', there is little the auditors can do. They can only be as effective as accounting standards allow, while finance directors hide behind these current standards. That point is reflected in the preface to the APB's 'going concern' draft, which calls on the ASB to develop a standard on the treatment of uncertainties. There is little sign yet that the ASB has taken the issue seriously in its own work programme. A final problem is how the new auditing standards will be policed. Mr Bill Morrison, chairman of the APB, talks about a 'twin barrel' approach. The Financial Reporting Review Panel is scrutinising companies, while the self-regulatory Joint Monitoring Unit of the accountancy bodies is watching the auditors, now armed with improved auditing guidelines. Unfortunately, like the deliberations between auditors and their clients, a great deal of the regulatory process remains behind closed doors. Whether that is inevitable or even desirable, it does little to remove the suspicion of accountants and auditors by the outside world. Users of accounts must hope that Stacy's red line does not open up new gaps below as it eagerly rises up the page of future APB documents.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Five appointed to PM's policy unit
DOC.TEXT: MR JOHN MAJOR took a further small step towards open government yesterday by announcing who had been appointed to the Downing Street policy unit. The five new members of the unit were appointed on the advice of the unit's head, Mrs Sarah Hogg. She took over within days of Mr Major becoming prime minister but inherited some colleagues from Mrs Thatcher's policy unit. Joining the Downing Street team are: Mr David Poole, on secondment from James Capel where he is a director; Ms Lucy Neville-Rolfe, a civil servant from the ministry of agriculture; Ms Katharine Ramsay, formerly a ministerial special adviser; Mr Damian Green, formerly industrial editor of the Channel Four Business Daily programme and unsuccessful Tory candidate in Brent East last month; and Ms Jill Rutter, a Treasury civil servant. Mr Nick True, the unit's deputy head, and Mr Alan Rosling, continue in their posts. While the announcement was the first formal press notice of such appointments, membership of the policy unit has scarcely been a matter of state secrecy in the past.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Government beat Labour charge by 52 majority
DOC.TEXT: THE government last night secured a majority of 52 (335-283) to defeat a Labour charge that it had failed to adopt economic policies to promote industrial and commercial investment, and improve education and training. Winding up the six-day debate on the Queen's Speech, Mr Tony Newton, leader of the House, promised full consultation about procedural changes in 'the most radical shake-up to our working practices for many decades'. The government's majority soared to 314 when, with Labour MPs abstaining, a Liberal Democrat attempt to condemn the omission from the Queen's Speech of a commitment to take Sterling into the narrow band of the Exchange Rate Mechanism was defeated by 332 votes to 18.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: MPs rebuffed on Maxwell appeal
DOC.TEXT: MPs campaigning on behalf of the Maxwell pensioners yesterday criticised the rejection by a junior minister of their suggestion that the government should seek ways of keeping pension funds open until investigations into the state of the Maxwell funds were complete. Mr Richard Page, Tory MP for Hertfordshire South-West, and Mr Frank Field, Labour chairman of the social security committee in the last parliament, will meet Mr Peter Lilley, social security secretary, on Tuesday to press for a 'lifebelt' for the pension funds. The talks follow a cross-party meeting on Tuesday, attended by more than 60 MPs, which called for an immediate Commons statement, and asked the government to consider how the funds might be kept open as 'a humanitarian as well as a practical gesture'. But Miss Ann Widdecombe, a junior social security minister, said it would be premature for the government to commit itself to any form of action, and questioned the usefulness of any move to 'drip-feed' the funds. The MPs believe that keeping the pension funds alive is critically important in increasing the prospects that the assets can be tracked down and retrieved by the trustees. The prime minister told pensioners of Maxwell-owned companies that compensation could be paid if there had been 'maladministration, either by the Department of Trade and Industry or Imro'. Sir Robert McCrindle, for Mr Major, said that if a complaint was made to the parliamentary ombudsman and an investigation proved maladministration had occurred, 'we may be in a similar situtation to that which prevailed in the case of the Barlow Clowes investors.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Waldegrave warns of threat to departments under Citizen's Charter
DOC.TEXT: MR William Waldegrave, the minister for the Citizen's Charter, warned last night that the careers of ministers and permanent secretaries could suffer if their departments fail to implement the charter. Mr Waldegrave told The Times that the prime minister was keen for the charter to receive a fresh impetus as part of his plans to reform the machinery of Whitehall.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Smith and Gould back reform
DOC.TEXT: LABOUR must reject the notion that minor policy changes will prove adequate to win the next election and instead develop a platform with an appeal that embraces the interests and aspirations of middle-class voters. That is the view held by both contenders for the party leadership in articles published in New Statesman and Society magazine today. Shadow chancellor Mr John Smith, the odds-on favourite, and Mr Bryan Gould, his challenger, definitively reject the so-called 'one last heave' notion, which argues that the party should simply repackage its current policies and improve on its communications with the electorate. But their approaches to broadening the party's appeal vary subtly, with Mr Gould delivering a thinly-veiled attack on his rival for his handling of economic policy. Mr Smith argues that Labour should play heavily on the argument of enlightened self-interest, a broad concept of freedom and economic logic. The shadow chancellor suggests that the 'comfortable and contented' are anxious about inner-city degeneration, unemployment and the decline in the quality of life. Mr Gould begins by criticising Labour's election campaign for failing to offer motives to middle-class voters to support the party. In a passage that will infuriate Mr Smith's supporters, he says the party endorsed Tory macroeconomic policies by accepting a simple goal of monetary stability, offering no route to full employment or recovery. He also asks why constructive proposals such as contributors' control over pensions funds, share ownership schemes and better employee rights were not proposed. In future, electors should not be treated as socio-economic groups but as individuals given the power that leaves them 'properly equipped to operate in a market place that would otherwise treat them unfairly'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Labour plans to abstain in Maastricht vote
DOC.TEXT: LABOUR MPs will be ordered to abstain in next week's vote on legislation to ratify the controversial Maastricht agreement on European Community treaty changes, the shadow cabinet agreed unanimously last night. Their decision guarantees the government a comfortable majority on the issue and brings to an end an impassioned debate within the Parliamentary Labour party. At a heavily attended weekly meeting of the PLP, about eight MPs argued vigorously that the party had several grounds on which it could justifiably vote against the government. But Mr Gerald Kaufman, the shadow foreign secretary, warned that to oppose the legislation would be inconsistent with Labour's stance at the general election. He was backed by Mr Neil Kinnock, the leader, who wound up the hour-long debate by reminding MPs that an opposing vote could be used against the party at the next election. Mr Stan Orme, the PLP chairman, argued that the Tory rebellion would be limited and the Liberal Democrats would almost certainly vote with the Conservatives. Liberal Democrat MPs agreed last night to support the Maastricht legislation on its second reading. But they will attempt to force debates during its passage on Economic and Monetary Union, the European parliament and the social chapter. The leadership's decision means Labour will table an amendment criticising the government's European stance, but will abstain on the main motion. But some Labour rebels can be expected to defy the whips and vote against. Liberal Democrat MP Archy Kirkwood was last night elected unopposed as the party's new chief whip. He replaces Mr Jim Wallace, the member for Orkney and Shetland, who becomes leader of the Scottish Liberal Democrats.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Parliament and Politics: Chancellor upbeat on growth aims
DOC.TEXT: BRITAIN'S return to economic growth would become 'firmly established' in 1992, Mr Norman Lamont, the chancellor, told the Commons last night. Confidently predicting a further reduction in inflation he said: 'We have a once-in-a-generation chance to push towards price stability'. The chancellor hoped for an increase in demand as the tax cuts made in the March Budget reached pay packets next week, and home-buyers used the extra money at their disposal through reductions in mortgage interest payments. He expected some of the increase in disposable incomes would 'feed through into higher consumer spending'. Mr Lamont's optimism contrasted with the judgment of Mr John Smith, shadow chancellor and front runner in Labour's leadership contest, who, on the final day of the debate on the Queen's Speech, led an attack on the government's continuing failure to halt the rise in unemployment. The chancellor also came under fire from Mr Neil Kinnock, the Labour leader, over his refusal to state the year in which the objective of returning to a balanced budget 'in the medium term' would be achieved. Mr Lamont stressed that he was not 'altering in any way' the forecast of a Pounds 28bn public sector borrowing requirement in the current financial year. The published figures for the PSBR in subsequent years - including the Pounds 32bn for 1993-94 - were 'assumptions' and not forecasts. The chancellor claimed that the projection for the last year covered by the table in the Budget Red Book - which Mr Kinnock emphasised was Pounds 6bn - was 'very close to balance indeed'. Mr Lamont said the uncertainty caused by the possibility of a Labour victory in the general election had held back company investment and orders, and subdued consumer demand. Now the message from forward-looking surveys of business and consumer confidence was clear, and the stock market and foreign exchange markets had signalled their renewed confidence in the government's policies. He emphasised,too, that with last week's 1/2 percentage point cut in bank rate the differential between British and German interest rates had been reduced from about 7 per cent to just a quarter of one per cent, lower than at any time in the past decade. Thanks to the government's refusal to bow to short-term pressures, Britain's inflation performance had improved out of all recognition, he said. Underlying producer-output price inflation was lower than at any time since the early 1970s, and he expected it to fall to below 2 per cent in 1993. The chancellor emphasised the need to control public expenditure, but Mr Smith deplored the lack of any reference in the Queen's Speech to unemployment and the recession, and accused Tory MPs of being interested only in 'the level of their shares on the Stock Exchange'. He said the government had failed to foster the manufacturing sector - the wealth-producing sector of the economy. To taunts from Tory backbenchers over the outcome of the election, Mr Smith said Labour's defeat did not alter the fact that investment was falling, unemployment rising and that the government had failed to support industry. He warned that Britain had no future as a low cost, low-skilled 'bargain-basement economy'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Dean to quit post in merged print union
DOC.TEXT: MS BRENDA DEAN is to resign from her job as deputy general secretary of the GPMU print union. She became a household name during the Wapping dispute with News International. Ms Dean, 49, failed to become leader of the new union last year when Sogat, the general print union which she had led since 1985, merged with the smaller NGA skilled print union. After she was beaten by Mr Tony Dubbins, the NGA leader, by 78,442 votes to 72,657, it was assumed she would not stay long as his deputy. Ms Dean said she was sad to leave after 32 years in the union movement but was going with 'no recriminations'. She added that the future was 'a blank sheet of paper' but she is expected to have no difficulty in finding a prominent position, probably in the public sector. According to some union officials Ms Dean might have left GPMU earlier but felt a duty to protect the senior officers of her former union after the merger. Sogat moved into the NGA's Bedford headquarters after the merger, reinforcing the impression that it was more a takeover by the NGA. Ms Dean accepted that there had been friction at national level after the merger, but added that overall 'it has gone much better than expected'. Observer, Page 19

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Investigator into BCCI is accused: MP names Abu Dhabi official
DOC.BYLINE: By RALPH ATKINS and RICHARD DONKIN
DOC.TEXT: AN ABU DHABI official actively involved in that country's investigation into fraud at the collapsed Bank of Credit and Commerce International was named in the Commons last night as having benefited from 'clearly fraudulent' transactions in BCCI shares. Mr Ghanem Faris Al Mazrui, who was the Abu Dhabi government's representative on the board of BCCI, gained from 'no risk' deals, according to a report by lawyers acting for BCCI creditors and disclosed by Mr Keith Vaz, Labour MP for Leicester East. Mr Vaz emphasised that he was convinced that Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan al-Nahyan, the ruler of Abu Dhabi, knew nothing about the deals. Similar accusations have been made in reports by Price Waterhouse, the auditors to BCCI, but their emergence last night could undermine the provisional agreement on a compensation deal for BCCI depositors which is awaiting the approval of creditors. The disclosure by Mr Vaz under parliamentary privilege of the report's contents is likely to upset the Abu Dhabi government at a critical point. It will also increase pressure on BCCI's liquidators. Mr Mazrui is a senior adviser to Sheikh Zayed and is still involved in Abu Dhabi's investigations into fraud at the bank. Mr Vaz called for Mr Mazrui to make a statement, 'either to deny knowledge of what this report refers to or to give an explanation of his actual involvement.' The MP read extracts from a report compiled by Norton Rose, the firm of solicitors commissioned by the BCCI interim creditors' committee to study the proposed compensation package, which includes Dollars 1.7bn (Pounds 937m) injected by the Abu Dhabi government. The leaked report said: 'Mr Al Mazrui, according to Price Waterhouse, admitted that he had benefited from 'no risk' transactions in which he purchased BCCI Group shares. Such transactions, including the manipulation of the BCCI Group share price, were clearly fraudulent. Mr Al Mazrui apparently informed other government officials of his involvement in April 1990.' Another passage, read by Mr Vaz and referring to the majority shareholders which included the Abu Dhabi government, said: 'We see no means by which Mr Al Mazrui's knowledge (if any) can be imputed to the majority shareholders.' Mr Vaz also protested about documents held in Abu Dhabi to which the creditors' lawyers had not been allowed access. He called for the UK government to intervene and also to provide more help for the 1,200 former BCCI employees and 40,000 depositors. Mr Vaz said that if the government 'was to support the view of depositors and creditors that more money should be made available, I believe the Abu Dhabi government would act positively.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / BBC launches subscriber service
DOC.TEXT: BBC SELECT, the subscription television service of the BBC, may launch family educational programmes including language tuition for children. A pilot programme on French for children aged seven to 11 has been produced, and talks on collaboration have started with publishers. Ms Angie Mason, senior commissioning editor for education at BBC Select, said: 'It's a question of which publishers we decide to go with.' She was speaking after the official launch of BBC Select, which plans to use spare capacity on BBC 1 and BBC 2 transmitters in the early hours to broadcast specialist programmes to businesspeople, accountants, lawyers, farmers and yacht owners. Ms Mason believes BBC Select may have identified a gap in the market by delivering a range of educational programmes direct to the home. The first BBC Select subscription service - the Executive Business Club - will start broadcasting on May 27. Professor Graham Robinson, chairman of the service, said yesterday he expected to reach Pounds 2m turnover in its first year of operation. Prof Robinson said he had 131 clients including three high street banks and Prudential Assurance. The charge for a company intending to make copies of the training programmes available to 2,000 staff is less than Pounds 10,000 a year. Meridian Television, which defeated TVS in last year's competitive tenders for ITV licences, has lost its director of news and regional programmes. Ms Dianne Nelmes resigned yesterday and said that after setting up programme structures and hiring key people she did not wish to remain.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Warning over costs in accounts proposals
DOC.TEXT: PROPOSALS unveiled yest-erday by the Auditing Practices Board may create extra costs and impose additional responsibilities on directors and auditors, experts warned yesterday. The plans were welcomed by Mr Roger Davis, head of audit at Coopers & Lybrand Deloitte, the accountancy firm. However, he warned that auditors would be put on the spot by the proposed requirement to express an opinion on whether a company was a going concern for the following 12 months. Mr Hugh Collum, chairman of the 100 Group of leading finance directors, said the going concern statement was an important contribution but 'it's going to need careful handling, particularly for companies in difficulties.' The Confederation of British Industry commented: 'It puts a heavy burden on directors and auditors.' The proposal for an expanded report spelling out that directors and not auditors are responsible for the accounts giving a true and fair view of the business was welcomed by the Institute of Directors. A report commissioned by the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales said that an expanded report would be useful in reducing the 'expectations gap' in public understanding of the role of auditors. The Expanded Audit Report. Technical Dept, ICAEW, PO Box 433, London EC2P 2BJ. Pounds 10. Accountancy Column, Page 10

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Commercial freedom for nuclear body urged
DOC.TEXT: THE UK Atomic Energy Authority should have more freedom to undertake commercial activities outside the nuclear industry, the Monopolies and Mergers Commission said yesterday. The authority is now known as AEA Technology, and it exploits expertise gained from the nuclear power programme. The commission said AEA was 'significantly inhibited' by constraints which prevent it manufacturing non-nuclear products and forming joint ventures outside the nuclear field. It has investigated AEA as part of its programme to review all public-sector bodies. The commission also said that AEA's businesses, which range from atomic research to petroleum services, 'rest uneasily in the public sector where their entrepreneurial activities are inevitably somewhat constrained'. The MMC concluded that AEA could generate higher net revenue. The report identified weaknesses in financial and project control, investment appraisal and marketing. Monopolies and Mergers Commission: UK Atomic Energy Authority. HMSO, Pounds 19.40.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Councils criticised over planning
DOC.TEXT: MOST councils are failing to meet government targets for faster planning decisions in spite of a fall in development activity, the Audit Commission says in a report published today. The government spending watchdog says only a handful of English councils are satisfying the target of deciding 80 per cent of planning applications within eight weeks. The target was set in 1982 by Mr Michael Heseltine, then environment secretary. The commission says the proportion of applications decided within eight weeks declined from 70 per cent in 1982-83 to 46 per cent in 1989-90. It adds that there has been only a small improvement since 1989-90 in spite of a fall in applications and a rise in staff. The commission says councils should take advantage of lower workloads to streamline and improve their planning procedures. The report was welcomed yesterday by the Conservative-led Association of District Councils; the Association of London Authorities, which represents most Labour London boroughs; and the Council for the Protection of Rural England (CPRE), the environmental group. Mr Tony Burton, senior planner at the CPRE, warned, however, that 'proper protection for the countryside cannot be secured by rushed planning decisions to meet artificial deadlines imposed by the government'. During 1990-91, English local authorities made decisions on 518,000 planning applications compared with more than 600,000 applications in each of the two preceding years. Applications last year, however, were still 40 per cent higher than 10 years before. Mr Bob Chilton, local government director at the commission, said: 'Having survived the pressures of the development boom of the late 1980s, local authorities should use the current easing in the volume of applications to assess the quality of the local service they provide and to prepare for the next surge in applications.' The commission said that time wasted in administration could be put to better use in improving assessment procedures and providing greater public consultation. It urged planning departments to avoid wasting time by setting clear objectives and providing opportunities for discussion and advice before developers submitted formal applications. Audit Commission: Building in Quality, A Study of Development Control. HMSO Pounds 8.50.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Ministers review London bus plans
DOC.TEXT: CONTROVERSIAL proposals for the deregulation and privatisation of the London bus network appear to be undergoing a review by the fresh ministerial team at the Department of Transport. The department yesterday announced that a working party comprising a range of interests in the capital had been set up 'to advise on the practical aspects of implementing deregulation.' Mr Steven Norris, minister for transport in London, said the government remained committed to extending bus de-regulation to the capital. However, the creation of the working party follows last week's surprise omission from the Queen's Speech of legislative proposals for London bus deregulation, which previous transport minsters had consistently promised early in the next parliament. Transport ministers seem unlikely to drop deregulation altogether, but some Conservative MPs in the capital are believed to be deeply concerned about the proposals in their present form.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Big rise reported in formation of company audit committees
DOC.TEXT: MANY British companies have created audit committees voluntarily in the past few years, but few disclose much about them in their accounts, according to a report commissioned by the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales. A sample of 300 organisations was polled and replies were received from 202 industrial concerns, including listed companies, and 44 financial institutions. Two thirds of the industrial concerns and 88 per cent of the institutions had audit committees, compared with 17 per cent of large UK companies in a 1985 study Mr Paul Collier, a lecturer in accounting at Exeter University who carried out the research for the institute early last year, said greater levels of control and the requirement for compliance committees explained the higher incidence among financial institutions. The typical audit committee has one executive director and three or four non-executive directors, appointed for an indefinite period. It meets three times a year and reviews company accounting principles and practice. Half of the committees in the survey review auditors' fees. But the annual reports of 45 per cent of the industrial concerns and 21 per cent of the institutions did not disclose even the presence of an audit committee. Among industrial concerns, many public-sector organisations and listed companies had audit committees, while other businesses and the subsidiaries of foreign-owned companies had very few. More than half of the committees had been created within the previous five years. The most frequently cited reasons for their creation were good corporate practice and strengthening the effectiveness of non-executive directors. Many companies without audit committees dismissed them as an additional layer of bureaucracy, and said that their costs would outweigh their benefits. Audit Committees in Large UK Companies. Technical Dept, ICAEW, PO Box 433, London EC2P 2BJ. Pounds 15.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Work experience western-style: Peter Norman reports on the Russian 'secondees' who are eager converts to capitalism
DOC.TEXT: THEIR resolve stiffened by an outward bound course in the Welsh mountains, the first of up to 1,000 young Russians will soon start working with British financial institutions under Mr Norman Lamont's scheme to spread practical knowledge of the market economy in the former Soviet Union. Last night the first pilot group of 20 'secondees' and their employers attended a reception in 11 Downing Street to mark the formal beginning of what has become known as the chancellor's Financial Sector Scheme. The idea, first put forward by Mr Lamont last October, is that banks, building societies, insurance companies, brokers, accountants and solicitors across Britain should provide jobs for financial services personnel from Russia and the other former Soviet republics for between six months and a year. On their return they will become an elite cadre that will help build the financial, legal and accounting infrastructure needed to modernise the former Soviet Union. 'A modern financial system is basic to the future of Russia,' Mr Lamont said. 'I think they need help there. By asking each company really to make a small sacrifice, just to pay somebody for a short period of time, it seemed to me that by harnessing private effort we really could achieve quite a lot.' Having met five of the Russians this week, it seemed more likely that the first group of employers - which range from NM Rothschild in the City to the Marsden Building Society in Nelson, Lancashire - will be gaining a valuable asset rather than making a 'small sacrifice' by employing the secondees. All were extremely keen to start work around the end of this month after completing an intensive course in business English and finance at Middlesex Polytechnic in Hendon. They also proved to be surprisingly knowledgeable, reflecting, in some cases, intensive study of capitalist ways in academic institutions under the communist regime. Mr Viatcheslav Butyrski, at 28 the head of securities trading at Promstroybank in Moscow, was looking forward to six months with Swiss Bank Corporation in London in which he would be able to relate his theoretical knowledge of share and bond trading to modern practice. He obtained a degree in capital market studies from the USSR Institute of Banking before joining the 70-year-old Promstroybank after it was converted into a joint stock bank a year ago. Ms Marina Krupina, 37, will be working in Cardiff with the Bank of Wales, where she hopes to learn how a medium-sized western bank operates. She says she has already gained some insight into western accountancy and taxation practices after working at Promstroybank for five years on joint ventures with foreign companies. Mr Igor Kostikov, 33, is already an entrepreneur in his own right as one of the owners and directors of Marka, a private sector financial consultancy and stockbrokerage. His varied career began with the study of Marxist political economy. But he claims that he has spent six years acquiring expertise about the British economy, including the privatisation of the oil and electricity supply industries. The main computer centre of the USSR Ministry of Finance may seem an odd apprenticeship for a stockmarket career. But Ms Elena Shakhurina, 26, is now a fervent advocate of equities and privatisation and looking forward to applying experience acquired with Nikko Europe when she returns to Moscow's International Stock Exchange in six months' time. Just a year ago Mr Max Diakonov, 22, graduated from Moscow's finance academy and joined the international department of Inkombank, one of the new Russian commercial banks, as head of correspondent banking. 'I have very good relations with western banks. But I don't have enough experience. That is why I am here. I will work in Lloyds Bank in London and Birmingham and try and find something really good for the Russian economy,' he says. 'I want to be an expert, the best in my sphere.' This first batch of secondees are impressive. But officials from the British Council, which is managing the scheme, point out that the first candidates 'self-selected' themselves, after hearing about the plan on the Moscow gossip circuit or having been tipped off by employers that were in close contact with the British Embassy or British Council in Moscow. They then had to go through a rigorous selection procedure, including a tough test in English. Sir Derek Thomas, European adviser to NM Rothschild, helped to interview the candidates. He has no doubt that Russia and the other republics will make the transition to the market economy if the pilot group is representative. So far about 300 UK companies have promised to take on a secondee. 'And if we can get 1,000 people, that actually is a very big thing,' Mr Lamont said. But the young Russians now in Britain are under no illusion that the hard work begins once they return home. As Mr Diakonov says: 'The main aim of the scheme is to help but not to solve our problems.' The Chancellor's Financial Sector Scheme, The British Council, Projects Division, 20 Bedfordbury, London WC2N 2BL, tel 071 389 8350, fax 071 389 8399. After September 1992 at Medlock Street, Manchester, tel 061 957 7000, fax 061 957 7111.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Holiday operators expect a tough year
DOC.BYLINE: By GARY MEAD and BETHAN HUTTON
DOC.TEXT: AN EXPECTED post-election boom in package holidays has failed to materialise, leaving tour operators facing a second difficult year. A number of tour operators have cut the price of holidays in May and June by as much as 60 per cent to fill empty seats - in some cases up to a quarter of their capacity. With Thomson, the largest operator, last-minute bargain-seekers can buy for Pounds 199 a fly-drive holiday to Florida which would normally cost more than Pounds 400. Analysts also point to a new trend for holidaymakers to wait longer before making bookings, depriving tour operators of the benefit of early deposits. The move to last-minute bookings means that tour operators now have less cash on deposit earning interest over several months. The Civil Aviation Authority yesterday published figures showing that tour operators had overcapacity of 1.6m holidays in the 12 months to September 30 last year and a turnover of Pounds 440m less than the tour industry had predicted. The 40 largest operators had obtained CAA licences for 11.9m passengers, but actually carried only 10.3m. This year, tour operators have told the authority they expect to carry 13.5m passengers, an increase of more than 30 per cent on last year's actual figures. Authority licences for this year project turnover of Pounds 4.44bn, a substantial increase on both the forecast for 1990-91 (Pounds 3.65bn) and the turnover achieved (Pounds 3.21bn). Thomas Cook, the travel agent, said yesterday that those in the industry who expected 'a post-election expansion of package holiday demand' had been disappointed. Holidays for May and June have 'not been selling as well as would have been liked' but Thomas Cook said the case would be different in the latter part of June through to September. Summer bookings - where discounting has not yet been necessary - are already 'full to the brim'. Thomas Cook believes that the projections by some operators of an increase of 20 per cent to 40 per cent in demand this year is over-optimistic. 'Those which are looking for a 7 per cent to 10 per cent increase are being more realistic', it said. Mr Harry Coe, group finance director of Airtours, the third largest operator, said the level of discounting was not unusual. 'Every year there is excess capacity in May and June, and every year there is price-cutting in the late bookings market in order to move it,' he said. Lex, Page 20

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Watchdog urges profit clawback
DOC.TEXT: THE government could have increased its proceeds from the privatisation of the electricity distribution industry in 1990 by clawing back part of the profits which the companies reported in the subsequent year, according to the National Audit Office. In a report on the sale of the 12 regional electricity companies the government spending watchdog says the Department of Energy considered introducing a provision for profit clawbacks over several years but decided against it because this could have affected the payment of dividends by the companies and cut the proceeds. The Audit Office says it would have been 'appropriate' for the department to explore whether higher proceeds could have been obtained by clawing back at least a portion of the profits that exceeded the companies' forecasts. The office also says that with hindsight the government could have earned more from the sale by retaining a portion of the shares to take advantage of the rise in the share price during the offer period. It recommends the government retains a substantial minority in future privatisations for this purpose. The sale of the twelve regional electricity companies. National Audit Office. Pounds 7.10. World electricity survey, separate section

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Companies act to exploit upturn
DOC.BYLINE: By MICHAEL CASSELL, Business Correspondent and JAMES BUXTON
DOC.TEXT: MANY MANUFACTURING companies have acted during the recession to take advantage of an economic upturn which is already under way, according to a survey published yesterday by Coopers & Lybrand Deloitte, the accountancy firm. The Gallup survey of 450 of Britain's biggest manufacturers shows that most have implemented cost-reduction programmes and have speeded up the introduction of new products. They have also invested more in new production processes, increased export business and improved delivery times. In spite of figures suggesting manufacturing investment has fallen during the recession, the survey shows that more than two thirds of manufacturers have maintained or increased the cash value of capital-investment programmes. More than a third of companies expect to have more employees in training within three years, and a quarter report that they are training more people than in 1989. Only 12 per cent of companies surveyed suggest that poor relationships with their workforces are affecting performance. Coopers says the survey provides evidence that many of the factors which contributed to the decline of manufacturing in the past decade are being reversed. It says manufacturing is making significant advances across all sectors. The survey also highlights some of the continuing problems which have weakened performance. It shows short-term attitudes on the development of businesses still prevail, with only one in 15 companies making any business plans for more than five years ahead, in contrast to Japanese competitors, which plan up to 25 years ahead. Nearly half of the companies surveyed cited Britain's 'roller-coaster' economy as an obstacle, while three quarters blamed high interest rates. Made in the UK. Coopers & Lybrand Deloitte, Harman House, 1 George Street, Uxbridge UB8 1QQ. Free. THE GOVERNMENT must change its attitude to manufacturing if British industry is to prosper, according to Mr Ron Garrick, chief executive of Weir Group, the Glasgow-based pump manufacturer, James Buxton writes. Its policies of the 1980s aimed at making Britain a post-industrial economy by fostering the growth of services were misguided, Mr Garrick said in his 1992 Engineering Manufacturing Forum lecture in Glasgow yesterday. He added: 'The most successful economies in terms of growth of gross domestic product also have the strongest manufacturing industries.' He wanted better policies for export credits, overseas aid and the Pounds 5bn the government spends on research. He said he was not seeking interventionist policies. British manufacturing had improved its performance substantially in the 1980s and now needed to regain ground lost to imported equipment.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Health trust managers strive for a new relationship: Lisa Wood and Catherine Milton on the effects of government reforms on industrial relations in the NHS
DOC.BYLINE: By LISA WOOD and CATHERINE MILTON
DOC.TEXT: ONE OF THE most immediate effects of government reforms to the National Health Service is likely to be on employee relations. Many personnel managers in the new self-governing trusts, which are allowed to set their own pay and conditions, are examining ways of leaving national agreements. But a Financial Times survey of more than half of the first 57 NHS trusts which came into existence just over a year ago shows that most are initially moving with caution. Mr Bob Rotchell, director of operations at West Dorset Community NHS Trust, said that nationally agreed terms and conditions in the health service had been a 'personnel manager's nightmare'. Like most trust managers, however, he said the devolution to trusts of managerial responsibility for industrial relations was not easy. 'Any group who thought when they established a trust that setting local pay and conditions would be easy must have been very naive,' he said. Nevertheless, greater flexibility should eventually mean a smaller, better-trained NHS workforce. Within weeks of becoming self-governing a year ago, Guy's and Lewisham Trust in London announced plans to shed several hundred jobs to cut Pounds 5m from labour costs. The trust is now balancing its books and has given lower-paid staff an extra Pounds 5 per week above national rates, but Mr Peter Griffiths, chief executive, expects the trust to operate with up to 20 per cent fewer staff in Guy's hospital in five years. Such reductions are likely to become widespread in the health service. The jobs of its many unskilled ancillary workers and of some laboratory and other technical staff will be at risk. The FT survey also highlights managers' ambitions for an overhaul of the traditional negotiating machinery. Most trusts want a single pay spine, or scale, for all their employees. That would replace the dozen or so present scales, including those negotiated by the Whitley Councils, which have traditionally set pay and conditions in the NHS. It would also replace the newer pay review bodies for nurses, doctors and professions allied to medicine. An overhaul would facilitate local pay bargaining. The government says it will not abolish national machinery, but it could become redundant or, at best, a 'benchmark' for local deals. Bradford Hospital Trust said: 'Nobody will be worse off. Whitley is regarded as a minimum.' All trusts in the survey agreed that pay would not be squeezed as a result of the changes. Most said they were affected by skill shortages and the need to attract staff, but Southend Health Care Trust warned: 'In some cases we will pay more than Whitley and, if we don't need to, we won't' Harmonising conditions for employees could, in the short-term, increase pay bills. But the process is likely to be linked to greater flexibility. Several trusts are taking on new healthcare assistants to assist trained nurses in wards from which student nurses are being removed. United Bristol Healthcare Trust said: 'As the number of people available as nationally trained nurses falls, so we will be forced to take on more people who are trained locally.' Other findings of the survey include: Only a few trusts have negotiated formal recognition agreements with unions. A few were reluctant to discuss the issue, including Central Middlesex Hospital and Nuffield Orthopaedic Trust. One, West Dorset Community Health Trust, has successfully agreed and implemented a pay package, including a local performance pay deal, with unions this year. Homewood Trust in Chertsey, Surrey, has agreed with unions a package that includes what is in effect a no-strike deal. But no local pay offer has yet been agreed. Northumbria Ambulance Trust has awarded employees a local pay deal this year, but it was negotiated with the Association of Professional Ambulance Personnel (Apap), a union not affiliated to the Trades Union Congress. Apap has been given sole negotiating rights at the trust. No other first-wave trusts plan to give sole rights to a union, although most want single-table bargaining, in which several unions appoint representatives to conduct joint negotiations. Cohse, the health-service union, says that only 15 trusts have signed formal agreements with unions to negotiate over pay and conditions. Acas, the conciliation service, sees great strides in employment relationship among trusts. It adds, however, that 'there often remains a lack of expertise in this area among local managers and trade union representatives alike'. Most trusts in the survey offered slightly different conditions of employment in contracts offered to new staff. Mr Brian Carpenter, personnel director of South Devon Healthcare Trust, said it had introduced changes to time off and had brought in performance-related pay for senior managers. Changes made by other trusts include limiting appeal rights and adjustments to maternity leave. Many trusts are using outside consultants to investigate job evaluation. Nine trusts in the south-west of England are working together on investigating job evaluation, a system trusts say could add to wage bills. Mr Rotchell of West Dorset said he had been told by consultants that the exercise could add 5 per cent. Most trusts want a single pay spine covering all staff although a few said such ambitions would be hard to realise because of the complexity of arranging so many groups of staff on one scale. Southend said it would like five or six spines and proposed big changes such as abolishing the increment related to length of service. It did not plan to introduce performance-related pay. Harmonisation of terms and conditions is favoured by trusts, but all agreed that such a move would incur costs.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Eggar seeks power price cut
DOC.BYLINE: By JULIET SYCHRAVA and ANDREW SLADE
DOC.TEXT: THE electricity industry must cut domestic bills to reflect cheaper coal prices, Mr Tim Eggar, energy minister, said yesterday. Mr Eggar, speaking during a visit to Rufford and Ollerton collieries in Nottinghamshire, said it was vital that consumers were given the benefit of any deal between the electricity producers and British Coal. He was confident British Coal would be able to produce coal at prices that would benefit electricity consumers. 'The challenge that faces this and other pits is to reduce their costs to produce coal competitively,' he added. 'It is a challenge I am convinced British Coal can meet.' Mr Eggar said it was important for British Coal to be privatised without delay. This meant that it must agree contracts to sell coal to the electricity industry as soon as possible. These contracts would determine how many British Coal pits would survive, Mr Eggar added. He would not confirm rumours that the government was about to negotiate an agreement between British Coal and the electricity industry. He saw a role for the government as a 'facilitator'. The government, British Gas, the regulatory body Ofgas and 11 of the regional electricity companies in England and Wales are to set up an independent Energy Savings Trust to promote the efficient use of energy, Andrew Slade writes. The initiative promised in the Conservatives' general election manifesto was announced yesterday by Mr Michael Howard, environment secretary. His department said the government expected funding to come from the electricity industry and consumers. a

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / CBI survey points to recovery areas: Yorkshire and Humberside region, east Midlands and Wales are expected to lead growth in services and manufacturing
DOC.TEXT: WALES, the east Midlands, and the Yorkshire and Humberside region are likely to lead the economic recovery, according to the Business Strategies consultancy. Its conclusion is based on a regional breakdown released yesterday of prospects for manufacturers, conducted by the consultancy with the Confederation of British Industry. Ms Bridget Rosewell, joint managing director of Business Strategies, said the three regions all combined relative strength in manufacturing with reasonably good prospects for services - which account for about three quarters of gross domestic product. The study is based on the CBI's quarterly industrial trends survey, which questioned 1,328 manufacturing companies between March 27 and April 13. According to the study, manufacturers across the UK are generally more optimistic than four months ago. Expectations about a recovery were particularly marked in East Anglia, the south-east and the west Midlands. All three areas were hit hard in the early stages of the recession in 1990. However, the north of England and Scotland - two regions relatively little affected in the early part of the recession - appear to be suffering more now in terms of depressed orders and output. Out of the 11 UK regions, five have seen a decrease in the past year in the proportion of companies working below capacity. These are the south-east, East Anglia, Yorkshire and Humberside, east Midlands and Wales. Most regions have continued over the past four months to see a fall in output and orders, but at a lower rate than last year. Another relatively gloomy conclusion is that all regions except the north expect a decline in investment in plant and machinery over the next 12 months. The expected rate of reduction in capital spending appears to be slowing in the east and west Midlands and Wales.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Fraud recoveries
DOC.TEXT: CITY of London Police said in its annual report that it recovered, or saved from fraud attempts nearly Pounds 1bn last year. The figure did not include the frauds involving Bank of Credit and Commerce International and Robert Maxwell.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Machine-tool sales
DOC.TEXT: JONES & Shipman, the machine tool manufacturer, yesterday announced more than pounds 500,000 worth of orders and claimed there were signs that manufacturing industry was beginning to pull out of the recession

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Freelance selling team for IBM
DOC.TEXT: INTERNATIONAL Business Machines is expected to announce later today that it is to use freelance salespeople to sell medium-sized computers on a commission-only basis. The UK subsidiary of IBM is training an initial 50 freelance salespeople, who will sell machines at the lower end of IBM's AS/400 medium-sized range.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / LSE planning permission
DOC.TEXT: THE London School of Economics' plan to move to County Hall, home of the former Greater London Council, won planning permission from Lambeth Council yesterday. The building, owned by the London Residuary Body, was sold in March to Shirayama, the Japanese property developer. The contract gives Mr Michael Howard, environment secretary, the option until next October of cancelling the deal.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Legal aid checks are criticised
DOC.TEXT: CRIMINAL legal aid is being granted without proper checks on applicants' eligibility, according to a report by the Commons public accounts committee. The matter was investigated after the qualification by Sir John Bourn, then comptroller and auditor-general, of the 1990-91 appropriation account of the Lord Chancellor's Department. Sir John cited 'uncertainty as to the propriety and regularity' of spending on criminal legal aid. Magistrates' courts - which account for more than half the Pounds 333m spent yearly on criminal legal aid - attracted particular criticism. Expenditure on Criminal Legal Aid. HMSO. Pounds 9.75.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Unions oppose relocation
DOC.TEXT: A CIVIL SERVICE union yesterday accused the government of spending public money to bail out private-sector property developers. The First Division Association, which represents senior civil servants, said it opposed plans to relocate 2,000 civil servants from the environment and transport departments to London's Docklands. The transfer is due to be completed by the end of next year, and is expected to be to Canary Wharf, the property development owned by Olympia & York.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Dismay over leak of Ulster proposal
DOC.TEXT: UNIONISTS in Northern Ireland were reported last night to be dismayed at the leaking of a submission to the round-table talks on the province's political future, our Belfast Correspondent writes. The submission from the nationalist Social Democratic and Labour party was tabled as part of the first phase of the talks. It proposes a European-style consultative assembly which would involve the appointment of commissioners for the province, including one by Dublin. Mr Peter Robinson, deputy leader of the Democratic Unionist Party, said he was furious at the breach of confidentiality. SDLP officers also expressed anger. Sir Patrick Mayhew, Northern Ireland secretary, said the leak 'rather strikes at the trust which has been maintained until now and I hope will be maintained in the future'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Job prospects up in first quarter
DOC.TEXT: JOB PROSPECTS improved in the first quarter of the year, the Alfred Marks recruitment agency said yesterday. It added that the number of temporary posts rose much faster than the total of permanent jobs. The employment department is expected to announce a further rise in unemployment today. Economists in the City of London are predicting a monthly increase of about 25,000, in line with the recent underlying trend of a slight improvement. Unemployment has risen steadily since March 1990. According to the Alfred Marks survey, temporary posts rose 13.2 per cent compared with 9.4 per cent in the same period last year. Permanent posts rose 1.2 per cent compared with a 6.6 per cent fall in the first quarter last year. Using temporary staff enables employers to respond more flexibly to fluctuations in demand. It is not clear, however, whether the increase in temporary work indicates a more flexible labour market or employers' continuing uncertainty about the strength of any economic recovery. The figures show more vacancies in the north and west of England than in the south and east. Vacancies rose 23.5 per cent in the west Midlands compared with a fall of 5.5 per cent a year before. In the north of England vacancies increased by 11.9 per cent compared with a fall of 4.4 per cent last year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / George warns on single EC currency
DOC.TEXT: A WARNING about the practical difficulties involved in the move to a single European currency was delivered last night by Mr Eddie George, deputy governor of the Bank of England. In a speech at Hull University, Mr George questioned both the timetable for European economic and monetary union, and the credibility of the proposed European Central Bank. The remarks by Mr George - a noted sceptic on Emu - may influence MPs ahead of next week's Commons debate on the Maastricht treaty, which last December set the general framework for a move to union later this decade. Mr George also held out little prospect of any early move by the government to reduce base rates further, following last week's 0.5 percentage point reduction to 10 per cent. In the longer term he hinted at the possibility of bringing UK rates lower than those in Germany, on condition that Britain kept its inflation low and retained the confidence of the financial markets. On Emu, Mr George said practical difficulties meant the schedule as set out at Maastricht looked ambitious. Under the Maastricht plan, the final stage of Emu will start up with or without Britain by 1999. The problems included converting national currencies into European currency units, and producing the necessary coins and notes. Another was establishing Ecu payments systems. Mr George was particularly sceptical about the operation of the proposed central bank. It is planned that in the final stages of Emu the bank would administer the single currency and set pan-European interest rates. He said that the central bank might be 'vulnerable to misjudgment and to outside influence'. In terms of determining the correct level of interest rates, the central bank would be faced with huge problems in monitoring how factors such as financial liberalisation affected the pan-European economy.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Smog shuts Chile factories
DOC.TEXT: OFFICIALS in the Chilean capital yesterday ordered five factories to shut down, and two out of every five vehicles off the road for the rest of the week, to fight smog, Reuter reports from Santiago. Levels of pollution which could affect the health of children, old people, the pregnant and the sick were registered, said a pollution commission. It closed three furnaces, a cement works and a metal foundry.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Ramos catches up with rival in Philippine poll
DOC.TEXT: MR FIDEL RAMOS, the former Philippine defence chief, last night caught up with his main rival Mrs Miriam Defensor Santiago, in the race for the presidency, according to latest unofficial counts based on a sixth of the votes cast in Monday's election. Earlier Mrs Santiago, a lawyer and anti-corruption campaigner, had claimed victory but her opponents had said her claim was premature. Quoting Winston Churchill, the outspoken Mrs Santiago said she would be magnanimous in victory. 'Certain losers among the presidential candidates might try to cheat, and may even have started doing so,' said Mrs Santiago, who hopes to undermine the country's oligarchy of influential families, 'but the youth and all the Filipinos who helped me to win will not allow the triumph of evil'. Mr Ramos had said yesterday afternoon that he expected the rankings to change in his favour as votes came in from the provinces following Monday's presidential, congressional and local elections. The lengthy manual process of counting ballot papers - each with up to 44 handwritten names - from as many as 27m voters has already given rise to several disputes in local political contests, but businessmen have reacted favourably to the relatively peaceful conduct of the poll. Both Mr Ramos and Mrs Santiago are regarded as candidates who would encourage private enterprise and foreign investment, and the twin stock markets of Manila and Makati rose more than 7 per cent yesterday from their levels on Friday after holidays on Monday and Tuesday. The Manila Stock Exchange composite index rose 93.02 points to 1,328.04. A glance at the official table of comparative statistics on violent incidents in recent elections helps to explain the euphoria. Between January 12 and yesterday morning there were only 12 'liquidations' (assassinations) throughout the islands, compared to 95 in the chaotic 1986 presidential elections and 93 in the local elections of 1988. Sceptics, however, have noted that the election cannot be said to be finished until the results are clear and have expressed fears about the destabilising effect of the long counting period. In an attempt to defuse the tension, the Commission on Elections yesterday warned candidates against making premature victory claims and announced an agreement with television and radio stations under which all unofficial counts - except for one authorised by the Commission - would cease from noon today.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Indian state institutions snap up shares
DOC.BYLINE: By DAVID HOUSEGO and R C MURTHY
DOC.TEXT: INDIA'S state-owned financial institutions took part in large-scale share purchases yesterday to reverse a price collapse on India's stock markets. The Bombay Stock Exchange 30-share index rose 11 per cent, adding 344.76 to 3,431.13, wiping out Tuesday's sharp decline. The two-week tumble in share prices had been triggered by revelations of a financial scandal that resulted in the syphoning of funds from the government securities market into equity purchases. The massive intervention by the financial institutions came after the stock exchange authorities overnight banned forward selling in 85 shares. In an effort to curb abuses in the interbank securities market the Reserve Bank, the country's central bank, yesterday issued fresh guidelines to commercial banks operating in the market. The central bank said banks should not hold an oversold position in a security - meaning that a bank should not sell a security which it did not actually hold. Finance Ministry officials say that some of the abuses in the securities market involve 'fraud and potential criminality.' The Reserve Bank is also probing securities dealing by ANZ Grindlays, Standard Chartered, Bank of America and Citibank, as well as 15 Indian state-owned banks. ANZ Grindlays, India's largest foreign bank and the one believed to be most exposed to losses from abuses in the securities market, last night declined to comment further on its involvement. It issued a press release which said that the bank sees 'no useful purpose in adding to speculation in the market'. According to widespread market reports, National Housing Bank issued a cheque to Grindlays for a large sum which was then credited to the account of Mr Harshad Mehta. Mr Mehta is the Bombay broker who was forced to repay Rs6.2bn (Pounds 122m) to State Bank of India to settle outstanding accounts in the interbank market in government securities. In its new guidelines the Reserve Bank also banned the use of brokers' accounts in interbank dealings. In the present financial scandal the worst abuses occurred as a result of connivance between brokers and bankers in what are normally direct transactions between banks.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Iraq assails Kurdish election
DOC.TEXT: Iraq yesterday denounced as illegal elections next Sunday in rebel-held Kurdistan, but ruled out the use of force to derail them, Reuter reports from Baghdad.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Nigerian students on rampage
DOC.TEXT: Nigerian students, angered by chronic fuel shortages, smashed cars during a rampage in a crowded, working-class area of Lagos yesterday, Reuter reports from Lagos. There were no immediate reports of clashes with riot police, who took up positions near Lagos University and in other areas late on Tuesday, after student leaders had called for two days of protests against the fuel shortage in the oil-producing country and to air other grievances.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Papua troops on Bougainville
DOC.TEXT: Papua New Guinea said yesterday its troops had landed in the south of the secessionist island of Bougainville for the first time since the national army and police withdrew in 1990, Kevin Brown reports from Sydney. Mr Rabbie Namaliu, prime minister, said 15 soldiers landed at the village of Siwai on Saturday and set up a base in the area. Mr Namalie said a further 60 troops have been stationed on a nearby island. Mr Namaliu said the troops were despatched in response to requests from local chiefs and village leaders. He said the leaders feared for their safety following executions this year by the secessionist Bougainville Revolutionary Army.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Kabul welcomes Russian minister
DOC.TEXT: Mr Andrei Kozyrev, Russian foreign minister, arrived in Kabul yesterday on a mission intended to help heal the wounds of Afghanistan's 14-year war, Reuter reports from Kabul. He was greeted by representatives of the mujahideen who fought Soviet troops for a decade. He congratulated them on having thrown off 'communist totalitarianism' by toppling the once Soviet-backed government of president Najibullah last month. He made a plea for the release of Russian prisoners of war believed to be held by Afghan guerrilla groups since Soviet troops withdrew in 1989. Later, he won a promise that one Soviet prisoner of war would be able to leave with him for Moscow today. The prisoner was not identified.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Commodity prices condemned
DOC.BYLINE: By DAVID DODWELL, World Trade Editor
DOC.TEXT: A steady fall in export prices for commodities is punishing people who are 'already on the margins of a decent human existence,' according to Rev Charles Elliott, one of the UK's leading development economists and former head of Christian Aid, writes David Dodwell, World Trade Editor. In a speech to be given in London last night, marking the 50th anniversary of Oxfam, the UK aid organisation, Mr Elliott argued that the international commodity price system 'has been a powerful process whereby wealth and income have been transferred from commodity producers to commodity importers/manufacturing exporters'. He said the import purchasing power of developing countries had fallen by 2 per cent a year since 1950 as a result of this process.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Bahrain to change commercial law
DOC.TEXT: BAHRAIN is planning big changes in commercial laws which have been in effect for nearly two decades, as part of wide-ranging plans to revive its economy, Reuter reports from Bahrain. Mr Habib Kassem, commerce and agriculture minister, said yesterday the laws -which will alter the rigid relationship between foreign companies and local agents - would be introduced by the end of May. He told the Gulf Daily News that the changes would address complaints from the international business community and promote free competition. One authorised trader in Bahrain has the monopoly of distributing any foreign product, and the contract drawn up between the two parties is unalterable. Bahrain last year broke with long-standing tradition by issuing laws that would allow wholly foreign-owned companies to operate in the country, providing they made it a regional base.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Iran pulls out the biggest plum from Afghan pie: Tehran has won influence via the Persian speakers who now control Kabul
DOC.TEXT: AS THE dust begins to settle over Kabul, the foreign players are counting their takings. Many countries have stuck their fingers into the Afghan pie during 14 years of civil war, but none has emerged with as much to show as Iran. Iran backed Afghanistan's Shia parties throughout the Afghan civil war, hosting the leaders and giving shelter to 1m refugees. It supplied arms to Shia mujahideen groups, vying with Sunni Saudi Arabia and Pakistan for control of the jihad (holy war). However, with the fall of the Soviet-backed regime last month, Tehran's primary aim in Afghanistan shifted. It turned from promoting Shia Islamic revolution to the promotion of Persian culture. As Afghanistan began to splinter along ethnic lines in the post-communist vacuum Iran placed its weight firmly behind the Persian-speaking Tajiks and Uzbeks who control Kabul. 'The Iranians support (defence minister Ahmad Shah) Masood,' said a moderate Afghan leader in Peshawar. 'They think Masood will take care of their interests because he speaks their language.' Mr Masood is not the only Persian speaker in Kabul. The ex-government militia controlling Kabul's streets are Persian-speaking Uzbeks. General Asif Dilawar, appointed commander-in-chief of the Afghan army forces by Mr Masood last week, is also a Persian speaker. Furthermore, Tehran hosted a meeting this year with Afghan president-designate Burhanuddin Rabbani and representatives from Tajikistan to promote Persian-based cultural links between Iran, Afghanistan and Tajikistan. With most power centres in Kabul filled by Persian speakers, the Iranians are sitting pretty. 'I'd like to say we've done very well out of the last 14 years,' said Iran's consul in Peshawar, Mr Hamid Reza Sherkhodai. A Persian-influenced government in Kabul is indeed a rare achievement. Afghanistan has been ruled almost continuously by the majority Pushtun tribe, who are spread throughout eastern Afghanistan and western Pakistan. In fact, only once has a non-Pushtun controlled Kabul, when Tajik waterseller Bacha Siqa ruled for six months in the 1920s. To bolster the new government in Kabul, the Iranians sent fuel and food to Afghanistan's western provinces. A religious delegation brought gifts and aid to Herat. Iran is also trying to open a supply route all the way to Kabul. The Iranians bring to the Afghans not only aid but a cultural influence. 'We have certain cultural roots with these people,' said Mr Sherkhodai. 'We have a common language and common religion.' Iran is encouraging these links, offering to fund academic study of Persian literature and celebrating the ancient Zoroastrian New Year in common with the Afghans. 'Iran is offering the Afghans a copy of Ferdowsi (a Persian poet) with every sack of wheat it sends,' said one western observer. Of course, Tehran has not abandoned the Shia parties entirely. It continues to back the Shia Hazara tribe in Afghanistan and provides moral and financial support to Shia mujahideen group Hezbe Wahdat and pressure groups such as the TNFJ in Pakistan. But Iranian hardliners elected in the fiery last days of Iran's war with Iraq who might have forced these groups higher up the Iranian agenda have found their influence waning in Tehran. President Rafsanjani's reformist supporters have just won a landslide victory in parliamentary elections characterised by an electorate more concerned with economic well-being than ideological purity. At the heart of Iran's acceptance of the status quo in Kabul is a fear of the alternative. Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, radical Pushtun and main recipient of Pakistani and US military assistance for the last decade, leads an informal coalition of parties opposed to the Kabul government. As the most powerful leader outside Kabul, Mr Hekmatyar would stand to take over the mantle if Kabul's new government fell. Tehran fears that Mr Hekmatyar, as a Pushtun, would favour Pakistani interests over Iran's. Iran is embroiled in tough competition with Pakistan and Turkey over the re-opening of trade routes with land-locked central Asia. Afghanistan borders three central Asian states of the former Soviet Union so any significant trade depends on stability in Kabul. In April, Iran announced the start of a new railway line from Turkmenistan to Iran's southern coast. It agreed to provide oil pipelines from Tajikistan and Turkmenistan through to Turkey to the west. And this week it joined an agreement to re-open the east-west silk road across Asia. Pakistan, meanwhile, is planning an Export Processing Zone in its North West Frontier Province bordering Afghanistan, providing 50 per cent relief on rail freight, duty-free import of raw material and reduced duty on exports. Iran's influence on Kabul is already bearing fruit. Iranian official sources said Kabul had this week ordered a significant supply of oil from Iran. A quick settlement in Kabul would also rid Iran of the financial burden of supporting refugees. With its inflation conservatively estimated at 30 per cent, and imports nearing an all-time high at Dollars 17bn (Pounds 9.6bn), Iran badly needs to patch its economy together. Turkmens in trade deal with Iran, Page 6

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Debts soar among Russian enterprises
DOC.BYLINE: By JOHN LLOYD and LEYLA BOULTON
DOC.TEXT: RUSSIA'S enterprises had piled up Rbs1.43 trillion (million million) in debts to each other and to the banks by May 1, the central bank said yesterday. This sum is greater than the country's gross national product for the first quarter. Mr Vyacheslav Solovov, the bank's vice-chairman, said inter-enterprise debts were increasing at the rate of Rbs27.5bn a day. Talks are under way between the government, central bank and parliament on ways to solve this rapidly gathering crisis - including debt forgiveness and a bigger budget deficit. Yesterday, the government more than doubled teachers' and doctors' pay after they had threatened to strike for a 10-fold increase. The two groups are among the poorest in Russia, earning about Rbs700 a month (the minimum wage has just been increased to Rbs900). The government also announced plans to levy import taxes of 5-10 per cent to reduce the import bill. These will come into effect in August, and they follow a 13 per cent increase in first-quarter imports, compared with a year ago. That pushed the balance of payments deficit for the period to Dollars 2bn. Mr Pyotr Aven, foreign economic relations minister, told Interfax news agency that the government was also considering an extra 28 per cent VAT on imports. Meanwhile, Mr Georgy Matiukhin, central bank chairman, said the system of trade between the main republics of the former Soviet Union was increasingly breaking down.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 14 MAY 92 / Havel tries to keep the family together: Ariane Genillard and Anthony Robinson set the scene for the Czechoslovak election
DOC.BYLINE: By ARIANE GENILLARD and ANTHONY ROBINSON
DOC.TEXT: THE FUTURE of Czechoslovakia's economic reforms and the fate of the Czech and Slovak federal state will be the main issues of debate in a hard fought general election campaign involving more than 40 political parties which began yesterday. The opening shot was fired by Mr Vaclav Havel, president of the Czech and Slovak Federal Republic. Addressing the nation from Bratislava, the Slovak capital, he warned against 'unconsidered and dangerous attempts' to break up the country's fragile federation. Moves to break up the union and reconstitute it as 'a vague dualist union' would lead to 'a chaotic break-up of the state which would exact as high a price as similar break-ups in Yugoslavia or the former Soviet Union'. The presidential warning was directed mainly at nationalists striving for greater autonomy for the Slovak republic, which holds a third of the country's 16m population.
