Despite Mr Major's assurances that Maastricht would not allow the Community to usurp the authority of British MPs, there are more un-welcome headlines to come. Mrs Thatcher's influence has been diminished by her departure from the Commons, but her speeches on Europe play still to receptive media. There will also be not insignificant rebellion when the Maastricht legislation is voted on. The best estimate at present is that about a dozen Conservative MPs will oppose it and perhaps half that number will abstain. The figures could rise. In theory that could comfortably rob Mr Major of his majority of 21. In practice the present disarray in the Labour party - it has not yet decided on its stance and may well abstain on the substantive vote - and likely support for the treaty from the Liberal Democrats appear set to guarantee the prime minister a comfortable majority. Yet even for a prime minister who has proved himself supremely adept at filling the philosophical divides in his own party, there is no such thing as a quiet life.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / British Rail holds up the Euston Stagecoach
DOC.TEXT: THE TRAIN arriving at London Euston's Platform One from Aberdeen every morning is the first regular privately operated passenger service to run on British Rail since nationalisation in 1948. But some things never change. The inaugural train, bearing public transport minister Mr Roger Freeman as passenger of honour, pulled in yesterday in much the same fashion as any ordinary BR train: 12 minutes late. In fairness, no blame could be attached to Stagecoach, the entrepreneurial bus operator providing the service. So far, its two carriages are merely appended to BR's existing sleeper service, so passengers remain at the mercy of BR timekeeping. Stagecoach stepped in when BR decided to drop seat-only accommodation on night trains between London and Aberdeen. It has taken over the seat-only carriages, repainting them in its own livery. Hostesses provide Stagecoach customers with a free hot meal in the evening, unlimited soft drinks and beverages (but strictly no alcohol) through the night and a bap with butter and jam for breakfast. Some fares are lower, too. BR charges Pounds 57 for a one-way ticket between London and Edinburgh, plus Pounds 25 for a sleeper berth. The price for Stagecoach's seat-only tickets, which can be bought from BR, is Pounds 33.50. On the inaugural run the worst advertisement for de-regulation turned out to be the minister himself. Under close questioning, Mr Freeman confessed that he had slipped away from the private-sector part of the train to grab a few hours' rest in the comfort of a public-sector sleeping compartment. 'I've got a full day's work in front of me,' he remarked, somewhat testily. 'I am 50 years old and I didn't feel like sitting up all night.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Threat seen to future of Drax
DOC.TEXT: BRITAIN'S biggest power station - Drax in North Yorkshire - may be forced out of business by the end of the century, according to National Power, the privatised electricity generator which owns the station. Drax, which supplies enough power for six cities the size of Liverpool, is on the River Ouse near British Coal's Selby colliery complex. National Power argues that Drax could be priced out of the new electricity market if negotiations with British Coal over coal pricing cannot be resolved. Mr Mike Grasby, manager at Drax, warned that the station could be switched off most of the time because of tough competition from gas-fired power stations.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Notts Tec warns over pit closures
DOC.TEXT: CONTINUED pit closures in Nottinghamshire would have a 'devastating' effect on the economic and social life of the county, the North Nottinghamshire Training and Enterprise Council (Tec) warned the government yesterday. It called for a national energy policy based on the use of coal as a strategic fuel. This is the first political intervention by a Tec, 82 of which have been set up to bring training closer to the needs of the private sector and to foster business growth. 'Everything we do on the training and enterprise front can be negated by a rapid reduction of the (coal) industry,' said Mrs Pat Richards, chief executive of North Nottinghamshire Tec. The stand taken by the Tec reflects disquiet in the region's business, voluntary and political circles about the plans of - and for - British Coal. Nottinghamshire County Council has this week published its coalfield strategy for this year. It opposes coal imports and urges support for deep-mined coal. The council and the Tec are to put pressure today on Mr Tim Eggar, energy minister, when he visits pits in the county. They will seek assurances about the future of the local mining industry under whatever organisation emerges after privatisation of British Coal. The council and Tec are seeking a meeting with Mr Michael Heseltine, trade and industry secretary, to urge a review of coal policy. Letters, Page 21

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Braque and Picasso lift market: Saleroom
DOC.TEXT: THE art market received a boost in New York on Monday night when Christie's sold 91 works from the collection of the late Bill McCarty-Cooper for Dollars 21.5m, (Pounds 12m), with an important late (1952) work by Georges Braque, 'Atelier VIII', making Dollars 7.7m. The other exceptional painting in the auction, 'Compotier et Guitare' by Picasso, went to a private US buyer for Dollars 3.85m. Not only did these two important paintings find buyers, but spirited bidding ensured that the auction was 95 per cent sold by value. Mr Christopher Burge, president of Christie's in the US, said the results were 'tremendous, sensational'. Christie's was fortunate in offering a collection with an excellent pedigree. It had been put together by Douglas Cooper, a friend of Picasso and Braque and one of the greatest collectors of 20th century art. In 1949 Cooper adopted McCarty-Cooper, then aged 25, who inherited the collection on Cooper's death in 1984. Many of the paintings were acquired directly from the artist. In the case of the Braque this included the provision that the work should never leave France. In addition to offering fresh paintings of undoubted quality, Christie's had the advantage of dealing with a deceased estate. That helped to ensure that reserves and estimates were kept low to encourage bidding. Three years ago, at the height of the art boom, the Braque might have sold for nearer Dollars 12m and the Picasso Dollars 10m. 'Guitare sur une Table' by Juan Gris sold for Dollars 1.485m, slightly below estimate, and another Picasso, 'Homme a la Sucette', for Dollars 968,000. Both went to US collectors. A Giacometti sculpture in bronze, 'Buste de Diego', almost doubled its estimate at Dollars 935,000. This was the first successful auction for two years in the troubled Impressionist and modern art sector. It will give confidence to the market, but the very high quality of the works makes it untypical.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / European blow to equal pension rights
DOC.TEXT: THE CAMPAIGN for equal pension rights for men and women in the UK suffered a setback yesterday. The European Court of Justice in Luxembourg gave a preliminary opinion that European Community law does not require equal treatment between men and women in National Insurance contributions. The advocate-general's opinion in a case brought by the Equal Opportunities Commission is not binding on the full court, which will give a final decision later. In most cases the court upholds the advocate-general's opinion. The EOC said it was disappointed by the opinion. It had sought a declaration that the UK government was in breach of an obligation in the EC social security directive to give equal treatment in statutory social security. To qualify for a state pension in the UK, men must have paid National Insurance contributions for at least 44 years. But for women the figure is 39 years. After the age of 60 women may not make any further NI contributions. But working men between the ages 60 and 64 must pay NI contributions even if they have already contributed for 44 years. The advocate-general's opinion is in stark contrast to recent European Court decisions on equal treatment in the employment and pension fields. In the Marshall case in 1986, the court ruled that women in public-sector employment had the right to remain in work until the same age as male colleagues. In the 1990 Barber case involving occupational pension schemes, the court ruled that men and women should receive equal pensions as well as equal pay for equal work. The stumbling block in the present case appears to be that the social security directive specifically permits member states to differentiate between state pension ages for men and women - though it also sets out a number of aspects of state pension schemes where equal treatment must apply. The advocate-general concluded that where a member state has a fixed pension age differing according to sex, it 'may still derogate from the principle of equal treatment laid down in the (social security) directive . . . unless such unequal treatment of men can be eliminated by the national court without unduly jeopardising the coherence or financial equilibrium of the national social security system concerned'. The government has already announced its intention to move towards a common state pension age. Letters, Page 21

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Mystery madonna
DOC.TEXT: An amateur collector yesterday issued a challenge to the art world, claiming a painting he bought for Pounds 360 is a Raphael. If genuine, the painting could sell for as much as Pounds 10m. Without expert endorsement it would fetch no more than thousands. Amid tight security and considerable secrecy, the Madonna And Child, pictured above with a security guard, was revealed to the world at a London hotel by Timothy Benoy, solicitor for Lester Winward, who owns the painting. Mr Winward did not attend. However, Nicholas Penny, the only Raphael expert yet to examine the painting, immediately dismissed it as the work of a copyist. Mr Winward, a Cheshire businessman who wants to sell the work, responded later by saying the tests he had carried out were the same as those used last year by Mr Penny to authenticate a Raphael owned by the Duke of Northumberland. The painting, bought in 1981 at an auction at Leeswood House, near Mold, north Wales, bears a strong resemblance to part of Raphael's Sistine Madonna. Mr Benoy said research suggested the picture might have come to England in 1636 as a purchase by Charles I, a keen art collector, or as a gift to his queen from the Vatican.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / TUC moves to avert row over recruitment
DOC.TEXT: LEADERS of the Trades Union Congress were yesterday trying to avert a fresh row over inter-union recruitment which could jeopardise the admission of the electrical section of the newly formed Amalgamated Engineering and Electrical Union to the TUC. Mr Norman Willis, general secretary of the TUC, yesterday wrote to all unions involved saying that the AEEU had agreed not to go ahead with a merger between its electrical section and Cabin Crew '89 while TUC-led discussions were continuing. Cabin Crew '89 is a 5,000-strong union of airline cabin-crew staff which broke away from the TGWU general union. The TUC hopes that the engineering section of the AEEU will veto any move by the electrical section, formerly the EETPU, to take Cabin Crew '89, or any other disaffected union splinter groups, into membership. Both sections of the AEEU are voting on TUC membership next year. Mr Paul Gallagher, general secretary of the electricians' section, responded to a sharply worded statement from Mr Bill Morris, general saecretary of the TGWU, by saying they would not allow other unions to run their affairs. Mr Morris had warned the TUC that unless it took firm action to stop the merger the TGWU would have to consider its own future in the TUC.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Auditors face radical shake-up of their role: Standard-setting body proposes enlarged report - Clear opinion on a company's chances of survival to be included
DOC.TEXT: AUDITORS will be required to comment on whether a company can survive for at least one year after its financial statements are approved, in a radical shake-up of their role proposed yesterday by the profession's new standard-setting body. The Auditing Practices Board is proposing that from early next year all annual company reports should contain a substantially enlarged audit report giving an unambiguous opinion on the financial statements provided by a company's directors. Details of the initiatives are in the first three draft documents produced by the board, which was created early last year. Mr Bill Morrison, board chairman, said: 'This is equivalent to trains moving from narrow gauge to wide gauge and coming out of a different station altogether.' Two of the new statements provide detailed standards for part of the statutory audit of all limited companies. They would fundamentally alter and lengthen the text of the report provided in accounts. The first addresses the issue of whether the company is a 'going concern' - to determine whether it is able to survive for a period of at least one year beyond the period to which the latest accounts refer. Auditors would be required to assess more actively the directors' view of their company as a going concern and use their judgment to identify 'material matters' such as inadequate borrowing facilities, litigation or significant debts falling due. They would also be required to look forward up to one year after the period to which statements refer, well beyond the timescale demanded under existing guidelines. The second statement deals more generally with the format of the audit report. It says the report should be addressed to the shareholders and state the date on which the opinion is expressed. It should describe and distinguish between the responsibilities of the directors for the preparation of the financial statements and the responsibilities of the auditors to express an opinion on these statements. It would have to contain a clear and unequivocal opinion on the financial statements. The third statement lays out the roles of the Auditing Practices Board. It has 18 voting members, including nine who are not practising accountants. The document says the board will issue two forms of document in the future: statements, which are mandatory, and practice notes, which represent best practice on emerging issues. The new standards establish six types of opinion with which the auditors' report can conclude: Unqualified opinion - no emphasis: the financial statements give a true and fair view. Unqualified opinion - with emphasis: the statements give a true and fair view but are affected by 'fundamental uncertainties'. Qualified opinion - partial disclaimer: all evidence reasonably expected to be available to the auditors has not been obtained and evaluated. Qualified opinion - disclaimer: the evidence has not been obtained and the effect is sufficiently material to make the statements as a whole misleading. Qualified opinion - disagreement: the statements are not prepared in accordance with accepted accounting principles or do not give a true and fair view, but the effect of the disagreement does not make the statements as a whole misleading. Qualified opinion - adverse opinion: the effect of the disagreement is so pervasive that the statements as a whole are misleading. The documents are open for comment until August 31, and the board aims to issue standards in the autumn applying to companies with year-ends after December 31 this year. Scope and Authority of APB Pronouncements, Pounds 4; Reports on Financial Statements, Pounds 4.50; Going Concern, Pounds 4. Accountancy Books. PO Box 620, Milton Keynes MK9 2JX. Letters, Page 21

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Pub body calls time
DOC.TEXT: uallers Association, which represents pub landlords, yesterday decided to wind itself up because of falling membership and subscriptions.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Complaints about travel adverts
DOC.TEXT: THE latest monthly report of the Advertising Standards Authority shows that dubious practices for holiday timeshares are still causing many complaints but that some travel companies have also recently been found to use misleading advertising. Three complaints against the travel company Airtours are upheld by the ASA. Dixons, the electrical goods retailer, is criticised for a camera advertisement.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Tube workers offered 4.5% rise
DOC.TEXT: LONDON Underground yesterday offered a 4.5 per cent pay rise to its rail and craft unions and appeared to make some progress on its disputed company plan with RMT, the transport union. The pay rise, the same as that offered and accepted at British Rail, is likely to be accepted by the unions. On the issue of London Underground's company plan, on which RMT members have voted 2 - 1 in favour of industrial action, 'there is still a long way to go', according to a union official. But both sides said that a useful start had been made in the discussions.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / SDLP outlines Ulster proposal
DOC.TEXT: THE nationalist Social Democratic and Labour party has proposed administrative machinery run by six commissioners for Northern Ireland. Three of the commissioners would be elected by the voters of Northern Ireland. One would be appointed by the British government, one by the Irish government and the other by the EC. They would preside over a system of power-sharing between the four main local political parties. All sides involved in the round-table talks refused to comment.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Lecturers to challenge EC rule
DOC.TEXT: A LEGAL test case on whether the European Community directive on the transfer of engagements applies to non-commercial public-sector bodies is expected in July. The Natfhe lecturers' union has been granted leave to pursue a judicial review following the refusal of the Department of Education to transfer some features of collective agreements from councils to the new further education corporations.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Outsider to head school inspectors
DOC.TEXT: MR JOHN PATTEN, education secretary, surprised the teaching establishment yesterday by appointing Professor Stewart Sutherland, a leading university administrator, as chief inspector of schools in England, Andrew Adonis writes. The chief inspector's powers were greatly increased earlier this year, giving control over the expanded - and soon to be semi-privatised - inspection regime for schools. Prof Sutherland will take up the post in September. A philosopher of religion, his career has been largely spent in academic posts and university administration. The appointment of an outsider was criticised by teachers' unions. Mr Nigel de Gruchy, general secretary of the NASUWT union, said: 'It shows that the inspectorate is going to be no more than an administrative machine.' The government released an extra Pounds 4.4m yesterday to help councils upgrade facilities in schools.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Water companies told to improve metering
DOC.TEXT: WATER COMPANIES have been warned by the industry's economic regulator they must make metering cheaper, fairer and simpler for customers, who are too often deterred by unreasonable installation charges and unfavourable tariffs. Mr Ian Byatt, director-general of Ofwat, has written to the companies emphasising that they must bring metered charges into line with other charges. Metered customers have been found in some cases to be paying more than those without meters for the same amount of water. Metering is likely to become much more widespread as the present charging system, based on domestic rates, is phased out by the end of the decade. All customers have the right to a meter, and Ofwat believes that many should benefit by controlling their consumption. Mr Byatt said: 'The choice of a meter must be made easier for customers, particularly those on low incomes and living alone, for whom current charges are disproportionately high by comparison with their actual use of water.' Mr David Gadbury, the industry's spokesman on metering, rejected the Ofwat criticism. He said customers who chose metering were likely to make savings, and the industry was making 'every effort' to extend metering.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Vauxhall to resist EC
DOC.BYLINE: By KEVIN DONE, Motor Industry Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: VAUXHALL, with second-biggest sales of new cars in the UK, has told dealers it sees no reason to adjust prices in the wake of last week's critical report from the European Commission. The study of car prices found large differentials between countries for some models at certain times between January 1988 and January last year. According to the EC report five carmakers - Ford, Honda, Citroen, Mazda and Audi - had at least one model with price differences greater than 40 per cent in one of the five time periods selected. Vauxhall, the UK subsidiary of General Motors of the US, said it had 'serious reservations' about the validity of some of the EC analysis. Mr David Wallis, Vauxhall director of business planning, said it was 'hard to accept the EC report, or to reconcile its detailed findings with the alleged 'high-price' character of the UK car market'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Council swaps case is settled out of court
DOC.TEXT: THE HIGH COURT action in which Hammersmith and Fulham Council in London faced a Pounds 2.94m claim by the US Chemical Bank over two interest rate swap transactions was settled out of court on undisclosed terms yesterday. A deal was agreed after only two days of what was expected to be a seven-week Commercial Court hearing. Opening the case for Chemical Bank last week, Mr Richard Southwell QC had said that the bank's policy was not to deal with rate-capped authorities. It would not have entered into the 1988 swaps deals with Hammersmith if it had known the council was trading for profit and acting as an intermediary for two capped authorities in London - Haringey and Camden. The case was the fifth of six test case actions to be settled out of court. A hearing has been fixed to decide whether new lead actions should be chosen to determine key issues in the swaps litigation between banks and local authorities. Mr Justice Hirst is to hear argument on June 8 as to whether further cases should be selected and, if so, which ones. In July last year, six lead actions were chosen with the aim of deciding key points and enabling the remainder to be resolved without recourse to the courts. Five of these settled and the sixth, between NationsBank, of North Carolina, and Hammersmith and Fulham Council, began last week and is still being heard. Mr Justice Hirst said there were still 196 live actions involving several dozen banks and a much larger number of local authorities.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Terminal plan will fly in face of local opposition: The need for expansion at London's main airport
DOC.TEXT: A fifth terminal at London's Heathrow Airport is an important but only partial step towards giving the London region capacity to meet passenger demand forecast to rise from just over 60m people this year to 170m by 2016. Although BAA, formerly the British Airports Authority, yesterday tried to focus attention on its plans to build the Pounds 800m-Pounds 900m terminal at Heathrow, it conceded that it would have to consider building a second terminal at Stansted Airport in Essex to cope with passenger growth in the next century. The Civil Aviation Authority also believes a new runway will be necessary in the south-east soon after the turn of the century. A working party is studying possible sites for the additional runway, which many in the industry believe is likely to be built at Stansted. But the fierce public debate and local opposition traditionally provoked by airport expansion has forced BAA to adopt a softly-softly approach to its long-term plans for its London airports. Local authorities reacted strongly to BAA's announcement. They fear that the new terminal would increase the number of flights at Heathrow, cause even greater noise and disturbance and worsen traffic congestion on the over-crowded M25 and M4 links to the airport. However, for BAA and the air transport industry as a whole, an additional terminal at Heathrow has become an urgent priority if the airport is to maintain its position as a leading international aviation hub and accommodate the steady growth in passenger numbers and a new generation of large wide-body aircraft. Mr Gunter Eser, director-general of the International Air Transport Association, said: 'Terminal 5 is the key to the continued development of air services to the UK. Without the terminal . . . Britain alone would stand to lose a billion dollars of economic activity every year.' Sir John Egan, BAA chief executive, warned that if the terminal was not built, the UK air transport industry risked facing 'the general decline we have seen in other industries'. Other European airports such as Paris or Amsterdam would take over some of Heathrow's share of the international passenger market, he added. The tortuous process of planning applications (there are expected to be several public inquiries) is expected to take five years. BAA hopes the government will give the go-ahead for the project in 1997. That will enable the first phase of the terminal to be completed by 2001. The new terminal would provide additional annual capacity at Heathrow for 10m passengers from 2002, giving the airport total capacity of about 60m passengers a year. The second phase would be completed by 2016, adding room for an extra 20m passengers a year. Even with the completion of the first phase of the project, demand is expected to exceed capacity in the London area by 2005. With the completion of the second phase, there would still be a capacity shortfall of 27m passengers by the year 2016, according to current traffic forecasts. That is likely to lead to construction of a second terminal at Stansted. Although the Pounds 400m Stansted complex opened last year is still struggling to attract traffic, BAA remains confident that the airport will eventually fill up as passenger growth recovers from last year's downturn in air travel caused by the Gulf war and the recession. Demand at Gatwick is also expected to grow during the next few years. Although a further runway will be necessary in the south-east, the expansion of Heathrow will not involve construction of a fourth runway there. 'The new generation of larger, quieter aircraft will help to deliver many more passengers without the need for any extra night flights or an additional runway at Heathrow,' Sir John said. Apart from accommodating the forecast 3.8 per cent annual growth in passenger traffic between now and 2016, the project will also be closely integrated with a broader scheme to improve road and rail access into Heathrow. In addition to the proposed fourth lane for the M25, BAA is discussing with the Department of Transport plans to improve other road links to the airport including the M4 and the A4. BAA is expected to be involved in the funding of these crucial infrastructure projects. BAA also intends to go ahead with its plans to open a Pounds 235m express rail link between Heathrow and central London in 1996. But BAA's original rail link project in partnership with British Rail has now been overtaken by the government's privatisation plans for BR. Sir John said he saw no big obstacle to halt the project, although it is likely to lead to a different partnership to finance and eventually operate the link. The new terminal would also be connected to the Piccadilly Underground line. Without improved road and rail links, the new terminal would do little to ease the growing stress levels of air travellers.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Civil servants to ballot on strikes over pay reforms
DOC.TEXT: MIDDLE-RANKING civil servants are to ballot on strike action in protest over the government's attempt to reform Civil Service pay. Delegates at the annual conference of the 110,000-strong NUCPS Civil Service union yesterday voted against an offer worth 4.5 per cent on the pay bill. The offer is in line with the government's attempt to strengthen the link between pay and performance and to decentralise negotiations for all 550,000 civil servants. The proposals mean they would lose their traditional right to annual earnings increments. The decision to renegotiate the existing pay agreements was announced last July by Mr Norman Lamont, the chancellor. It followed publication of the Citizen's Charter stressing the role of performance-related pay as an incentive for improving the quality of public services. So far the Treasury has calculated what it says are final offers for just two groups affecting 300,000 civil servants with settlement dates of April 1. The CPSA union, which represents clerical grades, is recommending that its members accept a basic offer of 4.25 per cent with an extra 0.5 per cent in performance-related pay. The NUCPS is opposed to its similar offer because it says that the 4.1 per cent basic increase, with 0.4 per cent in performance-related pay, breaches the spirit of the existing formula that ties settlements to private-sector deals. Under the formula, this year's offer should be at least 4.5 per cent but civil servants who are not eligible for performance-related pay are being offered only 4.1 per cent. The NUCPS also opposes the break-up of national pay bargaining and the principle of performance-related pay, which it says is divisive and open to abuse. Three other groups - senior managers, scientists and professionals and Inland Revenue staff - have settlement dates of August 1 and are still in negotiations. The result of the NUCPS ballot will not be announced until June 12, two weeks after the current agreement lapses on May 29. The government may simply impose the offer without waiting for the result and might then also abandon the link with private-sector pay, under which pay settlements must fall within the middle half of private-sector deals concluded in the previous year. Local government white-collar workers yesterday rejected a 3.6 per cent pay offer. Further talks covering the 740,000 group are planned for May 27.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Caterpillar in truck pact with Russians
DOC.TEXT: CATERPILLAR of the US, the world's biggest maker of earth-moving equipment, said yesterday it had reached an agreement with Zil, Russia's biggest truck manufacturer, to pursue an industrial and marketing arrangement for diesel truck engines and fuel systems. Neither side would disclose details of the agreement, the second between a big Russian truck producer and specialist US engine maker. Cummins, the world's largest independent producer of diesel engines, and Kamaz, the heavy truck maker, formed last year a joint venture aimed at the eventual manufacture of Cummins engines in the then Soviet Union. Zil produces about 200,000 trucks a year but its Moscow plant has suffered from under-investment since the 1970s. The trucks it has been producing are little changed from those of the 1950s. It is shortly to begin making 75,000 newly-designed diesel engine trucks, some expected to be fitted with Caterpillar's engines. Mr Donald Fites, Caterpillar's chairman, said he believed the two companies could build a mutually-beneficial truck diesel-engine business and 'together make a strong contribution to Russia's transportation system with engines that have good fuel economy and low emissions'. Mr Evgueni Brakov, Zil's general director, said that co-operation with Caterpillar could make his group's trucks more competitive in Russia as well as in the global market-place. The deal would appear to have similar potential to the Cummins-Kamaz venture. The latter envisages producing about 25,000 engines a year by the late 1990s. Local engine assembly could begin by the mid-1990s. Cummins has said that, at maturity in the next decade, production volumes could reach 150,000 engines a year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Bush draws up plan for inner cities: President will veto any bill with compensatory tax increases
DOC.TEXT: PRESIDENT George Bush yesterday announced a six-point Dollars 3bn-plus (Pounds 1.6bn) programme to relieve conditions in America's inner cities, but said he would veto any bill that included a compensatory tax increase. Speaking before a meeting with congressional leaders, Mr Bush was unable to put a sum on the cost of his proposals, which appeared mostly an amalgam of long-standing administration policies. Some exist in pilot form, some may be implemented by bureaucratic fiat and some require new legislation, but none had been a priority before the Los Angeles riots two weeks ago. The six points are: Expanding the Weed and Seed programme, designed to increase law enforcement and targeted social efforts in high-crime areas. Expanding home ownership for those in public housing. The creation of federal enterprise zones. Encouraging greater choice in public education. Allowing those on welfare to have savings of up to Dollars 10,000, 10 times the current limit, before becoming ineligible for welfare support. Job training, specifically the expansion of a youth apprentice scheme. Later, White House officials, while conceding the imprecision of some of their hurriedly compiled sums, gave a rough cost breakdown. The enterprise zone bill, consisting of tax breaks for inner-city investors, might come to Dollars 1.5bn; home ownership provisions about Dollars 1bn, up from Dollars 361m in the current budget; Dollars 500m for the Weed and Seed programme, now only in pilot form; and nearly Dollars 700m for job training. Emergency assistance to Los Angeles already amounts to about Dollars 600m, while unemployment insurance claims are likely to top Dollars 2bn. These, however, are covered under existing laws. With an eye on the November election, Mr Bush emphasised his opposition to tax increases to finance additional spending. 'The idea that you have to raise taxes at this time, when the economy is starting to recover, I'm sorry, I will not support that,' he said. Congressional reaction was guarded. Mr George Mitchell, Senate majority leader, promised co-operation with the president, but 'I don't promise we will enact precisely everything he proposes'. Mr Tom Foley, speaker of the House, said it would be worthwhile looking at transferring funds from the defence budget.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Accountancy firms to expand China ventures
DOC.TEXT: ARTHUR ANDERSEN and KPMG Peat Marwick, the accountancy firms, plan to expand their joint venture networks in China by opening offices in at least two other cities within the next year. Both firms are considering developing operations in Shanghai and Guangzhou to complement their first joint ventures approved by the Chinese authorities last month. Mr Eoghan McMillan, Arthur Andersen managing partner for Hong Kong and China, said the venture was considering opening branches in Shanghai and Guangzhou, possibly also in Shen Zhen. Peat Marwick signed documents formally approving a joint venture with a firm of certified public accountants in Beijing to be called KPMG Peat Marwick Huazhen on April 25 after two years' discussions with the Chinese. Arthur Andersen finalised a similar deal two days later, to be called Arthur Andersen Hua Qiang. The ventures have allowed foreign accountants to certify statutory audits on companies operating in China. Certification is required for tax returns and enterprises joining the Chinese stock market.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Reduced fiscal deficit sought: Pakistani Budget
DOC.TEXT: THE Pakistani government will unveil its annual budget tomorrow amid widespread expectations of measures to narrow a PR72bn (Pounds 1.61bn) budgetary deficit. These are expected to include cost-cutting efforts as well as possible tax rises. The deficit, estimated at 6.1 per cent of gross domestic product, has broken an earlier target ceiling of 4.8 per cent. It is regarded as a big pressure on the economy at a time when Pakistan is trying to encourage large-scale privatisation and deregulation. At the same time, though, the government yesterday claimed the growth rate for 1991-92 had risen to 6.4 per cent from 5.6 per cent a year earlier. According to Pakistan's official economic survey, announced before the budget, the manufacturing sector registered the largest growth rate of 7.7 per cent followed by 6.4 per cent in farming. The government is also expected to take credit for a 25 per cent increase in fresh private investment and a 13 per cent increase in exports. Inflation is down to 9.5 per cent from 12.5 per cent a year ago, the government says. Foreign exchange reserves stand at some Dollars 650m (Pounds 362m), up from Dollars 300m a year ago. However, failure to meet the earlier deficit target is attributed to an adverse international economic situation and lower than expected response in the privatisation programme which is eventually expected to raise up to PR250m. According to the economic survey, the current account deficit during 1991-92 is likely to end up higher than the Dollars 2.2bn last year. This has occurred because of a failure to meet an export growth target of 20 per cent, and a rise in imports of 10.5 per cent compared with an earlier projection of 2.5 per cent. A drop in international cotton prices and yarn has also affected export earnings. Remittances from overseas Pakistani workers have also fallen. But the current account deficit is expected to be made up in part by deposits in foreign currency accounts at Pakistani banks, allowed last year under government liberalisation measures. Under the privatisation programme, the government has partly sold 50 public sector factories with transfer of management to private owners, compared with an earlier target of 100. The programme has raised PR10bn through these partial sales while another PR15bn is expected to be raised through future sale of more shares in these factories. Among other economic constraints, the government is unlikely to cut the large defence budget, expected to stand at PR76.9bn. Some of Pakistan's foreign aid donors have expressed concern over defence expenditures, regarding this as an area where cuts would reduce the deficit. But resistance from the politically influential army together with continued tensions with India over Kashmir and instability in Afghanistan have prevented such reductions, officials say. Another PR79bn is expected to go towards debt servicing, where Pakistan's total external and internal debt stands at approximately PR900bn. Last week Mr Nawaz Sharif, the prime minister, said the country has accumulated a large debt burden, making it the biggest obstacle in the way of balancing the budget.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Europeans urge better Japan investment deal
DOC.TEXT: JAPAN must improve direct investment conditions for foreign companies or face 'increasingly strong' political pressure to redress the present imbalance in investment flows, according to a paper produced for European companies. Japanese investment in Europe had been more than 20 times larger than European investment in Japan in the past decade, the European Business Community (EBC), a Tokyo-based advisory committee to the EC, said in a paper. Tokyo had to ensure European companies had equal access to the Japanese market. 'If such opportunities are not created, this problem, which today has mostly commercial and economic dimensions, will develop an increasingly strong political dimension as well,' the EBC said. The paper focuses on the manufacturing and distribution sectors. It came as the Japan External Trade Organisation (Jetro) released a report suggesting the pace of Japanese manufacturing expansion in Europe is slowing. At the end of January, 721 manufacturing companies had operations in Europe, an increase of 69 over the year, against an increase of 132 the previous year. About 21 per cent of those companies procured all of their components in Europe, up from 15 per cent a year earlier, while 34 per cent had Europeans as chief executives, against 31.6 per cent in January 1991. European companies listed five conditions hindering investment in Japan: high cost of land; a relatively long wait for returns on investment; high corporate taxes; problems of attracting well-qualified Japanese staff; and 'extreme difficulty' in acquiring Japanese companies. EBC officials said Japanese mergers and acquisitions abroad last year totalled 294, while only 18 foreign transactions took place in Japan. There were no legal obstacles to acquisitions but the environment 'was not conducive to foreign investments'. The EBC asked that Japanese government agencies 'affirm their commitment' to an increase in European investment and, more specifically, that the Japan Development Bank increase its pool of funds available to foreign companies from Y88bn (Pounds 373m) to Y120bn (Pounds 508m). Tokyo was urged to lift formal curbs on foreign investment in farming, mining and the leather industry, and allow foreign lawyers more freedom.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Bilateral accords 'vital for Mideast progress'
DOC.TEXT: A political breakthrough in bilateral negotiations with Israel is vital for a wider discussion on the Middle East ecnomy to make progress, a Palestinian delegation said yesterday after a two-day session of the 35-nation working party on regional co-operation. Professor Youssef Sayigh, the Beirut-based leader of the Palestinian delegation, criticised Israel for not attending the meeting because Palestinian representation was not confined to those from the West Bank and Gaza. The EC, which chaired the working party, made the same criticism to Mr David Levy, Israel's foreign minister. The Brussels meeting was also boycotted by Syria and Lebanon, which are first demanding progress in their bilateral talks with Israel. Another Palestinian delegate, Mr Khalil Hindi said he understood the attitude of the Arab absentee countries, by 'the pros of attending outweight the cons'. All participants agreed that the multilateral discussions on regional co-operation would only blossom if and when there was a political breakthrough in bilateral Arab-Israeli talks. Mr Samir Hulaileh, a Jerusalem economist, admitted Palestinian disorganisation was partly to blame for not taking more advantage of the EC scheme to promote Palestinian fruit and vegetable exports to the Community. Israel was also frustrating such exports with systematic searches of Palestinians farm trucks.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Australia to reduce immigrant numbers
DOC.TEXT: Australia, one of the world's most popular destinations for European and Asian emigrants, yesterday announced plans to cut immigration by 27 per cent next year to about 80,000 people. Mr Gerry Hand, the immigration minister, said Australia would also require more skills and a higher level of competence in English from applicants other than refugees and close relatives of earlier migrants. The changes follow an anguished debate over the historically high level of immigration in the wake of an 18 month recession which has increased unemployment to 10.4 per cent. Immigrant organisations argue that high immigration benefits Australia by increasing economic activity. However, the government has accepted trade union arguments that immigration has worsened unemployment during the recession. Mr Hand said the level of immigration for future years would be decided in the light of 'national economic and social objectives'. He said the intake was likely to average 80,000 for several years. The cut was welcomed by Senator Peter Walsh, a prominent campaigner against high immigration, who urged a further cut to a maximum of 60,000 people in 1993-94. Immigrant organisations said the increased focus on English language skills was discriminatory, and would discourage applications from talented migrants from non-English-speaking countries.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / China announces special economic zone for Lhasa
DOC.TEXT: China is planning to set up a special economic zone in Lhasa, the troubled capital of Tibet, Reuter reports from Beijing. The zone will imitate those operating in China's flourishing coastal regions, the official China Daily said yesterday. It quoted Tibet's vice governor Gyamtso as saying lack of open-mindedness had impeded the region's development in the past. Tibet has been rocked by sporadic riots since Buddhist monks demonstrated against Chinese rule in late 1987, prompting police to open fire on protesters. The region's exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, syas more than 1m Tibetans have been killed since China took control of his country, now called the Tibet Autonomous Region, in 1950. China Daily said Tibet's local government is drawing up preferential investment policies for the Lhasa special economic zone, including tax breaks and low land-use fees. The isolated region plans to open several new border trading ports. Currently Tibet's sole air link is with Chengdu, in neighbouring Sichuan province.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Protectionist countries have become pollution havens
DOC.TEXT: SCANT evidence exists that pollutive industries migrate to countries where environmental standards are lax, the study concludes. Closed, protectionist countries have become 'pollution havens', it says, contradicting environmentalist views that economic growth and free trade lead to environmental degradation. The report shows developing countries have seen rapid growth of pollutive industry, due to the stage of industrialisation these countries are going through, rather than to investment targeted to escape tough environmental rules. Pollutive industry, that spends heavily on controlling or treating resulting pollutants, is still concentrated in First World countries. Industrial countries account for three-quarters of trade in products of 'dirty industry', with the EC accounting for 40 per cent. While North America has in the past 25 years cut its share of environmentally dirty goods by a third from 20.5 to 14 per cent, rapidly industrialising countries of south-east Asia more than doubled their share from 3.4 to 8.4 per cent. Concentrations of dirty industry are greatest in eastern Europe, where they accounted for more than a quarter of exports. 'There is clear evidence of a relative decline in the importance of these products in industrial countries' exports, while increases are observed in eastern Europe, Latin America and West Asia.' The report traced no evidence of investment decisions influenced by variations in environmental standards. Research in Chile, which has no controls on industrial emissions and is open to trade and foreign investment, shows the opposite. 'Openness to foreign investment and absence of barriers to technology imports encourage multinationals to invest in Chile, and ensure domestic producers will have to compete with them. Openness in Chile is associated with, if not contributing to, the opposite of the pollution haven effect.' Companion studies of Latin American countries show more open economies end up with 'a cleaner set of industries'. 'Developing countries selling their environment cheaply have little to offer investors, against those offering a cheap, efficient labour force, to take one example'. By contrast, east European protected economies show 'the extravagant carelessness with which the environment has been treated there'. Less than 5 per cent of Poland's river water is drinkable, with 40 per cent so polluted that it cannot even be used in industry. Czechoslovakia, east Germany and Poland have nitrous oxide emissions twice those of France, Italy or west Germany, with sulphur dioxide emissions 10 times higher. 'Environmental degradation of eastern Europe is mainly explained by political suppression of consumer choice.' Four reasons are given why dirty industry migration is not a matter of environmental concern: Scant evidence exists of such migration; Costs of compliance with environmental regulations are low as a proportion of total costs, so do not influence location; Legal liability and reputation in a company's home market weaken the temptation to cut environmental costs in a world of rising environmental standards; Companies anticipate rising environmental standards in developing country markets by introducing state of the art technology in the first place. To test whether tariffs should be used to induce countries to raise environmental standards, the report examines US industry demands for a 'pollution tax' on Mexican exports subject to laxer environmental regulations. It finds total pollution abatement costs across US industry amount to 0.54 per cent of total costs. The cement industry carries highest costs, at 3 per cent. The report concludes: 'It is not obvious that the threat or imposition of trade restrictions will have a positive effect on environmental quality.' The US policy would be flawed because it would be 'driven by considerations of competitiveness, not environmental quality'. That would amount to 'bad environmental policy and bad trade policy'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Environment: Deals set up trade in pollution permits
DOC.TEXT: THE first US deals to trade pollution rights were announced yesterday when the federally owned Tennessee Valley Authority said it had agreed to buy allowances to emit 10,000 tons of sulphur dioxide, a key cause of acid rain, from privately owned Wisconsin Power & Light. The Wisconsin utility, based in Madison, also said it sold allowances to Duquesne Light of Pittsburgh for emissions of between 15,000 and 25,000 tons. The exact terms of the sales were not disclosed but the price of each allowance was between Dollars 250 and Dollars 400 (Pounds 140 and Pounds 223), an official said. The deals are, in essence, forward contracts on allowances that will be issued next year by the Environmental Protection Agency as part of the implementation of the 1990 Clean Air Act. The act requires utilities to cut their sulphur dioxide emissions in half by the year 2000, or from a national total of 19m tons to 9m tons. The first deadline for partial compliance is in 1995. To help ease the high costs of converting to cleaner technologies, the US government has created a system under which 'dirtier' utility companies can buy allowances for sulphur dioxide emissions from 'cleaner' companies that have exceeded federal standards. The allowances have been allocated, but will not be in the hands of utilities until an auction in March 1993. Mr Erroll Davis, president of Wisconsin Power & Light, said the transactions 'clearly demonstrate that a market-based approach can be an effective way to address environmental problems'. If a market develops for the allowances, it is believed the public will save on rates because utility companies will be able to meet their clean air requirements at a lower cost than building scrubbers or switching to harder, lower-sulphur coal. There is, however, scepticism over how well such a market can work, as state and locally controlled utilities have been slow to set clear policies for trading allowances. Among other matters at issue, such as whether a given community wants to be 'dirty' even at a lower cost, is how to price the allowances. But Mr John Henry, president of Clean Air Capital Markets, a Washington-based investment banking firm that arranged the TVA transaction, said: 'It's a shot that will be heard around the utility world.' Its significance, he says, is that it will publicly set a price on the allowances which is below the cost of most scrubbers. He also said such transactions are less disruptive than switching fuel that must be transported from more distant sources. Soft, high-sulphur coal is produced largely in the eastern part of the US, where most of the offending utilities are located; hard, low-sulphur coal is produced in the western states. The Chicago Board of Trade, the world's biggest futures market, plans to begin trading futures contracts on the allowances, to be dubbed pollution futures.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Environment better served by free-trade carrot than protectionist stick - Co-operation produces better results than coercion, says a World Bank report intended to fuel debate at the Earth Summit next month
DOC.TEXT: PUNISHING poor countries through trade bans is unlikely to help protect the global environment, the World Bank concludes in a report published this month. While free trade is no panacea, co-operation will produce better results than coercion, it says. Developing countries, in particular, should not be forced to take action they cannot afford, such as stricter environmental legislation. 'In the case of worldwide global problems like global warming or in the case of regional problems like acid rain, there is no viable alternative to international co-operation,' says Mr Lawrence Summers, vice-president and chief economist, in his foreword to the report on trade and the environment. The study focuses on the pressure in the developed world for trade bans and other punitive action against countries whose environmental regulation falls below the standards of other countries. Blanket harmonisation of environmental regulation, sought to ensure fair competition between exporters, is inappropriate and runs counter to accepted principles of international trade, it argues. The report, intended to fuel debate at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro next month, acknowledges that the failure to take proper account of environmental costs has led in some cases to environmental degradation. It examines six broad themes: how trade and environment policy are linked; whether 'dirty' industries migrate in the face of higher environmental standards; whether higher standards hurt competitiveness; whether liberal trade, and the quest for economic growth underpinning it, necessarily results in degradation of the environment; how protectionists have captured environmental issues to aid their cause; and how international trade co-operation, including measures aimed at forcing harmonisation of environmental policies, can help to protect the environment. Attention should be paid to sustainable development, the use of unexploited natural resources, energy consumption, the possibility of environmental accidents, and threats to the 'global commons' including the oceans, the ozone layer and the world's forests, it says. Among its main conclusions, the report says: Companies have no environmental grounds on which to demand tariff protection against imports from countries with less rigorous environmental rules. Nor are there good economic grounds, since the cost of meeting environmental standards account for such a small proportion of total costs. There is no evidence that 'dirty' industries migrate to countries because their environmental standards are lax, and there is scant economic sense in doing so. International harmonisation of environmental standards is not necessarily a sensible aim, and may be used by governments to delay domestic environmental reform. In developing countries where poverty alleviation is a greater priority than environmental protection, different environmental standards may be valid. Trade bans, punitive tariffs or other forms of coercion are unlikely to be effective: 'Countries coerced into action by threats are unlikely to comply either very thoroughly or for very long, leaving the environmental outcome in doubt,' says Mr Summers. 'When consumption in the petitioning country is 20 times that of the country asked to bear additional costs for environmental improvement, or when countries are asked to forgo the benefits of their natural resources, equity more than economic logic suggests that threats to reduce poor countries' incomes further by trade restrictions are inappropriate.' A recurring theme in the report is the 'strong preference' governments show for 'direct command and control measures, which come far down in the efficiency hierarchy' when it comes to tackling environmental problems. Governments 'have omitted to give adequate consideration to the justification for measures they have adopted, or to the nature of the options available', the report concludes. Confirming the findings of a report by the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (Gatt) published in February, the World Bank accepts that trade measures may be justified as environmental policy 'in very narrowly defined circumstances', but that 'there is almost always a better way of meeting environmental objectives.' It rejects the 'deep ecology' view that environmental assets such as rain forests or endangered species have infinite value. From this, it follows that countries have a right to decide what value they give to environmental quality, traded against the need to provide jobs, relieve poverty, provide proper health care and education. 'Environmental standards and pollution abatement and control activities will be different among countries, and there is no valid presumption in favour of uniformity or harmonisation,' says Mr Patrick Low, the report's editor. While the report challenges the claim that a failure to harmonise environmental standards will result in 'dirty' industries migrating to countries with lax standards, it concedes that the amount of 'dirty' industry output in developing countries has grown steadily over the past two decades. It suggests, however, that this has more to do with the stage of industrialisation of many developing countries than any other factor. Studies in Chile and more widely across Latin America also contradict the claims that free trade leads to environmental degradation and that industries migrating to developing countries seek comparative advantage in their lower environmental standards. 'The more open an economy, the more rapidly clean technolsays. It also suggests that migrating companies have imported their technologies with them, rather than exploited lower local environmental standards. Several reasons are given for this: companies have become fearful of liabilities arising in the event of environmental accidents, and are sensitive to the demands of 'green' consumers in export markets. They economise by using common production standards in all plants, wherever they are based, and find it cheaper to start new plants with state-of-the-art technology rather than face the comparatively expensive prospect of 'retrofitting' ageing plant. They also have to anticipate that developing countries will over time demand more stringent environmental standards. The report attacks the case for protecting industries forced to meet high environmental standards because research shows the costs of pollution abatement and control to be small. Even in the US, which has generally high standards, these costs add up to an average 0.54 per cent of a company's overall costs. Even in the cement industry, which pays more for pollution control than any other, it accounts for just 3 per cent of costs. It argues that any attempt in the US to introduce a tax to 'level the playing field' would be 'strongly suggestive of a protectionist reflex, with little or no environmental justification'. It alerts environmentalists, who have often allied with protectionists in trade issues, that this provides a good example of how protectionist interests have no concern for better environment standards - only for the elimination of competitive disadvantage. 'Trade restrictions are an economically costly means for one country to use in trying to induce another to (take proper account of pollution costs), and they do not guarantee success in terms of the environmental outcome.' The report examines options to compensate developing countries undertaking environmental protection - including cash transfers, debt-for-nature swaps, technology transfers and sanctions for nature. It concludes that only the transfer of clean or pollution-reducing technology is without adverse side effects. *International Trade and the Environment, edited by Patrick Low. Available from the World Bank. The World Bank's annual World Development Report, to be published next week is dedicated to a study of environmental issues, and will be examined in the FT on Monday.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Environment: Bush will go to Earth Summit
DOC.TEXT: PRESIDENT George Bush confirmed yesterday he would go to the Earth Summit in Brazil next month, and rejected criticism that his demands have blocked chances for a breakthrough there, Reuter reports from Washington. White House officials have been divided over whether he should attend the conference, but concessions by other nations on a global warming treaty tipped the scales in favour of his going. In London, Mr John Major, UK prime minister, also to attend the meeting, sought to play down expectations of what might be achieved, saying there was 'bound to be a limited amount of success' at the Earth Summit.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Environment: Di Meana attacks UN over CO emissions timetable
DOC.TEXT: A STINGING new attack on the United Nations' dilution of the climate change convention, due to be signed at next month's Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, was launched by Mr Carlo Ripa di Meana, EC environment commissioner, yesterday. Mr di Meana was speaking on the eve of today's European Commission debate on its controversial energy tax as a means of combating global warming. The EC commissioner said he was bitterly disappointed that, in order to persuade the US to sign the convention, UN drafters had put aside any binding timetable to reduce carbon dioxide emissions. The EC is committed to stabilising CO emissions at 1990 levels by the year 2000, and Mr Ripa di Meana believes a mixed energy and carbon tax is an essential tool to meet this target. The tax would begin as Dollars 3 on the equivalent of a barrel of oil in 1993, rising to Dollars 10 by 2000. The US, which emits nearly twice as much CO as the EC, has until recently refused to accept any emissions target and at federal level has ruled out a carbon tax. Now that Washington appears to accept an emissions target, it is holding out against a timetable to achieve it. Wide-ranging exemptions from the carbon tax are proposed in today's Commission debate, adds David Lascelles. A draft which was being circulated yesterday would empower the Commission to exempt industrial sectors which voluntarily undertook to cut their carbon dioxide emissions, as well as companies which agreed to invest an equivalent amount to the tax in measures to cut emissions or conserve energy. Individual member states could also reduce the tax or seek temporary exemption if their economies were hard pressed or if they had made substantial progress in reducing carbon dioxide. This would require unanimous approval of the Council of Ministers.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Greece cuts taxes in fiscal reform package
DOC.TEXT: THE Greek government yesterday launched a wide-ranging fiscal package intended to boost revenues through broadening the tax base and curbing tax evasion. The new legislation, tabled in parliament, is also expected to promote growth by streamlining corporation tax, at present hemmed in by complex regulations which serve as a disincentive to investors, finance ministry officials said. Reduced income tax rates introduced in the bill will at first cause a sharp drop in revenues, estimated at about Dr50bn (Pounds 144m) for 1992. The top income tax rate will fall from 50 to 40 per cent, while the threshold for paying income tax rises to Dr1m, excluding junior civil servants and other white-collar workers. In 1993, the top income tax rate will drop to 30 per cent. Tax on corporate profits, currently between 42 and 50 per cent, is reduced to a single 35 per cent rate and companies are required to revalue fixed assets every four years. Stricter penalties for tax evasion include lifting of bank confidentiality, confiscation of professional licences and jail sentences for major offenders. Greece's most notorious tax evaders are self-employed professionals such as doctors and lawyers who avoid issuing receipts for their services. Under the new system, doctors must keep registers of their patients and lawyers are to be taxed under a co-efficient worked out with their union.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Divisions ease path in France for EC treaty
DOC.BYLINE: By IAN DAVIDSON and HILARY BARNES
DOC.TEXT: DEEP divisions in the ranks of France's opposition conservative parties yesterday seemed to promise the government a comfortable majority on its bill to revise the French constitution, as the prelude to ratification of the Maastricht treaty on European union. The leadership of the right-wing Gaullist party put forward four amendments to the bill in the hope of presenting a united front with the centre-right UDF umbrella grouping. But former President Valery Giscard d'Estaing, leader of the UDF, swung the prospects for the vote by breaking ranks with his ostensible Gaullist allies and advocated a Yes vote in Parliament. Ultimately, almost all of Mr Giscard d'Estaing's party, and all of the Centrists, were likely to vote with the government because they are in favour of European integration and the Maastricht treaty. Mr Giscard d'Estaing cut through the Gaullists' procedural manoeuvering, which was set to delay a vote until late last night or today, by dissociating himself from two of their four amendments. The Folketing yesterday approved the Maastricht treaty on European union by 120 votes in favour to 25 against with one abstention, Hilary Barnes reports from Copenhagen. The treaty will be submitted for approval to a popular referendum on June 2. The referendum result will be binding on the Folketing.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / UN sends mission to Nagorno-Karabakh
DOC.TEXT: The UN Security Council yesterday approved urgent dispatch of a fact-finding mission to study the conflict between Armenia and Azerbaijan over the enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh, Reuter reports. Mr Francesc Vendrell, a Spanish UN official, is expected to head the team. Mr Cyrus Vance headed a similar mission in March.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Banks press for Polish debt talks
DOC.BYLINE: By CHRISTOPHER BOBINSKI and ANTHONY ROBINSON
DOC.TEXT: POLAND'S commercial bank creditors want to start 'constructive negotiations as soon as possible' on re-scheduling the country's Dollars 11.8bn (Pounds 6.6bn) bank debt. However, Mr Jeffrey Stockley, head of a working group of the London Club of official creditors, said in Warsaw yesterday talks would not resume until the government reached agreement with the IMF. Poland is seeking a 50 per cent cut in commercial bank debt to match the 50 per cent cut in its Dollars 33bn official debt agreed last year with the Paris Club of western governments. Mr Andrzej Olechowski, acting finance minister, said final consultations with the IMF would take place next month. Officials from the IMF talks said an agreement with Poland could be completed by the end of July, provided the IMF board accepted a Polish letter of intent.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Delors denial on Brussels powers
DOC.TEXT: EUROPEAN Commission president Jacques Delors vigorously denied yesterday that he had any intention of trying to increase the powers of the Community's executive at the expense of small member states as the precondition for admitting new EC members. He made his denial in an interview with the Danish newspaper Politiken in an attempt to scotch rumours before next month's delicately poised referendum in Denmark on the Maastricht treaty. Mr Delors was reported to have been canvassing changes to make it possible for a bigger Community to function. Decisions are already slow in coming with 12 members in EC institutions set up to accommodate the original six member states. A smaller Commission, with greater supranational powers but more accountable to the Council of Ministers and the European Parliament, was the central idea Mr Delors is said to have been considering. The suspicion was that such a Commission would weaken the role of the six-month rotating presidency of the Community. This would weaken the position of small member states, which hold it just as often as the large, core countries, while the latter would maintain their influence through more prominence in the new executive. Mr Delors said yesterday that criticism of his alleged intentions was 'based on untruthfulness and lies. 'I have never put forward these proposals, because I do not intend them. On the contrary the meaning of the Community is that small and big countries are heard with the same interest.' Earlier this week, Mr Uffe Elleman-Jensen, Danish foreign minister, warned him that the widespread rumours were endangering the outcome of the referendum in Denmark and could cost Mr Delors his job.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Franco-German corps takes shape
DOC.BYLINE: By QUENTIN PEEL and DAVID WHITE
DOC.TEXT: FRANCE and Germany will next week finalise the concept and tasks of their planned European defence corps, including an independent command structure, which could run into strong objections by other Nato member states. A joint Franco-German military delegation yesterday met UK defence officials to try to allay British fears that the attachment of German units to the corps would conflict with Nato planning. The German embassy in London described the talks as 'constructive'. Chancellor Helmut Kohl said yesterday that the planning staff for the corps, intended to be the nucleus of a future fully-fledged European defence arm, would begin its work in July. According to government officials in Bonn, the two sides have ironed out their principal differences, and will set a timetable culminating in final establishment of the corps in October, 1995. They said Mr Kohl and President Francois Mitterrand would sign a treaty on the creation of the corps at a summit at La Rochelle in France on May 21-22. The chancellor said any other member states of the Western European Union were invited to join the unit, which will be built on the existing Franco-German brigade and is intended to be put under the WEU umbrella. The German troops in it will also remain assigned to Nato. The fear of some other Nato members, including Britain, is that the command arrangements for the new corps will dilute the German units' commitment to Nato and interfere in their full participation in Nato exercises. The German argument is that, on the contrary, the plan will bind the French contingent in the force more closely to Nato forces.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Fall in core inflation to 3.8 per cent
DOC.BYLINE: By PETER MARSH and JOHN THORNHILL
DOC.TEXT: THE GOVERNMENT revealed a lower than expected figure for core inflation yesterday but this potentially good news for the economy was accompanied by indications of continued weakness in consumer demand. The Central Statistical Office said the index of prices of manufactured products for domestic consumption rose in the year to April by 3.8 per cent. The rise was the lowest recorded for more than four years. But leading retailer Marks and Spencer - whose sales are tracked on a monthly basis by the Treasury - said in its annual results statement that consumer spending had yet to show an upturn. Indications that the removal of political uncertainty after the April 9 election has so far failed to stimulate the economy were reflected in a fall on the London stock market. It ended four successive days in which prices had closed at new records. The FT-SE 100 index of leading shares finished at 2,722.4, down 15.4. The inflation figure highlighted the lack of success of many manufacturers to restore profit margins - which have suffered since the recession started around mid-1990. Meanwhile Sir Richard Greenbury, the chairman and chief executive of M and S, said in announcing a 1.3 per cent increase in pre-tax profits to Pounds 623.5m that the recession had not ended as far as his company was concerned. Hopes of a sustained recovery later this year are linked to projections about a broad increase in consumer spending, which accounts for two thirds of gross domestic product. However, Mr John Major, the prime minister, put a more positive gloss on the economic outlook, emphasising the 'dramatic change' in business and consumer confidence since the Conservatives' general election victory. The inflation figure also contained good news for the government in that ministers believe the strong pressures on manufacturers to cut their prices, together with low wage settlements, will eventually spur increased output. Between March and April, the index of output prices at the wholesale level increased by 0.4 per cent, after a 0.7 per cent increase in March. That pushed the year-on-year rise in the index to 3.8 per cent, after 4.5 per cent in March. The extent of the reduction in the year-on-year figure was partly explained by this year's earlier than usual Budget statement on March 10. The early statement meant the normal Budget-time increases in excise duties for alcohol and tobacco showed up mainly in the March producer-price index number, rather than in April. The index of prices of products excluding food, drink and tobacco is the Treasury's favoured index for core inflation. It rose in the year to April by 2.8 per cent, as opposed to 2.9 per cent in March. Further indications of weak inflationary pressures emerged from the index for factory input prices. It showed a fall of 0.6 per cent last month compared with April 1991. Further figures for inflation - at the retail level - are to be released on Friday. The year-on-year change in the retail prices index last month is expected to be about 4.4 per cent, after 4 per cent in March. DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Stock and Currency Markets
FT 13 MAY 92 / Germany's engineering union gives employers ultimatum
DOC.TEXT: OPEN hostilities between Europe's biggest trade union and the mighty German engineering industry will break out on May 25 unless employers improve their 3.3 per cent pay offer. The industry - which produces annual sales of DM1,000bn (Dollars 606bn) - has been given until the end of this week. Announcing his ultimatum and the starting date for the long-expected strike, Mr Franz Steinkuhler, president of the IG Metall union, which represents 4m engineering workers, said yesterday that his only options now were 'capitulation or strike'. Gesamtmetall, the employers' association, said its 3.3 per cent offer remained the basis for any further negotiation. A deal approaching last year's 6.7 per cent would cost hundreds of thousands of jobs, added Mr Hans-Joachim Gottschol, the association president. Both sides have rejected arbitration. A structured deal giving more to the lower paid, similar to that agreed in the recent 5.4 per cent public sector settlement, is also ruled out. The union claimed yesterday that such 'social elements' were unsuitable in a workforce where pay ranged from DM2,000 to DM6,000 a month. In the absence of a new offer, Mr Steinkuhler said, an extraordinary union executive meeting would be called next Monday to decide which regional members would be balloted for strike action. Voting would be from May 20 to 22. The dates ann-ounced yesterday comprise the final data needed to complete the programming of a strike which seemed inevitable from the start of negotiations in early March. If it follows its tradition of seeking maximum effect with minimum outlay in terms of strike pay, IG Metall is most likely to start by calling out suppliers to the motor industry. The industry employs some 900,000 and has annual sales of almost DM300bn. Beyond the pre-strike rhetoric, there is wide agreement that German manufacturing industry faces a drastic slimming cure as it strives to restore competitiveness and cut unit labour costs. However, most plans are based on natural wastage and early retirement. Employers' threats of job losses have yet to make much impression on a workforce determined not to see living standards undermined. Forced redundancies are rare and difficult to implement in the rigid German labour market, and unemployment benefits are about two-thirds of basic pay. SPD attacks Kohl, Page 2

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / World News In Brief: America's Cup
DOC.TEXT: America3 beat Italy's Il Moro di Venezia by one minute 58 seconds to take a 2-1 lead in the best-of-seven America's Cup finals, pending a ruling on a protest flag hoisted by the Italians.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / World News In Brief: Five Britons missing
DOC.TEXT: Military helicopters were last night combing mountains west of Venice after a light aircraft with five Britons on board disappeared.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / World News In Brief: 'Friendly fire' inquest
DOC.TEXT: The US ambassador ruled out any hope that two US pilots, whose 'friendly fire' killed nine British soldiers, could appear at an Oxford inquest.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 13 MAY 92 / Japan laments loss of old work ethic
DOC.TEXT: JAPANESE executives are lamenting the disappearance of a breed of model worker delighted to do unpaid overtime, inspired by a passionate loyalty to the company and even 'genetically inclined' towards hard work. As part of an intensifying debate about whether the Japanese work ethic is being eroded by 'western-style' individualism and materialism, the Keidanren, the country's federation of economic organisations, surveyed 2,125 chief executives and senior managers. They agreed that the work ethic was changing but disagreed on the impact. The debate was inspired by Mr Akio Morita, the Sony chairman, who recently announced that managers should reduce working hours, raise workers' salaries, increase dividends and generally become more philanthropic. He also suggested that companies abandon their quest for market share and concentrate on profit quality. Mr Morita's comments were taken by some outraged executives as a direct attack on the terms and conditions of a social contract that had ensured Japan's success. There was also concern that employee enthusiasm may be undermined by a chairman's confession that they were under-compensated. The federation's survey showed that Japanese companies are indeed dependent on the enthusiasm of their staff, as 88 per cent of the companies rely on 'service overtime', that is, unpaid overtime. About 53 per cent of managers surveyed said unpaid overtime should decline but only 19.4 per cent supported an end to the practice, which makes the working year far longer than the official estimate of 2,052 hours. Japan's company-backed unions say the actual figure is closer to 2,400 hours. Asked to describe their employees' source of motivation, 30.9 per cent of managers said promotion prospects were most important and 26.9 per cent thought it was salary. But 37 per cent suggested that the love of work itself was the prime factor. A Nippon Steel executive said 'Japanese corporate energy' came from Japanese-style work values, self-realised desire and a now-declining, but essential love of teamwork. An executive at JR Tokai, the railway operator, said 'individualism' was replacing company loyalty as the most important motivation. Increasing wealth was seen as a threat to the old order, with 41 per cent of executives believing that work values were being eroded by material comfort, although 23 per cent disagreed, and 36 per cent were unsure.
