Mr Portillo said the government had been returned to power because it had gained the voters' trust by showing that it could reduce public borrowing, end the inexorable rise in public expenditure's share of national income, and bring about a massive reduction in personal taxation. Lower tax and a smaller role for the state fostered an environment in which business could flourish, industry prosper and the economy grow. Mr Portillo looked to resumed economic growth to 'enable the government to increase public expenditure on key areas, cut direct taxes and reduce public borrowing'. He underlined the government's commitment to reducing the share of the national income which was taken by the state and to balancing the budget over the medium term. Mr Portillo said medium-term policy would be designed to ensure that the convergence criteria agreed at the Maastricht summit were met. Taxes would be reduced 'when it is prudent to do so'. Mrs Beckett recalled that Mr Portillo had championed the poll tax and said he had 'absolutely no conscience' to preside over a steady stream of cuts affecting the poorest members of society. She renewed Labour's election charge that the government had caused a 'home grown' recession, and contended that the size of the public-sector borrowing requirement - 'Pounds 28bn and rising' - and the deficit on the balance of payments reflected the underlying weakness of the economy.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Fowler to be Tory chairman
DOC.TEXT: SIR Norman Fowler, former cabinet minister and political ally of the prime minister, is to become Conservative party chairman. His appointment from Monday, expected to be announced at the weekend, came as Mr Cranley Onslow appeared to have retained his chairmanship of the 1922 committee of backbench Tory MPs by promising to stand down after another year in the job. Sir Marcus Fox, Conservative MP for Shipley, had planned to stand in next Thursday's election but, after Mr Onslow's announcement, was reconsidering whether to force a contest. The post of Conservative party chairman fell vacant after the appointment of Mr Chris Patten as governor of Hong Kong. Sir Norman's acted as an adviser to Mr John Major's during the election. His biggest challenge will be to restore party finances, which were in deficit even before the general election. Sir Norman, who resigned from the government in 1990, will stand down as chairman of the Conservative backbench Europe committee. Observer, Page 17.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Labour chief whip faces challenge
DOC.TEXT: MR DEREK FOSTER, Labour's chief whip, looks likely to face a formidable challenge for his post as the party's Commons business manager in an election that may be brought forward to as soon as next month. Mr John Evans, at present Labour party chairman and MP for St Helens North, is canvassing support for the job that takes on a new significance as the Conservative majority has dropped from more than 100 to 21. Speculation is also mounting over the shadow cabinet elections amid reports that Mr Gerald Kaufman, the shadow foreign secretary, and Ms Jo Richardson, voice on women's issues, may have decided not to put forward their names for nomination. If they do step down - taken with the resignations of Mr Neil Kinnock and Mr Roy Hattersley - it will create four vacancies. Critics of Mr Foster say he has been unduly lenient with absentee MPs. His defenders reply that Labour's strategy in the last parliament was to concentrate on building support in the country by encouraging MPs to participate in regional campaigning. That will now come to an end as the Labour whips' office concentrates its efforts on devising ambushes and harrying tactics in Westminster aimed at wearing down the government and forcing compromises on legislation. Last year Mr Foster comfortably saw off a challenge by some 80 votes from Mr Peter Snape, the West Bromwich East MP. Mr Evans, who sits on Labour's national executive as the socialist organisations' representative, is said to have won a substantial body of support already. The timing of elections for the posts of chief whip and chairman of the parliamentary Labour party, at present Mr Stan Orme, is likely to be discussed at next Wednesday's shadow cabinet meeting. While normal practice requires an election shortly after a Queen's Speech, the contest for the Labour leadership and deputy leadership has left the party in limbo, with the shadow cabinet elections also postponed until the outcome on July 18. Mr Foster and Mr Orme, who may also face a challenge, are expected to propose to the shadow cabinet that the contest for their posts should go ahead now to allow for tactical planning of parliamentary business. Such a move would happen only if the candidates in the leadership race, Mr John Smith and Mr Bryan Gould, gave their blessing.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Rover sales drop by 9.6%
DOC.TEXT: ROVER, the vehicle subsidiary of British Aerospace, suffered a further sharp fall in UK sales of new cars in April in sharp contrast to the overall increase in UK new car demand, Kevin Done writes. Rover's sales volume last month fell year-on-year by 9.6 per cent to 15,854 compared with a 9.1 per cent jump in the overall market. Its market share last month plunged to only 11.5 per cent from 13.9 per cent a year ago. For the first four months, it remained narrowly in fourth place in the UK new car sales league behind Ford; Vauxhall, the UK subsidiary of General Motors of the US; and the Peugeot group of France, which includes Citroen. In the first four months Rover's sales, at 64,420, were 27.7 per cent lower than a year before. Its market share in the first few months plunged to only 11.8 per cent from 15.3 per cent in the same period a year ago. Ford, the UK new car market leader, again achieved a late surge in registrations in the final days of the month. It logged 38.2 per cent of its total April registrations in the last five days of the month. In the first four months this year the carmakers that gained most ground were Renault, Peugeot and BMW.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Dewhurst butchers chain faces shake-up
DOC.TEXT: DEWHURST, which runs the UK's biggest chain of butchers shops, will today disclose details of a substantial rationalisation of its 1,006 shops. Nevertheless the company, part of the privately owned Vestey business empire, yesterday refused to comment on the widespread reports that it planned to close up to 600 shops with the loss of 1,000 jobs. The company said it first had to inform its 4,234 staff of its decisions at regional meetings. There was disquiet, though, about possible closures at Dewhurst outlets yesterday. Dewhurst's plight may partly reflect the financial strains of the Vestey parent company, which was recently forced to make substantial provisions on its property portfolio. It also highlights the intense pressure that traditional butchers have experienced as a result of changing shopping habits and the growth of supermarket chains. According to estimates from Verdict, the retail research company, the big grocery chains now account for more than half of all carcase meat sold in the UK and about 92 per cent of bacon, ham, poultry and other meat products. Mr Richard Hyman, Verdict's director, said: 'I do not think it is too fanciful to suggest that this is at least partly due to the changing nature of society. 'Mothers do not pass on knowledge about cuts of meat to their children. It is pretty innocuous to go into a supermarket and choose a recognisable chunk of meat, whereas in a serviced butcher's shop you have to know what you are asking for.' Mr John Fuller of the National Federation of Meat Traders, which represents independent butchers, said butchers were trying to raise knowledge through educational programmes at schools. He added that, although butchers had undoubtedly suffered from supermarket competition, there were grounds for believing that smaller, family-owned butchers were experiencing a comeback, partly at the expense of the bigger chains - such as Dewhurst. 'Elements like the weather do have an impact on whether people buy stewing steak or barbecue meats,' he said. 'The private butcher is an entrepreneur and can respond a lot more quickly than the larger managed groups.' Nevertheless, the latest government figures showed that the number of registered butchers firms fell by 540 to 13,641 in the year ending April 1991. Thirty years ago there were more than 33,000 butchers shops on Britain's high streets.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Gas challenge date advanced
DOC.TEXT: THE GOVERNMENT is to introduce more competition into the gas market earlier than expected, it announced yesterday. Mr Tim Eggar, minister for energy, indicated that he would consider opening the household gas market to rival suppliers in May next year - three years sooner than expected. The government had previously said that domestic consumers would be offered a choice of supplier after 1996. Mr Eggar's comments followed the first meeting he has had with Mr Robert Evans, the chairman of British Gas, since taking up his appointment after the election. The meeting came after a fierce exchange on Wednesday between the company and Sir James McKinnon, the industry regulator, when Sir James threatened British Gas with legal action if it failed to cut its domestic prices immediately. Mr Eggar told Mr Evans he was surprised at the way in which British Gas had reacted and over its reluctance to cut household gas prices. He emphasised nevertheless that the issue should be decided between the regulator and the company. Mr Eggar said he would ask parliament to open up a greater segment of the industrial gas market for competitors to British Gas next month. That would allow 200,000 smaller commercial and industrial customers to negotiate gas supplies with competitors to British Gas in time for the new contract year, which begins in October. Mr Eggar's first step will be to lower the threshold for gas consumption under which rival suppliers will be allowed into the market. At present, customers must use 25,000 therms of gas a year before being allowed to choose a supplier. That will be reduced to 2,500 therms this year and possibly further next year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Abstract owned by Saatchi reaches Dollars 1.65m: Saleroom
DOC.TEXT: AN ABSTRACT painting by Cy Twombly, 'Untitled', loosely inspired by Leonardo da Vinci, sold for Dollars 1.65m (Pounds 917,839) at Sotheby's auction of contemporary art in New York on Wednesday. It was sent for sale by Charles Saatchi. Although it went for below its estimate, the fact that it found a buyer - the New York dealer Larry Gagosian - will help to restore confidence in what has been one of the weakest sectors of the art market. The auction totalled Dollars 12.32m with 24 per cent unsold. Charles Saatchi is selling many important pictures from his collection to release money to make purchases of younger artists, and most of the works he consigned to Sotheby's found buyers. They included 'Vermeer, Portrait Of The Artist In His Studio', a pastiche of an Old Master by the British artist Malcolm Morley, which sold for Dollars 627,000, an auction record for Morley. 'Bob's World', a 'plate' painting by the controversial Julian Schnabel, sold within forecast at Dollars 319,000. However, one important Saatchi picture, 'Night Interior' by Lucian Freud, failed to get anywhere near its Dollars 500,000 estimate. Other successes in the auction were Dollars 632,000 paid for a diptych by Brice Marden entitled 'The Dylan Karina Painting' and Dollars 577,000 for Andy Warhol's 'Most wanted man: No 11'. Christie's in south Kensington held a sale of rock memorabilia. The main lot, a rare video of Jimi Hendrix in concert, was unsold at Pounds 15,000, less than half its estimate, probably because of concerns about copyright; but Hard Rock International bought one of Hendrix's black felt hats for Pounds 4,950. A stage outfit worn by Prince on his Purple Rain tour sold for Pounds 9,020 and the instruments used by the band in the film The Commitments went for Pounds 3,300.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Building site safety hangs by a thread: Diane Summers on an initiative to reduce accidents in construction
DOC.TEXT: AN EVIL-looking hook is dangling from a piece of frayed rope. The contraption is supporting a plastic dustbin full of building materials which is being hauled by workmen up and down the outside of a three-storey building in north London. A short distance down the road, Mr Tim Small, Her Majesty's Inspector of Factories, is observing the scene from his car. 'This is a fairly typical set-up,' he says. 'It's cheaper to use old dustbins but they're not designed to be loaded like that. The work is close to the pavement - if the dustbin gives way, a member of the public could be seriously injured. We'd better take a look.' The work in progress is a re-roofing job, involving the addition of an extra storey to the building. Such work is among the most dangerous: one in five of all deaths in construction occurs during roof work. About three workers a month are killed falling off roofs and numerous passers-by are hit, sometimes fatally, by falling materials. Those figures are for the UK alone. Europe-wide, construction provides just 8 per cent of total employment but accounts for 16 per cent of serious accidents. Fatal accidents in construction occur at three to five times the rate of industry generally. EC directives aimed at tightening up site safety are on the way and this year has been declared the year of safety, hygiene and health protection at work by the European Commission. As part of the initiative, the Health and Safety Executive is 'blitzing' building sites involving roof work in an inspection campaign across the country. The campaign will not mean any more inspectors on the streets, but Mr Small and his colleagues will be concentrating their efforts on roofs during the next four months, the busiest period in the roof work industry. Outside the north London building, closer examination of the hook supporting the dustbin shows it to be an improvised job, fashioned out of a bent reinforcing rod. 'We'll have to put a stop to them using that straight away,' says Mr Small, leaping up a couple of ladders and some scaffolding in search of the workmen. At the top of the building he looks down for evidence of 'bombing' - debris thrown into the garden. This practice is strictly verboten, says Mr Small, except on sealed-off demolition sites. Thankfully, no bombing seems to have taken place. Back at ground level, a labourer grumbles that it is not his day: 'First the van's wheelclamped, now you lot. I've never even seen a factory inspector before.' Yes, they would have preferred to have used a proper chute instead of the dustbin, but the boss didn't want to spend the money and they were cutting corners all round on this job. No, they didn't have any hard hats but, as it happened, the boss would be around with some later. The boss arrives (no hard hats) to find out what is going on. Mr Small delivers a lecture on the dangers of improvised hoisting gear. He is told of a fatal case involving a falling bucket of boiling bitumen and a member of the public. A legal notice is served forbidding the further use of the dustbin-and-hook arrangement. The boss's attention is caught by the phrase 'fine of up to Pounds 20,000' if the legal notice is ignored. Mr Small promises to send a safety information pack. 'I don't expect he'll read it, but if there's an accident in future at least it'll be on file that he's had it. If there's a prosecution, we could bring that to the court's attention.' It is the sixth time in the week that he has served a legal notice at a construction site. He says it is good to keep the batting average up - everyone is impressed if you can point to an increased number of notices served and more prosecutions than in the previous year. But he has reservations about the time consumed in bringing cases to court and the paltry fines that often follow. 'It's not always the best use of time,' he says. 'There might be a Pounds 150 fine for not wearing a hard hat and the magistrate asks why you're picking on the guy. When you're in the office preparing paperwork for a case, you're not out there where you should be, stopping the things that are dangerous.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Heseltine order on drugs deal
DOC.TEXT: AAH HOLDINGS, the UK pharmaceuticals wholesaler, is to be asked to divest part of its acquisition of the UK business of Medicopharma NV, the Dutch pharmaceuticals wholesaler, on the ground that competition has been stifled. Mr Michael Heseltine, trade and industry secretary, yesterday instructed Sir Gordon Borrie, director-general of fair trading, to seek appropriate divestment undertakings from AAH after a Monopolies and Mergers Commission report that concluded that the merger was likely to operate against the public interest. The commission found that the acquisition made by AAH in November last year led to a reduction in competition in the Grampian and Highland regions of Scotland that was significantly greater than would have occurred if Medicopharma's UK subsidiaries had been placed in receivership. The commission did not consider that competition would be significantly affected at national level or in areas served by the other two depots of Medicopharma UK acquired by AAH - at Weedon, Northamptonshire, and Romford, Essex - or in the supply to hospitals, where AAH is by far the largest wholesaler. The commission recommended that AAH should be required to divest a business approximating as closely as possible to the business carried on by Medicopharma UK from its Aberdeen depot immediately before the acquisition. AAH and UniChem are the two largest UK wholesalers of pharmaceutical products, accounting for slightly more than 60 per cent of sales in 1990. AAH had 30 per cent of the market, valued at Pounds 2.84bn. Medicopharma UK was the third-largest wholesaler in 1990, accounting for 8 per cent of the market. AAH accounted for more than 70 per cent of sales of ethical drugs to hospitals by wholesalers in 1990 and about 33 per cent of total sales to hospitals, including direct sales. Medicopharma UK accounted for about 3 per cent of sales of ethicals to hospitals in 1990. Medicopharma entered the UK wholesale market in 1990 through the acquisition of two existing wholesalers, Butler, and the wholesale business of Macarthy. AAH said yesterday it was disappointed that the acquisition had been referred to the MMC but welcomed the commission's finding that there was no material effect on competition at a national level or in most of the UK. Mr Andrew Wallis, finance director, said the inquiry had delayed the integration of the Romford and Weedon warehouses into AAH's distribution network, but that could now proceed. AAH foresaw no difficulty in complying with the commission's recommendation in respect of the Aberdeen warehouse, Mr Wallis added. Mr Heseltine is making an order under the 1973 Fair Trading Act as a protective measure to guard against AAH's taking any action intended to frustrate the divestment.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Campaign for safer roof work launched
DOC.TEXT: THE HEALTH and Safety Executive warned the construction industry yesterday that it was mounting a safety drive on construction involving roof work, Diane Summers writes. Inspectors will order building sites to halt work and will take legal action in serious cases where safety rules are being breached, the HSE said. Dr Paul Davis, head of the HSE's construction group, said at the launch of its campaign: 'Cowboy roofers, like their namesakes . . . often die young.' Almost every roof work death could be prevented by simple precautions and the use of proper equipment. Roofers' deaths in building accidents make them the largest single occupational group for fatalities. Construction itself is the most dangerous of all industry sectors. Most roof work is done by about 7,000 contractors who provide work for 30,000 roofers. The sector is difficult to regulate because three quarters of the workers are self-employed and working for companies of three people or fewer.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Union threat of strikes on Tube
DOC.TEXT: LONDON Underground may suffer industrial action after a vote in favour of a strike by members of RMT, the transport union. The threatened action is over the loss of 5,000 jobs from the the 21,000 workforce. Changes in grading structures and working practices are also planned. London Underground said that the job losses will be phased over three years and there will be no compulsory redundancies. No date will be set for the action until the union has had a response from management, RMT said yesterday. One-day stoppages are more likely than an indefinite strike. The 11,000 RMT members at London Underground voted two to one in favour of a strike in a 65 per cent ballot turnout. London Underground said its message for the union was to 'stop posturing and start negotiating'. The restructuring would go ahead regardless, it added.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Surplus cash: whose money is it anyway?: Norma Cohen looks at the vexed issue of excess investment assets
DOC.TEXT: WHEN a pension fund has more money than it needs to pay benefits to members, just whose money is it? Is a surplus the property of pensioners, employees, former employees or the employer? Until now, the courts have taken the view that the owner of a pension fund's deficit also owns its surplus. Because employers have a nominal obligation to make good shortfalls, there have been no legal barriers to their use of surpluses for their own benefit. But in the aftermath of the Maxwell pension-fund scandal, in which more than Pounds 400m went missing from funds controlled by Robert Maxwell, that view looks increasingly unfair, or indeed, less sensible. The 100 Group of Finance Directors, representing Britain's largest companies, has just completed a review of pension issues, thus providing the first glimpse of the industry's response to some of the proposals to reform pensions law. Not surprisingly, the group opposes any attempt to yield pension-fund surpluses to members, saying that attempts to do so will only encourage employers to cut contributions and margins of cover available to meet pension liabilities. According to Caps, the pension-fund performance measurement service, more than two thirds of companies were taking pensions holidays last year - enjoying the use of surpluses built up in prior years and making no contributions towards their workers' retirement. The pensions fund industry had a net cash outflow of Pounds 2.5bn because investment income, rather than company contributions, was used to cover payments to beneficiaries last year. Two recent events have raised the temperature of the debate over who owns a pension fund's surplus. The first was a ruling by the European Court in May 1990 that, in establishing the need to set equal retirement ages for men and women, said that a pension was in effect deferred pay - and by extension, the property of employees. The second was the Maxwell saga itself. In the course of hearings conducted by the Commons social security committee, it emerged that Robert Maxwell was legally able to strip out millions of pounds of pension-fund surplus from companies he acquired - more in fact, than he paid to acquire them, according to evidence. The committee called for a royal commission to study the subject as part of a wider review of pensions law. Mr Frank Field, the committee's Labour chairman, said: 'My own view is that pensions are deferred pay. But that then raises serious questions about how they should be taxed.' Pension contributions of companies and workers are exempt from taxation, as are the income and capital gains of pension fund investments. Pensions industry professionals remain sceptical of industry threats to suspend or reduce benefits to workers if companies are forbidden to use surpluses themselves. Mr Alan Jenkinson, policy director at Noble Lowndes, an actuarial and pension fund consultancy, dismisses such threats as 'propaganda'. Mr Jenkinson believes there is little political support for allowing either employers or employees to secure the benefit solely for their own purposes. There is general agreement that surpluses should be shared, he said. Employers have argued their right to secure the surplus for their exclusive use on grounds that the surplus arose because they had contributed too generously in early years. Actuaries take issue with that, pointing out that surpluses arise for several reasons, including better-than-expected investment returns or failure to grant departing workers their fair share of pension assets. Mr Stewart Ritchie, pensions manager at Scottish Equitable, says: 'For many schemes, surpluses have arisen because the scheme has not kept pace with inflation. They have been relatively stingy with benefits while investment returns have soared.' Employers also argue that because they have ultimate obligation to make good a scheme's shortfall, they should also own the surplus. That view, too, is disputed. The Institute for Public Policy Studies, the leftwing think tank, has argued that employers can too easily evade their obligation to make up a shortfall by simply winding up a scheme. Mr Jenkinson says that has happened in relatively few cases. However, the plight of more than 4,000 Maxwell retired employees whose pensions disappeared overnight has heightened public concern about the strength of employers' promises to make good shortfalls. THE COURTS and politicians are increasingly challenging companies' rights to appropriate pension-fund surpluses for their own benefit, a leading pensions lawyer said yesterday. Mr John Cunliffe, a partner at McKenna and Company, called for clearer laws to end ambiguities over the ownership of surpluses at the conference. He said that until the question of surplus ownership was settled it would be impossible to draft legislation to safeguard pension-fund assets. Mr Cunliffe said politicians appeared increasingly to hold the view that pension-fund surpluses belonged to members, not the company. The courts, he said, had recently ruled that while members had no right to participate directly in a surplus, they had the right to be considered in relation to its use. 'All this comes pretty near to saying that surplus belongs to members,' he said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Funds told to be tougher against fraud: Call from Bank to pensions industry
DOC.TEXT: PENSION FUNDS must take a more active stand to prevent further Maxwell-style frauds, a Bank of England official told the annual conference of the National Association of Pension Funds in Glasgow. Mr Pen Kent, Bank of England director for finance and industry, said the association's members 'are not standing up to be counted'. Shareholders too often failed to exercise their right to vote and bore some responsibility for failing to insist on proper curbs on Robert Maxwell. Shareholders had not contributed enough to the debate over what companies should disclose in their corporate accounts, he added. 'We need to hear more from users of accounts about what is currently provided.' Mr Kent said that although there is 'no such thing as a risk-free society', there is a need to tighten regulation of the investment industry. Mr Brian McMahon, association chairman, outlined its support for pension reform. 'The days are gone, indeed if they ever existed, when this association could say that everything is fine, nothing wrong with the way we run our schemes, and especially nothing wrong with the way I run mine,' Mr McMahon said. 'Maxwell has cast a giant shadow over us.' The association is studying a compensation arrangement for pension scheme members similar to that available to private investors. Other reforms backed by the association include requiring boards of trustees to offer equal representation to employers and members. The association also says pension schemes should be required to pay for trustees to obtain training.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / New ferry is largest in Channel
DOC.TEXT: BRITTANY Ferries, the French cross-Channel ferry operator, has taken possession of the largest vessel yet to ply between the UK and France - the Normandie, weighing in at 27,000 gross tonnes (above), Richard Tomkins writes. The Pounds 80m vessel, which will make its maiden voyage on the Portsmouth-Caen route on May 18, can carry a total of 2,200 passengers and 630 cars. Built by the Kvaerner Masa shipbuilding company at its Turku yard in Finland, the ferry incorporates restaurants, bars, a children's playroom, two cinemas and a fully equipped hospital. The vessel forms part of a Pounds 350m investment programme being undertaken by Brittany Ferries on its fast-growing western Channel routes, which are less vulnerable to the threat of the Channel tunnel than the shorter routes to the east. Last month the company took possession of the 20,500 grt Barfleur, which has just gone into service between Poole and Cherbourg. This will shortly be followed by the introduction of the 31,400 grt Nils Holgersson - one of the world's 20 largest ferries - to the routes between Plymouth and Roscoff in Brittany and Plymouth to Santander in Spain.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Societies pressed on rescue pledges
DOC.BYLINE: By DAVID BARCHARD and JOHN WILLMAN
DOC.TEXT: BUILDING SOCIETIES were told yesterday that the government expects them to keep pledges made before Christmas to rescue mortgage customers facing possible eviction. Mr Anthony Nelson, the economic secretary to the Treasury, congratulated the Building Societies Association at its annual conference in Bournemouth for achieving a reduction in the likely number of mortgage evictions. 'We look to you, the lenders, to identify workable solutions to the problems which have emerged with these schemes, so that you will be able to deliver the commitments you made last December,' Mr Nelson said. Later Sir George Young, the housing minister, said mortgage-rescue measures should be a permanent fixture of the industry. First-time buyers considering a mortgage should be able to feel they would not be left 'stranded' if the economy and housing market moved against them. After talks with the government, the societies pledged more than Pounds 800m for mortgage-rescue schemes, intended to save at least 16,000 borrowers from eviction. Nearly six months later only a handful of borrowers have been saved directly by the schemes, although most societies have achieved a dramatic reduction in the number of evictions by improved debt counselling and similar services. Mr John Wriglesworth, a housing finance specialist at securities house UBS Phillips & Drew, said: 'I estimate that these techniques may be successful in cutting repossessions from 280,000 to around 80,000 this year.' Abbey National, Britain's second-largest mortgage lender, yesterday cut mortgage interest rates immediately for new borrowers and from July 1 for existing customers. Rates on mortgages of up to Pounds 60,000 go down from 10.9 per cent to 10.7 per cent; Pounds 60,000 to Pounds 100,000 loans from 10.55 per cent to 10.2 per cent; and mortgages above that from 10.4 per cent to 9.99 per cent.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Move to cut audits attacked
DOC.TEXT: PLANS to abolish the statutory audit requirement for small companies should be strongly resisted, the outgoing president of the Chartered Association of Certified Accountants said yesterday. Mr Ken Anderson attacked both the idea and its supporters at the association's annual meeting in London. The Department of Trade and Industry is considering abolishing the mandatory audit requirement for very small companies. Under the proposals, requirements could be eased for all companies below the Pounds 36,600 value added tax threshold. Mr Anderson accused the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales - which has supported the idea - of 'orchestrating' a campaign for abolition. 'In the current climate, with the audit side of the profession under such focus . . . it is surely not the time to seek to reduce the role of the audit,' he said. He argued that limited liability status imposed responsibilities on companies.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / MPs to meet SIB chief over Lloyd's inquiry
DOC.BYLINE: By DAVID OWEN and RICHARD LAPPER
DOC.TEXT: LLOYD'S OF London will come under political pressure again next week when a party of MPs visits Sir David Walker, chairman of the Securities and Investments Board, to discuss his inquiry into alleged malpractices. The authorities at the insurance market faced intense scrutiny earlier this year when MPs said Names working in the market were benefiting at the expense of Names outside. Names are the individuals whose assets support underwriting. The MPs will seek assurances that Sir David is gaining access to all the information he needs for his inquiries. The party is expected to include Mr Paul Marland, the Conservative MP for Gloucestershire West, who is also a Lloyd's Name. The credibility of the inquiry is critical to Lloyd's as it seeks to rebuild confidence in the face of its difficulties. Losses in 1989 are expected to amount to more than Pounds 1.35bn, with some recent estimates putting the figure as high as Pounds 2bn. At the time of Sir David's appointment in February, Mr David Coleridge, chairman of Lloyd's, commented: 'I needed a man who was so white that snow-white looked dirty.' Mr Marland is also expected to be at the forefront of calls for a fully fledged Commons debate on Lloyd's. He is understood to have written to Mr Neil Hamilton, a junior trade and industry minister, to request a meeting with him and other interested parties. In a separate development, Lloyd's has received a legal opinion from Mr Jonathan Sumption QC that it can admit corporate members without any alteration of the Lloyd's Act, which provides for the market's self-regulation. The opinion potentially clears the way for more rapid implementation of the proposals made by the Rowland report in January to bring corporate capital to the market. It had been assumed that changes in the act would be needed. However, Lloyd's will still need to talk to various regulatory bodies, including the US Securities and Exchange Commission, about the reforms. Potential investors may be encouraged by the findings of Mr Chris Hitchings, an insurance analyst with Hoare Govett, the securities house. Lloyd's has consistently outperformed both UK composite insurers and US insurers in terms of both its profit margins and the strength of its solvency margins, says Mr Hitchings in a report that analyses financial data from Lloyd's and the UK and US insurance industries on a like-for-like basis. Between 1950 and 1989, Lloyd's reported average annual profits (as a percentage of net written premiums) of 6 per cent, compared with 3.9 per cent for UK companies and 2.9 per cent for US insurers. Lloyd's losses for 1989 - which the market reports next month - are likely to be much worse than those experienced by the UK companies, partly because of its heavy exposure to natural catastrophes. However, had UK companies accounted on the same basis as Lloyd's, their results for 1989 would have been worse, says Mr Hitchings in his report. Many of the companies' 1990 and 1991 losses occurred because of the need to make provisions for claims made on policies underwritten in earlier years.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Acas reports slow growth in derecognition
DOC.TEXT: DERECOGNITION of unions, especially for supervisory, technical and professional jobs, is being considered by a 'slowly growing number of employers', according to the annual report of Acas, the conciliation service. Nevertheless, the report also points to a greater readiness on the part of individuals and unions to use the law against employers by taking unfair dismissal and discrimination cases to industrial tribunals. Acas, which has a statutory duty to conciliate between employee and employer before a case goes to a tribunal, saw a large increase in its workload in individual and collective cases last year. In the first quarter of this year, individual conciliation cases have increased by 40 per cent over the same period last year. Of the 60,605 individual conciliation cases last year, a 16 per cent rise over 1990, only 32 per cent went to tribunals. Sex discrimination cases rose by 119 per cent to 3,500. That was because of a wave of cases influenced by the European Court's Barber judgment, which extended the definition of equal pay to include pensions. Sir Douglas Smith, Acas chairman, also pointed to cultural changes that had led to a greater readiness by women to go to court. Unions, too, had changed their attitudes and 'are much more ready to ensure that members are aware of their statutory rights'. Although that is a sign of unions having less leverage through collective bargaining on matters such as election for redundancy, Sir Douglas said he did not believe unions were terminally weakened. He said national union leaders were more pragmatic than they used to be, but union strength often remained considerable at local level. Sir Douglas said he did not believe that employers wanted to scrap the Bridlington rules, through which the Trades Union Congress regulates disputes between unions. He also expects much more work involving the public sector - hitherto four fifths of Acas's work has been in the private sector - as new, more devolved industrial relations are introduced into many public services. The Acas report said it had already intervened in National Health Service trusts where 'there often remains a lack of expertise and experience (in industrial relations) among local managers and trade union reps alike'. The report also warns public-sector managers not to embrace uncritically performance-related pay at a time when the private sector's experience is becoming 'more mixed' and some employers are re-examining the advantages and disadvantages. Report 1991. Acas Reader, PO Box 797, London SE8 4JX. Pounds 1

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Settlement hope in council swaps case
DOC.BYLINE: By RAYMOND HUGHES, Law Courts Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: SETTLEMENT of Chemical Bank's Pounds 2.94m claim against the Hammersmith and Fulham council in London - part of the interest rate swaps litigation - appeared to be imminent last night. It will be the fifth of the six lead cases to have been resolved without the High Court having an opportunity to give guidance for the remaining disputes between banks and local authorities. The litigation stems from the House of Lords ruling in January last year that all swaps deals entered into by local authorities were void because they were outside councils' legal powers. Chemical Bank's case was opened on Wednesday. Its lawyers returned to court yesterday but went away without the hearing being resumed. Their places in court were taken by the lawyers for NationsBank of North Carolina - formerly NCNB National Bank of North Carolina - which is suing Hammersmith for Pounds 306,000, plus interest and costs, in the last lead case. Mr Robert Englehart QC, for NationsBank, told Mr Justice Hirst that, although a large US bank, it had been 'a veritable minnow' as far as the UK swaps market had been concerned. Its only swaps deals with local authorities had been two interest rate 'caps' transactions with Hammersmith, in which it had been intermediary between the council and Midland Bank and Salomon Brothers International. Mr Englehart explained that a 'cap' buyer paid a lump sum premium to the seller. In return, the seller agreed to make payments to the buyer if a variable interest rate such as Libor exceeded the fixed rate in the contract. It had been 'a most unfortunate dabbling' in the local-authority swaps market for NationsBank. It had received no payments from Hammersmith but had to honour back-to-back transactions in which it had sold the 'caps' to Midland and Salomon Brothers. The result had been that NationsBank had lost more than Pounds 1.75m instead of making an Pounds 81,000 profit. The hearing will continue on Tuesday.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Beer output cut
DOC.TEXT: BEER production in the 12 months to the end of February fell by 3.5 per cent, the Brewers' Society said yesterday. It added that the output of 37.1m barrels reflected depressed sales.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Leading index up
DOC.TEXT: THE Central Statistical Office said its longer leading index of economic indicators rose from 103.7 in March to 104.0 last month, supporting expectations of recovery this year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / BA launches promotion
DOC.TEXT: BRITISH Airways yesterday launched a Pounds 17.5m promotional campaign to increase business-class traffic. Mr Robert Ayling, marketing director, said that passenger figures had started to recover their pre-Gulf war levels. 'The moment is ripe for a major push of this kind,' he added.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Regalian proposes sale by tender
DOC.TEXT: THE depressed London property investment market has prompted Regalian, a property developer, to adopt the unusual tactic of selling an office block by tender. It hopes to choose four potential buyers to bid for Red Lion Court, an office building in Southwark near the City of London. The 128,500 sq ft building, which is let to Lloyds Bank, has a reserve price of Pounds 45m. In 1989 Regalian tried to sell the property for Pounds 65m. The reserve price of Pounds 45m would give a net yield of 9.3 per cent, slightly higher than that on long-dated gilts.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Mercury increases pay bill by 5.7%
DOC.TEXT: MERCURY Communications has increased its salary bill by 5.7 per cent, putting pay rises at the telecommunications group at the top end of current awards, Hugo Dixon and David Goodhart write. Mercury, BT's main rival in the telecommunications market, has also improved benefits, including paternity leave and a helpline for staff. Individual rises will vary because Mercury operates a performance-related pay scheme. The scheme takes account of market rates and the company's financial position as well as the performance of individual employees. Mercury, which does not recognise unions, prides itself on being at the forefront of industry in setting pay and conditions. The National Communications Union, the main BT union, claims that the generosity of the deal is in part a response to its present recruiting efforts. Mr Alan Harley, NCU national organiser, said Mercury responded 'in a friendly manner' before the general election. But since then 'it has stopped replying to our letters'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Theory on workforces is challenged
DOC.TEXT: ONLY 10 per cent of employers view their workforce as composed of a core of highly skilled, permanently employed workers and a periphery of less skilled, less secure ones, according to a Department of Employment survey. Such a view of workforces - known as the 'core-periphery' model - has been popular with labour market theorists since the early 1980s. But the survey, published in the government's Employment Gazette, suggests that far fewer employers hold that perception of their workforces than had been thought. The survey found only a third of employers guided by any strategic thinking in their deployment of non-standard or peripheral labour. Direct costs were not significant in distinguishing between full-time and other forms of labour. The hourly rates for full-timers, part-timers and temporary workers doing similar jobs were the same for nearly 90 per cent of employees. Coverage of the most important non-pay benefits - sick pay and pensions - was, however, significantly lower for part-timers compared with full-timers, and for temporary workers relative to part-timers. Working days lost through strikes last year, at 800,000, were the fewest since records began 100 years ago, according to another Employment Gazette study. There were 369 stoppages last year, compared with 630 in 1990. An initiative to train disabled people in information technology so that they can find employment by working from home was launched yesterday by Leeds Training and Enterprise Council. Housebound trainees will learn computer literacy, spreadsheet modelling, word processing, desktop publishing and databases during a six-month course.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Pigging out at the Cafe Royal
DOC.TEXT: THE Cafe Royal in London became a pig pen yesterday. It was the venue for the National Pig Development Company to show off its new Anglo-Chinese hybrid, the Manor Meishan. Lord Plumb, Conservative MEP for The Cotswolds and former president of the National Farmers' Union, described the hybrid as a 'quantum leap in pig breeding'. It combines the astonishing reproductive performance of the Meishan - each sow has 16 piglets a litter and produces two or three litters a year - with the lean meat characteristic of the British Large White and Landrace breeds. China sold 32 of its fat, wrinkly Meishan pigs in 1987 to a consortium of British pig breeding companies for use in a research programme co-ordinated by the Institute of Animal Physiology and Genetics Research in Edinburgh. The Manor Meishan is the first commercial result. It looks smooth and sleek, without the heavy folds of skin characteristic of its Chinese ancestors. Like them, it has 16 teats - and sometimes even 18 - to accommodate its large litters (a typical European pig has 12). National Pig Development, a private company based at Driffield, Humberside, will supply Manor Meishans 'exclusively to the UK market for the foreseeable future'. The company expects to deliver 2,000 pigs in the next year. Lord Plumb welcomed the 'cost-cutting' hybrid as a development that would help British farmers compete.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Protesters give Bush hostile reception in battered Los Angeles
DOC.TEXT: MANY Los Angeles residents gave President George Bush a hostile reception yesterday as he saw for himself the destruction wrought by riots last week. Walking through black, Hispanic and Korean areas of the city's downtown area, Mr Bush expressed his 'horror and dismay' at the results of the 'wanton lawlessness'. But the president also said he wanted to tackle the roots of the urban and social problems that had provided fuel for the rioting, which was triggered by the acquittal on charges of assault of four policemen who were videotaped savagely beating a motorist, Mr Rodney King. 'There must be no return to the status quo,' Mr Bush said as he arrived in the city late on Wednesday night. 'You have to get at the cause. You've got to do that,' he added yesterday. However, the president faced protests from those Angelenos who felt he should have come sooner to visit their battered city, as well as from those who felt that, by coming now, he was merely placing an unnecessary extra burden on the police and soldiers who are keeping the peace. He also met protests from the Korean-American community, which was in many instances singled out last week as the target of violence. Korean-American shopkeepers gathered outside Mr Bush's hotel, chanting: 'We want justice.' Banners proclaimed: 'We need money now' and 'Mr President - if you won't help, Clinton will.' Governor Bill Clinton of Arkansas, the presumptive Democratic presidential candidate, who had visited the riot-torn areas of Los Angeles on Monday, has criticised Mr Bush for blaming the problems of the inner cities on the Great Society welfare programmes introduced by President Lyndon Johnson in the 1960s. He has been cautious in his criticism of Mr Bush's response to the crisis in Los Angeles, however. Other demonstrators yesterday protested at the response of the police to the outbreak of violence last week. Mr Daryl Gates, the controversial chief of the Los Angeles Police Department, has come under renewed attack for having been inadequately prepared for an outbreak of unrest in response to the acquittal of his four officers. The department has been accused of having pulled its officers out of the area where violence first broke out, thus giving a green light to rioters. Many shopkeepers have also complained that police did not answer their calls for help and stood by as their stores were pillaged. Mr Gates has agreed under pressure to retire in June, after 14 years in his job, but local politicians yesterday called for him to leave immediately.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Climate treaty sets no emission limits
DOC.TEXT: A DRAFT treaty on climatic change, to be signed by world leaders next month, would commit rich countries to fight global warming by restricting greenhouse-gas pollution, but would stop well short of setting limits, Reuter reports from the United Nations in New York. According to a new text of the treaty, circulated yesterday, developed countries would agree to limit emissions of gases such as carbon dioxide and to protect 'sinks', such as forests, that absorb such emissions. The text, or a slightly amended version of it, was expected to be handed to UN negotiators today for approval by tomorrow. The treaty is to be a centrepiece of the UN's Earth Summit at Rio de Janeiro next month. By way of victory for the US, which has opposed the requirement of specific emission targets, the draft treaty contains only loose goals. One section recognises that reduction of emissions 'to earlier levels' by the end of the decade would contribute to fighting climatic change; another says countries should aim to return emissions to 1990 levels. Critics charged the draft could allow signatories to comply whatever they did. Mr Alden Meyer of the Union of Concerned Scientists said the UN negotiations had produced 'a toothless global warming treaty, totally inadequate to the threat posed by the continued build-up of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.' The language of the text was vaguer than an earlier European Community proposal to require stabilisation of carbon-dioxide emissions at 1990 levels by 2000, and was a far cry from the sharp cuts environmental activists say are necessary.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Brazil fails to achieve IMF aims
DOC.TEXT: THE BRAZILIAN government admitted yesterday it had failed to meet at least one of the five targets for the first quarter of its programme with the International Monetary Fund, and so would not request the second tranche of IMF funding due this month, reports Christina Lamb in Sao Paulo. Rather than ask for a waiver of the IMF conditions, so as to enable it to receive the Dollars 250m payment, Brazil has asked the fund for a rephasing of their agreement signed in January. The country's progress is now to be reassessed in August. Brazil's economic team believes targets will have been met by then.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Exxon executive 'held by ecological militants'
DOC.TEXT: A MILITANT environmental group, the Rainbow Warriors, has claimed it is holding Mr Sidney Reso, head of Exxon's international division, according to a New York press report yesterday. There was no official confirmation of the report but US law enforcement officers are investigating claims that a series of ransom messages has been received about Mr Reso, who disappeared on the morning of April 29 while going to work in New Jersey. His car was found at the end of his driveway, with the engine running and the door ajar. Mr Michael Murphy, the New Jersey prosecutor working with the FBI on the case, last night said it would be 'inappropriate' to discuss the report of an unverified communication from alleged kidnappers. He said that, without a photograph or voice recording, he could not conclude that Mr Reso was held by any group. A spokesman for Exxon, said it had 'no new information.' The company is seen as a prime enemy of militant environmentalists, who accuse the company of arrogance over the oil spill disaster caused by the Exxon Valdez tanker off Alaska in 1989. Rainbow Warrior was a protest ship owned by the Greenpeace environmental group. It was sunk by French secret service saboteurs in 1985.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Third World Environmental Fund to have wider role
DOC.TEXT: THE Global Environmental Facility, the fund administered by the UN and the World Bank to help developing countries protect the environment, is to be restructured so as to give it a wider role, writes David Lascelles, Resources Editor. The facility, set up as a three-year experiment in 1990, is to be given a more enduring status, after decisions at the World Bank meeting in Washington last week. It is to be altered in two main ways. Governance of the GEF is to be made more democratic by opening it to universal membership. At present, its policies are dominated by the wealthy countries which provide most of the money, and by its World Bank administrators. A new Participants' Assembly would be created. The facility will also be offered as a channel to fund projects under two conventions being negotiated for the Earth Summit next month in Rio de Janeiro.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / A fragile peace turns to dust on Beirut's blasted streets: Hopes of a new beginning are evaporating
DOC.TEXT: THE WAR was supposed to be over; the barriers were bulldozed by the Lebanese army last summer. Peace was supposed to mean freedom of passage - an end to barricades of burning cars and tyres. The Lebanese thought they had exorcised the bad memories of 1975, when the civil war started with riots similar to those that wracked the country this week. How quickly Lebanon's impoverished peace reverted to anarchy; how unnerving to see pistol-toting militiamen striding purposefully down Hamra Street again, among the small boys wielding sticks festooned with devalued Lebanese pound notes. They delighted in the sound of shattering windows, in the shouted obscenities against the government. When the riots which toppled Prime Minister Omar Karami's government were over, only the glass merchants would benefit from the orgy of breakage. There hadn't been such demand for new window panes since the artillery bombardments of 1990. Was it premature then, the refurbishing of shops and restaurants? Had Beirutis been too quickly seduced by an elusive peace? In the Unesco quarter, just 100 metres from the home of the speaker of parliament, the elegant, newly-erected facade of the Bank of Kuwait and the Arab World was devastated. Chunks of white marble, chipped off by the rioters' crowbars, lay in the street, alongside felled pink granite columns. The Middle East insurance executives who convened in Beirut this week will not forget their lunch at the seafront, marred by a crowd throwing empty bottles. 'Why should you eat when we have no food?' the people shouted. And -shades of Marie-Antoinette - President Elias Hrawi is sure to remember the housewives and children who marched to his home in Zahle in the Bekaa Valley crying, 'Give us bread, we are hungry.' Until this week, it was easy to forget those dispossessed by peace, the ragged thousands who took to the streets to the cheers of their better-off compatriots. Since the beginning of May, the street lamps were lit on the Mediterranean Corniche for the first time in nine years. On balmy evenings, families walked along the promenade, buying coffee from the sidewalk vendors while Arabic music blared from pushcarts offering audio-cassettes, the sesame-studded bread known as ka'ak, peanuts, sunflower seeds and pistachios. There was a profusion of florists and stalls offering exotic fruit. Smith's grocery store had revamped its facade with bright red awnings. For a price that few Lebanese could afford, there was duck liver pate, imported crab meat and champagne. In Hamra Street, the shopowners who yesterday assessed the damage had stocked the latest 'roulette' five-disc CD players, French designer clothes and copies of the same clothes from Turkey. But housewives bemoaned the price of tomatoes; from LPounds 600 per kilo in January to LPounds 2,000 this week. And Filipino maids were hard hit by government corruption. As the rioters began burning tyres on Tuesday night, the most wealthy member of an old Beirut Moslem family told his dinner guests that he had been offered Dollars 55m for his 19th century mansion and grounds, but wouldn't consider selling. The owners of a grand Ottoman house on the heights above Raouche were asking Dollars 12m - but of course the house would be torn down to make way for a high-rise building immediately after the sale. Like many of their fellow Lebanese, the dinner guests betrayed their nostalgia for the exiled Lebanese General Michel Aoun. 'There has never been any problem between the Lebanese - Moslems and Christians want to live together, if only the foreigners would leave us alone,' went the old, unconvincing refrain. The Syrians have launched a timid public relations campaign, prompting their clients in the Shia Moslem Amal militia to cover walls with posters showing clean-cut, smiling Syrian soldiers handing out toys to Lebanese children. 'The sons of (Syrian President Hafez) Al-Assad are here to protect the future of Lebanon,' the posters proclaim. But the Syrian soldiers melted away before the mobs who swarmed through Beirut on Wednesday. Former Prime Minister Karami's government said it wanted them to stay in Beirut beyond the September 1992 deadline set by the Taif peace accords. No one knows what the next government will say. No one knows whether the first parliamentary elections in 20 years will take place this summer. Once again, the Lebanese are mustering their famed skills of survival. The economic crisis has denied them simple pleasures that even the war never touched. Yet again, the promise of a new beginning lies in streets strewn with broken glass and burning rubbish.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Korean agreement
DOC.TEXT: South and North Korea took the first steps yesterday towards implementing their non-aggression and reconciliation pact, signed last December, John Burton reports from Seoul. The prime ministers of the two countries agreed, at a meeting in Seoul, to establish three committees by May 18 to help carry out the pact's terms.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Bangkok citizens rally to Mr Clean
DOC.TEXT: GENERAL Chamlong Srimuang, the opposition politician on the fourth day of a hunger strike to demand the resignation of Thailand's unelected premier, is a moralistic former general dubbed 'Mr Clean' by his supporters, Reuter reports from Bangkok. His uncompromising piety and idealism have made him hugely popular among Bangkok citizens grown tired of rampant corruption and influence-peddling in high office. They voted for his Palang Dharma or 'Moral Force' party in droves during the March 22 general elections and it swept 32 of the 35 seats contested in the city. Gen Chamlong's vow to fast to the death unless Gen Suchinda Kraprayoon resigns the premiership brought tens of thousands of people onto the streets in support of his protest. A devout Buddhist, Gen Chamlong won his spurs politically in two terms as Bangkok's governor where his efforts to fight corruption, clean up the city's streets and free them from annual floods won him a strong support base. He spurns the expensive suits, flashy cars and gold watches favoured by many other politicians. He wears the simple denim garb of a peasant and sandals cut from old tyres. His image as a politician untainted by corruption contrasts strongly with that of the new Thai cabinet, which includes ministers Gen Suchinda himself accused of corruption after staging a coup against the last elected prime minister in February 1991. Gen Chamlong has survived attacks by rivals who criticised him for failing to solve Bangkok's worsening traffic and air pollution problems and who tried to discredit him for associating with a renegade Buddhist sect deemed heretical by the religion's mainstream authorities. In a city known for its massive sex industry, Gen Chamlong abstains from sexual contact with his wife. He wakes before dawn and eats just one meal a day. 'Eat less, spend less, work harder' has become his catchphrase. Thais prefix his name with the title Maha - denoting a venerated Buddhist -because of his monkish habits. Gen Chamlong was born into a poor ethnic Chinese family, which his widowed mother struggled to support as a street vendor. Top grades in school took him into the army where he saw action in Vietnam and Laos and eventually rose to the rank of major-general. He left the military in the early 1980s to stand for the Bangkok governorship. Because of his steely character his vow to fast until death has been taken seriously. He has ordered his supporters to stand guard in shifts to prevent any attempts to force him to eat or take him to hospital. He vowed not to speak during his fast and instead communicated through signs.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Wellington offers railways for sale
DOC.TEXT: THE New Zealand government, struggling with high external debt, yesterday signalled that four state-owned enterprises, including the railways and the former ministry of works, will be sold by the middle of next year. They have a collective value of around USDollars 600m (Pounds 339m). State owned enterprises minister Mr Maurice McTigue said the government was looking into New Zealand Rail, the Works Corporation, Landcorp and the Government Computer Service to see whether privatisation was the best option. Mr McTigue stopped short of saying the sales were inevitable. But he said it was clearly the intention of the government to sell, providing there were no impediments. There are difficulties with a big Maori land claim under the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi, and privacy issues surrounding the computer company which manages the national register of all police, court and traffic offences. Parliament may need to pass urgent privacy legislation to permit a sale. Mr McTigue refused to give a breakdown of how much each of the businesses were expected to fetch. He said the sales would be used to retire external debt. Decisions to sell would be based on the likelihood of greater efficiency and financial gain for the businesses and a reduction of financial risk to the government and the taxpayer. He said that New Zealand Rail, which owns the ferries which link the North and South Islands, and the national network of tracks, trains and bridges, but not the land over which the trains run, is committed to a Dollars NZ350m (Pounds 106m) modernisation programme over the next three years. Mr McTigue said the government did not wish to pay for this. The other companies earmarked for sale include Workscorp, which operates large engineering, roading and construction companies, and Landcorp which owns 180 farms. The sale of the farms would be handled in such a way as not to depress the value of other farm properties, the minister said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Banda faces threat to grip on power: Two days of unrest leave 38 dead
DOC.TEXT: PRESIDENT Hastings Kamuzu Banda of Malawi was last night facing his most serious crisis since independence in 1964 after 38 people were reported killed as industrial unrest and looting continued for a second day. Earlier reports of a coup attempt against Dr Banda, who is in his 90s, seem unfounded, but the violence is a symptom of political tensions and a deteriorating economy. The combination of mounting opposition to his autocratic regime, led by the church and trade union movement, and external pressure from donors which are making aid conditional on human rights reforms, make it unlikely that Dr Banda can weather the storm. The unrest began in the commercial centre of Blantyre, say western diplomats in the country's capital, Lilongwe, when 3,000 workers on strike at a factory took to the streets on Wednesday. Looting broke out as the workers, demanding a pay rise, were joined by thousands of anti-government protesters, and para-military police opened fire. Demonstrations and looting continued yesterday, said diplomats and local residents, and the Blantyre offices of the ruling Malawi Congress party, the country's only legal political party, were reportedly ransacked. Earlier this year Catholic church leaders took the unprecedented step of criticising the government's human rights record in a pastoral letter read to congregations across the country. Last month a leading trade unionist, Mr Chakufwa Chihana, was arrested on his return to Malawi after calling for multi-party elections when addressing a meeting of Malawian dissidents in neighbouring Zambia. Mr Chihana was due to in court in Lilongwe yesterday, but failed to appear. Donors preparing for next week's meeting in Paris of the World Bank-chaired aid conference on Malawi have already warned the government that further help will be linked to political as well as economic reforms. Dr Banda has exercised a near-feudal control of Malawi since independence in 1964, ruthless in his treatment of opposition either real or suspected. In one notorious incident in May 1983, three cabinet ministers and a member of parliament died in what was officially described as a car crash. They were widely believed to have been assassinated. For several years the power behind the throne has been Mr John Tembo, minister in the president's office and uncle of Miss Cecilia Kadzamira, a long serving and influential figure with the formal title of official hostess.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Masood snubs Hekmatyar
DOC.TEXT: MR Ahmad Shah Masood, Afghanistan's defence minister, yesterday rejected demands by Mr Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, his rebel rival, to eject former government militiamen from the capital, praising them for having helped to depose the previous regime. Mr Masood, denouncing Mr Hekmatyar in his first news conference since he precipitated the collapse of the Soviet-supported government, also vowed to prevent the radical mujahideen leader making further attacks on Kabul in the latter's bid for ultimate power in the country. Some diplomats, however, predicted that the ceasefire would collapse, particularly given Mr Masood's uncompromising posture. 'Watch the rockets start falling Saturday morning,' one senior European diplomat said. 'Perhaps, for a short time, Mr Hekmatyar will be able to use his rockets and kill more innocent people,' Mr Masood said. 'But I assure you that soon we will push him so far back that his rockets won't reach the capital.' Mr Masood also claimed that, in addition to removal of the former government's militia, Mr Hekmatyar was demanding the removal of President Sibghutullah Mojaddedi. While confirming that negotiations were going on with Mr Hekmatyar, as part of a three-day truce that began on Wednesday, Mr Masood made no attempt at conciliation. He said that political leaders would decide what role Mr Hekmatyar could play in the government, but made no effort to hide his contempt for his long-time enemy. Mr Hekmatyar's refusal to join the government is a big reason why the mujahideen administration lacks stability.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Iran removes limit on foreign investment
DOC.TEXT: THE IRANIAN government is removing the limit on foreign investment in business and companies, according to Abrar, a Tehran daily newspaper. It reported yesterday that the Supreme Council for Investment had decided on Tuesday to drop the limit which restricts foreigners to a 49 per cent stake in Iranian ventures. It commented said decision was designed to attract funds from the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund for industrial projects and that these institutions had advised Iran to abolish limits on foreign ownership. Mr Mohsen Nurbakhsh, minister of economy and finance, and Mr Mohammed Adeli, governor of the central bank, returned this week from Washington, where they attended the spring session of the World Bank and IMF. Iran is seeking foreign investment in the fields of gas, energy, agriculture, transport and communications. The government of President Hashemi Rafsanjani has signalled that it is serious about trying to rebuild the country after its eight-year war against Iraq. The country, with a population of over 58m, remains an attractive market for trade but foreign companies have been less enthusiastic about investing in the country. Iranian delegations have been sent around the world, making presentations aimed at projecting an image of Iran as a friendly and stable country with which to do business.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Thais defy military with more pressure on PM to quit
DOC.TEXT: THAILAND'S most serious political unrest in more than 15 years deepened yesterday as more than 100,000 people defied military orders to end protests calling for the resignation of the new prime minister, former army commander General Suchinda Kraprayoon. After a day of high tension, confusion and apparent miscalculation by the military, the protesters moved from a narrow street in front of parliament to a much larger square in the centre of Bangkok. One reason for the move was to give more room for Major General Chamlong Srimuang, former governor of Bangkok, who has now completed three sweltering days of his hunger strike and was clearly suffering when the crowd at the round-the-clock vigil peaked each evening. Gen Chamlong, the simple-living former soldier known as the Mr Clean of Thailand has vowed to fast until he dies or forces the resignation of Gen Suchinda, who engineered a military coup 15 months ago and took over as prime minister last month. Mr Suriyant Oonnarkka, a member of Gen Chamlong's party, said the demonstrators would stay all night in defiance of the military. His aides said the four main opposition parties had written to King Bhumibol Adulyadej asking him to intervene. Students, workers, young professionals and old folk joined the protest, the largest since a student uprising toppled a military dictatorship in 1973. They are accusing the military of manipulating the electoral process to perpetuate its domination of Thai politics. An attempt by the prime minister to discredit Gen Chamlong clearly misfired, at least as far as public opinion in the capital was concerned. Gen Suchinda spoke briefly to parliament less than an hour into the second day of a debate on his new government's policy statement. He accused Gen Chamlong of being a religious deviant and implied that another opposition leader, Gen Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, wanted to impose a communistic leadership. The crowd outside parliament booed angrily when they heard what Gen Suchinda had said about Gen Chamlong, and speculators, watching the debate on television, dumped their shares. In the 10 minutes that he spoke the stock market index lost 30 points although it later recovered to close only 6.9 points down, the lowest level this year. The opposition booed the prime minister inside the parliament too and the debate was abruptly closed. Later in the day the military replayed tapes of the speech on television, editing out the booing. They also showed clips of some of the more aggressive gestures of the largely peaceful crowd before they started issuing orders for the demonstrators to disperse. They claimed the protesters were out to overthrow the legal government and to stir up unrest. All this has apparently only increased the numbers willing to join the demonstration. A sympathy rally was held in the northern city of Chiang Mai. Late last night more petitions were submitted to the king asking him to persuade Gen Suchinda to dissolve parliament and call another election. At least one member of one of the five coalition parties backing Gen Suchinda was reported last night to be defecting. Protest organisers predict more will follow.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Sweden seeks to enter EMS before joining EC
DOC.TEXT: MR Carl Bildt, the Swedish prime minister, yesterday held out his country's firm intent of seeking association with the European Monetary System before Sweden's planned EC membership in 1995. European finance ministers are expected at the weekend to have a preliminary discussion about Sweden's wish to link the crown to Europe's exchange rate stabilisation scheme, Mr Bildt said. He was speaking after talks in London with Mr John Major, the British prime minister. These centred on Sweden's desire for speedy accession to the EC, with negotiations expected to get under way early next year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Dail clears way for referendum
DOC.TEXT: AN Irish government white paper on the Maastricht Treaty was approved by parliament yesterday by a narrow majority, clearing the way for a national referendum on June 18 to seek backing for ratification. The opposition supported the bill, but criticised the government's wish to postpone legislation on the controversial abortion issue until after the referendum. A special Maastricht protocol preserves Ireland's ban on abortion. The opposition says legislation is needed to clear up confusion over women's right to travel abroad for abortion.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / EC threatens UK over border checks
DOC.TEXT: THE European Commission is threatening Britain with legal action if the UK does not remove border checks on travellers entering from other Community states by next January. The threat is contained in the Commission's latest report on the state of progress towards abolition of all controls on goods, services, capital and people crossing internal EC frontiers. The EC executive says, in its report issued this week, that it is 'resolutely determined to use all the legal and political means at its disposal' to ensure fulfilment of Article 8a of the 1986 Single European Act (SEA), which defines the internal market as 'an area without internal frontiers'. The Commission's maximalist interpretation of Article 8a has been known for some time, and its threat of legal action is by no means solely directed at the UK. Eight of the Community's continental members have already committed themselves to a free travel zone, through the 1990 Schengen Convention, and Greece has associated itself to the Schengen group as an observer. But Denmark and Ireland are also dragging their feet on plans to abolish border checks on intra-EC travellers - the former because of its passport union with Nordic countries, and the latter because of its passport union with the UK. Nonetheless, the chief target of the report - which the Commission delayed publishing during the recent UK election campaign - is Britain. The UK has always argued that the SEA's commitment to free movement of people applies only to EC citizens, and that controlling non-EC citizens coming into the UK inevitably requires checking the credentials of EC passport holders too. In addition, the UK government argues that the SEA's commitment to free movement is qualified by the treaty's explicit permission for member states to take action against crime, drugs and terrorism. 'Many other EC states agree that we need to keep controls' for these purposes, a senior UK official said yesterday. Increasing pressure from the Commission may embarrass the UK during its presidency of the EC Council. If the Commission takes the UK before the European Court it appears confident of winning.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Milan scandal deals a heavy blow to Craxi: 26 people have been arrested on corruption charges
DOC.TEXT: FOR a nation long inured to businessmen and politicians lining their pockets, the corruption scandal in Milan marks a watershed in the morality of Italy's public life. Milan magistrates are exposing, with fresh ramifications daily, a network of pay-offs on rigged public works contracts with the funds being channelled to the political parties. In the past two months 26 businessmen, municipal officials and politicians, including five over the past two days, have been arrested on corruption charges. Many more are under investigation including Mr Carlo Tognoli, a former Socialist mayor of Milan and outgoing minister of tourism, and Mr Paolo Pillittieri, also a former mayor of Milan, newly elected deputy and brother-in-law of Mr Bettino Craxi, the Socialist leader. Previous scandals in Italy have involved larger sums of money - like the collapse of the Banco Ambrosiano - or more prominent public figures, as in the unmasking of the masonic lodge, P-2. But the investigations were always obstructed by powerful vested interests and the truth was obscured. The Milan scandal is different. The large nationwide protest vote in the April general elections has weakened the traditional parties of power, the Christian Democrats and Socialists, obliging them to seek new partners in a yet unformed government. In Milan the emergent populist Lombard League became the second largest party, committed to clean out corruption. These two elements make it more difficult for the course of justice to be obstructed and indeed the post-electoral political climate in Italy is unprecedentedly favourable to a clean up of public life and the investigation has acquired a seemingly unstoppable momentum. Magistrates, egged on by the media immediately judging every accused to be guilty, have uncovered the following. On February 17, Mr Mario Chiesa, the head of the city's oldest charitable hospital, the Pio Albergo Trivulzio, was arrested allegedly in the act of taking a L7m (Pounds 3,160) bribe relating to work at the Pio Albergo. Enquiries by magistrates led to allegations that he possessed L12bn in cash and bank accounts. According to magistrates' charges, Mr Chiesa was the central figure in an elaborate system of rigged contracts, pay-offs and secret funding of political parties since the mid 1980s. Under investigation are some of the major public works contracts in Milan such as the enlargement of the metro, refurbishment of the San Sirio stadium, the rebuilding of Linate and Malpensa airports, and the new 'Piccolo' theatre. Officials of companies involved in these contracts are alleged to have handed over money to prominent members of the local Socialist and Christian Democrat parties as well as the Party of the Democratic Left (PDS). The Socialists and the Christian Democrats have set up special commissions to examine the affairs of Milan. Milan has long been run by a Socialist controlled administration and has been the power-base of Mr Craxi - his son, Bobo, is the local secretary. This city, the symbol and centre of modern Italy's wealth, has long prided itself on its efficient 'clean government'. The damage to Mr Craxi's reputation, the involvement of the 'uncorruptable' PDS and the undermining of the Milanese sense of propriety have given an added edge to the affair. Mr Craxi's once-fancied chances of heading the next government have been dealt a serious blow and the formation of a new government is expected to be further complicated by the divisions within, and among, the parties exacerbated by the effects of the scandal. In the case of the socialists, there are calls by anti-Craxi figures for a special congress to discuss thorough reform of the party. The Christian Democrats are split over what action to take, afraid that being too tough over Milan would oblige a further cleansing of the party apparatus elsewhere in Italy. The PDS leadership is distancing itself from its members under investigation in Milan. The revelations also coincide with Italy's economic recession and growing public demands for sweeping reforms of the political system. On the one hand, hard pressed businesses have begun to discover they can no longer pay 10-15 per cent 'commissions' on contracts. On the other, the Lombard League has put morality onto the agenda.
