But this rise in German pay inflation represents only a small erosion of the relative competitiveness gains made by German industry over the past five years. The rise in German unit labour costs since 1987 is still lower than that of France, Italy and the UK. German wage earnings have grown faster than those in France since 1987, the date of the last important realignments within the ERM. But German's superior productity growth record has meant that its unit labour costs, have lagged behind those paid by French industry. Both the UK and Italy have had faster earnings and unit labour cost inflation since 1987. But German unit labour costs have been catching up rapidly since German monetary unification in July 1990. In part, the rise in German wage inflation results from the economic consequences of German unification. The rise in consumer spending by east Germans following the fall of the Berlin wall - and funded largely by hand-outs from the western government - sparked a consumer boom. But this rise in west German wage inflation was, and remains, unsustainable. The Bundesbank has responded to rising inflationary pressures by pushing up interest rates across Europe; and the government, faced with a ballooning fiscal deficit, has pushing up income taxes. The recent crop of wage demands, and ensuing strikes, is the direct manifestation of the refusal of west German workers to accept a fall in their after-tax incomes. But the wage acceleration also results from pre-unification tensions. The latter half of the 1980s was a period of unusual wage restraint in west Germany. In return for a drop in working hours, the unions agreed to moderate their wage demands. With hindsight, the unions underestimated the cost of the fall in working hours. As a result the share of national income distributed to labour, as opposed to capital, fell to levels not seen since the early 1970s. The strikes partly result from their attempts to claw back their share. But if recent pay trends are worrying for German exporters, they are disastrous for those in the UK and Italy. Despite Germany's boom, and slow or zero growth elsewhere in Europe, UK and Italian wage inflation remains higher than in Germany. Unless wage inflation in these countries falls soon, their competitiveness will quickly start to deteriorate again once productivity growth returns to trend.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Ceasefire holds
DOC.TEXT: A ceasefire between the new Afghan government and dissident guerrillas held for the second day.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 08 MAY 92 / Horror videos seized
DOC.TEXT: A racket in horrific uncensored videos was believed smashed after thousands of tapes, including so-called 'snuff' killer movies - allegedly films of actual killings - were seized in police raids across the country.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / (CORRECTED) People: Insurance moves
DOC.TEXT: Correction (published 26th May 1992) appended to this article. Graham Ford is leaving Brown Shipley Insurance Brokers to launch a new national insurance broking venture. Ford, now 52, has been closely identified with the growth of the Brown Shipley broking business and had been involved in efforts to lead a management buy-out. After the failure of these, however, Ford has joined forces with Merseyside-based Berkeley Burke and Manson Reed, a broker which specialises in meeting the needs of sport centres, bowling alleys and other leisure installations. Ford will be managing director of the new venture, which is to be known as Burke Ford Reed Insurance Management. The group hopes to obtain a full Lloyd's registration within 18 months. ***** Michael Kier is to become chairman of CE HEATH on the retirement in July of Richard Fielding. John MacKenzie Green, group md, will become chairman of CE Heath (Insurance Broking). ***** Ralph Sneddon has been appointed md of BAIN CLARKSON's continental Europe operations; he joins from Sedgwick. ***** Roger Cooper has been appointed a director of BALLANTYNE, McKEAN & SULLIVAN; Charles Simpson has been appointed a director of its subsidiary BMS LMX. ***** John Clayton has been appointed company secretary of GUARDIAN ROYAL EXCHANGE on the retirement of John Evans. Correction (published 26th May 1992) The FT stated on May 7 that Burke Ford Reed Insurance Management had 'joined forces with Berkeley Burke'. This was incorrect. Burke Ford Reed has linked up with Berkeley Burke Northern Group, a former subsidiary of the Berkeley Burke Group, which also conducts insurance broking business and continues to trade independently.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: South African retail group improves 18 per cent
DOC.TEXT: Pepkor, the South African retail group, lifted attributable profits by 18 per cent in the year to February in which it took over Checkers, one of three largest supermarket chains in South Africa. Turnover rose by 118 per cent to R4.3bn (Dollars 1.5bn) following the takeover of Tradehold and its subsidiary Tradegro which controls Checkers. Operating profits was up by only 30 per cent, to R218.3m, reflecting the larger contribution from food sales relative to clothes on which margins were better. Attributable income was 18 per cent up to R93.8m and there were extraordinary profits of R75.3m. Pepkor's results included losses and large write-offs at Tradegro which made an operating loss of R30m on turnover of R2.2bn. It wrote off R46m in rationalisation and other costs related to its incorporation into Pepkor. Mr Christo Wiese, chairman of Pepkor and Pepgro, the holding company, announced that the two companies would be raising R398m through rights issues. Pepkor would raise R262.4m and Pepgro R135.5m. Mr Wiese said Pepkor's 18 per cent growth was satisfactory given the 'extremely difficult trading conditions still prevailing, especially since October 1991'. He forecast a turnaround in trading conditions in the third quarter and said he was confident of satisfactory results for the 1993 financial year. He added it would take two or more years to bring Shoprite and Checkers, the two food stores in the group, up to profitable levels. The dividend was lifted by 15 per cent to 244 cents per share.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Burlington Coat Factory Warehouse third-quarter earnings of dollars 1m
DOC.TEXT: Burlington Coat Factory Warehouse, the clothing retailer, had third-quarter earnings of Dollars 1m, or 6 cents a share, unchanged from a year earlier. Sales rose to Dollars 217m from Dollars 209m. For the nine months ended March 28, earnings rose to Dollars 31.4m, or Dollars 1.77 a share, from Dollars 27.8m, or Dollars 1.34, in the year ago period. Sales advanced to Dollars 809m from Dollars 759.4m.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Countryside sells site to Tesco
DOC.TEXT: Countryside Properties has sold a superstore site at its White Court, Braintree, project to Tesco Stores. Mr Alan Cherry, a chairman of Countryside, said it was good to have completed a major sale this early on, after only recently agreeing to acquire the land for the project at a fixed price over a six-year period, during which time 'we obviously expect the housing and property markets to improve.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Bass sells 16 pubs to JT Davies
DOC.TEXT: Bass has sold 16 pubs in London and the south-east to JT Davies & Sons, a Surrey-based wine merchant and pub operator. The deal, estimated to be worth between Pounds 2.5m and Pounds 3m, is part of a Pounds 4m expansion programme announced by JT Davies last year. The company, which runs the Davisons chain of 78 wine stores, now has an estate of 35 pubs.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Business park planned in N Wales
DOC.TEXT: A business park on the edge of the Snowdonia national park in north Wales is to be developed in a Pounds 15m joint operation between the Development Board for Rural Wales and the Royal Institute of British Architects, Anthony Moreton writes. The 300,000 sq ft park at Penrhyndeudraeth will create 750 jobs over the next five to 10 years, Mr Glyn Davies, chairman of the board, said. The board's annual report showed it paid Pounds 1.5m in grants during the year to support almost 1,000 jobs. It has budgeted to spend Pounds 2.3m this year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Charges allege N Sea corruption
DOC.TEXT: Three men were yesterday charged with corruption concerning a contract for supplying a North Sea accommodation vessel. The charges concern alleged payments totalling more than Pounds 30,000.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Ansaldo group in US rail deal
DOC.TEXT: Union Switch and Signal, the US subsidiary of Italy's state-owned Ansaldo Group, has won a L72bn (Pounds 32.6m) contract to build and install the first driverless light railway system in the US, writes Haig Simonian in Milan. The contract is for the new 'green line' of the Los Angeles subway system. The 20-mile line, covering 14 existing stations and two under construction, will be entirely run from a single control unit, which is also to be supplied and installed by the company. The line is expected to begin operation at the end of 1994.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Hoesch satisfied with performance
DOC.TEXT: HOESCH, the German steel and engineering group merging with its former rival, Krupp, says it is satisfied with its performance in the first third of the current year. Profits were slightly ahead of budget, and the core steel business made a profit during the period. The order book was stable, Mr Kajo Neukirchen, chief executive, said. Hoesch also released its profits for 1991, which were down by almost a half over the previous year at the operating level. It said it would hold 1991 dividend at DM10 per share. Operating profits fell to DM262m (Dollars 158.70m) last year, down from DM440m in 1990. Sales fell from DM16.14bn to DM13.31bn - reflecting not only poor steel prices but also the decision not to consolidate the O&K construction equipment subsidiary. Rationalisation measures meant that Hoesch Stahl, the core steel subsidiary, broke even despite the 'incessant' fall in steel prices. Profits from other areas - such as processing and industrial technology - were up but did not reach 1990 levels. The merger with Krupp is expected to be approved at the Hoesch annual meeting on June 22.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Hong Kong budget surplus increases
DOC.TEXT: THE Hong Kong government yesterday disclosed that its budget surplus for last year was HKDollars 6bn (Dollars 779m) higher than its provisional figure, revealed in March. The extra Dollars HK6bn brings the budget surplus for 1991/1992 to more than Dollars HK20bn. Legislative councillors expressed concern over the government's apparent inability to keep track of its finances. Financial secretary Mr Hamish MacLeod's statement on the windfall surplus was accompanied by a concession on his first budget. He said he would not raise property rates by half a point to 6 per cent, as proposed in his maiden budget speech two months ago. A number of legislative councillors had said earlier that they would vote against the rates increase, in spite of opposition by Mr MacLeod to any tampering with his first budget. He told the Legislative Council yesterday that the fall in revenue was 'roughly equivalent' to the windfall surplus. Mr MacLeod said the increase was due to higher-than-expected revenue from stamp duty, salaries and profits tax, first registration tax for vehicles, and a shortfall in public works spending.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Cairo budget cuts subsidies
DOC.TEXT: THE Egyptian government presented its 1992-93 budget to parliament yesterday, cutting subsidies but increasing both military spending and civil service salaries in line with inflation, Reuter reports from Cairo. Egypt is part-way through a radical programme of economic reform, agreed with the IMF last May. The budget put spending for the year from July 1 at Dollars 18.9bn, up only 14 per cent against inflation of nearly 20 per cent. The draft proposed a modest reduction in the budget deficit to Dollars 2.8bn. Targets agreed with the IMF include cutting the overall state budget deficit to 6.5 per cent of GDP in 1992-93 from 9.5 per cent in 1991-92. The draft budget covers only the central government and the IMF's targets are based on all state spending.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Followers of Nasser form new party: Surprise as Egyptian 'opposition' party is sanctioned by court
DOC.TEXT: WITHOUT any fanfare, a political party bearing the name of Egypt's late President Gamal Abdel Nasser has been quietly reconstituted in Egypt, but commentators doubt it will become a force in the land. Mohammed Sayed Ahmed, a columnist for the daily Al Ahram, said the decision of an Egyptian court to sanction a Nasserite party after years of rebuffs, reflected a desire by the government to extend Egypt's democratic base in the almost certain knowledge that the new party would not pose a serious challenge to the established order. 'The authorities no longer see it as a liability to have Nasserism as a symbol of opposition,' said Mr Sayed Ahmed. 'Rather, they view the secular Nasserites as a potential asset at a time when the religious trend is gaining momentum.' While the memory of Egypt's late president, who became a towering figure in the Arab and developing world until he was diminished by the Arabs' calamitous defeat in the 1967 war with Israel, remains strong at home, his socialist-era rule from 1952-1970 is generally regarded to have been deeply flawed, and to have contributed to many of Egypt's present ills. Mona Makram Ebeid, an independent member of Egypt's parliament and a sociology professor at the American University in Cairo, said the Nasserites, to be known as the Arab Democratic Nasserist party (ADN), may attract a 'nostalgia' vote, but doubted the party would become a rallying point for disaffection. 'They have yet to put their house in order,' she said. 'They don't have a charismatic leader, and their programme is still nebulous. One gets the impression that they were surprised that they were accepted by the court.' The Nasserites may, however, emerge as the main opposition bloc in Egypt's parliament, the 454-seat People's Assembly, dominated by the National Democratic Party with 348 seats. At present the leftist Tugammu, or National Unionist Progressive Party, with just six seats constitutes the only organised opposition. The remainder are independents, some of whom might join the Nasserites. Egypt's November, 1990, elections were boycotted by established organisations such as the nationalist Wafd party, the Moslem Brotherhood, the Socialist Labour Party and the Liberals. The main opposition groupings said they boycotted the poll because they could not be sure it would be free and fair. Mohammed Faik, a former information minister under Nasser and one of the leaders of the ADN, insisted this week that the party did not represent an 'idolisation' of Nasser. Rather, it wanted to use his legacy to promote Arab unity and the 'excellent ideal of independent development. 'Nasserism is not a reactionary movement, it's not a theory, nor does it mean a hero-worshipping,' he declared. 'It's just an experience affiliated to Nasser ..'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / EC aid of Dollars 496m to help redundant customs agents
DOC.TEXT: THE European Commission yesterday set aside Ecu400m (Dollars 496m) to retrain or re-employ 250,000 customs agents whose jobs will disappear when European Community trade barriers fall at the end of 1992, Reuter reports from Brussels. 'This is a very special sector,' tax commissioner, Ms Christiane Scrivener, said after the 17-member Commission approved the special aid package: 'Up to midnight December 31, 1992, they have to work.' The Commission estimates 240,000 people work in 16,000 companies handling internal Community customs documents and procedures. Tens of thousands are expected to lose their jobs and others will have to retrain once internal tax frontiers are abolished to create the single EC market. Strike action by customs agents protesting against the job losses has caused chaos at frontiers, ports and airports in France, Spain, Portugal and Belgium. Ms Scrivener said the funds would only cover about 20 per cent of the estimated Ecu2.3bn cost of the industry shakeout. She said member states and customs had only belatedly accepted that barriers would really disappear.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / EC applicants seek to speed entry: Czechs, Poles and Hungarians to step up co-operation
DOC.TEXT: THE three central European countries of Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Poland yesterday agreed to consider how their entry into the European Community could be co-ordinated. At the same time, Presidents Vaclav Havel of Czechoslovakia, Lech Walesa of Poland, and Jozsef Antall of Hungary said they would step up economic, political and security cooperation as as to speed up entry into the EC. 'We agreed that we will apply to the European Community together .. if we join our voices, our demands will be heard more strongly, than if we act individually,' said Mr Havel. The three presidents, who concluded a two-day meeting in Prague, the capital of the Czech and Slovak republic, also jointly expressed their readiness to recognise Macedonia, the former republic of Yugoslavia. On the subject of greater European integration, the three presidents also agreed to promote the possibility of Japan becoming an associated member of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe (CSCE). Formal relations between Japan and the CSCE, the pan-European body which includes former Soviet republics, were recently discussed between Mr Kiichi Miyazawa, the Japanese prime minister and heads of state in Paris and Bonn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / London Stock Exchange: Amstrad gains on rumours
DOC.BYLINE: By CHRISTOPHER PRICE, JOEL KIBAZO, PETER JOHN and COLIN MILLHAM
DOC.TEXT: HEAVY trading in Amstrad, for the second day running, left it 4 higher at 40 1/2 p, the biggest percentage gain in the London market yesterday. The rise was sparked by rumours that chairman Mr Alan Sugar was buying stock. More extreme talk even had him preparing to take the company private. Both stories were dismissed by analysts as highly implausible and denied emphatically by Mr Sugar, who put the rise down to 'speculative buying by investors trying to make a quick profit'. The 8.2m shares traded followed Tuesday's 7m. Amstrad shares have been hit hard over the past 12 months as the recession has begun to bite. A profits warning a year ago was followed by the group's first-ever loss six months later. 'Since the share price collapsed, Amstrad has been susceptible to all sorts of rumours,' said Mr Patrick Wellington at County NatWest. 'I doubt if this old chestnut has any truth in it either.' Gas deflated A demand for gas price cuts prompted a sharp fall in British Gas as traders assumed that any reductions would have a knock-on effect on profits. Regulator Ofgas told the company to cut prices for domestic customers or face possible regulatory action. The shares were down 8 at one stage before rallying to close 2 1/2 off at 262 1/2 p with 12m traded. A number of analysts said a price cut would have no effect at all as it was related to inflation, and if inflation fell costs would also come down. The share price was also hit by concern that first-quarter results, due next Thursday, may be disappointing. S & N downgraded Brewer Scottish & Newcastle lost 6 to 463p in an active market of 3.6m shares after Smith New Court downgraded its profits estimate for the current year and for 1993. Mr Mike McCarthy, drinks analyst at Smith, pointed out that Center Parcs, the company's leisure division, has a large exposure to Benelux countries and future profits may be influenced by problems involving the German economy. He added that in the short term the performances of Bass, up 26 at 637p, and Grand Metropolitan, 14 stronger at 496p, are likely to be better than S & N. Mr Christopher Wickham at Lehman Brothers noted that 20 per cent of S & N's volume is in the take-home trade, mainly involving off licences, and that margins are being squeezed by the amount of this business going through supermarkets. A statement that the chief executive of Johnson Matthey was resigning his post as non-executive director of Charter Consolidated raised a flurry of speculation and the shares in both groups responded sharply. Charter is the majority shareholder in Johnson and the resignation immediately sparked speculation that it was either considering selling its 38.5 per cent stake or launching a bid for Johnson. Apparently, the company said there was no significance in the management change and the share prices ticked back slightly at the close. Charter ended the day 11 ahead at 536p while Johnson Matthey closed 18 higher at 432p. A strong two-way pull was seen in Rolls-Royce shares, sending turnover to 14m as the stock firmed 2 to 172p. The interest was prompted by an announcement that China has placed an engine order worth around Pounds 100m. Smith New Court reiterated its buy recommendation on the stock. US buyers were also said to have been in evidence, but County NatWest said the shares had performed strongly since the beginning of the year and advised investors to 'pause for breath and take profits'. Disappointment with the tone of Tate & Lyle's statement accompanying the interim figures pushed the shares down 8 to 401p on turnover of 6m. Food manufacturer JLI Group reported a successful rights issue, with 96.1 per cent of the 13.28m shares offered taken up and the remainder placed in the market at a premium. JLI gained 4 to 124p. US buying was behind a good performance for Glaxo which, also benefiting from good news about its anti-nausea drug Zofran, climbed 23 to 774p. Good first-quarter figures from BAT Industries prompted the shares to rally 24 to 805p. Nervousness ahead of today's first-quarter figures left BP 1 1/2 easier at 262p. US investors bought British Steel, which added 3 at 85p on high turnover of 12m. Smiths Industries gained 3 to 316p as it held meetings with its leading investors. Car dealer Lex Service rose 11 to 245p after informing investors at the annual meeting that the UK car market had shown considerable improvement in April. The market appreciated Lex's Pounds 46m acquisition of Swan National Motor, formerly part of TSB. Improved air traffic figures prompted British Airways to gain 4 1/2 to 292 1/2 p. A larger than anticipated tax charge and higher than forecast borrowings caused Trafalgar House to buck the general trend as it reported interim profits in line with market forecasts. The shares eased 2 to 147p and brokers cut full-year forecasts. County NatWest trimmed its estimate by Pounds 15m to Pounds 120m and BZW's was cut by Pounds 8m to Pounds 125m. BZW became the latest broker to downgrade Rank Organisation. The securities house is looking for profits of Pounds 272m for this year, down Pounds 18m, and Pounds 340m, off Pounds 30m, for 1993. However, Rank, which was off 6 at one stage, rebounded to close 9 ahead on balance at 738p. NEW HIGHS AND LOWS FOR 1992 NEW HIGHS (297). DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / London Stock Exchange: Equity market surges to all-time high
DOC.TEXT: HEAVY overseas buying of June Footsie futures, principally by US investment banks, and a rethink by domestic institutions of the equity market's prospects after Tuesday's interest rate cut, saw the FT-SE 100-share Index burst through its all-time peak and launch a determined but ultimately unsuccessful attack on the 2,700 level. At the close of another session of heavy trading the index stood at a record 2,698.7, up 36.5 on the day. The market's previous all-time peak, an intraday level of 2,683.7, was attained last September, coinciding with a reduction in bank base rates to 10.5 per cent. Since the Tories' general election victory the Footsie has risen 262.3 points, or almost 11 per cent. Many dealers were caught on the hop by a sudden transformation in the market's fortunes which took place mid-morning. Share prices had opened with widespread but moderate losses as marketmakers, mindful of Wall Street's overnight decline and a general view of a period of consolidation, were happy to cut dealing levels in the hope that the lower prices would attract much needed stock into the market. Opening some five points down, the Footsie proceeded to drift back and registered a decline just exceeding nine points within an hour of the opening, reflecting bouts of profit-taking, before embarking on a remarkable rally which eventually propelled the index into virgin territory. A couple of indifferent trading results, from Tate & Lyle and Trafalgar House, added to the early uncertainty. The emergence of the big US-sourced buying orders in the Footsie future - one leading US house was said to have purchased 2,000 contracts and another was heavily involved on the buy side - triggered a scramble to cover short positions by other brokers, and the future promptly surged ahead. The cash market, where buying interest revealed widespread short positions in many stocks, went with futures and, by midday, was threatening to puncture the all-time high. Shortly afterwards the index sailed through the previous high and kept on going, helped by a firm opening on Wall Street, until it met a flurry of resistance just short of 2,700. The US buying was not confined to futures, but encompassed traditional North American investment favourites such as Hanson, Glaxo and SmithKline Beecham. BAT, after good first-quarter results, was also well supported. On the downside, Trafalgar House's halved interim dividend, in spite of the increased profits, induced exceptionally heavy selling, while Tate & Lyle's half-year results and the post-figures meeting with sector analysts saw the shares under pressure throughout the day. British Gas was another notable underperformer, with the shares persistently sold after Ofgas's demand for a cut in prices to customers. Mr Steve Turner, energy specialist at Smith New Court, said Gas's warning on prices was: 'An indication of a summer of discontent as far as relations between British Gas and the industry regulator are concerned.' Seaq turnover in equities totalled 637.1m shares.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets (America): Transport stocks lift Dow in modest volume
DOC.TEXT: Wall Street US STOCKS drifted higher yesterday, thanks partly to strength in the transportation sector, writes Karen Zagor in New York. The Dow Jones Industrial Average ended 10.06 higher at 3,369.41 after unexceptional total volume on the NYSE of about 200m shares. Rises outpaced declines by 1,012 to 680. The Standard & Poor's 500 was 0.05 easier at 416.79, but the Nasdaq composite gained 1.29 to 589.36. On Tuesday, the Dow fell about 19 points. Wall Street largely ignored the Federal Reserve's beige book of economic activity, which showed an increase in activity, although conditions were described as uneven. The market is more concerned with Friday's release of employment data for April, which will provide the first piece of significant economic news for the month and may indicate whether monetary policy is likely to be eased further. Transportation issues outpaced the general market for a second day, with the Dow Jones Transportation Average climbing 13.45 to 1,407.70, after adding 13.46 a day earlier in a declining market. USAir rose Dollars 1 1/2 to Dollars 14 3/4 in active trade amid speculation that the company had reached a tentative labour agreement with its pilots' union. Among other airline issues, AMR, parent of American Airlines, was unchanged at Dollars 68 7/8 , Delta Air Lines rose Dollars 1 to Dollars 60 3/4 and UAL, parent of United Airlines, gained Dollars 1/2 to Dollars 126 3/4 . Results continued to trickle in from the insurance sector, with Travelers reporting first-quarter net income of Dollars 63m or 58 cents a share, against Dollars 93m or 88 cents a year earlier. Shares in the company dipped Dollars 1/2 to Dollars 20. General Re, which fell sharply last week on the back of its quarterly results, recovered Dollars 1/4 to Dollars 80 5/8 . Unocal put on Dollars 5/8 to Dollars 25 7/8 after the Los Angeles-based energy group said it plans to sell or place in joint ventures at least Dollars 350m in non-strategic assets, eliminate at least 400 jobs and take other steps to improve efficiency and profitability. A number of blue chip stocks were active on the NYSE, including Exxon, down Dollars 5/8 to Dollars 59 1/4 , IBM, off Dollars 1/4 at Dollars 93 5/8 , AT&T, up Dollars 1/8 at Dollars 44 1/8 , and Ford, Dollars 5/8 firmer at Dollars 45 1/2 . In over-the-counter trading, technology and biotechnology stocks were active. Sun Microsystems rose Dollars 5/8 to Dollars 28 1/2 and Apple Computer improved Dollars 1 1/4 to Dollars 61 3/4 . Chiron declined Dollars 5/8 to Dollars 46 5/8 in heavy trading. The company has received US Food and Drug Administration approval to market its IL-2 Proleukin drug for use in cancer treatment. Canada TORONTO stocks closed mixed after the composite index shuffled within a 10-point range during a trendless session, but trading volume was a heavy 30.5m shares, well above Tuesday's 23m. The 300-share index was finally 3.2 off at 3,361.3, but advances narrowly exceeded falls by 278 to 264. Nine of 14 stock groups closed higher, led by transportation, up 2.1 per cent as Laidlaw 'B' gained CDollars 1/4 to CDollars 11 1/2 . The gold group climbed 2.0 per cent, led by American Barrick, CDollars 1 3/4 stronger at CDollars 28 3/4 .

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Foreign Exchanges: Dollar under pressure again
DOC.TEXT: THE DOLLAR was once again under pressure on foreign exchange markets yesterday because of its large interest rate differential with the D-Mark, writes James Blitz. Although most London dealers feel that the Bundesbank council will not lift the Lombard rate at its meeting today, overseas operators rushed to cover their positions, buying D-Marks and selling dollars. 'Deep down, most people are still bullish about the dollar,' said Mr Jim O'Neill, head of research at Swiss Bank Corporation. 'But with a 6 per cent differential between the dollar and D-Mark, investors are starting to get hurt.' The US unit was adversely affected by comments from Mr Helmut Schlesinger, the Bundesbank president, that it was too early to sound the all-clear on German monetary policy. And a repurchase agreement launched by the Bundesbank in the German money markets dealt a second blow: the bank drained nearly DM5bn from the money markets, and nudged up the 'repo' rate 5 basis points to 9.65 per cent. The dollar fell to a closing DM1.6305 in London, after opening at DM1.6405. It also lost considerable ground to sterling, which ended at Dollars 1.7945 compared to Dollars 1.7825 the night before, and the US unit dropped to FFr5.4950 from FFr5.5250. In New York the dollar closed lower at DM1.6287 and FFr5.4845, with the pound at Dollars 1.7975. Traders were starting to refocus their attention on the yen, after a string of public holidays had taken Tokyo dealers out of the market. The Japanese unit ended firmer against the dollar after traders considered the possibility of future intervention in its favour by the Group of Seven leading industrial countries. 'More and more people are thinking that the Japanese and the G7 are keen to get the yen higher,' said Swiss Bank's Mr O'Neill. Bullish sentiment over the yen was compounded by comments from the French finance minister suggesting it is undervalued in the market. In London the yen ended at Y132.40 against the dollar, after an opening Y133.10. In New York the dollar slipped to Y132.25. Sterling also appreciated yesterday, in spite of the Bank of England's 1/2 percentage point interest rate cut on Tuesday. It gained against all the major European currencies and lost no ground to a resilient D-Mark, again closing at DM2.9250. Dealers said the UK currency still has the advantage of a solid political background and brighter prospects for the economy. The French franc again performed strongly on thoughts that it might replace the D-Mark as the central anchor in the EMS if Germany's economic problems continue. Dealers took the suggestion with a pinch of salt, but the French currency ended firmly against the D-Mark at around FFr3.3662.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Money Markets: Sterling trade quiet
DOC.TEXT: AFTER A busy period in the sterling money market dominated by the Bank of England's 1/2 percentage point base rate cut on Tuesday, dealing resumed a much calmer tone yesterday. The volume of futures trading was exceptionally small. The combined trade in both the June and September short sterling contracts hovered around 16,000 lots yesterday. 'On a normally quiet day, trading in a front month contract would never be less than 18,000 to 20,000 lots,' commented Mr Nick Parsons, head of the Treasury Advisory Group at CIBC in London. 'But the general mood is that this level of base rates will be here for some time to come.' June short sterling ended the day at 89.93, implying that interest rates in June will be at 10.07 per cent. Traders believe that the floor for short sterling is now 89.88, indicating an interest rate of 10.12 per cent in June. 'The knowledge that interest rates will not go up means that nobody will sell it any way below that,' said one trader yesterday. In the interbank market there was only a little movement in period rates. Most of them, in the immediate aftermath of Tuesday's cut, were at 10 1/8 per cent. Yesterday, rates for everything from two months money to six months firmed up to 10 3/16 per cent. One week money was at the easier rate of 10 per cent, after forecasts of a much smaller shortage in the discount market for the first half of next week. Yesterday morning, the Bank of England forecast a shortage of around Pounds 1.05bn in the discount market. In early operations, the Bank purchased bills totalling Pounds 275m for resale to the market on May 27 at an interest rate of 9 15/16 per cent. In further operations, the Bank purchased bills totalling Pounds 262m, of which Pounds 200m were Band-1 bank bills at 9 7/8 per cent and Pounds 62m were for resale to the market on May 27 at an interest rate of 9 15/16 per cent. The bank operated in the market in the afternoon, purchasing Pounds 147m of Band-1 bank bills at 9 7/8 per cent and Pounds 10m of Band-2 bills at 9 7/8 per cent. In the German money markets, attention focused on the Bundesbank's decision to sell DM19.3bn of 28-day funds and DM7.8bn of 56-day money at 9.65 per cent, a rise of 5 basis points on previous rates.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: Brazil's coffee output decline
DOC.TEXT: THE NUMBER of trees producing coffee in Brazil has fallen from 4.2bn to 3.2bn since 1988, according to a survey by the National Coffee Council, a producer group. The study says that the country's output is expected to drop from the estimated 26m-28m sacks for last season to 18m-20m for 1992-93. International prices for the commodity, now at the lowest level for two decades, are primarily responsible for the decreased production, says Mr Luiz Sergio de Paiva Pereira, director of the coffee division of the Pocos de Caldas Regional Coffee Producers' Co-operative, in Minas Gerais state. 'Unless things turn around, we believe that output will continue to fall gradually,' he predicts. 'At current prices, income doesn't even cover production costs.' The CNC study reveals that 55 per cent of the country's coffee plantations are considered to be in a poor state of upkeep. Another 35 per cent are believed 'unsatisfactory'. Yields are low, with 60 per cent of plantations producing less than five bags (60 kg each) per hectare. Many producers are shifting, where feasible, to alternative crops - to sugar-cane and citrus fruits in the south-central state of Sao Paulo and to soyabeans and wheat in the southern state of Parana, says Mr Pereira. But in the mountainous regions in the states of Minas Gerais and Espirito Santo, 'it is often a case of pure and simple abandonment', he says. Generally, these farmers are using their land for cattle grazing, often without pulling up the coffee plants. The CNC is using the study to back its request for government assistance for the coffee sector. It has developed a 74-point plan that includes proposals for tax reductions, investment in productivity and the establishment of an official body to carry out many of the functions once handled by the Brazilian Coffee Institute, abolished by President Fernando Collor de Mello when he took office in March 1990. One of the sector's main requests, the roll-over of its debt, was fulfilled by the government last week.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: Pakistani government plans to increase sugar duty
DOC.TEXT: THE PAKISTANI government is considering an increase in import duty on sugar, in the country's annual budget to be announced next week, as a measure to boost the domestic sugar market. However, the new rate of duty has still not been decided. A senior government official said yesterday that the measure was a way to cut down on sugar imports at a time when a rise in domestic sugar production had already created a surplus. The country's sugar mills have produced at least 2.3m tonnes since October last year, while another 50,000 tonnes are expected to be produced this month. Surplus sugar stocks depress prices in the local market and therefore create economic difficulties for sugar mill owners and sugar-cane farmers, officials and traders say. Although wheat, cotton and rice account for about 70 per cent of the country's annual crop output, sugar-cane is right behind them as one of the more important crops of the remaining 30 per cent. The government has also been trying to promote sugar trading in the private sector as a way to reduce the public sector's participation in commodity trading. Pakistan's imports of sugar during the past 9 months have largely been secured through operators in the private sector, officials say.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: India aims to woo fishery investors
DOC.TEXT: INDIA IS aiming to build on the impressive growth it has achieved in the past two years in the export of marine products. It is planning to encourage the participation of foreign companies in deep sea fishing, coastal aquaculture and production and marketing of value-added sea food in consumer packs. Joint ventures, in which the foreign partners can have majority equity participation, will be allowed to import new as well old vessels for fishing and given freedom to hire 50 per cent of their crews abroad. The Indian Marine Products Export Development Authority has been assigned the task of wooing foreign investors. According to industry experts, India's 2m sq km (770,000 square miles) of sea area offers a potential catch of more than 4.5m tonnes of seafood a year. At present, however, the annual harvest is only about 2.3m tonnes. India has nearly 1.4m hectares (3,500 acres) of brackish, marshy lands on the sea coast offering vast scope for aquaculture, of which less than 70,000 ha has so far been brought into production. Out of the 60 varieties of shrimp found in Indian waters, six have so far been identified as suitable for aquaculture. A number of big Indian companies, including the Tatas, ITC, Larsen & Toubro, Thapars, DCM and Escorts, have plans for major investments in aquaculture. The government believes, nevertheless, that without foreign participation India's progress in capture and culture fishery will be less than satisfactory. The country's marine products exports in the year to March 1992 increased by 10.75 per cent to Dollars 557.42m. In terms of quantity, it shipped 171,989 tonnes representing a growth of 23.36 per cent. According to Mr CT Sukumaran, chairman of Impeda, Japan continues to be the single biggest market for Indian marine products, accounting for 50 per cent of exports by value. The other important markets for India are Western Europe, the US, Singapore and Hong Kong. The dominant export item is frozen shrimp, which constitutes more than 70 per cent of the total export value of marine products. India also exports lobster, squid, shark fins and fresh and frozen fish. If Impeda succeeds in its mission to attract adequate foreign investment and if Indian business houses' new-found interest in marine products is sustained, then India should be able to achieve its export target of Dollars 1.184m by 1996-97, the final year of its eighth five year plan.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Government Bonds: Bunds rally on speculation of end to 10-day strike
DOC.BYLINE: By SIMON LONDON and KAREN ZAGOR
DOC.TEXT: THE GERMAN government bond market staged a rally yesterday, buoyed by speculation that talks today would end the 10-day-old strike by public sector workers. The June bund futures contract on Liffe, the London exchange, closed at 87.16 from an opening level of 86.89 and close to the day's high of 87.21. Volume was a heavy 71,000 contracts for the second day running. In the cash market, the benchmark 8 per cent Unity Fund 10-year bond issue closed at around 100.08, from an opening of 99.85, for a yield of 7.99 per cent. Employers and union officials are due to hold talks today aimed at ending the dispute over pay. The Bundesbank council also meets today, although analysts are not expecting any change in monetary policy. Yesterday, the Bundesbank kept monetary conditions tight, draining a net DM5bn from the money market in regular repurchase operations. As a result, call money crept up to 9.70 per cent, from 9.65 per cent, and close to the 9.75 per cent Lombard rate - the emergency funding rate for financial institutions. The rise in the bund market helped other European markets to rally. For example, the benchmark French government 8 1/2 per cent OAT maturing 2002 closed the day 1/2 -point higher for a yield of 8.68 per cent, from 8.76 per cent on Tuesday. The French market also rose on speculation that the government would use today's money market tender by the Bank of France to signal a cut in interest rates following Tuesday's 1/2 point cut in UK base lending rates. As a result, the French market out-paced German bonds. The yield spread between the two markets at the 10-year maturity narrowed from 73 basis points at the opening to 69 basis points by the close. The Italian market was also lifted by speculation that interest rates may be lowered in line with the UK. The benchmark 12 per cent Italian government bond maturing January 2002 closed at 98.61, up from 98.42 on Tuesday. Trading volume in the cash market was L14,200bn, the highest recorded. THE UK government bond market was led higher by the strength of continental European markets yesterday, with trading volume light in the absence of new domestic factors. The long-dated cash benchmark, the 9 per cent gilt maturing 2011, closed up 5/16 of a point on the day at 99 23/32 for a yield of 9.02 per cent. On Liffe, the June gilts futures contract finished at 98.20, from an opening level of 98.13. Trading volume was light at 29,000 contracts. US TREASURY prices firmed across the length of the yield curve following the successful completion of the second stage of the Treasury's Dollars 36bn refunding auctions yesterday afternoon. In late trading, the Treasury's benchmark 30-year bond was up 15/32 at 100 7/16 , yielding 7.96 per cent. Gains were less pronounced at the short end of the yield curve, where the two-year note was 1/32 higher to yield 5.22 per cent. The Federal Reserve, as the market had expected, refrained from operating in the open market. Fed funds, the rate at which banks lend to each other, were changing hands at 3 per cent during the Fed's usual intervention period. Short-covering contributed to the higher prices after the afternoon's sale of Dollars 11bn of 10-year notes, which had a better-than-expected average yield of 7.53 per cent. JAPANESE government bond prices firmed overnight in Tokyo, having been closed for public holidays on Monday and Tuesday and suffering a run of negative sentiment last week. The benchmark 10-year government bond issue No 129 closed the Tokyo day on a yield of 5.635 per cent, a touch higher than the 5.675 per cent seen on Friday. Dealers said the authorities indicated that an auction of 10-year bonds scheduled for today would carry a higher coupon than last month's sale of 5.5 per cent paper. Analysts are now expecting a Y800bn auction of 5.7 per cent paper, although a smaller Y600bn issue of 5.6 per cent stock is still possible.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Chiron wins FDA approval for kidney cancer drug
DOC.TEXT: CHIRON, the US biotechnology company, has received approval from the US Food and Drug Administration to market Interleukin-2, a long-awaited treatment for aggressive kidney cancer. The approval marks the end of an eight-year struggle to bring to the US market what had widely been regarded as one of the most promising products of the US biotechnology industry. Interleukin-2, to be sold under the brand name Proleukin, was developed by Cetus, a biotechnology concern acquired by Chiron last year after the long and expensive approval process drained Cetus's resources. Proleukin, which harnesses the power of the body's immune system to attack cancer cells, was originally hailed as a breakthrough in cancer therapy. However in clinical trials the drug was found to benefit only a minority of patients and to have severe side effects. Proleukin shrank tumors in about 15 per cent of patients, with 4 per cent achieving complete remission, but another 4 per cent died from side effects of the drug. However, the trial results were better than for those patients receiving conventional chemotherapy treatment, of whom only about 5 per cent survived. Chiron's share price rose sharply on Monday, gaining Dollars 6 1/2 to close at Dollars 48 1/4 in anticipation of the approval. Chiron's stock fell Dollars 5/8 to Dollars 46 5/8 at close of trade yesterday.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Wesfarmers climbs 77%
DOC.TEXT: WESFARMERS, the diversified Australian agricultural group, yesterday said it was confident of meeting its full-year net profit target of ADollars 60m (USDollars 45.4m) after reporting a 77 per cent increase in profits to ADollars 38m for the first nine months, writes Kevin Brown in Sydney. Sales were up from ADollars 877m to ADollars 984m. The group said lower interest rates and greater efficiency in the fertilisers and chemicals division contributed towards the better performance. In addition, fertiliser sales were higher than in the comparable period of last year. Wesfarmers said demand for cropping fertilisers grew strongly in response to improved wheat prices. The coal, dairy and retail operations contributed improved results, while profits from the gas and transport operations remained steady. The group said it was confident of meeting its full-year profit target, but warned the result was difficult to predict because of the possible effect of weather between April and June, when most fertiliser sales take place.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Pepkor improves 18%
DOC.TEXT: PEPKOR, the South African retail group, lifted attributable profits by 18 per cent in the year to February in which it took over Checkers, one of three largest supermarket chains in South Africa. Turnover rose by 118 per cent to R4.3bn (Dollars 1.5bn) following the takeover of Tradehold and its subsidiary Tradegro which controls Checkers. Operating profit rose 30 per cent, to R218.3m, reflecting the larger contribution from food sales relative to clothes on which margins were better. Attributable income was 18 per cent up at R93.8m and there were extraordinary profits of R75.3m. Pepkor's results included losses and large write-offs at Tradegro which made an operating loss of R30m on turnover of R2.2bn. It wrote off R46m in rationalisation and other costs related to its incorporation into Pepkor.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Woolworth moves into the black
DOC.TEXT: WOOLWORTH, the US retailer, yesterday reported a small Dollars 17m profit after-tax in the three months to April 25. This compares with a Dollars 100m loss a year earlier, but the 1991 figure was struck after an accounting-related charge of Dollars 100m, writes Nikki Tait in New York. Sales during the first quarter, the least significant of a retailer's year, fell by 1.5 per cent to Dollars 2.01bn. However, the 1992 figure excludes sales from some 900 US stores which are to close. At the operating level, Woolworth's profits improved by 20 per cent to Dollars 59m.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: USAir reaches tentative deal with pilots
DOC.TEXT: USAIR said it has reached a tentative agreement with the Air Line Pilots Association on a four-year contract, Reuter reports. The company said the agreement calls for immediate salary reductions for a 12-month period, 'considerable improvements in pilot productivity and cost savings in health care', which will provide USAir with short-term cost savings. It said pilots would receive a series of pay increases at the beginning of September, 1993. USAir said the tentative deal would be submitted to the ALPA executive committee for ratification on May 13. It said it would provide no further details until then.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Canadian Pacific suffers CDollars 39m first-quarter loss
DOC.TEXT: CANADIAN Pacific suffered a first-quarter loss of CDollars 39.7m (USDollars 33.3m) or 12 cents a share, in spite of a strong performance by the group's railway business. The latest deficit at the Canadian conglomerate compares with a loss of CDollars 5.3m or 2 cents a share, a year earlier. Total revenues were CDollars 2.42bn, against CDollars 2.46bn last time. Canada's railways are busy moving record exports of grain, via Vancouver, in the first quarter and CP Rail almost doubled its operating income to CDollars 73.5m. The rail side was buoyed by the fact that expenses increased only slightly because of higher efficiency and lower fuel prices. CP Rail has just agreed to annual pay increases of 3 per cent in 1992 and 1993 with most of its unions. The improved railway results were more than offset by lower income from Pan Canadian Petroleum, the energy arm, and also contin-uing losses at Canadian Pacific Forest Products. The operating loss at CP Forest Products grew to CDollars 83.6m from CDollars 61.4m a year ago. CP Ships narrowed its loss with higher container rates, CP Trucks saw its loss increase, but Fording Coal managed to lift its income to CDollars 22.4m, up nearly CDollars 9m, because of lower operating costs. Marathon Realty's results were off slightly due to problems in the office building sector. This unit in April arranged the sale of CDollars 160m of properties, the proceeds of which will be used to repay debt. The hotels unit reduced its losses, though the market remains soft. The US Doubletree chain did better, with new management contracts and lower overheads. Telecommunications were unchanged, while the industrial products group improved. CP's 19 per cent interest in Laidlaw, the waste management group, generated income of CDollars 3.8m, against a loss of CDollars 3.9m a year earlier. CP expects some improvement in overall performance later this year, as the North American economy recovers from the long recession.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: General Dynamics plans sale of missiles operation
DOC.TEXT: GENERAL Dynamics, the second largest Pentagon contractor, aims to sell off businesses which contribute about one-quarter of its revenues - including its large missiles operation - in a radical plan to cope with the shrinking defence market. It is in the final phase of negotiating the sale of the missiles business, and could announce a deal soon, Mr William Anders, the chairman, said yesterday. Mr Anders, who has been sharply reducing the size of the company since he took over as chairman in 1991, told the annual meeting General Dynamics would adapt to the 'new realities' of the defence market by concentrating on four core areas: tactical aircraft, nuclear submarines, armoured vehicles and space launch systems. It recently sold its Cessna business aircraft subsidiary to Textron, and has adopted a 'plan of contraction' which involves selling other non-core businesses accounting for some Dollars 2.3bn of the group's Dollars 8.7bn of annual revenues. The list is headed by the missiles operation, which had sales last year of Dollars 1.3bn and consists of two parts: an air defence systems division, which makes tactical products such as the Stinger and Standard missiles; and a section of the group's Convair subsidiary, which makes the Tomahawk sea-launched cruise missiles used during the Gulf war. Mr Anders said the missiles business had been seriously considered as a potential core business. However, it could not become the leader in a field which included nearly a dozen firms in the US alone. During talks with numerous other companies, 'we found more interest in the purchase of our operations than the sale of their own'. Other parts of the group up for sale include the remainder of Convair, which makes fuselages for the McDonnell Douglas MD-11 commercial aircraft; the electronics division, which is a leading producer of avionics test equipment; and a materials division which produces aggregates, concrete, lime and coal. Mr Anders' strategy is radically different from that of most defence contractors, which have reacted to the shrinking Pentagon budget by trying to diversify into non-defence areas. He said yesterday the benefits of diversification were 'largely illusory'. The restructuring of the group has helped increase the company's cash and marketable securities to Dollars 1.2bn at the end of March. Mr Anders said the company was generating cash 'well in excess' of that needed to meet investment and debt reduction needs. He continued to favour some distribution to shareholders. The company's shares closed down Dollars 1 at Dollars 64 7/8 .

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Curtain falls on a Hollywood drama - Credit Lyonnais's ill-starred association with Giancarlo Parretti
DOC.TEXT: Shortly after 10 o'clock this morning, in the nondescript town of Wilmington, Delaware, the banging of an auctioneer's gavel should signal a most ignominious fate for MGM, the once legendary Hollywood studio. The auction is mainly a formality - the mechanism by which Credit Lyonnais of France forecloses on a huge loan default and takes possession of MGM stock by swapping around Dollars 400m of loans for 98.5 per cent of the studio's shares. In theory, anyone hoping to outbid the French state bank creditor and buy MGM could come along this morning with at least Dollars 570m of cash in hand -Dollars 400m for the shares and another Dollars 170m for related loan commitments. But MGM suffered a Dollars 347m loss last year, and will need a further Dollars 200m of cash to make it through the current year. It's no bargain. Rather, the foreclosure by Credit Lyonnais is intended as the definitive severing of ties between the Paris-based bank and Mr Giancarlo Parretti, the controversial Italian financier from whom the shares are being taken away. The mercurial Mr Parretti, who is still appealing a four-year jail sentence in Naples on fraud charges, refuses to accept defeat. As recently as this week he claimed he would win out over Credit Lyonnais, but as far as the bank is concerned, a recent US injunction has rendered Mr Parretti more of a nuisance than a threat. Worse, from Credit Lyonnais's point of view, the ill-starred association with the stocky former waiter has shocked many of its blue-chip clients and investors and is costing the bank dearly. The doubling of its 1991 bad debt provisions, to FFr9.5bn (Dollars 1.71bn), is believed to have included part of the MGM exposure. According to information obtained by the Financial Times, Credit Lyonnais's present loan exposure to MGM and to Mr Parretti's various companies amounts to Dollars 1.25bn. MGM was suffering long before November 1990, when Mr Parretti paid Dollars 1.3bn - most of it borrowed from Credit Lyonnais - to acquire the studio. The studio's difficulties were the result of the juggling of assets and repeated sacking of executives by Mr Kirk Kerkorian, the Las Vegas nightclub owner who had owned MGM since 1969. When Mr Parretti bought MGM, he had as a partial backer, Mr Steve Ross, the fast-talking chairman of Time Warner who promised Dollars 650m of loan guarantees in exchange for right to the MGM film library. Within months Time Warner claimed it had been betrayed and sued Mr Parretti for breach of contract. In yet another reversal, Time Warner then decided to make peace and do business again with Mr Parretti. Mr Ross and Time Warner have come under harsh criticism for the association with Mr Parretti, but they got a home video distribution deal on the cheap. From the very start most of Wall Street and Hollywood were betting Mr Parretti would not last very long at MGM, and rightly so. By March 1991 - just four months after Mr Parretti took over the desk once owned by Louis B. Mayer - a group of MGM unpaid creditors sued to force the studio into bankruptcy. Credit Lyonnais, alarmed at the deteriorating state of affairs, sent two top executives to Hollywood, provided MGM with an emergency Dollars 145m fresh line of credit and insisted as a condition that Mr Parretti give up his position at Pathe, his master company, and at MGM. In his place as chairman Mr Parretti put Mr Cesare De Michelis, the brother of his old friend and fellow nightclub habitue Mr Gianni De Michelis, Italy's Socialist foreign minister. Mr De Michelis lasted less than a month before Mr Parretti and the French bank began to sue one another. By the summer of 1991 the legal battle between Credit Lyonnais and Mr Parretti had degenerated into a slanging match. Lawsuits flew back and forth in America. By late December 1991 the chancery court in Delaware, where MGM is incorporated, had thrown out all of Mr Parretti's claims and upheld the right of Credit Lyonnais to remove him and his associates. Mr William Allen, the presiding judge, even declared that Mr Parretti 'did not give truthful testimony when he testified under oath in this court'. Mr Parretti could not be in Delaware to hear the verdict; he spent late December in a Sicilian jail, accused of tax evasion. Down, but not forgotten, the controversial Italian returned to the fray two months ago, claiming that a Rome judge had ordered the sequester of MGM stock and once again named the brother of Italy's foreign minister as MGM chairman. It was at this stage that Credit Lyonnais secured the binding Delaware injunction that ruled any Rome judge's views to be irrelevant under US law. With today's foreclosure auction, Credit Lyonnais is seeking to sever all ties to Mr Parretti. True to form, Mr Parretti yesterday told the Financial Times he considered the auction to be 'phony' and swore once again that Mr De Michelis would be named to MGM. The voluble Italian even argued he was not really in default on his loans from Credit Lyonnais. 'How can I be in default? They never really asked me to pay interest,' he maintained. Asked how much he had borrowed from the French bank, Mr Parretti then claimed: 'I can't remember.' Mr Parretti may not recall, but the amounts are considerable. It has been learned that the Dollars 1.25bn total of Credit Lyonnais loan exposure includes nearly Dollars 650m of loans to MGM itself, plus another Dollars 595m to three of Mr Parretti's holding companies - Comfinance, Melia and Pathe Communications. Credit Lyonnais is owed some Dollars 75m by Comfinance, a company that jointly controls MGM by way of two other vehicles - Melia and Pathe. Melia owes some Dollars 400m, including interest, while Pathe, owes Dollars 120m, including interest. Although Credit Lyonnais will convert about Dollars 400m of these loans into equity as payment in today's auction, the bank will still be left with Dollars 850m of combined MGM and Parretti-company debt on its books. The bank does not expect to be able to sell MGM until the shattered studio can begin producing profitable films, and that is likely to take at least another two years. Internal bank plans call for financial support of at least Dollars 200m this year, and probably as much again in 1993. That means that by early 1994, assuming MGM is profitable and saleable again -a big if in itself - Credit Lyonnais will be sitting on a total outlay of more than Dollars 1.2bn again. Put simply, Credit Lyonnais is likely to be stuck in Hollywood, with heavy loan exposure and a battered and loss-making studio on its hands, for quite some time. Today's auction thus may represent a new beginning for MGM, but at blockbuster cost.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Enlarged Morland rises 30%
DOC.TEXT: MORLAND & Co, the Thames Valley brewer which announced in March that it was talking to potential bidders, lifted interim pre-tax profits 30 per cent from Pounds 2.35m to Pounds 3.06m. 'At a time when there has been some speculation about the corporate future of the company, there has been no such uncertainty in our trading performance,' said Sir Humphrey Prideaux, the Morland chairman. However, The company's efforts to resolve problems stemming from the government's beer orders were reflected in an extraordinary charge of Pounds 236,000 for advisers' fees. The problems involve Whitbread Investment Company's 43.6 per cent stake. Unless this is reduced, WIC's sister company, Whitbread, will have to count Morland's 300 pubs as part of its tied estate and offload more pubs to meet the requirements of the beer orders. Morland's results for the six months to March 31 were boosted by last year's purchase of 100 pubs from Courage. Turnover rose some 23 per cent to Pounds 18.9m (Pounds 15.4m), and operating profit increased 49 per cent to Pounds 3.41m (Pounds 2.29m). Volume sales of Morland ales improved 13 per cent. Sales of Old Speckled Hen premium ale doubled and free trade volumes were 17 per cent up. Pub food sales rose 38 per cent. There was a provision of Pounds 250,000 against potential bad debts in its Pounds 3m free trade loans. Earnings per share rose to 10.5p (9.1p) and the interim dividend is lifted to 2.42p (2.11p).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Reflex Investments warns of deficit
DOC.TEXT: Reflex Investments, the Dublin-based computer leasing group, warned that it would report a loss for the year to end-April. The company said trading conditions in the second half of the year had remained difficult. It said it was taking all steps available to return the group to profitability. In the 1990-91 financial year Reflex made a pre-tax profit of IPounds 2.51m.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Aspen buys Dutch market consultancy
DOC.TEXT: Aspen Communications, the specialist print, communications and media services group, is acquiring Veenhuizen Reclame, a direct market consultancy in the Netherlands. The initial consideration is Pounds 760,000 cash, payable to Cumae Beheer, the vendor. Depending on profits performance, there could be further payments up to a maximum of Pounds 365,000.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Morgan Grenfell Equity Income
DOC.TEXT: In its first trading period Morgan Grenfell Equity Income Trust produced gross revenue of Pounds 565,000 and net income of Pounds 323,000. The trust was incorporated on September 24 1991. Accounts cover the trading period November 14 to March 31 1992. Earnings per share were 1.32p and an interim dividend of 1p is declared. At March 31 net asset value came to 89.7p.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: UniChem expands into Portugal
DOC.TEXT: UniChem, the pharmaceuticals wholesaler which in March withdrew from the battle for Macarthy, the retailer, has acquired two wholesalers in Portugal and has negotiated an option to buy a third. The consideration for the two acquired wholesalers, both based in Oporto, is Es1.2bn (Pounds 4.95m) cash. In the 1991 year, they had combined sales of some Es9.71bn, combined pre-tax profits of Es119m, and combined net assets of about Es371m. The exercise for the option on the third wholesaler, in Aviero, will involve a maximum Es1.05bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Forward Grp stages second-half recovery
DOC.TEXT: A recovery in the second half enabled Forward Group, the USM-traded printed circuit board manufacturer, to report profits of Pounds 622,000 pre-tax for the 12 months to January 31. The outcome compared with Pounds 955,000, including exceptional credits of Pounds 118,000, and was, according to Mr Ray Chamberlain, chairman, a 'most satisfactory' result given the economic climate. Interest charges fell from Pounds 399,000 to Pounds 231,000. The current year had continued the improvements of the second half, he said and trading subsidiaries had started the year 'materially better' although there was still 'fierce pressure' on prices reflecting competition. Turnover declined 11 per cent to Pounds 9.33m (Pounds 10.5m). Earnings per share emerged at 5.69p (8.95p) and a proposed final dividend of 1.5p brings the total to 2.5p (2.2p).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Overseas Investment asset value declines
DOC.TEXT: At March 31 1992 the net asset value per share of Overseas Investment Trust had slipped to 274.5p. Six months earlier it was 279.3p and the year before 277.6p. In the half year to end-March net income rose from Pounds 254,000 to Pounds 469,000 for earnings per share of 1.23p (0.67p). The interim distribution is lifted from 0.75p to 0.8p.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Brooks Bros staff to vote on strike
DOC.TEXT: New York-based staff at Brooks Brothers, the US menswear chain owned by Marks and Spencer, will vote tomorrow on a proposal which could authorise strike action. The 200 employees at the four New York stores who are members of the Amalgamated Clothing and Textile Workers Union have already rejected a new employment contract. The union said yesterday that no formal talks were taking place between the company and itself ahead of the strike vote, although it acknowledged that some informal contact was continuing.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: LIT recovers to Pounds 1.29m
DOC.TEXT: The strength of its UK operations helped LIT Holdings to produce a much improved result for 1991. Pre-tax profit of Pounds 1.29m for the year compared with a loss of Pounds 344,000 in 1990 for this financial services group. Turnover was Pounds 83m (Pounds 91.1m) but operating profits from Johnson Fry rose 50 per cent from Pounds 1.59m to Pounds 2.4m and LIT America contributed Pounds 2.39m (Pounds 2.52m). Both businesses are seasonal, so the bulk of profits were accrued in the first half when the pre-tax profit was higher at Pounds 1.92m (Pounds 838,000). Central charges fell to Pounds 3.5m (Pounds 4.45m) benefiting from the refinancing of short-term debt into medium-term debt and redeemable preference shares. Dividend payments on these shares took Pounds 203,000 after which losses per share were reduced to 1.4p (3p).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Beattie tackles tough times
DOC.TEXT: JAMES BEATTIE, the Wolverhampton-based department store operator, saw pre-tax profit decline by 14 per cent, from Pounds 9m to Pounds 7.73m, in the year to January 31 1992. Against the depressed background it was a commendable performance, said Sir Eric Pountain, chairman. Operating profit in the second half was only 6 per cent lower than last year, and compared with a drop of 34 per cent in the first half. The important Christmas trade was very late to develop. Sales edged ahead to Pounds 67.6m (Pounds 67m) excluding VAT, and operating profit was nearly 13 per cent lower at Pounds 5.25m. There had been tight control on costs and the group also resisted the temptation to secure sales volume by surrendering margins, Sir Eric said. Investment income and interest declined to Pounds 2.49m (Pounds 3m) reflecting the downward movement of interest rates. Earnings per share were 11.3p (13.03p) and the final dividend is 4.35p for a total of 5.75p (5.5p).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Silentnight ahead to Pounds 12.4m but loses sleep over first half
DOC.TEXT: SILENTNIGHT Holdings, Europe's biggest bed maker, yesterday warned over the outlook for profits in the first half, with deep discounting by retailers having eroded margins in the first three months of the year. Mr Bill Davies, chairman, said that sales were currently ahead of last year. However, he said high street discounting was affecting margins in the group's two middle market bed businesses - Silentnight and Layezee. 'The first half is going to be very difficult,' he said. Unless there was a change, 'profits will be affected.' The warning accompanied record profits of Pounds 12.4m (Pounds 11.5m) for the year to February 1. Turnover fell 9 per cent to Pounds 137.6m, following the disposal in 1990 of the upholstery division for Pounds 9m. On a like-for-like comparison, sales were 5 per cent higher at Pounds 137.8m. The profits advance was helped by interest gains of Pounds 690,000 on the group's Pounds 13m cash balance, compared with a charge of Pounds 97,000 last time. The final dividend is increased by 1p to 5.75p for a total of 8p (7p), payable from earnings per share ahead 7 per cent to 17.92p. Mr Barry McKenzie, finance director, said all four bed companies had improved their contributions with sales rising from Pounds 90.7m to Pounds 94.9m. He said that the group had, by his calculations, improved its market share in the UK from 30 per cent to 31 per cent. In the cabinet furniture division, sales rose by 18 per cent in a declining market. Homeworthy, the lower-to middle market range of furniture, was strongly ahead following heavy capital investment, although Silentnight Cabinets produced disappointing results. Gross margins improved from 34.8 per cent to 36.7 per cent due to a better product mix, said Mr Davies. The US division suffered losses, although Mr McKenzie said they were not significant in terms of the overall group. Sales in the US were down 20 per cent at Pounds 9.5m. Mr McKenzie added that Silentnight did not expect the US business to 'come back rapidly' this year. COMMENT These figures begin to show the benefits of Pounds 11.5m in capital spend, but there is more to come. The Pounds 8.5m pencilled in for this year will be spent on more plant and also on a TV advertising campaign to maintain the Silentnight brand. That is good news for the medium-term investors, who will be less shy of the fact that the shares have had a good run lately, rising by 88p in 12 months to last night's 245p. The balance sheet remains strong although critics would argue that the family-controlled company could use the cash to better effect. Forecasts are for Pounds 14m this year, in spite of the cautious noises about margins, and the shares look attractive with a prospective p/e of about 12 times.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Chelsea chief gives Fulham stern warning
DOC.TEXT: Mr Ken Bates, chairman of Chelsea Football Club which is planning to buy its west London ground from Cabra Estates, has warned Fulham Football Club that it should come to share the facilities by the start of next season - or not come at all. A move by Fulham to Stamford Bridge is a crucial part of Chelsea's agreement to buy the ground for Pounds 13m cash, plus the assumption of Cabra's liabilities to Fulham, worth Pounds 8.25m.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: BHH advises acceptance of Pounds 21m bid from chief's company
DOC.TEXT: THE BOARD of BHH Group has recommended a Pounds 21.3m cash bid from IM Group, a private distribution company controlled by Mr Robert Edmiston, chairman of BHH. The offer, which has been irrevocably accepted by shareholders representing 39.5 per cent of the equity, is worth 36p per share. BHH shares closed unchanged at 34p. The property company incurred a pre-tax loss of Pounds 4.7m on turnover of Pounds 25.8m in 1991. BHH said it was cutting costs, but was unlikely to return to profitability unless there was a sustained and significant improvement in the property market. It believed it would be better placed to continue with the support of, and access to, the funds of IM Group.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Lloyds takeover not in public interest, says Bifu - The Battle for Midland
DOC.TEXT: A LLOYDS takeover of Midland Bank would lead to monopoly banking in some towns and would not be in the public interest, Bifu, the banking union, will tell MPs today, writes Catherine Milton. The union is trying to increase support for a referral of the bid to the monopoly authorities because it believes 30,000 jobs and 1,100 branches are at risk if it succeeds. In a dossier sent to Mr Michael Heseltine, the trade and industry secretary, all MPs and British Euro MPs, the union explains why it believes the merger would not be in the public interest. 'Such a merger would be harmful to customers and staff and to the UK economy since it would lead to unemployment and reduce competition. A number of towns currently have only a Lloyds and a Midland branch and there would, in effect, be monopoly banking in those towns. The customer would lose a choice.' The union rejects the argument that the UK has too many bank branches, saying it ranks equal fourth with France among nine leading nations for the number of branches per head of population.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Suitors to lobby MPs next week - The Battle for Midland
DOC.TEXT: THE LOBBYING of members of parliament by Midland's two suitors will begin in earnest next week when senior executives from both Hongkong Bank and Lloyds are expected to meet Conservative backbenchers. A meeting with Mr William Purves has been provisionally arranged for next Wednesday or Thursday when the Hongkong Bank chairman is due in London. MPs are understood to have offered Lloyds a similar opportunity although details have yet to be finalised. It is expected that all Tory backbenchers will have the option of attending the meetings. The standard format is for those addressing such gatherings - usually scheduled to last about an hour - to be given up to 15 minutes to present their case before fielding questions. Mr Tim Smith, the Conservative MP for Beaconsfield and an officer of the Tory backbench finance committee in the last parliament, is understood to have played a leading role in arranging the meetings. Such is the geographic spread of the groups involved that interest among MPs is likely to be exceptionally widespread. Midland is next week expected to follow the example of its suitors in writing to all MPs. MPs recently received a letter from Sir Jeremy Morse, Lloyds chairman, arguing that the Hongkong offer failed to address 'the fundamental problems in the UK banking sector.' Hongkong Bank is expected to send out its own letter to MPs shortly. Meanwhile, Mr Michael Heseltine, President of the Board of Trade, will this week field his first written questions on the tussle for Midland. Ms Marjorie Mowlam, Labour front bench spokeswoman on City and corporate affairs, is to ask Mr Heseltine when he expects to be informed both of the EC competition directorate's views on the Hongkong proposals and of the Office of Fair Trading's opinion of the possible takeover of Midland by Lloyds. Mr Heseltine will also be asked whether he proposes any amendment to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission's present approach to potential takeovers in which the implication for competition is the sole criterion taken into consideration.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Buoyant BAT says US riots will not hit profits
DOC.TEXT: BAT Industries, the tobacco and financial services group, said yesterday the riots in Los Angeles should not affect the profits of its Farmers Group subsidiary, a leading provider of insurance to small businesses in California. The details emerged as BAT announced a 14 per cent increase in pre-tax profit to Pounds 262m in the first quarter of this year, with tobacco making a record Pounds 209m at the trading level. Group turnover advanced from Pounds 3.63bn to Pounds 3.87bn, and earnings per share from 7.9p to 8.7p. BAT was able to provide a snapshot of the riot claims coming in to the three reciprocal insurance exchanges which Farmers manages - obtaining its profit from fees on premiums, rather than from underwriting. By yesterday, about 300 riot-related claims had been received. The total amount was expected to reach at least Dollars 70m (Pounds 39.5m). Estimates of the total damage in all the cities affected have ranged from Dollars 1bn to Dollars 1.5bn, but it is not clear how much was insured. To put the riot claims in perspective, Mr Michael Prideaux, public affairs director, said claims arising from a hailstorm in Texas last week had amounted to Dollars 70m and the total for last year's Oakland fire was Dollars 130m. Bought for about Pounds 3.2bn in late 1988, Farmers increased its trading profit to more than Pounds 100m in the first quarter. Sir Patrick Sheehy, chairman, said that after financing costs there was a Pounds 60m contribution to group profits. Its profit and that of Allied Dunbar, the UK life business, were again eroded by losses at Eagle Star, the composite insurer hit by mortgage and other recession-related provisions. Overall, financial services saw its first-quarter trading profit fall from Pounds 112m to Pounds 95m. Tobacco was again a strong performer, increasing trading profit by 11 per cent to Pounds 209m. Sir Patrick said cigarette export volumes were 18 per cent ahead. Kent and Lucky Strike had maintained their success, while State Express 555 had become the UK's largest export brand. New markets included Hungary, while penetration continued to increase in Japan and Korea. Brazil had returned to profit and had recently ended 27 years of price controls on cigarettes. Lex, Page 24, Results, Page 26

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Trafalgar House halves dividend
DOC.TEXT: TRAFALGAR House, the property, construction and engineering group, halved its dividend as pre-tax profits for the six months to March 31 increased 18 per cent on the back of a strong performance from construction and engineering. Sir Eric Parker, chief executive, said the group would focus on construction and engineering which had an order book of almost Pounds 4bn as he unveiled pre-tax profits of Pounds 54m compared with Pounds 45.5m. Turnover increased from Pounds 1.5bn to Pounds 2.1bn. Sir Eric said the cut in the interim dividend, from 8.8p to 4.4p, which was signalled last year, would help mitigate its problems over unrelieved advance corporation tax. He added the group still needed another UK business to get rid of the problem once and for all. Trafalgar had further bad news for former shareholders in Davy Corporation, which the group took over last June. Although the group hopes to lease the Ocean Emerald oil rig to Midland and Scottish Resources for about Pounds 20m it held out little hope of Davy's former shareholders receiving the second payment, totalling Pounds 54m or 45p a share.
