This is because in Trafalgar's view MSR is still unlikely to be able to draw upon the Pounds 118m letter of credit with the project's bankers. Without the letter of credit Trafalgar House says it cannot make the second payment to the Davy shareholders. Operating profits from property and investment and shipping and hotels continued to fall. The former reported profits of Pounds 6.6m, compared with Pounds 19m, while the latter suffered a smaller profit fall to Pounds 5.9m from Pounds 7.6m. Sir Eric said property continued to experience depressed conditions, although the removal of political uncertainty and lower interest rates gave some prospect of a gradual UK recovery. Occupancy levels still remained disappointing at between 50 per cent and 60 per cent. Construction and engineering increased profits by 39 per cent to Pounds 53.3m. Sir Eric said the group would focus on these core businesses. Net borrowings fell from Pounds 450m to Pounds 328m, although debt increased since the year-end total of Pounds 182m. Fully diluted earnings per share before extraordinary items fell to 4.8p from 5.9p. Lex, Page 24 Observer, Page 23

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Canary Wharf fate lies with CIBC
DOC.TEXT: BANKERS yesterday accused Canada's second biggest bank, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, of threatening to put O&Y Canary Wharf Holdings, developer of Europe's biggest new office development, into administration under UK insolvency legislation. O&Y Canary Wharf is a subsidiary of Olympia & York Developments, which is today meeting its 15 biggest bank creditors to discuss its proposal to alleviate its difficulties by restructuring Dollars 12bn (Pounds 6.7bn) of debt. Today's meeting will discuss the prospects for the contributors to a Dollars 2.5bn 'jumbo' loan to an O&Y subsidiary, Olympia & York Resources Credit Corporation. A banker said yesterday that contributors to this loan could lose a third of their money. Hongkong and Shanghai Bank is understood to have lent Dollars 750m of the Dollars 2.5bn. Meanwhile there have been separate meetings of the 11 providers of bank finance for the Canary Wharf project in east London. At a meeting on Tuesday, 10 of the 11 lenders indicated they would be prepared to support a plan to provide Canary Wharf with Pounds 30m to meet its needs for the coming month, but bankers said CIBC refused to provide any new money. The banks will only provide the Pounds 30m if all 11 contribute. Without the Pounds 30m, O&Y Canary Wharf would go into administration. Bankers said CIBC was threatening to 'pull the rug' on Canary Wharf. The banks have until tonight to say whether they will provide the Pounds 30m, because Canary Wharf runs out of cash at the end of the week. CIBC is said to have told other banks that it was pessimistic about the long-term outlook for Canary Wharf and believed it would be wrong to inject any new money into the project. Bankers say CIBC's stance is surprising, as it is the biggest lender to O&Y's worldwide oper-ations, with about Dollars 1bn of loans outstanding, and it has the most to lose if O&Y's subsidiaries file for bankruptcy protection. Loans to Canary Wharf total about Pounds 1bn. However, these loans are guaranteed by the parent company in Canada. If Canary Wharf lenders face losses, they can demand reparations from the parent - with potentially damaging consequences for the rest of O&Y.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / German strike talks to resume today
DOC.TEXT: TALKS aimed at ending the 10-day-old public sector strike in Germany were adjourned last night until today, with no sign of a promised new offer from the employers. Union officials and representatives of federal, state and local authorities had just a brief meeting in Stuttgart after four hours of separate consultations by the two sides. 'We stood next to each other and did not have anything to say,' Ms Monika Wulf-Mathies, leader of the largest public service union, oTV, told reporters. Negotiators said they would meet this morning for 'further exploratory talks'. The Bonn government's chief negotiator, Mr Rudolf Seiters, the interior minister, added: 'We will have lots of time then.' Hopes had been raised by the public sector employers' indications that they would make a new offer to try to end what is already western Germany's most disruptive wave of industrial action since the Second World War. They previously offered a 4.8 per cent pay rise, while the unions originally demanded a 9.5 per cent increase. Ms Wulf-Mathies, said before the talks less than the 5.4 per cent proposed recently by arbitrators would be rejected. Both sides hinted earlier this week that a deal limiting wage rises for top earners and giving more to the lower-paid might be the best way forward. According to trade union estimates, more than 500,000 workers in both public and private sectors were on strike yesterday. While leading economists suggested that the stoppages would have to last at least a month before having any noticeable effects on economic output, tangible evidence of the strike's effects continued to mount. The national railway network was within days of collapse, a Bundesbahn official said. Only a quarter of its locomotives were still in service and losses had already reached DM100m (Pounds 34m). In Cologne 120 wagons of mail were standing in sidings. In Frankfurt an estimated 13,000 tonnes of uncollected refuse was piled in streets. At the same time unrest grew in the private sector. About 75,000 members of the IG Metall engineering workers' union defied threats of a lock-out and continued warning strikes as it became clear that employers were not yet prepared to increase their 3.3 per cent pay offer. IG Metall leaders will meet next Tuesday to decide on their next step. Building workers, members of the IG Bau union, threatened a work-to-rule until employers improved their 3.4 per cent offer. Printers demanding an 11 per cent increase continued token protests. Prof Hans Schneider, chairman of the 'five wise men', the group of leading independent economic advisers to the government, warned of dangerous consequences for the economy if the talks led to excessive pay rises. However, he added, a 5.5 per cent overall deal 'would not be the end of the world'. He agreed with the respected Ifo economics institute in Munich that a full month's stoppage in the public sector, with an average of 300,000 workers striking daily would cut the year's GDP growth by only between 0.1 per cent and 0.2 per cent.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Polish IMF deal put in jeopardy
DOC.TEXT: POLAND'S hopes of negotiating a new deal with the International Monetary Fund were in doubt last night following the resignation of Mr Andrzej Olechowski, the finance minister, in protest against a parliamentary vote for higher government spending. His departure weakens the minority centre-right coalition government of Mr Jan Olszewski, prime minister, which has been put in danger of collapse by the row over budget spending. The finance minister announced his resignation after two votes in parliament failed to overturn a 1991 constitutional court ruling which bars the government from cutting public sector pensions. The resulting rise in civil servants' pay and additional pension rights could cost the government Zl 28,100bn (Pounds 1.15bn), the prime minister said. This rise threatens to overwhelm the government plans to limit this year's budget deficit to Zl 65,500bn or 5 per cent of gross domestic product. This was the limit agreed two months ago after Mr Olechowski's talks in Washington with the IMF. IMF support for the government's economic policies is essential for the resumption of payments from the total Dollars 2.5bn three-year IMF extended loan facility granted last year. Disbursements were suspended in September when targets, including those for inflation and government spending, were exceeded. An IMF team is in Warsaw for talks with the government. Mr Olechowski said he was resigning because he could 'see no way of fulfilling these new obligations'. He added that those who had voted for the spending increases should be asked how they would pay for them. The former communists, the populist KPN party and the PSL peasants' party, refused to support either government attempt to secure the disputed cuts in public sector pay. The Democratic Union, the largest party, led by Mr Tadeusz Mazowiecki, a possible contender for the premiership if the government does collapse, voted against one of the motions. Yesterday's vote also raises the question of whether it will be possible to enforce the spending cuts of Zl 24,000bn agreed by the government to keep this year's budget within IMF-approved limits in the face of arguments that entitlements once granted by law cannot be taken away. Mr Olszewski said his government would not resign. He would try to have the draft budget accepted by parliament in two weeks. Editorial comment, Page 22

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Letter: Right ways for accountants to be regulated and improve image (2)
DOC.TEXT: Sir, The article 'Six ways to improve the profession's image' (Accountancy column, April 30) contained no reference to steps that have already been taken by the profession in these areas, namely: 1. The remit of the Accounting Standards Board undoubtedly includes the narrowing of options and the tightening of financial reporting standards. 2. Proposals from this institute to the Cadbury Committee include the role of audit committees in all public-interest entities. One of the duties of audit committees, containing independent non-executive directors only, would be to recommend auditor appointments and dismissals to the board. 3. We have recently published a paper recommending that auditors should approve the issue of interim accounts. 4. We (and others) also proposed to the Cadbury Committee that directors should report on the adequacy or otherwise of listed companies' internal controls and that auditors should attest the directors' statement. 5. The Auditing Practices Board is about to publish an exposure draft on a new form of auditors' report, including a proposal that the responsibilities of the directors for the preparation of financial statements should be distinguished from those of the auditors. Directors' responsibilities would therefore be highlighted. The need for auditors to draw attention to items of significance which may be buried in the notes to financial statements is also dealt with. 6. Procedures exist to cover the naming of members of the profession when serious 'public interest' cases result in disciplinary action against them. The coming months will see further progress on those matters that are still only at the proposal stage. Ian R McNeil, president, Institute of Chartered Accountants, Chartered Accountants Hall, Moorgate Place, London EC2

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Letter: Right ways for accountants to be regulated and improve image (1)
DOC.TEXT: Sir, Touche Ross is to be congratulated on calling for the regulation of auditors to be shifted from the Institute of Chartered Accountants to an independent body ('Touche attacks ICAEW audit role', May 1). The institute simply cannot be expected to be an effective regulator. Its primary role is that of a trade association; inevitably, its role as advocate of the immediate interest of members will take precedence over its role in upholding professional standards and increasing public confidence. I am glad I am not alone in knowing of cases where the two roles have been in conflict. The article by Geoffrey Holmes and Alan Sugden (Accountancy column, April 30) on 'six ways to improve the profession's image' would have carried more weight if it had endorsed the Touche Ross proposal. The article did, however, underline the importance of asserting the independence of auditors as a step towards better corporate governance. An audit is an integral part of good corporate governance and an independent regulator for auditors is but one of the steps we have to take in the UK to reach the goal of a truly independent audit. W B Kirkpatrick, 20 Abbotsbury House, Abbotsbury Road, London W14

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Observer: Till death. . .
DOC.TEXT: A lady who died left a note in her will that she should be cremated and her ashes scattered over Harrods to make sure that her daughter visited her at least twice a week.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Observer: Helm over
DOC.TEXT: How times change. Had it not been for Trafalgar House's opportunist bid for its smaller rival P & O 10 years ago, Lord Sterling of Plaistow would not have been press-ganged into taking the P & O helm. Today, a revitalised P & O is worth more than three times as much as Trafalgar House. Nor is it faced with the humiliation of having to halve its dividend to survive the recession. So does Trafalgar House now need the same sort of external shock to wake up its rather inbred management team? Certainly, it has hired a slick PR professional to patch up its accident-prone image, and there's no doubt that founder Sir Nigel Broackes looks reinvigorated on his new diet. But something more will be needed to convince the City that anything much has changed. A few fresh non-executive faces on the board would be a start, especially if the Trafalgar House really is intent on transforming itself into a world class engineering giant. It is the sort of company that the new president of the board of trade will need to keep an eye on.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Observer: Wendt away
DOC.TEXT: To be sure Henry Wendt, chairman of SmithKline Beecham, who attracted attention recently with his Pounds 1.8m remuneration package for 1991, does not need the money. But Arjo Wiggins Appleton, which made him a non-executive director 18 months ago, might reasonably have expected him to stay on its board a little longer. The paper company, the product of a 1990 merger between Wiggins Teape Appleton and Arjomari-Prioux, had hoped that his wisdom on a mega transatlantic merger would be of benefit in its Anglo-French endeavours. Now he has resigned and an Arjo spokesman says he does not know why. It goes to show the dangers of chasing trophy names to put on the company letterhead.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Observer: Musical allegory
DOC.TEXT: For more than a decade left-wing intellectuals have been puzzling over the reason for the halt in the forward march of labour. Now the letters column of the journal published by BT's main union, the NCU, offers a possible clue. Retired member Fred Hattley wrote asking what had happened to his union's brass band, once among the best in the land. Answer: the band is now owned by the employers and calls itself the BT band. 'BT took over sponsorship when the band's financial needs outstripped the NCU's ability to offer support,' writes the editor. Shame on the NCU.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Observer: Just relief
DOC.TEXT: Another Dollars 1.5m of Lloyd's names' money has just been sent down the tubes by a federal judge in America. But his ruling against the insurers' objection to paying a robbery claim by a US diamond wholesaler will bring relief to office workers everywhere else on the planet. Lloyd's policy with the NY Diaco diamond company stipulated that it must have a minimum of two employees on duty at all times. It turned out, however, that the robbery took place while one of the two staff present - the company president - had stepped out to the lavatory. Lloyd's therefore declared the policy void and refused the Dollars 1.5m claim. But Judge Louis Stanton has ruled the insurers' objection unreasonable. 'A brief trip to the restroom at various times during the day is not inconsistent with being on duty or attending the office,' he says.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Observer: Hard to swallow
DOC.TEXT: Age has its compensations - at least for wrinklies planning to holiday in the remoteness of New Guinea. They're less likely to end up on the locals' menu, according to an ex-cannibal now called Derek, just brought to public view by anthropological researchers in the Indonesian half of the huge island. 'Old ones are tough. Young men and women taste better,' the Christian convert reminisced when asked how his fellow humans had gone down. 'And babies taste like fish,' he added. 'The flesh is very soft.' But the last bit was just spicing things up for the occasion, one of the researchers said. 'There has been no documented evidence of babies being eaten.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Observer: Parallel rulers
DOC.TEXT: Like meets like at 10 Downing Street today with prime minister Major's first visit from his gangling Swedish counterpart Carl Bildt. Besides sharing the same dry sense of humour and conversational style, the two Conservative leaders aren't all that far apart in appearance, although the Scandinavian is fresher of face. Something else they have in common is an affinity with German chancellor Helmut Kohl, somewhat on the lines of two nephews to an uncle. Bildt sees John Major as a strong ally backing Sweden's bid for European Community membership by 1995. The UK premier wants to make widening the community a leitmotif of Britain's EC presidency in the second half of this year. While the Swede's election win came earlier - he took over last October - he also has a recent personal victory to celebrate. He has just struck a telling blow for his industrial policy by forcing the automobile group Volvo to back away from its controversial plan to take over the Procordia pharmaceutical and food company. But their talk won't be only of triumph. Yet another resemblance between them is that Bildt, too, is presiding over his country's worst recession since at least the Second World War.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Clash of wills over power for the people: The UK gas regulator has raised the stakes in his campaign for lower domestic prices
DOC.TEXT: Sir James McKinnon, the gas industry regulator, has come out of the trenches with his bayonet fixed, fighting for lower gas prices on behalf of UK households. He jolted the stock market, which immediately knocked 8p off the price of British Gas shares yesterday before they rallied to close 2 1/2 p down at 262 1/2 p. Stockbrokers reacted swiftly to Sir James's demands for British Gas to cut domestic gas prices by up to 2p a therm, calculating that this would slice at least Pounds 250m from the company's annual profits of more than Pounds 1bn. But the situation is more complex than the simple arithmetic implies. The public row is just the latest clash of wills between an aggressive regulator and a company that has yet to adjust to life under public surveillance. Relations between Sir James and British Gas have struck a discordant note since privatisation in 1986. Sir James sets the price British Gas can charge households for gas supply in a complicated formula which came into force last month. This limits gas price increases to 5 percentage points below the rate of inflation, which means that if the annual inflation rate is below 5 per cent, prices must fall. Sir James forecasts inflation will hover around the 4 per cent mark this year; so prices must be reduced now. He is threatening legal action against British Gas if it fails to comply with his request. 'Customers need a cut in price as soon as possible. British Gas should not be using customers' money to smooth out price rises and falls,' he said yesterday. But a smooth price decline is what British Gas wants: the company says it must avoid the 'yo-yo' effect of cutting prices now and possibly having to raise them again if inflation increases later in the year. When British Gas made its decision to freeze domestic prices at the beginning of last month, the company said its projections of inflation were rather shaky because it did not know the outcome of the general election. 'The prices are reviewed monthly and so at any time an adjustment can be made,' an official said yesterday. Part of the argument centres on Sir James's refusal to meet British Gas officials to discuss a price cut. He said a meeting was unnecessary as the evidence pointing to the need for a reduction was 'blindingly obvious'. The lack of communication between Sir James and British Gas points to a somewhat tense and combative relationship. Sir James is careful to maintain a distance between himself and the company he regulates, but British Gas accuses him of being aloof. The contentious nature of the relationship meant that British Gas only accepted the April price formula after a long-running dispute on pricing and faced with the threat of a referral to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission. But the company has now indicated that it wants the formula to be reviewed in the wake of a separate agreement reached with the Office of Fair Trading in January. The agreement requires it to relinquish half of its share of the industrial gas market to rival suppliers in a bid to encourage more competition. British Gas says its deal with the OFT changes its operating conditions to such an extent that the tough price formula for the domestic part of its business needs to be eased. A gas industry observer suggests that British Gas could be sticking to a clever strategy of freezing prices now in the hope of seeing the formula revised later in the year, thereby allowing it to keep prices steady or even to raise them. Sir James, however, does not sympathise with the request by British Gas for a revision to the formula. He believes the company should keep its domestic and industrial businesses separate and that a drop in profit in one should not affect prices in the other. His comments yesterday on prices could be the opening salvo in a much more serious disagreement later in the year over the actual level of the pricing formula. British Gas must tread carefully if it wants to avoid becoming embroiled in another distracting dispute over pricing. Sir James has found sympathy for his views among some politicians, and his arguments have struck a chord among consumers who resent the idea that they are being overcharged. The British Gas case against an immediate price cut is technical and not so readily absorbed by consumers, because it relies on complicated calculations in the price formula. However, some industry observers believe the company is right to be cautious and that Sir James has got his arithmetic wrong. They point out that the current rate of inflation indicates the need for a price cut of just 0.3p a therm rather than Sir James's 2p. Sir James himself is rather vague as to how he arrived at the 2p a therm figure and admits that a 1p reduction in price would probably be sufficient. But if the battle goes to court Sir James will have to prove the accuracy of his figures or risk a dent in his credibility. A cut of only 0.3p a therm would translate into a very small reduction in most domestic bills, and British Gas says it could make a more significant cut if it waited until later in the year. Overall the price paid for gas by UK consumers compares favourably with that in other western European countries. According to many international studies, British households pay lower gas bills than their German or Italian counterparts. Lower UK gas prices are, however, more a historical accident than a regulatory triumph. In the past, the price paid by British Gas to North Sea gas producers fluctuated with the rate of inflation, while prices on the continent were more closely linked to oil prices. When oil prices soared in the early 1970s, British consumers were paying lower gas prices than continental users. In the 1980s, there was a move to link UK prices more closely to the price of oil, but since then oil prices have been low and again gas prices have remained relatively low in real terms. Nevertheless, consumers need to be convinced they are getting a fair deal or they may switch to another energy supply. Mr Ian Powe of the Gas Consumers' Council, a consumers' lobby, said yesterday that Sir James's initiative is good news for customers. If Sir James loses any future dispute over pricing, consumers could lose an aggressive champion. By threatening British Gas with legal action, Sir James is taking a gamble on the basis of his own calculations which some observers believe are flawed. It is not clear whether Sir James would win a court case. 'This is a battle of wills and it is hard to see how both parties can emerge unscathed,' said Mr Peter Spring, industry analyst at Henderson Crosthwaite, the broker. Both the regulator and the company have much at stake. For Sir James, his reputation as an effective industry regulator and his credibility are on the line. For British Gas, the loss of Pounds 250m in profit would be extremely hard to justify to shareholders.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / A revolution on the runway: Boeing, the world's largest commercial aircraft manufacturer, is adjusting to tougher competition
DOC.TEXT: A cultural revolution is taking place at Boeing. For the first time in its 75-year history, the world's leading manufacturer of commercial jets has appointed a woman - Mrs Rozanne Ridgway, a career diplomat - to its all-male board of directors. More significantly, it is being forced to implement fundamental change in the way it does business. It has adopted a more open stance towards the outside world and is encouraging airlines, suppliers and subcontractors to participate actively in the design of its latest airliner, the 777 widebody twin engine jet. In the past, Boeing felt it knew what was best for its airline customers. 'But with the 777, Boeing has for the first time given us direct access to the process of designing a new aircraft,' says Mr James O'Sullivan, British Airway's chief project engineer on the 777 programme. Boeing is also openly talking for the first time of forging close ties, including equity partnerships, with other companies. 'We have always been a go-it-alone company with a fearsome amount of pride,' conceded Mr Frank Shrontz, Boeing's chairman. 'It has been difficult for us to share with others but we are changing that.' The reasons, according to Mr Shrontz, are the huge investments necessary to launch new programmes and the market risks which are forcing companies to pool their resources. 'I see more and more openness in that sense. I don't know where our next partners will come from but I am not ruling out partnerships with any other company in the world.' This new attitude reflects both the current conditions of the civil aviation market, which is still struggling to recover from its worst slump since the Second World War, and the changing nature of the competition facing Boeing. The biggest challenge has undoubtedly come from Airbus Industrie, the European aircraft consortium which has steadily built up market share during the past 20 years with advanced new aircraft and government subsidies. Airbus has now captured nearly 30 per cent of the world commercial jet market and has started making serious inroads into some of Boeing's traditional US airline customers. Airbus has not only developed a comprehensive family of aircraft to compete against Boeing, but has also sought to leapfrog its US rival by introducing new technological concepts to commercial jets. These include fly-by-wire controls, which enable the pilot's commands from the cockpit to be transmitted electronically rather than mechanically to the flaps and the rudder, and computer-aided design systems. The European consortium is now also threatening to challenge Boeing's dominance of the jumbo aircraft market by studying the development of a 600 to 800-seater aircraft for the end of the decade. But Boeing is facing a more immediate threat at the top end of the market from McDonnell Douglas. Boeing's American rival unveiled plans last week to build the MD12, a 430 to 510-seat double decker jumbo aircraft to compete against the Boeing 747-400 and the Seattle company's own longer-term plans to develop a 600 to 800-seater aircraft either by stretching the 747 or building an entirely new aircraft. Both McDonnell Douglas and Airbus are seeking partnerships in the Far East, one of the most promising markets for large jets, to help them develop their new jumbos. Airbus has already had preliminary talks with three Japanese manufacturers - Kawasaki Heavy Industries, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and Fuji Heavy Industries - to interest them in a possible equity partnership on its new jumbo project. McDonnell Douglas has been in negotiations for the past year to sell up to 49 per cent of its Douglas commercial aircraft business to Asian partners with Taiwan Aerospace leading the field. Last week, the Taiwanese company received qualified approval from its government to negotiate the purchase of up to 40 per cent of the Douglas business for Dollars 2bn. The proposed Taiwan Aerospace-Douglas deal has increasingly worried Boeing. It fears this could eventually lead to the emergence of what it calls an 'Asian Airbus'. Mr Shrontz said he hoped the deal would not force Boeing to fight another subsidised competitor. The tentative agreement reached last month between the European Commission and the US government on Airbus subsidies is expected to bring some discipline to the commercial aircraft market. The agreement will limit direct government support for future Airbus programmes to 33 per cent of their total development costs. 'We would have preferred zero subsidies and zero government involvement,' Mr Shrontz emphasised. While Boeing believes it has secured an acceptable compromise with Airbus, it fears Taiwan could distort the market because it is not a member of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (Gatt) nor of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), and therefore not bound by Gatt and OECD agreements on commercial aircraft trade. While Taiwan has made it clear that it seeks to join these organisations, it has also said it would finance up to 49 per cent of the Douglas deal with low interest loans and tax incentives. All these pressures have coincided with the worst slump in civil aviation in 40 years. And Boeing has not escaped the downturn. Although it has continued to report higher profits and sales (first quarter net profits of Dollars 441m this year represented a 43 per cent increase over the same period in 1991), Boeing is being forced to cut about 8,000 jobs this year and scale down production of its 737 narrowbody airliners from 21 a month to 14 a month next October. Rising profits have resulted from the high level of aircraft deliveries to customers and recovery in the company's military activities, while the job cuts reflect a slump in orders. Boeing does not expect any recovery in new orders until later next year. Some of its main US customers, including United Airlines, American and Delta, have announced deferrals of committed orders and significant cuts in spending. At the latest count, about 725 aircraft are lying idle in the Arizona desert. Mr Shrontz said he was optimistic about the longer-term prospects for the industry. In the short term, however, he acknowledged there was still considerable uncertainty. 'We need a couple more quarters to tell us that we are coming out of the recession and things are getting better,' he said. But Boeing says it cannot afford to wait for the recovery to be sure of retaining its 60 per cent share of the commercial jet market. Instead, the company has decided to act now. The strategy, reflecting the marketing and financial demands of airline customers, is most evident with the Dollars 5bn Boeing 777 programme. 'The real difference is the direct involvement of airline customers right at the start of the design of the aircraft,' said Mr Philip Condit, head of the 777 project and widely tipped to take over Boeing's commercial aircraft division if the new aircraft is a success. Boeing has formed 235 'design/build' teams grouping together airline designers and maintenance engineers, suppliers of components and subcontractors together with Boeing designers and engineers. These teams, devised by Mr Condit, use powerful computers which enable them to share their designs through a common database. International partners can therefore communicate directly from their headquarters. 'One of the things we are trying to do is to meet customer requirements as opposed to introducing technology for technology's sake,' Mr Condit said. This collaborative approach is also aimed at building what Boeing calls a 'consumer-driven service-ready aircraft'. Airlines have welcomed the change because it has helped them introduce specific improvements - such as the fitting of new overhead luggage bins and better-designed cabin lighting systems - more quickly. Boeing wants to reduce to a minimum the changes which normally have to be made to fix design problems during production of the aircraft and after it has been delivered to its first airline customers in 1995. In so doing, it is hoping to avoid repeating the mistakes made three years ago on the development of the 747-400, the newest member of its jumbo family. 'The scars of the 747-400 are still there,' Mr Condit conceded. Boeing was forced to delay delivery for several months of the 747-400 to initial customers because of teething problems and was also forced by airlines to make changes to its original design. 'With the 777, we want a fault-free introduction,' Mr Condit said. Boeing is introducing more electronics in the 777 than it has ever done on a new aircraft. The fly-by-wire system on the 777 will be as comprehensive as on any Airbus aircraft; Boeing is introducing liquid crystal displays in the cockpit; the 777 is the first aircraft Boeing has designed entirely by computers using a three-dimensional digital system called Catia developed by the French Dassault group; the US company is using computer-based training methods to prepare pilots and maintenance engineers; it is using new composite materials on the 777 tail and floor beams; it is also offering as an option a folding wing tip mechanism to enable the aircraft to park more easily at airport terminal gates. 'Boeing has been pushed by Airbus to develop a technically advanced aircraft. They want to overtake Airbus after the European group leapfrogged them,' explained Mr O'Sullivan of British Airways 'We are getting consistently better and cheaper Boeings because of Airbus and the competition,' he added. Mr Shrontz agreed. 'We would probably be a lot flabbier today without competition.' But with the launch of the 777 programme, 'it's bet your company time' all over again, added Mr Dick Albrecht, a Boeing executive vice-president. 'The development costs and lead times are so significant you really risk the health of the company every time you launch a new programme,' he said. And just as Boeing will start delivering the first 328-seater 777 widebody jets to customers in 1995, it will have to consider launching an even more expensive programme to develop its new jumbo aircraft. That aircraft is likely to cost more than the 777 and will inevitably force Boeing to accelerate its open-door strategy. For Boeing, survival as the industry leader will hinge on its ability to absorb such change.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Leading Article: A UK lead in Europe
DOC.TEXT: LESS THAN 18 months ago Britain was the perennial spoiler of plans hatched in Brussels and processed through the institutions of the European Community. Now it is well placed to be among the first to ratify the Maastricht treaty. Its economic policy is being shaped to ensure that in the medium term it meets the convergence criteria set forth in that document. The government remains determined to bring about the completion of the single market. It looks forward with enthusiasm to the enlargement of the EC. It wants to introduce budgetary discipline into community affairs and will try again to make sense of the agricultural policy. In sum, the United Kingdom seeks to be more than a good European; its aim is to be a leader of Europe. This is a reversal of postwar history, during which Britain has held back from, or opposed, every development proposed by France and Germany, starting with the coal and steel community. Now it is well placed to be the proposer itself, either with the two leading mainland powers, or in concert with other members. A British government has at last accepted that it is part of the European entity. This is the most striking inference to be drawn from the Queen's address to parliament yesterday. Mr John Major became prime minister in November 1990 as a result of the downfall of Mrs Margaret Thatcher; her political demise was brought about in large part by divisions among Conservatives over European policy. Those divisions persist, but Mr Major has done much to blunt the force of both the irreconcilable anti-Europeans (now reduced to a rump) and the romantic Eurofederalists. He has united most of his party around a centrist position defended with skill at Maastricht. Fundamental decisions The result was an agreement that recognises that the EC is a congeries of states, whose fundamental decisions are made in a continuing series of negotiations between its member governments. This concept has been eroded with the extension of majority voting, but the essence remains. Defence and security are not even within the EC structure. Britain stands alone in its refusal to sign the social chapter and its insistence on an opt-out clause on the single currency, but the community is learning to live with some of the idiosyncrasies of its most powerful offshore member. This general position will inform Mr Major's conduct of his government's presidency of the EC, which begins in July. To judge by his style in exploiting similar opportunities in the G7 and the security council last year, the prime minister will make the most of it. He will be helped by both pomp and circumstance. The Queen will visit the Council of Europe and address the parliament in Strasbourg next week - the first such royal visit. She will also make a state visit to France in June, and Germany in October; the European Council will meet at her palace in Edinburgh in December. Domestic discomfiture As to circumstance, the domestic discomfiture of the French president and the German chancellor, not to mention the disarray of the Italian government, weakens if only temporarily the influence of those countries. Britain is for the moment the only large European power with a stable government and sufficient energy to shape the next phase of the EC's development. The moment may, however, be short-lived. There is an apparent contradiction between the government's enthusiasm for enlargement of the community and its distaste, expressed by the foreign secretary in a speech last week, for any further structural negotiations before the agreed date of 1996. There may be only three new members by then, but that would make an already complicated structure even more unwieldy. The president of the commission, Mr Jacques Delors, will shortly circulate proposals designed to streamline the decision-making machinery before new members join the existing 12. These are likely to strengthen the commission and the parliament, probably at the expense of the intergovernmental committees that at present hold most of the reins of power. If Mr Major wants to lead opinion, and to retain the spirit of a Europe des patries, he had better come up with some proposals of his own.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Green grow the profits: Book Review
DOC.TEXT: CHANGING COURSE By Stephan Schmidheiny and the Business Council for Sustainable Development The MIT Press. Pounds 20.50 hardback, Pounds 9.95 paperback. 355 pages The business world faces a dilemma over the environment. In only a month, political leaders from more than 100 countries will gather in Rio de Janeiro for the grandly named Earth Summit. The conference halls will be packed with thousands of environmental pressure groups agitating for action. And the whole world - or such is the organisers' hope - will be watching. Who knows what will result? At the very least, the politicians will want to avoid a wasted journey by signing a commitment to get the world economy on to a more sustainable path. But they might also agree to more concrete measures, like taxation or regulation, to tackle the specific ills of global warming, deforestation and pollution. The chances of that are rather small. The run-up to the summit has exposed a world deeply divided on green issues; it cannot even agree an agenda, let alone a plan of action. But it is easy to see why some business people view Rio as an ominous prospect. They may welcome the fact that environmental issues have finally got on to the global agenda. But Rio will not simplify their life; it could make it more difficult. Much of the trouble lies in business's poor image, and the widespread view that protection of the environment and the pursuit of profit are fundamentally at odds with each other. A group of 50 top businessmen has got together to try to deal with these issues, and this book is the result of their labours. It comes very late in the day, and a lot of it will cut little ice with Mr Greenperson, but it is unquestionably one of the more important contributions to Rio. The prime mover is Stephan Schmidheiny, a little-known but highly successful Swiss businessman who was invited by the Rio organisers to become their adviser. Rather than do the job alone, he formed a business council with the top executives of companies such as Shell, ABB Asea Brown Boveri, Volkswagen, 3M, Nissan Motor and Dupont, and all have contributed from their experience. There are several strands to their message. The central ones are that business favours sustainable development, that it accepts the need for environmental policies, and that it recognises its responsibility to help the developing world out of its difficulties. In other words, greenery and profit-making can coexist. But these arguments are also highly qualified. Sustainable development must be achieved by means of free and open markets, environmental measures should be imposed through economic instruments (like taxes) rather than controls (which distort) or self-regulation (which encourages business cartels). And if business is to enrich the Third World with its technology, it must be on the basis of 'co-operation' (ie on commercial terms) rather than 'transfers' (terms mandated by government). None of this sounds specially surprising. But the book fleshes out these positions with 38 studies of businesses resolving conflicts with the environment. There is the case of New England Electric, the US utility which devised a system with its regulators that enabled it to profit if its customers reduced demand through conservation. Previously NEE's earnings had been based solely on the amount of electricity it had sold. Another case relates how Dow Chemical adopted a policy of eliminating harmful waste at source rather than by treating it at the end of the waste pipe, meaning that only a minimal amount now ends up in a landfill. In a quote that typifies much of this book, Dow's president, Frank Popoff, says: 'Surveys show that the public is sceptical of industry's efforts at environmental protection. If we fail to take the initiative, the result will be a regulatory crunch that costs us - and the public - dearly without achieving significant benefits.' Other cases show how Shell promoted local nationals in Nigeria, Henkel developed the phosphate-free detergent which eventually swept Europe, and Volkswagen designed the recyclable car. This book is undoubtedly well-intentioned, but the question is how much impact it will make. The case studies are rather predictable: the company always triumphs over adversity. This was a deliberate decision 'designed to provide positive examples to motivate others to take action', the authors say. But what a pity they did not develop a tantalising reference to 3M being forced to discard a water-based process for making audio tape because it was not good enough. This is not because, as the authors say 'too often the media focuses on errors and accidents'. It is because the world knows that business is having a tough time adjusting to environmental pressures, and it needs to be convinced that businessmen are acting out of genuine motives. As NEE chief executive John Rowe says in the book's most memorable quote: 'The rat has to smell the cheese.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Leading Article: Make Poland governable
DOC.TEXT: THROUGHOUT THEIR troubled history, Poles have found it easier to unite in common purpose against an oppressor than to work together constructively once liberation has been achieved. That pattern appears to be repeating itself. The resignation yesterday of Mr Andrzej Olechowski, finance minister in the minority coalition government headed by Mr Jan Olszewski, has underlined the fragile political basis on which post-communist Poland is built. It confirms that a continuation of economic reform will be impossible without fundamental changes to the country's political system. The immediate cause of Mr Olechowski's resignation is the inability of the government to secure a two thirds majority in parliament to overturn a controversial 1991 court decision that obliges the government to pay inflation-indexed pensions to millions of state employees. The higher social security bill will add an estimated Dollars 2.2bn to government spending and demolishes all hope of limiting this year's budget deficit to 5 per cent of gross domestic product, as agreed with the International Monetary Fund. Mr Olechowski resigned because he knows, and repeatedly told parliament, that without IMF backing Poland will not be able to make progress on debt reduction negotiations with the commercial banks, to which it owes more than Dollars 11bn. Without this, it will find it increasingly difficult to attract the private foreign equity investment it requires for future growth. Fragmented house Such considerations were ignored in yesterday's parliamentary votes, which reflected the fragmented nature of the 460-seat Sejm, or lower house of parliament. The apparent irresponsibility of parliamentarians is above all a function of the flawed electoral law under which members were elected. This has to be changed. The current system is a legacy of Poland's recent past. The electoral law, which provides for untrammelled proportional representation, was pushed through by the communists who dominated the previous parliament in a bid to improve their chances in the first free elections. The predictable result was a weak and divided parliament of 29 parties, many with only one elected member, which makes effective government impossible. This pleased the former communists, who emerged as the second largest party just behind the Democratic Union, home to many former Solidarity supporters. But it also allowed President Lech Walesa to step up his own campaign for greater presidential powers. Effective opposition Mr Walesa believes that Poland needs a new constitution, which would combine a Gaullist-style executive presidency with a parliament of fewer, but more coherent parties, capable of providing viable governments and effective parliamentary oppositions. His opponents are reluctant, however, to provide him with greater powers. They point to his unpredictable nature and his lack of understanding of economic and financial issues. After 45 years of totalitarianism, they say, participation in democracy is required, not another version of charismatic leadership. The resignation of Mr Olechowski, and the probable collapse of the government within the next few days or weeks, underlines the urgency of resolving the present conflict between the presidency and the government. This means, for a start, accelerating the work of the parliamentary commission working on a new constitution. One obvious target is to change the present proportional representation system, in particular by introducing German-style limits, to eliminate parties with less than 5 per cent of the vote. The inclusion of an element of first past the post voting would also help to create fewer but more substantial parties. Poland cannot afford a series of ineffectual governments and bickering parliaments. It needs effective government if it is to carry through the economic and social reforms required to achieve its goal of full European Community membership by the turn of the century. The EC, which has a strong interest in encouraging a stable transition in central Europe, should take every opportunity to help the Poles establish appropriate institutions.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Arts: Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme - Theatre
DOC.TEXT: In 1670 Moliere wrote the ultimate situation comedy about a man who wants to change situation, Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme. Moliere was, as Voltaire said, holding up views in general for the reprobation of mankind. The original is rapier sharp, but the National Theatre Company's latest version could not cut through a warm flan. This is theatre moyen sensuel, proud to be vulgar and undemanding, the essence of bourgeois. Moliere strove to entertain and to instruct. Gentilhomme finds him castigating the arriviste, warning against the advancement of yearning and suggesting proper self-culture instead. One sympathises with a man who wishes to better himself but does not know how. This message arrives as a series of moral choices neatly balanced, so one is instructed and flattered into recognising the dangers of pretence. One learns nothing, however, from this production. It lacks basic intelligence. The director Richard Jones succeeds in making Moliere au courant (with plenty of swearing), but has failed to use the resources of 17th-century France. This play was written in the midst of two decades which yielded Pascal's Pensees, La Rochefoucauld's Maximes and La Fontaine's Fables. Nothing of its intellectual milieu survives. The Gentilhomme has been reduced to pantomime. The production's strengths lie in its boldness: it is neither flawed nor ill-executed, just disappointing. It starts happily, with Monsieur Jourdain (very well played by Timothy Spall) amidst the competing pleasures offered by his hireling masters of Music, Dance, Fencing and Philosophy. Jourdain is quickly established as a boorish patron: 'It's always bleedin' shepherds' he says to the Maestro presenting a pastoral. His Tailor arrives to clothe him, a levee ensues; then Jourdain's unimpressed Maid (Janine Duvitski) and unimpressable wife (Anita Dobson) laugh at his pretention. The production's only joke turns on Jourdain constantly slipping into his bourgeois origins with 'You silly cow' or 'I beg you, please accept my humble apologies for the bloody behaviour of my repellent wife.' The earnestness for etiquette pervades every scene. His anxiety dominates the action and marginalises the sub-plot, in which he is duped into funding a spongeing aristocrat's amours and conned into marrying his daughter to her lover disguised as Turkish royalty. Moliere knew that manners govern general politeness, and change slowly; etiquette polices the class boundaries, and changes quickly to keep out the arriviste. But this production never probes at why Jourdain should want to recreate himself. Only once does he cry poignantly, 'There's so much I don't know.' Taste has more to do with manners than appearances, and so the best scenes of pretension, including a hugely excessive banquet, are conjured by word and deed. The brash design, however, is inventive: value-added Louis Quatorze, in pop-up storybook style, adds legs to the harpsichord and makes puffy clouds float by outside. The costumes (Nicky Gillibrand), particularly the beautifully accoutred swarm of cooks, dancers and singers, make a plain delight in a world of excess. The fine music (Jonathan Dove), altered from Moliere's collaborator, Jean-Baptiste Lully, shows that subtlety can make an impact, for the same reason that Vaux le Vicomte is a finer Chateau than Versailles: it never tries too hard. Lyttelton Theatre, in repertory (071 928 2252)

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Arts: Marlene Dietrich - Obituary
DOC.TEXT: The voice was a mellifluous foghorn. The languorous eyelids hung at half mast while the eyebrows were an elevated fantasy in mascara. And the well-lit cheekbones were rocks towards which infatuated men sailed knowingly to their destruction. Marlene Dietrich, who died yesterday in Paris, was the cinema's most exotic creation. Whether dressed for kitsch in her films with director Josef Von Sternberg or slumming it in low-budget Westerns and thrillers, she seemed a creature entirely composed of artifice. She was happy that we should see her that way. Dietrich claimed there was no connection between her public image and her well-guarded private life. Different versions of that life battled it out in the biographies. Was she born in Berlin on December 27 1901, as most books say? Yes - though she herself preferred later dates. Was The Blue Angel (1930) her first film, as she often insisted? No - it was merely her first film with Josef Von Sternberg. Before the icy master with the megaphone came on the scene, Dietrich had appeared in some 18 films in her native Germany. And as a little-known European actress she had even co-starred with another little-known European actress, Greta Garbo, in GW Pabst's 1925 Joyless Street. The Blue Angel made her world-famous: though the Dietrich she was to become later under Sternberg - haughty, mysterious, swathed in soft-focus - was a far cry from the piping cabaret vamp who sings 'Falling in love again' while doing strange things with her legs on a chair. Dietrich went to Hollywood in 1930, leaving her husband and daughter behind in Germany. An off-screen romance began between her and Sternberg, while on-screen they continued their partnership with six majestic films. The sublime and the ridiculous lie down happily together in movie romances like Morocco (1930), Dishonored (1931) and Shanghai Express (1932). And in the Sternberg-Dietrich masterpiece The Scarlet Empress (1934) Dietrich's beauty becomes merely one part, albeit the most plastic and haunting, of an astonishing fresco of scenic effects and design inspirations. The Sternberg-Dietrich films may be kitsch (her own favourite word of dismissal), but they have their own passion and conviction. Away from Sternberg, Dietrich never found the same creative spark, in either herself or her directors. She seems miscast or undercast in films like Destry Rides Again (1939), Manpower (1941), A Foreign Affair (1948) and Stage Fright (1950). And she seems worse than miscast - wheeled on as if to parody herself - in Hollywod's vain attempts to recreate the Sternbergian magic with other directors: Richard Boleslawsky's The Garden Of Allah (1936) or Mitchell Leisen's Golden Earrings (1947). In later years Dietrich's legend transferred itself effectively to the stage in her one-woman concerts. But in Hollywood after her heyday she came to be used as little more than a flavour-enhancer. Glorified cameo roles in films like Welles's Touch Of Evil (1958), Wilder's Witness For The Prosecution (1957) and Kramer's Judgment At Nuremberg (1961) showed that Dietrich, even if she could not exactly act, could smoulder interestingly. More: she could suggest better than anyone a whole non-Californian world of casbahs, cabarets and smoky enigma. Unlike Garbo, Dietrich retired reluctantly from the screen and even returned for an ill-judged guest role in Just A Gigolo (1978). Equally ill-judged, perhaps, was her cantankerous voice-only participation in Maximilan Schell's feature documentary Marlene (1985). Her bullying of interviewer-director Schell leaves a harsh aftertaste. But there is no denying the spell of that husky voice; nor, as we watch the vintage film clips, the power that those chiselled, shining, iconic features still have today.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Arts: Injuries inflicted on basic intelligence - Cinema
DOC.TEXT: A bisexual murderess stabs men to death with an ice pick just after they have sexually climaxed with her. Who is she? For adding this problem to the workload of the California police, the screenwriter of Basic Instinct Joe Eszterhas, formerly of Jagged Edge and Betrayed, was paid Dollars 3m: an all-time record for a Hollywood script. For playing the San Francisco detective who goes after her Michael Douglas was paid Dollars 14m. For directing the film, Paul Verhoeven was paid - enough: let us just say that the movie's budget was on the runaway side of Dollars 40m. As a film critic I feel an equivalent amount would compensate me for injuries to my intelligence. Basic Instinct is no Jagged Edge, even less a Fatal Attraction. It is a contrived, flashy, predictable crowd-puller, all the more disappointing for its early promise. As sexual aggression thrillers go, this one leaves the starting-block at 99 mph. We begin with a young man dying in flagrante with an unidentified blonde. We move on to Detective Douglas falling for lead suspect Sharon Stone, a bombshell who writes best-selling novels from her lavish Monterey retreat. And we are shocked as more ice-picked bodies hit the ground and Mr Douglas keeps hitting the sheets. He does so in startlingly explicit detail (for Hollywood) either with Miss Stone or with curvaceous police psychiatrist Jeanne Tripplehorn. When not being stoned or tripplehorned, Douglas occasionally does some police work. Here Basic Instinct shows its edgy best. Douglas displays a line in teeth-gritting angst worthy of father Kirk, and tension is spiced by the frequency with which the sleuths are outsmarted by the suspect. For Miss Stone discovers that by throwing nonchalant sexual candour at the Fuzz or by wearing no knickers during interrogation - five stunned police heads keep dipping whenever she uncrosses her legs - she can reduce the San Francisco PD to drooling incompetence. Yet for two hours the film asks 'Did she do the murders?' Since no definitive video evidence of them exists, whereby a Californian court could identify and acquit the culprit, Douglas must do much leg-work. And wheel-work too: a night car chase, a series of Vertigo-like trailings over San Francisco's rollercoaster hills, and a one-man shuttle service between the city and Stone's glass-and-stone mansion teetering above the Pacific whitecaps. Sadly, all this preludial stylishness gives way to hundred-horse-power hokum. Just when director Paul 'Robocop' Verhoeven has begun to prove that he can direct human beings - with fine use of focus-pulling to point up staged-in-depth conversation scenes - screenwriter Eszterhas piles on Mr V's shoulders one implausible plot twist after another. This is one of those films in which complete strangers turn out to have been at school together, or to have shared a common interest in ice picks, or to have been patrolling the same corridor when bloke X, Y or Z gets a sharp instrument through the jugular. Finally, the whole overwrought mess is cleared up, but not so tidily that a final 'twist' does not leave open the possibility of a lucrative sequel.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Management (Marketing and Advertising): Getting customers taped - Philips has discovered at last the value of promotion, and is belatedly looking for ways to win over the consumer
DOC.TEXT: Next month, an eye-catching dome big enough to house 80 people will go on the road in the UK, visiting shopping centres. The dome is a promotional gimmick from Philips, not best known for its clever marketing techniques. The 'Entechdome' as it is called, will carry demonstration booths for products which the Dutch group hopes will become hits in the consumer electronics market. Philips is demonstrating a new-found eagerness to reach out to consumers. After years at the mercy of its Japanese competitors, it has discovered that good marketing can make a difference. It reckons that the travelling demonstration booth - a technique borrowed from Japan - is a better way to publicise its products than conventional advertising. The change in attitude is reflected in 'Operation Centurion', which Jan Timmer, Philips' president, says will 'call entrenched views and habits into question' and shake the company out of its traditional complacency. When the programme was introduced a year ago, Philips was in dire need of a shake-up. Not only was it making heavy losses, it had become a symbol of what was wrong with much of European industry - it had superior technology but could not bring it successfully to the market. Its experience with video cassette recorders is a case in point. Philips was the first company to make VCRs commercially available. Yet its own machine, called V2000, which it confidently brought to the market as technically better than competing products, was a flop because of a shortage of pre-recorded tapes in the V2000 format. Meanwhile, the VHS format, which was widely judged to be technically inferior, was skilfully marketed by the Japanese, and has become the de facto industry standard. Philips had a similar experience with Laservision, its laser disc player which failed to win over consumers largely as a result of a distribution fiasco and marketing failure. Philips did not bother to ensure that the discs were sold with the players and, more often than not, salesmen could not even tell consumers where to buy them. While its Japanese competitors were busy brushing up their publicity acts, selling products which were largely based on foreign technology, Philips appeared to be sleeping unbothered in Eindhoven, the small Dutch town where it is based. But the group believes it has finally learnt its lesson. 'We've been through all the problems now,' says a spokesman. As a result, the group's philosophy has changed substantially, it says. No longer expecting products to sell on superior technology alone, it is paying more attention to consumer needs and preferences, industry trends and product design. It has set up a number of task forces charged with keeping up to date on trends in different markets and developing a greater awareness of customers' demands. Earlier this year it hosted a Customer Day when Timmer addressed 100,000 Philips employees throughout the world on the subject of customer responsiveness. The company's new approach, it says, is illustrated by its approach to the digital compact cassette. The cassette tapes, which will be available in September, were developed after extensive market research showed a need for a product to replace conventional audio tapes, which have seen sales fall in the past few years. 'You're actually starting from a marketing need rather than take a technology and try to find a market for it,' says a spokesman. Philips is also working to improve its corporate image and product design - two areas which, it now accepts, have an impact on competitiveness. Where it had - by its own admission - been old-fashioned in product design, it is now trying to revamp its image with products that are aesthetically satisfying as well as of high technical quality. Its new range of sophisticated audio and video products, called the Philips Collection, have a simple and elegant look. Consumers' perception of Philips' products will inevitably influence their view of Philips as a corporation. But Philips has no illusions about the challenge it faces in trying to revamp its image as a safe, if dull, company. The company is looking on enviously at the clever marketing of Sony, which is aiming electronic products at children with the catch-phrase 'My First Sony'. Those children who receive their 'First Sony' will grow up with a feeling of fondness for the Japanese manufacturer's products which they are likely to retain as adults. Philips hopes the purchase of Whittle, a US company which produces educational software, will help it in a similar way by introducing schoolchildren to Philips' products at an early stage. Many observers believe the steps it is now taking to shake up the group have been long overdue. Some still have their doubts as to whether the changes have come in time for the group to regain competitiveness in an increasingly difficult environment. Many of the changes have been accepted practice at Japanese electronics manufacturers for years. The success of those companies has been founded not only on the quality of their products, but on skilful marketing. If Japanese manufacturers are to be taken as a benchmark, Philips still has a lot of catching up to do.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Technology: Androids on the march - After years on the breadline, modern robots are finding gainful employment in Europe
DOC.TEXT: In the US fashion industry they call it 'localised abrasion' - the pre-worn look for denim jeans produced by applying potassium permanganate solution to the knee, thigh and seat areas. The faded effect has traditionally been achieved through manual spraying, but consistency and quality control have been hard to achieve. Now GMFanuc Robotics has perfected a robotic solution that is three times faster than manual spraying, can reproduce a spray pattern to an accuracy of 0.03 inch, and can be programmed easily to handle a wide range of garments. The system is a relatively simple example of recent trends in the industrial robotics industry, which is trying to reduce its dependence on comparatively mature automotive markets and find new applications elsewhere. It is a trend that is particularly important for robot suppliers in the European market, where the overall penetration of robots into industry is much lower than in Japan, and where a potentially huge market for non-automotive applications remains untapped. According to Massimo Mattucci, vice president for engineering and marketing at Comau of Italy, around 50 per cent of industrial robots installed in Europe are in use in the automotive industry and 20 per cent in electronics -the reverse of the situation in Japan. 'The automotive industry has more or less understood the potential of robots,' says Stelio Demark, head of ABB Robotics, Europe's largest producer, although he stresses, along with other robot industry executives, the potential of robots in the paint-spraying and final assembly area of European vehicle manufacturing. The inherent flexibility of modern robots, and the advances made in control systems and mechanics that have increased their speed and reliability, ought to increase their suitability for small-batch manufacturing in Europe, where model changes are frequent. Demark sees new opportunities for robots emerging in the European food, packaging, pharmaceutical and white goods industries. But the pace at which European industry accepts robots will depend partly on suppliers' ability to counter the mistrust caused by the hype of the 1970s and early 1980s, when the robot industry appeared to be carried away by euphoria over business prospects. There are other obstacles, too, for suppliers to surmount. In Japan, one of the driving forces behind the growth in the industrial robot population to 274,210 in 1990 - nearly 10 times the population in the former West Germany -has been labour shortages. 'Everything has to come back to economic considerations,' says Axel Gerhardt, an executive board member of IWKA, the holding company for Kuka, Germany's largest robot supplier. 'In Europe robots are used where it is economical to do so. In Japan the question is often whether to produce with a robot or not to produce there at all.' Mistakes have also been made in the installation of robots, for which the suppliers and customers have to share the blame. 'People have tended to put in a robot, then have an operator standing by watching,' says Demark. 'This is a half-way house that I wouldn't recommend.' Increasingly, robot suppliers are realising that if they are to make inroads into the small- and medium-sized businesses that still dominate European industry - especially outside the automotive sector - they have to understand better the customer's needs and worries. 'You have to enter into an economic calculation with the customer and demonstrate the ability to find a solution,' says Mattucci. That could mean being paid only for a feasibility study that comes down against the use of robots. But in the long run this approach makes more sense for an industry that wants to broaden its customer base and maintain its reputation. Comau, which sells most of its robots as part of an integrated automation package, is around 90 per cent dependent on the vehicle industry. Mattucci wants to expand the remaining 10 per cent of the business to 30 per cent over the next five years by exploiting the group's strengths in robotics for body-welding, mechanical assembly and difficult handling operations. The Italian company's most ambitious step away from the automotive sector is its involvement in the Columbus Automation and robotics Testbed (Cat) programme financed by the European Space Agency. The ground testbed for the automation and robotics on board the projected Columbus Space Station will incorporate a new Comau robot using advanced materials such as aeronautical alloys and composites. A more-down-to earth approach to broadening the customer base is in evidence at GMFanuc, the US/Japanese concern which is the world's second biggest supplier. The jean-spraying robot, developed in the US and now available in the UK, offers a high return on investment with a payback of less than a year, says Mike Wilson, the UK sales and marketing manager. Robotics are also in their infancy in the European food industry, partly because it has hitherto been difficult to turn a hose on to a robot to clean it without ruining its electrical circuits. In January, GMFanuc launched its 'Washdown' robot to conform to the strict hygiene requirements of the food industry and withstand all the chemical substances likely to be used in washdown or wipedown procedures. In the European electronics industry, robots are more frequent but applications are still developing. Data Packaging, an Irish supplier of plastic moulded components for the computer industry, recently installed an ABB Robotics painting cell to handle metallic paints used to provide an attractive finish, and assist in electrical shielding, on parts for the Apple Macintosh. Metallic paints are hard to handle because they block supply lines if not kept flowing continuously. The ABB system programs the robot to fire the spray gun if the system lays dormant for a given length of time. Advances such as these are often based on techniques originally developed for the automotive industry, which is not being neglected in suppliers' haste to exploit other markets. A number of fairly recent technologies have relevance to the use of robots in automotive and non-automotive fields. Laser welding, says Wilson, is attracting interest in a number of industries, including aerospace, because of its precision and speed. Unlike conventional spot welding, the robot does not have to reach both sides of the part to be welded. Another emerging technology, especially when combined with robotics, is water-jet cutting, which is likely to become increasingly important for cutting plastics quickly and cleanly. It is already being used in the automotive industry for cutting carpets, door panels and instrument panels. In both areas robot suppliers are forming partnerships with companies which have developed the technologies so that they can exploit the opportunities quicker. Comau has a co-operation agreement with Trumpf, the German machine tool builder best-known for its laser-cutting machines, while last year ABB Robotics formed a joint venture with Ingersoll-Rand of the US to develop and market a robotised water-jet cutting system in Europe. The search for a broader European customer base coincides with a much more price-conscious attitude over the past two to three years among customers, due as much to general business conditions as to scepticism about the early claims made by robot suppliers. Suppliers are rationalising their product ranges to give customers what they want and no more, but using developments in control systems to increase the applications available from each model. These conditions give advantages and disadvantages in more or less equal measure to European suppliers and Japanese/US importers, which control one third of the market. Demark and Mattucci strongly believe that the European suppliers benefit from a approach based on solutions rather than products. 'The Japanese do not have the solutions for European needs,' says Mattucci flatly. This is a view strongly disputed by the Japanese producers, but in a price-sensitive market the the Japanese do have the advantage of size - investment in control systems, in particular, can be spread over a bigger sales base. Ultimately, though, all the robot suppliers could benefit if they can persuade more European companies of the benefits of robots. And that is likely to be a gradual process where technology is only one factor in the equation.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Technology: Striking it rich in the deep blue sea
DOC.TEXT: 'WE GO where no one else dares,' boasts an engineer from the deep-sea drilling team of Petrobras, Brazil's state oil monopoly. At 625 metres, the company's Platform XIII in the Marlim oilfield off the coast of Rio de Janeiro is the world's deepest in production. Petrobras's efforts were rewarded earlier this week with the Offshore Technology Conference Award for Distinguished Achievement - the oil industry's most prestigious technology prize. The company has been breaking records for deep sea oil production since 1986 when it put into commercial operation a well at a depth of 384m. 'Having identified oil in deeper waters we realised we needed to develop the technologies to make this production viable,' says Roberto Jardim, director of deep-sea production at Petrobras. Since then the company has been going deeper and deeper, breaking depth records for installation of monobuoys, manifolds and submerged pipelines. In March of last year it broke through the 750m barrier at its Marlim field. Previously, 350m was considered the limit because it is the maximum depth at which divers can work. Most platforms in the North Sea and the Gulf of Mexico are at less than 200m. Petrobras was forced to go deeper because Brazil's main oil reserves lie in water as deep as 3,000m. Until the late 1970s the country was importing 80 per cent of its oil needs but the combination of two oil shocks sent the bill soaring. In addition, the debt crisis which cut off access to foreign capital made it imperative for Brazil to start exploiting its own reserves. 'Unlike other companies which test new equipment exhaustively before use we like to develop our equipment on site even though this may mean interrupting production. We can do this because we have the advantage of real fields to test in so we can move quickly to make the process economic,' says Jardim. Mainly as a result of its deep-sea successes Brazil now imports only 40 per cent of its 1.2m barrel per day needs. The Campos Basin, where Petrobras's wells are located, accounts for more than 60 per cent of Brazil's oil production. It has estimated reserves of 6bn barrels in a 100,000 sq km area ranging from the coast to a depth of 3,000m. The secret of the company's success, according to Petrobras technicians, is the combination of a 'wet Christmas tree' and a deep-sea robot. A 'wet Christmas tree' is oil industry jargon for the pipe and valve mechanism placed on a wellhead to control flow before oil can be pumped out. Conventional oilfields use steel-lines or divers to guide the positioning. But fields such as Marlim are too deep to use these methods - at 720m where the first Marlim well was completed the pressure is 14 times that of the earth's atmosphere. The Petrobras breakthrough was achieved by using a satellite signal to direct the tree into its place on the wellhead, guided by the giant eye (in the form of a video camera) of a robot lowered on to the seabed. Oil from such sub-sea wells is pumped to a floating pier to which ships can anchor in the open sea, making it possible to load safely in the Campos Basin. The company has 11 such floating production systems. 'These have been very important in leading our deep-sea drilling because they enable us to go into production within a year of discovery, giving quick returns,' says Jardim. According to Petrobras officials, production costs for Marlim are Dollars 8 per barrel - competitive with other offshore operations. Deep-sea production will be the biggest contributor in the company's plans to increase production from 650,000 barrels per day to 1m by the end of 1994. 'We want to go deeper still,' says Ernesto Weber, former Petrobras chief. The company aims to break the 2,000m depth mark by the end of this decade.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Accountancy Column: Outlook for merger mania in the early 1990s
DOC.TEXT: IF THE authoritative history of accountancy were ever yo bewritten, somewhere towards the end there would have to be a chapter called 'Merger Mania', charting the acquisitions of the late 1980s. A question now facing firms is whether it would also have to cover the more cautious era of the early 1990s. While the recession bites home and the taste of merged firms being digested grows increasingly bitter, rumours of a new wave of acquisitions are beginning to surface. The latest candidates to be mentioned are BDO Binder Hamlyn and Pannell Kerr Forster, which were respectively seventh and ninth by fee income last year. Both vigorously deny it. Whatever the truth of these particular cases, the consensus among managing partners is that many firms are coming under competitive pressure and the total number must shrink. None admits, though, that their own practice faces any difficulties. This has led to a new game played by journalists and the recipients of their telephone calls within accountancy offices. The Accounting Standards Board may be tightening up on the imaginative skills of the creative practitioners, but merger gossip has provided a new outlet for invention. Last season's version - which still continues - involved the issue of partner redundancies. Some firms adamantly deny that any have taken place. Most favour a more circuitous response: they stress that partners cannot be made redundant. Instead, they take early retirement, or depart voluntarily after deciding that their aims and those of the firm are no longer compatible. The 1992 variant - for countering talk of mergers - adopts the same technique. You can get a straight denial - though generally in a tone of voice that does not suggest the 'true and fair' pledge of an audit report. More typically, you hear an oblique comment using language which leaves the options open. 'We are not in merger discussions with anyone,' says an exasperated Mr Chris Swinson, national managing partner of Binder Hamlyn. 'I haven't even looked for the phone number of a dating agency .. But one keeps one's eyes open.' Mr Richard Pearson, national managing partner at Pannell Kerr Forster, sighs wearily: 'There is no strength to the rumours. From time to time one has discussions about discussions .. Of course, if the opportunity arises, we will certainly consider it.' There is no doubt that accountancy firms have been severely hit by the recession. Demand has dropped for non-essential services, such as management consultancy, and for activities linked to periods of economic growth like corporate finance. Insolvency work may have prospered, but it remains a small proportion of income for most firms.
