Statutory audits continue to command large revenues, but companies are increasingly putting this work out to tender and maintaining a tight ceiling on the fees charged. Meanwhile, costs have escalated sharply. Mergers have left the combined firms with substantial overheads including considerable surplus staff and excess property when they could least them. Corporate litigation is also fast expanding. Accountants, armed with professional indemnity insurance, have proved a tempting target for aggrieved users of accounts looking for recompense. When figures on fee income and employment are released by the top firms in June, they are likely to look bleak. Undisclosed internal accounts showing the falls in profitability will probably be gloomier still. This does not bode well for mergers driven by strategic reasons between two equal complementary partners, rather than as a panic-stricken survival measure by from ailing firms. But Mr Hugh Aldous, managing partner of Robson Rhodes, suggests that is nothing new. 'None of the mergers in the late 1980s was motivated by strategic cleverness. Despite all the hype from the firms' press offices about strategy, it is now clear that they were all driven by economic necessity.' He argues that the entire accountancy profession has come under pressure and many partners from leading firms are now on the job market. Mr Aldous believes the 'Big 6' - Coopers & Lybrand Deloitte, KPMG Peat Marwick, Ernst & Young, Price Waterhouse, Arthur Andersen, Touche Ross - are likely to survive because of their very strong reputation and the stranglehold they have on the largest clients. Some of the smaller firms will probably fade away, he thinks, while the group of six or eight firms below the premier league are likely to shrink to two or three over the next few years. Those which survive - among which Aldous naturally counts Robson Rhodes - will have to offer 'the same calibre of thinking' as the Big 6, while acting increasingly as advisers to individuals and private companies. A number of his competitors share the view of a shrinking middle tier, while putting up equally strong arguments for their own position as survivors. Among the most notable is Grant Thornton, eighth largest by fee income, which embarked three years ago on a strategy to concentrate on advisory work to small and medium-sized businesses. 'I don't think any firm outside the Big 6 which has a significant part of its income from the audit market can have a strong future,' says Mr David McDonnell, national managing partner. He believes two of the Big 6 firms may yet merge to create five large players, while a number of medium-sized firms are likely to have to seek partners in order to survive. The structure of Binder Hamlyn, by contrast, continues to be modelled in many ways on the Big 6 firms and it retains a number of large company audit clients. Mr Swinson is confident that such a role is sustainable. 'We have preserved a reasonable air of professionalism, and avoided the more rapacious moves of our competitors,' he says. Mr Paul Hipps, senior partner at Stoy Hayward, says: 'We have certainly sharpened up our act, putting enormous emphasis on quality and working hard talking to people to secure whatever business is around.' His firm has heavily cultivated family-owned businesses. Mr Peter Orenstein, senior partner with Casson Beckman, argues that his firm is not in the so-called 'second tier' but is at the top of a 'third tier'. He suggests that the second tier firms are coming under considerable pressure squeezed by both the Big 6 firms and the third tier. Many do not have the strong international networks of the larger firms, but have large overheads than their smaller competitors. 'We are small enough to be flexible and give clients the personal attention of individual partners, but large enough to have the specialist expertise they need,' Mr Orenstein says. 'We are certainly not under any pressure to merge. But that doesn't mean if a firm comes along with a proposal of some merit we would put up a brickwall. That would be foolish.' If further mergers do occur, one result will be a growing headache for regulators. Fewer firms will threaten both competition and independence. It is already difficult to find firms not subject to conflict of interest in a large and complex case such as the collapse of the Maxwell empire. Mr Swinson remains unconcerned by the rumours about BDO. He has flown off to Singapore on assignment and said before his departure: 'I would hardly be leaving if we were about to merge, would I?'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Wellcome supports gene map project
DOC.TEXT: THE Medical Research Council (MRC) and Wellcome Trust are joining forces to set up a genetic research centre in Cambridge. The centre, which will have a budget of several million pounds a year, will extend a research project led by Dr John Sulston of the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge. Early this year Dr Sulston was considering an offer to join a genetics company in the US - a prospect that dismayed British genetic researchers - but the prospect of new funding has persuaded him to stay in the UK. Dr Sulston is working out the genome - the entire genetic blueprint - of the nematode worm C. elegans, which provides a simplified model of the human genome. The centre will continue the worm genome project and begin to apply its lessons to the much larger task of finding the sequence of chemical 'letters' in the 100,000 human genes. Several sites in Cambridge are being considered for it. The research will have strong international links, especially with the US, France and Japan. The Wellcome Trust is the world's largest medical charity, with a budget of more than Pounds 100m a year - half as much as the state-funded MRC - derived mainly from its majority stake in the Wellcome drug company.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Warhol silkscreen sold for Dollars 2m: Saleroom
DOC.TEXT: A SILKSCREEN creation by Andy Warhol depicting 210 Coca-Cola bottles massed in seven lines sold for Dollars 2m (Pounds 1.17m) at Christie's in New York on Tuesday night. The buyer was Thomas Ammann, a Zurich dealer. The price was below Christie's optimistic estimate of up to Dollars 2.8m but the fact that the work sold for such a comparatively high sum will reassure the contemporary art market, which has suffered a two-year decline. The sale of 68 lots totalled Dollars 11.26m and was 18 per cent unsold. Christie's had turned away works it considered unsaleable and had insisted on low reserves on lots it did accept. That ensured that the great majority sold, often close to their low estimate. The painting 'Untitled' by Cy Twombly went for Dollars 660,000, also below estimate, but 'The Ocean' by Hans Hofmann was at the top of its forecast, making Dollars 550,000. Christie's also offered 25 works from the vast collection amassed by the late Frederik Roos. All but one sold and new auction records were set for two of the UK's leading contemporary sculptors, Tony Cragg and Barry Flanagan. Cragg's 'Three Cast Bottles', executed in 1988 and consisting of three vast bronze canisters, sold for Dollars 99,000. Flanagan's 'Acrobats', showing one of his famous hares balancing another, one of an edition of five, made Dollars 93,500 slightly below the Dollars 100,000-Dollars 150,000 estimate.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Business park
DOC.TEXT: A BUSINESS park at Penrhyndeudraeth on the edge of Snowdonia national park in north Wales is to be developed in a Pounds 15m joint scheme by the Development Board for Rural Wales and the Royal Institute of British Architects.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Esso raises petrol prices
DOC.TEXT: ESSO raised the price of four-star petrol by 4.6p a gallon to 240.5p from midnight last night. The price per litre is 52.9p. The price of unleaded rose 5.9p a gallon to 220.5p (48.5p a litre) and diesel by 4.5p to 212.3p (46.7p).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Nadir investment concern wound up
DOC.TEXT: SOUTH AUDLEY Management, the private investment vehicle owned by family trusts of Mr Asil Nadir, chairman of Polly Peck International, was compulsorily wound up in the High Court in London yesterday. The order was made on a petition presented by Kansallis-Osake-Pankki, a trade creditor for Pounds 300,000.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Warrant issued for De Lorean
DOC.TEXT: THE RUC Fraud Squad was yesterday granted a warrant for the arrest of Mr John De Lorean, the American whose Belfast car company crashed 10 years ago, after receiving Pounds 70m in government money. Last week Mr Fred Bushell, former Lotus Car Company chief, admitted he conspired with Mr De Lorean and others to defraud De Lorean Motor Company of nearly Pounds 10m. The US statute of limitations means Mr De Lorean cannot be brought back against his will.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Engineers urge better technology teaching
DOC.TEXT: AN EIGHT-POINT plan to promote technology teaching in schools was put forward yesterday by the Engineering Council, Andrew Adonis writes. The plan calls for a practical technology curriculum, based on the design and manufacture of products and systems. It was written by Professor Alan Smithers and Dr Pamela Robinson of Manchester University's education department. They say technology is poorly taught in schools in spite of its inclusion as a core subject in the national curriculum. It is mainly concerned with generalised problem solving without specific knowledge or practical application. Technology in the National Curriculum. Engineering Council, 10 Maltravers Street, London WC2R 3ER. Free.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Economic Indicators
FT 07 MAY 92 / Smithfield site row resolved in court
DOC.TEXT: THE High Court yesterday resolved a centuries-old dispute between the Crown and the Corporation of London concerning the Smithfield meat market in favour of the corporation. Mr Justice Hoffmann decided that the corporation owned a plot of land between St Bartholomew's Hospital and the meat market in the north of the City of London, the ownership of which has been contested for at least 350 years. The dispute came to a head with an idea to move the meat market and redevelop the Smithfield site. Moving the outdated market has been supported by many tenants, concerned about the rising costs of remaining in the City, and by alternative sites, such as New Covent Garden, the fruit and vegetable market in Battersea. Nevertheless the Corporation of London is determined to keep the meat market in the City and it recently approved a Pounds 50m refurbishment programme to comply with EC hygiene regulations. The land was given to the City under a charter granted by Henry VI in 1444. The High Court yesterday rejected the Crown's argument that it had retained the ownership of the site under the 1638 charter. The judge said that his reading of the charter was that it had given Smithfield to the City, although for the limited use of holding markets and fairs.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Sharp drop in company failures
DOC.TEXT: THE NUMBER of companies passing into receivership and administration last month dropped to the lowest level since December 1990, indicating possible economic recovery, figures from accountancy firm Touche Ross showed yesterday. There were 389 receivership and administration appointments, according to statistics derived from the London and Edinburgh Gazettes, compared with 527 in March and 441 in April last year. Mr Christopher Morris, national director of corporate special services at Touche Ross, said the decline was 'indicative' of support from banks towards companies to which they have loaned money. 'This shows grounds for very cautious optimism,' he said. 'But one swallow doesn't make a summer. We can be much clearer about a trend when we see the May and June figures.' The proportion of appointments for last month fell in London and the south-east - further evidence that the effects of the recession, which affected the region particularly badly, may be receding. There were 30 per cent fewer appointments in the service sector than last year, while there were sharp increases among wholesaling and distribution, hotel and catering, and retail. Mr Morris cautioned that business failures normally peak 18 months after the bottom of a recession, partly because companies are unable to borrow money as they expand. He said banks also sometimes called in receivers when they saw the prospect of recovering the value of assets in companies to which they had made loans. However, his recent discussions with banks had disclosed that a decreasing number of companies were in their 'intensive care' departments on the brink of insolvency. National Westminster was the bank that most commonly called in receivers and administrators, with 97 appointments, followed by Barclays, Lloyds and Midland. Bank of Scotland and the Royal Bank of Scotland also saw an increase in appointments, which Touche Ross said reflected the increase in failures in Scotland and the north. Coopers & Lybrand was awarded the largest number of appointments.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World standard training targets to be promoted
DOC.TEXT: THE GOVERNMENT is for the first time actively to support the promotion of world-class targets for training. Mrs Gillian Shephard, the employment secretary, in a letter to the chairmen of the 82 Training and Enterprise Councils, said one of her main goals was to raise awareness of national education and training targets. The targets were initially set by the government but were abandoned by her predecessor, Mr Michael Howard, who subsequently supported their voluntary resurrection by the Confederation of British Industry. Mr Howard never said they were one of his priorities. Tecs will be responsible at local level for working towards the ambitious targets, which include 80 per cent of young people reaching National Vocational Qualifications (NVQs) at level two by 1996. At present, 40 per cent achieve that level. Resources will be provided at national level to promote the targets through the National Training Task Force, a group of senior business leaders. Mrs Shephard, in her letter to the 82 Tecs, outlined six goals that she wanted to achieve in the Tec area. She will discuss them today when she meets G10, the group of 10 chairmen of Tecs that represents the common concerns of the movement to government. G10 will present its own agenda for change at the meeting. Tecs are concerned about various issues, including cuts in training budgets this year which they claim may affect the quality of training. Mrs Shephard will find it as difficult as her predecessor to fight for more funds from the Treasury but Tecs believe she may take a more active approach to promoting them. Mrs Shepard's goals are: raising awareness of and securing commitments to targets and securing their delivery; boosting the performance of Investors in People; promotion of Tecs, defence of their budgets and clarification of their relationship with government; and taking forward work on women's issues.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Stores' view of married women 'outdated'
DOC.TEXT: MARRIED WOMEN are finding themselves in a 'ghetto of part-time work' because of managers' outdated assumptions about attitudes to jobs, according to research by Lancaster University into employment in the retail sector. While married women were thought to be reliable, loyal and flexible, it was also assumed they would take time off because of their children and give their husbands' careers precedence, the report found. The majority of the supermarket employees studied were part-timers, and most of those were married women. Stores surveyed were Asda, J. Sainsbury, Marks and Spencer, Littlewoods and EH Booth branches in the Lancaster area. Employment Patterns in Contemporary Retailing. Roger Penn and Betty Wirth. Department of Sociology, Lancaster University, LA1 4YL. Pounds 50.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / House prices fall 1 per cent
DOC.TEXT: HOUSE PRICES fell 1 per cent last month, according to seasonally adjusted figures from Halifax Building Society. It was the sixth consecutive monthly fall, but Halifax said it expected the clear Tory win at the election to rekindle confidence, with prices stabilising later this year. That would be followed by a gentle rise before Christmas and a strengthening in 1993. The Council of Mortgage Lenders said the winter and election uncertainties had kept mortgage lending subdued in the first quarter but the interest rate cuts should help it to pick up. Gross mortgage advances in the three months fell to Pounds 12.8bn from Pounds 14.9bn in the previous quarter. New lending fell nearly 15 per cent to Pounds 4.6bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Smaller building societies complain over large rivals
DOC.TEXT: DOMINATION of the Building Societies Association by larger societies is forcing their smaller counterparts to consider new ways of representing their interests, chiefs of the smaller societies claimed yesterday. The smaller societies said at the annual BSA conference in Bournemouth that they were unable to secure adequate representation in the association and that the interests of the 20 largest societies had diverged from those of the smallest 65. They complain privately that the industry's leaders are putting pressure on them to surrender their independence through mergers. Many of the small ones are smaller than most branches of Halifax, the largest society. In the past two years, several informal gatherings of small building societies have begun to meet regularly outside the BSA. There is also a small-societies forum at which common issues are discussed. Some executives in smaller societies say privately that this week's cuts in mortgage rates by the larger societies are partly intended to put pressure on smaller lenders. The small societies are also unhappy at remarks by Halifax Building Society that it is not a lender of last resort guaranteeing savings deposits in smaller societies. However, they have not yet declared an open revolt and appear reluctant to face the possibility that they might eventually have to set up a trade association of their own. Halifax and BSA officials yesterday disclaimed any knowledge of unrest. Nationwide, the second-largest society, is cutting the rate for new borrowers by 0.29 points to 10.7 per cent on loans of up to Pounds 60,000; by 0.25 points to 10.3 per cent for Pounds 60,000 to Pounds 120,000; and by 0.4 points to 10 per cent for Pounds 120,000 to Pounds 300,000. TSB has cut its rate for new borrowers from 10.95 per cent to 10.65 per cent. Neither has announced when existing borrowers will see a reduction. Complaints against societies are expected to have doubled in the year to the end of March, building societies ombudsman Mr Stephen Edell said yesterday in Bournemouth. Changes to savings rates and difficulties with cash machines top the list.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Hammersmith in court over interest rate swaps
DOC.BYLINE: By RAYMOND HUGHES, Law Courts Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: CHEMICAL Bank went to the High Court in London yesterday to claim Pounds 2.94m from the London Borough of Hammersmith and Fulham in an action arising from the interest rate swaps debacle. The action is one of six lead cases selected from the multiplicity of litigation between banks and local authorities that followed the House of Lords ruling in January last year that all swaps deals were invalid because they had been outside councils' legal powers. The ruling left 80 banks facing losses of about Pounds 560m on swap transactions with 130 councils. Their only recourse was to try to recover about a quarter of their losses by suing councils for funds they earned by writing swap contracts. The lead cases were selected because they covered most of the points of law arising from the Lords' ruling. The intention was that they would enable the court to give guidance for the remaining cases and reduce litigation. That intention was frustrated when four of the lead cases were settled out of court. The opening of Chemical Bank's claim was delayed for an hour by last-minute discussions at the door of the court yesterday. Although they did not bear immediate fruit, negotiations are continuing and it seems unlikely that the case will run its estimated six weeks before terms are agreed. Mr Richard Southwell QC, for Chemical Bank, told Mr Justice Hirst that the bank, which had made two swaps contracts with Hammersmith in March 1988, had assumed that local authorities entering into such transactions were hedging their interest rate risks as end users. It had been a considerable surprise to the bank to learn during the litigation that led to the Lords' ruling that in its contracts with Chemical, Hammersmith had been trading for profit in the swaps market and acting as an intermediary between the bank and two rate-capped London councils, Haringey and Camden. If Chemical had known the true position, it would not have entered into the contracts. Its policy in relation to swaps had been not to deal with rate-capped councils. Hammersmith now contended that intermediation could be justified as amounting to the management of interest risks on its debts. The council's defence was that Chemical had voluntarily assumed the risk that the deals might prove to be beyond Hammersmith's powers and its payments to the council had therefore been voluntary and irrecoverable. Mr Southwell said it was a somewhat remarkable proposition that a bank would voluntarily hand over large sums on such a basis. He said Hammersmith had been party to 592 swaps deals involving a notional Pounds 6bn. The potential loss to its ratepayers - had the Lords not ruled such transactions void - would have been Pounds 194.2m. The fact that Hammersmith had been saved from making good that loss could be taken into account when considering whether it was reasonable for it to make restitution to Chemical Bank, Mr Southwell said. The hearing continues today.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Sega in Pounds 2m TV sponsorship deal
DOC.TEXT: SEGA Europe, the video games manufacturer, is to pay Pounds 2m to Independent Television for sponsorship rights of the European football championship, to be played in Sweden between June 10 and 26. Sega will use the deal to market its products in a variety of ways, including television commercials, a national consumer competition, point-of-sale promotions and dealership marketing drives.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Roadchef staff breach Pounds 3.40
DOC.TEXT: THE LOWEST-paid workers in Roadchef, the motorway services organisation, have breached the Pounds 3.40 an hour barrier - the level the Labour Party selected for a national minimum wage - after a 6 per cent pay rise for all staff. As part of the two-year deal it was agreed staff would get a rise related to the retail prices index next year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / BBC will face industrial action
DOC.TEXT: MEMBERS of Bectu, the broadcasting union, have voted narrowly for industrial action at the BBC in protest over cuts and restructuring. Bectu said a half-day stoppage on May 15 might affect some live television and radio news and current affairs programmes.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Rise in number of overseas visitors
DOC.TEXT: THE British Tourist Authority said 900,000 long-haul travellers visited the UK in the first two months of the year, nearly 50 per cent more than in the same period last year. In January and February the total number of overseas visitors was 2.1m, up 18 per cent.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Pit may be sold to rival bidder
DOC.TEXT: BRITISH COAL is to turn to the rival bidder in the competition to reopen Monktonhall colliery near Edinburgh after a consortium of mineworkers failed to produce the finance needed to operate the pit. It will invite Caledonian Mining, based at Newark, Notts, to pursue its interest.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Fininvest out of Channel 5 contest
DOC.TEXT: FININVEST Group, controlled by Mr Silvio Berlusconi, the Italian TV entrepreneur, yesterday said it would no longer submit a television licence bid for Channel 5, which is scheduled to start broadcasting by early 1995. Its decision leaves The Entertainment Channel - a consortium including the UK commercial breakfast broadcaster TV-am, the Daily Telegraph group and Time Warner - and Five TV - a company backed by Mr Moses Znaimer founder of City TV in Toronto - as declared intended bidders. Bids must be with the Independent Television Commission by July.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Early independence urged for central banks
DOC.TEXT: THE NATIONAL central banks of the European Community should be made independent as soon as possible after the planned start in January 1994 of stage two of European economic and monetary union, Mr Erik Hoffmeyer, the Danish central bank governor, said yesterday. Mr Hoffmeyer, who also chairs the committee of EC central bank governors, said central bank independence would improve the co-ordination of EC monetary policy, which is an important part of moves towards Emu. He was giving the 11th annual Mais lecture at the City University Business School in London. Mr Hoffmeyer was careful not to mention any EC central bank by name. However, his remarks are likely to renew controversy about the status of the Bank of England. The Bank has made no secret about wanting more independence. The Treasury acknowledges that the Bank will have to be independent if Britain moves with other EC member states to full monetary union in the third and final stage of Emu but the government has rejected earlier independence for the Bank because monetary policy will remain a national responsibility and it says that should be accountable to parliament. Mr Hoffmeyer also criticised the Emu provisions of the Maastricht treaty for being 'weaker than appropriate'. He noted that monetary policy would be concentrated in the European System of Central Banks once full Emu had been established, while governments would very largely retain responsibility for fiscal policy. As a result, a close relationship between the future European central banking system and 12 national decision-making units in fields other than monetary policy would be difficult. Although Mr Hoffmeyer said the proposed Emu blueprint 'is definitely a workable proposition', he expressed concern about how it would operate. Lines of liaison would have to be created between the future EC monetary authority and national economic policy-making units. Such lines would be weaker than existing links at the national level. 'This implies that the system will be more vulnerable,' he warned. 'There will be a higher risk that tensions will create dissatisfaction at the national level.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / GEC joins battle for Pounds 2bn deal: Three vie for helicopter order
DOC.TEXT: THE GEC group joined the US helicopter manufacturer, Bell Helicopter Textron, yesterday to compete for a Pounds 2bn contract to supply anti-tank helicopters to the British Army. The agreement between GEC and Bell brings a third leading contender to the contest, which is expected to be the biggest in UK arms procurement between now and the end of the century. The others are Westland, the UK helicopter maker, in collaboration with McDonnell Douglas of the US, and British Aerospace in association with the Franco-German Eurocopter consortium. The Ministry of Defence plans to invite formal tenders in October and to place a contract in June 1994. That would initially involve 12 helicopters, but the purchase is expected to total about 125. The contract, to replace the Westland Lynx helicopter now in service, would include weapons, ground equipment, training and support. GEC and Bell are offering a variant of Bell's AH1W Super Cobra, derived from the Huey Cobra and developed for use in the Vietnam war in the 1960s. The UK version, the Cobra Venom, would feature GEC electronics. GEC Avionics would lead the project. Westland has already reached agreement with McDonnell Douglas for a UK-assembled version of the AH64 Apache. BAe is preparing to lead a rival bid by the Franco-German Tiger helicopter, which is still under development. GEC's entry into the contest is part of a strategy aimed at securing a leading place for the group in prime contractorship for whole defence programmes. Last year GEC failed in a joint bid with BAe for a Pounds 1.5bn contract to manage the supply of EH101 Merlin helicopters to the Royal Navy. The British Army has indicated a strong preference for the Apache because of its impressive fire power. A recent report by US Congressional investigators, however, raised questions as to how reliably the helicopter performed in the Gulf campaign.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Confident Tories pin hopes on turnround: The prospects for political parties in the local elections in Scotland
DOC.TEXT: SCOTTISH Conservatives, long accustomed to keeping their upper lips stiff in the face of adversity, are suddenly beaming with confidence. They believe they will do well in today's district council elections and consolidate the turnround in their fortunes that began with the general election. In the prize target of Edinburgh, Mrs Christine Richard, leader of the Tory party, says: 'I am quite convinced that we are going to win here. I believe Conservative party supporters will turn out and the disaffected ones will come back to us.' The party is still basking in delight at confounding sceptics by winning two extra seats in the general election and increasing its share of the Scottish vote - admittedly by just 1.7 percentage points to 25.7 per cent. Tories gaze at the turmoil in the opposition parties, each of which lost a seat and failed to make promised conquests - although the Scottish National party's vote went up by 7.5 points to 21.5 per cent. Yet the Tories hold only three councils, the same number as the Liberal Democrats, while the SNP has only one. Labour controls 27 of the 53 Scottish districts and the rest are held by independents or non-Tory coalitions. The Conservatives believe they will win Perth and Kinross, run by an SNP/Lib-Dem/independent coalition, and Stirling, where Mr Michael Forsyth held his parliamentary seat on April 9 and where Labour rules thanks to the spin of a coin by the returning officer after a dead heat in 1988. They hold Berwickshire, where most of their councillors are unopposed, and should keep Eastwood, and Bearsden and Milngavie, both outside Glasgow. They hope to gain seats in Aberdeen and to remove the Liberal Democrats from power in Gordon, although they have no seats there at the moment. The main goal, though, is Edinburgh, which the Tories lost to Labour in 1984. In 1988 the Conservatives took 22 wards against Labour's 32 in spite of winning 70 more votes overall than Labour. To win a majority the Tories need a swing to them of 6 per cent, although a 1.5 per cent swing would be enough to rob Labour of its majority. Even the most enthusiastic canvassers of all parties admit that the voters are suffering from election fatigue. Yet the SNP is presenting the district elections as a re-run of April 9 and is fielding more candidates than any other party. Mr Alex Salmond, the SNP leader, sees it as a 'second chance' for Scots 'to vote in the light of the general election result'. The SNP has taken up the call raised after the general election for a multi-option referendum on Scotland's constitutional future. SNP councils and individual councillors will be committed to trying to organise the referendum - offering a choice of independence, a devolved parliament and the status quo - some time next year. It remains to be seen whether many voters will ignore local issues such as poll tax levels and housing to vote SNP on a national issue. So far the party controls only one council, Angus. It takes comfort from a System Three poll last week which put its support at 25 per cent, 3 points up on the general election. The SNP expects to win control of Banff and Buchan, and of Moray, from independents. Both are in the north-east, where the SNP's MPs are. It also hopes to capture Cumbernauld in the central belt, where Labour kept control in 1988, again on the spin of a coin in a dead heat. Further gains such as West Lothian, Clackmannan and Kilmarnock will still need substantial swings from Labour. The Liberal Democrats will be under pressure from the Tories in Gordon, in north-east Fife and in Annandale and Eskdale in the south-west. As in other parts of Britain they are strong in their own local-government areas. The big question is whether Labour can motivate enough of its supporters to go out and vote. Having failed to win power at Westminster and being unable to deliver the Scottish parliament it had promised, it is the most demoralised and divided of the Scottish parties. Last week's opinion poll put its support at 36 per cent, 3 points below the general election result. Labour is protected in many districts, however, by the large swings of votes needed by the opposition to unseat it. Provided its hardcore supporters turn out to vote, its losses should be limited. If not, there will have been a political earthquake.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Ford moves 300 R&D jobs to Germany
DOC.BYLINE: By KEVIN DONE, Motor Industry Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: FORD's restructuring of its European research and development operations will consolidate them at its sites at Dunton, Essex, and Merkenich, near Cologne in Germany. As part of the restructuring, announced earlier this week, about 300 jobs are to be transferred from the UK to Germany and 20-30 jobs will be moved from Germany to the UK. Ford's Aveley engineering site, about 10 miles from Dunton, will close. Ford said there would be no compulsory redundancies. In the UK, Ford plans to move by the end of 1994 1,200 engineering staff from satellite operations at Aveley, Basildon and Dagenham in Essex to the main R&D site at Dunton, where the total workforce will be increased to nearly 4,000. In Germany, about 1,300 staff are to be relocated to Merkenich from other sites in Cologne. That will bring the total at the site to about 3,300, including the 300 jobs transferred from the UK. The engineering reorganisation follows a far-reaching review by Ford of its European automotive operations, which had a net loss last year (including Jaguar) of Dollars 1.079bn (Pounds 605m) from a net profit of Dollars 145m in 1990. Mr John Oldfield, Ford of Europe vice-president for product programmes, vehicle and design, said the company was seeking to bring together design engineers and production engineers at one site so that 'we can achieve better communication and teamwork and thereby generate significant quality and efficiency gains'. Ford says it has to spend 10 per cent to 15 per cent more than rival carmakers in Europe to have its R&D operations split between the UK and Germany. However, it emphasised its continuing commitment to research and development in the UK yesterday. The company said it had invested heavily at Dunton, where the site facilities had a total capital value of about Pounds 500m. It was planning capital investment totalling Pounds 40m at Dunton this year, having spent an average of Pounds 20m a year there since 1985. Research and development expenditure at Dunton totalled Pounds 236m last year. Further jobs would be created at Dunton over the next three years.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Leaseholders to be given right to buy - Lease Reform
DOC.TEXT: THE GOVERNMENT is proposing to give many of Britain's 1.5m long-leaseholders of flats the right to buy a share in the freehold of their building. The proposal, to be included in a Housing, Land and Urban Development Bill, will end the centuries old system by which much of the country's property reverts to the original landlord once the lease expires. Flat-owners in blocks will get the right to buy their freehold at market value, provided two-thirds of householders in the block vote in favour. The buyers will become the joint freeholders for any tenants or leaseholders who do not participate. The right will only apply to properties where not more than 10 per cent of the floorspace, excluding common parts, such as staircases, is used for non-residential purposes. At least two-thirds of the flats must be held by long-leaseholders, those whose original lease was for more than 21 years. Crown property and charitable trust housing already let at a discount will be exempt, as will converted flats in houses where the landlord is resident. Flat-owners in blocks which do not qualify will get the right to extend their leases, at market price. The Bill does not include proposals to introduce a new system of common ownership or 'commonhold' of blocks of flats for new developments.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: No-win situation for Labour seats - Boundary changes
DOC.DATELINE: THE GOVERNMENT has angered Labour MPs
DOC.TEXT: and risked possible protests from its own supporters - by accelerating a review of parliamentary constituencies which would help the Conservative party at the next general election. The work of Boundary Commissions is seldom without controversy. Before the 1983 election, Mr Michael Foot, then Labour leader, tried to use the courts to prevent the last review's implementation. After the 1955 general election, when acrimoniously debated changes undoubtably helped the Tories to increase their majority from 17 to 60, there was a consensus that the period between reviews should be extended. The four Boundary Commissions (for England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland) were to report every 10 to 15 years, rather than every three to seven years. Now Mr Kenneth Clarke, home secretary, is risking charges of 'gerrymandering' by planning to reduce the period between reviews to eight to 12 years. More immediately, the Boundary Commissions' work, begun in 1991, will be speeded up. A statutory deadline of the end of 1994 will allow conclusions to be reached in 'good time' for the next election, the Home Office said. The work could probably be approved by parliament well before May 15 1997 - the latest date for the next general election. The consensus at Westminster is that the reviews will help the Tories to gain up to 20 seats. The 1983 review, which formed the basis for last month's general election, was drawn up on the 1976 electoral register. There have since been substantial movements of population out of inner cities - traditionally Labour's strongest areas. Mr John Major's constituency of Huntingdon, for instance, has an electorate of 92,913 while Birmingham Sparkbrook, held by Mr Roy Hattersley, Labour deputy leader, has only 51,677. But experience suggests that that will not stop complaints from Tory MPs who will lose out - such as in Chelsea which has an electorate of 42,371 - and even name changes could lead to local complaints.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Lottery angers pools workers - National Lottery
DOC.TEXT: USDAW, the union representing workers in the pools industry, voted unanimously yesterday to campaign against the introduction of a national lottery, warning that it could cost thousands of jobs. The long-awaited announcement of plans for a UK lottery was first made in March by the then home secretary, Mr Kenneth Baker, after a determined campaign by lobby groups and a number of prominent MPs and public figures. The new Department of National Heritage, under Mr David Mellor, is charged with setting up the lottery, with proceeds going to sport, arts, heritage, charities and a new Millennium Fund to celebrate the year 2000. It is estimated that the lottery could raise up to Pounds 1bn a year. An independent board will be responsible for distribution of the proceeds, with day-to-day management undertaken by the private sector under contract. Mr Garfield Davies, Usdaw's general secretary, warned that the lottery could have a serious impact on the pools industry. 'If the pools companies lose business then our members lose their jobs,' he told the union's annual conference in Blackpool. Delegates unanimously backed a motion to campaign against the lottery and to call for support from the TUC and the Labour party to block the bill. The pools industry has an annual turnover of Pounds 700m and employs nearly 7,000 people, mainly in Liverpool, with some in Glasgow and Cardiff. It also provides part-time employment for around 70,000 collectors around the country. Mr Malcolm Hughes, managing director of Vernons pools in Liverpool, said he was sceptical of the claim by lottery supporters that there was plenty of room in the market for both pools and a lottery. He said the argument that annual spending on gambling in the UK is considerably lower than in other countries did not take account of the true size and diversity of the British gambling market. Littlewoods, the biggest pools promoter, said it had been invited to make a joint submission about the lottery with Vernons and Zetters pools to the government by the beginning of June. A spokesman said he did not rule out the possibility that the pools industry might bid to run the lottery itself. 'We have raised billions of pounds over many years and would certainly be the most qualified to run it,' he said. Mr Denis Vaughan, the conductor, and head of the Lottery Promotion Company which has been lobbying for a lottery for more than a year, said he was delighted with the proposed format, but was anxious that the proceeds should be used only for capital investment and endowments. He dismissed the threat to the pools industry, saying that several thousand jobs were already at risk from a possible move towards online computer systems. He added that any job losses in that area would be more than offset by the estimated 85,000 jobs that could be created through investment of lottery proceeds.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Major's chance to show European heart - European Community
DOC.TEXT: MR JOHN Major likes to distinguish himself from his predecessor by saying that Britain is at 'the heart of Europe'. Britain's turn as president of the European Community for six months, which starts on July 1, will give him an unrivalled opportunity to show that the heart is beating at a measured but healthy pace. Political difficulties in other EC countries, combined with Mr Major's improved personal stature after the election, seem likely to provide the the prime minister with an ideal European springboard. The Queen's Speech made clear that the government will be giving priority to ensuring a brisk passage for the bill implementing the Maastricht treaty on European union agreed five months ago. UK officials are drawing quiet satisfaction from the recent spate of opposition to the Maastricht treaty in other countries such as Germany and France. Britain's view is that the government's well-known scepticism over a federal Europe has been vindicated by the anti-Maastricht flurry on the continent. At the same time, setbacks for government parties in elections in France, Italy and Germany will make Mr Major a more persuasive partner in dealing with his counterparts from other EC capitals. The resignation of Mr Hans-Dietrich Genscher, the long-serving German foreign minister, seems likely to weaken, at least temporarily, the cohesion of the traditional Franco-German alliance in the EC. This may boost the chances for Mr Douglas Hurd, the foreign secretary, to promote British views. Britain will be using the presidency to push forward enlargement of the Community, as well as to complete the establishment of the single market, due to come into force on January 1 1993. To stress its commitment to free markets, the government wants to make particular progress in breaking down trade barriers in life insurance, transport and energy, and public procurement. Even before the presidency has started, the aim of EC enlargement is being emphasised by a series of top-level visits to London from representatives of applicant countries. Mr Carl Bildt, the Swedish prime minister, will be in Downing Street today, while Mr Esko Aho, the Finnish prime minister, was in London last week. Both countries, along with Austria, want to join on January 1 1995. The government believes that the Community can continue to be 'deepened' - through the single market, as well as through greater co-operation in economic and foreign affairs - at the same time as it is being enlarged. But, as one official puts it, 'deepening is going to slow down as you go wider.' The UK believes that the timetable for European monetary union will be delayed by Germany's economic difficulties. The UK wants to hold out the hope of maximum access to EC markets, and eventual full membership, for former communist countries Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary. But there is little enthusiasm for the wide-ranging institutional reforms suggested by Mr Jacques Delors, the Commission president, as a way of managing a much more numerous Community. The UK is banking on support from Germany for toning down another Delors initiative - the plan for a large increase in spending on poorer regions, conceived as part of the 'cohesion fund' agreed at Maastricht. Germany's criticisms of Mr Delors' latest suggestions have been as strong as Britain's. British officials are banking on Mr Major's strong personal rapport with Chancellor Helmut Kohl to help revise downwards the Commission's proposals. Whitehall also opposes signs of growing trends in the Commission towards interventionism. These were highlighted by the recent row between Sir Leon Brittan, the competition commissioner, and Mr Martin Bangemann, the commissioner for industry, over aid for the automotive industry.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Changes to bankruptcy and parole - Scotland
DOC.TEXT: THE GOVERNMENT is proposing a light and relatively uncontroversial legislative programme for Scotland. The first of two bills is designed to close loopholes in bankruptcy legislation. Since the 1985 Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act, many debtors use sequestration to solve their debt problems. A debtor transfers his assets to a trustee, who then petitions for sequestration and for his appointment as permanent trustee under the 1985 Act. As the debtor's estate has few assets, the fees for the trustee managing the estate are met from public funds, at a total cost in 1991-92 of Pounds 18.5m. The government proposes that new powers be given to the accountant in bankruptcy (a civil servant) to administer sequestrations. The other measure will reform parole arrangements. Prisoners serving sentences of less than four years would be released after serving half their sentence instead of two-thirds as present. Prisoners serving sentences of four years or more would be eligible for parole at half-sentence instead of one-third. Prisoners who commit another offence between release and the end of their sentence would be recalled to serve the remaining part of their term. The legislation would bring Scottish practice roughly into line with changes in England and Wales under the 1991 Criminal Justice Act. A BILL will promote the use of Welsh in Wales by requiring public sector bodies to set out schemes for providing services in Welsh, and by establishing a statutory Welsh Language Board.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Crackdown on vote-rigging - Industrial relations
DOC.TEXT: THE GOVERNMENT will, as expected, go ahead with its sixth significant piece of industrial relations legislation since 1979, persevering with the core proposals in last July's industrial relations green paper. Only the plan to make collective agreements legally enforceable has been dropped. In 1990, the government announced it had completed its programme of industrial relations reform but then decided to have one more go. Nevertheless, the new Conservative government is expected to be less hostile to the unions than its three predecessors and further legislation of this kind is not expected in this parliament. One of the four areas for legislation that the government spelt out yesterday follows allegations of ballot-rigging in the TGWU general union in 1990 and misuse of National Union of Mineworkers funds during the 1984-1985 strike. The government will 'strengthen the rights of trade union members against fraud and vote-rigging in union elections and mismanagement of their union's finances'. Proposals include independent scrutineers for election and enhanced powers for the Certification Officer over union finances. The second area states that the government will 'give workers greater freedom to join the union of their choice and protect them against the unauthorised deduction of subscriptions from salaries'. The first part involves making the Trades Union Congress rules for controlling inter-union disputes - the Bridlington rules - inoperable. Some union officials fear that the proposal could release a wave of inter-union disputes, further discrediting trade unionism, and undermine the movement towards single-union deals. The second part will hurt union income, 65 per cent of which currently comes from union subscriptions 'checked-off' at source by employers. Instead of giving permission only when they join the system, as at present, union members are likely to have to give written permission for 'check-off' every three years and must be informed by employers every time the subscription is raised. Some observers think unions could lose 1m members as a result. Less controversial proposals include: giving users of public services the right to take action against unlawful strikes even when the employers do not; requiring seven days' notice of strike action; and extending the requirement for postal ballots to strike ballots.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Businesses win more rate relief - Local Government
DOC.TEXT: COUNCILLORS WILL be relieved to hear that for once local government, prominent in recent years, is notable for its virtual absence from the Queen's Speech. Virtual, because occupiers of 900,000 business premises will welcome the one minor measure proposed: to enact the concession announced in the last Budget extending transitional relief for payers of the uniform business rate, introduced in 1990. The concession will spare them any real terms increase in bills in the current year, with the existing limits on real annual increases to apply again from 1993-94. It will grant relief on the same terms to new occupiers when premises change hands. It will also increase the maximum reduction for businesses in transition to 3 percentage points higher than that applying now. These businesses will receive all their remaining gains in 1993-94. The existing transitional arrangements give businesses that face severe rate increases a year-on-year rise limited to 20 per cent in real terms for large premises, 15 per cent for small premises and 10 per cent for small premises with living accommodation attached. The reliefs apply to England and Wales, but business rate payers in Scotland and Northern Ireland - which have different systems - will gain reductions of a similar size. The legislation will backdate the the relief for new occupiers to March and other changes to April. Meanwhile, councils will have their hands full introducing the council tax, due to replace the poll tax next April. A few may also be visited by the local government commission, another fruit of Mr Michael Heseltine's brief stint at the environment department, which is examining the case for more single-tier authorities. Local councils will be keen to know whether Mr Michael Howard, the new environment secretary, shares his predecessor's enthusiasm for unitary authorities. The current signs are that he does not - but a strong Tory lobby is urging him to the contrary. With county council elections due next year, the outcome will soon be a hot issue in Britain's council chambers.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Radical schools syllabus based on opting out - Education
DOC.TEXT: AFTER FOUR years of radical but piecemeal tinkering, the government intends in the coming session to enshrine in legislation its blueprint for state schools in the 21st century. A white paper will be published before the summer, with legislation soon after. The regime for schools that have opted out of local education authority control will be the white paper's main preoccupation. Of the 25,000 state schools in England and Wales, only 217 are currently grant-maintained - funded directly from Whitehall, with their governors enjoying almost unfettered control over their management, budgets and recruitment, subject to fulfilling the national curriculum. A substantial increase in that number is top of the agenda for Mr John Patten, the new education secretary. He wants to see most of England and Wales's 4,000 secondary schools grant-maintained within a few years, and to make inroads into the primary sector, which currently boasts only 34 grant-maintained schools out of 21,000. The Tory election manifesto proposed that primary schools be allowed to opt out in groups - to share management and overhead costs, even budgets. A plan on those lines will doubtless feature in the white paper. It is also likely to include provision for a funding council for grant-maintained schools. The education department believes that if more than 1,000 schools opt out then it will be obliged to introduce some form of funding body. It is estimated that this number may be achieved within two years. However, Mr Patten will not only be concerned with numbers and funding. His white paper will have to address two other crucial issues: the future of local education authorities, shorn of day-to-day control of schools; and the type of education to be provided by grant-maintained schools. Some Tories would like to see local education authorities abolished outright once opting out has achieved a critical mass. Mr Kenneth Clarke, Mr Patten's predecessor, was no fan of local government. Mr Patten may be more sympathetic to retaining a distinct servicing and 'enabling' role for councils in a reformed system. The issue of selection is at the heart of the second aspect. The Tory manifesto pledged to allow grant-maintained schools to introduce selection 'if that is what parents clearly want and it fits in with the wider needs of the local area'. The wording was deliberately vague. Mr Patten will want to avoid the trauma involved in a wholesale return to selection through some newfangled 11-plus exam. Yet he recognises the popularity of grammar schools, particularly in the Tory shires (where most of the remaining 159 are located), and is keen to promote diversity and choice for parents. Extending the idea of 'magnet' schools and city technology colleges, specialising in particular areas of the curriculum, is the most plausible way forward. The Queen's Speech also promised 'to promote vocational training for young people and adults'. Although less divisive politically and requiring no legislation, this is as important an issue as opting out. The first general vocational qualifications - intended to offer a vocational alternative to A-levels for full-time students - are to be piloted over the coming year. Whether a success or failure, the fate of these qualifications may have a profound impact on the shape of post-16 year old education.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech (Analysis): Hurried along the track to privatisation - British Rail
DOC.TEXT: IF BRITISH Rail had harboured hopes that political and practical obstacles to its long-awaited privatisation were pushing the event ever further into the distance, it must have been sorely disappointed by the Queen's Speech yesterday. The government made it clear that it was determined not only to secure a large-scale hand-over of BR's operations to the private sector, but to do it much more quickly than had been expected. Within days, the British Rail and British Coal (Transfer Proposals) Bill will be put to parliament, seeking powers to do essential preparatory work for the privatisation of the rail and coal industries. This will be a purely technical measure: but in the case of the railways, it is expected to be followed within weeks by the much-delayed privatisation White Paper, and by full-blown legislation in the shape of a Rail Bill as soon as the autumn. Cynics will say they have heard that before, only to see see the plans founder amid ministerial wrangling or the sheer impossibility of finding a buyer for such a heavily loss-making operation. But if the government has at last found a successful formula, the result could be radical change for Britain's railways - not so much in the form of the 'big bang' privatisation originally envisaged by Mr Malcolm Rifkind, the former transport secretary, as in the form of a creeping denationalisation. The framework agreed by Mr John MacGregor, Mr Rifkind's successor, and the rest of the Cabinet follows the lines set out in the Conservative party's election manifesto. BR will be split into two bodies: one owning the railway tracks and associated infrastructure, and the other operating the trains. Separate accounting systems will be set up so that the track body knows how much to charge train operators for the use of its tracks. Once that charging system is in place, it will be possible to give private sector operators the right to run trains on BR's tracks provided they are prepared to pay the price. Several companies, including Mr Richard Branson's Virgin Group, have already expressed an interest in becoming train operators. The next step will be to start getting BR's own services into the private sector. To quell fears of line closures, ownership of the track infrastructure will stay with BR indefinitely, but the operation of the trains will gradually be handed to the private sector. The freight and parcels operations will be sold, and the operation of passenger services will be franchised to private sector operators, with subsidies to ensure the preservation of loss-making but socially necessary services. One possibility is that passenger services will be franchised in groups of routes, so paving the way for the re-emergence of regional companies such as the London Brighton and South Coast. An official regulator will be set up to award the passenger service franchises and to make sure that BR's track infrastructure body treats private sector entrants fairly. Safety, as now, will be administered by the Railway Inspectorate, part of the Health and Safety Executive. The government will also seek powers in the bill to sell stations outright to the private sector - not just to franchisees operating the trains that run through them, but to any private-sector operator which believes it can make more productive use of the assets than BR. Mr John Prescott, shadow transport secretary, said Labour favoured more private investment in the railways, but he opposed the break-up of the railways and the removal of strategic decision-making from the government. Trains and tracks needed to be upgraded together to get the best out of both, he said. Dividing the ownership of tracks and trains meant that investment in the two would not be co-ordinated. The break-up of the network would also lead to a fragmentation of services, swingeing cuts in fringe routes such as those in rural areas, and big fare increases. The omission from the Queen's Speech of controversial proposals for the deregulation and privatisation of London's buses is likely to be seen as a setback for Mr MacGregor. Transport minsters had repeatedly promised the extension of de-regulation to the capital's buses early in the next parliament. The plans have met strong resistance from bus user groups, the London boroughs, the London Tourist Board and others.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech (Analysis): Generators hold key to size - British Coal
DOC.TEXT: THE PRIVATISATION of British Coal was confirmed, although no timetable was given. Civil servants said yesterday that the sale could take place by the end of next year. The announcement provoked fresh criticism from the Labour party and mining communities, which believe that the controversial privatisation could lead to the closure of more of British Coal's 49 remaining pits. The government itself says that the size of the company will be determined not by privatisation, but by the contracts agreeing how much coal British Coal sells to the privatised electricity industry. The Queen's Speech announcement will intensify pressure for these contracts -which represent the bulk of British Coal's revenue - to be renegotiated within the next few months. Existing contracts expire in March 1993. But they are proving difficult to settle, because the two big electricity generators, National Power and PowerGen, believe that British Coal's product is too expensive. The signs are that they are reluctant to buy more than 50m tonnes - possibly falling to less over the life of the contract - compared with 65m in the old contracts. But this would force British Coal to close more pits. The electricity companies accept that the government will have to intervene to forge a deal that is acceptable to all the parties concerned. There are still many obstacles. The generators need to back their contracts with sales to the regional electricity companies, which supply domestic consumers. And the regional companies are waiting for the regulator to give them a sign of the kind of deal he thinks would be fair on domestic consumers. But the regulator said yesterday that the negotiations between British Coal and the generators were a matter for them alone. The government will have to resolve this issue before it can proceed with the privatisation. It can, however, proceed with legislation. The first stage, the Queen's Speech indicated, would be a 'paving bill'. This bill, which is expected shortly, will simply give British Coal powers to restructure itself in preparation for the sale. This will be followed, probably in the autumn, by the privatisation bill, or Coal Bill, itself - clearing the way for the sale late in 1993. A white paper, or policy document setting out the government's approach, would precede the bill, said officials at the Department of Trade and Industry, which is now responsible for energy. So far, the government has given few clues about how the privatisation will be structured, and ministers are still studying reports from N M Rothschild, the merchant bank advising on the privatisation. But a likely option is that the company will be split into two or more parts, and sold to trade buyers. One prospective buyer is the Union of Democratic Mineworkers (UDM), which, with Lloyds Bank, is planning an employee-led buy-out of the company.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech (Analysis): More measured approach - Political asylum
DOC.TEXT: THE POLITICAL momentum behind the Asylum Bill has fallen since it was first published last November. And while the government still regards the task of controlling flows of refugees into Britain as a serious problem it gave the bill little more than a passing reference in yesterday's legislative agenda. With the election out of the way, and with the first three months of the year showing a sharp fall in asylum requests, the government can adopt a more measured approach. The Bill was postponed by being withdrawn from the committee stage in the House of Lords in February. This followed fierce criticism from lawyers, church leaders and refugee organisations. Opponents claimed that plans for a highly restricted appeals procedure for applicants refused asylum could lead to refugees being unjustly returned to face persecution in their home countries. Government officials said yesterday that it was not clear when the bill would be resubmitted. If it were delayed until the autumn, the bill would not become law until next summer. The government has made clear that the Bill will be reintroduced with the amendments already made during its passage through the Commons earlier this year. The bill as originally tabled gave asylum-seekers only 48 hours to request leave to appeal against their applications being turned down. The government has since increased this to 10 days, a period which Amnesty says still does not give applicants sufficient time to prepare their cases. According to government figures, there were 44,700 applications for asylum in the UK last year, a 10-fold increase compared with 1988. Officials however recognise that a large proportion reflected requests by people placing more than one application in order to defraud the social security authorities. Applications in the first three months this year fell to only 1,730 a month against an average of 3,730 last year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech (Analysis): Scheme to spur inner-city renewal - Housing
DOC.TEXT: THE GOVERNMENT will renew its assault on inner-city dereliction in a Housing, Land and Urban Development Bill, which will also extend home ownership to more council tenants and strengthen their hands in getting repairs done to their homes. The headline-catching provision of the bill will be the creation of an Urban Regeneration Agency to co-ordinate the task of regenerating England's inner cities. The agency is to be headed by Mr Peter Walker, a former Conservative minister who retired from the Commons at the last election. The main function of the agency will be to bring back into use vacant and underused land. It will have compulsory purchase powers, in the same way as the existing urban development corporations in London's Docklands and other UK cities, including Liverpool and Birmingham. The corporations have had some success in using limited amounts of government finance to lever in private capital, attracting developers by reclaiming derelict land and putting infrastructure in place. The agency is expected to take over responsibility for administering much of the present government spending on urban programmes. However, ministers appear to have ruled out giving it responsibility for administering City Challenge, the competitive bidding by towns and cities for urban development funds. A second measure in the Bill will offer council tenants a chance to become part-owners of their homes, through rent to mortgage schemes. With more than 1.4m council homes bought by their tenants since 1981 under the hugely successful right to buy legislation, these schemes reach further down the income ladder to those who cannot afford full ownership. In return for accepting some obligations of ownership, the tenant's rent is converted into mortgage payments, buying part of the equity in the home. The intention is that tenants acquire full ownership by stepping up their payments at a later date, or cash in their equity when they move home. However, pilot studies in Scotland, rural Wales, Basildon and Milton Keynes have not indicated great demand for rent to mortgage schemes. Fewer than 400 tenants have taken them up in all four areas. 'Given the low level of take-up so far, there is no reason to believe that a national scheme will be popular,' said Mr John Perry, head of policy at the Institute of Housing. 'And rent to mortgage schemes will do nothing to address the urgent need to help homeowners move back to renting if they can no longer afford to buy.' Also to be strengthened is the right to repair, which allows council tenants to get essential and urgent repairs done when the local authority fails to do them in time. The existing scheme has not been a conspicuous success, mainly because it was administratively cumbersome and relied on the tenant to pay the bill and claim the money back. A consultative paper put out last autumn suggested that tenants should be able to get essential and urgent repairs done by contacting contractors on an approved list who would send the bill for the work to the council.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Kinnock attacks Tory lack of ideas
DOC.TEXT: THE GOVERNMENT had returned to office with no new ideas as to how to tackle Britain's underlying economic weaknesses or to build a sustained recovery, Mr Neil Kinnock told the Commons yesterday. In a confident performance, the Labour leader used his last important state occasion as leader of the opposition to highlight continuing high unemployment and the danger that tax rises or spending cuts will be needed to balance the budget. In spite of a jobless total of 2.7m, there was 'nothing new' in the government's approach and the word 'unemployment' was not even mentioned in the speech, he pointed out. Its strategy for growth was entirely consumption-led, included no measures to restore training funding, provide incentives for industrial investment or reverse the reduction in research-and-development spending. Meanwhile, Britain lay at the bottom of the Group of Seven industrialised nations' league table for growth, investment and employment. Rising to Labour cheers, Mr Kinnock began with a witty, if barbed, tribute to Mr Kenneth Baker, the former cabinet minister who moved the loyal address, and his seconder, Mr Andrew Mitchell, the MP for Gedling. In their choice of speakers, he remarked, the Tory whips had combined exuberance with experience and a loyal Heathite with a loyal Thatcherite - 'all together in the person of the Rt Hon member for Mole Valley'. Mr Baker, he added, had been described as 'capable of falling from grace without hitting the ground'. The Labour leader went on to compliment Mr Mitchell on his 'rare admission' of ambition. Some of the greatest love affairs he had ever seen in the Commons, he said, 'have been by one Honourable Member unaccompanied'. Turning to the Queen's Speech itself, Mr Kinnock said Labour could support the government's commitments to combating drug trafficking and terrorism. It also backed efforts to bring peace to Yugoslavia, push forward the process of nuclear disarmament and participate in the environment conference in Rio de Janeiro. He then went on to the attack, charging Mr John Major with failing to tackle adequately the issue of joblessness. Unemployment and the fear of unemployment were hanging over individuals, families and households, he said: 'Yet the prime minister cannot even bring himself to mention the word in this Queen's Speech.' He challenged Mr Major to say how he would rid the country of unemployment and reduce the budget deficit in the medium term. Such a goal required either growth rates in excess of those reached at the height of the boom in oil revenues, or tax increases, or public expenditure cuts. Mr Kinnock added: 'When the government says with such certainly they will get rid of the budget deficit in the medium term, they must know how they are planning to do that.' The National Lottery now to be set up was an apt symbol for policies that were making 'life itself' a gamble, with schools and hospitals opting out of local control in such a way as to make the provision of their services a matter of chance. Mr Paddy Ashdown, Liberal Democrat leader, urged the government to give a strong lead on Europe by moving to the narrow band of the exchange rate mechanism and ditching the 'unnecessary and damaging' opt-out clause on Britain's entry into European monetary union. Britain's European presidency was beginning at a crucial time, with many European countries facing internal difficulties. It would be 'very easy indeed' for Europe to lose momentum at this stage.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: MPs gain question time
DOC.TEXT: MEMBERS OF parliament will be able to ask questions directly about the Citizen's Charter for the first time under the new arrangements for departmental questions to be approved by the Commons today. There will also be an extended opportunity to ask questions on the arts, with Mr David Mellor, the national heritage secretary, having a 40-minute question slot once every four weeks. Mr William Waldegrave, the minister in charge of the Citizen's Charter, will face questions from MPs for 20 minutes once every three weeks. Mr John Taylor, the new junior minister in the lord chancellor's department, will answer MPs' questions for 15 minutes once every six weeks. Energy matters will be subsumed in the hour-long monthly slot for questions to trade and industry ministers. The new arrangements for questions have been made quickly, but there is some uncertainty about when the all-party committees that monitor departments can be set up. Mr Tony Newton, leader of the Commons, is keen to see them established early, but at present there are difficulties about the timing of opposition nominations. Labour party rules say that no frontbench spokesman can be a select committee member. Until the shadow cabinet elections are over - in late July -and junior spokesmanships agreed, therefore, it will not be clear who will be available and keen to serve on the committees, including perhaps those who may have lost places in the frontbench team. Other Commons committees such as the public accounts committee and the committee looking at European legislation are likely to be established more quickly. The parties will have to decide whether there should be a committee to monitor the national heritage department. The Opposition hopes that the two extra Tory MPs for Scottish seats will mean that in this parliament, unlike the last, a Scottish affairs committee will be appointed. Labour will also be pressing for the chairmanship of at least one additional departmental committee, beyond the four it holds already. As a further element in the Commons' becoming operational again, the three deputy Speakers, who will take turns at substituting for the Speaker in presiding over MPs' debates, were appointed yesterday. Mr Michael Morris, Tory MP for Northampton South, was appointed the senior deputy Speaker, as chairman of ways and means. Mr Geoffrey Lofthouse, the Labour MP for Pontefract, and Dame Janet Fookes, the Tory MP for Plymouth Drake, are the other two deputies.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: MI6 comes in from the cold
DOC.TEXT: MR JOHN MAJOR'S decision to bring the Secret Intelligence Service in from the cold was long overdue after the public recognition of organisations such as the KGB in Russia and the CIA in the US. For most people, the biggest surprise about SIS - better known as MI6 - was not that it exists but that Mr Major's reference to the service and Sir Colin McColl, it's head, during the Queen's Speech debate was the first time that it has been officially recognised by the government. Mr Stephen Dorril - whose book, In From The Cold, on the development of the intelligence services during the 1980s and the 1990s is published in October -said: 'We know quite a lot about MI5 and its structure, but we know very little about MI6, which seems to have escaped attention.' Like MI5, its sister organisation, MI6 developed from branches of British military intelligence during the First World War. It is responsible for the collection of foreign intelligence, particularly in the military and economic spheres. It also carries out counter-espionage, involving the infiltration of foreign intelligence services. The idea that the existence of a secret service should in itself be classed as a secret was exposed to ridicule in the 1980s with debacles such as the failed government prosecution of Mr Peter Wright for alleged breaches of the Official Secrets Act in the publication of Spycatcher, his account of his career in MI5. The announcement is part of a wider trend towards accountability. MI6 managed to maintain its cloak of secrecy longer than MI5 whose new head, Mrs Stella Rimington, was announced late last year. New MI6 offices close to Vauxhall Bridge in London are currently under construction. The organisation has about 2,000 staff and a budget of about Pounds 150m.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Major aims to avoid tax increases
DOC.TEXT: A FALL in Britain's budget deficit without the imposition of any increase in taxation was envisaged by Mr John Major, the prime minister, when he outlined the government's programme for the new parliament in the Commons yesterday. He insisted that the renewed confidence generated by the Conservative party's fourth successive general election victory was already being reflected in the economy. To government cheers, the prime minister underlined the favourable impact already made by Tuesday's 1/2 -percentage-point cut, which brought the bank rate down to 10 per cent. After the election, Mr Major said, business surveys had immediately reflected stronger prospects, the stock market had risen by 10 per cent, and sterling had risen to DM2.92. He emphasised that the policies endorsed by the British people were designed to encourage the creation of wealth - 'in Britain and for Britain'. He reaffirmed that the government intended to expand the 20p income tax band -introduced in the March Budget for the first Pounds 2,000 of taxable income - 'steadily' up the income scale so that it applied to more and more people. He emphasised that the 40 per cent upper rate was at a 'proper and sustainable level'. He announced that the Finance Bill, to implement the proposals from the Budget that could not be enacted before the election, would be introduced later this month. Mr Major promised to carry forward the 'crusade' against over-regulation and state interference, and renewed his commitment to opposing any pressure from the European Community to reimpose handicaps on industry removed during the Thatcherite era. Amid further government cheers he said: 'Not for us the interventionism that would put people out of work with minimum wages and artificial restrictions on working times.' The prime minister also highlighted the developments it would fall to him to set in train when Britain assumed the presidency of the EC in July - with ensuring the survival of 'fledgling' democracies in eastern Europe a top priority. Labour backbenchers caustically reminded the prime minister that the public-sector borrowing requirement for the current financial year was expected to exceed Pounds 28bn. Mr Major referred his critics to the figures in the Budget statement, or Red Book, and assured the House: 'We will seek to stick to them until we have a balanced budget.' He said the budget deficit reflected cyclical factors and added: 'As we come out of recession, that deficit will begin to fall.' Pressed for a detailed explanation of his stance on Scotland, the prime minister underlined his determination to prevent the break-up of the UK, stressing that the union was not negotiable. The government would seek to be 'more responsive' to Scotland's needs, and he undertook to report back to the House after fulfilling his pledge to take stock of the situation in the light of the outcome of the election. Mr Major said the Citizen's Charter would be at the centre of the government's decision making, with policies designed to make public services more accountable. Tougher performance targets would be set by Mr William Waldegrave, chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, and he would ensure that high-quality, responsive public services were provided for the individual citizen.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Other measures - Main Points
