DOC.TEXT: The non-domestic rating bill will allow implementation of non-domestic rate transitional arrangements; the boundary commission bill will set new deadlines for the completion of reviews; the social security bill aims to modernise the social security system; a Welsh language bill will promote the use of Welsh; the Scottish bankruptcy bill will close legislative loopholes; and a Scottish prisoners and criminal proceedings bill is intended to make legal practice conform with that in England and Wales.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Milk monopoly to end - Main Points
DOC.TEXT: Legislation to 'promote improvements in agricultural marketing' aims to speed the end of the Milk Marketing Board's 60-year monopoly.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Urban regeneration agency - Main Points
DOC.TEXT: An urban regeneration agency will be set up to co-ordinate the regeneration of England's inner cities. It will aim to bring back into use vacant and under-used land, and will have compulsory purchase powers similar to those of existing urban development corporations. The rents-to-mortgages proposals also contained in the bill will offer council tenants a chance to become part-owners of their homes.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Asylum Bill reintroduced - Main Points
DOC.TEXT: The Asylum Bill, withdrawn from the committee stage in the Lords in February, will be reintroduced, but government officials said yesterday that it was not clear when the bill would be resubmitted. If it were delayed until the autumn, it would not become law until next summer.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Brisk pace for Maastricht - Main Points
DOC.TEXT: The government intends a brisk passage for the bill implementing the Maastricht treaty on European union agreed five months ago. To stress its commitment to free markets, the government wants to make particular progress in breaking down trade barriers in life assurance, transport and energy, and public procurement.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Union reforms extended - Main Points
DOC.TEXT: Legislation has been pledged to strengthen rights of trade union members against ballot rigging and regulate the check-off procedure for union subscriptions so that members would have to give written permission for money to be taken from their salaries.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Opt-out schools a priority - Main Points
DOC.TEXT: The government intends to put into legislation its blueprint for state schools in the next century. A white paper will be published before the summer, and legislation will follow soon afterwards. It will focus on the regime for schools that have opted out of local education authority control. The government intends a substantial increase in the number of state schools funded directly by Whitehall.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Lottery aims to raise up to Pounds 1bn -Main Points
DOC.TEXT: The new Department of National Heritage, under Mr David Mellor (pictured), will set up the lottery with proceeds going to sport, arts, heritage, charities and a new Millennium Fund to celebrate the year 2000. It is estimated that the lottery could raise up to Pounds 1bn a year. An independent board will be responsible for distribution of the proceeds, with day-to-day management undertaken by the private sector under contract. The long-awaited announcement of plans for a UK lottery was first made in March by Mr Kenneth Baker, then home secretary.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Privatisation plans are put into motion -Main Points
DOC.TEXT: The government aims to secure the large-scale handover of BR's operations to the private sector much quicker than had been expected. Within days, the British Rail and British Coal (Transfer Proposals) Bill will be put to parliament, enabling essential preparatory work for the privatisation of the rail and coal industries. In the case of the railways it is expected to be followed within weeks by the much-delayed privatisation white paper and by full-blown legislation in the shape of a Rail Bill as soon as the autumn. The privatisation of British Coal was confirmed. Civil servants said yesterday the sale might take place by the end of next year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Queen's Speech: Realism steers PM's first agenda - Reduced majority forces caution; Balance of controversial and populist measures
DOC.TEXT: WHEN Mr Neil Kinnock began the unfinished task of returning the Labour party to the centre ground of British politics, somebody coined the phrase 'the new realism'. As Mr John Major set out yesterday the first legislative programme that he can call his own, it was from the comfortable position of a leader who has defied overwhelming odds to win a fourth term of office for the Conservatives. Yet as the prime minister's colleagues emerged from the pomp and ceremony of the state opening of parliament, the most frequent comment was that his programme's strength lay as much in its realism as its radicalism. Mr Major has not abandoned reform in favour of consolidation - but he has called a halt to the permanent revolution that proved the downfall of his predecessor. The programme for the next 18 months is radical in intent but realistic in its ambitions. It is intended to reinforce his reputation for achieving objectives by consensus rather than confrontation. It recognises that there is a world outside Westminster, that legislation is not the sole instrument of change. That does not mean it will be free of controversy. The short bill due within a few days to implement the treaties concluded at the Maastricht summit will provoke great public soul-searching on the right of the Conservative party. With his majority reduced to 21, Mr Major cannot afford more than a handful of rebels. Mr Major's promise to make the London government more responsive to Scotland's aspirations may do little to cap the rising tide of support north of the border for a new constitutional settlement. Legislation to privatise British Coal and parts of British Rail may not be free from political risk. The first will force a belated acknowledgement from the government that many more pits will be forced to close. The second will throw up more hidden horrors - and demands for public money - than ministers are ready to accept. The education bill planned for the autumn - designed to accelerate rapidly a move towards grant-maintained status for most of the nation's schools - will oblige the government to decide who or what will replace local authorities in making strategic decisions about educational provision. Some parents will welcome the return of selective education. Many more will not. Mr Major has been careful to balance the difficult with the more instantly populist. The National Lotteries Bill and legislation establishing the urban regeneration agency and extending further rights - including rents into mortgages - to council tenants promise some good headlines. Even without its present debilitating troubles over the party leadership, Labour would find it hard to stir public anger against the bill promising a further erosion of the power of trade unions. The pace will be more sedate. Ministers are desperately anxious to counter the impression that parliament could be twiddling its thumbs for much of the 18 months. They admit, though, that the programme has been designed to mesh with the proposed reform of MPs' working hours and with the political reality of a reduced majority. The prime minister's public avowal yesterday of the existence of the Secret Intelligence Service was designed to signal another break with the past by promising a more open, relaxed, style of government. But there was a more substantial shift. Much of the legislation has been framed around Mr Major's belief in individual choice, ownership and responsibility, but a single sentence emphasises the core of his own prospectus. The government, it says, will 'give priority to improving public services through the Citizen's Charter which will be at the centre of decision-making'. Translated, that means that the welfare state is to be preserved but its monolithic structure dismantled in favour of a more diverse pattern of locally managed services. Mr Major's ambition is to create a new consensus on the management of the public sector to outflank Labour in the 1990s, in much the same way as his party's approach to the economy left the Opposition stranded during the 1980s. It may prove a powerful brand of realism.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Environment protection pledge from top banks
DOC.BYLINE: By MICHAEL LITTLEJOHNS, UN Correspondent and DAVID LASCELLES
DOC.TEXT: COMMERCIAL banks in 23 countries, with combined assets of Dollars 1,500bn (Pounds 847bn), made a formal commitment at the United Nations yesterday to pursue common principles of environmental protection in all their operations, writes Michael Littlejohns, UN Correspondent, in New York. An official of National Westminster Bank of the UK, an initiator of this first such collective effort by the industry, told a press conference that environmental risk was now a vital element in credit risk. The group of 31 signatories did not include any US or Japanese banks. But Dr Mostafa Tolba, head of the UN environment programme, said Citibank had expressed an interest. The signatories included Germany's Commerzbank, Deutsche Bank and Dresdner Bank; Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp; Credit Suisse and Swiss Bank Corp; Westpac of Australia, Royal Bank of Canada, and Royal Bank of Scotland. Among the principles to which they have committed themselves is to ensure 'the best practices in environmental management, including energy efficiency, recycling and waste minimisation.' In a report published today the UN environment programme says that ecological destruction has accelerated over the last 20 years, David Lascelles reports from London. Malnutrition has increased, the gap between rich and poor has widened and children have become the worst victims of environmental mismanagement. The report predicts that the world's population, currently 5.4bn, will rise by a further 1bn by the end of the decade.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Brazil may request loan tranche delay
DOC.BYLINE: By STEPHEN FIDLER and CHRISTINA LAMB
DOC.TEXT: BRAZIL is likely to ask the International Monetary Fund to delay the second tranche of a Dollars 2.1bn (Pounds 1.18bn) loan agreed earlier this year because it has failed to meet some targets agreed with the Fund. Mr Marcilio Marques Moreira, the economy minister, does not want to ask for a waiver fearing this will reflect badly on Brazil, which has never previously come anywhere near completing an IMF programme, according to an Economy Ministry official. Instead, Mr Moreira has apparently suggested to Mr Michel Camdessus, managing director of the IMF, that the Dollars 250m payment due in May be delayed to August, when a six-month review of the programme is due. A collapse of the IMF standby programme would jeopardise the government's economic reform plan and severely set back Brazil's negotiations with creditor banks over a reduction in its foreign debt burden. Mr Pedro Parente, planning secretary, said yesterday the economic programme was going well. 'We have met the majority of targets but some have been missed by a small margin.' The problem lies on the fiscal side. As a result of falling tax revenues, Brazil's economic team has been unable to bring the operating deficit under control. An operating deficit means government revenues have fallen short of expenditures, including interest payments on its debt. Tax receipts fell by 14 per cent in real terms between January and March. Under the terms of the accord signed in January, Brazil must produce a primary surplus - which does not factor in interest payments - of 3 per cent of GDP by the end of this year. 'We already have a primary surplus but it's just not enough,' Mr Parente said. The economic team hopes that by delaying the second drawdown to August it will gain time for an increase in tax revenues as a result of tax reforms coming into effect this month. The news is likely to increase instability in the Brazilian financial markets. The central bank started intervening again in the gold and parallel (black) dollar markets yesterday after a six-month absence.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / White House reviews domestic policy in wake of riots
DOC.TEXT: THE Bush administration is working on a new domestic policy programme to deal with problems exposed by last week's violence in Los Angeles and to counter criticism of its lack of ideas or action. President George Bush, who left for Los Angeles last night for a two-day visit to tour the riot-torn areas of the city and discuss reconstruction measures with local officials and community leaders, said he wanted new ideas, not a continuation of existing welfare programmes that have not worked. 'It is far more important to give people a piece of the action than it is to have the federal government simply dump largesse on them,' he said. The Republican administration has been put on the defensive by criticism of its neglect of urban problems during 11 years in the White House. Party strategists had been hoping the violence in Los Angeles would rebound to their advantage by heightening concerns over law and order, a traditional Republican strength. But the haste with which the administration has struggled to define a new urban policy agenda reflects a worry that voters might blame the incumbent president for failing to tackle the underlying social problems. The debate over how best to respond to the Los Angeles riots has now erupted into a partisan argument over the social safety net programmes of the 1960s and 1970s. Mr Bush's Democratic opponents had at first reacted cautiously to the riots, fearful of the dangers of appearing to politicise the issue. Goaded by the White House's attack on President Lyndon Johnson's 'Great Society' programmes as the cause of today's urban problems, however, the Democrats have punched back. 'When domestic problems become too visible to ignore, all this administration does is look for somebody else to blame. First it was Jimmy Carter, today it's Lyndon John-son. Who is next? Grover Cleveland, maybe?' sneered Congressman David Bonior, Democratic whip in the House of Representatives. Mr Bush said yesterday that he did not want to 'play the blame game,' but went on to reaffirm his criticism of Great Society programmes. The administration has, however, shifted its position to emphasise that it has increased spending on many of these programmes, such as Medicaid and food stamps. 'Every single agency of the federal government is spending more today than it was in 1980 and spending more than it was in 1988,' said Mr Jack Kemp, secretary of housing and urban development. Mr Kemp has long been the principal, and sometimes only, advocate within the Bush cabinet of a more active domestic policy agenda, based on the 'empowerment' of poor people by helping them accumulate capital to buy homes and start businesses. His ideas are now likely to receive more enthusiastic support from the White House as it seeks to play up Mr Bush's response to domestic problems. The programmes have their critics, but the more devastating charge against the president is that he is once again following a pattern he has perfected in his three years in office: create a paper trail by proposing legislation, do nothing to push for its enactment, then blame the Democratic- controlled Congress for not passing it.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Task force looks to the private sector: How restoration plans for Los Angeles offer a national model
DOC.TEXT: REBUILD Los Angeles, the task force created by Mayor Tom Bradley to take charge of efforts to restore the riot-ravaged sections of the city, has set its sights on creating a model for urban renewal throughout the US. To be headed by Mr Peter Ueberroth, whose ties to Los Angeles stem from his role as chairman of the 1984 Olympics organising committee, the task force aims to revitalise the economically depressed parts of the city that suffered most of last week's destruction. Private-sector investment will be the key focus of the group. State and local government funding is limited. California is already facing a Dollars 9bn (Pounds 5bn) budget deficit that can only be worsened by the problems in Los Angeles, while the city is in the red to the tune of more than Dollars 800m. 'We will be out soliciting and wrenching out commitments from the private sector,' says Mr Barry Sanders, a prominent international business lawyer and counsel to the 'extra-governmental' non-profit group and a member of Rebuild LA. The task force will seek support from a wide range of businesses with established ties to Los Angeles, including foreign as well as US companies. 'We intend to reach out to the people who have investments in this community, or who ought to have, and that will include the British and the Japanese,' says Mr Sanders. 'There are Japanese car plants in southern California, for example. We want those companies to consider locating their next plant in Los Angeles. We will try to get tax breaks and low-interest loans for large and small businesses. We want them to go into this with a profit motive but at the same time train and employ people from this community.' But that will take time. 'By next week there are going to be people asking 'why hasn't this group done anything yet',' Mr Sanders predicts. Therefore, the initial thrust of the task force will be to have a visible impact on the hardest hit areas; to move ahead with demolition and clean up. Already there are tentative plans involving a landscaping industry group that has offered to plant grass and trees and install irrigation on demolition sites. Although such parks might be only temporary, at least they would improve the outlook of burnt-out neighbourhoods and, as Mr Sanders puts it, 'show that something is being done'. Longer-term efforts to attract investment to the area may prove difficult. 'The riots have dealt a serious blow to Los Angeles' image,' says Mr Jack Kyser, chief economist at the Los Angeles Economic Development Corporation. 'Foreign investors are hesitant. They are reconsidering the risks' in light of last week's events. Even US companies may 'sit back and assess whether they want to pump money into an area already besieged by problems of riots and earthquakes,' Mr Kyser adds. The more immediate problem may be to stem the outflow of businesses leaving the area, Mr Kyser suggests. In the past 18 months California lost half a million jobs, according to a report issued last month by the Council on California Competitiveness, chaired by Mr Ueberroth. Others are more optimistic. 'Los Angeles is still a huge market that will continue to attract investment,' argues Ms Mary Tuten, president of the Los Angeles World Trade Centre. 'Some businesses will leave, but some will view this as a tremendous new opportunity,' she predicts. 'In the long term you will see major reconstruction.' History would suggest otherwise. The Watts district of Los Angeles, the site of race riots in the 1960s, has never recovered despite reconstruction programmes. 'But they were driven by government spending and it did not work for business reasons. This is going to be different, this community is going to rebuild itself,' Ms Tuten maintains. Rebuild LA, however, has also yet to win the trust of key segments of the community. Black leaders, in particular, have voiced concerns that the task force may not provide opportunities for their people. 'Whatever we do, it must be done with the full involvement of all segments of the community,' Mr Sanders responds. 'This cannot be a bunch of downtown businessmen imposing their ideas on the community,' he stresses. People from all segments of the community will be invited to join the governing board of the task force. 'They have been at sword point with one another, but this is a chance for them to start over, to work together, if anything good is to come out of all of this.' Raising hopes are the commitments of Bank of America and smaller local banks to offer preferential loan terms to people affected by the riot. And other offers are 'flooding in' to Rebuild LA, says Mr Sanders. 'We have to capture this rush of enthusiasm and hope.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK set to sign new pact on boat people
DOC.TEXT: AN ACCORD is due to be signed next week to repatriate tens of thousands of Vietnamese boat people from Hong Kong, the UK Foreign Office said last night, PA reports. 'We are on the verge of signing an agreement to return to Vietnam all Vietnamese who arrived in Hong Kong before October 29, 1991, who, after careful screening, are judged not to be refugees,' an FO spokesman said. The accord covers over 20,432 people, and the operation could take three years. An agreement already exists between Britain, Vietnam and Hong Kong for repatriation of boat people - not deemed political refugees - who have arrived since October 29. The Hong Kong government yesterday disclosed that its budget surplus for last year was HKDollars 6bn (Pounds 437m) higher than its provisional figure, revealed in March, writes Simon Davies in Hong Kong. This brings the budget surplus for 1991-1992 to over Dollars HK20bn. Financial secretary Hamish MacLeod's statement on the windfall surplus was accompanied by a concession on his budget: property rates would not rise half a point to 6 per cent, as announced in the budget speech. The revenue fall was 'roughly equivalent' to the windfall surplus.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Riots force Lebanese premier to quit
DOC.TEXT: MR OMAR Karami, Lebanon's prime minister, and his 30-member cabinet resigned yesterday after anti-government riots spread throughout the country. The departure of the pro-Syrian premier after two days' civil unrest may diminish Syria's influence in Lebanon and presage a more independent line for his successor. It is the first time a Lebanese government has been toppled by civil unrest since the country's civil war began in 1975. Thousands of rioters took to the streets of Beirut and other Lebanese cities early yesterday, brandishing sticks, shovels and pistols. Main roads were blocked by heaps of blazing tyres. They smashed windows of government offices, banks and shops and set up barricades of burning tyres. Two teenagers were wounded when looters broke into Beirut's Arab Bank. Rioting broke out on Tuesday after radio reports that the Lebanese pound had collapsed to about LPounds 2,000 to the US dollar on the black market. But violence subsided after Mr Karami's resignation was announced. 'I have resigned to save the country,' the 57-year-old lawyer said after meeting President Elias Hrawi. The unrest has been sparked by Lebanon's economic crisis. For the first time, Lebanese of all faiths, trade unionists, industrialists, bankers and business people united in denunciation of the government and support for a four-day general strike aimed at ending its mandate. The country's main trade union is scheduled to reassess the strike today. Because the Karami half-Christian, half-Moslem cabinet was installed under Syrian supervision in December 1990, Lebanese rejection of the government constitutes a growing resentment of Syria's hold over the country. The Treaty of Brotherhood, Co-operation and Co-ordination signed with Syria last May required Lebanon to link its economic, foreign and security policies with those of Damascus, which keeps 40,000 troops in Lebanon. The Syrian presence made the disarming of Lebanese militias possible, but in recent months the Syrian embrace has choked public confidence and potential foreign investors. Lebanese leaders have made no important decisions without travelling to Damascus for 'consultations'. Mr Karami had sought Syrian approval in a trip to the Syrian capital on Tuesday before he resigned. Mr Karami, a Sunni Moslem, feuded openly with President Hrawi, a Maronite Catholic. When Mr Hrawi pleaded with Syrian officials for permission to replace Mr Karami in March, the Syrians refused, saying the Karami government would have to oversee parliamentary elections soon. A new cabinet is unlikely to be announced immediately. Officials in Beirut suggested the decision may take a few days. Most popular candidates to replace Mr Karami are Dr Selim El Hoss, the former prime minister, and Mr Rafiq Hariri, the Lebanese-born Saudi millionaire. Mr Hariri, a friend of the Saudi royal family, would appear well placed to obtain Saudi economic aid for Lebanon. Both men have in recent days met Syrian leaders in Damascus. Both are believed to have demanded greater independence from Syria as a condition for becoming premier. Syria's strategy regarding the crisis in Lebanon remains unclear. Many rioters in southern Lebanon and Beirut were members of the Syrian-backed Amal militia, and Syrian troops made no attempt to intervene during the disturbances. Damascus could seek to impose an even closer ally as prime minister, perhaps Gen Sami Khatib, interior minister, who was among those who resigned yesterday.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Thais urge general to resign as prime minister
DOC.TEXT: ABOUT 80,000 Thais surrounded parliament last night demanding that the general who engineered a coup last year resign from his new position of prime minister, police said. As room for compromise between Gen Suchinda and his critics appeared to dwindle, a group of academics appealed to the king to defuse the crisis by dissolving parliament and calling another general election. The Thai monarch would have the power to do that although he normally keeps strictly above politics. Some observers say his intervention might be the only way to break the deadlock. Maj-Gen Chamlong Srimuang, former Bangkok governor and leader of one of the opposition parties, continued the hunger strike he began on Monday. His threat to die if Gen Suchinda does not resign has brought a number of normally passive supporters out on to the street in front of parliament where he is encamped, communicating only in writing. He has predicted he will last only seven days, adding urgency to the crisis which has caused panic on the stock market, whose share price index shed 43.36 points yesterday to close at 717.62. So far, the protests have been peaceful, but observers fear there is a real danger of unrest if Gen Suchinda remains prime minister, as is his constitutional right, and Maj-Gen Chamlong dies. Maj-Gen Chamlong, whose party took 32 of the 35 seats in Bangkok in the March 22 general election, has gained popularity as a modest-living politician. For either to back down would mean a serious loss of face and reputation. Opposition MPs boycotted the start of yesterday's debate when the prime minister presented his first policy statement to parliament. After that, they launched a barrage of criticism, questioning his ability to fulfil promises to maintain democratic government. They accused him of destroying democracy by engineering last year's coup d'etat and putting himself and his military friends in key positions. Members of the five-party coalition defended their constitutional right to pick an outsider to be prime minister. Opposition MPs also addressed the rally outside parliament where the more emotive speeches concentrated on Gen Suchinda's earlier promise not to accept the premiership after this year's election. One MP said the planned 12-hour debate on the policy statement would be a waste of time because Gen Suchinda's word was 'worthless'. MPs, who were expecting to continue until midnight, were caught by surprise when Gen Suchinda left parliament shortly before 6pm and the debate ended abruptly without any explanation. Some opposition MPs said the prime minister feared for his safety because of the large numbers outside parliament. The debate is scheduled to to continue today.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / ADB renews call to fight Asian poverty
DOC.TEXT: THE Asian Development Bank closed its annual meeting yesterday with renewed calls to step up the war against poverty and environmental degradation in Asia's fast-growing economies, Reuter reports from Hong Kong. But some delegates privately attacked the bank for what they see as its flabby response to the region's growing social needs and inability to trim its bureaucracy. The task of meeting growing social and infrastructure needs at a time of shrinking funds from rich member-nations such as the US was a main theme at the ADB's three-day meeting of Asian finance ministers and international bankers. ADB president Kimimasa Tarumizu urged more efficient use of resources to tackle the bank's priorities for the 1990s. 'Global changes have created new demands on the flow of resources; the need to augment these flows becomes more important,' he said. The US delegation has vowed to oppose an early increase in the bank's capital until it sees more evidence to back the request. Last year, the bank proposed its capital base of Dollars 23bn (Pounds 12.9bn) be doubled by 1994.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Finland to buy US jet fighters
DOC.BYLINE: By ROBERT TAYLOR and GEORGE GRAHAM
DOC.TEXT: Finland has opted for McDonnell Douglas's F/A-18 Hornet to replace its ageing air force of Russian-built MiG-21s and Swedish Draken fighters, report Robert Taylor and George Graham. It will buy 57 single-seater Hornets and seven two-seater trainers for FM9.5bn (Pounds 1.2bn). McDonnell Douglas was in competition with General Dynamics, Dassault, Saab and the Russians. Total value of the deal, once training and weaponry such as the Sidewinder and Amraam air-to-air missiles are included, is expected to reach FM13bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Trade News: ABB-led consortium to build Iran plant
DOC.BYLINE: By MARK NICHOLSON, Middle East Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: IRAN has awarded a consortium led by Asea Brown Boveri (ABB), the Zurich-based engineering group, a Dollars 1.25bn (Pounds 700m) contract to build a 2,000MW hydroelectric plant on the Karun River. ABB said its German subsidiary, ABB Mannheim, would supply eight generators and all the electrical equipment for the project, giving it a Dollars 340m share of the Karun-3 contract overall. The hydroelectric plant, in south-west Iran, will be one of the world's largest and follows ABB's energetic pursuit of work in the Gulf. Gebruder Sulzer of Switzerland will supply turbines, valves and other equipment worth Dollars 230m, while Austria's Voest Alpine will provide hydromechanical equipment worth Dollars 145m. Brazil's Andrade Gutierrez will undertake work worth Dollars 530m on constructing the dam and other civil engineering. Financing for the project, which is due to have the first 500MW on stream before 1997, is still being negotiated, ABB said. The project is one of several power plants planned by the Iranian government on both the Karun and Arras Rivers, including a further, Karun-4, hydroelectric plant.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Corsican stadium disaster
DOC.TEXT: French policemen carry an injured soccer fan to a helicopter after the Corsican stadium disaster on Tuesday in which 700 spectators were injured. French authorities said 10 people were killed when the stadium collapsed, near Bastia, but the regional prefect's office and public prosecutor put the figure at 26. The International Football Federation (Fifa) is now likely to ban temporary football stands made of tubular scaffolding, writes Ian Davidson from Paris.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Minimum bank guarantees proposed
DOC.TEXT: ALL depositors in EC banks should have a minimum Ecu15,000 (Pounds 10,500) of their deposits guaranteed, the European Commission proposed yesterday. The EC executive began work on the draft directive before the failure of the Bank of Commerce and Credit International (BCCI) last year, but accelerated its initiative after the scandal surrounding the bank's collapse. The Commission suggests that bank customers should obtain their deposit guarantee reimbursement within three months, in contrast to the much longer period that many depositors with the Luxembourg-incorporated BCCI had to wait. Responsibility for deposit insurance would switch from the host to the home country of a bank. Mr Pierre Jaans, head of the Luxembourg Monetary Institute, said this would not pose a problem for the duchy. Very few Luxembourg-based banks, with the notable exception of BCCI, had branches abroad. Commission officials hope that EC governments will reach basic agreement on the guarantee scheme under the UK presidency of the EC later this year. The plan would require Greece and Portugal to institute deposit guarrantees for the first time.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Sweden wants its EC application speeded up
DOC.TEXT: MR Carl Bildt, Sweden's prime minister, will seek the British government's support in speeding up his country's application to join the European Community during a meeting with Mr John Major, the British prime minister, today. The meeting comes amid doubts over the feasibility of Sweden's self-imposed timetable for entry. Mr Bildt would like the British EC presidency, which starts its six-month term on July 1, to give EC enlargement top priority. He insists formal negotiations must start with Brussels early next year and be concluded by the end of 1993. This would ensure time for a national referendum on Sweden's entry to be held during the first half of 1994. Such speed is dictated by the Swedish constitution. Any change in the country's fundamental laws requires two identical approvals by the Swedish parliament, with the first given not less than nine months before a general election and the second after an election. Sweden will elect its next parliament on 20 September 1994, which means any EC entry agreement must be submitted by 18 December next year, or be delayed until 1 January 1998. It would need a majority of parliament's constitutional committee to waive this provision. Another concern for Mr Bildt is the sign of growing opposition within Sweden to EC entry. Observer, Page 22

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Bold action to transform Russia's 'wooden' rouble
DOC.TEXT: DIPLOMATS and businessmen in Moscow laugh about it. Russian enterprises are worried by it. The Russian people are bewildered. But the government is deadly serious about it. The announcement on Tuesday that the Russian government would make the rouble internally convertible this summer was a bold political statement following the west's decision to provide a Dollars 6bn (Pounds 3.3bn) stabilisation fund for the project. Politically, it served notice to the battered Russian people that the government would deliver its promise to transform the much-maligned 'wooden' rouble into a real currency. It told the world Moscow was on track with its bold plans to integrate Russia into the world economy. It warned the other republics that they would have to play by tough budgetary, financial and credit policy rules dictated by Moscow in order to continue using the rouble. The plan involves floating the rouble rate from July 1 and then defending it up to 7.5 per cent either side of the fixed rate from August 1. Russian officials admitted yesterday that many of the details had yet to be decided. But the general idea, as explained Mr Andrei Vavilov, the first deputy finance minister, is that if central bank intervention to defend the rouble becomes excessive, the government responds by either raising interest rates (to encourage people to convert dollars into roubles to earn interest) or by devaluing. Foreign diplomats and businessmen doubt whether the rate of Rbs80 a dollar at which the goverment hoped to start defending the rouble was realistic given the enormous demand for hard currency in Russia. But Mr Alexander Potemkin, head of the Russian central bank's international department, suggested that the rate might be as strong as Rbs50-Rbs60 with the moves towards convertibility. He pointed to three factors: if exporters were encouraged to sell hard currency earnings at a free market rate there would be more supply than at present. Secondly, if the government's macro-economic reforms stayed on track, the state-owned enterprises would have to become more efficient. Thirdly, he said, the exchange rate would continue to benefit from a physical shortage of roubles in the economy - yesterday the rouble strengthened to Rbs128 per dollar from Rbs143.6 last week. The reform will seek to create a single exchange rate, abolishing all other rates such as the punitive 'commercial' rate at which exporters are obliged to sell 40 per cent of their earnings to the state. This means doing away with favourable exchange rates for certain types of state-owned enterprises to purchase vital imports such as spare parts. Competition from imports is unlikely, since imports would probably remain too expensive for most Russian consumers for some time. But for foreign companies contracting to sell goods to solvent buyers in Russia, the system would be little changed. The Russian buyer converts roubles into currency and sends it to the seller's bank account. Another argument in favour of proceeding with convertibility is to encourage badly-needed foreign investment - investors will be less afraid of making mountains of roubles they cannot spend or convert to hard currency. It remains to be seen if the supply of currency can be vastly increased. Estimated annual export earnings are Dollars 25-Dollars 30bn, but only 2 per cent of that is sold voluntarily by enterprises to the state, with many avoiding the 40 per cent tax by keeping earnings in foreign bank accounts. The government plans to open exchange points around the country to encourage the ordinary citizen to part with dollars. It is unlikely that this will attract currency in itself. But what may have more of a role will be a proposed clampdown on the use of the dollar to buy and sell goods within Russia - if it can be enforced.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Tajikistan opposition militia seizes control of capital
DOC.TEXT: THE communist government of Tajikistan was in disarray yesterday after opposition militia groups seized most of the capital, Dushanbe. But there were signs of a possible compromise last night, with attempts to put together a coalition between the opposition and moderate members of the government. Opposition forces said up to 60 people had been killed in clashes in the republic since Monday. The government appeared to have lost control of all key structures of power in the capital, apart from the parliament buildings. Mr Rakhmon Nabiyev, the Tajik president, appeared to have vanished and a split was said to have emerged in government ranks between hardliners - including Vice-President Nazrullo Dustov and parliamentary speaker Safarli Kenjayev - and moderate factions. The opposition, a loose alliance of Islamic and democratic parties, set up roadblocks, guarded by nervous and shabbily dressed opposition militia carrying Kalashnikovs. The presidential palace was under opposition control, and the television station, captured earlier in the week, broadcast pro-opposition statements. Gun battles broke out in the tree-lined parks around the city's radio station, as the opposition sought to take away the government's last channel of mass communications. Many Interior Ministry troops appeared to have joined the opposition militia group. In an attempt to stop the bloodshed, leaders from opposition parties re-opened negotiations with some of the more moderate government figures, with the aim of forming an interim coalition. But with armed militia groups still roaming the city, finding a compromise appeared extremely difficult. Although the government's hand seemed weak, many key government figures remained bitterly opposed to the political reforms the opposition has been demanding, and seemed far from ready to give in peacefully. The conflict is exacerbated by bitter regional splits in the republic. Most government supporters come from the Kulyab and Khodjent regions in the north and south-east, while most Islamic party supporters come from the east and south. Another problem lies with the fragile nature of the opposition coalition of Islamic and democratic parties. For a month, the opposition had been peacefully demonstrating against the government before being provoked into a more radical stance by the arrival of thousands of government supporters bussed into the capital 10 days ago. Its official aim is establishment of a multi-party democracy. But with the Islamic party clearly the stronger partner, many fear the democratic leaders could soon be swept away by more radical Moslems. The square where thousands have been demonstrating for the last month is decorated with Islamic placards and slogans. Many of these have been copied from Iran. White-veiled women and determined young men declare themselves ready to die as martyrs for Islam. Opposition leaders continue to insist that these fiery sentiments will not be necessary. But with most of their supporters insisting that they will not go home until the communist government is completely overthrown, the opposition leaders will find it difficult to persuade them to accept any compromise.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Gorbachev blames East and West for Cold War
DOC.TEXT: MR Mikhail Gorbachev, the former Soviet leader, said yesterday that both east and west deserved blame for the Cold War and that the Soviet Union never intended to attack the west, Agencies report. He told a crowd of thousands in Fulton, Missouri, that the US mistakenly fed hostilities by believing in 'the probability of open' Soviet aggression. 'This could never happen, not only because Stalin ..was afraid of war and did not want war ..but primarily because our country was exhausted and destroyed.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Kravchuk reassures US over N-weapons treaty
DOC.TEXT: PRESIDENT Leonid Kravchuk of Ukraine assured the US yesterday that his newly independent republic would implement the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (Start) reducing long-range nuclear weapons. Speaking after talks with President George Bush at the White House, Mr Kravchuk denied reports in Moscow that all Ukraine's tactical - or short-range - nuclear weapons had been removed to Russia to be destroyed. But he promised they would be moved by the agreed July deadline. Mr Kravchuk said the US and Ukraine had worked out a protocol by which Ukraine, which inherited some of the Soviet Union's long-range missiles, would endorse Start. The US wants the former Soviet republics with nuclear weapons - Ukraine, Russia, Belarus and Kazakhstan - to commit themselves to the treaty, signed by Washington and Moscow last year but not yet ratified by either side. The confusion over the withdrawal of tactical missiles follows months of shadow boxing between Moscow and Kiev over this and other military issues dividing the two most powerful members of the Commonwealth of Independent States. Earlier this year Ukraine held up the transfer of tactical nuclear missiles, arguing that once in Russia it was not clear they would be dismantled. This objection was overcome by an agreement to do it under international supervision. The two republics have also been arguing over dividing the Black Sea naval fleet and control of the Crimean peninsula. The transfer of all tactical weapons would be widely welcomed in the west as a step towards ensuring a stable outcome for part of the vast nuclear arsenal inherited from the Soviet Union. The Crimean parliament yesterday took a big step back from a declaration of independence approved a day earlier and proclaimed the peninsula to be part of Ukraine.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Heseltine acts to cut gap in car prices
DOC.BYLINE: By KEVIN DONE and DAVID BUCHAN
DOC.TEXT: THE GOVERNMENT is to open talks with car manufacturers to remove restrictions on dealerships which have been blamed for keeping British car prices higher than those in other European countries. A two-year European Commission study of the EC car market has confirmed that many models were 30 per cent more expensive in the UK than on the continent. A so-called 'block exemption' allows carmakers to determine which dealerships can sell their brand of cars and where they can be sold. They generally prevent dealers from selling more than one brand of car and do not allow them to import cars themselves. 'I am seeking a better deal for consumers through the removal of some restrictions placed on dealers by car suppliers,' said Mr Michael Heseltine, trade and industry secretary, yesterday. He welcomed moves announced yesterday by the European Commission to ensure car companies do not abuse their selective dealership system. Mr Heseltine said the government would now push ahead with the recommendations of the recent Monopolies and Mergers Commission report on new car sales in the UK. This called for the removal of some restrictions placed by some carmakers on their franchised dealers, which the MMC claimed operated against the public interest. As part of the push for fairer pricing, manufacturers are being encouraged by Brussels to publish price lists to help consumers shop around the EC for models with the same specifications. 'We want to ensure people's right to buy the car they want at an undistorted price,' said Sir Leon Brittan, competition commissioner. He claimed his campaign for cross-border selling in the EC car market would lead to 'a substantial downward pressure on prices and to a more equal distribution of prices'. Sir Hal Miller, chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, claimed the EC report showed no evidence that selective distribution was responsible for price variations. Ford moves R&D jobs, Page 11

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Markets
FT 07 MAY 92 / Major cuts at secrecy by naming MI6 chief
DOC.TEXT: MR JOHN MAJOR yesterday foreshadowed a significant shift towards more open government with a pledge to provide a legal framework for Britain's Secret Intelligence Service. His public acknowledgement of the existence of the SIS, the first by any prime minister since the forerunner of the country's spy establishment was set up in 1909, came as he presented his legislative programme in the Queen's Speech. The programme includes bills to pave the way for the privatisation of British Coal and parts of British Rail, as well as to implement the Maastricht treaties on European union. A finance bill, due within the next 10 days, will reintroduce those measures in Mr Norman Lamont's Budget which were dropped because of the general election. Speaking in the House of Commons, Mr Major said one of his most immediate aims was 'to sweep away some of the cobwebs of secrecy which needlessly veil too much of government business'. He confirmed that among the first steps would be publication of the details of the cabinet committees which make most important government decisions and of the guidance issued to ministers on their personal financial interests. Mr William Waldegrave, chancellor of the duchy of Lancaster, had been asked to review other areas where 'excessive secrecy' might be removed. The prime minister then told MPs that it was time to acknowledge officially the existence of the SIS, commonly known as MI6. It was responsible for foreign intelligence designed to support the government's foreign, defence, security and economic policies. He confirmed that the service works directly to the foreign secretary and the prime minister, and that its current chief is Sir Colin McColl. Sir Colin is listed in reference books as a senior official at the Foreign Office. MI5, the domestic counterpart of the SIS, was given a legal basis in 1989. This year, Mr Major broke with tradition by making public the appointment of Mrs Stella Rimmington as its director. Between them the two services have a budget of Pounds 185m for the current financial year. Mr Major insisted that the government would continue to refuse to comment on the activities of the two services because of the risk that would bring to their effectiveness and staff. Senior Whitehall officials said this meant that the legislation to place the SIS on a statutory basis was unlikely to subject it to direct scrutiny by MPs. Instead the legislation is expected to be modelled on that introduced for MI5, which provided for limited rights of redress by the public. Mr Major's first legislative programme as an elected prime minister included a range of bills designed to enhance individual choice and ownership, and to improve the responsiveness to public sector services. Among the most significant measures in a parliamentary session which will last until the autumn of 1993 are bills to push ahead with the government's education reforms, to tighten the law on asylum and to set up an urban regeneration agency.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / OFT blow for Lloyds' plan to buy Midland
DOC.TEXT: THE OFFICE of Fair Trading plans to recommend that the Monopolies and Mergers Commission examine Lloyds Bank's proposal to buy Midland. It does not, however, believe the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation bid for Midland raises competition issues worthy of extended investigation. The disclosure of the OFT's view by a senior government official will come as a blow to Lloyds. It has been hoping that both its plan and Hongkong Bank's bid would be examined by the MMC. Lloyds has said it would only convert its takeover plan into a fully fledged bid if the MMC looked at the takeover approaches of both banks. The official stressed that the OFT had not made a final decision. By the end of the week it should have submissions from all three banks on the competitive issues raised by the takeover proposals. It will review these documents next week and make a recommendation to Mr Michael Heseltine, trade and industry secretary. However, OFT officials have had meetings with executives of all three banks and they have already assessed the effect on banking markets of both takeover proposals. The OFT believes that the Lloyds' approach may have a detrimental effect on competition in small business loans. The OFT decision on Lloyds and Hongkong Bank will be the last one taken by the director-general, Sir Gordon Borrie, who retires in June. Mr Heseltine has not instructed Sir Gordon to review the takeover by any other criteria than those he has been using for the past eight years which give the highest priority to competitive issues. In the Hongkong Bank case, the OFT believes it will not have the leading role in making a recommendation on whether there is a threat to competition. It has been told by DG4, the European Community's competition authority, that jurisdiction over the Hongkong Bank takeover offer is likely to rest with DG4. A decision is expected in the coming week. The government official said the question of which body has jurisdiction on the competition question may be less important than Lloyds believes. If the OFT were to have jurisdiction, the official said, it would not recommend that the Hongkong Bank bid was scrutinised by the MMC. Mr Heseltine does not have to follow the recommendation of the OFT. But in the past 16 years, Mr Heseltine's predecessors have done the opposite of what the OFT has recommended on only 14 occasions. On just two occasions have they ordered an MMC inquiry when the OFT recommended against one. Mr Heseltine could ask the MMC to investigate whether a Hongkong Bank takeover of Midland would be against the public interest for reasons other than competitive ones. But this would not be easy for him. If the EC decides it has jurisdiction on the competitive aspect of the Hongkong Bank bid, Mr Heseltine could ask for a separate UK review of whether the takeover was a threat to Midland's depositors. However, he would have difficulty making such a request, because the Bank of England has already said it does not believe Hongkong Bank's bid would put Midland's depositors at risk. Mr Heseltine could also argue, under Article 9, that the Hongkong Bank bid raises general issues of national concern and should therefore be reviewed in the UK. However, the European Commission has to date been reluctant to comply with requests for national reviews of takeovers under Article 9. Lloyds is putting pressure on Mr Heseltine not to deprive Midland shareholders of its takeover proposal by making a reference. However, the government official hinted this argument was unlikely to influence the government. Lloyds' condition that the bid will only be made if there is no MMC reference is self-imposed, he pointed out, and can therefore be dropped.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK shares reach record high as hopes of recovery rise
DOC.TEXT: SHARE PRICES in London closed at record levels last night on the back of optimism about recovery prospects and signs that sterling was holding on to its recent gains. The FT-SE 100 index of leading shares gained 36.5 at 2,698.7 as investors took heart from Tuesday's half-point cut in interest rates to 10 per cent. The reduction in borrowing costs is expected to lead to a gradual uplift in the retail and housing markets - developments seen as helping a sustained revival from the recession that started around mid-1990. Sterling was unchanged in London against a stronger D-Mark, closing at DM2.925. That underlined the perception of many investors that, in spite of the cut in UK rates, sterling is unlikely to encounter serious strain within the European exchange rate mechanism over the next few weeks. The currency was close to its London levels in late New York trading. The possibility, viewed as remote by many economists, that the Bundesbank council might decide to increase German rates at its regular meeting today led to some switching of funds into the D-Mark. This caused the dollar to drop 1 pfennig to DM1.6305 in London. It closed at DM1.6287 in New York. But the buying pressure buoying the D-Mark was not enough to disturb sterling's position within 3 pfennigs of its DM2.95 central ERM rate. Against the dollar, the pound gained more than 1 cent in London to Dollars 1.7945. It closed at Dollars 1.7975 in New York. The rise in share prices pushed the FT-SE index above its last closing high of 2,683.7, reached eight months ago. The rise contrasted to Tuesday's tepid stock market reaction to the UK's first base rate cut since September. Mr Richard Jeffrey, head of economics research at stockbroker Charterhouse Tilney, said investors had needed time to tell whether the rate cut would damage sterling. 'If you are confident an upturn is really going to happen, the stock market looks 10 per cent undervalued.' Lex, Page 24 London stocks, Page 44

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World News in Brief: Tunnel fears
DOC.TEXT: More Britons fear the prospect of travelling through the Channel tunnel than flying or using a cross-Channel ferry, according to consumer magazine Which?

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World News in Brief: Racketeering blitz
DOC.TEXT: Up to 1,000 police and troops in Northern Ireland launched a dawn swoop against paramilitary racketeering in border areas in a bid to curb financing for terrorism.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World News in Brief: Ryan arrested
DOC.TEXT: Former priest Patrick Ryan, who evaded extradition from Belgium and Ireland four years ago over an IRA bombing campaign, was arrested by police in the Irish Republic.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Switzerland (15): The nuts and bolts - Engineering is still the motor of the economy
DOC.TEXT: MANY PEOPLE still tend to think of Switzerland as a country of solid banks, delightful tourist retreats and quaint watchmakers. In fact, the country's outsize engineering industry is the motor of the Swiss economy. With 3,000 companies and a labour force of 370,000, it dwarfs the banking sector, and its exports of SFr39.3bn last year were worth six times those of the watchmakers. By the late 1980s, the Swiss engineering industry had become so large that it was having difficulty keeping up with its customers' demands. In particular, it was suffering from skilled labour shortages, and chafing at Switzerland's tough restrictions on immigrant workers. In the past year, however, the industry's concerns have changed dramatically as, like its counterparts elsewhere in the world, it has been hit by the downturn in capital spending in many of its important markets. While Asea Brown Boveri (ABB), by far the biggest group in the sector, managed to eke out a 2 per cent improvement in pre-tax profits last year, few others did as well. Von Roll, the steel and machinery group, and Rieter, the textile machinery group, slumped into loss, while others, such as Sulzer Brothers, the pumps and textile machinery group, George Fischer, the machine tool builder, and Schindler, the lifts and rolling stock maker, reported sharp declines in their profits. At the annual press conference in February of the Swiss Association of Machinery Manufacturers (VSM), concern about labour and skill shortages gave way to shock at the soaring jobless rate. By the end of 1991, the number of full-time unemployed in the sector had nearly tripled to 5,700 compared to the end of 1990, and short-time working, which was virtually non-existent in the late 1980s, was affecting 21,000. Hardly a week goes by without announcements of closures and redundancies. Perhaps the most significant last month was the closure by Sulzer Brothers of its large-piece grey iron foundry at Oberwinterthur. This was the last remaining large-scale iron foundry in the country, and even though its demise will eliminate only 520 jobs, it was a chilling indicator of how tough things have become in some industry sectors. Sulzer pointed out that the foundry's main clients were the machine tool and textile machinery industries and their combined orders tumbled from 10.7m tonnes in 1989 to only 5.3m tonnes last year. Surprisingly, output and order statistics do not yet fully reflect the agony that is being felt in many engineering sectors. Last year, new orders of 200 leading companies surveyed by the VSM were down only 1.4 per cent and their combined sales advanced a healthy 11.3 per cent to SFr26.1bn. Total industry exports were up 0.3 per cent. However, other figures are more revealing. The combined backlog of 260 companies in a VSM study dropped from 6.1 months in the fourth quarter of 1990 to 5.3 months in the fourth quarter of last year, the lowest level in 10 years. Capacity utilisation also fell from a record 91.5 per cent in 1990 to a seven-year low of 85 per cent last year. The hardest hit was textile machinery, which is the second largest sector in the industry after machine tools. Textile machine sales were down nearly 18 per cent, as clothing and home furnishings makers turned cautious. The machine tool industry's sales tumbled 11 per cent to SFr3.6bn, hurt by the virtual drying up of eastern European markets. Sales of electrical and precision equipment eased 2 per cent, but electronic industries' revenues were up, thanks in part to major modernisation programmes of the Swiss telecoms establishment. As for the outlook, there is little optimism for the near term. Mr Martin Erb, executive director of the VSM, noted in February that the slight upturn in orders in the fourth quarter of last year was due to a single large order received by ABB to build a power station in Indonesia. In the first quarter of this year, exports were up a surprisingly healthy 7 per cent by value, but VSM officials cautioned against reading this as an indication that there will be much improvement in the year as a whole. For one thing, the export figure is flattered by the sharp decline in the value of the Swiss franc in the past year. For another, the important machine tool sector is still sagging, with exports down 21 per cent. Another negative factor is that domestic demand is likely to be softer this year than last because of budget constraints at all levels of government. 'It is still difficult to tell if we will even achieve the same level of sales this year as last year,' a VSM official says gloomily. This sharp change in the industry's health has heightened its anxiety about Switzerland's position in Europe and the world. Nearly two-thirds of all its exports go to EC countries and over 70 per cent go to the 18 west European countries. The VSM has long officially supported the idea of Switzerland joining the European Community and major international organisations, and this year added its formal endorsement for the proposal to join the European Economic Area. Mr Erb said that the engineering industry, with its record exports to the EC, 'provided further proof of the absolute necessity of free access to the largest internal market in the world'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Switzerland (14): Wine goes upmarket - The country's last cottage industry
DOC.TEXT: IN THE mid-1980s Swiss winemakers awoke from a slumber worthy of Rip van Winkle to find the world utterly changed. Shifting consumer tastes and a domestic wine glut are forcing the country's last remaining cottage industry to become more efficient, professional and outward-looking. As a consequence, thousands of small vineyard owners are expected to bow out over the next few years. Traditionally, Switzerland has produced eminently quaffable but unremarkable wines with little staying power. About 60 per cent of its production, 140m litres last year, is white wine, mostly from the Chasselas grape. The dominant red grapes are Pinot Noir, Gamay and Merlot. Cushioned by high government subsidies and tight restrictions on competing imports, especially for white wine, Swiss growers had little need to worry about quality in what was essentially a captive market. For white wine, domestic production meets nine-tenths of consumption, against about one-third for red wine. Winemakers had little interest in exporting abroad and no incentive to do so. Things changed abruptly 10 years ago when a string of bumper harvests from 1982 created Switzerland's very own wine lake, one big Valais winery went to the wall, and the federal government was forced to implement a costly surplus disposal programme. In 1986, the mountain canton of Valais, Switzerland's main wine-producing area, became the first to impose stringent measures to rein back production and boost wine quality by restricting the quantity of grapes left to grow on the vines. Switzerland's first 'Appellation d'Origine Controlee' (AOC), wine conforming to strict quality standards, was introduced in 1987, also in the Valais. The Swiss parliament is currently discussing a draft federal decree that will restrain production and improve wine quality nationwide. At the beginning of this year the government scrapped import quotas for bulk deliveries of red wine, and it plans further liberalisation of wine imports in the light of the international trade talks under way in Geneva. Earlier government proposals to regulate wine production were thrown out by voters two years ago on the grounds that they did not go far enough to eliminate barriers to imports. The draft decree also classifies wines into three quality groups (with 'appellation d'origine', 'indication de provenance' and 'vins ordinaires'). This, too, is a big break with the past. In the Valais, for instance, most small growers sold their grapes to big wine distributors to be bottled simply under the generic names of Fendant (Chasselas), Johannisberg (Sylvaner) or Dole (Pinot Noir and Gamay). The effects on the structure of the Swiss wine industry will be far-reaching. Mr Francois Cordonnier, president of the Valais Federation of wine growers, thinks the number of vineyard keepers in the canton could shrink from 22,000 to just 4,000 over the next decade. One in five working adults has a vineyard, often no bigger than a tennis court, and 90 per cent of holdings are worked part-time. Equally revolutionary, the Swiss are turning their minds to markets abroad, and not just for offloading the odd surplus. Switzerland now exports under 2m bottles of wine a year, a tiny 1 per cent of production which the Association of Swiss Wine Exporters in Lausanne would like to see boosted to 5 or even 10 per cent in the longer term. The problem with exporting more, as Swiss growers concede, is that Switzerland has few distinctive wines, and even fewer distinguished ones, to entice sophisticated overseas palates. Yet with production costs in Switzerland two to four times those elsewhere in Europe, Swiss winemakers have little choice but to follow their compatriots in watchmaking, machine tools and other export industries in moving resolutely upmarket. The industry is split on how best to do this. Some growers in French-speaking Switzerland, which produces 80 per cent of the country's wine, propose abandoning the ubiquitous Chasselas grape in favour of more reliable varieties such as Chardonnay or Sauvignon Blanc. Others say the Chasselas gives Swiss wine its distinctiveness and advocate research to improve the grape's wine-making qualities. Mr Christophe Von Ritter, secretary-general of the wine exporters' association, thinks prospects are good for wines made from some of Switzerland's unique indigenous grape varieties, which could sell not only on quality but also on curiosity value. But, despite the association's best endeavours, exporting is likely to remain a marginal pastime for growers while subsidies and protection continue to provide easier rewards in the domestic market.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Switzerland (13): The prospect of a Swatch car - After the rescue of the watchmaking industry, there are more ambitious plans
DOC.TEXT: ON APRIL 1, the French language daily, Le Nouveau Quotidien, published an interview with Mr Nicolas Hayek, boss of SMH, the watchmaking company best known for the Swatch plastic watch. Referring to the current political row over the Swiss government's intended purchase of 34 US fighter planes, Mr Hayek said Switzerland should develop its own aeroplanes. Aircraft design needed rethinking to produce a high-performance, low cost, environmentally friendly machine. Of course, the 'Swatch fighter' was a spoof. But Mr Hayek's real-life project to build a Swatch car has met much the same kind of amused disbelief. In proving the scoffers wrong, he hopes to demonstrate a personal conviction that Europe, even high-cost Switzerland, need not surrender its manufacturing base to the Far East. This conviction underpinned Mr Hayek's rescue plan for the Swiss watchmaking industry in the early 1980s when it was in danger of obliteration by Japanese competition. An engineering consultant who had already built up a successful business, Hayek Engineering, Mr Hayek was brought in by the banks to guide the troubled merger of SSIH and Asuag, the two biggest watchmakers, to form SMH (Societe Suisse de Microelectronique et d'Horlogerie) in 1984. Rejecting the conventional wisdom that Switzerland should retreat to the luxury end of the watch market, he argued that a thriving industry needed the mass market to provide the impulsion for cost control, technological development and marketing. The Swatch, which first appeared in 1982, was to spearhead recapture of this market from the Japanese. Greeted sceptically at the time, the Swatch has become a classic success story. Last month, the 100 millionth Swatch came off the production line - making it the biggest selling watch in history. Early Swatches are collectors' items, fetching thousands of dollars at auction and contemporary Swatch variants like the chronograph are the object of a flourishing black market trade. Stylish, constantly changing designs, a careful distribution policy and clever marketing have kept the Swatch boom going. But at its heart rests the original Swatch innovation - a big cut in the number of watch parts and a way of assembling them in one operation, allowing fully automated production for the first time. Today, the basic Swatch still sells for its original price of SFr50. Sales of Swatches, which are all produced in Switzerland, topped 17m in 1991. SMH plans output of 25-30m this year, doubling to 50m within five years, including variants such as the Pop Swatch, chronograph and the Scuba diving watch. A Swatch automatic, with a self-winding mechanism, will be launched later in 1992. Swatch accounts for something over half SMH's finished watch output of 30m last year and about a quarter of its SFr2.37bn sales. But production and marketing skills honed on the Swatch have helped to revitalise SMH's higher-priced watch brands, such as Omega, Longines, Rado and Tissot. SMH is now a world leader in luxury watches, which are estimated to contribute over half its profits, though analysts think it may be losing money in the highly competitive medium-priced market. The company has also pursued an ambitious strategy of vertical integration, manufacturing its own components including state-of-the-art microchips and batteries. These, and some 50m watch movements produced by SMH last year, are sold for assembly by other manufacturers in Switzerland and elsewhere. Within a decade, SMH has become the world's most profitable watch company, according to James Capel, the London stockbrokers, and sales by value are poised to overtake Seiko of Japan within five years. Profits have risen steadily, jumping by a third last year to SFr252m, and in 1992 the company is expected to have cash in hand after repayment of debt. Taking watches and movements together, SMH accounts for some three-quarters of total Swiss production (about 13 per cent of the world total) and about a third of Swiss sales. The rest is accounted for by mainly top-of-the-range watchmakers such as Rolex and Patek Philippe, whose dominance in the luxury market gives Switzerland over half the total world watch sales by value. Mr Hayek, who with a group of investors, bought out the banks' controlling shareholding in 1985, says SMH is and will remain primarily a watch company. But he believes other, more dynamic markets are ripe for the Swatch formula of technological innovation combined with skilful design at a competitive price, that can capitalise on the company's experience with micro-electronic and micro-mechanical devices. About 5 per cent of SMH's sales are currently outside the watch sector, mostly accounted for by the Swatch twinphone (a dual handset model) in the US and Europe. However, initial problems with telephone type approval, marketing and distribution have now persuaded SMH to opt for tie-ups with established telecommunications companies. Mr Hayek plans to announce in June a deal with a major telecommunications manufacturer to produce the twinphone and the cordless, cellular and fax telephones SMH already has on the stocks. SMH hopes to produce 1m twinphones this year - assembled in south-east Asia - and in March launched the Swatchpager, a paging watch, in the US in partnership with BellSouth. More ambitiously still, SMH and Volkswagen, the German car maker, last year set up a joint venture to develop, manufacture and distribute the Swatchmobile, an ecological car intended to exploit the huge potential market for non-polluting vehicles, especially in the US. The rewards could be enormous for a car with the right price-performance combination, which has so far eluded the big car makers. A Swatchmobile prototype is already under test, and the two companies are hoping to start production in 1994 for launch in 1995. The details are a closely guarded secret but the car will have an electric or hybrid petrol-electric motor and, Mr Hayek claims, the performance and safety features of a normal petrol-driven model. Though the project seems fanciful, SMH is not taking too big a risk. VW is thought likely to put up most of the funds needed for the manufacturing operation, with SMH taking a royalty fee on sales and perhaps an equity stake. The companies, which are sharing development costs of around Dollars 20m, are planning production of 100,000 cars a year if the launch goes well. Analysts concede that Mr Hayek's track record makes it difficult to dismiss the idea out of hand. 'If VW and SMH can bring a car to market that is cheap, clean, handy and comfortable, it could be a nice surprise,' says Mr Roland Leutenegger of Bank Julius Baer in Zurich.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Switzerland (12): A radical package
DOC.TEXT: INVESTOR-FRIENDLY is the great buzz-word among Swiss quoted companies these days. They are all rushing to publish more - and more revealing - information about their activities and trying to make their shares more attractive to investors, including foreigners. In part, they are doing this to get their share prices up, so they can raise capital on better terms. But for the biggest companies, such as Nestle and Roche, the hard fact is that the Swiss capital market can no longer meet their needs, so they have no choice but to appeal to foreign investors. If there were an award for the Swiss company that has done the most in the shortest time to become investor-friendly, it would undoubtedly go to Holvis Holzstoff, formerly Holzstoff, a long-established, medium-sized group (SFr823m consolidated sales last year). Holvis has transformed itself in the past two years from a boring pulp and paper maker to a world leading producer of the non-woven polymer-based material for disposable nappies and dozens of other trendy products. Even the group's name is new, created to help it shed its identification with paper, which accounted for only 14.5 per cent of sales last year. Holvis used to be one of the most secretive Swiss companies. 'It was very conservative; there was almost no information,' Mr Rudolf Wenger, finance director, says. And when it finally decided last year to change its spots, it got off to a very bad start. Like many others before it, Holvis proposed eliminating restrictions on foreigners owning its registered shares but installing in its place a general restriction on anyone registering more than a 2 per cent stake. The idea was to prevent someone from secretly accumulating a bid stake, a move which is still possible in Switzerland because there is, in effect, no takeover code. To their surprise, Holzstoff directors ran into a barrage of criticism from Swiss institutional investors. 'The culture around us had changed,' says Mr Pedro Reiser, chief executive, ruefully. So the directors went back to the drawing board, and emerged in early March this year with the most radical package of proposals yet advanced by a Swiss quoted company. The proposals, which were to be approved at yesterday's annual general meeting, included the consolidation of capital into a single class of registered shares with no restriction on ownership, by numbers or nationality. In addition, the shares would be split 10 for one to make their price more accessible to small shareholders. In terms of disclosure, the group has also led the way, being one of the first Swiss companies to publish a breakdown of its profits last year by division. And the directors promise that this year's financial statements will be published in accordance with international accounting standards (IAS). Mr Reiser says that one of the group's objectives in liberalising was to improve the rating on its shares so that it could raise capital more cheaply in the future. It spent Dollars 175m in 1990 buying the non-woven assets of the US paper group, James River, and might need to return to the capital markets in the future. Since the announcement of the capital restructuring in early March, the group's bearer shares have risen from SFr5,040 to SFr5,600. Mr Wenger adds: 'Management has started to understand that shareholders are an important part of a company's life. In Switzerland, that has been neglected.' However, the group has taken a risk by going all the way, because it is now vulnerable to a surprise hostile takeover bid. Several other Swiss companies, including Nestle and Sulzer, intend to liberalise their capital structures this year. But they have decided to maintain a limit on the proportion of share capital that any individual may register until a proper takeover code is in place in Switzerland. Mr Reiser acknowledges the problem, but he says the rise in the market valuation of the group's shares since the announcement should drive away the opportunistic bidder. 'Even if we maintained restrictions, we could not stop a determined strategic bidder. We could only delay him,' he says.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Switzerland (10): The mobilisation of a diehard patriot - Profile: Christoph Blocher
DOC.TEXT: TO SOME, he is a right-wing eccentric, to others he is the conscience of the nation, the quintessential Swiss patriot. Christoph Blocher is a colonel in the Swiss army, a member of the federal parliament for the conservative People's Party and executive chairman of a successful speciality chemical company. He also led the forces that six years ago successfully opposed the proposal that Switzerland join the United Nations. And now he is in the forefront of efforts to block the federal government's plans to take the country into the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the European Community. If he were British, he would undoubtedly be a diehard Thatcherite. He distrusts bureaucrats and believes passionately that less is better when it comes to governments. He is also suspicious of corporate bureaucrats, and prefers to pay out big dividends to Ems-Chemie shareholders rather than use the company's strong cash flow for risky diversification projects or acquisitions. Next week, the Swiss are to vote in a referendum on joining the IMF and early next year they will have to decide whether or not to ratify the so-called European Economic Area (EEA) treaty, which would bring the six countries of the European Free Trade Area (Efta) closer to joining the EC. Mr Blocher is already mobilised for these campaigns, with beguiling negative arguments at the ready. On the IMF and World Bank, as on the UN, he h a s no particular complaints, but he thinks Switzerland is better off as a non-member. He insists that the country is not isolationist; it pays to support many of these organisations' projects and agencies, but it also reserves the right not to participate if it thinks a particular project is ill-conceived. 'If we were a member, we would have only one vote. We are a little country, so no one would listen to us. So it is better for us to be on the outside and decide on a case-by-case basis. I think also that our views are sought more than they would be if we were members.' Mr Blocher also resents the enthusiasm of what he calls 'official Bern' for joining these organisations. 'They say we must participate, that we must be in solidarity with other countries, but they really just want to be in the club so they can tell us, the people, that the club has decided something and there is nothing we can do about it. They like power, but Swiss democracy is against power.' His complaints against the EC are more numerous. Indeed, Mr Blocher opposes the EEA because he believes it is designed as a halfway house towards full EC membership. 'The government's policy is that the EEA is a first step towards EC membership. You cannot find many people in Switzerland who are for the EEA and against the EC. If anyone says he likes the EEA but not the EC, he is saying it for tactical reasons.'
