The basic problem with the EC, he says, is that it is an 'intellectual construction'. Viewing it with Swiss eyes, it appears very centralised, undemocratic and unfederal. 'We have a lot of difficulty finding out what officials in Bern are doing with our money. Brussels would be much worse.' He says the whole idea of a united Europe is fundamentally flawed. Europe is composed of several states with substantial differences in history, culture, language and economic and political systems. Several attempts have been made to unify it, but all have failed, and the EC will fail too. 'I am sure that it cannot function.' The current tensions between Germany and other countries in the European Monetary System (EMS) illustrate the difficulties. 'It is not that Germany has made a mistake or France or Britain; the mistake is having one system.' Mr Blocher thinks it is better to have competition between governments to prevent any one of them from getting too powerful or arrogant. He acknowledges that if it turns out that Switzerland is the only western European country to refuse to join the EC, Brussels might get tough. 'But they need Switzerland, too. This is not a new problem for us, and we have been in much more dangerous positions in the past than we are today. 'The EC wants to export. We are their largest single market after the US and they sell more to us than we sell to them.' Mr Blocher is not distressed either by the prospect of 'missing the train' by not joining the EC at the same time as the other Efta countries. 'Nobody can see what Europe will be like in 10 or 20 years. Perhaps it will be more decentralised, and then we could apply, if we wanted to. In a situation like this, it is better for a little country to wait and watch. 'This is not an egotistical stance. We want to be friendly with everyone, politically and economically open, but always maintaining our sovereignty.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Switzerland (11): A neutral force - Is the army that absurd?
DOC.TEXT: ONE NEVER knows whether to treat the subject of the Swiss army with humour or respect. The idea of a small, resolutely neutral, land-locked country of 6.8m people having a huge citizen army constantly at the ready to repel any invader and enough nuclear shelters to house every citizen somehow seems absurd. Yet historically, Swiss military achievements, up to and including the second world war, speak eloquently for the competence and courage of the country's armed forces and for the durability of the country's neutrality and democratic institutions. And the Swiss militia system, under which every able-bodied male is constantly on call and has to train for a few weeks every year, has long been admired for its contribution to the country's social fabric as well as to its military effectiveness. The system has even been copied, notably by Israel. And yet, and yet. The cold war is over and the prospect of nuclear conflagration on the European continent seems to have disappeared. Even before the fall of the Berlin wall, Switzerland's military stance had been questioned. After all, the military was still working under a security doctrine published in 1966. Did the country still need a 600,000-strong army? Did every strategic bridge and tunnel in the country still have to have vast quantities of high explosives strapped to it? Some even doubted that the country needed an army at all. In 1989, a referendum on the subject revealed that a startling 35.6 per cent minority favoured scrapping it. Perhaps that galvanised the federal government into action. In the spring of 1989, Bern launched a full-scale re-evaluation of the country's future military requirements, called Army 95. The result will be implemented towards the middle of the decade. The plan retains the principle of armed neutrality for Switzerland, claiming that an army contributes to the credibility of a country. It also accepts that Switzerland should continue to rely on an army composed almost entirely of part-timers. But it acknowledges that the potential missions of the military concerns about maintaining order at home in the event of natural catastrophes or shock waves from conflicts or disasters in neighbouring countries. 'The line between simple violence and warlike actions is a very moving one, notably when the development of a situation has not been understood quickly and responded to energetically,' the draft says. As a result, Switzerland needs a smaller, more flexible army. Troop numbers could fall by a third to 400,000 and the class system, dividing soldiers among elite, support and stormtroop cadres, should be eliminated. Time given over to military service could be substantially shortened. Now the minimum service consists of a 17-week basic training course at age 20 plus a further 12 sessions totalling 212 days taken up to the age of 50. Under Army 95, it would be reduced to an initial 15 weeks and only 10 additional sessions of 19 days, taken every two years up to the age of 42. There has been little public reaction to the Army 95 proposals, which would suggest that most Swiss are comfortable with them. Many men in their 40s are pleased because they are at points in their careers where the time given over to the military can be a real loss. Similarly, young people now envisage the possibility of doing some kind of civil service instead of joining the army. Up to now, this has been forbidden, but a referendum on a proposal to introduce it is being held next week. In March, a consultation process on creating a battalion of 600 armed 'blue helmet' forces to help in United Nations peacekeeping operations has also yielded positive results. Up to now, the country has supplied only unarmed 'blue beret' peacekeepers, but the political parties are agreed that the country must do more in the future. All this is not to say there has been no controversy on the military front. The country was gripped last month by a surge in opposition to the government's plan to invest Dollars 2.3bn in 34 McDonnell Douglas F-18 fighter aircraft to replace ageing Mirages. The plan was approved by one of the two parliamentary chambers in March and now requires only approval from the other in June to be put into effect. The pacifist Group for an Army Free Switzerland has launched a petition that would cancel the project, and hopes to raise the 100,000 required signatures before the June vote. The drive just might succeed. Many Swiss who are not pacifist still do not understand the need for a sophisticated fighter aircraft to face the kind of adversaries posited in Army 95. Another issue is the future of Swiss neutrality. In March, a group of experts submitted a report to the government, saying that the country's tradition of neutrality did not prevent it from joining the European Community or participating in UN mandated economic sanctions. EC entry would not conflict with Swiss neutrality as long as the EC did not have security and defence policy structures fixed by treaty. If the EC subsequently set up a military alliance, the Swiss might have to reassess their policy of neutrality but, 'even as a member of the EC, Switzerland could stand aside during conflicts between other states, maintain a credible and autonomous national defence and carry out its traditional humanitarian and mediating roles'. The foreign ministry is now assessing the report and may recommend policy changes to the cabinet.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Switzerland (8): Struggle to stay at the top - The problems of Swissair
DOC.TEXT: SWISSAIR may be a widely admired airline, but as a shareholder-owned company based in a small country, it has a struggle on its hands to keep pace with the giant groups taking shape in its industry. Last year, in common with most international airlines, the group suffered from a substantial slump in traffic. Total passengers carried were down 8.2 per cent to 7.9m and cargo volume eased 3.3 per cent to 271,000 tonnes. However, thanks to cost-cutting and more than normal aircraft sales, the group was able to show a substantial gain in net profit from SFr48m in 1990 to SFr83m last year. Still, as Mr Armin Baltensweiler, the retiring chairman said, this was 'not a brilliant result by any means', with return on equity a dismal 3 per cent. On the other hand, the group has a relatively strong financial position for an airline, with debts of SFr5.3bn supported by SFr2.8bn of shareholders' equity, and its fleet of 60 aircraft has an average age of only six years. Swissair's major problem is that it has a small national customer base. This makes it hard for it to muster enough passengers to fill the non-stop flights that customers demand these days. New medium capacity aircraft with long-haul capability, such as the McDonnell Douglas MD-11, have helped the group remain competitive, but its main strategy for dealing with this problem has been to form pacts with other airlines. Late in 1989, it formed one with Delta Airlines of the US and Singapore Airlines for long-haul routes. In May 1990, it formed another with Austrian Airlines and Scandinavian Airlines, called the European Quality Alliance. The idea was that the airlines would share facilities and route management and exchange strategic share- holdings, but they have found that working together is easier in good times than in a recession. 'Alliances are not enforceable,' Mr Paul Muller, a Swissair director, says wryly. 'And when things are bad, a company's first thoughts are for its own problems.' There were, for example, plans for SAS and Swissair to combine forces on aircraft purchases, but they have been scuttled because of SAS's financial problems. Similarly, the depressed state of the shares of both companies has delayed a planned share swap. Swissair's role as the distribution and collection point for Delta in Europe was undermined when Delta acquired Pan American's European routes. However, that does not mean the alliances have failed. Mr Muller claims the co-ordination of Swissair and SAS schedules has contributed to a big increase in Swissair's business from Scandinavia to and from Africa. SAS, Swissair and Austrian Airlines have set up a jointly operated station in Vilnius, thus saving costs. Also, Swissair has won a contract to service Delta's 21 Airbuses, 'our most important maintenance contract in 10 years,' Mr Muller says. Swissair's other big headache is a political one. The airline is terrified about being left out in the cold when EC-wide air transport policies are made. 'If Switzerland remains isol- ated from the rest of Europe, our ability to compete will be further handicapped,' Mr Otto Loepfe, the airline's president, said last month. 'Swiss integration in Europe is a matter of survival,' he added. Most other Swiss companies have already insulated themselves against the possibility that Switzerland will not join the EC by setting up subsidiaries and factories within EC countries. However, Swissair cannot do this, because EC transport policy requires that EC airlines be owned and controlled by EC nationals. The country will hold a referendum later this year on the plan to build new tunnels through the Alps. This is a vital element of the Alpine transit treaty negotiated last year with Brussels. Also in the treaty is a provision for bilateral air transport negotiations. Swissair desperately hopes the treaty will be approved by the Swiss people. 'We are telling all our employees to be sure to vote and to get their families to vote too,' Mr Muller says. 'It is not a matter of politics; it is a matter of jobs.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Switzerland (5): A tale of triumphs and disasters -Banks have scored bigger profits and record loan provisions
DOC.TEXT: THE SWISS banking industry has lived through a bewildering combination of triumphs and disasters in the past year. Many banks scored handsome increases in profits. The big three universal banks all recorded new records on the bottom line and showed that in spite of the unpopularity of the notion of global banking these days they could made significant progress in international markets. Yet most banks had to make record provisions for bad loans, some in connection with the embarrassingly well publicised collapses of companies controlled by Mr Werner Rey and the late Robert Maxwell. The Swiss banking community was also embarrassed by the spectacle of the forced closure of a sizeable regional bank, Spar und Leihkasse Thun, last October, something no-one ever expected to see in Switzerland. And early this year, the removal by Moody's of its triple A rating from the long-term debt of Credit Suisse, and its threat to do the same to Swiss Bank Corporation (SBC) caused further discomfort. Moody's cited the increased risk to banks caused by the liberalisation of Swiss banking and security markets in the past two years, but the indications are that over the period both the big universal banks and the top private banks have strengthened their positions in securities dealing and fund management. Probably the most important of these developments is the growing success of the big three banks in world markets. Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS), the largest, and Credit Suisse have had considerable troubles in the past with their foreign subsidiaries and SBC was slow in establishing an international strategy. But in the past year, aided by their strong balance sheets and no doubt also by the retreat of troubled Japanese and US banks from the key international markets, the big three have found profitable pickings in international lending, foreign exchange dealings and fund management. Credit Suisse said 30 per cent of its net income came from foreign operations, but Bank Julius Baer, in a recent study, argues that the figure would be more like 66 per cent if income from the group's Luxembourg-based mutual funds, which are managed from Zurich, were included. UBS said the foreign contribution to its earnings last year tripled to 25 per cent. SBC said that its association with the derivative specialists, the O'Conner Partnerships in Chicago, in which it invested about SFr90m a little over a year ago, yielded net income of SFr107m last year, but overall foreign earnings were depressed by large provisions on bad debts. In spite of the Thun failure, the country's regional banks also did well. The Union of Swiss Regional Banks (VSRB) said its 173 members increased their combined net profits by 12 per cent to SFr264m and enlarged their balance sheets by 5.1 per cent to SFr86.1bn. However, even their combined profits are tiny in comparison with UBS's SFr1.2bn last year, indicating the need for further consolidation. Mr Robert Studer, chief executive of UBS, startled a Zurich audience in March by predicting that 100 of the country's banks could disappear in the next 10 years. That seems a large number for a small country, but it makes more sense when you consider that Switzerland's total bank count is still a whopping 630. Indeed, some might think Mr Studer's proposed reduction too modest. Leaders of the country's financial services industry have known for a long time that rationalisation was inevitable, and that the need for action had intensified since various cartel-like conventions, providing protection for various types of banks, were abolished. But they preferred not to think about it much until the failure of Spar und Leihkasse Thun shocked them into action. It was the first time in memory that the Federal Banking Commission had closed a well-known bank without warning, and the sight of queues of depositors outside the bank's doors was not one anyone had ever expected in Switzerland. In the wake of the closure, the various bank associations in February agreed to set up a two-layer safety net designed to prevent any more forced closures. First, the VSRB, which represents many of the smaller local banks that are in the greatest difficulties, has formed an examining board to discover problem cases and try to solve them. Union officials say that about a dozen of their 185 member banks are now being examined. Ideally, another bank will be found to take on the problem bank or its assets. If a problem bank refuses to co-operate, the Federal Banking Commission will apply pressure. If no bank is willing to take over the troubled bank, a working group within the Swiss Bankers Association will move in to make sure that, whatever happens, creditors are protected. Meanwhile, rationalisation is also the order of the day among big banks. In his March speech, Mr Studer also shocked his audience by suggesting that one of the big three might decide to give up retail banking in the foreseeable future because profits were so thin in this area. Analysts immediately pointed the finger at Credit Suisse, the third largest of the big three, and a relatively recent player in the retail area. However, Credit Suisse officials denied that they had any intention of abandoning its retail network. Nevertheless, all three big banks are now looking carefully at their retail businesses for ways to raise revenues and trim costs. Thus, UBS announced in January that it would concentrate certain specialised services in a limited number of branches rather than have every branch offer every service. Credit Suisse said it had already made considerable progress on this front. Mr Franz Galliker, chairman of Swiss Bank Corporation, said last month that SBC too was thinking of 'streamlining' its branch network. In March, SBC announced that it was restructuring Banca della Svizzera Italiana, in which it acquired a majority stake last year, to become part of a private banking group, leaving it with retail activities only in its canton Ticino base. The big three banks have also participated in the trend among leading Swiss companies to greater transparency and investor friendliness in recent months. They have much stronger equity bases than most of their leading international competitors, but their return on equity, ranging from 7 per cent to 10 per cent, still leaves considerable room for improvement.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Switzerland (9): Trying to carve out a niche - Profile: Volksbank
DOC.TEXT: FEW PEOPLE outside Switzerland had heard of Swiss Volksbank until it emerged as a lender of Dollars 35m to a private company controlled by the late Robert Maxwell. The loan attracted wide attention abroad because it was made only after Mr Ian Maxwell and Mr Kevin Maxwell had pledged Berlitz shares owned by Maxwell Communication Corporation (MCC) to Volksbank. The brothers had previously agreed to sell the shares to a Japanese company. The loan also raised eyebrows because few people in Switzerland would have expected this rather sleepy and parochial bank to be involved with the likes of Maxwell. Although Volksbank is Switzerland's fourth largest commercial bank, it is a distant fourth behind the third largest, Credit Suisse, and does not have a particularly distinguished performance record. While Credit Suisse had total assets of SFr155.6bn at the end of last year, Volksbank had only SFr46.5bn. And Volksbank's after-tax return on equity was only 3.1 per cent, compared with 9.9 per cent at Credit Suisse. The bank has been trying to improve its performance, and the Maxwell misadventure is a curious footnote in the story. Volksbank has long looked a rather awkward player on the Swiss banking stage. Though it is in a different league from the big three Swiss commercial banks, it is more than just a building society. It is a full service bank with 191 branches and agencies throughout Switzerland and a strong presence in both retail and corporate lending. The fact that Volksbank does not fit neatly into a clear category has given rise to speculation that it might be taken over. But none of the big three banks - and they are the most likely potential bidders - is much interested in expanding its already large presence in the Swiss market. Volksbank's leaders recognised a few years ago that their main customers - Switzerland's army of small and medium-sized businesses - were expanding abroad. 'We did not want to lose them because we could not serve them any more,' says Mr Rudolf Bosshard, the bank's director responsible for international development. They knew that they could not match the big three in the world's leading financial mar- kets. But they thought they could build a sufficient inter- national presence to preserve their client base at home. The obvious first step was to set up offices in the key financial centres that could provide customers with export finance, foreign exchange, capital markets and portfolio management services on competitive terms. A London branch was opened in 1985, and offices in New York, Tokyo and Sing- apore followed in 1989. Early this year, Volksbank purch- ased a 20 per cent stake in Banque Odier Bungener Cour- voisier in Paris rather than try to build up from scratch there. Ironically, it was through the application of this strategy that the bank came into con- tact with Robert Maxwell. In 1987, one of its Swiss industrial customers won a contract to supply machinery to a Maxwell company and Volksbank's London branch provided a guarantee of delivery. The contact was maintained. Volksbank lead-managed a bond issue for MCC a few months later and participated in a syndicated loan for it. However, it then decided to back away a bit. 'We realised Maxwell was too big for us,' Mr Bosshard says. Even so, the bank still has some Maxwell business on its books, and last year made provisions for a Dollars 73m loan to MCC. No provision was made for the Dollars 35m loan to the private Maxwell company because it was covered by the Berlitz shares, which the bank has since claimed. The second stage of Volksbank's international strategy began to take shape last year. Under its expansion programme, it has concluded co-operation agreements with banks in Bavaria, Baden-Wurttemberg and France. Now, says Mr Bosshard, it is looking for a partner or acquisition in northern Italy.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Switzerland (7): Cloud over the cartels - Trade policy faces an overhaul
DOC.TEXT: PARTICIPATION in the European Economic Area (EEA) and eventual EC membership will give a substantial boost to the Swiss economy, but some sectors will suffer painful adjustments. Economists agree that the impetus to growth will come not so much from higher exports to more open European markets, but from greater efficiency due to stiffer competition in domestic markets. Though Switzerland's heavily protected agricultural sector is not directly affected by the EEA, it too is being forced to contemplate radical change in the light of the current round of global trade talks now nearing a close under the auspices of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (Gatt) in Geneva. A Gatt report on Switzerland's trade policy last autumn pointed out that, while Swiss per capita incomes were more than 25 per cent above those in the US and Canada in 1989, they lagged in terms of purchasing power. Swiss food prices are well above EC levels, with consumers bearing 80 per cent of the SFr7bn annual cost of farm support through guaranteed prices, tariffs and border restrictions. In industry too, while external trade policies are a model of liberal economic principles, a network of formal and informal cartels between domestic producers and traders keeps prices high and stringent regulations tend to restrict competition from new entrants. As a result, Swiss consumers pay over 40 per cent more for goods and services than their EC counterparts, according to the Swiss Bank Corporation. Unusually in Europe, Swiss law permits cartels, providing only for investigation of abuses. No-one knows for sure how many cartels there are, but one estimate puts the number at 900, many of which involve price-fixing. Some, as in brewing, have crumbled under competitive pressures and others, like the banking conventions, have been dismantled at government insistence. But the bulk have been untouched for many years. EEA membership will entail adoption of EC competition law which forbids cartels and curtails monopolies. The SBC study published last month estimated that the EEA could boost Switzerland's economic growth rate by 0.5 percentage points a year, a gain of 4-6 per cent by the end of the decade. The Basle-based Economic Research Institute (BAK) thinks the benefits would be even greater, with the Swiss economy growing by 2.3 per cent a year within the EEA to the year 2000 and only 1.1 per cent a year outside it. SBC's economists identified two vulnerable sectors: the construction industry, due to an opening of public procurement - especially at cantonal level - to foreign bidding; and medium-sized companies geared primarily to the domestic market, notably in commerce, the food and drink industry and services. Main beneficiaries would be pharmaceuticals, insurance companies and multinationals including the banks. Switzerland's successful export industries have undergone major structural adjustments over the past decade or so, shifting further to capital-intensive, high value-added products and services to economise on scarce and expensive skilled labour and land. Most already have a solid base in the EC. The Community accounts for nearly half Switzerland's foreign assets of SFr85bn, half the near-1m overseas employees of Swiss companies, and two-thirds of Switzerland's foreign trade. Useful but unspectacular gains will come from harmonisation of standards and common regulations throughout the 19-nation EEA, as well as freer movement of labour and an end to the Lex Friedrich which restricts land sales to foreigners. Industry will also welcome the assurance of future harmonisation of technical and environmental standards, which could otherwise pose trade barriers. Swiss farmers view the future with much more apprehension. They have turned out in their thousands to demonstrate in the capital, Bern, and in Geneva against Gatt proposals that would oblige Switzerland to scrap its import quota system on agricultural products in favour of tariffs, and reduce domestic subsidies for agriculture by some 20 per cent by 1999. These proposals, and future EC membership, could slash farm incomes by as much as half, according to farmers' groups. The government has said that the Gatt plan is not acceptable. But it has admitted that Switzerland's 'war economy' farm policy based on ensuring food self-sufficiency and maximising farmholdings is no longer tenable. The effect has been to generate chronic surpluses and encourage heavy use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides, while failing to protect farmers' incomes or stop the exodus from the land. The federal council is now proposing a shift from price supports to direct income payments which would be largely independent of production. These would be permitted under the Gatt plan. The intention is to target payments at services provided in the public interest, such as food security and care of the countryside, while ensuring that prices better reflect market conditions and come down further towards EC levels. This is bound to produce some restructuring and consolidation of Switzerland's 90,000 farms, 40 per cent of them part-time. While international pressures will lead to greater economic competitiveness, many of the economic and political constraints that handicap efficiency will require independent action by the Swiss government. The federal council has said that it plans to reduce the extent of regulation (for instance, it recently denoun- ced the International Labour Organisation convention banning night work for women in industry). But it is not obvious how it can reform the legal and political system that enables citizens to delay inordinately investment projects and other economic initiatives, while maintaining desired high environmental and health and safety standards. Mr Jean-Pascal Delamuraz, the economy minister, gave a telling example of Swiss dilatoriness to the upper house of parliament a couple of months ago. 'One Sunday, the Swiss people said yes to Rail 2000 (a programme to modernise and expand the rail network). The following Monday, the French government said yes to the construction of the Atlantic TGV. Result: we have constructed a few metres of Rail 2000 and Adolf Ogi (the transport minister) is fighting 80 appeals per kilometre. Meanwhile, the TGV is running at 514 kilometres an hour from end to end.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Switzerland (4): Worrying outflow of funds - Moves to stem the decline of a financial centre
DOC.TEXT: IF INTEGRATION with Europe is the biggest concern of the Swiss these days, the second biggest may well be the future of their country as an international financial centre. Hardly a week goes by without someone worrying about or proposing measures to secure the future of what is known in all the official Swiss languages as Finanzplatz Schweiz. The name itself reveals part of the problem. One does not discuss the future of Finanzplatz Zurich or Finanzplatz Basel, or even La Place Financiere de Geneve. The country's financial industry is typically Swiss; it is decentralised inconveniently among three centres (not to mention Lugano) and to propose any large-scale concentration is out of the question. Although precise statistics are hard to come by, there is no doubt that Switzerland has declined as a financial centre in the past decade. The country's big corporations have gone global for their banking and capital market needs, and the big Swiss banks have followed them. This year, some even held their financial results press conferences in London rather than Switzerland. While the Japanese provided a blizzard of equity-linked Swiss franc bond issues in the late 1980s, these have petered out as Tokyo's stock market has plunged. Many of the 42 Japanese banks and brokerage houses in Switzerland have been shedding staff in recent months, and observers expect more than a few to close their doors within the next year or so. Meanwhile, the heart of the equity market has decamped to more liquid London, where prices for most leading Swiss shares are now set. Mr Robert Studer, president of Union Bank of Switzerland, says that about 15 per cent of dealing in the top 18 Swiss blue chips now takes place in London. Dealers point out that the figure would be larger but for the reluctance of the big banks - which dominate equity trading - overtly to irritate the Swiss authorities by executing more deals in London. Ironically, Zurich is about to open a new spacious stock exchange building, planned more than a decade ago in anticipation of expansion that has gone elsewhere. Zurich's foreign exchange market is also fading, as trading is increasingly concentrated in three big global centres: London, Tokyo and New York. And the big three banks have tended to build up their trendy derivatives businesses outside Switzerland as well. The only sector in which the Swiss financial centre appears to be holding its own is in asset management, mainly in connection with private banking. According to Mr Jean Pierre Cuoni, president of Coutts & Co in Zurich, Switzerland still attracts about half of the world's cross-border private banking business - worth perhaps Dollars 1,500bn. The country also has outsize institutional pools of money because of its large insurance companies and legislation requiring every Swiss company to have a pension fund for its employees. Indeed, private banking is an area where even foreign banks, including Coutts, think they have a future in Switzerland. If that roughly is the state of play, perhaps the first question to ask is whether it is the result of a shift away of financial activity, especially to London, or whether things can be done to improve or restore some lost or weakened elements of Finanzplatz Schweiz. The consensus appears to be that some of the outflow, notably of mutual funds to Luxembourg, could have been stopped if the Swiss government had been more sensitive to the negative impact of some of its regulations and taxes in this area. Similarly, if the country's stock exchanges had combined forces sooner, they might have created a sufficiently liquid market in Switzerland so that London would not have snapped up so much of the dealing business. Even today, there are still three stock exchanges in Switzerland. However, in a book* published this week, Mr Hans-Dieter Vontobel, president of Bank J. Vontobel, a leading Zurich private bank, suggests that the departure of much financial activity from the country was inevitable because of the 'opening up and vitalising process of the foreign financial centres'. Mr Vontobel also blames the four big banks for being too willing to let the Swiss financial centre decay. He points out that the four opened only 10 branches in Switzerland in the 1980s, while they created nearly 150 offices abroad. In any event, he thinks there is not much point chasing after lost business. Instead, it would be better to concentrate on taking steps to help preserve the competitiveness of the Swiss asset management sector. His main argument is that competition should be allowed free rein. He claims that despite the elimination of various conventions in the banking sector in the past two years, there is still too much concentration and oligopolistic practice and the Swiss generally are too afraid of competition. But Mr Vontobel says there is not much point in waiting for the government to take action as the process is too slow. The international competitiveness of Swiss asset management has to be ach- ieved by the firms themselves, notably through productivity gains. He suspects that 20 per cent of the 115,000 jobs in the Swiss financial industry could be lost in the next five to 10 years, even if the government moved quickly to improve the regulatory environment. The next reform milestone comes in the autumn when a referendum will be held to approve a government proposal to reduce substantially the 0.3 per cent stamp duty that has been blamed for much of the weakening of the Swiss financial centre. Although the reform is endorsed by virtually all political parties, financial circles fear that it will be rejected by the people. Many Swiss see no reason why the big banks should receive a gift at a time when they are boasting about record profits. The irony is that more and more of the banks' profits are coming from abroad. *Wettbewerb als Chance (Competition as Opportunity), by Hans-Dieter Vontobel and Lukas Morscher, Verlag Neue Zurcher Zeitung, Zurich.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Switzerland (2): Decisions loom on Europe - Ian Rodger looks beneath the calm of the country's political life
DOC.TEXT: PERHAPS IT is the calm before the storm. In the past year, Swiss political life has been eerily quiet, especially in contrast to the previous turbulent three years of scandals and consequent debate about the effectiveness of the country's peculiar political institutions and traditions. Probably the biggest issue to disturb politicians in the past year has been dealing with the country's surprisingly large number of drug addicts. And while one would not attempt to underrate the seriousness of the drug problem, it is not a matter that is likely to influence the country's future. By contrast, everyone knows that vital decisions about Switzerland's place in Europe and the world are just around the corner, starting with next week's referendum on joining the International Monetary Fund and followed by another one in the autumn on whether or not to build new railway tunnels through the Alps. The tunnels are aimed at defusing the long-running dispute between Switzerland and the European Community over transit rights for EC lorries. That referendum is a prelude to another plebiscite, now expected in mid-1993, to approve a treaty uniting the six countries of the European Free Trade Association (Efta), including Switzerland, with the EC in the so-called European Economic Area (EEA). That, in turn, is seen by the government as merely a 'first step' towards Switzerland becoming a full EC member. Yet, so far, public debate on Europe has been muted, to say the least. In last October's general elections, for example, the issue was scarcely discussed. There was no clear theme in that campaign although, as in other European countries, extremist and single theme parties made gains at the expense of the four-party grand coalition that has been in power since 1959. The anti-immigrant Automobile Party, for example, raised its representation from two seats to eight in the 200-seat National Council, while the Swiss Democrats, another anti-immigration group, raised their tally from three to five. On the left, the Greens won 12 seats, three more than they won in the 1987 elections, while the Lega dei Ticinesi, a new populist formation from the Italian speaking canton of Ticino, took two seats. Among the coalition parties, only the Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party maintained their totals of 41 and 25 seats respectively. The conservative Radicals dropped from 51 to 44 and the Christian Democrats from 42 to 36. In all, the election result was seen as only a mild rebuke to the ruling parties for the scandals of the last parliament, notably that over Mrs Elisabeth Kopp, the former justice minister, who tipped off her husband that a company of which he was vice-chairman was under investigation for money laundering. She was acquitted in 1990 of breaching official secrecy, but the judgment was widely criticised. Another scandal raged over revelations that cabinet ministers were unaware that federal police maintained secret files on more than 900,000 Swiss citizens and foreigners living in the country. These scandals, together with other indications that the Swiss government system was no longer working effectively, led a number of critics to press more stridently for radical reforms. The fact that parliament sits for only four three-week sessions a year, for example, is considered an anachronism. It should become a full-time body, many argue, but the politicians themselves rejected the idea last year. Similarly, the size of the cabinet, with only seven members, one of whom takes a turn at being president under an annual rotation system, is considered hopelessly inadequate for today's needs. And many of its tasks, such as setting speed limits and appointing minor officials, could be delegated. The result is that the cabinet has trouble finding time to debate important issues, such as those thrown up by a group of experts in March on the compatibility of Swiss neutrality with membership in the European Community. Also, the cabinet's composition, according to the so-called magic formula that splits the ministerial portfolios among the ruling parties and representatives from regions and language groups, is considered by many to be far too rigid. However, critics admit that the cabinet is a fair representation of the bland combination of four parties making up the governing coalition. It is perhaps worth pointing out that the two conservative parties could, with the help of splinter parties, control parliament on their own. There have been suggestions from time to time that the grand coalition may collapse, but there is no sign of it at the moment. The Social Democrats threatened last month to take the government to court for making a SFr50m down payment on a Dollars 2.3bn order for 34 F-18 fighter aircraft, but they backed down when their coalition partners suggested this was an unfriendly move. Another complaint about the political system is that the conditions which a group of citizens has to fulfil so as to force a plebiscite have become too light. It is said that almost anyone with enough money to hire the right public relations agency can raise the required 100,000 signatures to force a vote on any issue. The figure has not changed in a century, except in 1977 when it was roughly doubled to take account of women being given the right to vote. But all these complaints have receded somewhat in the past few months, perhaps reflecting a feeling that, compared with some other countries in these tough times, Switzerland is not, after all, that badly governed. Also, the cabinet has at least twice shown an uncharacteristically high sense of purpose in recent months. Last October's decision to make membership in the EC official government policy and to declare that ratification of the EEA treaty was only a 'first step' towards accession to the EC itself startled many observers. Only two members of the cabinet, Mr Rene Felber, the foreign minister and this year's president, and Mr Jean-Pascal Delamuraz, the economics minister, are unconditionally enthusiastic about EC membership. Another, Mr Adolf Ogi, the transport and communication minister, is in favour, but cannot stray from his People's Party's negative stance. Mr Flavio Cotti, the interior minister, and Mr Arnold Koller, the justice minister, are unenthusiastic and Mr Otto Stich, the finance minister, is resolutely opposed. In March, Mr Felber, flanked by Mr Stich, Mr Delamuraz and Mr Markus Lusser, president of the Swiss National Bank, appeared before the press to make a passionate appeal to the people to endorse the government's plan to join the IMF and World Bank. 'It is in institutions like the IMF or World Bank which practise international co-operation on the basis of recognised rules that states see their rights best protected,' he said. It remains to be seen if this forceful presence is enough to win the day in next week's referendum. Many observers doubt it, but even if the government's policy is rejected, life will go on as normal. 'There is no opposition in parliament,' says Mr Christoph Blocher, the outspoken president of the People's Party in Canton Zurich. 'In our system, the people are the opposition.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Switzerland (3): A paragon is humiliated - The country's economic problems
DOC.TEXT: ONCE HELD up as a model for the industrialised world, the Swiss economy has lost its allure. Switzerland has suffered a deeper recession than any European Community country, its inflation rate is above the OECD average, unemployment is at its highest level in more than half a century, and the former rock-solid Swiss franc is looking feeble. An economy as open as Switzerland's could not hope to insulate itself from the world economic slowdown, which has been longer and more pronounced than predicted just a few months ago. Imports and exports account for some 40 per cent of Swiss GDP. However, the drop in national output last year of 0.5 per cent was tempered by buoyant exports to the booming German market, which takes nearly a quarter of all Swiss merchandise exports. By the same token, this year's recovery will be weakened by the slackening German economy, not only through the effect on exports but also through the higher Swiss interest rates necessitated by the German Bundesbank's tough monetary stance. Most economic forecasters are predicting export-led growth of 0.5-0.9 per cent in 1992, concentrated in the second half, as the world economy picks up steam. But even in 1993 GDP is not now expected to exceed 2 per cent, which will make little dent in the unemployment total. For the Swiss, accustomed to tight labour markets and negligible unemployment, the rapidity of the climb in joblessness has come as a shock. Just a year ago, 35,000 people - 1.1 per cent of the workforce - were registered as unemployed. Even this was high by comparison with the 0.5-0.8 per cent rate common for much of the 1980s. But in March 1992 nearly 76,000 -2.5 per cent - were out of work. The total is still rising. The surge in the numbers out of work contrasts with the recession in the early 1980s. Companies have been readier to lay off surplus staff this time around and redundant workers have been readier to register as unemployed. Unemployment benefits are more generous than 10 years ago, the social stigma attached to unemployment has lessened, and women and foreign workers have not withdrawn from the labour force as they did in the past. Most of the country's 1.2m foreigners - who make up a quarter of the workforce - now have long-term residence rights. Despite the mounting jobless total, the Swiss government has firmly rejected calls by the trade unions for reflation and large-scale job-creation. This refusal partly reflects a long-standing federal government policy of eschewing intervention in the economic cycle, as well as the need to curb government spending. But it also reflects fears that reflation would hinder necessary structural adjustments to reverse the country's declining long-term competitiveness. The high costs of doing business in Switzerland, a shortage of skilled workers and a legal system that permits projects to be held up for years by appeals, have led multinational companies to move production, and even research facilities, abroad. The decision last December by Ciba-Geigy, the country's biggest chemicals group, to locate a genetic engineering research centre just over the border in Alsace, was a recent example. But even at the end of 1990, the 15 biggest Swiss enterprises employed 684,700 people - 82 per cent of their total workforce - outside Switzerland. Government and industry are in accord that the Swiss economy suffers from excessive regulation and too much cosiness in business. Heading industry's wish list, aside from participation in the EEA and eventual EC membership, are a relaxation of strict restrictions on skilled foreign workers, a change in Swiss competition law to ban cartels, which are widespread, the introduction of VAT (rejected by Swiss voters last year) to replace the present unsatisfactory sales tax, and less regulation, especially in the labour market. These objectives are shared by the much-vilified Swiss National Bank (SNB), the central bank, which has been struggling to control an unruly bout of inflation sparked off by an inadvertent over-relaxation of monetary policy in 1987-88. The subsequent monetary tightening, accompanied by high interest rates, precipitated the recession by hitting investment, especially construction, and has prevented any decisive recovery. Inflation has subsided from its peak of 6.6 per cent last summer to just under 5 per cent in March, but is expected to fall only slowly to 3-3.5 per cent next year. Mr Markus Lusser, SNB president, says there is no room for any significant loosening of monetary policy. The Bank says its policies have been less effective than they should have been because of important structural rigidities in the Swiss economy. These include widespread indexation, notably of rents (tied to mortgage rates) and of wages (linked to prices), steep rises in public sector charges and the high degree of cartelisation in industry as well as one of the most protected farm sectors in Europe. The fight against inflation has also been hampered by the weak Swiss franc, which has lost about 10 per cent of its value against a trade-weighted currency basket since January 1991. The SNB decided not to follow the rise in German rates last December, so as not to squash the first signs of economic recovery. But it was subsequently forced to intervene heavily in the money and foreign exchange markets earlier this year when the currency tumbled, threatening to push up inflation once again. Some commentators, such as KOF, a leading economic forecasting institute, have suggested that counter-inflation policy would be more credible if the Bank abandoned the pretence of an independent monetary policy and declared a floor or band for the Swiss franc against the Deutschemark. The Swiss parliament has asked the government to examine Swiss membership of the European Monetary System. EC economic and monetary union may soon be the order of the day. But, as Mr Jean-Pascal Delamuraz, the economy minister, has said, Switzerland would not currently qualify for EMU because its inflation rate is too high. For a former economic paragon, this is humiliation indeed.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Switzerland (1): Gear after neutral - The government has firmly committed itself to joining the European Community. Line is overdrawn But doubts remain about whether the inhabitants of neutral Switzerland will want to follow this lead
DOC.TEXT: THE TIME for decisions has at last arrived. Over the next year, the Swiss will be called upon, after years of debate and soul-searching, to take a number of decisions that will set the framework for their relations with the rest of Europe and the rest of the world for the foreseeable future. At stake is whether the country will continue to pursue its detached stance, maintaining strict neutrality and avoiding foreign alignments. Or will it adopt a more conventional role for a small, landlocked, resource-poor country of 6.8m people, and join formally with its neighbours in building the European Community of the future? Opinion polls have consistently indicated that the Swiss are sharply divided on these questions, worried, on the one hand, that if they remain detached, their highly developed industrial base will suffer and their much-envied standard of living will decline. These worries are understandably acute at a time when the Swiss economy is having difficulty pulling out of a year-long recession, when inflation is uncharacteristically high and the country's role as a financial haven seems to be disappearing. But the Swiss are strongly attached to their decentralised style of self-government and they fear that their interests would be not be well-protected in an organisation such as the European Commission. They dread a further rush of immigrants and foreign property buyers if the country has to accept the EC principle of freedom of movement of people. It would be wrong to overdramatise the distance between the two options on offer. Even if it decides to maintain its autonomy, Switzerland would not be isolated or aloof from the problems of its continent or the world. It already participates as a non-member in the activities of most international organisations; it has an increasingly liberal and open economy and it shares the burdens of refugees that strain most western European countries these days. More than 16 per cent of Swiss residents are non-Swiss. Conversely, if the Swiss decide to move towards joining the European Community, they will still be able to maintain - at least at the local level -their unique and cherished political structures. The decision-making process on these issues begins as early as next week when the Swiss will vote in a plebiscite on whether their country should at last join the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. This will be the first test of Swiss sentiment towards international organisations since a majority rejected a proposal in 1986 to join the United Nations. In the meantime, Switzerland startled many observers by joining in the UN-led coalition to roll back Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait. A few weeks ago, it joined the sanctions against Libya over airline terrorism. In the autumn, the people will vote in another plebiscite on a mammoth project to drill two new rail tunnels through the Alps. This project, called NEAT, is the Swiss government's contribution to trying to solve the inflammatory dispute that pits Austria and Switzerland against the EC over the use of Swiss roads by EC lorries moving between Italy and Germany. The EC and the Alpine countries reached a comprehensive agreement on the problem late last year, subject to ratification by the Swiss and Austrians. The importance of the agreement for EC-Swiss relations is great enough in itself, but other factors make it even more important. For one thing, it includes an air traffic agreement, which is vital to the survival of Swissair, the Swiss national airline, especially if Switzerland later decides not to join the EC. The treaty is also part of the transport element in the agreement between the six European Free Trade Area (Efta) countries, including Switzerland, and the EC that was initialled last month to create what is called the European Economic Area (EEA). So if the NEAT proposal is rejected by Swiss voters, Switzerland will have reneged on its commitments under the EEA treaty. The final referendum of interest is on the EEA itself. This was originally going to be held in December, but because parts of the agreement had to be rewritten early this year to overcome the objections of the European Court of Justice, completion was delayed and so the referendum must be postponed until May 1993. The vote on the EEA has taken on increased importance since the federal cabinet's declaration last autumn that it considers the EEA nothing more than a first step towards full EC membership. Thus, the ground has been cut from under those Swiss who like the idea of the EEA - essentially a free trade area - but do not like the EC, at least in its present form. Since the cabinet's declaration, some political and business leaders have argued that the country should put in its application to join the EC immediately rather than wait for the EEA referendum result. They say that speed is of the essence if the country is to sit around the table with the likes of Sweden, Austria, Norway and Finland rather than having to apply in a few years' time with Czechoslovakia, Turkey and Hungary. In particular, the Swiss would like to be involved in the resolution of how neutral countries' interests will be protected in the EC. This will be sorted out in the negotiations with Austria, Sweden and Finland, so if Switzerland is not present, it will have to accept the same terms when and if it applies at a later point. There is also a tactical point. Some argue that if a majority of the Swiss vote against joining the EEA in next May's referendum, it would be awkward for the government to turn around and apply immediately for EC membership. Thus, these people say, it would be smarter to put the application in now. Then, if the EEA referendum was lost, the government could just move on to the EC negotiations. Even though the federal government and most top business leaders are recommending that the people endorse all the above steps towards integration with the European Community and the world, it is far from certain that they will do so. The Swiss tend to be very practical voters and, according to one Zurich banker, they will probably vote against joining the Bretton Woods institutions simply because they do not see what they will get out of them. Attitudes toward Europe are more complex and varied. In general, the Swiss do not like what they see as the concentration of more and more jurisdiction at the EC centre in Brussels. One is frequently told that if the EC were developing along the more decentralised lines that the British government has proposed, then the Swiss might be more enthusiastic. In the business community, the thousands of small wholesalers, retailers and contractors - not to mention farmers - who still benefit from protection from foreign competition obviously fear the potential arrival of the EC anti-cartel office and the Common Agricultural Policy. For totally different reasons, many of the country's large industrialists and bankers no longer seem terribly worried about the outcome, which means that they may feel free to vote with their hearts rather than their heads. This is because, at their level, life has already become very European and international. Switzerland exports 36 per cent of its output and imports an almost identical proportion of its consumption, with the great majority of its trade in both directions being with other European countries. Leading Swiss banks and industrial companies have large and successful operating bases abroad, and many leading EC companies, notably car makers, have substantial sales in Switzerland. More important, whatever unfair advantages they once enjoyed as a result of being based in Switzerland are rapidly being swept away. Perhaps the most significant of these advantages was the relatively closed Swiss capital market, which is now in serious decline. (Ironically, Swiss voters are expected to veto in yet another referendum later this year a government plan to help the capital markets by cutting an irritating stamp duty on securities transactions.) This decline has forced big companies to make their shares more accessible and attractive to foreigners and to become more transparent in their reporting so that they can attract foreign capital. In the past few months, several companies have split their shares and removed restrictions on foreign ownership. They are still feeling their way in the new, more liberal environment and there have been no hostile foreign takeovers of Swiss companies so far. Friendly sell-outs are starting to occur though. In January, German interests took control of the big Movenpick restaurants and hotels group and an Italian company took a strategic stake in the machinery group, Saurer. But one lesson that already seems to be emerging is that business will go on, whether or not companies are controlled by Swiss owners. It will also go on whether or not Switzerland joins the EC.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (16): Investors urged to behave like owners - Corporate governance is taking hold in the consciousness of UK pension funds
DOC.TEXT: AFTER YEARS of determined passivity, UK pension funds are finally waking up to their own power. With over Pounds 250bn in assets, they provide the largest single source of working capital for British industry. Thus, it should come as no surprise that pension funds are finally coming around to the view that they should act like owners, rather than simply passive investors. The issue of corporate governance - the way companies are governed by their directors - has slowly taken hold in the consciousness of UK pension funds in a way unimaginable just a few years ago. Shareholders are beginning to demand that managements tell them more about how their companies are run, and seeking the right to do something about inefficient, profligate or arrogant managers. In the US, where the corporate governance movement has been in full swing for years, pension fund activism has been assisted by the US Labour Department, which in 1988 determined that voting rights are an asset of pension fund trusts which must be exercised on behalf of members. Meanwhile, in Britain, the National Association of Pension Funds last year highlighted the passivity of its members, when it conducted a survey showing that fewer than 20 per cent of them regularly exercised their proxy rights. Mr Clive Gilchrist, deputy chairman of the NAPF and chairman of BesTrustees, a company which acts as an independent trustee on pension boards, has repeatedly urged members to use their voting rights. A survey conducted in 1990 showed that some 23 per cent of NAPF members did not even know whose responsibility it was to make voting decisions. 'By 1991, the numbers were only very slightly better,' he said. To encourage members to vote, the NAPF has just established a proxy voting service. In its initial stages, it will track all the companies in the FT-SE 100 index, preparing reports on matters to be voted at each annual general meeting. The reports make no effort to advise pension funds on how to vote; they simply inform readers whether or not the matter in hand is consider contentious. It will also inform readers whether they are being asked to approve a development which does not conform with NAPF guidelines on best practice on corporate governance. Mr Angus Matheson, chairman of the NAPF's investment committee, acknowledges that the group has not been deluged with demands for the new service, but says that, at Pounds 2,000 per participant, response has been better than expected. Currently, about six large institutions have signed up. 'So many of then haven't even given the matter of voting any thought,' said Mr Matheson. The debate about corporate governance has been spurred on by the recession of the past three years, which has exposed many managerial weaknesses covered up by the go-go years of the late 1980s. Shareholders began asking hard questions only when managements proved themselves unable to cope with the downturn in business. The NAPF, among other shareholder groups, has been busy developing codes of practice intended to promote shareholder influence and make companies more responsive to the interests of their owners. As a member of the Institutional Shareholders Committee, it has participated in the drafting of codes outlining the rights and responsibilities both of directors and of shareholders. Also, the NAPF has held discussions with the Accounting Standards Board, to urge new rules which would require companies to disclose more about their operations in their annual accounts. Meanwhile, the legitimacy of demands for better corporate governance is likely to get a boost from a report to be issued at the end of this month by the so-called Cadbury Committee. The Committee on the Financial Aspects of Corporate Governance, chaired by Sir Adrian Cadbury, is expected to recommend a wide range of measures, aimed at improving the quality of information offered to shareholders and improving board accountability. For hawks on the corporate governance issue, the report is likely to be disappointing, because it will have no enforcement mechanism other than a new rule from the London Stock Exchange requiring companies to disclose the extent to which they comply with its recommendations. But the report will underline the growing seriousness of investors in seeing to it that boards are held accountable for their own performance. But if those codes are to be any more than self-righteous posturing, shareholders will have to use their muscle in the form of votes to put their recommendations to the test. Mr Matheson notes that, for those pension funds that use external managers, the sheer mechanics of voting mitigate against it. 'For a large external manager with several hundred clients, there's quite a lot of paper to be signed,' he said. A manager unable to contact pension fund trustees may have to forgo a vote on their behalf. Also, many pension fund trustees may feel they are not well informed enough about each company's affairs to use their votes wisely. Thus, such decisions are better left to professional money managers who are paid fees for their judgments. Mr Matheson said that the NAPF's effort to encourage members to vote has been helped by the Institutional Fund Managers Association, a trade group, which urges the adoption of a standard management agreement authorising the manager to make voting decisions on the pension fund's behalf. Ann Simpson, co-director of the Pensions Investment Research Council, which largely advises local authority pension funds, notes that, when fund managers need to seek trustees' permission to vote, the typical 21-day notice period offered by most companies is inadequate. The PIRC has for some time been running a proxy voting service similar to that newly established by the NAPF. However, the PIRC's bulletins include a discussion of matters not on the agenda - such as companies' refusal to offer their executive directors for periodic renomination - and suggests that shareholders raise the issue with managements. Meanwhile, Mr John Wilcox, chairman of Georgeson, a US-based investor relations consultancy, argues that UK laws actually offer far more freedom to domestic institutions to influence managments than is offered to their US counterparts. US securities laws, for instance, prevent institutions from discussing joint courses of action without filing certain documents with the Securities and Exchange Commission. 'The barriers to the exercise of power are much lower here in the UK,' he said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (17): Morale lift for boutiques - A move towards specialist managers in the UK
DOC.TEXT: SOMETHING ODD seems to be going on among trustees when it comes to selecting pension fund investment managers. Are they, or are they not, abandoning the traditional UK preference for balanced managers in favour of US-style specialists? The latest evidence appears to point both ways at once. Until the late 1980s, British pension schemes not managed internally were nearly always entrusted to investment houses with a very broad brief - to invest at their discretion across the spectrum of equities, bonds and cash. Only property investment, always regarded as something of a law unto itself, was usually conducted by a specialist manager. This style of management, which produces a balanced portfolio, is in marked contrast to the US, where trustees themselves set a specific strategy for the fund and then hire numbers of specialist managers to carry out different aspects of the strategy. Only funds too small to warrant splitting up into separate tranches are generally managed by a broad-spectrum 'balanced' manager. By 1990 the UK picture had begun to change sufficiently for the National Association of Pension Funds' committee of inquiry into investment performance measurement to take note. In his report, the committee chairman, Maurice Stonefrost, commented on the 'move towards some specialisation of managers' briefs (and therefore greater trustee involvement in detailed asset allocation decisions).' Mr Stonefrost attributed this in part to the increasing availability of more detailed disaggregated information on managers' performance in the 'sub sets of balanced fund portfolios' - for example, in their international investment portfolios. He also believed that it reflected regulatory change. The Financial Services Act, for instance, requires trustees explicitly to define objectives as part of their contract with managers, because the ultimate responsibility for a fund's investment risk profile, and therefore broad asset allocation, lies with the trustees. That same year, a survey by Phillips & Drew Fund Managers (PDFM) of large pension schemes, produced some electric figures in support of this view. Although only 14 per cent used specialist UK equity managers and 20 per cent used international equity specialists, more than 10 per cent said they were actively considering such a move. The enthusiasm with which trustees appeared to be embracing specialists was a great morale booster for small or new niche managers, who could not hope to compete across the board with large 'balanced' houses. One such niche (though hardly small) boutique is Lombard Odier Investment Management, the London-based fixed income and continental equities investment arm of the Geneva bank. Paul Abberley, LO's head of fixed income, explained: 'We are seeing a trend towards funds splitting into a balanced core and specialist satellites as and when they review the structure of their operations. There is no reliable data yet, but the shift is quite strong whenever trustees undertake their reviews.' Even the established houses are prepared to concede that they may soon face competition from specialists. However, Chris Cheetham, director of investment strategy at the Prudential, warned that Mr Stonefrost may have overstated the change. 'We are seeing the growth of specialisation,' said Mr Cheetham, 'but it won't reach US proportions.' Today his caution seems more than justified. A second survey carried out by PDFM in 1991 showed little growth in the numbers of specialists actually hired. But, more important, the number of trustees actively considering their use had dropped sharply to under 4 per cent. And the initial figures from the 1992 survey, which will be published in the summer, are nearly identical to last year's. If PDFM's figures are reliable, 'the move from balanced to specialist, which most commentators expected to accelerate, appears to have come to a very sharp stop.' PDFM can throw little light on the turnround, although they speculate that there may be three factors at work: 1, The difficulty of controlling asset allocation within a specialist structure; 2, The difficulty of coping with innovation in a rigid specialist structure (except by adding more and more specialists); and 3, Lack of evidence of any improvement in performance. If trustees have abandoned their shift to specialists on the basis of poor performance over just two years, this will disappoint Mr Stonefrost's committee, which strongly advised that performance should be measured against a background of no less than five years. But it may be that PDFM's surveying equipment is not sensitive enough for what is going on. Lombard Odier, for example, has noticed a shift from balanced to regional bond and equity portfolios as updated computer facilities have introduced trustees to tactical asset allocation techniques. This in turn, they say, has meant that trustees who used to 'employ more than one balanced manager, now farm out the asset allocation decision to these professionals who in turn appoint a growing number of specialists'. Thus, in one sense, the trustees can still claim to be running balanced funds while simultaneously promoting the growth of specialists. PDFM's antennae have been able to pick up another curious fact: a clear tendency for larger schemes to go the specialist route, sometimes by appointing an internal specialist. It is possible that the internalising process may have taken the place of overt external specialisation to the point where the slow growth of external specialists does not tell the true story. If that is so, it suggests that trustees want to have their cake and eat it, carrying out specialist techniques under a balanced label.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (15): Consultants blamed for short-term view - Manager selection
DOC.TEXT: 'PIGS MIGHT fly,' said a leading fund manager wistfully, considering the demise of the pensions consulting industry. The role played by pension fund consultants does little to soothe fund managers who complain bitterly of the so-called 'beauty parade', which has become a ritual of the selection process. The fund managers claim that consultants urge clients to switch managers simply to justify their own positions. Worst of all, fund managers say, the role of consultants has caused pension funds to take too short a time-horizon into account when considering the performance of managers. Mr Robert Baker, a senior consultant in the asset planning department at the actuarial and consulting firm of Mercer Fraser, said that he urged pension fund clients to look at performance over at least a three-year period. Recently, he said, Mercer Fraser had conducted some research, and discovered that the top performers for one three-year period were unlikely to achieve that status in the following three-year period. Also, he said, pension funds should spend more time trying to understand the investment objectives of the fund managers they choose. When circumstances were particularly adverse for that strategy, performance would suffer for a time. 'What happens if a good firm goes through a bad patch - what happens if their style goes out of favour?' Mr Baker said. He generally urges clients to stick with the fund manager so that, when the pendulum swings back again, the client will benefit from the upside. This has particularly been the case in the recession when fund managers specialising in small companies or recovery stocks have been hard hit. Also, he argues, pension fund trustees do not spend enough time selecting a fund manager, even when they are advised by a consultant. 'The beauty parade is a very bad way of picking a manager,' he said. Mr Baker urges trustees, instead of inviting managers in to make a presentation, to visit the fund manager's own premises and see how he runs his business. But not all consultants have the same long-term time horizon, fund managers complain. 'These guys have set themselves up as judge, jury and executioner of fund managers. They earn fees for conducting searches, and its in their interest to shuffle the pack periodically,' said one investment director. The tension between the two groups is palpable. The power of pension consultants is such that fund managers are unwilling to speak candidly about them publicly, for fear that their views will damage future business prospects. But even they grudgingly admit that the consultants play a valuable role. 'We brought the consultants upon ourselves by being too complacent,' said one. The fund managers say there is wide variation in the quality of consultants, with most of the large actuarial consulting firms winning generally high marks for thorough research and sensible guidance. However, less well-known consultants, seen as more keen for the business, attract the greatest ire. 'I've been asked to fill out a 100-page questionnaire, only a small portion of which was sent on to the client,' said one fund manager, complaining that consultants, too, often stand between fund managers and their clients. 'Its a kind of a love-hate relationship,' said an official of the Institutional Fund Managers Association. And fund managers' insistence on displaying their own performance records in the most flattering light - to the complete confusion of potential clients - has only hastened the rise of an industry whose job it is to peer through the hyperbole to get at the performance below. In recognition of this, the National Association of Pension Funds last year produced an advertising code of conduct designed to coerce fund managers to standardise the way they advertised their track records. Among other things, it urges the display of a five-year time horizon. But even if comparison of performance becomes a simpler matter for the layman, fund managers and consultants agree that the average pension fund trustee is often badly equipped to make manager selections on his own. 'There is caveat emptor in the selection of fund managers, and that's where we come in,' said Mr Baker. He believes that tensions between investment managers and consultants may have increased in recent years, as consultants have taken on some of the tasks - especially that of asset allocation - previously within the strict remit of fund managers. Meanwhile, questions have also been raised about the role that pension fund consultants have played in directing larger and larger sums into the hands of just a few major fund managers. A recent study of pension funds by the 100 Group of Finance Directors, representing the UK's largest companies, found that just six fund managers and five internally-managed pension funds accounted for over half the funds surveyed. The survey covered roughly a third of the Pounds 300bn in UK pension funds. 'You have to have a track record to attract new business,' Mr Baker said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (14): Caution still needed -Property yields remain high
DOC.TEXT: 'IN THIS business you have to take the rough with the smooth. And last year was rough, believe me.' Thus Tom Heyes, head of ICI's pension funds, commenting on the market for investment property. He does not exaggerate. In mid-1989, average property yields took off vertically and did not stop rising until the last quarter of 1991, by when they were 30 per cent higher. Since then the decline from this all-time historic peak of 10.2 per cent has been barely measurable. Statistics from the Richard Ellis Monthly Index suggest that yields may have dipped to 9.9 per cent by the year end. No lower. Little wonder, therefore, that fund managers with the decades of experience of Mr Heyes are still advocating 'a great deal of caution', and categorise some sectors (notably offices) and regions (particularly the City of London) as disaster zones. New funds, which may have bought within the past five years at yields above 7 per cent, would have taken a bad enough hit if forced to sell properties last year. But pity those whose holdings go back a decade or more to the days when yields were under 5 per cent. Yet Mr Heyes and his counterparts at the other gigantic pension funds remain philosophical, and continue to believe that large funds should maintain an exposure to property, if only as a diversification from the dominance of equities in their portfolios. Outsiders will note that the large funds have little choice but to hold on. When times are hard, the property market dries up, its illiquidity making sales extremely difficult. That illiquidity, coupled with the fact that properties come in expensive lumps and require skilled and continuous management, is also the reason why significant property holdings are not really suitable for smaller funds (Jones Lang Wootton estimates that a fund needs a minimum of Pounds 15-20m in a property portfolio to give it reasonable diversity). With such different factors operating at either end of the scale, the statistics for pension fund property exposure need careful interpretation. Overall, they show a very significant run down in exposure. From a high of 19 per cent in 1974, average pension fund property holdings were only 7 per cent of total assets last year, according to the Phillips & Drew Fund Management annual figures. Many funds had no exposure at all. But that probably disguises the tendency for smaller funds to avoid going into the sector and/or to sell those smallish holdings which they had already bought. Independent figures reinforce the experience of JLW's in-house fund managers (whose clients are almost exclusively in the middle to large bracket) that large funds entered 1992 with property holdings amounting to between 8 and 12 per cent of their total assets. It is more difficult to draw a line through the different claims about current strategies. Malcolm Naish, a partner of JLW's fund management arm, says that more of his clients are today increasing their holdings if they have fallen below 10 per cent, than allowing them to continue to shrink. But other fund managers are adamant that they have no new money going into property at the present time. There may be a number of reasons for this: some have little or no new money arriving for any form of investment, as redundancy programmes continue to erode the number of contributors and cash-strapped companies gratefully take contribution holidays on the back of the outperformance of the late 1980s. Others are robbing Peter to pay Paul: that is, selling one form of investment (or property sector) to buy another. According to the latest in PDFM's Pension Fund Indicators series (whose publication should coincide with the National Association of Pension Funds conference) the tentative conclusion is that some net new money - about 4 per cent - was allocated to property last year, compared with the net 2 per cent disinvestment in 1990. The trend remains to be confirmed later this year and will bear close examination. For anecdotal evidence suggests fund managers have become highly selective in the forays into the property market. Although many, like the Prudential's pension fund management arm, now believe that the drop in property values has now been sufficient to compensate for the poor outlook for rental growth, they are still wary of the office market overall, and of the City's prospects in particular. Tom Heyes reserves real enthusiasm only for smallish retail units where demand has already begun to pick up. 'In the cathedral towns, there are five buyers for every Pounds 2m shopping centre investment,' he observes.
