In previous downturns in the UK cycle, British fund managers have been able to turn their sights abroad. This time the range of sparkling opportunities is small. The US is in a worse state than the UK, and may take more than five years to find its feet again. Forget Japan. Too many investors are trampling over one another in Berlin, though that is taking some of the pressure off Frankfurt. France is at best flat. Some are beginning to look again at Spain. As for east Europe, it's a case of: 'After you. . . No, after you, sir.' Jones Lang Wootton may accurately have pinpointed the turning point when British fund managers regained their appetite for property in the home market, but they are scarcely ravenous. When a pensions manager on the scale of the Prudential - which dramatically reduced the numbers in its property department in 1990 - now talks of a mixed programme of sales and purchases but makes no moves to increase staff numbers, it speaks volumes for the expected future exposure to property. Property unit trusts, the once-popular vehicle for funds too small to consider direct property holdings, have also fallen from favour as a result of a decade of under-performance. However, Medidian Funds Management, the global investment arm of NML, the Australian insurance group noted for its consciously counter-cyclical approach, will begin marketing this month a planned DM1bn closed-end European Property Fund, to be launched in September. The success of that launch may offer a pointer to whether mutual funds can be revived.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (12): Holidays reduce the flow of new money - Charges
DOC.TEXT: GIVEN THE current level of fierce competition in the fund management industry, pension funds ought to be in a better position than ever to get the service they want at attractive prices. Competition for pension fund management mandates has been heightened by, among other things, the recent surge of non-UK houses into the market. Major US firms, offering their expertise in index-matching and 'active quantitative' approaches to investment, have aggressively sought to mark out their stake in the pensions market. But also, competition has been heightened by a shrinking pie. The past three years' recession has caused so many companies to seek 'contributions holidays' from their pension funds that, in fact, pension funds under management in 1991 actually experienced a net outflow of roughly Pounds 2.5bn, according to figures compiled by Caps, the pension fund performance measurement service. Only 30 per cent of funds surveyed by Caps in 1991 had any new money to invest over the year. Since fund managers' fees are expressed as a percentage of funds under management, the shrinkage in pension pools hits them in the pocket. Mr Rob Collinge, director of compensation and benefits at SmithKline Beecham, said he had recently renegotiated management contracts with a number of his outside fund managers which, to his surprise, had resulted in lower charges for some. 'I was surprised at how successful we were,' he said, explaining that several of the managers involved had strong performance records and no shortage of clients. The problem with competition, he said, was that those fund managers with mediocre performance records were the ones most willing to cut fees. 'But for us, a few basis points of improved performance can far outweigh the advantages of slightly lower fees,' he added. The shrinkage has caused a pinch for investment managers who have now had to work harder to secure mandates away from their competitors. However, it has also provided the incentive for managers to find ways to cull fees from clients in ways which are not immediately obvious. Indeed, at least one US bank was said to have been offering its index-matching fund management services for no fee at all - provided the clients used the bank's global custody service. The use of hidden - or so-called 'dirty' charges - is an issue that has troubled pension fund trustees for a long time. But in recent years, publicity surrounding charges and the ensuing calls for regulators to do something about them has made trustees look even harder at them. Indeed, the National Association of Pension Funds has formed a committee on fee transparency, to examine dirty charges and make recommendations to members about how to deal with them. Pure charges on pension fund pools range from 0.2 to 0.5 per cent for balanced pools, depending on the size of funds under management. However, segregated pools or specialist and overseas accounts incur transaction charges of up to 1 per cent and additional charges above that, depending on circumstances. By international standards, particularly those of the US, UK pension fund management charges come cheap. In the US, fees can easily average 1.5 to 2 per cent, partly reflecting the wider use of specialist and boutique-type fund managers. But it is the hidden charges that are the bone of contention in the UK. The most significant of these are 'soft commissions' - the provision of services in kind to fund managers who transact a pre-agreed level of commission-generating business through a broker. Last month, the Securities and Investments Board, after vacillating for months over the matter, declined to outlaw soft commissions, on the grounds that fund managers can use them legitimately to obtain services which ultimately enhance returns to clients. However, it has required fund managers who accept soft commissions to begin disclosing the extent of these to clients. Among services typically received by fund managers in exchange for soft commissions are research, data retrieval systems and software packages. Because all commissions costs are deducted from the clients' total funds under management, effectively, it is one way of shifting overheads to clients from fund managers. Mr Nick Fitzpatrick, partner at pensions consultants and actuaries Bacon and Woodrow, said that there was no good reason for pension fund managers to pay soft commissions. 'Commissions are a voluntary cost, because many fund managers are able to negotiate transactions with no commission whatsoever,' he said. 'The only reason I can see for paying soft commission is to hide the charges from the customer.' In the US, where disclosure rules have been in place for some time, pension funds are increasingly demanding that soft commission payments be rebated to them by the managers which accept them. Also, fund managers are able to add on dirty charges by placing client funds in internal unit trusts, which carry charges of 0.5 to 0.75 per cent. While these are typically used for overseas assets, managers are often inclined to place clients with pools below Pounds 10m in domestic unit trusts as well. Mr Fitzpatrick says that he urges clients to seek 'clean' charging structures wherever possible. While these rarely mean lower costs for pension funds, they do clarify exactly what the service costs. In a clean structure, a client may not be charged for anything but the service fee. Mr Collinge said that almost all his fund management agreements were now 'clean'. 'Its a cost control mechanism - we know what we are paying,' he said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (11): Trust deeds may need amendment - Increased understanding of derivatives is paying off
DOC.DATELINE: UK PENSION funds are starting to make use of futures and options
DOC.TEXT: but slowly. Concern about the inherent risks remains a deterrent, but other issues also counter the shift towards derivatives. Trustees can prove resistant, particularly when they are not certain how to assess the use of such products, and fund managers themselves may be unsure how to report performance. However, efforts to broaden understanding of futures and options among both fund managers and trustees are starting to pay off. According to a recent survey by KPMG Management Consulting, five out of the 10 top UK pension fund organisations use futures and options in more than 25 per cent of their funds - an increase on last year, when eight out of the 10 funds surveyed used futures and options in less than a quarter of funds managed. However, the use of derivative products is far less widespread among smaller organisations. themselves aware of the benefits which might be derived from using futures and options,' said Mr Angus Matheson, chairman of the National Association of Pension Funds' investment committee. But from that starting point, the journey is not always straightforward. Once fund managers have decided to adopt futures and options, they must in turn convince trustees of the advantages. Trust deeds can prove a further pitfall. 'Check your trust deeds. Do not do anything unless you are empowered to do it,' advises Mr Clive Gilchrist, managing director of BES Trustees and vice president of the NAPF. 'If you want to play the game, learn the rules.' Some trust deeds specify which investments are not permitted; others define which investments are allowed. In the latter case, unless derivative products are specifically included, the trust deeds have to be changed. Some important barriers have been removed, however. Crucially, fund managers' tax position was clarified in the 1990 budget. Although there was no dramatic shift in attitudes, fund managers started to look at the market seriously after the tax change. There has been progress on other issues, such as performance measurement. A recent set of recommendations by the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (Liffe) for the reporting of financial futures and options in investment portfolios, provides an industry standard for the first time. The guidelines will allow trustees to assess more easily whether fund managers are using futures and options for investment or hedging purposes, or whether they are taking more speculative positions. '(These recommendations) will lead to a better understanding of the uses of these instruments, higher standards of reporting and more consistent performancecalculations,' said Mr Tim Gardener, head of planning services at Mercer Fraser, the actuarial consultancy firm commissioned to write the report. The educational effort by Liffe, which has run seminars with the NAPF for trustees, has fostered interest in derivative products. Where fund managers are using futures and options, their application is generally quite restricted. For the most part, UK fund managers do not regard futures and options as a separate asset class, but as part of the underlying asset class. (For example, a stock option is essentially an equity asset, not an option.) Derivative products are 'part of the armoury', says Mr Gilchrist. While a few US pension funds have started to allocate part of their funds to specialised managed futures funds, there are no signs of a similar trend in the UK. Managed futures fund managers consider futures an asset class in their own right, representing a diversification of portfolio risk. 'The idea of trying to persuade pension fund trustees to put a pot of money into a dedicated futures fund is very far away,' said Mr Peter Stanyer, head of investment for British Rail pensions. So far, futures fund managers and specialist trading advisers (particularly US-based commodity trading advisers, or CTAs) have been marketing UK pension fund managers to little avail. The poor performance of futures funds this year is unlikely to encourage any change of heart. Most pension funds use futures and options in two ways: to hedge exposure - that is, to reduce potential losses on cash holdings by taking a contrary position in the futures market; and for asset allocation - to shift exposure from one market to another. These uses come under the concept of efficient portfolio management, under Securities and Investment Board rules. A future obliges the holder to buy or sell at a set price at a future date; an option gives the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell at a set price at a set date. Futures are of particular use in asset allocation, while options can be used for stock selection. The use of derivatives for asset allocation is attractive, because buying and selling large holdings of stocks or bonds can be both time-consuming and expensive. It is often cheaper and more efficient to shift exposure by, for example, buying FT-SE index future contracts and holding a cash deposit, so creating a synthetic equity asset. There is a growing use of index products on foreign markets, which is likely to increase as portfolios become more international. Funds which aim to match the performance of stock indices often use index futures rather than stocks. Because UK pension funds are broadly UK equity-based, they have so far been most active in Liffe's FT-SE contracts. Liffe's gilt futures are also widely used. They are less active in individual stock options, but if the market picks up following the merger of the Liffe and the London Traded Options market earlier this year, activity could increase. UK pension funds remain for the most part resistant to over-the-counter products offered by banks, partly because of the credit implications, and also because they fear such products will lack liquidity.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (13): New code agreed - Performance measurement
DOC.TEXT: PENSION FUND performance measurement has moved into a new era this year, with the publication of a code which has the backing of many pension industry interests. But, ironically, the whole idea of league tables and performance comparisons could be undermined by a slowly emerging trend towards individual fund benchmarks. Performance measurement is now a highly developed service, which has become concentrated into two main specialist operations. One is the World Markets company, which started as a soft commissions venture of a stockbroking firm but is now owned by Bankers Trust, the US commercial banking group. The other is Combined Actuarial Performance Services (Caps) which, as its name suggests, is the result of merging the separate measurement service of various actuarial firms such as R Watson, Bacon & Woodrow, Mercer Fraser and Noble Lowndes. WM is the market leader in terms of the size of funds measured. Last year its WM All Funds Universe consisted of over 2,000 UK pension fund portfolios worth Pounds 241bn, said to represent about three-quarters of the industry. Caps measured rather more portfolios, at 2,760, but a rather smaller aggregate of Pounds 156bn. While Caps has a slightly smaller - although clearly overlapping - coverage, in some respects its funds are more typical of the industry. The WM results tend to be affected by the performance of a few huge funds which may have rather different characteristics, such as a significantly higher investment in property. The WM Universe had an 8 per cent property content in its aggregated portfolio last year, against only 2 per cent for Caps. However, the performance of property can be separated out. Moreover, WM now also divides its funds into the WM Very Large Funds Universe, worth over Pounds 1bn each, and the WM Average Funds Universe. A dismal property market meant that the giant funds did worse than average in 1991. The WM Very Large Funds earned an average rate of return of 16.2 per cent (income plus capital growth) compared with 17.8 per cent for the WM Average Funds. Meanwhile, the Caps median fund earned 18.3 per cent including property, and 18.6 per cent excluding it. Despite an element of harmonisation within the past year or two, the WM and Caps services retain slight technical differences. WM tends to talk about averages, and Caps about medians, for instance. But these are of little consequence, and there will be no repetition of the minor embarrassment two years ago, when the rate of return on the FT-Actuaries All-Share Index for was measured as 36.1 per cent by WM and 35.5 per cent by Caps. The discrepancy related to the timing of dividend receipts. For 1991, however, both services measure the All-Share return as 20.7 per cent. Possibly the methodology still needs to be refined in specialist areas such as index-tracking funds. Last year, for instance, the presence of a significant element of recently-privatised stocks within the All-Share tended to flatter the index funds, because they held these shares in partly-paid form, and outperformed because prices rose. However, such details may be a matter for interpretation rather than changes in technique. At any rate, a code of practice for both methodology and the presentation of historical performance records has now been agreed. The code was developed because of complaints that performance measurement figures have been misused by fund managers, particularly when soliciting for new business. There has been a tendency to choose funds selectively for inclusion in the records, and to pick particular periods, indices or measurers. Fund managers have developed a kind of Orwellian tendency to rewrite history, notably by dropping poorly-performing funds from their records, on various pretexts. Accordingly, a National Association of Pension Funds inquiry in 1990 recommended the establishment of a voluntary code; and the simple outline of the code has now been published by a working party, which included the representatives of various industry bodies. A further working group has been set up to monitor compliance with the code, and consider how it might be further developed in the future. Already many investment management houses have begun issuing figures which they certify to be in accordance with the code. This means, inter alia, that the standard performance presentation should cover five calendar years, should include all discretionary balanced funds under management, and must state the name of the measurer. At the very least, the industry is therefore now developing a standard format for performance data. But there remain some grey areas, particularly in the selection of funds and the definition of 'discretion' as applied to management mandates. From next year, however, the performance league tables which have been appearing in various journals and consulting actuaries' circulars will have a little more credibility, although gaps may remain. The biggest pension fund manager, Mercury Asset Management, has refused to publish any aggregate figures, probably because it fears that clients underperforming the published house median would complain. Moreover, the whole idea of developing comparable performance statistics may be torpedoed by a trend towards the setting of individual performance benchmarks by pension funds. In time, the idea of discretionary balanced management may fade away. Already, WM has divided its Universe into two. In future, the measurers may need to set up a series of specialist universes (global equities, say, and international bonds, or UK index trackers). Beyond that, increasing numbers of funds may give their managers individual briefs in terms of investment risk and return in relation to specific scheme liabilities. It could be that the industry league table could will begin to lose its relevance almost as soon as it has emerged into statistical daylight.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (9): Opportunities for overseas players - Japan's rapidly ageing population will oblige funds to place greater emphasis on performance
DOC.TEXT: PENSION FUND management in Japan, traditionally the exclusive territory of Japanese life assurers and trust banks, is changing as the emphasis in fund management appointments shifts towards performance. The shift in attitudes is expected to provide opportunities for foreign companies, which have been unhappy with the limitations due to appointments ruled by the complex and cosy corporate networks. The recent appointment of Invesco MIM Asset Management, the Japanese arm of the UK asset management group, by Nagasakiya, a leading retail company, to manage a portion of its pension funds, came as a surprise to the industry. Foreign managers have only managed to win appointments from quasi-government organisations, and Nagasakiya became the first single private Japanese company to appoint a foreign-based fund manager. Nagasakiya indicated that it was dissatisfied with the returns of investments by trust banks, and allotted Y1bn of its Y23.7bn (Dollars 178m) pension fund to Invesco MIM. Foreign fund managers and more aggressive Japanese managers believe that the rapid ageing of the country's population will force company funds and the Japanese government to put more emphasis on performance. Other leading Japanese companies have also started to indicate interest in allowing foreign companies, which have more expertise in fund management. For those companies wishing to diversify their investments internationally, foreign fund asset managers are attractive, because foreign asset management companies are permitted to invest up to 70 per cent of assets overseas, compared with 50 per cent for domestic asset managers. The weakness of the Tokyo stock market has made Japanese companies wary of the deployment of funds. The uncertainty over Japanese share prices has made overseas investments all the more attractive. Last year, Japan's 1,400 pension fund schemes had Y38,500bn in assets. This figure is expected to hit Y161,000bn by the year 2000. Public pension funds and mutual aid programmes boasted another Y127,000bn. Foreign companies also hope that the government's own concern about the financial burden of expected demographic changes in Japan will stimulate further reforms of pension fund management. About 11 per cent of Japanese are now aged 65 or over, but the ratio is expected to jump to 16 per cent by 2000. Given such figures, the momentum for pension management reform is mounting. Asset management firms were allowed limited access to pension fund management in 1990. Investment advisers were permitted to manage only new pension contributions in portfolios with a minimum value of Y1bn and up to one third of total assets. The finance ministry responded to US pressure last year by allowing foreign affiliated asset managers to handle pension funds with as little as Y500m in assets and to hold up to 70 per cent in foreign investments. SG Warburg, Jardine Fleming and Fidelity were appointed to handle a fraction of the Pension Fund Association's own account, and part of the schoolteachers' fund was handed over to Jardine Fleming and Merrill Lynch. Foreign trust banks, which have been in the pension fund management business since 1985, now manage Y59bn, of which Y29bn is handled by Bankers Trust. Mr Noboru Terada, of the Pension Fund Association, says there is a change in attitude among Japanese companies towards appointing foreign managers. However, he points out that companies are still worried about the commitment the fund management company has made to Japan and the efficiency of administration and reporting procedures. Mr Haruaki Deguchi, at Nippon Life, Japan's largest life assurer, says that pension fund management will shift to be more 'western style' in the future. 'Japan's pension fund system is relatively new compared with that of Europe and the US. As the pension liabilities of companies start growing, managers will become more severe about investment returns,' he adds. Corporate pensions have usually been allotted to trust banks in the same keiretsu (corporate group), or to life assurers which in return would be buyers of the company's equity in times of fund raising. Until recently, trust banks held 65 per cent of the market, while life assurers held 35 per cent. Winning an appointment would be virtually impossible for a fund-managing company without such links. This arrangement has started to become a burden for the life insurers. The slump in share prices and low dividend payments has made long-term shareholdings unattractive investments. Mr Deguchi says that if companies start to base fund management relationships on performance, the nature of the funds will become more unstable. Selling life assurance policies, roughly 80 per cent of the total funds in the life assurance industry, will be the main focus of business, rather than pension fund management. However, changes in Japan do not happen overnight. Objective performance analysis of the industry has yet to be established, and performance data is not available to western consulting firms in Tokyo, including Intersec Research and Frank Russell. Once the growth in pension liabilities starts to affect a company's profits, the improvement of return on assets will become a more pressing matter for the companies. To wait for this to happen may require patience, because it could be at least another five to 10 years.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (10): Protectionism and suspicion of equities - A genuinely open market for pensions in Europe is still some way off
DOC.TEXT: THE CURTAIN on a single European market formally goes up in less than eight months' time. But so far as pension funds and their managers are concerned, the long anticipated drama will take rather longer to unfold. It is not just that the draft EC directive on pension fund freedoms - likely to be adopted by member states later this year - will not be implemented in many national legal systems until the mid-1990s. The challenge of securing a genuinely open market for pensions will only be achieved when cultural barriers, local protectionism, and continental suspicion of equities as a suitable investment medium are finally overcome. Major UK groups, such as Morgan Grenfell Investment Management (part of Deutsche Bank), Warburg Asset Management and the merchant bank Robert Fleming, are all chipping away. It seems, however, that some of the UK investment management industry's earlier expectations of picking up mainland European business were overdone. 'The European marketing chaps are the ones with the big expense accounts and glamour lifestyles,' observes an employee in one leading fund management business, a touch irreverently. 'The amount of money which they have brought in is pitiful compared with what we can pick up in the UK.' Signs that the French government, for one, may introduce tax-efficient money-purchase schemes to take pressure off the state - notwithstanding recent opposition from unions and others - is one good reason not to lose heart over Europe. Others are the EC pension fund directive, and pressure which continues to be exerted on Brussels by multinational companies seeking a more efficient way of organising their employees' pension arrangements. Ironically, last October's draft EC pensions directive omitted the freedom which the likes of IBM would most dearly appreciate, namely cross-border membership of funds. The Commission insists that it has not abandoned this principle for the longer term, but acknowledges that the inherent tax complications could hold up progress on the other morestraightforward issues. These are the freedom for pension funds to choose an investment manager anywhere in the Community, and the removal of national restrictions on where and how funds should invest their money. Neither of these will fundamentally alter the UK market per se, but they are highly relevant in countries such as Belgium and Portugal. One question constantly raised by the approaching single market and the reduced currency risk of the exchange rate mechanism is whether the EC should be seen by pension funds as a single area for investment purposes. At the end of last year, however, the split of UK to continental European investments was roughly 6:1, suggesting that old preconceptions die hard. One measure of the appropriate split, for instance, might be individual stock market capitalisations, which showed the UK as 42 per cent of total European stock markets at the end of December 1991. It is not as though historic performance justifies UK pension funds' bias in favour of their domestic territory. Another consideration is whether multinational employers will ultimately want to take advantage of the possibilities for consolidating the pension fund assets of their various European subsidiaries. IBM and Digital Equipment Corporation are among those looking at the options, but Ford Motor company is among those adopting a more cautious approach. The companies which are pursuing consolidation plans clearly think that they will be in a strong position to negotiate a competitive fee structure and reap the advantages of economies of scale. Within the EC, there are signs that some pension funds are beginning to look beyond traditional boundaries for new opportunities - the Dollars 90bn Dutch civil servants pension fund ABP being one cited by the leading consulting group Watsons. Wells Fargo Nikko was a beneficiary to the tune of a Dollars 600m account, but generally the sums involved tend to be much smaller as companies put their toes in the water. Many managers admit that their continental fees are smaller, not least because of competing local banks' ability to take advantage of dealing spreads. The Netherlands is the one market which is recognisable from an Anglo-Saxon point of view. As Mr Patrick Gifford, a director of Fleming Investment Management, puts it: 'Everyone in Holland has a funded pension, and the country is open to non-resident managers.' At this stage, though, it looks as though Europe's big banks and insurers are fiercely protecting their patches from the incoming hordes. Another problem is that the cult of the equity is only slowly catching on, while the saga of employees dependent for their pensions on companies controlled by the late Robert Maxwell has hardly advanced the cause. Some have not been slow to point out that the German system of accounting for pensions on a company's balance sheet has its advantages after all. Reaching clients, meanwhile, is not easy, given that the UK's consultant-led marketing structure is not familiar in continental Europe. Firms such as Watson and Wyatt have blazed a trail, but they are not retained by companies in the same way as in the US and the UK.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (7): UK funds hesitate to leap in the dark - The progress of quantitative management
DOC.TEXT: LONDON'S QUANT scene is hotting up. A number of new quantitative managers, such as Pareto Partners, Quorum and Barr Rosenberg European Management, have opened up, joining the slightly longer-established operators like PanAgora and GMO Woolley. Many of these have American connections. Domestic leaders include clearing bank subsidiaries like County NatWest Investment Management and Barclays de Zoete Wedd Investment Management. These dominate the basic quant product area of index funds. And there are clear ambitions on the part of several houses to move into higher value added sectors, involving active, rather than passive, management, for which much higher fees can be charged. But British pension funds appear to be rather cautious. Quant managers seek to exploit electronic technology and statistical analysis to achieve enhanced investment performance. Index management is still in a growth phase. Its characteristic is that it involves large economies of scale so that, untypically of investment management in general, indexation has become concentrated amongst a few large players. The UK market leader is BZWIM, which has been putting on new business at the rate of Pounds 1bn or more annually for the past few years. It now runs almost Pounds 10bn in indexed portfolios tracking various equity and bond indices. It is estimated that about 15 per cent of the assets of UK pension funds are now indexed, formally or informally. There is still some way to go to reach the US indexed proportion of more like 25 per cent; the US penetration has changed little for five years, suggesting that it represents something of a natural ceiling, which may also eventually apply in the UK. Indexation is a cheap, low-risk option for pension fund trustees disappointed by traditional active managers. This is no strategy for trustees aiming to top the performance league tables, but it has obvious appeal for those fed up with featuring in the fourth quartile. For more ambitious clients, however, the quants have plenty of second-generation products. Some of these are bottom-up stockpicking systems, which aim to add several percentage points a year to investment performance without adding risk. There has also been a lot of emphasis recently on top-down models to control tactical asset allocation - basically, bond-equity switching - and handle currency exposures for global portfolios. County NatWest has found UK pension fund clients for its Value-Based Investment Service, an asset allocation system. But generally its more advanced and weirdly-named products, like Dynamic Currency Hedging and Ratcheted Multi-Bond Option (call it Rambo for short), are only selling in Japan and the US. Japanese houses have become quite keen on quant. Nikko's London asset management arm, for instance, has this year launched a so-called Return Reversal Fund, aimed at exploiting stock rotation effects in the Tokyo market. But it has not been fortunate with its timing. Several of the US-owned houses in London are basically selling global products back into America. Pareto, which has only been running for about a year, but is backed by Mellon Bank, has already won over Dollars 2bn of currency overlay business, mainly from US pension funds. Mr Ronald Liesching, a director of Pareto, suggests that many US institutions may already have becoming disillusioned with 'black box' stockpicking products, some of which have had enough time to go wrong for American clients. 'Those approaches which have been devised to fit history are shortly doomed to join it,' he says. In the UK, he adds, quant is only making very slow progress. In fact, there are signs that continental European clients are more receptive, being ready to make the quantum leap from low-performing life assurance contracts or Swiss bank fiduciary accounts to state-of-the-art high technology investment products. In contrast, British pension funds have generally received excellent returns from traditional balanced managers in the 1980s, and have little reason to take a leap in the dark. Barr Rosenberg is nevertheless trying to sell to UK as well as continental funds, seeking to exploit the poor relative performance achieved by British managers in US and Japanese equities. Ms Jennie Paterson, the firm's marketing director in London, tends to play down the technological wizardry. She describes Barr Rosenberg's method as 'using an expert computer system to duplicate the thought processes of the typical investment manager'. British pension funds have been 'very receptive to the idea' but have yet to sign up. Certainly, active quant has had an uncertain reception in the UK. There was the example of Lazard Investors, which imported an American value-based system in the late 1980s just when growth stocks were beginning to take off and value stocks wilted. Lazard dumped the system at the end of 1990 in favour of a traditional style, with which apparently it has enjoyed considerable success. Nevertheless, some active quant products have begun to achieve a breakthrough. Hill Samuel Investment Management, for instance, a few weeks ago picked up a Pounds 50m account from the Cable and Wireless pension fund. It will run the UK equity portfolio, using its established quant product called Active Value Management. HSIM has now built up a five-year record for AVM, outperforming the All-Share Index return by some 4 per cent a year on average, albeit with some significant short-term fluctuations. AVM portfolios now total Pounds 360m. Mr Alan Greenhorn, HSIM's quant director, says: 'Many quantitative managers are single-factor strategists. With AVM, we do not expect any one strategy to be successful for ever.' Various tilts have been used in practice over the five years, starting with high asset value, then moving to high overseas earners, with a recent shift from high to medium market capitalisation. This restless search for new values and insights could be said to be true of quant management as a whole. And with computer brainpower and memory capacity becoming ever cheaper, no traditional manager can afford to ignore the trend.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (8): Futures gain respectability - US funds are beginning to diversify
DOC.TEXT: A WIND of change is blowing through the huge pension fund industry in the US. For years, there has been much talk of portfolio diversification, particularly into international stocks and bonds, and correspondingly little action. Now, industry observers believe some real developments are taking place. For example, Greenwich Associates, the Connecticut-based consultancy, has noted recently* that 'the proportion of funds using smaller capitalisation stocks, international stocks and international bonds is up sharply'. Extrapolating from its annual survey of the 2,000 largest tax-exempt pension funds and endowments, with a projected Dollars 2,200bn in plan assets, the firm suggests that the percentage of funds using small capitalisation stocks last year was up from 48 to 54 per cent; for international stocks, from 38 to 44 per cent; and for international bonds, from 15 to 17 per cent. This, adds Greenwich Consultants, may only be the beginning. Its consultant, Joe Purcell, notes that an additional 6 per cent of pension funds plan to start using small cap stocks in 1992; another 13 per cent plan to start using international stocks; and another 5 per cent plan to start using international bonds. The figures in last category, he says, represent 'a particularly large leap relative to the proportion already using such bonds'. The last point is pertinent. The use of international equities, say, in US pension fund portfolios may be on the rise, but it still accounts for a very small proportion of total assets - perhaps 4.4 per cent among all funds, with a rather higher 5.8 per cent in corporate funds and under 3 per cent in public funds. Still, boldness seems to be becoming fairly endemic. A good deal of attention has focused recently on the increasing willingness of large public pension funds to commit funds to the often-volatile futures market. This is progressive thinking, by anyone's reckoning. Convention dictates that futures are a risky game for large public pension funds. Some states, including New York, even go so far as to prohibit the investment of public pension money in futures contracts. But, such prudence notwithstanding, there is a growing school of thought within the industry which believes that forays into the financial futures arena at least, will become commonplace for public pension funds in the decade ahead, and that funds which reject this notion will be denying their beneficiaries the chance of significant additional returns. Still, no matter how advanced a pension fund trustee's thinking, the road to diversification can be littered with all kinds of problems. For example, much attention centred on the hiccups encountered by the Californian State Teachers Retirement System, the Dollars 34bn state teachers' pension fund, as it tried to invest Dollars 1.5bn in foreign stocks last spring. California has particularly tough affirmative-action laws. Among other things, these require state contractors - including money managers - to set goals of subcontracting with women and minority-owned firms for goods and services equal to one-fifth of the fees which they receive from the state. When the state pension fund invited money managers to submit applications to handle the international diversification, it found that only 36 of the 91 firms chasing the contract had met the affirmative-action law requirements. Indeed, to a money management business based overseas the affirmative-action requirements might seem almost impossible to fulfil. Such hassles aside, the current move towards more diversified portfolios contrasts sharply with the demand for passive equity management, or indexation. In 1990, the proportion of total funds using passive equities stood at 41 per cent. Last year, the figure fell to 36 per cent. Total funds which expect to start using passive equities in 1991 stood at 6 per cent, unchanged from the previous year. Overall, it is currently reckoned that index funds account for about one quarter of US pension funds total assets. Finally, it is interesting to note that the proportion of US employees actually covered by corporate pension funds is steadily declining, although assets handled by such funds have tripled over the past decade, thanks largely to the rise in market levels. It has been estimated, for instance, that only 43 per cent of workers participated in US company pension plans last year, compared with a peak of 49 per cent in 1979. This receding coverage has been variously attributed to the anti-union climate, a declining role for low-paid blue-collar workers who would have had pension coverage in the past, and the associated expansion of small business jobs. But whatever the cause, it is scarcely a comforting development - for employees or fund managers. *Greenwich Reports: Strengthening Relationships, Improving Performance.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (5): Erisa might be a welcome transatlantic hurricane - Was Maxwell uniquely crooked, or are all funds vulnerable to criminal damage? The possible legislation
DOC.TEXT: WHEN THE scale of Mr Robert Maxwell's plundering of his companies' pension funds became clear, the entire UK pensions industry caught its breath. Not unnaturally, thousands of individual pension scheme members began asking whether their own investments were safe from a similar theft. A previously quiet backwater of pensions management was swamped by a wave of interest. Suddenly, a parliamentary committee was probing the arcane world of pension fund security and asset administration. It produced a report which highlighted the gaps in pension fund security. Pensioners and scheme members alike began to question the ultimate ownership of pension fund assets. Who controls funds, and what limits are there on the investment and transfer of assets? It is perhaps unsurprising, then, that pension funds are at the centre of a passionate debate among rival groups of financial intermediaries. The question is whether Maxwell was uniquely crooked, or whether all funds are vulnerable to criminal damage. One school of thought believes that a few simple changes in rules governing fund trustees should suffice to make the Maxwell affair unrepeatable. Another school thinks changes need to be widespread. In particular, the aftermath of the Maxwell affair has been a tense time for fund trustees and fund managers. It is too early to predict whether legislation will follow the rush of interest, but it seems likely the pressure for reform will not disappear. Legislation could be modelled on US laws passed in 1974. The Employee Retirement Investment Security Act (Erisa) demanded the separation of fund management from the custody of the assets, and completely redrafted US pension fund law. If anything like it were adopted in the UK, it would overturn decades of self-administration and regulation by London's fund management community. It would also blow like a hurricane through the arcane world of the fund trustee. Erisa made it compulsory for fund trustees (known in the US as plan sponsors) to demonstrate in an annual report that they had managed their fund prudently. In addition, it meant that funds would have to appoint a so-called master custodian or trustee, to oversee the fulfilment of its requirements, by providing appropriate records and adequate security against prohibited transactions. Indirectly, the prudent investment principle enshrined in Erisa led to diversification outside the US by its massive pension plans. And the plan sponsors' need for better information led to huge investment by their banks in the administrative and reporting systems which became the core of the global custody product. Although UK fund managers are often at one remove from administration of the assets they invest, some of the UK's largest houses do their own safe custody and are substantial players in the custody business in their own right. Erisa-style legislation would require them to pass that function to external specialists. That might sound undramatic, but it would have far-reaching implications, not least for costs. The fund managers might not have the option of setting up their own subsidiaries to take over the custodial function - Erisa specifies that the custodian must be an entirely independent entity. Thus, the recent creation by SG Warburg, for example, of a custody division separated from its Mercury Asset Management subsidiary, would be made redundant - it would still have to be sold or closed. Fees would inevitably rise. Small wonder that the commercial banks, particularly the large US banks which specialise in custody and trustee services, have been aggressively marketing their products to nervous trustee boards of UK pension funds. For the custodians at least, Maxwell has provided a welcome marketing opportunity. A notable example was a seminar on pension fund security held by Chase Manhattan in February, at which Mr Colin Grimsey, managing director, said: 'I have no doubt that changes in legislation will present significant challenges and opportunities for custodian banks.' Mr Grimsey, one of the pioneers of global custody, also made a prediction: 'Whatever the outcome of anticipated legislative changes, there is little doubt that the role of the independent professional trustee will be expanded.' The fund management community is not so sure. It has produced a series of defensive measures, notably a letter published in the Financial Times from the chairman of the Institutional Fund Managers' Association. He argued that the IFMA would broadly welcome any strengthening of restrictions on self-investment, as well greater powers for trustees. But the letter went on to point out that wholesale changes along the lines described above would be expensively aimed at the wrong target. The UK pension industry as a whole has functioned safely for decades without over-elaborate restrictions. That is a view shared by Michael Robarts, a director of Robert Fleming Investment Management. He points out to the example of local authority pension funds. Only when the notorious Hammersmith & Fulham swaps case focused attention on local authority funds did it emerge that the rules governing them were so narrowly written as to make questionable even the appointment of external fund managers. Local authorities have largely withdrawn from stock-lending markets, because some legal opinion suggests such transactions are disallowed.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (6): Bonds may prevail, unless the ERM crumbles - After a decade of exceptional real returns, short-term prospects are less encouraging
DOC.TEXT: THE CONSERVATIVES' emphatic election victory may be about to deliver UK investors into a promised land of low and stable inflation; but no one is quite sure how the investment landscape will change as the UK adjusts to membership of the European exchange rate mechanism. The real returns earned by UK pension funds on their equity portfolios over the past decade have been exceptional. The average annual nominal return on UK equities over the 10 years to the end of 1991 was 19.6 per cent. Deflated by the average earnings index, which is the best indicator of the change in their liabilities, this implies a real return of 11.3 per cent on UK equities, compared with 6.3 per cent on UK fixed-interest securities and 1 per cent on index-linked gilts. Little wonder, then, that UK pension funds have both accumulated large surpluses in recent years and orientated their portfolios towards equities. But the short-term prospects for real returns do not look so encouraging. The rate of economic growth is the most important long-run determinant of real returns on equity investments. But current tensions within the ERM, and the pain of adjustment to a low inflation regime, may depress real equity returns over the next few years. The total return on equity investments is equal to the dividend yield plus the capital gain. The capital gain depends, in turn, on the expected future stream of profits. Assuming that the share of profits in national income remains stable, the main determinant of real profitability, and thus the long-term real return on equity investments, is the real growth rate of the economy. History confirms the central role of GDP growth in determing long-run real returns, according to a recent paper from Lombard Street Research. Mr Tim Congdon and Mr Simon Ward show that the combination of an expected trend rate of real economic growth of 2-2 1/2 per cent, added to an average dividend yield of 5.2 per cent over the period 1955-90, implies an annual real return of 7-8 per cent, before management fees. A recent BZW study confirms their expectations: the average annual real return on equities, with gross income reinvested, was 7.2 per cent over the 70 years to 1988, higher than target real return of 4-4 1/2 per cent normally set by pension funds, but much below the real yield on equities in the 1980s. Yet this relationship between real returns on equities and trend GDP growth tends to hold true only over very long periods: several decades, rather than a few years. Real returns in the 1990s could stray from this long-run trend for a number of reasons: sluggish economic growth; changes in the profit share in GDP; or changes in market expectations. ERM and European growth: The clearest threat to UK economic growth, and thus real equity returns, is the high level of nominal and real interest rates that Germany is imposing on its ERM partners. Because Germany sets the floor for Europe's monetary policy, the rest of Europe remains stuck with a combination of slow growth and tight monetary policy. Even if the Bundesbank feels able to cut its rates by the end of this year, as inflationary pressures abate, it is unlikely to cut rates very far, very fast. ERM and the UK: UK rates may have to remain above those in other European countries. The interest rate premium against German rates has narrowed to just half of a percentage point. But if UK imports surge and the trade deficit widens, the markets may become nervous once more about sterling's ERM parity. In addition, there is still some way to go before UK industry fully adjusts to life in the ERM. Annual wage inflation is still above 7 per cent, and therefore remains higher than the European average. There may have to be a few years of high unemployment and squeezed profits before UK unit labour cost inflation falls to European levels. Corporate profitability: But UK productivity growth in the 1980s grew faster than in every main industrialised country, except Japan; and output per person-hour in British manufacturing is still only two thirds of the German level, suggesting that there is room for further improvement. UK equities benefited from the rise in the share of value-added that was distributed in profits in the 1980s. According to the OECD, capital's share rose from 30.3 per cent in 1975-79 to 31.5 per cent in 1980-87. Yet the rate of return on capital in the latter period was virtually unchanged at 9.5 per cent, well below the OECD average of 14.2 per cent. Capital gains: The main determinant of the rate of return on equities is likely to come from short-run movements in share prices, as investors reassess their expectations of the future. Congdon and Ward find that, over one-year periods, changes in the return on equities come about largely through swings in the dividend yield. Only over five-year periods do changes in dividend growth matter. But even over 20 years the correlation between share-price indices and output is weak, as the charts shows. At first sight, the UK equity market does not appear over-valued. The average price-earnings ratio of UK equities is broadly in line with long-run trends; the prospect of low inflation could boost profitability; and the ratio of nominal yields on bonds to equities has fallen to 1.95:1, lower than its past average of 2.25:1 Yet low inflation combined with high and stable yields on bonds may reduce the need for such a high nominal premium on fixed interest investments. If inflation were to fall to 2-3 per cent a year, and economic growth remained below trend for the first half of the decade, the current nominal yield gap of 4 1/2 percentage points between bond and equity yields would make bonds an attractive investment. The market is not yet convinced that the UK will move into this low-inflation world: the yield gap between nominal and index-linked gilts remains nearer to 5 percentage points. The capital gains from falling nominal yield may make bonds portfolios outperform equities during this adjustment. The strength of the UK's ERM commitment remains a central uncertainty. If tensions in Europe were to boil over, the ERM were to crumble and the UK were to return to its inflationary ways, then the short-term case for bonds would quickly disappear.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (4): Maturity may point to gilts - Investment strategy
DOC.TEXT: THERE WAS a phenomenal change in the investment strategy of UK pension funds during the 1980s. Back in 1982, Combined Actuarial Performance Services (Caps) found that the average pension fund had 19 per cent of its portfolio in UK fixed-interest securities and 10 per cent in property; by the end of 1991, those proportions had dropped to 3 and 2 per cent respectively. The cult of the equity appears to have triumphed, with combined UK and overseas equity holdings rising from 65 per cent in 1982 to 83 per cent at the end of 1991. But could those statistics be about to change? Many might argue that the prospects of a low-inflation low-growth decade in the 1990s means that bonds will offer attractive returns. A shift may be inevitable. The Conservative government's efforts to reduce the budget deficit in the 1980s (which succeeded in creating a budget surplus in the latter part of the decade) meant that the supply of gilt issues dried up. There were few gilts for pension funds to buy. Now that the budget deficit is back and the government is issuing around Pounds 2bn of gilts a month - a figure which may increase in future financial years - UK pension funds will have plenty of gilts to choose from. There is a further point. Pension funds need to match their assets to their liabilities. If a large proportion of members of the fund are receiving pensions, then the fund is described in industry jargon as 'mature'. Mature funds need to place a greater emphasis on income than capital growth, and therefore tend to invest a greater proportion of their funds in gilts. According to John Clamp, of Caps, UK pension funds are more mature than they were in 1982, so one would logically expect a greater proportion of gilts in pension funds. Part of the reason for the low proportions of gilt investment may be the memories of the 1970s, when inflation, and a soaring budget deficit, savaged the returns for those managers who invested in gilts. But for those who bought fixed-interest securities in the 1980s, the returns were pretty respectable. Caps figures show that the cumulative annual return on gilts over the 10 years to the end of 1991 was 14.7 per cent. That was behind the return available from UK equities (19.6 per cent) and overseas shares (16.9 per cent), but was well ahead of both retail price and average earnings growth. Some would argue that, in the 1990s, there will be lower nominal returns across all the investment categories, and that the gap between bond and equities will be much smaller than in the recent past. Whether pension funds will re-discover their enthusiasm for property is a more thorny question. The well-publicised problems of many property companies, plus the apparent over-supply of office space in the City, might discourage many funds from increasing their exposure to this area. (Some, of course, will see this as the low point of the cycle and therefore the time to buy). But property has recorded only an average annual return of 9 per cent over the 10 years to end 1991; well behind the 11.9 per cent earned on sterling cash. If there is going to be a shift away from equity investment in the 1990s, there was no sign of it in 1991. Caps found that new money invested by pension funds last year was largely placed in the UK and overseas equities sectors. Cash levels fell substantially from the figures at the start of 1991. Overall, Caps figures show that the average fund at the end of 1991 was invested in the following proportions (all per cent): UK equities (58.6); Europe (9.4); US (5.9); overseas bonds (5.5); sterling cash (4.3); UK fixed interest (3.2); Japan (5.3); property (1.9); Pacific (ex Japan) (2.8); index-linked gilts (1.9); other overseas (0.7); other assets (0.5). The 1990s could see a shift in the balance of the equity element of the average pension fund portfolio. As the UK gradually becomes used to the exchange rate mechanism of the European Monetary System, the currency risk in holding continental assets will gradually diminish. If a single currency were instituted then, of course, currency risk would vanish altogether. At least in foreign exchange terms, there would be no reason to differentiate between UK and European assets. A pension fund which kept all its equity assets in the UK would be akin to a Norwich-based fund confining its investments to Norfolk. There may be practical difficulties, however. Many continental markets are less liquid than in the UK. And by comparison with Britain, publicly quoted companies play a relatively small part in other big European economies. So there may be good technical reasons for funds to retain a UK bias. It is also possible to gain some measure of exposure to European economies by investing in one of the UK companies with continental subsidiaries. However, the scope for doing so is limited by the fact that the US has traditionally been the main area for overseas investment by UK companies, partly for cultural reasons and partly because the US has been far more open to acquisitions than Europe. While complete integration of UK and European assets may not occur, it seems likely that pension funds will own may more European equities by the end of the decade. Given that the proportion of UK equities in the average portfolio is currently six times bigger than that in European shares, there is plenty of scope for a shift.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (2): To those that have - The leading managers
DOC.TEXT: LINDSAY Tomlinson, UK investment chief at Barclays de Zoete Wedd Investment Management, is waiting for the giants of the balanced pension funds investment business to crack. His company, an offshoot of Barclays Bank, is the UK leader in index fund management, with portfolios worth nearly Pounds 10bn linked via computer programmes to the All-Share and various other UK and international stock and bond market indices. 'Over the past three or four years the industry has polarised on four or five top managers,' he says. 'It only needs one or two of them to fall over, and you will find that a group of trustees will move towards indexation.' It is a fact that a handful of managers is winning almost all the new business. According to the newsletter Global Money Management, the top mandate winner in 1991 was Phillips & Drew Fund Management, with about Pounds 1.4bn net. Mercury Asset Management, easily the biggest in terms of existing funds under management, pulled in another Pounds 1.2bn. Schroder received Pounds 0.7bn and Gartmore over Pounds 0.5bn, confirming its position as the industry's current rising star. In the past four years, Gartmore has leapt from nowhere to eighth in the FT's annual league table of UK pension funds under management. Mr David Watts, head of pension funds at Gartmore, reports that the new mandate scene is quite busy, despite the greater concentration in the market-place. 'We have not seen the volume of new enquiries going down recently,' he says. This year Gartmore has picked up a new balanced mandate worth Pounds 125m from Northamptonshire County Council. Few managers are fortunate enough to be able to report much activity, however. Most managers in the list are losing clients, and the overall scene is likely to be quiet this year as trustees focus on the security and governance questions arising from the Maxwell pension funds scandal. Still, there is currently a so-called externalisation under way, as the previously internally managed Universities Superannuation Scheme seeks two to four external managers. Several local authorities besides Northants are also revising their arrangements, a round of restructuring that reflects the breakdown of the old relationships between local authorities and stockbrokers that were characteristic of the pre-Big Bang era. How far can the polarisation of pension fund investment around a handful of managers go? Five years ago, the then top four accounted for 41 per cent of the funds managed by the top 20. Now the proportion is 51 per cent. The trend has yet to change. And, while BZWIM may hope that the pacesetters will falter, the beneficiaries might not just be the index fund managers. There is a whole group of management companies which hope to improve their performance and get back into a position where they can start winning significant numbers of mandates again. An example is Prudential Portfolio Managers, which had a poor couple of years for performance in 1989 and 1990 but picked up speed again in 1991 when it claimed a 21.8 per cent return, against the Caps median of 18.6 per cent (excluding property). Others with good performance numbers for 1991 included Baring, Henderson and Lazard, but it takes more than one good year to get back on to the short lists, let alone to start winning new mandates. Another top City name which would like to claw its way back up the table is Robert Fleming. It achieved an above-median performance in 1991 through an emphasis on UK blue chips. Like Henderson, Fleming suffered a few years ago from becoming too big too quickly; but, according to its investment boss, Mr Iain Saunders, a new structure in the investment department is working smoothly. In 1991, he says, 'the emphasis was on increasing the level of discipline in investment management.' Across the industry, fund managers wait eagerly to see if the industry leader, Mercury Asset Management, will falter. It appears to have had an indifferent year for performance in 1991, although only hearsay evidence is available because MAM refuses to disclose its performance - a policy it has stuck to in the past, even when the numbers have generally been good. The number two house, PDFM, also dipped slightly below median performance last year, although it is not unusual for PDFM to underperform in conditions of high average returns and more than make it up in more difficult years. As an industry giant, MAM is under pressure to move ahead of the herd. Moreover MAM cannot hope to deliver the same consistency of performance to all its client funds as can a smaller manager. Still, it has always managed to please most of its clients and disappoint its competitors in the past. Yet little is predictable in the fickle business of pension fund investment management. Look at the varying performances of two Scottish independents, Murray Johnstone in Glasgow losing significant numbers of clients, but Baillie Gifford in Edinburgh powering ahead with a 40 per cent jump in assets under management. As the industry giants get even bigger, there is certainly scope for well-managed and well-marketed smaller houses to find their niches. 'We are seen as an interesting alternative,' says Mr Jimmy West, chief executive of Lazard Investors, part of the City merchant bank. He can offer features such as 'tight dispersion' - that is, all the funds perform closely in line - which the big managers find harder. 'I think a lot of people are now looking for a house with a more individual style,' he says. A lot of other bosses of smaller pension fund management firms hope so, too. But not Mr Tomlinson at BZWIM.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (3): Big players sink in the pool
DOC.TEXT: THOUSANDS of smaller pension schemes which cannot economically justify their own segregated investment portfolios are clients of the life companies and other investment houses which provide pooled investment products. Top performer last year was Lloyds with a rate of return (given full investment discretion) of over 20 per cent. But curiously the big contenders in the field - Scottish Widows, Provident Mutual, Confederation Life and Scottish Amicable - were well below average. The Caps survey suggests that the median return was 17.4 per cent for 1991 (a little below the median of 18.3 per cent for segregated funds), while the WF Corroon performance evaluation service reports an average of 16.2 per cent. On a long-term view, Confederation Life stays top of the 10-year rankings, according to Caps, returning 18.4 per cent a year on average.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Survey of Pension Fund Investment (1): Consensus at risk - Investment performance does not currently cause concern, though there are warning signs in Japan. UK funds must decide how to respond to an increase in gilt issues, and any stumble in the equity market might lead to a change in strategy
DOC.TEXT: MANAGERS OF Britain's near-Pounds 300bn pension funds are still obsessed with the consensus. The handful of top management companies which have played the game of balanced discretionary management to perfection in the past few years have wound up with an unprecedented proportion of the available business. But is the game about to change? The collapse in the Japanese stock market could be a warning sign. With the typical fund holding 5 per cent of its assets in the Tokyo market at the end of last year, the market's tumble has knocked more than a percentage point off portfolios. It is not a loss which in itself will greatly concern pension fund trustees. They have other, bigger, worries on their minds: the implications of the Maxwell scandal, for instance, which will soon lead to new pensions legislation; and the growing pressure for pension funds to act as good corporate citizens, exercising votes and behaving like responsible proprietors. Investment performance is not currently a source of concern. Most schemes have healthy surpluses. The long run of years of strong equity market performance during the 1980s was resumed last year after a hiccup in 1990. Professional investors mostly remain highly optimistic: last month, according to an opinion survey by Godwins, the pensions consultants, 84 per cent of top fund managers thought that UK equities would be high in a year's time. At the end of 1991, the typical British pension fund, according to the Caps measurement service, had 59 per cent of its assets in UK equities and another 24 per cent in overseas equities. The 83 per cent commitment to equities in aggregate is the highest ever in the UK, and is much greater than for pension funds in other countries: the corresponding figure is some 48 per cent in the US and about 25 per cent (though rising) in the most comparable European country with large and mature pension funds, the Netherlands. At the end of the 1970s, British pension funds were much more diversified than they are now, with some 25 per cent of their assets in sterling bonds (almost entirely UK government securities, or gilts) and a significant direct investment in property, too. The main diversification now is that overseas equities have replaced gilts, which in their fixed-interest form account for only 3 per cent of the average fund today. The justification for this strategic shift is that equities have given splendid performance and are the natural form of investment for final salary-linked pension schemes, which are the most common in Britain. In price terms over the past five years, however, UK equities have performed only in fits and starts. The average annual rate of return of 11.7 per cent achieved in UK equities by pension funds has only just exceeded the gilt return of 11.5 per cent. Overseas equities have lagged badly, returning only 4.4 per cent a year. A few fund managers are starting to look again at the strategy, but there is no inclination on their part to begin with a clean sheet. Most managers regard the performance of the median fund as their benchmark, and indeed this is often part of their contract with the trustees. A modest, but increasing, number of schemes have undertaken asset-liability modelling exercises and have established customised benchmarks. For most external managers, however, to diverge very far from the consensus asset allocation would constitute a severe business risk, more important in practice than the investment risk being borne by the client. Consider the view of Mr Hugh Jenkins, chief executive of Prudential Portfolio Managers, with around Pounds 10bn of corporate pension fund assets under his care. 'We are the people who challenge the consensus,' he claims. But what he means is that the Pru, like other managers, will diverge only slightly from the norm; the intention is to add a percentage point or two of performance without greatly exposing the managers to the risk of serious divergence from the median. For example, the Pru recently had something of a bet on UK equities over the election period, raising its exposure to 63-64 per cent instead of the standard 59 per cent. This has paid off for the Pru, continuing its good run which began last year. But it is far from being a radical formula. One of the few mavericks who rejects the whole approach of trying to be slightly ahead of everyone else year by year (or even quarter by quarter) is Mr Bruce Campbell, an Australian who runs a global management boutique in London called Pyrford International. Much of Pyrford's Pounds 800m-plus under management comes from overseas, but it recently picked up a Pounds 40m mandate from Fisons. At present Pyrford's strategy for UK pension fund clients is to hold only 40 per cent in equities (about half in the UK), with 30 per cent each in bonds and cash. It has nothing in either the Japanese or US stock markets. It was the best performing manager of all in 1990, but was a long way down in the bottom quartile last year, underperforming the Caps median by some 7 per cent. Is this a high-risk approach? 'No, it is the other managers' strategy that carries extremely high risks,' Mr Campbell insists. It is true, however, that conventional managers have been diversifying modestly into international bonds, with the average exposure rising from zero to 6 per cent over the past four years. International bond portfolios, in fact, outperformed UK equity portfolios last year. Specialist international bond managers, however, see little interest so far from UK pension funds. Mr Paul Abberley, fixed income director at Lombard Odier in London, hopes that opportunities will come for his company now that the UK is firmly established in the low inflation EMS currency bloc. 'Fixed income instruments may be more appropriate for UK pension funds than in the past,' he argues. But he admits that there are few global bond briefs from UK pension funds. 'It is slow progress at present.' But UK funds inevitably face a decision about how to respond to the huge prospective increase in gilt issues as the British government moves into the forecast budget deficit - of Pounds 28bn this year. As in the 1970s, it looks as though a substantial proportion of future issues will have to be taken up by domestic pension funds. So far, though, life insurance companies and foreign investors appear to be dominating the gilt-edged auctions. The pension fund strategy consensus survives. So far equities, especially UK equities, have done what has been required of them. The stock market revival after the election on April 9 has put a spring back into the step of fund managers. But successive collapses on Wall Street and in Tokyo - and the fear that the US market may again have departed seriously from fair value - must cast doubt on the wisdom of the current extreme strategy. If the UK equity market falters, the consensus may encounter a real challenge.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / London Stock Exchange: Equity Futures and Options Trading
DOC.TEXT: A SERIES of large buying orders early in the session sent stock index futures sharply forward and led the underlying cash market higher, writes Joel Kibazo. Early trading in the June contract on the FT-SE had pointed to a quiet session as it retreated 9 points with dealers digesting the poor overnight performance on Wall Street and the weakness in the gilts market on Tuesday. However, a turnround was staged mid-morning as James Capel, along with several leading US houses, went on a shopping spree. June moved ahead on the orders, but it was a large early afternoon order from international futures trader Cargill, said to have been acting for a US investment fund, that triggered a further squeeze. A firm Wall Street only served to underline the positive mood. June closed at 2,737, up 35 from the previous session and around 24 points above its estimated fair value premium to cash of about 18. Turnover reached 9,006 lots. Volume in the traded options market reached 32,794 contracts, of which the FT-SE 100 option accounted for 8,914 contracts. Amstrad was the busiest stock option, trading 2,831 lots, with the June 30 calls the most traded series.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets (Asia Pacific): Nikkei advances 3.3% on arbitrage buying
DOC.TEXT: Tokyo ARBITRAGE-related buying lifted the Nikkei average by 3.3 per cent, but volume remained subdued after the recent holidays, writes Emiko Terazono in Tokyo. The 225-issue average gained 575.27 to 17,878.66. The index opened at the day's low of 17,325.77, and hit the day's high of 17,929.65 in the afternoon. Volume picked up modestly to 280m shares from Friday's thin 230m. The market was closed on Monday and Tuesday. Trading was dominated by arbitrage-related activity ahead of today's option exercise day. The yen's firmness against the dollar and a higher bond market provided support. Light bargain hunting by foreigners and investment trusts was noted. Advances outscored declines by 893 to 125, with 107 issues unchanged. The Topix index of all first section stocks moved up 26.02 to 1,339.43. In London the ISE/Nikkei 50 index put on 2.11 to 1,086.31. Speculative issues were in the limelight. Teac, the electronics company, was the most active issue of the day, gaining Y10 to Y1,090. Some high-technology exporters have been promoted by brokers as beneficiaries of the US economic recovery. Canon, the precision instruments maker, advanced Y40 to Y1,440. Short-term buying also lifted capital goods manufacturers on reports of an increase in plant construction projects in south-east Asia. Chiyoda added Y40 at Y1,610 and JGC rose Y40 to Y1,970. Biotechnology issues were firm, with Morinaga Milk up Y8 to Y792 and Okamoto climbing Y30 to Y1,240. Toyo Trust & Banking was an exception in a generally firm banking sector, losing Y10 to Y890 on reports that it will cut dividend payments for the last fiscal year ended March due to an increase in bad loans to real estate concerns and non-bank financial companies. In Osaka, the OSE average improved 429.05 to 20,275.69 in volume of 18.8m shares. Roundup PACIFIC RIM markets were generally weaker, with Bangkok registering its steepest loss in a single day since the military coup in February 1991. HONG KONG declined on profit-taking. The Hang Seng index retreated 50.01 to 5,581.20 in turnover of HKDollars 3.8bn. Cheung Kong fell 50 cents to HKDollars 24.20 and Hutchison Whampoa slipped 30 cents to HKDollars 18.10. HSBC Holdings was HKDollars 1.25 firmer at HKDollars 43.50. BANGKOK fell sharply as the political crisis increased. Yesterday anti-government demonstrators surrounded the parliament building and called for the resignation of Prime Minister Suchinda Kraprayoon. The SET index dropped 43.36, or 5.7 per cent, to 717.62 in turnover of Bt3.34bn. Bangkok Land receded Bt14 to Bt140. SEOUL weakened, with most activity coming in small-capitalisation issues. The composite index fell 8.48 to 611.85 in turnover of Won351.8bn. TAIWAN lost ground after the central bank announced that it was tightening money supply. The weighted index relinquished 54.28 to 4,482.25 in TDollars 17.67bn turnover (TDollars 16.8bn). MANILA's composite index slipped 35.78 to 1,209.74 in combined turnover of 240m pesos. AUSTRALIA gave an unenthusiastic response to the one percentage point cut in interest rates. The All Ordinaries index edged forward 3.3 to 1,668.9 in turnover of ADollars 261.18m. NEW ZEALAND's NZSE-40 index put on 2.97 to 1,473.09 in turnover of NZDollars 15m. Telecom gained 3 cents to NZDollars 2.01. BOMBAY fell on fears that a central bank enquiry would lead to tightening of credit for brokers. The BSE index lost 327, or 8.42 per cent, to 3,560.72. KUALA LUMPUR advanced on selective buying of major stocks. The composite index gained 1.44 to 604.46.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets: Risk of corruption worries IFC
DOC.TEXT: WORLD Bank officials are concerned that the lack of legislation and regulation has exposed some emerging stock markets to the risk of scandal and corruption. Mr Peter Tropper, author of the International Finance Corporation's (IFC) emerging markets factbook, said yesterday: 'A stock market does not exist in a vacuum, it has to be part of the economy and has to be effectively regulated.' While declining to name offenders, Mr Tropper said that the IFC, part of the World Bank, was working with them to improve the situation. Looking back on 1991, Mr Tropper noted that the Gulf war had brought many regional funds to a discount to their net asset value. The IFC's 1992 Emerging Stock Markets Factbook is available from 1818, H Street, NW, Washington, DC, 20433 USA, priced at Dollars 60.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets (Europe): Frankfurt rises in confident trading
DOC.TEXT: BOURSES made a broad advance yesterday, writes Our Markets Staff. FRANKFURT regained confidence on expectations of an early end to the public sector strike. Sentiment was also lifted by comments by the Bundesbank president, Mr Helmut Schlesinger, that inflation could fall below four per cent this year. The DAX index gained 10.86 to 1,743.50, its biggest rise in a single day for nearly three weeks. The FAZ index advanced 6.70 to 704.70 while turnover rose to DM6.3bn from DM4.3bn. Volkswagen closed up DM5.50 at DM386 following pleasing first quarter results and the company's positive comments for the rest of the year. There is an analysts' meeting today. Other car stocks were mixed: BMW advanced DM4.50 to DM574 while Porsche fell DM5 to DM530. Deutsche Bank gained DM6.10 to DM712.30 following its announcement after the close on Tuesday of a restructuring of its US operations and plans to issue profit-participating certificates with warrants attached.
