The reopening of Frankfurt airport after Tuesday's closure helped Lufthansa regain DM5.50 or 3.7 per cent to DM152. Among steels, Hoesch shed DM3.50 to DM247 on lower first quarter sales while Kloeckner-Werke put on DM1.40 to DM121.40 on confident expectations for 1992. PARIS came off the day's highs on profit-taking but analysts said the market was likely to move higher as international investors continued to switch funds out of Germany. The CAC-40 touched a year's high of 2,054.50 before closing up 0.22 at 2,047.15. Volume was a heavy FFr3.1bn. The strong rise in Matra and Hachette shares, which were both re-quoted yesterday, surprised the market. Matra jumped FFr15.50 or 9.5 per cent to FFr178.90 on expectations of a favourable merger with Hachette, which added FFr3.20 to FFr150.70. Hopes of lower interest rates lifted the financial sector. UAP added FFr18 or 3.3 per cent to FFr558 while CCF rose FFr10.50 or 5.7 per cent to FFr196.50. Rhone-Poulenc rose FFr18 or 2.9 per cent to FFr646 ahead of next week's first quarter results. MILAN got some comfort from Generali's 1991 results. The Comit index rose 3.57 to 495.75 in turnover estimated at less than Tuesday's L122.4bn. Generali gained L370 to L29,510, while Olivetti rose L75 to L2,910 following favourable press coverage of its Dollars 300m contract to install computers in McDonald's restaurants in the US. The telecommunications sector recovered after its recent drop, with Stet gaining L22 to L1,949. Italcementi, another recent casualty, put on L750 or 5 per cent to L15,590. But the construction sector was harmed by the growing corruption scandal in Milan. Cogefar lost L80 to L3,720 and Grassetto lost L380 to L9,250. ZURICH maintained its rally to close at another 1992 high. The SMI index rose 16.8 to 1,937.3. Industrial companies saw strong foreign buying, with Nestle bearers gaining SFr20 to SFr10,000. Roche certificates advanced another SFr100 to SFr3,710 on Tuesday's good results and the planned issue of ADRs. Brown Boveri bearers put on SFr70 to SFr4,300 on news that Asea Brown Boveri, in which it holds a 50 per cent stake, had won a Dollars 1.25bn contract to build a hydroelectric facility in Iran. AMSTERDAM followed other bourses higher and the CBS Tendency index closed up 0.7 at 130.0 in turnover of Fl 771.1m. Philips disappointed some analysts with its first quarter figures and shed 60 cents to Fl 38.00. Some switching into Polygram was noted: its shares advanced Fl 1.30 to Fl 50.40. Ahold, which lists in Zurich today, was Fl 2.60 stronger at Fl 164.50. STOCKHOLM saw Volvo B free shares rise SKr10 to SKr430 on reports of an early merger with the French auto maker, Renault. The Affarsvarlden General index added 10.6 to 1,004.3, as turnover remained heavy at SKr768m after SKr746m. Ericsson B shares added SKr2 to SKr135 ahead of its first quarter earnings report today. The market expects a pre-tax loss of SKr100m. MADRID's general index gained 0.94 to 250.11. Banks were generaly weaker with Banco Central Hispano losing Pta30 to Pta3,670 after reporting a 8 per cent rise in first quarter net profit. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- FT-SE EUROTRACK 100 - MAY 6 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Hourly changes ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Open 10 am 11 am 12 pm 1 pm 2 pm 3 pm close 1180.81 1180.57 1180.60 1181.18 1180.89 1181.57 1182.24 1182.62 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Day's High 1182.75 Day's Low 1180.30 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- May 5 May 1 Apr 30 Apr 29 Apr 28 1178.23 1175.00 1174.96 1174.59 1169.61 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Base value 1000 (26/10/90). -----------------------------------------------------------------------

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets: New listing rules to put listing ship on even keel - The efforts of private managers to give weight to the Jakarta exchange
DOC.TEXT: First impressions of the Jakarta stock exchange do not inspire confidence. Surly lobby attendants sit on battered chairs, their feet planted on desks, and a hand-written paper sign is taped to the wall outside the office of Bursa Efek Jakarta (BEJ), the private managers who took over the running of the exchange from the government last month. BEJ's adjoining offices are a building site, indicating that some kind of transformation is under way. Indeed, the aim of Mr Hasan Zein Mahmud, the BEJ president, is to inject life and confidence back into the stock market. Jakarta attracted the attention of international investors in 1990 when the official index rose 70 per cent in the first three months to peak at 638.8. It subsequently suffered a severe fall, as a series of accounting scandals tarnished the market's image, and is now trading just below 290. Mr Mahmud faces a big challenge in overhauling the stock exchange. The biggest problem is the lack of liquidity. As one foreign broker comments: 'Try and buy a reasonable stake in some companies and you could double their share price.' Domestic investors, such as the state pension funds, have opted to place money on deposit or invest in property rather than in shares. Deposit rates have peaked at 20 per cent, pushed up by the government's tight monetary policy imposed after bank credit grew by more than 50 per cent in 1990. The central bank has recently eased controls on money supply, but there will be some delay before commercial bank rates fall. Lending rates of 26 per cent, coupled with an economic downturn in export markets, have squeezed company profits and further depressed share values and trading volume. The value of daily transactions last year averaged Rp24.9bn (Dollars 12.4m). This increased to Rp29.6bn in January and Rp39.5bn in February but fell back to Rp25.3bn in March. BEJ has tightened the listing requirements in an effort to improve investor confidence and liquidity. From June 18, the qualifications for a listing are: an operating profit for two consecutive years; minimum assets of Rp20bn; equity capital of at least Rp7.5bn and paid-up capital of more than Rp2bn; at least 200 public shareholders; and a free-float of at least 1m shares. Companies may be struck off if: they record losses for three consecutive years; their shares are not traded for more than six months; they cannot produce scheduled financial reports; or accounting standards are not met. Brokers had estimated that up to 40 companies of the 141 currently listed were liable to be struck off. But last week BEJ said the new requirements would only apply to companies entering the exchange. Brokers now expect fewer than five companies, which have failed to produce annual reports, to be delisted. The tighter listing procedures have been welcomed by brokers, except for the threat to remove loss-making companies. 'The temptation for loss-makers will be to falsify accounts, a problem BEJ should be deterring,' explains a local broker. Mr Mahmud, however, says the main purpose is to provide an early warning system to the investor. Furthermore, the removal of loss-making companies will not be automatic but at BEJ's discretion. Brokers complain that there are too many of them - 189 domestic brokerages and 26 joint ventures - for the size of the stock market. Mr Mahmud reckons 75 to 100 firms would be sufficient, but denies that BEJ will limit numbers: 'I do not like the idea of directly intervening in the market.' BEJ has a paid-up capital of Rp12.3bn, owned equally by 205 stockbroking firms. The venture will be financed by a 0.1 per cent commission on every share transaction, and an annual listing fee for listed companies of 0.1 per cent of the face value of their shares. Under new rules, local stockbroking firms must have a paid-up capital of Rp500m, or Rp5bn if they want to act as underwriters. The requirement is double for joint ventures, in which foreign companies can hold up to 85 per cent. BEJ also intends to streamline clearance and settlement, which currently takes five days or more, but there are no immediate plans to computerise the exchange.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets: South Africa
DOC.TEXT: JOHANNESBURG was lifted by strong demand for blue chips and positive economic and political sentiment. The overall index rose 48 to 3,581 while industrials gained 45 to 4,453. The gold index advanced 22 to 1,073.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: LME plans recycled aluminium contract
DOC.TEXT: THE LONDON Metal Exchange is to launch a contract in secondary (recycled) aluminium alloy in early October. The contract - the first totally new product since the launch of the nickel contract in 1979 - has been the subject of hot debate in both the industry and the exchange for nearly two years. During metals week last October some LME members put the chances of getting the contract off the ground at only 50-50. But the odds shortened considerably earlier this year when a special LME committee recommended its introduction. In a short statement yesterday the LME said trading in three month secondary aluminium will begin on October 6, and trading in cash metal on January 4. The exchange has not confirmed the grades of metal to be traded, but they are likely to be the Japanese ADC12, the German DIN 226 and the US 380. The contract is expected to be in US dollars, cover lots of 20 tonnes and be traded 15 months forward. Secondary aluminium was an obvious choice for the LME as it searches for ways to expand its business. Secondary production is a large industry, with output of about 4.5m tonnes a year, mainly of automotive grade alloy. The motor industry uses more than 70 per cent of production. The secondary industry has been growing at 5 per cent a year, compared with only 1 per cent for the primary industry. Mr Angus MacMillan, of Billiton-Enthoven Metals, said the contract would be good for both the LME and the secondary aluminium market. 'It's another example of how the LME has started to drag itself into the 20th century since the tin crisis.' Mr Robin Bhar, consultant to Carr Kitcat & Aitken, also welcomed the contract. Hedging secondary metal against the primary contract was difficult, he said. In theory the two should move in parallel, but in practice they do not.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: Coffee and cocoa futures prices slide to fresh lows
DOC.TEXT: LONDON ROBUSTA coffee and cocoa prices continued their declines to new lows yesterday, while in New York the July arabica coffee contract had fallen below 60 cents a lb by midday. London's July robusta contract plunged nearly Dollars 40 a tonne to a 22-year low of Dollars 678 a tonne before recovering to Dollars 690, down Dollars 26 on the day. July cocoa closed only Pounds 1 above a new 16 1/2 year low of Pounds 574 a tonne. Producers with abundant supplies of both coffee and cocoa have this year been faced with the stark fact that consumers have high stocks, and see no need to buy. 'Producers have to sell for what they can get,' said Mr Lawrence Eagles, analyst with London futures broker GNI. Stocks of coffee held in importing countries have now reached 90m bags (60 kg each) - probably twice the required level, according to Mr Peter Kettle, analyst with ED & F. Man, the London trade house. Mr Eagles also pointed out that the markets had become increasingly oligopolistic, with few trade houses and few consumers. He cited a recent Unctad report pointing to 'a shrinking number of participants in many commodity markets' with increasing power to influence prices through actions such as holding stocks.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: Jobs to go at London Fox
DOC.TEXT: THE LONDON Futures and Options Exchange (Fox) is to decide by the end of this week on a number of redundancies needed if it is to break even in 1992-93, a memorandum by the exchange's chief executive said, reports Reuter. 'In order to achieve break-even for the exchange, the executive director decided it was necessary to examine every item of projected expenditure and decide whether or not it was vital to the functioning of the exchange,' said the memorandum, sent out yesterday. 'Regrettably. . . it is necessary to eliminate some jobs from the exchange and to combine others,' the memorandum said. An executive group meeting will be held tomorrow, when a final decision will be made on redundancies, which traders suggest could affect 15 to 20 people. The drafting of the 1992-93 budget proved time-consuming and difficult, with previous drafts rejected by the board of directors as it would not agree to London Fox budgeting at a loss, the memorandum said. 'We came to the conclusion the exchange must move from its current structure and operating approach to a maintenance-only basis,' it added. The exchange will in future provide only those services absolutely necessary for the safe operation of its markets, which include coffee, cocoa, sugar and other agricultural products.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Commodities and Agriculture: Spice trade put through the mill - Problems posed by tighter food safety regulations
DOC.TEXT: THE INTERNATIONAL spice trade is being ground down at present by a range of non-tariff barriers imposed by some of the major importers. But producers are hopeful that they will see a recovery in 1993. Reports by the International Trade Centre of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development and the Commonwealth Secretariat, say that the increase in the number and type of non-tariff barriers coincided with the lowering of tariffs under several rounds of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade negotiations and the introduction of special market access for some of the least developed countries. 'The most important non-tariff measures imposed by developed countries usually relate to health and phytosanitary (plant health) regulations,' says a report from the International Trade Center that was presented to a meeting in Jamaica of the International Spice Group, made up of producers and consumers. 'The public concern in these countries about food safety has led to stricter regulations on food items, including spices.' The report says that in the US specifications on cleanliness established by the American Spice Trade Association 'are considered the most stringent among developed countries'. The regulations, which differ from country to country 'are so diverse and standards vary so much that spice exporters in developing countries frequently experience great difficulty in obtaining up to date, comprehensive information about them.' Mr Hernal Hamilton, chairman of the International Spice Group, says that some spice exporting countries have encountered problems because of the cleanliness requirements, but many have overcome these by implementing more rigid inspection systems. The industry is also worried about the effects on the major markets of the banning of fumigants, particularly by European consumers, and a reluctance to accept irradiation to improve cleanliness and remove bacteria. Successfully meeting the US demands for cleanliness is considered by the industry to be crucial to hopes for expanded trade, as that country is the world's largest market. In 1990, US imports, including spice herbs, mustard and sesame seeds, amounted to 238,949 tonnes, valued at Dollars 355m. Although the volume imported by the US in 1990 was 12,277 tonnes more than in 1989, the value was Dollars 19m less. The volume of spices traded internationally in 1990 reached 400,000 tonnes, valued at USDollars 1.5bn, according to the International Spice Group. But producers are unhappy that prices for key products are low, with pepper fetching about Dollars 1,200 a tonne, a third less than six years ago. 'Sixty per cent of global imports are for the food industry, so any projections for higher volumes and better prices must be based on the performance of this industry,' says Mr Fazli Husain, a senior marketing adviser on spices for of Unctad's International Trade Center. Consequently, producers are laying great store by the performance of the food processing industry in the industrialised countries, mainly the US and Europe. An improved market will ease the concerns of those producers who have suffered from recent developments in Europe. Exporters have been affected by the instability of imports into eastern Europe and the CIS, because of a lack of foreign exchange to maintain imports. This has been particularly painful to Jamaica, the leading producer of pimento (allspice), with exports averaging of 2,500 tonnes a year, accounting for 70 per cent of world output. The industry earns the island about Dollars 7m a year. The Jamaican industry suffered a setback with the loss of an important market for pimento in what was the Soviet Union. 'The purchasers in what was the USSR did not buy any pimento last year because of the political upheaval, but we expect this to be a temporary problem,' says Mr Hamilton, who is also managing director of the Jamaica Export Trading Company, which markets the spice. 'They need the pimento for their fish processing industry and we expect this industry to be in touch with us again soon. We have not lost that market and I am optimistic that shipments will resume when the political situation settles down.' Hopes in the trade for significant increase in the consumption of spices in non-traditional industries are unlikely to materialise, according to the International Spice Group. 'The consumption of spices in the non-food sector, in pharmaceuticals and perfumery, is not in general appreciable, and does not have any significant effect on overall demand,' it says. Despite this, consumers and producers are likely to take comfort from indications that the size of the market could be increased significantly by two developments that promise an expansion of the trade. The creation of a single European market at the end of the year will bring changes in import patterns and could lead to increased demand, the ISG says. The second development expected to affect that trade is the Uruguay Round discussions. These will be of benefit, says the International Trade Centre, 'provided the trade liberalisation objectives for tropical products. . . are attained and maintained'. In the background, however, lurks a threat from modern technology. The ISG says that except for vanilla, spices have not so far been threatened by synthetics and substitutes. It says substitutes for pepper have been developed, but have not yet made an impression on the market. 'However, the availability of spices in forms other than the 100 per cent natural spice needs to be monitored. In recent years, spices in other forms, such as encapsulated spices and spice drops, are entering the market, which could influence not only the usage pattern, but also affect the actual amount of spices used, particularly in the industrial sector in the longer term.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Commodities Prices: Market Report
DOC.TEXT: ZINC prices fell at the London Metal Exchange yesterday, although the tightening squeeze on supplies available for nearby delivery was reflected in the further widening of the backwardation (cash premium over forward metal). The cash price fell Dollars 8.50 to Dollars 1,379 a tonne, but with the three months position slipping another Dollars 17.50 to Dollars 1,273 a tonne the backwardation climbed to Dollars 106 a tonne. Traders said that, while zinc chart indicators were bearish, nervousness about the technical tightness might discourage fresh sales for the time being. ALUMINIUM staged an early rise, which traders thought might be linked to May option declarations, but quickly ran into resistance when the three months price moved above Dollars 1,321 a tonne. By the close three months metal was quoted at Dollars 1,317.50 a tonne, up Dollars 5 on the day, and the cash position was up Dollars 5.50 at Dollars 1,291.50 a tonne. TIN prices also rose in early trading. Gains were trimmed by profit-taking but three months metal closed Dollars 37.50 up at Dollars 5,937.50 a tonne and traders said the near-term target of Dollars 6,000 could reached soon. Compiled from Reuters

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Commodities Prices: Wool
DOC.TEXT: Wool prices for wool at recent auctions have been almost static. After dipping very slightly when sales were resumed after Easter the Australian Wool Corporation's market indicator has stabilised at 577 cents a kg. This is said to be around 100 cents below the level needed for woolgrowers to be persuaded to maintain output and forecasts at present indicate a further decline next season. The absence of any clear direction in the market as the selling season draws to its close in June is causing quiet trading throughout. The recession is showing slight signs of lifting in the severely affected sectors.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Capital Markets: Italy absent from international market for last 14 months
DOC.TEXT: FOR A country with a burgeoning public sector borrowing requirement, Italy has been notable by its absence from the international bond market over the past year. The last Eurobond issue by the Republic of Italy was in February 1991, a Ecu2.5bn 20-year issue lead managed by Paribas Capital Markets. The deal marked the culmination of an increasingly ambitious borrowing programme in the Euromarket, which saw Italy's international bond market borrowings rise from Dollars 1bn - Dollars 2bn a year in the mid-1980s - to Dollars 5.4bn in just the first two months of last year. Italy's absence from the international market over the last 14 months is partly due to a deterioration in it's public finances and credit quality. Shortly after the Ecu issue last year, Moody's Investors Service, the US credit rating agency, lowered Italy's top triple-A credit rating. The deterioration of public sector finances continues to worry credit analysts. Yesterday, Standard & Poor's, which does not rate with the co-operation of the authorities, said that the outlook for its AA+ rating of Italy (the same level as Moody's) was now negative. The rating agency said 'the continued delay in reducing large fiscal imbalances and the lack of strong political leadership' meant that Italy's credit quality was likely to diminish over time. Analysts estimate that the 1992 deficit is now likely to top L170,000bn, against a budgeted L128,000bn. Parliamentary elections last month failed to produce a strong government. President Francesco Cossiga resigned two weeks later, reducing the likelihood of strong measures to curb government spending. The decline of Italy's credit rating has made borrowing in the international bond market less attractive. Italy would certainly have to pay a premium over top-rated sovereign borrowers in the international market. Syndicate officials said yesterday that a 10-year Eurodollar deal should be priced to yield around 45 basis points more than US Treasury paper, against a yield spread of perhaps 25 basis points for a borrower such as Austria. Ironically, Italy's reluctance to tap the international bond market may be a positive factor, according to the rating agencies. With only Dollars 22bn foreign currency borrowings, Italy is not reliant on international investors. While foreign investors are nervous about the prospects for Italy, the government has continued to raise funds successfully in the domestic bond market. Last week, for example, the Italian Treasury successfully auctioned L18,000bn of fixed and floating rate bonds.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Bonds: Enthusiastic response to Compagnie Bancaire Dollars 400m issue
DOC.TEXT: THE DOLLAR sector of the international bond market had its first sell-out for some time yesterday when Compagnie Bancaire came to the international bond market with its first big dollar issue. 'It was one of the deals of the year so far,' said a rapturous banker, echoing the sentiment elsewhere. 'People are clamouring for more.' The reason: the Dollars 400m issue, later raised to Dollars 500m due to demand, was priced at a seemingly generous level, given the poor state of the dollar swaps market. The indicated spread over US Treasuries of the 10-year issue, to be priced today, was 75-78 basis points, though the final pricing is expected to be at a 75 basis points spread. That was seen as a fair spread for the AA-rated borrower. However, were the proceeds to be swapped into floating rate dollars at that level, the cost to the borrower would be about 45-50 basis points over the London inter bank offered rate (Libor) - some 20-25 basis points above the level at which Cie Bancaire might normally expect to borrow, according to bankers close to the deal. The Cie Bancaire transaction, its first attempt to generate a following among institutional investors in the international bond market, has been planned for some weeks, perhaps helping to explain its pricing. In spite of the deterioration of the swaps market, the borrower was keen to push ahead with the deal, its main aim being to complete its first substantial transaction successfully. It is not known if the proceeds were swapped, though bankers close to the deal believed they had not been. The generous spread against Libor was said in some quarters to have prompted a degree of asset swapping - that is, banks taking fixed rate paper and selling on floating rate paper to investors. The co-lead managers to the deal are thought to have agreed not to engage in asset swapping, but other banks involved commented that it was impossible to prevent the process if the attractions were significant, as in this case. JP Morgan, which led the Cie Bancaire deal, was also credited yesterday with an Ecu150m issue for Johnson & Johnson which was reported to have sold well. The five-year issue, yielding 9 per cent, was almost guaranteed to find a market among retail investors in Europe given the big-name, AAA-rated borrower, other bankers said. The yield was nine basis points above the level at which Credit Local's five-year benchmark Ecu issue was re-opened yesterday by UBS Phillips & Drew, taking the total size of the issue to Ecu900m. Meanwhile, the World Bank brought its first dollar floating rate issue priced against Libor, with a Dollars 250m 10-year issue organised as a block trade through Salomon. Banco Comercial Portugues (BCP) has launched an Ecu140m convertible bond issue, led by UBS Phillips & Drew, Merrill Lynch International and Companhia de Investimentos e Servicos Financeiros (CISF), the BCP group's investment and financial services company. The bonds are convertible into BCP shares, and offer 8.75 per cent interest and a conversion premium of 16 per cent above BCP shares market price at issue date. The issue is the first convertible issue launched on the international market by a Portuguese financial institution. It forms part of a wider programme aiming to raise Esc50bn (Dollars 357bn) on the international markets and domestically to build up its international position and shareholding base.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Capital Markets: Danish overseas debt set to fall
DOC.TEXT: DENMARK's overseas state debt is expected to fall to DKr77bn at the end of the year from DKr92.3bn at end-1991, provided the current account remains in surplus and private capital movements are at worst in balance, Reuter reports from Copenhagen. The central bank said the share of dollar-denominated debt rose to 19 per cent from 13 per cent in 1990 and that of Ecu debts rose to 20 per cent from 15 per cent.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Unilever sets its sights on satisfying Mrs Jones - The new co-chairman
DOC.TEXT: It is not often that a change at the top of a well-managed multinational as big as Unilever coincides neatly with a shift in the company's direction. But Michael Perry, who this week succeeded Sir Michael Angus as British co-chairman of the Anglo-Dutch consumer products manufacturer, talks like a man who stands on the verge of a new era. 'If you ask what characterised the Angus years, clearly it was the single-minded focus on improving Unilever's profitability by driving out inefficiency and low margin businesses,' Mr Perry says. Boosting the bottom line will remain as important as ever - his aim is to improve on last year's 8.7 per cent operating margin by 'a percentage point or two' during his four-year chairmanship. 'But it will have to happen by different means,' he says. The challenge now is to move forward by seizing the initiative much more aggressively in all Unilever's markets: 'We have got to do better than our competitors and better than we have ever done before at harnessing our global technological resources to individual markets. It's my firm belief that restoring the all-important focus on leading and setting the agenda is what it's all about.' That does not imply any let-up on cost cutting. In Europe, where Unilever is rationalising extensively its food business to prepare for the single market, Mr Perry says the biggest pay-off is still to come: 'You ain't seen nothing yet. There's a hell of a lot more to come in margin improvement.' Unilever is also still ploughing a lot of effort into straightening out US businesses acquired in the 1980s. Profitability at its Cheseborough Ponds subsidiary should be 'exactly where we want it in the next 12 months or so'. The big wave of restructuring, disposals and acquisitions of the 1980s, when Unilever shed many established businesses and expanded into new ones such as perfumes and cosmetics, is unlikely to be repeated. Further acquisitions are likely to be closely related to the company's four 'core businesses' of food, detergents, personal products and speciality chemicals. One imperative dominates the 58-year-old Mr Perry's strategic vision for Unilever. It is sharply to accelerate the company's rate of innovation, showering markets worldwide with new products. The goal is particularly urgent because some of Unilever's biggest traditional businesses - notably edible fats, in which it is the world market leader - have grown mature and face increasingly tough price competition. To restore margins and growth, the company needs to diversify into new products with higher added value. Mr Perry is counting heavily on Unilever's extensive investments in modern information technology to tighten internal communications. But its ability to innovate and respond faster will depend, above all, on the success of radical moves under way to reorganise some of its biggest operations. These have gone furthest in detergents, where Unilever's previous patchwork of national baronies has been replaced by a more unified executive intended to drive the business worldwide. A slightly less sweeping shake-up has been instituted in European foods, while the personal products division is seeking to co-ordinate its operations more closely from an office recently established in Paris. Although Mr Perry is satisfied with results to date, he admits that the company is still experimenting. The trick will be to strike a balance which produces coherent global strategies without endangering Unilever's much-prized entrepreneurship in the field. As Mr Perry puts it: 'Innovation and creativity only happen successfully close to markets - not in Brussels or any other central place.' Above all, it is essential to keep attention riveted on the consumer. 'The moment you focus anywhere else, you are lost. Everything that drives you must be with the sight of Mrs Jones looking you straight in the eye. If you get that right, all the rest will be in place.' If Mr Perry has his way, the Unilever of the 1990s will reach more Mrs Joneses in more countries than ever before, as its reliance on Europe - 60 per cent of its business today - is gradually diminished by faster growth in other parts of the world. He is particularly excited by prospects in South America, south-east Asia, India and China, where he is going in September for 'a first-hand look see'. China, he says, will be the biggest growth market of them all 'if things come together, if there are no more Tiananmen Squares'. Meanwhile, Unilever will keep plugging away at the more mature markets of the US, Europe and Japan. Although it has yet to show a profit in Japan, Mr Perry says the company cannot afford not to be in one of the world's most innovative markets. However, he concedes that Unilever needs to focus its operations there more selectively. His expansionist vision owes much to a 35-year career with Unilever which has included postings in the Netherlands, Thailand, Argentina and Japan. He expects his international experience - far more varied than that of Sir Michael Angus - to be a big advantage in steering Unilever through the challenges of the 1990s. A self-confessed hands-on manager, whose biggest anxiety is not to grow remote from the business, he also relishes getting out and meeting people around the world. 'I've got to be down there talking to people, walking through stores, looking at what my competitors are doing, sniffing around. Not second-guessing management, but just asking them bloody tough questions and making sure they've got sensible answers.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Hafslund Nycomed advances 46%
DOC.TEXT: HAFSLUND Nycomed, the Norwegian company which makes radiology products to improve the clarity of X-rays, yesterday announced a 46 per cent rise in pre-tax profits to NKr367m (Dollars 57.29m) for the first quarter of 1992. Operating profit, after research and development costs, improved by NKr66m to NKr410m. R&D costs rose by NKr27m to NKr168m. Sales rose 10 per cent to NKr1.415bn. Hafslund made a NKr43m loss on securities, bonds and foreign currency trading during the three months, against a NKr111m loss last year. Hafslund reiterated plans to spin-off its shipping operations into a separate company, Actinor Shipping. The group plans to retain a 25 per cent stake and around the middle of the year take a listing for Actinor on the New York Stock Exchange. Among individual business units, Nycomed Imaging made satisfactory progress in all markets in the quarter although operating revenue was up NKr4m to NKr567m. Nycomed Pharma saw steady growth in pharmaceutical sales and improved operating revenue by NKr78m to NKr613m with operating profit NKr25m higher at NKr123m.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Loblaw will push into US if bid for Steinberg fails
DOC.TEXT: IF Loblaw, Canada's biggest food distributor, fails to buy the Steinberg chain in Quebec soon, it will push further into the US, said Mr Galen Weston, chairman of Loblaw's parent company, George Weston. Loblaw is negotiating with Steinberg's owners for all or part of its Montreal operations. It is the third time Loblaw has tried to enter the Quebec grocery market over the past 20 years. It already has a large automated bakery in Montreal. Mr Weston said his group has CDollars 500m (USDollars 420m) or more available for a Canadian or US acquisition. Its north-eastern US bakery operation is succeeding after a restructuring and is expanding its long-term supply contracts. The Weston group has large cash resources but its earnings are being held down by its forest products and fisheries divisions. First-quarter earnings fell nearly 50 per cent to CDollars 6.1m on revenues of CDollars 2.5bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Christiania Bank seeks NKr2.05bn capital increase
DOC.TEXT: CHRISTIANIA Bank yesterday disclosed reduced first-quarter losses but warned it needs NKr2.05bn (Dollars 320m) in fresh state support if it is to meet new capital adequacy regulations. The bank, Norway's second biggest, reported a decline in net loss to NKr86m for the first quarter of 1992 from NKr279m in the same period last year, helped by lower operating costs, lower credit losses and higher earnings. Christiania said it had been given assurances by the state-backed Bank Insurance Fund (BIF) that it will assist the bank in meeting capital adequacy regulations as defined by the Bank for International Settlements. The bank said that at the end of March its core capital had fallen to 1.9 per cent of risk-weighted assets, or NKr1.92bn. But the new rules demand core capital of 4 per cent by the end of the year. Christiania said a fresh state capital injection would bring core capital up to 4 per cent as of end-March. Contributing to Christiania's improved trading performance was a reduction of credit losses to NKr565m from NKr610m and a NKr56m rise in net interest income to NKr780m. Operating costs were cut NKr137m to NKr750m and Christiania said that the reduction was in line with the bank's goal to cut costs by at least 15 per cent, according to demands by its owner, the state, in 1992. Net profits on securities trading were reduced, however, by NKr13m to NKr205m. The bank said that as a consequence of changes in strategy it had reduced its short-term equities portfolio since the end of 1992 by NKr269m to NKr816m. Christiania warned, however, of considerable risk for future losses and pointed specifically to the negative development in the shipping industry in which ship values have fallen considerably along with charter rates since the start of the year. As a result the bank had increased general loan loss provisions by NKr150m to NKr2.66bn, the equivalent to 3.4 per cent of the group underlying loan portfolio.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Sandvik plans expansion in metal-cutting tools
DOC.TEXT: SANDVIK, the Swedish engineering group, is hoping to expand its presence in the SKr50bn (Dollars 8.45bn) world metal-cutting tool market over the next five years through acquisitions of specialist companies and internal product development. The Sandvik Coromant division, which had sales last year of SKr4.88bn, is the world's largest producer of cemented-carbide tools, but has a relatively small presence in high-speed steel tools. Each sector accounts for half the total market, and Mr Clas Ake Hedstrom, Sandvik Coromant president, predicted this week the company would have 'a bigger chunk' of business in high-speed steel, and in small-hole drilling tools, in five years. The company already produces 12,000-13,000 types of tools, of which around 1,500 are replaced each year. But Mr Hedstrom wants to be able to serve the needs of big manufacturing customers that use both types of cutting tool. Mr Hedstrom said there were a number of small cutting tool companies with a specialised product or market which could come up for sale. But he doubted whether Coromant would acquire Valenite, the big US tool company, because the two companies lacked the necessary product and marketing fit. Valenite's owner, the US telecommunications group GTE, said in September it was considering various options including the sale of its electrical products group, which includes precision materials. Mr Hedstrom also wants to increase the proportion of Coromant's sales which derive from fast-growing automation products such as tool changing systems. These currently account for 10 per cent of sales, but also have a beneficial knock-on effect on sales of consumable cutting tools known as 'inserts'. Coromant's sales fell 7 per cent last year, with Germany the last European market to succumb to the downturn. Mr Hedstrom indicated the German outlook was clouded by the current political and industrial uncertainty, but said the US market for consumable cutting-tools had 'passed the bottom'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Chicago insurer falls to Dollars 29.9m
DOC.TEXT: KEMPER, the Chicago insurance and financial services company, suffered a drop in first-quarter net income to Dollars 29.9m, or 61 cents per share, from Dollars 51.5m, or Dollars 1.08 per share, last year. Mr David Mathis, chairman, said a decline in net investment income, particularly from the company's life insurance segment, hurt first-quarter operating earnings, which dropped to Dollars 35.1m from Dollars 49.3m last year. Included in the first-quarter results are after-tax realised investment losses of Dollars 5.2m, or 11 cents per share, compared with after-tax investment gains in the year ago quarter of Dollars 2.2m, or 5 cents per share. The company had after-tax charges of Dollars 2.6m, against potential losses on properties, and Dollars 1.8m to write down below investment grade securities. Kemper life insurance investment portfolios were more conservatively positioned late last year in moves which included reductions in below investment grade securities. Kemper Securities, once the poor sister of the corporation, was its star performer in the first quarter. It reported net income of Dollars 3.6m, or 7 cents per share, up from Dollars 929,000, or 2 cents per share, for the same period last year. Performance in the insurance side was mixed. Life insurance reported a net loss of Dollars 4.7m, against net income last year of Dollars 8.5m; reinsurance's net income declined to Dollars 7.3m from Dollars 10.2m; property-casualty also reported a decline to Dollars 9.8m from Dollars 13m in the first quarter of 1991. The company's asset management operations reported net income of Dollars 20.7m, up marginally from Dollars 19.3m last year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Delta debt rating may be downgraded
DOC.BYLINE: By NIKKI TAIT and ROBERT GIBBENS
DOC.TEXT: MOODY'S, one of the largest US rating agencies, said yesterday it was considering downgrading the debt ratings of Delta Air Lines, one of the three US 'mega-carriers', writes Nikki Tait in New York. Its review was prompted by 'the outlook for continued losses in the intermediate term'. Last year, Delta bought the east coast shuttle and transatlantic routes owned and operated by Pan Am. The benefit from last November's acquisition of Pan Am's European routes 'have fallen short of Moody's expectations, and Delta's domestic business has reflected weak conditions in the US'. Mr Donald Carty, executive vice-president of American Airlines, says a deal to inject CDollars 200m-CDollars 250m into Canadian Airlines International should be finalised within 30 to 45 days, writes Robert Gibbens in Montreal. But American might not necessarily end up with 25 per cent of CAIL's voting equity, he said, and the deal might lead to American forging links with several other airlines. 'Such alliances are primarily concerned with administration and computerised booking systems, where tremendous economies of scale are possible,' Mr Carty said after a service club speech. Under the alliance CAIL and American would also co-ordinate flights and develop strong cross-border connections to improve the Canada-US service. CAIL is insisting on an investment by American, either in equity or other securities.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Hopewell raises HKDollars 2bn for Chinese development
DOC.TEXT: HOPEWELL Holdings, the Hong Kong-based property development and construction company, has raised HKDollars 2bn (USDollars 259m) from a private placement to fund a toll bridge and property developments connected to its 304km super-highway in China. The company issued 400m new shares at HKDollars 5 each, representing 9 per cent of its enlarged share capital. Response was enthusiastic, reflecting demand from international institutions for China 'plays'. Hopewell's shares have been the best performing among the Hang Seng Index constituents this year. Although it had a net cash position of about Dollars HK4bn, it is undertaking several ambitious projects throughout the region, including the Guangzhou-Shenzhen toll road project in China, its HKDollars 25bn Bangkok mass transit system and power stations in China, the Philippines and Malaysia. The latest China property developments are all linked to the company's super-highway. Hopewell plans to develop a 3.12m sq ft site adjacent to the toll road's border crossing with Hong Kong at a cost of HKDollars 300m. A further 7.75m sq ft of retail and commercial space will be developed on 12 intersections of the super-highway, taking up HKDollars 1.15bn of the new capital.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Unocal details disposal plan
DOC.TEXT: UNOCAL, the US oil group, said yesterday that its exploration and production division would sell or place in joint ventures Dollars 350m in assets and cut at least 400 jobs to boost profits, Bloomberg reports. Unocal said it would narrow its exploration focus worldwide, consolidate regional offices and consider the sale of its geothermal and power generating operations. The oil company will incur most of the cost from its restructuring over the next four months. The plan has been designed to boost the division's after-tax cash flow by Dollars 100m annually next year, the company said. The moves are part of a restructuring announced last week. Unocal plans to sell more than Dollars 700m in assets over the next few years, slash its work force and boost after-tax cash flow by Dollars 200m a year. Additional asset sales and job cuts are expected to follow in other divisions. Unocal joins a host of other leading oil companies planning to sell domestic oil and gas assets to concentrate on newer fields abroad.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: DAF unveils key truck ranges
DOC.TEXT: DAF, the loss-making Dutch commercial vehicle maker, is spending Pounds 170m (Dollars 302.6m) to bring into production two new truck ranges, which the company described yesterday as 'crucial' to its future. The new ranges, under development for four years, were unveiled at a dinner to mark the retirement of Mr Aart van der Padt, DAF's chairman. However, the trucks are not due to enter commercial production at DAF's Eindhoven plant until the final quarter of this year. The west European market for such vehicles is 110,000 to 120,000 a year, of which DAF has 8 per cent. Its total truck output last year was 24,000. The new ranges offer the prospect of a production boost for Leyland DAF, the company's UK subsidiary. This is in spite of a decision to concentrate production of all trucks over 17 tonnes in the Netherlands, and production of lighter trucks and vans in the UK - at Leyland DAF's plant in Leyland, Lancashire, and at the former Freight Rover facility near Birmingham. 'This is a very comprehensive and far-reaching range of vehicles. There is every prospect the Leyland plant will need to share some of the (production) load,' said Mr David Gill, Leyland DAF's managing director, sales and marketing. He said common material supply systems developed for DAF's British and Dutch plants over the past two years had given DAF greater flexibility to switch production between the two countries. DAF, in which British Aerospace holds a 16 per cent stake, has been one of Europe's hardest-hit manufacturers, mainly because of its heavy dependence on the UK market, which accounts for nearly 30 per cent of group turnover. Fiat, Italy's largest car maker, is studying the possibility of manufacturing four-wheel-drive vehicles in the former Soviet republic of Kazakhstan, AP-DJ reports. Mr Renato Ruggiero, Fiat's international affairs director and Italy's former foreign trade minister, recently led a Fiat delegation to Kazakhstan to explore the opportunity of developing industrial ties with the republic as part of its strategy to expand in eastern Europe. 'We examined the possibility of developing a plant to assemble the Panda four-wheel-drive and light commercial vehicles,' Mr Ruggiero was reported as saying. He also said Fiat had reached an agreement with Mr Nasultan Nazarbaev, Kazakhstan's president, to conduct a feasibility study for the project. Mr Ruggiero said that the project 'could be expanded to include other sectors: tractors, earth moving equipment, civil infrastructure and treatment of agricultural products.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Travelers set back in first quarter
DOC.TEXT: TRAVELERS, the US composite insurer, has reported first-quarter profits of Dollars 63.1m after tax, down from Dollars 93.1m in the same period last year. The profit figure is struck after realised investment losses of Dollars 1.6m, against a loss of Dollars 2.4m in the first quarter of 1991. Travelers has been badly hit by souring property-related investments, and said a further Dollars 23m was added to reserves to cover potential real estate losses during the first three months of 1992. However, the insurer noted that overall earnings from the property-casualty operations were improved, 'driven by the continued turnaround in personal lines'. Profits from the life and pensions businesses continued to suffer from the real estate difficulties, while lower interest rates reduced net investment income across the board. Travelers said that the property environment had remained much as expected, and the under-performing portfolio increased to Dollars 5.1bn, compared with Dollars 4.9bn at the end of 1991. The real estate valuation reserves at the end of the first quarter were Dollars 856m. Net profits from the property-casualty commercial lines increased to Dollars 51.7m, compared with Dollars 42.5m a year ago, while personal lines turned in Dollars 19.2m, against Dollars 1.9m. Life, health and annuities made a net loss of Dollars 4.1m, against a Dollars 16.7m deficit a year earlier, while managed care/employee benefits produced Dollars 19.3m, against Dollars 30.4m a year ago.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Philips up 29% in first term
DOC.TEXT: PHILIPS, the Dutch electronics company, posted a 29 per cent rise in net profit in the first quarter of 1992, although operating profit showed a much smaller increase because of the continuing malaise in the company's key consumer electronics sector. Net profit climbed to Fl 174m (Dollars 94m) in the first three months of 1992 from Fl 135m a year earlier. The rise was substantially aided by a Fl 65m decline in financing charges, which helped to compensate for the more modest 5 per cent increase in operating profit to Fl 685m from Fl 655m. Sales were up 4 per cent at Fl 12.96bn. Philips' biggest product group, consumer products, saw operating profits plummet to Fl 106m from Fl 298m, as losses in colour televisions and other types of consumer electronics more than outweighed the advances achieved by domestic appliances and PolyGram, the group's 80 per cent-owned London-based music company. Mr Henk Appelo, group finance director, described the operating losses in consumer electronics, at less than Fl 100m, as 'satisfactory', given the fierce, world-wide competition which led to a 5 per cent decline in the price of consumer electronics early in 1992. A year earlier, consumer electronics had posted operating profits of around Fl 100m. Apart from consumer electronics, the company's other three main businesses turned in strong profit improvements. Philips' lighting division - the world's largest manufacturer of light bulbs - posted a 74 per cent rise in operating profits, while professional products and semi-conductors/components improved 85 per cent and 50 per cent respectively. The 'Centurion' cost-cutting programme launched by Mr Jan Timmer, Philips president, in late 1990 is producing results. The workforce of 240,000 was, on average, 27,000 lower than a year earlier, producing savings of Fl 450m. However, half of these savings were eliminated by average wage rises of 5 per cent for the remaining employees. Mr Appelo repeated the group's forecast of 'limited' increases in sales and net profits from normal business activities for the full year 1992.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Unilever steps up European expansion
DOC.BYLINE: By GUY DE JONQUIERES, Consumer Industries Editor
DOC.TEXT: UNILEVER, the Anglo-Dutch consumer products company, plans to increase further its presence in central Europe by making three more acquisitions in Poland and Czechoslovakia this year. If the deals go through on schedule, Unilever expects to expand its annual sales in Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary from about Pounds 200m (Dollars 356m) this year to almost Pounds 700m in less than five years. Without the planned acquisitions, sales in the region would rise to almost Pounds 500m. The deals involve the purchase of a margarine and food manufacturing business in Poland, and of foods, detergents and soap operations in Czechoslovakia. Total investment, including planned spending on plant modernisation, would be almost Dollars 70m. Mr Hans Eggerstedt, Unilever's regional director for continental Europe, said negotiations on all the deals had been completed and were awaiting approval by the Polish and Czech governments. He said the investments would largely complete the company's acquisition drive in Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary, and that any further deals would be small. He said more than three-quarters of Unilever's sales in central Europe were locally produced. Its operations in the region would be profitable in five years if they achieved their growth targets. The acquisitions would make Unilever one of the most active western investors in central Europe. They would come on top of the Dollars 120m which it has invested, or agreed to invest, in central Europe since it began acquiring there last year. Its first acquisition was of an 80 per cent stake in Lever Polska, a Polish detergents producer. In Hungary, Unilever this year bought the ice cream business of the state-owned VMTV dairies. Background, Page 32

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: VW net edges ahead to DM202m
DOC.TEXT: PROFITS growth at Volkswagen, the German motor concern, lagged behind turnover expansion in the first quarter of this year, with domestic earnings showing a sharp drop. VW, which is cutting jobs and reducing costs to improve competitiveness, said group net income in the period was 3.5 per cent higher at DM202m (Dollars 122m). Turnover grew by 11 per cent to DM21bn. Earnings at the parent company, which reflect profitability of VW cars in Germany, dropped 35 per cent to DM103m; last year, these were 33 per cent lower at DM447m. In the first four months, group vehicle deliveries were 5 per cent higher at 1.2m units. Mr Carl Hahn, chief executive, said VW would have a good year in 1992. Mr Dieter Ullsperger, finance director, said VW had made full use of special depreciation allowances carrying tax advantages. These were mainly related to the geographical situation of VW's Wolfsburg headquarters, near the border with the former East Germany, and previously subject to state assistance. He said profits were reduced by nearly DM3bn due to: DM340m in start-up costs of new projects; the DM1.3bn expense of bringing the new Golf and Vento family cars into production; and the special depreciation of DM1bn. Pre-tax profits fell 25 per cent last year to DM1.8bn. Mr Ullsperger said they would have shown a 25 per cent rise, to DM2.8bn, if the group had not raised its depreciation provisions considerably. Earnings per share were flat at DM36, while cash-flow was 25 per cent higher at DM7.1bn. VW's high depreciation also cut its tax bill. Net profits, therefore, showed a 2.6 per cent rise to DM1.1bn. Turnover in 1991 was 12 per cent higher at DM76bn. Group capital spending was 84 per cent higher at DM9.9bn; Mr Hahn said this year's figure would be around DM12bn. Total VW group output - including the up-market Audi subsidiary in Germany, Seat in Spain, and Skoda in Czechoslovakia - would rise from 3.3m to 3.6m units. In the US, where VW makes a loss, competitiveness would be restored by production of the new Golf and Vento models in Mexico. Sales in the first four months were 4 per cent higher in the US, while Audi gained 40 per cent. Audi's net profits last year were 30 per cent higher at DM370m. Mr Ferdinand Piech, head of Audi, will become the new chief executive of the VW group next year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Renault, Volvo closer to merger deal
DOC.BYLINE: By WILLIAM DAWKINS, IAN HAMILTON-FAZEY and ROBERT TAYLOR
DOC.TEXT: RENAULT, the French state-owned carmaker, and Volvo, its Swedish partner, have confirmed they are exploring ways to deepen their successful two-year-old alliance - possibly through a merger. The pair would not comment on Swedish television reports, sourced to Volvo, that a deal - under which a majority French government-owned holding company would control both groups - would be in place before the summer. However, they carefully avoided denials. Mr Raymond Levy, Renault chairman, said in Manchester yesterday: 'We are getting closer and closer to each other. We definitely share a strong will to go on tightening the alliance by any means. A merger is one possible means. I don't say there will be a merger, but I don't say there won't be.' Volvo has repeatedly underlined its eagerness to get closer to Renault, though it said yesterday it would not comment on speculation. Only last week, Mr Pehr Gyllenhammar, Volvo's chairman, hinted strongly at a shareholders' meeting that Volvo would accept a minority stake in a merged car and truck making group. Volvo agreed to take 20 per cent of Renault in February 1990, in exchange for which the French group took a 10 per cent stake in its Swedish partner's parent. They declared then they would act as one company. A full merger would create the world's fourth largest automotive industry grouping after General Motors, Ford and Toyota, and the world's biggest bus and truck maker. Whatever the actual state of talks between the partners, the ground is ready for them to deepen their alliance for several reasons. Politically, the French government has switched from scepticism about the alliance to support, with the recent change of prime minister to Mr Pierre Beregovoy making the difference. Unlike Mrs Edith Cresson, his predecessor, he does not believe in intervening in the decisions of state-owned companies' professional management. The Swedish government has also become less interventionist. It scrapped the obligation for foreign mergers to seek official clearance at the beginning of the year, and confirmed yesterday it would not interfere. The French government, which owns 80 per cent of Renault, now looks likely to allow Mr Levy, due to retire on May 22, to hand over to his preferred successor, Mr Louis Schweitzer, managing director and one of the main architects of the alliance with Volvo. A French ministerial meeting is due to name the new Renault chairman on May 27, said Mr Levy, who thought Mr Schweitzer had a 'fair chance'. Renault has the government's consent, under the original accord, to sell only another 5 per cent of its shares to Volvo, giving the Swedish car group a maximum 25 per cent stake. Any more would require an act of parliament, since Renault's statutes are governed by its own individual law, dating back to its 1945 privatisation. Renault, then, will have to ask the government's support before it can stage a merger with Volvo or make any big change to its ownership. According to Renault officials, no decision has yet been taken. Industrially, both sides are ready to go further, in that they are pleased with the alliance, which has permitted greater-than-expected cost savings from joint component purchasing and exchanges of engines and gearboxes. Renault executives, basking in last year's net profits recovery, privately say they would love to be privatised. The partners agree at the same time that their brand identities must be kept separate, otherwise they would both lose market share. Volvo now has its hands free, following its settlement with the Swedish state over the future of Procordia, the Swedish food and pharmaceuticals conglomerate earlier this week.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / International Company News: Salomon warns of extra provisions for bond affair
DOC.TEXT: SALOMON INC, the New York securities house, warned yesterday it expected to make new provisions, on top of the Dollars 200m already set aside, to cover a settlement with the US government of last year's bond trading scandal. The announcement came as it reported a drop in first-quarter net income - from Dollars 273m, or Dollars 2.30 a share, to Dollars 190m, or Dollars 1.51 a share - as repercussions from the scandal continued to drag down its earnings. Salomon reserved Dollars 200m in the third quarter of last year to cover the likely fines, damages and other costs of settling the bond scandal with government regulatory authorities and private parties suing the firm. It said yesterday that although the outcome of its negotiations with the government was uncertain, it believed any agreed resolution would require an additional charge, to be taken after the first quarter. However, it did not expect this charge to 'adversely affect the long-term economic prospects of the company'. Salomon's lawyers have been discussing a settlement with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the government agency investigating the bond scandal, since February. The SEC has faced strong pressure from Congress to impose a large fine on the firm, which has admitted to falsifying bids in Treasury bond auctions. Salomon gave no indication when a settlement might be reached. Uncertainty over the outcome has made many clients wary of giving business to Salomon in sensitive areas such as investment banking and the underwriting of new issues of equity. This was reflected in its first-quarter earnings decline, which contrasted sharply with the record income figures reported by several Wall Street rivals, which have been enjoying a boom in the issuance of new corporate equity and debt. Salomon Brothers, the group's securities arm, reported earnings before tax of Dollars 374m, down 26 per cent from the Dollars 503m reported a year ago. However, the firm said its securities trading and debt underwriting results were 'highly satisfactory'. Phibro Energy, its oil subsidiary, reported a pre-tax loss of Dollars 30m, compared with profits of Dollars 5m a year ago, due to weak demand for crude oil and refined products, narrow refining margins and relatively low price volatility. It also warned it might be unable to recover the Dollars 116m it has invested in Russian oil development and production joint ventures, due to unfavourable Russian taxes and pipeline tariffs, as well as unpaid balances due from various Russian entities. Nevertheless, analysts were pleasantly surprised by the cost-cutting achieved by the new management team at Salomon, headed by chairman Mr Warren Buffett. It has radically overhauled its management systems and pay structures since last autumn. Non-interest expenses in the quarter totalled Dollars 584m, compared with Dollars 696m a year ago, while revenue net of interest expense dropped from Dollars 1.18bn to Dollars 915m. Mr Perrin Long, analyst with First of Michigan, said the cost reduction figures were 'quite positive for the future'. He said any additional provisions for the scandal were 'highly unlikely to significantly impair Salomon's operating ability'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Worcester holders challenge aspect of Bosch bid
DOC.TEXT: A LOBBY of shareholders in Worcester Group, the central heating boiler maker which has agreed to a Pounds 71.8m offer from Robert Bosch, the German conglomerate, has appealed to the Takeover Panel over an aspect of the bid. The full panel will meet next Monday to hear the appeal and a decision could be announced that day. The shareholders, thought to account for about 25 per cent of Worcester's equity, have appointed Cazenove, the stockbrokers, to represent them. They are concerned about the offer Bosch has made to the Worcester management which would give them a continuing equity interest in the business. Worcester's management would be bought out in 1996 at a price up to 384p, or as low as 100p, while other shareholders are being offered 225p in cash or loan notes. The panel executive had approved the arrangement, but the shareholders believe that it breaches the fundamental principle of the Takeover Code that all shareholders should be treated similarly in a bid. Mr Christopher Smith of Cazenove said the shareholders felt that it was a point of principle which they wanted to test. It is a relatively unusual case, as managements rarely have such a large stake as the 38.4 per cent held in Worcester's case. It is also rare for shareholders to appeal to the panel. There is some time pressure as the offer's first closing date is May 21. The bid can go unconditional with acceptances of more than 50 per cent, and Bosch already has commitments to accept from holders of 51.4 per cent of the shares, including the management's portion.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Cresta slides into Pounds 11.3m loss
DOC.TEXT: HEAVY PROVISIONS against potential losses on its property portfolio left Cresta Holdings with a Pounds 16.6m fall for 1991. There is no final dividend. The group has been disposing of its property portfolio and concentrating on its CrestaCare nursing and retirement homes business in the Isle of Man - where it is currently resident - and the UK. That business increased profit by 53 per cent to Pounds 3.5m, which contributed to a group operating profit of Pounds 1.78m (Pounds 5.44m). But exceptional costs of Pounds 12.6m and heavier interest charges resulted in pre-tax losses of Pounds 11.3m, against a profit of Pounds 5.3m. Losses per share were 15.6p (earnings 9.1p). An interim dividend of 0.7p had been paid (last year's total was 2p). Of the costs Pounds 12.1m represented potential losses on property pending disposal. 'These provisions should protect us against further losses, and the future growth prospects for CrestaCare look set to continue,' claimed Mr Brian O'Connor, chairman. Since the year-end the Northampton development was sold for Pounds 6.3m, along with certain other properties. Realised losses have been fully provided for in the 1991 accounts. Mr O'Connor said CrestaCare had reached its target of 1,400 nursing home beds with the opening of eight new homes over the past 12 months. Expansion was being constrained, however, by the recession which was hampering property disposals. Directors plan to move the company's residence to the UK, where most profits are generated, and change the name to CrestaCare. There will also be a capital reconstruction to eliminate the Pounds 13.6m deficit on revenue reserves.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Meggitt bids Pounds 17.3m for Micrelec
DOC.TEXT: MEGGITT, the specialist engineering group, yesterday announced an agreed bid for Micrelec Group, valuing the USM-traded petrol pump controls company at Pounds 17.3m. The offer of 141 new Meggitt shares for every 100 Micrelec values the target's shares at 130p, against last night's close of 122p, up 10p. There is a cash alternative of 62 new shares and Pounds 65 for every 100 Micrelec shares. Meggitt has received irrevocable acceptances from directors holding 35.6 per cent of Micrelec's shares and undertakings from institutional shareholders to accept, subject to no higher offer, representing a further 12.2 per cent. Mr Nigel McCorkell, Meggitt's managing director, said Micrelec's electronics systems for retail petrol distribution would fit with systems developed by Triscan, his company's commercial fuel management subsidiary. Micrelec also had substantial service and maintenance business with the likes of BP and Shell which was growing and profitable. Mr McCorkell said Triscan and Micrelec's retail fuel management businesses would not be merged although some departments, like R&D, would be brought together. The market has known for some time that Micrelec would accept sensible offers and was is believed to have been approached by interested foreign buyers in January. It has suffered in the recession from oil companies cutting back on capital expenditure. Micrelec estimates that in the year to March 1992 it achieved sales of Pounds 16.5m and incurred a pre-tax deficit of Pounds 1.7m. Mr McCorkell said that for the deal to be non-dilutive in 1993, its first full year, Micrelec would have to make pre-tax profits of Pounds 2m, a figure he thought was attainable. Micrelec, which sold its Normand subsidiary in January for Pounds 7m, has cash balances of Pounds 5m. Mr David Willis, one of the two main shareholders, will stay on as managing director. Gearing after the bid is likely to be about 10 per cent, down slightly from the 12-15 per cent position after the Dollars 53m acquisition in March of Endevco, the US maker of pressure sensors and other electronic equipment. The acquisition will bring sales in Meggitt's electronics division to Pounds 60m, still behind its controls and aerospace activities.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Profits warning hits Andrews Sykes
DOC.TEXT: SHARES IN Andrews Sykes fell from 160p to 140p after the plant hire company warned that profits in the year to March 31 would be significantly below the level previously anticipated. In the previous year, the company made pre-tax profits of Pounds 1.32m on turnover of Pounds 62.6m. The board said that although it was disappointed by the fall in hire demand, it intended to recommend a maintained final dividend of 3p when its annual results are announced on May 26. Strong cash flow had reduced group borrowings by Pounds 3.3m to Pounds 14.5m, cutting gearing from 110 to 90 per cent.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Smurfit pleased to see decline limited to 9%
DOC.TEXT: JEFFERSON SMURFIT, the Irish paper, packaging and financial services group, yesterday reported surprisingly good results for the year to January 31 1992. Pre-tax profits fell 9 per cent from IPounds 173m to IPounds 157.5m (Pounds 143.8m), on turnover of IPounds 1.23bn (Pounds 992.6m). Diluted earnings per share declined 6 per cent to 48.7p (52p), only the second time in a decade they have dropped. However, Mr Dermot Smurfit, joint deputy chairman, said: 'We are pleased and proud of these results given the market conditions. Of course, we are not happy with the reduction in earnings, but we have been doing better than everybody else, so we have a right to be pleased.' Mr Smurfit predicted that next year would be a strong one for the paper business. Sales growth last year had mainly been achieved through acquisitions and a 5 per cent rise in the value of the dollar. The group spent IPounds 50m on four acquisitions Operating profits increased in four of the five geographical regions. The one decline was caused by a collapse in prices in the US and Canada. Mr Smurfit said these businesses, which represented 10.5 per cent of turnover, had caused significant heartache. The timely restructuring of JSC/CCA in late 1989 had reduced the group's dependence on US earnings, he added. The price of linerboard in the US had recently fallen from Dollars 410 to Dollars 330 per tonne, said Mr Smurfit. Similarly, the price of newsprint had been in free-fall and had now reached about Dollars 100 a tonne. Recent attempts to push through price increases had failed. A final dividend is not proposed, leaving the 1991-92 total at 2.202p (5.05p); however, there will be a first interim of 4.872p (2.202p) for the current year. Mr Smurfit explained this was being done for tax reasons. Later in the year there will be a 1-for-1 scrip issue. The group had IPounds 919m in cash and no debt, said Mr Smurfit. These funds were not invested in Ireland. He said the group had plenty of investment opportunities, but it was unwilling to pay unrealistic prices for businesses. It was planned to expand in mainland Europe and have 10 per cent of the corrugated cardboard market, said Mr Smurfit. The group presently had about 3 per cent, with little presence in France and none in Germany. The group had written off its Pounds 15m investment in bonds issued by Brent Walker, the leisure group. Mr Smurfit said they may eventually be worth something, but it was better to reduce the uncertainty surrounding them.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Interest turnround pushes Stanhope to Pounds 15.3m loss
DOC.TEXT: STANHOPE PROPERTIES, the London office developer which is one third owned by Olympia & York, the troubled Canadian company, more than halved its pre-tax losses from Pounds 33.8m to Pounds 15.3m in the six months to December 31. However, excluding exceptional items, the losses almost doubled from Pounds 8.77m. The deterioration resulted from an swing from interest receivable of Pounds 6.61m to interest payable of Pounds 7.09m. This followed an increase in borrowings from Pounds 35m to Pounds 165m and the waiver of the interest on outstanding shareholder loans to the Rosehaugh Stanhope Developments joint venture. The share of the losses of associated undertakings shrank from Pounds 14.7m to Pounds 9.43m, partly as a result of this waiver. A charge of Pounds 1.19m resulted from the abortive merger talks with Rosehaugh, its partner on the Broadgate development in the City, which were broken off early this year. 'By common consent the property sector is experiencing the most difficult conditions in living memory,' said the company. 'While there are few, if any, signs of an early improvement, the anticipated further lowering of interest rates coupled with increasing economic activity should, in due course, bring a return of confidence to, and the recovery of, the London office market.' Stanhope said that it was actively pursuing a number of low risk partnership developments in the UK and Europe. It had recently been appointed by British Rail to act as its partner in a 12-acre mixed use scheme at Oxford Station. Turnover grew to Pounds 24.3m (Pounds 19.6m), helped by a rise in the rent roll to Pounds 6.5m (Pounds 4.5m). A subsidiary that specialises in fitting out offices accounts for 70 per cent of turnover. Administration costs were cut to Pounds 4.79m (Pounds 5.83m). Losses per share fell from 20.37p to 9.21p.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: BAT sees encouraging signs at Eagle Star
DOC.TEXT: EAGLE STAR, the insurance subsidiary which has been a drain on profits at BAT Industries, showed some encouraging signs in the first quarter of this year, when the tobacco and financial services group increased its pre-tax profit from Pounds 230m to Pounds 262m. Although Eagle Star's pre-tax loss for the period increased from Pounds 2m to Pounds 40m, the previous year's figure included no losses on domestic mortgages. These were not provided for until the interim stage, when they amounted to Pounds 121m for six months. Between the fourth quarter of last year and the first quarter of this year, mortgage indemnity provisions were reduced from Pounds 44m to Pounds 25m and the average claim per repossessed home fell from Pounds 15,000 to Pounds 11,000. Sir Patrick Sheehy, chairman, said the encouraging signs included an easing in the number of repossessions and anecdotal evidence of more activity at estate agencies. It was, however, too early to say whether the improvement was a genuine trend rather than a quirk. Eagle Star's total underwriting losses showed little deterioration at Pounds 104m from the previous year's Pounds 102m. In the third quarter of last year -normally better for seasonal reasons - they had amounted to Pounds 147m. General insurance, which includes part of Farmers' activities in the US, had staged a recovery from a Pounds 105m loss in the second quarter of last year to a Pounds 40m trading profit in the first quarter of this year. This was down from Pounds 65m in the comparable period when the figures also benefited from a stock market rally, whereas this year the London market had been in pre-election doldrums. Discontinued activities lost Pounds 17m. On premiums, Sir Patrick said that although they had been raised by 30 per cent since last year, revenue was flat because some business had been lost. There was also a lag in the benefits coming through from the increases. In the life business, where Allied Dunbar is the group's largest concern, trading profit improved to Pounds 71m (Pounds 60m) helped by higher premium income and investment returns. At Allied, advances were made in lump sum investment, bonds and personal equity plans, but life assurance and pensions were down. The group benefited from a Pounds 25m reduction in net interest payments thanks to lower rates in the US and the UK, and to higher investment income, particularly in Brazil. The tax charge continued to be high at 44 (43) per cent, aggravated by unrelieved ACT. Sir Patrick said the main route to easing this would be a return to profits at Eagle Star. Growing exports of cigarettes from the Southampton factory were also an alleviating factor.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Tate & Lyle slips to 'satisfactory' Pounds 92m
DOC.TEXT: POOR WEATHER conditions and pressure on cereal sweetener margins were mainly to blame for a slight fall in interim profits at Tate & Lyle, from Pounds 94.7m to Pounds 92m pre-tax. The shares fell 9p to 401p. Mr Neil Shaw, chairman, predicted a 'satisfactory year in the prevailing conditions'. He said the six month period, to March 28, had been a good one in terms of enlarging the group's foundations. Mr Shaw said that the acquisition last year of Bundaberg in Australia gave the group a way into the south-east Asian market, and the company had more than covered its financing costs. In the half-year Tate invested more than Pounds 30m in central Europe which Mr Shaw said was an important market. The group has high hopes for two products - Splenda and Stellar - which are low calorie alternatives to sugar and fat. Splenda is being sold in Canada and is awaiting approval from the US authorities, which Mr Shaw hoped would come this year. A number of competitors had appeared to Stellar and the build-up in production would be slower than earlier hoped. Group sales were almost 10 per cent higher at Pounds 1.63bn and operating profits were up 2.5 per cent to Pounds 115.6m. Associates chipped in Pounds 3.1m (Pounds 1.3m) but higher net interest charges of Pounds 26.7m (Pounds 19.4m) cut the pre-tax figure. The tax rate was lower at 26 per cent (30 per cent) and Mr Paul Lewis, finance director, said he expected that rate to apply for the year. Minority interests took Pounds 10.5m (Pounds 9.6m). Earnings per share were slightly higher at 13.2p (13.1p) on a fully diluted basis. The interim dividend is increased by 8.1 per cent to 4p (3.7p). Trading profits fell in two important divisions, both in the US, with the impact softened by exchange gains. The US sugar division saw a fall from Pounds 23.7m to Pounds 17.6m, caused by poor weather affecting sugar beet which was awaiting processing at Western Sugar. Profits at Western fell 80 per cent, but were somewhat offset by a good result from Domino Sugar, based in the eastern US. Also in the US the cereal sweeteners and starches business saw profits down from Pounds 34.6m to Pounds 29.9m, with margins cut from 11.9 to 9.5 per cent, as cool weather and overcapacity affected volumes. Pre-interest profits from the Canadian sugar business rose 15 per cent to Pounds 4.7m; in the UK sugar profits were up 6.4 per cent to Pounds 25.1m; Bundaberg made Pounds 5.3m before financing costs and sugar profits from elsewhere, such as Europe and Africa, were up 39 per cent at Pounds 8.5m.
