The European starch business increased profits by 14 per cent to Pounds 26.2m. Profits from sugar by-products, such as molasses, rose to Pounds 11.3m (Pounds 9.1m). Commodity trading made Pounds 100,000 (loss Pounds 300,000) and other activities, which includes Splenda, lost Pounds 10m (Pounds 9.7m). COMMENT After five years of double-digit earnings growth Tate can be forgiven a period of consolidation. There is plenty to look forward to in the longer term if the promise of Splenda and Stellar is realised and Tate wins its share of the annual growth in the world sugar market. But meanwhile, this year's profits depend heavily on the weather, and are likely to be a few million pounds one side or the other of last year's Pounds 234.6m. If they were unchanged, the lower tax rate would lift earnings a touch, giving a p/e of about 11.8. The shares are unlikely to do well until there are signs of a return to growth.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: Time Products down to Pounds 7.62m
DOC.TEXT: TIME PRODUCTS, the watch and jewellery distributor, yesterday reported a 19 per cent fall in profits but increased the dividend after deciding to close Remex, its uncompetitive Hong Kong subsidiary. Pre-tax profits in the year to January 31 fell from Pounds 9.37m to Pounds 7.62m on sales down 5 per cent at Pounds 51.1m. Earnings per share dipped from 12.16p to 9.74p but the final dividend is increased to 4.85p, giving a total of 7.5p, up 3 per cent on the year. Mr Marcus Margulies, managing director, justified the increase in the dividend on the grounds that the company had never been too generous in the past, had Pounds 20m of cash and was still covering the payment with earnings. Following the restructuring, including the closure of Remex, Mr Margulies said he was confident about the future. The closure of Remex led to a Pounds 4.9m extraordinary item. 'Against the Swiss and Japanese, it was almost impossible to compete,' Mr Margulies said. 'We would have had to jack up the sales in Hong Kong or reduce costs and we just couldn't have done it.' Last year Remex had sales of Pounds 12.2m but made a trading loss. It only reported an operating profit, of Pounds 78,000, after inclusion of property rental income. Margins in the UK were maintained at 12 per cent. 'Whilst the board is not expecting a rapid resurgence of consumer demand, it remains confident in the future of the company as the economy improves,' said Mr Richard Langdon, chairman. The group ended the year with higher stock and debtor levels, and a lower cash position. Mr Margulies said there had been no deterioration in working capital control; one large debtor had paid a bill three days after the year-end and the company had needed to build stock levels at Apollo, the watch strap manufacturer which was acquired last September.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: TJ Hughes heads for USM
DOC.TEXT: TJ HUGHES, the Liverpool-based discount retailer founded in 1912, aims to lure investors with a homespun philosophy of value for money as it prepares to join the USM next Tuesday. The group - which operates a chain of 11 stores selling a wide range of both branded and generic clothing, household goods and toiletries at low prices - yesterday announced plans to raise Pounds 8m via a placing of 11m shares at 75p. Hughes is expected to be valued at about Pounds 15.2m when the total of 20.2m shares begin trading. Mr Gurth Hoyer Millar, chairman, said the company was stopping off on the USM, en route to its goal of a full listing in 1993. The proceeds of the USM placing would be used to pay off Pounds 3.4m in debt and to reduce the holding of LET, the international property and development division of SPP, the Swedish mutual life company. The flotation was partly prompted by the demands of Swedish law, which restrict the scope of investments held by insurance companies. As a result, LET will receive about Pounds 4m from Hughes in return for preference and ordinary shares, leaving the investment group with a holding of 45 per cent. This stake would be subject to review, and possibly further reduced, at the end of June 1993, Mr Millar said. The management and staff of the company would hold a further 7 to 8 per cent, including options, after the flotation. Profits for the year to January 25 were up 35 per cent at Pounds 1.1m on sales 39 per cent higher at Pounds 28.4m.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / UK Company News: RBS sinks to Pounds 48m after more debt charges - Decision to sell all or part of Charterhouse confirmed
DOC.TEXT: A FURTHER rise in provisions for bad debts hit pre-tax profits at Royal Bank of Scotland in the six months to March 31. The charge increased Pounds 33.8m to Pounds 168.1m and pre-tax profits fell 34 per cent from Pounds 72.4m to Pounds 48m. But the bank said that the figures were a slight improvement compared with the second half of last year, and is maintaining its dividend at 2.8p. Earnings per share fell to 2.9p (6.1p). Profits before provisions and tax rose by 5 per cent from Pounds 206.7m to Pounds 216.1m. Branch banking, the bank's biggest sector in terms of capital employed, saw its contribution drop from Pounds 34.2m to Pounds 7.8m, although profits from corporate and institutional banking rose from Pounds 26.9m to Pounds 36.5m. Mr George Younger, chairman, said the last year had experienced the worst world recession in post-war years. There were no clear signs of an end to recessionary conditions, and the rest of the financial year would be difficult, with bad debt provisions likely to remain high. However, the restructuring, which involved the loss of 1,000 senior posts, had achieved its aim of introducing a new culture to the bank. Costs were being brought under control and lending procedures improved. Mr Younger confirmed the bank's decision to sell all or part of Charterhouse, the merchant bank which achieved a marginal increase in profits from Pounds 11.2m to Pounds 11.3m. Charterhouse would benefit from 'a larger European dimension.' Mr George Mathewson, chief executive, said that owning a merchant bank was not 'synergistic' with a clearing bank and prevented the latter from developing services. He would not comment on progress in selling Charterhouse, beyond saying 'we are moving forward in measured fashion.' The financial services division increased its profits from Pounds 2.4m to Pounds 7.9m. There was good growth from Direct Line, the motor insurance company, and Royal Scottish Assurance. In the US, Citizens Financial Group increased its profit from Pounds 6.5m to Pounds 8.9m despite higher provisions. Royal Bank's total expenses rose 7.9 per cent. Reduced staff numbers helped offset a 7 per cent pay rise. The cost:income ratio rose from 64.9 per cent to 65.6 per cent. Assets rose to Pounds 34.2bn (Pounds 32.2bn). Mr Mathewson said the bank's performance would improve as the economy recovered and reduced bad debts, insurance earnings rose - to account for 20 per cent of pre-tax profit by 1995, and higher fee income and lower costs, particularly in branch banking. See Lex

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / WPP and banks near deal on plan to reduce Dollars 1bn debt
DOC.TEXT: WPP, the London-based inter-national marketing services group, yesterday appeared to be close to an agreement with its 28-bank syndicate on an equity-for-debt swap of some Dollars 200m (Pounds 111.7m), to reduce its Dollars 1bn debt. WPP anticipated that a formal proposal for recapitalisation could be concluded by the end of next week, ready for presentation to WPP's shareholders and perhaps finally in place by mid-June. The co-ordinating committee - JP Morgan, Bankers' Trust, Citibank and Barclays - last week presented options to WPP's 28-bank syndicate, but it is understood that the banks and WPP favour the equity-for-debt swap. Mr Martin Sorrell, chief executive, announced in March his wish to dispose of a US advertising agency, Scali McCabe Sloves, along with market research subsidiaries and the flotation of WPP's minority share in its Asian advertising businesses. He had wanted to raise Dollars 200m from such moves, but no deals have yet been concluded. The difficulty of making disposals for the price Mr Sorrell seeks, especially during economic recession, has exacerbated uncertainty over the group's financial health. Disposals would reduce overall group revenues. Although in March WPP reported pre-tax profits of Pounds 56.1m for 1991 (compared with Pounds 90m), analysts suggested at the time that without the release of Pounds 17.8m of exceptional items to boost 1991's figure, the group would have breached its banking covenants. At the end of 1991, WPP - which owns the Ogilvy & Mather and J Walter Thompson advertising agencies - had net debt of Dollars 334m on its balance sheet and negative shareholders' funds of Dollars 268m. These factors have contributed to some of WPP's banks wishing to reduce their exposure. With the apparent determination of ABN, the Dutch bank, and Fuji, its Japanese counterpart, not to renew an Dollars 85m discounting receivables facility when it runs out in June, WPP is approaching serious cash-flow difficulties. Analysts expect that any recapitalisation will involve three items: conversion of the 213m convertible preference shares to ordinary shares (of which there are 60m); a rights issue to existing shareholders; and the banking syndicate taking equity in WPP for a portion of debt.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Building a new image in the City: The importance of a seminar with a difference
DOC.TEXT: Trafalgar House plans a seminar with a difference for analysts and fund managers next Tuesday. Senior line managers from the construction and engineering division, rarely seen in the City, will take part as it outlines its strategy for the 1990s. Sir Eric Parker, chief executive, says: 'We want people to understand us better, particularly the core businesses of construction and engineering. 'This is the division which we will be focusing on for the future.' Most people following the company know that Trafalgar specialises in building roads and bridges, so an announcement, expected today, that the Trafalgar-led Anglo-Japanese consortium has won a HKDollars 8bn (Pounds 583m) contract to build one of the world's biggest suspension bridges will come as no surprise. 'But did you know that 25 per cent of the new pharmaceuticals plants are being built by us?' asks Sir Eric. 'I bet you didn't know we were building any pharmaceuticals plants. That's part of the problem.' Sir Eric hopes those attending next week's meeting will come away with a better appreciation of the group's construction and engineering businesses which he claims are like no other in the UK. 'These are technology-led businesses' he says. Trafalgar will take analysts through the detailed strategy of each business within its core division. This will range from the construction of the first plant in the world producing artificial blood, to the more mundane business of transport and oil and gas. At the end of the presentation Sir Eric hopes it will be clear that Trafalgar is no longer a sprawling conglomerate, but a property, construction and engineering-based company. By using that description he is acknowledging that in the 1990s conglomerates are no longer in fashion. With more than 80 per cent of the group's half-year Pounds 65.8m operating profit related to construction and engineering, compared with a mere 20 per cent in 1989, Trafalgar has changed direction. This is just as much a result of circumstances as it was of planning. The group accepts it became too dependent on property development and some of its acquisitions, such as the ailing shipbuilder Scott Lithgow, could not be described as great buys. A change of direction, however, does not mean the sale of its non-core businesses. Sir Eric is adamant there are no leisure disposals in the pipeline. 'We are not in negotiations to sell anything, nor have there been any decisions to do so, although we are not committed to it forever.' Trafalgar signalled its intention a year ago to leave the hotels business but only at the right price. It does not believe that time has arrived and does not see it arriving for several years. Its fleet of seven ships is also likely to remain unchanged for the foreseeable future. In spite of the disappointing result from property, Trafalgar wants to keep its property and investment division to take advantage of recovery in the UK. In Sir Eric's opinion disposals are not needed to reclassify Trafalgar as a specialised property, construction and engineering company.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Lex to buy Swan National retail arm
DOC.BYLINE: By KEVIN DONE, Motor Industry Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: LEX SERVICE, a leading UK motor retailer, is to acquire the Swan National motor group, the UK's 11th largest dealership concern, in a deal worth around Pounds 46m. Swan National motor group, the retail motor distribution arm of Swan National, a wholly-owned subsidiary of the TSB banking group, has 23 UK dealerships. The deal will make Lex the second-largest publicly quoted car retail group in the UK with 86 dealerships. The planned acquisition is the latest move in a radical restructuring of UK motor retailing. Late last year Inchcape, the international motor distribution and motor retailing group, took over Tozer Kemsley & Millbourn (TKM) making Inchcape one of the world's biggest independent car distribution and retailing groups. At the same time, the privately-owned AFG motor dealer group, controlled by Mr Octav Botnar, reduced its 160-strong dealer network to 127 and aims to retain more than 100 dealerships with a range of franchises. Lex Service's planned takeover of Swan National motor group follows its expected loss of the exclusive UK importer/distributorship for Volvo in the UK. Lex said the Swan National deal was conditional on the Volvo transaction, worth a net Pounds 77m to Lex, being approved by its shareholders and given clearance by the European Commission competition authorities. Under the deal Lex will acquire the Swan National dealerships for Pounds 26m in cash and repay inter-company loans of about Pounds 20m. Swan National sold about 18,500 new vehicles in the year to the end of September. It holds dealer franchises for Ford (4), Vauxhall (6), Peugeot (3), Mercedes-Benz (3), and Rover (2) as well as single outlets for Fiat, Jaguar, Land Rover, Renault and Volvo. The acquisition of the Swan National operations would raise its share of the UK new car market from 1.7 per cent to 2.6 per cent. The existing Lex Retail group has a turnover of Pounds 594m, 3,600 employees, 57 dealerships and a sales volume of 27,000 new and 17,000 used cars. Swan National has a turnover of Pounds 309m, 1,200 employees, 23 dealerships and a sales volume of 18,500 new cars and 7,400 used cars.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / British Gas told to cut prices: Watchdog's tough line over charges to domestic customers provokes row
DOC.TEXT: BRITISH GAS was told yesterday to cut its prices to 18m domestic customers or face court action, prompting a further row between the company and Ofgas, the industry's watchdog. Sir James McKinnon, Ofgas director-general, demanded average cuts of Pounds 15 a year in household gas bills. If British Gas did not reduce charges, it would break an agreement which came into force last month, he said. British Gas said in March that it would freeze residential prices with a view to cutting them later in the year. The company is bound by a tough formula imposed by Sir James which limits price rises to 5 percentage points below the rate of inflation. Sir James said that, since inflation was forecast to remain at 4 per cent this year, British Gas should cut prices now by up to 2p a therm. 'We are talking here about customers being knowingly overcharged,' he said. British Gas said its decision to freeze prices was taken before the election when the outlook for inflation was unclear. 'These prices are reviewed every month and an adjustment can be made at any time,' the company said. Nevertheless, British Gas said it was disappointed with the way the row had broken, as the company had requested a meeting with Sir James to discuss prices. Sir James said there was no need for a meeting as the need for a price cut was so obvious. 'It looks like they're trying to hold on to their money as long as they possibly can,' Sir James said. 'A price cut of up to 2p a therm was right at the beginning of April and now needs to be introduced urgently.' Mr Ian Powe, chairman of the Gas Consumers' Council, welcomed Sir James' initiative. 'This is a battle that neither side can afford to lose; the outcome will prove whether or not British Gas puts profit before customer commitment,' he said. A cut of 2p a therm would trim Pounds 250m from British Gas's annual pre-tax profit of over Pounds 1bn. The stock market reacted immediately to the profits threat and the company's share price had fallen 8p by mid-morning, but it recovered to close 2 1/2 p down on the day at 262 1/2 . British Gas said it did not want to be boxed in by making an early cut in price, only to have to raise prices again if the inflation rate increased later in the year. The company still wants a meeting with Ofgas to discuss the issue. Some analysts questioned Sir James's calculations on prices, saying they were not consistent with the price formula. Rather than pointing to a required price cut of as much as 2p a therm, the current level of inflation indicated the need for a price cut of just 0.3p a therm, they argued. Clash of wills over power for the people Page 23

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Lex Column: BAT Industries
DOC.TEXT: The 14 per cent jump in BAT's first-quarter pre-tax profits fully justifies the re-rating which its shares have enjoyed this year. The question after yesterday's 25p rise is whether investors ought to switch to one of the composite insurers with which the group now tends to be compared. The faint-hearted will cut and run ahead of a key US Supreme Court ruling on tobacco liability expected this summer. But the scope for BAT to use its relentless tobacco cash flow to increase dividends, combined with Eagle Star's turnaround potential, more than merits a prospective 6 per cent yield.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Lex Column: Royal Bank
DOC.TEXT: Royal Bank of Scotland's interim results ought to be encouraging news for the banking industry as a whole. Bad debt provisions were lower than expected and sharply below the preceding six months. But the trend should not be exaggerated. Royal's provisions tend to be weighted towards the second half of its business year. Those for the six months to March are still 25 per cent ahead of the first half of 1990-91. If that suggests caution about the pace of Royal's recovery, so should its poor underlying profits. Operating income before provisions rose only 4.5 per cent. Admittedly this partly reflects more stringent treatment of non-performing loans, but management appears optimistic in its expectations for overheads and for financial services, which contributed only 16 per cent of first half profits. Last, but not least, is the ominous ring to its warning of a possible claim arising from transactions by a former customer now in liquidation. There are thus grounds for doubt about the real dividend growth which is Royal's traditional attraction. It has plenty of spare capital to pay a higher final this year from reserves if necessary. Indeed, selling Charterhouse would improve ratios further. But the risk might then be that low growth prospects in the UK would set it off on a spree in the US, where Citizens Bank is obviously itching to expand.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Lex Column: Trafalgar House
DOC.TEXT: Stories of Trafalgar wanting out of Cunard and the Ritz are far from fanciful, official denials notwithstanding. Here, it would seem, is a company at the crossroads, anxious to throw off the unfashionable conglomerate tag and focus investor attention on its newly enlarged and probably underrated construction and engineering skills. After years of dabbling in newspapers, luxury cruise ships and North Sea oil, a proper Trafalgar identity may finally be to hand. The actual restructuring process may not be so smooth. The market was clearly disappointed by the vague commitment to sell peripheral assets, which on top of the dividend cut left the shares 8 per cent lower at 147p. No doubt it is hard for Sir Nigel Broackes to contemplate leisure and hotel sales given the prices on offer, but Trafalgar's balance sheet raises the question of whether the company will ultimately have much choice. Gearing by the September year-end is likely to be 60 to 70 per cent and heading higher -in part due to working capital demands for construction and engineering - just when the commercial property side may be needing new investment. Another rights scarcely seems a realistic option.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Lex Column: British Gas
DOC.TEXT: The market was largely unimpressed by yesterday's feisty reminder from Sir James McKinnon that he is not about to let British Gas alone. But the regulator was also threatening that the fundamental differences between the two sides may yet develop from mere niggling into a full-blown monopoly reference. Even by its previous standards, Ofgas's challenge on domestic gas prices was an aggressive and not fully merited swipe. Gas can fairly argue that when it froze prices ahead of the election, it was working on a much more cloudy inflation outlook. But that does not help its case while the two sides are not talking. The threat is not that a price cut would be devastating for Gas's profits. More worrying for investors is that the burden of regulatory changes is starting to slow the company down. This could expose a strategic problem. Gas has been trying to counteract domestic pressure by building an exploration division and a global supply company. These businesses are supposed to account for 60 per cent of profits by the end of the decade, but already the weak oil price augurs badly. If that approach looks like failing, the long-term progression of Gas's dividend will be in doubt. The market might find that prospect rather more unnerving than yesterday's sabre-rattling.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / The Lex Column: Braving the heights
DOC.TEXT: The strength of the UK equity market continues to astonish. Since the election, the FT-SE is up by more than 300 points, or 13 per cent. At the time of the election result, the more bullish broking houses predicted 3,000 by the year end. The market is half way there already. It only needs another 150 points on the index for the return on equities to match that on cash between now and the end of the year. Even now, the ratio of gilt yields to equity yields is only just above two, which puts it at the low end of the historic range. Over the past 12 months, the UK market has risen only half as fast as Wall Street. Now that the UK economic recovery, like that of the US, is tentatively established, can the FT-SE match the Dow by pressing into record territory? Part of the difficulty in answering lies in gauging overseas demand. US buying was reportedly strong yesterday, presumably on the grounds that the combination of interest rate cuts and a right-of-centre government appeals to any US fund manager out to diversify away from a possibly overvalued domestic market. But US investors have proved fickle already this year in such modish sectors as pharmaceuticals. There is also the risk that UK finance directors will be lured by these heady levels into cash calls, which will fall mainly on the UK institutions. Given that the gilt market recovered only modestly yesterday and that the money market still seems sceptical about whether Tuesday's rate cut will hold, it may yet prove that the equity market is more bullish than sober reflection can justify.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Letter: Search for a new job
DOC.BYLINE: From Mr DUNCAN I BROWN and Ms FIONA L BELL
DOC.TEXT: Sir, Michael Dixon (Recruitment, April 29) considered why a recent opinion survey carried out by the Wyatt Company showed a significant increase in the proportion of employees intending to find a new job now in comparison with a similar survey in 1988. However, the conclusion that there is an increase in employees with 'itchy feet', dissatisfied with their current jobs is not the only explanation which can be drawn. Rather, it may be that in a more buoyant job market four years ago, more employees thinking about a move could actually do so and therefore fall out of the statistics. Nowadays, with continuing high employment, many of those wanting a move for positive or negative reasons can only stay put, waiting for a suitable opportunity - filling surveys while they wait. Duncan I Brown, Fiona L Bell, 41 Copthall Gardens, Twickenham TW1 4HH

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Letter: A German example on competition
DOC.TEXT: Sir, Mr Jacques Calvet's personal view (April 30), as well as your report on EC Commission proposals to subsidise training programmes in the automobile industry ('Shake-up urged in EC car and aircraft sectors', April 30), are hardly believable against the background of German experience. Am I really being ideological or a 'competition fundamentalist' if I point out that the German automobile industry has performed pretty well without subsidies and without protection against Japanese competitors? And is it on the basis of their experience and expertise that Mr Bangemann and his staff conclude that the cause of the European industry's inefficiency is simply lack of training? Or is it, rather, that political activism and populism makes them want to spend taxpayers' money? Can they really be sure that the deficiencies of industry and of specific companies do not have their roots elsewhere, and that subsidies will not be a waste of our money? Or will they concentrate subsidies on those companies which, so far, have performed best and can be expected, therefore, to make a good use of our money? Competition forces companies to rely on themselves. It is the only guarantee against the states or the EC wasting money on an industrial policy they are not qualified to handle. We must be aware that the evidence collected by governments and as well as the Commission in support of such policies regularly comes from those who have had no success and want to extricate themselves from inefficiency at the expense of others. Ernst Steindorff, Hofbrunnstrasse 25, 8000 Munchen 71, Germany

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Letter: Prosecution not measure of success
DOC.TEXT: Sir, I welcome Nigel Wilkins' support (Letters, April 29) for the introduction of penalties for the late filing of company accounts. However, he incorrectly equates Companies House compliance effort with the number of directors prosecuted. We aim to secure compliance with the filing requirements of the Companies Act rather than to prosecute. Companies House has an active compliance programme, which includes the issue of letters and explanatory leaflets, regular roadshows and seminars around the UK, national advertising campaigns, and a video. Where these measures fail, we do, of course, prosecute. But a truer measure of our success is the fact that, currently, 8 per cent more companies are filed up-to-date than at the same time last year. This figure is encouraging, but the introduction of late filing penalties should be seen as an indication that Companies House is determined to improve upon this figure even further. In this way, we can offer a better service to the many customers who are entitled to the up-to-date information. Lynne Beal, assistant director (compliance), Companies House, Crown Way, Cardiff CP4 3UZ, Wales

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Arts: Today's Television
DOC.TEXT: The curio of the day promises to be True Stories on C4 (9.30). When Dennis O'Rourke's marriage broke up he went to Bangkok to make a programme about different attitudes to love and sex. In a bar at 3am a pimp introduced him to Aoi: 'Only 500 Baht, do anything you want, no worries'. O'Rourke stayed in Bangkok for nine months, recorded Aoi's life and, according to the billing, 'his feelings for her deepened into love'. He filmed the punters and pimps as well as the bar girls and says of his programme that it is 'about prostitution as a metaphor for capitalism'. In the end he offered to buy Aoi a rice farm because Aids had made her life so dangerous, but she says that prostitution is her fate. In the last of its BBC2 series Taking Liberties has yet another appalling story in which tragedy was not only predictable but predicted. Two mentally handicapped patients in Greaves Hall Hospital, Southport, were killed by another patient during one weekend in 1991. It seems the parents of the murderer had expressed disquiet every night for a week before these events occurred and an external report had already called urgently for more staff (8.00).

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Arts: Proms 1992 season announced
DOC.TEXT: Eleven overseas orchestras, seven BBC commissions plus another ten premieres, works by 104 composers of whom 23 are living and 22 (including Handel) are British - the statistics of the 1992 Proms came spilling forth from director John Drummond yesterday. There will be 66 concerts (all at the Albert Hall) in the 58 eight day season. It all starts on July 17 with the Princess of Wales in the audience for a Verdi Requiem and it ends on September 12 with Dame Kiri singing operatic arias - and 'Rule, Britannia ]'. Among the highlights are the visits by the Vienna Philharmonic, under both Abbado and Pierre Boulez, and the St Petersburg Philharmonic also with two conductors, Jansons and Temirkanov; new works by Richard Rodney Bennett and John Tavener; plenty of Rossini, including arrangements from his operas by jazzman Mike Westbrook; and the British premiere of William Walton's suite Christopher Columbus. There will be more early music, slightly less opera this season, although Glyndebourne will bring a semi-staged version of The Queen of Spades. Ticket prices are only marginally higher than last year but the top price for 55 of the concerts remains a reasonable Pounds 15.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Arts: The Bacchae - Opera
DOC.TEXT: John Buller (b. 1927), whose adaptation of Euripides's Bacchae is the latest new opera to be presented by English National Opera, is an extraordinary and peculiarly attractive figure among postwar British composers. He spent much of his working life outside the world of music, as an architectural surveyor, and came to it late, driven by personal need. At least one piece on his short work-list - Proenca (1978), a tautly spun, richly appealing stretch of orchestral song-setting from medieval Provencal poetry - has already achieved international circulation. Buller's broad intellectual interests have fed fertile imaginative inspiration into each one of his artistic conceptions. The Theatre of Memory, the large orchestral work first given at the 1981 Proms, may be seen as the direct ancestor of the new opera in its marriage of ancient Greek theories of memory and Renaissance conventions of drama. Buller's insistence on the original ancient Greek words for his ENO Bacchae -already widely publicised - should be seen not as a dotty elitist quirk, but as consistent with an intense artistic response to the 'feel' of language (as shown in Proenca), and with an out-of-time approach to composition. It is no surprise to learn, from an interview in the programme, that previously he had had no desire to write an opera at all, and that the subject of his Bacchae was chosen as a sort of 'just response' to Henze's Bassarids - a very different Euripides opera - as also mounted (in 1978) by ENO. For this, as shown at Tuesday's opening performance, is by no means a straightforward new Bacchae opera to add to the 20th-century list. (Last year Andrew Porter reported on the Stockholm premiere of Daniel Bortz's Backanterna, produced by Ingmar Bergman, and in 1990 Andrew Clark described the 1990 Bielefeld revival of Egon Wellesz's 1931 Bakchantinnen.) My gut reaction, indeed, is that it is not really an opera at all but, rather, a type of enacted Bacchae frieze, expertly arrayed, which may well come to be more fittingly displayed in concert-hall circumstances. It's hard to imagine a more confidently composed frieze. Buller, whose only imposition on the play has been to condense it into an unbroken 100-minute structure, avoids entirely the faults of inexperience - overscoring, over-extension of material, uncertainties of pacing and word-setting - that usually stamp first stage-works. The beguiling sound-world of this Bacchae is its most memorable achievement: Lutoslawski-like in absolute cleanliness of line, beautifully spaced and contrasted for both voices and instruments, never clotted or uncertain of purpose or contour. The work is planned in the form of 17 linked scenes, and marked out in 'realms' of distinct atmospheric texture - by, for example, Dionysus's liquidly trickling celesta and woodwind, Pentheus's fractious brass consort, or the frequent unisons and snapping intervallic leaps of the female chorus. The main characters have their particular vocal styles; Dionysus and Pentheus are both high tenors differently treated (Dionysus, in addition, is the only character to use English, when speaking as a god rather than to the other personages on stage). Exotic, rather Roussel-like streams of modal harmony, motivic influences from ancient Greek scales and a fastidious richness of colouristic detail all aid in supplying the score with its highly individual patina. The treatment of the play is coolly sophisticated, with absolutely none of the Expressionist gesture-thrusting and Grand Opera noise-making that other 20th-century composers have thought fit for Greek subjects. What to my mind this Bacchae lacks is any of the unrepeatable combustion of dramatic subject and music that is the root characteristic of many different kinds of opera. The effect of listening to an opera in a dead language is, as we know from Stravinsky's 'opera-oratorio' Oedipus rex, to repose fullest concentration upon the dramatic workings of the music. (The libretto promises more interventions from a narrator than on Tuesday we were given.) In this case, I felt that the result was to heighten awareness of an oversimplification of the dramatic subject. With its long scenes built upon immobile pedal points and its characterisation devoid of psychological perspective, this seems to me a static Bacchae, whose presentation in a theatre adds nothing 'kinetic' to my understanding of it, or of the Euripides play. By this I mean disrespect neither to the fine, confident musical realisation under Martin Andre nor to the grippingly intelligent, economical ENO staging by Julia Hollander in Hildegard Bechtler's rough-hewn angled-box set and Nicky Gillibrand's bold costumes. The producer has devised a sinuous, startlingly effective kind of sculptural body-language, derived from Indian dance, which Dionysus and the Bacchantes employ to contrast with the bans. This inspires Thomas Randle (Dionysus) to give a sensational performance, glamorously embodied and lustrously sung, that is alone worth the ticket price. Sarah Walker, whose mezzo Agave enters the scene only at the seven-eighth point, sings with moving eloquence; the less obviously grateful roles taken by respectively Graeme Matheson-Bruce, Gregory Yurisich and Richard Van Allan with notable authority, and the singing of the nine-strong female ensemble is thrilling. London Coliseum (071-836-3161): in repertory until May 28

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / People: Bringing intelligence to bear on buildings
DOC.TEXT: Doug Oughton, a director of Oscar Faber Consulting Engineers, is the first chairman of the European Intelligent Building Group, which spreads the message across the continent about the merits of what is termed 'intelligence' in building design and construction. The EIBG grew out of the Intelligent Building Group, a co-operative that claims to have gained considerable momentum in recent years. It counts among its members consultant engineers such as Oscar Faber, architects including DEGW, Lloyd's of London as a 'user', a selection of suppliers to the building trade and a coterie of academics. The first European members in the expanded operation include Legrand, the French electrical supplies manufacturer. Oughton, who is well known in the industry and a long-serving fellow of the Chartered Institute of Building Services Engineers, specialises in energy conservation at Oscar Faber. He will be chairman of EIBG for a year. While no-one can quite agree on a definition of exactly what constitutes the intelligent building, Oughton stresses that it is more than state-of-the-art technology. 'It is rather a case of looking at everything that improves the productivity of the workplace.' The Lloyd's representative cites for instance the dividends paid by flexibility - as when Lloyd's immediately offered a workable home to the Baltic Exchange after the latter's City premises were destroyed by the recent IRA bomb. DEGW has just completed a 1,100 page study devoted to intelligent buildings in Europe. While this started off as an IBG idea the group did not then have the resources to effect it itself. Now it would, says Oughton, who says such studies are an important way of influencing consultants.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / People: Wakeling's move: 'routine tidying-up'
DOC.TEXT: Richard Wakeling, chief executive of Johnson Matthey, is stepping down from the board of Charter Consolidated, JM's biggest shareholder. The move led to renewed speculation that Charter might be close to deciding what to do with its 38.5 per cent stake in JM which is worth more than half Charter's stock market capitalisation. However, Charles Parker, who is the remaining Charter man on the JM board, describes the move as a 'routine tidying up operation'. Wakeling, 45, had been Charter's acting chief executive before moving across to JM as part of a major management shake-up of Charter's most important affiliate. Parker says Charter is happy with JM's performance and described the relationship between the two companies as 'really stable'. He says there are no plans to nominate additional Charter directors to the JM board and notes Wakeling's appointment as a non-executive director of Costain. Nevertheless, Wakeling's departure is a further sign of the growing independence of the two groups. David Davies, JM's chairman, used to be deputy chairman of Charter but no longer sits on the Charter board. Charter has net cash of Pounds 130m and if it chose to sell its JM stake, which provides around a third of its profits, it could have close to Pounds 400m to spend on an acquisition.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / People: Non-executive directors
DOC.TEXT: Alex Hammond-Chambers, former chairman of Ivory & Sime, at CONTRA-CYCLICAL INVESTMENT TRUST. ***** Sir John Garlick and Michael Heap have retired from ABBEY NATIONAL. ***** John Anderson, who has just retired as deputy head of the Bank of England's banking supervision division, at The NIKKO BANK (UK). ***** John Hudson, group chief executive of Wagon Industral Holdings, at TEMPLE BAR INVESTMENT TRUST. ***** Sir Tom McDonald and Richard Boddy are resigning from SCOTTISH HERITABLE TRUST. ***** Christopher Honnor, who retired last year as director of Kleinwort Benson Securities, as chairman of DILLON, READ SECURITIES. ***** Sir William Barlow (below), who retired as chairman of BICC last year, as chairman of BARKING POWER, one of whose five shareholders is BICC. ***** Jaime Carvajal y Urquijo (above), chairman and chief executive of Kleinwort Benson Iberfomento and chairman of Ford Espana, at KLEINWORT BENSON GROUP. DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Management (Marketing and Advertising): Desert island discs
DOC.TEXT: Britain's commercial television viewers may be surprised to see a 30-second advertisement promoting the services of Andersen Consulting sandwiched between promotions for instant coffee and cars. In the advertisement, a man stranded on a desert island finds a wooden crate containing a desktop computer. The castaway ingeniously constructs a raft from the crate and paddles off towards the horizon - using the computer keyboard as an oar. The message - echoed in newsprint and poster adverts featuring the slogan 'metamorphosis in a world of change' - is that Andersen Consulting can help its clients profit from change. The campaign is evidence of increasing competition among management consultants, particularly in technology, which is attracting not just the big management consultants, but also computer hardware and systems companies. Although similar marketing campaigns by service companies are familiar in the US, they are only just catching on in Europe. However, most of Andersen's competitors are dubious about the value of television advertising, which they argue can be useful to promote knowledge of a firm's name, but is ineffective in generating new business. Keith Burgess, Andersen's UK managing partner, says the Pounds 1m-plus mass-media campaign is aimed at raising general awareness of Andersen Consulting. 'We want people to know we are not just another (consultancy) arm of an accounting firm,' he says. Because the firm's consultancy work in the public and private sectors directly affects thousands of workers, Burgess also hopes the campaign will convey 'our personality' to a wide audience. One of Andersen's press advertisement juxtaposes the artist Jackson Pollock's style of 'abstract expressionism' with the 'realism' of Roy Lichtenstein in order to show how the complex abstract can be transformed into the tangible. Burgess is delighted with the 'metamorphosis theme' which he says 'gets across what we are trying to do with our clients'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Management (Marketing and Advertising): Turning to television for the power and the glory - How a Scottish electricity group is planning to broadcast its message to shareholders
DOC.TEXT: Ian Preston, chief executive of the recently-privatised Scottish Power, is built with the solidity of one of his power stations. He does not look the sort of man who throws money around lightly. 'Prudent is the word,' he says. Yet the practical Preston has recently been spending time in the media village of London's Soho discussing new ways of getting his message across. In July, Scottish Power will become the first user of The Business Channel, which will use BBC television transmitters in the early hours of the morning to broadcast corporate meetings. A half-hour edited version of Scottish Power's 1992 annual general meeting on July 29 will be broadcast at 5.30 the next morning. And although the programme may catch a few early risers, the main hope is that people will record it and watch it later. Scottish Power's agm is not going to make much of a splash in the ratings but Preston hopes it might help to solve a rather tricky problem - how to communicate with his 900,000 shareholders. The company - the first big privatisation in Scotland - has shareholders all over the UK. Although some of the original shareholders are likely to sell, Preston believes his permanent roster is likely to be around 750,000. Preston is afraid that many of the company's letters or brochures 'arrive with the junk mail and many get the same kind of treatment'. He was initially sceptical about The Business Channel, run as a joint venture between a new company, BMH Communications, and BBC Select, the subscription television arm of the Corporation. BMH was set up by Bryan Hall, the film producer who believes that eventually it could be broadcasting up to 250 hours a year on both BBC 1 and BBC 2 between 2am and 6am. 'I think we have all warmed to the idea as we began to think what the pluses are in communicating with both shareholders and staff,' said Preston. The half-hour programme will cost Scottish Power Pounds 30,000, not including production costs, but for that they will be able to show an eight-minute corporate video as well as the highlights of the meeting all over the UK, albeit it an unearthly hour. Preston is determined that the programme will be 'a fair representation of what takes place. Otherwise there is no point in it'. If there is a riot at the agm in Glasgow that will be shown too. The programme will be listed in both the Radio Times and TV Times but Scottish Power will also publicise its experiment in corporate communications to try to make sure as many shareholders set their video recorders as possible. BMH says it is talking to a number of large companies about using the new channel. Under the agreement with the BBC, it is possible to broadcast any valid public meeting whether annual or extraordinary or part of a campaign to fight-off a predator. Straight advertising of products is not allowed but a meeting to launch a new range of products or fashions to buyers could be broadcast on The Business Channel using BBC transmitters. Preston views his move into national television very much as an experiment and will be watching carefully to see what kind of audience and reaction he gets to Scottish Power: The AGM. Before he hands out another Pounds 30,000, the Scottish Power chief executive will want to be sure the message was spread a bit more widely than at his first agm last year when the company catered for an audience of 6,000 and actually got 600.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Business Law: Tangled skein of tax adjustments
DOC.TEXT: The differing legal systems and currency fluctuations of nations create burdens on cross-border investment and commerce. These discrepancies often cause the greatest inefficiencies when they involve the taxation of international business transactions. Most developed countries have long recognised the seriousness of tax inefficiencies and have adopted a network of bilateral tax treaties, based on models developed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, which are intended to reduce the potential for double taxation of income from cross-border transactions. The US has been a leader in this effort but, over the past several years, has pursued a course that, if not properly contained, has the potential fundamentally to undermine these arrangements. The US Internal Revenue Service has become increasingly concerned that many foreign-owned US companies are systematically under-allocating the portion of their worldwide income that should properly be attributable to sales and other activities in the US. The source of this IRS concern is data gathered in the late 1980s which tend to establish that foreign-controlled US corporations earn a substantially lower rate of return in the US than do US-controlled companies. IRS data indicate that while US-controlled corporations had a ratio of taxable income to assets ranging from 1.6 per cent to 1.9 per cent during the period 1983-87, the ratio for foreign-owned US corporations ranged from minus 0.2 per cent to plus 0.8 per cent. There are plausible explanations for statistical discrepancies: the fact that many foreign-owned US companies were acquired within the past decade and thus have relatively high book asset values; that foreign investors may be willing to accept a lower return to gain market share in the US; and so on. But US Treasury and academic economists have not been able to establish to their satisfaction a statistical basis for any alternative explanations to the under-allocation of worldwide income to the US. Responding in part to this data, the IRS has assigned a large part of its audit and legal staff to foreign-owned US company cases. These auditors are often aggressive, and suspicious of the audited taxpayer. This has resulted in cases that are beginning to overload IRS administrative appeals channels and the US Tax Court. The IRS readily admits that dealing with these cases through litigation is inefficient and prefers to resolve them through government-to-government negotiations under the so-called 'competent authority' provisions of various bilateral US tax treaties. The average competent authority case requires two to four years to be resolved. Because resolution requires the voluntary agreement of both governments and the taxpayer, success is unlikely unless the foreign government is willing to refund a portion of any tax payments made to it by the parent multinational as an offset to the US adjustment. The US and Japan, for example, agreed in the late 1980s to competent authority settlements resulting in Japanese refund payments for Toyota, Nissan and Honda that have been reported to total hundreds of millions of dollars for each company. Since that experience, Japan's National Tax Administration has been reluctant to accommodate further US adjustments. It is thus difficult to see how voluntary competent authority proceedings are likely to resolve the flood of IRS-initiated adjustments. It may not be long before other governments decide to follow the IRS example and initiate their own adjustments against US-based multinationals. The revenue stakes are potentially enormous. The techniques developed by the IRS to analyse the activities of foreign-based multinationals can readily be applied by foreign governments to US-based companies. Given that US tax rates are generally lower than those of other leading industrial countries, it is possible that any corporate under-allocation of income to non-resident jurisdiction applies outside as well as inside the US. The problem results in part from the internationally agreed tax rules for related party cross-border transactions, which were largely developed in the 1960s. These rules establish the standard of 'arm's length' dealings between related parties. The quest is to determine what unrelated parties dealing with each other at arm's length would have charged for the relevant goods, services or use of intangibles. Finding persuasive evidence of what such unrelated parties would have charged in similar circumstances is often impossible. Many industries, such as cars, electronics and pharmaceuticals, are dominated by integrated companies where there are few transactions between unrelated parties at the same level of trade. Moreover, multinational related parties enter into specific arrangements that unrelated parties are often unwilling or unable to obtain - such as exclusive supply and purchase arrangements or long-term licences of existing and future technology. Finally, the efficiencies and long-term perspective of many integrated multinational corporations often make their expectations of returns in specific markets at any given time much different from those of an independent company doing business only in a few geographic markets. For these reasons, no third-party transaction prices or formula for determining prices can be identified as correct for any particular multinational. Instead, a broad range of prices is likely to command nearly equal merit, even though the price chosen within that range has a substantial impact on the allocation of income between taxing jurisdictions. In this setting, IRS auditors can identify a set of reasonably correct prices that create a substantial allocation of income to the US during the years under audit. Similarly, in a wide variety of cases, other governments can no doubt identify adjustments that create a substantial income re-allocation to their country. Thus new solutions to income allocation disputes are required. One possible approach has recently been implemented on a trial basis by the IRS. It is a procedure for advance pricing agreements (called APAs) among the IRS, relevant foreign governments and a specific multinational taxpayer. Each agreement would apply for three or more years subject to further renewal. It can cover the pricing of specific transactions involving goods, services or intangibles or can establish a more global allocation of income generally between two or more related entities. The IRS has discussed this procedure with various foreign governments and has found a willingness to entertain negotiations for specific agreements from Australia, Canada, Germany and the UK, among others. The first agreement has recently been completed, involving a US-based manufacturer and its sales affiliate resident in Australia. This APA procedure holds out much hope as a prototype for avoiding the spread of inter-company pricing controversies. It is customised to each taxpayer's circumstances, permitting the creation of specific formulas for pricing and income allocation that meet realistic expectation of the revenue authorities of each country. Because any agreement is achieved in advance of the years in question, the APA procedure resolves a problem with the current system: the fact that governments are reluctant to part with revenues that have already been collected. Moreover, if the procedure is applied to a large enough group of taxpayers, a series of informal guidelines may evolve that can be applied on a broader industry or other basis. Over time, elements of agreed standards might be developed to apply even to taxpayers not choosing to participate in an APA procedure. Any solution to current problems will only work if foreign governments perceive that their interests are served as well. If that perception is developed through negotiation, a source of potentially serious tax barriers to cross-border commerce can be eliminated. The author is the senior partner of the New York based international law firm of Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Edinburgh award takes on business
DOC.TEXT: THE Duke of Edinburgh award scheme, which operates in more than 50 countries, is branching out into the business world and getting a facelift in the process. The London design company Basten Greenhill Andrews (BGA) has designed a new logo and a new element in the award - the Charter for Business - was launched yesterday. It is a response to companies which are increasingly calling for business-oriented skills from young school leavers. The original scheme started in 1956 and so far about 1.25m participants have been awarded badges and certificates. Participants undertake voluntary activities for the completion of which they may win bronze, silver or gold awards - as well as a claim to personal achievement. The scheme is almost entirely funded by business contributions, including membership fees to an exclusive golf club. Last year Pounds 4m all told was raised. Ten companies - Mars, Rover, Glaxo, Kwik-Fit, Bernard Matthews, Halina, Compaq, Littlewoods, Philips and TNT - have joined the new Charter for Business to promote it in the workplace. For the past 18 months Mr Jim Andrews, BGA's managing director, has worked with Mr Robin Wight, chairman of the advertising agency WCRS, Mr Bob Clarke, chairman of the business film production company Visage, and the scheme's small staff to attract business support. The companies have undertaken to recruit 100,000 new young people from business as members of the award scheme over the next five years. They have committed themselves to promoting, supporting and developing the scheme. Mr Andrews hopes that more companies will join. According to Mr Eric Worrell, deputy chairman of the scheme, the companies did not wish to disclose what cash they were putting into the new charter. 'But they have all been very supportive,' he said. The companies had various reasons for joining the scheme. Some were 'genuinely philanthropic' and others worried about their own young employees. All were keen to employ people who could demonstrate personal initiative and tenacity. 'The gold award means giving up two hours a week for two years, and the great thing about it is that it is something young people do in their own time,' Mr Worrell said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Engineers urge better technology teaching
DOC.TEXT: AN 'EIGHT-POINT plan' to promote technology teaching in schools was put forward yesterday by the Engineering Council. The plan calls for a practical technology curriculum, based on the design and manufacture of products and systems. It is written by Professor Alan Smithers and Dr Pamela Robinson of Manchester University's education department. They say technology is poorly taught in schools in spite of its inclusion as a core subject in the national curriculum. It is mainly concerned with generalised problem solving without specific knowledge or practical application. 'Technology lacks an identity in the national curriculum,' they say. 'But Britain is the first country to make technology part of the compulsory curriculum for all pupils aged five to 16 . . . and some false starts are perhaps inevitable.' The report points to the difficulty experienced in devising suitable technology assignments as part of the compulsory tests being introduced for 14-year-olds. Mr Denis Filer, director general of the Engineering Council, told a press conference that the plan had to be implemented if school technology 'is to be given credibility and respect among the community at large and with industry'. Technology in the National Curriculum, A. Smithers & P. Robinson. Engineering Council, 10 Maltravers St, London WC2R 3ER. Free.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Fininvest pulls out of contest for Channel 5
DOC.TEXT: FININVEST Group, controlled by Mr Silvio Berlusconi, the Italian TV entrepreneur, yesterday said it would no longer submit a bid for the Channel 5 television licence, which is scheduled to start broadcasting by early 1995. Its decision leaves The Entertainment Channel, a consortium of TV-am - the UK commercial breakfast broadcaster linked with the Daily Telegraph group - and Time Warner, and Five TV, a company backed by Mr Moses Znaimer, founder of City TV in Toronto, as the declared intended bidders. Bids must be lodged with the Independent Television Commission by July. Most estimates suggest that at least Pounds 200m is needed to launch Channel 5. Some critics suggest Fininvest might not have sufficient resources. Yesterday's decision is believed to be related to the uncertainty in Italian politics.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Line to the Continent
DOC.TEXT: Line to the Continent: track laying started this week at the new international rail terminal which will link London Waterloo and the Channel tunnel

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Local council elections held today
DOC.TEXT: TODAY 3,798 council seats will be contested as about 23m voters are able to give their first political opinion since the general election. There are no contests in London, while all the 53 Scottish districts are being fought. Four of the 37 Welsh districts are being contested. A third of the seats are to be contested in all England's 36 metropolitan areas and 114 of the 296 non-metropolitan districts. The seats were last contested in 1988, which left Labour with 1,286, the Conservatives with 943 and the Liberal Democrats with 303. The opposition parties have a strong showing in town halls. Only one of England's metropolitan districts is Tory-controlled. Labour has 69 per cent of all metropolitan district councillors and the Tories controlling just 18 per cent of seats.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Queen's Speech: Missing agency - Environment
DOC.TEXT: A CONSPICUOUS absentee from the Queen's Speech was any commitment to set up an Environment Agency, as promised in the Tory election manifesto. This is a thought to result from a disagreement between the Department of the Environment and the Ministry of Agriculture over who should be responsible for water pollution controls. Mr Bryan Gould, the shadow environment secretary, said the omission showed 'just how shallow is the Conservative commitment to the green agenda'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Queen's Speech: Freeing the market for milk - Agricultural marketing
DOC.TEXT: THE drawn-out process of bringing to a close the Milk Marketing Board's 60-year-old monopoly right to buy milk appears to be gathering pace. The announcement in the Queen's Speech that legislation would 'be introduced to promote improvements in agricultural marketing' is mainly aimed at the reform of the MMB - a long-term aim of the government. Shortly after the election last month, and only a few days before the government's Easter deadline, the MMB submitted to the Agriculture Ministry its plans to turn itself into a single voluntary co-operative with pooled prices. The ministry said the legislation would be intended to help the MMB's move 'to a new structure better able to protect the interests of producers and consumers in the European single market.' The ministry has not yet made a formal response to the plans, which will also have to be approved by the European Commission. The MMB, which has put up stiff resistance to reforming itself, was debating the reforms for two years. The plans include the spinning off of Dairy Crest, its wholly owned subsidiary with a 25 per cent share of the UK's manufactured dairy products market. Yesterday Mr Bob Steven, MMB chairman, said: 'In changing a structure that has existed for nearly 60 years, future legislation must seek to preserve as many benefits of the current system as possible.' It must give farmers and dairy companies 'a fair opportunity to adapt their businesses to changed circumstances,' he added. Legislation is also being introduced to end government guarantees for the Potato Marketing Board and British Wool Marketing Board intervention schemes. The government has not spent any money on the potato scheme since 1984, but the ministry said yesterday that the wool scheme had cost Pounds 40m last year. However, the wool board said yesterday it was well prepared for the end of the wool scheme, as the government first announced its intention to reform it at the opening of the previous Parliament.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Queen's Speech (Analysis): Push for personal provision - Pensions
DOC.TEXT: THE GOVERNMENT'S legislative programme heralded few surprises on the pensions front. Indeed, it may have been more notable for what it did not say about pensions than what it did. The speech made no reference to pension law reform - an issue that had been rising on the political agenda since the disappearance of more than Pounds 400m from pension funds controlled by the late Mr Robert Maxwell. Instead, it focused exclusively on personal pensions. As foreshadowed in February by the then social security minister, Mr Tony Newton, the government has pledged to maintain the increase in personal pensions which its tax breaks first inspired in 1988. The 2 per cent incentive payment to those opting out of the government's State Earnings Related Pension Scheme, which expires in April 1993, will be replaced by a more modest rebate of 1 per cent on tax payments. Only those over the age of 30 - roughly 40 per cent of the nation's 4.6m personal pension holders - will benefit from the new rebate. The total cost of the new rebate, at Pounds 175m per year, is considerably below the estimated Pounds 685m annual cost of the current pension incentive payment. The rebate will apply to the national insurance payments of individuals between the lower and upper wage bands (currently between Pounds 54 and Pounds 405 a week). At best, this will cut an individual's payments by Pounds 182.52 per year under the current tax structure. The Department of Social Security says the new lower tax incentive is intended to run for 'at least three years', suggesting that no more efforts to tinker with private social security schemes are envisaged. The new 1 per cent incentive payment has angered occupational pension schemes, the members of which will not benefit from it. The National Association of Pension Funds, the trade body representing those schemes, has condemned the policy, saying it unfairly promotes private pensions at the expense of employer-sponsored plans.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Queen's Speech (Analysis): 'My lords and members of the House of Commons . . . - The Queen's Address
DOC.TEXT: I look forward with great pleasure to receiving the state visits of His Majesty the Sultan of Brunei and Her Majesty the Raja Isteri in November and His Excellency the President of the Portuguese Republic and Senhora Soares in 1993. I look forward to my forthcoming visit to the European Parliament and the Council of Europe at Strasbourg, and to my visit to Malta later this month, France and Canada in June and Germany in October. My government attaches the highest importance to national security. It will continue to give full support to the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, and will work with our allies to adapt it to changing risks. It will aim to develop the Western European Union as a means of strengthening the European pillar of the alliance and the defence component of the European Union. The United Kingdom's armed forces are being restructured to reflect these changes. Britain's minimum nuclear deterrent will be maintained. My government will work for a comprehensive and verifiable ban on chemical weapons, to prevent the proliferation of biological weapons and other weapons of mass destruction and to encourage greater international responsibility in conventional arms transfers. It will help the Russian federation in the task of dismantling surplus nuclear weapons. My government will work to strengthen the United Nations. It will require full Iraqi compliance with UN Security Council resolutions. It will work for a peaceful settlement in Yugoslavia. It will support moves to bring lasting peace to the Middle East. It will lay before Parliament the Treaty of Maastricht and introduce a bill to implement it. My government looks forward to welcoming the European Council at our Palace of Holyroodhouse in Edinburgh towards the end of the United Kingdom's presidency of the Community in December. During the presidency, my government will attach particular priority to enlargement of the Community and completion of the single market. It will promote sound finance and budgetary discipline. With our Community partners it will continue to strive for a successful conclusion to the Gatt trade negotiations, and to press for changes in the Common Agricultural Policy. My government will encourage Community agreements with central and eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union and will support democratic reform there. It will maintain the fight against terrorism in the United Kingdom and elsewhere. It will energetically pursue policies to combat the trafficking and misuse of drugs. My government will play an active part in the Commonwealth. It will support efforts to build a democratic society in South Africa. My government will maintain a substantial aid programme to reduce poverty in developing countries. Its objectives will include promoting good government, sensible economic policies and respect for human rights. It will continue to press creditor countries for a further reduction in the official debt of the poorest countries. The United Kingdom will work for a successful outcome to the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development. My government will continue to administer Hong Kong justly and efficiently, in the interests of its people, and to co-operate with China on the basis of the Sino-British Joint Declaration to promote the political and economic development of the territory. Members of the House of Commons, estimates for the public service will be laid before you. My lords and members of the House of Commons, my government will pursue, within the framework of the exchange rate mechanism, firm financial policies designed to achieve price stability and maintain the conditions necessary for sustained growth. It will set policy in the medium term to ensure that the United Kingdom meets the convergence criteria set out in the Maastricht Treaty. It will reduce the share of national income taken by the public sector and balance the budget over the medium term, reducing taxes when it is prudent to do so. It will promote market mechanisms and incentives and improve the working of the economy. To help business, legislation will be introduced to amend the non-domestic rate transitional arrangements. A bill will be introduced to improve further the law on industrial relations. My government will pursue vigorously its programme of privatisation. Legislation will be introduced to return British Coal to the private sector. My government is committed to increasing the role of the railways in meeting the country's transport needs. Legislation will be introduced to enable the private sector to operate rail services. My government will give priority to improving public services through the Citizen's Charter, which will be at the centre of decision-making. Steps will be taken to apply Charter principles throughout the public service. My government will continue to work to raise standards at all levels of education, to promote vocational training for young people and adults and to improve teacher training. A bill will be introduced to extend choice and diversity in education. Action will be taken to combat crime and promote law and order. A bill will be presented to enable applications for asylum in the United Kingdom to be determined quickly and effectively. Legislation will be presented to facilitate the work of the Parliamentary Boundary Commissions. My government will work to enhance the quality of life provided by our nation's cultural and sporting heritage. A bill will be introduced to establish a national lottery to raise money for good causes. My government will continue to improve the quality of the National Health Service and community care and their responsiveness to patients' needs. My government will work both at home and abroad to protect the environment. It will ensure that the environment remains a key issue in all policymaking and will continue to publish annual reports. Measures will be introduced to enhance the rights of local authority tenants in England and Wales and in Scotland, to establish an Urban Regeneration Agency and to enable leaseholders either to acquire the freehold or to extend the lease. My government will continue to improve and modernise the social security system with sustained emphasis on those groups with the greatest need. Legislation will be introduced to maintain an additional rebate for holders of personal pensions age 30 or over. Legislation will be introduced to promote improvements in agricultural marketing. A bill will be presented to promote the Welsh language. For Scotland, legislation will be introduced to amend the laws relating to bankruptcy and early release of prisoners. In Northern Ireland, my government will continue its efforts to eliminate terrorism through resolute enforcement of the law, combined with progressive economic, social and political policies. It will promote the re-establishment of stable institutions of government, within a framework of positive relations with the Republic of Ireland. Other measures will be laid before you. My lords and members of the House of Commons, I pray that the blessing of Almighty God may rest upon your counsels.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Clinton closes in on party nomination
DOC.TEXT: GOVERNOR Bill Clinton of Arkansas notched up his biggest victory margins of the electoral season in three primaries on Tuesday, and is now within sight of a first-ballot nomination to be the Democratic party's presidential candidate. He won 74 per cent of the vote in the District of Columbia, 64 per cent in North Carolina and 63 per cent in Indiana, picking up 144 of the 178 convention delegates allocated on Tuesday. He now has about 1,740 delegates of the 2,145 needed for the nomination, with about 1,100 still to be selected. In DC and North Carolina, Mr Jerry Brown, his only active challenger, failed to pass the 15 per cent vote threshold and won no delegates. He conceded the numbers were running heavily in Mr Clinton's favour but promised to take his cause to the final primaries, including his native California, on June 2. For President George Bush, already mathematically assured of the Republican nomination, the biggest satisfaction was his 71-20 per cent margin of victory in North Carolina over Mr Patrick Buchanan, who put in two weeks of solid campaigning in the state. Mr Ross Perot, the prospective independent candidate who is on no primary ballot, appeared to attract the support of about 25 per cent of those interviewed in Indiana and North Carolina.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Recovery in US uneven
DOC.TEXT: THE US economy is picking up but the recovery is uneven, the Federal Reserve said yesterday, Reuter reports from Washington. The latest Beige Book survey of economic conditions by the Fed's 12 district banks gave a guarded assessment of the economy. The report said manufacturing had picked up in most parts of the country, along with home construction, although the rate of building appeared to have slowed. Many districts had reported gains in retail sales and more optimism among retailers about future sales. Loan demand was beginning to increase, but it remained uneven. Most banks across the country reported an increase in mortgage originations and a slowdown in refinancings. Demand for non-mortgage loans was soft. On inflation, the report said producer and consumer prices were generally stable.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Japan announces big increase in payments surplus
DOC.TEXT: JAPAN'S current account surplus for March more than trebled to Dollars 13.58bn (Pounds 7.6bn), bringing the surplus for the 1991 fiscal year to Dollars 90bn, a 167 per cent increase and a likely source of trade friction with Washington. The leap in the surplus, which was not far below the peak of Dollars 94bn in 1986, included a record surplus of Dollars 113bn in the trade account, and is expected to prompt renewed international demands that Japan stimulate a slowing domestic economy. Balance of payment figures released by the finance ministry also showed the long-term capital account had a surplus of Dollars 40bn for fiscal 1991, a turnaround from a deficit of Dollars 16.8bn in the previous year and the first surplus since 1980. The surplus followed a sharp increase in foreign net purchases of Japanese securities, which rose from Dollars 60bn in 1990 to Dollars 101bn, and a smaller rise in Japanese net purchases of foreign securities, up from Dollars 48.8bn to Dollars 61bn. Bonds were Japanese investors' main target, as net purchases of foreign stocks fell from Dollars 847m to only Dollars 118m, while foreign capital was used to purchase a net Dollars 36.77bn in Japanese stocks, up from Dollars 15.92bn in fiscal 1990. Finance ministry officials said the current account surplus had peaked, and blamed the surge in March surplus on the payment of Japan's Dollars 9bn contribution to the Gulf War effort in the same month last year. But the government fears that the large total for Japan's 1991 fiscal year, which runs to the end of March 1992, will be an easy target for foreign criticism of Japanese trade and fiscal policies. Mr Matthew Berlow, economist at Credit Lyonnais Securities (Japan), said that the large current account surplus, in theory, should have been accompanied by an outflow of capital from Japan, but foreigners' purchases of Japanese securities in recent months had upset the trend. 'In the longer term, these figures must even out. There has been a lot of fears about Japanese pulling money out, but they are still buying foreign securities. We will have to see what happens in April,' Mr Berlow said. Japanese direct investment in 1991 was Dollars 23.6bn, down from Dollars 44.9bn, showing the effects of tougher financial conditions at home and the international recession. Foreign direct investment in Japan, as recorded by the ministry, doubled from a year earlier but was still a mere Dollars 2.2bn. The Japanese deficit in invisible trade, including tourism, fell 14.5 per cent from 1990 to Dollars 19.2bn, following an increase in transfers to Japan of investment income. In the overall balance of payments, the surplus soared from Dollars 961m in 1990 to Dollars 114bn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Hekmatyar halts assault on Kabul
DOC.TEXT: RADICAL Mujahideen leader Gulbuddin Hekmatyar halted his assault on Kabul yesterday so that peace talks could be held with his rivals in the new Mujahideen government. Mr Hekmatyar's five-man delegation demanded, among other things, that President Sigbutulla Mojaddedi's powers to select cabinet ministers be eliminated. He also wants an 8,000-man Uzbek militia backing his chief rival, defence minister Ahmad Shah Massoud, to leave the capital region. Mr Massoud's chief deputy, Mr Abdur Rahaman, said in an interview that the ruling 51-member council would negotiate with Mr Hekmatyar, 'but one-way demands are not reasonable. He should accept the decisions of the council.' Mr Masoud's political leader, Mr Berhanuddin Rabbanni, who will assume the nation's presidency in six weeks, is expected to meet Mr Hekmatyar on the outskirts of Kabul today. The peace talks are expected to lead to Mr Hekmatyar's admission to the interim government in some form. Although Mr Hekmatyar had appeared to isolate himself from nearly all major Mujahideen leaders by continuing to fight despite Kabul's fall two weeks ago, it has become clear that his rivals are not ready to sever ties with him. This means that a member of Mr Hekmatyar's organisation, Hezb-i-Islami, will probably assume the post of prime minister. Mr Hekmatyar has nominated one of his northern commanders, Ustad Fareed, to take the position, and he seems to have been accepted by most of the rebel factions participating in the government. Analysts believe Mr Massoud is reconciled to his bitter enemy joining the government, but that he would like to delay the move as long as possible. 'Masoud doesn't want to annihilate Hekmatyar. Basically his strategy is to weaken him sufficiently, then let him join the government,' said an Asian diplomat. Mr Hekmatyar, 39, is believed to have huge stockpiles of weapons from his 14 years as the chief recipient of Dollars 9bn (Pounds 5bn) in US aid to the Mujahideen. A gifted organiser and orator with fierce determination, Mr Hekmatyar has been able to stall and bully his way into powerful positions throughout the war. Meanwhile, Mr Abdul Wakil, the deposed regime's foreign minister, was said to have fled to Tashkent. Mr Wakil became the face of the government after ex-president Najibullah went into hiding.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Australia cuts interest rates again
DOC.TEXT: THE Reserve Bank of Australia yesterday cut official interest rates for the 12th time since 1990, ignoring signs that recovery from 18 months of economic stagnation or decline is already under way. The Bank announced a cut of one percentage point in official cash rates to 6.5 per cent, the lowest since the mid-1970s. Rates have now been cut by 11.5 percentage points since peaking at 18 per cent in January 1990. Mr Bernie Fraser, the reserve bank governor, said the cut was justified by zero growth in the consumer price index in the three months to the end of March. Inflation is currently 1.7 per cent a year. Mr Fraser said the economic recovery was uneven, and forecast that excess capacity would restrain upward pressure on prices. 'A reduction in rates will help business cash flow, and provide some encouragement (to companies) to undertake new investments,' he said.
