Mr John Dawkins, the federal Treasurer (finance minister), said inflation expectations were on 'a downward trend,' and forecast that inflation would average less than 2 per cent for the remainder of 1992. Mr Dawkins said the outlook for inflation would be 'very important for the future stance of monetary policy.' He said the government 'will stand ready to increase rates if circumstances require.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Hong Kong budget surplus increases
DOC.TEXT: THE Hong Kong government yesterday disclosed that its budget surplus for last year was HKDollars 6bn (Pounds 437m) higher than its provisional figure, revealed in March. The extra Dollars HK6bn brings the budget surplus for 1991/1992 to more than Dollars HK20bn. Legislative councillors expressed concern over the government's apparent inability to keep track of its finances. Financial secretary Mr Hamish MacLeod's statement on the windfall surplus was accompanied by a concession on his first budget. He said he would not raise property rates by half a point to 6 per cent, as proposed in his maiden budget speech two months ago. A number of legislative councillors had said earlier that they would vote against the rates increase, in spite of opposition by Mr MacLeod to any tampering with his first budget. He told the Legislative Council yesterday that the decrease in revenue was 'roughly equivalent' to the windfall surplus.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Angola poll timetable in jeopardy
DOC.TEXT: ANGOLA'S transition to multi-party elections at the end of September is in jeopardy, the country's opposition Unita movement warned yesterday. In a strongly worded statement which reflects increasing tension between the two parties, Unita accused the MPLA government of 'deliberate delay' in implementing a programme scheduled to culminate in Angola's first democratic poll since independence in 1975. It cited the government's failure to establish a National Electoral Commission, or to appoint an election commissioner. The government had also failed to provide guidelines for voter registration, due to begin this month. This criticism is echoed by western diplomats and UN officials who are monitoring the transition programme. Government inaction is attributed to a weak bureaucracy rather than a lack of political will, but there are growing doubts about the country's ability to meet the election timetable. Western officials also fear that the monitoring exercise is under-staffed and inadequately financed. The Dollars 100m (Pounds 56m) budget and 600-strong UN force is well short of what the exercise requires, they say, pointing out that Angola's 10m population is scattered across a country five times larger than the UK.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Tired Nigerian leadership battling to limit economic damage: How Lagos must strive for fiscal stability while attempting to bring about a smooth transition to civilian rule
DOC.TEXT: WITH just eight months to go before he hands over power to an elected civilian administration, Nigeria's President Ibrahim Babangida has lost his image as the mercurial Maradona of Nigerian politics. Instead, a tired, leaden-footed administration is battling to contain the impact of depressed oil prices, the ravages of rampant inflation, a generation of fiscal irresponsibility and an unsustainable debt burden, domestic as well as foreign. On the economic front, his government is preoccupied with damage limitation while still determined to ensure that the transition to civilian rule goes ahead as smoothly as possible. The brave, if unavoidable, March 5 decision to devalue the Naira from N10.5 to the dollar to the current rate of N18.6 brought down the wrath of vested interests on the President's head. The timing was doubly unfortunate; coming after a period of excessive monetary growth, the inflationary impact has been lethal. The latest official figures show inflation running at 29 per cent in January in the wake of 1991 credit growth of over 40 per cent. Devaluation was seized upon by all and sundry as justification for sharp price increases, and according to one survey, retail prices rose 12 per cent during March alone. Devaluation was all the more unfortunate too, since after a decade of stagnating living standards and nearly six years of structural adjustment, it was hailed by the administration's many critics as concrete evidence of the decisive failure of economic reform. Nor has a subsequent series of own goals helped matters. In a newspaper interview, the President said he kept asking his advisers 'why the Nigerian economy has not collapsed until now', adding: 'I have still not found an answer'. In a statement tying the hands of his officials who at the time were negotiating a standby agreement with the IMF, the President ruled out any increase in the domestic price of petrol - currently less than four US cents a litre. The sensitivity of the issue has been underlined over the past few days. The riots that broke out on Sunday were over fuel shortages rather than the fuel price but Nigeria's history shows that any increase in petrol pump prices provokes an angry reaction. The pricing issue, he said, was best left to the future civilian government to resolve - confirmation, as critics were quick to point out, of his administration's lame-duck character. Government hypersensitivity to criticism was reflected in the two-week long closure of Concord press, whose news magazine African Concord's critical 17-page survey of the economy has been banned. As time runs out, crisis management is the only strategy to hand. Western diplomats and bankers believe the best Nigeria can expect in talks with the IMF is a year-long standby which might just enable the government to secure a conventional debt-rescheduling agreement from the Paris Club of official creditors before the handover in January. Although Nigeria is now eligible for an IMF Extended Structural Adjustment Facility, (ESAF), negotiations for such a concessional facility must await the emergence of a new administration that can take a three-year view of the economic situation. In last week's negotiations in Washington with the Fund, the Nigerian team apparently had little to offer. Naira devaluation removed the major obstacle, but agreement on fiscal management is likely to be extraordinarily difficult, especially given the probability that in its final months in power the Babangida administration will seek to buy off its increasingly-vocal opponents. With inflation set to reach 50 per cent later in the year, according to local economists, the government will come under intense pressure to grant compensatory pay awards to public servants. Wage inflation is already on the march in the private sector as employers react to the post-devaluation price surge. Weak though Nigeria's bargaining hand may be, the Fund negotiators are also in a bind. If they press too hard for Nigerian concessions especially on the entirely rational but intensely emotive issue of phasing out the petroleum subsidy, they run the risk of being accused of contributing to civil unrest that could derail the return to democracy. At the same time, both the IMF and the World Bank know that throughout the main flaw in their Nigerian game plan has been their inability to achieve fiscal stability. It is not just a matter of the size of the budget deficit nor the manner of its financing, but the lack of accountability and transparency in public spending programmes. Fiscal policy is the key to short-term stability too. Devaluation in March did no more than bring the official - subsidised - exchange rate into line with that ruling in the marketplace. Although officials claim to have deregulated the foreign exchange market, bankers say that the rate is still being closely managed. 'Its now a fixed rate system,' said one Lagos banker; 'pegged at N18.6 to the dollar, despite strong fluctuations in the demand for foreign currency'. The Central Bank no longer publishes the details of the weekly foreign exchange auction, though it does announce the exchange rate and how much currency is being sold. Money market liquidity has tightened a great deal since March largely because the banks now need almost twice as many Naira to buy their dollar requirements, but also because the Central Bank issued N5 billion (Dollars 269m) of stabilisation securities to mop up excess liquidity. This might result in brief respite for the Naira though it may soon be overtaken by escalating inflation on one hand and increased public spending on the other. The familiar Nigerian syndrome of the central bank trying to contain inflation while the government spends as if there were no tomorrow seems all too likely to repeat itself during the administration's dying months. Donors insist that any debt-relief package must be linked to a closely-monitored reform programme agreed, not with a lame-duck military administration, but with the incoming civilians. As one donor put it bluntly last week: 'There is nothing in this administration's recent track record to merit Trinidad-style debt-relief terms.' With so little room for manoeuvre on either side both the IMF and the government seems set to fudge the issues. Its clear that Nigeria cannot meet its debt-service obligations - of more than Dollars 5bn during 1992 - from export earnings of around Dollars 9bn. A one-year IMF standby and a conventional Paris Club rescheduling would avoid a new build-up in arrears, giving the incoming civilians the breathing space - but no more than that - to try and put together a coherent economic strategy. But in the run-up to the national assembly elections in mid-year and the presidential primaries in September there is little evidence to suggest that more than one or two of the literally dozens of presidential aspirants yet accepts that, whoever wins in December, will have to continue to implement the military government's highly unpopular economic reforms.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Trade News: OECD in campaign to harmonise export credit insurance
DOC.TEXT: THE Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has launched a campaign to reduce huge differences in export credit insurance premiums charged by its members, which distort free competition in sales from the industrialised to the developing world. OECD headquarters in Paris has invited trade officials from its 24 member countries to meet next autumn to share information on 'six or seven' Third World countries, to which the costs of export credit insurance vary widely between different OECD exporters. Meetings to exchange information on commercials risks in other Third World markets are expected to follow. Officials are unwilling to give precise examples of which countries charge too little or too much. However, a recent OECD study shows that premiums on export credit insurance to one African country vary between OECD members from a minimum of 6 per cent to a maximum of 26 per cent of contract value. 'It is complete chaos. There are very large differences which are commercially inexplicable,' said an official. If the meetings are successful, OECD officials believe export credit insurance premiums within the industrialised bloc should converge over the next few years. Patchy information on Third World market risks accounts for most of the differences, said an OECD expert. The study shows no evidence of attempts by the governments of exporting countries to subsidise overseas sales by encouraging providers of export credit guarantees - often state-owned - to charge unrealistically low premiums. However, the move is consistent with a separate OECD campaign which is aimed at preventing governments from mixing aid funds with commercial credits, so as to win export markets.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Dunkel says 'fatigue' is new danger
DOC.TEXT: THE Uruguay Round faces the danger of unravelling because of 'fatigue, frustration, disenchantment and missed deadlines', Mr Arthur Dunkel, director general of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (Gatt), said in Lausanne yesterday. Addressing the Business Council for Sustainable Development, Mr Dunkel called for trade negotiators to 'display political courage' by recognising that nothing can be achieved by further delay in completion of the long-blocked round. He pointed to a recent assessment by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) that the draft Uruguay Round agreement, tabled at the end of last year, would increase trade flows by Dollars 195bn (Pounds 110bn) a year - with Dollars 90bn of that benefiting developing countries, and the hard-pressed countries of central and eastern Europe.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Trade News: US Eximbank to adjust fees it charges for contract cover
DOC.BYLINE: By DAVID DODWELL and NANCY DUNNE
DOC.TEXT: THE US Eximbank is to adjust the fees it charges exporters when it provides them with insurance cover on export contracts. The changes are the result of a programme of comprehensive credit reform and link with efforts by other leading export credit agencies to provide a 'level playing field' for exporters to compete for foreign contracts. The adjustments come into effect on May 15 and will 'somewhat increase costs at the higher risk end', according to Mr Ray Albright, the bank's new executive vice-president. The fees are not intended to cover fully the bank's exposure to possible default on contract payments, but are intended to reflect more accurately the level of risk involved in exports country by country. Any scale that aimed at full recovery of liabilities would result in 'killing exports where you still want to do business', Mr Albright said. A month ago, Bonn revealed that Hermes, its leading export credit agency, would abandon a long-standing practice of offering exporters a standard fee for providing export credit insurance. This had become a source of controversy because it gave German exporters a competitive advantage in high-risk countries, but penalised them in competing for contracts in countries regarded as low credit risks. The Eximbank's new charges will range on a scale from 'A' and 'A-minus' down to 'F' and 'F-minus'. Fees at the highest-risk end of the scale could rise to 10 per cent on a 10-year contract. Once the Eximbank has fixed a basic country rate, then fees will vary depending on the type of deal: sovereign public-sector purchasers will get the best country rate, with non-sovereign public-sector purchasers and creditworthy banks being ranked as slightly more expensive, and creditworthy borrowers a little higher still. 'It has taken us four to five years to get a handle on this,' Mr Albright said. 'We are very comfortable with the (new system) and feel we are technical leaders. 'We now have an integrated country risk assessment process covering all US government agencies, with Exim as lead drafter. 'We are keen to accelerate international harmonisation, and if this can move the system up a little bit, we will be happy to do that.' Mr Albright was also comfortable with a recent Berne Union workshop in which the Eximbank and Britain's Export Credit Guarantee Department ran their country risk assessment models in parallel on a variety of countries and 'found our results were very close'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Egypt moves to help its exporters
DOC.TEXT: EGYPT'S parliament has approved the establishment of an export credit organisation with capital of EPounds 100m (Pounds 17m) to help promote exports. Dr Hazem Beblawi, chairman of the Export Development Bank of Egypt who will also head the new Export Credit Guarantee Company of Egypt (EGCE), said credit support would put Egyptian exporters on the 'same footing' as their competitors. EGCE is expected to begin operations before the end of this year, and its establishment coincides with heightened efforts by Egypt to improve its trading performance. The World Bank, which helped fund studies into requirements for a credit agency, has been pressing Egypt to expand non-traditional exports.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / World Trade News: German grain blamed for Gatt stalemate
DOC.BYLINE: By DAVID DODWELL and NANCY DUNNE
DOC.TEXT: GERMAN refusal to agree to cuts in grain prices lies at the heart of the stalemate over farm trade reform in the Uruguay Round of world trade talks, according to a senior US administration official. 'Everyone thinks the French are the problem - and the French obviously do have a problem - but they are not the only or even the worst problem,' the official said. 'The Germans are the ones who are resisting the decline in grain prices.' The German government has failed to provide a lead in breaking the farm trade deadlock in spite of mounting international expectations that they would do so. Hopes of a breakthrough in March during a state visit to Washington by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl were frustrated when he arrived and departed with no initiatives. The chancellor has apparently been 'very distant' even at summit meetings where Mr Jurgen Mollemann, Germany's economics minister, has spoken on trade matters on the country's behalf. Germany's role will come into sharp focus in July when it hosts a summit of the Group of Seven industrialised nations in Munich. Two previous G7 summits have made commitments to resolve the farm trade problem with no effect, and a third failure would be both an embarrassment to Germany and a blow to the standing of the G7. Mrs Carla Hills, the US trade representative, was not willing this week to endorse explicitly the complaint against Germany. She nevertheless conceded: 'The Germans have the capacity to facilitate an outcome.' She emphasised that the EC's failure to find a common position on farm trade reform was the critical obstacle to progress in the long-stalled Uruguay Round. 'Since the problem is agriculture, and that is the impediment that has to be swept away and the Europeans have the broom, we have to wait until they have a consensus as to how they are going to treat with it,' she said. Mr Arthur Dunkel, the director-general of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (Gatt), released at the end of 1991 a comprehensive plan for the reform of the world trading system. This included proposals to cut subsidised farm production and agriculture export subsidies and to open all markets to farm exports. Within days, the plan was rejected by the EC, which has been hobbled by its own efforts to reform Europe's Common Agriculture Policy. A frustrated US agriculture official recalled: 'It was as if the Dunkel Final Act fell out of the sky.' Intensive talks between the US and EC have brought negotiators close to agreement. It has been widely assumed that France, which is a leading farm exporter, was the principal impediment. However, the US official said: 'Whether it is export subsidies or rebalancing or internal supports, it comes down to the price of grain . . . and the Germans are the primary obstacle.' The mood in Washington improved from 'despondency' to 'mere frustration' after the visit of Mr Jacques Delors, the EC president. Mr Delors convinced US officials that he was determined to reach a settlement and agreed to intensify bilateral negotiations. 'I believe that they want to achieve a deal,' said Mrs Hills. 'I didn't have that feeling five or six months ago.' Officials hope to arrange a EC-US ministerial meeting in Washington later this month followed by discussions at the OECD.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Economic growth to top European finance ministers' talks
DOC.TEXT: ECONOMIC growth in Europe is likely to top the agenda at this weekend's informal meeting of European Community finance ministers in Oporto, northern Portugal. High European interest rates, rising public sector indebtedness, and sluggish growth prospects prompted Mr Pierre Beregovoy, the French prime minister, to write to his EC counterparts urging a high level discussion on promoting EC growth. Mr Jorge Braga de Macedo, Portugal's finance minister, yesterday said that the ministers would seek concerted action through a Community-wide 'non-inflationary growth policy'. He also said that the ministers would examine several structural impediments to European growth and review concerted means of eliminating these obstacles. Ministers are expected to examine developments towards the single market and ways to promote competition in the non-tradeable goods sector, including services, distribution and the labour and capital markets. 'There is scope for initiatives in these areas,' Mr Braga de Macedo said. A paper from the Committee of Central Bank governors on stage two of European Monetary Union, due to start in January 1994, will attempt to define some of the steps involved. The thorny issue of choosing a site for the European Monetary Institute (EMI), which would be converted into a European central bank by 1999 at the latest, is expected to be raised separately. Other topics include requests by non-EC countries for their currencies to be linked formally to the exchange rate mechanism of the European Monetary System. Ministers are also expected to discuss broadening EC economic assistance to all the republics of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), as well as the possible extension of European Investment Bank activities to Latin America. Discussion of the Community's 1993-97 budget is expected to focus on improving budgetary discipline and transparency by raising efficiency and reducing bureaucracy. 'Some (Community) procedures are far too slow, and we want to find ways to ensure that taxpayers' money is not wasted,' Mr Braga de Macedo said.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Minimum bank guarantees proposed
DOC.TEXT: ALL depositors in EC banks should have a minimum Ecu15,000 (Pounds 10,500) of their deposits guaranteed, the European Commission proposed yesterday. The EC executive began work on the draft directive before the failure of the Bank of Commerce and Credit International (BCCI) last year, but accelerated its initiative after the scandal surrounding the bank's collapse. The Commission suggests that bank customers should obtain their deposit guarantee reimbursement within three months, in contrast to the much longer period that many depositors with the Luxembourg-incorporated BCCI had to wait. Responsibility for deposit insurance would switch from the host to the home country of a bank. Mr Pierre Jaans, head of the Luxembourg Monetary Institute, said this would not pose a problem for the duchy. Very few Luxembourg-based banks, with the notable exception of BCCI, had branches abroad. Commission officials hope that EC governments will reach basic agreement on the guarantee scheme under the UK presidency of the EC later this year. The plan would require Greece and Portugal to institute deposit guarrantees for the first time.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / French assembly split on Maastricht
DOC.TEXT: THE French debate on ratifying the Maastricht Treaty on European Union heated up yesterday after the French national assembly voted down two procedural attempts to have the whole exercise thrown out as being unconstitutional. Both these fundamentally anti-Maastricht moves, one from the Gaullist right-wing and one from the communists, were rejected by wide margins. The motion tabled by Mr Philippe Seguin, a standard-bearer of the nationalist wing of the Gaullist Party, was defeated by 396 to 101; while the communist motion was defeated by 411 to 54. The votes against the Maastricht Treaty were much larger than the government had been expecting, and suggest that the necessary constitutional reform and ratification of the Treaty could after all turn out to be closely-run. As it is, the government has already been forced to give ground to opposition protests that it tried to ram through the constitutional revision at unreasonable speed during the preliminary committee stage. As a result the full national assembly debate, which was to have been concluded tonight, is being extended with an additional day's discussion next Tuesday, and will then be wound up with a vote. But if the size of the two anti-Maastricht votes in the national assembly is moderately worrying for the Socialist government, it is deeply disturbing for the right-wing Gaullist party, because it has again opened up the deep split over the issue of Europe which has traditionally run right down the middle of the party. Before the debate, Mr Jacques Chirac, the leader of the Gaullists, attempted a compromise with tepid support for the Treaty and modest criticism of the constitutional revision, which he hoped would satisfy both the pro- and anti-Europeans in the party. But his attempt to forge a facade of unity in the party has now been blown apart by the fiercest debate on France's European destiny since the Treaty of Rome in 1957. Nearly half the Gaullist contingent in the national assembly (58 out of 126 members) voted for the Seguin motion, and 16 Gaullists even voted for the communist motion. Some commentators play down the operational significance of yesterday's votes. The Gaullists knew the anti-European motions would be defeated, so they could afford a display of anti-European and anti-government ill-temper; but next Tuesday the more prudent members may fall back into line behind the leadership. As a potential candidate in the next presidential elections, Mr Chirac will find it more difficult to pose as a constructive if prudent European statesman when nearly half his parliamentary party appears implacably opposed to the whole enterprise.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Brussels draft budget shows money to spare: Main saving to come on farm subsidies
DOC.TEXT: THE European Commission yesterday presented its 1993 draft budget which at first sight shows the EC has money to spare, thereby undermining its own controversial plan to increase Community revenue 35 per cent by 1997. The full 'appropriations' budget would rise from Ecu66.6bn (Pounds 46.62bn) this year to Ecu67.3bn in 1993, a rise of only 1.1 per cent, against average spending rises in the member states of 7 per cent. This compares with an 11.3 per cent rise in last year's EC budget and a 19 per cent increase the year before. Actual spending this year is forecast at Ecu63.1bn, and Ecu64.3bn next year. This means that spending in 1992 is below target and that the Commission is in real terms pitching next year's target below this year's likely outcome. The EC's revenue ceiling is equivalent to 1.2 per cent of Community gross national product. This year's forecast outcome would be well within the ceiling at 1.11 per cent, whereas next year's target would be 1.1 per cent. Mr Jacques Delors, the Commission president, however, still wants to raise the revenue base to 1.35 per cent of GNP by 1997, under its new five-year finance plan. Net contributors to the budget, led by Germany and the UK, will see the draft budget as confirming their argument that the revenue base should not be raised that high because there is enough 'headroom' under the existing ceiling to accommodate EC spending ambitions. These ambitions are reflected in the planned 19 per cent rise in regional spending, from Ecu18.6bn this year to Ecu22.1bn next. This includes Ecu1.6bn for the 'cohesion fund' to help poorer member states catch up with average EC living standards. Spending on external aid and foreign policy, and on research, rises 13 per cent, from Ecu3.6bn to Ecu4.1bn, and from Ecu2.5bn to Ecu2.8bn respectively. These priorities and the cohesion fund were agreed at December's Maastricht summit, but the only attempt to attach sums to them is the so-called 'Delors II' five-year finance plan which is likely to be whittled down by member states. The main saving for 1993 is on farm spending, forecast to drop from Ecu35.3bn to Ecu32.1bn - the first time since the EC was founded that agriculture has absorbed less than half the budget. This estimate is based on current world prices and the strength of the dollar, and also incorporates modest savings from the Commission's farm reform plan which has yet to be agreed. But this picture could easily change. Lower farm spending and more 'cohesion' finance are also likely to increase pressure on the UK to give up some of the budget rebate it won from 1985, conceded because it did relatively badly out of a bigger agriculture budget. Germany, by far the largest net contributor, intends to press for a reduction of this Ecu2bn rebate, and Mr Delors on Tuesday told Socialist Euro-MPs that 'consideration of the British situation could be different from in the past'. Commission budget officials said yesterday they would recommend whether to 'continue, modify or abolish' the rebate later this month.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Albania to launch economic reform package
DOC.TEXT: ALBANIA'S new government plans to launch an economic package this month aimed at reassuring the International Monetary Fund and other potential lenders that the country's transition to a market economy is finally under way. The Democratic party's March election victory over the communists opened the door to reform. But the economic and social chaos accompanying Albania's emergence from half a century of self-imposed isolation has prompted western governments and international financial institutions to move cautiously. Yesterday Mr Sali Berisha, Albania's first democratically elected president appealed to Europe for aid to rebuild his country. On his first European tour since he was elected president last month, he promised shock treatment to revive his country's 'ruined' economy. The first measure will be to cut payments to unemployed industrial workers, who still receive 80 per cent of their wages, despite the closure of most factories after supplies of raw materials ran out last year. Unemployment now exceeds 150,000, which is over 50 per cent of the urban workforce. Under the new government's programme, wage subsidies will be reduced by 10 per cent a month until they are eliminated. By that time, the government hopes that industrial plants will be producing basic goods. According to Mr Genc Ruli, the economy minister, about Dollars 100m (Pounds 56.4m) pledged in aid or loans from Germany, Italy, Turkey and Greece will be spent on importing raw materials for industry. 'Our economic situation is tragic. We shall be dependent on food aid for months to come. But we must stop the subsidies if we are to get structural loans,' he said. Albania is negotiating a Dollars 9m stand-by arrangement with the IMF, to be followed by a World Bank adjustment loan. 'We are hoping for several hundred million dollars, in a series of instalments,' Mr Ruli said. The government is already concerned about meeting a major condition for the stand-by loan: the liberalisation of prices for a basket of subsidised goods, including bread, sugar and cooking oil. The economy ministry forecasts that bread prices alone will rise fourfold. With higher wages and steadily rising food prices, inflation has reached 500 per cent. Following a disastrous 60 per cent decline in agricultural output last year as collective farming collapsed, Albania survived the winter on food aid provided first by Italy, then by the European Community. Despite severe shortages, remittances in cash and consumer goods from about 150,000 migrant workers in Greece have helped the south of the country to subsist. Elsewhere, Albanians from Kosovo in Yugoslavia took advantage of the launch of privatisation to invest in property and start small businesses. The Albanian diaspora in the US is believed to have sent more than Dollars 1m in private aid. Yet despite the introduction of import taxes on popular items such as colour televisions and second-hand cars, government revenues cover only 20 per cent of expenditure. The public deficit has reached Lek10bn (Dollars 100m), equivalent to 15 per cent of GDP. However, new fiscal arrangements are being drawn up under the Phare programme, the vehicle for EC technical assistance to eastern Europe.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / US calls on CSCE to exclude Serbia
DOC.BYLINE: By LAURA SILBER and JUDY DEMPSEY
DOC.TEXT: THE US and other western countries yesterday stepped up the pressure on Serbia by refusing to recognise it as the legal successor of the former Yugoslavia, and calling for its exclusion from the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe (CSCE) The moves to isolate Serbia - and Montenegro, its tiny ally - came as CSCE members met in Helsinki to discuss the civil war in the independent republic of Bosnia-Hercegovina and as European Community officials tried to consolidate the latest ceasefire there. Mr Haris Silajdzic, Bosnia's foreign minister, repeated his plea at the CSCE meeting for some form of military intervention from the international community. But several west European countries were sceptical about intervening. Growing international criticism of Serbia coincided with the reconvening of the EC peace conference in Brussels. Although Mr Alija Izetbegovic, the president of Bosnia-Hercegovina, remained in Sarajevo, the talks were attended by President Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia and President Franjo Tudjman of Croatia, who over the past year have held secret negotiations on dividing Bosnia. The EC-brokered ceasefire was agreed on Tuesday just hours after Mr Marrack Goulding, the United Nations special envoy, arrived in Sarajevo to assess whether any UN peace-keeping forces would be sent. Mr Goulding, whose convoy came under fire last Tuesday, was yesterday again attacked. Radio Sarajevo said a bullet hit the envoy's car. In other parts of the republic, there were reports of heavy fighting. Radio Sarajevo said Mostar, southern Bosnia, was pounded by some 500 grenades. Radio Belgrade reported fresh clashes around Zvornik, eastern Bosnia, one of eight mainly Moslem towns seized by Serb irregulars on or near the River Drina, Bosnia's eastern frontier with Serbia.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Angry SPD threatens to boycott budget crisis talks
DOC.TEXT: GERMANY'S Social Democratic opposition yesterday threatened to boycott cross-party talks on the country's budget crisis in protest at the government's plans for drastic cuts in unemployment benefits and job creation schemes. The hostile response to the first government proposals for long-term budget austerity was fuelled by an equally angry reaction at the Federal Labour Office, which declared that any large-scale savings would only increase the numbers of fully unemployed - above all in east Germany. The plan put forward by Mr Theo Waigel, the finance minister, would curb growth in government spending to a bare 2.5 per cent per year until 1996, and would abolish any central subsidy for the Labour Office, currently standing at some DM5bn (Pounds 1.7bn). Spending by the states and local authorities would be kept to a 3 per cent annual growth rate. Mr Waigel's aim is to cut his central government budget deficit, a factor behind the country's current high interest rates, from DM45bn this year to DM25bn by 1995. The plan yesterday split the German political and economic establishments on predictable lines, winning solid support from the Chamber of Trade and Industry and the ruling coalition partners, and outright hostility from the Social Democrats (SPD) and the trade union federation (DGB). Both Mr Bjorn Engholm, the SPD leader, and Mr Hans-Ulrich Klose, the Bonn parliamentary group leader, called into question their planned talks with the government on May 27. Mr Klose said the talks would be pointless on the basis of the 'sloppy and socially unjust' proposal put forward by the finance minister. The most disturbing response for Mr Waigel, however, was the reaction of the Federal Labour Office's conservative president, Mr Heinrich Franke, who suggested that substantial savings in training and job creation schemes would simply boost outright unemployment in the east, without any significant budget saving.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 07 MAY 92 / Last tactical nuclear missiles leave Ukraine
DOC.TEXT: MOSCOW announced yesterday that the last tactical nuclear missiles had been withdrawn from the Ukraine to Russia in record time, ending suspense over whether Kiev would fulfil a promise to get rid of them by July 1. Lt-Gen Sergei Zelentsov, of the Commonwealth of Independent States joint command, said the transfer was completed on Tuesday night. It would help ensure that the number of nuclear states did 'not grow,' he said. The announcement is a first success for the republics' attempts to reassure the west over the future of the vast nuclear arsenal which they inherited from the Soviet Union. A Russian foreign ministry representative said he hoped the four republics with strategic missiles - Russia, Belarus, Ukraine and Kazakhstan - would soon agree a formula for jointly ratifying the Start treaty on reducing long-range missiles. It was signed last year but not ratified by the US and the Soviet Union. Apart from Russia, Ukraine has 176 strategic missiles, Kazakhstan 104 and Belarus 54. The announcement on tactical missiles was confirmed by an aide to the Ukrainian defence minister, Mr Konstantin Morozov, who said: 'Ukraine is trying to behave in such a way as to inspire trust in its policies.' The news coincided with a US tour by Ukraine's President Leonid Kravchuk, who sent alarm bells ringing two months ago when he said he was suspending the shipment of tactical missiles to Russia because he was not sure they would be dismantled. A Ukrainian spokesman in Moscow said Ukraine, would be seeking international guarantees for its security. In Washington, Mr Kravchuk merely said Ukraine would transfer all the tactical nuclear weapons on its territory by July as originally planned. He said he expected Ukraine to sign the Start treaty. President Nursultan Nazarbayev of Kazakhstan, who has made no such promise, was quoted by Itar-Tass news agency as saying he would give up all nuclear weapons if he received guarantees for his republic's security from the US, China and Russia. Lt-Gen Zelentsov said it would take from next month until the year 2000 to dismantle the tactical weapons and recycle for civilian use the weapons-grade plutonium contained in the warheads.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / International Company News: MIM declines 12 per cent to Adollars 46m
DOC.TEXT: MIM HOLDINGS, the Australian resources group, yesterday blamed weak metal prices for a 12 per cent fall in net profits to ADollars 46m (dollars 34.8m) for the nine months to April 5, on sales down 12.6 per cent to ADollars 1.2bn. The result represents a significant improvement over the first six months, when MIM reported a 76 per cent cut in new profits to ADollars 16m, on sales down 10 per cent to ADollars 840m. After including a second-quarter abnormal profit of ADollars 45.7m from the sale of its interests in Teck Corporation, net profits rose to ADollars 91.8m, from ADollars 52.8m the previous comparable period. However, net profits fell to ADollars 70m after including foreign exchange losses and minority equity interests. The equivalent profit in the first nine months of last year was ADollars 30m. MIM said profits had continued to be affected in the third quarter by weak metals prices, but reported excellent results from the Porgera gold mine in Papua New Guinea, which is 30 per cent owned by Highlands Gold, an MIM subsidiary. The group said gold operations at Tick Hill also performed well, and coal operations at Oaky Creek returned to profitability during the quarter. Oaky Creek suffered a loss of ADollars 24m in the first six months, mainly because of operational difficulties. MIM said average copper prices during the nine months were 12 per cent lower than in the comparable period of last year. The equivalent falls in prices for other metals were 27 per cent for lead, 12 per cent for zinc and 10 per cent for gold. The directors said the weakness in prices was likely to continue in the absence of signs of economic recovery in the metal consuming countries. It said recent data on housing starts and retail sales in the US were encouraging, but this was offset by worsening economies in Germany and Japan.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / International Company News: US media boss predicts recovery
DOC.TEXT: A RECOVERY in earnings in the second half of 1992 was forecast yesterday by Mr Daniel Burke, president and chief executive of Capital Cities/ABC, the US television and newspapers group. Mr Burke, speaking at the annual shareholders's meeting in New York, said the second-half results would benefit from an improvement in local and national advertising demand in the broadcasting division. The company's shares reacted with a rise of dollars 7 3/4 to dollars 448. 'We cannot make predictions beyond that for the balance of the year, although we expect the company's expense growth to be modest,' Mr Burke explained. The media group's 1991 net income declined by 28.1 per cent to dollars 343.5m, on revenues of dollars 5.4bn. In the first quarter of 1992 net profits at Capital Cities/ABC plunged by 45 per cent, to dollars 58.6m, on unchanged revenues of dollars 1.26bn. Mr Burke promised that ABC would remain 'a player of consequence' in the global television market, having established partnerships in seven international media-based ventures to date. In the US, ABC Television ended the 1991-92 prime time season in last place, just behind NBC. 'While I live for the day I can report to you that the network ranked first or second, I would rather that it made a respectable profit,' Mr Burke told shareholders. He noted that the broadcasting division had earned dollars 669.7m of operating profit last year. Mr Burke said while Capital Cities was considering acquisitions, it might be 'entering a period where internally developed businesses make more sense for us'. He cited several internally generated ventures such as new magazine and fashion shows that have cost the company dollars 42m pre-tax in start-up expenses.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Usdaw to fight Sunday law
DOC.TEXT: THE SHOP WORKERS' union, Usdaw, has moved to counter government proposals for legislation to expand Sunday trading, expected in today's Queen's speech. Delegates at the union's annual conference unanimously backed their executive committee's call to move the focus of the anti-Sunday trading campaign to influencing new legislation and away from simple condemnation of shops trading illegally. Mr Bill Connor, deputy general secretary, said the union would continue to call for law enforcement, but delegates had to realise that large stores would continue to trade illegally, especially over the Christmas period. The union gave qualified support for the so-called 'rest' proposals, formulated by Keep Sunday Special (KSS), the anti-Sunday-trading lobby. Mr Connor said the proposals were acceptable because they meant most shops would be closed on Sundays, law-breaking employers would face fines of up to Pounds 50,000, and boards of directors would be held legally liable. He criticised KSS for having little to say about Scottish shopworkers and for suggesting that illegal traders be closed for up to 14 days, without clarifying the position of staff during that time. The union will press EuroFiet, the body that represents the interests of shop workers at European community level, to join Usdaw in sponsoring a conference on trading hours legislation. Earlier, the union reaffirmed its support for wages councils, the bodies that set minimum statutory pay levels for about 2.5m workers, of which more than 1m are shop workers. Mr Tony Blair, shadow employment secretary, told the conference he would fight the abolition of wages councils line by line and comma by comma in the House of Commons. He said the government had no mandate to abolish wages councils because the Conservative manifesto did not refer to that.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Record for Post Office deliveries
DOC.TEXT: A RECORD 89.7 per cent of first-class letters were delivered the day after postings during the past financial year, Sir Bryan Nicholas, Post Office chairman, said yesterday. The figure was an improvement on the previous of 85.5 per cent, beating targets agreed with the Post Office User's National Council (Pounc), he said. Pounc welcomed the figures and said it hoped improvements would continue.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Canadians approve new Arctic region
DOC.TEXT: About 27,000 voters in Canada's Northwest Territories have narrowly approved the setting up from 1999 of the region of Nunavut, a vast area including most of the eastern Arctic, Robert Gribbens reports from Montreal. It is seen as the first step toward creating a homeland for the Inuit. Most of the inhabited Arctic islands are included in Nunavut, but the Beaufort Sea remains in the western NWT. Mr Robert Bourassa, Quebec's premier, is returning to the constitutional negotiating table with a four-day visit to western Canada and direct talks with the four western premiers. He wants to put a federal constitutional offer before Quebec voters this autumn, rather than hold a referendum on Quebec's sovereignty. He is now trying to ensure the offer will be at least as generous to Quebec as Ottawa's Meech Lake proposals, which failed to get unanimous provincial consent in 1990.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / International Company News: DnB cuts losses to NKr601m in first quarter
DOC.TEXT: DEN NORSKE Bank, the troubled Norwegian bank, has reduced its first-quarter net losses to NKr601m (Dollars 93.6m) from NKr798m in the same period last year. It attributed the improvement to lower credit losses, growth in net interest income and a reduction in operating costs. Group operating profit, before credit losses and taxes, rose by NKr17m to NKr424m. The bank said a NKr45m charge was made against accounts to cover write-downs and losses arising from the sale of fixed assets. Credit losses were reduced by NKr172m to NKr1.02bn but non-performing loans rose by NKr105m from the end of last year to NKr10.27bn. Group net interest income increased NKr113m to NKr1.14bn but other operating income fell by NKr117m to NKr545m. A reduction of NKr28m to NKr13m in income from securities trading contributed to the decline, as trading in foreign exchange and other financial instruments fell NKr92m to NKr70m. DnB said that results of Realkreditt, a mortgage company acquired last year, were included for the first time in the group's accounts. Realkreditt contributed NKr58m to total net interest income. The bank said that, as a percentage of total assets, first-quarter net interest income rose to 2.28 per cent from 2.04 per cent a year earlier. DnB said that the previously announced preferential share issue to raise NKr2.38bn will be launched in late May or early June, and that shareholders would soon receive a subscription offer.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / International Company News: Moller Group doubles turnover to DKr47bn
DOC.TEXT: AP MOLLER Group, the Danish shipping, shipbuilding and oil and gas business, and its associated companies, last year doubled turnover to DKr46.9bn (Dollars 7.8bn). Turnover in the core shipping and oil and gas operations amounted to DKr23.72bn. The group's results include the turnover, profit and equity capital figures for 18 associated companies. These include: Maersk Air, the airline; a big supermarket chain; and the Odense Steel Shipyard. Turnover in the associated companies totalled DKr23.26bn, which includes DKr13.71bn in the supermarket chain. While the core companies made a net profit last year of DKr1.92bn, the associated companies, four of which incurred losses, reported combined profits of DKr173m. Equity capital in the core companies at the end of last year was DKr16.52bn, while equity in the core companies was DKr4.06bn. The Moller Group's figures are still incomplete as they do not reveal turnover in the group's foreign subsidiaries. Neither does the group make it clear which of the associated companies are wholly or partly owned by the group.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Campaign to swap debt for drugs aid gathers pace: The third world has told UN it cannot afford the fight against narcotics
DOC.TEXT: A LARGE group of third world countries has told the United Nations they cannot afford to fund the fight against drugs. They want to swap some of their international debt to help pay for combating illicit drug growing, production, trafficking and abuse. The move is being opposed by most developed nations, particularly the US and Britain, which regard third world debt as a bilateral matter between individual borrowers and lenders, not as something on which the UN can act collectively. They also say the global fight against drugs and drug-related crime is embedded in international treaties which all nations have a duty to implement. Their efforts cannot be made conditional. Nevertheless, the UN is being forced to investigate and develop the 'debt-for-drugs' concept after Bolivia, Colombia, Egypt, Nigeria and Peru this month forced a motion through the UN Commission on Narcotic Drugs in Vienna. Nigeria acted on behalf of the Group of 77, the third world's counterweight to the smaller, but more powerful, grouping of developed nations. The Group of 77 is gradually increasing its representation on the commissions and committees that formulate UN policy, so as to have a voting majority wherever it can. The UN International Drug Control Programme, which gets most of its Dollars 100m-plus budget from the US, Japan Australia and east European countries, has to report back to the commission in 12 months on making the debt-for-drugs concept work. One idea canvassed is for some government-to-government debt to be converted into local currency, forgiven but frozen in place, and the former interest payments diverted into anti-drug projects. Bolivia is being suggested for a pilot scheme with some of its Dollars 200m debt to US agencies retired for the purpose. A parallel is being drawn with 'debt-for-environment' schemes which UN and other agencies are also exploring. Here, third world countries can agree, for example, not to clear areas of rain forest in exchange for debts being forgiven. However, opponents of the debt-for-drugs idea say the parallel is false. The debt-for-environment swap would work through a value being placed on a section of rain forest not being developed and being designated a conservation area or international nature park. This would turn it into an asset for the country concerned, making money-earning development, such as tourism, possible. Debt-for-drugs is being seen as more like blackmail because international crime and widespread corruption are involved. At best, countries with debts would be tempted to let their anti-drug performance deteriorate so as to force a debt-for-drugs agreement on the international community. Illicit drug producers could then simply transfer operations over the nearest border, thus compounding the problem in a neighbouring country and encouraging debt-for-drugs swaps there. The UN already has experience of unexpected side effects from anti-drug initiatives. When it started crop substitution programmes, some farmers started growing opium for the first time in order to qualify for the subsidies that then enabled them to switch back to their original crops. The Group of 77 nations says, however, that diverting already scarce resources into fighting drug cultivation, reduction, trafficking and abuse strains the countries' national economies. At the same time, debt burdens diminish their ability to promote alternative economic development to persuade people away from the easy money drugs provide. There is also a view in the UN that much third world debt is never going to be repaid anyway, so debt-for-drugs would at least give the developed world some benefit from writing off what is in effect dead money. However, the 'blackmail' connotations have already registered strongly with several developed nations. This is thought likely to make some of them wary of channelling money to UN agencies, using instead bilateral agreements with individual third world countries, with close monitoring of the anti-drug projects involved. Illust. Specially chosen Guarijos Indian troops carry out a drugs search in the Colombian town of Riohacha, but they are failing to keep pace with the traffickers

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / US steps up threat to seize Iraqi assets
DOC.BYLINE: By MARK NICHOLSON, Middle East Correspondent
DOC.TEXT: WASHINGTON has stepped up talks with its Gulf war allies on a proposal to appropriate frozen Iraqi assets to pay for humanitarian needs and United Nations programmes in the country. The US is pressing Britain and France to consider framing a Security Council resolution to enable the spending of some of the Dollars 5bn in Iraqi overseas assets frozen since the August 1990 invasion of Kuwait. Washington's renewed vigour in pursuit of a proposal which has been in the air for some weeks is aimed at forcing Baghdad into accepting the terms of a UN-permitted sale of Dollars 1.6bn worth of Iraqi oil to buy food and medicines. A western diplomat in New York said: 'Iraq is being told, either do a deal with the UN, or we'll spend your assets.' Talks between Iraq and the UN on a limited sale of oil have remained deadlocked, with Iraq maintaining that the UN supervised terms for the sale, and for spending the revenues, are an unacceptable abrogation of its sovereignty. Mr Abdul Razzak al-Hiti, Iraq's oil minister, said at the Opec summit last month that an agreement on the oil sale could take only 'a few days' to work out, but no date has been set for further talks and oil analysts believe Iraq is unlikely to resume any oil sales before the end of this year. Mr Abdul Amir al-Abnari, Iraq's representative at the UN who has led negotiations over the permitted oil sale, has flown to Baghdad for talks with Mr Tariq Aziz, Iraq's deputy prime minister, and is expected to escort him on a trip within the next few days to non-aligned UN member countries. Mr Aziz is expected first to visit Rabat, capital of Morocco, the sole Arab country presently on the UN Security Council. US officials say an appropriation of frozen Iraqi assets could easily be enacted. However, Britain and France have been less enthusiastic about the possible legal ramifications of such a move. Bankers and lawyers in London say an assets appropriation would have to be backed up by passage of domestic legislation to protect banks against potential future Iraqi claims on the seized assets. Just over Dollars 530m of frozen Iraqi money lies in London banks. Bankers also say that they would be unhappy about the effect any such appropriation would have on the view of London as a financial centre: 'It's Iraq this time - but who might it be later? That would be the thinking,' said one banker. The US treasury is also understood to be worried that any Iraqi assets spent on humanitarian needs would not then be available to offset claims by US companies against Iraq. 'The problem is we have more claims against Iraq than we have money,' said one US official. More than Dollars 1.4bn of Iraqi assets are locked in US banks. Money secured, either through an oil sale or appropriation of assets would be spent largely on food and medicine, with 30 per cent used to pay for compensation to victims of the invasion of Kuwait and for UN programmes in the country. Syria denied a report that it was importing Iraqi oil, which is under a UN embargo, and exporting it mixed with its own crude, Reuter reports from Damascus. Dadoud Hido, president of Sytrol, the body responsible for marketing Syrian oil, said the increase in his country's oil exports was a result of newly discovered oilfields coming onstream. He denied a report in Petroleum Intelligence Weekly last month that Syria was mixing its oil with Iraqi crude.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Record exports for Taiwan
DOC.TEXT: Taiwan's exports last month totalled a record Dollars 7.25bn, bringing the value of exports so far this year to Dollars 26.3bn, according to finance ministry figures released on Monday, Luisetta Mudie reports in Taipei. The March figure represents an increase of about 29 per cent on the same month last year. The US remained the largest importer of Taiwanese exports, accounting for 26.4 per cent of the total and running a Dollars 700m trade deficit which increased by 135 per cent year-on-year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / ABB wins turboset contract
DOC.TEXT: Asea Brown Boveri, the Swedish-Swiss engineering group, announced yesterday that it had secured a Dollars 210m contract from the German company VEAG to design and supply two turbosets with a total output of 1,600MW for a power plant to be built at Boxberg in Saxony, writes Robert Taylor in Stockholm. The first turboset is scheduled to supply electricity from mid-1996 and the second from six months later. The order for ABB follows one worth Dollars 50m a few weeks ago for the same Saxon plant. The contract will be carried out with ABB Bergman Borsig of Berlin.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Ukraine goes to GPA for jets
DOC.TEXT: GPA, the Irish-based aircraft leasing company, is negotiating a Dollars 400m deal with the new Ukrainian government to re-equip its national airline with between five and seven modern narrow and wide-bodied jets, reports Tim Coone from Dublin. Mr Leonid Kravchuk, the Ukrainian president, met senior GPA executives at the company's Shannon headquarters yesterday during a stopover en route to the US. Negotiations are apparently at an advanced stage with two other republics in the Commonwealth of Independent States to supply one Boeing 757 and one 737 on leasing contracts. Lithuania and Hungary have already received nine jet aircraft from GPA.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / China and Russia in trade pact
DOC.TEXT: Russia plans to trade machinery, aircraft and factory equipment for Chinese food and consumer goods under a pact on economic ties signed in Beijing yesterday, Reuter reports from Moscow. The protocol, according to the Itar-Tass news agency, specified the volume of goods that the two will supply to each other through direct trade, local deals over the border, barter and exchange agreements and other means.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / London Stock Exchange: Footsie falters on brink of record
DOC.TEXT: CONFIRMATION of the widely expected half-point cut in UK interest rates saw the FT-SE 100-share Index burst through its previous all-time closing high but fail by less than one point to penetrate its record intraday high. After failing to push through the peak, the market quickly ran out of steam and saw an early strong rise turn into a minor loss, before closing moderately higher. Dealers kicked off the shortened trading week by pushing share prices up sharply, anticipating another flurry of institutional buying interest after the rate reduction. Further impetus to the London market came from Wall Street, which had raced up to record levels during London's bank holiday period. The Footsie topped its previous closing high - 2,679.6 reached on September 2 last year - opening some 20 points stronger at 2,679.8 and quickly moving up to 2,683.0, or 23.2 ahead, within minutes of the start. But the market was unable to build on this, as profit-taking from institutions anxious to lock in big profits achieved on the general election result saw equities retreat for most of the remaining session. Specialists said the market's reversal stemmed from a general feeling of anti-climax and worries that the market may well need to consolidate before launching another attempt at piercing its all-time high. There was also widespread concern about the German economy and the possibility that Wall Street may have run too far too quickly. The US stock market opened easier yesterday and continued to drift off as London closed. Dealers also spoke of at least two programme trades in London, both weighted on the sell side, and lingering worries about the possibility of sizeable rights issues. Selling pressure in London reached its peak just before Wall Street opened. At that time the Footsie fell into negative territory, reaching the day's low of 2,658.4, or down 1.4. Thereafter it managed to claw its way back to end a busy session a net 2.4 higher at 2,662.2. The trading session was spiced by another big placing. Smith New Court, the London market's bought deal specialist, acting in conjunction with Panmure Gordon, acquired and easily placed Sir Ron Brierley's 29.7 per cent stake in BSG International. The placing of the BSG stake, comprising some 60m shares, accounted for 120m of the market's turnover, which reached 638.1m shares. Pharmaceuticals were in the spotlight, with Glaxo delivering another sparkling performance as the UK authorities granted approval for the group's Zofran anti-nausea drug. SmithKline Beecham moved higher in sympathy with Glaxo, but Fisons was aggressively sold late in the session following news that the group had failed so far to win US approval for its Opticrom drug. Most senior dealers said the market had already factored in the rate cut and was seeking further stimulation. 'We have had the good news for the time being; short of some bid activity we are due a period of consolidation,' said one.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / London Stock Exchange: Zofran boost for Glaxo
DOC.BYLINE: By CHRISTOPHER PRICE, JOEL KIBAZO and COLIN MILLHAM
DOC.TEXT: AFTER feeling the wrath of American investors on Friday, Glaxo returned to favour yesterday as encouraging weekend press comment in the US restored the reputation of the group's leading drug, Zantac. In fact, it was Glaxo's new drug Zofran which took centre stage yesterday as UK approval - the first in the world - was received for the post-operative anti-nausea product. Analysts estimate that Zofran could generate sales of around Pounds 400m a year by 1995. Glaxo was also boosted by a series of institutional meetings in London arranged by Canadian group Biochem Pharma, which is developing an anti-Aids drug on behalf of the UK company. The new drug, 3TC, is seen as a potential market threat to Wellcome, which declined 8 to 1058p. Glaxo surged ahead 31 to 751p in busy turnover of 4.5m. SmithKline Beecham rose in sympathy with Glaxo to end 15 stronger at 870p. Expected approval by the US Food and Drugs Administration of Fisons' Opticrom facility failed to materialise, the drugs group merely announcing that the inspection had been completed. The shares receded 11 to 379p. Williams weak Conglomerate Williams Holdings lost more than 4 per cent of its equity value as the market responded to suggestions that the company may launch a white knight bid for Dowty Group, the aerospace concern currently under attack from TI Group. The shares tumbled 15 to 329p on turnover of 3.1m, with the market particularly concerned about the cash underwriting in the event of a bid from Williams. Mr Matthew Sutherland at County NatWest said: 'I would not rule out the fact that Williams may be looking to do a white knight deal with Dowty. But it is unlikely that they will make an acquisition that will dilute earnings.' Shares in leading retailers failed to respond favourably to yesterday's 1/2 point cut in bank base rates, the Bank of England's endorsement of lower rates having been widely forecast. Trading in Sears was fairly active, at 6m shares, and the stock dipped 4 to 101p ahead of tomorrow's results. Turnover in other leading stores was not heavy, although the recent disappointment at retail sales performance tended to push prices lower. WH Smith 'A' slipped 6 to 476p, while Boots gave up 7 to 465p and Dixons 7 to 249p. Ratners eased a penny to 20 1/2 p on lower turnover of 4.4m shares as bid speculation faded. Technical factors tended to weaken Tesco, on completion of the buying in of shares for its employee profit sharing scheme. BZW's recent advice to switch into J. Sainsbury also weighed on Tesco, as well as adverse comment from Credit Lyonnais Laing about the sector's policy on property valuations. Tesco shed 4 to 274p. Shoprite, whose shares were valued at under 400p a month ago, climbed a further 33 to 504p, following recent visits from securities houses. The shares have risen on optimism about a proposed store opening programme. Saatchi & Saatchi was the day's second most busiest stock with 30m traded, the shares easing 1/2 to 22 3/4 p. US and continental European buyers were most evident on expectations of a recovery in advertising revenue. Turnover in PowerGen was a hefty 4.1m shares, with the price falling 6 to 228p, and National Power lost 5 to 221p on trade of 2.1m shares, amid reports that overseas investors were selling shares in the power generators. Scottish generating companies were steady, however, responding to a positive note from Smith New Court. The Electricity Package gave up Pounds 15 to Pounds 3178, Friday's rumour that MEPC had let the remainder of its Alban Gate office block continued to lift the shares, in a generally positive property sector. MEPC, which touched 369p, was finally 3 up at 361p. British Fittings plunged 48 to 105p after the building group announced losses, trading difficulties and the need for a new chairman. Broker Hoare Govett decided that Thorn EMI was undervalued, citing the potential for expansion in the music market, and in particular new music formats such as Digital Compact Cassette. The shares rose 6 to 857p. Lehman Brothers' downgrading of Allied-Lyons continued to weigh on the drinks and food giant, pushing the shares 9 lower to 630p. Speculation about a possible takeover bid has also faded of late. BAT Industries, which reports first-quarter figures today, was wanted, the shares advancing 14 to 781p as turnover rose to 2.8m on speculation that profits may be higher than anticipated. P & O moved ahead 10 to 515p after Smith New Court reiterated its buy recommendation on the stock. Mr Clive Anderson at Smith said the company has 'an undemanding multiple for a recovery play and an attractive yield'. Motor components manufacturer BSG International closed 1 1/2 firmer at 64p after Smith New Court and Panmure Gordon successfully placed the 29.7 per cent stake held by Sir Ron Brierley with institutions. The majority of the 60m-share holding, which was bought by the brokers at 61 1/2 p, was placed at 62p, while a block of 13.5m was placed in ex-dividend form at 59 1/2 p. DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / World Stock Markets (America): Late program selling causes Dow to recede
DOC.TEXT: Wall Street US EQUITIES moved in a narrow range in quiet trading throughout most of the day, before a late round of program selling pushed the Dow Jones Industrial Average lower after closing at a record high on Monday, writes Karen Zagor in New York. The Dow ended 18.78 off at 3,359.35, but advances led declines at the close by 934 to 779 after NYSE volume of 200m shares. The Standard & Poor's 500 edged down 0.07 to 417.40, but the Nasdaq composite of over-the-counter stocks gained 4.53 at 588.07. Blue chip issues dominated the actives list on the NYSE, with PepsiCo slipping Dollars 1/2 to Dollars 36 1/8 , American Express rising Dollars 1/4 to Dollars 22 1/2 and Sears Roebuck losing Dollars 1/4 to Dollars 43 3/4 Transportation issues were strong, with the Dow Jones Transportation Average up 13.46 to 1,394.25. AMR, parent of American Airlines, added Dollars 2 at Dollars 68 7/8 and UAL, parent of United Airlines, rose Dollars 1 1/4 to Dollars 126 1/4 . Delta Air Lines lost Dollars 3/8 to Dollars 59 3/4 . Shortly before the close of trading, Moody's Investors Service said it was reviewing Delta for a possible downgrade. Cigna put on Dollars 3/4 to Dollars 52 1/2 . The insurance company's first-quarter earnings of Dollars 1.48 a share, against 67 cents a year earlier, were released after the close of trade on Monday. Glaxo Holding's American Depositary Receipts rose Dollars 3/8 to Dollars 27 in heavy trading. The company's Zofran drug received marketing approval in the UK for use in preventing and treating post-operative nausea. The approval comes only days after UK regulators approved marketing of Glaxo's migraine drug. April car sales figures from Ford and Chrysler spurred active trading in both issues. Chrysler turned in a 38 per cent jump in truck sales for the month while car sales rose 5 per cent. The company said April was its best month for total vehicle sales in nearly two years. Ford's car sales advanced 5.5 per cent while truck sales rose 19.2 per cent. Shares in Ford eased Dollars 1/8 to Dollars 44 7/8 and Chrysler dipped Dollars 1/8 to Dollars 18 5/8 . ITT climbed Dollars 2 5/8 to Dollars 66 5/8 in active trading on news that it is planning a new share repurchase programme for common and convertible preferred for up to 25m equivalent common shares. The repurchase plan is intended to help the company achieve a 15 per cent return on equity by 1996. Santa Fe Pacific slipped Dollars 1/4 to Dollars 12 7/8 on news that it had filed for a secondary offering with the Securities and Exchange Commission to allow beleaguered Canadian property developer Olympia & York to sell its 18 per cent stake in the railway company. Technology issues performed well on both the big board and in over-the-counter trading. On the NYSE, IBM climbed Dollars 1 3/8 to Dollars 93 7/8 and Hewlett Packard Dollars 1 1/8 to Dollars 81 5/8 . In over-the-counter trading, Microsoft moved ahead Dollars 2 1/2 to Dollars 116 1/2 but Apple Computer held steady at Dollars 60 1/2 . Canada TORONTO stocks retraced early gains to end flat. An analyst said the market is waiting for results from Olympia & York's meeting in London with its bankers, the end to the US Treasury refunding tomorrow, and Friday's US and Canada unemployment figures for April. The composite index closed just a point up at 3,364.5, while falls finally outnumbered rises by 282 to 262. Volume was 23m shares. The gold group stood out with a 2.7 per cent rise. Ipsco fell CDollars 1 1/8 to CDollars 18 7/8 . The company said it will sell 2.4m common shares to a group of underwriters for CDollars 18.75 a share.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Foreign Exchanges: Sterling slips after rate cut
DOC.TEXT: STERLING held most attention in the foreign currency markets yesterday, after the Bank of England signalled a 1/2 percentage point cut in UK base rates, writes James Blitz. The UK currency dipped below DM2.92 shortly after lunch as investors who had bought sterling at around DM2.88 after the April general election took profits. However, traders reported a large amount of corporate buying of the currency shortly afterwards to help sterling finish at DM2.9250, half a pfennig down from its previous close. It also ended down against the dollar, at Dollars 1.7825, off 1/4 cent. Against its trade weighted index, the pound closed at 92.2 after opening at 92.4. In New York, sterling rallied to end at Dollars 1.7863. Analysts believe that, in spite of its late recovery yesterday, the rate reduction carries some downside risk for the UK currency. 'The gap between German and UK rates is now wafer thin,' said Mr Neil MacKinnon, chief economist of Yamaichi International, 'and leaves sterling with little by way of support. The move has also shown the market that the UK authorities are prepared to use any chance they can to lower interest rates.' Mr Gerard Lyons, chief economist of DKB International, also believes that the cut carries risks. 'It showed that the authorities are more worried about the weakness of the economy than anything else,' he said. High German rates were yesterday unsettling the US dollar as well. In European and North American trading, the US currency eased against the D-Mark, partly due to renewed hopes of a solution to the German labour strike. But the interest rate differentials between German and American rates were irresistible. As one dealer said: 'Germany may have its industrial problems. But it is hard to ignore that you can get 9 3/4 per cent interest on the D-Mark compared to about 3 3/4 per cent with the dollar.' In Europe, the dollar finished at DM1.6405, against DM1.6410. In New York it closed at DM1.6370. The only major currency not to lose out to the D-Mark yesterday was the French franc, which still enjoys investor popularity. An article in Le Monde, the French daily paper, suggested that there could be an impending revaluation of the currency. The D-Mark ended at around FFr3.3690, after opening at FFr3.3696. The dollar's difficulties stemmed mostly from last week's indifferent economic indicators. Analysts believe that employment data due at the end of this week should show a modest but positive improvement, but that investors will have to wait until further into the month of May before seeing clear signs of a recovery. The US unit closed at Y133.10, against a previous Y132.70. It was finally Y132.85 in New York.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Money Markets: Bank cuts base rate
DOC.TEXT: THE BANK of England signalled a 1/2 percentage point cut in UK interest rates yesterday by offering lower rates at the short end of its dealing operations in the discount market. The base rate reduction to 10 per cent was the first rate cut for nine months, but the market appeared unsure as to what time scale to put on money at this level of interest. After signalling a shortage of around Pounds 900m, the Bank purchased Pounds 10m of Band-1 Treasury bills at 9 7/8 per cent, Pounds 659m of Band-1 bank bills at 9 7/8 per cent, and Pounds 5m of Band-2 bank bills at 9 7/8 per cent. That interest rate compared with a rate of 10 3/8 per cent offered for short-term bills in Bands-1 and 2 last week. The forecast was later revised to a shortage of around Pounds 950m before taking account of the early operations. The bank subsequently purchased Pounds 300m of Band-2 bank bills at 9 7/8 per cent. The overnight rate fell in line with the rate cuts, reaching a low on the day of 7 3/4 per cent and finishing at around 9 7/8 per cent. Other period rates, however, indicated, if anything, that the market expects this to be the last rate cut for some time. The rate for three-month money finished at 10 3/16 - 1/8 per cent, compared with 10 1/2 - 3/8 per cent one week ago. Further out, the rates ended at 10 3/16 - 1/16 per cent for everything from four-month money to one year. In the futures market, volumes were high in the wake of the base rate cut. After trading in a 12-tick range, the June short sterling contract finished at 89.92, after a high of 89.99. The closing price indicates an implied interest rate in June of 10.08 per cent, roughly in line with a 10 per cent base rate. The market's eyes are now fixed on whether the German Bundesbank might raise rates, a move that would put pressure on sterling following yesterday's reduction. Close attention will be paid to Thursday's meeting of the Bundesbank's general council. 'Nobody in the market expects the Bundesbank to raise rates on Thursday,' said Mr Gerard Lyons, chief economist of DKB International. 'But there is a fear that German money supply figures for April will ratchet up again.' As a result, the market's focus is even more firmly set on the Bundesbank meeting in two week's time, after the M3 figures have come out.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Government Bonds: Reduction in lending rates prompts selling of gilts
DOC.BYLINE: By SIMON LONDON and KAREN ZAGOR
DOC.TEXT: THE UK government bond market gave a cool reaction to yesterday's easing in monetary conditions, with cash bond and futures prices closing lower. Dealers said trading was dominated by investors taking profits following the strong performance of the gilts market since the Conservative election victory. The Bank of England signalled a 1/2 -point cut in base lending rates in morning money-market operations, supplying short-term liquidity to the banking system just below 10 per cent. The move was widely anticipated in the gilts market, but caused significant selling. The long-gilt futures contract on Liffe, the London exchange, opened at 99.00 but quickly fell to 97 15/16 following the rate cut. Through the afternoon session sentiment improved and the contract stood at 98 7/32 in late afternoon. Volume was heavy at 51,000 contracts. In the cash market, selling was concentrated at the longer maturities. The 9 per cent gilt maturing 2011, the benchmark long-dated government stock, opened at 99 31/32 and closed at 99 13/32 for a yield of 9.06 per cent. Shorter-dated stocks fared better. The 10 per cent gilt maturing 1994 closed down 1/16 of a point on the day at 101 1/8 , for a yield of 9.44 per cent. In addition to profit-taking, the market was unsettled by uncertainty over the outlook for UK inflation as the economy pulls out of recession. Analysts' forecasts for the annual rate of inflation during April range from 4.2 per cent to around 5 per cent. Official data is due to be released on May 15. Lower interest rates were also seen as threatening the position of sterling within the European exchange rate mechanism. The UK currency fell from DM2.93 before the easing was signalled to just above DM2.92 by late afternoon. Moreover, yesterday's interest rate reduction may be the last for some time. Most economists are forecasting one more rate cut before the year-end. 'There is not much good news on the horizon now,' said Mr Phillip Tyson, gilt market analysts at UBS Phillips & Drew. 'There is no incentive now to chase yields lower.' Another factor depressing gilts prices at the medium maturities is a partially unsold tap issue announced by the Bank of England on Friday. Dealers estimated yesterday that only around half of the Pounds 800m issue of 8 3/4 per cent gilts maturing 1997 had been sold. GERMAN government bonds moved lower yesterday with investors concerned over continued public sector strikes and plans to introduce withholding tax on interest income from bond market investments. The 8 per cent Unity fund bond maturing 2002 was trading at 99.64 in late afternoon, for a yield of 8.06 per cent, from around 99.68 at the opening. The June bund futures contract on Liffe opened at 87.11 but moved down to 86.70 during the day, before recovering to close at 86.86. Volume was very heavy at 83,000 contracts. Analysts said the government was likely to increase its 4.6 per cent pay offer to striking public sector workers at talks this week. A final settlement much above this level would increase fears of wage inflation, driving up prices throughout the economy and higher interest rates. The Bundesbank council holds its bi-weekly meeting on Thursday, although few analysts are expecting an immediate rate increase. The market was unsettled by indications that the opposition Social Democratic party, which controls the lower house of parliament, would vote against the government's compromise withholding tax proposals. If the current package of measures is rejected, more stringent measures may be applied. US TREASURY prices firmed slightly yesterday afternoon, on the back of a satisfactory three-year note auction in the first leg of the Treasury's Dollars 36bn refunding auction. In late trading, the Treasury's bellwether 30-year bond was 3/16 higher at 99 15/16 , yielding 8.00 per cent while the two-year note was up 1/32 to yield 5.26 per cent. The Federal Reserve added liquidity to the banking system by arranging Dollars 1.5bn in customer repurchase agreements in the open market when Fed funds were trading at 3 3/4 per cent. The move was widely expected. The Treasury sold Dollars 15bn of three-year notes at an average yield of 5.96 per cent with a coupon of 5.875 per cent.
