The prime minister is sympathetic to the growing criticism of the civil and military honours, which many mandarins, MPs and members of the armed forces receive almost by right - rather than for their contribution to society. Downing Street officials emphasised, however, that 'nothing is going to happen in the immediate future'. Mr Major believes he made a start in changing the priorities for awards in last June's Gulf war honours list, when he deliberately put emphasis on rewarding meritorious service regardless of rank. Reforming the honours system would fit Mr Major's pledge to push for a 'classless' society. Mrs Margaret Thatcher, the former prime minister, reinstituted political honours, including hereditary peerages, for long-serving politicians. Changes to the system would, however, be supported by many Tory MPs. Sir Peter Emery, chairman of the Commons procedure committee, said: 'The honours system has a role to play in British society but it should be based on merit and the individual contribution of a person - rather than the length of time they have served in a particular job.' Mr Richard Shepherd, Conservative MP for Aldridge-Brownhills, said on BBC Radio: 'The automatic assumption that you get knighthoods or gongs is, I think, very out of date.' Other senior backbench Conservative MPs would also back reform of the honours system but, perhaps looking at their own prospects, refused yesterday to comment publicly.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Northern Ireland talks resume
DOC.TEXT: ROUND-TABLE talks between Northern Ireland party leaders on the political future of the province resumed in Belfast yesterday. A news blackout was maintained as leaders of the Ulster Unionists, Democratic Unionists, Social Democratic and Labour party and the Alliance party arrived at Stormont for the second session under the chairmanship of Sir Patrick Mayhew, Northern Ireland secretary. On Monday, Unionists and the SDLP were at loggerheads over the SDLP's decision to travel to Dublin to brief Irish Prime Minister Mr Albert Reynolds on the recently restarted search for an agreed system of devolution. If the political leaders agree an agenda for the talks, they will meet again tomorrow and from next week are expected to meet on Mondays, Tuesdays and Wednesdays.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Doctor seeks political cure for Belfast's ills: The difficult task facing Dr Joe Hendron in Gerry Adams' former constituency
DOC.TEXT: THE political landscape has changed in West Belfast, where the predominant Roman Catholic population lives in gritty red-brick houses, in a physical landscape not helped by bomb damage and metal grilles on traffic lights and pub windows. Dr Joe Hendron, the freshly elected Social Democratic and Labour party MP, is a moderate nationalist who cheerfully provokes republican hardliners after narrowly winning the seat on April 9. 'They are extremely hostile to me because they were beaten in the election,' he says. Dr Hendron, who will work within the UK political system, has replaced Mr Gerry Adams, president of Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, who would not. Because it supports violence, Mr Adams' party is excluded from round-table talks on the province's future which began again yesterday. Dr Hendron estimates that he was helped by about 1,500 Protestants in Unionist enclaves who voted tactically. Sinn Fein said those voters supported loyalist paramilitaries; Dr Hendron says that is 'an extreme insult'. Smouldering tensions in his constituency flared with the murder by loyalist terrorists last week of a 26-year-old mother, Mrs Philomena Hanna, at a chemist's shop on Springfield Road. Dr Hendron was jostled by Sinn Fein supporters as he visited the site. 'Hendron's voters killed Philomena,' read posters. If Dr Hendron, aged 59 and a GP since the 'troubles' began, was supposed to be a conciliator, his first action, prompted by Mrs Hanna's death, was regressive. After urgent consultations with the Royal Ulster Constabulary, the gates along the 'peace line' - a spiked barrier that rises as high as bedroom windows on houses along the Protestant and Roman Catholic divide - were closed. In justification, the loquacious MP shows a card he was given at an interdenominational service after the killing. 'This was handed out to all the people. 'The walls of separation do not reach to Heaven.' That is what I would say. 'So many politicians are screaming 'These gates must be kept open', but they are not living on the peace line. People are very frightened.' A greater test will be Dr Hendron's performance over coming years. Non-participation in the Westminster system has been ingrained among radical Irish nationalists for decades. Dr Hendron wants to work with Northern Ireland Office ministers to encourage investment in West Belfast, drumming up interest in the US, Canada and elsewhere. He also wants to talk with the police and Army about ending harassment. Mr Adams did nothing, he says. Mr Richard McAuley, Sinn Fein's spokesman, responds: 'We have a very well-run constituency service which provides a useful service in West Belfast. Unlike Joe Hendron, we did not engage in making promises we could not keep.' Dr Hendron is also part of the SDLP delegation at the round-table talks - hoping to deliver a deal by which local politicians can be given real political control. When he canvassed on Unionist housing estates, the 1985 Anglo-Irish Agreement - supported by the SDLP but despised by Unionists because of the role it gives the Irish republic - was top of the agenda. 'I said, 'But isn't that what the talks are about?' I said that the Anglo-Irish Agreement is not a sacred cow.' Success in the talks would require huge compromises with the Unionist community. West Belfast would need much convincing.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Mortgage lenders to follow lead: Immediate response to base rate cut IoD welcomes 'stimulus' Retail confidence encouraged
DOC.TEXT: HALIFAX, the largest UK building society, cut its standard mortgage interest rate by 0.3 percentage points to 10.65 per cent within an hour of the base rate cut being announced. Mr Jim Birrell, Halifax chief executive, described the latest base rate cut as good news for home buyers. The reduced rate applies immediately to new borrowers but the society declined to say yesterday when the 0.3 point cut would be applied to existing mortgage customers. The reduction means a saving of Pounds 10.63 a month on a Pounds 50,000 endowment mortgage and Pounds 8.91 on a repayment mortgage of the same size. Halifax's move took the rest of the mortgage industry by surprise. Mr John Bayliss, managing director of Abbey National, the second-largest UK mortgage lender, said later in the day that Abbey National would also reduce its rates by 0.3 of a point. Leeds Permanent, the fifth-largest society, said it would lower its rates later this week. The other societies have little option but to follow Halifax and Abbey National, but they will do so with serious misgivings about the effect on their balance sheets. Although most mortgage lenders agree that some sort of stimulus is needed to encourage the housing market to revive, many building societies are under strong market pressure on both the lending and the savings sides. In January, following Abbey National's lead, Halifax and the other building societies cut their rates to borrowers to about 10.95 per cent, less than 0.5 of a point above the base rate. Some societies have said privately that they would like to put up mortgage rates to be able to pay savers more. Halifax's move means that this will not now be possible. The flow of retail savings into building societies accounts been disappointing for several months, partly because of competition from National Savings. By cutting their rates to mortgage customers now, building societies will also have to reduce their rates to savers. Mr Dick Spellman, general manager for marketing at Halifax, said yesterday that it was too early to say how the savings market would settle down. He said Halifax and other societies were experiencing a reduced inflow of savings because they were having to compete against 'overpriced' one-year and two-year offers from National Savings. Mr John Simson, chairman of Connell, the estate agency chain owned by Scottish Widows, said he was uncertain how much difference the latest interest rate cut would make to the housing market. He said there had been no sign of a recovery in April. The clearing banks yesterday said that they had their mortgage rates under review, but the centralised lenders are likely to have more difficulty in making a reduction. Mortgage lending was very subdued in the first quarter of the year, growing by only 1.5 per cent over the previous, the Council for Mortgage Lenders said yesterday. New lending during the quarter was Pounds 4.6bn, down from Pounds 5.4bn during the final quarter of 1991. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- MORTGAGE PAYMENT CHANGES ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Monthly payments on a 25 year mortgage Endowment Loan size Previous rate New rate Difference pounds percent pounds percent pounds pounds 30,000 10.95 205.33 10.65 199.70 5.63 50,000 10.95 387.83 10.65 377.20 10.63 APEX 80,000 10.50 634.38 10.20 616.25 18.13 100,000 10.30 793.96 10.00 770.84 23.12 150,000 10.30 1223.13 10.00 1187.50 35.63 200,000 10.30 1652.30 10.00 1604.17 48.13 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Repayment 30,000 10.95 238.47 10.65 233.96 4.51 50,000 10.95 424.52 10.65 415.61 8.91 APEX 80,000 10.50 697.24 10.20 682.03 15.21 100,000 10.30 874.95 10.00 855.57 19.38 150,000 10.30 1344.62 10.00 1314.60 30.02 200,000 10.30 1814.28 10.00 1773.63 40.65 ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Source: Halifax Building Society based on a 0.3% cut in rates -----------------------------------------------------------------------

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Pay fall lends hope for training
DOC.TEXT: THE PAY of young adults aged between 18 and 20 has fallen sharply as a proportion of adult wages since 1979, according to data collected by the Low Pay Unit, the research group. The fall, from 61 per cent of adult wages to 53 per cent, has been greeted by some economists and employers as an important step towards increasing the number of training places for young people. Ms Vivien Marshall, head of education and training at the Engineering Employers Federation, said: 'This is an encouraging sign, which could lead to more, and better-quality, training places.' She said there was a widely accepted correlation between young people's pay and the training opportunities employers offered. Youth pay in Germany used to be almost half the UK rate, which was one reason for some German employers overtraining, to the benefit of the economy as a whole, she added. The Low Pay Unit, which backs moves to restore income support for people aged 16 to 19, cut in 1988, also found that pay for those aged 16 and 17 had fallen from 43 per cent of adult pay in 1979 to 33 per cent. Young, Gifted and Broke. Low Pay Unit, 27-29 Amwell Street, London EC1R 1UN.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Wary traders see signs of modest recovery
DOC.BYLINE: By JOHN THORNHILL, PHILIP RAWSTORNE and GARY MEAD
DOC.TEXT: THE HESITANT twitchings of life in high streets across the country since the general election have been encouraged by yesterday's cut in interest rates. Mr James May, director-general of the British Retail Consortium, which represents nine tenths of the retail sector, sees modest recovery in most sectors. He says: 'It is hard to say what the figures are with certainty but there does seem to have been a sustained pick-up in demand over the past two to three weeks.' Special factors cloud the picture: last April's increase in VAT to 17.5 per cent from April 1, this year's late Easter, the uncertainty caused by the election, and the recent fine weather. Yet confidence is recovering, although no one expects a rapid switch in mood. Mr Brian Stewart, chief executive of Scottish & Newcastle, the brewing, retail and leisure group, said: 'As yet, we have seen only spasmodic signs of recovery and I do not think anyone should expect a sudden surge in consumer confidence and spending - but this is a positive and timely move.' Mr Terry Maher, chief executive of Pentos, which runs Dillons bookshops and Ryman stationery shops, predicts only an 'anaemic' recovery. 'People's confidence has been shattered and that does not change suddenly or dramatically,' he says. 'In my view there is nothing more important than that interest rates are now brought down as rapidly as possible. There will be no sustained improvement in consumer demand unless and until that happens.' Other voices still urge restraint. Mr May, of the BRC, says: 'Many retailers would like to see a bigger and quicker reductions in interest rates, but the cautious approach is right in the long run. It is vitally important that interest rate cuts are sustainable and sustained.' That largely depends on what happens elsewhere in Europe. As Mr Derek Bowden, media director at the Saatchi & Saatchi advertising agency, says: 'Until the German economy has fully resolved its problems, this does not herald a significant move for the UK economy.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Industry faults size of cut
DOC.TEXT: INDUSTRIAL reaction to the cut in interest rates yesterday was mixed. All sectors welcomed the cut but there were complaints about its timing and size. Many said the real impact would be in terms of confidence rather than immediate cash. The Institute of Directors was most bullish, saying that it was the 'best possible stimulus' for British business to pull the economy out of recession. The Confederation of British Industry said the base rate cut was 'not before time'. Sir John Banham, CBI director-general, said the move reflected the underlying strength of the economy as well as the progress on inflation. 'It will provide a useful boost to business confidence at an important time,' he said. 'But real interest rates remain very high for manufacturers especially. It is important the downward trend is maintained.' In the construction sector, Mr Peter Parkin, chief executive of Raine, said: 'A slow thaw appears to have begun in the housing market. The latest cut in base rates can only help this progress.' Mr Colin Hope, chairman of motor components group T&N and president of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, emphasised the psychological importance of the cut. He said: 'It's a question of confidence, not cash. I detect a sense among business people that we're moving in the right direction. People are more optimistic. But perhaps most helpful is the extent to which we are winning business in Germany, whose costs are going out of control. This latest cut will help further.' Mr Ian Coomber, Vauxhall's director of sales, said the reduction should serve a useful role 'in transforming already reviving customer interest into customer orders'. As a result of slowly reviving confidence, the company now believes the UK market for new cars might reach about 1.7m units, up from 1.59m last year. Many companies felt the impact would be negligible, however. Some have built up exports to such an extent that a cut in domestic rates would have little impact on demand. Others have long fixed-term loans and are unaffected in the short term. Many were more interested in the effect of the cut on the strength of sterling. Mr Graham Hearne, chairman and chief executive of Enterprise Oil, the UK oil exploration and production company, welcomed an interest rate cut that would stimulate demand for oil, but said a weakening in sterling against the US dollar would have a more meaningful effect on his business. Alps Electric, the Japanese electric and electronics group, said the rate cut affected it inasmuch as it affected the strength of sterling, since the group directly or indirectly exported about 80 per cent of products it manufactured in the UK. Courtaulds, the chemicals and materials group, said the effect of the cut would be negligible. It was simply too little. Mr Martin Smith, finance director at Witton, a small speciality chemicals company, agreed that the cut was too little, too late. Although the company was not heavily borrowed, he argued the real problem was the D-Mark, which was keeping real interest rates far too high. Electronics manufacturers expressed limited hope that the rate cut would have a significant positive effect by encouraging business investment and consumer spending. Canon, the Japanese camera and office equipment maker, has suffered from a tendency among business to postpone investment decisions during the recession. It said: 'Obviously it's good in that hopefully it will stimulate some kind of recovery.' Many electronics manufacturers do not think the 0.5-percentage-point rate cut is large enough to boost spending significantly at once. Panasonic said: 'It means (the UK economy) is moving in the right direction.' But the cut was not big enough to have a significant effect because people still felt the economy was depressed and would take more time to recover. Mr Malcolm Chatwin, chief executive of Yorkshire Electricity, said the cut would have little impact on the regional electricity companies, which are typically long-term investors.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / National Savings trims rates
DOC.BYLINE: By PHILIP COGGAN, Personal Finance Editor
DOC.TEXT: NATIONAL Savings is cutting the returns on most of its products. The government department said the rates it offered had diverged from the rest of the savings market. The main changes are: The 36th issue of certificates (which paid 8.5 per cent a year tax-free if held for five years) has been withdrawn from sale and will be replaced by the 37th issue on May 13. The new issue will pay 8 per cent. The return on the yearly plan will also fall from 8.5 per cent to 8 per cent. The series C capital bonds (which paid a taxable 11.5 per cent a year if held for five years) have been withdrawn. They will be replaced by series D bonds paying 10.75 per cent. The rate on income bonds will be reduced from a taxable 10.25 per cent to 9.25 per cent from June 18. The rate on the investment account will be reduced from 9.5 per cent to 8.5 per cent from May 18.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Usdaw to fight Sunday law
DOC.TEXT: THE SHOP WORKERS' union, Usdaw, has moved to counter government proposals for legislation to expand Sunday trading, expected in today's Queen's speech. Delegates at the union's annual conference unanimously backed their executive committee's call to move the focus of the anti-Sunday trading campaign to influencing new legislation and away from simple condemnation of shops trading illegally. Mr Bill Connor, deputy general secretary, said the union would continue to call for law enforcement, but delegates had to realise that large stores would continue to trade illegally. The union gave qualified support for the so-called 'rest' proposals, of the Keep Sunday Special, the anti-Sunday-trading lobby. It will also press Euro-Fiet, the body that represents the interests of shop workers at European community level, to join Usdaw in sponsoring a conference on trading hours legislation. Earlier, the union reaffirmed its support for wages councils, the bodies that set minimum statutory pay levels for about 2.5m workers, of which more than 1m are shop workers.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / PowerGen workers balloted on wages
DOC.TEXT: UNIONS at PowerGen, one of the privatised electricity companies, are balloting their members on the first local pay package in the electricity industry. The 6,500 employees are expected to accept the package, which has been negotiated over the past year with the five unions representing the majority of employees. The last national pay settlement in the electricity supply industry was negotiated this year, with a 5.5 per cent settlement for 1992-93. Employers then gave 12 months' notice of their intention to negotiate locally next year. PowerGen is believed to be the first of the 19 main employers to have drawn up an offer. According to Personnel Today, the specialist magazine, a single document has been drawn up to replace the three existing agreements for industrial, engineering and administrative workers. PowerGen said yesterday the deal proposed harmonisation of terms and conditions for all employees, with a single pay structure for all staff. Holiday entitlement, for example, would be harmonised so that entitlement would be related to the grade an individual was on within a job category. In addition flexible working and single-table bargaining with the unions were proposed. The electricity companies are likely to pursue widely differing strategies because of their local situations.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Rise seen in company ethics codes
DOC.TEXT: THE PROPORTION of large companies with a written ethical code is rising sharply and stands at nearly 30 per cent, according to a survey published yesterday. Policies on relations with employees and customers and on sexual harassment dominate ethical codes, says the study by the Institute of Business Ethics, a think tank. There has also been a sharp growth in statements on environmental policy in the past two years, said Mr Simon Webley, author of the report. Twenty-nine per cent of the replies from 164 leading companies said that they had a statement of business ethics in 1991. That compared with 18 per cent when the survey was last conducted in 1987. A fifth of companies with codes were UK subsidiaries of foreign-owned corporations, most of which were American. Those had more detailed and lengthy codes than British parent companies, and discussed staff involvement in the community more frequently. Most companies with written codes commented on their obligations to employees, including equal opportunities, remuneration and development, and listening to staff. By contrast, very few mentioned duties to shareholders. Some discussed obligations to customers, such as the provision of high-quality products. A smaller number mentioned their responsibilities to suppliers, such as prompt payment or policies on giving and receiving gifts. In 37 per cent of cases, the chief executive or chairman was the person who felt responsible for the company's ethics. Lord Laing, institute president and former chairman of United Biscuits, urged all companies to produce a code and said that shareholders should call for the introduction of codes at companies' annual meeting. Eleven per cent of companies gave reasons why they did not have written codes, including a belief that it was unnecessary because they always acted ethically, or that policies should be determined by individual subsidiaries. Business ethics and company codes. Institute of Business Ethics, 12 Palace Street, London SW1E 5JA. Pounds 15.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Staff discounts freed of VAT
DOC.TEXT: EMPLOYERS selling discounted goods to staff will be required to levy VAT only on the reduced price. This is a reversal by Customs and Excise of its position. The decision follows complaints from employers and comes into effect from May 15.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Outhwaite action is stepped up
DOC.TEXT: NAMES ON Lloyd's troubled Outhwaite syndicate who missed out from February's Pounds 116m out-of-court settlement yesterday agreed to step up their own legal action to recover losses. Writs alleging negligence by the Outhwaite Underwriting Agency and 81 other members' agencies, were issued last week on behalf of 393 Names - the individuals who provide backing for the insurance market. Mr Eddie Kulukundis, yesterday elected chairman of the 1992 Outhwaite Names' Association, said the group would now aim to enlist as many as possible of the 627 non-litigants to the February action before serving the writs.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Cheques found in rubbish skip
DOC.TEXT: BANK OF Scotland said last night that it could not explain how 20 envelopes containing cheques for payment for the second instalment of ScottishPower shares had come to be dumped in a rubbish skip in Edinburgh last week. According to the Edinburgh Evening News, a refuse worker opened some of the envelopes and saw cheques, including one for Pounds 26,000. Bank of Scotland is handling the payment of the second instalment of 70p on shares in ScottishPower and Scottish Hydro-Electric, which was due by April 29. Bank of Scotland said shareholders who did not receive certificates by May 15 should contact the bank.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / BT and Visa agreement
DOC.TEXT: HOLDERS of Visa credit and debit cards will soon be able to pay for domestic and international telephone calls on their card account under a deal between British Telecom and Visa International. VisaPhone, which is already available in the US, allows callers to provide their card number and an identification number to pay for calls. The system will be fully introduced in the UK early next year. Visitors to the UK will be able to bill calls to their Visa card in local currency. UK banks which issue Visa cards are expected to offer the service in the next few months.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Gold reserves rise by Dollars 63m
DOC.TEXT: BRITAIN'S gold and foreign currency reserves rose by an underlying Dollars 63m last month, the Treasury said yesterday. The overall level - which includes cash gained from sales of Ecu-denominated Treasury bills and other changes - rose by Dollars 748m to reach Dollars 45.8bn on April 30.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Car deal will create 500 jobs in Wales
DOC.TEXT: NEARLY 500 jobs are to be created in West Glamorgan, south Wales, as a result of a contract to supply wiring systems to Japanese car plants in the UK, John Griffiths writes. The contract - the second won by the joint venture company between Lucas and Sumitomo Electrical Industries of Japan - is worth Pounds 20m a year. Lucas SEI Wiring Systems' plant at Ystradgynlais will supply Honda's manufacturing plant at Swindon, Wiltshire, due to go on stream in the autumn.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Channel 5 writ against TV-am
DOC.TEXT: FIVE TV, one of the companies planning to bid for the Channel 5 licence, yesterday issued a writ against TV-am, the breakfast television company, for alleged breach of contract. Last week TV-am signed an agreement to bid for the franchise in a consortium that included Time Warner, the world's largest media organisation, and Mr Conrad Black's Daily Telegraph group. Mr Bruce Gyngell, TV-am chairman, was to be chairman of the consortium, to be called The Entertainment Channel. Yesterday Five TV, whose investors include Mr Moses Znaimer, founder of City TV in Toronto, said TV-am had signed a document in January agreeing not to invest in any other applicant for the Channel 5 licence other than Five TV. TV-am - which lost its ITV franchise in last year's competitive tenders - last night conceded that it had signed what appeared to be such an undertaking, but by mistake. The company said Mr Stratis Zographos, the TV-am finance director, had signed what he thought was a normal confidentiality agreement in order to be able to see the proposed Five TV business plan. It had then discovered a line about not investing in a rival Channel 5 bid. It said it would defend any legal action. Mr Gyngell said: 'We signed what we thought was a normal confidentiality agreement. We regard that line (about a rival bid) as a restraint of trade and that is also senior counsel's opinion.' TV-am is surprised at the timing of the legal action because both Mr Jeremy Fox, the chief executive of The Entertainment Channel, and Mr David Frost, the broadcaster and TV-am founder, have been in Toronto for talks with Mr Znaimer about a possible merger between the two bidders. The main choice for the Channel 5 licence may turn out to be between Five TV, which plans a mainly city-based service, and something like The Entertainment Channel, offering a largely national service.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Wandsworth set to axe comprehensives
DOC.TEXT: TORY-controlled Wandsworth council in south-west London last night voted to abandon comprehensive education and make its secondary schools selective. The council endorsed a decision by its education committee which will allow three of the borough's schools to organise their own admissions, with 11-plus-style entry tests, possibly by September 1993. Under the controversial plan, drawn up by director of education Mr Donald Naismith, Wandsworth hopes its schools will become 'centres of excellence' specialising in subjects such as languages or design. Mr Naismith denied, however, that the change represented a return to secondary-modern and grammar schools. The proposals will allow schools to select pupils on the grounds of aptitude and compatibility with the school. Parents whose children are unsuccessful in obtaining a place at their chosen school would be able to appeal to the council, which will keep a register of unfilled places. But the Department of Education and Science has advised against the council being able to nominate pupils for 10 per cent of the places at each school. Mr Edward Lister, chairman of the council education committee, said Wandsworth was 'turning its back on 30 years of centralised planning because it doesn't work'. The National Union of Teachers said the plan failed to recognise that comprehensive schools brought wider opportunities for all children - not just expanded opportunities for the selected few. Editorial Comment, Page 18

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Prince Charming finds his Cinderella: Michael Heseltine outlines his strategy for the trade and industry department
DOC.TEXT: WHEN Mr Michael Heseltine was offered the job of trade and industry secretary three weeks ago he chose to revive the title of president of the board of trade. It is a potent symbol of the political clout he has brought to a job that had become one of the Cinderellas of successive Conservative administrations. Already his staff refer to him simply as 'the president'. But Mr Heseltine is also a political realist. If he is to deliver a partnership between government and industry - mapped out during his political exile under Mrs Margaret Thatcher - there will be battles to be fought, not least with the Treasury. So yesterday it took 30 minutes to prise from him a phrase to encapsulate his new role in Mr John Major's government: 'My job is to help British industry to win . . . commerce and industry to win.' Speaking to the FT in his first interview since his appointment, Mr Heseltine was concerned to damp speculation that he had arrived with a bagful of instant solutions. 'I know that industrial success, commercial success is essentially a long-term phenomenon,' he said. 'The great danger is to try to adopt the psychology of the fairy godmother.' He intends to build a closer relationship between government and industry - to establish over time what he calls an industrial strategy. Yet he is not in the business of raising expectations that he cannot meet. His starting point is that his advocacy of such a strategy is still misunderstood. For others it conjures up images of 'picking winners' or subsidies for sunset industries. He said: 'What I have always meant by an industrial strategy is an awareness in government of the impact that government can have on industry as a consequence of the many interfaces between the role of government and the wealth-creating process.' That rather long-winded explanation can be condensed as follows: since government decisions are constantly impinging on the nation's businesses, it is up to the DTI to introduce some coherence into the process. Mr Heseltine promises to be a sympathetic listener. His predecessors - Mr Peter Lilley and Mr Nicholas Ridley - never managed to persuade industrial leaders that they particularly cared about anything beyond deregulation. Their successor likes dialogue. 'I've always believed in all government departments, including this one, that you should talk and listen carefully to the industries, to the companies, which you sponsor.' It was such dialogue, he added, that led to the creation of the European Space Agency and brought lucrative contracts for British industry from the European Fighter Aircraft project. 'Some people believe that talking to people is a sign of weakness,' he said. 'I've never believed that.' What about action? In his books, Mr Heseltine had after all set out in some detail how the DTI should co-ordinate government industrial strategy. It should replace the Treasury in the lead role at a strengthened National Economic Development Office. A cabinet committee should be established to take a broad view of departmental decisions which affect business. Mergers policy should be less tightly drawn to include a wider judgment of the national interest as well as the impact on competition of proposed mergers and takeovers. Here Mr Heseltine became distinctly cagey. He did not disavow completely such ambitions but was careful to stress that they were not prerequisites. A new cabinet committee under his direction was a matter 'for the prime minister'. It was perfectly possible to take a strategic view of government's relations with industry within existing cabinet committees. On mergers policy - perhaps the most sensitive of his responsibilities - he will say practically nothing. His approach to the battle for Midland Bank between Lloyds Bank and Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation should reveal some of his thinking. For now, though, he insists that any change in the so-called Tebbit doctrine would require a collective decision by the cabinet. 'I have inherited a set of (merger) policies, Until and unless any announcements are made those policies prevail.' So what were his immediate priorities? Some set themselves. Britain's forthcoming presidency of the European Community will put Mr Heseltine in the driving seat of efforts to complete the single market. His concern was that the regulations that gave force to that market did not end up representing a 'cloying intervention in the marketplace'. The legal framework had to be sufficiently flexible to adapt to a fast-moving competitive environment. Completion of the stalled Uruguay round of trade talks was also essential if British industry was to take full advantage of the opportunities on the international horizon. Closer to home, Mr Heseltine was unsure whether industry appreciated the scale of the opportunities that were already there to be taken. His suspicion was that the government's advice had too often been getting through to only a 'relatively thin strata'. He would be looking closely at improvements in the 'delivery' of advice from Whitehall. He then came up with a phrase that is likely to figure prominently in his public pronouncements - 'incremental excellence'. Instead of looking for instant solutions, the government needed to look constantly and comprehensively at all its policies to ensure that they helped to foster wealth creation. On one level, that meant sticking with macro-economic policies that provided stability and fostered enterprise. On another, it meant ensuring that policies such as those for education and training provided industry with the quality of recruits they needed. He would also be constantly on the alert to ensure that government decisions did not inadvertently impede industrial success. It was, he concluded, 'the aggregation of all these policies that adds up to an industrial strategy'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Parties rely on traditional voters in local elections
DOC.TEXT: THE THREE main political parties sought to portray themselves as efficient providers of services yesterday as the local-election campaign entered its final stretch. At the end of a low-key election campaign, marked by the parties' determination to get their supporters to vote, rather than to make mass converts, each re-emphasised its traditional areas of appeal. Mr John Redwood, the local-government minister, illustrated the Tories' central message, that Conservative councils cost less, with figures showing that most of the Labour and Liberal Democrat-controlled councils up for election were spending above standard spending assessments (SSAs) - government estimates of what councils need to spend to provide services - while most of the Tory ones were budgeting below SSAs. Labour countered by highlighting the provision in areas such as personal social services by Labour-controlled authorities, and warning that some Tory councils chose not to provide a service in, for example, nursery education. Both opposition parties insist that the political complexion of councils still matters because they can act as 'buffers' against the decisions of central government. In a signal that ministers intend to maintain their tight controls on local-government spending, Mr Redwood also emphasised the importance of local authorities' discretion in deciding how to allocate the funds within the total spent. The parties also clashed over the defection to the Conservatives of Mr Alan Winmill, leader of the Labour group on Wiltshire County Council. Mr Chris Patten, Tory party chairman, welcomed Mr Winmill's decision, but Mr John Cunningham, Labour's campaigns co-ordinator, dismissed him as 'a somewhat obscure Labour councillor', and said his decision was of little consequence. Mr Paddy Ashdown, Liberal Democrat leader, spoke of 'restrained optimism' as the party repeated its claims of low morale among Labour workers. The Liberal Democrats predict, however, that they will make more gains from the Tories, as they hold more of the seats being contested this time. Mr Cunningham referred to potential demoralisation among Liberal Democrats, saying that the party 'spent the (general election) campaign boasting about how well it was going to do, and actually lost ground significantly'. Mr Jim Wallace, MP for Orkney and Shetland, is to become leader of the Scottish Liberal Democrats, it was announced yesterday. Mr Wallace takes over from Mr Malcolm Bruce, MP for Gordon.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / World Trade News: North America free trade deal could be initialled next month
DOC.BYLINE: By DAVID DODWELL and NANCY DUNNE
DOC.TEXT: AGREEMENT on a North American free trade area (Nafta) could be initialled as early as next month as a result of significant headway made by negotiators last week in Mexico City. 'It is within the art of the possible to have an agreement this summer,' Mrs Carla Hills, the US trade representative, said in Washington yesterday. 'But I'm not betting my next paycheck on it.' It is understood that several chapters of the negotiating text were 'locked up' last week. These include customs regulations, standards, principles for services, intellectual property, textiles food safety regulations, and land transport. Close to agreement were tariffs, rules of origin, safeguards, and financial services and insurance and telecommunications. There appears to have been a breakthrough on Canadian reservations concerning local-content rules for car production. The main problem areas remain farm trade, especially Canada's supply management and subsidy regimes, government procurement and energy. On the question of Mexico's reluctance to open its energy sector to foreign investment, advisers to the negotiators say Mexico has signalled a willingness to compromise by opening its petrochemical sector, pipelines and petrol stations to foreign investment. Last week's surge in progress came after a disappointing ministerial meeting in Montreal in early April, when some participants said talks had moved backwards. A visit to Washington by Mr Jaime Serra Puche, Mexico's commerce secretary, after Easter apparently revived the momentum. 'It was a very productive week,' said Mr Jules Katz, deputy trade representative. He predicted a ministerial meeting would be scheduled later this month 'depending on progress made'.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Israel extends its arm to tie up central Asian links - Following success elsewhere, the Jewish state finds open doors in unlikely places
DOC.TEXT: TURKEY and Iran attract most of the headlines in the battle for influence in the central Asian republics of the former Soviet Union. But Israel has wasted little time in establishing links it hopes will blossom into lucrative trade. The Jewish state is anxious that the Moslem republics should not line up against it with fellow-Moslem Arab states and Iran, the most strongly anti-Israel state in the region. It has moved quickly to establish official relations with five of the six republics - Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan, Tajikistan and Kirghizia - but not Turkmenistan, and may soon have representative offices in the first two. To underpin the diplomatic relationship - and establish a foothold in what is seen as a big potential export market - there are efforts to build trade links. It is a pattern Israel has followed in the past in regions such as South America and Africa and recently in China. As many as 18 Israeli companies are said to have visited Kazakhstan, with at least three 'doing serious business'. Israel was one of the first countries to be put on a direct-dial telephone link by Kazakhstan. Several Kazakh government delegations have been to Israel in recent weeks, including one led by the agriculture minister which held talks with Mr Yitzhak Shamir, the prime minister, and was given lavish treatment. The Kazakh prime minister is expected this month. Similar links have been established with Tadjikistan, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan. In a typical Israeli scheme, cotton yields at a farm in Uzbekistan were reported to have increased by 40 per cent on one-third of previous water consumption in one season through improved irrigation techniques. Mr David Kimche, a former director general of the foreign ministry who specialises in fostering delicate relationships such as that with China, has been building contacts in the central Asian republics in recent months. He says he has found 'no hesitation' among them in forging links with Israel. In South America, Africa and China, much of what Israel has offered has been military supplies. In public at least, the emphasis in central Asia has been on the republics' outmoded agriculture and communications systems - both areas Israel reckons it is ideally placed to upgrade. 'They believe we have a lot to offer in agricultural technology and food production,' said Mr Kimche. He said there was interest also in studying the experience of Israel's collective - but independent - Moshavim farms. Although these farms have been in difficulties, the Asian republics are said to be thinking of using the Moshav model in scaling down their huge collective farms left over from the Soviet era. The risk for Israel is that the current secular-oriented regimes it is now getting close to will be replaced later, perhaps by more militantly Islamic governments. But that has not deterred the drive into the republics. One Israeli company which has signed agreements for four projects in Kazakhstan is Merhav, part of an Israeli-owned international private group Metropolitan Investments Corporation. With widespread experience in debt settlement, project development and trading in regions such as South America and Africa, it has taken the plunge in central Asia enthusiastically. The four turnkey projects to refurbish outdated agricultural systems signed in January - one in cotton and one in tomato production are already underway - have a total value of Dollars 35m. But, as Mr Yosef Maiman, the company chief, admits, the deal is a calculated risk. It was concluded with the Kazakh government in three days in mid-February, barely a month after first contacts were made. 'You have to take decisions on the spot. A lot goes on intuition and you have to be fast to implement. We started ordering millions of dollars worth of equipment before the deal was finalised,' said Mr Maiman. Merhav has had to spend a lot up front to get the projects moving. It has established a 25-person office in Alma Ata in Kazakhstan. Getting equipment shipments to the distant, land-locked republic has been a logistical nightmare. The company uses its own private jet and charter flights to speed things up. In early April, a 14-truck convoy was sent back to Turkey from Iran causing a 20-day delivery delay. Only a 'small part' of the price is paid in hard cash. For the rest, Merhav gets to pick from a Kazakh list of commodities which, like a menu in a flagging restaurant, has fewer items available than it first appears. Cotton and tomato paste will make up some of the payment, says Mr Maiman. But he insists Merhav will make money on these initial projects and foresees future business for Merhav in Kazakhstan of up to Dollars 100m a year. 'Yes, there is a particular value for Israel to be in a predominantly Moslem republic which has natural resources Israel may need over time,' Mr Maiman says. 'But we are a business operation aiming to penetrate a market and to be profitable doing it. We wouldn't have got into it otherwise.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / World Trade News: UK-led group likely to win HK bridge deal
DOC.TEXT: THE Hong Kong government is expected to announce tomorrow that a British-led consortium has won an HKDollars 8bn (Pounds 583m) contract to build one of the world's biggest suspension bridges. An Anglo-Japanese consortium, led by Trafalgar House, is believed to be the successful bidder to build a 1,377m bridge to connect Tsing Yi and Ma Wan Islands as part of the HKDollars 114bn (in March 1991 prices) airport and related infrastructure programme. The contract will be the biggest single one awarded so far for the colonial government's infrastructure development of Hong Kong. As well as the Anglo-Japanese consortium, three others were in the bidding: an all-Japanese group and one led by the French construction company Dragages et Travaux Publics; the third, a South Korean grouping led by Hyundai, was some HKDollars 2bn cheaper than the Trafalgar House bid. The HK government is expecting to be criticised by local politicians and probably China, which had an interest in the Hyundai consortium, if it awards the contract to Trafalgar House. Hyundai's troubles in South Korea, where some senior executives have been accused over taxes, and the highly-geared nature of Hyundai Construction and Engineering, the main bidder, are understood to have concerned the HK government. It raised doubts about the company's ability to enter into a long-term commitment to build the bridge. The government's critics say it should never have pre-qualified Hyundai. UK consulting firms have done well in bidding for consultancy contracts for the airport programme. They have done less well in previous building contracts, but the award of the bridge to a predominantly British consortium will be seen as favouritism in some quarters. The Anglo-Japanese group would be asked to build one of the world's longest suspension bridges in the shortest possible time. It will have to be completed by mid-1997, at the latest, when the airport is expected to be opened.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Olivetti Dollars 300m computer deal with McDonald's
DOC.TEXT: OLIVETTI, the Italian computer and office equipment group, is to supply point-of-sales computer technology to the McDonald's fast food group in the US in an agreement worth over Dollars 300m (Pounds 169.4m). The order, won against competition from IBM, Panasonic and NCR, is Olivetti's biggest contract from the the US and one of the largest deals in its history. Under the plan, eight or nine Olivetti personal computers will be installed in each of McDonald's 8,800 US outlets, which will be linked via local area networks. The deal envisages the installation of over 50,000 computer workstations, along with a variety of peripheral equipment. The system will allow full automation both for customers, who will be served by staff using new touch-screen terminals, and for back-office uses. Computers in each McDonald's outlet will handle accounting, administration and record keeping. Using the local area networks will also allow each outlet to report regularly on its performance to McDonald's headquarters, providing information on sales and payroll records, or receive instructions on new menu items or prices.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / World Trade News: Southern EC states fight move to end tied aid
DOC.TEXT: SOUTHERN EC states have opposed a European Commission proposal, backed by the Dutch, for the EC to remove curbs tying much of their national development aid to purchase of goods and service within their own countries. The first serious debate for years by EC aid ministers on the issue of 'untying' development aid ended on Monday night, with France, Spain and Italy opposing any weakening of 'national procurement' restrictions still attached to Dollars 10bn (Pounds 5.6bn) aid that EC states give the Third World each year. The southern three argued that, while untying aid might give developing countries better value for money if they could shop around the EC for the best deal, it would cut overall aid because taxpayers in one EC state would not want to see aid-related contracts going to the industry of another EC state. The Commission proposal won full backing only from Mr Jan Pronck, Dutch aid minister, who had commissioned it when the Dutch held the EC Council presidency last autumn. Lady Chalker, UK aid minister, with some German and Danish support, suggested a gradual untying of aid. Ministers asked the Commission to make a further study, but the EC executive seems unlikely to produce a formal draft directive to abolish tied aid, as Mr Pronck has urged. This week's debate showed France, Italy and Spain form a blocking minority in the EC Council. EC aid, via the Community and national budgets, amounted to Dollars 26.7bn in 1988, (not including small amounts from Greece, Luxembourg, Spain and Portugal which do not belong to the OECD's Development Aid Committee). Some 60 per cent is untied, including money channelled through Brussels to some 70 developing country members of the EC's Lome Convention. The remaining aid from EC states is totally tied (requiring all contracts be placed with companies, or contain a minimum national content, from the donor country), or partially tied.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Boutros Ghali warns on troop deployment delays in Cambodia
DOC.TEXT: Delays in the UN's troop deployment in Cambodia could have a negative effect on its peace-keeping operation unless they were soon remedied, Mr Boutros Boutros Ghali, secretary-general, warned last night, writes Michael Littlejohns. In a report to the Security Council, he mentioned the slow pace of recruiting and deploying civilian administrators, which could impair the UN's ability to maintan supervision and control.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / ADB considers its first loan to Cambodia for 21 years
DOC.TEXT: THE Asian Development Bank is discussing its first loan to Cambodia for 21 years, marking the country's return to the international financial community after the ravages of the Khmer Rouge regime in the 1970s and the subsequent 13-year civil war. Officials said the bank is considering a special rehabilitation loan of Dollars 50m to Dollars 70m (Pounds 28m to Pounds 39m) for emergency support for transport, irrigation, fertiliser and health care. The financing will go before the ADB board within two months if legal and bureaucratic obstacles can be overcome. Cambodia must still repay a small amount of arrears, and the legal entity receiving the loan must be determined, as the country still has an interim government structure. New loans would also depend on continuation of the UN-sponsored peace process. Yesterday, Khmer Rouge guerrillas launched attacks on government-held positions in the worst violations yet of the ceasefire begun last autumn. The scale of the rebuilding task awaiting Cambodia's new government is revealed in a report by the ADB released at its annual meeting in Hong Kong. Production of most goods, such as rice, rubber and fish, though they recovered in the 1980s under the Vietnamese-installed government, is below 1969 levels. By 1979, after the genocidal reign of the Khmer Rouge in which 1m people died, life expectancy was down to 31. By 1989, it was still only up to 48. Annual per capita income is guessed to be between Dollars 150 and Dollars 200, though even this low figure masks wide disparities between relative prosperity in Phnom Penh, the capital, and poverty elsewhere. What the ADB does not mention is the need for successful UN-monitored elections of a new government, rehabilitation of over 300,000 refugees, and clearing of land-mines. Mr Ou Orhat, vice-minister of planning and head of the Cambodian delegation to the ADB meeting, said yesterday: 'After twenty years of destructive war, the reconstruction needs are enormous.'

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Hunger strike in Thailand adds to pressure on PM
DOC.TEXT: ABOUT 5,000 Thais rallied in Bangkok yesterday in support of a popular politician who has pledged to starve himself to death unless Prime Minister Suchinda Kraprayoon resigns. His hunger strike increased tensions in the city on the eve of a parliamentary session in which Gen Suchinda is due to set out his government's policies. Pressure on the government of Gen Suchinda, the former army commander and leader of last year's coup d'etat, has increased steadily since his appointment was announced on April 7. It escalated on Monday when 50,000 Thais protested against the appointment of an unelected prime minister and Major General Chamlong Srimuang, former governor of Bangkok, started his hunger strike . Business leaders expect stocks to fall sharply when the market reopens this morning, accelerating a steady decline in the stock exchange's share price index. The index has lost 71.41 points or 8.6 per cent since Gen Suchinda's appointment. Businessmen say Gen Suchinda should never have appointed to his cabinet allegedly corrupt MPs who were in the government which the military overthrew last year. Gen Chamlong's threat to die if the premier does not stand down is being taken seriously. He has gained popularity because of his near-ascetic way of life and his reputed hon-esty. The party he leads won 32 out of 35 seats in Bangkok in the general elections which took place on March 22.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Russia, India face US action over missile deal
DOC.TEXT: RUSSIA and India faced the possibility of sanctions by the US after they decided yesterday to go ahead with a Dollars 250m (Pounds 141m) contract for the sale of Russian rocket technology for India's space programme. The Russian decision was announced yesterday by Mr Gennady Burbulis, Russian secretary of state, after three days of bilateral talks. Mr Burbulis ridiculed US attempts to assume the role of global lawmaker on missile technology and said Russia would go ahead with its contract with India. The Bush administration warned both countries they risk US sanctions if the deal goes through. Ms Margaret Tutwiler, state department spokeswoman, said the US would decide soon on its response to the rocket deal, which she said was inconsistent with guidelines of the Missile Technology Control Regime, an accord among western states to limit the spread of missile technology. Russia did not sign the pact, but has agreed to abide by its provisions. Penalties could involve suspension of access to US government contracts and to US technology requiring export licences. A Russian foreign ministry spokesman yesterday called for international experts to examine the deal to show that it should not incur sanctions. 'We insist on an international expert examination of the contract to prove that it doesn't undermine the Missile Technology Control Regime in any way,' Mr Sergei Yastrzhembsky told reporters. Under the deal, the Russian space agency is to sell India technology needed to build rocket booster engines for launching communications satellites. The US apparently feels the Indian space programme has military objectives but Russia has rejected this view. Russia has been collaborating with India on its space programme for a long time. With the help of the then Soviet Union, India has launched several satellites. Russia has now openly resisted US pressure to revise the accord. Mr Burbulis's visit was the first by a Russian leader since the political changes in that country. It has laid the basis for a visit to India by Mr Boris Yeltsin later this year. India has very close ties with the former Soviet Union and faced the possibility of losing an important ally because Indian officials misjudged events that led to the break-up of the Union. They have been busy ever since trying to restore Indo-Russian relations to their former level. Mr Burbulis's remarks at the end of his visit are reassuring to India's ears. As well as defying the US over rocket technology, Mr Burbulis said Russia would continue to supply defence equipment spares. Mr Burbulis said Russia has confirmed its intention to continue defence co-operation that the former Soviet Union had with India. He also said that disruption of Russian crude oil supplies would end soon. During his visit, Mr Burbulis signed a five-year trade agreement with India which envisages payments in hard currency instead of rupees. He also offered India a Rbs2.5bn (Pounds 14.3m) credit for supply of defence equipment and paper.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / US stance rattles Asian Development Bank consensus
DOC.TEXT: THE Asian Development Bank, with its president and many senior officials coming from Japan, is traditionally run by consensus and without open confrontation. These qualities were difficult to find yesterday, however, with officials of shareholding countries, speaking at the bank's annual meeting in Hong Kong, advancing deeply contrasting views of the bank's future role as a regional development institution. Mr Olin L. Wethington, assistant secretary for international affairs in the US Treasury, said bluntly that the US, as equal largest shareholder with Japan, would not countenance a replenishment of the ADB's capital resources until it had radically altered its lending policies. The opposing view was provided by Mr J B Sumarlin, finance minister of Indonesia, by far the largest borrower from the ADB. He urged rapid approval of the bank's request for a capital increase, arguing that its loans 'represent the most cost-effective way of delivering development financing'. The ADB will not in fact need new money - it is seeking a 110 per cent capital increase representing new commitments of Dollars 25bn - (Pounds 14bn) until 1994 and the approval process is likely to take at least a year. However, the opening arguments appeared to signal a fundamental debate about the role of development institutions in fostering growth, and about the role of the state, which remains significant in most Asian economies despite their dynamic growth and healthy private sectors. The ADB has begun to direct financing at the private sector and has carried out numerous studies on the issue. But the bulk of its lending continues to finance public sector works. The US has lost patience. 'Any new capital increase should await the formulation of a clear and effective strategy for encouraging private sector development,' Mr Wethington said. The US also wants: loans to be conditional on adherence to policy reforms, for example to support reforms which opened up financial markets; an end to co-financing deals with commercial banks which could threaten the ADB's credit standing; and a re-assessment of which countries should get loans. The arguments stem partly from Asia's remarkable growth, which has pushed the four 'dragons' - Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan and South Korea - beyond the point where they can borrow from the ADB. Thailand and Malaysia are approaching that stage. This leaves a concentration of loans outstanding to a few countries: Indonesia (34 per cent), India (17), Philippines (14), Pakistan (14), Malaysia (6), China (5) and Thailand (4). A 46 per cent rise in new loans last year was largely because of increased borrowing by India and China. The US says, however, China's large current account surplus should enable it to borrow more from commercial sources and less from the ADB. The US attitude to the ADB is viewed as dogmatic and blinkered by many regional countries which see Washington as increasingly out of step with Asia and isolated on issues such as financing for Vietnam, which it blocks.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Australia claims US support over Apec
DOC.TEXT: AUSTRALIA yesterday claimed to have won US support for proposals to strengthen the Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) process by establishing regular meetings of regional heads of government, writes Kevin Brown in Sydney. Australian officials said US president George Bush endorsed the plans in a letter to Mr Paul Keating, prime minister and also supported the establishment of a permanent Apec secretariat. Mr Keating proposed upgrading Apec on a visit to Indonesia last month. The plan was received cautiously by President Suharto, and is thought to be regarded with suspicion by other south-east Asian nations. Malaysia, in particular, has opposed Australian attempts to strengthen Apec because of concerns that it might undermine the Association of South-East Asian Nations (Asean). Asean, grouping Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Brunei, Thailand and the Philippines, is planning a south-east Asian free trade zone in response to the emergence of trading blocs in Europe and North America. Apec, launched two years ago by Mr Bob Hawke, former Australian prime minister, was envisaged as a forum for informal discussion of regional trade and development. However, the process has become an symbol of Australia's increasing trade and foreign policy focus on the Asia/Pacific region since Mr Keating replaced Mr Hawke last year. Mr Keating has increased pressure on the US to keep a security presence in the region. In recent talks with Mr Dick Cheney, US defence secretary, Mr Keating supported continuation of US facilities in Australia, and offered use of a bombing range when the US leaves the Philippines this year.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Threat to Cuba investment
DOC.TEXT: ATTEMPTS by President Fidel Castro to rescue Cuba's battered economy through foreign investment was dealt a blow yesterday when 11 Cuban exile groups, representing all shades of exile opinion, said that were they to come to power 'these (foreign) investments would be considered as state property and disposed of accordingly', writes Damian Fraser in Mexico City. In an open letter to foreign investors, the 11 groups said the investments served to 'prolong the tragic situation' of the country and its people.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Clinton lead stretched by primary victories
DOC.TEXT: GOVERNOR Bill Clinton yesterday took another step towards the Democratic party's presidential nomination, winning more delegates in primary voting and gaining the support of the US trade union movement, writes George Graham. Early returns and exit polls showed Mr Clinton soundly defeating former Californian Governor Jerry Brown in Democratic primaries in Indiana and North Carolina. He was also expected to win by substantial margins in the District of Columbia, where polls closed later. In Republican party primaries President George Bush was projected to have won in Indiana and to have scored a three-to-one victory over Mr Patrick Buchanan in North Carolina. With Mr Bush now mathematically assured of his party's nomination, and Mr Clinton more than 80 per cent of the way towards becoming the Democratic candidate, yesterday's primaries were fought with little fire. The endorsement of the AFL-CIO, the US trade union confederation, came as little surprise as the labour movement has endorsed every recent Democratic candidate except Mr George McGovern. But Mr Clinton has had his differences with the trade unions, notably over his support for the North American Free Trade Agreement which labour leaders believe will lead to US jobs being transferred to Mexico.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Two more charged with corruption in Milan
DOC.TEXT: TWO LEADING figures in the Italian construction industry were yesterday added to the lengthening list of those charged in connection with the two-month-old Milan corruption scandal. Magistrates ordered the arrest on corruption charges of Mr Mario Lodigiani, vice-president of the construction company of the same name, one of the country's best known, and Mr Roberto Schellino, formerly technical manager of Cogefar Impresit and chief executive of Iacorossi, a Milan general contractor. Six prominent people involved with the Milan construction business have already been charged on various counts of corruption. The latest arrests confirm that Milan magistrates are beginning to allege a direct link between the large number of public works contracts awarded in the city over the past decade and an elaborate system of pay-offs also involving the funnelling of funds to political parties. Italy's overall balance of payments deteriorated sharply in the first quarter, according to official figures. The L737bn (Pounds 333m) deficit compares with a L7,778bn surplus during the same period last year. The deficit has been blamed on a big rise in capital outflows and a decline in the level of inflows, especially in March, the month before the general election.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Appeal for more US aid to east: Kohl warns there is no 'rational alternative to continuous support'
DOC.BYLINE: By CHRISTOPHER PARKES and GEORGE GRAHAM
DOC.TEXT: CHANCELLOR Helmut Kohl of Germany yesterday made an impassioned appeal for more US help for the crumbling economies of eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union. 'If the new democracies are left to cope alone with their difficulties, then there could be a new flood of refugees to the west and other uncontrollable political developments,' he warned in a speech prepared for the annual congress of the American Newspaper Publishers' Association in New York. 'The west has no choice. There is no rational alternative to comprehensive and continuous support,' Mr Kohl added. Germany, meanwhile, was already committed to DM105bn (Pounds 35.7bn) in aid and had reached the limits of its ability to help. The issue would be 'right at the top' of his agenda at the Group of Seven world economic summit planned for Munich in July. The chancellor, who will chair the summit, had been concerned that his plan to focus the meeting on what he considers Germany's greatest foreign policy issues would be marred by top-level wrangling over the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. Now, he indicated, there was reason to hope the negotiations would be over by the end of June. The current situation in eastern Europe was comparable with the 'great upheavals' which followed the First and Second World Wars, he said, pointing to the 'dangerous expansionist tendencies' in countries like the former Yugoslavia. By 1945 the US government had learnt from the mistakes of President Woodrow Wilson, who withdrew from Europe after the First World War. America's success story in post-war Germany should now be a model for its policies towards former Cold War enemies in the east, the chancellor said. 'We Germans are experiencing in our country just how difficult the task is. In spite of enormous transfers to the former GDR the process of growing together is not progressing either as quickly or as free of friction as we would wish,' Mr Kohl said. George Graham adds: Mr Ross Perot, the Texas businessman who is seeking to enter the US presidential elections as an independent candidate, complained yesterday of a dirty tricks campaign by the Republican party to discredit him, and said he would stop most of his public appearances over the next few weeks so he could work out where he stood on policy issues. Mr Perot, who is best known for his Dollars 3bn (Pounds 1.6bn) fortune, was speaking at the American Newspaper Publishers' Association congress in New York.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / French delay debate on Maastricht pact
DOC.TEXT: THE FRENCH government yesterday postponed debate in the national assembly on constitutional amendments required for ratification of the Maastricht treaty. Mr Pierre Beregovoy, prime minister, yielded to opposition demands for more time and sent the bill back to committee. The debate, which had been set to end on Thursday, will now resume next Tuesday. Opening yesterday's session, Mr Beregovoy called for a 'great movement of national agreement'. Amid catcalls from right-wing Gaullist members, he promised the government would be receptive to detailed amendments and said the assembly would in future be fully consulted throughout the transition towards economic and monetary union, scheduled towards the end of this decade. But he made clear that there could be no question of renegotiating the Maastricht treaty, warning that if parliament seemed likely to obstruct the necessary constitutional revisions the president would put the revisions before the electorate in a referendum. 'If there is any risk that the reform might be buried,' he said, 'we shall go to a referendum. I should regret it; but if a referendum is necessary, neither the president nor the government fears the result of an appeal to the people'. Mr Beregovoy rejected opposition arguments that the single European currency would mean the abandonment of French independence. On the contrary, he said, the Emu system would strengthen French influence over economic policy. Mr Roland Dumas, the foreign minister, followed the prime minister at the rostrum of the National Assembly, with a strong plea for a more politically united Europe.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / BCCI: First American's trustee plan set in motion
DOC.TEXT: US banking and law enforcement authorities yesterday set in motion the procedures needed to transfer control of First American Bankshares - the troubled Washington bank that was secretly controlled by the Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI) - to an independent government-approved trustee, writes Alan Friedman in New York. Once the trustee is appointed he will work to facilitate the sale of First American. The nominee as trustee is Mr Harry Albright, a former New York State banking superintendent and former special counsel to the late Vice-President Nelson Rockefeller. The Washington bank has been co-operating with the Federal Reserve, the New York district-attorney, the BCCI liquidators and the Justice Department to achieve the trustee plan in order to sever all ownership links between BCCI and First American. To approve the trusteeship plan, First American has called a special shareholders' meeting of Credit and Commerce American Holdings NV (CCAH), the offshore vehicle controlling First American and featuring several nominees described by the Fed last year as 'front men' for BCCI. Among the BCCI figures being called to the meeting, to be held on May 12 in Curacao, is Sheikh Kemal Adham, a key shareholder and the US-trained former head of Saudi Arabia's intelligence agency. Mr Albright will be named as the sole trustee - enabled by a court order to exercise the powers of an owner of all the shares of First American - once the plan is approved by CCAH shareholders.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Bush to see Los Angeles devastation
DOC.TEXT: PRESIDENT George Bush will fly to Los Angeles today to visit the devastated South Central area where riots killed 58 people last week. Mr Bush met cabinet advisers and congressional leaders yesterday to work out his administration's plans for rebuilding the shattered city, where he is expected to stay until Thursday night. In the wake of the riots, Mr Jack Kemp, secretary of housing and urban development and the administration's enfant terrible, has been given more leeway to press his free-market solutions to the nation's urban problems. Mr Kemp advocates - with little support from Mr Bush until now - programmes to reform the welfare system and help the inner-city poor accumulate capital and buy their own homes. 'People do not trash their own property,' he said. Los Angeles remained calm yesterday after three days and nights of burning and looting, and schools and businesses returned to near normality. No serious incidents were reported on Monday night despite Mayor Tom Bradley's decision to lift the dusk to dawn curfew that he had imposed last Thursday. Soldiers in battle dress continued to patrol the streets, however. Police said many of those who took part in the pillaging of shops last week were now returning their booty or leaving it out on the street. Cardinal Roger Mahoney's appeal for looters to return goods to Roman Catholic churches has found a strong response, and police indicated they were offering an informal amnesty to those who voluntarily returned their loot. 'If they tell us, they get a free ride. If we find them, they get arrested,' said one police officer. Arrests are limited, however, for the city's jails are already overflowing and its police courts working overtime to deal with the 13,379 people arrested during the rioting. The costs of containing the rioting and cleaning up afterwards have put a new burden on the already strained finances of Californian state and city authorities. Besides damage to its own property, the city of Los Angeles is estimated to face a bill in excess of Dollars 12m (Pounds 6.7m) for police and firefighters' overtime pay. The greatest cost, however, is likely to come in the shape of falling revenues from property taxes levied on the damaged areas.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Halt called to Tajik clashes
DOC.TEXT: SUPPORTERS and opponents of Tajikistan's conservative authorities clashed in and around the capital of the former Soviet republic yesterday and at least four people were believed to have been killed, Reuter reports from Dushanbe. But after several hours of violence, the first in a month of political confrontation, the two sides in the republic concluded a truce. They agreed to talks and called for the withdrawal or disarming of militia units. President Rakhmon Nabiyev declared a state of emergency, imposing a 9pm-5am curfew, putting troops on alert and banning rallies, political activity and strikes. But neither he nor the speaker of parliament, Mr Safarali Kenjayev, the main target of opposition anger, appeared in public. Moslem and liberal opponents of the conservative government have been demonstrating for five weeks in different parts of Dushanbe. But yesterday's shooting, amid pouring rain in and near the capital, was the first serious violence in what has been largely a standoff. Opposition groups demanded, and secured, several concessions, including the resignation as speaker of Mr Kenjayev, seen as the power behind President Nabiyev's leadership. But he was appointed to the post of security chief last week, sparking fresh protests, and was given back his job as speaker at the weekend, enraging anti-government protesters.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Gunfire greets Bosnian truce: Mortars land close to United Nations envoy in Sarajevo
DOC.TEXT: INTENSE gun and mortar fire was heard around Sarajevo, the Bosnian capital, last night within minutes of the signing of a truce between the Bosnian presidency and representatives of the Yugoslav army. The accord, which came only hours after heavy shelling hit the city, was reached at the United Nations headquarters there in the presence of the European Community envoy, Mr Colm Doyle. It said both sides would be able to recover their dead and wounded with International Red Cross help, and the free flow of food and medicines to military installations would be guaranteed. Earlier, two mortar shells landed close to the building as UN special envoy Marrack Goulding arrived after a seven-hour delay in Pale, a Serb stronghold outside the city. A third shell landed near his car as he was driving away in a UN convoy to see President Alija Izetbegovic. He was not hurt and there appeared to be no injuries. Mr Goulding was escorted into Sarajevo late yesterday afternoon by General Satish Nambiar, commander of UN peace-keeping forces, after being blocked in Pale. The first UN convoy which tried to meet him had to turn back because of fighting. A second convoy, with Gen Nambiar, got through but with further delay. 'The first convoy came under fire up close and had to turn back. The second expedition was held up for three hours at a Serbian road block and this is really not acceptable behaviour,' said Mr Goulding. 'Terrible things have been happening in Sarajevo and elsewhere in Bosnia. It is a tense and dangerous situation with the risk it might spread. There are strong feelings. . . . that the international community must do something about this.' Mr Goulding's mission to assess the feasibility of sending a peace-keeping force to the republic coincided with an ultimatum from the largely Moslem Bosnian militias to the Yugoslav federal army to withdraw from the capital by midnight tonight. The continuing violence forced 25 monitors to pull out of Sarajevo, leaving a nine-member crew. Responsibility for the killing of a Belgian EC monitor last Saturday was denied yesterday by the federal army, which implied that Croatians had done it. In an apparent effort to stave off international criticism, the presidency of the new Serb-dominated Yugoslavia yesterday ordered its citizens - Serb and Montenegrin soldiers and officers - to withdraw from Bosnia within 15 days. However, the call was rhetorical since more than 80 per cent of 80,000 federal soldiers stationed in Bosnia are Bosnian Serbs. The republic's Moslems are backed by Croats who have joined forces against the Serbs and the federal army in a battle for control of strategic parts of Sarajevo. However, the Moslem-Croat coalition which supports Bosnian independence looks fragile. Serb leaders hinted yesterday that Serbia and Croatia could reach agreement on dividing Bosnia-Hercegovina, leaving Moslems without a homeland.

DOC.HEADLINE: FT 06 MAY 92 / Base rates cut to 4-year low of 10%
DOC.TEXT: THE UK government yesterday cut interest rates to their lowest level for four years in an effort to strengthen the so far fragile signs of recovery. Commercial bank base rates fell from 10.5 per cent to 10 per cent - the first fall since September - after the Bank of England reduced its short-term money market rates in a move widely welcomed by industry. The cut, which may help the Conservative party in tomorrow's local council elections, is expected to boost consumer confidence. It cuts the margin between borrowing rates in Britain and Germany to the lowest level for 11 years and underlines the perception among UK policy makers that Germany's anchor role within the European exchange rate mechanism may be less important than it was. The cut led to some mortgage cost reductions. Halifax Building Society, the market leader, cut its rate for new borrowers to 10.65 per cent from 10.95 per cent. The Halifax's move will shave Pounds 13.13p a month off the cost of a Pounds 60,000 endowment-linked mortgage. Other lenders will probably follow suit. They are also likely to follow Halifax's lead and not pass on the full reduction in base rates to mortgage-holders.
